title: Care of the Older Person in Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject enhances students’ knowledge and skills in caring for older adults in paramedicine practice settings. Using evidence-based practices, students will learn to assess and manage medical, traumatic, and psychological conditions and social situations affecting older people. They will also prepare and administer medications in accordance with NSQHS standards and other relevant regulations. By integrating pathophysiological principles with assessment outcomes, students will be equipped to formulate and implement effective management plans for older people in paramedicine practice environments. Additionally, students will develop skills in collaborating with other health professionals to care for older people in palliative care and using Advance Care Directives.
learning_outcomes: Determine appropriate evidence-based treatment plans and interventions for older people experiencing medical, traumatic, psychological conditions and social situations.
Advocate on behalf of the older person for their safety and well-being, supporting their rights in social situations and healthcare.
Explain the medical, traumatic, psychological conditions and social situations that commonly affect the older person encountered in paramedic practice.

Collaborate effectively with other interdisciplinary professionals to provide comprehensive person-centred care for older people, including those in palliative care and using Advance Care Directives as per the NSQHS standards.
Prepare and administer medications in accordance with NSQHS standards and other relevant legislation and regulatory requirements for the older person.
prerequisites: PAR103: Introduction to Contemporary Paramedic Practice

title: Clinical Biochemistry 1 (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces units, reference ranges and specimens used in clinical biochemistry. The subject also covers the patho-physiological and patho-biochemical rationale for routine clinical biochemistry tests and the interpretation of data. Biochemical techniques associated with the various routine tests covered include principles of the methods and the analytical performance. Technology, including point of care testing is important in healthcare and is also included. Students will gain knowledge of the requirements of the various specimens and measurements and will acquire theoretical skills to carry out routine testing using various methods and equipment. Students will also interpret routine clinical biochemistry data. Such knowledge is useful, in further studies in this discipline, routine and specialist medical laboratory sciences, forensic sciences, biotechnology, dentistry, medicine, veterinary and animal sciences, research and in industry that develops and/or supplies diagnostic technology and consumables.
learning_outcomes: Describe and justify the importance of units and reference values for various measurements in health and in diseases and their use in interpretation of data.

Evaluate methods (including but not limited to evaluating accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, linearity), to identify and analyse sources of errors, to implement quality control and quality assurance for good analytical practice.
Explain the applications of technology, automation and information systems and to analyse their usefulness.
Identify, describe and justify the utility of the various specimens, conditions of specimen collection and preservation as well as other requirements for analysis.
Describe principles of various measurements and the rationale and usefulness of the tests in diagnosis and management of diseases.

title: Evidence in Practice 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students begin to undertake safety assessments and apply clinical reasoning for safe clinical decision making. Students will explore learning experiences within simulation learning environments, including the knowledge, behaviour and attitudes required for safe practice and the purpose of feedback. Students will begin to integrate knowledge of human anatomy and physiology across the lifespan to undertake evidence based foundational nursing skills and assessments. Students will demonstrate readiness for their first professional experience placement subject through practising within the framework of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice and the Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) in the simulation learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Discuss best practice for providing care across the lifespan for hygiene, elimination and nutrition.

Apply knowledge of human anatomy and physiology across the lifespan when performing the skills and techniques required to safely obtain, interpret and document basic assessment data including vital signs.
Describe the purpose of simulation and feedback for developing safe practice in readiness for professional experience placement.
Demonstrate the ability to establish person centred, therapeutic relationships while maintaining professional boundaries.
Discuss a range of factors that impact on safety and the strategies applied to identify and address risk in the healthcare environment.

title: Doctoral Research (Allied Health, Exercise and Sports Sciences) FT
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a research subject available only to students enrolled in an appropriate Higher Degree by Research within the School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences. Students enrolled in this subject will work directly with their supervisory team to undertake an appropriate research project, culminating in completion of a thesis to be submitted for examination.
learning_outcomes: Develop a research hypothesis or question that is soundly embedded in the context of the current body of knowledge in the field.
Systematically and critically evaluate relevant literature, philosophical approaches, and data collection and analysis techniques in the broad research field.

Independently plan and undertake an approved research project, including data collection, analysis, interpretation and presentation, which leads to a highly substantial and original contribution of new knowledge to the research field in the form of a research thesis.
Demonstrate an expert level of theoretical knowledge and be able to critically reflect on that knowledge and its applications.
Develop an appropriate conceptual framework and research design that forms the basis for the conduct of the research project.
Demonstrate research, analytical, critical, reflection and communication skills through research outcomes such as seminar presentations and publication and/or thesis and/or portfolio submissions.
prerequisites: EHR702: Doctoral Research (Human Movement Studies) FT

title: Evidence in Practice 4
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds directly from the previous Evidence in Practice subjects. A systems based approach is used to support students develop the psychomotor skills required to undertake a range of holistic assessments and interventions for people with common health conditions across the lifespan, including vulnerable people. Further to this, students evaluate the outcomes of interventions and adapt plans for care. Students are asked to critique the clinical significance of policies, procedures, pathways, guidelines and other evidence-based resources for translation into practice. Students will demonstrate readiness for their next professional experience placement subject through practising in within the framework of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice and the Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) in the simulation learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate person-centered, therapeutic communication strategies when working with vulnerable people.
Critique policies, procedures, pathways, guidelines and other evidence based resources for translation into practice.
Evaluate the outcomes of interventions with consideration to clinical risk, patient safety and progress toward person-centred goals.
Justify the indication for a range of interventions using clinical reasoning.
Apply a reflective framework to critique your practice and identify areas for further development to support future professional experience placements and practice as a registered nurse.

title: Accounting 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Accounting 1 introduces students to key accounting information that business managers and accountants use to make decisions and manage a business. Students will develop skills that enable them to analyse and interpret accounting reports and to communicate the results of this analysis to interested parties. The subject focuses on the use of accounting information rather than on the recording of financial transactions and events (book-keeping). Students will learn various tools and techniques to enable them to make important business decisions.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe sources of business finance.
Implement various management accounting tools and techniques in making business decisions.
Use a computer spreadsheet to assist in the preparation of business information and be able to generate and analyse a range of business results and reports.
Define the role of accountants and explain how accounting can assist in making decisions.
Employ research and report writing skills.
Analyse and interpret a range of accounting and financial transactions and reports.

title: Accounting 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the ability to analyse and interpret accounting information developed in ACC100 Accounting 1 by teaching students to prepare accounting information using manual and automated accounting information systems. All aspects of the financial statement preparation process are covered with a focus on accounting for key assets.
learning_outcomes: Record accounting transactions using manual and automated accounting information systems.
Explain, prepare, analyse and interpret the following major financial statements: income statement, statement of changes in equity, statement of cash flows, and statement of financial position.
Calculate, account for and report values of key assets including: receivables, inventory; and property, plant, equipment.

title: Academic English for Australian Tertiary Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to introduce Australian academic culture and to enhance the level of Academic English skills of those students from Language Backgrounds Other Than English (LBOTE) entering the University. Both International and Domestic students, who may have studied English for some time, often find it challenging to write for academic purposes in the Australian academic context. This subject aims to provide students with opportunities to develop additional skills in critical thinking, listening, speaking, reading and writing necessary for tertiary studies.
learning_outcomes: Identify and use appropriate language for academic writing
Recognize how ideas and concepts are expressed and connected through effective language use
Identify an author's stance and to evaluate evidence and sources
Explain the academic expectations of tertiary study in the Australian context
Use the structural conventions of academic writing
Identify and engage with different text types
Structure and present opinions and information in an oral presentation
Apply effective listening and note-taking strategies

title: A Deeper Dive Into Marketing Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Marketers need to be adaptive and be able to apply their skills and knowledge in a range of contexts. In this subject, students will take a deep dive into several important marketing contexts. In each context, students will be asked to critically examine the marketplace, recognise opportunities, and select and apply appropriate marketing theories, justifying their choices. Students will also be asked to address specific issues, and create and communicate, appropriate, imaginative and engaging market-based solutions.
learning_outcomes: Communicate in a range of mediums to a diverse group of stakeholders and audiences.
Utilise their expertise to interpret and assess the impact of marketplace factors on marketing practice.
Critically analyse essential marketing capabilities, skills and knowledge necessary for effective strategy development in different marketing contexts.
Engage in research skills to collect, collate and use secondary data as evidence to support their argument.
Evaluate key marketing frameworks and theories and to communicate coherent and theoretically rigorous arguments about how and when these theories can be applied.

title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Cultural Education Program
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject has been designed to facilitate opportunities for students in the Bachelor and Master of Teaching degrees to develop respectful relationships with their local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community through participation in a placement in a local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community organisation or an authorised cultural immersion program. The local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community cultural education experience is part of the cultural competence program embedded within the degree. It allows for authentic engagement with the community to broaden students' understanding of issues confronting the local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community and to further understand the role of education in achieving reconciliation and improving educational outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their experience in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community cultural education program using the Australian Professional Standards for Teaching Graduates standard to annotate strategies for teaching Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students and describe how importance of relationships and community engagement can promote reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians.
Successfully participate in a placement with an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community organisation or authorised cultural immersion program.

title: Academic Writing Skills
school: School
syllabus_overview: Academic Writing Skills aims to provide students with an intensive writing workshop in which the key skills required to write successfully at university are presented and practised. The subject content covers the broad academic categories of style and structure, with a focus on complexity and formality, referencing, punctuation, grammar, as well as writing an essay introduction, body, and conclusion. This subject will be delivered to students via a two-day (week-end) face-to-face workshop. During the workshop, students will deconstruct exemplar texts in order to identify and analyse the features of quality academic writing. They will complete a number of written activities, individually and in groups, including composing simple and complex sentences as well as extended texts displaying coherent, logical arguments. There will also be an online component providing students with the opportunity to participate in CSU's online learning environment. The Subject Coordinator will be available via the online forum before and after the workshop to guide and support students
learning_outcomes: Write an introduction to an academic essay.
Use punctuation to organise meaning in a text and be able to edit a text to ensure that correct punctuation is used.
Demonstrate effective strategies for note taking.
Use the conventions of academic writing to produce texts.
Identify the features of academic writing.
Write a concluding paragraph.
Plan and structure a text that presents and supports a point of view based on research.
Demonstrate the ability to integrate sources into a body paragraph.
Write a coherent body paragraph that includes a topic sentence, elaboration and evidence.
Write a variety of simple, compound and complex sentences.
Identify some basic grammatical terms and understand their relevance to formal academic writing.
Demonstrate the ability to write formal and complex structures, where appropriate.
Find resources or services that support further development in academic writing skills.
Critically evaluate evidence.
Demonstrate an understanding of the purpose of referencing at university and be able to produce correct in-text citations and an end-of-text reference list.

title: 300 Level Placeholder
school: School

title: Academic Literacies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Academic Literacies is a core subject in the Undergraduate Certificate in University Preparation. It explicitly teaches the essential academic skills required for successful university completion. Students learn to independently apply skills of critical reading and textual analysis. They are supported to source, curate and evaluate information to support their position on a given topic. Through a progressive series of scaffolded research, writing and presentation tasks they will engage with and apply the principles of academic integrity including referencing. Assessment tasks incorporate the planning, drafting, and refining of an academic essay including incorporating feedback. At the conclusion of the subject students will be effectively prepared to manage research and writing tasks at an undergraduate level.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of academic integrity to developing oral and written texts.
Independently apply academic skills of text analysis and critical reading.
Source, curate and evaluate information to support an argument.
Plan, draft and refine an academic essay, including incorporating feedback.

title: Professional Experience Placement 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will apply their learning from other Bachelor of Nursing subjects during 160 hours of professional experience placement. The placement is supervised by registered nurses in low acuity settings. Students focus on implementing person-centred care, undertaking risk assessments and planning and implementing safe foundational nursing care which includes vital sign assessment and support for mobility, hygiene, elimination and nutrition.
learning_outcomes: Describe personal and professional experiences, actions, attitudes, feelings and beliefs.

Demonstrate safe practice by adhering to individual student registered nurse scope of practice and relevant university, profession and industry policies, guidelines, standards, regulations and legislation.
Establish, sustain and conclude professional relationships while maintaining clear boundaries between professional and personal interactions.
Undertake holistic and systematic person-centred assessments.
Respond actively to feedback in order to improve own nursing practice.

title: Accountability and Policing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject allows serving police officers to reflect on their sworn policing duties with a view to enhancing ethical practice and accountability within that work. The issue of being accountable for what they do - ie. acting with integrity - rather than simply being held accountable will be a central theme throughout the subject. At all times, students attention will be directed to their actual experiences in the workplace and to ways of critically evaluating those experiences.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an enhanced understanding of the ethical issues raised by various policing methods and be able to explain what constitutes the ethical use of those methods.
Analyse and evaluate both formal and informal accountability mechanisms.
Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Analyse and evaluate various institutional values and the impact of those values on personal and professional values.
Analyse and evaluate the impact of ethical decision making in the course of their sworn policing duties and private lives.

title: Academic Integrity at Charles Sturt University
school: Division of Learning and Teaching
syllabus_overview: At Charles Sturt University great importance is placed on academic integrity. All Charles Sturt University students are expected to understand the Academic Integrity policy and the concepts of plagiarism, cheating and collusion. In this subject you will be introduced to the key concepts, terms, policies and support services related to Academic Integrity at Charles Sturt University. It is a self-paced subject, working through the content in an online environment. You will be assessed through a series of formative and summative quizzes. All students will be automatically enrolled in this subject. This subject must be successfully completed during their first session of enrolment. A hold is placed on all grades until successful completion of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Use and reference digital media (e.g. images and video) with academic integrity.
Demonstrate understanding of the importance of academic integrity when evaluating different sources and making notes.
Demonstrate academic integrity through the appropriate use of referencing.
Identify ways to show academic integrity when working with other students.
Discuss why academic integrity is important for study and future professional practice.
Explain the key concepts, principles and practices of academic integrity.

title: Oral Health Sciences 1B
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject continues students' knowledge of oral biology. This subject develops the knowledge needed to differentiate landmarks of the oral cavity, head and neck. Students will learn congenital and developmental orofacial defects and injuries. Knowledge of oral and peri-oral anatomy will be further developed. Students will explore basic embryological processes and the macro and microscopic interactions that lead to the development of the craniofacial complex and oral region. The subject is focused on the healthy development of the oral cavity at this stage of study, so the student acquires sound foundational knowledge needed to distinguish health from disease and provide optimal oral health care as an oral health care practitioner.
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the macroscopic anatomy of the head and neck structures, their functions, and clinical relevance using anatomical terminology with a focus on oral and peri-oral structures.
Describe and explain the basic embryological processes and their macro and microscopic interactions that lead to the development of the craniofacial complex and oral region.

Apply anatomical knowledge in identifying disease processes and clinical manifestations of congenital and developmental orofacial defects, and be able to explain the clinical manifestation of defects affecting the craniofacial complex.

title: Accounting and Finance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject integrates the study of the accounting and finance functions of the firm in the context of a global financial institutional environment. The subject examines the objectives of corporate finance and develops specific student competencies pertinent to corporate treasury management and institutional finance.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate mainstream financial theory and concepts.
Explain and critique the objectives of financial management in contemporary organisations.
Evaluate and explain the congruence of accounting, finance and treasury functions.
Demonstrate appropriate communication skills in the context of corporate finance.
Demonstrate specific technical competencies and skills in utilising quantitative techniques in financial analysis.
Discuss and evaluate ethical considerations in financial dealings.

title: Accounting and Financial Literacy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the need for accounting and financial literacy for anyone interested in business. The subject introduces students to key accounting information that business managers and accountants use to make decisions and manage a business. Students will develop skills that enable them to analyse and interpret accounting reports and to communicate the results of this analysis to interested parties. The subject focuses on the use of accounting information rather than on the recording of financial transactions and events (book-keeping). Students will learn various techniques to enable them to make important business decisions. Students will gain a foundation understanding of accounting as an information system, professional ethics, computer applications, business communication and report writing, through the preparation and basic analysis of financial and management accounting reports. This subject is esential for any business manager and for those seeking to become a professional accountant to empathise with the needs of their client.
learning_outcomes: Implement various management accounting tools and techniques in making business decisions.
Identify and describe sources of business finance.
Explain the importance of ethics in accounting and the accounting profession.
Employ research and report writing skills.
Define the role of accountants and explain how accounting and utilising critical thinking can assist decision-making and add value to organisations.
Contextualise and evaluate accounting information for ethical decision making purposes including sustainable accounting.
Analyse and interpret a range of accounting and financial transactions and reports.
Use computer software to assist in the preparation of business information and be able to generate and analyse a range of business results and reports.

title: Accounting and Financial Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the accounting and financial management disciplines in an integrated manner dealing with financial accounting, management accounting, social and environmental accounting and finance and business decision making using quantitative information technology and business communication skills. Students will gain an understanding of the accounting principles underlying the accounting process and the uses and limitations of financial statements published by business entities. Accounting and financial management issues faced by management and some of the techniques used by managers in decision making will also be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Integrate skills in information technology, communication and the use of quantitative techniques for management decision making.
Critically evaluate and analyse some of the interpretative techniques used in accounting and financial management.
Explain and evaluate the concepts behind the management decision making processes associated with the efficient allocation of business resources.
Critique basic accounting and financial management ideas that underlie and limit the usefulness of accounting and finance information.
Explain the nature of, and apply, the measurement of assets, equities, revenues, expenses and income.

title: Accounting and Tax for Estates and Trusts
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Finance professionals working in the area of estate planning and trusts will, at some stage in their career, need to source, critically analyse and make decisions involving accounting information. Further they will be involved in the distribution of money to beneficiaries and tax authorities. The subject aims to increase students' knowledge and understanding of the accounting and tax principles and practices underlying the administration of trusts and estates. The emphasis of the subject is on applying relevant frameworks and techniques to real life cases, to ensure that students can practically apply the knowledge gained in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the financial and other records required and explain the rationale for the administration of an estate or trust.
Apply appropriate accounting frameworks and techniques to real life cases involving accounting for trusts and estates.
Prepare a distribution statement from a given set of information.
Critically analyse a given set of transactions and accounting information relating to an estate or trust and compile a set of accounts.
Distinguish between capital and income in the case of a trust or estate and calculate the tax payable including capital gains.
prerequisites: ACC585: Financial Statement Analysis and Valuation

title: Accounting Information Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory accounting information systems subject designed to provide students with an overview of computerised accounting information systems (AIS), some practical skills in using an AIS, and an understanding of the scope and types of different AIS.
learning_outcomes: Explain and understand the impact of information technology on the nature and development of accounting.
Analyse and evaluate business processes and model them using systems documentation.
Analyse organisational processes for risk, and design appropriate control mechanisms to.
Record business transactions using computerised accounting information systems.

title: Accounting Information Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the role of information systems in providing support to organisational business processes and decision making. It is designed to provide students with an overview of computerised Accounting Information Systems (AIS), an understanding of the scope and types of different AISs; and some practical skills in using an AIS. The subject also considers information controls and business processes and their impact on the reporting of accounting information.
learning_outcomes: Understand and apply foundation principles relating to computerised information systems in contemporary organisations.
Illustrate typical network configurations and identify the components of a network.
Evaluate accounting information system architecture and generate models of business events.
Analyse, synthesise and apply the concepts underpinning systems planning development and implementation.
Identify organisational risk and generate systems that control that risk.
Explain the role of data analysis tools and data mining.

title: Accounting For Strategic Decision Making
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to financial accounting, management accounting and finance for those working in a business environment. Students will gain an understanding of the accounting principles underlying the accounting process and the uses and limitations of financial statements published by business entities. Accounting and finance issues faced by management and some of the techniques used by managers in decision making will be also addressed.
learning_outcomes: Explain and evaluate the concepts behind the management decision making processes associated with the efficient allocation of business resources.
Explain and apply the definitions, recognition criteria and measurement bases of assets, equities, revenues, expenses and income.
Critique basic accounting and financial management concepts,principles, techniques and conventions that underlie and limit the usefulness of accounting and finance information.
Critically evaluate and analyse financial information using a range of interpretative techniques used in accounting and financial management.
Integrate skills in information technology, communication and the use of quantitative techniques for management decision making.

title: Accounting Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory information systems subject designed to provide students with an overview of computerised accounting information systems (AIS). Students are required to develop practical skills in using AIS, and an understanding of the scope and types of different AIS. This subject also covers information controls and business processes, and their impact on the reporting of accounting information.
learning_outcomes: Explain the impact of information technology on the nature and development of accounting.
Analyse and evaluate business processes and model them using systems documentation.
Record business transactions using computerised accounting information systems.
Analyse organisational processes for risk, and design appropriate control mechanisms to mitigate identified risk.

title: Accounting Standards Interpretation and Disclosures
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject delves more deeply into the sources of international financial reporting regulation and the conceptual framework, both crucial to informing the global debate regarding financial reporting standard formulation and application. The subject develops student ability to research, interpret and apply accounting standards to a range of specific real world business issues including the raising of capital, impairment of assets and financial statement disclosures. Students will gain an appreciation of the dynamic and contested arena of financial reporting standard setting.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and apply generally accepted accounting principles and specific financial reporting standards relating to concepts of recognition, measurement, disclosure, revaluation and impairment of key financial statement elements.
Discuss critically and comprehensively the statutory and professional requirements upon which published financial statements are based.
Interpret and communicate clearly and concisely, in a range of formal and informal situations and settings, the relevant principles and accounting standards to a diverse audience.
Prepare financial statements for reporting entities in accordance with relevant professional and statutory reporting requirements.

title: Accounting in a Global Environment
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject presents concepts dealing with more complex financial accounting issues in an international context. Students will explore consolidated financial reporting and account for the impacts of foreign currency translations and transfer costs across international borders. The subject will also consider the impacts of related-party international dealings from a social accountability perspective.
learning_outcomes: Explain the relationships that exist between a parent company and its subsidiary(ies), an investor and its investee, a company and its overseas subsidiaries.
Discuss the relevant accounting standards and statutory reporting requirements for foreign currency dealings and segment reporting.
Critically assess and report upon the information contained within published financial statements.
Prepare accounts for each of the above-mentioned business combinations in accordance with relevant professional and statutory reporting requirements.

title: Accounting Standards, Application and Disclosures
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will acquire the skills to interpret the underlying accounting standards and apply them to challenging business problems. Based on International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and their Australian equivalents (AASB) the subject develops students' capacity for professional and personal judgement and initiative through the application of the accounting standards. Graduate capabilities are centred upon critical, analytical and integrative thinking, research and problem solving as students explore the issues and concepts involved in the preparation and presentation of Financial Statements.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and critique the statutory and professional requirements upon which published financial statements are based and their impact on practical situations and recent developments in accounting.
Apply professional judgement in the preparation of financial statements for reporting entities in accordance with relevant ethical, professional and statutory reporting requirements.

Apply and analyse generally accepted accounting principles and specific financial reporting standards relating to concepts of recognition, measurement, disclosure, revaluation and impairment of key financial statement elements.
Critically analyse and communicate clearly and concisely the relevant principles and accounting standards to a diverse audience.

title: Accounting Systems and Processes
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the accounting discipline in an integrated manner dealing with financial accounting and developing and applying critical thinking, information technology and communication skills. The subject provides the basis for an iterative and spiral approach to accounting, exposing students to areas of accounting including accounting as an information system, ethics, business communication and report writing, computer applications, the accounting cycle, financial reports and the fundamentals of management accounting.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of ethics in accounting.
Appraise the use of information technology including spreadsheet software in accounting problem solving, and evaluate the Internet as a professional resource.
Contextualise and evaluate accounting information for decision making purposes.
Demonstrate relevant business communication skills including report writing.
Discuss the historical development of accounting.
Apply conceptual and technical aspects of accounting and prepare relevant business financial statements.

title: Accounting Theory
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Drawing on prior knowledge of accounting, ACC341 is designed to examine accounting theory in the global economy. This subject covers the nature and function of theories and their application to accounting; a historical examination of accounting and its development to its present as interpreted from different perspectives; and an examination of the application of theoretical perspectives to particular issues in accounting such as financial accounting, professionalism, environmental accounting and behaviour. Throughout the subject, students are encouraged to consider ethical dimensions of the theories applied within the discipline of accounting.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of theory in the nature and development of accounting as a discipline.
Evaluate ethical implications of theory in relation to current practice.
Compare and contrast the diverse perspectives which can be used to explain the development of accounting theory including the impact of social change on accounting and vice versa.
Deconstruct specific accounting issues that have been the subject of theoretical analysis.
Engage in the accounting discourse including critical analysis of the various theoretical approaches applied within the accounting discipline.
Describe and apply the process of theory development.

title: Acute Care Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students completing this subject will develop knowledge and skills required for physiotherapy practice in acute care settings. Assessment, clinical reasoning and practical skills relevant to the physiotherapy management of health problems affecting individuals admitted to acute care settings such as hospitals, will be addressed. Additionally, students will evaluate the experience of a client in accessing and utilising health care services. A major component of this subject will address core competencies expected of entry-level practice in the specialist area of cardiorespiratory physiotherapy practice. Students enrolling in this subject are expected to have achieved a substantive level of background knowledge of the anatomy and physiology of the cardiorespiratory system, and foundation levels of knowledge of physiotherapy practice.
learning_outcomes: Use best available evidence to critically evaluate information and derive recommendations for a target client group.
Demonstrate professional behaviour appropriate to cardiorespiratory physiotherapy practice.
Demonstrate and articulate sound clinical reasoning processes which explore, explain and analyse assessment findings.

Demonstrate knowledge of the pathophysiological basis of common cardiorespiratory conditions and the interplay between structure and function of the cardiorespiratory systems in health and disease states.
Demonstrate understanding of the impact of pain on cardiorespiratory function and how this may impact physiotherapy management.
Reflect on professional practice and take timely and appropriate action to recognise situations outside of competence and determine the actions required to continually improve.
Plan and apply safe and effective physiotherapy intervention for cardiorespiratory physiotherapy practice.
Plan and apply a range of physiotherapy assessment and evaluation techniques using tests, tools and outcome measures relevant to cardiorespiratory physiotherapy practice.
Communicate effectively to involve the client and relevant others in the planning and implementation of acute care physiotherapy.

title: Adaptive Leadership for Intersectionality
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines leadership for cultural and behavioural change within organisations or places of work with an intersectional lens. It specifically considers how leadership influences, creates and maintains wellbeing.
learning_outcomes: Identify aspects of proactive goal setting.
Communicate the systemic and structural benefits of an intersectional approach.
Determine healthy leadership and followship styles for institutional change.

title: Adaptive Leadership in Cybersecurity and Emerging Technologies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject seeks to equip industry leaders with the skills to navigate rapidly evolving cybersecurity threats and technologies. It introduces the fundamentals of cybersecurity, emphasising the critical human-cyber interactions that drive both vulnerabilities and solutions. Drawing from the latest research in cybersecurity, behavioural science, human-data interaction, human-computer interaction, governance, and artificial intelligence, students will develop decision-making capabilities that anticipate threats before exploitation occurs. Students will learn to examine complex digital threats, mobilise internal expertise, and foster innovation to build a practical cyber defence toolkit. This framework enables executives to systematically identify, assess, and counter emerging risks across their organisation, establishing security approaches that adapt alongside technological change.
learning_outcomes: Interpret cybersecurity findings, and effectively explain them to both technical and non-technical audiences.
Assess both human and technological risks and vulnerabilities within dynamic real-world settings.
Discuss basic security principles, strategies, and frameworks in the context of cyber-, information and data security.
Analyse, assemble and evaluate qualitative and quantitative methods for understanding and addressing cybersecurity issues in real-world scenarios.

title: Administrative and Government Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the judicial review of administrative decisions and actions of government. The role of the Ombudsman, freedom of information and anti-corruption legislation is also discussed. In addition, consideration is given to how administrative law meets the challenges of privatisation, outsourcing and the adoption of human rights protection.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the legal framework, including common law and statutory remedies, together with the importance of statutory construction and interpretation in the exercise and supervision of government powers.
Evaluate critically the role played by the Ombudsman in the resolution of administrative disputes.

Analyse critically the separation of powers, the doctrine of ministerial responsibility, merits review tribunals, investigative tribunals and tribunal procedure in order to formulate legal advice or opinion relating to hypothetical scenarios or real-world contextual problems.
Demonstrate an understanding of how law can affect the behaviour of governmental decision makers and organisations in such a way as to promote important social objectives.
Identify and articulate democratic theories, legal doctrines and remedies that courts utilise in constraining the decision-making power of administrators and apply them to practical scenarios.
Discuss critically the ways public and private organisations are required to comply with substantive and procedural laws pursuant to conferred powers under Commonwealth and State legislation.
Analyse critically non-judicial mechanisms of accountability, including merits review by tribunals, and freedom of information, and to reflect upon social policies underpinning this area of the law.
Develop a critical perspective upon the accountability of government decision-makers.
prerequisites: LAW112: Introduction to the Australian Legal System
LAW116: Writing and Communication for Legal Professionals

title: Addiction - clinical practice in human services
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The subject will introduce students to a range of clinical assessment and treatment modalities for alcohol and other drugs addictions as well as for comorbidity of addiction with mental health disorders including development of treatment plans, care coordination and case management, pharmacotherapy and psychosocial approaches such as brief intervention, CBT, motivational interviewing etc. Assessment and treatment modalities for Culturally and Linguistically Diverse and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients are also included. Students will also learn how to apply the Readiness for Change Model to prevent and address alcohol and drug issues in specific groups and communities.
learning_outcomes: Independently research and develop their knowledge base regarding a variety of pharmacotherapies used to treat addictions based on best available evidence.
Independently research and develop a sound knowledge and understanding of the main psychosocial approaches used to address addictions based on best available evidence.
Develop client specific Alcohol and Other Drugs treatment plans with special consideration for co-morbidity based on best available evidence.
Critically approach a range of Alcohol and Other Drug assessment frameworks, care coordination approaches and case management plans and procedures.
Independently develop community intervention plans to address Alchool and Other Drug issues using the Readiness for Change model.
Independently conduct a community assessment, have an sound understanding of the Readiness for Change Model and its applications for addiction issues at community level.

Independently research and develop a critical understanding of culturally secure assessment and treatment modalities for Culturally and Linguistically Diverse groups as well as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients.

title: Adult Assessment
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to the psychological assessment of adults. Students will become familiar with the theoretical and empirical foundations of contemporary adult assessment, and the application of these theories and research findings to the development of empirically-based assessment practice. Students will be introduced to best practice in the assessment of cognition, behaviour, mood, personality, and other psychological constructs, and popular psychological measures of these functions will be critically evaluated. Students will be instructed in the integration of assessment data into clinically-useful reports. Different approaches to psychological assessment will be compared and evaluated. Ethical and professional issues in psychological assessment will be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Administer, score and interpret the results of major measures of adult intelligence, achievement and other cognitive domains.
Demonstrate knowledge of the theoretical and empirical foundations of psychological assessment.
Identify ethical issues in psychological assessment.
Select assessment methods and measures appropriate to the needs of a client.
Effectively interpret and communicate the results of a psychological assessment.
Critically evaluate psychological tests and questionnaires.

title: Administrative Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the relationship between legal persons (including corporations) and government agencies and instrumentalities. It examines the legal controls on administrative action, remedies available to aggrieved persons, grounds for judicial review of administrative decisions (including the concepts of ultra vires and procedural fairness), the role of Appeals Tribunals, Ombudsmen and Freedom of Information and Privacy legislation.
learning_outcomes: Identify the kinds of errors that administrative bodies make.
Apply an understanding of the rights individuals have in relation to Government bodies.
Identify and apply available remedies and methods and grounds of review to fact situations, using case law and legislation.
Compare the differences between courts and tribunals, the functions they perform in administrative law review and the differences between the concepts "review" and "appeal".
Explain and apply the reforms of the "new" administrative law and assess their effectiveness.

title: ADPP Bridging
school: School
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to prepare prospective policing students for the academic requirements of the Associate Degree in Policing Practice.(ADPP) The subject introduces students to the most recent developments in policing studies in a University environment and develops the academic skills needed to become both a successful policing student and an officer in the NSW Police Force. The subject provides opportunities for students to learn to manage their study time effectively, think critically, undertake basic research, organise and summarise information to meet assessment requirements, write essays and reports, reference correctly and use information and communication technology for learning in a policing studies context. The professional demand for graduates to have exposure to the most immediately relevant content requires that a student may only attempt completion of this subject twice and that there should be a currency period of not more than two years for any successful graduate of this subject.
learning_outcomes: Undertake basic research on a topic or issue relevant to policing studies.
Plan and write a short essay or report on a topic relevant to policing studies.
Use information and communications technology, particularly within the CSU online learning environment, to support learning.
Reference correctly according to CSU requirements.
Think critically about selected topics and issues within the Associate Degree in Policing Practice.
Identify their learning style and discuss how that style may be utilised for effective learning in the Associate Degree in Policing Practice.
Prepare a study plan designed to assist in achieving study goals whilst also meeting personal and family commitments.
Organise and summarise information for the purpose of meeting the types of assessment requirements within the Associate Degree in Policing Practice.

title: Adult Assessment
school: School

title: Adult and Vocational Education in Australia
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Quality training and assessment requires practitioners to have a thorough understanding of the Australian Vocational Education system. This subject explores the theoretical, regulatory, and practical factors that influence training. The training system is examined in terms of the analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation cycle. The subject then presents a model of scholarship that allows a teacher-practitioner to identify, investigate and propose opportunities for improvement in their teaching practice. This subject assumes background knowledge of content covered in the Certificate IV in Training & Assessment and experience working within the context of Australian Qualifications Framework Training Packages.
learning_outcomes: Discuss theoretical, regulatory, and practical factors that influence training within the Australian vocational education and training sector.
Design, conduct and present the findings of a small basic research project focusing on one aspect of the training cycle that addresses an issue of importance in your area of professional practice.
Discuss the vocational training system in the context of the training development cycle.
prerequisites: EMV501: The Adult and Vocational Education System in Australia

title: Adult Interventions 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the theory, practice and historical foundations of evidence-based psychotherapy with adults, with a focus on the application of cognitive-behaviour therapies for the treatment of anxiety, mood and related disorders. It links the development of individualised formulations to the planning and implementation of interventions for specific psychological disorders. Students will be introduced to specific cognitive-behavioural intervention skills and develop a critical appreciation of the effectiveness of the interventions across a number of applications.
learning_outcomes: Competently conduct cognitive-behavioural assessments of adults with anxiety, mood and related disorders.

Critically analyse and synthesize the information obtained during cognitive-behavioural assessments in order to be able to develop individualised cognitive-behavioural formulations for adults with anxiety, mood and related disorders.
Articulate treatment plans, based on individualised cognitive-behavioural formulations, that nominate appropriate targets for intervention, specifically targeting identified maintaining factors.
Evaluate the effectiveness of cognitive-behavioural therapies for anxiety, mood and related disorders, modifying formulations as necessary.
Demonstrate competence in the application of cognitive-behavioural interventions for anxiety, mood and related disorders.
Understand the roles and effectively communicate with other professionals involved in patient care.

title: Adult Interventions 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject extends upon the content covered in PSY564 Foundations of Professional Psychology and PSY536 Adult Interventions 1. The emphasis will be on case and problem formulation-driven treatment planning, treatment implementation, and treatment outcome evaluation. Empirically-supported individual and group psychological interventions for adults presenting with a range of conditions, including psychotic disorders, bipolar disorders, personality disorders, sexual dysfunctions and disorders, eating disorders, and dissociative disorders will be included. Recent developments in the conceptualisation of psychological treatments, including transtheoretical and transdiagnostic approaches, will also be introduced.
learning_outcomes: Describe and critically evaluate various therapeutic approaches, techniques, and procedures with respect to theoretical origin, hypothesised change processes, indications, contraindications, and precautions in implementation.
Design, implement, and evaluate individual and group-based psychological interventions for clients from a range of these clinical populations.

Outline the general nature and aetiological formulation of complex psychopathological syndromes, including psychotic disorders, bipolar disorders, personality disorders, eating disorders, sexual dysfunctions, paraphilias, and dissociative disorders.

title: Advanced Arabic Grammar
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to the development of the study of the Arabic language after the advent of Islam. Main figures, critical books and different methodologies in the study of Arabic will be explored to gain an appreciation of the importance of the study of Arabic for different Islamic disciplines and other fields. Students will continue to advance their knowledge in vocabulary, syntax and morphology as well as begin to access classical non-vowelised textbooks.
learning_outcomes: Formally analyse sentences incorporating the new rules of syntax.
Demonstrate measurable improvement in reading and composition skills.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the development of the study of Arabic language post-632AD.
Conjugate common weak-letter verbs in the appropriate tense, gender, number and person.
Demonstrate intermediate to advanced level comprehension of technical and non-technical prose.

title: Advanced Arabic Grammar
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to the development of the study of the Arabic language after the advent of Islam. Main figures, critical books and different methodologies in the study of Arabic will be explored to gain an appreciation of the importance of the study of Arabic for different Islamic disciplines and other fields. Students will continue to advance their knowledge in vocabulary, syntax and morphology as well as begin to access classical non-vowelised textbooks.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the development of the study of the Arabic language post-632 CE.
Formally analyse sentences incorporating the new rules of syntax.
Conjugate common weak-letter verbs in the appropriate tense, gender, number and person.
Demonstrate intermediate to advanced level comprehension of technical and non-technical prose.
Demonstrate intermediate to advanced level proficiency in reading and composition skills.

title: Advanced Arabic Morphology
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject involves the critical reading of classical texts on morphology. Students will gain an advanced understanding and appreciation of the classical discourse on morphology along with its application in advanced level texts. Students will focus on the irregularities of weak letter verbs and learn how to explain and justify their occurrence.
learning_outcomes: Examine, critique and infer information from texts on morphology at the advanced level.
Articulate and discuss advanced concepts of Arabic morphology with reference to its technical literature.
Explain and justify the irregularities of weak letter verbs.
Compose complex analyses of morphological features in Arabic texts at the advanced level.
Analyse and investigate Arabic literature at the advanced level using morphological tools.

title: Advanced Biblical Exegesis
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject involves detailed exegesis of a portion of the Bible, in its original language, at an advanced level. The student will engage with contemporary critical views of biblical interpretation, and undertake a thorough exegetical and hermeneutical exploration of a specific biblical passage. The student will translate the selected passage and examine a range of critical issues (text-critical issues, literary and historical context, literary structure, relevant critical approach(es), e.g., form, narrative, sociological, ideological, etc., as appropriate to the chosen passage, together with engagement with select hermeneutical questions raised by the passage.
learning_outcomes: Undertake detailed exegesis of a portion of the Bible, in its original language, at postgraduate level.
Demonstrate independent research, writing and communication skills through preparation and presentation of substantial exegetical essay.
Provide a detailed exegesis of a chosen biblical passage, in which methods specified are applied to the text at postgraduate level.
Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and discussion skills through interaction with the subject co-ordinator.
Provide a critical analysis of the hermeneutical issues involved in an advanced reading of the biblical text.

title: Advanced Biblical Exegesis
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject involves detailed exegesis of a portion of the Bible, in its original language, at an advanced level. The student will engage with contemporary critical views of biblical interpretation, and undertake a thorough exegetical and hermeneutical exploration of a specific biblical passage. The student will translate the selected passage and examine a range of critical issues (text-critical issues, literary and historical context, literary structure, relevant critical approach(es), e.g., form, narrative, sociological, ideological, etc., as appropriate to the chosen passage, together with engagement with select hermeneutical questions raised by the passage.
learning_outcomes: Provide a critical analysis of the hermeneutical issues involved in an advanced reading of the biblical text.
Provide a detailed exegesis of a chosen biblical passage, in which methods specified are applied to the text at postgraduate level.
Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and discussion skills through interaction with the subject co-ordinator.
Demonstrate independent research, writing and communication skills through preparation and presentation of substantial exegetical essay.
Undertake detailed exegesis of a portion of the Bible, in its original language, at postgraduate level.

title: Advanced Arabic Syntax
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject involves the critical reading of classical texts on syntax. Students will gain an advanced understanding and appreciation of the classical discourse on syntax along with its application in advanced level texts. There is a focus on iʿrab (syntactic parsing) and the theory of ʿamal (syntactical governance).
learning_outcomes: Analyse and investigate Arabic literature at the advanced level using syntactical tools.
Compose complex analyses of morphological features in Arabic texts at the advanced level.
Explain and utilise the theory of ʿamal (syntactic governance) during syntactic parsing.
Examine, critique and infer information from texts on syntax at the advanced level.
Articulate and discuss advanced concepts of Arabic syntax with reference to its technical literature.

title: Advanced Breast Imaging
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Breast imaging is a broad term used to describe the screening, diagnosis, treatment and review of breast disease using medical imaging techniques. This subject builds on practitioner knowledge of 2D mammography and adjunct breast ultrasound as the cornerstones of routine breast imaging and presents advanced theoretical knowledge across the existing modalities of mammography, digital breast tomosynthesis, ultrasound and MRI. It also considers new and emerging technologies including contrast mammography, automated whole breast ultrasound screening, cone beam breast computed tomography, positron emission mammography and molecular imaging, as well as artificial intelligence. Individualised imaging and advanced practitioner roles in breast imaging will be explored.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate image acquisition across core modalities and describe features of common normal and abnormal variants.
Use research skills to undertake literature searching, review, and critique, and apply evidence-based breast imaging research within a range of contexts.
Synthesise knowledge of routine mammographic positioning and image quality analysis with the current evidence base for new techniques and technology.
Apply advanced knowledge of the principles and applications of Advanced Practice in breast imaging using new technologies and artificial intelligence.

Apply evidence-based discussion of the principles and decision making involved in constructing individualised imaging regimes from the context of breast cancer risk, new and emerging technologies, artificial intelligence and patient outcomes.
Critically evaluate the role and future applications of Advanced Practice in breast imaging across a wide range of patient presentations and settings.
prerequisites: MRS501: Breast Imaging Physics and Instrumentation

title: Advanced Care Practicum
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject requires students to undertake clinical placements in an advanced clinical setting. In this subject, students have an opportunity to integrate theory into practice under supervision. It develops the role of the paramedic as a clinician and builds on the model of paramedic clinical competence in the context of advanced paramedic clinical practice. During the period of 120-140 hours on clinical placement, students will have the opportunity to practice and develop their clinical skills in the management of patients with health conditions in a supervised clinical placement.
learning_outcomes: Be able to use discipline-specific language necessary to assess and interpret data, convey ideas, develop plans of care and implement therapeutic interventions.
Be able to apply relevant theoretical knowledge in the implementation of advanced paramedic management, clinical tasks and techniques in the health care clinical environment.

Be able to articulate the paramedic role in the advanced clinical setting and demonstrate autonomy, leadership, advanced clinical judgement, professionalism, responsibility, accountability and reflection.

Be able to critically appraise and identify professional capabilities, identify own learning needs and suitable experiences to maintain current clinical knowledge and skill in the paramedic environment.
Be able to perform as an effective team member and work with other health care professionals to provide appropriate patient care.

title: Advanced Clinical Options
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject is undertaken by final year students whilst they are on clinical placement. The subject is largely a directed student learning and self-learning subject requiring students to undertake independent reading and literature searches on assigned topics in dentistry, to evaluate literature, to demonstrate critical thinking skills and to demonstrate high level analytical and written communication skills. Although not a formal part of the subject students' clinical experiences also inform this subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced skills in written communication to provide a coherent and comprehensive review of the literature.
Use databases effectively and systematically to search for relevant literature.
Evaluate literature related to a topic/s in clinical dentistry and discuss the application to general or specialist dental practice.
Demonstrate developing critical thinking skills in relation to a topic/s in clinical dentistry.

title: Advanced Clinical Assessment of the Older Person
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will enhance the assessment skills of registered nurses who work with older people which will be evidenced by a portfolio. Physiological age-related changes mean that pathophysiology may present differently in an older person making the task of assessing the physical needs of an older person a complex and challenging task for registered nurses. Students will develop an awareness of the skills required in the assessment of an older person. The challenges of the rural and remote environment in aged-care will be explored as students develop skills in using appropriate technology to work with interdisciplinary teams and astutely link assessment to referrals, in conjunction with the person. The complexities of age-related cognitive, psychological and emotional, and the related social and spiritual needs will also be explored with a focus on First Nations peoples.
learning_outcomes: Explain the appropriate technology to support rural and remote practice and engage with virtual teams in the provision of care and services.

Critically reflect on the effectiveness of the clinical reasoning cycle to provide an advanced, systematic and theory- based approach to assessment of the older person within an ethical and legal framework.
Evaluate communication skills involved in aged care assessments.

Formulate an appropriate care plan for the older person based on an integrated knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and cognitive, social and spiritual needs giving specific attention to First Nations peoples.
Engage in collaborative communication within an inter-professional health care team.

title: Advanced Cardiology and Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to extend the students' knowledge and clinical skills required for the care of the patient experiencing acute health emergencies focusing on cardiovascular and respiratory emergencies. Students will need to integrate pathophysiological principles and assessment findings to implement management plans for the patient with cardiovascular and respiratory disease or ventilation-perfusion failure.
learning_outcomes: Make informed evidence-based clinical decisions in cardiovascular emergencies.
Apply a knowledge of the characteristics, consequences, and pathophysiology of cardiovascular and respiratory emergencies to the treatment of patients.
Interpret basic, intermediate, and advanced ECG tracings and use these to inform patient care.
Perform advanced clinical protocols and procedures for patients with cardiovascular and respiratory emergencies.
Explain and critique the evidence base of current management protocols and guidelines for cardiovascular emergencies.

title: Advanced Clinical Podiatric Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on student's prior experience to enable clinical practice with a more consultative level of supervision, including direct instruction as appropriate, based on the complexity of the client. Students will be expected to treat a range of cutaneous pathology independently, in the on-campus clinic. Students will also have the opportunity to observe clinical practice in a private practice setting. Students will apply theoretical knowledge of biomechanical principles, pathophysiology, medicine, pharmacology, medicines prescription and podiatric best clinical practice to inform their assessment and management of a range of clients. Students will consult with the Clinical Educator (CE) when formulating a diagnosis, developing and reviewing an appropriate client management plan. This subject also addresses environmentally sustainable practice in the manufacture of orthomechanical devices.
learning_outcomes: appropriately prescribe, fabricate and modify a range of orthomechanical devices under supervision, with attention to environmental sustainability;
develop a person-focused podiatric management plan with both short-term and long-term goals;
comply with applicable professional standards, codes of conduct and guidelines relevant to prescribing to inform evidence-based decisions in the context of the person's needs.
demonstrate safe and professional management practices in a clinical environment when managing cutaneous and musculoskeletal presentations;

understand management options, recognising when it is clinically appropriate to prescribe or not to prescribe medicines, and negotiate therapeutic goals that enhance self-management for a range of podiatry patients; and
independently evaluate a person's social, medical, neurological, vascular, musculoskeletal and cutaneous status, and use that information to formulate differential diagnoses;

title: Advanced Clinical Podiatric Practice (Honours)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is offered to students in the Honours stream. It builds on student's prior experience to enable clinical practice with a more consultative level of supervision, including direct instruction as appropriate, based on the complexity of the client. Students will be expected to treat a range of cutaneous pathology independently, in the on-campus clinic. Students will also have the opportunity to observe clinical practice in a private practice setting. Students will apply theoretical knowledge of biomechanical principles, pathophysiology, medicine, pharmacology, medicines prescription and podiatric best clinical practice to inform their assessment and management of a range of clients. Students will consult with the Clinical Educator (CE) when formulating a diagnosis, developing and reviewing an appropriate client management plan. This subject also addresses environmentally sustainable practice in the manufacture of orthomechanical devices.
learning_outcomes: Comply with applicable professional standards, codes of conduct and guidelines relevant to prescribing to inform evidence-based decisions in the context of the person's needs.
Appropriately prescribe, fabricate and modify a range of orthomechanical devices under supervision, with attention to environmental sustainability.
Develop a person-focused podiatric management plan with both short-term and long-term goals.
Demonstrate safe and professional management practices when managing cutaneous and musculoskeletal presentations in a clinical environment.
Independently evaluate a person's social, medical, neurological, vascular, musculoskeletal and cutaneous status, and use that information to formulate differential diagnoses.

Understand management options, recognising when it is clinically appropriate to prescribe or not to prescribe medicines, and negotiate therapeutic goals that enhance self-management for a range of podiatry patients.

title: Advanced Clinical Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: Key areas of clinical specialisation covered in this two year subject include: cultures and clinical practice, culture and behaviour, interpersonal issues in mood and anxiety disorders, the impact that clients' beliefs have on adherence and compliance with treatment, the impact that mental illness has upon parenting capacity, research methodology for applied settings, and advanced psychometric theory. Additional topics chosen by staff and students are examined through "on-line" seminar discussions. Students undertake an advanced placement in a clinical setting where they can combine both their clinical and research skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to undertake research in applied settings, using a range of methodologies and techniques.
Demonstrate an understanding of the scientist practitioner model in relation to all professional work.
Demonstrate an awareness of the importance of combining clinical and research skills to facilitate advances in clinical practice.
Demonstrate the ability to develop and validate psychometric instruments for use in clinical settings.
Demonstrate knowledge of the key areas covered during this subject.
Demonstrate skill in a broad range of psychological assessments.
prerequisites: PSY527: The Clinical Psychologist in Practice

title: Advanced Clinical Research Internship
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to develop clinical research skills relevant to professional clinical practice. This will include development of advanced clinical knowledge relevant to clinical research questions, research methodologies, problem-solving skills and reflective skills allowing critical appraisal of existing and new research knowledge relevant to the discipline. Students will concurrently undertake veterinary clinical training while undertaking this subject allowing development of clinical research skills, methodologies and data collection and translation of generated knowledge. Candidates will develop communication skills through which clinical research knowledge and critical enquiry is communicated and disseminated to peers.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate cognitive skills to critique existing and new clinical research knowledge relevant to the professional discipline.
Demonstrate substantial knowledge of research principles and methods to undertake systematic investigation and plan and execute original research relevant to the discipline.
Demonstrate intellectual independence, accountability and responsibility for personal outputs and initiative for application of knowledge and research skills.
Demonstrate effective communication skills to explain and critique theory, methodologies, results and conclusions of existing scientific literature.

title: Advanced Dynamics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject builds upon the fundamental principles of dynamics studied in the first year. It delves deeper into the analysis of motion and forces, focusing on advanced topics such as particle dynamics, systems of particles, and rigid body dynamics.
learning_outcomes: Use advanced mathematical techniques to solve dynamic problems.
Analyse the dynamics of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions.
Evaluate problem-solving skills for engineering applications involving dynamic systems.
Apply the principles governing the motion of particles and systems of particles.
