title: Advanced Enquiry Methods
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed specifically for postgraduate students who will undertake a research project in agriculture and related fields. Students will be able to develop appropriate methodological design, apply suitable research techniques and analyse data with appropriate discipline-specific statistical tools. This subject will enable students to become proficient at specific research methodologies, experimental techniques and data analysis suitable for a research discipline of their interest.
learning_outcomes: Design discipline appropriate experiments.
Implement a process of establishing a research project.
Understand the research process and the ethical considerations in undertaking research.
Undertake data analysis experiment on experimental data.
Determine suitable research techniques for a specific discipline.

title: Advanced Geostatistics
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates and extends core concepts and algorithms in geostatistics, in the context of spatial modelling as applied to geosciences. Students will learn about geostatistical simulation and uncertainty assessment, building on their previous knowledge of variography and estimation. New avenues in geospatial modelling will also be explored in this subject. The practical component provides students with an in-depth knowledge of different simulation algorithms and the skills to quantify and communicate uncertainty. On completion of this subject, students will be able to select, apply, validate, and evaluate appropriate geostatistical modelling approaches to characterise and quantify the spatial distribution of an attribute and its uncertainty.
learning_outcomes: Quantify and assess uncertainty associated with geostatistical modelling outputs.
Select, apply and analyse a range of different geostatistical simulation algorithms to propose authentic applications in practice.
Effectively communicate uncertainty to a range of stakeholders in the context of geoscience applications.
Examine, validate, and evaluate geostatistical simulation outputs.
Contrast, assess and justify different geostatistical modelling approaches for geoscience applications.

title: Advanced Ethics
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an in-depth understanding of some central issues and debates in theoretical and applied ethics. The subject explores what is fundamentally characteristic of, and at issue between, consequentialist, deontic and agent-based ethical theories. Various practical and applied implications of the ideas and values that underpin and motivate our different ethical views are examined in detail.
learning_outcomes: Assess and apply different and conflicting ethical claims in practical affairs.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of what characterises and contrasts our major ethical theories.
Demonstrate a clear understanding of the theoretical landscape in normative ethics.
Have a well developed understanding of core ideas and values that ground or arise from our ethical theorising and practice.
Be well prepared for further study in philosophical ethics.
Have developed a good theoretical understanding of the different and conflicting views about the nature of ethical reasons.

title: Advanced Graphics for Games
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject presents advanced graphics topics relevant to game programming. Specifically, it presents the use of programmable shaders to implement lighting, texturing and other visual effects, and 3D animation through the use of hierarchical mesh models and skeletal animation. As a result of successfully completing this subject students will be able to create and navigate within a scene of animated 3D models.
learning_outcomes: Apply concepts of 3D modelling to design and create parsers to load 3D models.
Apply concepts of skeletal animation to animate a mesh and to blend between animations.
Apply mathematical and programming techniques to select objects in 3D scenes.
Apply advanced graphical programming techniques to implement shadows and reflections in 3D scenes.
Apply principles of programmable shaders to design and create shaders which implement lighting texturing of 3D models.
Integrate knowledge to create a 3D scene of animated and lit 3D models and to navigate within it.

title: Advanced Graduate Entry Credit Package - 128
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Advanced/graduate entry Up to 128 points of credit may be granted to students who have a 3-year Social Science-related degree or its equivalent, or who have successfully completed two-thirds of such a degree, including completion of at least 16 session-long subjects, with one session-long subject in each of the following areas: Developmental psychology (or equivalent) Sociology Australian Government and politics and/or welfare politics, social policy and social philosophy, or Australian economic and social history Research methods The credit which will apply to those who fully meet this requirement is as follows: POL01C Social Work Politics Studies PSY01C Social Work Psychology Studies SOC01C Social Work Sociology Studies SWK02C Social Work Prelim Studies (96 points) WEL01C Research Methods Maximum Total: 128 points

title: Advanced Human Exercise Physiology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject applies physiological principles to explain acute responses to exercise and chronic adaptations to training, with emphasis on the muscular and cardiovascular systems. The laboratory component is designed to provide students with the skills and knowledge necessary to conduct standard physical fitness assessments, which are applicable for employment in clinical, corporate and community fitness programs, as well as exercise and sports science research. It is compulsory for students studying online to attend a three (3) day intensive school for this subject.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate evidence-based literature to determine best practice recovery strategies and ergogenic aids for exercise performance.
Undertake appropriate exercise physiology-based testing for healthy and athletic populations autonomously.
Explain the biochemical and molecular responses to exercise and the influence on training adaptations.
Analyse results from laboratory-based projects and deduce appropriate findings and recommendations.
Explain the cardiovascular and respiratory responses to acute and chronic exercise of various modes and intensities.
Explain the role of fatigue during exercise and the influence on behaviour.

title: Advanced Haematology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in depth study of advanced haematological concepts in areas of blood cell kinetics and regulation of cell cycle, haemopoietic malignancies, anaemias, and disorders of haemostatic systems (primary haemostasis, coagulation system and fibrinolytic system). Furthermore, quality control and quality assurance measures related to haematology are integrated into this subject. Students will also develop advanced knowledge and skills in conducting laboratory tests including but not limited to the examination of blood and/or bone marrow films, and the investigations of haemoglobin abnormalities and coagulation disorders. Distance Education students are required to attend a compulsory Intensive School.
learning_outcomes: explain the pathogenesis, clinical features, classification, laboratory diagnosis, and principles of treatment of haemopoietic malignancies;
demonstrate an understanding of key issues regarding quality control and quality assurance in the haematology laboratory;
demonstrate high levels of academic communication and team working skills.
explain the pathogenesis, clinical findings, laboratory diagnosis and treatment of anaemias;
demonstrate an understanding of the current impact of advances in molecular techniques relevant to haematology;
explain the pathogenesis, classification, clinical features, laboratory diagnosis, and treatment of disorders of the haemostatic system;
conduct haematological tests including but not limited to blood film examinations, investigation of abnormalities in haemoglobin synthesis, and coagulation studies; and

analyse, interpret and apply the results of haematological tests, as well as some clinical findings, to problem-solving activities including but not limited to case studies in regard to haematological disorders;
prerequisites: BMS441: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion
BMS341: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion
BMS336: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion
BMS318: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion

title: Advanced Integration of Theory, Knowledge and Practice
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is undertaken over one session. The aims of the subject are to develop expert skills in the integration of theory and new knowledge into the context of professional practice. Through this subject, students develop cognitive skills and the capacity for the advanced application of a body of knowledge and skills integral to evidence-based professional practice and investigation of new knowledge. Specific aims include (1) advanced training and development of expert cognitive and technical skills and substantial knowledge in the context of professional practice, (2) systematic investigation and critical reflection and integration of the theory of current and new knowledge in the context of professional practice, (3) development of communication skills to explain, conceptualise and critique theoretical propositions, knowledge advancement and application and conclusions and (4) develop research methodologies to advance knowledge in the context of professional practice.
learning_outcomes: be able to demonstrate expert technical, cognitive and creative skills applicable to the field of learning and research.
be able to demonstrate written and verbal communication skills to explain the critical appraisal and integration of theory and knowledge in professional contexts;
be able to reflect critically on theory and knowledge in the context of professional practice and the integration of current and new knowledge and evaluate common practices in the clinical field;

be able to demonstrate expert cognitive skills and use of intellectual independence to think critically, evaluate existing knowledge and ideas, undertake systematic investigation and reflect on theory and professional practice; and

title: Advanced Pastoral Counselling
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject integrates the student's prior knowledge and skills in pastoral counselling with the advanced knowledge, skills and critical reflection required for pastoral counselling involving complex issues. It includes critical reflection and rigorous examination of theological and pastoral counselling concepts, professional issues and skills apposite for advanced study in pastoral counselling.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate sensitivity, creativity and flexibility in their approaches to multicultural, interfaith, abuse, trauma, sexuality and gender issues in pastoral counselling.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the challenges involved in the development of a pastoral counselling practice, including core competencies, advanced skills, ethical and administrative issues, limitations, specialisations and practical considerations.
Clearly articulate an integrative model of pastoral counselling which is appropriate for the student's pastoral setting.
Critically reflect on their own process as a pastoral counsellor.
Demonstrate an ability to assess and work therapeutically with the client's complex issues including those requiring longer term pastoral counselling.
Demonstrate advanced skills in the choice and use of techniques assessed as appropriate for pastoral counselling from a wide range of psychological theories.
Reflect critically on theological and psychological understandings of human development and human nature.
Demonstrate a rigorous and responsible approach in addressing ethical and professional issues in pastoral counselling situations.
Critically reflect on the theological and psychological implications of the key issues in pastoral counselling of pain and suffering, forgiveness, hope, shame, grace, and despair.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of spiritual and psychological dimensions within a pastoral counselling setting integrating with interpersonal and intrapersonal theory and practice.

title: Advanced Nursing Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a platform to develop their knowledge, and expertise for advanced nursing practice. Students will critically analyse the concept of advanced nursing practice and link this to their own and other specialty areas in nursing. The scope of advanced nursing practice will be explored in the context of contemporary models of care and relevant policies as students evaluate their current practice. Students will also link advanced nursing practice with leadership in nursing and evaluate the importance of advanced nursing practice to the provision of care for First Nations people and other vulnerable minority groups.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of contemporary models of care and policies relevant to advanced nursing practice.
Evaluate the applicability of advanced nursing practice for First Nations peoples and other vulnerable minority groups.
Reflect upon assumptions that influence the delivery of advanced nursing practice.
Critically examine current national and international trends and research findings in advanced nursing practice.
Articulate the scope of advanced nursing practice.
Critically analyse advanced nursing practice in relation to ethical and professional responsibilities.

title: Advanced Pharmacology and Prescribing
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the student's knowledge of pharmacology, to develop an understanding of the issues associated with the prescription, administration and dispensing of medicines. Students will study the clinical use of a range of scheduled medicines (S2, S3 and S4) of relevance to podiatric practice. Medico-legal and ethical implications of prescribing will be addressed and students will consider their professional responsibilities as a potential podiatrist prescriber. Areas of study are informed by the NPS MedicineWise Prescribing Competencies Framework and will comprise: understanding the person and their clinical needs; understanding treatment options and how they support the person's clinical needs; working in partnership with the person to develop and implement a treatment plan; communicating the treatment plan clearly to other health professionals; monitoring and reviewing the person's response to treatment. This subject will provide students with a firm foundation from which to apply for endorsement of scheduled medicines and to work towards becoming safe and competent prescribers.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the context of responsible prescribing for podiatric practice.
Write a prescription for the correct scheduled medicine with the appropriate dosage.

Subsequent to prescribing a scheduled medicine, be able to develop a client management plan that demonstrates interprofessional collaboration to monitor, assess and evaluate the efficacy of the intervention with particular reference to adverse reactions.

Synthesise a podiatry client medical and social history, their own observations and diagnostic testing to appropriately prescribe the required scheduled medicines (S2, S3 & S4) with attention to ethical, social and financial considerations.
Formulate appropriate podiatric prescriptions within the relevant medico-legal frameworks, both state and national.
prerequisites: BMS263: Foundational Pharmacology and Pathophysiology for Allied Health Practice

title: Advanced Pastoral Counselling
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject integrates the student's prior knowledge and skills in pastoral counselling with the advanced knowledge, skills and critical reflection required for pastoral counselling involving complex issues. It includes critical reflection and rigorous examination of theological and pastoral counselling concepts, professional issues and skills apposite for advanced study in pastoral counselling.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to assess and work therapeutically with the client's complex issues including those requiring longer term pastoral counselling.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of spiritual and psychological dimensions within a pastoral counselling setting integrating with interpersonal and intrapersonal theory and practice.
Clearly articulate an integrative model of pastoral counselling which is appropriate for the student's pastoral setting.
Demonstrate advanced skills in the choice and use of techniques assessed as appropriate for pastoral counselling from a wide range of psychological theories.
Reflect critically on theological and psychological understandings of human development and human nature.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the challenges involved in the development of a pastoral counselling practice, including core competencies, advanced skills, ethical and administrative issues, limitations, specialisations and practical considerations.
Demonstrate a rigorous and responsible approach in addressing ethical and professional issues in pastoral counselling situations.
Demonstrate sensitivity, creativity and flexibility in their approaches to multicultural, interfaith, abuse, trauma, sexuality and gender issues in pastoral counselling.
Critically reflect on their own process as a pastoral counsellor.
Critically reflect on the theological and psychological implications of the key issues in pastoral counselling of pain and suffering, forgiveness, hope, shame, grace, and despair.

title: Advanced Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject critically evaluates the methodologies of Practical Theology in the lived experience of the Church and provides an opportunity for students to engage with foundational texts of the discipline. Students will develop more complex theological reflection practices that demonstrate the interdisciplinary and transformative nature of Practical Theology as it informs ministry and mission.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and critically evaluate the relevance of other disciplines to practical theology, including Indigenous studies, gender studies and the social sciences.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including research, writing and communication skills relevant to the discipline of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate the application of a variety of theological praxis models.
Evaluate critically the work of significant contributors to the field of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the methodologies of Practical Theology.

title: Advanced Plant Protection
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the development and evaluation of integrated plant protection programs for horticultural, pastural and broadacre cropping systems in Australia. Students will build on their pest knowledge from introductory plant protection studies to develop integrated pest management (IPM) plans. Students will also develop skills to evaluate the risks and economics of different management options, potential yield impacts and direct and indirect costs associated with different management options. Finally, students will investigate issues around biosecurity and regulation with respect to a part of the plant protection industry.
learning_outcomes: Outline Australia's approach to plant biosecurity and implications for management and research.
Evaluate a range of strategic and tactical pest management options.
Develop an integrated pest management plan.
Evaluate pesticide modes of action and recommend appropriate pesticides.
Implement monitoring techniques and use economic pest thresholds to determine potential yield loss.
Explain the application, economics and risks associated with key pest management approaches and their interaction with environmental factors and other management activities.

title: Advanced Principles in Computed Tomography
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the concepts of physics and instrumentation in the field of computed tomography (CT). It briefly reviews the foundational physics principles of CT and considers the physics of advanced principles and techniques. The subject will extensively cover image quality parameters and other quality factors in CT. It will cover such areas as Dual-Energy CT (DECT), Cone-Beam CT (CBCT), 4D CT and image reconstruction; modern tube designs and other associated instrumentation, such as pressure injectors. Radiation dosimetry in CT, methods of measurement and relationship to image quality will be covered with emphasis on justification and optimisation.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and apply the basic principles of CT in making clinical decisions.
Explain and communicate the principles of modern scanners and detector configurations to non-specialist audiences.
Critically discuss the differences between image reconstruction methods and reformatting options.
Solve problems regarding the interaction of primary image quality factors and their impact on radiation dose.
Analyse, review and synthesise appropriate literature in relation to current CT practice and Medical Radiation's interdisciplinary learning.
Discuss the primary radiation dosimetry measures and justify how they can be used to improve practices in CT.
prerequisites: MRS564: Computed Tomography Practice And Trends

title: Advanced Principles in Magnetic Resonance Imaging
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers advanced physical principles and imaging techniques including instrumentation in the field of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). It briefly reviews the foundational physics of MRI and extensively considers the physics of advanced principles and techniques. The following subject topics will be covered: perfusion, fMRI, non-proton imaging, MR angiography, MR spectroscopy, diffusion, 3D sequences, MR contrast, fat suppression techniques and K-space sampling as well as coil design, MRI safety and MRI quality assurance.
learning_outcomes: Explain and assess coil and other MR hardware designs taking into account safety considerations.
Discuss and apply the foundational physics principles of MRI.
Assess quality in MRI and recommend improvements in clinical protocol designs.
Evaluate, analyse and critically discuss the advanced principles of MRI covered in this subject and professionally communicate this information using discipline terminology.
prerequisites: MRS555: Advanced Principles in Magnetic Resonance Imaging

title: Advanced Psychological Practice 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: PSY570 Advanced Psychological Practice 1 and PSY571 Advanced Psychological Practice 2, together, introduce students to the core elements of professional psychological practice. PSY570 is the first of two 350 hour placements which students are required to undertake in an area of professional psychology practice. As professional placements may be undertaken in any of a variety of settings (public health, forensic institutions, educational organisations, private practices etc), the specific content of the placement will be negotiated between the external placement supervisor and the student, and will be approved by the School of Psychology's Placement Coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in the delivery of evidence-based psychological interventions, and the conduct of appropriate evaluation of outcome.
Demonstrate applied knowledge of theories of psychopathology.
Conduct practice in accordance with professional and ethical standards.
Demonstrate proficiency in diagnosis and case formulation.
Demonstrate proficiency in applied psychological assessment.

title: Advanced Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject critically evaluates the methodologies of Practical Theology in the lived experience of the Church and provides an opportunity for students to engage with foundational texts of the discipline. Students will develop more complex theological reflection practices that demonstrate the interdisciplinary and transformative nature of Practical Theology as it informs ministry and mission.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the methodologies of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate the critical application of a variety of theological praxis models.
Evaluate critically the work of significant contributors to the field of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills relevant to the discipline of Practical Theology.
Articulate and critically evaluate the relevance of other disciplines to practical theology, including Indigenous studies, gender studies and the social sciences.

title: Advanced Remote Sensing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on core remote sensing concepts and techniques, focusing on the processing, transformation, classification, interpretation, and evaluation of optical and radar imagery. Students will gain hands-on experience using both specialised desktop software and open-source, cloud-based platforms to independently develop projects addressing contemporary issues across real-world applications. A key emphasis of this subject is the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into project workflows to enhance remote sensing analysis, improve interpretation accuracy, and automate processes for efficiently managing large datasets. By the end of the subject, students will be able to confidently select, apply, validate, and evaluate a range of remote sensing techniques, incorporating AI tools to design and implement projects using optical and radar imagery.
learning_outcomes: Design, implement and critically evaluate a project using image classification techniques applied to optical and radar imagery.
Apply, compare and evaluate appropriate transformation methods to enhance optical imagery interpretation.
Identify, apply and discuss techniques for optical and radar imagery processing.
Apply, critically evaluate and justify the use of AI tools to automate workflows and improve remote sensing analysis and efficiency .
prerequisites: SPA442: Remote Sensing 2: Image Processing and Analysis
SPA217: Remote Sensing of the Environment

title: Advanced Psychological Practice 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: PSY570 Advanced Psychological Practice 1 and PSY571 Advanced Psychological Practice 2, together, introduce students to the core elements of professional psychological practice. PSY571 is the second of two 350 hour placements which students are required to undertake in an area of professional psychology practice. As professional placements may be undertaken in any of a variety of settings (public health, forensic institutions, educational organisations, private practices etc), the specific content of the placement will be negotiated between the external placement supervisor and the student and will be approved by the School of Psychology's Placement Coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in diagnosis and case formulation.
Demonstrate proficiency in the delivery of evidence-based psychological interventions, and the conduct of appropriate evaluation of outcome.
Demonstrate proficiency in applied psychological assessment.
Conduct practice in accordance with professional and ethical standards.
Demonstrate applied knowledge of theories of psychopathology.
prerequisites: PSY570: Advanced Psychological Practice and Research 1

title: Advanced Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject covers complex research designs used in psychological research, as well as the statistical techniques that deal with them. Advanced univariate and multivariate techniques such as Factorial Analysis of Variance, MANOVA, multiple regression, factor analysis and reliability of scales are investigated. Students learn how to use the SPSS statistical program to apply these techniques to analysing data for research. They apply their learning in evaluating published research in terms of results and methodology. Emphasis is also placed on students undertaking key steps in analysing and reporting the results of research data in an area of psychological investigation. Students will apply their learning in further study and professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of statistics and methodology to undertake various key steps (e.g., design, data screening, preparation, analysis of data, and write-up of research results) in producing research of a high quality in an area of psychology.
Critically evaluate research papers both from a methodological and a statistical perspective.
Explain and critically evaluate the different types of research design used in psychological research and identify the strengths and weaknesses of different designs.
Apply knowledge of statistics and methodology in professional practice.
Identify the wide range of statistical procedures available to the researcher; and choose the most appropriate statistical procedures for a research design.
Interpret the analysis outputs of the statistical procedures covered in the subject.
prerequisites: PSY201: Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology

title: Advanced Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject covers complex research designs used in psychological research, as well as the statistical techniques that deal with them. Advanced univariate and multivariate techniques such as Factorial Analysis of Variance, MANOVA, multiple regression, factor analysis and reliability of scales are investigated. Students learn how to use the SPSS statistical program to apply these techniques to analysing data for research. They apply their learning in evaluating published research in terms of results and methodology. Emphasis is also placed on students undertaking key steps in analysing and reporting the results of research data in an area of psychological investigation. Students will apply their learning in further study and professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify the wide range of statistical procedures available to the researcher, and choose the most appropriate statistical procedures for a research design.
Interpret the analysis outputs of the statistical procedures covered in the subject.
Critically evaluate research papers both from a methodological and a statistical perspective.
Explain and critically evaluate the different types of research design used in psychological research and identify the strengths and weaknesses of different designs.

Apply knowledge of statistics and methodology to undertake various key steps (e.g., design, data screening, preparation, analysis of data, and write-up of research results) in producing research of a high quality in an area of psychology.
prerequisites: PSY451: Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology
PSY301: Advanced Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology

title: Advanced Social Inequality
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Inequality is one of the big social and political issues of the new millennium. This subject focuses on current patterns of social inequality in contemporary society. The subject critically analyses and evaluates diversity, social justice, social change, human rights and ethical dimensions of social inequality using principles evident in sociological theory. Sociological theories of inequality are presented and applied to national and global social inequalities. Topics covered include: socio-biology, the family, age, gender, race and ethnicity, regional inequality, income and wealth distribution, social class, social mobility, unemployment and the underclass, nationally and globally.
learning_outcomes: Identify, evaluate and critically review where and how social inequality occurs in Australia and globally.
Construct a sociological argument explaining and analysing social inequalities and communicating these in writing using appropriate referencing skills.
Investigate and analyse current events, past injustices, and patterns of social inequality using sociological theory.
Demonstrate cognitive and creative skills to exercise critical thinking and judgements in identifying and solving problems of social inequality with intellectual independence.
Demonstrate an ability to critically review, analyse, summarise and synthesise sociological scholarship and research.

title: Advanced Seminar in Mission and Evangelism
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to advanced study in mission and evangelism founded in Biblical and theological principles, together with a critical review of the history of mission and specifically its impact in the Australian, Asian and Pacific regions. Particular models of mission and evangelism are addressed together with their critical application within a given ministry context. Students will be challenged to develop a personal ethical approach to contemporary mission and to implement more effective models of mission and evangelism relevant to their cultural and ecclesial context.
learning_outcomes: Discuss critically contemporary approaches to mission and evangelism across a range of contexts, such as Asian, Pacific, Multi-cultural and Indigeneous Australian perspectives.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the theological and ecclesial basis for mission and evangelism.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of ethical approaches to mission and evangelism and articulate a personal ethical approach to contemporary mission.
Analyse critically the impact of evangelisation on Indigenous peoples.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the social, cultural and contextual issues in the mission of the church in the world.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the influences of the human sciences to the study of mission and evangelism.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the relationship of mission, evangelisation and evangelism to social justice and systemic inequity.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of historical perspectives on Christian mission.
Engage critically with biblical models and theology of mission and evangelism.

title: Advanced Social Work Practice Theory
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to critically review a number of theories which currently influence social work practice, policy and research and reflect on the theories and values which influence their own practice and the settings within which they work. The subject aims to enhance understandings of practice knowledge, values and skill issues that arise in the tension between managerial and professional approaches, and other issues facing contemporary social work so that a more thoughtful and reflective practice base is attained.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate principles and processes of critical reflection in examining the role of theory in their own professional practice experience.
Assess contemporary organisational and socio-political contexts and examine contextual tensions in applying theory to practice.
Apply principles and processes of critical thinking to identify and critique underpinning paradigms and practice theories in their own professional practice experience.
Apply principles and processes of reflection and critical reflection to their own professional practice experience.

title: Advanced Social Work Theory and Reflective Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject enables candidates to begin the process of developing their research topic, in the context of exploring contemporary theory and critically reflecting on their professional practice. Together with their supervisor/s, candidates reflect on the foundations of their research project and develop a plan for progress within the structure of the Doctor of Social Work.
learning_outcomes: Investigate critically identified issues in the professional practice of social work.
Demonstrate an understanding of the research process.
Actively and constructively engage with the supervisory team.
Demonstrate higher order skills in critical reflection on the strengths and weaknesses of contemporary theory, practice and philosophy relevant to the area of research.
Articulate a research topic of significance.

title: Advanced Social Research Methods
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores research methodology, epistemology, axiology and ontology relevant to the candidate's research topic. Opportunities are provided for candidates and their supervisor/s to extend and reflect on the relationship between research ethics and advanced methodological processes required for research and to gauge progress as the foundations of the research project are developed.
learning_outcomes: Understand the issues involved in formulating a research question.
Actively and constructively engage with the supervisory team.
Undertake initial planning of a research process to explore a research topic.
Identify and use appropriate research tools (software programs such as, but not limited to SPSS, NVivo, and the like).
Demonstrate a critical awareness of the principles of ethical social research.
Demonstrate an understanding of methodology, epistemology, axiology and ontology.
Critically evaluate published research.
Demonstrate an understanding of the research process.
Demonstrate an understanding of a range of data collection and analysis methods at an advanced level.

title: Advanced Structural Design
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject builds upon the foundational knowledge acquired in Engineering mechanics, mechanics of materials, and the introductory structural analysis. This subject focuses on structural design, and Australian codes and standards’ application. Topics covered include advanced structural analysis methods, and the design of concrete, steel and timber structures.
learning_outcomes: Design concrete, steel and timber structures in compliance with Australian codes and standards.
Apply advanced structural analysis methods and tools to analyse the behaviour of, and design structural systems under various loading conditions.

title: Advanced Statistical Modelling
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides specialised knowledge in order to perform advanced statistical modelling through a range of generalised regression analyses and spatial analyses. The subject will focus on generalised linear models based on the exponential family of distributions, including the Binomial, Poisson and logistic regression, and highlight some basic techniques for spatial data analysis. A feature of this subject will be the analysis of practical problems with real life data using modern computer packages, and interpretation of results for a variety of audiences.
learning_outcomes: Perform statistical analyses associated with generalised linear models including the Binomial, Poisson and Logistic Regression models.
Produce a report that interprets the output for an academic or professional audience.
Explain the role of Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) and their applications.
Evaluate a given situation to select the appropriate generalised linear method by checking assumptions.
Sample spatial features, test their patterns, and estimate their densities using appropriate statistical techniques in spatial data analysis for a range of applications.

title: Advanced Studies in Industrial Relations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines the major elements of the Australian industrial relations system. Students will systematically study the parties, processes and outcomes of Australia's industrial relations system, paying particular attention to the intersection with an organisation's strategic goals.
learning_outcomes: Critique and appraise ideas and perspectives of other students by creating and sharing information and knowledge in online moderated spaces.
Synthesise and apply theoretical frameworks and scholarly research to critically analyse issues relating to the practice of industrial relations in Australia.
Employ academic writing and information literacy skills to produce robust, well-supported argument related to industrial relations issues.
Apply specialised knowledge to solve complex problems relating to the Australian industrial relations system and the interrelationships among the parties and processes in the system.
Communicate specialised industrial relations knowledge and ideas to a variety of audiences.
Produce informed, relevant and well-communicated business advice and/or research papers relating to industrial relations issues.

title: Advanced Studies in Policing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This advanced policing subject seeks to address a series of contemporary, critical and emerging issues in policing. Various aspects of policing, both in Australia and internationally, along with the broader socio-political context in which policing operates, will be considered. The subject further seeks to extend upper level student knowledge of policing to contemporary, critical and emerging domestic and international issues relevant to professional practice, focussing on the most cutting edge innovations in the field. Students will apply theoretical and practical approaches to considering issues such as the use of force, mental health in the policing context and the role of forensic science in policing practice. This subject builds on the learning experiences offered in first year in which critical reflection on the role, function, styles and techniques of policing is enhanced.
learning_outcomes: Explain and analyse the interaction between policy and research.
Analyse various policing problems and their resolutions at a theoretical, policy and practical level.
Analyse and evaluate strengths and weaknesses in the policing response and provisions for each issue from a theoretical, policy and practical standpoint.
Demonstrate an awareness of the fluid nature of both the discipline and practice of policing.
Analyse and evaluate strengths and weaknesses of research in the areas being studied.

title: Advanced Study of Hadith Literature
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the knowledge and skills developed in ISL232. It involves the study of a selected range of Hadith from the canonical collections, and will allow students to critically examine the text (matn) and the chain (sanad) of these selected reports together with their commentaries (sharh) from various angles. It will expose students to the most well-known and relevant Hadith and enable them to develop the ability to apply the Hadith methodology developed in ISL232. Selected Hadith will have theological, moral, spiritual and legal implications within the context of Islamic studies.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate Hadith traditions.
Critically discuss the level of authenticity of Hadith for its social, theological and spiritual application.
Investigate and discuss the primary source of Hadith material in the analysis of religious issues.
Discuss the criteria for Hadith preference in legal applications.

title: Advanced Tomographic Imaging
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the advanced concepts and innovations associated with tomographic imaging. It will examine the principles and applications of frontier technologies in computed tomography (CT), single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), positron emission tomography (PET), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and hybrid technologies. Tomographic imaging principles and procedures will be explored and critically analysed within the context of clinical applications associated with advances in computer and data science, instrumentation, and physics. State-of-the-art protocols and procedures that optimise efficiencies, outcomes, costs or radiation dose will also be explored.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-based insight and knowledge to the principles of tomography within the clinical and research environments to optimise protocols and outcomes.
Analyse and explain the use of the principles and applications of tomographic imaging.
Identify and evaluate opportunities for, and applications of, advances in tomography to inform protocol development.
Critically evaluate the concepts of the technological advances in CT, MRI, SPECT, PET and hybrid systems.
prerequisites: MRS564: Computed Tomography Practice And Trends
MRS565: Advanced Principles in Computed Tomography

title: Advanced Study of Tafsir (Qur'anic Exegesis) Literature
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject exposes students to different Qur'anic exegeses. It also includes development of different forms of exegeses, helping students to see how Muslims have benefitted from the Qur'an. It considers the different ways in which the Qur'an has been interpreted as a source of understanding and implementation for Islamic jurisprudence and theology. It explores traditional and contemporary interpretations of the Qur'an in the Islamic world and the West. It also presents example passages from each classical exegetical work to show how they complement each other.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate exegetical methodology by studying selected passages from a range of exegesis works covering various genres.
Discuss the major Qur'anic exegetical types and works in the past and present.
Critically deduce theological, legal and spiritual meanings from the Qur'anic verses by following exegetical methodology.
Critically discuss multiple meanings of the Qur'an in terms of how it is a source for multiple Islamic disciplines.
Critically articulate theological, legal and spiritual knowledge and insights inherent in the Qur'an for everyday life.

title: Advanced Topics 1
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides in-depth study at an advanced level of topics related to the discipline area selected by a student for a Graduate Certificate, Graduate Diploma or Master coursework program. As such for some courses it is used as a capstone subject (i.e. a subject that integrates your prior learning in other subjects). The subject contains no intensive and students should arrange a project supervisor before enrolling in this subject. Students completing this subject will: i) have demonstrated an ability to apply their knowledge and skills with creativity and initiative to new situations in professional practice and/or for further learning and ii) shown an ability to plan and execute a substantial research-based project, capstone experience, and/or piece of scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Have communication and technical research skills to justify and interpret theoretical propositions, methodologies, conclusions and professional decisions to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Have demonstrated they have a body of knowledge that includes an in-depth understanding of a discipline and/or area of professional practice.
Have demonstrated the application of knowledge and skills to plan and execute a substantial research based project, capstone experience and/or piece of scholarship.
Have demonstrated the application of knowledge and skills with creativity and initiative to new situations in professional practice and/or for further learning.
Reflect critically on an in-depth and comprehensive body of knowledge of (or specialised technical skills in) a nominated topic area relevant to their degree.

title: Advanced Topics in Civil Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to extend their technical knowledge of civil engineering through further self-directed study. This could be through additional material offered by CSU staff, research seminars, or cross-institutional enrolment in other engineering programs.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate achievement of aggregate objectives in the individual topics chosen by the student.
Possess a comprehensive, theory based understanding of the underpinning natural and physical sciences and the engineering fundamentals applicable to the engineering discipline.
Fluently and critically apply engineering techniques, tools and resources.
Critique and use, a specialist body of knowledge within the engineering discipline.
prerequisites: ENG471: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Cadet Engineer
ENG473: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Senior Cadet Engineer

title: Advanced Topics 2
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides in-depth study at an advanced level of topics related to the discipline area selected by a student for a Graduate Certificate, Graduate Diploma or Master coursework program. As such for some courses it is used as a capstone subject (i.e. a subject that integrates your prior learning in other subjects) that is taken towards the end of a degree. The subject contains no intensive and students should arrange a project supervisor before enrolling in this subject. Students completing this subject will: i) have demonstrated an ability to apply their knowledge and skills with creativity and initiative to new situations in professional practice and/or for further learning and ii) shown an ability to plan and execute a substantial research-based project, capstone experience, and/or piece of scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on an in-depth and comprehensive body of knowledge of (or specialised technical skills in) a nominated topic area relevant to their degree.
Have a body of knowledge that includes the understanding of recent development in a discipline and/or area of professional practice.
Demonstrate the application of knowledge and skills with creativity and initiative to new situations in professional practice and/or for further learning.
Communication and technical research skills to justify and interpret theoretical propositions, methodologies, conclusions and professional decisions to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Advanced Topics in Food Science and Nutrition
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will integrate prior knowledge and skills derived from previous studies to plan, implement and evaluate a project with due consideration of any ethical aspects, and reflect on how this will inform their future practice in the food science and/or nutrition profession. Experience in industry may form a component of the project.
learning_outcomes: Collect, analyse and interpret relevant research data using methods appropriate to the project being undertaken.
Describe in depth a specific area of food science and/or nutrition through the medium of a literature review or report.
Critique the scientific literature and its application to practice.
Identify, collate and critically review scientific information to inform planning, implementation and evaluation of a project.
Apply scientific conventions commonly used in the presentation of both an oral seminar and in a written report.

title: Advanced Topics In Civil Engineering 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students select a specialty area of engineering in which they will extend their technical knowledge of engineering through completing a required set of advanced topics and further self-directed study. This further advanced technical knowledge could be gained through additional material offered by CSU staff, research seminars, conferences, and industry and professional training opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Critique and use a specialist body of knowledge and design practices within the engineering sub-discipline.
Demonstrate achievement of aggregate objectives in the set of topics for their choen specialty of engineering.
Possess a comprehensive, theory and practice based understanding of the underpinning natural and physical sciences and the engineering fundamentals applicable to the engineering siub-discipline.
Fluently and critically apply engineering techniques, tools, resources and methods in a specialised sub-discipline of engineering.

ENG471: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Cadet Engineer
ENG477: Topic Tree - Senior Cadet Engineer 4

title: Advanced Topics In Civil Engineering 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students continue to extend their technical knowledge in their chosen specialty area of engineering. Students will deepen their understanding of the sub-discipline through independent study avenues such as supplementary materials, research seminars, conferences, industry and professional training opportunities, or cross-institutional enrolment in other engineering programs.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and analyse engineering techniques, tools, resources and methods in a specialised sub-discipline of engineering with fluency and critical insight.
Synthesise a comprehensive, theory-based comprehension of the foundational principles in natural and physical sciences relevant to the engineering sub-discipline.
Demonstrate an in-depth mastery of a specialist body of knowledge and design practices within the engineering sub-discipline, while critically reflecting on its application and implications.
