title: Advanced Veterinary Clinical Skills
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject allows candidates to develop advanced clinical skills and knowledge in a selected discipline, develop cognitive and technical skills, abilities to synthesise and increase theoretical knowledge in professional practice and integration of research activity for investigation and development of new knowledge.
learning_outcomes: be able to work with initiative, full responsibility and accountability and intellectual independence for professional development.
be able to demonstrate advanced cognitive and technical skills, expert understanding of theoretical knowledge and research skills for application to professional practice;
be able to demonstrate a substantial body of knowledge relevant to the chosen discipline and capacity to apply knowledge in the context of professional practice;
be able to demonstrate communication skills integral to specialised professional practice, and

title: Advanced Virology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This advanced virology subject will allow students to further investigate the biology and pathogenesis of medically important viruses at the cellular and molecular level. The subject will also study how viruses can be used in the biotechnology industry and gene based therapeutic approaches to treat disease. The subject will also focus on the technology used in the modern diagnostic virology laboratory and recent advances in pathogen detection and disease epidemiology. The subject will also study viruses from a public health perspective including preventing transmission and control of disease outbreaks, including vaccination and pharmacological intervention strategies.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate how principles of virology and virus replication can be applied to development of new drugs, vaccines and diagnostic techniques.
Explain the design of and use of appropriate molecular techniques for the diagnosis for viral diseases.
Critically evaluate recent published data relating to research in virology.
Explain the rationale of current anti-viral treatment strategies with particular reference to immunodeficiency viruses.
Comprehensively explain in detail how virus structure and replication relates to the pathogenesis of medically important viruses.
Critically interpret the safety issues associated with the use of viruses for gene therapy.
Integrate data from phylogenetic analysis of viral evolution and its application to epidemiology of disease outbreaks.

Describe the pathology of virus infections with particular reference to immunodeficiency diseases, latent and reactivation diseases, malignancies and development of new drugs and vaccines for their treatment.

title: Advances in Clinical Practice and Prescribing
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject equips students with the necessary knowledge and skills for safe and therapeutically appropriate prescribing and management of specific clinical conditions. The subject is designed to provide registered pharmacists with the skills to undertake an extended scope of clinical practice in keeping with advances in the profession.
learning_outcomes: Apply clinical skills in a Work Integrated Learning (WIL) environment, while collaborating effectively with experienced prescribers and other health care practitioners to support patient care, including referral arrangements and care coordination when necessary.

Develop management plans through clear and respectful communication with patients, incorporating both pharmacological and non-pharmacological options, and determine when referral to other healthcare practitioners is required.
Apply knowledge of epidemiology, anatomy, physiology, and pathophysiology to patient care, and integrate evidence-based guidelines, clinical protocols, and practice standards into decision-making.
Identify, evaluate and interpret relevant clinical investigations, including pathology where relevant, to support clinical decision-making and patient care management.
Evaluate patient care management including medication use, side effects, and preventive strategies, and maintain accurate and timely clinical documentation.
Conduct thorough patient history-taking, identify risk factors, and perform relevant examinations and assessments to formulate differential diagnoses and initial management plans.

Apply the pharmacist’s scope of practice guidelines and principles of culturally safe practice in evaluating and managing individual patient presentations, including relevant legislative frameworks and ethical considerations, while respecting patient diversity.

title: Advancing Emergency Care Nursing Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the development of advanced knowledge and skills in the triage, assessment, and management of emergency presentations in the rural and remote environment. Students will use state, rural and remote clinical guidelines as a foundation for exploring the underlying pathophysiology, common assessment findings and collaborative management of common emergency presentations across the lifespan. Students will analyse the unique features and challenges of the rural and remote environment on the provision of timely, definitive emergency care and explore care delivery models to improve patient outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Analyse legal and ethical principles related to the provision of emergency care in the rural and remote environment, including scope of practice of the registered nurse.
Evaluate the role of the registered nurse in preparing the patient for retrieval across the lifespan.
Analyse the impact of the rural and remote environment, and models of emergency care delivery, on the provision of timely care and patient outcomes.
Apply advanced communication skills, including the use of technology to access, present, interpret and document relevant information.
Apply the principles of triage to assess urgency in relation to emergency presentations across the lifespan.
Integrate clinical reasoning, clinical guidelines, and knowledge of underlying pathophysiology to undertake focused assessment and time-critical interventions for common emergency presentations.

title: Advertising and Design
school: School

title: Ageing and Professional Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on development of professional practice knowledge and skills to be able to work ethically and in partnership with older people in health and human services contexts in Australia. A bio-psycho-sociocultural approach to ageing and professional practice is utilised. A number of contemporary practice models applicable to contexts of ageing at home, residential and home care services will be examined, including a focus on interdisciplinary collaboration and working in partnership with family caregivers. The concept of Yindyamarra Winhanganha and its foundational concepts will be introduced as a way of engaging in respectful relationships with First Nations Elders, families and communities. The historical context of colonisation, policy and practices and the impacts on the health and wellbeing of older Indigenous Australians will be examined. Ways of ‘walking together with’ First Nations Elders and communities will be explored as will opportunities to extend these knowledges to broader practice. Students will engage in reflective practices applying ethics and values, awareness of own positionality and critical re-evaluation of the standpoint which they bring to their own practice. Students will develop a professional development plan for ongoing education and career progression.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the impact of historical events and policies in relation to the health and wellbeing of older First Nations Australians and their communities, drawing on decolonising approaches and Indigenist Standpoint theory.

Examine, compare and evaluate a range of professional practice models and ethical approaches to working in partnership with older adults, their families and in collaboration with other health and human services professionals.

Critically reflect on contemporary professional practice models and develop an individual practice model that incorporates principles of cultural awareness including Yindyamarra Winhanganha that is applicable to professional practice with older adults.
Analyse, reflect on and critique own current professional practice, identify opportunities for interdisciplinary communication and collaboration and plan for future professional development.

title: Agile Project Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce the principles and practices of Agile Project Management. Students will learn the background and origins of various Agile concepts and methodologies. Scrum will be examined in detail, as well as the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe®). Students will also study the strengths and weaknesses of Agile, and the steps involved in managing an Agile project.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the differences between Agile and other project management methodologies.
Interpret and apply various principles, phases and activities of the Scrum methodology.
Create elements of an Agile project management plan and apply the practical decisions and management actions of an Agile project within context.
Understand stakeholder strategies and create engagement plans for the different people in an Agile project.
 be able to identify the strengths and weaknesses of Agile and leverage or mitigate them in the correct situations.
Implement SAFe® principles to larger projects.

title: Agile Project Management and Recovery
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce the principles and practices of Agile Project Management and also address recovery issues. Students will learn various Agile concepts, methodologies and practices. Scrum will be examined in detail as well as the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe). Students will evaluate the strenghts and weaknesses of Agile approaches, the steps involved in managing an Agile project and recovery options for projects that go "off track".
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the differences between Agile and other project management methodologies.
Implement SAFe principles to larger projects.
Create elements of an Agile project management plan and apply the practical decisions and management actions of an Agile project within context.
Examine stakeholder strategies and create engagement plans for different people in an Agile project.
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of Agile and leverage or mitigate them in the correct situations including recovery.
Intrepret and apply various principles, phases and activities of the Scrum methodology.

title: Agribusiness Systems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the holistic nature of agricultural industries from both an Australian and a global perspective. A supply/value chain approach is taken as a way of studying the components of and the interrelationships between resources, functions and processes and consumer products of agribusiness systems. Emphasis is placed on identifying issues affecting the sustainability of agribusiness systems in a dynamic global environment.
learning_outcomes: Describe how Quality Assurance and Quality Control systems are integrated throughout an agricultural value chain.
Describe an agricultural value chain in a simple diagrammatic form from farm to retail.

Demonstrate an understanding of the principles of value chain analysis, the concept of market failure and identify examples of organisations established to support the functioning of an agricultural value chain.
Demonstrate an understanding of the differences between vertical and horizontal integration in supply chains.
Identify the various forms of information and associated communication flows that occur along a value chain and describe their purpose.
Identify, analyse and recommend a response to an external issue impacting an agricultural value chain.
Identify the key principles of marketing and supply chain management.
Identify the key non-financial drivers of a successful agricultural business.

title: Agribusiness Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a comprehensive subject aimed at introducing the principles and practice of business management with particular emphasis on financial management of small agribusinesses. Major topics of study include: management concepts; understanding financial statements, evaluating past performance planning ahead; financing the business; the taxation system in Australia; investment appraisal and business structure. The subject material is applied to businesses involved in the equine sector, agriculture, viticulture and issues in farm forestry.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the particular problems of small business management.
Demonstrate an understanding of and apply business planning procedures and investment analysis to long-term investments.
Show an appreciation of and account for the taxation procedures that apply to small business.
Demonstrate comprehension of the forms of business structure available to small business and explain their advantages and disadvantages.
Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of management and management activities.
Demonstrate an understanding of business finance, sources of finance and financial planning.
Prepare, analyse and interpret financial statements in an agribusiness context.

title: Agribusiness Planning
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Agribusiness Planning is a 16 point capstone subject in which students prepare a business plan for an agribusiness. It is a project-based study where students will analyse an existing agribusiness and create a strategy for its improvement; or develop and evaluate a new agribusiness proposal through to a steady state position. In each case, the focus will be on the achievement of pre-defined goals. Analysis and planning will be strategic and holistic, taking account of the multiple contexts in which the agribusiness will operate. Students will also reflect on the development of their capabilities relative to the subjects learning objectives and to the agribusiness planning process, and plan for ongoing personal development.
learning_outcomes: Review the strategic direction of an agribusiness and assess opportunities that can achieve improved financial; human; environmental; and marketing and production outcomes.
Prepare and analyse the production and financial forecasts of the business plan.
Develop a marketing, operations and human resource plan based on new opportunities that are tailored to the specific industry context of the agribusiness.
Review the proposed project outcomes relative to the business mission and goals and suggest changes to the business plan in the light of this review.
Use a holistic model to analyse financial, human; environmental; and marketing and production issues that need to be factored into holistic and strategic business planning.

Conduct a risk assessment of financial; human; environmental; and marketing and production factors, plan contingency strategies for risk events and undertake scenario analysis from a whole of business perspective.
Reflect on the development of their capabilities and prepare a plan for personal development.
Undertake a situation analysis examining the feasibility of the revised strategic direction by conducting an audit of the external and internal environments.
Prepare and present a business plan.
Review the mission, goals and outcomes by undertaking an issues analysis based on SWOT.

title: Agile Thinking For Marketers In a Disrupted World
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will identify and examine the key societal and market-based issues facing marketers. Students will analyse the influence and impact of a range of transformative and disruptive factors on markets. Then students will assess the need for marketers to engage in practices that are agile, consistent, reflective, responsive and ethical. Students will explore emerging technologies and their effect on the marketplace. Finally, students will develop and exercise their judgment to build a portfolio of responsive marketing strategy solutions to contemporary issues using predictive and forecasting scenario planning techniques.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and reflect on the impact and influence of revolutionary changes in existing and evolving markets.
Work effectively within groups to brainstorm, negotiate and develop convergent solutions.
Exercise judgement to create and communicate responsive and engaging solutions for marketing practice.
Synthesise a range of issues to map their impact on the organisation's value proposition, marketing strategies and tactics.
Explore, evaluate and draw conclusions regarding complex ethical, societal and market based issues.
Identify and critically analyse assumptions and biases within social structures.

title: Agribusiness Planning
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students prepare an in-depth 5 year business strategic plan for an existing agribusiness. It is a project-based study where students will analyse an existing agribusiness, determine the long term goals and objectives with the owners or managers, and create a strategy for its improvement and/or development. In each case, the focus will be on the achievement of the owners or managers pre-defined goals. Analysis and planning will be strategic and holistic, taking account of the multiple contexts in which the business operates. Students will also critically analyse and explore deeper engagement of agribusiness planning as part of their development relative to agribusiness planning strategies and personal development.
learning_outcomes: Review, analyse and document the strategic direction of an agribusiness and assess opportunities that can achieve improved financial; human; environmental; and marketing and production outcomes.
Analyse, explain and review the mission, goals and outcomes by undertaking an issues analysis based on Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats ('SWOT').
Explain and review the project outcomes relative to the business mission and goals and suggest changes to the business plan in the light of this review.
Design, prepare and present a business plan.
Discuss, analyse and report on the development of their capabilities and using integrated engagement prepare a plan for personal development.
Prepare and analyse production and financial forecasts of enterprise and business performance and compare the outcomes to internal and industry key performance indicators.
Conduct a risk assessment of financial; human; environmental; and marketing and production factors and plan contingency strategies for risk events nominated by the students project supervisor.
Demonstrate the use of an holistic model to analyse financial, human; environmental; and marketing and production issues that need to be factored into holistic and strategic business planning.
Undertake a situation analysis examining the feasibility of the revised strategic direction by conducting an audit of the external and internal environments.
Design and develop marketing, operational and organisational/human resource plans based on new opportunities that are tailored to the specific industry context of the agribusiness.

title: Agricultural and Sustainable Development Goals
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines the key issues and links between agriculture and sustainable development in a global context, using case studies in Australia and internationally. Upon completion, students can critically assess the relationship between agriculture and sustainable development, drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives and approaches.
learning_outcomes: Review, consolidate and synthesise knowledge from several case studies to critically understand the effectiveness of various approaches to agriculture.
Make sound judgments on the use and application of some current methods of social and science research.
Critique and assess factors influencing the application of interdisciplinary perspectives and approaches to agriculture.
Explain the terminology, concepts, principles, and theory associated with global sustainable development.
Reflect on and discuss the key challenges associated with implementing sustainable development in a global context.

title: Agricultural Biotechnology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce students to the critical aspects of biotechnology in agriculture. Students will learn the key principles behind the fundamental biochemical processes and their underlying genetic basis. The application of these skills is essential in all aspects of food production, and is of increasing importance for nutritional security.
learning_outcomes: Outline the social and regulatory issues relating to recombinant DNA technology in an agricultural context.
Relate the implications of genetic change to improvements in agricultural production, particularly regarding conventional and molecular breeding.
Apply the principles and extensions of Mendelian genetics to agricultural production systems, and describe the link between genotype and phenotype.
Describe the structure and function of the four major classes of biological macromolecules and apply this knowledge to describe the properties of enzymes and cofactors in biological systems.

title: Agricultural Business Risk and Investment
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject addresses the application of financial business management, economic and risk management principles to decision making in agribusiness and agricultural systems. Major areas of study include: agribusiness management and decision making principles; managing risk and decision making under uncertainty; historical and projected agribusiness productivity and financial analysis; benchmarking and best practice analysis; analysing and acquiring capital resources; and accounting for sustainability and environmental agribusiness assets. The subject also develops a framework on how to assess and measure risk, and formulate strategies to reduce it from a qualitative and quantitative perspective. The influence of the decision maker through individual bias and decision making heuristics are also examined.
learning_outcomes: Understand and examine the roles of qualitative and quantitative analysis in risk management.
Identify the sources of risk to an agribusiness and their management implications.
Demonstrate how to develop and apply principles of historical and projected performance analysis for agribusinesses.
Demonstrate how to carry out formal procedures of capital investment appraisal in agriculture and be able to interpret the answers of these analyses.
Demonstrate how to develop and apply basic principles of management and decision making in relation to agribusiness.
Define risk, differentiate between risk and uncertainty, and explain and detail the key variables influencing risk.
Carry out benchmarking and best practice analysis of individual agribusiness and understand industry expectations, including the consideration of environmental assets and agribusiness sustainability.
Apply techniques for the assessment of risk and develop strategies to enhance decision making under uncertainty.
prerequisites: AGB352: Agricultural Business Risk and Investment

title: Agricultural Business Management Dissertation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject gives the student the opportunity to investigate in depth an area of personal interest in relation to Agricultural Business Management. This is the capstone subject in the Master of Agricultural Business Management program for students and is designed to develop skills in building a research question, formulating strategies to answer that question, and gathering evidence to develop a well reasoned treatise that addresses the research question. The Agricultural Business Management Dissertation principally involves an evaluation of information from a wide range of sources enabling students to formulate a view or perspective on a chosen topic. Field studies may be included but are not expected and would be a minor component.
learning_outcomes: Disseminate the outcomes of the dissertation through a seminar presentation and preparation of a draft journal publication.
Demonstrate how to access data or information on a specified topic from a wide range of sources including databases of primary sources of information.
Develop a focused research question and a framework or methodology of enquiry.
Prepare a written report, dissertation that develops a well-reasoned proposition for which evidence has been gathered and discussed in a logical manner.
Critically appraise and evaluate collected data.

title: Agricultural Business Risk and Investment
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be introduced to the application of financial business management, economic and risk management principles to decision making in agribusiness and agricultural systems. Major areas of study include: agribusiness management and decision making principles; managing risk and decision making under uncertainty; historical and projected agribusiness productivity and financial analysis; benchmarking & best practice analysis; analysing and acquiring capital resources; and accounting for sustainability and environmental agribusiness assets. Students will develop a framework on how to assess and measure risk, and formulate strategies to reduce it from a qualitative and quantitative perspective. Students will also examine the influence of the decision maker through individual bias and decision making heuristics.
learning_outcomes: Carry out formal procedures of capital investment appraisal in agriculture and be able to interpret the answers of these analyses.
Apply techniques for the assessment of risk and develop strategies to enhance decision making under uncertainty.
Apply principles of management and decision making in relation to agribusiness.
Define risk, differentiate between risk and uncertainty, and explain and detail the key variables influencing risk.
Compare and examine the roles qualitative and quantitative analysis in risk management.
Define and apply principles of historical and projected performance analysis for agribusinesses.
Explain industry expectations, including the consideration of environmental assets and agribusiness sustainability.
Identify the sources of risk to an agribusiness and their management implications.
Carry out benchmarking and best practice analysis of an individual agribusiness.

title: Agricultural Communication for Impact
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Start your investigation into a chosen field of study with the guidance of staff by finding and critically analysing past agricultural research communications and assessing the impact on the expected target audience. This subject is designed to promote the development of critical thinking in developing a change plan and communicating agricultural research to allow you to become confident in reviewing communications critically but constructively. You will work with the guidance and support of staff to undertake a broad review of methods for communicating agricultural research results and critique the impact. Based on this analysis, you will develop a communication plan for your field of study that is expected to suit the target audience to ensure maximum impact. You will develop communications about your field of study using at least two different methods. Core curriculum principles informing this subject include your transition toward independence in being able to source and review communication critically and constructively, and to utilize evidence to form a change plan and as a result a suitable communication plan and then develop communications for impact.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical thinking in developing a change plan and a communication plan suited to a target audience.
Assess the impact of research communications on an expected target audience.
Analyse research communications with reference to theory.
Evaluate and rate the work of their peers.
Demonstrate excellent verbal communication skills e.g. through developing research communications in at least two different methods.

title: Agricultural Economics
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Agricultural economics is the application of economic and financial management principles relating to the economic, social and environmental performances of agricultural businesses. This extends beyond the farm gate to include a broader range of food- and fibre-related activities contributing significantly to the nation's output. Students will be introduced to the key economic theories and financial management tools for decision-making in Australia's agricultural industries from domestic and international perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Describe various agricultural industries and the characteristics of their market structures.
Describe the forces of supply and demand and explain how they determine price in the market.
Explain the relevance of private and social costs in agricultural production and market failure.
Identify core principles of microeconomics, especially relating to agricultural production, cost analysis and prices, and apply these principles to selected farm management problems.
Interpret and apply basic algebra and graphical representation to present economic concepts.

title: Agricultural Finance and Business Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a comprehensive subject introducing students to principles and practice of accounting and managing finances for agribusinesses engaged in primary production. Students will develop their knowledge of the annual accounting cycle and producing Cash Flow, Depreciation, Trading, Income, Financial Position and Gross Margin Statements for primary producers and associated agribusinesses. Students will analyse the financial performance of sole proprietor agricultural businesses with comparisons to alternative business structures. The subject has been designed to be adaptable to the needs of students irrespective of the agricultural industry with which they most closely affiliate, with examples provided from various agricultural crop, animal, equine and viticulture enterprises.
learning_outcomes: Utilise financial performance indicators to analyse the profitability, liquidity and long-term stability of an agricultural business.
Identify the financial resources and the financial management objectives of agricultural businesses.
Explain the impact of business structures and taxation procedures on small agricultural businesses.
Construct, analyse and interpret the meaning of biophysical and financial statements that define the performance of an agricultural business.
Apply interest rate and discounting procedures for financing agricultural businesses.

title: Agricultural Industry Practicum
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this subject is to prepare students to enter their chosen career in a supported manner that encourages personal and professional development. This subject allows students to take the knowledge gained in previous subjects and apply it within a business context. Students apply for and sit interviews with businesses (with which the School has an ongoing relationship) to gain a place with the business for a 12 week practicum. Within the business, trained staff are assigned to each student to act as a mentor and to assess the students development within the workplace. During practicum and the teaching periods before and after, students are evaluated on a range of assessment tasks designed to encourage reflection of the students own professional/personal development. These tasks are also designed to improve a students communication and interpersonal skills, technical competency, and self-learning and problem solving skills in the context of a business.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively and show formed linkages with the part of Industry towards which they have a career orientation.
Demonstrate excellent verbal and written communication strategies when engaging with people, including clients, work colleagues and other industry professionals.
Discuss the complexities of industry practice in context.
Demonstrate an understanding of how to identify problems within the workplace or region and demonstrate problem-solving skills.
Obtain a level of technical competency to allow them to operate effectively and independently within the workplace.
Observe and critically analyse a commercial business and suggest potential ways in which to develop practice.
Participate effectively as part of a team.
Extend and give practical application to the knowledge gained in previous subjects.
Demonstrate professional conduct within a workplace.
Clearly identify personal goals and learning needs with regard to professional practice and development including an ability to learn independently.
Demonstrate and effectively convey appropriate skills during practice job interviews.
Write an effective job application and curriculum vitae.
Maintain a portfolio identifying practicum experiences and the learning that has taken place as a result of these experiences.

title: Agricultural Marketing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The modern food and fibre system is complex, dynamic and international, with revolutionary changes taking place. The system is becoming highly demand-driven with marketing being very important. The purpose of this subject is to examine agriproduct marketing (raw commodities, food, fibre and agricultural services) in this new global environment. Agriproducts can be categorised into undifferentiated products (also called commodities) and differentiated products. Students will examine the marketing of these two types of agriproducts in detail, focusing on both conceptual and practical aspects. Students will also develop a marketing plan and carry out real-time research for a selected agriproduct.
learning_outcomes: Create a marketing plan and conduct primary research for differentiated agriproducts.
Review how commodity markets work, how future markets work and how to analyse price movements in commodity markets.
Identify how and explain why agriproduct marketing has undergone such revolutionary changes in recent times.

title: Agricultural Production and Food Systems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject the students will investigate global agricultural production and food systems. Students will reflect on previous technical knowledge components of agricultural production systems but also analyse the complex relational interactions that occur. To undertake this process, agricultural production and food systems will be investigated through the lens of biophysical, economic and social systems. This subject will also describe food production and utilisation as it relates to food security. Students completing this subject will gain a thorough understanding of the complexity of agricultural production and food systems.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate social factors affecting agriculture production and value chains.
Differentiate biophysical agricultural production systems including nutrient flows.
Explain key aspects of global food systems and to develop solutions to food insecurity.
Analyse value chains operation from farm input supply to final end consumers.

title: Agricultural Research Dissertation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a research subject available only to students enrolled in the Master of Agricultural Science (with specialisations). This subject gives the student the opportunity to investigate in depth an area of personal interest in relation to agriculture. This is the capstone subject in the Masters program, and is designed to develop skills in building a research question, formulating strategies to answer that question, and gathering evidence to develop a well reasoned treatise that addresses the research question. Students enrolled in this subject will work directly with their supervisory team to undertake an appropriate research project and complete a dissertation.
learning_outcomes: Design a research project, including the appropriate application of research methodologies, and articulate this design in a research proposal.
Demonstrate how to access data or information on a specified topic from a wide range of sources including databases of primary sources of information.
Obtain human/animal ethics approval (if required).
Demonstrate proficiency in the execution of a research project through submission of a high-quality dissertation.
Critically appraise and evaluate collected data.
Effectively communicate the research project in written and verbal formats.

title: Agricultural Marketing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The modern food and fibre system is complex, dynamic and international. The changes taking place in this system are revolutionary. The system is becoming highly demand-driven with marketing being very important. The purpose of this subject is to examine the question of agriproduct marketing (raw commodities, food, fibre and agricultural services) in this new global environment. Agriproducts can be categorized into undifferentiated products (also called commodities) and differentiated products. The marketing of these two different types of agriproducts are examined in detail, focusing on both conceptual and practical aspects.
learning_outcomes: Accurately explain how and why agriproduct marketing has undergone such revolutionary change in recent times.
Accurately explain how differentiated product markets work and how to go about market planning of differentiated agriproducts.
Demonstrate how commodity markets work, how futures markets work and how to go about analysing price movements in commodity market.

title: Agricultural Industry Internship
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this subject is to prepare students to enter their chosen career in a supported manner that encourages personal and professional development and integrates them into the agricultural network. Students will work beside a mentor within Industry, applying their academic learning in a professional setting and developing a portfolio of their employability and technical skills. Students will be prepared for their time in industry by addressing topics around reflective practice, workplace dynamics, communication, safety in the workplace and professional conduct. It is intended that students will leave this subject with a refined resume and renewed awareness of professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Explore and enhance personal brand development through academic application, self-development and life-long learning.
Develop and enhance communication skills to various audiences within the industry.
Prepare an effective job application for the Agricultural industry.
Critically evaluate and reflect on practical and technical competency development through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.
Implement professional standards within the Agricultural industry.

title: Agricultural Value Chains
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to factors unique to agri-food and fibre value chains, value chain analysis and opportunities to improve value chain performance. Students will employ a supply/value chain approach to study the components of and the interrelationships between resources, functions and processes and consumer products of agribusiness systems.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and apply key value chain functions including; agriproduct transformation and value adding, quality assurance and quality control systems, marketing and communication, supply chain management and commodity trading.
Evaluate the principles of value chain analysis and the concept of free market failure intervention.
Research, analyse and recommend a response to an issue or opportunity impacting an agricultural value chain.
Describe an agri-food or fibre value chain in a simple diagrammatic form from farm to retail.

title: AI and Machine Learning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces applied machine learning techniques and workflows used in contemporary AI applications, including cloud-enabled environments and services. In this subject, students explore supervised and unsupervised machine learning techniques through applied case studies and practical experimentation. The subject focuses on how machine learning models are developed, evaluated, and applied to solve real-world problems using contemporary tools and datasets. Ethical considerations, bias, transparency, and responsible AI practices are embedded throughout. Students develop practical skills in selecting, interpreting, and evaluating machine learning techniques within software and organisational contexts.
learning_outcomes: Explain fundamental concepts and workflows used in applied machine learning.
Interpret machine learning outputs and assess their reliability, limitations, and potential bias.
Analyse ethical, social, and organisational considerations associated with machine learning applications.
Evaluate machine learning model performance using suitable validation and testing approaches.
Apply appropriate machine learning techniques and tools to solve practical problems using real-world datasets.

title: Akhlaq (Morality) and Adab (Manners) in Islam
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject explores Islam in everyday human interactions. It introduces the two concepts; akhlaq (morality) and adab (manners) from an Islamic perspective and the importance of their application in developing human virtue and perfection. The subject commences with akhlaq and adab in the everyday life of a Muslim, followed by immediate family, and then other common relationships such as neighbours, work colleagues and friends. One's relationship with the environment, animals and worship will also be covered. An important part of this subject is to study the traditional understanding of akhlaq and adab through the lens of the Qur'an, Hadith and the traditional scholars. The traditional understanding of each relationship type will then be analysed, considering the benefits and the challenges of their application in the contemporary context.
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the relationship between good character, akhlaq (morality) and adab (manners).
Understand the role of akhlaq (morality) an adab (manners) in the life of a Muslim.
Critically analyse the application of the traditional understanding of akhlaq (morality) and adab (manners) in today's world.
Explain the traditional understanding of akhlaq (morality) and adab (manners) in different relationship types.

title: Algorithms and Programming for Geospatial Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students are introduced to key mathematical concepts and programming techniques to design and implement solutions to real-world geospatial problems. Open-source programming languages are introduced to develop a life-long learning capability in spatial programming while facilitating the learning in the development of algorithms for GIS and Remote Sensing. Open-source software is also explored to equip the student with a comprehensive geospatial science toolbox beyond the use of commercial software. Programming techniques are demonstrated by solving selected real-world problems related to spatial modelling, and imagery processing and classification.
learning_outcomes: Utilise open-source software to carry out spatial analysis, imagery processing and classification.
Design and implement programming techniques to solve a real-world spatial problem.
Construct and implement GIS and Remote Sensing algorithms for common data processing tasks.
Apply mathematical concepts required for the development of algorithms relevant to GIS and Remote Sensing.
prerequisites: SPA215: GIS 1: Geographic Information Science Foundations

title: Algorithms in GIS and Remote Sensing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students learn the advanced mathematical knowledge and skills required to analyse and develop mathematical algorithms for GIS and Remote Sensing. This includes developing a good understanding of mathematical concepts required for the development of GIS-related algorithms, developing skills in solving linear algebra problems, having an ability to analyse, modify and design various GIS algorithms.Students also learn important mathematical concepts and algorithms commonly used in processing of multispectral remote sensed imagery. This includes understanding the sources and characteristics of remote sensed data and the geometric and radiometric corrections to remote sensed imagery. Students who complete this subject will have advanced knowledge and skills in constructing and implementing spatial algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Construct and implement GIS algorithms for common spatial processing tasks.
Construct and implement remote sensing algorithms for common image processing tasks.
Implement mathematical concepts required for the development of remote sensing-related algorithms.
Implement mathematical concepts required for the development of GIS-related algorithms.
prerequisites: SPA403: Algorithms in GIS and Modelling

title: An Introduction to Data Management: Governance, Standards and Ethics
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Data has always been an organisational asset, however, with organisations and individuals now producing vast amounts of real-time heterogeneous data (ie Big Data), there is greater demand than ever to manage and use data effectively. In this subject, students will develop an understanding of the issues involved in data management, including planning, infrastructure, and governance, driving the control of data and its lifecycle. Students are also challenged to consider the range of issues related to handling data, including privacy, security, data preservation, ethics, data storage and data distribution.
learning_outcomes: Discuss governance, standards and ethics for data (business, scientific, governmental, and scholarly).
Investigate data management research and technological trends.
Critically analyse the challenges associated with data management and data sharing for collaboration and re-use.
Define data and identify the role of data in organisational, cultural, technological, legal, business and other contexts.
Describe data concepts, terms, tools and technologies.
Demonstrate understanding of the variety of data types generated and used.
Demonstrate understanding of both theoretical and practical issues in data management.

title: Aligning Learning, Teaching and Assessment
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The alignment of curriculum, pedagogy and assessment within the context of students’ learning needs is core to effective teaching and learning. In this subject, teacher education students will be introduced to the purpose of assessment, related conceptual frameworks, principles and policies and their influence on assessment requirements and practices. Students will extend their knowledge and skills in assessing student learning through informal and formal, diagnostic, formative and summative strategies. They will use a range of student, class, school and system data and evidence to assess learning and to inform planning. This subject will cover approaches to feedback and feedforward, comparable judgements and moderation, and ongoing evaluation. Additionally, students will develop skills in reporting assessment information to enable decision-making and recommendations for multiple stakeholders including students, parents/carers, teachers and schools.
learning_outcomes: Apply their knowledge of student learning, curriculum, pedagogy, assessment and reporting to plan learning sequences.
Interpret and analyse student assessment data and appropriately modify teaching programs.
Create learning goals that provide achievable challenges for all students.
Identify processes for timely and appropriate feedback to students about their learning.
Discuss assessment moderation and its application to support consistent and comparable judgements of student learning.
Assess student learning through informal and formal, diagnostic, formative and summative approaches.
Identify strategies for reporting to students and parents/carers.
Apply fitness for purpose and principles of inclusion in assessment design.
prerequisites: EEE505: Aligning Learning, Teaching and Assessment

title: Aligning Learning, Teaching and Assessment
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The alignment of curriculum, pedagogy and assessment within the context of students’ learning needs is core to effective teaching and learning. In this subject, teacher education students will be introduced to the purpose of assessment, related conceptual frameworks, principles and policies and their influence on assessment requirements and practices. Students will extend their knowledge and skills in assessing student learning through informal and formal, diagnostic, formative and summative strategies. They will use a range of student, class, school and system data and evidence to assess learning and to inform planning. This subject will cover approaches to feedback and feedforward, comparable judgements and moderation, and ongoing evaluation. Additionally, students will develop skills in reporting assessment information to enable decision-making and recommendations for multiple stakeholders including students, parents/carers, teachers and schools.
learning_outcomes: Create learning goals that provide achievable challenges for all students.
Critically reflect on assessment moderation and its application to support consistent and comparable judgements of student learning.
Analyse and evaluate student assessment data and appropriately modify teaching programs.
Identify strategies for reporting to students and parents/carers.
Apply fitness for purpose and principles of inclusion in assessment design.
Identify processes for timely and appropriate feedback to students about their learning.
Apply their knowledge of student learning, curriculum, pedagogy, assessment and reporting to plan and justify learning sequences.
Assess student learning through informal and formal, diagnostic, formative and summative approaches.
prerequisites: EEE315: Aligning Learning, Teaching and Assessment
EED422: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development

title: Analogue Electronics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principles and applications of modern analogue electronics. Students will learn the fundamentals of semiconductor devices, operational amplifiers, and their application in analogue circuits. The subject also covers basic analysis and design techniques.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and design basic analogue circuits using operational amplifiers.
Apply circuit analysis techniques to solve simple analogue circuit problems.
Understand the principles and characteristics of semiconductor devices.

title: Analysing Learning: The Early Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The first part of this subject focuses on the analysis and interpretation of documentation for children's learning, and explores various assessment practices relevant to the early childhood context. Students will then undertake 240 hours of professional experience in an early childhood setting with children aged 3-to-5 years. The professional experience placement is designed to meet the Graduate level requirements of the seven Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST). While on placement, students will be required to build positive relationships with children, families, educators and community members. The Early Years Learning Framework (or equivalent) will be used to analyse and interpret observations and documentation, to guide the design and implementation of effective learning experiences, and to assess and evaluate children’s learning. Students will also create safe and supportive learning environments, implement leadership skills, evaluate and reflect on their teaching, and the contribution of this experience to their professional growth.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret observations and documentation as evidence about what children aged three to five years know, can do and understand.
Demonstrate authentic and ethical assessment for learning for children aged three to five years.
Analyse the learning of children aged three to five years by applying a range of theoretical perspectives.
Reflect on their professional development through the compilation of a teaching portfolio demonstrating their achievement of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers at graduate level.
Develop a situational analysis of the early childhood context, including descriptive observations and analyses of children, staff and the environment to inform practice and learning design.
Evaluate learning plans through authentic annotations and amendments to plans, following the implementation of learning experiences.
Build positive relationships with children aged three to five years, and interpersonal engagement with professional stakeholders within the learning context.
prerequisites: EPT328: Professional Experience 4 Extended Placement: Early Childhood and Primary
EED110: Child Development: The Early Years
EEP101: Historical and Social Contexts of Early Childhood Education

title: Analysing Learning: The Early Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In the first part of this subject, students will focus on the analysis and interpretation of documentation for children's learning, and explore various assessment practices relevant to the early childhood context. In the second part of the subject, students will undertake 200 hours of professional experience in an early childhood setting where students will participate in learning experiences that require them to: observe and interact with children, gather, analyse and interpret observations and documentation, design learning experiences, assess, evaluate and reflect on their teaching and the contribution of this experience to their professional growth.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their professional development through the compilation of a teaching portfolio demonstrating their achievement of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers at graduate level.
Develop a situational analysis of the early childhood context, including descriptive observations and analyses of children, staff and the environment to inform practice and learning design.
Analyse and interpret observations and documentation as evidence about what children aged birth to five years know, can do and understand.
Evaluate learning plans through authentic annotations and amendments to plans, following the implementation of learning experiences.
Analyse the learning of children aged birth to five years by applying a range of theoretical perspectives.
Build professional relationships with children aged birth to five years, and interpersonal engagement with professional stakeholders within the learning context.
Demonstrate authentic and ethical assessment for learning for children aged birth to five years.

title: An Introduction to Research, Ethics and Reasoning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principle of ethics, the process of logical reasoning, research methods and the ways of describing and displaying data. Students will explore the basic principles of ethics and how they apply to research with human and animal participants. Different ways of thinking in relation to research are examined. Students will learn about logical reasoning and reflexivity and the importance of these processes for research. Quantitative and qualitative research methods and how these are applied to specific research questions will be examined. The subject will examine the basic methods researchers use to describe and display quantitative data, and some of the methods used to analyse qualitative data. Students will also be introduced to data analysis packages including SPSS and NVivo.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the general principles of ethics as they apply to research.
Demonstrate critical evaluation skills.
Discuss why logical reasoning and reflexivity are important in research.
Demonstrate an understanding of the different ways of thinking in relation to research.
Identify the method, quantitative or qualitative, required to answer specific research questions.
Demonstrate an understanding of some of the methods researchers use to analyse qualitative data.

title: Analytical Chemistry
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop a practical and conceptual understanding of analytical chemistry by actively engaging with the principles and applications of commonly used analytical methods. Students will learn key analytical terminology—such as accuracy, precision, sensitivity, detection limits, selectivity, and specificity—and use these concepts to evaluate and compare analytical techniques. Through guided exploration of the analytical method, students will build skills in method selection and performance assessment. The subject provides practical and theoretical exposure to core analytical techniques, including electrochemistry, chromatography, and spectroscopy, while also reinforcing foundational knowledge through a review of classical wet chemical methods.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competence and safety in the application of analytical methodologies and operation of instrumentation relevant to chemical analyses.
Evaluate and apply analytical methodologies to qualitative and quantitative chemical analyses, incorporating principles of accuracy and precision.
Explain and apply the principles of wet and instrumental techniques for quantitative and qualitative chemical analyses.
Interpret, and perform calculations on, gravimetric, volumetric, chromatographic, electrochemical and spectroscopic data.
prerequisites: CHM102: Chemistry for Dental and Veterinary Sciences

title: Analytical Chemistry Industry Experience
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this subject is to prepare students in the Analytical Chemistry major of the Bachelor of Science to develop technical and professional skills that employers are seeking. Students will work beside a supervisor within a technical or research laboratory, applying their academic learning in a professional setting. There will be opportunities for the development of independent employment skills through obtaining a placement, negotiating the work to be done and reporting on the outcomes. It is intended that students will leave this subject with an increased skill set relevant to employment in Analytical Chemistry.
learning_outcomes: Compose written reports that meet industry requirements and conventions of academic and scientific writing.
Use practical skills in the safe handling of a variety of chemicals relevant to chemistry laboratories.
Apply theoretical principles of analytical techniques and procedures in a commercial or research chemical laboratory.
Demonstrate practical skills, competencies and attitudes consistent with industry expectations of entry level practice as an analytical chemist.
Act in a professional manner to meet expectations of ethical and legal behaviour especially confidentiality.
Undertake responsibilities in independent work and as part of a team.
Demonstrate a capacity for self-directed learning, professional development and learning from experience.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundation study of the human body using an integrated systems approach. The primary focus of this subject will be on the physiological processes underlying the function of each body system. After an introduction to anatomical terminology and cell biology, the emphasis of the subject is on the physiology of the nervous, endocrine, skeletal and muscular systems.
learning_outcomes: Identify and define anatomical and physiological concepts using discipline specific terminology and illustrations.
Apply and interpret anatomical and physiological concepts and how they support the normal functioning of the body.
Identify and describe the principal structures, features, functions, and location of the nervous, endocrine, skeletal, and muscular systems.
prerequisites: BMS161: Health and the Human Body: Cells, Immunity and Musculoskeletal System

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject continues the foundation study of the function of the human body. Students will examine the physiology of various systems such as the cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, renal and reproductive systems including pertinent medical considerations.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe the principal structural features and locations of each component organ of the following body systems: circulatory, respiratory, digestive, renal and reproductive systems.
Describe the functions of each component organ of the following body systems: circulatory, respiratory, digestive, renal and reproductive systems.

Demonstrate application of the principles of physiological regulation in each of the following body systems, by explaining the integration of these systems in the entire organism: circulatory, respiratory, digestive, renal and reproductive systems.
prerequisites: BMS162: Health and the Human Body: Systemic Human Physiology

title: Anatomy and Physiology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to the anatomical structure and physiological function of the human body. Students will develop a knowledge of anatomy and physiology of the cells, tissues, skeletal, muscular, integumentary and nervous systems and the integration of various systems in maintaining health, physical activity, and wellbeing.
learning_outcomes: Identify the chemical and cellular components of the human body and explain how these components regulate integrated bodily functions.
Describe the neurophysiological processes associated with communication within the body.
Identify the anatomical sub-divisions of the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Outline the characteristics of tissues and how these characteristics relate to function.
Outline the structure and function of the integumentary system.
Describe the anatomy of the muscular system, application of muscle to movement, and the physiological properties associated with muscular contraction.
Outline the anatomy of the skeletal system using appropriate terminology and the physiological processes associated with bone development, growth and remodelling.
Define anatomy and physiology and describe the scope relevant to exercise science.
Describe different skeletal and joint structures and demonstrate how anatomical structures support movement throughout the body.

title: Anatomy and Physiology for Health & Physical Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the central topics in anatomy and physiology for health and physical education. The key elements include the structure and function of the organ systems in the human body. Emphasis is placed on students developing an understanding of anatomy and physiology from an atomic level through to the integration of various systems for effective movement and the importance of nutrition in the maintenance of health and wellbeing.
learning_outcomes: Describe the anatomy and physiology of the musculoskeletal system and the reproductive system.
Portray the structure and function of the cardiorespiratory system in relation to homeostasis and human function.
Outline the anatomy of the lymphatic system and describe the role this system plays in immune function.
Explore the role of energy systems and the importance of nutrition in how the body physiologically adapts to training.
List the anatomical structures and describe the functions of the digestive system and define the relationship with nutrition, metabolism and temperature regulation in the human body.
Map the components that contribute to the chemical and cellular basis of life and how these regulate integrated body function.
Define anatomy and physiology and interrelationships between body systems for efficient movement.
Define the structural organisation and the regulatory functions of the urinary system, endocrine system and the nervous system.

title: Anglican Foundations
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the development of Anglican faith and life within the broad catholic tradition of the Church. It examines the distinctive features of method and content in Anglican theology through selected studies in ecclesiology, ethics, worship and spirituality. Special attention is given to the analysis of the writings of major Anglican theologians and influential commentaries on Anglican history and tradition. Anglicanism in the Australian context is also explored.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a broad and coherent knowledge of the work of either a major Anglican theologian or a significant movement within Anglicanism.
Demonstrate a broad and coherent knowledge of major developments within the history of the Anglican communion from its early origins in England to its current global expressions.
Articulate the relevance and implications of Anglicanism in the Australian context.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Contextualise and communicate a variety of recent interpretations of the significance of Anglican contributions to contemporary world Christianity.

Analyse and critically review distinctive features of Anglican theology and theological method, particularly in relation to an understanding of the church and its ministry, ethics and spiritual disciplines.

title: Android App Development
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to develop skills and knowledge in native mobile applications development for the Android platform. The subject starts with a review of the Java programming language, which builds on students' previous knowledge of object oriented programming. The subject teaches the fundamentals of Android app design, as well as examining advanced programming concepts such as Model-View-Controller (MVC), controls and the user interface, Google APIs, content providers and intents.
learning_outcomes: Write, examine and critique Java program code for Android applications.
Develop advanced applications for the Android platform.
Publish an Android application.
Build and develop a user interface for the Android platform using sound user interface design principles.
Implement various app components for the Android platform.
Compare and analyse different types of Model-View-Controller patterns.

title: Anglican Foundations
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the development of Anglican faith and life within the broad catholic tradition of the Church. It examines the distinctive features of method and content in Anglican theology through selected studies in ecclesiology, ethics, worship and spirituality. Special attention is given to the analysis of the writings of major Anglican theologians and influential commentaries on Anglican history and tradition. Anglicanism in the Australian context is also explored.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Analyse and critically discuss Anglicanism in the Australian context.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of a variety of recent interpretations of the significance of Anglican contributions to contemporary world Christianity.
Discuss critically major developments within the history of the Anglican communion from its early origins in England to its current global expressions.
Demonstrate a detailed and critical appreciation of the work of either a major Anglican theologian or a significant movement within Anglicanism.

Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the distinctive features of Anglican theology and theological method, particularly in relation to an understanding of the church and its ministry, ethics and spiritual disciplines.

title: Animal Anatomy and Physiology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Animal Anatomy and Physiology introduces students to the principles of physiology and anatomy as it relates to animals, in particular mammals and birds. The integration and control of all major organ systems, including endocrine, nervous, musculoskeletal, digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal and immune will be examined, from micro to gross anatomical levels and normal physiological processes. The importance of blood, cellular communication and the principles of thermoregulation will also be covered. Homeostasis is central to this subject and the linkages between each of the organ systems and how they contribute to maintaining homeostasis, thereby allowing an animal to cope with, or thrive in, its environment is explored. Examples from a range of animal species are used to assimilate and demonstrate concepts learnt in lectures and applied in practical classes.
learning_outcomes: Describe and relate the anatomy and physiology of these animals to the maintenance of homeostasis.
Describe and relate the anatomy and physiology of these animals to their lifestyles and environments.
Identify and explain important anatomical and physiological features of the various major organ systems.
Communicate effectively, using the specialised language of anatomy and physiology.
Compare and contrast the normal anatomy and physiology of various species including mammals and birds.

school: School of Theology
