It examines the distinctive features of method and content in Anglican theology through selected studies in ecclesiology, ethics, worship and spirituality. Special attention is given to the analysis of the writings of major Anglican theologians and influential commentaries on Anglican history and tradition. Anglicanism in the Australian context is also explored.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.

Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the distinctive features of Anglican theology and theological method, particularly in relation to an understanding of the church and its ministry, ethics and spiritual disciplines.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of a variety of recent interpretations of the significance of Anglican contributions to contemporary world Christianity.
Discuss critically major developments within the history of the Anglican communion from its early origins in England to its current global expressions.
Demonstrate a detailed and critical appreciation of the work of either a major Anglican theologian or a significant movement within Anglicanism.
Analyse and critically discuss Anglicanism in the Australian context.

title: Animal Behaviour, Welfare and Ethics
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a broad introduction to the study of animal behaviour, animal ethics and animal welfare science. The behaviour of an animal is one of the most obvious and widely adopted indicators of its welfare. This subject introduces students to the fundamental processes controlling behaviour, and will assist in interpreting what observed normal and abnormal behaviour patterns indicate about animal welfare. This subject also introduces students to the study of animal welfare which, in simple terms, aims to provide the scientific evidence to answer the question of how animals should be treated. The latter question is actually an ethical question, and this subject will introduce the principles of animal ethics. Knowledge of animal ethics will allow students to defend and reflect on their own ethical judgements, and critique those of others regarding the use of animals.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the main indicators of animal welfare, and using these indices, describe the welfare of the animal.
Apply knowledge of fundamental animal behaviour processes to interpret normal and abnormal behaviour patterns.
Discuss the principles of animal ethics, defend one's own ethical judgements and critique those of others regarding the treatment of animals.

title: Animal Biotechnology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a comprehensive theoretical and practical understanding of animal biotechnology, emphasising hands-on experience with laboratory techniques commonly used in the biotechnology industry. Students will participate in practical exercises, including nucleic acid extraction, restriction endonuclease digestion of a plasmid, DNA cloning, transformation, molecular diagnostic techniques such as PCR, immunological methods like ELISA, microbiological culture, gene expression analysis, protein purification, and bioinformatics. These practical activities are complemented by lectures that cover key theoretical concepts and their applications in real-world scenarios, including animal molecular biology, recombinant DNA technology, the production of transgenic animals, reproductive biotechnology, biotechnology in animal breeding, bioinformatics, and ethical considerations in the field.
learning_outcomes: Describe the contribution 'functional genomics' is making and is likely to make in animal biotechnology now and in the future.
Describe basic principles and techniques in genetic manipulation and genetic engineering.
Describe how genes are expressed and what regulatory mechanisms contribute to control of gene expression.
Describe the structure of animal genes and genomes.
Describe gene transfer technologies for animals and animal cell lines.
Describe techniques and problems both technical and ethical in animal cloning.

title: Animal Diversity
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the classification and identification of invertebrates and vertebrates. The emphasis is on the major groups in Australian fauna, their evolutionary relationships, and the use of keys for identifying them. The subject provides a good, solid grounding in what types of animals exist, how they are distinguished from other animals, and what their form and functions are. The subject also gives students a solid foundation in how animal anatomy, physiology, morphology, and behaviour are related to the environments in which these animals live through laboratory work. On completion students will have skills in the collection, identification, and description of animals and be able to apply these skills to interpret and communicate the finding of a fauna survey or collection within an ecological and management context.
learning_outcomes: Have specialised skills in the classification and taxonomy of animals including the ability to use dichotomous keys.
Have specialised skills in the collection, preservation, storage and description of reference collections.
Have the ability to interpret and communicate the finding of a fauna survey, collection, and list clearly and coherently these findings within an ecological and management context.
Have a comprehensive understanding of the key features of major animal groups worldwide.
Critically apply evolutionary theory to identify the relationships among different animals groups.

title: Animal Genetics
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces core genetic principles, including molecular and Mendelian genetics, and builds on these to explore population and quantitative genetics used in livestock breeding. Students will learn about quantitative traits, associated genetic parameters such as heritability, selective breeding, and the consequences of inbreeding. Students will apply these principles to the genetic improvement of livestock populations and develop an understanding of how genetic theory informs breeding decisions. The knowledge and skills gained are also relevant to the study of quantitative traits in companion, performance, and wild animal populations.
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss the important genetic decisions to be made in different breeding enterprises.
Identify and apply basic principles and concepts of DNA structure (and sequence), central dogma and chromosome structure including their significance in the context of health and disease.
Identify and apply principles and concepts associated with the interaction between genes and alleles, and how this results in the occurrence of commonly observed traits and diseases in animals.
Use mathematical expressions which are common in quantitative genetics to predict the outcomes of particular approaches to genetic improvement.
Devise a practical breeding program for breeders of livestock or other animals.
Identify and apply principles underlying inheritance of genes in populations, and apply these principles to predict the impact of breeding decisions on gene and genotype frequencies in populations.

Summarise the industry structures commonly in place for the breeding of production animals and to provide informed advice to lay persons and scientists about the merits of particular genetic selection programs.

title: Animal Handling and Health Care
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the animal care and veterinary services industry. It is designed to provide key foundational knowledge and skills that will enable appropriate handling and restraint of common companion animals and provide for their behavioural and nutritional needs, especially when they are patients in a veterinary clinic or hospital. In addition, students will develop digital literacy skills, analyse and evaluate information, and complete a range of activities including problem solving of real-life veterinary scenarios. Students will be introduced to GOTAFE and Charles Sturt University learning platforms whilst developing effective learning styles and time management strategies for university study. ASC180 is the first of a suite of subjects (four in total) which are used for the basis of the awarding of a Certificate IV in Veterinary Nursing.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate within the workplace with peers, clients and supervisors by understanding and applying appropriate language to attain optimal outcomes.
Administer treatments under appropriate veterinary supervision and provide nursing to hospitalised animal patients.
Provide daily care of animals, including cleaning of housing and patient hygiene, and to describe and provide for animal husbandry and welfare needs.
Describe and provide high standards of hygiene and infection control and to demonstrate safe workplace practices.
Recognise, respond to and assist with animal emergencies.
Describe the structure of the animal care and veterinary services industry and the different roles within the industry.
Gather information on products and services for animals and relate these to individual animal requirements by identifying customer needs.
Observe and monitor animal patients and identify and describe 'normal’ and ‘abnormal’ parameters.
Identify animals from a range of different species and breeds, and to safely handle and restrain these animals.

title: Animal Growth and Development
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the processes of growth and development from conception through to maturity in domesticated and non-domesticated species. Factors that control growth will be examined from genetic, epigenetic, nutritional, and hormonal perspectives, including reference to growth disorders and growth manipulation.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the ways in which animal growth and composition are manipulated in the interests of livestock production or animal health.
Explain how hormones, nutrition and epigenetics influence animal growth and body composition.
Describe the process of differentiation and the growth of bone, muscle and adipose tissue, and specialised tissue structures such as wool and mammary gland.
Describe foetal development and the factors that can have a lifelong influence on the newborn animal.

title: Animal Nutrition
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principles of ruminant and monogastric nutrition. Students will examine the nutrients in animal feeds, and the processes of nutrient digestion, absorption and metabolism in monogastrics and ruminants. Students will also explore the use of quantitative feeding standards, using ruminant animals as an example, and the application of these to cattle and sheep production systems.
learning_outcomes: Describe the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins in monogastrics and ruminants.
Categorise different carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins and minerals.
Identify ingredients commonly used in rations for livestock.
Describe the key factors associated with the practical application of science to the feeding of animals, including supplementary feeding.
Describe the functions of minerals and vitamins in the nutrition of animals; list the sources of these nutrients; and identify the clinical signs associated with a deficiency of these nutrients.
Use and apply feeding standards to calculate the nutrient requirements of ruminants and to formulate rations meeting these requirements
Describe how a feedstuff is analysed for dry matter, organic matter, lipid content, protein and fibre contents.
List and describe key nutrients for animals and analyse rations based on their ability to meet these key nutrients.
prerequisites: BCM210: Foundations and Techniques in Biochemistry

title: Application of Precision Agriculture
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be introduced to geospatial science concepts and technologies that underpin the application of precision agriculture within a variety of agricultural contexts. Students will develop a range of basic analytical and digital skills for geospatial data processing and mapping that will prepare them to design and implement a precision agriculture project relevant to a range of common agricultural enterprises. The subject is written for students with no prior knowledge in geospatial science and serves as an introductory subject for the application of precision agriculture and geospatial science to any course related to land productivity, sustainability and/or environmental management.
learning_outcomes: Perform and explain basic data processing for a range of data acquisition technologies used in precision agriculture (GPS and remote sensing imagery).
Identify, describe and select geospatial technologies and methodologies used in current precision agriculture applications for a range of agricultural enterprises.
Use software to visualise, interpret and map geospatial data in the context of precision agriculture applications.
Select, justify and implement methodologies suited to mapping spatial variability relevant to precision agriculture management.

title: Animal Health
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles of health and disease in farm production animals, horses and zoo animals. Students will learn to differentiate between the various types of immune responses in animals, undertake a disease outbreak investigation, and analyse and interpret parasitology studies. Students will appraise risks posed by exotic and endemic diseases, and apply animal health economic principles to common scenarios. Students will have opportunities to explore particular interests in horses, production or companion animals and wildlife, with an overall enterprise health and strategic planning focus. Students will develop a holistic approach to animal health and disease prevention, with a firm foundation in management and husbandry practices.
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the key concepts involved in herd or collection health, including biosecurity, vaccination, strategic treatments and disease epidemiology.
Describe the role of economic decision making in animal enterprises, and defend animal management decisions using economic rationale.
Apply effective scientific writing and animal health communication skills.
Identify and appraise the differences between healthy and unhealthy animals within an enterprise, including physical and post mortem changes.

Identify common internal and external parasites important for animal health and disease management within animal enterprises, and conduct tests required to determine the parasite burden of individuals and groups of animals.
Describe the impact of stress on animals and their health, appraise animals for signs of stress, and develop practical, evidence-based solutions to mitigate stress in captive animals.

Discuss and discriminate between important examples of endemic and exotic infectious diseases (and their causative agents - prions, viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites), non-infectious diseases (including metabolic and genetic conditions) and zoonotic diseases.

title: Appendicular and Axial Skeleton Image Interpretation
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to develop fundamental image interpretation knowledge and skills for planar appendicular and axial musculoskeletal radiographic images using a systematic approach. Image interpretations will be correlated with relevant clinical history and informed by evidence based practice. The role and appropriateness of imaging will be considered holistically within the context of the patient's care pathway and patient centred care. The image interpretation knowledge and skills developed within this subject will directly complement current and future clinical practice for practitioners routinely using planar appendicular and axial musculoskeletal radiographic images.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and justify the efficacy of planar imaging correlating with the clinical history, using evidence based practice and with consideration of patient centred care.
Critically analyse image quality and radiographic positioning when reviewing planar appendicular and axial musculoskeletal radiographic images.

Perform interpretations of planar appendicular and axial musculoskeletal x-rays using a systematic approach to accurately describe normal, variant and abnormal radiographic appearances correlating with the clinical history.
Critically reflect on individual learning needs to inform professional practice.
Apply clinical reasoning to identify clinical problems and formulate potential solutions to inform patient management.
Recognise, justify and apply ethical, legislative and regulatory principles to communicate information related to significant findings.
prerequisites: MRS575: Appendicular and Axial Skeleton Image Interpretation

title: Animal Production and Welfare
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Humans have an ethical responsibility to provide appropriate care for animals under their care, and veterinarians have particular obligations and responsibilities in this area. Animal Production and Welfare (VSC110) presents an introduction to animal production systems and provides an integrative link for the study of animal health and husbandry, welfare, behaviour, agricultural economics, intensive and extensive production systems, as well as introducing the principles of scientific writing, literature research and review, skills in numeracy and referencing. Basic information on livestock production systems is presented, and the application of this information to informed consideration of health, welfare, productivity, market access, public health and environmental impact. This subject is foundational to study of the sciences underpinning animal health, welfare and productivity, including genetics, nutrition, physiology, pathology, microbiology, parasitology and epidemiology. Animal handling skills are developed in the context of animal behaviour, health and welfare and operator safety in both classroom and practical settings as preparation for student participation in animal husbandry extramural (AHEMS) placements.
learning_outcomes: Outline the characteristics of a simple handling facility appropriate for common production animal species.

Describe animal production systems at a basic level in terms of nutritional and environmental requirements, husbandry procedures, breeding, annual production cycles, disease management, behaviour and welfare.
Compare and contrast the impact of intensive and extensive animal production systems on productivity and profitability, resources, public health, public perception and animal welfare and behaviour.
Recognise, evaluate and utilise different types of literature to develop knowledge relevant to this subject and to communicate appropriately with differing audiences.
Explain how animal welfare can be assessed in animal production systems using the Five Domains of animal welfare.
Describe and analyse the key issues in relation to the livestock industries globally including supply, demand, productivity and profitability, environmental impacts, welfare and public health.
Safely and capably handle common production animal species, and carry out a basic health assessment of individual animals and groups of animals.
Recognise and describe the characteristics of common breeds of animals used in farm animal production.

title: Annual Crop Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the production and management of annual crops in agriculture. Students will learn about agronomic principles in the context of annual winter and summer crops. Students will also further develop their knowledge of marketing, financial management and alternative production methods that are central to this important part of Australian agriculture.
learning_outcomes: Describe the growth cycle for a range of annual crops.
Determine market requirements for selected annual crops or their by-products.
Identify the agronomic requirements for a winter and a summer crop.
Plan a cropping system for a dryland and irrigated annual crop production.
Manage and evaluate the performance of annual crops.
Outline the specialised technology or management interventions necessary for the production, processing and/or distribution of selected annual crops or their by-products.
Determine business and production goals for annual crop enterprises.

title: Animal Reproduction
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Reproduction is central to the efficiency of livestock production industries and the breeding and management of companion animals and wildlife. Successful reproduction is dependent on managers and carers having a sound knowledge of reproductive principles. This subject is designed to develop the basic understanding of the reproductive anatomy, physiology, endocrinology and behaviour in selected farm, companion animals and wildlife species. Students will have the opportunity to examine strategies to control reproduction and gain hands on experience in reproductive evaluation and fertility management of livestock.
learning_outcomes: Apply reproductive principles to control reproductive potential in animals.
Discuss and explain basic artificial breeding protocols for domestic animals.
Describe reproductive anatomy and its relation to function in various species.
Evaluate the reproductive potential and identify factors that limit reproduction in males and females.
Discuss the processes of gametogenesis, fertilisation, foetal development, placentation, parturition and lactation.
Discuss and explain basic methods of contraception.
Explain the endocrine mechanisms that regulate reproduction and the physiological and behavioural changes that occur during the oestrous cycle.
Work collaboratively with peers in both practical and theoretical settings.

title: Applications of Equine Science: contemporary issues
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to investigate and evaluate the issues that currently affect the equine industry in general and equestrianism in particular. In the course of this subject students will develop and enhance their communication skills using a range of modalities suitable to the topic and audience in question. Students will also gain an appreciation of the complexities of the equestrian world, including impacts of tradition, the complexities of integrating differing cultural and traditional beliefs and how these integrate to facilitate human behaviour change. By the end of this subject students will be able to evaluate contemporary research findings from a growing number of academic disciplines in relation to equine industry practice and the equid, and be able to communicate effectively with equine-based practitioners in order to enhance existing practitioner understanding and assist with effecting any necessary changes across a wide range of equestrian disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the findings from other non-equine areas of investigation in relation to equine based activities.
Summarise, justify and communicate the results of contemporary equine research to a wide range of equestrian-audiences.
Assess and interpret the issues that currently affect the equine industry against a scientific evidence-based framework.
Critically appraise the significance of contemporary developments in equine science to the equine industry.
Devise strategies and activities to support and acknowledge tradition of Indigenous Australian and cultural influences on human behaviour change regarding equine practice.
Create meaningful information and communicate it in an effective way using social media and smart-technology within the equine industry.

title: Applied Animal Nutrition
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject the study of ruminant nutrition is extended, particularly applied nutrition, with the review and analysis of rations and the management of major nutritional disorders. The nutritional requirements of non-ruminant animals including companion animal species, performance animals and animals of intensive production are investigated as well as discussion of nutritional deficiencies, imbalances and potential toxicities that may occur in these species. The relationships between animal nutrition, health, and production are examined. Feed contaminants including potentially toxic plants, plant secondary metabolites, mycotoxins and other environmental contaminants are also investigated.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and describe the interactions between animal nutrition, health and production.
Critically evaluate scientific literature and complex concepts presented in a scientific format and be able to apply and assimilate information from disparate sources to novel situations.

Identify plants and their associated toxic agents that commonly cause poisoning of farmed and companion animals, describing the toxin's mode of action and their direct and indirect effects on farmed and companion animals.
Formulate rations for farmed and companion animals for various physiological states based on the nutrient requirements of the species and the nutrient content of potential feed ingredients.
Analyse rations and commercial foods fed to farmed and companion animals and comment on the suitability of the ration/food.
Provide advice to clients on the nutritional requirements of companion animal species, including animals with special needs.
List potential feed contaminants and describe their mode(s) of action when animals ingest these contaminants.

title: Applied Animal Pharmacology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject investigates why pharmacology is important in animal industries. It covers the principles of pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics and the action of the major classes of therapeutic agents used in animals. Issues of the correct use of drugs, including dose calculation, drug resistance, detection times, withholding periods, and export slaughter intervals, are addressed. Traditional Australian First Nations treatments will be explored, including bioethical and intellectual property challenges. Drug registration and regulation are examined as well as the role of good clinical practice in drug development.
learning_outcomes: Explore the unique pharmacological contributions of Australian First Nations traditional treatments and discuss strategies to respectfully address bioethical considerations and safeguard intellectual property rights.
Discuss issues arising from drug resistance in animal industries.
Describe the major classes of drugs used in animals and their modes of actions.
Describe how these drugs can be used to enhance animal health and welfare, and to improve animal production.
Explain the principles of drug discovery and development, and the design of clinical trials.
Explain the principles or pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and drug administration, including drug dose rate calculations development.
Analyse, interpret and present clinical trial data, including basic pharmacokinetic analysis.

title: Applied Clinical Sciences 1
school: School of Rural Medicine
syllabus_overview: Applied Clinical Sciences 1 is the first major clinical year of the Bachelor Clinical Science (Medicine) / Doctor of Medicine program. Students will apply and extend the knowledge and skills gained in previous subjects by undertaking a longitudinal integrated rural generalist clerkship (clinical placements). The focus of the subject is on the medical disciplines of General Practice, General (Internal) Medicine, Surgery, Critical Care (focusing on Emergency Medicine and Anaesthetics) and Oncology (including Palliative Care). In addition, the subject incorporates a dedicated week of tuition to help prepare students for their MD Project. Online, self-paced theoretical modules support student experiential learning and research skills development. The subject also includes structured learning designed to support the clinical placements using small group learning facilitated at the relevant clinical schools. During the year, students will be based at hospitals, health, and community-based services.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and develop professional skills, responsibilities and attitudes.
Promote the health and wellbeing of individuals and populations, with particular focus on regional, rural and remote communities and First Nations Peoples.
Develop and apply a sound understanding of the scientific foundations (social, basic and clinical domains) of medical practice.
Provide patient-centred care as a member of an interdisciplinary team under appropriate supervision.

title: Applied Clinical Sciences 2
school: School of Rural Medicine
syllabus_overview: MED411 is the second major clinical year of the MD program. It continues the students' longitudinal Rural Generalist clinical placement with a shift in focus to the subspecialties of Paediatrics, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Mental Health. In addition, MED411 incorporates focused time for students to complete their Doctor of Medicine MD Scholarly Project. Theoretical modules support student experiential learning and research skills development. MED411 also includes structured learning designed to support the clinical placements using a combination of online learning and small group learning facilitated at the relevant clinical schools. During the year, students will be based at hospitals, health, and community-based services. Students will also undertake three longitudinal online learning modules (Scientific Streams) and continue work on their reflective professional portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Communicate empathically and effectively with patients, families and health care team members to interact, negotiate, learn and foster understanding.
Integrate the contextual needs and perspectives of health, illness and risk factors for ill-health in planning patient-centred care.
Apply knowledge of pathophysiology in clinical assessment and management in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Mental Health, and Paediatrics.
Formulate management plans based on patient assessment in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Mental Health, and Paediatrics.
Adapt to working and learning within health care teams in the hospital and community setting.
Apply ethical principles and legal responsibilities in professional practice and research in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Mental Health, and Paediatrics,.
Collate, analyse, interpret and present scholarly research project in academic writing style.
Engage in self-directed learning and self-care, teaching and peer review.

title: Applied Clinical Sciences 2
school: School of Rural Medicine
syllabus_overview: This subject is the second major clinical year of the Bachelor of Clinical Science (Medicine) / Doctor of Medicine program. It continues the students' longitudinal Rural Generalist clinical placement with a shift in focus to the subspecialties of Paediatrics, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Mental Health. In addition, the subject incorporates focused time for students to complete their MD Project. Theoretical modules support student experiential learning and research skills development. The subject includes structured learning designed to support the clinical placements using a combination of online learning and small group learning facilitated at the relevant clinical schools. During the year, students will be based at hospitals, health, and community-based services.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of pathophysiology in clinical assessment and management in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Mental Health, and Paediatrics.
Engage in self-directed learning and self-care, teaching and peer review.
Apply ethical principles and legal responsibilities in professional practice and research in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Mental Health, and Paediatrics.
Formulate management plans based on patient assessment in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Mental Health, and Paediatrics.
Communicate empathically and effectively with patients, families and healthcare team members to interact, negotiate, learn and foster understanding.
Integrate the contextual needs and perspectives of health, illness and risk factors for ill-health in planning patient-centred care.
Adapt to working and learning within healthcare teams in the hospital and community setting.
Collate, analyse, interpret and present scholarly research project in academic writing style.

title: Applied Clinical Sciences 3
school: School of Rural Medicine
syllabus_overview: MED511 is the third major clinical year of the Bachelor of Clinical Science (Medicine)/Doctor of Medicine program. It continues the students' longitudinal Rural Generalist Placement program and consists of six weeks in each of Medicine, Surgery, General Practice, Critical Care (focus on Emergency Medicine, Anaesthetics and Intensive Care); one week of Medicine in Context Community Placement; two weeks in Indigenous Health; and four weeks of selective clinical rotation. During the year, students will be based at hospitals and health and community-based services.
learning_outcomes: Promote the health and wellbeing of individuals and populations in a hospital setting, with a particular focus on regional, rural and remote communities and First Nations Peoples.
Demonstrate professional skills, responsibilities and attitudes.
Demonstrate preparedness for practice as a post graduate year one trainee.
Provide patient centered care as a member of an interdisciplinary team under appropriate supervision in a hospital setting.
Apply a sound understanding of the scientific foundations (social, basic and clinical) of medical practice.

title: Applied Cryptography
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the foundational principles, protocols, and practices used to secure modern digital systems and communications. Students will develop practical knowledge and skills in network security protocols and standards while exploring the core concepts of cryptography, including encryption algorithms, digital signatures, cryptographic hash functions, and key management techniques. This subject will introduce students to how cryptographic methods support security goals such as authentication, confidentiality, integrity, and secure communication across contemporary computing and networked environments. The subject will also explore emerging security trends in modern IT infrastructure, alongside ethical and professional responsibilities related to cyber security practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the various digital threats to IT networks and computing devices
Compare and contrast the features of various authentication protocols
Describe cryptographic algorithms, both symmetrical and asymmetrical, and explain how they are used to improve network security
Propose and justify mitigating techniques against cryptographic and network security threats.
Examine and communicate current and emerging trends in cryptography and network security

title: Applied Computer-Aided Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth understanding of computer-aided engineering (CAE) applications used in the analysis and design of engineering systems. Students will explore various CAE tools and techniques, focusing on their practical application in solving real-world engineering problems.
learning_outcomes: Develop Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulations to solve structural engineering problems.
Construct Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations to analyse fluid flow problems.
Select optimisation techniques to enhance engineering designs.
Integrate CAE tools into the engineering design process.

In addition, MED311 incorporates a dedicated week of tuition to help prepare students for their MD Project. MED311 also includes structured learning designed to support the clinical placements using a combination of online learning and small group learning facilitated at the relevant clinical schools. During the year, students will be based at hospitals, health, and community-based services. Provide patient-centred care as a member of an interdisciplinary team under appropriate supervision.
Develop and apply a sound understanding of the scientific foundations (social, basic and clinical) of medical practice.
Demonstrate and develop professional skills, responsibilities and attitudes.

title: Applied Clinical Sciences 3
school: School of Rural Medicine

It continues the students' longitudinal Rural Generalist Placement program and consists of placements in Medicine, Surgery, General Practice, Critical Care (focus on Emergency Medicine, Anaesthetics and Intensive Care); Medicine in Context (Community Health); Indigenous Health; and four weeks of directed clinical placement according to identified student learning needs. During the year, students will be based at hospitals and health and community-based services.
learning_outcomes: Provide patient-centered care as a member of an interdisciplinary team under appropriate supervision in a hospital setting.
Promote the health and wellbeing of individuals and populations in a hospital setting, with a particular focus on regional, rural and remote communities and First Nations Peoples.
Demonstrate professional skills, responsibilities and attitudes.
Demonstrate preparedness for practice as a post graduate year one trainee.
Apply a sound understanding of the scientific foundations (social, basic and clinical domains) of medical practice.

title: Applied Ecological Conservation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Applied ecological conservation is a subfield within ecology, which considers the application of the science of ecology to real-world (usually management) questions. This subject is intended to allow students to develop an understanding of the main ecological concepts fundamental to conservation theory, and to present tools and models that are important to the application of conservation ecology. This will give students the necessary theoretical and applied skills required for them to assist in the management of ecosystems, habitats or species. As this subject discusses a range of tools and models, there is a statistical and mathematical component. There is no intensive associated with the subject. In completing this subject students are able to use initiative and decision making skills to make professional judgements about the implementation of conservation strategies in a variety of contexts.
learning_outcomes: Have the ability to identify and analyse the relative influence of the major ecological processes that influence scarcity and diversity of flora and fauna.
Exercise critical thinking and sound judgments to identify and evaluate solutions to issues associated with scarcity and survival.
Use initiative and decision making skills to make professional judgements about the implementation of conservation strategies in a variety of contexts.
Have an in-depth understanding of the key principles, concepts, and philosophy associated with ecological conservation.

title: Applied Entrepreneurial Projects
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for enterprising students to develop and evaluate entrepreneurial ideas, projects and ventures. This subject combines the application of entrepreneurial theory with practical business/management knowledge. The subject explores social and commercial entrepreneurship, and addresses issues including micro-enterprise, mini-preneurship, intrapreneurship as well as corporate entrepreneurship. The focus is on innovation and entrepreneurship in relation to both product and process.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the opportunities for a value proposition of an entrepreneurial idea and assess the viability of a project for development.
Describe the pros and cons of venture finance in a start-up business model vs. a sustained growth business model.
Identify and analyse current theory and research in entrepreneurship and entrepreneurial behaviour.
Make recommendations for a entrepreneurial project or venture based on sound and justified evidence.
Identify and evaluate start-up processes to a lean business model and apply to a potential start-up idea.
Develop and present a pitch of a business idea for a start-up for potential investors.
Develop and present a business plan for an entrepreneurial venture that is appropriate for different audiences.

title: Applied Forwarding Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: Applied forwarding systems are crucial for managing the complex logistics, documentation, and regulatory requirements involved in global trade. This subject provides students with an understanding of international freight forwarding and its interaction with customs in the real-world online environment by examining the role, functionality and key outcomes of applied forwarding systems and provides students the opportunity to become familiar with a leading software platform.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and compare different software platforms used in cross-border freight-forwarding contexts, applying advanced criteria to select appropriate solutions tailored to specific organisational needs.

Demonstrate advanced proficiency in utilizing industry-specific software tools, such as CargoWise, to create, complete, and lodge essential documentation, such as Global Manifests and Customs Declarations.

Apply advanced analytical techniques to leverage software solutions for addressing complex customs and freight forwarding related challenges, such as determining customs valuation and optimizing trade compliance processes.

Critically evaluate the potential of industry software to enhance professional practice and address emerging trends and challenges in the customs and freight-forwarding contexts, demonstrating innovative thinking and foresight and report writing skills.

Analyse critically the evolving landscape of the international freight-forwarding industry by evaluating the increasing role of software platforms in enhancing operational efficiency and cross-border regulatory compliance.

title: Applied Geostatistics
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers fundamental concepts and algorithms in geostatistics in the context of spatial modelling applied to geosciences. Students will acquire foundational knowledge in spatial continuity modelling and estimation required to become competent practitioners. Students will develop in-depth practical skills in exploratory data analysis, variography, and different estimation algorithms. On completion of this subject, students will be able to select, apply, validate, and evaluate appropriate geostatistical approaches to characterise and quantify the spatial distribution of an attribute.
learning_outcomes: Explain and illustrate the importance of using geostatistics for geoscience applications.
Select, apply, contrast and critique geostatistical estimation approaches for geoscience applications.
Select, apply, validate, justify and evaluate spatial continuity models.
Validate and evaluate geostatistical modelling results.

title: Applied Geotechnical Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject builds upon the knowledge acquired in the Soil and Rock Mechanics subject. The topics include slope stability analysis, earth retention systems, and foundation improvement techniques. Emphasis is on developing advanced analytical and design skills to address complex geotechnical challenges in civil engineering projects.
learning_outcomes: Design and evaluate various earth retention systems.
Assess the suitability and effectiveness of ground improvement techniques.
Apply advanced analytical methods to evaluate slope stability and mitigate slope instability hazards.

title: Applied Islamic Psychology and Counselling
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject covers counselling interventions for various mental health conditions using principles of Islamic psychology. It utilises current theories, research and culturally-competent practices in the delivery of effective counselling interventions. The subject provides the essential Prophetic principles of giving counsel and its application. Islamic value systems in relation to mental health issues are explored, giving consideration to scriptural, spiritual, ethical, social and cultural contexts. The subject develops skills to enable counselling and therapeutic support for the well-being of the diverse Muslim community.
learning_outcomes: Critically apply practical skills within Islamic counselling.
Critically discuss theological, Prophetic, professional and ethical issues relevant to Islamic counselling for mental health conditions.
Critically reflect on Islamic counselling work with increasing self-awareness.
Critically rationalise appropriate counselling skills within a religiously-informed setting.
Justify decisions in applying Islamic therapeutic principles in counselling using case studies.
Justify evaluations based on individual differences and coping responses.
Establish a safe Islamic counselling environment and relationship.

title: Applied IT Ethics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop students skills and knowledge in identifying and analysing ethical issues in cybertechnology. The subject will cover areas such as critical thinking, professionalism, ethical theories, privacy, intellectual property, regulation of the cyberspace, social and ethical issues associated with Artificial Intelligence (AI), and emerging technologies. Finally, we shall explore the impact of AI from an Indigenous perspective. By the end of the subject, students should be able to argue consistently and rationally about the moral problems raised by the adoption and use of cybertechnology, and propose solutions to those moral problems.
learning_outcomes: Assess the implications of ethical problems.
Argue consistently and rationally about the moral issues raised by the adoption and use of cybertechnology.
Critically evaluate solutions to ethical problems.
Analyse ethical problems from the point of view of information and communication technology (ICT) professionals using the Australian Computer Society (ACS) Code of Ethics.
Identify ethical issues related to cybertechnology.
Analyse various ethical impacts of AI from an Indigenous perspective, with a focus on data sovereignty, digital divide and AI algorithmic bias.
Apply ethical theories to ethical problems.

title: Applied Logic (Mantiq) and Critical Reasoning
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: Proficiency in persuasive reasoning and objective analysis of arguments presented by others is indispensable in the field of Islamic studies, as well as in modern academia. This discipline provides students with essential tools for critical reasoning and guides them in their application to both written and oral work. By engaging with this subject, students will cultivate the ability to distinguish between valid and invalid arguments. They will also have ample opportunities to practice constructing logical arguments and identifying logical fallacies within diverse texts and discussions. Additionally, this subject delves into the significance of mantiq (logic) within the context of Islamic scholarship. It explores the remarkable contributions of Muslim logicians throughout history, who have developed a distinct system of logic tailored specifically to scrutinise concepts, ideas, and structures derived from divine revelation. The instrumental role of logic in Islamic studies will be thoroughly examined, highlighting its inherent value and relevance.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate deep understanding of the role of reasoning and mantiq (logic) in Islamic studies.
Demonstrate the ability to construct sound and valid logical arguments.
Apply critical reasoning in their spoken and written work.
Investigate and critically assess the reasoning of others and identify logical fallacies.
Comprehend effective techniques for persuasive reasoning in a discourse.
Demonstrate appreciation for Muslim scholars of mantiq (logic).

title: Applied Pastoral Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to develop, clarify and refine their theology of pastoral work. Students will be required to reflect on pastoral practice with a view to their own and other's theology, and to explore the dialectical relationship between theory and practice within their own work and ministry.
learning_outcomes: Articulate their understanding of pastoral theology.
Demonstrate an integration of psychological, sociological, anthropological and education theory with theology relevant to their pastoral practice.
Critique various contemporary theories of pastoral theology.
Demonstrate their understanding of how Scripture, Tradition, Reason and Experience shape their pastoral work.
Articulate an understanding of the nature of God and humanity.
Reflect critically on selected theological writings on pastoral ministry issues.
Demonstrate an understanding of the Classical Theological Tradition.

title: Applied Health Management and Leadership
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject offers students a comprehensive exploration of the dynamic field of healthcare leadership, focusing on practical skills and knowledge essential for successful management and leadership within healthcare organisations. This subject combines theoretical foundations with hands-on applications to equip students with the ability to navigate challenges, drive innovation, and lead effectively in today's complex healthcare landscape. Students will be equipped with practical skills and knowledge necessary for effective leadership and management within the healthcare sector that includes analysing health policy landscapes, applying advocacy principles, implementing project management strategies, and honing communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Apply advocacy and engagement principles to practice.
Discuss barriers and enablers to managing talent within healthcare.
Implement project management principles.
Apply communication skills within a healthcare context.
Examine the health policy landscape and its impact on service delivery.

title: Applied Oral Health Psychology and Research
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject expands on foundational learning of DOH106 to further develop and refine the relevant skill-sets and psychosocial considerations required of a competent person-centred oral health practitioner. Learners will explore an in-depth application of interpersonal processes, communication, and counselling strategies to support the development of positive therapeutic alliances. In addition, learners will develop the fundamental knowledge of research methodologies and the practical interpretation and dissemination of research literacy. Students will begin to develop critical appraisal of research by applying learned knowledge to contemporary psychosocial issues and how to effectively communicate complex subject matter to suit a wide range of population needs and understanding.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic skills developed throughout the subject including: sourcing, reading and evaluating scientific research articles and academic literature; academic writing; referencing; and critical thinking.
Effectively communicate complex knowledge to a wide range of population groups.
Identify and critically appraise the appropriateness of research methodologies in the context of oral health practice.
Understand and recount key research principles, methodologies, design, and reporting conventions.
Demonstrate the ability to formulate person-centred strategies for the management of health and behaviour.
prerequisites: DOH106: Psychology and Society in Oral Health

title: Applied Pharmacology for Paramedicine
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will expand upon the student's general understanding of pharmacology by applying these principles to paramedic practice. Students will be introduced to medications used in managing a wide variety of clinical conditions encountered in out-of-hospital settings.
learning_outcomes: Formulate comprehensive medication treatment plans for simulated patients with a variety of medical complaints.
Describe interactions, common prescription and home medications have with the medications commonly administered by paramedics and the affects these may have on the treatment of patients.
Safely and effectively administer medication to patients and perform accurate advanced medical calculations.
Explain the indications, contraindications, mechanism of action, dose, route of administration and adverse effects of the most common medications used in paramedic practice.

title: Applied Management in Law Enforcement and Security
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the theoretical foundation of contemporary management thinking in the unique context of law-enforcement, emergency service and security organisations. It draws upon the history of management theory, the evolution in thinking about management in the public sector and the major developments in governance and accountability in law enforcement and security organisations in Australia and overseas.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically upon the application of management theory to law enforcement and security organisations.
Research and apply established management theories to law enforcement and security organisations.
Apply knowledge and skills to demonstrate autonomy and expert judgment to management of a law enforcment, emergency service or security organisation.
Synthesise complex concepts and theories related to contemporary approaches to public sector management.

title: Applied Photovoltaics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the practical application of photovoltaic (PV) technology. Students will gain experience with the design, installation, and optimisation of PV systems, as well as an understanding of their integration into various applications and energy grids.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the integration of PV systems into existing energy infrastructures and evaluate their sustainability and economic viability.
Design and optimise photovoltaic systems for various applications, including residential, commercial, and industrial settings.
Critique photovoltaic technology, including components and operational principles.
Evaluate the performance of PV systems considering factors like efficiency and energy output.

title: Applied Principles of Church Leadership
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to responsible leadership practice, which is grounded in biblical and theological principles, together with a critical review of church leadership practices. Particular models of church leadership are addressed together with their critical application within varied ministry contexts. Students are challenged to develop and implement more effective and context sensitive models of leadership for ministry.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the application of biblical and theological principles of responsible leadership in transformative practice.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of leadership and authority in the Christian tradition, with particular reference to Australian church contexts.
Demonstrate advanced skills in the development of new models of leadership.
Analyse critically the place of leadership within various ministry contexts.
Demonstrate an evidence-based approach to the transformation of leadership practice within a given ministry context.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of particular models or practices of leadership and their application in various contexts.
prerequisites: MIN521: Applied Principles of Church Leadership

title: Applied Psychology for Sport and Exercise
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to enhance student understanding of current research and practice in applied sport and exercise psychology. It introduces students to behaviour change models, psychological skills training program development and a range of psychological interventions to improve the performance, satisfaction and personal growth of athletes and exercise participants. Students also examine psychological characteristics of optimal performance and intrinsic motivation across a range of population groups, and analyse psychological skills and mental strategies for sport performance and psychosocial and behavioural tools for exercise adherence. This subject will involve creative solutions to issues with sport and exercise clients or groups, which also enables students to reflect on their personal capabilities in their chosen career area.
learning_outcomes: Apply various techniques of a psychological skills training program that addresses the needs of a sport or population-specific group or individual.
Identify the influences that selected psychological factors have on adherence, performance and personal growth in sport and exercise settings.
Evaluate the process of developing and implementing an applied sport psychology program.
Apply critical thinking in order to identify and adapt training environments to maximise adherence and performance.
Analyse a range of techniques for developing psychological and mental skills, including models of behaviour change.
Apply reflective judgement to determine when clients require referral to other allied health professionals.

title: Applied Python for AI and Data Science
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the applied use of Python for data analysis, visualisation, and introductory artificial intelligence techniques in applied contexts. Students will develop skills in advanced Python programming, numerical computing, and data manipulation, and apply widely used data science libraries to analyse, model, and interpret datasets. Through hands‑on projects, students will learn to apply ethical data practices and communicate data‑driven insights effectively using code, visual representations, and clear narrative explanations for both technical and non‑technical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Analyse datasets using appropriate data structures and established Python libraries to extract meaningful insights.
Design Python programs to import, clean, and transform real world datasets for data analysis tasks
Apply introductory modelling concepts using Python to support predictive analysis
Evaluate the quality, limitations, and assumptions of datasets, analytical methods, and resulting outputs.
Communicate data-driven results clearly using code, visual outputs, and narrative explanations tailored to the intended audience.

title: Applied Social Media and Digital Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Social media and digital marketing is now embedded in many organisations ranging from SME to global companies. Individuals also have a vested interest in communicating their personal brand for commercial benefit through online tools. This subject is designed to provide an introduction to the world of digital and social media marketing, and help students to develop strategic and tactical skills that are required by industry. Students will examine how communication practices influence company motivations for creating a digital marketing strategy and the tactics to embed message across various networks. Further, students will learn how to assess the way digital technologies can be used in personal and professional settings. Students will also examine how digital technologies and social marketing tools comply with legal requirements and engage with ethical guidelines. Finally, students will explore key issues in measuring and evaluating social and digital media campaigns.
learning_outcomes: Map and conceptualise cross platform communications and strategy and tactics.
Examine individual digital platforms and evaluate how they are used for personal and professional marketing practices.
Create an effective social and digital marketing plan.
Implement and evaluate digital marketing strategies and tactics.
Reflect on ethical and legal issues facing social and digital activities and analyse how they impact on marketing practice.

title: Applied Veterinary Epidemiology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subjects provides extended opportunities to strengthen evidence based veterinary decision making skills, and lays the foundation for the development of clinical epidemiological skills, including interpreting diagnostic tests, investigating disease outbreaks, and modelling of diseases in populations. This subjects supports the development of clinical reasoning skills and the prevention, diagnosis and management of diseases in populations.
learning_outcomes: Appropriately use the basic concepts and terminology applicable to epidemiology.
Define, select and explore a range of appropriate sampling methods and conduct calculations of sample size.
Interpret and make appropriate inference from epidemiological outcomes.
Apply different epidemiological approaches to disease management scenarios taking into account varied production systems.
Explore and understand the importance of the hierarchy of evidence, define and critically appraise each level of evidence.
Calculate, interpret and compare measures of diagnostic test accuracy.
Determine and apply different methods to measure disease frequency, dynamics and associations.
Demonstrate knowledge of and apply the steps of an outbreak investigation.
Demonstrate knowledge of and appropriately apply principles of study design.

title: Applied Statistics and Animal Epidemiology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the fundamental research and analytical skills required to answer questions posed by practitioners and scientists within the equine and veterinary technology industries. Students will examine the principles of experimental design which ensure that research conducted is well planned and able to provide useful and reliable results. Students will develop expertise in the correct formulation of hypotheses that are fundamental to statistical testing along with the requirements for data collection, collation and preparation for analysis. A range of appropriate descriptive and analytical statistical methods will be covered, along with an introduction to quantitative animal-based epidemiology to assess and analyse problems in animal populations. On successful completion of this subject, students should be able to develop a well-designed study, apply appropriate statistical analysis and appraise the conclusions with respect to the statistical outcomes for a range of industry-based problems.
learning_outcomes: Reach informed statistical-based conclusions and communicate these appropriately to a range of audiences.
Design research studies in order to generate usable data.
Apply basic epidemiological concepts to the assessment of contemporary problems within the animal industries.
Identify appropriate data collection, collation (management) and analysis methods and apply these in order to test hypotheses and reach statistically valid conclusions about research questions.
Apply appropriate interpretation and inference skills based on the hierarchy of evidence for epidemiological investigations.
Explain the research cycle and plan research studies.
Use statistical software to conduct simple descriptive and analytical statistics of industry related data.
prerequisites: ASC114: Applied Statistics and Animal Epidemiology

title: Applied Veterinary Nutrition and Production
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In the veterinary profession the role of nutrition in health is often overlooked. This subject will examine the relationship between animal nutrition, production and health for a range of animals commonly seen in veterinary practice. Applied ruminant nutrition is further developed, with the review and analysis of production systems, rations and veterinary management of major nutritional disorders. The nutritional requirements of companion animal species, performance animals and animals of intensive production are also investigated, including discussion of nutritional deficiencies, imbalances, therapeutics and potential toxicities that may occur in these species. Feed contaminants including potentially toxic plants, plant secondary metabolites, mycotoxins and other environmental contaminants are investigated in this subject.
learning_outcomes: List potential feed contaminants and describe their mode(s) of action when animals ingest these contaminants.
Describe the basis of therapeutic nutrition for common disorders of farmed, companion and performance animal species.
Evaluate scientific literature, analyse data by using common statistical methods and integrate them with valid conclusions into a scientific report.

Formulate rations for farmed, companion and performance animals for various physiological states based on production goals, the nutrient requirements of the species and the nutrient content of potential feed ingredients.
Analyse rations and commercial foods fed to farmed, companion and performance animals and comment on the suitability for production and health.
Recognise and describe the interactions between animal nutrition, production, management, housing, environment and health.
Describe the mode of action of plant toxins and/or anti-nutritional factors and their direct and indirect effects on farmed and companion animals.
Identify plants and their associated toxic agents and/or anti-nutritional factors that commonly cause poisoning or have adverse effects on farmed and companion animals.

title: Applying an Intersectional Lens to Research
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with a broad framework for undertaking research and research design. It enables the student to design research with an intersectional lens which aids in meaning-making to apply strategies to practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify research design and literature that utilises an intersectional approach.
Discuss the elements of research design incorporating an intersectional approach.

title: Applied Veterinary Nursing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will apply the practical skills and knowledge gathered from previous veterinary nursing subjects and work-integrated learning (WIL). Students will consolidate the competencies required of a veterinary front-line para-professional, including reception, triage and communication skills to deal with real-life scenarios. This subject will assist students to develop self-reflection and self-assessment skills in order to develop strategies for professional lifelong learning. This is the final subject used for awarding the Certificate IV in Veterinary Nursing and requires 15 days (minimum 120 hours) of work-integrated learning placement.
learning_outcomes: Prepare and process clinic correspondence and maintain veterinary pharmaceutical and stock inventory.
Apply veterinary nursing knowledge to provide advice on animal nutrition, behaviour and reproduction.
Prepare and assist with the provision of veterinary drugs and poisons within current veterinary practice legislation.
Apply veterinary nursing knowledge to provide advice on preventative animal health, disease, and grief support.
Demonstrate competency in triage, patient admission and discharge procedures.
prerequisites: ASC183: Foundations in Veterinary Surgical Nursing

title: Applying Criminology To Crime Reduction
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the application of criminology to crime reduction. The study of criminology in the context of crime aims to develop reflective criminal justice professionals who can apply evidence based best practice to selected crime problems. It will critically analyse traditional and post-modern crime prevention strategies and equip police, community managers, and those working in crime prevention roles to work collaboratively with community groups to achieve crime reduction. Emphasis is also placed on the development of academic literacy and learning skills to assist course participants with successful transition to tertiary study.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the strengths and weaknesses of various crime prevention strategies.
Devise appropriate crime prevention strategies relevant to particular communities.
Apply criminological theory to crime prevention.
Relate current crime theories, particularly those concerning social issues, to selected crime problems.
Develop academic literacy and learning skills essential for successful tertiary study.

title: Applied Veterinary Physiology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Applied veterinary physiology continues the study of normal renal, neurological and special sense systems and then explores applied physiology of acid-base regulation, cardiovascular/respiratory and endocrine systems during stress, performance and adaption to new situations. Physiology's application to meat production is examined. Comparative studies will expand the finer understanding of physiology for the veterinary clinician. The student will then be prepared to integrate physiology into pathophysiology and medicine.
learning_outcomes: Apply and assimilate information from disparate sources to novel situations.

Critically evaluate scientific literature, analyse data by using common statistical methods and integrate them with valid conclusions into a scientific format in a critical manner; and complex concepts presented in a scientific format.
Work as a team to achieve a group or individual goal.
Explain the normal function of renal and nervous systems in common domestic species.
Identify and explain interactions between different body systems required for complex physiological processes such as production, locomotion, acid-base balance, exercise and thermoregulation.

title: Approaches to Enquiry in Ministry
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject covers those research strategies and methods of data collection most suited to the field of Christian Ministry and its sub-disciplines. It provides an overview of contexts within which enquiry is undertaken, and introduces students to the role and potential of research in the specific disciplines of Christian Ministry, history and practice. The subject focuses on research traditions and paradigms relevant to the chosen field of research, and the nature of the research process, including planning and designing a research project. Students study the use of qualitative and quantitative methods and their application to the field of Christian Ministry.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of qualitative and quantitative research methodologies and their application to the field of Christian Ministry.
Demonstrate familiarity with the role and potential of research in the field of Christian Ministry and/or its discipline areas.
Apply critically knowledge gained to define and refine a proposed area of study.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the professional contexts in which the enquiry within ministry is undertaken.
Possess the research skills necessary to prepare a research project or major research paper in the field of Christian Ministry.

Demonstrate a critical understanding of the ethical issues in research and their particular relevance to Christian Ministry, including recognising the significance of consent, confidentiality and other ethical considerations in relation to research.

title: Approaches to Enquiry in Ministry
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject covers those research strategies and methods of data collection most suited to the field of Christian Ministry and its sub-disciplines. It provides an overview of contexts within which enquiry is undertaken, and introduces candidates to the role and potential of research in the specific disciplines of Christian Ministry, history and practice.The subject focuses on research traditions and paradigms relevant to the candidate's discipline, and the nature of the research process, including planning and designing a research project. Candidates study the use of qualitative and quantitative methods and their application to the field of Christian Ministry.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of qualitative and quantitative research methodologies and their application to the field of Christian Ministry.
Demonstrate familiarity with the role and potential of research in the field of Christian Ministry and/or its discipline areas.
Demonstrate the research skills and expertise necessary to prepare a thesis or Portfolio.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the professional contexts within which the enquiry is undertaken.

Demonstrate a critical understanding of the ethical issues in research and their particular relevance to Christian Ministry, including recognising the significance of consent, confidentiality and other ethical considerations in relation to research.
Critically apply knowledge gained to define and refine their proposed area of study.

title: Aquatics and Track and Field
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is comprised of two modules preparing students to teach aquatics and track and field in Year K-10 contexts. These modules provide students with the opportunity to develop skills in planning for and presenting safe, fun, age appropriate and challenging aquatics and track and field activities. These modules will also assist students to critique the inclusion of aquatics and track and field in school and community programs. Opportunities to develop an array of pedagogies relating to the teaching of and assessment approaches for aquatics and track and field movement experiences are explored. Students learn to devise strategies which expand the development of young people through water and land-based activities.
learning_outcomes: Sequence concepts and learning experiences for specific stages of learners.
Design stage-appropriate, safe, creative and challenging learning experiences which cater for a variety of student learning styles and special needs.
Accurately engage with the literacies applicable to aquatics and track and field.
Appreciate the meaning and cultural relevance of aquatics and track and field in Australian society and in the lives of young people.
Affirm, celebrate and respond to the cultural and social difference of their learners.
Develop observational, instructional and assessment abilities for skills in aquatics and track and field.
Recognise the inherent risks in both aquatic and athletic environments and plan accordingly.
Value physical activity as a lifelong learning experience.
Develop formative assessment strategies which reflect NSW Years K-10 PDHPE learning outcomes.

title: Arabic Grammar 1
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces Arabic focusing on grammar and grammatical analysis of sentences. Students will learn the different categories of words, phrases and sentences, and how to identify them through form, meaning and context. Various relevant contexts such as the Qur'an, Hadith and everyday scenarios will be explored in order to apply the grammar rules learnt.
learning_outcomes: Grammatically analyse sentences from an Arabic text.
Translate an Arabic text into English.
Interpret information from an Arabic text.
Conjugate simple verbs in the appropriate tense, gender and person.
Identify the different types of words, phrases and sentences in an Arabic text.

title: Arabic Grammar 2
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will build upon the knowledge they gained from ISL461 Arabic Grammar 1. Students will broaden their knowledge of the syntax of Arabic words, phrases and sentences. They will also enhance their proficiency in grammatical analysis by applying it to a variety of contexts and more complex sentences. Classical Arabic-styled stories with Islamic, cultural and moral themes will be explored to acquire new vocabulary, build comprehension and expand proficiency in grammatical analysis.
learning_outcomes: Compose prose using appropriate syntax and vocabulary.
Interpret information from an intermediate level text.
Articulate understanding of the different forms of verbs.
Grammatically analyse sentences from an intermediate level text.
Conjugate simple verbs in the appropriate tense, gender, number and person.

title: Arabic Language and Culture 1
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces Arabic as a living language. Students will explore Arabic through common scenarios and everyday interactions. They will also focus on vocabulary acquisition and developing their practical skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking. They will also reflect and analyse their perceptions of Arabic through a case study examining the parallels between Arabic and Wiradjuri language.
learning_outcomes: Write passages related to everyday interactions.
Interpret meaning from passages that include frequently used vocabulary and sentence structures.
Recall vocabulary related to everyday interactions.
