Analyse how national discourses over countries’ history impacts perception of language: case study of Wiradjuri and Arabic language.
Communicate in conversation involving everyday interactions.

title: Arabic Language and Culture 1
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces Arabic as a living language. Students will explore Arabic through common scenarios and everyday interactions. Students will also focus on vocabulary acquisition and developing their practical skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking.
learning_outcomes: Read simple passages that include frequently used vocabulary and sentence structures.
Demonstrate vocabulary acquisition related to everyday interactions.
Communicate in simple conversation involving everyday interactions.
Write simple passages related to everyday interactions.
prerequisites: ISL140: The Arabic Script and its Sounds

title: Arabic Language and Culture 2
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject continues from Arabic Language and Culture 1 and covers new topics related to everyday interactions including education, work, sport, travel and food. Students will also learn about the culture, geography and dialects of major Arab regions. Students will continue to develop their practical skills by exploring more complex sentence structures and verb conjugation in the different tenses.
learning_outcomes: Read passages at the intermediate low level that include newly introduced vocabulary and sentence structures.
Communicate in conversation at the intermediate low level involving the new topics introduced.
Compose short passages related to the topics covered while expressing correct usage of nouns, verbs and sentence structures.
Accurately use verbs that are related to everyday interactions in different tenses, person, number and gender.

title: Arabic Language and Culture 3
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject continues from Arabic Language and Culture 2 and introduces new topics of greater complexity such as the media, environment, politics and further explores culture. This subject will continue to focus on developing practical skills where sentence structures are more complex. Students will also use higher form verbs in different tense, person, number and gender options. Writing skills will also be covered to develop the student's ability to write short to medium length stories and passages.
learning_outcomes: Present in spoken Arabic form the topics covered.
Use the vocabulary acquired to form new sentences based on the sentence structures covered.
Compose 500 to 700 word stories and passages in Arabic related to the topics covered while expressing correct usage of nouns, verbs and sentence structures.
Appropriately use higher form verbs that are related to everyday interactions in different tense, person, number and gender options.

title: Arabic Language and Culture 2
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject continues from Arabic Language and Culture 1 and explores new topics related to everyday interactions including education, work, sport, travel and food. Students will also learn about the culture, geography and dialects of major Arab regions. They will continue to develop their practical skills by exploring more complex sentence structures and verb conjugation in the different tenses. They will also reflect and analyse Arabic from the lens of culture and identity preservation through a case study examining the parallels between Arabic and Wiradjuri language.
learning_outcomes: Compose passages related to the topics covered while expressing correct usage of nouns, verbs and sentence structures.
Interpret meaning from passages at the intermediate high level that include newly introduced vocabulary and sentence structures.
Comprehend the importance of language to preserve culture and identity: case study of Wiradjuri and Arabic language.
Communicate in conversation involving the new topics introduced.
Accurately use verbs that are related to everyday interactions in different tenses, person, number and gender.

title: Arabic in Islamic Texts
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject involves the critical reading of Islamic texts from a variety of genres. Students will gain an appreciation of the classical discourse surrounding the Qur'an and Hadith and the Islamic sciences such as theology, law and ethics. There is a focus on conducting research utilising Arabic-Arabic lexicons as well as developing the skill of differentiating between technical and lexical meaning of words in a given text.
learning_outcomes: Independently research, analyse and critique texts related to key Islamic sciences.
Critically analyse the lexical and technical meanings of words.
Examine, critique and infer information from Islamic texts at the advanced level.
Compose complex analyses of lexical features in Arabic texts at the advanced level.

title: Arabic Language and Culture 3
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject continues from Arabic Language and Culture 2 and focuses on topics of greater complexity such as the media, environment, politics and further explores Arab culture. Students will engage with Arabic in various mediums such as social media, print material, video and audio. They will continue to develop their practical skills by exploring more complex sentence structures and conjugation of higher form verbs in the different tenses.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate and evaluate the appropriate use of vocabulary and expressions in multiple varied contexts.
Compose passages at the intermediate high level while expressing correct usage of nouns, verbs and sentence structures.
Interpret meaning from texts at the advanced level.
Communicate in conversation involving topic areas such as media, environment, politics and Arab culture.

title: Arabic Literature 1
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This reading subject is for students who have completed both Arabic Language and Culture 3 and Arabic Morphology. Students will engage deeply with classical Arabic literature to further develop their vocabulary and language skills. They will also continue to advance their knowledge and skills in syntax and morphology in application to these texts. Focus is on the morphology of verbs and derived nouns, and syntactic structures related to the manṣūb nouns.
learning_outcomes: Examine and infer information from parables and moral stories at the advanced level.
Analyse Arabic texts with reference to syntactic structures related to the mansub (accusative) nouns.
Clarify words and expressions in the context of parables and moral stories with reference to Arabic-English dictionaries.
Articulate the morphology of Arabic verbs and derived nouns.

title: Arabic Literature 2
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This reading subject is for students who have completed both Arabic Language and Culture 3 and Arabic Morphology. Students will engage deeply with classical Arabic literature to further develop their vocabulary and language skills. They will also continue to advance their knowledge and skills in syntax and morphology in application to these texts. Focus is on the morphology of weak letter verbs, and syntactic structures related to the harf jarr (preposition).
learning_outcomes: Examine and infer information from poetry and Islamic texts at the advanced level.
Clarify words and expressions in the context of poetry and Islamic texts with reference to Arabic-English dictionaries.
Analyse Arabic texts with reference to syntactic structures related to the harf jarr (preposition).
Conjugate weak letter verbs accurately in the appropriate tense, number, gender and person.

title: Arabic Morphology
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will build upon the knowledge they gained from ISL462 Arabic Grammar 2. They will engage in a detailed study of Arabic morphology exploring the tri-literal Arabic root system and the various complex verb and noun forms that can be derived. Students will continue to engage with classical Arabic-styled stories to acquire more sophisticated vocabulary and deepen their comprehension.
learning_outcomes: Interpret information from an intermediate-high level text.
Grammatically analyse sentences from an intermediate-high level text.
Articulate understanding of the system of word derivation.
Conjugate higher form verbs and nouns in the appropriate tense, gender, number and person.
Compose intermediate-low level prose using appropriate syntax and vocabulary.

title: Arabic Literature 3
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This reading subject is for students who have completed both Arabic Language and Culture 3 and Arabic Morphology. Students will engage deeply with classical Arabic literature to further develop their vocabulary and language skills. Focus is on the author's style and frequently used words and expressions in classical Arabic. Students will also continue to advance their knowledge and skills in syntax and morphology in application to these texts.
learning_outcomes: Examine and infer information from creative non-fiction texts at the advanced level.
Compose a text at the intermediate level in the creative non-fiction genre.
Clarify words and expressions in the context of creative non-fiction with reference to Arabic-English dictionaries.
Evaluate usage of frequently used Arabic phrases and expressions.

title: Arabic Skills 3
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject continues from Arabic Skills 2 and introduces new topics related to everyday interactions including travelling, pilgrimage, health, holidays, looking after our health and leisure time. This subject will focus on the speaking of Arabic where the sentence structures are more complex, using higher form verbs in different tense, person, number and gender options. Writing skills will also be covered to develop the student's ability to write short to medium length stories and passages.
learning_outcomes: Compose 500 to 700 word stories and passages in Arabic related to the topics covered while expressing correct usage of nouns, verbs and sentence structures.
Present in spoken Arabic form the topics covered.
Use the vocabulary acquired to form new sentences based on the sentence structures covered.
Appropriately use higher form verbs that are related to everyday interactions in different tense, person, number and gender options.

title: Art and Books
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject offers a thematic study of art and books. It focuses on the relationships between image and text, between form and content, and between conception and construction. These concepts are introduced through the study of key examples, including illuminated manuscripts, livres d'artiste, children's illustrated books, and the 'new comic' and artists' books in the twentieth century. The subject also introduces students to the literature and contemporary debate about art and books and discusses the future of the book in a digital age.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the definitions of 'book', 'illustrated book', 'artists' book', 'booklike object'.
Analyse and critique artists' books and illustrated books.
Debate the issues surrounding the book in a digital age.
Discuss the relationship between image and text in the book format.
Identify key episodes in the evolution of the book and discuss the factors what contributed to the evolution of the book form.
Discuss the relationship between form and content in the book format.

title: Architecting Cloud Solutions
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will help students prepare for the Amazon Web Services (AWS) Certified Solutions Architect industry certification. Students will study important characteristics of a successful cloud-based implementation, including those that relate to scalability, security, reliability, durability, and cost effectiveness. This learning will be applied through the design of an optimal cloud-based system in accordance with a set of project requirements.
learning_outcomes: Create and implement procedures for secure cloud deployment and maintenance.
Design a cloud-based system, including associated processes and procedures for compliance, control and operation.
Critically analyse and Implement appropriate data storage architectures within a cloud computing context.
Evaluate a cloud migration strategy.
Plan and manage the lifecycle of a cloud application.
Plan and execute a cloud migration strategy.

title: Asia-Pacific Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject studies recent developments in the Asia-Pacific region and their implications for international business. A thematic approach is used to analyse economic systems, political systems and business culture in the region. Physical geography and natural resource endowments are discussed. Case studies provide detailed analysis of issues and problems in a number of countries. Australia's changing role in the region is assessed.
learning_outcomes: Identify and interpret key economic and social trends in the Asia-Pacific region.
Assess the current roles of the major political associations and trading groups operating in the region.
Assess alternative strategies for managing political risk.
Discuss the importance of business culture in conducting international business.
Explain the ethical dimensions of conducting business in the Asia-Pacific region.
Analyse the economic and political roles of Australia in the region.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an in-depth study of the issues surrounding the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) systems. It will examine the basic mathematical foundations and logic requirements for developing AI and ML systems. AI and ML will be examined in detail together with the need for data analysis, data matching, decision trees, and Bayesian networks. The role of Neural networks in AI and ML will be considered. The subject will provide students with design and development experience in AI and ML programming and will include a practical section using AI and ML techniques.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop an AI/ML application.
Critically evaluate the preparation and processing of data for analysis and data matching.
Explain the role of several techniques including Bayesian and Neural networks in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning systems.
Perform the basic mathematical and logic calculations for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning systems.
Critically analyse a proposed AI/ML development proposal.

title: Assessment and Analysis of Sensory-Motor Skills in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop competence in speech pathology assessment of hearing, voice, swallowing, speech and fluency. Students critique theory, empirical research and holistic frameworks to plan and justify assessment for clients across the lifespan. A key focus of this subject is the development of skills in the collection, analysis and interpretation of assessment data using both standardised and non-standardised procedures. Students critique the holistic context to evaluate and justify the appropriateness of assessment planning, procedures and interpretation. Clinical reasoning and communication skills are developed through communicating assessment outcomes with a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences.
learning_outcomes: Use clinical reasoning and communication skills appropriate to a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences to report and discuss assessment procedures, analysis, interpretation and professional recommendations regarding hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation.

Demonstrate technical skills in the assessment of hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation while adhering to professional ethical standards and medico-legal requirements.

Analyse and interpret data from hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation assessment, based on critical reflection, analysis and synthesis of theory, concepts and holistic client data.

Justify the selection of assessment procedures for assessing hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation based on critical reflection, analysis and synthesis of theory, concepts and holistic client data.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Image Analysis
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the advanced concepts and innovations associated with artificial intelligence, neural network algorithms, machine learning and deep learning in medical image analysis. It will examine the foundation principles and explore the landscape associated with these concepts in artificial intelligence. The applications of machine learning and deep learning will be investigated, with the opportunity to critically discuss relevant concepts within the context of clinical and research medical image analysis. The subject aims to arm students with foundation understanding of the principles and working knowledge of artificial intelligence in medical image analysis.
learning_outcomes: Develop robust artificial intelligence frameworks to support decision making and application of algorithms in medical image analysis.
Critically discuss the principles and technologies underpinning neural networks, machine learning, and deep learning in medical image analysis.
Identify, justify and evaluate opportunities for, and applications of, artificial intelligence augmented medical image analysis.
Design, evaluate and implement an artificial intelligence application for medical image analysis.
Demonstrate command of, and critically reflect on the legal, social and ethical implications of artificial intelligence in image analysis and appraise applications or proposals within this context.
Investigate and apply advanced knowledge of the principles and applications of artificial intelligence in medical image analysis.
Apply principles of artificial intelligence in medical image analysis within the clinical and research environments.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Business Applications
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide valuable insights into emerging applications of Artificial Intelligence for modern day businesses and industry. It covers the fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence, deep learning and reinforcement learning, and applying these technologies to solve complex business problems. This subject will also prepare students to develop business design thinking to optimise business processes by harnessing AI's capabilities.
learning_outcomes: Interpret Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning concepts in the context of industry specific business applications.
Critically evaluate different Artificial Intelligence approaches for optimising complex business processes.
Analyse advanced algorithms to design and develop complex business applications using Artificial Intelligence.
Discuss the fundamental concepts behind Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.

title: Assessment and Analysis of Language and Cognition in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop competence in assessment of the speech pathology practice areas language and cognition. Students critique theory, empirical research and holistic frameworks to plan and justify language and cognition assessment for clients across the lifespan. A key focus of this subject is the development of skills in the collection, analysis and interpretation of assessment data using both standardised and non-standardised procedures. This subject facilitates students' critique of speech pathology assessment practices in the context of multilingual and multidialectal Australia, and enables them to identify and justify speech pathology assessment approaches for clients from diverse cultural and social backgrounds. Clinical reasoning and communication skills are developed through communicating assessment procedures and outcomes with a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate technical skills in the assessment of language and cognition while adhering to professional ethical standards and medico-legal requirements.

Use clinical reasoning and communication skills appropriate to a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences to report and discuss assessment procedures, analysis, interpretation and professional recommendations regarding language and cognition.
Analyse and interpret language and cognition assessment data based on critical reflection, analysis and synthesis of theory, concepts and holistic client data.
Critique the appropriateness of assessment practices including the analysis and interpretation of data in the context of Australia's linguistic and cultural diversity.
Justify the selection of assessment procedures for assessing language and cognition based on critical reflection, analysis and synthesis of theory, concepts and holistic client data.

title: Assessment and Crisis Management
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Mental health is about the study, diagnosis, treatment and management of mental illness and mental disorders. This subject examines mental illness and mental disorders. It focuses on the causes, prevalence, clinical features, classification, assessment, treatment and management issues. Using the DSM 5 and ICD 11 (which are the two diagnostic classification systems used in Australia) diagnostic criteria will be explored. In addition, students will also look at a range of assessment tools that are used in the assessment process including the Mental Status Examination (MSE) and Risk Assessment. The subject will provide students with the theoretical knowledge and the practical skills to assess, contribute to the clinical formulation, and develop treatment and management plans in collaboration with significant others i.e., carers, partners identified support workers. Furthermore, culturally responsive models of assessment, diagnosis and care within existing legislative frameworks and industry standards in mental health will be included. Holistic health encompasses spirituality as well as the physical, social, and emotional well-being of the individual and community.
learning_outcomes: Explain the recovery and resilience framework for mental health and the inclusion of family in contemporary mental health services.
Describe mental health classification systems and mental health legislation used throughout Australia.
Discuss a range of treatment modalities used in mental health including medication groups prescribed for different mental illness and mental health disorders.
Describe the principles involved in providing culturally responsive care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experiencing mental health disorders.
Initiate and document a comprehensive mental health assessment including a mental status examination and a mental health risk assessment.
Define the key mental health disorders/illnesses and describe their prevalence, clinical features and treatments.
Critically discuss within a team environment, management and treatment options for clients with a range of mental health disorders and to effectively advocate for these clients.

title: Assessment and Evaluation for Learning
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds students' capacity with curriculum-based, authentic assessment and the use of standardised assessment. With a focus on literacy and numeracy, these approaches can be employed to differentiate the learning for all students. The subject addresses assessment at both school/setting and classroom levels and how assessment and evaluation information can be employed at whole-of-organization scale for instructional decision-making using a Master Teacher approach to inclusive settings.
learning_outcomes: Self-evaluate their current knowledge of standardised testing and measurement principles and apply that evaluation using a knowledge audit tool to build technical knowledge of test development and use.
Apply knowledge of standardised testing to make a recommendation about a test for use with students in an inclusive school setting.

Build an assessment schedule/matrix for a classroom/school for the purpose of making a valid and reliable determination of student growth and then build a rationale for the schedule/matrix as described. The experience draws together learning about curriculum-based and standardised tests and outcome measurement in schools/settings.
Evaluate the utility and limitations of standardised testing.

Identify the distinct features of curriculum based assessments and curriculum based measurement and use that information to design a CBM or research and apply an existing curriculum-based measure. The tool should be specific to a specific curriculum area/aspect of difficulty and include all of the details required for classroom use including guidance for scoring, space for student demographic information and level.
Understand and evaluate contemporary standards for the design and use of standardised tests with students who have disabilities or cultural differences.
Develop a scholarly position on the use of standardised testing in schools and settings.
Identify and describe the different purposes of assessment types and their utility in instructional decision making. Demonstrate their roles in a preliminary annual assessment plan.
Evaluate the role of classroom ecology in the assessment process and build a device for measuring classroom ecology.

title: Assessment and Reporting
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Assessment and reporting are significant aspects of school education. Educational achievement and reporting of this is crucial to ongoing success for learners. Assessment monitors learning progress and reporting makes the results available to a range of audiences. Understanding the complexities surrounding assessment and reporting is essential for effective teaching. This subject compares and contrasts assessment and reporting strategies relevant to school education. Skills and practices required for effective assessing and reporting are explored with specific attention to identifying and understanding the challenges and complexities encountered by teachers when assessing and reporting on academic performance. Assessment as learning occurs when students reflect on and monitor their progress to inform their progress. Assessment is the ongoing process of gathering, analysing and reflecting on evidence to make informed and consistent judgments to improve student learning. Assessment for improved student learning and deep understanding requires a range of assessment practices to be used. Reporting is the process by which assessment information is communicated to help students, parents and teachers to make decisions by providing information about what students know and can do, together with recommendations for their future learning.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of moderation and apply standards to form consistent and comparable judgements.
Construct a critical position on how social and political trends have shaped the National Assessment Program.
Discuss a range of strategies for reporting on student achievement and engaging parent/carer support in the educative process.
Explain multiple ways to assess and inform student learning.
Explain the role of feedback on student learning.
Research, analyse and interpret student data to evaluate student learning and plan subsequent teaching practice to improve student outcomes.

title: Assessment Design for School Improvement
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines the contemporary assessment landscape in schools, with a particular focus on the intersections of official assessment requirements and local assessment practices. In this subject, students will evaluate the relationship between school improvement policies, metrics and evidence and how these influence local assessment practices. Students have opportunities to engage with a range of case studies profiling diverse assessment practices and challenges and evaluate the ethical dimensions of diverse assessment practices. Students will also debate how diverse assessment practices can make unique contributions to school improvement. A key focus is on responsive assessment design to strengthen teaching and learning in response to diverse learner needs.
learning_outcomes: Map the relationships between school reform agendas, education policy and assessment.
Analyse a range of ethical implications for assessment design, particularly for diverse learners including First Nations young people.
Propose how assessment designed for diverse learners, including First Nations young people, can drive school improvement.
Critically review the contemporary assessment landscape and identify key stakeholders and how these shape hierarchies of being, knowing and doing.
Critically reflect on and evaluate approaches to assessment design in a specific educational context.

title: Assessment and Reporting: The Primary Years (K-2)
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will explore assessment practices in primary school settings and critically discuss the purposes, methods, strengths and challenges of assessing learning. Students will become familiar with the grading systems commonly used in primary school settings in Australia. The students will develop a critical awareness of the usefulness of different approaches for recording children's learning for planning purposes, and to reflect on teacher professional practice to improve student learning outcomes. This subject examines skills and practices required for effective assessment and reporting. Students will complete a 240 hour placement in a K-2 classroom. They will plan sequences of learning based on observation and assessment of children's abilities. Based on the Charles Sturt University student's area of specialisation, either literacy or numeracy, lessons should include catering for differentiation and the use of formative and summative assessment strategies that guide teaching and learning. Students will have the opportunity to reflect on practice to guide future planning for improved learning outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Use assessment results to modify teaching practice, inform planning of teaching, and progress learning.
Identify the role of assessment in teaching and learning.
Reflect on their professional development through the compilation of a teaching portfolio demonstrating their achievement of the Australian Professional Teaching Standards at graduate level.
Interpret assessment data to evaluate children's learning.
Assess children's learning using a variety of assessment strategies, including informal and formal, diagnostic, formative and summative approaches.
Build professional relationships with children and interpersonal engagement with professional stakeholders within the learning context in a school setting.
Identify a range of strategies for reporting on student learning.

title: Assessment in Clinical Education
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject applies the principle of transformative learning to explore the role that assessment and feedback plays in clinical education for students and clinicians, and ultimately, the provision of safe and competent patient care. The different categories and purposes of assessment will be examined, along with the necessary features of a valid and reliable assessment tool. Students will learn how to identify and implement an evidence-based assessment tool to assess a clinician and then reflect on this experience to expand their skills as an assessor in the clinical context. The use of constructive alignment between assessment, learning objectives and learning activities will be considered, as well as the role of the clinical educator in identifying and managing underperformance in the health sector.
learning_outcomes: Critique the uses of formative and summative assessment in clinical education.
Analyse the role of the clinical educator in identifying and working with under-performance.
Contrast the role of a clinical educator during an assessment, and the role of a clinical educator during a teaching and learning experience.
Examine self-assessment and peer assessment in clinical education.
Select and implement an evidence-informed competency assessment tool that is aligned to a specific learning outcome.
Apply evidence-informed strategies to deliver constructive and timely feedback to a learner.

title: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will extend their understanding of assessment strategies and practices in the adult and vocational education context. Students will critically engage with current assessment theories and link these to their practice. The learning design for this subject is based on the principles of critical reflection on experience which leads to improved practice. The modules address the theoretical underpinning of good assessment practices in a range of adult and vocational education contexts.
learning_outcomes: Explain how assessment activities operate with the Australian Quality Training Framework (AQTF).
Explain the issues associated with assessment practices within the adult and vocational education context.
Critically reflect on their own performance as an assessor in their professional setting.
Critically examine assessment practices within their own professional context.
Articulate the professional ethical issues associated with assessment practices in the adult and vocational education context.
prerequisites: EEE304: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education
EEE506: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education

title: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will extend their understanding of assessment strategies and practices in the adult and vocational education context. Students will critically engage with current assessment theories and link these to their practice. The learning design for this subject is based on the principles of critical reflection on experience which leads to improved practice. The modules address the theoretical underpinning of good assessment practices in a range of adult and vocational education contexts.
learning_outcomes: Explain the issues associated with assessment practices within the adult and vocational education context.
Examine assessment practices within their own professional context.
Reflect on their own performance as an assessor in their professional setting.
Articulate the professional ethical issues associated with assessment practices in the adult and vocational education context.
Explain how assessment activities operate with the Australian Quality Training Framework (AQTF).
prerequisites: EEE404: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education
EEE506: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education

title: Assessment of Animal Welfare
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The welfare of all animals - companion, domestic, captive and wild - is a matter of increasing concern in Australia and internationally. This subject, on the rapidly developing science of animal welfare, provides the skills necessary to apply a multidisciplinary approach for the assessment of animal welfare. Moving beyond basic husbandry, students will critically analyse the interplay between an animal’s internal biological state and its external environment. Students will evaluate the validity and reliability of established markers of welfare, such as behaviour, and neuroendocrinology as well as emerging biomarkers arising from advances in genetics and neuroscience. A significant portion of the subject is dedicated to emerging methodologies, including cognitive bias testing, qualitative behavioural assessment (QBA), and the use of real-time sensor and artificial intelligence technologies for continuous monitoring. By developing a broad knowledge of relevant physiological and psychological domains and emerging technologies, students will be well placed to apply a multidisciplinary, collaborative approach to design robust welfare assessment protocols across diverse contexts (research, domestic/companion animal and conservation).
learning_outcomes: Apply ethological principles to design and execute a behavioural assessment protocol, including Qualitative Behavioural Assessment (QBA) and ethograms.
Communicate and work effectively as part of a research team.
Appraise the efficacy of emerging technologies, such as real-time sensors and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for the continuous and non-invasive monitoring of animal welfare in a range of environments.
Appraise the biological validity and reliability of behavioural, physiological and morphological markers of animal welfare.
Analyse the efficacy and role of emerging measures of animal welfare, including those arising from advances in genetics and neuroscience.
Design robust animal welfare assessment plans that integrate multidisciplinary methods with appropriate technologies to meet industry, legislative or conservation needs.

title: Assessment, Diagnosis and Risk Management
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Mental health is about the study, diagnosis, treatment and management of mental illness and mental disorders. This subject focuses on clinical features, classification, assessment, treatment and risk management issues of mental illness and mental disorders from a trauma focused perspective. Using the DSM 5 and ICD 11, diagnostic criteria will be evaluated. Students will look at a range of assessment tools that are used in the assessment process including the Mental Status Examination and Risk Assessment. Students will be equipped with the theoretical knowledge and the practical skills to use these tools to undertake an assessment, contribute to clinical formulation, and develop treatment and management plans in collaboration with significant others i.e. carers, partners and identified support workers. Culturally responsive models of assessment, diagnosis and care within existing legislative frameworks and industry standards in mental health will be examined.
learning_outcomes: Initiate and document a comprehensive mental health assessment including a mental status examination and a mental health risk assessment.
Analyse the principles and practices involved in providing culturally responsive care for vulnerable and at-risk populations experiencing mental health disorders.
Examine the recovery, resilience and trauma informed care frameworks for mental health care and the inclusion of family in contemporary mental health services.
Discuss a range of treatment modalities used in mental health including medication groups prescribed for different mental illness and mental health disorders.

title: Assessment, Design and Delivery of Exercise
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to equip students with the essential skills and knowledge to competently conduct health and fitness evaluations, perform common health, exercise and sport-related assessments and provide appropriate exercise prescription and delivery outcomes. Emphasis will be placed on the need for accurate measuring devices, corrective exercises, critical evaluation of established assessment for exercise interventions, and the communication skillset needed for service delivery. In addition to these core areas, the subject emphasise adherence to professional standards and ethical practices, integrates evidence-based and technological approaches, and offers practical, hands-on experiences to ensure safe, individualised client care in the dynamic field of exercise science.
learning_outcomes: Implement behavioural strategies and provide effective communication, respecting client needs and professional standards.
Utilise and critique scientific literature, applying basic data analysis for informed exercise science prescription and delivery.
Apply evidence-based tools to prescribe and evaluate exercise interventions, ensuring client safety and progress.
Conduct comprehensive client assessments considering health, sport and exercise determinants, with accurate use and calibration of equipment.
Interpret assessment data to recognise, apply, and monitor personalised corrective exercise prescription.
Identify contraindications in health and exercise assessment settings, ensuring appropriate technology integration for client care.

title: Astrophysics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to astrophysics, extending topics from PHY299 Introduction to Astronomy and is suitable as a basis for further astrophysics research, it will also be suitable for students in other areas of science teaching, and for students who wish to take the subject for general interest. The subject covers most areas of astrophysics including solar system astronomy, stellar astronomy (formation, evolution and the fate of stars and stellar systems). The subject will also cover galactic evolution and kinematics of galaxies, extra galactic astronomy and cosmology. Students will be able to complete this subject by distance with no intensive.
learning_outcomes: Identify the areas of physics involved in precision astrophysics.
Describe and explain the structure, formation and evolution of galaxies.
Combine the various astronomical observations of the universe to compose a coherent picture of universal structure and evolution.
Classify the various components of the universe.
Identify and explain the various physics processes associated with astrophysics.
Conceptual and mathematical problems associated with the topics covered in Astrophysics.
Describe and explain stellar formation and evolution.
Identify, describe and relate the various components of the universe over a range of astrophysical scales.

title: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will extend their understanding of assessment strategies and practices in the adult and vocational education context. Students will critically engage with current assessment theories and link these to their practice. The learning design for this subject is based on the principles of critical reflection on experience which leads to improved practice. The modules address the theoretical underpinning of good assessment practices in a range of adult and vocational education contexts.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on their own performance as an assessor in their professional setting.
Critically examine assessment practices within their own professional context.
Explain the issues associated with assessment practices within the adult and vocational education context.
Articulate the professional ethical issues associated with assessment practices in the adult and vocational education context.
Critique how assessment activities operate with the Australian Quality Training Framework (AQTF).
prerequisites: EEE304: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education
EEE404: Assessment Practices in Adult and Vocational Education

title: Audiovisual Archiving
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Audiovisual media have given rise to entirely new forms of expression through recording, communicating and entertaining. While sharing intellectual, physical and contextual characteristics with traditional media, they have distinctive physical formats and storage needs and can only be comprehended via appropriate technology. Their management must take into account traditional principles and methods of managing information resources, and new principles, methods and paradigms arising from the nature of the audiovisual media themselves. This subject provides an overview of the discipline, including its history, philosophy and ethics, the development of and models for audiovisual archives, and international organisations responsible for audiovisual heritage.
learning_outcomes: Explain the underlying rationale for collecting, preserving, and providing access to audiovisual materials.
Describe the structures, strategies and skills by which audiovisual management activities are pursued.
Provide a perspective on the future of audiovisual management.
Discuss underlying values, principles, ethics, and legalities associated with AV collections.
Discuss the history and nature of audiovisual media.

title: Audiovisual Archiving 2
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Audiovisual materials have specialised management requirements in terms of collection development, intellectual control, access and preservation because of their very nature. This subject considers a range of contexts, comparing systems that have been developed specifically for these media with those adapted from library, archival or museum approaches. It also examines how policies, criteria and mechanisms have been devised to ensure appropriate coverage of evidential and research material in line with organisational objectives. Practical sessions focus on the complexities of providing access to audiovisual materials, from individual research requests through to product development and marketing.
learning_outcomes: Apply the body of knowledge to workplace scenarios.
Explain the principles and practices underlying collection development, collection management and access within the audiovisual environment, particularly as they relate to audiovisual archives.
Critically discuss many of the complex issues that can arise in dealing with audiovisual materials in the workplace.

title: Auditing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject adopts a risk-based approach to auditing and assurance services, exploring the practice and theory of auditing as it applies to Australia within a global environment. The concept of risk management is emphasised as it permeates all functions of management, audit and corporate governance.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the expanding scope of assurance services and providers in today's international business environment.

Explain and critically evaluate influences on audit and assurance services including: Australian and international professional standards, statutory and common laws, regulatory bodies, and public expectations within a global market.
Exercise critical and reflective judgement and appreciate the value of ethical practice.
Demonstrate risk management methodologies and the role of internal controls in an audit context.
Design an audit plan and select and apply appropriate audit procedures for a financial statement audit.

title: Auditing and Assurance Services
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject adopts a risk-based approach to auditing and assurance services, exploring the practice and theory of auditing as it applies to Australia within a global environment. Emphasis is placed on the application of auditing concepts to financial statement audits.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of assurance services and providers.

Identify and evaluate the influences on the audit processes, including the Corporations Act, Common Law, Australian and International professional standards, professional bodies and public expectations within a global market.
Appraise the expanding scope of auditing in the current international business environment.
Explain, select and apply procedures involved in the audit process.
Appraise the client's business environment and apply the risk model.

title: Australia and Asia
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the history of Australia's political, cultural and economic relations with Asia, aiming to provide an understanding of the complex issues involved in Australians' present-day attempt to come to terms with their region. Changing perceptions of Asia are emphasised: from alien source of threat, both 'Yellow Peril' and 'Red Peril', to Asia as a region inextricably bound to Australia's future. Particular attention is given to the roles of race, culture and ideology in Australian attitudes to Asia and to tension in Australia's history between the nation's British and Western cultural heritage and political and economic interests arising from its geographical location in the Asian-Pacific region.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the importance of historical perspective for the present day debate on Australia's relations with Asia.
Demonstrate developed skills of critical thought and expression.
Demonstrate an understanding of the main interpretations of the history of Australia's relations with Asia.
Demonstrate a sound knowledge of the main developments in Australia's relations with Asia since the 1880s.

title: Auditing and Assurance Services
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject adopts a risk-based approach to auditing and assurance services, exploring the practice and theory of auditing as it applies to Australia within a global environment. Emphasis is placed on the application of auditing concepts to financial statement audits.
learning_outcomes: Explain, select and apply procedures involved in the audit process.
Appraise the expanding scope of auditing in the current international business environment.

Identify and evaluate the influences on the audit processes, including the Corporations Act, Common Law, Australian and International professional standards, professional bodies and public expectations within a global market.
Explain the role of assurance services and providers.
Appraise the client's business environment and apply the risk model.
prerequisites: ACC395: Risk Based Audit and Assurance

title: Australia in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries: Times of Debate and Change
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop students' understanding of Australian history during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Through a selection of key historical periods, events and individuals, students will analyse, discuss and form conclusions on how elements of Australian society instigated, influenced and enacted change in politics, social attitudes and behaviour. Students will investigate and interpret history where selected moments and causes evoked different voices towards activism and change including Indigenous Australians, gender groups, the family, workers, youth and the counter-generations, and immigrants. Students will learn how contemporary historians and revisionist history accounts have interpreted key moments and individuals; how the contexts and events of former times are viewed and interpreted today; and in what ways such views may alter, and why, into the future.
learning_outcomes: Make informed arguments on how historical interpretations may change in the future.
Evaluate attitudes and debates in historical source material together with those of contemporary historians and revisionist history accounts.
Analyse how Indigenous Australians and other minority groups were denied a voice and/or had a distorted representation in Australian history through power, the media and popular perceptions.
Analyse where particular moments and individuals in Australian nineteenth and twentieth century Australian history caused debate and changed attitudes and action.
Assess how relevant historical themes and interpretations may be represented in community story-telling, cultural sites and collections.
Communicate in oral and/or written form complex ideas in relation to history using research, critical thinking and theoretical application.

title: Australian Art from 1939
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a survey of Australian art from 1939 to the present. It traces the shifting sources of overseas influence, from Europe to the USA to a recent rich variety. Themes discussed include the 'Angry Decade' (1937 - 1947), the Antipodeans, abstract expressionism, the function of international exhibitions and art magazines, Pop Art, Minimal and Conceptual Art, Neo-Expressionism, and postmodernity.The opening up of the processes of art to include new forms and to represent groups previously marginalised because of gender, class, or ethnicity is discussed via the examples of specifically feminist art and contemporary Aboriginal painting.
learning_outcomes: Propose reasons for artistic change.
Recognise some styles and artists.
Understand contemporary concerns in the arts.

title: Australian Art To 1939
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the development of Australian art from its beginnings to the outbreak of World War II, giving particular emphasis to modernism and its sources. Central concerns are: the primacy of British and European influences; the effect of expatriatism; the role of women artists in bringing early modernism to Australia; and the impact of international art movements on major Australian modernists between the wars. The focus is on painting and sculpture, but photography and the decorative arts are introduced where they are relevant. Attention is also given to art history methods and critical writings.
learning_outcomes: Extend their grasp of art history methods.
Trace the development of modernism in Australia.
Demonstrate an overview of early Australian art and its sources.

title: Australian Cultural Dialogues
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This introductory subject explores the rich, ancient and dynamic visual culture of Australia, including the many Indigenous First Nations and the complex relations between artworks, artists, audiences and cultural institutions. Using peer to peer discussion informed by research from diverse Australian sources, students will review case studies from the late 18th through to the 21st century, culminating in a reflection on emerging directions in Australian art. Throughout this subject, Indigenous art and non-Indigenous art will be discussed in dialogue, to generate holistic perspectives on Australian cultural identity.
learning_outcomes: Research Australian artworks in the context of wider historical events, debates and political issues that have affected and continue to affect Indigenous Australians and Australian cultural identity.
Investigate, compare and discuss the work of specific Australian artists, including Indigenous and non-Indigenous art, both historical and contemporary.
Demonstrate an understanding of the importance of precedent, protocols and copyright, as well as cultural and commercial values in relation to Indigenous and other Australian artists.
Ethically and accurately utilise Australian cultural institutions and their collections as research sources.

title: Australian History and Politics
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop students' broader understanding of contemporary Australian history and politics, including how history and politics affect the lived experiences of Indigenous Australians from British invasion to the present. From a political history disciplinary perspective, this subject will ask students to analyse and interpret the impact of social forces on Australian government processes and policies, influenced by factors that include migrants, women and international relations. Students will learn to investigate how history and politics are determined, by whom and for what reason. Students will develop skills to analyse and debate, interpret and communicate complex ideas and express these ideas to their student peers, and in academic writing.
learning_outcomes: Articulate how Australian governments and democracy operate, including links to policy and influence, past and present.

Analyse the key political and historical themes and influences in Australia in relation to the impact of past policy and practice on Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians from pre-invasion to today.
Apply knowledge and skills to communicate complex ideas in relation to history and politics using research, critical thinking and be able to demonstrate these in academic writing.
Analyse how power and privilege operates in relation to the self and to the experiences of Indigenous Australians, migrants and women.
prerequisites: POL112: Understanding Australia: History, Politics and Society

title: Australian Civics and Citizenship
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the functions of democracy and concepts of citizenship in Australia. It provides knowledge of the concepts of democracy, citizenship and leadership within the relevant historical contexts. Students will examine the role and influence of both groups and individuals in Australian democracy.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role of the media and other outside influences in the political process.
Demonstrate knowledge and skills to participate in the Australian democratic system.
Demonstrate an understanding of changes in citizenship policies and practices since Federation.
Discuss concepts of democracy, citizenship and leadership in Australian politics.
Demonstrate an understanding of the historical context of Australian civics and citizenship.

title: Australian Law and Legal System
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the nature of law in society, the major schools of legal philosophy, the major features of the Australian legal system including the Australian Constitution, sources of law, statutory interpretation, the judicial process and the doctrine of precedent, an introduction to techniques of legal research and problem-solving.
learning_outcomes: Understand the difference between common and civil law and be able to comment on the merits of each.
Apply the law relating to the jurisdiction of the courts and apply the doctrine of precedent in complex situations.
Understand and be able to engage in critical analysis of law as a system of norms.
Understand the history of the reception of common law into Australia and the status relating to Indigenous law.
Be aware of the sources of law in Australia and be able to explain the relationship between them.
Explain the basics of the Commonwealth Constitution and suggest areas in need of reform.
Explain the main schools of legal philosophy and assess their relative merits.
Undertake advanced legal research and solve legal problems.
Apply rules of statutory interpretation to complex fact situations.

title: Australian Literature
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a survey of the development of Australian literature up to the 1970s through a study of significant novels, short stories and poetry. From the entries of the diaries of Captain Cook to contemporary multicultural writing students will be introduced to the diversity of Australian literature, focussing on key authors such as Henry Lawson, Judith Wright, Patrick White as well as a range of lesser-known writers and movements.
learning_outcomes: Have continued the development and refinement of their literary competence through a reading of selected Australian works.
Place the literature in its social, political and cultural context.
Be aware of the relationship between reader and text in the creation of literary meaning.
Have an introduction to the major lines of development in Australian prose and poetry from 1788 to the 1990s.

title: Australian Theatre
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject, plays from contemporary Australian theatre are studied through the lens of colonisation - with particular focus on Australian Indigenous and other cultural contexts. Special attention is paid to periods of intensive activity in playwriting and the role of theatre in reflecting constructed Australian cultural standpoints. Students read and critique a range of texts selected for their engagement with Indigenous Australians, class, gender, sexual orientation, and the migrant experience.
learning_outcomes: Apply the position of contemporary Australian theatre practice within Australian and global arts industries.
Apply, evaluate and compare Australian theatre forms, practices and issues - including approaches to decolonisation of Australian stages.

Investigate the development of Australian theatre in a colonised land: with special reference to the relationship between Australian First Nations theatre and performance and theatre created by settler Australians.

Identify, acknowledge and analyse the construction of Australian cultural standpoints with respect to: Indigenous Australian perspectives, experiences of migrants and people of colour, class difference, sexual orientation and gender.

title: Avian Evolution and Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Recent advances in bird fossil discoveries and studies of extant bird taxa have significantly deepened our understanding of avian evolution, including the origins, diversification of modern birds, and their interrelationships. This subject explores the early evolutionary history, phylogeny, and systematics of birds, providing a foundation for understanding species evolution and the drivers of population divergence. Students will examine broad-scale patterns of avian distribution and diversity, as well as the underlying mechanisms shaping these patterns. Students will also explore population and community ecology of birds, with a focus on temporal and spatial variations in population size, structure, and demographics, as well as the factors regulating populations. Finally, students will investigate bird assemblages and the species interactions that shape community composition, offering a comprehensive study of avian ecology and evolution.
learning_outcomes: Review, relate and synthesise knowledge of avian evolution and ecology.
Integrate advanced concepts in avian evolution, phylogeny and classification, and apply the methods and processes by which classifications and phylogenies are deduced.
Explain and analyse the structure and dynamics of bird populations and communities and appraise the factors that influence the abundance and distribution of bird populations and communities.
Explain and evaluate different approaches to studying avian distribution and diversity patterns, and synthesise insights on the interplay between phylogeny, ecology and biogeography.

title: Avian Systematics and Biogeography
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of evolutionary biology, taxonomy, systematics and biogeography with an emphasis on their application to the study of birds. Included in this subject are a number of fundamental topics: the origin of birds as a whole and their relationship to dinosaurs and other reptiles, the early evolution and radiation of birds, and current ideas about the relationships of modern birds. It examines distributions of different bird groups, explores large-scale patterns in diversity, and the basis of these patterns. Results of recent research are combined with existing theories to give an up-to-date introduction to this dynamic field, and an insight into the history of evolutionary ornithology. The subject has an intensive school. On completion, students have a comprehensive understanding of the principles of phylogenetic systematics and can read and critically interpret cladograms.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the principles of avian systematics including the theories and current ideas about the origin and early radiation of birds and the various species concepts and their application to ornithology.
Use a phylogeny to infer patterns of character evolution and selection.
Apply different approaches to studying distribution patterns, and understand the interplay between phylogeny and biogeography.

Describe extant orders of birds, their phylogenetic and biogeographical origins, their distinguishing characteristics and apply the methods and processes by which these phylogenies and taxonomies are deduced.
Apply their knowledge of avian systematics in order to describe the evolutionary origins of Australian bird taxa.
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the principles of phylogenetic systematics and can read and critically interpret cladograms.
Explain how modern evolutionary and landscape processes affect the population genetics of birds.

title: Avian Biology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive overview of the biology of birds. This includes the structure and function of feathers, the skeletal, muscle and physiological adaptations allowing flight, the highly efficient respiratory, circulatory, gastrointestinal and excretory systems, and the structure of the brain and sensory organs that influence bird behaviour. Special attention is paid to how the anatomy and physiology has evolved differently across species to support endurance and to allow birds to survive in a particular environment. During the second part of this subject, students will gain in-depth knowledge about the main, annual events that marks a bird's life: reproduction, moult and migration. On completion of this subject, students will know and understand the fundamentals of bird biology and be able to apply this knowledge to further study bird ecology, evolution, behaviour and conservation.
learning_outcomes: Describe the sensory and neural mechanisms underlying bird behaviour.
Demonstrate extensive knowledge of migration, navigation, avian life histories and reproduction.
Demonstrate a broad knowledge of the internal and external anatomy of birds, bird physiology, and avian respiratory, circulatory, gastrointestinal, excretory and reproductive systems.
Review, relate and synthesise their knowledge of avian biology to bird behaviour, ecology, evolution and conservation.

title: Bachelor of Engineering Capstone Thesis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject helps cadet engineers to enhance their research skills by working in a research project to develop an appropriate research strategy to fill an identified knowledge gap, collect relevant literature data systematically, generate, analyse and interpret the data accurately. Cadets should apply their theoretical and technical knowledge gained elsewhere in the curriculum and the previous workplace to justify the usability of their research findings in civil engineering applications. The outcomes will be delivered in both written (thesis) and oral (thesis defence) formats. Bachelor of Engineering Capstone Thesis is supervised by an academic engineer from Charles Sturt University.
learning_outcomes: Apply research in accordance with established research methodologies based on the theories underpinning the engineering discipline.
Apply knowledge of systems thinking methodologies and engagement as a platform for creative, sustainable, and socially responsible engineering practice.
Synthesise and use specialist bodies of knowledge within the engineering discipline and demonstrate the capacity to independently generate new knowledge in the context of existing literature.

Use and manage information in a professional and ethical manner, analyse and appraise raw information, and draw appropriate conclusions in context with due consideration of the knowledge, methods, and assumptions within the engineering discipline.
Apply communication, research, and technical skills to justify, critique and interpret theoretical propositions, methodologies, results and conclusions to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
prerequisites: ENG375: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Bachelor of Engineering 1

title: Bachelor of Vocational Education and Training or Bachelor of Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is applicable for students who have completed a Bachelor of Adult and Vocational Education course or, a Bachelor of Vocational Education and Training course, and are awarded credit in the Master of Adult and Vocational Education (Articulated Set).
learning_outcomes: This is a credit code only - no learning outcomes apply.

title: Balgargal: Indigenous Cultural Immersion Experience
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to spend a minimum of two days in country with Australian Aboriginal Elders and/or Cultural guides, learning about local Aboriginal culture. Development of cultural competence requires not just knowledge, but also engagement of attitudes, values and skills. The subject facilitates this engagement by taking students out of the classroom and involving them in first-hand experience. Activities such as storytelling, yarning and walking in country are examples of Aboriginal teaching approaches which will provide an authentic way for transformative learning to occur. Through direct contact with Aboriginal Elders and/or cultural guides, the subject provides a way to foster a deeper understanding of the experiences of Aboriginal Australians and the contemporary issues faced by Aboriginal people which impact upon their social and emotional wellbeing. This in turn will lead to reflection on attitudes and values.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the way in which people in Australian Aboriginal cultures identify themselves in terms of family and the significance of this for psychological practice.

Demonstrate an understanding of the local history of the country that they visit, the significance of Australian Aboriginal relationships with land and the implications of these for psychological practice.

Demonstrate critical reflexivity on their cultural identity, values and ways of working and the way in which this will influence their future professional relationships with Australian Aboriginal people.

Demonstrate critical reflexivity on the way that their experience at camp challenges their assumptions and the way in which they will use this experience to consider an Indigenous standpoint when working with Aboriginal Australians as future psychologists.
Demonstrate an understanding of the issues impacting upon the social and emotional well being of Aboriginal Australians today and the implications of this for psychological practice.
Demonstrate knowledge and the use of protocols, codes of behaviour and skills that are relevant for interacting with Australian Aboriginal people in a culturally sensitive and respectful manner.

Demonstrate critical reflexivity on the culture, values and history of the discipline, and the way in which this will influence their future professional relationships with Australian Aboriginal people.

title: Basic Mathematics Skills
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide a comprehensive review of basic mathematics skills for students who wish to study a university course which assumes a basic level of numeracy. This self-paced, short subject will enable students to build on their prior knowledge and develop the basic mathematics skills required for success in their course. It is particularly useful for students about to begin their CSU studies in theBachelor of Education (Early Childhood and Primary), Bachelor of Education (K-12), Bachelor of Nursing and Bachelor of Paramedicine.
learning_outcomes: Be familiar with pre-algebra concepts.
Be familiar with techniques for data collection and reporting.
Confidently, without the use of a calculator, work with all types of numbers.
Work with concepts of space and measurement.
Be comfortable with using the language of mathematics.

title: Beginner Arabic Language 1
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the Arabic language adopting the methodology of the classical grammarians. Students will learn the different types of words and move onto forming phrases and eventually sentences. Various examples will be derived from different sources such as the Qur'an, Prophetic traditions and everyday scenarios. Reading and writing skills acquired in the previous unit will be further developed.
learning_outcomes: Formally analyse sentences at a beginner's level.
Distinguish between different types of words, phrases and sentences at a basic level.
Fluently read long vowelised passages.
Translate simple sentences into English.
Conjugate basic singular verbs in the appropriate tense, gender and person.
Compose basic sentences using appropriate syntax and vocabulary.
prerequisites: ISL140: The Arabic Script and its Sounds
ISL160: Arabic Language I: Language Essentials And Qur'anic Script

title: Beginner Arabic Language 2
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will begin to engage with a basic text called 'Stories of the Prophets'. This text will be used to acquire new vocabulary, improve comprehension and further develop the skill of syntax analysis. Students will continue improving on their knowledge of syntax and morphology. Various examples will be derived from different sources such as the Qur'an, Prophetic traditions and everyday scenarios. Reading and writing skills acquired in the previous unit will be further developed.
learning_outcomes: Conjugate basic verbs in the appropriate tense, gender, number and person.
Compose non-technical prose using appropriate syntax and vocabulary.
Demonstrate sufficient comprehension of non-technical prose.
Formally analyse sentences incorporating the new rules of syntax and morphology.
Demonstrate basic understanding of the different scales of verbs.

title: Behavioural Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Behavioural Ecology is the discipline devoted to understanding animal behaviour within an ecological and evolutionary context. Behavioural Ecology emerged from a synthesis of many scientific disciplines including animal behaviour, ecology, evolutionary biology, psychology and anthropology. In this subject, we will first examine various aspects of animal behaviour and consider the developmental, genetic, neural and physiological bases underlying these behaviours. Then we will investigate how and why behaviours vary among animals, how these behaviours may enable animals to thrive in their environments and how such behaviours evolved over time. By examining examples from wild animals across major animal groups, we will study predation, competition, migration, communication, sexual selection, parental care and eusociality. Participants of this subject come from a wide variety of backgrounds, ranging from professionals with tertiary-level qualifications to experienced amateurs without university training. Regardless of background, students enrolled in this subject are exposed to advanced levels of behavioural ecology allowing them to transfer their knowledge to the appropriate context.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate specialist skills in the identification, description and measurement of animal behaviour.
Design a basic behavioural study, collect meaningful behavioural data and interpret results of behavioural ecology studies.
Apply specialist skills in recognising and interpreting animal behaviours.
Synthesise and analyse peer reviewed literature on animal behaviour.
Articulate in-depth knowledge about why behaviours vary among animals and how these behaviours have evolved.

title: Being the Church
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the scriptural, theological and sacramental bases for the identity and mission of the church in the twenty-first century. The emergence of the ecumenical movement will be discussed, as will contemporary critiques of the church related to the history of colonialism, the abuse of power and the end of Christendom.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on the relations between the mission of the church and its varied contexts: cultural, political and geographical.
Demonstrate an understanding of contemporary critiques of the church related to the history of colonialism, the abuse of power and the end of Christendom.
Discuss theological issues relating to the unity and diversity of the church across history.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills.
Articulate the scriptural, theological and sacramental foundations of the Christian church.

Articulate and critically evaluate the scriptural, theological and sacramental foundations of the Christian church.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Analyse critically the relation between the mission of the church and its varied contexts: cultural, political and geographical.
Discuss critically theological issues relating to the unity and diversity of the church across history.

title: Biblical Hebrew 1
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to Biblical Hebrew as a basis for enhanced study of the Old Testament (Hebrew Bible) and for further study of Biblical Hebrew. Its primary focus is foundational Hebrew vocabulary, grammar and syntax. Translation of selected biblical texts into English is an important component of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competence in the use of print and digital resources for the study of Biblical Hebrew.
Translate selected texts from the Hebrew Bible and discuss relevant issues relating to vocabulary, grammar and syntax.
Demonstrate knowledge of the historical context and cultural significance of Biblical Hebrew.
Read, write and pronounce simple Biblical Hebrew phrases.
Demonstrate self-guided learning.
Demonstrate the acquisition of a basic vocabulary of Biblical Hebrew and an understanding of basic Biblical Hebrew grammar.

Demonstrate a sound grasp of the verb system and all major features of Biblical Hebrew grammar and syntax.

title: Big Data and Marketing Analytics
