faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The emergence of big data accelerated by the internet, e-commerce and social media provides opportunities for better business/organisational management and a better society through evidence-based decision-making and the provision of new services and products. This subject introduces the conceptual and practical issues in developing models to aid in decision making in marketing. Students will be introduced to the discovery and analysis of social networks, social trends, and relationships amongst industry factors using spreadsheets and data visualisation software. Students will also translate these analytic models into competitive strategy models by making policy for strategic and other decision recommendations.
learning_outcomes: Apply intermediate skills in spreadsheets and data visualisation software to identify trends and relationships among factors in industry and society.
Analyse government, industry and social media data to identify relationships and trends.
Create interactive models using appropriate software.
Effectively communicate findings, implications and conclusions to aid decision-makers from a range of big data sources.
Critically evaluate data from a range of data sources and using analytic tools to draw conclusions and a create a coherent marketing story.
Critically examine different methods of data analysis and presentation for social networks, complex systems and relational links.

title: Bioethics: Birth, Death, Love and Sex
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject we think philosophically about some of the biggest practical issues that give shape to people's lives. Examples include the following: Should you have children? Should you fear death? Should you get married? What forms of sex are morally permissible?
learning_outcomes: Apply their skills of analysis and argument and their understanding of theories to the clarification and resolution of the particular practical moral problems/issues addressed in the Syllabus.
Demonstrate a significant degree of understanding of the practice of addressing philosophical and ethical problems.
Demonstrate a significant degree of understanding of philosophical and ethical techniques of analysis and argument.

title: Biology in Agriculture
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the subject of biology as it relates to Agriculture. Students will be taken on a journey through the key biological concepts associated with the cell; including biochemistry, structure, function (including respiration and photosynthesis) and the cell cycle. This leads on to genetic principles and the mechanism of inheritance. This subject investigates plant and animal anatomy and physiology in relation to agricultural production and then grounds this work in a study of the principles of ecology. Students integrate their knowledge of biological diversity with their understanding of farming and biodiversity at the landscape level. Students will learn to use equipment and techniques for biological investigations and practice the skill of observation and recording.
learning_outcomes: Describe diversity from single-celled to multi-celled organisms and how our taxonomic system allows us to classify life.
Describe the interactions between organisms and their biotic and non-biotic environment.
Explain and apply ecological principles in the study of simple and biodiverse farming systems with respect to their connection and impact on broader ecological systems.
Describe key biological concepts related to plant and animal cells, including the molecules of life, genetics and metabolic processes, especially photosynthesis and respiration.
Describe animal anatomy and physiological systems and processes, especially in relation to agricultural production animals.
Describe plant anatomy and physiological systems and processes, especially in relation to agricultural plants.
Use basic equipment and techniques to investigate plant and animal form and function and be able to observe and record the information gained from these investigations.

title: Biomechanical Analysis of Human Movement
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject will develop a student's capability to apply biomechanical theoretical concepts and methods to analyse the causes and effects of movement tasks. A problem-focused learning design will require students to review and interpret literature to construct, apply and justify the research design, which will include performing data collection, analysis, interpretation and presentation of kinetic, kinematic and/or electromyography data. At the completion of this subject, students will be able to perform a three-dimensional biomechanical analysis of a human movement task to identify biomechanical issues attributing to an injury and/or potential injury risk factor, or to improve performance to provide critical information to assist clinicians and/or coaches to develop and implement effective injury prevention and/or rehabilitation program, and/or improve performance.
learning_outcomes: Describe and apply biomechanical principles in relation to the understanding of injury, disability and disease as they relate to movement.
Interpret and communicate results obtained from a biomechanical analysis.
Apply and utilise various biomechanical methods and equipment to perform movement analysis.
Evaluate biomechanical principles contributing to sporting injury and performance optimisation.
Explain and apply biomechanical principles using a scientific approach in relation to data collection, analysis and interpretation.
Identify movement asymmetry and movement errors during human movement based on biomechanical analysis and evidence-based literature.

title: Biomechanics
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the opportunity to gain an understanding of the fundamental underpinning mechanical principles of human movement and to be able to apply them in a practical context. Students learn how various kinetic (forces) and kinematic (description of motion) principles can be applied to improve movement skill technique and equipment design to maximise performance and/or reduce injuries across a broad range of populations. A practical-focused learning design will allow students to apply mechanical concepts to identify and describe why the body moves in certain ways.
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the kinematic and kinetic patterns during the gait cycle.
Distinguish between and undertake qualitative and quantitative approaches for describing human movement.
Apply the fundamental concepts and principles of biomechanics as they relate to a specific movement skill.
Solve basic quantitative problems related to linear and angular kinetic and kinematic concepts involving motion.
Describe the mechanical principles of the centre of gravity, equilibrium, balance, levers, mechanical advantage, projectile motion, muscle mechanics and fluid motion.
Understand and explain basic kinetic and kinematic biomechanical principles, and how they can be applied to motion, performance and injury prevention.

title: Biblical Hebrew 3
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates the studies completed in Biblical Hebrew 1 and 2. It entails a close examination of the grammatical and literary qualities of selected passages from the Old Testament (Hebrew Bible) as well as the completion of a substantial translation project demonstrating advanced proficiency in working with Biblical Hebrew.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate engagement with critical scholarship.
Demonstrate proficiency in Biblical Hebrew grammar and vocabulary.
Demonstrate familiarity with linguistic and literary features of Biblical Hebrew.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including well developed research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate use of the critical apparatus in critical editions of the Hebrew Bible.
Demonstrate facility in translating Biblical Hebrew prose and poetic texts.
Demonstrate advanced skills in translation, including an ability to discuss critical issues involved in translation choices.

title: Biopsychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: The aim of Biopsychology is to introduce students to paradigms for the explanation and study of behaviour that are characterised by a focus on the functioning of the nervous system. This subject will introduce students to basic principles of neuroscience, including neuron structure and function, neurotransmission, and functional neuroanatomy. These will be examined within the broader framework of the structures of behaviour (innate and acquired), as well as functional systems (eg. sensation, perception, motor control and memory).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to draw and describe the structure and function of neurons within the central nervous system (CNS).
Demonstrate ability to describe the major components of the CNS involved in sensation, perception and movement and how they interact.
Demonstrate knowledge of current explanations of behaviours from a biological perspective.
Demonstrate an understanding of the consequences of brain damage resulting from psychopathological disorders and other trauma on the functioning of the CNS and on behaviour.
Demonstrate an understanding of methods of research in neuroanatomy.
Demonstrate an understanding of the structures and pathways involved in higher level functions such as motivation, emotion, learning and memory and language.

title: Biopsychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: The aim of Biopsychology is to introduce students to paradigms for the explanation and study of behaviour that are characterised by a focus on the functioning of the nervous system. This subject will introduce students to basic principles of neuroscience, including neuron structure and function, neurotransmission, and functional neuroanatomy. These will be examined within the broader framework of the structures of behaviour (innate and acquired), as well as functional systems (eg. sensation, perception, motor control and memory).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the structures and pathways involved in higher level functions such as motivation, emotion, learning and memory and language.
Demonstrate an understanding of methods of research in neuroanatomy.
Demonstrate ability to describe the major components of the CNS involved in sensation, perception and movement and how they interact.
Demonstrate knowledge of current explanations of behaviours from a biological perspective.
Demonstrate an understanding of the consequences of brain damage resulting from psychopathological disorders and other trauma on the functioning of the CNS and on behaviour.
Demonstrate ability to draw and describe the structure and function of neurons within the central nervous system (CNS).

title: Birth, Death, Love and Sex
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject we think philosophically about some of the biggest practical issues that give shape to people's lives. Examples include the following: Should you have children? Should you fear death? Should you get married? What forms of sex are morally permissible? Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
learning_outcomes: Apply their skills of analysis and argument and their understanding of theories to the clarification and resolution of the particular practical moral problems/issues addressed in the Syllabus.
Demonstrate a significant degree of understanding of philosophical techniques of analysis and argument.
Demonstrate a significant degree of understanding of the practice of addressing ethical problems.

title: Books change your life: Improving literacy through literature
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to a range of literary forms and genres so they gain a deep understanding of how language works. It fosters immersive reading experiences whilst also cultivating language-based skills. It is particularly concerned with the relationship between reading and writing and how the development of high-level literacy skills are achieved through the improvement of both in tandem. The ability to articulate, verbally and in writing, is an important dimension to student learning and as such students undertake tasks designed to help them communicate clearly and effectively. The Basic Key Skills Builder (BKSB) resources are built into the pedagogy of the subject to prepare students for the LANTITE test — an examination that must be passed by all Pre-Service Teachers across all States and Territories in Australia. Finally, this subject provides students with a foundational knowledge of English literature and language in education which is essential to their development as communicators, writers, readers, and future teachers.
learning_outcomes: Describe and analyse a range of language forms, features and structures of texts and explain the ways these shape meaning and influence responses in a variety of texts.
Demonstrate a working knowledge of Australian and non-Australian literature.
Present a sound critical response showing developed skills in interpretation and analysis of texts.
Demonstrate improved skills in literacy (reading, writing and comprehension).

title: BIS Online Intensive Introductory Learning
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This course-based intensive subject introduces undergraduate students to tertiary study, distance education, the discipline of information studies, the structure of the Bachelor of Information Studies course, and to Charles Sturt University services and online systems.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role, importance and availability of a range of University services.
Explain how the University's online systems will facilitate their studies.
Show that they can apply a range of study skills.
Prepare a study schedule for themselves.
Demonstrate an understanding of the structure, aims and content of the degree program.

title: Border Management Ethics and Governance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an overview of the governance and integrity issues raised by the regulation of cross-border trade and how that can impact adversely on all aspects of border management. The subject will focus on the Customs environments where high levels of corruption can significantly reduce the effectiveness of Customs administrations and affect trade policy and development. The subject will examine international efforts and other policies and strategies that will help improve governance and integrity in Customs and the other regulatory authorities at the border
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically existing levels of ethical behaviour and integrity in a border management environment and make recommendations for improvement in standards.
Assess critically issues arising from the lack of good governance.
Identify and communicate effectively the role of the WCO in improving border management ethics and governance and be able to analyse the key initiatives promoted by that organisation.
Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge and understanding of the concepts and principles pertaining to governance issues in the border management environment.

Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge and understanding of the aims and objectives of the Revised Arusha Declaration, including the codes of conduct, and be able to apply its principles in selected border management contexts.
Research, locate and interpret information pertaining to corruption in the public domain.

title: Border Security
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates the students' understanding of a range of procedures and responses used by Customs to regulate trade and people flows across national borders and to consequently protect the community. The contemporary environment and the challenges posed in protecting the community are introduced and the subject addresses customs enforcement/interdiction activities in respect of illicit drugs, other prohibited imports, people smuggling and counter-terrorism responses.
learning_outcomes: Formulate practical solutions to both regulate and facilitate trade and passenger processing flows in a disaster relief or pandemic environment.
Evaluate critically various operational approaches to the clearance of international consignments that may contain illicit drugs and to identify good practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of contemporary and emerging threats facing customs administrations.

Evaluate, analyse and prioritise potential risks to effective border management regulation and enforcement with respect to people and goods, and to identify a range of appropriate risk mitigation treatments.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the key tools, controls and responses available to Customs to detect illicit/harmful goods at the border.

title: Botany
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject investigates the structure and function of the flowering plants (the angiosperms), the most successful plants on the planet and vital for our survival. Students will gain an appreciation for the role that plants have in human history and culture, and will learn about plant evolution, including how plants are named and classified. Students will be introduced to plant biochemistry, including photosynthesis, plant hormones, and signalling. Finally, students will learn about the structure and function of plant cells, tissues, and organs, and concepts of whole-plant biology such as water and sugar transport.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe the structure of plant cells, tissues and organs, and relate these to their functions.
Describe plant metabolic, cellular and developmental processes.
Explain the importance of flowering plants for life on earth.
Classify and distinguish between major plant groups and features, and name plants using binomial nomenclature.
Collect, record, interpret and communicate experimental results.
Apply knowledge from discrete topics to interpret and explain whole-plant biology.

title: Botany
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject investigates the structure and function of the flowering plants (the angiosperms), the most successful plants on the planet and vital for our survival. Students will gain an appreciation for the role that plants have in human history and culture, and will learn about plant evolution, including how plants are named and classified. Students will be introduced to plant biochemistry, including the process of photosynthesis, plant hormones, and signalling. Finally, students will learn about the structure and function of plant cells, tissues, and organs, and concepts of whole-plant biology such as water and sugar transport.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge from discrete topics to interpret and explain whole-plant biology.
Identify and describe the structure of plant cells, tissues and organs, and relate these to their functions.
Describe plant metabolic, cellular and developmental processes.
Collect, record, interpret and communicate experimental results.
Explain the importance of flowering plants for life on earth.
Classify and distinguish between major plant groups and features, and name plants using binomial nomenclature.

title: Brand Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Strong brands are key assets for companies. This subject will focus on the management of brands, including developing brands that resonate with consumers, building brand equity, measuring brand performance and managing brands over time. It has been designed to provide students with the capabilities to evaluate, design and make recommendations for branding programs across a diverse range of large and small organisations.
learning_outcomes: Make recommendations for the design and implementation of brand marketing programs.
Conduct a brand audit and use the information generated for brand planning.
Create and effectively communicate a brand positioning strategy.
Apply relevant theoretical concepts of branding to analyse specific problems and challenges in brand management.
Examine and critically evaluate current branding activities in the marketplace.

title: Border Revenue
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an in-depth study of the international legal instruments which guide the tariff classification and the determination of origin and value of internationally traded merchandise and is aimed at providing students with a strong appreciation of the principles and practices relating to border revenue determination and collection in a constantly changing cross border trade environment.
learning_outcomes: Use relevant sources, analyse critically the practical and legal aspects of the key elements of calculating border revenue and the attendant impact on international trade flows and border regulation.

Identify and critically assess the practical impact of international trade obligations relating to border revenue collection and to apply those obligations to both theoretical and practical situations/scenarios in respect of tariff classification, customs valuation and rules of origin.

Solve complex problems addressing the border management interactions of revenue collection, control and facilitation on the movement of goods across borders and to be able to communicate those solutions to others.
Locate and use relevant sources of information concerning tariff classification, customs valuation and the determination of origin of goods.

Explain and commentate critically on the fundamental principles, policy objectives and role of border agencies collecting revenue on cross border trade in an increasing globalised and/or regionalised context.

title: Border Management Theory and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to key features of managing a customs administration in the contemporary globalised world, including the role and responsibilities of Customs, customs policy and practice, strategic and operational management issues, relevant international conventions and agreements, risk management in the customs context, and international trends that impact on Customs such as social expectations, emerging technologies and the global economy.
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically the roles and policy objectives of Customs administrations.
Evaluate critically different approaches and operational practices to managing the import, export and transit of goods.
Identify and explain key international instruments affecting Customs operations.
Evaluate and analyse critically supply chain security issues and ways in which they may impact on Customs authorities.
Apply specialised knowledge and skills to identify appropriate responses to strategic management issues and policy objectives including management of risk, information and informed compliance.
Evaluate critically the regulatory framework of a particular Customs authority against established international standards.

Formulate appropriate and well-developed approaches to address complex problems such as control, revenue protection and environmental change in the border management context and be able to communicate those approaches to others.
Evaluate and transform information to mitigate risks at the strategic and operational level.

title: Branding and Identity
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the function of corporate identity and explore the process of logo design, brand development and management and how it is incorporated into a range of design solutions including collateral, advertising and packaging.
learning_outcomes: Understand and demonstrate a variety of research techniques and creative approaches in logo and brand development and management.
Understand and apply a critical approach to design briefs.
Create a logo and relevant brand touch points and associated guidelines.
Identify and critically analyse attributes of successful logos and brands.
Apply creative, theoretical and technical skills already acquired in the creation of computer based design solutions.

title: Breast Imaging
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject commences with breast embryology, anatomy, physiology, pathology at both a microscopic and macroscopic level, and epidemiology. Students will gain a thorough understanding of breast disease, including causes, prevention and management as well as being able to recognise normal and abnormal variants of the breast. In addition, the subject introduces students to mammographic techniques and protocols as required for breast imaging. Ancillary and specialised techniques, such as breast tomosynthesis, lesion localisation, interventional procedures and alternative imaging modalities are studied, as well as image analysis, including radiographic and mammographic image interpretation, with review criteria. All aspects of mammography imaging will be covered as well as principles and techniques of MRI, ultrasound and sentinel node scintigraphy. Students will develop the theoretical knowledge and skill set to enable them to perform as competent, independent mammographic technologists within a multidisciplinary breast care team.
learning_outcomes: Explain both benign and malignant disease under the following headings: i. disease aetiology, mechanics and clinical manifestations; ii. pathological tests used to identify and evaluate the disorders; iii. current methods of treatment.
Develop research skills such as literature searching, review, critique and apply evidence-based breast imaging research within a range of contexts.
Critically evaluate the role of various imaging procedures and apply their procedural use as appropriate to a given examination.

Explain the rationale for the use of interventional and sonographic examinations under suitable guidance and supervision and critically evaluate the role of alternative modalities and the future applications of such.

Critically evaluate images and recognise normal and abnormal variants on the basis of their mammographic properties and apply the principles of image quality control in order to avoid, rectify and identify problems.
Examine the theory of positioning techniques used in mammography, including standard and specialised positioning and apply these in clinical mammography practice to a consistently high standard.

title: Breast Imaging Physics and Instrumentation
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the fundamental principles of radiation production, safety and protection, and the instrumentation used in breast imaging. It extensively considers the physics of mammography and advanced mammography and explores alternate breast imaging modalities covering digital image formation and recording methods. The design and maintenance of breast imaging instrumentation will be reviewed, with a focus on quality assurance and quality control procedures, as well as key considerations in visual perception, image processing and analysis. Finally, this subject deals with fundamental considerations of breast dosimetry, radiation biology and radiation protection.
learning_outcomes: Explain the structure of matter along with the fundamental principles, types and units of radiation; describe the physical principles underlying the generation of breast X-ray and alternative modality images; and evaluate the foundations of the visual perception system in order to synthesise their implications for breast image analysis.
Identify the way in which imaging equipment and associated technology embraces the above principles, and apply this knowledge of the various equipment types into the practice of mammography.
Explain the fundamental radiation quantities and units relevant to breast dosimetry, radiation biology, and radiation protection, and differentiate the methods used to assess breast dose.
Evaluate the potential bioeffects and recommendations pertaining to some alternate imaging modalities.

Analyse fundamental radiobiological event sequence and their effects at the molecular, cellular and tissue level; explain the principles of risk evaluation; and calculate probable population outcomes based on predetermined irradiation dose conditions.

Synthesise and apply foundational and practical knowledge to minimise risk in mammography, incorporating both legislative requirements and recommended best-practice controls - legislative and recommendatory.

title: Budgeting and Financing for Project Managers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject will teach students about the ways in which projects are selected and managed from a financial perspective. Students will learn how to evaluate different projects on the basis of their projected financial return and how to evaluate different sources of finance to fund the project. Students will then learn how to apply budgeting principle(s) to the selected project and how to incorporate different budgeting techniques and processes into the overall management of the project.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate different sources of finance and recommend a preffered option based on the projects characteristics.
Demonstrate knowledge of accounting budgeting techniques in the context of managing a project.
Evaluate the viability of competing project options using financial project evaluation techniques.
Apply budgeting processes to project management.

title: Building Community Resilience
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the range of community processes and their implications for community resilience. It investigates and evaluates ways in which innovative and inclusive approaches to supporting and building community resilience can be implemented, and considers implications for students' professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply a sustainable model of community resilience to a known community problem and identify implications for professional practice.
Define resilience in the context of communities.
Critically appraise the ways that processes of community stratification can impact on community resilience.
Identify a range of approaches to building community resilience in order to ensure communities are strengthened through innovative and inclusive practices.

title: Building Emotional Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: To be able to work with others, we must first understand ourselves and how we are perceived in the workplace. This subject will explore your role in the workplace, challenge you to reflect on and develop your self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills, as well as your ability to understand and manage your impact on others.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate their personal change management initiatives.
Create an action plan to develop their emotional intelligence, including their impact on others.
Recognise and critically reflect on their personal and social skills in the workplace through the lens of emotional intelligence theory.

title: Border Agencies and Principles of Border Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to an extensive range of border management issues including policy, legislation, compliance management, and economic and social impact. Comparative international studies and the application of international norms and legislation in areas such as migration, security, customs and quarantine are a key aspect of this subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the internationally recognised government structures for border management.
Apply international legal principles and best practice administrative approaches to border management issues.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of international organisations, treaties and conventions on border management.
Critically assess the challenges faced by customs and border agencies in the delivery of their services.
Identify and articulate solutions to selected issues and problems in the border management context.
Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the policy responses of government to border issues.
Analyse and interpret international and national developments affecting border integrity and security.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the principles of strategic planning in border management.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of the role of customs and border agencies and their environment.

title: Building Resilience for the Workplace
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: Resilience encompasses a set of behaviours that help people to process and adapt to change and uncertainty in their environment. Understanding and using resilient behaviours can support both individuals and organisations to effectively navigate today’s complex, dynamic and constantly evolving workplaces. This subject introduces students to concepts and theories of resilience, helping them to understand and use strategies to build personal and organisational resilience.
learning_outcomes: Identify challenges to resilience in workplace settings and apply appropriate strategies to manage the challenges.
Critically evaluate theories of resilience in relation to the workplace.
Define the concept of resilience.
Discuss the role of resilience in the workplace.

title: Building Sustainable Communities
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the role of human services in relation to governance and policy for a more sustainable world. Using a global citizenship framework, local and global policy contexts will be appraised with reference to the multidimensional impacts of environmental issues on wellbeing. A critique will be undertaken of all systems of governance including nation states, global entities, markets and institutions. This subject provides an opportunity for students to discover how professional practice can actively contribute to sustainable planning and policy development in communities.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate systems of governance in relation to social and environmental policy at local and global levels.
Describe global citizenship and ecological justice in the international context.
Describe roles for human services professionals in relation to ecological and social justice.
Apply principles of holistic human services practice to address governance and policy issues.

title: Business Accounting and Finance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed as an introduction to financial accounting, management accounting and finance for those working in a business environment. Students will gain an understanding of the generally accepted accounting principles underlying the accounting process and the uses and limitations of financial statements published by business entities. Accounting and finance issues faced by management and some of the techniques used by managers in decision making will be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and apply basic accounting ideas that underlie and limit the usefulness of accounting information.
Explain and analyse the nature, and measurement, of assets, equities, revenues, expenses and income.
Implement and critique analytic and interpretative techniques used in accounting and finance.
Explain and implement financial analysis and management accounting procedures.
Apply computer software to quantitative business decisions.
Discuss and critique the concepts behind the decision making processes associated with the efficient allocation of business resources.

title: Business Analysis and Data Analytics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The increasing availability of data provides opportunities to support evidence-based business decision-making. Students will be introduced to a range of data sources and analytical tools currently used in industry such as social networks and media. Students will also be asked to apply analytic models to create insight and from this insight develop ideas for further analysis.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant business analytics models.
Collate data and explain the implications of the findings on business operations and tactics.
Track and report industry trends.
Utilise data to make recommendations on insights and ideas for further analysis.
Identify and evaluate a range of data sources.

title: Building your Professional Profile
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to introduce students to the professional practice of communication and employment in the sub-disciplines of strategic communication, news and media and design and content creation. It is designed to provide a broad understanding of contemporary communication practice in a national and international context. Students will learn how to present themselves as a personal brand, how to begin developing professional networks and reputational concepts to inform the building of their professional profile and e-portfolio. This subject is one of four introductory subjects that build the theoretical and discipline specific skills essential for communication professionals.
learning_outcomes: Produce evidence of developing skills in academic learning and professional practice competencies and attitudes conducive to employment in the communication profession.
Plan and design an e-portfolio and digital identity as an emerging practitioner.
Identify and describe the key competencies required of communication professionals.
Analyse, create and reflect on the components parts of a digital identity.
Describe and explain current social, economic, political and technological issues shaping communication practice.

title: Business and Corporations Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines key Australian legal concepts and issues directly relevant to business operations. It covers the structure of the Australian legal system, sources of law, statutory interpretation, the court system and the doctrine of precedent. It then examines substantive areas of tort, contract, agency, and the difference between various types of business organisations before focusing on corporations law, including the way in which corporations are formed, rules regulating internal relationships within corporations, relationships with outsiders, the duties of directors and other officers, fundraising and the termination of corporations, with a particular focus on liquidation.
learning_outcomes: Anlayse the rules of statutory interpretation and the law relating to torts, contracts, property, agency, partnerships and corporations.
Distinguish between rules of law and exercise judgement in applying the law to complex legal problems.
Analyse matters so as to evaluate which court has jurisdiction and differentiate between courts in applying the doctrine of precedent .
Appraise and discuss the Australian and other legal systems.

title: Business Economics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the economist's way of thinking about the activities of individuals and institutions (both private and government) which determine the nature of our business and social environment. The subject presents, applies and assesses the key theoretical principles in microeconomics and macroeconomics that enable us to make sensible decisions in a complex world.
learning_outcomes: Apply economic concepts and principles to daily life activities.
Recognise and outline market related decisions in the context of the conditions of demand and supply.
Discuss the nature of market failure and the role of government intervention.
Describe assessments of the health of the economy as a whole.
Explain why government intervention in the economy may be necessary.
Explain the price and output decisions of a firm under different market structures.

title: Business Data Analytics and Storytelling
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Data and analytics can help decision makers in public, private and not-for-profit organisations transform operations, cut costs, improve efficiency, predict customer behaviour, enhance employee satisfaction, improve recruitment and employee-organisation fit, generate forecasts, and generally make informed strategic decisions. This subject teaches leaders and senior executives how to use analytics to make data-driven decisions for competitive advantage and how to communicate the findings to various stakeholders. Students will draw on a range of modern visual tools and interactive media to present a compelling narrative for action.
learning_outcomes: Individually or collaboratively synthesise and integrate diverse data sources and discuss implications for strategic business operations.
Evaluate ethical issues associated with data collection and usage.
Individually or collaboratively make recommendations to resolve business problems;and.
Individually or collaboratively utilise visual tools and interactive media to communicate and engage with diverse stakeholders.
Individually or collaboratively identify and evaluate a range of data sources.
Track and report industry trends.

title: Business Economics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the economist's way of thinking about the activities of individuals and institutions (both private and government) which determine the nature of our business and social environment. The subject presents, applies and assesses the key theoretical principles in Microeconomics and Macroeconomics that enable us to make sensible decisions in a complex world.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine and demonstrate why it might be necessary for government to intervene in the production of goods and services and in the distribution of income.
Identify and critically evaluate opportunities for specialisation and exchange.
Apply demand and supply analysis to make a range of market related decisions.
Examine critically the health of the economy as a whole through the analysis of major economic variables and advise on likely policy alternatives.
Explain and defend why it is important to understand the structure of the market in which a firm operates.
Make decisions that incorporate the relevant benefits and cost analysis.

title: Business Ethics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Ethical issues arising in business and professional life are addressed from the standpoint of western moral philosophy. Topics covered include the ethical limitations of the corporation under capitalism, appropriate conduct in the workplace, moral choices for employees, job discrimination, the crisis in the natural environment, social responsibility, and dilemmas facing professionals.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the various theories that underpins, values, morality and the main Western approaches to ethics.
Appraise how leadership and decision making impacts on corporate social responsibility including sustainability.
Assess and determine the impact of business and national cultures on ethical behaviour in organisations.
Critically examine the decision making process within business in light of recent ethical dilemmas, corportate scandals and government conduct.

title: Business Ethics a Global Perspective
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject students explore the nature of ethics within the context of the global economy. They will develop an understanding and explore ways of ethically responding to culturally diverse ways of conducting business. Major ethical theories are studied and applied to a range of business issues, including corporate social responsibility, ethics in the workplace, and discrimination. Environmental sustainability is considered from ethical, business and cultural perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Describe the issues and critique the debates associated with the concept of corporate social responsibility in a global business environment.
Distinguish different views of justice, and outline opposing arguments about justice and economic distribution.
Critically reflect on the effects of climate change, ecology and the environment in a global business context.
Critically reflect on their role as business professionals and how their future actions as business professionals can affect society in positive and negative ways.
Outline ethical theories in western moral philosophy and apply them in inter and intra cultural organisational contexts.
Resolve a range of real life ethical dilemmas.

title: Business Honours Dissertation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Students will carry out a supervised research project in an area that falls within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science approved fields of research; accounting, finance, economics, marketing or management. The student will be able to test his/her ability to use management theory and research techniques in a business environment.
learning_outcomes: Successfully design and complete a research project that involves the application of relevant theories and frameworks to the solution of a significant management problem or situation that falls within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science approved fields of research; accounting, finance, economics, marketing or management.

title: Business Honours Project/Dissertation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Students will carry out a supervised research project in an area that falls within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science approved fields of research; accounting, finance, economics, marketing or management. The student will be able to test his/her ability to use management theory and research techniques in a business environment. This subject is the first of BUS416 and BUS417.
learning_outcomes: Successfully design and complete a research project that involves the application of relevant theories and frameworks to the solution of a significant management problem or situation that falls within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences approved fields of research; accounting, finance, economics, marketing or management.

title: Business Organisations Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the difference between various types of business organisation before focusing on corporations law, including the way in which corporations are formed, rules regulating internal relationships within corporations, relationships with outsiders, the duties of directors and other officers, fundraising and the termination of corporations with a particular focus on liquidation
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles of good governance and a governance framework, including the rights and responsibilities of owners, investors, and those charged with governance including the concepts of disclosure and transparency.
Identify the different types of business organisation and the law regulating them.
Explain the characteristics of different business organisations.
Apply the law to legal problems.
Explain the rules of law regulating the internal relationship between the participants in business organisations and between the organisation and third parties.

title: Business Honours Project/Dissertation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Students will carry out a supervised research project in an area that falls within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science approved fields of research; accounting, finance, economics, marketing or management. The student will be able to test his/her ability to use management theory and research techniques in a business environment. This subject continues and completes the dissertation started in BUS416.
learning_outcomes: Successfully design and complete a research project that involves the application of relevant theories and frameworks to the solution of a significant management problem or situation that falls within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science approved fields of research; accounting, finance, economics, marketing or management.

title: Building Personal Resilience
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the concept of resilience. It will explore how resilience is different to recovery, and that there are multiple and sometimes unexpected pathways to resilience. Students will learn about models of stress, trauma, and coping, and factors that predict resilience. The subject highlights the importance of coping and positively adapting to stressful life experiences. Students will explore the three features from scientific resilience discourse: recovery, sustainability, and growth.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of recovery, sustainability, and growth in resilience.
Define the concept of resilience.
Critically evaluate models of resilience and the factors that may predict resilience.
Describe the different pathways to resilience.

title: Business Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines key Australian legal concepts and principles directly relevant to business operations and their legal underpinnings. It explores the structure of the Australian legal system, sources of law, principles of statutory interpretation, the court system and the doctrine of precedent. It then examines the law of negligence and substantive areas of contract and property law.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the law relating to data protection and privacy.
Compare and contrast the Australian legal system with other legal systems.
Synthesise knowledge of the doctrine of precedent with knowledge of the hierarchy of the courts at a state and federal level, to explain which court has jurisdiction in a particular matter.
Compare different methods of dispute resolution and evaluate their effectiveness.
Independently apply rules of statutory interpretation, including Latin maxims, common law approaches and the legislative provisions that apply at a state and federal level.
Describe the Australian legal system, including its history, development, and the current theoretical frameworks within which it and its institutions operate.
Investigate the different sources of Australian law in order to contrast these sources and explain their significance and interrelationships when applying them to legal problems.

Demonstrate knowledge of tort, contract, and property law by identifying the relevant issue(s) arising out of novel factual situations, stating the relevant legal principles, and explaining how these relate to the legal issue(s), in addition to suggesting potential remedies when providing a conclusion.
prerequisites: LAW112: Introduction to the Australian Legal System

title: Business Scenario Solutions
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Today's organisations operate in a market place where change occurs at a magnitude and duration that has not been seen before. The role of information, globalisation and the global digital economy now sees worldwide events quickly translated into our local economy. Business scenario planning is about implementing processes that allow businesses to source some certainty or predictability in an uncertain world. Scenario planning links with strategic management and involves developing differing scenarios; interpreting signals and then reframing these signals into the strategy and future plans of the business. Scenario planning covers all aspects of the business operations - people, finance, operations, stakeholders, customers, government, and looks at all signals large and small. This subject develops a framework for undertaking business scenario planning. It includes defining a business scenario, examining different planning methods used, identifying the principles of scenario planning, and reviewing how these principles link with business strategy.
learning_outcomes: Interpret market based signals and their likely impact on an organisation.
Utilise appropriate sources of data.
Apply theoretical models of forecasting to predict trends.
Critically analyse the impact of crisis conditions and develop responses to sudden market changes.
Justify decisions based on market data and make reasoned recommendations.

title: Business Transformation Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the complexities of managing changes in the rapidly evolving modern business landscape with emphasis on market and competitive analyses, emerging technologies, and effective digital leadership. Students will explore various aspects of business transformation, including technological advancements, process reengineering, organisational restructuring, and cultural shifts. The subject integrates theoretical frameworks with practical applications, preparing students to tackle real-world challenges and implement sustainable transformation strategies. Students will learn how to manage risk in the digital age, perform business analytics in a responsible and ethical manner, and identify and apply relevant emerging technologies to transform business processes.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically evaluate different technologies and strategies for effective risk management.
Interpret transformative business analytics outcomes, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.
Devise a range of strategies that facilitate digital transformation in various scenarios.
Apply and discuss fundamental concepts in business transformation management.

title: Business Strategy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In today's changing world, strategy is critical to organisational success. Business Strategy is a capstone subject examining theories and practices of strategic business management. It provides practical insight for approaching strategic issues by evaluating organisations' existing strategies and performance to create innovative strategies. The subject critically views a variety of perspectives of strategic management contexts and processes such as industry trends, business intelligence, strategic thinking and evaluating strategies. This subject is designed to enhance students' knowledge and capability to develop critical thinking, analytical skills and professional practice-oriented skills in the context of strategic business management.
learning_outcomes: Identify and understand contemporary theoretical concepts of strategic business management.
Create innovative strategies to improve organisation performance.
Assess industry issues and the impact on organisational strategies individually or collaboratively.
Critically reflect on and assess business strategies.
Critically analyse and apply strategic models and evaluate how they should act conjointly to achieve organisation's strategic aims and objectives individually or collaboratively.

title: Capstone Subject: Your Discipline, Your Region and the World
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The subject applies the principles of a capstone subject. It integrates prior knowledge and skills from the whole course into a cohesive framework for practice and further research. Students will be encouraged to apply their particular disciplinary knowledge to the subject's themes and also engage with other disciplinary perspectives. In this subject students are encouraged to interrogate and reflect upon the concepts of 'place' and 'region' and what these might mean for them and their specialised discipline. The subject will analyse the interaction between individual, regional and global spheres of influence and explore non-geographic notions of 'place' and 'region'. Accordingly, the subject will meaningfully engage with the university's ethos of 'Yindyamarra Winhanganha' - the wisdom of respectfully knowing how to live well in a world worth living in. It is advised that students take this subject only after completing a recognised specialisation or major sequence of subjects.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced research and writing skills to a given topic of enquiry.
Apply their particular disciplinary knowledge to the subject's content.
Communicate and engage effectively with peers and colleagues from various disciplines.
Critically reflect upon the concepts of 'place' or 'region' and the interaction between individual, regional and global spheres of influence.

title: Captive Reptilian Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the general principles of the management of reptiles in captivity. The general principles of housing, husbandry, nutrition, diet, breeding, and health and disease will be examined for each of the reptilian groups. These studies will lead into more specialised studies of selected groups including enrichment, captive breeding for conservation including reintroduction case studies, and the care and rehabilitation of injured reptiles.
learning_outcomes: Have an understanding of the general breeding requirements of captive reptiles, and for a specific species, the detailed breeding requirements.
Have an appreciation of the importance of enrichment in keeping captive reptiles, and for a specific species, design appropriate enrichment protocols.
Describe the general principles of housing and husbandry in keeping captive reptiles, and in detail, the requirements of a specific species or group.
Have an understanding of health and disease issues in keeping captive reptiles, and for a specific species, a detailed understanding of these issues.
Have an understanding of the importance of appropriate methods of keeping records, including breeding records.
Have an understanding of the role of keeping reptiles in captivity in conservation.
Have reviewed in detail, at least one reptilian reintroduction study.
Have an understanding of the general principles/protocols in the care and rehabilitation of injured reptiles.
Describe the specialised management requirements for a specific species.

title: Cardiac Critical Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students’ previous education and experience to advance the knowledge and skills needed to provide critical care paramedicine for cardiac emergencies across the lifespan. Students will further develop their ability to integrate assessment and diagnostic data, and knowledge of relevant anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, and pharmacology to apply evidence-informed practice to propose critical care paramedicine treatment plans. To foster the professional attributes required in critical care paramedicine, students will integrate leadership strategies and communication skills as part of managing cardiac emergencies.
learning_outcomes: Interpret clinical data derived from advanced patient diagnostics, assessment and history taking to inform clinical decision-making for cardiac emergencies across the life span.
Integrate advanced knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology to critical care paramedic management of cardiac emergencies.
Formulate evidence-informed critical care paramedic treatment plans for cardiac emergencies across the life span.
Integrate leadership skills, including communication in a team while managing cardiac emergencies.

title: Career Skills in Focus
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to the broad range of skills and knowledge students require to move forward with their career in business. It allows students to focus on transferable skills and career planning. This subject has a particular emphasis on enhancing knowledge related to working in a professional business environment, and promoting an in-depth understanding of the value of workplace learning and lifelong learning. Students will carry out an audit on their current transferable skills, and reflect on how they can expand their knowledge and skills in preparation for advancing their career.
learning_outcomes: Determine key personal and transferable skills and requirements, and create an action plan for transferable skill development; and
Describe the relationship between workplace learning, lifelong learning, career development and life balance, and identify personal impacts;
Reflect on personal career and life choices, and discuss the factors influencing potential future direction.

title: Case Management
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Case management is designed to provide advocacy, support and services to vulnerable people and communities. This subject examines case management and its increasing application to diverse and interdisciplinary human service and health settings and organisations. The origins and development of case management models are examined and a model applicable across many fields of practice is applied. Students examine case management systems, their underlying ethos, theory, functions, structures and practices and apply this knowledge within a case study approach.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the theoretical underpinnings of the functions of the case management model.
Identify and discuss case management systems within agency and community contexts, including provider driven vs client driven case management practices.
Demonstrate an understanding of several models of case management with a specific focus on a designated human services model.
Apply the designated model of case management to a simulated situation via a case study.
Explain case management.
Apply case management theory to practice including analysis of skills and tensions in case management practice.

title: Cartography
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on students' existing GIS abilities by introducing them to techniques for the mapping presentation of spatial, numerical and table-based data in order to maximise their effectiveness and simplify their interpretation. Students will learn how to design visualisations of information, taking into account the problems of human perception, variations in audience type, and the media or presentation environment selected including when working with and mapping Indigenous Australian data and knowledges. They will learn how to classify spatial and non-spatial, multi-dimensional, discrete and continuous data to elicit the most information. Dynamic methods such as animation, interactive atlases and data exploration tools will also be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Apply and describe methods of symbolisation, map elements and typography.
Critically evaluate colonial impacts on mapping and cartography, especially in relation to Indigenous Australian knowledge systems.
Apply and describe methods of thematic and statistical map classification.
Demonstrate a professional understanding of ethical considerations when working with Indigenous Australian data and data sovereignty in cartography.
Produce and critically evaluate univariate and bivariate analysis maps.
Explain how maps can used to manipulate public understanding of geospatial information.
Apply and describe web publishing methods for cartography.
Compare map projection characteristics and apply these appropriately in cartographic outputs.

title: Caring in Nursing
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the Caring Science principles and examine ways in which they can be linked to the Clinical Reasoning Cycle and applied to the practice of registered nurses. It will also focus on concepts such as transpersonal care, emancipatory intent and creative problem-solving in diverse settings.
learning_outcomes: Explain how Caring Science principles can be linked to the Clinical Reasoning Cycle and applied to practice in diverse settings.
Demonstrate understanding of Caring Science principles.
Demonstrate knowledge of the application of value assumptions in caring moments.
Explain how transpersonal care principles can be applied to patient care.

title: Cartography
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on students' existing GIS abilities by introducing them to techniques for the mapping presentation of spatial, numerical and table-based data in order to maximise their effectiveness and simplify their interpretation. Students will learn how to design visualisations of information, taking into account the problems of human perception, variations in audience type, and the media or presentation environment selected including when working with and mapping Indigenous Australian data and knowledges. They will learn how to classify spatial and non-spatial, multi-dimensional, discrete and continuous data to elicit the most information. Dynamic methods such as animation, interactive atlases and data exploration tools will also be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Compare map projections characteristics and its appropriate use in cartographic outputs.
Identify, apply and justify effective visual communication methods using multiple spatial datasets in cartographic outputs.
Describe and apply methods of symbolisation, map elements and typography.
Describe and apply methods of thematic and statistical map classification.
Explain how maps can used to manipulate public understanding of geospatial information.
Evaluate colonial impacts on mapping and cartography, especially in relation to Indigenous Australian knowledge systems.
Demonstrate a professional understanding of ethical considerations when working with Indigenous Australian data and data sovereignty in cartography.

title: Case Management
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Case management is designed to provide advocacy, support and services to vulnerable people and communities. This subject examines a contemporary paradigm of case management and its increasing application to diverse and interdisciplinary human service and health settings and organisations. The origins and development of case management models are examined and a generic model that is applicable across many fields of practice is applied. Through a case study approach students differentiate and critically evaluate case management systems, their underlying ethos, theory, functions, structures and practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to apply the generic model of case management to a simulated situation via a case study.
Demonstrate critical thinking in application of case management theory to practice including analysis of skills and tensions within case management practice.
Define case management and compare different models and contexts.
Critique case management systems within agency and community contexts, including provider driven vs client driven case management practices.
Articulate the theoretical underpinnings of the functions of the case management model.
Demonstrate critical analysis of key models of case management with specific focus on a generic model.

title: Case Management and Coordinated Care in Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the context of case management practice. The broad spectrum of functions of case management, the skills required for client assessments and collaborative decision making. It will consider a range of opportunities and challenges experienced when providing person-centred care within diverse contexts including understanding concepts of vulnerability, living with a disability, culture, socioeconomic and political concerns and the geographic factors. Students will reflect on the application of practice during all stages of case management intervention. Consideration will be given to developing a culturally competent workforce that increases the capacity of clinicians or workers to engage authentically with Indigenous Australian peoples across the lifespan in various health care and practice settings.
learning_outcomes: Develop innovative and advanced methods of planning, implementing and evaluating interdisciplinary approaches to case management.

Critically analyse the complexities that impact on person-centred care in the context of case management and demonstrate advanced skills required to comprehensively assess the needs of patients/clients.
Critique their own values and beliefs in relation to case management and evaluate its impact on practice.
Identify and apply theoretical frameworks that inform case management practice.
Integrate and apply Indigenous Australian cultural competence to practice.
Apply professional behaviours relating to global citizenship to work effectively in transcultural contexts.

title: Certificate IV TAE40110/40116
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is applicable for students who have completed a Certificate IV in Training & Assessment (TAE40110 or TAE40116) and are awarded credit in the Bachelor of Adult and Vocational Education (Articulated Set) and the Master of Adult and Vocational Education (Articulated Set).

title: Challenges of Global Sustainable Development
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the concepts and underlying principles of global sustainable development. Students investigate the issues raised in the application of sustainable principles by exploring real situations and case studies. A key focus is on the importance of the knowledges and understandings of the Indigenous Peoples of Australia in both historical and contemporary environmental management. On completion students are able to critically appraise the lessons learned from the experience of implementing sustainable development in a global context.
learning_outcomes: Explain the terminology, concepts, principles and theory associated with global sustainable development.
Critically appraise the lessons learned from the experience of implementing sustainable development in their profession, the issues raised, and the proposed effective solutions.
Discuss the key challenges associated with implementing sustainable development in a global context.
Critically reflect on and discuss ideas on how the knowledge and cultural property of Indigenous Australians relate to global sustainable development.
Critique and assess factors influencing the application of tools for sustainability in real situations.
Recognise a range of theories and concepts available for minimising our impact on the environment and society and how these might be applied to achieve sustainability.

title: Chemical Fundamentals
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the core principles of chemistry, providing a foundation in the language of the discipline, modern theories of atomic structure, and the principles of chemical bonding that underpin the formation of molecules. Students will examine how different types of bonding influence molecular properties and how these, in turn, determine the behaviour of bulk matter, including chemical reactions, the characteristics of gases, liquids and solids, chemical equilibrium, and the behaviour of acids and bases. In addition, students will develop practical skills in laboratory techniques, chemical safety, and the use of standard analytical equipment essential for chemical investigation.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of chemical equilibrium and carry out basic calculations.
Describe the states of matter in terms of chemical bonding and molecular behaviour that account for observed macroscopic properties.
Apply appropriate practical techniques and be familiar with equipment used to understand chemical investigations.
Work safely in a laboratory, generate, record and interpret data, and calculate quantities of matter in solutions.
Use the language and nomenclature of chemistry.
Name and identify the major classes of organic compounds as a large, diverse and important class of covalent compounds necessary to life/plant processes.
Apply fundamental physical laws to chemical systems and perform relevant calculations.
Describe the properties and behaviour of acids and bases and perform basic calculations.
prerequisites: CHM102: Chemistry for Dental and Veterinary Sciences

title: Chemical Safety and Laboratory Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: A thorough knowledge of laboratory safety is essential for anyone who either works directly in a laboratory or has Work, Health and Safety (WHS) responsibility for others. In this subject, students will learn essential information regarding statutory regulations governing health and safety, laboratory design and accreditation, hazard identification and managing, waste minimisation and disposal, and chemical storage. Excellent communication skills are an industry expectation and this subject reinforces those skills with an emphasis on report writing and presentation of written/oral submissions.
learning_outcomes: Conduct a laboratory chemical health and safety audit on a chemical laboratory and prepare a safety audit report.
Implement chemical waste minimisation programs, considering the problems associated with waste disposal.
Distinguish the ways by which chemicals may pose a hazard, and apply potential actions and controls of incompatible chemicals.
Recall and apply different measurements of chemical toxicity, monitor various chemical hazards and complete hazardous chemical risk assessment and laboratory risk assessment.
Present information, articulate arguments and conclusions, in a variety of modes, to diverse audiences, and for a range of purposes.
Demonstrate capacity and ability to work safely in a laboratory and demonstrate competence in using equipment for monitoring laboratory safety.
prerequisites: CHM102: Chemistry for Dental and Veterinary Sciences

title: Chemistry 1A
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers many of the fundamental principles of chemistry and introduces students to the language of chemistry, current theories on the nature of atoms, and the principles of bonding to form molecules. Students will explore the relationships between bonding and the properties of molecules, and relate those to the behaviour of bulk matter including: chemical reactions; the properties of gases, liquids and solids; chemical equilibrium; and the behaviour of acids and bases. Students will also develop knowledge and skills in laboratory and chemical safety, as well as a broad range of laboratory techniques and equipment used for chemical investigations.
learning_outcomes: Explain states of matter with respect to bonding and associated molecular behaviour that accounts for observed macroscopic properties.
Apply the laws of equilibrium and perform related calculations.
Apply the language of chemistry.
Apply appropriate practical techniques and be familiar with equipment used to conduct chemical investigations.
Describe relevant acids and bases and perform related calculations.
Work safely in a laboratory, generate, record and interpret data, and calculate quantities of matter in solutions.
Apply known physical laws and perform related calculations.

title: Chemistry 1A
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers many of the fundamental principles of chemistry and introduces students to the language of chemistry, current theories on the nature of atoms, and the principles of bonding to form molecules. Students will explore the relationships between bonding and the properties of molecules, and relate those to the behaviour of bulk matter including: chemical reactions; the properties of gases, liquids and solids; chemical equilibrium; and the behaviour of acids and bases. Students will also develop knowledge and skills in laboratory and chemical safety, as well as a broad range of laboratory techniques and equipment used for chemical investigations.
learning_outcomes: Describe relevant acids and bases and perform related calculations.
Apply the laws of equilibrium and perform related calculations.
Apply the language of chemistry.
Work safely in a laboratory, generate, record and interpret data, and calculate quantities of matter in solutions.
Explain states of matter with respect to bonding and associated molecular behaviour that accounts for observed macroscopic properties.
Apply known physical laws and perform related calculations.
Apply appropriate practical techniques and be familiar with equipment used to conduct chemical investigations.

title: Chemistry 1B
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the fundamental language and concepts of chemistry presented in Chemistry 1A. Students will learn about redox reactions—a key chemical process with widespread applications—and organic chemistry—the chemistry of the building blocks of life. Students will be introduced to the fundamental driving forces for all chemical transformations through the study of thermodynamics and kinetics.
