Students will continue to develop knowledge and skills in laboratory and chemical safety, as well as a broad range of laboratory techniques and equipment used for chemical investigations. This subject prepares students for later subjects in biochemistry, physiology, pharmacology, and their applications in wine, viticultural, animal, and medical sciences.
learning_outcomes: Balance redox equations, use the Nernst Equation, and calculate Gibbs free energies and equilibrium constants from electrochemical data.

Classify and name the various types of organic compounds, the type of bonding within them, and the various forms of isomerism, and apply a selected range of standard chemical transformations to common organic functional groups.
Work safely in a laboratory, generate, record and interpret data, and calculate quantities of matter in solutions.
Explain the catenation ability of the element carbon, the nature of covalent molecular compounds, and their chemical properties.
Explain the fundamentals of chemical kinetics and determine rate equations from kinetic data.
Apply appropriate practical techniques and use standard laboratory equipment competently to conduct chemical investigations.
Apply the three laws of thermodynamics to solve thermodynamic calculations.

title: Chemistry for Medical Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be introduced to current theories of the nature of atoms, molecules and bonding to explain the behaviour of bulk matter. Students will apply their mathematical skills with respect to chemical relationships and processes. This subject provides foundational knowledge for medical science, including clinical chemistry.
learning_outcomes: Calculate equilibrium relationships.
Calculate chemical amounts of matter.
Describe relevant acids and bases and solve calculations.
Identify and calculate quantities of matter in solutions.
Use and apply the language of chemistry.
Describe molecular behaviour of matter that explains observed macroscopic properties.
Describe states of matter with respect to bonding.
Apply known physical laws and solve related calculations.
prerequisites: BMS132: Medical Science Communications and Methods

title: Chest Image Interpretation
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to develop fundamental image interpretation knowledge and skills for conventional thoracic radiographic images using a systematic approach. Image interpretations will be correlated with relevant clinical history and informed by evidence based practice. The role and appropriateness of imaging will be considered holistically within the context of the patient's care pathway and client centred care. The image interpretation knowledge and skills developed within this subject will directly compliment current and future clinical practice for practitioners routinely using conventional thoracic radiographic images.
learning_outcomes: Perform interpretations of conventional thoracic x-rays using a systematic approach to accurately describe normal, variant and abnormal radiographic appearances correlating with the clinical history.
Apply clinical reasoning to identify clinical problems and formulate potential solutions to inform patient management.
Critically reflect on individual learning needs to inform professional practice.
Critically evaluate and justify the efficacy of conventional imaging correlating with the clinical history, using evidence based practice and with consideration of client centred care.
Recognise, justify and apply ethical, legislative and regulatory principles to communicate information related to significant findings.
Critically analyse image quality and radiographic positioning when reviewing conventional thoracic radiographic images.
prerequisites: MRS574: Chest And Abdomen Image Interpretation

title: Chemistry for Dental and Veterinary Sciences
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide foundational knowledge and skills in chemistry as scaffolding for further studies in many fields relevant to animal, dental and veterinary sciences including, but not limited to, biochemistry and physiology. Current theories of the nature of atoms, molecules and bonding, to explain the behaviour of bulk matter, will be investigated. Topics include thermodynamics; kinetics; gases; an introduction to organic chemistry and organic functional group chemistry, with specific applications. A practical component will enhance understanding of theoretical concepts as well as develop problem solving abilities.
learning_outcomes: Develop an awareness of the catenation ability of the element carbon, the nature of covalent molecular compounds, and of their chemical properties and nomenclature.
Accurately describe molecular behaviour of matter that explains observed macroscopic properties.
Understand the three laws of thermodynamics and be able to perform thermodynamic calculations.
Understand equilibrium and perform calculations.
Understand acids and bases and perform calculations.
Describe states of matter with respect to bonding.
Understand the fundamentals of kinetics and be able to determine rate equations from kinetic data.
Recognise the various classes of organic compounds, the type of bonding within them, the various forms of isomerism, and some of the typical industrial applications made of organic substances.
Calculate chemical amounts of matter.
Be familiar with a selected range of standard chemical transformations between common organic functional groups.
Understand the language of chemistry.

title: Child Abuse and Child Protection
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a core knowledge base about the definition, identification and consequences of all types of child maltreatment. It also provides information on the legal, organisational and professional responsibilities placed upon professionals to respond to such maltreatment. This is an introductory subject for undergraduate students about child abuse and child protection. The subject deals with a major social problem, child abuse, and the complex and often controversial policy and community response to that problem, child protection. The subject will explore how these matters are socially constructed in an Australian context. Students should be aware that the content of this subject deals with case studies, and descriptive content about how children are abused and the consequences of that for the child and family and professionals that may be confronting and/or upsetting. The subject must not be used as an avenue for investigating personal experiences of abuse or child protection practices.
learning_outcomes: Understand the significance of child maltreatment as a social problem in Australia and elsewhere.
Demonstrate understanding of the complexity of child protection responses and the significance of inter-disciplinary processes in giving effect to those responses.
Demonstrate understanding of the significant contextual aspects of child maltreatment including; poverty, social displacement and disadvantage, violence, authority and power.

Articulate the common operational definitions of physical, emotional/psychological, sexual abuse and neglect of children including the major physical, social and behavioural indicators of these types of maltreatment.
Articulate the role and responsibilities of different professional groups in the identification of and response to child maltreatment as defined by law and policy.
Demonstrate understanding of the significant effects of a child's experience of maltreatment in terms of their health, education, and wellbeing.

title: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the foundational aspects of child and adolescent development, covering physical, socio-emotional, and intellectual growth. Students will engage with contemporary research and explore the ways these major developmental domains interact with each other and their surrounding context to shape learning and development. Key theories—including cognitive, constructivist, behavioral, and ecological perspectives—will be examined and applied to educational settings. Additionally, students will examine the factors influencing academic achievement in primary and secondary education, addressing common developmental challenges and high-incidence disorders. Throughout, students will consider the implications of these topics for classroom teaching and learning, with an emphasis on evidence-based strategies to support effective pedagogical practice across various stages of development.
learning_outcomes: Apply major theories of learning and development and explain how they apply to effective pedagogical practice in primary and secondary school contexts to address the needs of diverse learners.

Articulate a range of evidence-based strategies that teachers can employ to address various issues and challenges faced by children and adolescents, including strategies tailored to meet the learning needs of diverse learners.
Discuss a range of high incidence child and adolescent disorders and explain their causes using the bio-psycho-social model.
Explain the role of families, culture and community in child and adolescent development and evaluate a broad range of strategies to engage learners and their families in the learning process.
Discuss the major physical, socio-emotional and cognitive changes that occur during childhood and adolescence.
Identify underlying social and pedagogical implications of ICT for education.
Interpret research into how students learn and explain the implications for teaching and learning that is culturally and linguistically appropriate for diverse learners.
prerequisites: EPT125: Child Development: Foundation to Year 6

title: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the foundational aspects of child and adolescent development, covering physical, socio-emotional, and intellectual growth. Students will engage with contemporary research and explore the ways these major developmental domains interact with each other and their surrounding context to shape learning and development. Key theories—including cognitive, constructivist, behavioral, and ecological perspectives—will be examined and applied to educational settings. Additionally, students will examine the factors influencing academic achievement in primary and secondary education, addressing common developmental challenges and high-incidence disorders. Throughout, students will consider the implications of these topics for classroom teaching and learning, with an emphasis on evidence-based strategies to support effective pedagogical practice across various stages of development.
learning_outcomes: Analyse major theories of learning and development and explain how they apply to effective pedagogical practice in primary and secondary school contexts to address the needs of diverse learners.
Analyse the role of families, culture and community in child and adolescent development and evaluate a broad range of strategies to engage learners and their families in the learning process.
Evaluate underlying social and pedagogical implications of ICT for education.

Identify and analyse a range of evidence-based strategies that teachers can employ to address various issues and challenges faced by children and adolescents, including strategies tailored to meet the needs of diverse learners.
Apply research into how students learn and explain the implications for teaching and learning that is culturally and linguistically appropriate for diverse learners.
Evaluate a range of high incidence child and adolescent disorders and explain their causes using the bio-psycho-social model.
Interpret the major physical, socio-emotional and cognitive changes that occur during childhood and adolescence.
prerequisites: EED216: Child Development: The Primary Years

title: Child and Adolescent Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development of children and adolescents. Influences on such developmental processes from family, school, and society are examined using psychological theory. Students should note that this subject does not contribute to an APAC (Australian Psychology Accreditation Council) accredited sequence in psychology.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain issues related to the physical, cognitive, emotional, and social development of children and adolescents, including those who come from adverse circumstances
Explain physical, cognitive, emotional, and social development of children and adolescents
Reflect on and articulate how knowledge of child and adolescent development informs future practice in human service contexts.
Apply theoretical and evidence-based information on child and adolescent psychology to human service contexts
Explain the influence of different contexts including family, school, and society on the development of children and adolescents

title: Child Assessment
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to the psychological assessment of children and adolescents. It is designed to assist students to develop theoretical knowledge and practical skills in the assessment of clients. Students will become familiar with the current theoretical and empirical foundations of child psychological assessment, and the application of these theories and research findings to the development of empirically-based assessment practice. Contemporary practice in the assessment of cognition, behaviour, emotions, and other psychological constructs will be explored, and popular psychological measures of these functions will be critically evaluated. Students will be instructed in the integration of assessment data into clinically-useful reports. Different approaches to psychological assessment will be compared and evaluated. Ethical and professional issues in psychological assessment will be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Administer, score and interpret the results of major measures of child and adult intelligence, achievement and other cognitive domains.
Select assessment methods and measures appropriate to the needs of the client.
Demonstrate knowledge of the theoretical and empirical foundations of psychological assessment.
Effectively interpret and communicate the results of a psychological assessment.
Critically evaluate psychological tests and child and parent questionnaires.
Identify ethical issues in the psychological assessment of children and adolescents.

title: Child Development: The Early Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn about a range of theories of child development and how they can be applied to understand children’s development and learning. This includes the study of prenatal, brain, physical, cognitive, language, moral, social and emotional development, in infants, toddlers and pre-school children. Theories of development and child observations will be used to extend understandings of children's growth and development. Students will use the Early Years Learning Framework (EYLF), with specific reference to the five learning outcomes for children from birth to 5 years. They will apply these through the lens of child development theories to analyse and interpret the growth and progress of children from birth to five years old.
learning_outcomes: Analyse early childhood scenarios through multiple theories of development.
Apply the Early Years Learning Framework when analysing the development of children aged birth to five years.
Discuss major theories of development relevant to children aged birth to five years.
Describe the major physical, socio-emotional and cognitive changes that occur between birth and five years.
Explain the role of the child, families, peers and society in child development.

title: Child Development: The Primary Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the major theories of physical, socio-emotional and intellectual development of primary school aged children. Students draw on contemporary research to study how individual, social-cultural and environmental factors interact to influence children's development across these domains. Implications for learning and well-being are emphasised. Students will explore factors related to high incidence disorders of childhood and the implications for practice. Current developmental and educational research is applied in considering the implications for classroom teaching and learning in contemporary classrooms.
learning_outcomes: Explain underlying social and pedagogical implications of ICT for primary school education.
Interpret research into how students learn and explain the implications for teaching and learning that is culturally and linguistically appropriate for diverse learners
Discuss the major physical, socio-emotional and cognitive changes that occur during childhood.
Discuss a range of high incidence child disorders using the bio-psycho-social model and the implications for teaching and learning.
Apply major theories of learning and development to children in the primary school context.
Describe a range of evidence-based strategies teachers can use to address childhood issues and concerns.
Explain the role of families, carers and peers in child development and explain the broad range of strategies to engage them in the learning process.
prerequisites: EPT125: Child Development: Foundation to Year 6
EED215: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development
EED422: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development

title: Child Health Care and Promotion
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides opportunity for students, as professionals working in multidisciplinary environments, to explore the promotion and maintenance of health and wellbeing for children to ensure they reach their potential. Students will interrogate evidence-informed practices and frameworks to meet the healthcare needs of children with illness, injuries, disabilities, and those affected by maltreatment. Child healthcare will be considered across global, national and local healthcare contexts with particular attention to rural settings. Students will explore a range of multidisciplinary/interdisciplinary frameworks for care; theories and strategies for optimising growth and development; theories and strategies to acknowledge the rights of the child and child safety. Students will extend their existing professional knowledge and experience to include the health care of First Nations children and their children in the first two years of life.
learning_outcomes: critically analyse current issues that affect the health and wellbeing of children globally, nationally and locally;
compare and contrast evidence-informed strategies for promoting and maintaining child health and wellbeing at individual, family and community levels;

analyse and acknowledge the impact of colonisation on the health and wellbeing of First Nations children and families and identify strategies to address the health inequities experienced by First Nations children and families; and
apply the International Convention on the Rights of the Child to professional roles including responsibilities for keeping children safe from maltreatment;
apply evidence-informed frameworks, theories, and practices to enable children to reach their potential for growth and development;
critically evaluate their role in the interdisciplinary context of promoting and maintaining children's health.
critically analyse the role of the family in child wellbeing;
prerequisites: NRS325: Child Health Care and Promotion

title: Child Health Care and Promotion
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the opportunity for students, as professionals working in multidisciplinary environments to explore the promotion and maintenance of health and wellbeing for children to ensure that they reach their potential. Students will review and critique evidence-informed practices and frameworks to meet the healthcare needs of children with illness, injuries, disabilities, and those affected by maltreatment. Child healthcare will be considered across global, national and local healthcare contexts. Students will explore a range of multidisciplinary/interdisciplinary frameworks for care; theories and strategies for optimising growth and development; theories and strategies to acknowledge the rights of the child and child safety. learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast evidence-informed strategies for promoting and maintaining child health and well-being at individual, family and community levels.

Discuss and acknowledge the impact of colonisation on the health and well-being of First Nations children and families and identify strategies to address the health inequities experienced by First Nations children and families.

Apply the International Convention of the Rights of the Child to professional roles including responsibilities for keeping children safe from maltreatment.
prerequisites: NRS528: Child Health Care and Promotion

title: Child Interventions 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students' knowledge of complex internalising and externalising disorders in children and adolescents. Students will examine the diagnostic classification, epidemiology and aetiology of a range of complex conditions, including traumatic stress disorders, eating disorders, psychosis and sleep disorders. The assessment, diagnosis and formulation of complex disorders will be discussed, and advanced techniques for treating these conditions will be introduced and evaluated. Consideration of the unique challenges of specific populations and strategies to work in different ways with some of these groups will also be included.
learning_outcomes: Develop and implement cognitive-behavioural interventions for complex emotional and behavioural disorders.
Critically evaluate research concerning the efficacy of psychological therapies for these problems.
Identify the characteristics of a range of complex emotional and behavioural disorders in childhood and adolescence.
Incorporate information from multiple assessment methods into detailed case formulations.

title: Child Interventions 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the nature, assessment and treatment of psychological disorders in children and adolescents. Students will examine the diagnostic classification, epidemiology and aetiology of common psychological problems, including anxiety disorders, behaviour disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder and related conditions, mood disorders and suicidality. The theoretical and empirical foundations of a range of cognitive and behavioural techniques will be discussed, along with a number of major conceptual and practical issues in the treatment of psychological disorders in childhood and adolescence.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate research concerning the efficacy of psychological therapies with children and adolescents.
Identify the characteristics of the common emotional and behavioural disorders in childhood and adolescence.
Develop and implement cognitive-behavioural interventions for a range of emotional and behavioural disorders.
Employ reliable and valid methods of assessing children and adolescents with psychological disorders.

title: Child Safety: Awareness and Mandatory Reporting of Child Sexual Assault and Abuse
school: School
syllabus_overview: This training module fulfils key recommendation 62f of the Final Report into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (CSA). The module will prepare Charles Sturt students and graduates entering child-related professions to understand their responsibilities as mandatory reporters. The course will familiarise participants with policy requirements for reporting within a reflexive framework that enables them to understand their roles in the hierarchy of mandatory reporting. On completion of this training participants will have an increased awareness of the significance of mandatory reporting contextualised for current or future professional roles.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on their skills and dispositions as they relate to mandatory reporting of CSA.
Examine the diverse contexts within which assessments and reporting of CSA occur.
Understand patterns of abuse and identify those that are potential indicators of CSA.
Review legislative requirements for mandatory reporting of CSA.

title: Child, Family and Community: EC Contexts
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will use a strengths based approach to explore educationally challenging and supportive environments for young children. It explores concepts such as resilience and risk through an ecological perspective which focuses on the interaction between context and the individual. Strengths based approaches recognise strengths as well as the challenges faced by people in families and communities. It also draws on social justice principles to support self determined goals as the basis for effective change. The subject recognises the pivotal role of quality early childhood education to the wellbeing of children, families and communities.
learning_outcomes: Focus on the application of strengths approaches to the educational workplaces and to the community settings in which they are working.
Understand the development and implementation of strengths based approaches to working in early childhood education.
Identify, develop and justify an appropriate range of solutions based, resilience raising strategies to identify and address risks affecting children, families and communities.
Understand and critically analyse the use of a strengths approach and an ecological theoretical perspective when working in early childhood contexts.

Develop ability to identify, and cater for, the strengths and needs of children and families, including children from rural and remote, low SES and Indigenous communities; culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds; and children with special and complex support needs.
Identify social justice issues and challenges surrounding early childhood contexts that affect the wellbeing of children, families and communities.

title: Christian Chaplaincy in Context
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the role and function of the Chaplain in institutional and workplace settings; the development of a theological framework for chaplaincy; exploration of professional and personal issues and their bearing upon ethical practice; the goals and tasks of the chaplain; and the challenging issues that arise in the chaplaincy context. In addition, this subject introduces students to critical reflection on their own experience of being a Religious Practitioner in their chosen field of specialisation, and it integrates theological reflection with theory, professional issues, vocational observations and professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on their own experiences of being a Religious Practitioner in their chosen field of specialisation.
Articulate a well-developed theology of workplace chaplaincy.
Evaluate critically professional issues in chaplaincy.
Integrate and apply pastoral care theory with the function and role of the chaplain.
Reflect critically on the role and function of the chaplain in institutional and workplace settings.
Demonstrate skill in analysis of their strengths and growth areas as a Religious Practitioner in their chosen field.
Exhibit an in-depth understanding of the role of the chaplain in diverse contexts, and the application of that understanding to the practice of the ministerial profession.

title: Children and Family in Theological Perspective
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject looks at two important and surprisingly neglected themes in theology, namely, children and human family and relationships, from a theological perspective. In light of the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Sexual Abuse, it examines the place of children, child development, child abuse and its impact, and the response of denominations to the Royal Commission findings. It also considers the resources that Scripture, Trinitarian theology and ecclesiology offer.
learning_outcomes: Articulate key features of childhood and family in contemporary multicultural society and to develop relevant pastoral and ministerial strategies.
Analyse and reflect on the causes and effects of institutional abuse and to apply these findings to church and community institutions.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the theology of children and family across the spectrum of Christian thought and practice.
Articulate the effects of child abuse on individuals, families and institutions.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.

title: Christian Ethics
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to engage with work by prominent Christian ethicists. In particular, students will engage this material with a view to pressing contemporary ethical challenges in Australia and elsewhere. In addition, students will engage with and reflect upon material from a range of different theological perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on the relationship between texts in Christian ethics and their diverse historical and theological contexts.
Engage critically with and assess some major texts in Christian ethics.
Demonstrate research and writing skills appropriate for theological study at the Masters level.
Identify and discuss critically the diverse positions and views in contemporary Christian ethics.
Begin showing the relevance of Christian ethical thinking for understanding and responding to pressing challenges.

title: Christian Education
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores a range of approaches to Christian education and the philosophical, psychological, theological, ethical and biblical ideas upon which they depend.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Articulate an informed theological position in relation to more than one model of Christian education.
Discuss critically the role of the Christian educator as mentor, teacher, advocate and disciple.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the significance of faith development theory for Christian education.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of a variety of approaches to Christian education.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of ways of integrating and contextualising models of Christian education.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the significance of Christian education for the life and ministry of the Christian community.

title: Christian Ministry
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject students explore the practice and theory of Christian ministry, both lay and ordained. The church engages in a range of ministries within the church and in the wider community. The context of contemporary ministry includes awareness of heightened public standards, cultural context, issues of justice, and the status of churches within society. While students bring a range of experiences to the subject, they will be challenged to develop their understanding in light of changed expectations in the community, as well as developments in the theology and practice of ministry.
learning_outcomes: Critique ministry practice in light of contemporary awareness of issues of abuse, violence, coercion, power.
Analyse and critically evaluate the range of ministries practised by the church in its ministries of pastoral care, Christian education, social justice, worship and evangelism.
Articulate an understanding of the partnership between lay and ordained in ministry, including an understanding of the ethics of ministry.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the principles and practices of Christian Ministry (lay and ordained), including an understanding of models of leadership and spirituality appropriate to Christian ministry.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Analyse critically and articulate new models of ministry available to the Christian church in a changing world.

title: Christian Spirituality
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the nature and history of Christian spirituality within the context of contemporary interest in spirituality. It focuses particularly on Western spiritual traditions, including the desert fathers and mothers, the monastic and mendicant traditions, Reformation spiritualities and mystical traditions. Orthodox and Pentecostal spiritualities are considered briefly. The subject addresses questions concerning the relationship between Christian spirituality and issues relating to justice, ecology, culture and interfaith understanding. It also requires students to engage with and to reflect upon a range of Christian spiritual disciplines or practices.
learning_outcomes: Identify major elements in the history of Christian spiritual traditions.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding and critical appreciation of one strand of the Christian spiritual tradition.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.

Demonstrate an appreciation of the significance of the relationship between Christian spirituality and a range of contemporary issues, including justice, ecology, culture and interfaith understanding.
Reflect critically on a range of Christian spiritual disciplines or practices in the context of their own spirituality and practice.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the concept of specifically Christian spirituality.

title: Christian Worship
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the history and practice of worship across a variety of Christian traditions, including contemporary and blended worship. The subject centres on the effects and interrelationships of rites, symbols, words, music, gesture and space in facilitating worship. Key issues considered include liturgical forms, symbol, language, music, architecture and mission. In the context of human ritual activity, the importance of worship in the formation of Christian identity is analysed, including the relationship of worship to questions of power and abuse.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and discuss critically the nature of Christian worship in the context of human ritual activity.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of particular forms in worship across the wider Christian tradition, including blended and contemporary forms.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the effect of form, language, space, body and music on the experience of worship.
Discuss the relationship between worship, mission, identity and pastoral care, including the relationship of worship to questions of power and abuse.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the origins of Christian worship.

title: Christianity in Australian History
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the history of Christianity in Australia from 1788 to the present. Drawing upon historical and sociological studies of the Christian churches in Australia, this subject considers the distinctives of immigrant religious traditions and the effects on churches of drought, pluralism, economic depression, two world wars, post-war immigration and exposure to American culture. The subject also investigates interaction between Christianity and Indigenous peoples, and the engagement of the churches in education, welfare, intellectual and cultural life, and politics. That engagement is further considered within the framework of contemporary historical and theological discussion of mission in a post-Christendom context.
learning_outcomes: Review and articulate the historical relevance and implications of Christian beliefs in forming an Australian sense of identity.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the principal movements in theology, social context, ecclesiology and politics in Australia since European settlement.
Demonstrate a broad and coherent knowledge of the history of Christianity in Australia informed by empirically grounded sociological and historical research.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills relevant to history as a discipline.
Analyse and evaluate historiographical approaches to the church across different cultures, ecclesial communities, and worldviews.
Analyse and evaluate some of the changing roles played by various Australian Christian communities and movements since European settlement.

title: Church Governance and Management
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the key aspects of governance and management in an ecclesial context. The student will examine the role of boards and councils in their own ecclesial setting with particular reference to the responsibilities and duties of board and council members. Students will examine the basic models and theological perspectives associated with church governance and management and develop an understanding of the legal and ethical issues associated with governance and management of churches.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge and skills in meeting procedures and the management of conflict in board/council meetings.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the legal and ethical issues associated with ecclesial governance and management.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the role of boards and councils in their ecclesial setting.
Articulate the duties and responsibilities of board and council members.
Demonstrate skills in understanding and interpreting reports to governance boards or councils.
Demonstrate an understanding of the place of theological reflection in ecclesial governance and management.

title: Church History Methodology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to foster a self-critical religious historiography by exploring how and why history is written and re-written principally within Christian traditions in the modern era. It seeks to identify the dominant concerns and emphases of past and recent historiography to uncover widely recognised criteria for good history writing; to focus on perennial methodological issues in religious history writing; to survey critically recent Australian religious history writing; and to demonstrate the central part that history as a discipline plays within theological studies.
learning_outcomes: Assess the competence of any history writing by formal historiographical standards.
Show understanding of how emphases and perspectives of religious and wider historiography have changed during the past century.
Discuss the problems posed by historical methodology in vindicating or corroborating religious faith.
Evaluate critically the perspectives and preoccupations of contemporary works on Australian religious history.
Demonstrate recognition of how perspectives of history writers are shaped by their culture and religious interests.
Evidence enhanced research and historiographical skills.

title: Church History Methodology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to foster a self-critical religious historiography by exploring how and why history is written and re-written principally within Christian traditions in the modern era. It seeks to identify the dominant concerns and emphases of past and recent historiography to uncover widely recognised criteria for good history writing; to focus on perennial methodological issues in religious history writing; to survey critically recent Australian religious history writing; and to demonstrate the central part that history as a discipline plays within theological studies.
learning_outcomes: Show understanding of how emphases and perspectives of religious and wider historiography have changed during the past century.
Evidence enhanced research and historiographical skills.
Assess the competence of any history writing by formal historiographical standards.
Demonstrate recognition of how perspectives of history writers are shaped by their culture and religious interests.
Discuss the problems posed by historical methodology in vindicating or corroborating religious faith.
Evaluate critically the perspectives and preoccupations of contemporary works on Australian religious history.

title: Circuit Theory
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: The subject covers fundamental principles, laws, and analysis techniques necessary for the analysis and design of basic electrical circuits. Emphasis is placed on developing problem-solving skills and the ability to analyse and interpret circuit behaviour.
learning_outcomes: Determine power in AC circuits and discuss power factor concepts.
Explain fundamental electrical circuit concepts and terminology.
Discuss transient responses of Resistor-Inductor (RL), RC Circuit (RC), and Resistor-Inductor-Capacitor (RLC) circuits.
Analyse sinusoidal steady-state responses of circuits using phasor techniques.
Apply Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff's Laws, and network theorems to analyse DC circuits.

title: Civil Engineering Design Challenge
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates student engineers' knowledge and skills in the specialised civil discipline through a team-based practical project. Student engineers will deliver workable solutions to real-world civil engineering problems. Student engineers will apply fundamental principles, methods and tools in the civil discipline when formulating the solutions. Student engineers continue to improve their skills in, but not limited to, project management, designing, researching, and evaluating, implementing, teamwork, and communication. This subject offers student engineers in the civil discipline opportunities to practice and reflect upon their identities and practices as future civil engineers, both individually and in groups. This subject serves as a bridging pathway for civil students to embark on their first work placements.
learning_outcomes: Create workable solutions to real-world problems by applying principles, methods, and tools in the civil discipline.
Apply systematic design processes, considering legal, social, economic and environmental factors.
Research, evaluate and synthesise information from a range of credible and current resources.
Exercise effective communication and teamwork skills to ensure the successful implementation and delivery of the project.

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the principles and practices of engineering experimentation specifically tailored for civil engineering applications. Students will learn to design, conduct, and analyse experiments related to structural, geotechnical, and environmental engineering. The subject will cover experimental design, data collection and analysis, and the communication of findings. Emphasis will be placed on practical applications and problem-solving in civil engineering contexts.
learning_outcomes: Collect, process, and analyse experimental data using civil engineering tools and techniques, including statistical methods and software.
Communicate experimental methods, results, and conclusions effectively.
Develop and implement experimental designs to investigate civil engineering problems and validate engineering hypotheses.
Critically evaluate experimental results, identifying potential sources of error and uncertainty and assessing the implications for engineering practice.

title: Civil Procedure
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the procedural rules governing civil litigation in NSW as exemplified in the rules of the superior courts. Students will critically examine the civil litigation workflow of courts including court adjudication under an adversarial system, the types of processes available to start a case, how they must be served, joinder of claims and parties, summary disposition, the transfer of matters between courts, time limits, pleadings and notices to admit, the duty to exchange information, as well as interlocutory orders. It also provides an introduction to alternative forms of dispute resolution practised in civil disputes.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse conflicts and ethical dilemmas that occur in pre-trial process and propose solutions by applying substantive law to procedural steps.

Articulate the chronology of a civil dispute from the time it is referred to the lawyer until the matter is ready for trial, including demonstrating an understanding of the reasons for and content of pre-trial rules relating to discovery, inspection of documents and evidence gathering in general.
Engage critically with the principles of civil procedure including identifying and solving problems within real world contexts.

Demonstrate an informed understanding of the rules, principles and standards of civil practice articulated in the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW), the Uniform Civil Procedure Rules 2005, the NSW Court practice notices and identified case law.
Critically analyse legal argument for compulsory disclosure of evidence that is relevant and otherwise admissible, including identifying the relevant doctrines.
Demonstrate an understanding of the legal principles governing pre-trial process and its relationship to issues of access to justice.
Critically analyse joinder of claims and parties and causes of action, including the objectives of the pleading system and the principal rules of pleadings.

Demonstrate personal autonomy in the use of professional judgement relating to mediation and other alternative dispute mechanisms, including extra judicial determination of issues arising in the course of litigation.
Critically analyse service process and interim measures including orders to preserve property, evidence or assets in general.

Present a clear and coherent exposition of the way civil procedure is regulated in Australia (particularly NSW), including demonstrating in depth knowledge of the abuse of civil procedural devices, especially costs and delay.

title: Class, Global Capitalism and Social Change
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Australian culture tends to downplay the relevance, or even existence, of social class. Yet, class and global capitalism influence all aspects of our social world from everyday injustices to popular uprisings and climate change. This subject examines different ways of thinking about class and how it shapes personal identities, lived realities, communities, whole societies and the planet. Historical and contemporary examples of class formations, inequalities, power and conflict in Australian and international contexts will be explored. By learning how class is a major force of social change and resistance in a capitalist-dominated world, this subject empowers students to recognise and become social change agents.
learning_outcomes: Explain class and global capitalism from a sociological perspective.
Use sociological theory and concepts to explain how class influences social change in the context of global capitalism.
Think critically about class in the context of historical and contemporary global capitalism.
Demonstrate familiarity with key sociological research on class and global capitalism.

title: Classical Performance and Mediated Production
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject students collaborate within a series of workshops to present a production of a classical play text. Plays are studied through a systematic approach to dramaturgical research and analysed as texts for performance. Special attention is paid to the discussion and analysis of dramatic structure, and how the development of dramatic tension is associated with the ethical and moral dilemmas that confront the central characters within a play.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and demonstrate a practical working knowledge of theatrical forms and performance traditions from different classical genres.
Effectively collaborate with others to analyse the dramatic structure of plays.
Clearly articulate and demonstrate a personal performance or production process.
Research, select, and interrogate key decision-making moments for characters within a classical play.

title: Classic Texts in Christian Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject enables students to engage in the study of systematic theology at an advanced level by exploring critically texts that have had a formative influence on the Christian tradition. By engaging with selected classic Christian texts, their historical and theological contexts, and their reception and influence on later Christian thought, students will be encouraged to reflect deeply on the coherence, diversity, and continuing tensions within the Christian theological tradition.
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss critically the reception and influence of classic texts in the later Christian tradition.
Reflect critically on the relationship between Christian theology and its diverse historical and theological contexts.
Demonstrate a capacity for theological reasoning at an advanced level.
Discuss critically the continuing significance of classic texts for issues in contemporary theology.
Demonstrate research and writing skills appropriate for theological study at the Masters level.
Provide an independent scholarly interpretation of classic theological texts at an advanced level.

title: Classroom Technologies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores how classroom digital technologies can be used in pedagogically effective ways to engage students in their learning, to expand learning opportunities, and to facilitate student-centred learning. As well as developing the ability to plan research-based classroom activities using technology, the subject also covers ways to enable school student achievement of Australian curriculum outcomes through utilisation of a range of digital technologies. This subject will enable teacher education students to identify and understand a range of social, legal, and ethical issues, and know how to use digital technologies in a safe, responsible, and ethical way in their teaching. The ability to locate, select, and evaluate digital technology-based resources for use in their teaching, and how to use such resources in the classroom is also addressed.
learning_outcomes: Identify social and legal issues, and explain the safe, responsible, and ethical use of ICT for teaching and learning.
Plan research-based classroom activities using ICTs that engage students in their learning.
Locate, select, and evaluate ICT-based learning materials and software resources that engage students in their learning.
Develop teaching strategies that effectively support and expand opportunities for students' learning of curriculum outcomes.
Explain how ICTs can be used in pedagogically effective ways to facilitate student centred learning.

title: Climate Change Impacts, Mitigation and Adaptation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to give a comprehensive overview of the science and policy issues surrounding current and likely global Climate Change.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of current Government policy and management systems and develop problemsolving skills as applied to Climate Change adaptation and mitigation options.

Demonstrate a thorough knowledge of past and present climates, the science behind anthropogenic global warming, the current state of knowledge on likely Climate Change scenarios, and mitigation and adaptation efforts.

Accurately assess the significance of new Climate Change research and will gain sufficient knowledge to be able to adjudicate between conflicting evidence and theories on anthropogenic global warming.
Demonstrate broad skills in climatology, geomorphology, soil science, landscape history and environmental science as they affect climate change issues.

title: Climatology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the major topics of climate science. Fundamental energy and water exchanges are covered for several different climate surface types with a focus on evaporation. Processes at a larger scale are then explored to explain the major influences of climate and weather on the Australian landscape. The subject has no intensive. The final section of the subject builds on this framework so that on completion students will have an in-depth understanding of contemporary climatic variability and climate change processes.
learning_outcomes: Have a broad and coherent understanding of a range of fundamental climate processes such as energy and mass exchanges.
Critically discuss the scientific basis of climate change predictions and models and recent developments in this area.
Explain previous climate change and variability.
Have advanced knowledge of the differences between climates of simple non-vegetated surfaces to those of vegetated surfaces.
Have advanced knowledge of weather systems in Australia and global climatology.

title: Clinical Bacteriology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of infectious bacteria, their collection, detection and diagnosis of infection. In-depth studies of the infectious bacteria of selected organ systems are conducted. Practical sessions and case studies simulate 'real life' medical situations, with the emphasis on laboratory diagnostic methodology in which the student microbiologist is consulted in order to diagnose the aetiological agents of infection.
learning_outcomes: Describe the principles behind antibacterial chemotherapies.

Describe the causative bacterial pathogens, pathogenesis, epidemiology and clinical signs of diseases affecting the urinary tract, the integument and haematopoietic system, the digestive tract, the respiratory tract, the eye, sexually transmitted diseases, obstetric and perinatal infections, vector borne infections, multisystem zoonoses and the immunocompromised host.
Describe the principles of diagnosis, specimen collection and specimen quality.
Identify the kinds of bacteria that cause disease.
Demonstrate an understanding of the basic taxonomy of medically significant bacterial agents and how it is used for diagnosis.
Demonstrate an understanding of the underlying principles of bacterial genetics with emphasis on antibiotic resistance and spread.
Competently perform microbiological techniques for diagnosis of infection.

title: Clinical Biochemistry 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces units, reference ranges and specimens used in clinical biochemistry. The subject also covers the patho-physiological and patho-biochemical rationale for routine clinical biochemistry tests and the interpretation of data. Biochemical techniques associated with the various routine tests covered include principles of the methods and the analytical performance. Technology, including point of care testing is important in healthcare and is also included. Students will gain knowledge of the requirements of the various specimens and measurements and will acquire theoretical skills to carry out routine testing using various methods and equipment. Students will also interpret routine clinical biochemistry data. Such knowledge is useful, in further studies in this discipline, routine and specialist medical laboratory sciences, forensic sciences, biotechnology, dentistry, medicine, veterinary and animal sciences, research and in industry that develops and/or supplies diagnostic technology and consumables.
learning_outcomes: Explain the applications of technology, automation and information systems and to analyse their usefulness.
Describe principles of various measurements and the rationale and usefulness of the tests in diagnosis and management of diseases.

Evaluate methods (including but not limited to evaluating accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, linearity), to identify and analyse sources of errors, to implement quality control and quality assurance for good analytical practice.
Work independently and collaboratively in data interpretation and in measurement of analytes and to write a scientific report on findings and data interpretation.
Describe and justify the importance of units and reference values for various measurements in health and in diseases and their use in interpretation of data.
Identify, describe and justify the utility of the various specimens, conditions of specimen collection and preservation as well as other requirements for analysis.

title: Clinical Biochemistry 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is a continuation of Clinical Biochemistry 1 and covers techniques in measurements of endogenous and exogenous metabolites found in low levels in biological specimens. These metabolites include (but are not limited to), hormones and drugs that are used in therapy and/or that are abused. Techniques inclusive of the various types of immunoassays as well as mass spectrometry are therefore covered. Monogenic diseases are learnt with emphasis on cystic fibrosis and phenylketonuria. Clinical endocrinology is studied and various endocrine disorders are emphasised to illustrate development of endocrine diseases and the importance of clinical biochemistry in diagnosis and management of endocrine disorders. On completion of this subject, a student is equipped with theoretical skills for clinical biochemical investigation of endocrine disorders, monogenic diseases and drugs. Such knowledge is useful for example in further studies in this discipline and also other disciplines such as forensic sciences, dentistry, medicine and veterinary as well as animal sciences, routine and specialist pathology, research and in industry that develops and/or supplies diagnostic technology and consumables.
learning_outcomes: Describe how endocrine diseases and monogenic diseases (e.g. cystic fibrosis and phenylketonuria) arise and to describe and evaluate the patho-biochemical/patho-physiological rationale for screening, diagnosis and management of these diseases.
Describe and evaluate toxicological exposure involving chemicals and metals.
Describe and analyse the rationale for measuring drugs and describe pharmacokinetic principles and their importance to clinical biochemistry.

Describe and evaluate the various techniques (including but not limited to recognition techniques and mass spectrometry) utilised in measurement of endogenous metabolites and drugs found in low concentrations in biological fluids/tissues in various diseases.
Interpret results/data in measurement of drugs and in diagnosis and management of endocrine and monogenic diseases.
Work independently and collaboratively in measurement of analyses and to write a scientific report on experimental findings and data interpretation.

Interpret results/data in measurement of drugs and in diagnosis and management of endocrine and monogenic diseases.

title: Clinical Education and Supervision in Medical Radiation Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the fundamental principles of clinical supervision and their role in this facet of advanced Medical Radiation practice. Students will critically evaluate supervision and support strategies in the Medical Radiation clinical setting including student and peer assessment, mentorship and developmental support. A focus of this subject will be the enrichment of clinical supervisors' understanding of the principles and practice of assessment in relation to Medical Radiation students' clinical capability.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate the concepts of clinical competence and clinical capability in the context of Medical Radiation practice.
Apply research-based approaches to meet the diverse needs of students in the clinical supervision environment and integrate culturally safe practices of supervision and assessment.
Apply principles of adult learning to workplace learning in the Medical Radiation Sciences.
Organise and implement an advanced evidence-based program of supervision and mentorship for students in the workplace.
Formulate appropriate strategies to effectively supervise students and deliver feedback to students and education providers.
Formulate strategies to apply the principles of assessment in the workplace and appropriately assess clinical capability.
prerequisites: HLT542: Professional Practice in Clinical Education
HLT541: Teaching and Learning in the Clinical Setting
HLT539: Foundations of Teaching and Learning in Clinical Education

title: Clinical Biochemistry 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is a continuation of Clinical Biochemistry 1 and covers techniques in measurements of endogenous and exogenous metabolites found in low levels in biological specimens. These metabolites include, but are not limited to, hormones and drugs that are used in therapy and/or that are abused. Techniques inclusive of the various types of immunoassays as well as mass spectrometry are therefore covered. Monogenic diseases are learnt with emphasis on cystic fibrosis and phenylketonuria. Clinical endocrinology is studied and various endocrine disorders are emphasised to illustrate development of endocrine diseases and the importance of clinical biochemistry in diagnosis and management of endocrine disorders. On completion of this subject, a student is equipped with theoretical and technical skills for clinical biochemical investigation of endocrine disorders, monogenic diseases and drugs. Such knowledge is useful for example in further studies in this discipline and also other disciplines such as forensic sciences, dentistry, medicine and veterinary as well as animal sciences, routine and specialist pathology, research and in industry that develops and/or supplies diagnostic technology and consumables.
learning_outcomes: measure competently the levels of drugs and constituents associated with endocrine and monogenic diseases;

describe how endocrine diseases and monogenic diseases (e.g. cystic fibrosis and phenylketonuria) arise and to describe and evaluate the patho-biochemical/patho-physiological rationale for screening, diagnosis and management of these diseases;
describe and evaluate toxicological exposure involving chemicals and metals; and

describe and evaluate the various techniques (including but not limited to recognition techniques and mass spectrometry) utilised in measurement of endogenous metabolites and drugs found in low concentrations in biological fluids/tissues in various diseases;
work independently and collaboratively in measurement of analyses and to write a scientific report on experimental findings and data interpretation.
describe and analyse the rationale for measuring drugs and describe pharmacokinetic principles and their importance to clinical biochemistry;

title: Clinical Concepts in Oral Surgery
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject follows on from the 3rd year foundational oral surgery subject. In this subject, students will further develop diagnostic and surgical skills in in simple exodontia, suturing and wound management. Introductory concepts in surgical aspects of specialised surgical procedures, such as periodontal and endodontic surgery, and aspects of maxillofacial surgery will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the surgical principles that underpin mucosal and osseous surgical procedures in the oral cavity (eg surgical removal of teeth, periodontal and endodontic surgery, and the placement of dental implants).
Differentiate and discuss the diagnosis and surgical management of infections in the oral cavity and surrounding anatomical spaces.
Describe the scope of specialist surgical treatments that are available to support the practice of general dental practitioners in their management of patients in need of such services.
Demonstrate knowledge in assessment, diagnosis, and treatment planning for minor oral surgery, commensurate with the scope of practice of an intermediate-level student practitioner.
prerequisites: DOH337: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 3
DOH412: Medicine and Surgery for Dental Practice

title: Clinical Health Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an advanced understanding of the application of clinical psychological principles and techniques to the promotion and maintenance of health and to the prevention and treatment of illness. Clinical health psychology requires an understanding of the biological, psychological, and social characteristics of people with chronic and acute illness, the nature of their symptoms, the medical interventions they receive, and the appropriate psychological interventions to help manage their conditions and enhance quality of life. Students will examine the role of diet, exercise and sleep in a healthy lifestyle, and review the psychological aspects of a range of chronic conditions.
learning_outcomes: Identify factors that influence individual differences in response to physical conditions.
Assess the nature and challenges of clinical health psychology in practice, and develop effective ways to deal with them.
Recognise and assess the role of psychological, social, and biological factors in physical conditions.
Implement effective psychological interventions across physical conditions and health care settings.
Describe and discuss the theoretical and empirical foundations of health psychology.

title: Clinical Implant Dentistry
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: The Clinical Implant Dentistry subject draws together the learning from previous parts of this course to facilitate students providing implant treatments to their own patients with the assistance of mentors in both the surgical and restorative phases of treatment. Students will select appropriate cases, plan treatments, and then carry out both the surgical and restorative procedures needed.
learning_outcomes: Discuss implant restoration design for cases involving the replacement of multiple teeth.
Discuss the importance of implant maintenance and the protocols employed in this phase of case management.
Discuss the advantages/disadvantages of fixed versus removable implant prostheses.
Provide implant treatment and maintenance care to patients.
Critically discuss the timing and loading considerations associated with implant placement of missing teeth and the implant replacement of teeth requiring extraction.
Critically discuss factors which may influence the success or failure of implants, and potential complications that may arise.
prerequisites: DOH554: Advanced Concepts in Implant Dentistry

title: Clinical Leadership in Nursing
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Strong leadership is essential if the vision of a transformed health care system is to be achieved and nurses have a crucial role in this endeavour. Being able to design, implement, evaluate and advocate for ongoing reforms to the system are essential activities for nurse leaders in the 21st Century. This subject focuses on the knowledge and behaviours required to be a successful nurse leader in a rapidly changing health environment. Key knowledge areas include systems thinking, quality, safety and clinical governance, information and communication technologies, how to translate new research evidence into practice and evaluation. Opportunities will be provided to apply aspects of clinical nurse leadership that are relevant to students' area of practice and enhance understanding of leadership and management specific to the challenges faced by nurse leaders. Students will explore and integrate theoretical knowledge of transformative leadership approaches that support their current or future roles as leaders and managers. The subject is designed for nursing and midwifery leaders (expert clinicians, nursing and midwifery managers at all levels of health care) and will enable them to develop their leadership capacity in a way that leads to transformative change. Students will distinguish between different theories/models of leadership and management and apply their knowledge by developing a healthcare improvement proposal. Content including ethical and legal issues, cultural safety, evidence-based practice, resilience, quality improvement and recruitment and retention of an emerging multigenerational workforce will be examined within the context of health care.
learning_outcomes: investigate the concepts of complexity and systems thinking and how they apply to leadership;
apply principles of change management in their current work environment.
examine the role of teamwork in healthcare improvement; and
demonstrate and apply knowledge of the role of nurses in leading healthcare improvement and project management;
apply contemporary healthcare management theories and practices to the administration and evaluation of care delivery systems and facilitation of collaborative models of care;
prerequisites: NRS538: Leadership and Management for the Nurse 2
NRS537: Leadership and Management for the Nurse 1
NRS537: Leadership and Management for the Nurse 1
NRS538: Leadership and Management for the Nurse 2

title: Clinical Neuropsychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to contemporary neuropsychological theories, methods and measures, including aspects of the neuropsychological assessment, diagnosis and understanding of developmental and acquired cognitive disorders likely to be encountered by clinical psychologists. The functional neuroanatomy of the brain will be discussed, with consideration of basic neuroanatomy, vascular systems and neurochemistry. The nature of the cognitive systems involved in attention, memory, language, spatial processing, and executive functions will be reviewed, with discussion of the neuropsychological assessment of each of these systems. The application of neuropsychological theories and methods in clinical psychological practice will be explored, with consideration of a range of developmental and acquired disorders, neuropsychiatric disorders and other common conditions. Ethical and professional issues in clinical neuropsychological practice will be discussed. The unit also includes coverage of mechanisms of psychoactive drug action and the classification, use and efficacy of common psychopharmacological agents for psychological disorders.
learning_outcomes: Describe the mechanisms of psychoactive drug action.
Conduct a basic assessment of a client.
Appraise the use and efficacy of common psychopharmacological treatments for psychological disorders.
Apply neuropsychological knowledge and skills to the management of clients with cognitive impairments.
Demonstrate knowledge of neuropsychological theories, methods and measures.
Explain the neuropsychology of developmental disorders and acquired brain injury.

title: Clinical Pastoral Education
school: School
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for an Advanced Unit of Clinical Pastoral Education training as delivered by the NSW College of CPE or equivalent. The advanced program should be 400 hours in duration and contain at least 10 hours of individual supervision and 80 hours of group supervision. 'Advanced CPE requires a heightened level of personal awareness, pastoral formation and professional development in a pastoral care specialisation. Professional competency is the focus of an Advanced Unit.' (NSW College of CPE)
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for an Advanced Unit of Clinical Pastoral Education training as delivered by the NSW College of CPE or equivalent. The advanced program should be 400 hours in duration and contain at least 10 hours of individual supervision and 80 hours of group supervision.

title: Clinical Pathology for Veterinary Technologists
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will expand on their understanding of veterinary diagnostics. Students will learn how to maintain and quality check veterinary laboratory equipment and collect samples appropriately for laboratory tests. Students will also learn to apply their knowledge to correctly perform diagnostic test procedure, analysis of specimens and test results, and interpreting results for further Veterinarian evaluation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the current impact of advances in molecular techniques relevant to veterinary clinical pathology.
Demonstrate an understanding of key issues regarding quality control and quality assurance, equipment maintenance in the clinical veterinary laboratory to ensure accurate results.
Identify and apply basic principles and concepts of DNA structure (and sequence), central dogma and chromosome structure including their significance in the context of health and disease.
Describe appropriate diagnostic procedures associated with assessing the health status of animals.

Analyse, interpret and apply the results of veterinary diagnostic tests, as well as some clinical findings, to problem-solving activities including but not limited to case studies related to veterinary clinical pathology.
Collect, prepare, handle and process samples for diagnostic analysis in order to ensure maximum accuracy of results.
Identify and apply principles and concepts associated with the interaction between genes and alleles, and how this results in the occurrence of commonly observed traits and diseases in animals.
prerequisites: ASC183: Foundations in Veterinary Surgical Nursing
ASC182: Foundations in Clinical Procedures and Veterinary Nursing
BCM210: Foundations and Techniques in Biochemistry

title: Clinical Placement and Authentic Learning 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on healthcare workplace learning. Students will engage in Work Integrated Learning (WIL) experiences within the healthcare setting. Within this subject, students will apply paramedic skills under supervision in a clinical setting. Detailed protocols, procedures, and pharmacology's will be used during the WIL experience.
learning_outcomes: Identify and reflect on ethical and legal issues that arise in paramedic practice and within the work intergrated learning experience.
Develop and reassess the appropriateness and real impact of treatment plans tailored to the individual patient.
Perform patient assessments in a range of environments that are a paramedics work setting.
Show sensitivity towards the patient and family members by identifying and dealing with areas of potential distress while working in a clinical setting.
Practice clinical skills under supervision.

title: Clinical Podiatric Residency
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject commences the final series of clinical podiatry placements for students enrolled in the Honours stream. Students will consolidate their professional knowledge and skills, and demonstrate their ability to apply theoretical concepts in the workplace. Students will have the opportunity to undertake work-integrated learning with external podiatry providers in the public healthcare sector, working collaboratively with clinical educators and other practitioners to provide person-focused care. Through this subject, students will be supported to further develop skills in clinical reasoning and reflect on their own clinical practice to demonstrate principles of life-long learning that are required for continuing professional development.
learning_outcomes: Develop, implement and/or review evidence-based management plans in consultation with the patient and others in the healthcare team.
Apply skills in clinical reasoning to discuss management options relevant to the needs of the patient, their carers, and the broader community.
Negotiate therapeutic goals that enhance self-management for a range of podiatry patients, recognising when it is clinically appropriate to prescribe or not to prescribe medicines.
Critically reflect on personal learning and the application of this learning to future professional practice.
Comply with applicable professional standards, codes of conduct and guidelines relevant to prescribing medicines to inform evidence-based decisions in the context of the patient’s needs.
Practice in a manner that aligns with legislative and regulatory requirements and ensures patient safety is protected.

title: Clinical Placement and Authentic Learning 2
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are required to complete authentic learning placements in the healthcare environment. In this subject, students will apply knowledge learned from previous subjects to further develop skills, attitudes and values relevant to the delivery of care in the out-of-hospital environment. Students will build upon foundational knowledge and education covered to date.
learning_outcomes: Maintain an effective audit trail of their own paramedic practice.
Complete an accurate health assessment and effectively manage out-of-hospital patients.
Explain / demonstrate the concepts of advanced life support, advanced airway management and drug administration.
Undertake patient care activities related to the role of the paramedic as per clinical record book objectives.
Continually reflect on and improve their practice.
prerequisites: CLS206: Clinical Placement and Authentic Learning 1

title: Clinical Podiatric Residency
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject commences the final series of clinical podiatry placements for students enrolled in the Pass stream. Students will consolidate their professional knowledge and skills, and demonstrate their ability to apply theoretical concepts in the workplace.
