title: Communication and Human Services
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This is the first communication subject relating to work in the Human Services and is for students who have either not studied at university previously, and/or require further orientation to communicating in the Human Services profession. The subject incorporates the concepts of being, thinking and doing, and provides challenging learning experiences that cover a range of topics to illustrate communication on personal, social, organisational / political, and even spiritual levels. Students are required to actively do two things: to describe and to reflect critically upon their understanding and experience of communication; and to critique how and where, when and what, is communicated in those experiences. In doing so, students consider their own values and ethics in the context of the values and ethics of the helping professions, in order to demonstrate critical judgement about what content /information is appropriate in decision-making. The subject commences the process of critiquing research and arguments, through teaching thinking skills, including structured thinking, critical thinking, systemic thinking and lateral thinking. Students develop communication skills in the written form necessary for human services work, as well as knowledge about different levels of communication, including: intra-personal, inter-personal, trans-systems, and extra-dimensional communication.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to study in an academic environment by applying basic principles of learning and research required for university study.
Communicate in writing as required for successful university study and a career in the Human Services.
Demonstrate the acquisition of introductory skills in critical thinking, critical reasoning, research and various forms of communicating in an academic environment.
Demonstrate an identification with, and have a basic understanding of, the values needed in the Human Services and an understanding of own values and approaches.
Apply knowledge of the different levels of communication competence, including intra-personal, inter-personal, trans-systems, and extra-dimensional layers, to study and work in the Human Services.

title: Communication and Information Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to develop and refine communication skills within the workplace. It focuses on intra- and inter-personal factors which underpin effective communication. It provides guided practice in oral, written and electronic communication which includes skills of listening, speaking, reading, writing and use of associated technologies.
learning_outcomes: Identify the components of the communication model.
Select an appropriate communication style and technique when delivering a message in different settings and to different audiences.
Discuss the impact of non-verbal communication.
Critically assess the main issues associated with ethical communication.
Explain the fundamental concepts of the communication process.
Practise, develop, refine and demonstrate written language skills so students are able to write clearly, correctly and concisely.

title: Communication and Police Professional Standards, Conduct and Values 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on key capabilities required of a professional police officer, including the following range of capabilities: making ethical decisions in accordance with the law, community expectations and organisational policies; communicating with a range of individuals and groups; understanding and dealing with the customer base of the police organisation and recognising potential risks and avenues of corruption inherent in policing. The subject considers these capabilities in relation to key NSW Police Force policies-the Statement of Values, the Code of Conduct and Ethics, the Oath of Office and other associated policies. Corruption resistance strategies used by the NSW Police Force are also addressed.
learning_outcomes: Explain the NSW Police Force Customer Service Strategy and how it applies to general duties policing.
Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking framework in policing scenarios.
Identify the potential for corruption in policing and explain key corruption resistance strategies used within the NSW Police Force.
Explain the principles of professionalism and decision-making accountability as they apply to policing in NSW.

Explain NSW Police Force ethical standards as articulated in the Statement of Values, Code of Conduct and Ethics and the Oath of Office and other associated policies and apply these to policing scenarios.
Use effective written and oral communication techniques appropriately in a range of policing situations.
Explain the crucial role of lawful discretion in the police decision-making processes.
Apply the principles of effective victim care to a range of policing scenarios.

title: Communication and Police Professional Standards, Conduct and Values 1A
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on key capabilities required of a professional police officer, including the capabilities for making ethical decisions in accordance with the law, community expectations and organisational policies; communicating with a range of individuals and groups; understanding and dealing with the customer base of the police organisation and recognising potential risks and avenues of corruption inherent in policing. The subject considers these capabilities in relation to key NSW Police Force policies-the Statement of Values, the Code of Conduct and Ethics, the Oath of Office and other associated policies.
learning_outcomes: Use effective written and oral communication techniques appropriately in a range of policing situations.
Explain the crucial role of lawful discretion in police-decision making processes.
Explain the principles of professionalism and decision making accountability as they apply to policing in NSW.
Explain the NSW Police Force Customer Service Strategy and how it applies to general duties policing.
Apply the principles of effective victim care to a range of policing scenarios.
Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking framework in policing scenarios.
Identify the potential for corruption in policing.
Explain NSW Police Force ethical standards as articulated in the Statement of Values, Code of Conduct and Ethics, the Oath of Office and associated policies and apply to policing scenarios.

title: Communication and Police Professional Standards, Conduct and Values 1B
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on key capabilities required of a professional police officer, including the capabilities for making ethical decisions in accordance with the law, community expectations and organisational policies; communicating with a range of individuals and groups; understanding and dealing with the customer base of the police organisation and recognising potential risks and avenues of corruption inherent in policing. The subject considers these capabilities in relation to key NSW Police Force policies-the Statement of Values, the Code of Conduct and Ethics, the Oath of Office and other associated policies. Corruption resistance strategies used by the NSW Police Force are also addressed.
learning_outcomes: Identify the potential for corruption in policing and explain key corruption resistance strategies used within the NSW Police Force.
Explain NSW Police Force ethical standards as articulated in the Statement of Values, Code of Conduct and Ethics, the Oath of Office and associated policies and apply to policing scenarios.
Explain the principles of professionalism and decision making accountability as they apply to policing in NSW.
Explain the NSW Police Force Customer Service Charter and how it applies to general duties policing.
Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking framework in policing scenarios.
Apply the principles of effective victim care to a range of policing scenarios.
Use effective written and oral communication techniques appropriately in a range of policing situations.
prerequisites: PPP154: Communication and Police Professional Standards, Conduct and Values 1A

title: Communication and Police Professional Standards, Conduct and Values 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject continues to develop critical thinking and decision-making. Communication strategies, customer service and victim care are reinforced to ensure an ongoing understanding of these critical areas in policing. They are extended to a wider range of offences and situations especially in investigations and domestic violence. Another key area of policing to be considered is making sound ethical decisions. Decisions related to scrutiny, fairness and in compliance with legislation and NSW Police Force policies and procedures are addressed in policing scenarios. The NSW Police Force guidelines for professionalism are considered generally with a specific focus on domestic violence along with the lawful use of police discretion.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of effective customer service and victim care in a range of complex policing scenarios.
Identify and apply appropriate and effective oral and written communication techniques in a range of complex policing scenarios.
Identify and explain the characteristics of a professional police officer.
Apply NSW police force ethical standards to practical scenarios as articulated in the Statement of Values, the Code of Conduct and Ethics, the Oath of Office and other associated policies.
Understand potential barriers to effective communications in a range of complex policing scenarios.
Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking decision-making framework in policing scenarios.
Explain the crucial role of lawful discretion in the decision-making process within policing scenarios.

title: Communication and Technology: digital connectivity
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the technologies/channels of communication and the impact of the digital on communication theory and practice, as well as the behaviour of communicators, both professional and 'citizen'. The impact of technical change is explored at all levels of the communication process, from individual to societal and global impacts,
learning_outcomes: Locate the practice of communication as a global (or local)/digital (or non-digital) phenomenon, and relate this to their particular research project.

Consider the behaviour changes required by all parties in the creation and dissemination of digital communication content, at individual, local, national and global levels, as well as alternative non-digital forms.
Critically evaluate the impact of technological developments on traditional/historical approaches to communication in their field.
Speculate about the impact of impending technological/digital changes (positive and negative) on their field of practice.

title: Communication for Case Managers
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Through this subject students will develop skills in clear and persuasive communication within the diverse and dynamic practice fields in which case management and coordinated care is provided. Spanning a wide range of contexts, disciplines and theories, this subject will help students to map and critically reflect on important trends and influences on and within communication including social, technological, ethical, legal, cultural and practice issues. This subject will focus on professional writing, inter-personal skills, inter-cultural communication, communication etiquette, negotiation, meeting processes, interagency collaboration, conflict management, team management and electronic communications (e.g. social media). Students will develop communication skills based on critical thinking, reflective, analytic and strategic skills linking theory-informed practice, case analysis and strength based learning.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to work effectively with, and when required, lead teams applying conflict resolution, negotiation and mediation skills where necessary.

Use technical and communication skills to communicate with clients, families, carers, health practitioners and organisations within contemporary health, community and other settings within which case managers and care coordinators work.
Recognise and discuss their own strengths and areas for development and improvement in communication for case management and coordinated care.

Use person-centred, communication strategies to build effective working relationships with people from all backgrounds, including working with interpreters, people with communication difficulties and a variety of lived experiences and values.
Use communication to facilitate behaviour change, empowering clients to make decisions about their lives and their health.

title: Communication Development Across The Lifespan
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students explore the development of communication across the lifespan. Students gain an understanding of the role of language and cognition, as well as sensory-motor skill development in the development of communicative competence focusing on oral language and literacy development. Students develop skills in the analysis of communication data and apply this to describe communication skills of infants, children and adolescents. Students reflect on their personal experiences and knowledge of communication across the lifespan and extend this knowledge through critical reflection on linguistic and developmental theories, as well as cultural/social beliefs. Throughout this subject, students will engage with different types of evidence as used in evidence-based speech pathology practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of typical communication development including milestones of language, cognition and sensory-motor skill development.
Use a range of academic and digital literacy skills to communicate with specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Critique theory of communication development based on individual variation and the role of individual, social and cultural contexts and knowledges.
Synthesise and interpret knowledge of developmental milestones, cultural/social beliefs and critique of theory to identify and justify strategies to support and promote communication development.

title: Communication for Occupational Therapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will facilitate the development of respectful and effective communication skills for occupational therapy practice in various health, community, social, and educational settings. Key skills include professional writing, interviewing, and adapting communication to effectively interact with people at various life stages, from diverse backgrounds, and in different practice contexts. The subject will include communication partner skills for engaging with people using alternative strategies, and culturally responsive considerations when engaging with First Nations Australians. Students will identify their personal communication strengths and areas for improvement, setting goals and strategies for ongoing development. This subject will also enable students to further develop their academic, digital, information and research literacies to support occupational therapy practice. Within this subject, students will complete 75 hours of work integrated learning (WIL) placement. This provides the opportunity for students to demonstrate suitable professional behaviour, self-management and communication skills within a practice context.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate communication, professional behaviour and self-management skills required for occupational therapy practice.

Identify and implement occupational therapy techniques used in culturally responsive communication across the lifespan with a particular focus on respectful communication with First Nations Australian peoples.
Reflect on communication skills to articulate personal strengths, identify areas for improvement, and develop realistic strategies for ongoing development.

Identify, describe and demonstrate a range of verbal, non-verbal and written communication skills relevant to occupational therapy practice, and describe the link between effective communication and health and wellbeing outcomes.
prerequisites: OCC104: Person, Environment and Occupation Foundations

title: Communication for Occupational Therapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will facilitate the development of respectful and effective communication skills for occupational therapy practice in various health, community, social, and educational settings. Key skills include professional writing, interviewing, and adapting communication to effectively interact with people at various life stages, from diverse backgrounds, and in different practice contexts. The subject will include communication partner skills for engaging with people using alternative strategies, and culturally responsive considerations when engaging with First Nations Australians. Students will identify their personal communication strengths and areas for improvement, setting goals and strategies for ongoing development. This subject will also enable students to further develop their academic, digital, information and research literacies to support occupational therapy practice. Within this subject, students will complete work integrated learning (WIL) placement. This provides the opportunity for students to demonstrate suitable professional behaviour, self-management and communication skills within a practice context.
learning_outcomes: Identify, describe and demonstrate a range of verbal, non-verbal and written communication skills relevant to occupational therapy practice, and describe the link between effective communication and health and wellbeing outcomes.
Reflect on communication skills to articulate personal strengths, identify areas for improvement, and develop realistic strategies for ongoing development.

Identify and implement occupational therapy techniques used in culturally responsive communication across the lifespan with a particular focus on respectful communication with First Nations Australian peoples.
Demonstrate appropriate communication, professional behaviour and self-management skills required for occupational therapy practice.
prerequisites: OCC103: Communication for Occupational Therapy Practice
OCC104: Person, Environment and Occupation Foundations

title: Communication in Organisations
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines communication in organisations from a range of standpoints. Students apply different models and theories to analyse professional communication, individual communication styles and communication management. Functionalist, interpretive and critical approaches are used to underpin analysis of communication in contemporary organisations. Students develop critical thinking, reflective, analytic and strategic skills through theory-informed observation, case analysis and problem-based learning.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to critically and systematically assess communication requirements and make high level judgments concerning communication processes in organisations.
Demonstrate specialised knowledge of theories and frameworks for analysing interpersonal and professional communication in organisations and other contexts.
Evaluate organisational communication and construct a strategic communication plan.

title: Communication in Practice
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the detailed practice of the student's field, whether the construction of news stories or advertisements, the gestation of performance or the creation and dissemination of organisational communication, for example. The emphasis is on understanding how communication practice is organised and constructed, its points of similarity and divergence from comparable practices or similar societies, past or present. The focus here is on the individual or team producing the communicative or creative work.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate assumptions about practice.
Consider and apply a range of practices relevant to the student's research project, with rationale for selection.
Identify shortcomings, developments, opportunities in current professional practice and suggest how student's research project would address such issues.
Compare and contrast practices over time or space.

title: Communication in Society
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject considers a research project in its wider societal context. It explores how communication research is framed by sociological, professional, economic, technological and other dynamics. The relationship aspects of research are highlighted and these paradigms are applied to the student's research project. Note: subjects may be taken in any order; all subjects include a literature review, research approaches and a presentation to faculty and peers
learning_outcomes: Locate their research project in a wider social context.
Draw upon relevant literature to develop research questions and defend these choices to Faculty and peers.
Discriminate between methodologies appropriate for studying communication in a social context.
Critically evaluate the role of the researcher in research and their relationship to the object of study.
Articulate the social impact on and social implications of their research.

title: Communication Project
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to equip students with the necessary skills and understanding to effectively plan, produce and evaluate a complex communication project. Students will examine the technical, social and communicative dimensions of managing a project in their chosen major.
learning_outcomes: Critique both their own work and that of their peers.
Plan a project in response to a brief from a client, commissioner or audience.
Reflect on and justify their disciplinary approach including cultural diversity within the project.
Design, develop and execute a complex project.
Work independently as an individual practitioner, and collaborate effectively to achieve goals.
prerequisites: CCI303: Communication and Creative Industries Project 1
CCI304: Communication and Creative Industries Project 2

title: Communication Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles and techniques used in modern communication systems, including modulation techniques, transmission media, multiplexing, digital communication fundamentals, and introduction to wireless communication systems. Emphasis is placed on theoretical concepts, practical applications, and the importance of communication systems in various engineering disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the performance of communication systems in the presence of noise and interference.
Apply multiplexing techniques to efficiently utilise communication channels.
Describe the properties and characteristics of different transmission media used in communication systems.
Analyse and compare various analogue and digital modulation techniques used in communication systems.
Understand the fundamentals of wireless communication systems, including wireless channels, modulation techniques, and multiple access techniques.

title: Communication Styles in Multiplatform Media
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject offers theoretical and applied learning in the preparation of communication tactics in multiplatform media environments. The subject develops students' ability to understand the multiplatform media environment and the range of communication styles adopted in this environment. Students plan, design and propose a media campaign for this multiplatform environment. The subject is designed for delivery to an industry partner so students apply the learning and communication proposition to their own industry situation. The subject is offered via an online program with a one week face to face intensive (residential) workshop program.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate specialised knowledge of approaches to designing communication for multiplatform media.
Demonstrate an ability to critically evaluate the effectiveness of specific communication styles and tactics in multplatform campaigns.
Propose relevant communication tactics as appropriate to multiplatform media campaigns.
Understand the multiplatform media environment.

title: Community Analysis
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The subject looks at community as a means of addressing social, environmental and economic problems in a globalising world which is seeing a strong social and political push for action to be taken by local communities. Starting from the perspectives of local professionals and active citizens, the subject applies sociological tools to community capacity in terms of social capital, interaction, organization, inequality, conflict and power relationships both within and beyond the community. We conclude by looking at the implications of globalisation and cultural change for local communities.
learning_outcomes: Apply sociological theory and concepts to real world cases of issues that occur in communities.
Understand some of the sociological theories that have been developed to help us understand the variety of forms of community we have in our society.
Understand sociological ways of describing and investigating communities.
Explain sociological research about communities clearly in writing.
Think critically about community.

title: Community and Public Health Nutrition
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject provides an introduction to the use of epidemiological, socioeconomic, and behavioural evidence-based data in community and public health. Students will develop skills in health promotion planning aimed at addressing health inequities, using a food and nutrition lens. A focus on community health, public health and health promotion strategies and solutions is core to enhancing health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable groups such as Australian First Nations and rural communities. This subject provides a foundation for community health, public health and health promotion practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the principles of public health approaches and delivery as they apply to food and nutrition, including key public health policies/mandates and possible roles for food and nutrition professionals.

Apply skills in health promotion planning, informed by an analysis of food and nutrition related health problems and chronic disease in Australian communities, with particular focus on enhancing health outcomes for Australian First Nations and rural communities.
Analyse the cause of health inequities, specifically in relation to social determinants of health.
Collate and evaluate demographic, epidemiological and other data for a health needs assessment to identify and justify priorities for health promotion programs.

title: Community and Stakeholder Engagement
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Community and stakeholder engagement are key professional skills for environmental science practitioners in contemporary workplace settings. This subject examines how to strategically implement public participation as both a professional moral imperative and as a legal requirement. It will also look at how to respond to such opportunities as a member of the public with a desire to influence decision makers. On completion of this subject, students will possess a range of stakeholder and community engagement skills as well as possess an understanding how to respond as a member of the community when such opportunities arise.
learning_outcomes: Respond like a member of the community to a consultation opportunity.

Outline the five different forms of 'participation' according to the International Association for Public Participation (IAP2) Spectrum and have the professional skills to know how to apply this concept in a range of situations.
Evaluate the nuanced professional skills required when applying the spectrum to marginalised groups with the broader community.
Explain the key conceptual frameworks used to distinguish different types of public participation.
Contribute to a small team that are developing a wider community advocacy strategy.

title: Community and Stakeholder Engagement
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Community and stakeholder engagement are fundamental skills for environmental science practitioners in contemporary work place settings for the public, not-for-profit and private sectors involved in the management of environments and natural resources. This subject examines how social values, attitudes and behaviours are related to how we maintain, protect and sustainably grow our environment and natural resources. A critical element will consider how to incorporate these attitudes and values into policy making, strategy development and project management so as to arrive at robust decision making. During the minimum 40 hours of workplace learning, students will design and evaluate a workplace stakeholder engagement project. On completion of this subject, students will possess a range of skills in stakeholder and community engagement management, processes and capabilities.
learning_outcomes: Discuss how social values, attitudes and behaviours are related to how we maintain, protect, enhance and use our environments and natural resources.
Demonstrate skills in a variety of stakeholder and community engagement management, processes and capabilities including conflict avoidance and resolution.
Participate in and reflect on a placement related to environmental science and management as a developing professional.
Critically consider how to apply different stakeholder and community engagement models in environmental management across a spectrum from policy to service and project delivery.
Explain and illustrate governance of environments and natural resources, including individual and government decision making processes.
Make sound judgments on the use and application of some contemporary methods of stakeholder engagement.

title: Community Contexts
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an examination of the social contexts that influence community leadership and resilience. It begins by considering the contested nature of concepts like community, community resilience and community leadership and related social theories. Socio-cultural, political, economic and environmental factors influencing the lived experience of community leadership and resilience are also analysed. This includes the impacts of socially inequitable patterning of leadership and resilience among communities, for example by social class, gender and cultural background. Attention is also paid to institutional, community-led and partnership-based initiatives to foster community leadership and resilience. The subject is designed with adaptable delivery models, which may include combinations of condensed online sessions and one-off workshops.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and discuss the contested nature of key concepts like community, community leadership and community resilience.
Critically explain how social structures and human agency influence experiences and practices of community leadership and resilience.
Apply theoretical concepts to the development of community leadership and resilience initiatives.

title: Community Disaster Recovery
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the concept of community disaster recovery and it's focus within the emergency management context. It will explore the principles of community disaster recovery and examine how contemporary practice in community disaster recovery is evolving.The use of electronic technologies for communication is becoming more widely used within emergency management practice, and this subject provides students with the opportunity to use digital technologies to analyse and report on innovative contemporary community disaster recovery practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify, critically evaluate and reflect on innovative community disaster recovery practices.
Produce an audio-visual presentation on a selected innovative community disaster recovery practice.
Define what is meant by community disaster recovery.

title: Community Cultural Education Program
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for teacher education students to engage in community educational programs and experience educational opportunities that are linked to wider social issues and contexts. Teacher education students are required to complete 24 hours of community based service learning in an educational setting catering for adolescents or pre-adolescents other than a classroom. Students will broaden and deepen their understandings of issues confronting the wider education community and gain a greater awareness of the needs of diverse students through participation in a community educational program eg. holiday STEM programs, youth camps, PCYC, Sport and Recreation camps, Robocup, community literacy programs. Alternatively students may meet subject requirements through the completion of an international placement registered through CSU Global or an authorised cultural immersion program. The Community Cultural Education Program will provide teacher education students with the opportunity to develop respectful relationships and increase their familiarity with community based organisations, resources, policies and strategies which will potentially improve their professional abilities and broaden their professional knowledge and practice as a teacher.
learning_outcomes: Develop respectful relationships and have knowledge of community based organisations, resources, policies and strategies.
Employ strategies to support inclusive participation and engagement in learning activities in diverse settings.
Employ strategies to work effectively, sensitively and confidentially with carers/leaders/instructors/managers/supervisors/teachers.

Submit evidence of having satisfactorily completed a 24 hour placement in a structured community setting (other than a school classroom) catering for adolescents or pre-adolescents or an authorised cultural immersion program or a CSU Global registered placement or short term program.
Seek and apply constructive feedback received from supervisors.
prerequisites: EEB443: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Cultural Education Program

title: Community Histories
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the development and management of community history collections. Community history collections range from those in formal collecting institutions to the collections of local family, community and cultural groups and organisations. Such collections include those that seek to preserve histories within a specific community or cultural group or geographic area; the historical records of a specific community organisation; or the historical records of a community which is not confined to a specific geographic location, such as online common interest groups. The subject also examines the nature and significance of community history collections and reflects on the interplay between library and archival practices and the implications of community histories existing in a digital world in developing and managing such collections.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the nature and significance of community history collections.
Strategically apply a foundational understanding of library and archival practices integral to the development and management of community history collections in the digital environment.
Evaluate and apply policy requirements for a community history collection.
Identify and evaluate funding and development opportunities relevant to community history collections.

Assess and justify the need for community organisations to maintain their historical records in a sustainable, inclusive, and accessible manner which accurately reflects the evolution of that community.

title: Community Histories
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the development and management of community history collections. Community history collections range from those in formal collecting institutions to the collections of local family, community and cultural groups and organisations. Such collections include those that seek to preserve histories within a specific community or cultural group or geographic area; the historical records of a specific community organisation; or the historical records of a community which is not confined to a specific geographic location, such as online common interest groups. The subject also examines the nature and significance of community history collections and reflects on the interplay between library and archival practices and the implications of community histories existing in a digital world in developing and managing such collections.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and explain the need for community groups and organisations to maintain their historical records in a sustainable, inclusive, and accessible manner which reflects the evolution of that community.
Describe and discuss the nature and significance of community history collections.
Identify and review funding and development opportunities relevant to community history collections.
Identify policy requirements for a community history collection.
Apply a foundational understanding of library and archival practices integral to the development and management of community history collections in the digital environment.

title: Community Outreach
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the concepts of community and diversity (including age, socio-economic, mental and physical health, rural and remote communities, linguistic and cultural diversity) in the context of providing localised information-related community outreach services to diverse populations. Students are encouraged to explore diversity-related issues from within a framework of equity and social justice. Students will choose to explore these ideas from the perspective of a range of professional information settings (such as public libraries, academic libraries, specialised information agencies).
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on the concepts of community and diversity.
Appraise cross-cultural communication methods to support collaboration with diverse populations.
Evaluate the community outreach roles of a range of information organisation types.
Conceptually map the sociocultural makeup of a community.
Critically review the relationship between information services, and equity and social justice issues.
Design and justify an information related community outreach plan to meet the needs of a community group.

title: Community Law and Culture: Regional, Rural, Remote and Indigenous Contemporary Issues
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject is a capstone subject in the Bachelor of Laws. It addresses the classification of regional, rural, remote and very remote areas and particular legal and social issues that are relevant to regional, rural, remote and very remote Australia, and to First Nations communities. It covers topics such as legal need and access to legal services, the legal assistance sector, Indigenous law and culture, sovereignty and legal pluralism, and includes a focus on preparing for practice by investigating professional skills for legal practice, innovation and entrepreneurship, career planning and development.
learning_outcomes: Address critically the issues relating to legal need and access in regional, rural and remote Australia.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the nature of entrenched social patterns evident in some regional, rural and remote communities, and the limitations of the laws ability for addressing these contemporary social issues.
Reflect critically on the role of the lawyer in regional, rural and remote Australia.
Reflect on issues of Indigenous social justice, Indigenous dispute resolution, women and the legal system, and access to justice for those living in regional, rural and remote Australia.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the community issues that arise regularly in a regional, rural or remote legal practice, for example, domestic violence and agricultural-based crime.
Demonstrate an understanding of law reform processes and apply research and critical thinking to devise law and policy solutions to community issues .
Discuss critically the role of Indigenous law and culture and its relationship to the policy and legislation of the three tiers of government.
prerequisites: JST123: Indigenous Australians and Justice: An Introduction
LAW112: Introduction to the Australian Legal System
LAW116: Writing and Communication for Legal Professionals

title: Community Outreach
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the concepts of community and diversity (including age, socio-economic, mental and physical health, rural and remote communities, linguistic and cultural diversity) in the context of providing localised information-related community outreach services to diverse populations. Students are encouraged to explore diversity-related issues from within a framework of equity and social justice. Students will choose to explore these ideas from the perspective of a range of professional information settings (such as public libraries, academic libraries, specialised information agencies).
learning_outcomes: Explain the concepts of community and diversity.
Explore and describe the sociocultural makeup of a community.
Develop knowledge of effective cross-cultural communication methods to support collaboration with diverse populations.
Design an information related community outreach plan to meet the needs of a community group.
Articulate the community outreach roles of a range of information organisation types.
Reflect on the relationship between information services, and equity and social justice issues.

title: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 1
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 1 will be presented in a Problem Based Learning (PBL) format over four weeks based around authentic case studies. It will present cases related to companion animals, particularly illustrating the management of cases with a surgical focus. This subject addresses in particular the integration of pre- and para-clinical principles in order to diagnose and treat disease in individual companion animals. This subject will assist students to develop skills in researching and applying best-evidence to support life-long learning.
learning_outcomes: Integrate and act on information regarding client expectations, financial considerations, ethics and welfare specific to common scenarios in companion animals with a surgical focus.
Develop and refine the differential diagnoses associated with common presenting complaints in companion animals with a surgical focus.
Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with peers and staff.
Identify and explain the aetio-pathogenesis of common conditions of companion animals with a surgical focus.

Apply and integrate literacy and numerical knowledge from the pre-clinical and para-clinical disciplines, along with best evidence, to diagnose and manage clinical cases in companion animals with a surgical focus.
Identify risk factors for the occurence of common diseases or conditions in companion animals with a surgical focus.
prerequisites: VSC331: Diagnosis and Critical Thinking in Veterinary Science

title: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 2
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 2 will be presented in a Problem Based Learning (PBL) format over four weeks based around case studies. It will present cases related to companion animals, particularly illustrating the management of cases with a medical focus. This subject addresses in particular the integration of pre- and para-clinical principles in order to diagnose and treat disease in individual companion animals. This subject will assist students to develop skills in researching and applying best-evidence to support in life-long learning skills.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the aetio-pathogenesis of common conditions of companion animals with a medical focus.
Develop and refine the differential diagnoses associated with common presenting complaints in companion animals with a medical focus.
Identify risk factors for the occurrence of common diseases or conditions in companion animals with a medical focus.
Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with peers and staff.
Integrate and act on information regarding client expectations, financial considerations, ethics and welfare specific to common scenarios in companion animals with a medical focus.

Apply and integrate literacy and numerical knowledge from the pre-clinical and para-clinical disciplines, along with best evidence, to diagnose and manage clinical cases in companion animals with a medical focus.
prerequisites: VSC417: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 1

title: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 3
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 3 will be presented in a Problem Based Learning (PBL) format over four weeks based around case packages. It will present cases related to companion animals with a focus on requirement for acute and rapid response, particularly illustrating the management of complex medical and/or surgical cases in the individual animal. This subject addresses in particular the integration of pre- and para-clinical principles in order to diagnose and treat emergency disease in individual animals. This subject will assist students to develop skills in researching and applying best-evidence to result in life-long learning.
learning_outcomes: Integrate and act on information regarding client expectations, financial considerations, ethics and welfare specific to common scenarios in companion animals with a focus on requirement for acute and rapid response.

Apply and integrate literacy and numerical knowledge from the pre-clinical and para-clinical disciplines, along with best evidence, to diagnose and manage clinical cases in companion animals with a focus on the requirements for acute and rapid response.
Develop and refine the differential diagnoses associated with common presenting complaints in companion animals with a focus on the requirements for acute and rapid response.
Identify risk factors for the occurrence of common diseases or conditions in companion animals with a focus on the requirements for acute and rapid response.
Identify and explain the aetio-pathogenesis of common conditions of companion animals with a focus on the requirements for acute and rapid response.
Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with peers and university staff.
prerequisites: VSC425: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 2

title: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 4
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 4 will be presented in a Problem Based Learning (PBL) format over four weeks based around case packages. It will present complex cases related to companion animals, particularly illustrating the management of complex medical and/or surgical cases in the individual animal. This subject addresses in particular the integration of pre- and para-clinical principles in order to diagnose and treat complicated disease in individual animals. This subject will assist students to develop skills in researching and applying best-evidence to result in life-long learning.
learning_outcomes: Apply and integrate literacy and numerical knowledge from the pre-clinical and para-clinical disciplines, along with best evidence, to diagnose and manage complex clinical cases in companion animals.
Develop and refine the differential diagnoses associated with complex presenting complaints in companion animals.
Identify risk factors for the occurrence of complex diseases or conditions in companion animals.
Integrate and act on information regarding client expectations, financial considerations, ethics and welfare specific to complex scenarios in companion animals.
Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with peers and university staff.
Identify and explain the aetio-pathogenesis of complex conditions of companion animals.
prerequisites: VSC425: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 2

title: Company Accounting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the financial reporting skills and knowledge gained in successful completion of ACC222 External Reporting. The subject is designed to prepare students for sought after financial reporting roles in both business and practice. A range of challenging financial reporting topics including accounting for company income tax, consolidating financial statements, and accounting for foreign currency transactions and translations will be presented in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Prepare consolidated financial statements for economic entities where the parent has a 100% ownership interest in subsidiary and where a non-controlling interest is involved.
Compute and account for company income tax.
Translate the financial statements of an overseas controlled entity which have been denominated in a foreign currency.
Account for foreign currency transactions.
Account for and prepare relevant financial report disclosures in relation to investments in associates and business combinations.

title: Company Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the law governing the formation, regulation and termination of companies in Australia within the context of modern commercial practice. The internal operation of companies is discussed, particularly the role of members, meetings, the corporate constitution, the board of directors, and the duties of corporate directors and other officers. The topic of separate corporate personality is also discussed. In addition, students are introduced to contemporary legal and ethical issues in respect to corporate reporting and fundraising, along with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.
learning_outcomes: Understand different corporate governance structures, including Indigenous corporations.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the origins of companies and their role in society.
Interpret critically the rules of corporate governance, especially in respect to company financing and security arrangements.
Demonstrate an understanding of the roles, functions and duties of the board of directors, management and shareholders, and their relationships with other corporate stakeholders.
Discuss the role of agency law, including the creation of agency and the duties and rights of an agent.

Engage critically with the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) and the main case law relevant to its operation, including analysing the effect and operations of these laws on corporations and their stakeholders.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of a complex body of legal principles of corporate law and their relationship to the Australian legal landscape.
Demonstrate the application of legal principles relating to the management and control of a company, and the processes of winding up.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the incorporation process.
Think critically, strategically and creatively in preparing advice on corporate legal matters.
Identify and discuss the legal constraints imposed on different types of business structures, including partnerships.
Demonstrate professional communication skills through the development and presentation of a persuasive argument.
Analyse critically different types of companies, including not for profit entities, and reflect upon social policies underpinning this area of the law.
Demonstrate an understanding of the reason behind the concept of separate legal personality.

title: Comparative Anatomy
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Comparative anatomy continues the study of normal body organs and structures undertaken in Veterinary Anatomy but extends it to study systems not studied in the dog including special senses and reproductive anatomy and of features of veterinary interest in a wide range of species including birds and wildlife.
learning_outcomes: Relate these major anatomical characteristics to superficial features on the body of live animals.

Describe the normal structure, development and disposition of major organs and systems of veterinary significance of the following species. Ruminants, Horses, Chickens, Fish, Amphibians and Reptiles, Rodents and lagomorphs, Pigs and Tylopods.
Be familiar with basic anatomy, how it develops embryologically and understand the relationship between form and function, for organs of special sense and for the reproductive systems of mammals.
Relate the anatomy of these animals to their lifestyles, particularly their feeding strategies.
Use information presented on these species to understand and explain the anatomy of a range of vertebrate species not specifically studied in this course.
Integrate information from concurrent physiology subjects and apply this information to material covered in Comparative Anatomy.

title: Comparative Animal Anatomy and Physiology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject involves the study of the anatomy and physiology of a wide range of vertebrate species. An integrated approach is taken to explore the functional (and otherwise) anatomical and physiological similarities and differences between species including evolutionary, environmental and current societal perspectives. Central themes focus on homeostasis and the linkages between the environment and the context in which animals live. Physiological and anatomical adaptations of animals to their environment will be covered from both a systems (e.g. cardiovascular) and environmental (e.g. marine) perspective.
learning_outcomes: Identify, assess and predict how animals may cope and adapt to changing environments/environmental extremes.
Evaluate and predict how physiological mechanisms to maintain homeostasis may vary or differ in animals living in different environments.
Apply and demonstrate the use of appropriate scientific methods to design, conduct basic physiological research, effectively communicating the findings for diverse audiences.
Provide a justified evaluation of how specific adaptations in form (anatomy) or function (physiology) allow particular animals to survive in different environments.
Distinguish and consider the physiological mechanisms underlying animal physiology.
Identify and evaluate the anatomical adaptations of animals enabling them to survive in different environments.
prerequisites: ASC111: Comparative Animal Anatomy and Physiology

title: Comparative Indigenous Studies
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: Adopting a comparative method of inquiry, this subject introduces students to the cultures, histories and contemporary realities of the indigenous peoples of North America and New Zealand (Aotearoa) and explores the commonalities and differences of experience between Indigenous Australians and these Nation groups subjected to the processes of British colonisation. A range of contemporary issues which impact upon the indigenous peoples of North America and New Zealand will be examined, including indigenous struggles for recognition of rights in relation to land, self-determination and treaty rights, allowing students the opportunity to learn from international developments in indigenous affairs and how these developments may apply to the Australian context.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and articulate commonalities and differences of experience of the indigenous peoples of North America and New Zealand with those of Indigenous Australians.

Apply a comparative approach to the examination of commonalities and differences of experience of colonisation of the indigenous peoples of North America and New Zealand and a range of contemporary issues which impact upon or are of concern to them.
Describe the cultures, and post-invasion histories of the indigenous peoples of North America and New Zealand.
Relate the history of Treaty systems in North America, Canada and New Zealand and the benefits and weaknesses today in empowering rights and self determination for indigenous peoples.

title: Complex Analysis
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject allows you to appreciate how complex analysis extends the ideas of calculus to the complex plane, and throws light on real number problems. It generalises the concepts of calculus (limits, derivatives, Taylor series and integrals) to functions of complex variables. The subject culminates with residue theory and its applications to both complex and real integration. This subject enables you to be more familiar and comfortable with mathematical background, concepts and language necessary for the study of applicable mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concept of function as applied to complex numbers, and the ideas of limit, continuity, and differentiation of complex functions.
Apply residue theory to evaluate closed contour integrals.
Explain the nature of complex numbers, and their representation in the complex plane.
Identify elementary functions defined in terms of complex numbers.
Write complex functions as Taylor and Laurent series and.
Apply the techniques of integration in the complex plane.

title: Comparative Industrial Relations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is concerned with the structure and operation of industrial relations systems in different national contexts, such as Asia, Europe and the United States of America. A comparative approach with the Australian context is used to develop an understanding of the differences and similarities in industrial relations systems in different countries, and some of the factors that explain these differences.
learning_outcomes: Investigate industrial relations arrangements and activity in a number of countries.
Explain the potential benefits, problems and pitfalls associated with the study of comparative industrial relations.
Evaluate the similarities and differences in industrial relations arrangements and activity between countries.
Critically analyse Australian industrial relations system using the knowledge of comparative industrial relations gained in this subject.

title: Comparative Labour Relations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the employment relations systems of a collection of developed and developing countries. A key focus of comparative study is to gain insights into the strengths and limitations of different institutional arrangements, as well as to inform professional practice in a globally-interdependent world. Countries studied will vary according to contemporary issues.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the employment relations systems of selected countries, with reference to current issues in global business.
Critically reflect on the application of a comparative method in studying employment relations systems.
Apply industrial relations theory to analyse patterns of convergence and divergence in national employment relations systems.
Demonstrate the ability to prepare analytical, evidence-based argument in academic and business settings.

title: Complex Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject allows you to appreciate how complex analysis extends the ideas of calculus to the complex plane and throws light on real number problems. It generalises the concepts of calculus (limits, derivatives, Taylor series and integrals) to functions of complex variables. The subject culminates with residue theory and its applications to both complex and real integration. This subject enables you to be more familiar and comfortable with mathematical background, concepts and language necessary for the study of applicable mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Apply residue theory to evaluate closed contour integrals.
Explain the concept of function as applied to complex numbers, and the ideas of limit, continuity, and differentiation of complex functions.
Write complex functions as Taylor and Laurent series and.
Identify elementary functions defined in terms of complex numbers.
Apply the techniques of integration in the complex plane.
Explain the nature of complex numbers, and their representation in the complex plane.

title: Complex Clinical Pharmacology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will expand upon your previous clinical pharmacology studies. You will evaluate medication literature to determine the safety and efficacy of medication in polypharmacy cases. Case studies will increase in complexity through exploration of age variation, changes in clinical state, pharmacogenomics, pregnancy and breastfeeding. You will also have the opportunity to manage complex cases with other health professionals. You will further develop your literature evaluation skills by educating your colleagues on the pharmacotherapy of a medication that is not yet registered in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Detect medication related issues and justify medication related recommendations to ensure the quality use of medicine.
Identify adverse drug reactions and drug interactions, explain their mechanisms (if known), describe their consequences and recommend steps to manage or minimise their impact.
Interpret patient information and make recommendations to improve a patient's medication regimen.
Communicate and collaborate effectively in a team environment.
Identify and justify evaluation and monitoring steps to minimise patient harm and ensure effective use of medicine.
Recommend patient centred medication changes appropriate for the patient's age, clinical state, allergies, sensitivities, or whether the patient is pregnant or breastfeeding.
Explain how drugs can alter the progression of a pathophysiological condition or reduce the signs and/or symptoms associated with that condition.

title: Complex Mental Health Presentation and Management
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop students’ skills in caring for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples living with complex health and mental health concerns, and the communities in which they live. Students will examine the long-term outcomes of serious mental illness including medication side effect profiles and non-responsiveness to treatment, with a particular focus on the relevance of ageing and comorbidities. This subject will also explore neurodevelopmental disorders and neurocognitive disorders. Students will study forensic mental health and the Mental Health Act to enhance their understanding of the complexity of mental health, including classification of dual disability and dual diagnosis, for many of the people who are managed within the forensic mental health system.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate neurodevelopmental disorders and current treatment modalities to support people with dual disability.
Explain the pharmacology of medicines used in the management of complex mental illness.
Critique the forensic mental health care system in relation to the experience of people living with mental illness, substance misuse and dual disability.
Interpret aspects of neurocognitive impairment including causes and treatment options.
Explain other complex mental health presentations such as genetic disorders and dual diagnosis disorders.

title: Comprehensive Literature Review
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will progress and sharpen both the practical strategies necessary for the successful construction of a literature review, and the content knowledge relevant to the proposed research. Students will become thoroughly conversant with the literature of their intended area of study and understand the major processes, techniques, issues, problems and knowledge within their field of research that will enable them to complete a major draft literature review for their doctoral thesis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate intellectual independence to think critically, and in relation to the research problem evaluate existing knowledge and ideas, reflect on theory and practice and thereby make an original contribution to their field of research.
Identify and analyse existing sources of information that relate to the chosen research problem.
Plan and execute a framework which demonstrates knowledge of the processes and methods for a critical exploration of the literature pertaining to their research.
Communicate effectively the theoretical justifications for the research in a draft of a literature review chapter for their doctoral thesis.

title: Complexities in Midwifery Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will continue to develop the knowledge and skills required for woman-centred, evidence-informed midwifery care as they focus on complex childbearing and participate in simulation experiences to support their learning during their midwifery practice experience. Students will focus on accurate assessment, stabilising care, timely referral, and escalation within the interprofessional and intraprofessional teams. Students will also extend their capacity to plan strategies to empower women and their significant others to play an active role in decision-making when they experience complex childbearing.
learning_outcomes: Apply strategies to ensure that women experiencing complex childbearing remain central to decision making about themselves and their foetus.
Demonstrate advancing midwifery knowledge and skills required for safe, woman-centred care during complex childbearing and initiate appropriate action when there is an emergency.
Apply knowledge of the anatomical, physiological, social and emotional changes that occur during complex childbearing to provide woman-centred, culturally safe and evidence-informed midwifery care.
Identify deviations from normal and consult, refer and collaborate with other healthcare professionals to initiate appropriate action in an obstetric emergency.

title: Computed Tomography
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with a detailed understanding of the principles and practice of Computed Tomography (CT). The subject explores the physics and instrumentation of CT, techniques and protocols employed in CT, and clinical applications utilised for CT in clinical practice. The subject also explores relevant regulations, quality assurance, department planning and radiation/hazard protection involved in the application of CT. The subject specifically provides insight and understanding into stand-alone CT devices, hybrid CT devices (SPECT/CT, PET/CT), CT for therapeutic use (planning and verification) and innovative CT designs.
learning_outcomes: Explain radiation risks, international best practice and statutory requirements for CT, and plan / strategies to control and minimise risk, recognising and describing appropriate safety management in the workplace, explaining legislative and regulatory requirements for managing radiation and incidents, and applying and explaining the principles of ALARA and TDS (MRPBA Domain 5.1).
Explain the reconstructions and use of 3D datasets including demonstrating management of data (MRPBA Domain 1B.4f and 1.2).
Understand, explain and apply principles for appropriate CT parameters and dose based on patient presentation (MRPBA Domain 1B.4b-c, 1.4 and 1.5).
Recognise, describe and apply knowledge of radiation physics and instrumentation to operate CT systems safely and effectively (MRPBA Domain 1B.4a).
Understand, explain and apply principles for contrast and non-contrast CT performance, and demonstrate capacity to modify protocol where appropriate (MRPBA Domain 1B.4e and 1.3).

Perform quality control of 3D datasets, identify limitations and recognise artefacts in 3D datasets, including identifying and reporting artefacts that represent urgent or unexpected findings (MRPBA Domain 1.2).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1).
Describe, explain, evaluate and develop CT protocols in a collaborative manner (MRPBA Domain 1B.4d and 3.2).
Implement techniques for patient/client stabilisation and reproducibility of procedures and outcomes (MRPBA Domain 1.6).

title: Computed Tomography Practice And Trends
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the theoretical components to the modality of Computed Tomography (CT), and also examines new techniques and applications of CT. The aim of this subject is to provide the theoretical basis of the practice, new techniques and applications of CT scanning, and the mechanism to acquire information in order to perform as a professional in the field of CT. Emphasis will be placed upon the scanning techniques, scan protocols, clinical indications of the scan, pathology shown, and patient management. Emerging developments, whether they be in clinical practice, contrast agents, equipment or safety practice, will be examined. The subject also offers theoretical mechanisms to develop CT management policies and CT safety procedures for practice in CT scanning.
learning_outcomes: Review and synthesise appropriate literature in relation to current CT practice and medical radiations interdisciplinary learning.
Apply and discuss the technical knowledge required to perform the specialised procedures used in clinical CT.
Analyse the relationship between radiation dose, clinical practice and image quality in relation to best practice.
Apply knowledge and skills, and critically reflect on the clinical practice of CT in the areas undertaken in this subject.
prerequisites: MRS564: Computed Tomography Practice And Trends
MRS564: Computed Tomography Practice And Trends

title: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to calculus and linear algebra, with an emphasis on understanding and applications addressed in geometry, physics, economics and environmental modelling. A symbolic algebra package, Maple, is used to assist with computation. Every topic will be presented geometrically, numerically and algebraically. Formal definitions will be based on investigation and practical problems.
learning_outcomes: Use derivatives in applications, including rates of change, graphing, optimisation and approximation.
Use differentiation, integration and linear algebra to solve a wide range of applied problems.
Graph and solve equations involving the most common functions including algebraic, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions.
Solve systems of linear equations.
Calculate a determinant of a matrix.
Calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix.
Differentiate simple functions, including implicit functions.
Integrate simple functions, analytically and numerically.
Use integrals in applications, including area, volume, arclength and average.
Use Maple to help solve mathematical problems.
Calculate limits.
Describe the connections between a function, its derivative and its integral.
Perform addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, matrix multiplication, transposition and inversion of matrices.
prerequisites: MTH401: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to calculus and linear algebra, with an emphasis on understanding and applications addressed in geometry, physics, economics and environmental modelling. A symbolic algebra package, Maple, is used to assist with computation. Every topic will be presented geometrically, numerically and algebraically. Formal definitions will be based on investigation and practical problems
learning_outcomes: Describe the connections between a function, its derivative and its integral.
Formulate and evaluate integrals for area, volume, arc length, and average.
Analyse complex problems, transform them into mathematical forms and solve them using appropriate methods.
Perform addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, matrix multiplication, transposition and inversion of matrices.
Differentiate simple functions, including implicit functions.
Graph and solve equations involving the most common functions including algebraic, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions.
Integrate simple functions, analytically and numerically.
Solve systems of linear equations.
Use derivatives in applications, including rates of change, graphing, optimisation and approximation.
Calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and interpret these in linear transformations.
Calculate a determinant of a matrix.
Calculate limits.
Use mathematical software for solving and communicating complex mathematical problems.
prerequisites: MTH101: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Computer Aided Mathematics 2 with Applications
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to continue to develop students' ability to apply commonly used techniques in applied mathematics. Topics include integration, differential equations and modelling, series (including Taylor series), vectors and functions of several variables and complex numbers. The subject will also enable students to develop their skill in using a computer based algebra system.
learning_outcomes: Use a computer algebra system to assist with calculations and graphs.
Use techniques of integration.
Calculate and use Taylor series approximations.
Use techniques of calculus for functions of several variables.
Solve simple differential equations.
Perform calculations with complex numbers.
prerequisites: MTH402: Computer Aided Mathematics 2 with Applications
MTH101: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Computer Aided Mathematics 2 with Applications
school: School of Education

Topics include integration, differential equations and modelling, series (including Taylor series), vectors and functions of several variables and complex numbers. The subject will also enable students to develop their skill in using a computer-based algebra system.
learning_outcomes: Analyse complex problems, transform them into mathematical form and solve them using appropriate methods.
Calculate and apply Taylor series approximations.
Perform calculations with complex numbers.
Use mathematical software for solving and communicating complex mathematical problems.
Solve simple differential equations.
Apply techniques of integration.
Apply techniques of calculus for functions of several variables.
prerequisites: MTH401: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications
MTH102: Computer Aided Mathematics 2 with Applications

title: Computer Graphics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students learn how to write interactive computer graphics programs using a standard graphics library. An understanding of the graphics system architecture provides a sound basis for application program design. Students study how to model objects in 2D and 3D, and how to transform and project them for viewing. Algorithms for clipping, rasterisation, hidden-surface removal and antialiasing are covered.
learning_outcomes: Write well-designed interactive graphics programs, using a standard graphics library, which may include 2D objects, 3D objects, basic animation and arbitrary projection points.
Describe, explain and analyse algorithms for common graphics system processing operations.
Describe, implement and analyse data structures and algorithms for transforming and projecting objects for viewing in 2D and 3D.
Describe, implement and analyse data structures and algorithms for modelling objects in 2D and 3D.
Interpret and assess the features and operations of a graphics system.

title: Computer Networks
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students learn the architectures, models, protocols, and networking elements that connect users, devices, applications and data through the Internet and across modern computer networks - including IP addressing and Ethernet fundamentals. Students design, test and analyse the elements of small to medium-sized networks. The concepts covered in this subject enable students to develop skills related to cabling, IP addressing, configuring and routing. This subject is the first in a series of three subjects that incorporate the Cisco Networking Academy Program.
learning_outcomes: Explain critical concepts in Local Area Networks.
Analyse the communication processes across different levels in the layered architecture.
Design, calculate and apply subnetting in IP networks.
Describe and design the addressing and naming schemes of data networks.
