Perform and analyse tasks related to basic network configuration for routers and switches and testing.
Implement foundational network security.

title: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation FT
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop practical insights into real-world research writing and dissemination processes. Students will be enabled with supported autonomy to apply advanced knowledge and skills in research practices to produce a completed research dissertation. This will involve planning and executing a research project through the completion of a literature review, data collection and analysis of results culminating in the research dissertation.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the research process and progress.
Complete and analyse a research project.
Write a final dissertation that brings together all the parts of the project and can be understood by experts in the field.
Critically review, appraise and synthesise academic literature relevant to the chosen research problem.
Communicate effectively in ways appropriate to the discipline, audience and purpose.
prerequisites: HRC417: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation PT Part A
HRC418: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation PT Part B

title: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation PT Part B
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will complete their planned Honours research. Students will be guided by their supervisor(s) to develop their knowledge, skills, and confidence as a researcher, particularly in relation to data analysis and interpretation. Through regular communication with their supervisor(s), students will have opportunities to reflect on their collected data, analyses, and interpretations to produce a completed research dissertation.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate the rationale, method, and results of a research project via a research dissertation.
Demonstrate knowledge of research methods and sound study design, including how study design can impact on the interpretation of data.
Reflect on the impact of the research findings.
Demonstrate knowledge and skills of data analysis and interpretation.
prerequisites: HRC417: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation PT Part A
HRC432: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation FT

title: Computer Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the function and characteristics of various computer system components necessary to process information digitally. It develops knowledge of computer hardware, and computer organisation and architecture, and their relationship to software performance. Current trends in computing technologies are also introduced.
learning_outcomes: Describe the essential elements of computer organisation and discuss how the elements function.
Describe the basic instruction set architecture of a simple computer.
Apply Boolean algebra and digital logic to understand computer operation.
Discuss various programming tools available and their relationship to the computer architecture and.
Define and appropriately use computer systems terminologies.
Describe the concepts of data representations and use appropriate methods of implementation.
Discuss the general trends in computing technologies including examples of leading edge developments.
prerequisites: ITC577: Information and Communication Technology Fundamentals

title: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation PT Part A
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will begin their planned Honours research activities, under the guidance of their Honours supervisor(s). Through engaging in their research project, students will develop their knowledge, skills, and confidence as a novice researcher. This may include knowledge and skills to obtain the ethics approval required to commence their data collection. Through regular communication with their supervisor(s), students will also have opportunities to reflect on their research practices, experiences, and learning.
learning_outcomes: Succinctly report on their research progress in a way that shows increasing independence as a novice researcher.
Demonstrate the ability to obtain ethics approval with supervisor guidance (if necessary) and begin collecting and/or analysing data to address a research question.
Reflect on their research progress during regular supervision conversations including strengths and skills they are developing, issues they have encountered, and problem-solving they have engaged in.
Critically use theory in the development of an individual research dissertation.
prerequisites: HRC432: Computing and Mathematics Honours Dissertation FT

title: Concepts in Image-Making
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject expands on fundamental skills within visual communication by exploring what it means to make and read images. Through the consideration of diverse perspectives on a core problem, students will gain a deep appreciation of historical and contemporary creative practices. They will learn to develop and refine their own creative practice, and constructively critique the work of others.
learning_outcomes: Develop, maintain and complete creative projects in response to conceptual stimuli.
Interpret and critically approach visual problems, based on investigative research using historical and contemporary sources.
Creatively respond to visually orientated conceptual problems.
Combine image, text, and format to convey ideas and information.
Demonstrate an understanding of the effect of different technologies upon processes and outcomes.

title: Computing Placement 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on prior industry experience gained in ITC317 Computing Placement 1 by supporting students in undertaking increasingly independent professional practice in computing and information technology settings. Students critically reflect on workplace experiences, apply and extend technical and problem-solving skills to industry projects, and demonstrate professionalism, collaboration, and career readiness through the completion of a professional portfolio and reflective industry engagement activities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective professional communication, collaboration, and initiative within multidisciplinary workplace teams.
Apply computing concepts, technical skills, and problem-solving approaches to real-world industry tasks and projects.
Critically reflect on professional practice, workplace experiences, and personal development within computing environments.
Refine and present a professional portfolio demonstrating technical capability, workplace achievements, and career readiness.
Demonstrate ethical conduct, cultural awareness, critical thinking, and professional responsibility when contributing to workplace activities and projects in diverse professional environments.

title: Concepts of Biology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to the study of biology. The syllabus covers seven key topics relevant to first year students commencing a degree in the life sciences and therefore effectively offers an introductory biology subject for all science courses, particularly animal science, as well as an introduction to plant science. The topics covered include: the cell, biomolecules and cellular biochemistry, cellular reproduction and genetics, animal anatomy and physiology, plant anatomy and physiology, evolution, ecology, and the biodiversity of life. Contemporary learning materials and an emphasis on real-world applications encourage students to engage with the topics, irrespective of their course.
learning_outcomes: Describe the importance of diversity, evolution and the basic ecological drivers and interactions in populations, communities and ecosystems.
Apply basic techniques and become familiar with the equipment used to conduct biological investigations.
Observe and record scientific information.
Explain key biological concepts related to the cell, biochemistry and inheritance.
Explain key biological concepts related to both animal and plant anatomy and physiology.
Describe and classify the biological basis for life.

title: Conservation Biology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Conservation biology is the scientific study of the Earth's biodiversity with the aim of protecting genetic diversity, species, their habitats and ecosystems. In this subject, students build on their understanding of ecology to learn about genetic, species and ecosystem diversity, the main threats to biodiversity, and the current mass extinction crisis due to anthropogenic influences. We review a range of management approaches that are used in conservation biology to increase genetic health, population numbers and ecosystem functioning. Current and emerging conservation issues with potential socio-economic consequences are explored and discussed. On completion students are able to make professional judgments to generate possible strategies and courses of action to address conservation issues.
learning_outcomes: Explain and discuss the current biodiversity crisis, threatening processes and the need for conservation.
Analyse conservation strategies and evaluate the effectiveness of strategies that are implemented for the conservation of biodiversity.
Explain and summarise the key terminology, principles and concepts underpinning conservation biology.

title: Conservation Management of Birds
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Bird populations worldwide are experiencing dramatic declines due to habitat loss, poaching, climate change, invasive predators, and diseases. This subject investigates conservation strategies designed to mitigate and reverse these declines and prevent species extinction. Students will examine hands-on conservation management techniques for birds, both in their natural habitats (in situ) and in captivity (ex situ). Students will start by examining the key threats to bird populations, followed by an in-depth exploration of conservation strategies, including habitat restoration, species translocations, reintroductions, and captive breeding programs. Through the analysis of real-world case studies, students will investigate how successful bird conservation programs integrate community engagement with evidence-based research.
learning_outcomes: Appraise appropriate avian husbandry and discuss disease management.
Apply in-depth knowledge of conservation biology to develop, discuss and communicate effectively future approaches to address regional and national bird population declines.
Evaluate and synthesise the current threats to bird populations and develop appropriate management techniques for birds in the wild and in captivity.
Analyse and evaluate community and governmental support needed to address logistical and financial challenges in bird conservation and management.

title: Conservation Biology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Since prehistoric times, humans have been concerned about their environment. However, over the last few centuries, an ever-increasing human population and associated technologies have had a profound impact on Earth’s biological diversity. Conservation biology is the applied science discipline that aims to reduce any further losses of biodiversity by protecting populations, species and ecosystems. In this subject, students build on their understanding of ecology to learn about threats to biodiversity, extinction processes, and how to maintain and manage populations effectively. A range of case studies and management approaches from around the world will be presented and discussed. On completion, students are able to make professional assessments on possible strategies and courses of action to address conservation issues.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of scientific methods used in biology to design conservation studies and critically review conservation management strategies.
Explain key terminology in conservation science and synthesise principles and processes underlying the current biodiversity crisis.

Apply in-depth knowledge of conservation biology and conservation case studies to develop, discuss and communicate effectively future policies and approaches to address sometimes complex conservation issues at a regional, national and international level.
Analyse, synthesise and present a broad range of scientific evidence on conservation issues with an integrated understanding of the underlying theory to non-specialist and specialist audiences.

title: Consolidation of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will further develop fundamental principles and practical skills for the physiotherapy management of musculoskeletal presentations (including sports injuries). Students will apply a problem solving approach in the assessment and management of specific presentations that may affect the musculoskeletal system. Learning in this subject will focus initially on the upper limb and progress to the cervical spine and systemic inflammatory conditions. This subject builds on skills learnt in PHS313 in communication, professional and ethical behaviour, and other elements of professional practice including reflection and critical analysis.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively to involve the client and relevant others in the planning and implementation of musculoskeletal physiotherapy practice.
Demonstrate and articulate sound clinical reasoning processes which explore, explain and analyse assessment findings.
Reflect on professional practice to determine the actions they need to undertake to continually improve; to recognise situations outside their competence; and to take timely and appropriate actions.
Critically analyse resources, synthesise the information and communicate effectively according to the context and audience.
Justify situations in which physiotherapy management is no longer required and cease physiotherapy or refer to another practitioner.
Plan and apply a range of physiotherapy assessment and evaluation techniques using tests, imaging, tools and outcome measures relevant to the upper limb, thoracic and cervical spine.
Plan and implement safe and effective physiotherapy management for disorders of the upper limb, thoracic and cervical spine.
Make and act on informed and appropriate decisions about acceptable professional and ethical behaviours.
Apply evidence-based, person-centred self-management strategies for pain that promote a person's general well-being.
Locate, evaluate and use evidence-based information to inform decision making and develop and guide their own knowledge, learning and practice.
prerequisites: PHS313: Foundations of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice
BMS271: Functional Anatomy of the Head, Neck, Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limb

title: Constitutional Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses state, territory and Commonwealth constitutional law in Australia. It provides students with an understanding of the relationships between the differing levels of government in Australia, and addresses a range of constitutional law issues, including sovereignty, separation of powers, rule of law, and human rights. In addition, the role of the High Court in shaping Commonwealth legislative powers over States is addressed, as well as the limitations of legislative and executive power of the Commonwealth over states and territories. It provides an historical and cultural context for the application of constitutional law in the rapidly changing contemporary state, territory and Commonwealth governments.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an informed understanding of the origins and formation of the Commonwealth constitution.
Plan and apply legal research skills in the interpretation of constitutional law in order to resolve hypothetical legal problems.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of constitutional law, including the role of the High Court in formulating constitutional law reform.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the points of difference between the various state, territory and Commonwealth constitutions and constitutional systems.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the processes and challenges involved in federation.
Demonstrate an understanding of specific 'heads of power' such as trade, commerce, taxation, corporations and external affairs powers.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of the origins and formations of the Commonwealth constitution including the exclusion of specific groups such as Indigenous Australians and women.

Demonstrate an understanding of the procedures and processes of the High Court's ability under the Commonwealth Constitution to declare valid or invalid state, territory and Commonwealth government legislation, and its potential impact on Australian society.
Demonstrate an understanding of the constitution and operation of the legislature, executive and judiciary.
Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between different institutions of government and separation of powers.
Critically reflect on the diversity amongst Indigenous Australians with reference to constitutional law reform.

title: Constructing Effective Learning Environments for Adults
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops the students' understanding of their role as a manager of the learning setting and the importance of creating a motivating learning environment. This involves recognising the impact of the teacher and the importance of relationships within the learning setting. This subject addresses learning management issues and develops critical thinking around the theory and practice of the management of different adult and vocational learning contexts.
learning_outcomes: Apply effective teaching and learning strategies in the management of different adult and vocational learning contexts.
Evaluate a variety of theoretical models and approaches to the management of learners and the learning environment.
Examine key policy documents and resources that assist teachers to create effective adult and vocational learning environments.
Apply theoretical perspectives to group and individual learning management situations.

title: Consumer Behaviour
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Consumer behaviour explores the consumer decision-making process. This process is affected by situational, internal and external factors. This subject is designed to help the student see consumer behaviour from the marketer's perspective. Therefore, students will be able to link consumer behaviour theory to marketing strategy.
learning_outcomes: Apply consumer behaviour models to a range of diverse, real life situations for an organisation's marketing strategy.
Identify the components of consumer behaviour models and illustrate how those components work together.
Identify and describe the behaviour of consumers in the marketplace.
Predict consumer behaviour using relevant theoretical models.
Gather and interpret information from a range of academic and industry sources related to consumer behaviour.

title: Consultancy for Farming Systems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will take their problem-solving skills to a higher level. Students will learn to analyse the farm manager's personal attributes, their considerations in decision making, and incorporate these features into their analysis of real-world farm management scenarios. Students will also develop project management skills and be exposed to the professional community of Agricultural consultants to ensure high relevance of consultancy skills upon entering the workforce.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the development of consultancy skills for practice.
Integrate agricultural knowledge to address real-world problems.
Appraise farm management and decision-making styles and evaluate its impact on the consultancy process.

Apply skills in project management, situation enquiry, systems analysis, problem identification and analysis, time management, holistic evaluation of management options, recommendation formulation and communication as consistent with professional consultancy practice.

title: Containers and Virtualisation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on container virtualization using open-source technologies that automate the deployment of applications. Students of the subject will create and run their own custom container environment, from the base operating system through to the entire container platform. Students will also study the appropriate use of different container types and how to apply them in a business context.
learning_outcomes: Configure networking between containers.
Design a secure container environment.
Design and manage a cluster of containers.
Build and maintain a container for a custom application.
Determine the appropriate use of different container types and/or virtual machines.
Install and configure a container engine.
Apply containers to business workflows.

title: Contemporary and Emerging Issues in Animal Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is the capstone subject for all students in the final year of the Bachelor of Animal Science degree, allowing for a culmination of experiences, and the synthesis and application of knowledge from across the various aspects of Animal Science studied in the preceding years. In this subject, students will investigate and evaluate contemporary local and global influences on animal production and wildlife conservation, including major emerging issues affecting policy and practice within the animal science sphere. Students will also gain an appreciation of the complexities of the interrelationships between humans, animal production and wildlife conservation, including the impacts of differing human cultural values and beliefs. Through the use of workshops and discussion groups, individual involvement and engagement with the subject matter will be fostered. These activities will provide students with an opportunity for discussion, debate, problem solving and thinking about the future. This subject also includes reflection and assessment of work place learning undertaken prior to enrolment in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Develop and explain strategies or solutions applicable to animal enterprises that address challenges identified in the relevant industries.
Summarise, justify and communicate information effectively in a style appropriate to the audience.
Work effectively and with initiative both independently and as part of a team to meet individual, team or class outcomes.
Prepare and present a workplace learning portfolio that encompasses experiences, skills, knowledge, capabilities and reflective practice.

Investigate and evaluate complex issues through innovative and critical use of a variety of available data sources, and the scientific literature, and then synthesise the information to form and defend a cogent argument supporting a viewpoint on these issues.
Critically evaluate one's own ideas and those of peers.

Critically discuss and appraise the complexity of, and interrelationships between environmental, ethical, cultural and social issues relevant to the animal sciences and their incorporation into decision making.
prerequisites: ASC308: Contemporary and Emerging Issues in Animal Science
ASC307: Critical Reviews in Animal Science

title: Contemporary and Emerging Issues in Crime and Justice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This Applied Criminology Subject seeks to address a series of contemporary and emerging issues in criminology and criminal justice. Various aspects of the criminal justice system (CJS), both in Australia and internationally, along with the broader socio-political context in which the systems operate, will be considered.The subject further seeks to extend upper level student knowledge of criminology and criminal justice to contemporary and emerging domestic and international issues relevant to professional practice, focussing on the most cutting edge innovations in the field. Students will be exposed to a range of contemporary and emerging issues in crime and justice in which the impact on private individuals, communities, corporate entities, government, law enforcement agencies, regulatory agencies and the criminal justice system will be examined. Students will apply theoretical and practical approaches in considering issues such as modern slavery, Trafficking in Cultural Property, Risk Screening and Creative Corrections.
learning_outcomes: Analyse various criminological problems and their resolutions both at a theoretical and practical level.
Explain and analyse the interaction between policy and research.
Demonstrate an awareness of the fluid nature of the discipline.
Explain and analyse the interaction between criminological theory and policy.
Analyse and evaluate strengths and weaknesses of research in the areas being studied.
Analyse and evaluate strengths and weaknesses in the CJS response and provisions for each issue.

title: Contemporary Approaches to Biblical Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject compares and contrasts major contemporary approaches to the study of the Old and New Testaments. It traces recent developments in Biblical Studies, paying particular attention to methodology, both in a theoretical framework and through an analysis of a variety of concrete exegetical problems.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique selected methods and their contribution to the solution of particular exegetical or theological problems.
Demonstrate independent research and writing skills.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of major methodological options in contemporary Biblical Studies.
Show advanced skills in biblical exegesis.

title: Contemporary Cost Accounting for Management Decision-making
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on management accounting for cost and control purposes in an organisational context. The subject builds on the introductory topics in ACG511 and assumes knowledge of the management tools for data analysis in ACG512. Emphasis is placed on the use of quantitative techniques and computer software including spreadsheets. The subject includes an overview of management accounting perspectives with an emphasis on systems design and provides a framework for problem solving and analysis of conventional and modern cost accounting paradigms.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and critique the historical and ethical development of management accounting.
Critically evaluate the design and operation of performance management systems.
Critique how managers make decisions.
Use quantitative techniques and computer software including using the Internet as a professional source.
Apply cognitive skills in the design and operation of costing systems.

Apply analytical and synthesis skills in report preparation in order to communicate clearly and concisely in a range of formal and informal situations and settings that engage, persuade, motivate and inform stakeholders using a range of technologies and presentation strategies.
Explain the role of management accounting in organisational contexts and the implications for management accounting of different paradigms.
Use information and communication technology advances that support data analysis and decision making to create and implement computerised decision models.
prerequisites: ACC512: Management Accounting for Costs and Control

title: Contemporary Approaches to Biblical Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject compares and contrasts major contemporary approaches to the study of the Old and New Testaments. It traces recent developments in Biblical Studies, paying particular attention to methodology, both in a theoretical framework and through an analysis of a variety of concrete exegetical problems.
learning_outcomes: Show advanced skills in biblical exegesis.
Demonstrate independent research and writing skills.
Analyse and critique selected methods and their contribution to the solution of particular exegetical or theological problems.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of major methodological options in contemporary Biblical Studies.
prerequisites: THL411: Contemporary Approaches to Biblical Studies

title: Contemporary Education Professionals
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This compulsory subject is designed to introduce students to Masters level study in education and the concepts, skills and capacities necessary to ensure success in future learning at this level. Students in this subject will examine core concepts about being a contemporary education professional across a range of contexts in order to formulate personal professional learning goals. They will investigate issues, and develop skills of critical analysis and reflection, as they engage with diverse materials and with each other during the subject. Students will reflect on their new understandings and learnings through the lens of their own contexts, experiences and beliefs. A further core element of this subject is the development of skills to use ICTs and digital technologies to support learning throughout the Masters program, and in the preparation of an ongoing e-Portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Formulate personal professional learning goals through a reflection on personal capabilities, research, professional standards and feedback.
Evaluate information, concepts and theories that justify professional practice.
Demonstrate critical reflection in the preparation and maintenance of an e-Portfolio as a learning and assessment tool.
Analyse developments in education with reference to research and evidence from a range of contexts.

title: Contemporary Curriculum, Policy and Practice Landscapes
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines contemporary debates relevant to curriculum and policy networks and their influence on curriculum work in schools. Students will explore contemporary curriculum and policy trends and the international networks that shape them. Students will map education policy priorities relevant to their educational setting and analyse how these policies shape curriculum development and practice. From these investigations, students will critically engage with policy representations of educational ‘problems’ and propose alternative approaches to addressing contemporary educational challenges. This subject is foundational to understanding the complex networks of educational policy and politics from elsewhere that shape education in ‘the local’ today.
learning_outcomes: Critically review the social, historical, cultural, political and economic conditions that shape local and international educational policy trends, including in relation to First Nations people.
Critically evaluate practices of curriculum and policy interpretation, translation and enactment in context.

Critically evaluate how curriculum and policy positions First Nations young people, people from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, and young people with a range of additional learning needs.
Map local curriculum landscapes and the policy settings that shape them.

Analyse the intersections and competing priorities across the UN sustainable development goals and local policy texts such as the Education Declaration, Close the Gap, and the National School Reform Agreement.

title: Contemporary Employability and Learning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is the first of a series of employability and professional practice subjects which focus on employability skills, personal skills and career planning. This subject has a particular emphasis on enhancing professional knowledge of working in a business environment, and understanding the value of workplace learning and lifelong learning. Students will also audit, reflect on, and expand on their employability skills.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on personal career and life choices.
Discuss the relationship between workplace learning, lifelong learning, career and life development, and apply this personally.
Identify personal examples of key employability skills, evaluate where personal skills require development and create a plan of action to show how skills will be developed.
Understand and evaluate the needs and drivers of regional businesses.

title: Contemporary Employability Skills and Reflective Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the employability and personal skills critical for professional practice. The subject has a particular emphasis on enhancing professional knowledge of working in a business environment, and understanding the value of workplace learning and lifelong learning. Students will also audit, reflect on, and expand on their employability skillset.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on personal career and life choices.
Create an action plan to address existing skills and capabilities gaps.
Critically evaluate personal employability skills, knowledge and capabilities.
Analyse the relationship between workplace learning, lifelong learning, career and life development, and apply this personally.

title: Contemporary Indigenous Australian Realities
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject has been designed in module format to provide students with knowledge and understanding of contemporary issues which are of interest to Indigenous Australian people. Students will reflect on their own standpoints as they explore the topics and Indigenous perspectives will be prioritised throughout this exploration. Students will explore the colonial foundations of a relevant discipline and will apply decolonising practices as a way to contribute to a more socially just society.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the links between contemporary circumstances as the trans-generational legacies of colonisation.
Outline a range of contemporary circumstances which impact on Indigenous Australians.
Identify ways to activate human rights and contribute to social justice both individually and professionally in ways which are informed by Indigenous Australian perspectives.
Examine the relationship between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples' contemporary experiences through an exploration of standpoint.
Explore the colonial foundations of a relevant discipline and apply decolonising practices.

title: Contemporary Issues in Agriculture
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a systems theory framework for analysing and applying critical thinking to contemporary global issues in agriculture. Students will investigate complex agricultural issues including globalised trade networks, food-based social movements, Indigenous Australian knowledges, sustainability challenges and the economic, social, cultural and political influences affecting change in agricultural systems, practices and policies. The subject focuses on local-global integrated dynamics of agriculture, with specific attention to people and the people-centred nature of agriculture. Students will be introduced to social research methodology and will have the opportunity to investigate a case study in-depth. Students will explore multiple techniques for communicating their findings via a range of media.
learning_outcomes: Apply systems thinking approaches, informed by ethical decision making, to identify creative solutions to wicked agricultural issues.
Develop a problem-solving strategy to address an agricultural issue.
Communicate to a professional audience.
Explain and critically analyse a range of social, economic, environmental and political issues affecting the practice of agriculture globally.
Critically analyse the role of Indigenous Australian cultural practices in contemporary agriculture.
Locate, critically evaluate, manage and use information and research to synthesise and guide their own knowledge and learning.
Apply skills in social research and analysis to investigate an issue.

title: Contemporary Issues in Community Development
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores community development theory and practice as it relates to human services. Students examine key concepts in community development and practice, including grassroots engagement, empowerment pedagogies, the role of new social movements, critical perspectives in community development and practice, the relevance of post-colonial theory to community development practices and Indigenous Australian perspectives of community development. It also covers a range of community development skills and strategies as well as contemporary barriers and threats to community development. The subject equips students to be able to engage diverse communities at different scales and to engage in community development aimed at promoting empowerment, social justice, environmental and ecological justice and human rights.
learning_outcomes: Explain and analyse the role and focus of community development in relation to contemporary issues associated with social, ecological and environmental justice.
Apply community development knowledge and skills, including from Indigenous Australian perspectives to human services practice.
Discuss and analyse key concepts in community development.
Evaluate a range of contemporary community development strategies, including barriers and threats to community development practice, and apply this knowledge to a range of human service contexts.

title: Contemporary Issues in Gerontology
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores a range of contemporary issues of significance to healthy ageing, for example: impacts of and planning for the ageing population; identity and ageing in place; ageing and climate change; indigenous experiences of ageing in Australia; gender aspects of ageing and aged care. An alternative contemporary topic of relevance to student may be chosen in negotiation with subject coordinator. Students will research their topic and critically analyse the representations of this issue in the public domain, including within news and current affairs commentary, entertainment media, in government policy, in gerontological literature and research and within expert and public debate. Themes underlying the examination of the chosen topic include how issues are represented in contemporary debate, rights, anti-discriminatory practice and advocacy. Assessments enable practice of skills including high level critical analysis, advocacy and formal report writing.
learning_outcomes: Utilise a relevant formal report format to present findings on the selected topic.
Define, explain and analyse the topic selected for their intensive study.

Examine and critique the current status of knowledge, policy and practice within the topic selected, and identify areas for development and implementation of new knowledge and policy and/or improved practice.
Research, interpret, analyse and contribute to community and professional debate on contemporary and changing needs of older people.
Identify and employ a range of skills to engage in advocacy for older peoples rights and needs.

title: Contemporary Issues in Financial Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines money laundering, terrorism financing and financial crime prevention within organisational settings, both public and private. Theoretical perspectives on the incidence, and control of these crimes will be examined, along with the contemporary implementation of related standards, policies and processes. Students will be introduced to the role of the financial crime prevention manager and explore the intricacies involved in the development of a financial crime prevention framework. The effectiveness of these systems will be examined.
learning_outcomes: Critique the nexus between AML/CTF and financial crime prevention strategies and criminological explanations of crime.
Create and communicate a financial crime control plan that incorporates regulatory, technological and social controls.
Evaluate the effectiveness of AML/CTF and financial crime prevention strategies implemented in modern organisational settings.

title: Contemporary Issues in HRM
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: As human resource management (HRM) is an evolving field this subject seeks to explore a variety of contemporary issues and challenges. The topics covered will reflect the changing organisational and societal expectations of HRM and its contribution to organisations and their sustainable operations. This subject is the capstone unit for the Graduate Diploma/Masters of HRM
learning_outcomes: Research and critically analyse contemporary and emergent HRM issues and evaluate their impact on business performance.
Develop skills to foster collaboration and communication, transfer knowledge and ideas, build teams and influence stakeholders on issues relevant to HR operations and organisational sustainability.
Appraise, evaluate, and prioritise HR issues and consider implications including those impacting on a productive, sustainable and engaging workplace.
Apply industry specific good practice frameworks and processes in developing HR policies, procedures and recommendations in response to emergent and contemporary issues.

title: Contemporary Issues in Industrial Relations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines a selection of contemporary issues in the operation of the industrial relations framework for addressing the challenges facing workforces in Australia, amidst changing competitive and wider social pressures.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise and integrate multiple perspectives to evaluate the impact of current issues on the workplace.
Critically analyse a selection of current issues in Australian industrial relations.
Explain some of the current challenges facing the operation of the Australian industrial relations framework.
Communicate information to a range of stakeholders on workplace policy, practices, risks or issues.
Analyse the application of these issues to students' own organisations and/or workplace experiences and for their professional practice.

title: Contemporary Issues in Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject explores local, indigenous and international leadership thinking and practices. It invites students to reach beyond westernised cultures to apply novel perspectives on the perplexing leadership challenges of a globalised world. There is a particular emphasis on the ethical and ecosystem dimensions of leadership for healthy organisations, communities and other social systems. Students will explore the dynamic nature and complexity of contemporary issues and how leadership can respond. Students will reflect on historical, cultural, economic and sociocultural influences on leadership and use these insights for planning culturally appropriate and sustainable interventions in the face of contemporary global challenges.
learning_outcomes: Build a theoretical framework for the practice of leadership in the face of contemporary challenges.
Critically evaluate interventions for contemporary global leadership challenges through analysis, planning and self-reflection.
Research and evaluate how leadership is mobilised in relation to a range of contemporary global challenges.
Develop and apply ethical, ecoleadership interventions in response to leadership challenges.

title: Contemporary Issues in Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students engage critically with the foundational theoretical and practical texts underpinning the discipline of Practical Theology. Students are enabled to apply cross disciplinary research, critical perspectives and a variety of methods to examine issues and questions of church practice, with a view to developing new approaches and understandings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to understand and evaluate critically theological models of praxis, and appropriately apply them in given contexts.
Demonstrate research and writing skills relevant to the discipline of Practical Theology.
Evaluate critically significant contributors to the field of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a chosen contemporary issue from a perspective of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the relevance of other disciplines to Practical Theology including Indigenous, Feminist and Social Science perspectives.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the breadth of thinking represented by the term Practical Theology.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the place of Practical Theology within the discipline of Theology.

title: Contemporary Issues in Physical Activity and Sport
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable students to develop knowledge of pertinent and contemporary issues in physical activity, sport and recreation in education and in the sports industry both in Australia and globally. Students are provided with a range of theoretical tools with which to critically analyse issues and to develop a strong appreciation of the complex place of physical activity in society. Students evaluate sources of knowledge related to physical activity and sport and further develop skills in critical thinking. In addition, students will explore, assess and evaluate the relationship between theory and current issues in their preferred field.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the challenges, barriers and enablers for participating in exercise and sport to inform culturally safe practice.
Critique the ways in which knowledge about physical activity influences the teaching of, and narratives surrounding, physical activity and sport.
Integrate relevant information and effectively communicate their opinions.
Collect, synthesise and evaluate sources of information.
Utilise theories as tools to critically examine current issues in physical activity, such as issues of gender, race, religion, socialisation through sport, deviance in sport and the future of sports.
Identify and respond to issues surrounding sustainability related to the global sports industry.
Examine the origins and significance of personal biases when evaluating sources of information and forming opinions.

title: Contemporary Issues in Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject students engage critically with the foundational theoretical and practical texts underpinning the subdiscipline of Practical Theology, especially as these relate to ministry practice. Students are enabled to apply cross disciplinary research, critical perspectives and a variety of methods to examine issues and questions of church ministry practice, with a view to developing new approaches and understandings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical comprehension of contemporary issues in ministry from a practical theological perspective.
Demonstrate an ability to understand and evaluate theological models of praxis and also apply them appropriately in various ministry contexts.
Demonstrate a critical appreciation of the role of Practical Theology within the context of church ministry.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the breadth of thinking represented by the term Practical Theology.

Demonstrate advanced knowledge and skills relevant to the discipline of Practical Theology, including critical reflection on ministry practice, social research methods, and appropriate communication skills.
Evaluate significant contributors to the field of Practical Theology, especially in relation to the practice of ministry.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the relevance of other fields of enquiry to Practical Theology, including indigenous studies, feminist hermeneutics, and the social sciences.
prerequisites: THL519: Contemporary Issues in Practical Theology

title: Contemporary Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' knowledge and understanding of contemporary management theory and practice. Students will be challenged to think critically about core management theories and evaluate and communicate their relevance to contemporary management practice in a complex, diverse and rapidly changing globalised workplace. Students will be invited to embrace the subject innovatively and encouraged to develop and reflect on their own management competencies and experiences.
learning_outcomes: Research and communicate effectively and professionally in a variety of organisational settings.
Reflect on and develop their own management competencies required for today's complex, diverse and globalised workplace.
Critically analyse and evaluate a variety of management and organisational theories and practices in the context of the contemporary business environment.
Reflect critically on management issues such as ethics, sustainability, innovation & digital disruption and how they are shaping 21st century organisations.

title: Contemporary Issues in Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students engage critically with the foundational theoretical and practical texts underpinning the discipline of Practical Theology. Students are enabled to apply cross disciplinary research, critical perspectives and a variety of methods to examine issues and questions of church practice, with a view to developing new approaches and understandings.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically significant contributors to the field of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate an ability to understand and evaluate critically theological models of praxis, and appropriately apply them in given contexts.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a chosen contemporary issue from a perspective of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the relevance of other disciplines to Practical Theology including Indigenous, Feminist and Social Science perspectives.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the place of Practical Theology within the discipline of Theology.
Demonstrate research and writing skills relevant to the discipline of Practical Theology.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the breadth of thinking represented by the term Practical Theology.

title: Contemporary Mission and Evangelism
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject facilitates advanced critical reflection on mission and evangelism grounded in biblical and theological principles, together with a critical review and appraisal of the history and impact of mission and evangelism in the Australian, Asian and Pacific regions. In light of key social, cultural, and contextual challenges associated with the mission of the church in the world, particular models of mission and evangelism are addressed, together with their critical application within a range of ministry contexts. Students are challenged to develop a personal ethical approach to contemporary mission and to implement more effective models of mission and evangelism relevant to their cultural and ecclesial contexts.
learning_outcomes: Engage critically with biblical and theological models of mission and evangelism.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the relationship of mission and evangelism to issues of social justice and systemic inequity.
Demonstrate critical appraisal of the impact of mission and evangelism on Indigenous peoples.
Demonstrate a critically informed understanding of historical perspectives on Christian mission and evangelism.
Discuss critically contemporary approaches to mission and evangelism across a range of sociocultural and ministry contexts.
Demonstrate a critically informed understanding of ethical approaches to mission and evangelism and also to articulate a personal ethical approach to contemporary mission and evangelism.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of social, cultural and contextual challenges for the mission of the church in the world.

title: Contemporary Perspectives of Health
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will examine the multi-dimensional and dynamic nature of health and explore the factors that determine health status and influence 'meanings of health'. The notion of health as a social construct will be investigated by examining international frameworks of health promotion. Young people will act as a case study population for investigation, and healthy eating habits and physical activity will act as study foci. Through the design of a health promotion strategy that responds to the health needs of young people, this subject offers students the opportunity to apply both a settings and population approach to health promotion, and incorporate the principles of social justice.
learning_outcomes: Argue the efficacy of the socio-ecological approach in promoting social responsibility for health.
Explain the factors that determine health status and influence meanings of health.
Critique the role of epidemiology in informing strategies for health promotion.
Evaluate the impact of key health promotion policies on health status.
Apply the settings and population approaches to the design of a health promotion strategy to support the health of young people.
Describe the multi-dimensional and dynamic nature of health.
Employ the principles of social justice to the design of a health promotion strategy to support the health of young people.
Explore the notion of health as a social construct.

title: Contemporary Performance and Mediated Production
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to contemporary performance practices from a theoretical and practical perspective. The subject uses a thematic approach to analyse performance concepts including: postmodern performance, the body as text, post-dramatic theatre and the space and place of performance. Students engage in critical discussion and reflection about the work of leading practitioners and apply their understanding of concepts by creating their own thematic mediated performance.
learning_outcomes: Apply theories of performance to creative practice using mediated forms.
Analyse the performance methods of leading practitioners.
Identify and explore theories and practices of contemporary performance.
Research and facilitate seminars in contemporary performance.

title: Contemporary Performance and Production
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to contemporary performance practices from a theoretical and practical perspective. The subject uses a thematic approach to analyse performance concepts including: postmodern performance, the body as text, post-dramatic theatre and the space and place of performance. Students engage in critical discussion and reflection about the work of leading practitioners and apply their understanding of concepts by creating their own contemporary mediated performance production.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the performance methods of leading contemporary practitioners.
Apply theories of performance to creative practice using mediated forms.
Work in a team to produce a contemporary mediated performance production.
Identify and explore theories and practices of contemporary performance.

title: Contemporary Practice in Emergency Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the key themes and concepts of emergency management and examines contemporary practice in the emergency management arena. Emergency management is an important consideration in any organisational management context. The complexity and dynamic nature of emergency management practice in today's world requires emergency management professionals to be constantly aware of latest developments, innovation and practices being conducted and undertaken in the emergency management discipline.
learning_outcomes: Generate draft policy and practice documents on an aspect of the EM process for industry, and critically reflect on the potential implementation of this.
Identify key challenges for emergency mangers, including the variety of perspectives and approaches of the stakeholders involved.
Think critically about the perspectives of the various stakeholders and provide suggestions to be able to effectively manage these.
Demonstrate a broad appreciation for how emergency management fits into the role of a range of professions.
Review analyse, consolidate and synthesise theory and best practice in advanced emergency management preparedness, response and recovery practices.

title: Contemporary Theology in a Global Context
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to engage critically with some major figures and movements in twentieth and twenty-first century theology. Students will engage with theological voices from Western and non-Western contexts. Attention will be given to understanding figures and movements as part of broader developments in the theological landscape.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a selection of contemporary theologies and the contexts in which they emerged.
Discern and evaluate critically the contribution of particular theologies to their global and historical contexts.
Demonstrate independent research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a chosen contemporary theological figure or movement.
Evaluate critically selected theologies in reference to their contexts, tasks and methods.

title: Contemporary Theology in a Global Context
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to engage critically with some major figures and movements in twentieth and twenty-first century theology. Students will engage with theological voices from Western and non-Western contexts. Attention will be given to understanding figures and movements as part of broader developments in the theological landscape.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate independent research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a chosen contemporary theological figure or movement.
Discern and evaluate critically the contribution of particular theologies to their global and historical contexts.
Evaluate critically selected theologies in reference to their contexts, tasks and methods.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a selection of contemporary theologies and the contexts in which they emerged.

title: Contemporary Theories for Case Management
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject critically analyses theories and strengths-based frameworks informing case management practice, and seeks to critique those that stem from a colonising ideology. Students will benefit from learning how colonisation impacts on contemporary human services case management. Case management is a widely accepted and effective model of practice in health, human services, and other community-based sectors supporting people with complex needs. This subject will examine the generic skills used in case management and their application by a range of disciplines, and associated practice settings. It will explore the diverse contexts where case management is delivered including, but not limited to, the disability sector, person directed care and commissioning frameworks, and how these contexts are impacted by certain discourses and policy that come from initiatives such as Reconciliation, and Closing the Gap. An analysis of those frameworks will help identify the delivery of models of practice.
learning_outcomes: Independently analyse and apply practice principles of case management including person centred care, strengths-based models, human rights, social justice and advocacy to meet the needs of diverse and vulnerable client groups.

Independently research, apply and critique the theories and frameworks that inform case management practice in diverse practice settings considering the contribution that different disciplines make to this mode of practice.

Locate and evaluate social policies (including those that are underpinned by colonial ideologies and/or cultural bias) that inform case management practice and provide strategies informed by critical reading for case management implementation to meet policy requirements.

Independently research and critique specialised knowledge for the implementation of case management with specific client groups to address specific needs, including evaluation of how case-management policy and practice can be structured to support the aspirations of First Nations peoples.

Independently research contemporary frameworks directing service delivery, and examine the strategies for implementation of case management that meets current service delivery expectations, including from the impacts on Indigenous Australians that arise from Reconciliation, and Closing the Gap.

title: Contemporary Topics in Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to allow students to explore contemporary empirical and theoretical topics in psychology. The subject will consist of a series of seminars delivered by research staff in the school and students will prepare by reading articles set by the relevant staff member. It will provide higher level critical analytic skills that will prepare students for engagement in research and practice in the science of psychology.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of the theoretical and substantive issues relating to contemporary empirical and theoretical topics in psychology.
Demonstrate effective research skills.
Demonstrate higher level critical analytic skills and the ability to produce an original and coherent argument.

title: Contexts of Language, Literacy, Numeracy and Digital Literacy in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Through this subject, students will extend their knowledge and skills in the development of language, literacy, numeracy and digital literacy (LLND) capabilities in a variety of current contexts within theoretical frameworks. Students will evaluate the LLND needs of a particular cohort, examine a range of possible delivery settings, analyse the stated outcomes, select from a range of approaches and practices, and justify their preferences.
learning_outcomes: Develop and defend a language, literacy, numeracy and/or digital literacy approach for a particular context.
Compare and contrast various LLND teaching and learning practices, from traditional approaches to innovative approaches and technologies, and discuss how these may best suit a given context.
Evaluate models of LLND provision with reference to a range of teaching and learning settings.
Analyse and determine the LLND demands of training in a specific context for a particular cohort using known frameworks.
Discuss and compare the different purposes of provision of LLND capabilities, which may include vocational, preparatory, workforce development, self-efficacy and community and further education.

title: Contexts of Midwifery Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates midwifery knowledge, skills and application for practice in a variety of diverse settings in which midwives provide care to a range of populations in primary healthcare contexts. The role of midwifery and maternity care in improving perinatal outcomes for women and families will be discussed, including the provision of culturally safe midwifery care for diverse populations. The subject will also address the dimensions of culturally safe healthcare for First Nations peoples in a decolonising framework.
learning_outcomes: Develop strategies to provide culturally safe midwifery care, inclusive of First Nations people, that recognises the specific needs and preferences of diverse women and families.
Critically reflect on how each woman's circumstances and belief systems might influence her experiences and perceptions of midwifery care.
Apply understandings of socio-cultural determinants for First-Nations peoples and develop strategies for culturally safe midwifery care for First Nations communities.
Apply the principles of primary health care to midwifery practice.
prerequisites: MID452: Midwifery as Primary Health Care

title: Contexts of Nursing
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the profession of nursing and Caring Science theory. Students will consider the diverse nature of the work of the nurse; and explore important issues that have shaped and continue to shape the profession today. Issues such as the history of nursing, the role of professional nursing bodies, nursing ethics, and technology in nursing will be considered. Professional skills such as literacy, numeracy, and the use of evidence-based practice will be introduced.
learning_outcomes: Describe factors contributing to the current professional status of nursing.
Describe and give examples of professional frameworks and standards for practice that underpin the nursing scope of practice.
Demonstrate literacy skills necessary to understand, interpret, and communicate effectively according to the context at an introductory level.
Demonstrate the skills required to locate, describe and interpret existing information to support development of disciplinary knowledge at an introductory level.

title: Contract Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: The subject addresses the universal elements of contract law, including parties to a contract, formation of contract, contractual capacity, contract enforcement, possible breaches and remedies for breach under contract. Contemporary case law is examined to assess the ways in which the rules of contract are being modified by courts to reflect a changed understanding of the purpose of contracts. Particular attention is placed on decisions of appellate courts, and on key legislation such as consumer law, unfair contracts and unconscionable contracts.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the important elements in the formation of a contract.
Articulate the consequences for breach of contract and the possible defences that may be available to the parties.
Identify and evaluate the implied and express terms of a contract.
Evaluate and advise upon relevant remedies in statute, common law and equity.
Demonstrate an understanding of the structure and rationale of contract law, and its related legal doctrines, that arise from statutes and common law.
Demonstrate the application of contractual doctrines to hypothetical fact scenarios.
Evaluate the historical, social, political, and ethical factors underpinning contract law.
Identify and assess possible breach of contract scenarios.
Discuss critically the influence of a changing society on the law of contract.
Interpret contractual documents.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of public policy and law reform within the field of contract law.

title: Control Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principles, analysis, and design of control systems, with a focus on practical applications. It covers classical and modern control theory, including transfer function and state-space representations, stability analysis, controller design, and frequency domain techniques.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast different control system architectures and controller designs, considering their advantages, limitations, and suitability for specific engineering applications.
Compare the effectiveness of control system design strategies through simulations and experiments, assessing factors such as stability, transient response, and steady-state error.
Analyse the behaviour of dynamic systems using time and frequency domain techniques, demonstrating proficiency in stability analysis and response characterisation;.
Test and implement control systems using classical and modern control techniques, including PID control, state feedback, and frequency domain methods, to achieve desired system performance.

title: Corporate Finance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the key financial decisions faced by businesses in a modern economy. These decisions relate to funding business operations, evaluating investment proposals and the distribution of profits to providers of funds. It provides the basic concepts and theory for further studies in finance.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and analyse financial data at an appropriate level for post-graduate finance students.
Assess critically the scope of the finance function and its role in corporate management.
Apply acquired skills in the evaluation of financial data to enable informed decision making.
Synthesise relevant finance theories that will assist in the evaluation of investment, financing and dividend policies of firms through critical analysis and evaluation.

title: Corporate Culture, Stakeholder and Change Communication
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Understanding of organisational culture and change are essential for organisational communication professionals. This subject critically examines external pressures to change, such as sustainability, employee and community engagement, demographics, responsibility, reputation and gaining competitive advantage. It explores methods used by organisations to identify, meet and manage stakeholder expectations. It explores and critiques concepts of corporate culture, and the implications of organisational change for organisational communication professionals. Students explore principles, theory and case studies of contemporary practice and strategies for meeting and managing stakeholder expectations.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to identify and critically evaluate stakeholder theory and practice, and external pressures on organisations, and develop strategies intended to support and effect organisational change.
Demonstrate cognitive skills to critically evaluate theories and contemporary communication practice concerning organisational culture.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the role of communication in organisational culture and organisational change.

title: Corporate Governance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The subject examines the role of corporate governance in the fight against financial crime. It explores models of corporate governance and examines how organisational standards are established and maintained. The role of legal frameworks, self-regulation and corporate criminal liability are examined along with external factors that have an impact on the intersection between corporate governance and financial crime including the impact of technological change, global pressure against corruption and the role of media. Issues of institutional change, whistleblowing, autonomy, accountability, individual and organisational responsibilities for driving and institutionalising cultural improvements will also be explored.
learning_outcomes: Analyse external factors that shape the efficiency of corporate governance models to prevent fraud and financial crime.
Evaluate and discuss the major mechanisms in corporate governance used to prevent fraud and financial crime.
Analyse a range of issues that drive and institutionalise organisational cultural improvements.
Assess the ability of ethical frameworks embedded in corporate governance mechanisms to combat fraud and financial crime.

title: Corporate Investments
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The principal focus of this subject is on the financing and risk management aspects of corporate finance, and security and portfolio analysis. Valuation techniques introduced in financial management are applied to various investment situations incorporating current theories in finance.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrated financial research and analytical skills.
Communicate effectively about security analysis and portfolio management.
Solve financial problems within the context of a dynamic market place.
Undertake financial research.

title: Counselling Skills for Human Services
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the theoretical and practice skills necessary for students to undertake a counselling role. It enables the practice of skills and strategies compatible with the contemporary counselling frameworks and theories studied. Specific techniques relevant to working with diverse individuals and groups in the human services field are introduced and applied. Application of professional ethics, boundaries and the importance of self-care when engaging in professional helping relationships are examined and practised.
learning_outcomes: Conduct a client interview applying relevant skills and knowledge.
Apply understanding of diversity and demonstrate cultural responsiveness within the helping relationship.
Articulate, discuss and apply contemporary counselling theories, models and frameworks.
Reflect on their own practice and develop strategies to enhance counselling skills.
Demonstrate core communication and counselling skills.

title: Counselling Skills
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to provide students with a systematic introduction to the theory and practice of counselling. Students will acquire knowledge and skills concerning ethical, legal, and professional issues relating to working with clients from different age groups and cultural backgrounds, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and presenting concerns in a range of settings.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and evaluate the ideas and theories that inform counselling practice.
Demonstrate knowledge and practice of basic counselling micro skills with diverse populations including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Reflect on their own strengths and weaknesses as a counsellor.

Demonstrate an understanding of the process of professional regulation for psychologists including: familiarity with the National Law; familiarity with the Commonwealth and State laws; familiarity with the PsyBA code of ethics and ethical guidelines for psychologists; and familiarity with the appropriate requirements for data collection, storage, and destruction.

title: Counselling Theory and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject develops professional counselling skills. It covers the essential micro skills of counselling and develops these skills through training exercises. It will enable students to conceptualise clients' problems from the standpoint of a professional counsellor and develops some interventional strategies based on a theoretical conceptualisation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an integration of these skills into a considered, unique and personal counselling style.
Demonstrate an understanding of the nature and efficacy of a problemmanagement model of the counselling process.
Demonstrate practical competence in these counselling skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of the nature of the developmental stages of the model and its component skills.
Demonstrate an awareness of the ethical and professional issues inherent in the practice of counselling.
Demonstrate an insight into their own personal potential strengths and weaknesses as a counsellor.

title: Counter Terrorism
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Countering terrorism is not an act, but a process. In a post-9/11 world, counter terrorism is no longer within the ambit of few, but the responsibility of many. This responsibility spans intelligence, law enforcement, corrections, and the military as government representatives, and crosses into private industry, encompassing business, legal analysis, the media, and community organisations. This subject will introduce you to the complex counter terrorism challenges that are intrinsic to the current terrorism threat. You will explore the different approaches to counter terrorism through the lens of government and non-government actors, in order to consider the practical, ethical and legal challenges in countering evolving and diverse threats.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse counter terrorism theory and practice to provide insight and make recommendations.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of diverse counter terrorism approaches, theories and principles to evaluate recent developments.
Identify and evaluate challenges to professional and ethical practice in the field of counter terrorism.
Develop effective research methods and methodologies to make strategic assessments of counter terrorism approaches.
Demonstrate leadership through innovating professional practice by challenging existing knowledge and proposing alternate theories; and,.

title: Counterintelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
