school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the contribution counterintelligence makes to securing intelligence in an operational and organisational context. It is suitable for current and future practitioners in law enforcement, military, national security and business intelligence contexts; as well as students of the Master of Intelligence Analysis program. Subject content is delivered by blending theory with scenario based learning experiences, thus positioning students to recognise and apply counterintelligence knowledge and skills.
learning_outcomes: Gather and interpret data, construct knowledge and influence stakeholder groups in multiple domains.
Apply technical and critical analysis to complex counterintelligence ideas, concepts and problems.
Synthesise and apply advanced counterintelligence theory, principles and knowledge areas to address trends and threats.
Critically evaluate contemporary legal and ethical frameworks applicable to analytical judgement and reasoning in counterintelligence.

title: Creative External Production
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This interdisciplinary collaborative subject introduces students to techniques and issues specific to screen production in a location environment. Within this concept students will undertake projects, which involve single camera production from concept to final presentation through advanced instruction in the imaginative creation and practical production of creative works. Specific areas of practice include script analysis, working with actors, designers and television production teams, location production methodologies and discipline interaction.
learning_outcomes: Develop and critically reflect on personal process.
Be fully conversant with location Work Place Health and Safety and Risk Assessment.
Demonstrate a competent understanding of the pre-production, production and when required post-production; processes.
Analyse and interpret scripts using discipline specific skills learnt to date.
Creatively problem solve complex situations.
Manage and execute the discipline specific skills required for an external location production.
Interact and effectively communicate with your peers as part of the collaborative process.
Synthesise practical execution with imaginative expression.

title: Credit Package
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is the Entry level credit for the Bachelor of Teaching (Primary) where the prior completion of relevant undergraduate bachelor's degree that meets the NESA requirements for appropriate prior studies.

title: Creativity and Innovation
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will learn how to integrate the needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and the objectives of organisations with creative thinking to develop new ideas and solve problems.
learning_outcomes: Communicate an understanding of the methodologies that drive creativity and innovation.
Demonstrate an understanding of and apply creative processes to develop strategies and solve problems.
Demonstrate knowledge of, and capacity to integrate, the needs of people with the possibilities of technology and organisational objectives.

title: Credit Package
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is the Entry level credit for the Bachelor of Teaching (Primary) where the prior completion of a relevant undergraduate bachelor's degree that meets the NESA requirements for appropriate prior studies requires the completion of an additional 16 subject points to meet Charles Sturt University course requirements.

title: Credit Package 1 - Community College of Qatar
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have completed the Associate of Applied Science Degree in Customs Management (AASCM) conducted jointly by the Centre for Customs and Excise Studies (CCES) and the Community College of Qatar (CCQ)
learning_outcomes: Receive transfer credit on a block basis (96 credit points) to allow this particular student stream the opportunity to pursue in greater depths aspects of border management that will best cater to their particular interest and their professional aspirations.

title: Credit Package 2 - Maldives Customs Training Academy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have completed the Diploma in Customs Management conducted by CCES in the Maldives. The Diploma has been accredited by the Maldives Qualifications Authority (MQA).
learning_outcomes: Qualify to be granted transfer credit on a block basis (64 credit points) to allow this particular student stream the opportunity to pursue in greater depths aspects of border management that will best cater to their particular interest and their professional aspirations.

title: Credit Package 6 - NCE Summer School I
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have completed Summer School I conducted jointly by the Centre for Customs and Excise Studies (CCES) and the Namibia Customs and Excise (NCE).
learning_outcomes: The objectives of this subject are to grant eligible admitted students proficiency credit on a block basis (16 credit points) upon their successful completion of NCE Summer School I.

title: Credit Package 3 - Kotelawala Defence University (UG)
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have been admitted to the Bachelor of Border Management and who are studying concurrently at the Kotelawala Defence University (KDU), Colombo, Sri Lanka.
learning_outcomes: The objectives of this subject are to grant eligible admitted students forward credit on a block basis (40 credit points) to allow this particular student stream the opportunity to pursue their CSU qualification in Border Management by distance education while undertaking concurrent and complementary studies at their home institution.

title: Credit Package 4 - Kotelawala Defence University (PG)
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have been admitted to the Master of Customs Administration and who are studying concurrently at the Kotelawala Defence University (KDU), Colombo, Sri lanka.
learning_outcomes: The objectives of this subject are to grant eligible admitted students forward credit on a block basis (16 credit points) to allow this particular student stream the opportunity to pursue their CSU qualification in Customs Administration by distance education while undertaking concurrent and complementary studies at their home institution.

title: Credit Package 7 - NCE Summer School II
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have completed Summer School II conducted jointly by the Centre for Customs and Excise Studies (CCES) and the Namibia Customs and Excise (NCE).
learning_outcomes: The objectives of this subject are to grant eligible admitted students proficiency credit on a block basis (16 credit points) upon their successful completion of NCE Summer School II.

title: Credit Package 8 - NCE Summer School III
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have completed Summer School III conducted jointly by the Centre for Customs and Excise Studies (CCES) and the Namibia Customs and Excise (NCE).
learning_outcomes: The objectives of this subject are to grant eligible admitted students proficiency credit on a block basis (16 credit points) upon their successful completion of NCE Summer School III.

title: Crime Reduction
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The reduction of crime is a core law enforcement and security function, which can be achieved through adopting an evidence-based investigative and problem-solving approach. By working in a collaborative manner with a variety of community and law enforcement sources, some of the underlying causes of a wide range of criminal activities can be identified and efficiently addressed. This subject explores the evidence based approach of gathering intelligence, in addition to the current methods of investigation that are available, to effectively deal with existing volume crime problems within a problem-solving framework. It provides students with an understanding of intelligence functions to identify crime and disorder problems as well as proactive problem-solving approaches necessary to reduce crime and community fear.
learning_outcomes: Explain the intelligence process and information management and apply to crime reduction.
Utilise community and law enforcement sources in crime reduction.
Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Design a crime reduction plan drawing upon strategies of best practice from various sources within a national and international context.
Analyse and utilise the intelligence structures within law enforcement agencies nationally and internationally.

title: Crime, Media and Culture
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Media representations of crime, both real and fictional, have a significant impact on our understandings of, and responses to, crime. This subject introduces students to the relationship between the criminal justice system and media. Students will examine key criminological and media theories as applied to the relationship between media and crime, including representations of vulnerability, gender, race and class. This subject will also look at representations of crime in fiction. Students will analyse the representations of offenders, police, crime, prisons and the courts in image and text. The subject will also look at the impact of social media on the perception and representation of the criminal justice system.
learning_outcomes: Analyse representations of crime, offenders, police, prisons, courts and the criminal justice system in both the news media and in fiction.
Describe the relationship between the media and the criminal justice system.
Describe the key theories of crime, media and culture and apply them to media content.
Apply self-reflection skills and demonstrate ability to assess their own learning of criminological topics.
Evaluate the impact of representations of crime, including in television and film, on our understanding of crime and responses to crime.

title: Crimes of the Powerful
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Taking a national and international approach, this subject introduces students to criminological debate and theory on crimes of the powerful through an examination of the role of power in the criminal justice system and wider society. It questions definitions of crime and harm, using case studies to illustrate these debates. This subject reviews issues of white collar and corporate crime, industrial and environmental harms, state crime, genocide, war and war crimes, modern slavery and labour exploitation. In this subject, students will critically analyse the relationship between power and crime on a local and global level.
learning_outcomes: Apply key theories of power, control and harm to the criminal justice system.
Critically analyse the definitions of crime and harm, with case studies as illustrations.
Demonstrate an interdisciplinary approach to understanding power and crimes of the powerful.
Critically analyse relevant contemporary issues in the context of crime, harm and power.
Critically analyse the relationship between power, crime, and the criminal justice system.
Evaluate key debates in criminology regarding power and the criminal justice system.

title: Crime, Risk and Control
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Students will examine the evolution of risk in line with financial crime control theory, contrasting holistic with specific approaches. Students will synthesize financial crime control approaches drawn from different jurisdictions and industries to formulate an innovative approach to risk and crime control within a defined operational setting.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the evolution of crime control theories and contrast holistic and specific approaches to financial crime control.
Analyse the effectiveness of existing financial crime control approaches and select appropriate controls within a defined setting.
Identify and analyse criminological, organisational, and cultural risk factors that contribute to financial crime.

title: Criminal Investigations in Culturally and Ethnically Diverse Societies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject will identify and explore various ways in which racial and ethnic diversity can impact on criminal investigations. In particular, subject participants will focus on the ways in which such diversity can create competing pressures for an investigation, and the effects which traditional investigative practices may have on members of ethnic and racial minorities. Subject participants will be required to apply their more general learning to the specific investigative situations which may be faced in their own jurisdictions.
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate the ways in which racial and ethnic diversity impacts on contemporary criminal investigation.
Develop and critique strategies for minimising any negative impacts, and maximising any positive impacts, of racial and ethnic diversity on a criminal investigation.
Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Demonstrate a professional capacity to conduct criminal investigations in ethnically and racially diverse societies while protecting the legal rights of their members.

title: Criminal Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the general principles of substantive criminal law in NSW, the doctrines and rules that define criminal liability, and it examines these in their historical, contemporary, social and political context. This area of study includes a selection of substantive offences: the offences of dishonesty, unlawful homicides, and sexual and non-sexual non-fatal offences against the person. Students will examine the extended forms of criminal liability and the defence of criminal matters. Public policy implications and contemporary law reform initiatives in respect of criminal defences will also be considered.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish civil wrongs from criminal wrongs by defining crime and the criminalisation process within the Australian criminal context.
Explain the effect of general doctrines of complicity and preparatory offences.
Plan and apply effective strategies in the research of substantive criminal law scenarios including offences and appropriate defences.
Identify and evaluate the historical, social, political, and ethical factors that impact upon our contemporary understanding of the operation of substantive criminal law.
Explain the impact of public policy and law reform.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the structure and rationale of New South Wales substantive criminal law that arise from statutes and common law.
Identify and explain the relevant provisions of the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW).

title: Criminal Law and Criminology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to the major areas of Australian substantive and procedural criminal law with a focus on New South Wales. The subject builds on developing and demonstrating applied skills of legal analysis and research. The subject covers the application and process of criminal law through case studies on major areas of crime such as Offences against the Person. In this subject students will examine the relationship between criminal law and the criminal justice system and critique the application and process of the law. The subject will also examine the limits and potentials for the law to achieve what it intends, e.g. through law reform.
learning_outcomes: Explain and critique the processes of the criminal law of New South Wales.
Describe the substantive and procedural criminal laws of New South Wales.
Explain the practices and procedures of institutions of criminal justice in New South Wales.
Utilise applied skills of legal analysis and research.

title: Criminal Law and Investigation Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The effective management of investigations is a forensic exercise governed by criminal law and actioned through informed practice. This subject focuses on investigation management practices that are utilised broadly across all areas of criminal law. These include crime scene control and exhibit management, victim care and preparation of the evidence for presentation at court. The subject examines these and other current management issues within the law of homicide, drug trafficking, sexual assault and property offences.
learning_outcomes: Apply sound management decisions to investigations based on current research and good practice.
Utilise investigation management practices broadly across all areas of criminal law encountered by front line investigators.
Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Effectively manage investigations of homicide, drug trafficking, sexual assault and property offences, through the application of informed practice and within the principles of law.

title: Criminal Procedure
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to criminal procedure. It is concerned with the procedures relating to criminal justice which are separate to the substantive hearing. It addresses police powers, arrest and bail, sentencing, access to justice, and contemporary issues relevant to regional, rural, remote and Indigenous communities. Students will consider the issue of 'targeted' law reform and its implications for diverse communites and vulnerable groups.
learning_outcomes: be able to demonstrate critical awareness of the benefits, limitations and injustices connected to the imposition of criminal law;
be able to demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the elements of criminal procedure, together with the operative framework of criminal trials;
be able to identify and discuss ways in which law responds to particular social problems;
be able to demonstrate an understanding of institutional bias and the role of the legal profession in facilitating access to justice for Indigenous people and communities.
be able to analyse the impact on regional, rural, remote and indigenous communities of 'targeted' law reform; and
be able to demonstrate the impact of public policy and law reform;
be able to explain and critically analyse the relationship between criminal law and other branches of law as systems of social control;
prerequisites: LAW112: Introduction to the Australian Legal System

title: Criminal Law in Context
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on a foundational understanding of criminal law and justice processes for the benefit of those needing to engage with the Australian criminal justice system. It provides a critical analysis of how the state chooses to use criminal law and justice processes to regulate behaviour. It considers development of criminal laws and opportunities for law reform. Students will critically examine criminal justice processes including investigation, arrest, bail, court proceedings, and sentencing. They will critique the way crimes are prosecuted through the courts. Students will follow defendants on their path through the criminal justice system.
learning_outcomes: Examine the various criminal justice processes including investigation, arrest, bail, court proceedings (pre-trial and trial), sentencing, and appeals process.
Examine the key elements of criminal offences, defences and legal procedures.
Explain how criminal law and justice processes are used to regulate criminal behaviour.
Describe how the criminal laws are made and the law reform processes.
Critically analyse the impact of criminal law upon individuals and groups in society.

title: Criminology and Vulnerability
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: The subject examines how criminology and vulnerability interact across different contexts in Australia. It examines how social, economic, and structural inequalities contribute to both offending and victimisation, particularly among marginalised groups within society. Students will study vulnerability and justice theories to evaluate criminal justice system responses towards people and communities labelled as ‘at risk’. The subject will examine systemic biases, over-policing and the disproportionate impacts of incarceration through case studies, policy analysis, and empirical research. The focus will be on recognising vulnerability as a socially constructed condition resulting from power dynamics and historical injustices instead of an inherent trait. Students studying the subject will be able to critically evaluate criminological policies and promote fairer and more inclusive justice methods in modern Australia.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the role of ethics and cultural awareness in understanding individual experiences of trauma, victimisation, marginalisation and/or discrimination.

Explain what vulnerability means in criminology, and analyse how factors like disability, health, poverty, race or culture, can increase individuals exposure to crime and the risk of inequitable treatment within the justice system.
Effectively communicate complex ideas, drawing on academic research and evidence to identify opportunities to improve access to justice and support for vulnerable groups in society.
Compare key criminology theories that help explain how vulnerability, victimisation and crime are connected.

Evaluate the criminal justice system’s responses to vulnerable individuals and communities, considering the extent to which these responses are accessible, fair, respectful, and free from discrimination.

title: Criminology of Financial Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This foundation subject examines criminological explanations for fraud and financial crime and is instrumental in grounding students in the study of this discipline. It explores research paradigms that have shaped the understanding of how and why financial crimes occur in different organisational and jurisdictional settings. The subject highlights and critiques connections between theoretical explanations for financial crimes and how those crimes are controlled to identify why some fraud prevention strategies are more successful than others. It also examines the role of the media and societal perceptions in shaping financial crime policy.
learning_outcomes: Investigate the suitability of theoretically informed controls to prevent financial crimes.
Analyse how the underpinning theory informing white-collar crime shapes societal perceptions.
Identify and distinguish between key criminological theories and research paradigms.
Demonstrate the communication, literacy, numeracy, research and digital skills required of a competent professional financial crime practitioner.
Synthesise and critique financial crime literature to identify strengths and weakness in criminological explanations for financial crime.

title: Criminology Workplace Learning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject utilises an integrated workplace learning approach to develop the students' professional knowledge of working in a criminal justice environment whilst expanding on their employability skills and building on their practical experience. The subject is also aimed at developing students' self-reflection and self-monitoring skills to help build their efficacy and confidence in the work place. As part of this subject, students will gain practical experience and apply their academic learning in a professional setting through a 70 hour work placement.
learning_outcomes: be able to apply knowledge of contemporary employability skills, career planning and development to enhance personal skills applicable to the work environment;
be able to demonstrate practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement; and
be able to evaluate personal development across a range of professional practice skills.
be able to critically reflect on and evaluate the application of theory in a criminal justice workplace setting;

title: Critical Analysis of Disaster Response
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will enhance their understanding of current emergency operations management and specifically what actions could be taken during the pre-impact and impact phases of any emergency to enhance the management of an emergency event. The subject will examine current legislation, emergency prevention strategies, communications during emergencies, current pre-impact arrangements, and the roles, responsibilities and authority of the Emergency Services. The subject will specifically identify what actions could be taken during the impact phase of an emergency or disaster to influence the operational management of an emergency event.
learning_outcomes: Examine and analyse emergency management prevention and mitigation practices.
Identify and examine communication and media management during emergency events.
Identify and analyse the command, control, and coordination structures in emergency management.
Analyse and evaluate the management of an emergency event in the pre-impact and impact phases.
Explain and apply the relevant legal, ethical, and governance frameworks to emergency management.

title: Criminology: History and Theory
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Why do people offend and how should we respond to offending? Criminology: History and Theory introduces the major theoretical approaches within criminology and provides students with the theoretical tools to answer these questions. Theories about the causes of crime play a central role in criminology and in criminal justice practice. This subject examines a range of historical and contemporary approaches within criminology and considers the social and political factors that influenced their development.
learning_outcomes: Apply criminological theory to understand crime and responses to crime.
Explain the development of contemporary criminological theory.
Evaluate contemporary criminological theories.
Describe the major criminological theories that have influenced criminology over the last 200 years.
Explain the development of theory within political and social changes over the last 200 years.

title: Critical Care Retrieval and Transport
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on providing students with specialised knowledge of aeromedical retrieval and critical care transport environments and systems of care for fixed-wing, rotary wing and ground transport. Students will learn foundational concepts including flight physiology, stressors of flight, aircraft types and retrieval team configurations. The subject will explore how critical care paramedics work as part of an interprofessional team to prepare patients for transport while applying culturally responsive practice and inclusive practices including the application of cultural safety to First Nations peoples during emergent transportation. Students will learn about the specialised equipment used in the air ambulance transport setting such as transport ventilators and IV pumps and clinical considerations relevant to transport. The subject will also address specialty transports including paediatric, neonatal, bariatric, acute behavioural disturbances, and intensive care interfacility transfers involving specialised equipment such as Intra-aortic balloon pumps.
learning_outcomes: Apply safe, ethical, patient-centred and inclusive practices relevant to critical care aeromedical retrieval and transport, inclusive of culturally safe care to First Nations peoples.
Apply advanced knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology relevant to critical care aeromedical retrieval and transport.

Apply and demonstrate in simulation specialised technical skills using specialised technology as appropriate to implement safe and evidence-informed critical care paramedic practice in the aeromedical retrieval and transport settings.
Integrate leadership and communication skills into interprofessional collaborative practice during aeromedical retrieval and transport.

title: Critical Care Skill Integration
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject facilitates students’ integration of advanced theoretical knowledge and skills into critical care paramedic practice. The subject allows students to integrate specialised technical skills into evidence-informed critical care paramedicine treatment plans for medical and traumatic emergencies across the lifespan. Extending upon their previous education and experience, students perform technical critical care skills in complex simulated scenarios. They also apply theories and frameworks of leadership, critical thinking, clinical reasoning, and communication to various authentic complex paramedic situations. Students in this subject further develop their ability to teach and mentor others while growing as an autonomous and reflective practitioner.
learning_outcomes: Integrate leadership, critical thinking and communication skills into interprofessional collaborative and reflective practice in critical care paramedicine.
Apply specialised technical skills using technology as appropriate, to implement safe and evidence-informed critical care paramedic practice.
Justify evidence-informed critical care paramedic treatment plans for respiratory, cardiac and traumatic emergencies.
Integrate specialised paramedic knowledge, theories and frameworks for contemporary critical care paramedicine as relevant to leadership, critical thinking, technical and/or communication skills.

title: Critical Issues in Research
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students an introduction to the Doctoral research process and the administrative supports that they will be expected to engage with. Attention is given to the nature of the research process, including the steps to be followed in planning and designing a research project. An outline of the philosophy of research and the means by which researchers identify issues and acquire knowledge is also provided. At completion students will be able to clearly articulate the purpose of their research, have a working knowledge of the major chapter-forming components of a dissertation and be cognisant of the ethical issues they will need to address.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the requirements of a professional doctorate, including the role and responsibilities of research students and supervisors.
Have a clear understanding of the nature of research as a process of speculative inquiry.
Appreciate the importance of transparency, accountability, academic writing standards, the ethics process and codes of conduct in research.
Articulate the social impact on, and social implications of, their research.
Independently reflect upon and apply the key planning and design steps in research.
Identify a research problem that is current and/or related to professional practice.
Critically discuss an initial broad range of literature applicable to their research, and from that discussion draw research question(s) and a corresponding rationale.

title: Critical Reasoning
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to informal logic and the nature of argument, especially as it relates to real-life settings. It is designed to develop the intellectual virtues of clear thinking and rational decision-making. Students will learn to accurately interpret the many types of arguments they encounter on a day to day basis, from the mundane to exotic. They will learn not only to distinguish good arguments from bad, but also to consistently construct good arguments for themselves. In this course we shall also be introducing several advanced topics, including the nature of conductive arguments, counter-considerations and confirmation bias. From common sense to abstract reasoning, this subject promises to help each student develop the tools necessary for all other rational pursuits.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced familiarity with the scope and content of modern applied logic.
Show that particular arguments are unsound, or have unnoticed or unwanted implications.
Be equipped to diagnose fallacies in reasoning and to avoid fallacies in their own writing.
Construct and evaluate conductive arguments with counter-considerations.

title: Critical Studies in Education and Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on and explores significant theory, concepts and developments in the study and practice of education. Students' study, discussion and research is situated around the aims and purposes of education, social justice, ethics, citizenship, and social sustainability. In today's world, teachers' work is increasingly complex. Teachers must therefore be cognisant of the complex web of social and cultural relations in educational settings given that schools exert considerable influence upon children, young people, their families and communities. This subject foregrounds cultural factors which influence educators, teaching practice and student learning. Factors specifically related to gender, sexuality, social class, ethnicity, power, policy, and globalisation will be considered. Students will be able to critically evaluate existing knowledge and scholarship, identify theoretical perspectives in current practice enabling continued professional engagement, reflection, and reflexivity as they develop as teaching professionals and individuals in a global world.
learning_outcomes: Explore their own positionality through reflection and reflexive practice as students and educators.
Communicate abstract and complex theoretical ideas and arguments to a professional audience.
Apply ethical decision making and reasoning to discussions on current issues in education.
Examine current literature with an informed, critical perspective.
Discuss and evaluate the role of education in global and sustainable futures.
Discuss and evaluate current theory and research.
Recognise and interpret how structural influences impact equity, access, and social justice in education.
Analyse and evaluate contemporary education policy and practice.

title: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australian Cultures, Histories and Contemporary Realities
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of Indigenous Australian peoples' varied and diverse realities. It will enhance understandings of the effects of historical and contemporary policy and practices on the lives of Indigenous Australian peoples. It examines a range of social, cultural, historical, and institutional factors that impact on the contemporary experiences of Indigenous Australian and non-Indigenous Australian peoples using a relational framework. Students will apply critical thinking, analysis, and reflexivity skills to examine and evaluate how dominating systems impact effectiveness of engagement and service provision for Indigenous Australian peoples.
learning_outcomes: Create, evaluate and present a professional practice framework that demonstrates ethical professional practice, and to apply principles to develop respectful partnerships with Indigenous Australian communities.
Critically analyse and theorise individual and collective standpoint in relation to Indigenous peoples' experiences of Australian history.

Analyse the factors that have shaped historical and contemporary engagement with Indigenous communities and Indigenous peoples and analyse effects of deficit paradigms as they relate to Indigenous Australians.
Examine critical race and culture theories to identify the function of hegemonic structures and analyse the impact on Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians in the past and present.
Reflexively critique professions such as health, policing, education, law, and social work to analyse the benefits of cultural competency.
prerequisites: IKC502: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australian Cultures, Histories and Contemporary Realities

title: Critical Studies in Education and Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on and explores significant theory, concepts and developments in the study and practice of education. Students' study, discussion and research is situated around the aims and purposes of education, social justice, ethics, citizenship, and social sustainability. In today's world, teachers' work is increasingly complex. Teachers must therefore be cognisant of the complex web of social and cultural relations in educational settings given that schools exert considerable influence upon children, young people, their families and communities. This subject foregrounds cultural factors which influence educators, teaching practice and student learning. Factors specifically related to gender, sexuality, social class, ethnicity, power, policy, and globalisation will be considered. Students will be able to critically evaluate existing knowledge and scholarship, identify theoretical perspectives in current practice enabling continued professional engagement, reflection, and reflexivity as they develop as teaching professionals and individuals in a global world.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical decision making and reasoning to discussions in education.
Examine current literature to gain a critical perspective which will inform practice.
Recognise and interpret how structural influences affect equity, access, and social justice in education.
Discuss the role of education in global and sustainable futures.
Communicate abstract and complex theoretical ideas and arguments to a professional audience.
Discuss and evaluate current theory and research.
Explore positionality through reflection and reflexive practice as students and educators.
Apply knowledge into educational practice and settings.

title: Critical Studies in Education and Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores significant theory, concepts and developments in the study and practice of education. Social justice, ethics, citizenship, sustainability and the aims of education are examined in the context of complex social and cultural relations in educational settings. These interactive cultural factors are centred in relation to educators, teaching practice, and student learning to foster holistic understanding of complex community needs in education. Factors specifically related to gender, sexuality, social class, ethnicity, power, policy, and globalisation will be considered. Students will develop critical thinking and reasoning skills and engage with existing knowledge and scholarship, identify theoretical perspectives in current practice, and develop professional reflexive skills as emerging teaching professionals and individuals in a global world.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the role of critical and creative thinking skills in education.
Apply ethical decision making and reasoning to discussions in education.
Explore positionality through reflection and reflexive practice as students and educators.
Recognise how structural influences affect equity, access, and social justice in education.
Discuss current literature to gain a critical perspective which will inform educational practice.
Reflect on the aims and purposes of education and schooling.
prerequisites: EEP425: Critical Studies in Education and Practice

title: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australian Cultures, Histories and Contemporary Realities
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of Indigenous Australian peoples' varied and diverse realities. It will enhance understandings of the effects of historical and contemporary policy and practices on the lives of Indigenous Australian peoples. It examines a range of social, cultural, historical, and institutional factors that impact on the contemporary experiences of Indigenous Australian and non-Indigenous Australian peoples using a relational framework. Students will apply critical thinking, analysis, and reflexivity skills to examine and evaluate how dominating systems impact effectiveness of engagement and service provision for Indigenous Australian peoples.
learning_outcomes: Reflexively critique the professions to interrogate the impact of dominating social and cultural norms on intercultural engagement and service provision.

Create, evaluate and present a professional practice framework that demonstrates ethical professional practice, and to apply principles to develop respectful partnerships with Indigenous Australian communities.
Critically analyse and theorise individual and collective standpoint in relation to Indigenous peoples' experiences of Australian history.
Analyse and evaluate the factors that have shaped historical and contemporary engagement with Indigenous communities and evaluate the effects of deficit paradigms.
Examine critical race and culture theories to identify the function of hegemonic structures and analyse the impact on Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians in the past and present.
prerequisites: IKC403: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australian Cultures, Histories and Contemporary Realities

title: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australians and the Politics of Control
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject frames policy developments in Indigenous Australian affairs since first British contact and beyond from Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australian standpoints. It critically examines Indigenous Australian politics in relation to hegemonic political structures. Specific policy developments and legislative determinations are critically examined from Indigenous Australian perspectives and considered in light of Indigenous Australian pursuits of rights and self-determination. Students will examine the evolution of Indigenous Australian policy and analyse evident discourses. This subject explores the workings of policy implementation and how this impacts on the pursuit of Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australian interests. Students will be asked to examine and reflect on standpoint in relation to Australian policy.
learning_outcomes: Reflexively analyse how Indigenous Australian issues are positioned by and within dominating political structures and social and cultural discourses in Australia.
Critically analyse and evaluate the benefits of political self-determination for Indigenous Australian peoples and how political structures can operate to disenfranchise non-dominant groups.

Analyse the features and impact of historical and contemporary policy and legislation in Indigenous Australian affairs and critically evaluate the social, historical, and political discourses that informed them.
Research and evaluate distributions of power in Indigenous policy development in relation to human service industries.

title: Critical Thinking
school: School
syllabus_overview: Being able to think and read critically are key skills required for success in university studies. Moreover, they assist with all areas of life. This subject will teach students, via extensive practice, how to think critically about claims and reasons as well as how to adopt a critical approach to reading, both of which are particularly relevant for responding effectively in assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Identify arguments.
Know how to be critical of claims.
Know when to be critical of claims and reasons.
Know how to be critical of reasons.
Read critically.
Participate effectively in academic debate.
Identify credible sources relevant to particular discussions.
Critically evaluate.

title: Critical Thinking
school: School

This subject will teach students, via extensive practice, how to think critically about claims and reasons as well as how to adopt a critical approach to reading, both of which are particularly relevant for responding effectively in assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate.
Read critically.

Identify credible sources relevant to particular discussions.
Identify arguments.

They will learn not only to distinguish good arguments from bad, but also to consistently construct good arguments for themselves. Students will also have the opportunity to apply their reasoning skills to a particular field of practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical reasoning skills to a relevant field of practice.
Demonstrate some familiarity with the scope and content of modern applied logic.
Diagnose fallacies in reasoning and to avoid fallacies in their own writing.
Show that particular arguments are unsound, or have unnoticed or unwanted implications.

title: Critical Thinking Skills in Context
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Being able to think and read critically are key skills required for success in university studies as with all other areas of life. This subject will teach students how to interpret and evaluate information from a variety of sources and think critically about claims and reasons. An ability to take a critical approach is developed through a range of activities relevant to university study.
learning_outcomes: Identify arguments and lines of reasoning
Interpret and evaluate information and sources
Evaluate arguments and lines of reasoning
Participate effectively in academic debate
Identify the importance and role of critical thinking in university study

title: Critical Thinking - A Philosophical Approach
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Being able to think and read critically are key life skills. This subject adopts a higher level philosophical approach to critical thinking. It will teach students, via extensive practice, how to think critically about claims and reasons as well as how to adopt a critical approach to reading, both of which are particularly relevant for responding effectively to issues presented in a tertiary context.
learning_outcomes: Read critically to identify points and arguments.
Identify how to critically evaluate arguments.
Identify how to critically evaluate information, source and claims.

title: Crop Agronomy
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject deals with the management of broadacre field crops in southern Australia. The subject will deal with topics such as yield parameters, climate and crop adaptation, crop rotations, crop nutrition weed and fertiliser management, tillage and stubble management and current issues in crop production. In addition, critical aspects of the agronomy of the main field crops of southern Australia are covered. This subject is presented in a way that will encourage students to conduct and interpret experiments, develop computer skills, use decision support systems, and be able to relate to 'onfarm' management issues.
learning_outcomes: Recommend basic strategies for the management of common field crops in southern Australia.
Explain the role of climatic, edaphic and management factors that influence the distribution of crop species.
Have developed skills in the assessment of crop development by routine application of current developmental scales.
Apply the principles that influence crop rotations to a range of diverse cropping systems.
Use basic principles and decision support tools to calculate and recommend fertiliser strategies for winter crops.
Explain the important management strategies in field crops.
Apply basic principles of precision agriculture.
Have developed skills in the use of crop monitoring systems in crop management.

title: Cross Cultural Ministry in Australia
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores methods and selected themes relating to the practice of cross cultural ministry in the Australian context. It assesses issues relating to understanding and appreciating the challenges and opportunities which arise in multicultural and cross cultural ministry settings. It enables students to become more familiar with critical issues relating to ministry and mission in multicultural contexts, with both theoretical understanding of cross cultural dynamics and practical skills in cross cultural relationships.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically a range of models for doing cross cultural theology.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the challenges facing Australia as a nation of cultural and ethnic diversity.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of a range of cross cultural issues.
Articulate and analyse critically the role of ministry in building inclusive communities.
Articulate and evaluate critically the understanding and practice of multicultural ministry within the Australian churches.
Demonstrate self-guided reading, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
prerequisites: THL230: Cross Cultural Ministry in Australia

title: Cross Cultural and International HRM
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject explores how multi-national organisations manage HR functions across multiple locations while sustaining the culture of a dynamic global workforce. The role of HR within multinational organisations, such as managing human resources in cross-border network structures; global legal regulations; identification, preparation and relocation of talent; career management; turnover and employer branding will be examined. A key component of this subject is in developing cross-cultural awareness, competence and potential for convergence.
learning_outcomes: Research emerging issues in international business and make responsive, culturally relevant human resource management recommendations.
Critically analyse international business activity in the context of current and emerging international HRM theory.
Examine the impact of cross-cultural diversity on the international business operations and international human resource management practice.
Critically evaluate global human resource management practices to determine effective HR strategies for multinational organisations.

title: Crop And Pasture Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject presents the basic physiology and ecology of plant-based production systems and develops skills in plant taxonomy relevant to agricultural production systems of southern Australia. The subject matter will deal with the science of plant production systems. In particular physiological topics such as water use, nutrition, photosynthesis, respiration, development, partitioning and yield formation will be examined at the single plant and crop/pasture levels. Likewise, those aspects of plant community ecology that are relevant to crops or pastures will also be covered. These include: competition, life-history, population dynamics and biodiversity.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic physiology and ecology of agricultural plant production systems.
Recognise all the major families of flowering plants utilised in agricultural and pastoral production in southern Australia.
Key out plants that they cannot readily recognise.

title: Cross Cultural Ministry in Australia
school: School of Theology

It assesses issues relating to understanding and appreciating the challenges and opportunities which arise in multicultural and cross cultural ministry settings. It enables students to become more familiar with critical issues relating to ministry and mission in multicultural contexts, with both theoretical understanding of cross cultural dynamics and practical skills in cross cultural relationships.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically a range of models for doing cross cultural theology.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the challenges facing Australia as a nation of cultural and ethnic diversity.
Articulate and evaluate critically the understanding and practice of multicultural ministry within the Australian churches.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a range of cross cultural issues.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Articulate and analyse critically the role of ministry in building inclusive communities.
prerequisites: THL486: Cross Cultural Ministry in Australia

Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of a range of cross cultural issues.

Demonstrate self-guided reading, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.

title: Cryptocurrencies and Anti Money Laundering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the link between cryptocurrencies and money laundering by providing an introduction to the functionality of cryptocurrencies and evaluates global and domestic efforts to mitigate the criminal risks these technologies present. Drawing on case studies this subject examines the evolution of cryptocurrencies and the criminal affordances presented by these technologies. The subject also examines regulatory and industry efforts to protect the integrity of these technologies and minimize the possibility of their use to launder the proceeds of crime.
learning_outcomes: Identify the susceptibility of cryptocurrencies to money laundering and terrorist financing.
Evaluate industry responses to cryptocurrency money laundering risks.
Demonstrate the communication, literacy, numeracy, research and digital skills required of a competent professional financial crime control practitioner.
Explain how cryptocurrencies function.
Evaluate domestic and international regulatory responses to cryptocurrency money laundering risks.

title: CSU Connect: Preparation for Studying Business
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop essential skills required for study in selected business courses within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science. The first part of the subject develops students' basic skills in maths and statistics within a business context through a closely guided, paced, supportive learning process. The second part of this subject introduces students to the use of conceptual frameworks in business studies. The preparation of students during this subject is enhanced by learning experiences that simulate those required for successful participation in the first year of undergraduate study.
learning_outcomes: Communicate in a mathematical way.
Perform a variety of functions using the Microsoft Excel software program.
Demonstrate an understanding of the mathematical standards and techniques required for some subjects in a Business degree.
Apply methods of reasoning and argument to critically analyse information.
Explain how theories and models are used to make sense of business data.
Use a calculator proficiently to solve problems.

title: CSU Connect: Introduction to Tertiary Study
school: School
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Tertiary Study is designed to better prepare you for an undergraduate degree course with the University. This subject offers you an entrance into an academic culture, and will allow you to become familiar with the University, its support systems and the expectations of tertiary study. Knowing a little bit about CSU and its learning environment should mean that you'll have fewer anxieties or uncertainties about studying at university. Also, a greater confidence in yourself as a learner should lead to improved chances for your future academic success.
learning_outcomes: Identify key resources that enhance adjustment to undergraduate study.
Apply the principles of good academic writing.
Access a range of university facilities, services and resources using online skills.
Develop self awareness for learning how to learn.
Demonstrate an understanding of academic integrity and referencing conventions.
Apply relevant critical thinking strategies.

title: Cultural Competency and Community Development as Speech Pathology Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students engage with the history and current realities of Indigenous Australian peoples and critically reflect on the influence this has on the accessibility and appropriateness of speech pathology services. Students further develop their reflective practice skills by exploring their own values and beliefs, and critiquing speech pathology practices when working with linguistically and culturally diverse populations. This subject has a specific focus on Indigenous Australian peoples, languages and cultures. The role of language and cultural maintenance in health and wellbeing is explored. Students develop their knowledge of Indigenous Australian languages and their skills in linguistic analysis, to facilitate their provision of culturally responsive speech pathology services. This subject is taught collaboratively by the School of Indigenous Australian Studies and the School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sports Sciences.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the socio-historical context including individual and institutional racism embedded within Australia's health and education systems, including speech pathology.
Reflect on learning across the subject to create personal and professional learning goals and strategies for achieving those goals.
Apply Indigenous research principles and methodologies to the evaluation of knowledge, policy and professional practice.

Apply standpoint theory to critically reflect on social, cultural and historical dimensions of knowledge, values, and experiences and the impact of these on development of culturally responsive speech pathology practices.
Describe Indigenous Australian relationships with language and the role of language maintenance in health and wellbeing.
Apply skills and knowledge of cross cultural communication and linguistic analysis to facilitate linguistically and culturally responsive speech pathology assessment and intervention practices.

title: Cultural Competency in Security Studies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth exploration of cultural competency and its critical role across various domains, including law enforcement, national security, emergency response, and globalised interactions. It begins by defining cultural competency and highlighting its significance in understanding socio-cultural environment. Students will develop self-awareness of cultural biases, enhance cultural aptitude, and refine cross-cultural communication skills. The subject examines cultural competency’s role in conflict resolution, ethical decision-making, and intersectionality, emphasising the impact of diverse cultural identities on professional practice. Case studies on First Nations peoples, migrants, and multicultural communities offer practical insights into applying cultural competency frameworks. Through theoretical and applied learning, students will gain essential skills to navigate cultural diversity effectively, fostering inclusive and ethical approaches in their respective fields.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the role of cultural competency in understanding human geography and apply this knowledge to scenarios in law enforcement, national security, emergency response, and globalised interactions.

Apply knowledge of the intersections of cultural identities and critically engage with cultural competency frameworks through case studies on First Nations peoples, migrants, and multicultural communities, evaluating their implications for practice.
Apply cultural intelligence principles to effectively communicate and collaborate in first nations and multicultural settings, considering verbal and non-verbal cultural variations.
Demonstrate knowledge of the intersections of cultural identities and apply cultural competency frameworks through case studies on First Nations peoples, migrants, and multicultural communities.
Analyse the influence of cultural factors in conflict situations and develop culturally competent approaches to mediation, negotiation, and ethical problem-solving.
Identify and critically reflect on cultural biases and apply strategies to engage respectfully with diverse cultural perspectives.

title: CSU Connect: Preparation for Studying the Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop essential skills required for study within Agriculture, Food and Nutrition, Wine Science or Viticulture. The first module develops students' basic skills in mathematics and statistics through a closely guided, paced, supportive learning process. In the second module students are introduced to chemistry and learn to solve problems through the application of foundation principles. The preparation of students during this subject is enhanced by learning experiences that simulate those required for successful participation in the first year of undergraduate study.
learning_outcomes: Calculate percentage composition of elements in compounds.
Use a calculator confidently and correctly.
Determine atomic weights and molecular weights.
Understand how chemical compounds are named.
Chemistry.
Appreciate the diversity and complexity of organic compounds; and identify and name simple hydrocarbons.
Mathematics and Statistics.
Understand and work with algebraic expressions.
Express concentration of a solution in various ways.
Write and balance chemical equations.
Understand basic atomic structure, chemical bonding and the formation of compounds; and distinguish between ionic and molecular compounds.
Understand and use trigonometry in a variety of applications.
Understand concepts of basic statistics and probability.
Understand and work with arithmetic and other basic concepts of mathematics.
Define and give examples of various chemical terms.
Interpret and apply a variety of graphical techniques.

title: Culture and Heritage
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Culture is a way of understanding and living in the world. Heritage is the environment, objects and places that we inherit from the past and pass on to future generations to use, learn from and be inspired by. Together these frame our understanding of the past and influence the decisions we make about what is worth keeping. In this subject, students learn both the practical and theoretical skills of dealing appropriately with our heritage and the culture around them. The subject also provides the students with hands on experience in the identification, classification and recording of Aboriginal and historic sites and places. An intensive school explores these issues through a range of practical activities, site visits and presentations by stakeholders (e.g. Indigenous Australians).
learning_outcomes: Have a broad understanding of the characteristics of people who have a relationship to heritage and what makes 'heritage'.
Apply specific practical methods and procedures to assess, conserve, protect and manage heritage sites and cultural resources.
Exercise critical thinking and sound judgments in considering the philosophies and approaches to managing our heritage.

Have a broad understanding of how their discipline and or profession might impact on the culture and heritage of people from diverse backgrounds (For example: European, Ethnic, Indigenous backgrounds).

title: Current Topics in Natural and Physical Sciences
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Science is a dynamic and essential element of everyday and global life. This subject explores current issues in the natural and physical sciences that will have major impacts on the environment, communities and individuals, both now and into the future. Students will experience the scientific process, develop their knowledge in foundational science disciplines, and expand skills in applying scientific methodology to have informed discussions about everyday and global issues.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply key concepts of natural and physical sciences including foundation chemistry, physics and biology.
Use appropriate terminology and communication strategies to analyse and discuss current issues affecting the natural and physical world to peers and the scientific community.
Describe the scientific method and explain how it is used to address issues affecting the natural and physical world.

title: Curriculum Method 1: Drama
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides teacher education students with the professional knowledge and pedagogical practices that will enable them to be a teacher of secondary drama. In this subject students will engage with the ideas, issues and practical considerations of classroom drama curriculum for Stage 4 and 5 (years 7-12), examine how these are represented in curriculum documents, and investigate the role and value of drama in the context of the broader curriculum. Teacher education students will design a range of learning opportunities to facilitate individual and collaborative learning about the elements of drama and the practices of making, performing and appreciating drama in a range of contexts. They will apply the theory, practice and processes of experiential learning in their planning for the teaching of a range of dramatic forms, performance styles, dramatic techniques and theatrical conventions. The emphasis in this course is upon the teaching, planning, programming and assessing classroom drama related to the NSW Year 7 - 10 Drama Syllabus. Teacher education students will explore learning and assessment strategies and resources (including digital resources) that are used in drama to engage learners with diverse needs and abilities. Attention is also given to the literacy and numeracy demands of this curriculum area. Throughout this semester students will keep a self-reflective journal to assist students in understanding, planning and decision-making in the experiential learning context.
learning_outcomes: Critique and apply pedagogical models for teaching drama, including strategies explicitly designed to develop students' ICT, literacy, numeracy and digital literacy skills in drama.
Apply the theory, practice and processes of experiential learning in the planning of learning activities aligned with stage 4/5 drama syllabus outcomes.

Explain the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of drama teaching and learning and the role and value of drama (Stages 4-5) in the broader K-12 school curriculum.
Identify and apply elements of the secondary drama curriculum including drama metalanguage.
Develop effective teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that incorporate cross-curriculum priorities / general capabilities in drama (Stages 4 and 5).
Integrate opportunities for individual and collaborative learning and assessment in drama, and are inclusive of students with diverse needs and abilities (Stages 4 and 5).

title: Current Developments In Accounting Thought
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject covers a critical review of developments in accounting theory and professional standards including the search for a conceptual framework, the evaluation and comparison of various accounting models and discussion of contemporary management accounting and financial reporting issues.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the possible usefulness of alternative measurement systems to historical cost.
Critically evaluate selected current financial reporting and management accounting issues.
Critically appraise the objectives of accounting and relate them to the various concepts of accounting discussed in earlier subjects.
Critically evaluate attempts to develop and apply a conceptual framework.

title: Curriculum Method 1: English
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject requires students to critically engage with conceptualisations of the English curriculum and examine how these are represented in mandated curriculum documents. This subject examines the wide-ranging nature of English curriculum content with attention given to each of the three significant strands in the English curriculum, namely language, literature and literacy, and including multiliteracies and multimodal texts. Students develop knowledge and skill in applying professional principles and practices appropriate to the design, implementation and assessment of high quality Stage 4 and 5 English curriculum teaching and learning programs that cater for the needs of diverse learners.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the place of secondary English across the continuum of learning in English K-12 and in the broader school curriculum including the development of students' literacy, digital literacy and numeracy capabilities in English.
Examine and explain principles, practices and models of pedagogy for teaching and learning in Stages 4 & 5 English.
Plan secondary English lessons to include quality teaching, learning and assessment strategies, including ICT strategies, and provide for differentiation of learning strategies for diverse learners.
Critically evaluate the structure and organisation of the Stage 4 & 5 English curriculum.
Plan for and apply the range of modes employed in multimodal text design.

title: Curriculum Method 1: HSIE/HASS
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides teacher education students with the professional knowledge and pedagogical practices that will enable them to be a teacher of secondary Human Society and its Environment (HSIE) / Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS). In this subject, students engage with conceptualisations of the HSIE/HASS curriculum teaching area, examine how these are represented in curriculum documents, and investigate the role and value of HSIE/HASS subjects in the context of the broader curriculum. Particular attention is given to History and Geography, together with electives, and an understanding of the teaching and assessment strategies and resources (including digital resources) appropriate to HSIE/HASS teaching and learning sequences to cater for the diverse needs of learners. Attention is also given to the literacy and numeracy demands of this curriculum area and application of cross-curricular priorities (including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures), general capabilities, and differentiation strategies in the teaching of HSIE/HASS subjects in Stages 4 and 5.
learning_outcomes: Develop effective HSIE/HASS teaching, learning, and assessment sequences (Stages 4 and 5) that incorporate cross-curriculum priorities / general capabilities and the vision, values, principles, and pedagogical practices of HSIE/HASS (Stages 4 and 5).
Identify appropriate historical and/or geographical issues and develop teaching and learning activities aligned with current pedagogical practices of HSIE/HASS and syllabus outcomes.
Develop effective teaching resources for HSIE/HASS teaching and learning sequences (Stages 4 and 5).
Describe strategies, including literacy and numeracy strategies, for teaching, learning and assessment in HSIE/HASS, to meet the diverse needs of students (Stages 4 and 5).

Explain the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of HSIE/HASS teaching and learning and the role and value of HSIE/HASS (Stages 4-5) in the K-12 school curriculum.
Analyse sample HSIE/HASS lessons in the light of authentic learning principles.

title: Curriculum Method 1: Mathematics
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces teacher education students to the discipline of mathematics, its nature, history, philosophy and place in secondary education. Students will reflect on the processes of mathematics learning and engage with, explore and explicate ideas about mathematics pedagogy, curriculum and the assessment of school students' acquisition of mathematical concepts. The focus of this subject will be the years 7-12 mathematics curriculum and in particular the development of content from the number and algebra strands within the mathematics K-10 syllabus. Students will explore the primary/secondary school transition and the relationship between mathematics, numeracy and literacy in the mathematics classroom and in the wider curriculum. Students will select and plan learning activities and lesson sequences which are inclusive, engaging and supportive of school student learning in years 7-10 mathematics. Particular attention is devoted to the application of contemporary theories of learning in mathematics, authentic pedagogies and assessment for learning in the planning of secondary mathematics curriculum.
learning_outcomes: Develop and explain engaging strategies (including the use of ICT) for teaching secondary mathematics from late Stage 3 through to Stage 6.

Describe the structure and content of the mathematics 7-10 Syllabus for NSW or the Australian Curriculum, including assessment and reporting requirements and apply this in the development of a sequence of learning activities.
Design contextualised teaching and learning activities for mathematics 7-10, which integrate literacy and numerary strategies and cater for a diversity of learners' needs and abilities.
Identify and design a range of assessment strategies to assess and provide feedback to students on their achievement of learning outcomes.
Apply contemporary models of pedagogy in planning a sequence of learning activities that develop a foundational mathematical concept from late Stage 3 through to Stage 6.

Articulate the role of secondary mathematics in the K-12 curriculum (focusing on the links between Stage 3 and 4) and in the development of students' literacy, digital literacy and numeracy capabilities.

title: Curriculum Method 1: Information Technology
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores a range of approaches to information and technology (IT) education in Years 7-12. It aims to assist teacher education students to construct Computing Technology specific lessons, and to program units of study that are challenging, engaging, and supportive of student learning. Students will be introduced to practical student-centred project-based learning in IT education. Particular attention will be devoted to the implementation of relevant state syllabus documents, authentic pedagogies, and assessment for learning in the context of secondary school IT education. Students will learn about safety, control and risk assessment in IT environments as well as strategies for the management of resources and equipment.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of project-based learning, authentic pedagogy, and assessment for learning in their planning for teaching.
Explain technological literacy as it relates to contemporary curriculum expectations.
Review the contemporary literature on project-based learning.
Apply IT concepts and metalanguage.
Develop Computing Technology syllabus-aligned lessons and units of study.
Integrate cross-curriculum and cross-cultural content into units of work.
Determine the appropriateness of software and hardware resources for teaching secondary school IT classes.
Identify strategies for managing students and resources to help create a safe teaching and learning environment.
