title: Curriculum Method 1: Science
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores a range of pedagogical approaches to science education in Years 7-10. It examines current Science 7-10 syllabus documents and identifies the place of science in the school curriculum. It promotes skills in selecting, planning and implementing learning activities and lesson sequences which are inclusive, engaging and supportive of student learning. Particular attention is devoted to the application of contemporary theories of learning in science, authentic pedagogies and assessment for learning in the context of secondary science education in diverse classes. An understanding of the nature of science, safety in science, risk assessment and the application of information and communications technologies in science teaching are also explored.
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of assessment strategies to assess and provide feedback to students on their achievement of learning outcomes.
Apply the structure and content of the Science 7-10 Syllabus for NSW or the Australian Curriculum in the development of a sequence of lessons.
Integrate pedagogies afforded by scientific and educational technologies into teaching/learning activities for Science 7-10.
Apply contemporary models of pedagogy, including inquiry based strategies, in the planning of sequences of teaching/learning activities and assessment in science.
Design contextualised teaching and learning activities for Science 7-10, which integrate literacy and numerary strategies and cater for a diversity of learners' needs and abilities.

Plan teaching and learning sequences for Science 7-10 that utilise learners prior experience of scientific ideas and will provide learners with opportunities to develop or apply their conceptual understandings through the application of Working Scientifically skills and open, inquiry questions.

title: Curriculum Method 1: PDHPE
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: As the first of two curriculum and pedagogy subjects, EMR441 Curriculum Method 1: PDHPE will provide opportunities for teacher education students to develop an understanding of and apply the curriculum inclusions in the K-10 continuum of the NSW Personal Development, Health and Physical Education (PDHPE) Key Learning Area. The subject aims to challenge students to justify the role and value of PDHPE in the broader school curriculum. Students will explore and apply current theories relating to pedagogy and practice, including the safe use of digital resources and tools, protective strategies and sexual safety, and accommodate the diversity of learners' needs, interests and abilities. In this subject, students will examine and apply contemporary, evidence-based practices relating to curriculum design, literacy and numeracy, digital literacy, differentiation, authentic assessment, quality teaching, and reporting in a range of contexts and settings.
learning_outcomes: Critique and apply pedagogical models for teaching PDHPE, including strategies explicitly designed to develop students' literacy, numeracy and digital literacy skills in PDHPE.
Design and employ strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment to cater for the diverse needs of learners.
Assess student achievement by designing real-world, meaningful, stage appropriate tasks, which engage learners in acts of intellectual quality and provide opportunity for all students to succeed.
Develop positive and safe learning environments that promote the social and emotional wellbeing of students.
Prepare and apply standards-referenced marking criteria and meaningfully report learner achievement to key stakeholders.
Evaluate the role and value of personal development, health and physical education within the whole school curriculum; including an understanding of the continuum of learning from K to 10.

Apply the structure and content of the NSW Stage 4 and 5 PDHPE/Child Studies/PASS/Life Skills syllabus to effectively program learning sequences, being mindful of issues of risk and safety, including e-safety, sexual safety and protective strategies.

title: Curriculum Method 1: Visual Arts
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop a foundational understanding of secondary Visual Arts education, Years 7- 12, with a focus on the NSW Stage 4 and 5 syllabi. Continuums of learning in Creative Arts K-12 and NSW Visual Arts, Photographic and Digital Media Years 7-10 and Visual Design Years 7-10 syllabi are explored. The subject begins with an examination of Visual Arts as a discipline and the self as learner. From this foundation, the subject then addresses understandings of teaching and learning in Visual Arts, local and global curriculum, the nature of Visual Arts teaching in schools and sites of learning beyond the classroom. Through engagement with these topics, students will develop an understanding of approaches to Visual Arts education, theories and practice with a focus on how to engage students in the secondary years in meaningful, rigorous and purposeful learning. Formal assessment focuses on the development and expression of knowledge in relation to Visual Arts education and the application of developing knowledge and skills through authentic practice-based tasks
learning_outcomes: apply pedagogical models for teaching Visual Arts, including strategies explicitly designed to develop students' literacy, numeracy and digital literacy skills in Visual Arts; and
identify, use and develop resources for secondary Visual Arts, creating connections between Visual Arts and the wider community;
discuss the role and value of Visual Arts (Stages 4-5) in the continuum of learning in Creative Arts K-12 and in the broader school curriculum;
develop effective teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that incorporate cross-curriculum priorities / general capabilities in Visual Arts (Stages 4 and 5);

discuss the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of teaching and learning visual arts as exemplified in the NSW Visual Arts 7-10 Syllabus, the NSW Photographic and Digital Media Years 7-10 Syllabus and the NSW Visual Design Years 7-10 Syllabus;

plan learning activities, aligned with Stage 4-5 Visual Arts syllabus outcomes, and apply strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment in visual arts for students with diverse needs and abilities;
effectively employ ICT applications to support learning and teaching of content and processes in Visual Arts.

syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop a foundational understanding of secondary Visual Arts education, Years 7- 12, with a focus on the NSW Stage 4 and 5 syllabi. Continuums of learning in Creative Arts K-12 and NSW Visual Arts, Photographic and Digital Media Years 7-10 and Visual Design Years 7-10 syllabi are explored. The subject begins with an examination of Visual Arts as a discipline and the self as learner. From this foundation, the subject then addresses understandings of teaching and learning in Visual Arts, local and global curriculum, the nature of Visual Arts teaching in schools and sites of learning beyond the classroom. Through engagement with these topics, students will develop an understanding of approaches to Visual Arts education, theories and practice with a focus on how to engage students in the secondary years in meaningful, rigorous and purposeful learning. Formal assessment focuses on the development and expression of knowledge in relation to Visual Arts education and the application of developing knowledge and skills through authentic practice-based tasks.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role and value of Visual Arts (Stages 4-5) in the continuum of learning in Creative Arts K-12 and in the broader school curriculum.
Effectively employ ICT applications to support learning and teaching of content and processes in Visual Arts.
Develop effective teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that incorporate cross-curriculum priorities / general capabilities in Visual Arts (Stages 4 and 5).

Explain the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of teaching and learning visual arts as exemplified in the NSW Visual Arts 7-10 Syllabus, the NSW Photographic and Digital Media Years 7-10 Syllabus and the NSW Visual Design Years 7-10 Syllabus.
Identify, use and develop resources for secondary Visual Arts, creating connections between Visual Arts and the wider community.

Plan learning activities, aligned with Stage 4-5 Visual Arts syllabus outcomes, and apply strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment in visual arts for students with diverse needs and abilities.
Apply pedagogical models for teaching Visual Arts, including strategies explicitly designed to develop students' literacy, numeracy and digital literacy skills in Visual Arts.

title: Curriculum Method 2: Drama
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Teacher education students will explore experiential learning theory and critically apply this methodology to Stage 6 classroom drama education. This subject develops the skills of programming, planning, implementing and assessing classroom drama learning experiences for stage 6 students with a range of abilities and backgrounds. It builds on the knowledge and understanding introduced in the previous subject EML343, developing an appreciation of the K-12 continuum of learning in the discipline of Drama. Teacher education students will design teaching and learning sequences that require learners to engage in the practices of Making, Performing and Critically Studying and to create and test ideas, generate creative works with confidence, shape inquiry and to critically evaluate and reflect on what they do. Students apply teaching and assessment strategies which are appropriate to Stage 6 drama, inclusive of the needs of diverse learners and address cross-curricular priorities / general capabilities.
learning_outcomes: Identify pedagogies and resources for stage 6 drama, including differentiated teaching, learning and assessment strategies to meet the needs of diverse students in Stage 6 drama.
Organise teaching resources that feature experiential activities and stimulus material and include strategies to cater for a diverse range of learners.
Apply curriculum metalanguage and dramatic language to unit and assessment design in senior drama.

Implement a selection of teaching resources for drama teaching and learning (Stage 6) including the selection of digital resources and tools with appropriate digital content to meet Stage 6 curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements.
Execute teaching programs that use a range of teaching and assessment strategies and are constructively aligned to the stage 6 drama syllabus outcomes.
Discuss the models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of drama teaching and learning and the drama theory & practice K-12 continuum.
Analyse and implement assessment and feedback strategies for assessing drama curriculum outcomes.

title: Curriculum Method 2: English
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject requires teacher education students (TESs) to examine professional perspectives on the teaching of secondary English. TESs examine the structure and organisation of Stage 6 English curriculum content, with attention given to each of the three significant strands in Stage 6 English curriculum, namely language, literature and literacy, and including multiliteracies and multimodal texts. TESs develop knowledge and skill in applying professional principles and practices appropriate to the design, implementation and assessment of high quality Stage 6 English curriculum teaching and learning programs that cater for the needs of diverse learners.
learning_outcomes: Compose a pedagogical position statement on teaching and learning in secondary English.
Plan Stage 6 English lessons that include quality teaching, learning and assessment strategies, including ICT strategies, that provide for differentiation of learning strategies for diverse learners.
Describe how secondary English curriculum content is organised, including the teaching of language, literature and literacy.
Examine and justify evaluate teaching and learning principles and practices for Stage 6 English.
Select and examine literary texts and/or non-literary texts for teaching and learning in Stage 6 English.

title: Curriculum Method 2: HSIE/HASS
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject builds upon the first curriculum method subject and incorporates an analysis of the major strands of Human Society and Its Environment (HSIE) / Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS) at a senior secondary level. Teacher education students learn to plan and explain teaching and learning sequences which draw upon principles of authentic pedagogy, and incorporate ICT. Students engage with conceptualisations of the Stage 6 HSIE/HASS curriculum teaching areas and examine how these are represented in curriculum documents. This subject examines the wide-ranging nature of Stage 6 HSIE/HASS curriculum content and incorporates content from all NSW Stage 6 board developed courses. Students apply teaching and assessment strategies which are appropriate to Stage 6 HSIE/HASS, inclusive of the needs of diverse learners and address cross-curricular priorities / general capabilities.
learning_outcomes: Explain the selection of teaching resources for HSIE/HASS teaching and learning sequences (Stage 6) that are culturally appropriate and inclusive, including the selection of digital resources and tools with appropriate digital content to meet Stage 6 curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements.
Discuss the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of HSIE/HASS teaching and learning and the place of HSIE/HASS (Stage 6) in the K-12 school curriculum.
Analyse current issues, pedagogies and resources that relate to the teaching of stage 6 HSIE/HASS, and justify their use in HSIE/HASS teaching and learning (Stage 6).
Apply strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment in Stage 6 HSIE/HASS.

Develop HSIE (Stage 6) teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that incorporate cross-curriculum priorities/general capabilities and explain their learning design with respect to the vision, values, principles, and pedagogical practices of HSIE and HASS.

title: Curriculum Method 2: Information Technology
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores a range of approaches to teaching Information Technology subjects in a senior secondary school (Years 11-12). It aims to assist teacher education students to construct lessons and units of study that are challenging, engaging, and supportive of school students' learning. Particular attention will be devoted to the implementation of relevant state syllabus documents, quality teaching strategies, and assessment for learning. In NSW these documents refer to two syllabi, namely, Enterprise Computing (EC) and Software Engineering (SE).
learning_outcomes: Differentiate a range of approaches to teaching and learning.
Realise and apply the principles authentic pedagogy, and assessment for learning, in their planning for teaching senior secondary Information Technology.
Develop assessment tasks that will differentiate student learning.
Critically review the function and place of EC and SE.
Evaluate software and hardware resources appropriate for teaching.
Develop classroom management strategies.
Develop EC and SE lessons and unit of study.
Integrate cross-cultural content into units of work.

title: Curriculum Method 2: Mathematics
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject extends teacher education students' knowledge and practice of mathematics teaching and learning with a focus on Year 11 and Year 12 NSW Mathematics syllabuses and the Australian Curriculum. Particular attention is devoted to issues in the teaching and learning of mathematics and the application of contemporary theories of learning in mathematics in planning of units of work for Stage 6. In this subject students will explore a range of strategies and ICTs for teaching and assessing Stage 6 mathematics, with a focus on ways of differentiating the curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners. The role and value of mathematics in the broader school curriculum and strategies to embed the cross-curricular priorities and general capabilities are also explored. The subject builds upon the previous secondary mathematics curriculum and pedagogy subject and assumes students have a deep understanding of the discipline content associated with Stage 6 mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Plan teaching and learning sequences for Stage 6 mathematics that apply appropriate pedagogical models for learning mathematics and provide learners with opportunities to develop or apply their conceptual understandings through the application of Working Mathematically skills.
Apply the concepts, content and structure of a Stage 6 Mathematics syllabus in the development of a detailed teaching program for a sequence of lessons.
Identify and describe an issue relevant to the teaching and learning of secondary mathematics in the Australian context for the diverse range of learners.
Describe appropriate strategies for addressing an issue relevant to the teaching and learning of secondary mathematics in the Australian context for the diverse range of learners.

Identify and use resources for Stage 6 mathematics that are culturally appropriate and inclusive, including the selection of digital resources and tools with appropriate digital content to meet Stage 6 curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements in mathematics.
Describe classroom environments and teaching and assessment strategies that support inclusive student engagement and achievement in Stage 6 mathematics.

Design contextualised teaching and learning activities for Stage 6 mathematics, which align with cross-curricular priorities and the general capabilities and cater for a diversity of learners' needs and abilities.

title: Curriculum Method 2: PDHPE
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This curriculum subject focuses on the NSW Stage 6 Personal Development, Health and Physical Education syllabus offerings (Health and Movement Science and Community and Family Studies). The subject provides opportunities for teacher education students to apply contemporary evidence-based knowledge and pedagogies to plan, assess and report on student achievement of curriculum outcomes. Students further learn to differentiate outcomes, content, processes and assessments to cater for the needs of diverse learners. Students will embed digital resources into lesson design and assessment, while ensuring learners' e-safety. The subject supports students to design learning experiences to assist their learners develop critical inquiry and research skills.
learning_outcomes: Describe strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment to be inclusive of learner ability and needs.
Design engaging pedagogies that promote collaboration, creative thinking, communication, analysis, research and problem solving.
Select digital resources to enhance student achievement of outcomes, taking into consideration students' e-safety.
Design learning experiences aligned with assessment and reporting processes that incorporate the social justice principles of equity, diversity and inclusive environments.
Communicate the structures, content and assessment requirements of the syllabus inclusions in the Stage 6 NSW PDHPE Key Learning Area.
Select strategies to enhance students' literacy, digital literacy and numeracy skills appropriate to PDHPE (Stage 6).
Develop teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that apply Stage 6 NESA curriculum requirements.

title: Curriculum Method 2: Science
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject examines Year 11 and Year 12 NSW science syllabuses and the Australian Curriculum. A major focus of the subject is on planning teaching and learning sequences for Stage 6 science that will provide learners with opportunities to develop science understandings through the application of Working Scientifically skills and inquiry questions. A range of strategies for teaching and assessing senior science subjects are considered including critical scientific thinking, problem-solving techniques, and the planning, conducting and communicating results of investigations. Strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment to meet the diverse needs of students in Stage 6 science and to embed the cross-curricular priorities and general capabilities are explored. The use of digital resources and tools, including the selection of appropriate digital content, to complement teaching strategies, enhance learning sequences and lesson plans, and to meet curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements in Stage 6 science is also included. The subject builds upon the first curriculum method subject and a deep understanding of the discipline content in one or more areas of science (biology, chemistry, physics, earth and environmental science) is assumed.
learning_outcomes: Design an assessment item, including a marking rubric, for a chosen area of content in senior secondary science.
Embed literacy, digital literacy and numeracy in teaching/learning activities in senior secondary science teaching programs.
Develop a detailed teaching program for a sequence of lessons from an area of content in senior secondary sciences.

Identify and appraise teaching resources for Stage 6 science that are culturally appropriate and inclusive, including the selection of digital resources and tools with appropriate digital content to meet Stage 6 curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements in science.
Implement senior secondary science curriculum and syllabus documents for NSW or the Australian Curriculum into a teaching program.
Apply appropriate pedagogical models within a teaching program, including inquiry-based strategies, for teaching senior secondary sciences.
Critically assess the suitability of a range of digital resources to support teaching and learning and assessment requirements in senior science.

title: Curriculum Method 2: Visual Arts
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop and deepen their understanding of secondary Visual Arts education, 7-12, with a focus on the NSW Stage 6 Visual Arts syllabus. The curriculum involves a practice-based approach that models, analyses and approximates teaching and learning. Students develop their understandings of Visual Arts curriculum, continuums of learning, approaches to pedagogy and assessment in Visual Arts. Students explore the perspectives of learners in Visual Arts, engage in collaborative examinations and approximations of teaching and develop connections to the community. Learning culminates in involvement in a documented online student event and development of a portfolio of professional teaching resources. Forms of assessment include digital presentations, curriculum documents, collaborative learning space development, investigative processes along with simulated assessment and reporting. Assessments focus on the application of knowledge and skills in a series of integrated and authentic practice-based contexts and tasks.
learning_outcomes: Describe the management practices required of Visual Arts teachers including safety and risk management, budgeting, selecting, storing, maintaining and replacing materials, equipment and other resources.

Describe the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of Visual Arts teaching and learning and the place of Visual Arts (Stage 6) in the continuum of learning in Creative Arts K-12.
Employ information and communication technologies (ICT) applications to assess and report on student learning and achievement of specific syllabus outcomes.
Contribute to a community of professional practice to achieve educational goals.
Plan teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that apply curriculum requirements and the concepts, values, principles, and pedagogical practices of Visual Arts (Stage 6).
Describe strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment to cater for the needs and abilities of diverse learners.

Design and evaluate learning experiences aligned with assessment processes that incorporate the social justice principles of equity, diversity and inclusive environments as appropriate to Visual Arts (Stage 6).

title: Curriculum Method: Agriculture
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores agricultural education as a medium for secondary school students' development. It examines current Years 7-12 syllabus guides and outcomes, curriculum material and recent research in technology and agricultural education and provides the context for a developmental framework for education. The focus of the subject is on promoting skills in selecting, planning and implementing teaching sequences within a constructivist learning model and productive pedagogies frameworks. It further incorporates the cross-curriculum priority area of sustainability and the general capabilities of critical thinking, ethical understanding, digital literacy, literacy, and numeracy. In addition, it addresses catering for and difference and diversity, programming units of work, and standards referenced assessment practices.
learning_outcomes: Select and source appropriate resource materials to support quality teaching and learning.

Develop project-based teaching units from appropriate syllabuses that incorporate strategies that enhance literacy, numeracy, and digital literacy capabilities, utilise information and communication technologies, and meet the needs of diverse student cohorts.

Develop formative assessment strategies and standards referenced summative assessment tasks and rubrics.
Develop a safe work method statement to create safe learning experiences and working environments.

title: Curriculum Method: Design and Technology
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores a range of approaches to Design and Technology education in Years 7-12. It identifies the position of design and technology in the school curriculum and explores design and the design process as concepts and their role in teaching and learning. It assists students in constructing technology context-specific Design and Technology lessons and units of work that are challenging, engaging, and supportive of student learning. Students will be introduced to practical student-centred learning in Design and Technology education. Particular attention will be devoted to the implementation of relevant technology syllabi, authentic pedagogies and assessment for learning in the context of secondary technology education in diverse classes. Issues of literacy, numeracy, safety/risk assessment and resource management strategies in Design and Technology classroom environments are addressed.
learning_outcomes: Develop teaching and learning activities that integrate the general capabilities and cross-curriculum priorities.

Prepare and explain detailed lesson plans and units of work that include appropriate resources and suitably aligned research-based pedagogical strategies to effectively teach concepts and other content.
Interpret the requirements and expectations in the Design and Technology curriculum.
Design and explain strategies that are designed to effectively assess and provide feedback on student achievement of identified learning outcomes.
Develop appropriate teaching and learning strategies for diverse learning environments and contexts.
Apply professional written and other communication skills.
Explain design projects from a risk assessment and ethical perspective and develop corresponding project management plans.

title: Curriculum Method: Senior HSIE/HASS
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject builds upon the first curriculum method subject and incorporates an analysis of the major strands of Human Society and Its Environment (HSIE) / Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS) at a senior secondary level. Teacher education students learn to plan and explain teaching and learning sequences which draw upon principles of authentic pedagogy, and incorporate Information and Communication Technology (ICT). Students engage with conceptualisations of the Stage 6 HSIE/HASS curriculum teaching areas and examine how these are represented in curriculum documents. This subject examines the wide-ranging nature of Stage 6 HSIE/HASS curriculum content and incorporates content from all NSW Stage 6 board developed courses. Students apply teaching and assessment strategies which are appropriate to Stage 6 HSIE/HASS, inclusive of the needs of diverse learners and address cross-curricular priorities / general capabilities.
learning_outcomes: Explain the selection of teaching resources for HSIE/HASS teaching and learning sequences (Stage 6) that are culturally appropriate and inclusive, including the selection of digital resources and tools with appropriate digital content to meet Stage 6 curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements.

Develop HSIE (Stage 6) teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that incorporate cross-curriculum priorities / general capabilities and explain their learning design with respect to the vision, values, principles, and pedagogical practices of HSIE and HASS.
Apply strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment in Stage 6 HSIE/HASS.
Discuss the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of HSIE/HASS teaching and learning and the place of HSIE/HASS (Stage 6) in the K-12 school curriculum.
Analyse current issues, pedagogies and resources that relate to the teaching of Stage 6 HSIE/HASS, and justify their use in HSIE/HASS teaching and learning (Stage 6).

title: Curriculum Method: Senior HSIE/HASS
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject builds upon the first curriculum method subject and incorporates an analysis of the major strands of Human Society and Its Environment (HSIE) / Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS) at a senior secondary level. Students learn to plan and evaluate teaching and learning sequences which draw upon principles of authentic pedagogy, and incorporate ICT. Students engage with conceptualisations of the Stage 6 HSIE/HASS curriculum teaching areas and examine how these are represented in curriculum documents. This subject examines the wide-ranging nature of Stage 6 HSIE/HASS curriculum content and incorporates content from all NSW Stage 6 board developed courses. Students apply teaching and assessment strategies which are appropriate to Stage 6 HSIE/HASS, inclusive of the needs of diverse learners and address cross-curricular priorities / general capabilities.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the knowledge base and models of pedagogy underpinning the principles and practices of HSIE/HASS teaching and learning and the place of HSIE/HASS (Stage 6) in the K-12 school curriculum.
Apply strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment in Stage 6 HSIE/HASS.

Justify the selection of teaching resources for HSIE/HASS teaching and learning sequences (Stage 6) that are culturally appropriate and inclusive, including the selection of digital resources and tools with appropriate digital content to meet Stage 6 curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements.
Analyse current issues, pedagogies and resources that relate to the teaching of Stage 6 HSIE/HASS, and justify their use in HSIE/HASS teaching and learning (Stage 6).

Develop HSIE (Stage 6) teaching, learning, and assessment sequences that incorporate cross-curriculum priorities / general capabilities and justify their learning design with respect to the vision, values, principles, and pedagogical practices of HSIE and HASS.

title: Curriculum Method: Senior Science
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject examines Year 11 and Year 12 NSW science syllabuses and the Australian Curriculum. A major focus of the subject is on planning teaching and learning sequences for Stage 6 science that will provide learners with opportunities to develop science understandings through the application of Working Scientifically skills and inquiry questions. A range of strategies for teaching and assessing senior science subjects are considered including critical scientific thinking, problem-solving techniques, and the planning, conducting and communicating results of investigations. Strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment to meet the diverse needs of students in Stage 6 science and to embed the cross-curricular priorities and general capabilities are explored. The use of digital resources and tools, including the selection of appropriate digital content, to complement teaching strategies, enhance learning sequences and lesson plans, and to meet curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements in Stage 6 science is also included. The subject builds upon the first curriculum method subject and a deep understanding of the discipline content in one or more areas of science (biology, chemistry, physics, earth and environmental science) is assumed.
learning_outcomes: Identify opportunities to embed literacy, digital literacy and numeracy in teaching/learning activities in senior secondary science teaching programs.
Identify and appraise teaching resources for Stage 6 science that are culturally appropriate and inclusive.
Apply appropriate pedagogical models within a teaching program, including inquiry-based strategies, for teaching senior secondary sciences.
Design an assessment item, including a marking rubric, for a chosen area of content in senior secondary science.
Assess the suitability of a range of digital resources to support teaching and learning and assessment requirements in senior science.
Incorporate senior secondary science curriculum and syllabus documents for NSW or the Australian Curriculum into a teaching program.
Develop a detailed teaching program for a sequence of lessons from an area of content in senior secondary sciences.

Identify and appraise teaching resources for Stage 6 science, including the selection of digital resources and tools with appropriate digital content to meet Stage 6 curriculum, assessment and reporting requirements in science.

title: Curriculum Method: Technologies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on earlier technology curriculum and pedagogy subjects. The focus in this subject is on the Years 7-12 TAS classroom and a broad range of Technologies subjects; agricultural, food, graphics, industrial, information and textiles technologies. It aims to assist teacher education students to construct scope and sequence plans, units of work, assessment plans and tasks that are challenging, engaging, and supportive of student learning. Particular attention will be devoted to the implementation of relevant syllabus and related support documents, quality teaching strategies and assessment design practices for specific contexts with diverse students (EAL/D, Aboriginal, literacy/numeracy, low SES) and students with special needs. Students will study the syllabus associated with their specific area of discipline.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and integrate ICT resources for TAS teaching.
Analyse stage 5 and 6 TAS syllabi and support documents.
Develop strategies for managing and supporting students completing project-based learning.
Plan appropriate differentiated teaching and learning resources, activities and tasks.
Design standards-referenced assessment tasks, rubrics and feedback.
Construct practical activities, create units of work, and develop scope and sequence plans.
Plan a range of approaches to teaching and learning in TAS.
Implement the Quality Teaching principles, and Assessment for Learning.

title: Curriculum Method: Technology Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The focus in this subject is on the Years 7-12 classroom for a broad range of Technologies courses. It engages with the development of context appropriate lesson plans, units of work, scope and sequence plans, assessment plans and tasks that are challenging, engaging, and supportive of student learning. Principles and strategies for feedback will also be addressed. Particular attention will be devoted to the implementation of relevant syllabus and related support documents, effective teaching strategies and assessment design practices including those for contexts with diverse student populations and literacy and numeracy priorities. Students will study the syllabus associated with their specific area of discipline.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate teaching and learning experiences for students with diverse needs and develop effective strategies to meet literacy and numeracy priorities.
Design effective teaching and feedback strategies.
Integrate a range of information and communication technologies into Technology teaching.
Interpret stage 5 and 6 Technology syllabi and support documents.
Plan a project-based approach to teaching and learning in Technology courses.
Assess and manage risk to create safe learning experiences and environments.
Design standards referenced assessment plans, tasks, and feedback.
Construct school community and syllabus-aligned Technology lesson plans, units of work, and assessment and scope and sequence plans.

title: Curriculum Method: Technology Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The focus in this subject is on the Years 7-12 classroom for a broad range of Technologies courses. It engages with the development of context appropriate lesson plans, units of work, scope and sequence plans, and assessment plans and tasks that are challenging, engaging, and supportive of student learning. Principles and strategies for feedback will also be addressed. Particular attention will be devoted to the implementation of relevant syllabus and related support documents, effective teaching strategies and assessment design practices including those for contexts with diverse student populations and literacy and numeracy priorities. Students will study the syllabus associated with their specific area of discipline.
learning_outcomes: Design standards referenced assessment tasks, plans, and feedback.
Differentiate teaching and learning experiences for students with diverse needs and develop effective strategies to meet literacy and numeracy priorities.
Plan a project-based approach to teaching and learning in Technology courses.
Construct and justify technology lesson plans, units of work, and assessment and scope and sequence plans.
Assess and manage risk to create safe learning experiences and environments.
Analyse stage 5 and 6 Technology syllabi and support documents.
Effectively integrate a range of appropriate information and communication technologies into Technology teaching.
Design effective teaching and feedback strategies.

title: Curriculum Studies: Creative Arts
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject the students will be introduced to the concepts and ideas that underpin the Key Learning Area of the Creative Arts, which includes the four art-forms of dance, drama, visual arts and music. The students will acquire knowledge, skills and experience and develop appropriate strategies for planning, programming and teaching art, music, dance and drama curricula in schools. The students will experience the materials and subject matter of the four art-forms and develop skills in their use.
learning_outcomes: Have demonstrated competence in the development of learning experiences which illustrate a differentiated curriculum that meets the diverse needs of learners in the Creative Arts.

Illustrate understanding of the child's artistic and conceptual development, theories of learning and knowledge of pedagogies through the design of sequenced, integrated lessons as delineated in the NSW Creative Arts Syllabus.
Develop, implement and assess student learning through integrated arts learning experiences across the curriculum with particular reference to literacy.
Have developed an understanding and appreciation of art, music, dance and drama through reading, classroom observations, looking at artworks and immersion in arts-based activities.
Demonstrate knowledge, skills and a range of strategies for teaching, learning and assessing in the K6 school Creative Arts classroom, including the use of ICTs.
Have an understanding of classroom management and safety issues with arts-based activities.

title: Curriculum Studies: Personal Development, Health and Physical Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The students will develop a broad, critical knowledge and understanding of the discipline area of PDHPE. It focuses on examining and critiquing the content, principles, practices, and pedagogical approaches associated with physical activity and movement education, personal development and health education. Students will design differentiated inclusive experiences for all learners including those from diverse cultural and social contexts. Students will also appreciate the diverse social factors which impact upon the nature of PDHPE for supporting the development of health, well-being, and a positive sense of self and others. Students will link PDHPE with literacy and all Key Learning Areas.
learning_outcomes: Value PDHPE as a lifelong learning experience.
Compose academically informed positions and judgements on the nature and role of PDHPE for supporting the development of health, wellbeing, and a positive sense of self and others.
Select an array of children's literature and other visual stimulus to address sensitive and social issues in the K6 syllabus.
Design, implement and report on quality assessment for and assessment of learning tasks that assist in developing descriptive profiles of student learning outcomes.
Investigate the place of PDHPE in the continuum of learning from K12, with particular emphasis on the links between Stage 3 and 4.
Justify the inclusion of PDHPE as a valuable educational experience in the broader school curriculum.

Critique, select and apply a variety of pedagogical models to design stage appropriate, creative, challenging and inclusive learning experiences which cater for the varying learning styles and needs of their learners.
Accurately engage with the literacies applicable to the KLA.
Examine and critique the content, principles and practices, and pedagogical approaches, associated with teaching physical activity and movement education.
Affirm, celebrate and accommodate the cultural and social difference of their learners.
Investigate the aims, objectives, outcomes, content, course requirements, and key terms in the PDHPE K6 syllabus.
Differentiate the curriculum to include the interests, motivations, abilities and sociocultural backgrounds of their learners.
prerequisites: EMR205: PDHPE: Health and Movement Studies
EMR302: Personal Development, Health and Physical Education Curriculum

title: Curriculum Studies: Primary HASS
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students to teach in the primary curriculum area, Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS) and the NSW Key Learning Area of Human Society and Its Environment (HSIE). The subject aims to give students an understanding of the relevant syllabus documents and the rationale for teaching HASS, wider research skills, an understanding of the inquiry process, and knowledge and understanding of practical approaches for teaching HASS/HSIE in the classroom.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and apply a range of strategies and resources for teaching and assessing Primary HSIE in a sequence of learning.
Embed cross-curriculum priorities and general capabilities in HASS learning sequences.
Critically discuss a rationale for teaching HASS in primary classrooms, which includes inquiry-based and place-based pedagogies.
Plan and use a range of literacy, numeracy and digital technologies capabilities in HASS learning programs.
Plan learning experiences that comply with the requirements of HASS and the NSW HSIE K-6 Syllabus (2024), Early Stage 1-Stage 3.
Incorporate meta-cognitive skills into planning and teaching decisions as a means of building reflective practice.
Design engaging learning experiences that connect the HASS curricula with the community.
prerequisites: EMH205: HSIE: Teaching About People, Places and the Past

title: Curriculum Studies: Primary HASS
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students to teach in the primary curriculum area, Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS) and the NSW Key Learning Area of Human Society and Its Environment (HSIE). The subject aims to give students an understanding of the relevant syllabus documents and the rationale for teaching HASS, wider research skills, an understanding of the inquiry process, and knowledge and understanding of practical approaches for teaching HASS/HSIE in the classroom.
learning_outcomes: Articulate a rationale for teaching HASS in primary classrooms, which includes inquiry-based and place-based pedagogies.
Incorporate literacy, numeracy and digital technologies capabilities in HASS learning programs.
Plan learning experiences that comply with the requirements of HASS and the NSW HSIE K-6 Syllabus (2024), Early Stage 1-Stage 3.
Incorporate a range of strategies and resources for teaching and assessing Primary HSIE in a sequence of learning.
Embed cross-curriculum priorities and general capabilities in HASS learning sequences.
Design meaningful learning experiences that connect the HASS curricula with the community.

title: Customs Field Education - Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject the emphasis will be on the practical day to day activity of customs officers and current domestic practice/legislation. Students will transition knowledge and skills gained from earlier subjects in the course from the international law basis, upon which these subjects have been founded, to their own domestic law and practice under supervision.By reflective practice students will apply and integrate their existing technical knowledge and skills to their workplace and further develop their technical and non-technical communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, interpret and practically apply international (principles and best practice)and national developments affecting border integrity and security applicable to their own customs jurisdiction.
Critically assess the challenges faced by customs in the delivery of their services.
Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the policy responses of government to customs issues.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of the role of customs and their environment.
Identify and detail current domestic practice/legislation and communicate the results to others.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of international organisations, treaties and conventions on their own customs jurisdiction.

title: CUS05C Credit Package 5 - University of Texas at Brownsville (PG)
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject forms a credit package for students who have been admitted to the Master of Customs Administration and who have completed the Graduate Certificate In Customs and International Trade delivered and developed by the Centre for Customs and Excise Studies (CCES) at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB).
learning_outcomes: The objectives of this subject are to grant eligible admitted students forward credit on a block basis (16 credit points) to allow this particular student stream the opportunity to pursue in greater depths aspects of customs administration that will best cater to their particular interest and their professional aspirations.

title: Customer Due Diligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Students will explore the importance of Customer Due Diligence (CDD) in identifying, mitigating, and preventing financial crimes and how it can be applied as a key control to comply with regulatory requirements including monitoring and reporting of suspicious activity. Students will examine the notion of a risk-based approach and understand how to implement various CDD measures to mitigate and manage Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (ML/TF) risk. The subject will also explore the concept of Enhanced Customer Due Diligence (ECDD) and the role it plays in detecting, disrupting ML/TF
learning_outcomes: Analyse knowledge and skills relating Ongoing Customer Due Diligence (OCDD) and Enhanced Customer Due Diligence (ECDD).
Examine the role of CDD as a risk-based compliance approach within a AML/CTF Program.
Apply CDD knowledge and skills to customer identification procedures.

title: Customs Management Theory and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to key features of managing a Customs Administration in the contemporary globalised world, including the role and responsibilities of Customs, Customs policy and practice, strategic and operational management issues, relevant international conventions and agreements, risk management in the Customs context, and international trends that impact on Customs such as social expectations, emerging technologies and the global economy.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically different approaches and operational practices to managing the import, export and transit of goods.
Apply specialised knowledge and skills to identify appropriate responses to strategic management issues and policy objectives including management of risk, information and informed compliance.
Analyse critically the roles and policy objectives of Customs administrations.
Evaluate and analyse critically supply chain security issues and ways in which they may impact on Customs authorities.
Evaluate and transform information to mitigate risks at the strategic and operational level.
Identify and explain key international instruments affecting Customs operations.
Evaluate critically the regulatory framework of a particular Customs authority against established international standards.

Formulate appropriate and well-developed approaches to address complex problems such as control, revenue protection and environmental change in the border management context and be able to communicate those approaches to others.

title: Customs Field Education - Policy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject the emphasis will be on the application of the students skills and knowledge to allow a critical evaluation of current domestic practice and their ability to demonstrate their capability to develop and guide policy determination and be an 'arbiter of change'. Students will transition knowledge and skills gained from earlier subjects in the course from the international law basis, upon which these subjects have been founded, to their own domestic law and practice under supervision.
learning_outcomes: Identify and articulate solutions to selected issues and problems in the customs context and communicate the results to others.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of international organisations, treaties and conventions on their own customs jurisdiction.
Analyse, interpret and practically apply international (principles and best practice)and national developments affecting border integrity and security applicable to their own customs jurisdiction.
Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the policy responses of government to customs issues.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of the role of customs and their environment.
Critically assess the challenges faced by customs in the delivery of their services.

title: Customs Procedures
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the range of procedures used by customs to regulate and facilitate trade flows across national borders. The subject addresses the range of regulatory activities and procedures which must be carried out by the trading community and by Customs in order to comply with the Customs law.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically various operational approaches to the clearance of international consignments and identify good practice, including the use of information technology.
Formulate practical solutions to mitigate potential bottlenecks in trade flows resulting from customs procedures.

Demonstrate an understanding of the roles and responsibilities of the various members of the international trading community relating to customs formalities, including private sector organisations and international organisations such as the UPU.
Evaluate the WCO's methodology for measuring clearance times.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the key border management concepts of control and release, including documentary and physical controls.
Demonstrate an understanding of the broad range of Customs procedures and evaluate the procedures used in different operational settings.

title: Customs Reform and Modernisation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an in-depth study of the key aspects of customs reform and modernization including the rationale for modernisation, the relevant international conventions and agreements and best practice responses to external pressure to reform from the trading environment and the heightened focus on customs performance.
learning_outcomes: Explain and discuss critically the key concepts and rationale for customs reform and modernisation in the context of the otherwise negative impact on international trade flows and border regulation.
Formulate appropriate and well-developed approaches to border policy, practice and procedure relating to reform and modernisation and to be able to communicate those approaches to others.

Locate and use key international instruments and research appropriate best practice responses to reform and modernisation and apply that research to practical and theoretical situations that they may face as border regulators and/or managers.

Identify and explain the practical impact on border regulation and management of the key concepts and the international trade obligations relating to reform and modernisation including identifying the major impediments to the change process and the techniques and strategies for design and implementation of a successful program of organisational change.

title: Customs Research Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: Under the guidance of a supervisor/mentor, the student will be required to undertake research and prepare a dissertation/project on an approved area of customs administration and/or international trade facilitation and regulation. The subject will require completion of a dissertation/research project of approximately 10,000 words and will require demonstration of competence in research and the capacity to present a well-written piece of work which analyses or critically reviews the approved topic in depth.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate good analytical skills and the ability to present well-developed arguments relating to the question posed and supported by logical, compelling premises/evidence, evaluation and critique.
Demonstrate appropriate research techniques, showing the use of primary and secondary sources and depth and quality of research.
Formulate a written contribution to existing knowledge/practice, or an original re-examination of existing knowledge/practice, with a coherent structure that contributes to argument.

Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of their selected topic and familiarity with, and citation of, existing quality literature and the effective relationship of their paper to other scholarship in the area.
Demonstrate literary skills at a high level.

title: Customs Research Methods
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject introduces students to research methodology and planning in the context of the Customs Administration and its related disciplines. The subject focuses on research traditions and paradigms relevant to the student's discipline, and the nature of the research process, including planning and designing a research project. In consultation with their supervisor/mentor students will be required to propose/select a research topic, develop appropriate research method(s) and undertake a preliminary literature review.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the ethical issues in research and their particular relevance to Customs Administration, including recognising the significance of consent, confidentiality and other ethical considerations in relation to research.
Select, evaluate, justify and communicate appropriate research methods for their chosen topic area.
Demonstrate the research skills and expertise necessary to prepare a major paper or a work-based project.

Demonstrate familiarity with the role and potential of research in the field of Customs Administration and related disciplines, including concepts and theories in a professional and/or academic context.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the importance and various roles of the literature review in research.
Formulate and articulate well-developed approaches to a research project, including specificity of purpose and a clear set of objectives.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of the broad body of knowledge in the specialist field of customs administration, including recent developments in theory and practice.
Develop a research plan to explore critically the issues in their chosen topic area in depth and with balance.

title: Customs Workplace Improvement Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: Under CSU supervision students will undertake a workplace improvement project. Students will identify a workplace issue/problem and over the course of the session conduct a situation analysis, develop solutions and prepare and present an implementation plan for their executive management.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate literary skills at a high level.
Demonstrate appropriate research techniques.
Work within a team to achieve results.
Communicate the results of their findings with clarity in a professional setting.
Formulate a written original re-examination of existing knowledge/practice, with a coherent structure that contributes to argument.
Demonstrate good analytical skills and the ability to present well-developed arguments relating to the question posed and supported by logical, compelling premises/evidence, evaluation and critique.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of their selected topic and familiarity with, and citation of, international obligations and best practice.

title: Customs Workplace Planning and Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the strategic leadership necessary in modern customs administrations and seeks to develop their capabilities to formulate planning in a customs workplace, recognising inherent tensions, and be an 'arbiter of change'.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the importance of measuring organisational performance, reviewing strategic performance and activities for future planning.
Analyse leadership styles and the appropriateness of styles for particular strategic activities in the Customs context.
Select and discuss an appropriate strategic planning framework for their Customs administration and understand the components within that framework.
Discuss the importance of stakeholder consultation and customs/business partnerships.
Demonstrate and understanding of the fundamental principles and applications of team leadership and management in a team context tailored to the Customs environment.
Identify the corporate governance framework within their Customs administration and evaluate the effectiveness of existing strategies in respect of structures, policies and procedures.

Analyse existing planning strategies and evaluate against contemporary approaches including reform and modernisation, human resource management, contemporary compliance and change management best practice and risk management concepts and techniques.

title: Cyber Ethics Foundations
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Cyber Ethics Foundations is one of the suites of non-award micro-subjects offered in Studylink. This subject introduces students to foundational ethical theories, equipping them with the skills to identify and analyse ethical issues in the digital world. By applying these theories to case studies, students will develop the ability to navigate and address ethical dilemmas in cyberspace.
learning_outcomes: Identify some common ethical Issues in cyberspace
Demonstrate awareness of fundamental ethical theory
Apply ethical theory to some cyberspace scenarios.

title: Cyber Security Fundamentals
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students explore core cyber security concepts and terminology through applied scenarios, guided activities, and practical examples. The subject focuses on identifying common cyber threats, risks, and unsafe digital behaviours, as well as applying safe computing practices in both personal and workplace contexts. Students analyse cyber security scenarios, covering human, ethical, and organisational factors, to develop a broader understanding of digital risk and responsibility. The subject also develops students’ ability to communicate cyber security risks and responsibilities clearly and appropriately, preparing them to engage responsibly with digital systems and to progress into applied cyber security studies.
learning_outcomes: Communicate cyber security risks and responsibilities clearly and appropriately.
Explain fundamental cyber security concepts and terminology;
Identify common cyber threats, risks, and unsafe digital behaviours;
Analyse cyber security scenarios involving human, ethical, and organisational factors; and
Apply safe computing practices in personal and workplace scenarios;

title: Cyber Incident Response
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of the key concepts, tools, and techniques necessary for effective cyber incident response management. Students will learn how to detect, contain, and mitigate cyber incidents, as well as how to develop and implement an incident response plan. The subject will cover different types of cyber incidents, including malware infections, data breaches, and distributed denial of service attacks, as well as provide practical guidance on how to respond to each.
learning_outcomes: Collect threat intelligence to prepare for cyber incidents.
Describe the principles of cyber incident response management.
Develop and implement an incident response plan.
Manage cyber incidents through the various response phases including detection, containment and investigation.

title: Cyber Security
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides in depth analyses of some of the key cyber security concepts. Students will be introduced to the security threat environment as well as various defensive mechanisms, with a focus on operating system security, program security, host and application hardening and data protection techniques. Some of the emergent information and communication technology security related topics, such as, dark web, Internet of Things (IoT) security and digital forensics will also be briefly discussed.
learning_outcomes: Analyse fundamental cyber security concepts.
Discuss basic concepts of emergent cyber security topics, such as digital forensics, the dark web and IoT security.
Explore and critique some of the security implications of operating systems and computer programs.
Compare and contrast authentication and access control mechanisms.
Propose measures for data protection, host hardening, application security and physical security.

title: Cyber Security Fundamentals
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with knowledge of cyber security principles along with industry-based vendor-neutral IT security knowledge and skills. In particular, the subject helps students prepare for the Security+ industry qualification which has been developed by the International Computer Technology Industry Association (CompTIA). Students will also be introduced to a broad range of cyber security related topics such as infrastructure security, communications network security, cryptography, access control, authentication, external threats, and operational and organisational security. At the completion of this subject, students will be able to apply these concepts to protect computing infrastructure from cyber security threats and attacks.
learning_outcomes: Formulate approaches for incident analysis and response, risk management and disaster recovery/business continuity.
Analyse typical cyber security requirements, formulate and implement technical and procedural strategy to provide enhanced security solutions.
Analyse approaches to implementing secure networks, firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems and identity and access management systems.
Describe key terms, concepts and implementation considerations of fundamental cyber security systems, processes, and tools in a contemporary business context.
Analyse and describe vulnerabilities, threat actors and threat vectors within a contemporary context.

title: Cyber Security Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Cyber security is primarily a management and not a technical problem. Identifying risk and implementing effective policy and practice to secure information is recognised as a management issue. This subject is comprised of a series of topics that investigate cyber security and the implications for the management of Information and Communications Technology (ICT) and primarily management aspects of cyber security to provide a practical insight into ICT security practices. The foundational concepts of cyber security management models and practices are included.
learning_outcomes: Explore and analyse the principle components of enterprise information security governance and planning.
Develop an enterprise information security policy.
Discuss the legal and regulatory environment in the context of cyber security.
Describe the key concepts associated with management of cyber security.
Propose risk management and risk mitigation strategies.

title: Cyber Security Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject helps prepare students for the Certified Information Security Manager Certification (CISM), which is an international industry certification developed by ISACA. Students in this subject will investigate how to establish and maintain an information security governance framework along with the supporting processes to ensure that an organisation's information security strategy is aligned with its goals and objectives.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate appropriate risk treatment options as part of a risk management program.
Formulate a framework to enable an organisation to classify its information assets.
Create and maintain an information security strategy that aligns with organisational goals and objectives.
Identify, define and manage requirements for internal and external resources to execute the information security program.
Establish, monitor and report on a set of security metrics that are appropriate to an organisation's business mission.
Create and maintain an incident response plan to ensure an effective and timely response to information security incidents.

title: Cyber Security Practices
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces applied cyber security practices used to support secure digital environments in organisational and professional contexts. In this subject, students will explore access management, authentication practices, system and device hygiene, data handling, and common defensive controls through guided activities, practical examples, and applied scenarios. Students will develop foundational knowledge and practical skills relevant to entry-level cyber security roles and further study in cyber security and related disciplines. The subject also introduces ethical responsibility, professional conduct, and cultural awareness within cyber security practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain common defensive cyber security practices used in personal and organisational contexts.
Analyse cyber security risks affecting users, devices, systems, and data.
Apply access control and authentication principles to everyday computing scenarios.
Evaluate ethical, professional, and organisational responsibilities in preventing cyber security incidents.
Communicate appropriate responses to basic cyber security risks and incidents to technical and non-technical audiences.

title: Cyber Threat Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: As cyber threats continue to increase, it has become even more important to have a proactive approach to identifying security gaps and have effective measures in place to close those gaps. The availability of data from past cyber incidents provides a vital source of information about the type of adversaries and trajectory of cyber-attacks. That data can be used along with intelligence measures to prevent and mitigate future cyber-attacks. In this subject, students will gain knowledge to become proactive and predictive about cyber-attacks and develop skills to assess the likelihood of cyber threats. Students will learn to apply modelling techniques to become proactive and stay ahead of cyber adversaries. The subject will have a strong focus on hands-on exercises and practical use cases to demonstrate cyber activity attribution, and threat monitoring and countering skills.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and evaluate the countermeasures involved in implementing controls and to follow best practice for reducing cyber threats.
Identify and analyse emerging cyber threats and vulnerabilities to gain a deeper understanding of complex cyber threat situations.
Differentiate frameworks and standards, and to devise a plan to detect and respond to targeted threats.
Develop skills in operational, tactical, and strategic-level threat intelligence, and apply those skills in various threat scenarios.
Evaluate intelligence data sources, and to formulate threat modelling and undertake predictive threat analysis.

title: Cybersecurity and AI
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and cybersecurity within contemporary business environments. Students analyse security threats both posed by AI/ML systems and directed at those systems, including adversarial attacks, data compromise and misuse. The subject develops practical capability in mitigating risks arising from authorised and unauthorised AI/ML usage, implementing governance controls, and protecting AI-enabled business processes.
learning_outcomes: Assess and mitigate threats posed by authorised and unauthorised AI/ML usage in a business environment
Analyse and evaluate security threats posed by and to AI and ML systems in business environments
Critically analyse and address ethical challenges associated with AI/ML use in business environments
Critically evaluate the approaches for managing sanctioned and unsanctioned AI/ML usage in a business environment

title: Cybersecurity Foundations 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Cybersecurity Foundation 1 is the first of two consecutive micro-subjects providing students with an initial introduction to the essential concepts of cybersecurity. Students will understand the digital landscape and learn how to protect themselves from common cyber threats. The subject focuses on basic cybersecurity principles, such as recognising different types of cyber-attacks, understanding data protection, and practicing safe online behaviour. Through a range of learning activities, students will develop awareness and critical thinking skills that highlight the importance of cybersecurity in daily life. Students are recommended to progress their foundational learning by subsequently undertaking Cybersecurity Foundations 2 and Cyber Ethics Foundations.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate safe online practices.
Identify and describe common cyber threats and their potential impact.
Explain and apply basic data protection measures.
Develop awareness of cybersecurity's role in society.

title: Cyberwarfare and Terrorism
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the increasing threats to personal, corporate and national security from the cyber warfare and terrorism perspectives. Students commence by studying the principal motivations behind cyber attacks, which may be political, ideological, vengeance oriented, or profit based. The increasing incidence of such attacks is explored, and examples given of key military and government computing systems being subverted through digital warfare or terrorism. Students also learn how it may be possible to defend and prevent such attacks through the use of policy, procedure and technical controls. The subject will conclude with an analysis of future trends in the nature of cyber warfare and terrorist activities.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the main types of cyber attacks and the various tactics and strategies used during attacks.
Analyse examples of actual cyber terrorist attacks and to explain their motivations, method of operation, and impacts.
Compare and contrast the different types of cyber security threats, including cyber terrorism, cyber crime, and cyber warfare.
Distinguish between private, corporate, and national cyber attack events and their motivations.
Discuss and analyse trends in cyber warfare and terrorism and the increasing impact of such events on the security landscape.
Propose security policy, procedural and technical controls to mitigate the threats of different types of cyber attacks and the risks they present.

title: Cybersecurity Foundations 2
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Cybersecurity Foundations 2 is the second of two consecutive micro-subjects providing students with an initial introduction to the essential concepts of cybersecurity. The subject expands on the principles introduced in Cybersecurity Foundations 1, delving into more complex cybersecurity topics, emphasising network security, ethical considerations, and the practical implementation of security measures. Students will learn how to analyse security risks, understand ethical hacking basics, and explore the legal aspects of cybersecurity. Through a range of learning activities, students are challenged to apply their skills in real world contexts. This subject prepares students for further study in cyberspace learning or for workplace related cybersecurity applications. Students are recommended to first undertake Cybersecurity Foundations 1 and may also benefit from undertaking Cyberethics Foundations.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and assess more complex cyber threats.
Develop problem-solving skills through practical applications.
Implement basic network security measures.
Explore ethical and legal considerations in cybersecurity.

title: Dark Markets
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the dark side of the internet. Students will explore key features of the dark web, dark markets, the role of anonymity and the challenges law enforcement and national security agencies face when operating in these ever-evolving crime-scapes. This subject approaches these challenges as a ‘wicked problem', acknowledging the difficulty in defining the nature of the problem itself, its innumerable causes and the absence of one correct answer. Drawing on the latest research and industry best practice, students will use problem-solving skills to navigate this socially complex area in new and innovative ways as they formulate recommendations, triggering deep reflections on both content and process.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the evolving nature of fraud related dark-market products.
Critically reflect on and make recommendations to reduce the harms linked to financial crime threats posed within dark markets.
Research and design a systematic dark web access protocol.
Explain the role and scope of dark web anonymity.

title: Dashboarding, Visual Analytics, and Digital Storytelling
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject explores Visual Data Analytics (VDA) and provides a comprehensive overview of principles and toolkits for analysing complex real-world data. The strength of VDA lies in its ability to translate enormous volumes of data into a format that can be intuitively understood, thereby enhancing the decision-making processes. The subject combines insights from various fields to visualize data and introduces essential statistical and data analysis techniques. These methods include data reduction, visual mining, smoothing, clustering, and validation techniques. Students will learn how to create high-integrity visuals that enable fast and precise business decision-making. The subject also covers the limitations of visual perception and teaches students how to design impactful visuals that take advantage of human’s cognitive preference for visual information.
