learning_outcomes: Apply and discuss fundamental concepts in visual data analytics, dashboarding, and digital storytelling.
Design interactive data visualisation techniques for use in various business scenarios.
Identify and critically evaluate a range of data visualisations that facilitate the discovery and presentation of data-driven stories for various business use-cases.
Interpret outputs from visual data analytics, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.

title: Data Analysis and Insights
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Being able to interpret data and make informed decisions is an essential skill in a world that is constantly changing. This subject is designed to familiarise students with the varying kinds and uses of data. It begins by introducing the various types of data that can be used, and progresses into exploring how different types of data can be analysed and presented.
learning_outcomes: Employ appropriate techniques to analyse data and present conclusions.
Evaluate the different types and sources of data available.

title: Dark Web
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a broad overview of emerging malicious and cybercriminal activities inside the dark web. The subject also analyses dark web content and investigates anonymising networks in the dark web using publically available tools. Students will also learn dark web forensics and mitigating techniques to defend against cybercrime.
learning_outcomes: Investigate the usage of anonymising networks in the dark web using publically available tools.
Investigate the threat landscape in the dark web and appraise mitigating techniques used to combat cybercrime.
Analyse the malicious and cybercriminal activities inside the dark web.
Evaluate forensic techniques used to defend against cybercrime.
Analyse dark web content and create web logs.

title: Data Analysis for Financial Decision-making
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the application of quantitative management tools to data analysis in order to assist management decision makers within organisations. It introduces relevant statistical, research and operations management techniques which can be used to enhance the ability of managers to make informed decisions. Use is made of computer software designed to support the analysis, reporting and decision making functions.
learning_outcomes: Communicate clearly and concisely in a range of formal and informal situations and settings including delivering engaging presentations that persuade, motivate and inform stakeholders using a range of technologies and presentation strategies.
Describe how information and communication technology advances that support data analysis, decision making, can enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of communication.
Explain and use simulation and probability concepts for complex decisions.

Demonstrate understanding of the application of statistical hypothesis testing to decisions, with particular emphasis on quality control and interpreting the significance of regression coefficients in cost estimation.
Apply sustainability management accounting tools and decision theory to business situations.
Demonstrate problem-solving skills in assessing, organising, summarising and interpreting relevant data from a variety of sources and apply critical thinking skills for decision making purposes.
Apply cost-volume-profit analysis and linear programming to product mix decisions,.
Use accepted time-series forecasting methods.

title: Data Analytics for Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the students to the role of data and data analysis in decision making in organisations, including methods of sourcing, collecting and examining relevant data. Commonly used tools and techniques for data analysis, interpretation and presentation are then introduced, through the practical consideration of authentic data sets using relevant software. The emphasis is on effective communication of the findings. The subject's objective is on the development of a professional with the capacity to access, organise and analyse data in order to effectively make and convey decisions within the contemporary business context.
learning_outcomes: Present and communicate relevant decisions arising from the analysis of data.
Discuss the basic concepts relating to data analytics (including big data).
Identify and determine the appropriate statistical technique to analyse data.
Apply relevant software tools to summarise and analyse data.
Extract value from data sets for informed decision making.
Recognise the various types and sources of data.

title: Data Analytics for Non-Data Minds
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Data analytics is powerful in understanding and unlocking value from data. This micro-subject will provide an introduction to the fundamentals of data analytics. Covering key topics such as data types and data quality, basic data analytics, data visualisation, and ethical considerations, this subject is ideal for individuals without a strong data background who wish to understand what data analytics is about and how to perform basic data analytics tasks. By exploring concepts, techniques, and practical applications, you will gain essential knowledge and skills to draw meaningful insights from data, make informed decisions, and communicate findings to non-technical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and communicate data insights effectively to non-technical audiences, while evaluating relevant ethical considerations for data collection and analysis.
Demonstrate the importance of data analytics and its relevance in various industries.
Appraise the quality of data and apply data pre-processing techniques.

title: Data and Knowledge Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The subject provides students with in-depth study of data and knowledge engineering and their use in real life business. It looks into interpreting data through advanced approaches such as an ensemble of trees and clustering. Given the importance of clean and useful data for knowledge discovery, it offers thorough discussion on data pre-processing tasks including missing value imputation, corrupt data detection, discretization, and feature selection. The subject offers a study of the preservation of privacy when data mining, publishing and sharing among business organisations. It uses the current tools for knowledge discovery and future prediction.
learning_outcomes: Compare and evaluate various knowledge discovery techniques.
Compare and critique various data pre-processing techniques.
Critically analyse privacy preservation in data mining, data publishing and data sharing.
Evaluate the usefulness of data cleansing and pre-processing in discovering useful knowledge necessary for critical business decision.
Identify and design approaches for knowledge discovery from data for making critical business decision.
Evaluate and compare time series data mining approaches for business decision making.

title: Data Analytics for Business Success
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Data has become a vital asset for businesses which is increasingly being capitalised upon to advance their business objectives. The challenge in this data driven economy, is how businesses can position themselves strategically to unlock potential from data at their disposal. This micro-subject presents a non-specialist overview of the role of data analytics in businesses and provides a comprehensive foundation for businesses and organisations to understand and leverage data driven technologies to attract the right talent. The subject will provide an overview of data roles, technologies, and strategies to help organisations effectively position themselves for the future.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate between various data roles and assess an organisation's data needs and goals.
Identify the key technical and non-technical skills required for data professionals.
Explore emerging trends in data roles and understand the impact of AI and automation to prepare for future hiring needs in the data domain.

title: Data Driven Storytelling
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Professional communicators are increasingly required to have competency in using data to tell stories of all kinds. From journalistic work, to community engagement and community management, to organisational reporting and more, data-driven stories are in high demand. This micro-subject delivers practical skills in data-driven storytelling using up-to-date tools and techniques for all professional purposes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate user experience principles in data-driven storytelling artefacts.
Incorporate the principles of data-driven storytelling into artefacts of relevance to professional practice.
Develop and present a piece of original data-driven storytelling.

title: Data Mining and Visualisation for Business Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides in-depth coverage of the principles of data mining and the traditional machine learning techniques used for deriving business intelligence. It focuses on the need for developing timely and accurate descriptive and predictive models from large datasets to present accurate views of complex data trends and patterns. Students will also learn to assess model credibility and employ probabilistic modeling, decision trees and clustering techniques to unearth meaningful information from data by exploring the mathematical underpinnings of the widely used data mining models.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the different approaches and categories of data mining problems.
Identify and analyse business requirements for the identification of patterns and trends in data sets.
Compare and evaluate output patterns.
Compare and evaluate appropriate techniques for detecting and evaluating patterns in a given data set.
Identify and evaluate the security, privacy and ethical implications in data mining.
Explore and critically analyse data sets and evaluate their data quality, integrity and security requirements.
Explain the importance of current and future trends likely to affect data mining and visualisation.

title: Data Structures
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the students' previous knowledge of programming in a high-level language. It provides a study of abstract data types and classical data structures, including their implementation and their use in applications. Students will use their knowledge of object-oriented design techniques and extend these to solve programming problems.
learning_outcomes: Apply a variety of abstract data structures to the solution of welldefined problems.
Implement selected data structures in the Java language.
Design well structured solutions to programming problems and implement these solutions in the Java language.

title: Data-Informed Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the knowledge and skills required to engage with the policy and practice of data-informed practice. The subject will distinguish the approach as applied to education from its use in other fields highlighting the strengths, limitations and potential uses of the data available in educational contexts. Knowledge management, learning analytics, emergent feedback, the data-definition matrix, and data-based decision-making cycle will be defined and interrogated as a context for knowledge and skill-building in the ethical use of data to inform planning, instruction and learning. Key basic psychometric concepts and existing data repositories and approaches will be investigated using a problem-based approach focused on curriculum-based measurement. The subject involves the analysis and resolution of problem-based case studies that provide an opportunity to apply the skills and knowledge learned in the modules of study. A background in measurement and statistics is not required to successfully complete this subject.
learning_outcomes: Apply basic principles of measurement to data-based decision-making processes.
Build a professional capacity building session on Data-informed Practice (DIP) that demonstrates their knowledge of the key concepts and processes of DIP.

Explain and apply the data-definition matrix including the distinction between proximal and distal data and low and high power interventions as the key elements of a schema for data-informed practice and as a context for completing a self-assessment of your or a known school or setting.
Understand and be able to apply the key elements in the cycle of data-informed planning including the screening, progress monitoring and action planning approaches applied to the case study setting.

Build and articulate a personal position on the role of evidence and data and be able to provide feedback to the perspectives of their peers. The perspective will explore the assumptions on which data-informed practice resides including data quality, data capacity and data culture. This includes distinguishing between leaning, analytics, analytics and knowledge management.
Develop an implementation action plan for the case study setting.

Build an understanding of the Response to Intervention framework (RTI) as a methodology for taking up the situational analysis and critical actions in screening and progress monitoring at and for Validity Public School.

Conduct a situational analysis of a setting to determine its baseline circumstances with respect to data-informed practice. The situational analysis is used to develop theories of action for Assessment Task 2.
Identify commitments and theories of action that will enable the setting to become a data-informed learning environment. The commitments are included in Assessment Task 2.
Demonstrate an understanding of the difference between analytics, learning analytics and data-informed practice in education and their role in a data-informed school or setting.

title: Data-Driven Decision Making for Leaders in Emerging Technologies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject seeks to empower industry leaders with the confidence to make informed decisions grounded in the latest advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging technologies. It provides a comprehensive introduction to mental models for systematic data-driven thinking and decision making, alongside foundational knowledge in machine learning (ML) and AI. By cutting through the noise and hype, the subject offers an unbiased perspective on the latest developments in ML and AI, emphasising their practical applications in modern business analytics and modelling. Students will explore a range of state-of-the-art ML algorithms and AI techniques, learning how these tools can support intelligent business decision-making. The course focuses on real-world business applications, utilising carefully selected datasets to ensure relevance and applicability.
learning_outcomes: Design and create machine learning and AI models for studying relationship amongst business variables.
Discuss fundamental concepts in data science and machine learning, and compare different data science and machine learning methodologies.
Identify and critically evaluate machine learning and AI techniques for effective and ethical business decision making.
Interpret data science, machine learning and AI findings, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.

title: Deadly Start for Uni Success
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Deadly Start for Uni Success is a short, asynchronous university preparation subject offered on the Studylink platform. The subject guides students through a series of tasks and activities designed to develop the skills, strategies and knowledge which will support successful university study, with a focus on creating a culturally safe and inclusive learning experience for First Nations students. Students are introduced to university tools and systems and become familiar with the expectations of the higher education environment. The subject incorporates a scaffolded introduction to a range of support services available at university, highlighting the First Nations support services that are offered.
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and expectations of university learning and teaching, recognising a diverse range of perspectives and ways of sharing knowledge.
Explain and apply the concept of time and task management in a learning environment by balancing personal, cultural and community responsibilities.
Choose and apply some learning and help seeking strategies to support successful participation in university with a focus on First Nations support services available.
Access and navigate relevant university systems and tools to support inclusive and culturally safe learning experiences.

title: Database Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide a solid grounding in database design . It will examine the importance of database design in the development of applications that meet business needs. There will be an emphasis on modeling a database using Entity Relationship Diagrams (ERDs), optimising its design using normalisation techniques and implementing it and querying it using Structured Query Language (SQL).
learning_outcomes: Research a recent development in the field of database technology.
Apply normalisation techniques to optimise a database design.
Use complex Structured Query Language (SQL) commands to query a database.
Model complex business rules using Entity Relationship Diagrams (ERDs).

title: Decision Support Tools
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the application of quantitative management tools to data analysis in order to assist management decision makers in organisations. It introduces relevant statistical, operations research and operations management techniques which can be used to enhance the ability of managers to make informed decisions. Use is made of computer software designed to support the decision making function.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the application of statistical hypothesis testing to decisions, with particular emphasis on quality control and interpreting the significance of regression coefficients in cost estimation.
Use accepted time-series forecasting methods.
Explain the use of simulation in complex decisions.
Apply cost-volume-profit analysis and linear programming to product mix decisions.
Apply decision theory to business situations.
Demonstrate problem-solving skills in assessing, organising, summarising and interpreting relevant data for decision making purposes.
Apply probability concepts to decision making.
Solve scheduling problems.

title: Decision-making in Occupational Therapy
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop knowledge of models, theories and frames of reference that underpin occupational therapy practice. They will identify decision points and considerations, make and justify decisions in various occupational therapy scenarios, and reflect on the professional decision-making processes. Students will understand how professional decision-making is integral to their future occupational therapy practice, learning how different types of knowledge, models of practice, theory, professional concepts, and ethical frameworks inform this process. Factors including client goals, professional and research evidence, legal and ethical requirements, and the practice and social contexts will be considered in the decision-making process. Students will develop skills to apply these concepts to make informed and respectful decisions to facilitate occupational participation across the lifespan and in diverse contexts.
learning_outcomes: Identify ethical challenges and apply a suitable process to justify professional decision making.
Describe issues of occupational justice and how these influence occupational therapy practice.
Describe and apply models, theories and frames of reference relevant to working with individuals, groups, and/or communities.
Demonstrate the application of models, theories, frames of reference and professional decision making to a range of clients and contexts.
Reflect on and describe the rationale for practice decisions to clients and/or relevant others.
Demonstrate an understanding of legal considerations and requirements relevant to occupational therapy practice.
prerequisites: OCC106: Communication for Occupational Therapy Practice

title: Delivering Projects, Events and Experiences
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' ability to plan a project or event, emphasising the strategic importance of planning at every stage. This subject provides students with comprehensive theoretical knowledge of project management processes and practical skills through the planning, development and individual execution of a real or virtual project or event.
learning_outcomes: Plan and evaluate a project, event or experience.
Implement the project management process to execute a project, event or experience.
Understand the legal, cultural, social and ethical parameters informing projects, events and experiences.
Identify and describe the significance of contextual factors impacting the planning and execution of projects, events and experiences.

title: Deferment Approved
school: School
syllabus_overview: Administration subject - Deferment Approved

title: Dental Clinical Practice 4
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject is a continuation of Dental Clinical Practice 3 and is designed to provide students with the skills necessary to provide complex and comprehensive clinical care. Students will continue to develop the requisite skills in diagnosis, treatment planning and case selection at a general dental practitioner level, as well as develop an appropriate understanding of the referral pathways essential for optimal patient care.
learning_outcomes: be able to analyse patients' expectations, desires and attitudes when planning and delivering treatment, and propose the least invasive therapy, based on sound evidence-based principles, necessary to gain a successful outcome for the patient.

be able to demonstrate skills and knowledge required for the examination, diagnosis, treatment planning and management of prosthodontic, endodontic, advanced restorative, advanced periodontic and exodontia cases;
be able to demonstrate the ability to perform laboratory procedures required at various stages in the fabrication of the prostheses for patient work;
be able to demonstrate practice time management skills in the clinical environment and operate ethically and professionally when delivering patient care; and

title: Dental Clinical Practice 4
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject is a continuation of Dental Clinical Practice 3 and is designed to provide students with the skills necessary to provide complex and comprehensive clinical care. Patient clinic, simulation clinic and dental technology laboratory sessions are utilised to help students continue developing the requisite skills in diagnosis, treatment planning and case selection at a general dental practitioner level. Students will also develop an appropriate understanding of the referral pathways essential for optimal patient care.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate time management skills in the clinical environment to operate safely, ethically and professionally when delivering patient care.

Demonstrate skills and knowledge required for the examination, diagnosis, treatment planning and management of prosthodontic, endodontic, advanced restorative, advanced periodontic and exodontia cases.

Analyse patients' expectations, desires and attitudes when planning and delivering treatment, and recommend the least invasive therapy, based on sound evidence-based principles, necessary to gain a successful outcome for the patient.
Demonstrate the ability to perform laboratory procedures required at various stages in the fabrication of the prostheses for patient work.

title: Dental Clinical Practice 5
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: Students participate in a clinical placement program in the provision of clinical care in varied settings in regional NSW. Each clinical site will have students providing dental care under supervision. Clinical learning is reinforced by means of case analyses, case reviews and clinical session reviews by clinical staff.
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss the scope of oral/dental health needs of different societal and cultural groups within rural and regional communities.
Demonstrate competence in the provision of treatment for patients with multidisciplinary needs.
Demonstrate competent comprehensive treatment planning.
Manage the decision-making and provision of acute-care treatment as required in a clinical setting.
Apply professional, ethical, and legal principles to the full range of duties and responsibilities of a dentist, as defined by the Dental Board of Australia.

title: Dental Biochemistry
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundation level understanding of the structure and function of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids) and the major metabolic and bio-energetic pathways within cells. The subject also includes study of calcium and phosphorus metabolism and an introduction to nutritional biochemistry. Oral biochemistry provides the basis for further studies by Dentistry students in applied genetics, immunology, pathology, pharmacology-therapeutics and in clinical dental subjects.
learning_outcomes: Describe the major metabolic pathways used to synthesise and consume ATP.
Describe the properties of enzymes as biological catalysts.
Describe the role of energy in living cells, with particular reference to the concept of free energy and the role of ATP.

Describe the structure and function of the four major classes of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids) and understand the relationship between structure and function.

Demonstrate an understanding of normal calcium and phosphorus metabolism and its relationships to tooth and bone formation, mechanisms of mineralisation and its roles in relation to the maintenance of calcified dental tissue integrity.
Demonstrate an understanding of common techniques used in the study of biochemistry.
prerequisites: BCM210: Foundations and Techniques in Biochemistry

title: Describing and Analysing Education Resources
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles and processes of analysing and describing resources within the school context. It examines traditional and emerging means of providing access to learning resources, and the application of metadata standards to ensure effective information organisation. While the focus is on schools, the broad principles apply to a variety of information environments.
learning_outcomes: Apply national and international metadata standards.
Understand the importance of effective organisation of learning resources for successful information retrieval.
Understand the relationship between information retrieval systems and the description and analysis of resources.
Utilise these standards to provide effective access to information for the school community.

title: Design and Content Creation Perspectives 1
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject develops students’ knowledge, skills and abilities in the discipline of Design and Content Creation. This subject expands on key concepts of content design, production and publication for a range of media channels. Students will develop the research and production skills and understanding of ethical and legal frameworks necessary for a content creation professional and demonstrate capacity to work in a content creation team.
learning_outcomes: Conceptualise ideas and undertake research to inform the development of diverse content for a variety of media.
Demonstrate and illustrate the developing skills of a content creation professional.
Plan, produce and manage the design and production of content for a variety of media channels.
Demonstrate the skills of a content creator to work collaboratively in a team to meet a deadline.

title: Design and Digital Technologies: Curriculum and Pedagogy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to foundational aspects of teaching as a profession. To contextualise this positioning, students engage in investigation of design and digital technologies, and consideration of computational, design, and systems thinking, and their relationship to each other. These concepts and processes are then examined in light of their links to, and application in, the NSW Technology 7-8 curriculum. Planning for teaching in a project-based context with attention to meeting the needs of diverse learners, and the development of literacy, numeracy, sustainability, and ethical understanding are also a major focus.
learning_outcomes: Design teaching and learning activities to develop numeracy, literacy, sustainability, and ethical understanding capabilities in the context of design and digital technologies.
Demonstrate clear and accurate writing, effective research skills, knowledge and use of appropriate educational terminology, and current APA referencing and citation conventions.
Explain the use, development, nature and impact of technologies and design and their relationship to society and the environment.
Describe and plan strategies to meet the needs of diverse learners.

Identify curriculum links and explain pedagogical application of technological and design concepts, and computational, design and systems thinking across a range of technology contexts including the ways in which products, systems, services and environments operate and develop.
Apply the principles of project-based problem-solving and authentic learning in their planning for teaching and learning.
prerequisites: EMT447: Design and Digital Technologies Curriculum

title: Design and Content Creation Perspectives 2
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject continues to progress students’ knowledge, skills and abilities in the discipline of Design and Content Creation. Students undertaking this subject will work on real-world projects to further enhance their ability as a developing content creation professional. Students will work in a content creation team to produce and publish content for a range of media channels and reflect upon their practice as an emerging content creation professional.
learning_outcomes: Undertake research, assess information and manage the production of content for media in response to deliver a project.
Assess, critique and reflect on your practice as an emerging content creation professional.
Differentiate the discipline and interpersonal skills to work efficiently as part of a content creation team to deliver a project.
Demonstrate advanced skills and judgement of a content creator in making evidence-based decisions.
prerequisites: DCC200: Design and Content Creation Perspectives 1

title: Design and Digital Technologies Curriculum
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to foundational aspects of teaching as a profession. To contextualise this positioning, students engage in investigation of design and digital technologies, and consideration of computational, design, and systems thinking, and their relationship to each other. These concepts and processes are then examined in light of their links to, and application in, the NSW Technology 7-8 curriculum. Planning for teaching in a project-based context with attention to meeting the needs of diverse learners, and the development of literacy, numeracy, sustainability, and ethical understanding is also a major focus.
learning_outcomes: Discuss curriculum links and explain pedagogical application of technological and design concepts, and computational, design and systems thinking across a range of technology contexts including the ways in which products, systems, services and environments operate and develop.
Justify and apply the principles of project-based problem-solving and authentic learning in their planning for teaching and learning.
Discuss the use, development, nature and impact of technologies and design and their relationship to society and the environment.
Explain and plan strategies to meet the needs of diverse learners.
Demonstrate clear and accurate writing, effective research skills, knowledge and use of appropriate educational terminology, and current APA referencing and citation conventions.
Design teaching and learning activities to develop numeracy, literacy, sustainability, and ethical understanding capabilities in the context of design and digital technologies.
prerequisites: EMT203: Design and Digital Technologies: Curriculum and Pedagogy

title: Design and Production
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject utilises practice-based education principles of situated authentic learning and reflective practice. It engages students in the process of designing and creating various outputs in creative and performing arts. Students are introduced to a range of roles and responsibilities in environmental design, including computer aided design (CAD) skills and drawing for a range of spatial design outcomes. Students undertake projects through the use of designer-led approaches to the analysis, visualisation and construction of environments, and undertake projects responding to site-specific contextual needs.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply research, explorations and experimentations in order to creatively problem solve.
Describe a range of roles and responsibilities in spatial design.
Produce concept designs, including technical drawing/illustration, that utilise computer-aided design (CAD) and modeling software.
Apply knowledge and skills in various design and production media.
Demonstrate knowledge of the impact of technology on creative and performing practices.

title: Design Thinking and Ideation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores a variety of methodologies for problem solving in design, including Design Thinking, Human-Centred Design and User Experience Design. Students will explore through practice how collaboration, research and prototyping are fundamental to the design process and how these methodologies support the creation of collaborative, innovative and strategic solutions.
learning_outcomes: Apply targeted research methods related to a design problem, its stakeholders and clients.
Describe the potential of design to instigate innovation and change within organisations and communities.
Explain the role prototyping and testing possible design outcomes.
Work independently and collaboratively.
Apply a range of creative, theoretical and technical skills to solve design based problems.
Demonstrate practical capacity to apply design processes that arrive at strategic or innovative solutions.

title: Design and Technology Project
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on prior learning in the practice of design and use of technologies, tools, materials and equipment, as students demonstrate skills of designing and managing a coherent design project. Students will: understand the relationships between design, technology, creativity, innovation and enterprise; apply design concepts, criteria and considerations to technology processes and production skills; and implement ways of communicating, evaluating, assessing, reporting on and presenting a designed product, system, service or environment. The subject also enables students to consider emerging technologies and preferred futures.
learning_outcomes: Make judgements about appropriateness of planning and management decisions.
Apply design concepts, criteria and considerations to design ideas.
Produce a coherent product or system or environment.
Explain the relationship between design, technology, creativity, innovation, and enterprise.
Demonstrate a range of strategies to communicate, assess, evaluate, report on and present designed solutions.

Demonstrate clear and accurate writing and professional written and other communication skills including: effective research skills; use of appropriate educational terminology, and the ability to use referencing and citation conventions.

title: Designing and Creating Usable Websites
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the web technologies used to manage information in today's digitally connected world and explains the importance of web usability in the design and development of a website. Students will research and learn the concepts, tools and techniques of website creation, design and some practical applications while taking into consideration the organisational contexts and design standards to effectively transmit and share information. Learning will also focus on user behaviour, user needs, information content and use, and other design factors to make the online content informative and engaging so that it attracts and holds website visitors' attention. Therefore, practical knowledge of fundamental web design concepts and their application in real world context is the main focus of this subject.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, evaluate and select appropriate web design elements and features for creating, transmitting and sharing information.
Critically analyse the organisational context to reflect upon and synthesise issues that affect web design and publishing.
Evaluate different aspects of web interface design to ensure effective information retrieval and effective information delivery.
Research and apply good design techniques to improve readability, user friendliness, and general usability of online content.
Apply web design standards to create a website for specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Designing and Delivering Programs for User Engagement
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Libraries and other cultural institutions worldwide play a unique role in delivering training, education and lifelong learning opportunities for their communities. This subject provides an introduction to the strategies and skills required to facilitate the effective design, dissemination and delivery of education and training programs within the information and cultural sectors. Marketing, advocacy and building practical funding partnerships are also examined in the context of effective program delivery. Students are encouraged to become reflective practitioners, employing the research and professional literature to inform their understanding of training and education in these sectors and as a lens for shaping practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify a learning need appropriate for a particular community and apply this to practice.
Recognise and apply strategies for marketing, advocacy and funding to support public programs.
Identify key stakeholders in the information and cultural sectors and critically evaluate their differing roles and needs.
Appraise the appropriateness in practice of a variety of delivery formats and instructional delivery types for both formal and informal learning situations.
Identify and describe a number of key theoretical, professional, historical and social contexts in which education and training in the information and cultural sectors are situated.
Reflect critically and discuss relevant national and international agendas in the information and cultural sector.

title: Designing and Managing the Inclusive Learning Environment
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a context for managing student behaviour in inclusive settings. The content of this subject is anchored in research from the Applied Behaviour Analysis literature and is focused on the design of interventions for individuals with challenging behaviours. The subject focuses on individual student behavioural needs in relation to ecological, cognitive and behavioural theories and the way the principles and practices associated with individual planning can be anchored in classroom and school-wide approaches to supporting positive social and academic behaviour.
learning_outcomes: Take hypothetical data for prioritised behaviours over 3-5 days and provide a summary of the results that can be used to justify the criteria in a performance objective.
Write performance objectives for new target behaviours.
Choose and deploy an appropriate system for observing and recording behaviour.
Build a position on the continuum of behavioural strategies available to reduce inappropriate behaviour and justify their position.
Use information from various stakeholders to complete a functional analysis/ (FBA or ABC) form and analyse the antecedents and consequences of inappropriate behaviour.
Devise methods to accommodate reduction of inappropriate behaviour.
Plan stimulus and response generalisation of target behaviour.
Develop an individual behaviour plan for students in inclusive settings (using case studies from their own settings).
Describe potential positive and negative reinforcers to use to encourage a target behaviour.
Describe, prioritise and target inappropriate behaviour.
prerequisites: EEA402: Learning Environments in Early Childhood

title: Designing Blended Learning Environments in Higher Education
school: Division of Learning and Teaching
syllabus_overview: The subject provides opportunities for participants to examine the changing nature of tertiary learning and teaching in the digital age and the implications of these changes for the roles of teachers and students, the development of generic skills, capabilities and attributes, and emerging professional identities. Participants will consider key educational philosophies that underpin contemporary approaches to 'blended learning design', drawing in particular on 'constructive alignment' (Biggs & Tang, 2011) and 'affordances' (Gibson 1977) as a foundation for designing blended experiences for 21st century learners. Participants will also examine concepts such as: the networked learner, digital citizenship, lifewide and lifelong learning, authentic learning, Open Education Resources, technology-enabled learning, and e-assessment. They will engage in critiquing existing learning designs, as well as designing small-scale authentic and blended learning and teaching experiences.
learning_outcomes: Consider key educational philosophies and ideals that underpin 'blended learning design'.
Justify the generic skills, capabilities and attributes required when designing, facilitating, enhancing or supporting lifelong learning experiences in the 21st Century.
Design and justify, using constructive alignment, a learning and teaching experience.
Critically discuss the affordances of different learning activities, spaces, technologies and assessments in tertiary education taking into account participants' disciplines and professions.
Critique the design of a learning and teaching experience.
Identify the changing nature of learners and learning in tertiary education in the 21st Century, including both formal and informal learning experiences.
prerequisites: EEC403: Designing Learning Environments in Higher Education

title: Designing Inclusive Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject teacher education students will develop their understandings of inclusion and inclusive teaching practices that supports learner agency and access to engaging learning. Students will be introduced to contemporary thinking around inclusive education including the importance of disability-affirming perspectives, and the central role that people with lived experience of disability have in shaping this space. In addition, students will review the relevant legislation and evidence-based foundations of inclusive practice and be introduced to approaches and strategies that maximise the potential for a wide range of learner variability. The principles of universal design for learning, strategies for differentiation and the use digital technologies to support inclusion will be explored. Students will also engage in 40 hours of classroom observation in a school context and design universal supports for literacy and numeracy. Students will also develop strategies to engage and collaborate with other professionals, support services, students, parents and/or caregivers in planning for inclusion and participation to create safe and positive classroom cultures.
learning_outcomes: Develop a lesson within a teaching area using the principles of universal design for learning in order to teach to a wide range of learner variability.

Apply the essential characteristics of explicit teaching and other effective teaching strategies to support academic inclusion of students with disabilities with a specific focus on supporting literacy and numeracy.
Develop appropriate goals and actions to support a range of learner variability (including learning difficulties and giftedness), based on an IEP meeting.
Apply ICT and other strategies in their planning to support inclusive student participation and engagement.
Review the research-based evidence of a tiered approach to differentiation as a reasonable adjustment, and evaluate its applicability.
Describe strategies and processes for collaborating with students, parents/caregivers and other professionals in planning for inclusion and participation.

Outline the implications for teaching and learning arising from contemporary thinking about inclusive education, the broader impacts of disability on learning and the legislative requirements and policies that support the inclusion and participation of students with disabilities in educational settings.
Describe and apply disability affirming and trauma informed approaches to behaviour support for all children including those with complex learning profiles.
prerequisites: EPT455: English Curriculum: Understanding Language and Literacy
ESS440: Teaching and Learning in the Differentiated Classroom

title: Designing, Implementing and Evaluating Projects
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject introduces the role of project management in the contemporary business environment. The subject examines the key principles of designing, implementing and evaluating projects through the wider project lifecycle. The role of various stakeholders is also introduced. This subject may include some face to face workshops and activities depending on the student cohort.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role that projects play in the strategic management of organisations.
Develop a completed and comprehensive project plan that includes all relevant stakeholders.
Evaluate project progress through application of project management measurement tools and techniques.
Apply project technical aspects across the project lifecycle.

title: Designing the Inclusive School
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the way schools/settings can be designed to be more responsive to individual difference. The subject will examine contemporary national and international literature on school reform, improvement, and organisational change as a context for the study of the way schools/settings can be designed for inclusion. The design approach employed in the subject applies principles derived from the study of self-organising systems and their application in education. The subject will focus on the way the schools/settings can self-organise and plan for learner diversity. Assessment items focus on the use of the principles and practice of self-organisation to design solutions and solve problems that relate to making schools/settings more inclusive.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the reform context generating a set of drivers that account for the challenge of school reform and improvement.
Select an evidence-based whole school intervention that will be the target of reform at scale in a school or setting.
Develop an organisational structure (network of teams) for decision-making in the school that is capable of supporting the commitment to evidence-based inclusive practice.
Build an emergent feedback model for Positive Behavioural Support (PBS).

Demonstrate an understanding of scale in school reform and improvement and what it means for a learning organization. Students will develop a set of characteristics of an inclusive school that should exist at scale across the organization.
Explain how your design framework serve as a response to the issues described in your initial problem analysis.

Write a reflection that links their design effort to the broader focus of a multi-tiered approach to school design evaluating the design's merits/limitations in light of the issues, benefits and challenges associated with Multi-Tiered Approach (MTA).

Apply the embedded design principle to a school commitment. This includes specifying the knowledge and skills required of teachers and the developmental career trajectory for teachers at the school/setting and the foci of the key areas for feedback associated with the commitment.
Identify five design factors that would create better practice at scale in school design.
Undertake a SWOT analysis that reflects all other outcomes in the subject including the reform context, getting to scale and the specifics of the design created.
Frame the professional capacity building required within an embedded design framework to build teacher capacity with evidence-based practice that underpins the commitment.

title: Desk-Top Research Critical Analysis
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Start your investigation into a chosen field of study with the guidance of staff by finding and critically analysing past research and publications. This subject is designed to promote the development of critical thinking and review skills and to allow students to become confident in reviewing the work of others critically, but constructively. Students will work with the guidance and support of staff to undertake a range of broad reading and literature review. Core curriculum principles informing this subject include a transition for students toward independence in being able to source and review literature critically and constructively, and to utilize the published evidence base to identify research gaps, and to form research questions or hypotheses.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate recent literature on a topic of interest and report this using effective written communication.
Demonstrate an enhanced knowledge of their discipline area through in-depth literature review.
Effectively conduct an academic literature search in a field of interest to synthesise knowledge and identify gaps in the research and publications reviewed.
Demonstrate excellent verbal communication skills e.g. through seminar presentation.
Critically evaluate the work of their peers.

title: Developing a Disaster Recovery Plan
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop an understanding of the strategies to be implemented to assist a community to recover after a disaster. This involves students learning how to apply the Community Analysis process to a community of their choice in order to develop and generate a genuine community recovery management plan. This also includes the use of emergency/ disaster event management case studies to identify strengths and weaknesses relating to the management of recovery activities within those events and the identification of strategies that will enhance the community recovery management in future emergency/ disaster events.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the social characteristics and infrastructure of a community.
Recommend strategies for enhanced community recovery capabilities, based on contemporary community development concepts and theory.
Evaluate and prioritise the recovery management needs of a community.
Implement the Community Analysis Process.

title: Developing as a Police Educator
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: EEL409 introduces participants to new teaching and learning concepts, and outlines standards for teaching into the Associate Degree of Police Practice with a specific focus on foundation teaching concepts and classroom skills. The subject will introduce learning and teaching theory whilst engaging participants with contextual examples relevant to police education. This subject will encourage the construction of an ongoing teaching development plan, a personal teaching philosophy, and provides context and opportunity for reflection.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate reflective practice, professionalism, and academic integrity to make informed judgements and decisions on the student learning experience.
Analyse their individual learning and development priorities and develop a professional development plan to guide their professional practice.
Demonstrate effective preparation and performance in teaching that is informed by the needs of the ADPP curriculum and multi-modal pedagogy and reflection.
Demonstrate effective mentoring practices and participate in the NSWPF Academy Community of Practice arena to enhance professional development.
prerequisites: EEL522: Foundations of Learning and Teaching in Higher Education
EEL516: Foundations of Learning and Teaching in Higher Education

title: Developing Cross Cultural Competencies
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to key concepts relating to service provision and service delivery and will explore the strategies and competencies required when working with a range of culturally diverse communities throughout Australia. The relationship between cultural diversity and policy development as well as its implementation will be analysed in the context of the social welfare field. The subject looks at the complex field of working with people from diverse cultural backgrounds. Content of the subject includes looking at topics to do with: anti-discriminatory practices; structural issues of racism, discrimination and policies; and individual practice issues focusing more on how to work with individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds.
learning_outcomes: Assess the impact of policies on special needs groups with possible reference to young people within families.
Analyse critically the key issues that have influenced service provision and service delivery to culturally diverse communities.
Demonstrate an understanding of cross cultural competencies in delivering services to individuals, groups and communities from diverse cultural backgrounds.
Understand the strategies and policy implications of access and equity in relation to welfare programs throughout Australia.

title: Developing Human Resources
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Effectively developing human resources is an essential component in attracting, building and retaining high performing individuals and teams that better meet organisational needs. Evaluating individual and organisational needs, and developing and applying knowledge, skills, experience and performance are essential tools to achieve individual development and organisational outcomes. Drawing on industry best practice, methodology and theory, this subject covers the major human resource development approaches from an individual and organisational perspective.
learning_outcomes: Identify, explain and evaluate challenges to human resource development in the context of individual and organisational development.
Utilise suitable needs analysis methodology to analyse organisational contexts and identify relevant human resource development needs.
Plan a human resource development program for an individual and/or organisational context with the assistance of emerging technologies.
Select, discuss and apply appropriate learning theory and practice in the design, operation, assessment and evaluation of human resource development programs.

title: Developing Media Relationships
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to the fundamental theory and practice of establishing and maintaining effective and valuable relationships with media partners. It situates media relationship building within existing strategic goals of the organisation. The subject includes targeted development of content for media agencies. This subject is designed with adaptable delivery models, which may include combinations of condensed online sessions and one-off workshops.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and understand potential media partners within contemporary practice.
Research, plan and pitch content to media partners.
Identify strategies for maintaining and adding value to media relationships.

title: Developing Skills in Information Technology
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop essential information technology skills required for a student to undertake study within the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science. The first part of the subject develops students' basic knowledge with a personal computer. Next, it guides the student to understand how to manage files on a computer system and then provides skills to effectively use the internet. Finally the subject will develop a student's working knowledge in the use of word processing and spreadsheet application software.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of computing from a personal computer platform perspective.
Identify and use appropriate application software for specific tasks or activities.
Demonstrate an ability to effectively use internet resources from an academic perspective.
Manage files stored on a personal computer.

title: Developing Solutions
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will learn how to research business problems and priorities using current solution-based investigation and sales principles. Students will learn how to define clear objectives and strategies for managing and leveraging a business relationship and generating stakeholder buy-in and alignment for preferred solutions. This subject will offer students a detailed knowledge of the most effective and current solution-based sales techniques and methods, and how to apply them to influence stakeholder decisions.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast current solution-based sales techniques and apply them within a business context.
Design and implement clear objectives and strategies for managing a business relationship.
Identify customer issues and opportunities and develop buy-in and alignment amongst decision makers.
Research the objectives, culture and environment of a business and create effective solutions based on this analysis.
Recognise and critically evaluate the influences that political, economic and social factors have on a business.
Independently develop and promote customer-oriented sales solutions.

title: Developing the Clinical Exercise Practitioner
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In Australia, Exercise Physiologists are allied health professionals who prescribe clinical exercise interventions for people at high-risk of developing, or living with, existing complex medical conditions and/or injuries. This subject will develop students' understanding of the Exercise Physiology profession and build a foundation for effective clinical practice and learning across the course. Emphasis is placed on developing students' comprehension of Exercise Physiology practice within the context of the Australian health care system. Students will also reflect on their standpoint and evaluate the relevance of language, policy, workplace culture and history to develop skills required to practice in a culturally safe manner. Students will develop the skills required to facilitate behaviour change with clients across the lifespan, work within a multi-disciplinary team and build their capacity for reflexivity and reflective practice.
learning_outcomes: Assess client readiness for change and apply models of behaviour change to support appropriate exercise and physical activity.
Examine the core principles of culturally responsive health partnerships to explore the complexity of working with diverse communities.
Critically evaluate relevant literature and appropriately apply conclusions to inform evidence-based practice, clinical reasoning and professional decision making.
Examine the social, cultural, historical, and institutional factors that challenge discourses and impact professional practice as an Exercise Physiologist.
Evaluate and review the Australian health care system and how the scope of the Exercise Physiology profession contributes to improving health outcomes for individuals and communities.

title: Development, Security and Operations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an overview of integrating security practices into the software development lifecycle using the Development, Security and Operations (DevSecOps) approach. Students sill learn and apply a range of topics including chain of trust, Linux security, container security, open-source dependency security, application security testing and monitoring.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate security testing and how to integrate it into the development process.
Describe the principles of DevSecOps and how to integrate security into the software development lifecycle.
Describe the chain of trust and how to cryptographically ensure secure boot, operating system, containers and patching.
Demonstrate understanding of open-source dependency security and compliance and how to secure open-source libraries.

title: Developmental and Social Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines developmental and social psychology. Developmental Psychology examines human development across the life-span. Descriptions, explanations, and predictions of developmental stages/changes are covered through an investigation of major theories and research findings. Practical implications and applications of this material are considered, with some topical current issues. Social Psychology examines the influence of society, groups, and interpersonal relationships on the individual, and their location within society. This includes theoretical/empirical examination of how we perceive others, social influences on the individual and interpersonal relationships ranging from attraction/love to aggression/hate. The relevancy of dominant developmental and social psychological theories for Indigenous Australians are also considered.
learning_outcomes: Understand research methods and analyses of data commonly used in the study of developmental and social psychology.
Evaluate whether western conceptualisations of developmental and social psychology are universal or culturally specific, with a specific focus on First Nations Australians.
Demonstrate an understanding that human development across the lifespan results from an interaction of changes in biological, cognitive, and social processes.
Critically evaluate previous research and theoretical positions in developmental and social psychology via assessment.
Apply major theories of developmental and social psychology, and an awareness of their applications in everyday life.
Demonstrate an understanding of social psychology's fundamental issues and controversies.
Understand key research findings within developmental and social psychology.

title: Developmental Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines human development across the entire life-span. Descriptions, explanations, and predictions of developmental stages and changes are covered through an investigation of major theories and research findings. Practical implications and applications of this material are also considered, along with some topical current issues.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a familiarity with research methods and analyses of data commonly used in the study of developmental psychology.
Demonstrate a familiarity with major theories of developmental psychology.
Demonstrate an ability to evaluate critically theories and research findings in developmental psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding that human development across the lifespan results from an interaction of changes in biological, cognitive, and social processes.
Demonstrate a knowledge of key research findings within developmental psychology.

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology

Demonstrate an understanding that human development across the lifespan results from an interaction of changes in biological, cognitive, and social processes.
Understand research methods and analyses of data commonly used in the study of developmental and social psychology.
Critically evaluate previous research and theoretical positions in developmental and social psychology via assessment.
Understand key research findings within developmental and social psychology.
Apply major theories of developmental and social psychology, and an awareness of their applications in everyday life.
Evaluate whether western conceptualisations of developmental and social psychology are universal or culturally specific, with a specific focus on First Nations Australians.

title: Developmental Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines human development across the entire life-span.
