learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a familiarity with major theories of developmental psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding that human development across the life-span results from an interaction of changes in biological, cognitive, and social processes.
Demonstrate a knowledge of key research findings within developmental psychology.
Demonstrate a familiarity with research methods and analyses of data commonly used in the study of developmental psychology.
Demonstrate an ability to evaluate critically theories and research findings in developmental psychology.

title: Developments in Ethics Governance and Accounting Thought
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject students examine developments in accounting theory and professional standards through the lens of ethics and governance. Using prior research the subject provides insight into the search for a conceptual framework, the evaluation and comparison of various accounting models and discussion of contemporary management accounting and financial reporting issues.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of theory in the nature and development of accounting as a discipline.

Compare and contrast the diverse perspectives which can be used to explain the development of accounting and the accounting profession including the impact of social change on accounting and vice versa.
Critically evaluate selected current financial reporting and management accounting issues.
Critically appraise the objectives of accounting and relate them to the various concepts of accounting discussed in earlier subjects including attempts to develop and apply a conceptual framework.
Discuss and critically reflect on the role of ethics, professionalism and corporate governance and the underpinning theories to support the role of accounting as a profession.

title: Diagnosis and Critical Thinking in Veterinary Science
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Diagnosis and Critical Thinking in Veterinary Science will provide students with the tools to embark on the remaining components of the veterinary science degree. This subject will be taught in a Problem-based learning (PBL) format where students will work in teams to solve authentic, ill-structured problems, working though a set of Situation Analysis and Critical Thinking questions. PBL is student centred learning, rather than teacher centred learning. Therefore, students will be required to determine what they need to know in order to solve the problems presented, and then using prior knowledge, experiences and references, identify information that can be utilised to advance the case or solve the problem. PBL is collaborative; students do not work alone, but in a team for the entire session, and are therefore able to develop their communication and team skills. Knowledge acquired previously and knowledge and skills taught concurrently during the session in the other subjects will be applied to the PBL cases. There will be a strong connection between these clinical subjects and this subject, where students will be able to apply this knowledge to the case in a safe and supportive environment. Animal Husbandry Extra Mural Studies marks will also be collated into this subject. Students cannot progress to Phase 2 (Year 4 of the course), without the completion of Phase 1 (Years 1 to 3 inclusive).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate time management and organisational skills to permit completion of all PBL activities and assessment tasks.

Utilise the PBL approach to develop a plan to investigate, diagnose and manage diseases of animals, and gather and interpret this relevant information to progress the cases; taking into account financial, clinical, welfare and social factors.
Demonstrate the development of self-directed learning skills, utilising appropriate quality references and sharing this knowledge with PBL team members in a collaborative and timely fashion.

Work according to the principles of Evidence Based Veterinary Medicine in applying knowledge from the pre-clinical, para-clinical and clinical disciplines, to the health management, prevention and treatment of diseases of animals.
Demonstrate developing critical appraisal skills in self and peer evaluation of PBL performance.
Engage in the Problem Based Learning (PBL) process, working as part of an effective PBL team by demonstrating developing skills in team management, team communication and team efficiency.
Communicate veterinary knowledge and information clearly, effectively and efficiently to a variety of audiences utilising appropriate terminology, both verbally and in writing.
prerequisites: VSC333: Applied Veterinary Nutrition and Production

title: Diagnostic Imaging for Veterinary Technologists
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will expand on their knowledge of veterinary diagnostic imaging and modalities. Students will learn how to maintain and quality check veterinary diagnostic imaging equipment. Students will gain knowledge of the background to, and application of, radiation safety for all imaging modalities. Students develop skills in performing diagnostic imaging procedures, processing of images and optimising image quality and recognising possible pathology for further Veterinarian evaluation.
learning_outcomes: Identify and minimise risks to personnel and patients during ionising radiation procedures according to the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency.
Operate a range of veterinary diagnostic imaging equipment and provide maintenance and quality control of imaging equipment necessary to ensure optimal images.
Identify and describe appropriate diagnostic imaging procedures associated with assessing the health status of animals.
Compare and contrast the case application of imaging modalities such as but not limited to CT, MRI, nuclear scintigraphy, and ultrasonography.
Ensure safety compliance of both the individual and the workplace according to the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency.
prerequisites: ASC182: Foundations in Clinical Procedures and Veterinary Nursing
ASC183: Foundations in Veterinary Surgical Nursing

title: Difference and Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The construction of difference and how differences between people are mobilised are key challenges facing leaders today. This subject explores theories of difference and diversity from an organisational and societal perspective as well as critical and philosophical perspectives. It also examines interdisciplinary leadership concepts, perspectives, and theories. Students will consider the challenges, drivers and strategic issues leaders face when working interculturally and globally. Issues of structural, cognitive and behavioural diversity will be explored through theory, case studies and critical reflection. Opportunities are provided to reflect on the practical organisational and societal challenges which impact respectful and effective leaders working across lines of difference.
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate how leadership is mobilised in relation to a range of cultural, racial, ethnic, identity and other demographic differences.
Build a theoretical framework for the practice of leadership in the face of difference and diversity challenges.
Apply learning about difference and leadership in the face of challenges in relationships, workplaces and society.
Critically engage in self-reflection about difference and how it constructs opportunities and limitations in the practice of leadership.

title: Diagnostic Radiography Residency
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This year-long subject is a capstone residency that consolidates learning (knowledge and skills) across the entire degree into practice-based capabilities. The subject formalises the learning, development and assessment of MRPBA-defined capabilities as the minimum standards for general registration with Ahpra. The residency is underpinned by professional practice in diagnostic radiography in the clinical setting (1 x 18 weeks plus 1 x 15 weeks; 5 x 7.5 hour days per week = 1200 hours). Clinical skills are consolidated to demonstrate work-ready capabilities with appropriate professional and ethical conduct to care and advocate for their patients. In this subject, students are able to demonstrate and refine their existing written, verbal and aural communication skills, demonstrating cultural sensitivity with both staff and patients within a range of contexts, enabling safe work environments. Students are able to apply their decision making skills and critical thinking in general practice of medical radiation science, specifically in diagnostic radiography, and demonstrate required radiation safety and risk management capability.
learning_outcomes: Prepare patients and delivery systems for fluoroscopy and angiography examinations, including positioning patient for best diagnostic outcomes, checking for contrast contraindications, and loading delivery devices using aseptic technique (MRPBA Domain 1A.2c and g).

Describe and apply principles of practice in diagnostic radiography, with specific reference to implementing fluoroscopy in a range of settings, explaining the principles and clinical applications of angiography and interventional techniques, and explaining the principles of mammographic imaging within the clinical context (MRPBA Domain 1 and 1A).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence-based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical and reflective thinking to resolve clinical challenges and identify professional learning needs / life-long learning (MRPBA Domain 4).
Recognise near misses and their consequences, adverse events, and relevant contributing factors, and report on these in a timely and appropriate manner (MRPBA Domain 5.1g).

Explain and implement professional practice with specific reference to applying anatomy, physiology and pathology, applying the principles of physics and instrumentation, utilising patient information management systems, determining appropriate procedures, patient assessment and due diligence, deliver appropriate care, and manage / manipulate 3D datasets (MRPBA Domain 1 and 1A).

Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with specific reference to clear, sensitive, effective and culturally appropriate communication to support culturally safe environments, and when collaborating with other health practitioners (MRPBA Domain 3).
Understand the processes of peer assessment, standard setting, mentorship, and developmental support to other members of the healthcare team. (MRPBA Domain 2.5a).
Manage and adapt to limitations and restrictions in the use of techniques and devices for reproducibility of procedures concerning patient condition and presentation (MRPBA Domain 1.6a).

Identify, explain and implement non-discriminatory, professional and ethical conduct with specific reference to practising in an ethical, professional and legal manner, providing appropriate care, assuming accountability and responsibility, and patient advocacy (MRPBA Domain 2).

Ascertain the suitability and application of a proposed medical radiation examination/treatment, to recognise when an alternative pathway may be more appropriate, and make suitable recommendations to other members of the healthcare team (MRPBA Domain 2.4c, 3.2d and 4.1d).
Recognise the need for appropriate decisions about the care of patients before, during, and after the examination/treatment. (MRPBA Domain 1.7d; 2.3a).

Apply knowledge of medical equipment and prostheses used in the angiography and operating theatre setting, collaborating in the design of fluoroscopy and angiography protocols (MRPBA Domain 1A.2h and i).

Describe and apply the principles of radiation safety and risk management with specific reference to safe radiation practice, protecting/enhancing patient safety, ensuring safe operation of equipment, maintaining safety of self and others and safely managing radiation and radioactivity (MRPBA Domain 5).
prerequisites: MRS333: Digital Systems, Sustainability and the Global Community
MRS367: Radiation Biology, Protection and Dosimetry
PHY115: Physics for Medical Radiation Science
MRS413: Pharmacology for Medical Radiation Science

title: Digital Agriculture in Practice
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Digital disruption to Agricultural practice is causing transformative change in some sectors of the Industry. In this subject students examine the range of current applications of digital technology to Agriculture globally and its likely impact in the future. The aim of this subject is to provide students with the opportunity to apply their new-found skills in global positioning systems (GPS), remote sensing, information technology and database management to a case study in agriculture.
learning_outcomes: Articulate digital citizenship in professional practice.
Appraise the appropriateness of key digital tools to current farm systems.
Develop and implement a strategy for project delivery.
Integrate knowledge and apply skills in digital technology to an agricultural situation and reflect on the outcomes.
Describe the range of digital agriculture applications occurring globally in agriculture and debate their productive, environmental, social and human impact on agricultural systems.

title: Digital and Social Media Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Digital marketing is now ubiquitous. This subject develops students' abilities to plan and implement digital marketing strategies in a social media world and to integrate these with the organisation's broader marketing strategies. Students will examine how communication practices influence an organisation's approach when creating a digital marketing strategy. Students will assess how digital spaces are being used in the context of business to business (B2B), business to consumer (B2C) and consumer to consumer (C2C). They will also critically examine online consumer behaviour, investigate legal and ethical issues, identify appropriate analytics and measurement tools, and evaluate evolving contemporary issues that need to be addressed within digital and social media marketing programs.
learning_outcomes: Conceptualise digital marketing as it applies across multiple digital platforms.
Plan, implement, measure and evaluate digital marketing strategies and.
Critically review digital marketing concepts in a broader social and market context.
Assess and evaluate how different communication practices influence strategic decision making in a digital marketing environment.

title: Digital Audio
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will gain an understanding of the digital audio landscape and be able to interpret future trends. You will also learn how to critically reflect on audio content for a variety of formats and platforms. This subject will include a virtual or physical study visit.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the digital audio landscape and future trends.
Critically reflect on audio content for a variety of platforms.
Demonstrate an understanding of the different audio programming formats.

title: Digital Citizenship in Schools
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the concept and practice of digital citizenship. Technological, political and ethical issues concerning digital citizenship are examined, including intellectual property, plagiarism, cybersafety, freedom of information, transliteracy and the effective use of a range of technologies to support learning and teaching. Issues in policy and practice are examined to understand how learning programs and school community practices can build capacity and resilience in students to enable them to become effective and responsible digital citizens in global online learning environments.
learning_outcomes: Incorporate a range of digital experiences in learning and teaching to promote digital citizenship in schools.
Identify and discuss the wide range of social, political, ethical and technological issues affecting the development of a digital citizen.
Articulate and reflect on the role of an information leader in the development and management of digital citizenship and information policy within an organisation.
Evaluate the use of a range of information sources and delivery modes that support effective digital citizenship.
Understand professional and ethical standards and social responsibility in information environments.
Develop an information policy or a set of guidelines that support the development of digital citizenship in schools.
Develop transliteracy skills and engage in professional dialogue in online environments.
Demonstrate an understanding of key concepts of digital citizenship.

title: Digital Forensics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth study of the rapidly changing and fascinating field of computer forensics. It combines both the technical expertise and the knowledge required to investigate, detect and prevent digital crimes. The subject covers the knowledge on digital forensics legislations, digital crime, forensics processes and procedures, data acquisition and validation, e-discovery tools, e-evidence collection and preservation, investigating operating systems and file systems, network forensics, art of steganography and mobile device forensics, email and web forensics, presenting reports and testimony as an expert witness.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the technology in digital forensics to detect, prevent and recover from digital crimes.
Critique and compose technical tactics in digital crimes and assess the steps involved in a digital forensics investigation.
Prepare and defend reports on the results of an investigation.
Analyse data on storage media and various file systems.
Collect electronic evidence without compromising the original data.
Formulate a digital forensics process.
Evaluate the functions and features of digital forensics equipment, the environment and the tools for a digital forensics lab.
Determine and explain the legal and ethical considerations for investigating and prosecuting digital crimes.

title: Digital Curation and Preservation
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores digital and data curation and preservation from the point of creation through the lifecycle of description, use, storage, accessibility and understandability over time, to future usability and use. Digital information and data surround us in organisations and our personal lives. They are inherently impermanent due to their dependence on rapidly changing technology. The curation and preservation of digital information and data involves ensuring their usability and accessibility into the future. Curation and preservation also require new strategies, practices, tools and techniques and is a burgeoning area of employment. Consideration of Indigenous Australian data sovereignty is also covered in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the digital curation and preservation lifecycles and identify the activities associated with each stage.
Demonstrate understanding of the need for digital curation and preservation in public and private organisations.
Explain digital curation and preservation concepts, terms, tools and technologies.
Examine and critically analyse the challenges associated with data and information sharing, including how it applies in the context of Indigenous Australian content.
Identify and critically assess theoretical and practical issues in digital curation and preservation.

title: Digital Forensics: Principles and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles, methodologies, and practical tools of digital forensics, with a focus on investigating cybercrime and handling electronic evidence within the Australian legal context. Students will learn how to identify, acquire, preserve, analyse, and present digital evidence in a forensically sound manner. The subject balances theoretical foundations with hands-on experience, covering topics such as forensic imaging, cybercrime typologies, computer and mobile device forensics, network investigations, and ethical considerations. By the end of the subject, students will be prepared to conduct basic forensic investigations, support criminal cases involving digital evidence, and navigate the complex intersection of technology, law, and ethics.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate digital evidence for its relevance, reliability, and admissibility in legal contexts, with reference to Australian and international frameworks.
Prepare professional forensic documentation and reports for both technical and non-technical stakeholders, including simulated expert testimony.
Identify and explain the legal, ethical, and privacy considerations involved in digital forensic investigations, with attention to emerging technologies and evolving privacy concerns.
Demonstrate a thorough understanding of digital forensics concepts, terminology, and methodologies, including data recovery, evidence handling, and chain of custody.

Apply and set up forensic tools and techniques within a virtual digital forensics laboratory environment, simulating real-world investigations to acquire, analyse, and interpret data from computers, mobile devices, and networks

title: Digital Futures: Questioning Texts in Media, Literature and Philosophy
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The rise of artificial intelligence, virtual reality, social media, deep fakes and cybernetics pose vital questions about how we make meaning and shape our conceptual understanding of the world. Can computers write poems? Can humans be fully digitised? Is it wrong to murder in computer games? In this subject, we will explore and investigate the complex ideas raised by such questions, as we analyse, critique and evaluate a range of literary, philosophical and media texts (e.g. computer games, novels, films, papers, podcasts, poems and social media posts). In critically examining these texts, we will be grappling with philosophical and literary ideas concerning the future of humanity and its relationship with technology.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate research methods derived from literary/media studies and analytical philosophy.
Apply knowledge and skills to communicate complex ideas within the context raised by future digital technologies.
Examine, analyse and discuss a range of texts using research methods derived from literary/media studies and analytical philosophy.
Critically investigate the key problems and opportunities raised by future digital technologies.

title: Digital Health Leadership
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Digital health leadership involves strategic decision-making to drive the successful adoption of data and technology in the health ecosystem. Leaders in the healthcare industry face challenges such as financial constraints, maintaining service quality, and improving standards of care, all important contributors to health system performance. In this subject students will explore digital health leadership, Australian health system performance, digital health safety, ethics and quality as well as digital maturity and consumer digital health. This content will allow leaders to navigate a landscape that includes digital transformation, informatics, research, innovation, and analytics.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the principles of consumer digital health in the design and delivery of health systems today and for the future.
Analyse the legal, ethical, social, and cultural factors in the use of digital health to inform leadership decision making.
Compare and contrast digital maturity models in Australia and internationally.
Advocate the need for digital health leadership, and the implications of data and technologies, on health system performance.

title: Digital Health Management
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to explore the foundations and principles of digital health, which is the dynamic intersection between data, technology, management, and health. By understanding how digital health can be a powerful and potentially challenging force in healthcare, students will gain the expertise to effectively navigate the evolving landscape of healthcare technology. This subject will examine these contrasting facets, emphasising the importance of effective governance and management, health equity and digital literacy, co-design principles, data security and safety, and the need for responsible integration. Students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how to leverage digital health solutions to drive improvement while addressing the associated risks and ethical considerations.
learning_outcomes: Examine corporate, clinical and information governance in digital health.
Apply and promote the principles of digital health literacy.
Analyse the use of digital health solutions to support delivery, decision- making, innovation, quality improvement and research.
Apply the foundational concepts of digital health, including security, safety and organisational risks of adopting digital health solutions.
Co-create a digital health solution using co-design principles.

title: Digital Marketing Analytics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn about the analytics that drive decision making in the digital media landscape. For all types of organisations, the ability to collect data in the digital sphere - from websites, the Internet of Things, apps and mobile usage - is having a major impact on strategy. With tools of analysis becoming more widely available, organisations look to data-driven decision making as critical to business effectiveness. From initial set-up to interpreting reports, students will learn how to analyse data to gain an understanding of the behaviour of visitors and the performance of their website and campaigns. This subject will also help students prepare for certification with the Digital Analytics Association (DAA).
learning_outcomes: Design workable personas for a digital analytics project.
Calculate digital campaign KPIs and create a KPI report.
Analyse user experience digital data, trends, and patterns and evaluate their impact on the digital experience.
Create and define baseline metrics for impact analysis.
Determine a website's effectiveness in maintaining the interest of organic search engine visitors and use that interest to drive conversion.
Design and recommend a multimedia digital campaign.

title: Digital Marketing and Social Media
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Social media and digital marketing is now embedded in many organisations ranging from SME to global companies. Individuals also have a vested interest in communicating their personal brand for commercial benefit through online tools. This subject is designed to provide an introduction to the world of digital and social media marketing, and help students to develop strategic and tactical skills that are required by industry. Students will examine how communication practices influence company motivations for creating a digital marketing strategy and the tactics to embed message across various networks. Further, students will learn how to assess the way digital technologies can be used in personal and professional settings. Students will also examine how digital technologies and social marketing tools comply with legal requirements and engage with ethical guidelines. Finally, students will explore key issues in measuring and evaluating social and digital media campaigns.
learning_outcomes: Implement and evaluate digital marketing strategies and tactics.
Examine individual digital platforms and evaluate how they are used for personal and professional marketing practices.
Reflect on ethical and legal issues facing social and digital activities and analyse how they impact on marketing practice.
Map and conceptualise cross platform communications and strategy and tactics.
Create an effective social and digital marketing plan.
prerequisites: MKT211: Applied Social Media and Digital Marketing

title: Digital Media - Level 5
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for the Master of Communication (generic and with specialisations) Articulated Set.

title: Digital Literacy
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' data literacy in order to make evidence-based decisions. Students will develop an understanding of data sources and constructs, analytical methods and techniques to clearly communicate information to others.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of and participate in conversations about data.
Read, write, and communicate data to others using words and visual representation.
Clearly communicate information to others in a particular context.

title: Digital Media Practice
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Students undertake a practice-based exploration of emerging models of media creation, distribution and consumption and consider the impact of these models on existing communication and creative industries from an industry-specific perspective. Students research audiences and markets to develop a complex digital artefact of relevance to their professional practice and engage with the major controversies, issues, and ethics around social media in society. This subject encourages experimentation with digital media and introduces students to key concepts in project and product development.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect upon the role of social and digital media in society, including major ethical concerns.
Examine the impact of emerging models for media creation, distribution and consumption upon existing media, communication, and creative industries.
Demonstrate key project and product development principles in the design of a complex, experimental digital artefact.
Research, plan, develop and pitch a complex digital artefact of relevance to professional practice.
Critically reflect on appropriate research and evaluation methodologies for defining and working with digital media audiences and users.

title: Digital Photography Studio
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on skills attained in prerequisite subjects by encouraging students to explore a variety of digital solutions to more complex photographic problems. The creation and enchancement of digital images is expanded in greater depth to equip students with a sound foundation for producing more sophisticated photographic projects. This is supported by significant investigation into technical and theoretical issues in areas such as colour, digital camera files and formats, digital image processing and studio lighting.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate their understanding the principles of artificial flashlighting and effectively apply these in and out of the studio in a creative context.
Demonstrate the creative application of sophisticated digital imaging processing and enhancement skills.
Articulate conceptual and practical synthesis between analogue and digital methods and techniques in photoimaging.
Manually operate a digital SLR camera system competently.
Understand more complex methodologies in creating and acquiring digital photographs for application in specific photographic related creative projects.

title: Digital Social Selling
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn how to create engaging marketing content as well as how to achieve selling success. They will study the difference between traditional and digital and social selling methods and the benefits that can be gained from adopting a digital and social selling approach to their current sales activities.
learning_outcomes: Utilise the research tools and techniques needed to develop a well-informed digital and social selling strategy for their product or service.
Devise holistic digital social selling strategies and plans for online business.
Develop relevant, informative content that engages potential and existing buyers.
Develop relevant sales messages and content by using digital tools to analyse social media platforms.
Identify different customer types and recommend how to build relationships in the most effective way over an entire customer life-cycle.
Forecast and establish targets based on a comprehensive assessment of their digital sales pipeline.

title: Digital signal processing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the theory, algorithms, and applications of processing digital signals. It covers essential concepts such as discrete-time signals and systems, convolution, Fourier analysis, Z-transforms, digital filter design, and spectral analysis.
learning_outcomes: Use models to simulate and analyse digital signal processing algorithms.
Apply discrete-time signal processing techniques.
Compare and contrast various multirate signal processing techniques.
Evaluate the effectiveness of different spectral analysis techniques for estimating signal properties.
Apply digital filters using appropriate design methods.

title: Digital Society and Global Citizenship
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the broad challenges and opportunities that digital and networked media technologies bring to societies. Throughout this subject, students will explore issues around practising in a digital society and engage with global issues that include diverse cultural voices and perspectives. This subject is one of four introductory subjects that build the theoretical and discipline specific skills essential for communication professionals.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate digital media content from the perspective of both the consumer and the producers.
Analyse the role of media.
Apply communication theory to critique participation in digital media.
Define and describe key concepts relevant to studying digital society and global citizenship.
Identify and reflect on the risks and opportunities of global digital communities.

title: Digital Systems, Sustainability and the Global Community
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students explore current and emerging digital technologies in medical radiation science, including image informatics, data reconstruction, and data management systems, in order to develop an applied understanding of the application and management of digital technologies within the clinical environment. Translational knowledge and skills in digital technologies will provide insight and understanding of development of sustainable practices and in connecting to a global community. The principles of evidence-based practice will be utilised to allow students to develop critical thinking, analytical appraisal, and reflective skills, and apply these in the global digital environment.
learning_outcomes: Recognise opportunities to develop new knowledge through research and enquiry, and contribute to the improvement of local and global social, economic and environmental sustainability (MRPBA Domain 4.1d).

Describe, explain and implement professional practice with specific reference to utilising clinical information management systems and managing and /or manipulating image datasets, including 3D (MRPBA Domain 1.2).
Identify and seek opportunities to progress the MRS profession and one's own professional learning (MRPBA domain 4.2 and 2.5).

Apply digital technology and digital literacy skills for professional practice and research and demonstrate digital citizenship in online learning, professional and social communities (MRPBA Domain 4).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1).
Identify and respond to the impact of variations in clinical workflow on clinical information management systems, and ensure data security through appropriate access management (MRPBA Domain 1.2).
Describe and explain the application of digital systems to work effectively with local and global communities and workplaces.
Identify and respond to clinical information errors, data errors, and data failures utilising clinical information management systems (MRPBA Domain 1.2).

title: Dirty Money
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject contrasts the reality of money laundering with its portrayal across popular culture mediums. Focusing on the main players in money laundering operations, students will explore the implications this contrast has on public perception and ultimately contemporary crime-control policy and practice debates.
learning_outcomes: Critique contemporary anti-money laundering policy.
Critically reflect on the impact of public perception on crime control policy and practice.
Evaluate popular culture representations of money laundering against the reality of money laundering.

title: Disaster Recovery, Sustainability and Resilience
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Sustainability, vulnerability and resilience are now key words for emergency managers. Disaster plans must incorporate the philosophy of sustainable development. Increasingly communities are being encouraged to find ways to build their resilience, rather than 'waiting for help to arrive'. The degree to which a community is considered resilient is often spoken about in terms of its 'vulnerability'. Through the use of case study examples, this subject explores the concepts of sustainability, vulnerability and resilience in the context of both western and developing countries.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles and process of recovery in emergency management within a community.
Examine the relationship between environmental sustainability and disaster recovery.
Evaluate the level of social vulnerability and resilience in a community.
Assess the impact of trauma of communities, industry, and individuals.
Design strategies for building the resilience of communities.

title: Disaster Recovery: A Human Services Perspective
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: 'Disaster recovery' often focuses on the technical, practical and physical aspects of recovery, leaving social, psychological, spiritual and communal aspects under-explored. This subject takes a holistic eco social approach and focuses on the multidimensional nature of recovery from disasters. Students will explore the current environmental context in relation to different types of disasters, including natural disasters and those influenced by environmental degradation and climate change. Students will be encouraged to critically reflect on community context, discourses, policy, governance, service systems, resilience and approaches to disaster recovery from a human services perspective.
learning_outcomes: Analyse how 'sense of place', community context, notions of resilience and social structures impact on disaster recovery.
Explain different types of disaster in the context of climate change.
Apply multidimensional perspectives of human services practice in the context of disaster recovery.
Explain disaster recovery as a multidimensional, human services issue.
Analyse impacts of discourses, policy, service systems and governance on disaster recovery.

title: Discrete Mathematics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Discrete mathematics explores finite mathematic objects such as the integers, graphs and logical statements which assume distinct and separated values. The importance of discrete mathematics has greatly increased with the development of digital computers which themselves operate in discrete steps and store data in discrete units (bits). Students will learn the concepts and notation which are fundamental in studying several areas of computer science, including computer algorithms, data structures, programming languages, cryptography and software development.
learning_outcomes: Work with discrete probabilities, and the related statistics such as expectations and variances.
Recognise and use mathematical notation and operations to simplify expressions and prove properties of sets, formal logic and computer circuits and other discrete objects.
Understand that numbers can be represented in several bases, and be able to reason in non-decimal bases such as binary and hexadecimal.
Understand the basic algorithms for analysing graphs, apply them to examples, and to estimate running times.
Analyse growth rates in terms of recursions and recurrence equations.
Follow and apply simple mathematical statements and proofs.

title: Disease Processes
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject examines the processes of disease development in humans, together with the way that such processes are detected and monitored using laboratory tests. Emphasis will be placed on the role of common point-of-care tests which may be utilised.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the role of genetic factors in the development of both monogenic disorders and multifactorial human diseases.
Describe and demonstrate knowledge of the biomedical rationale of routinely encountered laboratory and point-of-care tests.
Perform point-of-care tests.
Interpret results presented in routine pathology laboratory reports.
Integrate and demonstrate knowledge from various biomedical science disciplines to gain an understanding of disease processes of the human body.
Know the range of clinical disorders commonly encountered by practising pharmacists.
Demonstrate knowledge of the need for drug therapy arising from an understanding of disease processes.

title: Dispute Resolution
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the range of dispute resolution methods that are available (eg adjudication, arbitration, conciliation, mediation, negotiation and hybrid methods) and how to use them to achieve desired results in various settings. Comparisons of methods and systems design are undertaken; and alternatives to court processes are scrutinised including the use of Ombudsman schemes and conflict management in both public and private settings.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate systems and methods to resolve complaints and disputes in various settings, both public and private.
Critically analyse both the role and the dispute resolution methods of courts and lawyers and compare adversarial with non-adversarial legal systems.

Differentiate between alternative methods of dispute resolution and evaluate when they might be applied, either separately or in conjunction with one another, in different institutional and private settings.

title: Dispute Resolution: Methods and Results
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the range of dispute resolution methods that are available (eg adjudication, arbitration, conciliation, mediation, negotiation and hybrid methods) and how to use them to achieve desired results in various settings. Comparisons of methods and systems design are undertaken; alternatives to court processes are scrutinised including the use of Ombudsman schemes and conflict management in both public and private settings.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse both the role and the dispute resolution methods of courts and lawyers and compare adversarial with non-adversarial legal systems.
Design and evaluate critically systems and methods to resolve complaints and disputes in various settings, both public and private.

Differentiate between alternative methods of dispute resolution and evaluate when they might be applied, either separately or in conjunction with one another, in different institutional and private settings.

title: Disruptive Media
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces a wide range of foundation concepts for experimentation and professional practice in the creative industries. These include perception and the use of images, narrative design and analysis, the history of the stage and screen, and other innovative interactions between technology, the creative arts and performing arts. In particular, this subject reviews the impact, ethics and limitations of generative AI through creative practice research.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse narratives through image and text.
Demonstrate the limitations of generative AI systems.
Analyse the structure and content of diverse forms of visual communication.
Explain fundamental principles for creative and performing arts.
Discuss technological and cultural factors that have shaped creative and performing arts.
prerequisites: CCI103: Perspectives on the Creative Industries

title: Dissertation (32) in Health or Medical Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students build upon their resarch skills to undertake original independent research, under the guidance of research supervisor(s), involving critical evaluation of existing data and/or new data collection, analysis and interpretation. The student prepares a manuscript, based on the research undertaken, for publication in a peer reviewed journal.
learning_outcomes: Produce a research portfolio that includes, at a minimum, ethics approvals and other approvals as required and a manuscript written according to the guidelines of the intended journal.
Analyse, interpret and present research findings.
Undertake independent scholarship and/or research applicable to biomedical or health related sciences.
Prepare a manuscript for publication in an appropriate peer reviewed journal in accordance with the journal's publication guidelines.

title: Dissertation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This dissertation will require students to examine a specific aspect of their Course of studies. The dissertation must result from original and independent research conducted by the student for this course and have prior approval of the Academic Supervisor. The research should examine aspects of practice with reflection on best practice and the development of policy.
learning_outcomes: Complete empirical research in an area of practice related to specialist area of investigation or practice.
Discuss results of research and formulate recommendations for 'best practice' in the area of research and specialisation.
Write concise research report and critically discuss research undertaken.
prerequisites: JST530: Research Methodology and Dissertation Proposal

title: Dissertation for Islamic Studies
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to undertake a research on Islamic Studies. It comprises of a 12,000 word research project on a topic which has been touched upon by one of the subjects they have studied so far in their Islamic Studies course. The research will advance theoretical and/or practical understanding of the chosen topic.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a deeper level of knowledge in a particular area of Islamic Studies.
Produce a thorough, carefully reasoned report which demonstrates an in-depth understanding of a specific area of knowledge or inquiry.

title: Diversity and Difference in Early Childhood Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject takes as foundational the value of diversity and difference in early childhood education contexts. Students will examine national policies and curriculum frameworks to unpack cultural factors, social justice and equity issues that may impact on children, educators, families and communities. The subject aims to critically examine assumptions that frame practice, shape identities, and to offer alternatives so that early childhood professionals can realise their role as agents of change around issues of diversity, difference, social justice and equity.
learning_outcomes: Develop positive strategies, pedagogies and curricula for inclusive and socially just practice in early childhood contexts and the broader community.
Recognise the power and place of early childhood education in the struggle for social justice and act to provoke thought in others.
Develop and articulate a critical disposition towards assumptions about children in relation to issues of diversity and difference in multicultural education.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of issues related to identities, diversity, intersectionality, social justice and equity for children, families and communities.

Critique professional practice that involves prejudices, biases, structural and institutional inequalities in relation to white privilege, ongoing colonisation, racism, gender diversity, sexism, homophobia, ableism, class position and socioeconomic status.

title: Doing Theology on Indigenous Australian Countries
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject situates theological inquiry within extant custodianship of the land by Indigenous Australians and the impacts of settlement and immigration. Listening to––and learning from––the language, Country, kinship, and ceremony of Indigenous peoples, these experiences, traditions, stories, and spiritualities challenge and deepen contemporary theological exploration in 21st century Australia. The subject stimulates deeper critical self-reflection and inquiry for new relational positions for Indigenous and non-Indigenous theology students.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique continuing issues of land justice which Indigenous Australians face in contemporary Australian society.
Articulate how knowledge of how Indigenous Australian languages, Countries, kinships and ceremonies shape Indigenous cultures and spiritualities.
Critically evaluate the impact of Christianity and the church on the dispossession and dislocation from the land for Indigenous Australians.
Adopt a reflexive framework for doing theology on Indigenous Australian Countries.
Critically engage with the implications of connection to Country for non-Indigenous expressions of Christian faith.
prerequisites: THL362: Doing Theology on Indigenous Australian Countries

title: Drawing to Design
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject students develop experimental drawing skills, both to produce independent works of art and as a means of 'drawing-to-design' applied towards different disciplines in the creative industries. The subject investigates a range of approaches to drawing, including perceptual, conceptual, sculptural and performative drawing modes. Students develop the ability to align hand-work with computer based strategies for application in fine art and design contexts.
learning_outcomes: Create visual imagery based on observational and conceptual drawing skills.
Demonstrate the ability to undertake research and investigative visual research using historical and contemporary sources.
Evidence an understanding of historical and contemporary drawing to design strategies.
Demonstrate visually coherent developmental studies and finished thematic drawings.
Demonstrate an individual visual language of process.
Refine presentation and practice to match means and ideas in a related body of works.

title: Drugs, Crime and Society
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: The link between drug use and crime remains a central issue for contemporary criminal justice. This subject examines social, legal and political responses to illicit and licit drug use and abuse in contemporary society. Students will examine domestic and international debates on the current 'war against drugs' and the policing of illicit drugs. The relationship between key social concepts such as race, gender and ethnicity, and official and unofficial interventions, will be explored. Also considered are a range of interventions inside and outside the criminal justice system.
learning_outcomes: Describe the main issues concerning the policing of drug markets.
Identify and compare the political, social and economic implications of contemporary drug policies.
Explain the history, social construction and criminalisation of drug use including concepts such as addiction.
Critically analyse a range of political, criminal justice and medical AOD use/abuse interventions.
Describe patterns of drug use and abuse across a variety of historical, cultural, national and international settings.

title: Duty Suspension Regimes
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject students examine the range of Duty relief programs provided by governments as part of their cross border trade policy. Duty suspension regimes are designed to remove or reduce the tariff burden to give exporters access to required inputs at world prices and, as a consequence, improve the competitiveness of the country's exports. Students will examine the consistency of such suspension regimes with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, the various types of schemes, policy imperatives, best practice as set out in the Revised Kyoto Convention and compliance aspects and issues.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and examine the procedural requirements surrounding the issue and use of an ATA Carnet.
Identify sources guiding the practical application of duty suspension schemes, particularly recommended and best practice approaches, and apply these sources to specific customs procedures.
Assess critically the advantages and disadvantages in the operation of duty suspension schemes in particular contexts, particularly in respect of bonded warehouses and free zones.

Demonstrate the ability to assess and discuss critically the differences between the operation of duty suspension schemes in respect of inward processing, outward processing, manufacturing in bond and drawback.
Discuss and evaluate critically the way these schemes are designed and administered.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the concepts and characteristics of duty suspension schemes.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the principles and practices associated with temporary admission.

title: Early Childhood Leadership and Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Leaders have a powerful influence on the quality of early childhood education (ECE) programs, yet many challenges exist for leadership development within ECE. Challenges include inadequate preparation for positional leadership roles, few opportunities for professional development for emerging leaders, and an absence of workforce planning for cultivating leaders within the early childhood education profession. This subject addresses those challenges by contextualising early childhood leadership and practice, locating early childhood leadership within the history of leadership theory and philosophy, and exploring the emergence and practices of leading within early childhood education. Students will apply a body of knowledge to their role and practices as emerging or positional leaders within early childhood education.
learning_outcomes: Apply theoretical knowledge in leadership practice.
Analyse the challenges and disruptions to leadership cultivation in early childhood education.
Synthesise knowledge of theory and practice to formulate individualised standpoints on leadership identity.
Critically reflect on the social, political and economic history of early childhood education and its impact on leadership emergence and development.
Demonstrate practice changes to leadership through dialogic processes and critical reflection.

title: Early Childhood Professional Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject comprises a Work Integrated Learning (WIL) placement designed to meet the Graduate level requirements of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST). While on placement, Pre-Service Teachers (PSTs) will be required to build positive relationships with children, families, educators and community members. The Early Years Learning Framework (EYLF) V2.0 will be used to analyse and interpret observations and documentation, to guide the design and implementation of effective learning experiences, and to assess and evaluate children’s learning. PSTs will also create safe and supportive learning environments, implement leadership skills, evaluate and reflect on their teaching and the contribution of this experience to their professional growth. PSTs will complete 320 hours (8hrs/day for 40 days) of WIL placement in an early childhood service with three-to-five-year-old children. Eligible PSTs are able to apply for a reduction of 160 hours (20 days) placement based on recent experience of at least 12 months duration in a leadership role within an early childhood setting.
learning_outcomes: Link child development theory to early childhood pedagogical practices and programs (including supporting transitions) for 3-5 year olds.
Plan, implement and evaluate responsive learning experiences for children aged 3–5 years, using documented observations to inform practice.
Observe and document children’s play and learning, and analyse this evidence to identify individual and group strengths, interests and developmental needs.
Engage in reflective practice with other professionals in their work with children to inform future practice.
Develop positive relationships with children and use responsive pedagogical approaches to create inclusive environments and guide behaviour for children aged 3-5years.

Explain the use and implications of the relevant curriculum framework, early childhood education and care policy and regulations (including child safety) in relation to children, families and educators.
Access and create resources to enhance the learning and development of 3-5 year old children.
Demonstrate a range of pedagogical, social, and administrative skills (including pedagogical leadership) in line with the professional experience setting.
prerequisites: EMC305: Investigation: Mathematics, Science and Technology

title: Early Childhood Studies Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This is a credit code for the Bachelor of Education (Birth to Five Years) Articulated Set for credit upon entry for students who have completed an equivalent Bachelor of Teaching (Birth to Five Years) tertiary qualification at another institution.

title: Early Childhood Studies Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is the Entry Level Credit for Bachelor of Education (Birth to Five Years) Articulated Set.

title: Early Church History
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This foundation subject introduces students to skills appropriate to studying church history, including the use and analysis of early sources, both written and non-written, and later historical interpretations. It encompasses the contributions of the Apostolic Fathers and early Christian Apologists, and explores early challenges to the Christian movement from within and without. Close attention is given to church-state relations and the formulation of Christian theology by prominent theologians and significant councils, especially those convened at Nicaea and Chalcedon. The subject also examines early Christian monasticism, issues of ethnicity and gender, mission and the claims of the Bishop of Rome to supremacy. Consistent attention is given to understanding the broader context of the Graeco-Roman world in which Christianity developed.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of primary source documents from this period.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of principal movements in theology, ecclesiology and politics in the Christian Church prior to 600 CE.
Demonstrate an advanced ability to use contemporary documents in making critical judgements about the past and in testing the judgements of others.
Demonstrate an advanced critical understanding of Christians who lived in different times, cultures and with different worldviews.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills relevant to history as a discipline.
Assess critically historians interpretations of early church history.
Demonstrate advanced understanding of methods of historical study.

title: Early Intervention and Inclusion
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds knowledge and skills in the theory of early intervention and inclusion, including an understanding of the concepts informing inclusion, current practice in the early childhood field, the examination of developmental theory, and application to practice. Students will build their capacity to address the needs of children with disabilities in a non-categorical fashion employing approaches that focus on individual needs and context. Principles of inclusion and consideration of various service delivery models are investigated in relation to the creation of an inclusive environment. Child and family-centred inclusive practice is emphasised with a focus on empowering families in decision-making and planning for early intervention. The importance of collaboration, the ability to work with other professionals, and the role of the early childhood educator as an advocate for children with disabilities and their families underpins the design of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Explain national and international trends in inclusive early intervention.
Articulate a rationale for child and family-centred models and the value of a team approach to early intervention.
Demonstrate an understanding of what constitutes an inclusive curriculum and setting.
Design an inclusion plan that incorporates the involvement of the family, available support services and other professionals.
Critique research on current practices in inclusion and reflect on their practice.
Explain individual differences in young children with reference to developmental theories informing practice.
Articulate a rationale for child and family-centred models and the value of a team approach to early intervention.

title: Early Church History
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This foundation subject introduces students to skills appropriate to studying church history, including the use and analysis of early sources, both written and non-written, and later historical interpretations. It encompasses the contributions of the Apostolic Fathers and early Christian Apologists, and explores early challenges to the Christian movement from within and without. Close attention is given to church-state relations and the formulation of Christian theology by prominent theologians and significant councils, especially those convened at Nicaea and Chalcedon. The subject also examines early Christian monasticism, issues of ethnicity and gender, mission and the claims of the Bishop of Rome to supremacy. Consistent attention is given to understanding the broader context of the Graeco-Roman world in which Christianity developed.
learning_outcomes: Review critically and analyse the contribution of historians and historiographical perspectives from a variety of denominational and historical contexts.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the primary source documents of this period and be able to analyse, interpret, and critically review these documents.
Analyse and critically evaluate historiographical approaches to the Christian faith across different cultures and ecclesial communities.
Research and communicate the relevance of historical documents for understanding the historical origins of contemporary churches in Australia and Asia.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills relevant to history as a discipline.
Demonstrate a broad and critical understanding of the principal movements in theology, ecclesiology and politics in the Christian Church during its formative period.

title: Ecological and Environmental Soil Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The properties of soil are a major influence on the functioning of natural ecosystems. This subject explores how natural soil and landscape features affect plant and animal communities. The subject examines Australia's natural soil properties and the relationships between geology, biology, geomorphology, climate and time that have influenced the development of Australia's soil. A general underpinning of soil related topics relevant to the environmental and ecological sciences is presented so that ecological and environmental professionals can apply soil knowledge to the exploration of Australia's unique flora and fauna.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the role of soils in sustainability.
Describe, explain and critically evaluate solutions to some environmental problems related to soils.
Describe the major landform development processes affecting the Australian landscape.
Describe the main features of Australia's natural soil systems.
Describe the relationships between soil properties and native fauna and flora.

title: Earth System Processes
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will learn about the processes operating in Earth's lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere. You will learn how geological processes have shaped the Earth's landforms and how to interpret geological features and the shape of the landscape to develop a historical perspective on landform development. You will also learn about the relationships between the Earth's hydrological cycle and the atmosphere to be able to demonstrate an understanding of the processes affecting weather on a global and local scale including how to forecast the weather.
learning_outcomes: Describe the key principles and concepts associated with hydrological processes.
Interpret geological features to develop a historical perspective on landform development.
Read, interpret and use topographic maps.
Describe the key principles of atmospheric processes and climate.
Describe the key principles and concepts associated with geological processes.
Interpret weather maps and forecast the weather.

school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds knowledge and skills in the theory of early intervention and inclusion, including an understanding of the concepts informing inclusion, current practice in the early childhood field, the examination of developmental theory, and application to practice. learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the range of community resources that can be accessed to support a child and their family.
Critique research on current practices in inclusion and reflect on their practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of what constitutes an inclusive curriculum and setting.
Articulate a rationale for child and family-centred models and the value of a team approach to early intervention.
Explain national and international trends in inclusive early intervention.
Design an inclusion plan that incorporates the involvement of the family, available support services and other professionals.
Explain individual differences in young children with reference to developmental theories informing practice.
prerequisites: ESS508: Inclusion and Early Intervention 0-8 Years

title: Ecological Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an opportunity to engage and reflect upon the climate crisis and its implications. Attention will be given to contemporary work in the area of ecological theology, as well as to insights from the natural sciences and other disciplines. In addition, close attention will be given to the insights of climate activists and the experiences of those most affected by climate change.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and reflect on the realities of the climate crisis.
Draw on a variety of hermeneutical approaches to Scripture and the Christian tradition for understanding and responding to ecological challenges.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Articulate and communicate ecotheological methodologies in a variety of theological contexts.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the barriers that prevent people from engaging with the climate crisis.
prerequisites: THL210: Additional New Testament Exegesis in Greek

title: Ecological Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an opportunity to engage and reflect upon the climate crisis and its implications. Attention will be given to contemporary work in the area of ecological theology, as well as to insights from the natural sciences and other disciplines. In addition, close attention will be given to the insights of climate activists and the experiences of those most affected by climate change.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and communicate ecotheological methodologies in a variety of theological contexts.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the barriers that prevent people from engaging with the climate crisis.
Draw on a variety of hermeneutical approaches to Scripture and the Christian tradition for understanding and responding to ecological challenges.
Critically analyse and reflect on the realities of the climate crisis.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
