learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of the barriers that prevent people from engaging with the climate crisis.
Articulate ecotheological methodologies.
Draw on Scripture and the Christian tradition for understanding and responding to ecological challenges.
Identity and discuss the realities of the climate crisis.

title: eCommerce
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject is about conducting business in the digital environment. The origins, growth and technical operation of the Internet are examined with respect to business practices, strategies and performance. This subject introduces the use of computerised information systems specifically in the area of eCommerce. These systems are useful business tools which enable an organisation to record, summarise and report events arising from interactions with its environment including customers and suppliers. In addition, this subject examines the legal, ethical, security, social and global implications of eCommerce. No prior knowledge of computers is required to successfully complete this subject.
learning_outcomes: be able to evaluate applications of electronic commerce in organisations and analyse the barriers to successful implementation of these technologies;
be able to discuss electronic commerce planning processes and the managerial and organisational contingencies affecting the relationship between technology and the organisation; and
be able to identify the effects of technology on business results and measure the contribution of technology to firm performance;
be able to evaluate problems posed by utilising electronic commerce, including security, legal jurisdictions and effectiveness;
be able to analyse technology needs in specific situations and develop customer-focused plans and correspondence.

title: Economics for Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the economist's way of thinking about the activities of individuals and institutions (both private and government) which determine the nature of our business and social environment. The subject presents, applies and assesses the key theoretical principles in microeconomics and macroeconomics that enable us to make sensible decisions in a complex world.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the nature of market failure and the role of government intervention.

Apply critical thinking skills to identify and solve problems, inform judgments, make decisions, reach well-reasoned conclusions and make recommendations regarding the health of the economy as a whole through the analysis of major economic variables and advise on likely policy alternatives.
Describe how information and communication technology supports data analysis and decision making, and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of communication.
Apply economic concepts and principles to evaluate data and information from a variety of sources and perspectives through research, integration, and analysis to daily life activities.
Evaluate demand and supply conditions to make a range of market related decisions.
Analyse the price and output decisions of a firm under different market structures.
Determine the circumstances in which government intervention in the economy is necessary.

title: EDU35C Credit Package
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is the Entry level credit for the Bachelor of Teaching (Primary) where the prior completion of a relevant undergraduate bachelor's degree that meets the NESA requirements for appropriate prior studies requires the completion of an additional 24 subject points to meet Charles Sturt University course requirements.

title: Education Policy Analysis
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Where does this policy come from? What does it mean? How can I respond? What implications does this policy hold for teachers and educational leaders? This subject provides a framework to address these questions from which an understanding of education policy and its intended and unintended effects can be built. Given the increased scrutiny on educational systems to deliver solutions to political problems, this subject builds an understanding of the way that education policy problems are constructed, and the processes by which these policy problems come to influence the lives of teachers, students, parents and educational leaders. The structure of the subject encourages students to test the theories and tools introduced against cases in their regions, and apply these theories and tools to local and regional policy developments.
learning_outcomes: Identify national and global trends in the adoption of education policy themes.
Describe typical policy problems associated with governing education in Modern Nationstates.
Describe and analyse the operations of education policy from influence, text to practice.
Outline different perspectives on the role and function of policy.
Apply policy frameworks in the construction of policy texts and processes.
Identify and describe traditions in the analysis of education policy.
Identify sites of action for different policy agents.
Categorise, analyse and critique historical and contextual changes in the development, application and uses of education policy.
Describe the contextual assumptions of policy problems.
Identify and analyse changing trends in the application of education policy.
Describe, utilise and identify the limits of tools emanating from different education policy analysis traditions.
Describe the influence of the following themes on educational practice: globalisation; innovation; knowledge economy; contractualism; marketisation; social justice; mediatisation.

Utilise education policy literature to construct models that help in explaining the intended and unintended effects associated with the introduction of different education policies on educators, students, parents and education leaders.
Utilise educational policy literature to analyse cases of policy development and implementation.

title: Education Studies: Child Development and Learning
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with discipline-based knowledge of the psychology of child development within a variety of social contexts: family, socio-cultural and school settings. The focus of the subject is on child development across the primary school years (4-12 years), with an emphasis on cognition and reasoning. All developmental/theoretical bases delivered will incorporate a philosophical framework (humanism) acknowledging preventative management and including among other things, the rights of the child-as-learner in terms of the UN Charter: The Rights of the Child. Professional ethics provide another part of this framework.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the developmental and psychological bases of managing difficult behaviour.

Understand developmental issues within the context of humanism and preventative approaches including: professional ethics, the UN Charter: The Rights of the Child plus the obligation of schools to provide safe, positive learning settings.
Articulate an understanding of all areas of child development and the interdependence of these from childhood to early adolescence.
Understand and progressively demonstrate an ability to critique developmental theory and research literature.
Understand children's development in terms of their family/neighbourhood and sociocultural contexts (ecological perspectives).
Demonstrate a sound knowledge of cognition-problem solving and reasoning, plus developmental patterns and inconsistencies (4-12 years).
Acknowledge and understand that developmental diversity is an expected aspect of growth and development.

title: Education Professionals for the Future
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Students will reflect on their learning throughout the Masters course, consider the transformation that has taken place in their thinking and their professional practice, and draw this learning together to inform their future professional practice. The subject also provides the opportunity for students to identify an issue or challenge in their own professional context that they consider to be unreasonable, unjust, or inadequate, and develop a plan for improvement. This subject is a capstone subject which will be undertaken by students who have completed all or most of their study for the Master of Education.
learning_outcomes: Generate, collect, analyse and apply evidence to inform context specific approaches to educational/learning situations.
Critically reflect on learning throughout the Masters course to inform your own philosophy of teaching.
Synthesize and evaluate understandings developed throughout the Masters course to inform present and future educational practices.
Analyse relevant research, scholarship and professional practice to inform future educational practices of self and others.

title: Education Studies: Inclusive Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds knowledge and skills in the theory and practice of inclusive education. This includes the theoretical, philosophical and applied underpinnings of the practice of inclusion, the current state of practice in the field and the design of inclusive pedagogy. Students will build their capacity to address learner diversity in their own classrooms employing an approach that focuses on learner need and context rather than label. The intent of the subject is to assist students to become self-organizing inclusive educators through the processes of research, design, reflection and collaboration.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate how the use of quality teaching, curriculum differentiation and curriculum based assessment intersect in practice.
Recognize and describe the characteristics of a successful inclusive learning environment.

Have designed and organized strategies and adaptations, including writing individual educational plans (IEPs) that can be implemented within classroom settings that promote learner access to the academic and broader life skills curriculum.
Have built a personal position on inclusive education based upon research in the field and their professional beliefs and values.
Have briefly described the history of the development of inclusion as an educational philosophy/phenomenon.
Have demonstrated a knowledge of the legislative underpinnings of inclusion, with particular reference to (although not limited to) the Australian context.
Develop an applied understanding of the theoretical and research-based underpinnings of inclusive strategies and pedagogy as they relate to classroom practice.
Describe how having a disability may impact on a student's access to and participation in education.

title: Educational Application of Digital Technologies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will consider a range of digital technologies which influence learning, methods for gathering data about learning, and ways of improving and/or expanding learning using digital technologies. Students will explore and develop a range of digital technology methods for assessing the educational needs of learners, and be confident in selecting appropriate courseware to meet learners' needs. The subject provides opportunities for students to use a range of software in assessment and diagnosis to support learning.
learning_outcomes: Plan quality learning experiences across a range of educational scenarios and contexts using digital technologies.
Discuss the contemporary role of digital technologies in a socio-political context.
Evaluate the nature and purpose of using digital technologies for learning.
Evaluate software and hardware resources for learning experiences across a range of educational scenarios and contexts.

title: Educational Leadership in Contemporary Organisations
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the changing nature of educational leadership from the perspective of educational and training organisations. It examines the nature, characteristics and dynamics of global, national and local forces on contemporary educational and training organisations. It analyses how these influences shape and define the contemporary context for educational leadership, drawing on a range of theoretical perspectives including social justice and critical approaches to educational leadership and training. It provides the opportunity for students to reflect on the nature and characteristics of these influences within their own organisation and the moral and ethical implications of these influences for their own leadership practices. This subject provides the basis for further study concerning policy development and implementation, organisational change and the politics of education in the 21st Century.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the varying global, national and local contexts and forces which are impacting upon leadership in educational and training organisations.
Investigate the economic and social forces, internal and external to formal organisations, which impact upon contemporary educational and training organisations.
Apply concepts of ethical educational leadership to a local context.
Use a range of critical theoretical perspectives to exemplify their application within an organisation, in terms of their implications for leadership at both the informal and formal levels.

title: Educational Transitions in Multiple Contexts
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject investigates principles, practices and policies underpinning educational transitions, with particular focus on the transitions made by children and families as they commence attendance in educational settings outside the home. Transitions are recognised as times of educational and social change for all involved: children, families, educators, other professionals and communities. Transitions are also points at which support and engagement are established and renegotiated, providing opportunities for relationship building and intervention. Students will consider a range of issues-social, cultural and educational-that impact on transition; explore the perspectives of all involved in transitions; and examine their own role in promoting positive transitions.
learning_outcomes: Apply subject knowledge to the educational workplaces and to the community settings in which they are working.

Identify, and cater for, the different needs of children and families in transition, including children from rural and remote, low SES and Indigenous communities; culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds; and children with special and complex support needs.
Critically analyse current theory, research and practice to gain an understanding of the needs of children and families in transitions.
Identify, develop and justify an appropriate range of pedagogical strategies to support educational transitions.
Identify the issues surrounding transitions for children and families moving from home to early childhood settings, and from early childhood settings to school.
Demonstrate knowledge of the multiple contexts for, and which influence, transitions for children and families, incorporating an ecological theoretical perspective.

title: Educational Transitions in Multiple Contexts
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject investigates principles, practices and policies underpinning educational transitions, with particular focus on the transitions made by children and families as they commence attendance in educational settings outside the home. Transitions are recognised as times of educational and social change for all involved: children, families, educators, other professionals and communities. Transitions are also points at which support and engagement are established and renegotiated, providing opportunities for relationship building and intervention. Students will consider a range of issues-social, cultural and educational-that impact on transition; explore the perspectives of all involved in transitions; and examine their own role in promoting positive transitions.
learning_outcomes: Identify the issues surrounding transitions for children and families moving from home to early childhood settings, and from early childhood settings to school.
Be aware of the multiple contexts for, and which influence, transitions for children and families, incorporating an ecological theoretical perspective.
Focus on the application of knowledge to the educational workplaces and to the community settings in which they are working.
Critically analyse current theory, research and practice to gain an understanding of the needs of children and families in transitions.
Identify, develop and justify an appropriate range of pedagogical strategies to support educational transitions.

Have an ability to identify, and cater for, the different needs of children and families in transition, including children from rural and remote, low SES and Indigenous communities; culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds; and children with special and complex support needs.

title: Electrical Engineering Design Challenge
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the principles and practices of electrical and electronic systems. Students will engage in designing, analysing, and optimising electrical systems and components. The subject combines theoretical knowledge with practical design experience, emphasising problem-solving, creativity, and functional applications.
learning_outcomes: Develop comprehensive designs for electrical systems and circuits, addressing specific engineering problems and constraints.
Effectively communicate design solutions and engineering concepts.
Perform detailed analyses of electrical designs to assess performance, efficiency, and reliability.
Produce and interpret technical documentation, including drawings, specifications, design reports.

title: Electrical Engineering Experimentation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides hands-on experience with experimental techniques and instrumentation used in electrical engineering. Students will design, conduct, and analyse experiments related to electrical circuits, signals, and systems. Emphasis is placed on developing practical skills, critical thinking, and data analysis.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate experimental results, identifying potential sources of error and uncertainty and assessing the implications for engineering practice.
Communicate experimental methods, results, and conclusions effectively.
Develop and implement experimental designs to investigate electrical engineering problems and validate engineering hypotheses.
Collect, process, and analyse experimental data using electrical engineering tools and techniques, including statistical methods and software.

title: Electrical Machines
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principles and designs of electrical machines. Covering DC and AC machines, transformers, and special machines. Students gain the skills to analyse, design, and apply these devices. With a blend of theory and practical examples, this course equips students for practical engineering challenges.
learning_outcomes: Design and optimise electrical machines considering factors such as efficiency, voltage regulation, torque-speed characteristics, and power factor correction.

Analyse the construction, working principles, and performance characteristics of various electrical machines; including DC machines (including Brushless dc Motors), transformers, induction motors, and synchronous machines.
Apply mathematical modelling techniques to analyse the behaviour and performance of electrical machines under different operating conditions.
Discuss control techniques to regulate and optimize the operation of electrical machines, including speed control methods and power factor correction strategies.

title: Electricity and Waves
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject gives a thorough exploration into the fundamental areas of static and dynamic electricity, electromagnetism, wave motion as well as geometric and physical optics, forming a crucial component of calculus-based physics education. It delves into the fundamental principles that govern these fields, strengthening theoretical knowledge with a strong emphasis on practical experimentation. An integral part of this course is the inclusion of laboratory work, which serves multiple purposes in the physics education of students. The practical component allows students to translate abstract theoretical concepts into observable phenomena. It also develops critical thinking skills as they analyze experimental data and draw evidence-based conclusions. The practice of writing detailed laboratory reports enhances their communication skills, requiring them to articulate their findings in a clear, concise manner. This collaborative learning environment also encourages peer-to-peer communication, further refining students interpersonal skills.
learning_outcomes: Conduct experiments which demonstrate some of the concepts developed during the study.
Understand the physical phenomena of wave motion.
Understand the concept of capacitance and the manner in which it is utilised for the storage of energy.
Understand the concepts of geometrical optics and apply them to simple optical instruments.
Have a basic understanding of the manner in which charged bodies behave in an electric field.
Present experimental results in an acceptable manner, indicating the likely sources and magnitudes of any errors involved.
Understand the nature of the direct electric current and how it is affected by various circuit components.

title: Emergency Decision Making
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will analyse the decision making processes used by emergency management professionals in managing emergency situations. Through the exercise of reflective practice, students will be further equipped in their approach to critical decision making as emergency management practitioners dealing with the prevention, preparedness, response and recovery aspects of emergency management.
learning_outcomes: Explain the various models of decision making, concentrating on those applicable to time critical, emergency situations.
Identify factors that hinder or help decision making under stress.
Describe the theory and concepts of decision making.
Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts of decision making within the context of managing emergency situations.

title: Electronic Commerce

school: School of Business

These systems are useful business tools which enable an organisation to record, summarise and report events arising from interactions with its environment including customers and suppliers. In addition, this subject examines the legal, ethical, security, social and global implications of eCommerce. No prior knowledge of computers is required to successfully complete this subject.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate problems posed by utilising electronic commerce, including security, legal jurisdictions and effectiveness.
Analyse technology needs in specific situations and develop customer-focused plans and correspondence.
Identify the effects of technology on business results and measure the contribution of technology to firm performance.
Discuss electronic commerce planning processes and the managerial and organisational contingencies affecting the relationship between technology and the organisation.
Evaluate applications of electronic commerce in organisations and analyse the barriers to successful implementation of these technologies.

title: Emergency Management Plan Development
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the skills and knowledge to develop an emergency management plan for a community/enterprise. This will include an examination and application of the emergency management planning process, the specification of emergency management needs for a community/ enterprise, resource availability, needs ratification, emergency management organisational design, the selection of emergency management strategies and planning implementation.
learning_outcomes: Work with communities/enterprises to develop emergency management plans in response to risk assessment and vulnerability analysis.
Critically analyse and reflect on own professional performance.
Select, explain, and apply the techniques and strategies of risk management in emergency management planning.
Analyse contemporary emergency plans in order to maintain and improve practice.
Develop recovery strategies to address areas of risk and vulnerability.

title: Emerging Issues and Professional Practices in Trans-national Crime Investigations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The subject analyses the theory of transnational crime, the emerging trends and practices of transnational crime investigations in addition to the policing of these types of global crimes. This study focuses upon the existing forms of (complex and sophisticated) criminal activity such as drug trafficking, human trafficking, illegal arms trade and financial crime and also examines emerging forms of criminality such as environmental crime, trafficking of cultural property, piracy and organ trafficking. Students will explore local education programmes along with the dynamics of operational, strategic and tactical demands for enforcement response and political and social influences.
learning_outcomes: Have an advanced level of knowledge and understanding of the emerging trends within transnational crime in association with globalisation.
Understand and critically analyse recent developments within the criminological theory of transnational crime.
Critically analyse the emerging practices of transnational organised crime groups and investigative responses.
Critically analyse and reflect upon the growth of collaboration strategies between global enforcement agencies and other organisations in the fight against transnational crime.
Demonstrate a mastery and critical understanding of the theoretical, legal and regulatory approaches to transnational crime.

title: Emergent Professional
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject students undertake self-directed study towards the generation of an individual value proposition, future work or study plan and consolidated professional portfolio. Students are required to explore and critique their current research and professional interests and consider how as emergent professionals they can maximise their individual impact in existing, emergent, future or speculative professions. Students will have developed a network of industry and/or academic contacts relevant to their individual aspirations and have constructed, under supervision/guidance, a plan for their future.
learning_outcomes: Have developed an evidenced network of industry and/or academic contacts relevant to their individual professional aspirations.
Independently identify and critique the political, cultural, economic and environmental factors currently affecting their discipline/s.
Critically evaluate and speculate on the future of their discipline/s.
Identify and justify their current research and creative/professional practice within existing, emergent, future or speculative professions.
Construct, describe and illustrate an individual value proposition and future work or study plan.

title: Emerging Practitioner
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject requires students to be able to reflect on all course learnings and to integrate those reflections into their approach to professional practice and pursuit of life-long learning. Students will review the e-portfolio developed throughout the course and reflect on their progress in developing the competencies of a professional communicator. Students reflect on the graduate learning outcomes they take into professional practice as they conclude their studies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate evidence of a network of industry and/or academic contacts relevant to professional aspirations.
Develop a professional portfolio that includes an e-portfolio and professional CV.
Evaluate and discuss pertinent professional issues.
Reflect on all course learnings as they enter professional practice.

title: Emerging Technologies and Innovation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject requires research and project work, at an advanced level, on a topic related to emerging technologies and innovation. In the context of professional practice, students will draw upon prior learning in their Masters course to execute an independent capstone project in a selected topic related to their course and specialisation(s) within their course (where applicable).
learning_outcomes: Apply project management and information and communication technologies (ICT) tools to plan, execute, record and present their research and project work as a capstone experience.
Critically reflect on and synthesize complex information, problems, concepts and theories in the chosen topic.
Apply established research methodologies with autonomy.
Justify to an audience of peers any conclusions and professional decisions made that contribute to creating new knowledge.
Interpret and evaluate an overview of recent trends in emerging technologies and innovation.
Demonstrate advanced communication skills in transmitting their capstone experiences and ideas.
Perform literature searches and critically analyse the literature in the chosen topic.

title: Emerging Technologies for Operational Efficiency
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject empowers industry leaders to operate with efficiency by optimising for resilience, scale, and agility. It introduces students to change engineering in the context of emerging technologies, providing a comprehensive overview of theoretical frameworks and practical methodologies for orchestrating transformative changes within organisations and business processes. The subject imparts the necessary knowledge and skills to effectively manage the changes that emerging technologies bring to modern businesses and society. Students will learn about the principles and practices of change engineering, the challenges and risks associated with emerging technologies, and the analytics skills and strategies needed to successfully navigate technological disruptions. Real-world case studies will be used to illustrate these concepts and provide practical insights.
learning_outcomes: Understand and interpret change impact analytics outcomes, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.
Identify and critically evaluate competing strategies to effectively manage technological changes for business decision making.
Design transformative change orchestration processes for effective adoption of emerging technologies with minimal risk.
Utilise and discuss fundamental concepts and principles in change engineering for emerging technologies.

title: Employability and Professional Practice 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject is designed to develop students' employability skills and their understanding of professional practice, including the job application process. The subject is also aimed at developing students' self-reflection and self-monitoring skills; skills which are utilised to develop a career action plan and to help build efficacy and confidence in the workplace. The subject provides students with an opportunity to build upon the skills, knowledge and personal insights gained from BUS114 Contemporary Employability and Learning.
learning_outcomes: Explore and enhance personal brand development through academic application and self-development.
Prepare an effective job application.
Define, evaluate, and reflect on employability skills and graduate attributes.
Assess and learn through reflective practice.
Explore, develop and evaluate a career action plan.

title: Employability Skills
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to enhance students' understanding of the common skills that all ICT professionals must possess as specified by the Australian Computer Society in their Core Body of Knowledge (ACS CBOK). Students will develop an understanding of core CBOK knowledge areas. This includes problem solving skills, teamwork, ethics, professionalism and interpersonal communication. The knowledge and skills gained from this subject will help students to launch a successful career post-graduation.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate job search strategies and methods to identify appropriate IT job opportunities.
Evaluate and interpret Australian workplace legislation, including Workplace Health and Safety regulations.
Identify and articulate the knowledge and skills required for successful IT professionals.
Synthesise the knowledge gained from academic learning in readiness for application in the workplace.
Analyse complex information to devise solutions to a range of problems within the IT workplace.

title: Employability and Professional Practice 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on ‘people at work' through the development and application of a personal reflection on diversity, tolerance and forms of bias; Australian Indigenous Cultural Competency; and the development of cultural competence in general. The Indigenous Australian content in this subject builds on students' completion of IKC101 and considers Australian Indigenous perspectives and contributions to workplace and business practices. Students will also develop their language and communication skills, in the context of diversity in the workplace, and reflect on the learnings from this subject. This subject expands upon the skills, knowledge and personal insights gained from BUS114 Contemporary Employability and Learning and BUS224 Employability and Professional Practice 1.
learning_outcomes: Present an integrated view of the various disciplines of business: to understand how a multi-disciplinary perspective can be used to address issues relevant to Australian Indigenous communities.
Evaluate and reflect on personal and professional development.
Use appropriate language and communication strategies to inform the resolution of workplace challenges related to cultures or diversity.
Demonstrate an understanding of Australian Indigenous perspectives and contributions to workplace and business practices.

Use self and professional critical reflexivity to develop discipline specific and culturally appropriate skills for working effectively with Indigenous Australian and a range of diverse colleagues, clients, businesses, persons and/or communities.
Reflect on and question personal values and ethics in developing a social justice lens, and in relation to areas such as tolerance, forms of bias, diversity and power.

title: Electrical Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principles and applications of electricity and electrical power systems. Emphasis is placed on understanding electrical systems, analysing circuits, and applying electrical principles to engineering problems.
learning_outcomes: Solve simple electrical circuits using circuit analysis techniques.
Apply electrical principles to analyse and design basic electrical systems.
Describe the fundamentals of electromagnetism and its engineering applications.
Explain power generation, transmission, and distribution systems.
Explain basic electrical machines and their operation.

title: Enabling Strategies: Contemporary & Emerging Occupational Therapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject will enable students to expand their theoretical and practical knowledge of the scope of occupational therapy practice. Students will critique five contemporary and/or emerging areas of occupational therapy practice, relevant to working with individuals, families, groups, communities, and/or populations. Students will extend their professional reasoning skills to collaboratively develop, apply, evaluate and reflect on occupational therapy interventions for a range of practice areas. They will develop skills in the presentation and dissemination of the information and evidence that underpins professional decision-making. This subject provides students with the opportunity to demonstrate a professional level of proficiency for practice, and an understanding of the need to be responsive to changes within practice contexts and the profession.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise the scope of occupational therapy practice including contemporary and emerging practice areas for individuals, families, groups, communities and/or populations.
Critically appraise, integrate and apply knowledge, skills and attitudes to effectively communicate occupational therapy concepts and demonstrate proficiency for entry-level practice.
Consistently demonstrate a collaborative, culturally responsive and inclusive approach to occupational therapy practice.
Apply, analyse and reflect on evidence-based practice and professional reasoning skills to meet the needs and the contexts of individuals, families, groups, communities and/or populations.

title: Enabling Strategies: Contemporary and Emerging Occupational Therapy Practice (Honours)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject will enable Honours students to expand their theoretical and practical knowledge of the scope of occupational therapy practice. Students will critique three contemporary and/or emerging areas of occupational therapy practice, relevant to working with individuals, families, groups, communities, and/or populations. Students will extend their professional reasoning skills to collaboratively develop, apply, evaluate and reflect on occupational therapy interventions for a range of practice areas. They will develop skills in the presentation and dissemination of the information and evidence that underpins professional decision-making. This subject provides students with the opportunity to demonstrate a professional level of proficiency for practice, and an understanding of the need to be responsive to changes within practice contexts and the profession.
learning_outcomes: Consistently demonstrate a collaborative, culturally responsive and inclusive approach to occupational therapy practice.
Apply, analyse and reflect on evidence-based practice and professional reasoning skills to meet the needs and the contexts of individuals, families, groups, communities and/or populations.
Critically appraise the scope of occupational therapy practice including contemporary and emerging practice areas for individuals, families, groups, communities and/or populations.
Critically appraise, integrate and apply knowledge, skills and attitudes to effectively communicate occupational therapy concepts and demonstrate proficiency for entry-level practice.

title: Enabling Strategies: Facilitating Therapeutic Groups
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students' knowledge of occupational therapy theory and practice to develop knowledge and skills in group therapy programs for a range of client groups (for example children, families, older adults) and purposes (for example therapy, education). Students will develop skills in designing and facilitating effective occupation-based groups by applying knowledge and design principles based on relevant theories such as occupational therapy theory and group theory. Students will experience working as a collaborative team member and will have opportunities to practice managing group dynamics and group facilitation skills, and to further develop their communication skills and strategies as a way to engage people in occupations in a group setting.
learning_outcomes: Understand and justify the purpose/s of occupation-based group therapy programs for a range of clients and outcomes.
Facilitate an occupation-based group by applying knowledge developed through the practice, observation and self-reflection on group-based therapy programs.
Apply therapeutic communication strategies to facilitate effective group development and cohesion, and to enable therapeutic outcomes.
Work collaboratively as an effective team member to plan and facilitate a group activity.

Apply professional reasoning and relevant evidence to justify and design an occupation-based group therapy program, including proposed facilitation strategies to be used, for a particular client group and outcome.
Design an occupation-based group therapy program through applying knowledge of group dynamics and health and wellness issues for a range of client groups.

title: Enabling Strategies: Working with Assistive Technologies
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to environmental assessment and assistive technology devices, strategies and processes, relevant to occupational therapy practice. Students will apply their knowledge of the person, environment and occupation, and analyse these interactions to inform assistive technology decision-making. Students will develop practical skills in the assessment of different environments and in the selection and use of a range of assistive technologies. This subject will extend students’ skills in professional written and verbal communication to work effectively with people and report relevant findings and recommendations.
learning_outcomes: Use a feature-matching process and investigate appropriate assistive technology options from a range of sources, to make suitable person-centred recommendations.
Describe the components of an effective assistive technology solution and articulate the role assistive technology has in enabling occupational participation.
Conduct environmental assessments, apply relevant Standards, and develop accurate technical drawings to convey the identified environment.
Effectively communicate the selection, use and implementation of a range of assistive technology for different purposes and audiences.
Identify person-environment-occupation interactions and articulate how this influences assistive technology recommendations to facilitate occupational performance.

title: Enabling Strategies: Working with Communities and Populations
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students’ understanding of the inter-relationship between social determinants and the health and wellbeing of people, communities, and populations. Students will explore the principles of health promotion and community development in the context of occupational therapy practice. Students will build on their knowledge of diversity within communities, Australian history and Indigenous Australian culture, in order to design programs for communities and/or populations that are meaningful and culturally responsive.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on cultural responsiveness and how this influences personal and professional decision-making.

Analyse a health promotion and/or a community based program for cultural responsiveness and identify if strategies used have been developed respectfully, and in partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Justify how design decisions for a community program reflect the principles of health promotion, community development, and cultural responsiveness.
Collaborate to design an occupation-based community program that applies the principles of health promotion, community development, and cultural responsiveness.

Analyse and evaluate a contemporary community health, population, and/or social issue, and synthesise connections between the issue and the social determinants of health to prepare and present a researched argument.

title: Enabling Strategies: Working with Individuals (Consolidation)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends first and second-year concepts to consolidate the occupational therapy process when working with individuals across the lifespan. Students will apply theoretical models and utilise research skills to identify relevant enabling strategies (interventions) to use when working with people experiencing a range of physical, neurological and psychosocial conditions. They will integrate and critique evidence to inform professional decision-making. Students will further their understanding of occupation and recognise the importance of utilising meaningful occupations to enable participation. They will use occupation-focused enabling strategies (interventions) to promote the health and wellbeing of people at different life stages, and consider the impact of social, cultural and practice contexts. Throughout the subject, students will articulate their decision-making in assessment, intervention, service delivery, and outcome measurement, and communicate this effectively with various audiences.
learning_outcomes: Apply the occupational therapy process to work with people across the lifespan with a range of health conditions.
Demonstrate a person-centred approach and dynamic, flexible problem solving skills.
Articulate decision-making informed by theory and evidence.
Consolidate professional written and verbal communication skills and demonstrate the ability to adapt these for different audiences.
Demonstrate, using an occupation-focused approach, how to enable people to engage in life activities.
Adjust for service-delivery contexts and integrate culturally responsive and respectful strategies for engaging people from diverse backgrounds in all stages of the occupational therapy process.
Research, justify and implement contemporary occupational therapy enabling strategies/interventions relevant to a range of people and practice settings.
Demonstrate internal strategies to examine and monitor personal responses to cultural and social differences.
Demonstrate effective self-management skills and professional behaviours when working individually and/or as part of a team.
prerequisites: OCC206: Enabling strategies: Working with Individuals (Fundamentals)

title: Enabling strategies: Working with Individuals (Fundamentals)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to guide students through the application of the occupational therapy process, when working with individuals. This subject will enable students to apply principles of evidence-based practice and further develop skills in professional reasoning, to inform person-centred, occupation-focused intervention plans. Students will integrate knowledge and understanding of occupational therapy practice for people from diverse backgrounds and contexts. Occupational therapy models, practice theory, frames of reference, and research evidence will be used to inform and support students’ application of the occupational therapy process and to articulate their professional reasoning.
learning_outcomes: Access and appraise relevant evidence to generate evidence-informed hypotheses to describe the impact health conditions may have on occupational participation.
Access, appraise and apply contemporary theory and evidence to develop occupation-focused strategies/interventions to enable the occupational participation of individuals.
Interpret and apply findings from assessments and observations to develop person-centred, occupation-based interventions to facilitate occupational participation.
Demonstrate a person-centred, culturally responsive, and respectful approach to occupational therapy practice.
Apply and justify a professional decision-making process for working with a diverse range of individual clients and contexts.
Demonstrate professional responsibility through engaging in self-reflection, and responding to feedback.

title: Endodontics
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be given an introduction and opportunity to develop their knowledge and skills in the management of simple dental endodontics, incorporating diagnosis, treatment planning and post-operative follow up. The subject will emphasise an evidence-based approach to the management of the patient's endodontic requirement in the context of their overall dental and systemic health. Using a mastery learning approach, students will develop the clinical skills and manual dexterity required to deliver endodontic treatment. The treatment includes patient assessment, differential diagnosis, treatment planning and provision primarily of non-surgical endodontic treatment using contemporary technology.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate mastery of the clinical skills required to deliver simple endodontic treatment.
Apply a patient-centred approach to endodontic care by integrating the patient’s overall health status, values, and needs into endodontic treatment planning and clinical decision-making.

Apply knowledge and skills to perform all stages of root canal therapy safely and effectively on permanent teeth in a simulated clinical setting, adhering to health, safety, and infection control protocols, and prioritising patient-centred decision making.

Explain and analyse the principles related to the management of a patient related to simple endodontic treatment from diagnosis to treatment planning with an evidence-based approach to the management of the patient's endodontic requirement in the context of their overall dental and systemic health.
prerequisites: DOH233: Pathological Basis of Human Disease

title: Engaging Audiences and Social Media Communities
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores how to identify, connect and build relationships in a professional communication context. Students will explore a range of specific strategies to understand the importance of audiences needs and behaviours in developing communication for impact in a digital age. This subject is one of four introductory subjects that build the theoretical and discipline specific skills essential for communication professionals.
learning_outcomes: Research and develop strategies for optimal user engagement.
Identify and explain target audiences, demographics, and related datasets.
Plan an audience engagement activity for a real-world context.
Develop a communication response to an audience problem/issue.
Analyse the relationships between audience engagement and social connection.
Evaluate and reflect on approaches to audience engagement on and off line.

title: Engineering Capstone Thesis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: The cadet engineer will conduct research on a current problem/issue relevant to the engineering industry and report results in a dissertation. Cadets must demonstrate advanced theoretical, professional and methodological knowledge and the work must demonstrate an original contribution to professional practice, policy or knowledge. Cadet engineers must justify and get prior approval for the topic for their thesis and they will present their findings formally to CSU Engineering and their peers in an oral conference format, where they may anticipate a careful examination of their work and be expected to display a thorough knowledge of their thesis.
learning_outcomes: Identify and act on areas for improvement in civil engineering, initiate to develop innovative solutions and evaluate and report their potentials.

Use and manage information in a professional and ethical manner, and discern, analyse and appraise raw information, and draw appropriate conclusions in context with due consideration of the knowledge, methods, and assumptions within the engineering discipline.

Critique and use specialist bodies of knowledge within the engineering discipline and demonstrate the capacity to independently generate new knowledge in the context of existing literature and new developments in engineering.
Apply knowledge of systems thinking methodologies and engagement as a platform for creative, sustainable and socially responsible research and engineering practices.
Plan and execute original research in accordance with established research methodologies based upon the theory underpinning the engineering discipline.

Reflectively apply communication and technical research skills to justify, critique and interpret theoretical propositions, methodologies, conclusions and professional decisions to specialist and non- specialist audiences.
prerequisites: ENG471: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Cadet Engineer
ENG473: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Senior Cadet Engineer

title: End of Life and Palliative Care Issues in Ageing
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the complex bio/psycho/social/ethical/legal and political aspects of end of life care of older people and contemporary issues facing health professionals in this field. A diversity of social and cultural interpretations of death and dying will inform study of palliative care models within community, hospital and residential settings. Topics will include experiences of diagnosis of a terminal illness, person-centred care in palliation, communication about death and dying, working with families, professional self-care, duty of care and professional ethics. The subject also offers a specific focus on palliation in dementia care.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique contemporary models of palliative care applicable to different practice settings.
Apply person-centred care principles in end of life care.
Describe and explain complex palliative care and end of life issues for older people within a social framework.
Interpret and apply ethics to practice in end of life care.
Explore and articulate their own personal, spiritual and cultural values on death and dying, and evaluate the influence of their beliefs and values on practice.

title: Engineering Capstone Thesis 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: The Engineering Capstone Thesis comprises two integral components geared towards nurturing a comprehensive skill set in research, analysis, and communication within the engineering discipline. This first subject initiates with a preliminary research phase. Here, students immerse themselves in existing scholarship to pinpoint a pertinent research problem or question within their chosen engineering field, ideally aligning with their work placement. As the outcome of this phase, students develop a promising research proposal. This approved proposal serves as the launchpad for the second component of the Engineering Capstone Thesis.
learning_outcomes: Engage with basic concepts of systems thinking and its application in engineering contexts, fostering an initial appreciation for holistic problem-solving approaches.

Synthesise and critically evaluate fundamental theories, principles and methods, and current knowledge development and research directions within the specialised engineering discipline, laying the groundwork for independent exploration and knowledge generation by identifying gaps, contradictions, and opportunities for further exploration or innovation. knowledge development, research directions.

Develop foundational skills in research design and methodology, including review of literature and current practices, data collection, and analysis techniques, to plan an original entry-level research project in a specialised field of engineering.
Cultivate effective communication skills for conveying technical information to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, emphasising clarity, coherence, and relevance.

title: Engineering Capstone Thesis 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In the second part of the Engineering Capstone Thesis, students translate their approved research proposal into practice. Utilising credible methodologies and techniques, they address the identified problem or question. This phase involves activities such as data collection, analysis, and interpretation, culminating in the development of innovative insights or solutions within the civil engineering domain. The results of their research are manifested in written formats such as theses or journal manuscripts, as well as oral presentations. Throughout both segments of the thesis, students receive continual support and feedback from their supervisor, fostering a collaborative and iterative approach to scholarly inquiry and research.
learning_outcomes: Lead interdisciplinary collaborations and communicate research findings effectively to stakeholders, demonstrating leadership, professionalism, and ethical responsibility in engineering practice.

Synthesise and critically evaluate specialised bodies of knowledge, knowledge development, research directions and evolving methods related to the identified engineering problem to deliver innovative findings and solutions.
Deliver an original entry-level research project in a specialised field of engineering.
Apply advanced systems thinking methodologies to analyse and optimise complex engineering systems for enhanced performance, sustainability, and societal impact.

Demonstrate proficiency in advanced research methodologies, such as experimental design, modeling, and simulation, to address a complex engineering challenge and contribute to cutting-edge developments.

title: Engineering Capstone Thesis – Part A
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to prepare students for their capstone thesis project in their chosen engineering discipline. Through a combination of seminars, and individualised guidance, students will develop the necessary skills and knowledge to formulate a research question, conduct a literature review, and design a feasible research plan for their capstone project.
learning_outcomes: Develop a comprehensive research proposal outlining the methodology, timeline, and resources required for the capstone project.
Explain the research process and methodologies relevant to engineering.
Interpret and critically analyse relevant literature in the chosen engineering field.
Demonstrate critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for engineering research.
Formulate a well-defined research question and objectives for the capstone thesis.

title: Engineering Capstone Thesis – Part B
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: The Engineering Capstone Thesis Part B builds upon the knowledge developed in Part A, enabling students to execute their research plan, collect data, analyse findings, and present their capstone thesis.
learning_outcomes: Develop appropriate data analysis techniques.
Interpret findings and draw conclusions based on evidence.
Communicate research findings effectively through a written thesis and oral presentation.
Formulate experiments, simulations, or other research methods.
Execute a research plan and collect relevant data.
prerequisites: ENG410: Engineering Capstone Thesis – Part A

title: Engineering Challenge 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject draws upon the Engineers Without Borders annual challenge to provide teams of student engineers the opportunity to solve real world problems with human dimensions. Student engineers work in teams to respond to the Engineers Without Borders challenge, and will then have to communicate their achievements to both engineers and non-engineers. The development of technical, teamwork and communication skills are supported as student engineers begin to develop the Charles Sturt Engineering mindset.
learning_outcomes: Implement and evaluate planning processes and employ project management skills to solve an engineering problem.
Apply the principles of sustainable design in a development context.
Reflect on the strengths and weaknesses of the team approach to problem solving in order to enhance teamwork.
Articulate and incorporate considerations of the ethical, social, cultural, global and environmental responsibilities of the professional engineer in solving an engineering problem.
Communicate achievements to engineering and non-engineering audiences.
Apply a systems thinking approach to an engineering problem, and utilise the human-centred design process.
Identify information needs and locate, select, use and reference information from a variety of sources to effectively inform design process.

title: Engineering Challenge 0
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: The Charles Sturt Engineering course is structured very differently to other engineering programs. This subject introduces commencing student engineers to the Charles Sturt Engineering structure and philosophy. By focusing immediately and fully on a single project that exemplifies the principles of Charles Sturt Engineering, the incoming students are familiarised with the culture and expectations of Charles Sturt Engineering, while also taking the opportunity to establish their relationships with other student engineers.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and describe the Charles Sturt Engineering course, and the way in which the degree differs from traditional engineering degree programs.
Create a social connection as preparation for working together effectively in a team.
Work collaboratively to creatively solve a well-defined engineering challenge.

title: Engineering Challenge 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will continue to develop the student engineers' professional identities and capabilities from ENG161, while drawing upon the technical skills developed via the topic tree. Student engineers will work in teams to tackle a session-long engineering challenge in the civil context with social, environmental, economic and human dimensions. In particular, this challenge will focus student engineers' efforts on the norms of engineering practice, the management of engineering projects, the feasibility of their solutions, the engagement with people outside of their design team, and the communication of their ideas and designs to both technical and non-technical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Plan solutions to engineering problems that incorporate understanding of the interrelationships between social, environmental, economic, human and technical factors and apply appropriate methodologies throughout the design process to produce a creative and sustainable engineering design.
Produce technically feasible solutions to real world engineering problems through the application of mathematics and numerical analysis.
Conduct background research on applicable engineering content and synthesise the knowledge to apply to the design project.
Objectively reflect upon one's work, the work of others and the management of the project.
Present technical information in a professional manner, in written, verbal, numerical and graphical formats, both synchronously and asynchronously.
Demonstrate initiative, accountability and effective communication as members of an engineering team.

Demonstrate understanding of the scope and professional accountabilities of civil engineering practice on the design project and integrate the norms of practice into the conduct and management of the project.

title: Engineering Challenge 3
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will further develop the student engineers' identity through a team-based session-long practical project. Student engineers will deliver workable engineering solutions to real world problems sourced from community clients. Student engineers are to apply engineering fundamental principles, methods and tools when formulating the solutions. Skills in, but not limited to, the following aspects will be further enhanced beyond what has been introduced in ENG160, ENG161 and ENG162: project management, designing, researching, implementing, teamwork, communication, and offering and receiving feedback. This subject offers student engineers opportunities to practice and reflect upon their practice as engineers, both individually and in groups. This subject serves as a bridging pathway for student engineers to embark on their first work placements.
learning_outcomes: Apply underpinning sciences and engineering fundamentals to systematically devise a workable solution to a real-world engineering problem, considering social, economic and environmental sustainability.
Articulate and follow systematic engineering design processes.
Develop and reflect on their emerging identity as student engineers, and how this will change as they move into placement in industry.
Offer constructive feedback to peers, incorporate comments from peers/mentors and justify their acceptance and rejection.
Identify the hallmarks of high performance teams and the necessity for varieties of roles, and identify strengths and opportunities for improvement in a team environment.
Research, assess and synthesise information from a range of engineering resources, use appropriate artifacts within the engineering discipline to communicate with and engage different audiences.

title: Engineering Challenge 4
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop students’ engineering design skills to an advanced stage through a team-based session-long practical engineering design project. Students will identify their strengths and weaknesses based on experience so far in their degree, then work on a project aimed to develop their expertise in areas underdeveloped so far in their engineering education. Student engineers will deliver workable engineering solutions, competently applying engineering fundamental principles, methods, and tools to design suitable solutions to a complex engineering problem. This subject offers student engineers opportunities to practice and reflect upon their practice as engineers, both individually and in groups, and serves as a capstone design project to further develop their essential design skills.
learning_outcomes: Reflect objectively upon one's work, the work of others and the management of the project.
Develop and maintain collaborative, accountable and collegial relationships within the engineering team and external parties.
Present complex technical information in a clear and professional manner, suited to the technical and non-technical audiences.

Apply underpinning sciences and engineering fundamentals to systematically devise a workable solution to a complex engineering problem considering technical, social, economic factors, and environmental sustainability.
Devise, articulate, justify and follow systematic engineering design processes.

title: Engineering Challenge 5
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: Students entering the Master of Engineering (Civil Systems) program bring a range of experiences and expectations of engineering. In this subject we bring the cohort together, and introduce them to the CSU engineering mindset by working in teams to define, solve and report upon a term-long project.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively in teams to deliver a workable solution to an engineering problem.
Demonstrate an awareness of the broad range of document types encountered by engineers in their professional practice, and the distinctions between the different audiences they are targeted towards.
Apply a systems thinking approach to an engineering problem, and utilise the human-centred design process.
Create a social connection as preparation for working together effectively in a Team.
Articulate and incorporate considerations of the ethical, social, cultural, global and environmental responsibilities of the professional engineer in solving an engineering problem.
Identify the hallmarks of high performance teams and the variety of roles that team members play within them, as well as their own preferred roles in a team environment.

title: Engineering Challenge 5
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: Students entering the Master of Engineering (Civil Systems) program bring a range of experiences and expectations of engineering. In this subject we bring the cohort together, and introduce them to the Charles Sturt engineering mindset by working in teams to define, solve and report upon a term-long project.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the hallmarks of high performance teams and the variety of roles that team members play within them, as well as their own preferred roles in a team environment.
Utlilise a broad range of document types encountered by engineers in their professional practice targeting different audiences.
Work collaboratively in teams to deliver a workable solution to an engineering problem.
Apply a systems thinking approach to an engineering problem, and utilise the human-centred design process.
Incorporate considerations of the ethical, social, cultural, global and environmental responsibilities of the professional engineer in solving an engineering problem.

title: Engineering Construction
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the concepts and practices of construction systems and processes. It covers topics in construction activities, theory of production, planning and control for construction, materials procurement and handling, and recycling, waste and environmental issues and sustainable construction. Emphasis is on developing knowledge and skills needed for the collaborative delivery of construction projects.
learning_outcomes: Apply technical, managerial and collaborative skills, methods and tools required for construction activities.
Analyse management problems in construction that affect project performance.
Plan and implement construction projects.

title: Engineering Cornerstone Thesis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject 'Engineering Cornerstone Thesis' helps cadet engineers to enhance their civil engineering design skills by working in an engineering design team to solve a multidisciplinary, integrated, complex, civil engineering design project, identified in their intermediate work placement. Cadets must apply their theoretical and technical knowledge gained elsewhere in the curriculum and the workplace learning to the design. The outcomes should be delivered in both written (thesis) and oral (thesis defence) formats. Engineering cornerstone thesis will be jointly supervised by an academic engineer from CSU engineering and with a supervisor from their work placement, in addition to the subject coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate in-depth knowledge and understanding of engineering design practices, reflective applications and contextual factors impacting on multi-disciplinary engineering challenges and creative application of systematic engineering synthesis and design processes.

Define a complex engineering problem accurately and comprehensively in a workplace context and creatively apply systematic approaches to pro-active conduct and management of engineering projects as part of a team.
Formulate an appropriate method for investigating a complex civil engineering problem and correctly and innovatively apply established engineering methods and design processes to create a solution.

Communicate the problem definition, design processes and outcomes clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences and project a creative, innovative, entrepreneurial, and pro-active disposition.
Apply systems thinking and specialist engineering bodies of knowledge in sustainable and socially responsible engineering practice.

Use and manage information in a professional and ethical manner. Analyse raw information and draw appropriate conclusions in context with due consideration of the knowledge, methods, and assumptions within the engineering discipline.

title: Engineering Cornerstone Thesis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject helps cadet engineers to enhance their civil engineering design skills by working in an engineering design team to solve a multidisciplinary, integrated, complex, civil engineering design project, identified in their intermediate work placement. Cadets must apply their theoretical and technical knowledge gained elsewhere in the curriculum and the workplace learning to the design. The outcomes should be delivered in both written (thesis) and oral (thesis defence) formats.
