learning_outcomes: Use and manage information in a professional and ethical manner. Analyse raw information and draw appropriate conclusions in context with due consideration of the knowledge, methods, and assumptions within the engineering discipline.
Apply systems thinking and specialist engineering bodies of knowledge in sustainable and socially responsible engineering practice.

Define a complex engineering problem accurately and comprehensively in a workplace context and creatively apply systematic approaches to pro-active conduct and management of engineering projects as part of a team.

Demonstrate in-depth knowledge and understanding of engineering design practices, reflective applications and contextual factors impacting on multi-disciplinary engineering challenges and creative application of systematic engineering synthesis and design processes.
Formulate an appropriate method for investigating a complex civil engineering problem and correctly and innovatively apply established engineering methods and design processes to create a solution.

Communicate the problem definition, design processes and outcomes clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences and project a creative, innovative, entrepreneurial, and pro-active disposition.
prerequisites: ENG273: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Junior Cadet Engineer

title: Engineering Cornerstone Thesis 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This is the first of two subjects in which cadet engineers enhance their civil engineering design skills by working in an engineering design team to solve a multidisciplinary, integrated, complex, civil engineering design project, identified in their intermediate work placement. Part one of the Engineering Cornerstone Thesis entails scoping, research and planning their design strategy. Throughout both parts of the thesis, students receive guidance and feedback from their workplace and academic supervisors.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of specialised bodies of knowledge and established design practices within the engineering discipline.
Define and scope a complex engineering problem accurately and comprehensively in an industry context.
Creatively apply systematic engineering synthesis and design processes to formulate an appropriate design strategy for a complex civil engineering problem.
Communicate the problem definition and design strategy clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences.

title: Engineering Cornerstone Thesis 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In part two of the Engineering Cornerstone Thesis, students apply their theoretical and technical knowledge to execute their design strategy and deliver a multidisciplinary, integrated, complex, civil engineering design project in their intermediate work placement. Throughout both parts of the thesis, students receive guidance and feedback from their workplace and academic supervisors. The outcomes will be delivered in both written (thesis) and oral (thesis defence) formats.
learning_outcomes: Creatively apply systematic engineering synthesis and established engineering design processes and methods to correctly and innovatively carry out the design strategy and delivery a complex engineering project.
Apply systematic approaches to pro-actively conduct and manage the engineering project as part of a team.
Communicate the outcomes clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences.

Use and manage information in a professional and ethical manner. Analyse raw information and draw appropriate conclusions in context with due consideration of the knowledge, methods, and assumptions within the engineering discipline.

Demonstrate innovative application of specialist engineering bodies of knowledge knowledge and understanding of engineering design practices, reflective applications and contextual factors involved in and impacting on multi-disciplinary engineering challenges, including sustainability and socially responsibility.

title: Engineering Design Challenge 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject draws upon the Engineers Without Borders annual challenge to provide teams of student engineers the opportunity to solve real world problems with human dimensions. Student engineers work in teams to respond to the Engineers Without Borders challenge and will then have to communicate their achievements to both engineers and non-engineers.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate collaboration and teamwork skills in addressing the Engineering challenge and be able to reflect and discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the team approach to problem solving.
Implement and discuss planning processes to solve an engineering problem.
Apply systems thinking and utilise the human-centred design process.
Explain the ethical, social, cultural, global and environmental responsibilities of the professional engineer.
Apply the principles of sustainable design in a development context.
Explain achievements to engineering and non-engineering audiences.

title: Engineering Design Challenge 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This challenge will focus students' efforts on the norms of engineering practice, the management of engineering projects, the feasibility of their solutions, the engagement with people outside of their design team, and the communication of their ideas and designs to both technical and non-technical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Apply appropriate methodologies throughout the design process to produce a creative and sustainable engineering design.
Review one's work, the work of others and the management of the project.
Explain technical information in a professional manner, in written, verbal, numerical and graphical formats.
Describe technically feasible solutions to engineering problems through the application of mathematics, science and engineering fundamentals.
Demonstrate initiative, accountability and effective communication as members of an engineering team.

title: Engineering Design Challenge 3
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: Engineering Design Challenge 3 is a multidisciplinary subject that focuses on engineering design and problem-solving skills through collaborative, hands-on projects. Students from electrical, mechanical, and civil engineering disciplines will work together to tackle complex, real-world challenges. The subject emphasises the integration of knowledge from different engineering fields to develop innovative solutions, considering technical feasibility, cost, sustainability, and societal impact.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to integrate electrical, mechanical, and civil engineering principles to develop comprehensive solutions to complex engineering problems.
Produce clear, professional documentation and presentations that effectively communicate design processes, solutions, and results to a diverse audience.
Effectively manage project resources, timelines, and team dynamics to achieve project goals and deliverables within set deadlines.
Apply design methodologies and tools to create, test, and refine designs that address a project's requirements and constraints.

title: Engineering Materials
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces fundamental concepts in engineering materials, focusing on the properties, structure, processing, and applications of various materials used in engineering. The subject aims to provide students with a solid foundation in materials science and engineering principles applicable across different engineering disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the basic principles of materials science and engineering.
Identify material selection criteria and apply them to engineering design and applications.
Discuss common manufacturing processes and use material testing techniques.
Explain the relationship between material structure, processing, properties, and performance.
Identify and describe the properties and characteristics of different classes of engineering materials.

title: Engineering Mechanics - Dynamics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the principles of engineering dynamics, focusing on the analysis of the motion of particles and rigid bodies under the influence of forces and moments. Emphasis is placed on developing problem-solving skills and applying theoretical concepts to practical engineering problems.
learning_outcomes: Apply Newton's laws to solve problems involving the motion of particles.
Solve work, energy, impulse, and momentum principles in dynamic systems.
Apply rotational dynamics principles to analyse motion and forces in rotating bodies.
Solve the motion of particles and rigid bodies using kinematic and kinetic principles.
Explain the fundamental principles of engineering dynamics.

title: Engineering Mechanics - Statics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the principles and fundamental concepts of engineering statics, which form the basis for understanding the behaviour of stationary bodies under the action of forces. It emphasises the development of problem-solving skills and the application of static equilibrium principles to engineering systems.
learning_outcomes: Determine centroids and moments of inertia of geometric shapes.
Use principles of friction to analyse contact forces between surfaces.
Explain the fundamental principles of static equilibrium.
Use vector algebra and trigonometry to solve engineering statics problems.
Solve problems involving forces and moments acting on stationary bodies.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Advanced
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject students draw upon their experience in industry to demonstrate that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of a CSU Engineering graduate. Whilst ENG492 takes place in the context of a paid work placement, it does not meet the CSU definition of WPL. During their work placement students will continue the portfolio from ENG491. Progress in the portfolio will show that they are exhibiting the required graduate attributes at an advanced level. The subject assesses the experience and practice of students and the way in which this experience is presented to both technical and non-technical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Creatively and critically apply systematic engineering synthesis and design processes.
Critically apply established engineering methods to complex engineering problem solving.
Evaluate their accountability in the ethical delivery of engineering projects.
Use and manage information professionally and ethically.
Demonstrate effective oral and written communication in professional and lay domains.
Collaborate, share and co-create information with others to arrive at effective solutions to complex problems.
Describe how their work placement experiences have helped advance their identity as a CSU Engineer.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Consolidating
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students draw upon their experience in industry to demonstrate that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of a CSU engineering graduate. During their work placement, students are expected to advance their portfolio from ENG292, and show that they are exhibiting the required graduate attributes at a consolidating level; the level at which they are more certain and confident about their job responsibilities. The subject assesses the experience and practice of students and the way in which this is presented to both technical and nontechnical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of engineering synthesis and design processes and practices and contextual factors impacting on the engineering discipline.
Critically analyse the application of a range of engineering techniques, tools and resources in solving practical problems.
Communicate effectively to professional and lay domains through a range of different communication channels, such as technical report writings, oral presentations, engineering drawings, user manuals.
Evaluate how working as a reflective practitioner has improved their professional practice.
Demonstrate accountability for the ethical delivery of engineering projects.
Appropriately apply mathematics, numerical analysis, statistics, computer, and information sciences which underpin the engineering discipline.
prerequisites: ENG380: Performance Planning and Review - Intermediate Cadet

title: Engineering Portfolio - Developing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject students draw upon their experience in industry to demonstrate that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of a CSU engineering graduate. Whilst ENG292 takes place in the context of a paid workplacement, it does not meet the CSU definition of WPL. During their workplacement students need to prepare a refective, informative portfolio detailing their work experience and skills mastered. Progress in the portfolio will show that they are exhibiting the required graduate attributes at a developing level. This subject assesses the experience and practice of students and the way in which this is presented to both technical and non-technical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Apply established engineering methods to broadly-defined problem solving within the technology domain.
Display a conceptual understanding of the mathematics, numerical analysis, statistics, and computer and information sciences which underpin the technology domain.
Fluently apply a range of engineering tools to practical problems.
Demonstrate engineering design practices as applied in industry.
Demonstrate effective communication through a range of different communication channels, such as technical report writing, oral presentations, engineering drawings, user manuals.
Recognise information needs and locate, evaluate and use information effectively in a range of contexts, acknowledging the impact of that context upon the interpretation of that information.
Describe how their work placement experiences have helped develop their identity as a CSU Engineer.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Introductory
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject students draw upon their experience in industry to demonstrate that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of a CSU engineering graduate. Whilst ENG291 takes place in the context of a paid workplacement, it does not meet the CSU definition of WPL. During their workplacement students will be required to construct a professional online portfolio to provide evidence of their development. Progress in the portfolio will show that they are exhibiting the required graduate attributes at an introductory level. This subject is assessed by a portfolio of work and experiences representing their preparedness for engineering practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply standard engineering methods to well-defined engineering problems.
Describe and analyse workplace episodes in Professional Episode Reports.
Identify the ethical dimensions of a range of engineering problems.
Communicate how your work placement experiences have helped develop your identity as a CSU Engineer.
Demonstrate knowledge of the stages of the engineering design process.
Apply a range of engineering tools to practical problems.
Use critical reflection to justify the compilation of appropriate artefacts to demonstrate developing engineering competence.
Document professional skills obtained and improved in the workplace.
prerequisites: ENG180: Performance Planning and Review - Student Engineer

title: Engineering Portfolio - Junior Cadet
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, junior cadet engineers document their engineering learning and experiences gained in their first workplace or during their time on campus, to claim, demonstrate and justify that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of an engineering graduate. This is performed referring to a list of essential engineering skills and competencies, divided into categories, with an ultimate aim of achieve all these essential competencies by the completion of all Engineering Portfolio subjects. Accordingly, junior cadet engineers assess sample/exemplar competency claims using a rubric. Additionally they can peer review the work of other cadets and write their own claims of competency supported by evidence, based on the skills, experiences and knowledge they have gained during undergraduate studies. The competency claims will form an introductory professional engineering portfolio corresponding to the stated essential engineering skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate reflective practice by creating a portfolio of their work placement experiences and describing how these experiences have helped develop their engineering identity and practice.

Demonstrate effective communication of engineering works to professional colleagues and the broader community through a range of different communication channels, such as technical report writing, oral presentations, engineering drawings, and work orders.
Apply established engineering methods to defined problems.
Relate workplace projects to engineering design processes and practices in the context of the industry.
Display a conceptual understanding of the mathematical and physical sciences which underpin the engineering discipline.
Apply a range of engineering techniques, tools and resources to practical problems.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Junior Cadet 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, junior cadet engineers document their engineering learning and experiences gained in their first workplace or during their time on campus, to claim, demonstrate and justify that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of an engineering graduate.
learning_outcomes: Experiment with a range of basic engineering techniques, tools, and resources to tackle practical engineering tasks, fostering hands-on learning and skill development.
Explore the application of fundamental engineering methods to address well-defined problems, honing problem-solving skills and analytical reasoning.
Demonstrate a foundational understanding of advanced mathematical and physical science concepts relevant to the engineering discipline.
Analyse workplace projects within the framework of engineering design processes, discerning their alignment with industry standards and best practices.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Junior Cadet 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: Junior cadet engineers compile their engineering experiences from their workplace or campus activities to demonstrate their progression towards expected engineering competencies. They refer to a categorized list of essential engineering skills, aiming to fulfill them by completing all Engineering Portfolio subjects. Additionally, they evaluate sample competency claims, engage in peer reviews, and create their own competency claims supported by evidence from their undergraduate studies, forming an introductory professional engineering portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Utilise established methods and technologies to solve well defined problems in the engineering workplace.

Demonstrate effective communication of engineering works to professional colleagues and the broader community through a range of different communication channels, such as technical report writing, oral presentations, engineering drawings, and work orders.
Utilise established approaches in the conduct and management of engineering projects.
Apply mathematical and physical science principles to formulate innovative engineering solutions for complex, real-world challenges.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Professional
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will undergo a mock evaluation against the Engineers Australia Stage 2 competencies for chartered status. Drawing upon their experience and their portfolios they will be required to undertake the assessment process, assembling responses to the 16 criteria from their portfolios and undergoing the same interview process as professional engineers seeking CPEng recognition. This will serve as a reflective exercise for students to capture their achievements throughout the course, and to guide them for continuing professional development needs after graduation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate progress towards achieving CPEng recognition.
Practice ethically as a graduate engineer.
Reflect upon their practice as professional engineers and their preparedness to enter the profession as independent, autonomous professionals.
Manage a portfolio of evidence to enable them to effectively evidence their capabilities to a technical audience.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Senior Cadet
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, senior cadet engineers continue documenting their engineering learning and experiences gained in their previous and current workplaces, to claim, demonstrate and justify that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of an engineering graduate. Considering their existing introductory professional engineering portfolio, such demonstration is performed referring to a list of essential engineering skills and competencies, divided into categories, with an ultimate aim to achieve all those essential competencies by the completion of all Engineering Portfolio subjects. Accordingly, senior cadet engineers critique sample/exemplar competency claims or the work of other cadets and write their own claims of competency supported by evidence, based on the skills, experiences and knowledge they have gained at their previous and current workplaces. The competency claims will form an advanced professional engineering portfolio corresponding to the stated essential engineering skills.
learning_outcomes: Appropriately apply mathematics, numerical analysis, statistics, computer, and information sciences which underpin the engineering discipline.
Critically apply established engineering methods in complex engineering problem solving.
Critically analyse the application of a range of engineering techniques, tools and resources in solving practical problems.
Demonstrate and evaluate their accountability in the ethical delivery of engineering projects.
Creatively and critically apply systematic engineering synthesis and design processes and practices and appraise contextual factors impacting on the engineering discipline.
Demonstrate reflective practice by creating a portfolio of their work placement experiences and evaluating how these experiences have further developed their engineering identity and practice.
Professionally manage, compile, collaborate on, and co-create information to implement effective solutions to complex problems.
Appraise effective communication with professional colleagues and the broader community through a range of different communication channels.
prerequisites: ENG474: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Conversion Masters

title: Engineering Portfolio - Senior Cadet 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, senior cadet engineers build on their previous and current workplace experiences, documenting their engineering learning to demonstrate progression towards expected skills. They refer to a list of essential engineering competencies, aiming to achieve them by the completion of all Engineering Portfolio subjects. Through critiquing sample competency claims and reflecting on their own experiences, they create an advanced professional engineering portfolio aligned with these essential skills.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate the use of engineering synthesis and design processes, nurturing creativity and critical thinking skills while considering contextual factors influencing engineering practice.
Demonstrate knowledge of engineering methodologies and tools, enabling the critical application of established techniques to address engineering challenges effectively.
Utilise diverse engineering techniques and resources through practical applications, fostering an understanding of their relevance and limitations in solving real-world problems.
Apply mathematical, numerical, and statistical concepts to engineering problems, supporting effective realistic analysis and problem-solving.

title: Engineering Portfolio - Senior Cadet 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, senior cadet engineers continue documenting their engineering learning and experiences gained in their previous and current workplaces, to claim, demonstrate and justify that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of an engineering graduate, including completing engineering design projects.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate application of engineering synthesis and design processes in the workplace, with consideration of the contextual factors influencing engineering practice.
Demonstrate understanding of the scope, principles, norms and accountabilities of sustainable engineering practice in the context of engineering industry practice.
Professionally manage, compile, and co-create information to implement effective solutions to complex problems.

Demonstrate competent application of advanced mathematical, numerical, and computational techniques, enhancing capabilities in modelling, simulation, and analysis for tackling complex engineering problems.

Demonstrate adeptness in interdisciplinary communication and collaboration, effectively conveying complex engineering knowledge to diverse stakeholders to establish and maintain effective collaboration towards a shared outcome.

title: Engineering Project Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth understanding of the principles and practices involved in managing engineering projects. It covers project lifecycle management, resource allocation, risk management, and effective communication strategies. Students will learn to apply project management methodologies and tools to real-world engineering scenarios to ensure successful project delivery within scope, time, and budget constraints.
learning_outcomes: Understand and Apply Project Management Frameworks.
Develop and Implement Project Plans.
Manage Project Risks and Communication.

title: Engineering Residency 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: Engineering Residency 1 is designed to provide students with practical experience in real-world engineering settings while developing essential workplace skills and creating a professional design portfolio. Through a combination of industry placement, and portfolio development exercises, students will gain insight into engineering practice, enhance their technical skills, and prepare for future career opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Examine practical experience in engineering workplaces through industry placements.
Create a design portfolio showcasing skills, accomplishments, and reflections on workplace learning experiences.
Apply engineering principles and techniques to real-world projects and challenges.
Utilise professional communication and collaboration skills within multidisciplinary teams.
Apply critical thinking and problem-solving abilities in diverse engineering contexts.
prerequisites: ENG212: Workplace Performance Planning and Review
IKC101: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country

title: Engineering Residency 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: Engineering Residency 2 builds upon the foundational experiences and skills developed in Engineering Residency 1. This provides students with advanced opportunities for workplace learning, project execution, and portfolio refinement. Students will deepen their understanding of engineering practice, further develop their professional competencies, and enhance their design portfolios.
learning_outcomes: Critique practical experience and proficiency in engineering workplaces through advanced industry placements.
Test advanced engineering concepts and techniques to complex real-world projects.
Examine professional communication, teamwork, and leadership skills in diverse engineering environments.
Demonstrate critical thinking, problem-solving, and innovation in engineering design and execution.
Build a design portfolio to effectively communicate accomplishments, skills, and career aspirations.

title: Engineering Residency 3
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to immerse students in cutting-edge engineering practice and foster innovation in their work. Through an advanced industry placement, innovation projects, and interdisciplinary collaboration, students will deepen their technical expertise, refine their problem-solving skills, and cultivate an entrepreneurial mindset.
learning_outcomes: Judge emerging technologies and trends shaping the future of engineering practice.
Collaborate effectively within multidisciplinary teams to tackle complex engineering challenges.
Critically analyse engineering problems in industrial settings.
Appraise leadership skills and project management capabilities in engineering contexts.
Judge their proficiency in creativity, innovation, and entrepreneurial thinking in engineering design and problem-solving.

title: Engineering Residency 4
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on preparing students for leadership roles in engineering organisations and fostering lifelong professional growth and development. Through an industry placement, students will enhance their leadership capabilities, refine their professional skills, and position themselves for success in the engineering profession.
learning_outcomes: Adapt a strategic mindset and decision-making capabilities in engineering contexts.
Navigate ethical dilemmas and societal responsibilities as future engineering leaders.
Design avenues for continued professional growth and lifelong learning in engineering.
Develop leadership skills and competencies relevant to engineering practice.
Critique professional communication, negotiation, and interpersonal skills.

title: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop and consolidate their understanding of English content knowledge in the strands of language, literature and literacy with a focus on the early years of schooling (ages 4-8) in the context of the broader curriculum. They will consider the acquisition of reading and writing processes with an added focus on catering for the specific strengths and needs of individual students, including First Nations and English as an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D) learners. Students will examine models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, talking, viewing and representing in the early years, with a particular focus on the explicit and systematic teaching of reading and writing. They will develop their knowledge of the ways digital technologies impact literacy practices in the early years. Students will also develop skills in the analysis of young children's literacy (reading and writing) work samples to determine students' strengths and needs and identify teaching priorities related to relevant curriculum documents.
learning_outcomes: Analyse young children's assessment data and literacy work samples to determine teaching priorities that address the needs of diverse learners.
Accurately describe the reading and writing processes at acquisition and the early stages of development, and explain the ways different theoretical models impact the teaching of reading and writing.
Articulate how digital technologies impact literacy practices and develop ability to use digital technology for teaching purposes.

Accurately assess students against the outcomes in the NSW English syllabus and the Australian Curriculum for English in years K-2 and plan meaningful and accessible instruction so all students can work towards the outcomes in this stage.

Design teaching experiences based on in-depth knowledge of how young children develop as speakers, listeners, readers and writers, viewers and creators, and be able to describe a diverse range of literacy capabilities for K-2 students.

Select appropriate models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, speaking, viewing and representing in the early years, including the ability to develop literacy teaching that is culturally and linguistically appropriate for EAL/D learners and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander learners.
prerequisites: ESL201: Literacy Studies in the Primary School
EML210: Primary English Curriculum: Reading Process and Pedagogy
EML433: Primary English Curriculum: Reading, Process and Pedagogy
ESL102: Foundations in Literacy Studies K-2
EML322: Literacy Studies in the Primary School : 2
EPT127: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning
EPT455: English Curriculum: Understanding Language and Literacy
EML453: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning.

They will consider the acquisition of reading and writing processes with an added focus on catering for the specific needs of individuals and examine models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, talking, viewing and representing in the early years, with a particular focus on the explicit and systematic teaching of reading and writing. Students will develop their knowledge of the ways digital technologies impact literacy practices in the early years. Students will also develop skills in the analysis of young children's literacy (reading and writing) work samples to determine students' strengths and needs and identify teaching priorities related to relevant curriculum documents.
learning_outcomes: Explain how young children develop as speakers, listeners, readers and writers, viewers and creators.
Analyse young children's assessment data and literacy work samples to determine teaching priorities that address the needs of diverse learners.
Examine the reading and writing processes at acquisition and the early stages of development including the specific needs of diverse individuals.
Articulate how digital technologies impact literacy practices.
Examine and apply the English syllabus content knowledge in the strands of language, literature and literacy with a specific focus on the early years (ages 4-8/K-2).
Select and evaluate models of pedagogy for teaching the modes of English in the early years with a particular focus on the explicit and systematic teaching of reading and writing.
prerequisites: EML210: Primary English Curriculum: Reading Process and Pedagogy
EML433: Primary English Curriculum: Reading, Process and Pedagogy
EML222: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning
EML322: Literacy Studies in the Primary School : 2
ESL201: Literacy Studies in the Primary School
ESL102: Foundations in Literacy Studies K-2

title: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning.
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop and consolidate their understanding of English content knowledge in the strands of language, literature and literacy with a focus on the early years of schooling (ages 4-8) in the context of the broader curriculum. They will consider the acquisition of reading and writing processes with an added focus on catering for the specific strengths and needs of individual students, including First Nations Australian learners and English as an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D) learners. Students will examine models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, talking, viewing and representing in the early years, with a particular focus on the explicit and systematic teaching of reading and writing. They will develop their knowledge of the ways digital technologies impact literacy practices in the early years. Students will also develop skills in the analysis of young children's literacy (reading and writing) work samples to determine students' strengths and needs and identify teaching priorities related to relevant curriculum documents.
learning_outcomes: Develop, use and interpret a variety of appropriate assessments to better understand diverse learner capabilities and inform appropriate evidence based approaches, including instruction for all students in K-2 literacy classrooms.
Critically evaluate how digital technologies impact literacy practices and construct ways to use digital technology for teaching purposes.

Accurately assess students against the outcomes in the NSW English syllabus and the Australian Curriculum for English in years K-2 and use assessment data to plan meaningful and accessible instruction so all students can work towards the outcomes in this stage.
Justify teaching approaches based on in-depth knowledge of the different ways young children develop as speakers, listeners, readers and writers, viewers and creators.
Clearly explain the reading and writing processes at acquisition and the early stages of development, to evaluate the appropriateness of different theoretical and pedagogical models.
Develop opportunities for literacy learning that are culturally and linguistically appropriate for EAL/D learners and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders.
prerequisites: EML449: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice
EML210: Primary English Curriculum: Reading Process and Pedagogy
ESL102: Foundations in Literacy Studies K-2
ESL201: Literacy Studies in the Primary School
EPT127: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning
EML433: Primary English Curriculum: Reading, Process and Pedagogy
EML322: Literacy Studies in the Primary School : 2
EPT455: English Curriculum: Understanding Language and Literacy

title: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Primary Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops and consolidates students' understanding of English content knowledge in the strands of language, literature and literacy with a focus on the primary years of schooling and the diversity of literacy classrooms in Australia. Students will revise and expand their understandings of current research in literacy for Stages 2 and 3 and apply that research to their own practice. Students will engage in learning experiences that promote their abilities to critically analyse texts and resources for their use in Stage 2 and 3 classrooms, with a specific focus on digital and multimodal texts and their implications for critical literacy, text deconstruction, manipulation, and reconstruction. They will engage with culturally sustaining literacy pedagogies that promote understanding of and respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, languages, and histories. Students will evaluate and choose resources to plan literacy activities that are sequential, align with the NSW syllabus and related resources, and promote dynamic literacy instruction in Stages 2 and 3; they will explore ways feedback and assessment work in unit and lesson planning. Students in EML530 will also explore and develop metacognitive teaching skills that are foundational tools in reflective practice.
learning_outcomes: Determine and explain the literacy demands of Stage 2 and 3 classrooms, including the diverse literacy capabilities of students across these Stages, with special attention to students who come from multilingual backgrounds.
Use the NSW Syllabus and additional state and federal curriculum resources to design, plan and differentiate multimodal literacy instruction for learners in Stages 2 and 3.
Incorporate meta-cognitive skills into planning and teaching decisions as a means of building reflective practice.
Evaluate and use a range of resources, including multimodal and digital texts and ICT-based learning materials, for the development of students' literacy capabilities.
Plan and use a range of literacy assessments to inform instruction and offer focused feedback for Stage 2 and 3 learners.

Evaluate and apply current literacy research to Stage 2 and 3 classroom practice, with a specific focus on critical literacy and digital literacy, anti-racist pedagogies, explicit instruction and culturally sustaining literacy instruction.
Identify and evaluate culturally safe and inclusive literacy resources that promote understanding of and respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories, cultures and languages.
prerequisites: EML439: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the primary years
EML449: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice

title: English Curriculum: Primary
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops and consolidates students' understanding of English content knowledge in language, literature and literacy to enable Stage 2 and Stage 3 learners to appreciate the value of the English language for communication, knowledge and enjoyment. Students revise and build on their understandings of current research in language, literature and literacy, including the explicit teaching of speaking, listening, reading, writing, viewing and representing. Students will examine a range of theoretical perspectives and models for teaching English in order to teach to diversity. Learning experiences will promote students' abilities to critically analyse diverse texts, including a specific focus on digital and multimodal texts and their implications for critical literacy, text deconstruction, manipulation, and reconstruction. They will engage with culturally responsive literacy pedagogies that promote understanding of and respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, languages, and histories. Students will evaluate and choose resources to plan literacy activities that are sequential, align with Australian curriculum documents, including the NSW English K -10 syllabus and related resources, and promote dynamic literacy instruction in Stages 2 and 3. Students will also explore the role of feedback and assessment in planning for units and lessons.
learning_outcomes: Plan and use a range of literacy assessments to inform instruction and offer focused feedback for Stage 2 and 3 learners.
Examine and apply, in their planning for teaching, English syllabus content knowledge in the strands of language, literature and literacy with a specific focus on Stage 2 and Stage 3 students.
Identify and evaluate culturally responsive and inclusive literacy resources that promote understanding of and respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories, cultures, and languages.
Examine a range of theoretical perspectives and select appropriate models of teaching to support the teaching of English content knowledge in contemporary Stage 2 and Stage 3 classrooms.

Differentiate instruction in English for varying learning needs, with including students who come from multilingual backgrounds (EAL/D) within the guidelines of the NSW English Syllabus and other State and Federal curriculum resources.

Examine and apply current literacy research to Stage 2 and 3 classroom practice, with a specific focus on critical and digital literacy, anti-racist pedagogies, explicit instruction, and culturally responsive literacy instruction.
prerequisites: EML322: Literacy Studies in the Primary School : 2
EML439: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the primary years
EML309: Primary English Curriculum: Text Construction, Pedagogy and Processes

title: English Dissertation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This is a research subject involving critical analysis of texts or other literary topics as approved by an appointed supervisor. The dissertation will be written over two semesters and not exceed 15000 words in length.
learning_outcomes: Undertake independent research in the field of literature.

title: English for Academic Studies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is intended for international students. This subject focuses on providing students the opportunity to develop and improve their English academic literacy writing and communication skills aligned to business disciplines and to be better prepared for their academic studies.
learning_outcomes: Locate, paraphrase, summarise and comprehend simple to complex English texts.
Write in a range of academic formats, following English writing mechanics and appropriate academic referencing styles.
Develop an effective academic argument based on information gained from a range of sources.
Develop speaking and listening communication skills.
Apply their communication skills to debate differing points of view using verbal and non-verbal communication methods.

title: English Grammar in Context
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: English Grammar in Context is a foundational subject that introduces diverse schools of English grammar and explores the place of grammar in learning English as an additional language or dialect. The subject enables students to develop a proficiency of grammar metalanguage in order to further their participation in, and investigation of, grammatical practices in diverse social contexts.
learning_outcomes: Appropriate grammatical theories in professional practice.
Identify, analyse, and discuss grammatical features of different English texts.
Critique various grammatical theories.
Assess applications of English grammar in professional contexts.

title: English Curriculum: Understanding Language and Literacy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop and consolidate their understanding of English content knowledge in the strands of language, literature and literacy with a focus on the early years (ages 4-8) through online study with an embedded classroom experience focus. They will consider the acquisition of reading and writing processes with an added focus on catering for the specific needs of individuals and models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, speaking, viewing and representing in the early years. Students will develop their understandings of how technology influences literacies. Students will also develop skills in the analysis of young children's literacy work samples to determine students' strengths and needs and identify teaching priorities related to relevant syllabus documents.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-based approaches that include instruction on how to teach phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary knowledge and text comprehension, concepts of print, grammar, punctuation, spelling, and handwriting.
Develop, use, and interpret a variety of appropriate assessments to better understand diverse learner capabilities and inform instruction for all students in K-2 literacy classrooms.

Analyse the reading and writing processes at acquisition and the early stages of development and explore models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, speaking, viewing and representing in the early years.
Identify the diverse literacy capabilities of K-2 students and explain how technology influences these literacies.
Develop K-2 literacy experiences that are sequenced and supported in current literature.

Identify, evaluate, and use a range of resources to support students' literacy learning in years K-2 contexts, with special attention to understanding effective strategies for meeting the literacy and learning capabilities of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and English as an Additional Language/Dialect (EAL/D) students.
Use the NSW and Australian Curriculum documents for English in years K-2 to plan meaningful and accessible instruction for all students in this stage.
prerequisites: EML449: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice
EML440: English Curriculum: Understanding Language and Literacy
EML222: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning
EML453: English Curriculum: Pedagogies in the Early Years of Learning.

title: English Language for University Preparation 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to enhance the Academic English skills of students from language backgrounds other than English (LBOTE) at the university preparation level. The syllabus structure provides students with opportunities to develop the necessary skills in listening, speaking, reading and writing prior to undertaking further university preparation studies. Students completing the subject will have improved their capacity to use English for academic purposes in the Australian context. The subject also functions as an initial preparation for attempting the International English Language Testing System (IELTS). Students are recommended to progress to enrolment in English Language for University Preparation 2.
learning_outcomes: Apply appropriate speaking skills for class discussions and short presentations.
Identify and begin to apply appropriate language and conventions for academic writing.
Use listening and note-taking strategies to engage with general information presented in the university context.
Use text identification and reading strategies to engage with course materials and simple academic texts.

title: English in the World
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the global spread of English over time and its implications for TESOL. It adopts a historical perspective to look into the formation of contemporary English while adhering to a critical perspective to examine the position of Englishes in the world in relation to power, identity, community, and knowledge economy. The subject provides an opportunity for students to critically reflect on their own life experiences and performances in the context of language teaching and learning.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on and change their perceptions and practices.
Understand various sociopolitical, economic, and cultural influences on English and its varieties.
Understand English language history including the main influences and phases.
Understand the implications of World Englishes for TESOL.
Become familiar with varieties of English and their implications.
prerequisites: EML503: English as an International Language: Cultural and political issues

title: Enhancing mathematical learning in the early years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Early childhood teachers need to be knowledgeable, confident, and intentional in their approach to facilitating early mathematical learning within play-based environments. This subject will extend students’ understanding of early mathematics and build capability to respond to rich opportunities for mathematical learning within early childhood environments. Students will consider the barriers of practice, theoretical underpinnings of mathematical pedagogy, and the ‘everydayness’ of mathematics, including First Nations Australians perspectives of mathematical learning and the importance of learning on Country. This subject will also support students to work in partnership with families to build capacities to notice and explore powerful mathematical knowledge and skills with children in ways that develop positive dispositions to learning, connect with the home learning environment and empower families.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of early mathematical ideas, skills and concepts aligned with frameworks of early childhood practice and culturally appropriate approaches to learning.
Explain the barriers of mathematical pedagogy in the early years including the impact of attitudes, beliefs, and confidence on educator practice.
Articulate the importance of mathematical learning in the early years as foundational and predictive of later success.
Apply effective communication skills and relationship building strategies in partnership with families to enhance mathematical learning in the home learning environment.
Apply knowledge of mathematics to notice, explore and enhance learning in early childhood environments through play and intentional practice.
prerequisites: EMC305: Investigation: Mathematics, Science and Technology

title: Enhancing The Skilful Higher Education Teacher.
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides learners with the opportunity to consolidate their learning by undertaking deliberate practice to integrate and synthesise their course learnings into their context via a capstone project. The capstone project gives learners the opportunity to demonstrate autonomy, creativity, adaptability, and responsibility as both practitioners and developing higher education scholars. Learners will create and submit evidence of their evidence informed project, disseminate the findings and participate in an Oral Assessment that explores their higher education learning and teaching practices and approaches within their discipline area. This subject supports learners to meet the challenges of practice in their higher education context and encourages their continuing professional development.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their personal and professional learning as a result of the capstone project.
Utilise an evidence informed approach to their capstone project and disseminate their findings.
Explore how the current higher education context influences learning and teaching practices within their discipline area.
Develop a plan for the implementation of their educational leadership development priorities.

title: Entry Level Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is applicable for students who have completed a Bachelor of Adult and Vocational Education course or, a Bachelor of Vocational Education and Training course, and are awarded credit in the Master of Adult and Vocational Education

title: Entrepreneurship Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for enterprising students to formulate, evaluate and develop entrepreneurial ideas, projects and ventures. This subject integrates entrepreneurial theory and research with practical business/management knowledge, and is designed for prospective entrepreneurs to develop, launch and grow an entrepreneurial idea, project or venture. The subject explores social and commerical entrepreneurship, and addresses issues including bootstrapping, micro-enterprise, mini-preneurship, intrapreneurship as well as corporate entrepreneurship. The focus is on innovation and entrepreneurship in relation to both product and process, and is suitable for those working as individuals or within organisations.
learning_outcomes: Prepare and present an entrepreneurial venture plan and pitch.
Recommend growth and/or harvest strategies for entrepreneurial projects or ventures.
Identify and evaluate individual and organisational entrepreneurial opportunities.
Identify and critique current theory and research in entrepreneurship and entrepreneurial behaviour.
Assess the value proposition of an entrepreneurial idea, project or venture.

title: Entry Level Discipline Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is the Entry level credit to the Bachelor of Teaching (Secondary) where disicpline content requires the completion of an additional 8 subject points to meet CSU course requirements.

title: Entry Level Discipline Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is the Entry level credit for the Bachelor of Teaching (Secondary) where the prior completion of relevent undergraduate bacehlor's degree that meets the ESA discipline content requirements.

title: Entry Level Vocational Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: A standard entry-level credit package of 64 points. This is represented as VET08C Entry Level Vocational Credit and is based on the following entry criteria: Certificate III as part of a completed apprenticeship leading to trade recognition and accreditation, and a minimum of three years relevant industry experience; or an advanced certificate (Certificate IV), associate diploma, diploma or the appropriate tertiary qualification and a minimum of three years relevant industry experience.

title: Entry Level Discipline Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is the Entry level credit for the Bachelor of Teaching (Secondary) Articulated Set where discipline content requires the completion of an additional 16 subject points to meet CSU course requirements

title: Entry to CSU Global
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject serves as a prerequisite to enrol into the subjects for Short-term International Mobility Program (SIMP) for participants from the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences. Students participate in Faculty of Business, Justice & Behavioural Science. SIMPs are eligible for a zero point TCR credit in either BUS201 or BUS202 subjects. This subject will act as prerequisite gatekeeper subject for students to enrol in BUS201 and BUS202 subjects only and there are no concepts in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Enrol in BUS201 and BUS202.

title: Entry to CSU Global Post Graduate
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject serves as a prerequisite to enrol into the subjects for CSU Global Programs for participants from the Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Science. Students accepted into Faculty of Business CSU Global postgraduate programs will be awarded a zero point transfer credit for this subject.
learning_outcomes: Enrol in MBA551.

title: Environment Taxation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject introduces students to the areas of excise law and administration relating to the taxation of certain products or processes that impact upon the environment. There is a particular focus on the differing types of approaches to the taxation of these products and processes through the excise system; including levies, off-sets, rebates and incentives, as well as other fiscal instruments such as emissions trading and product stewardship. The subject considers such contemporary issues as impact on local industry and consumers, development of environmental protection technology, and cross border issues.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the different types of approaches available under an indirect taxation system, including carbon tax, levies and excises, for implementing environmental policy outcomes.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the impact of these taxation measures on business and consumers, and the implications of this.

Demonstrate an understanding of some of the issues in relation to climate change being a global problem, and that certain aspects of international trade are impacted by the need to address the cross border movement of carbon and other hazardous products.
Focus on one industry (motor vehicles) directly impacted by environmental taxation and work through the various taxation issues.

title: Environmental Assessment and Auditing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to environmental assessment and environmental auditing. This includes Local, State and Federal environmental planning, environmental protection and pollution laws, as well as methodologies associated with impact prediction, environmental assessment, and environmental auditing. On completion of this subject, students are able to step through the process of environmental assessment from project inception, identification of relevant legalisation and planning structures, through to impact prediction, impact documentation, mitigation planning, approvals and project consent conditions, through to the development of environment audits.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the current legislative systems that underpin environmental planning processes, environmental assessment, reporting and auditing in Australia.
Outline processes associated with environmental assessment and environmental auditing.
Develop professional and appropriate documentation to document project impacts and support consent authorities deliberations on the proposal.
Make a professional judgement on how to develop and prepare for an environmental audit.
Apply the processes professionals use to evaluate proposed developments in the context state and federal planning and conservation laws and identify and apply other relevant legalisation.

title: Environmental Assessment and Auditing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to environmental impact assessment and environmental auditing in Australia. This includes local, State and Commonwealth environmental protection and planning frameworks, environmental auditing and controls. Methodologies associated with impact identification, evaluation, reporting and auditing are also outlined. On completion of this subject, students are able to step through the process of environmental impact assessment from project inception, identification of relevant legislation and planning structures, through to impact prediction, impact documentation, mitigation planning, approvals and project consent conditions, and auditing.
learning_outcomes: Coherently articulate the current legislative systems that underpin environmental planning processes, environmental assessment, reporting and auditing in Australia.

Select and adopt the correct skills and processes professionals use to evaluate complex proposals for development in the context state and federal planning and conservation laws and identify and apply other relevant legalisation.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the processes associated with environmental impact assessment and environmental auditing.
Generate appropriate professional documentation to document project impacts and support consent authorities deliberations on complex proposals.
Make professional and well-developed judgements on how to generate and prepare for an environmental audit.

title: Environmental Impact Assessment
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to environmental impact assessment in Australia. This includes the relevant local, State and Commonwealth environmental protection and planning frameworks, as well as methodologies associated with impact identification, evaluation and reporting. On completion of this subject, students are able to step through the process of environmental impact assessment from project inception, identification of relevant legislation and planning structures, through to impact prediction, impact documentation, mitigation planning, approvals and project consent conditions.
learning_outcomes: Coherently articulate the current legislative systems that underpin environmental planning processes, environmental assessment, and reporting in Australia.

Select and adopt the correct skills and processes professionals use to evaluate proposed developments in the context state and federal planning and conservation laws and identify and apply other relevant legalisation.
Generate appropriate professional documentation to document project impacts and support consent authorities deliberations on the proposal.
Broadly and coherently outline processes associated with environmental impact assessment.

title: Environmental Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the way the law regulates and imposes legal constraints on environmental management and land use planning. This regulation is then critically analysed and examined by undertaking a study of the regulation that affects a chosen industry. Students are encouraged to evaluate the effectiveness of the law in regulating environmental values and consider alternative methods of managing the legal issues that confront the conservation and protection of the environment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse legal attempts to regulate environmental planning and development by applying the relevant laws to a planning situation.
Critically evaluate the effectiveness of the law in regulating environmental values and laws in a chosen area.
Assess and evaluate the legal constraints on environmental management.

title: Environmental Law and Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject has a dual focus. The aim is firstly to examine the way the law regulates and imposes legal constraints on environmental management and land use planning. This regulation is then critically analysed and examined by undertaking a study of the regulation that affects a chosen industry. Students are encouraged to question the effectiveness of the law and to suggest alternative methods of managing the legal issues that confront the conservation and protection of the environment.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the effectiveness of the law in regulating environmental values and laws in a chosen area.
Analyse how the law attempts to regulate environmental planning and development by applying the relevant laws to a planning situation.
Assess and evaluate the legal constraints on environmental management.
Determine the ability of the law to foster the sustainability of the environment.

title: Environmental Internship
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject seeks to develop skills related to a number of management systems in environmental science. In particular, the focus will be on skills in asset, risk, financial and capacity management incorporating key administrative and workplace skills appropriate to environmental science graduates. This is a capstone subject (i.e. a subject that integrates prior learning from other subjects in the course) for the Bachelor of Environmental Science and Management. Assessment tasks are based on the industry project undertaken, where the student investigates and reflects upon the context and processes of management in the work environment that they observe and experience and an analysis of management outcomes.The subject contains a total estimated workload of 480 hours. On completion the student will have demonstrated the ability to apply their knowledge and skills to professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Take responsibility and accountability for their own professional practice and in collaboration with others within broad parameters.
Demonstrate communication skills to present a clear, coherent and independent exposition of knowledge and ideas in the workplace.
Adopt appropriate courses of action to achieve career aspirations.
Demonstrate the ability to apply a broad and coherent body of knowledge to a range of contexts in professional work.
Apply critical thinking and problem solving methods to a field of work.

title: Environmental Management of Mine Sites and Contaminated Lands
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the theoretical and practical aspects for understanding the environmental management of mine sites and the management of contaminated land. The subject focuses on industry perspectives of biodiversity and water management, environmental systems, monitoring and audit and rehabilitation of mine sites. Contaminated land management is introduced focusing on typical contaminants and their behaviour, the regulatory environment and case studies. The subject has no intensive.
learning_outcomes: Describe example contaminants and their behaviour.
Describe a range of approaches to biodiversity and water management.
Describe the regulatory framework with respect to contaminated land management.
Discuss the purpose of environmental systems and plans.
Apply sustainable development principles in mining.

title: Doctoral Dissertation FT
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This is a research subject. Content will be determined by the candidate in consultation with their supervisor.
learning_outcomes: Research and prepare a professional Doctorate dissertation in consultation with their supervisor/supervision team.

title: Environmental Policy
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Environmental policy is a planned course of action to manage human activities with a view to prevent, reduce, or mitigate harmful effects on nature or natural resources. This subject explores the nature of policy development and implementation and the cultural, environmental, political, legal and ethical issues that can influence the process. It provides an understanding of the policy making process, policy instruments and the skills necessary to analyse policies related to environmental management. There is no intensive associated with this subject. On completion students have an in-depth understanding of the principles, processes, and complexity associated with environment policy.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise and apply a range of methods to evaluate public policy.
Understand the roles of key institutions and stakeholders involved with environmental policy.
Have an in-depth understanding of the principles, processes, and complexity associated with policy.
Critically understand how environmental policy relates to other areas of public policy.
Identify and make critical judgements about a range of policy instruments available to address environmental problems.

title: Environmental Practice
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the planning, management, and evaluation of projects in environmental management. Through a role play that has an emphasis on working within the current public sector, a range of planning and budgetary contexts are provided, and students will authentically apply administrative processes. This includes understanding the logic behind human resource management, organisational structures, organisational risk assessment and management, budgeting planning and grant applications. These themes are addressed in tandem and are woven together through a narrative based around a regional natural resource management agency. Students complete a workplace learning requirement, enabling them to apply these concepts in a professional environmental management setting and reflect on the practical realities of project implementation.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse funding opportunities available to an organisation in relation to potential organisational risk and capacity, with specific consideration of environmental management requirements, sustainability impacts, and compliance obligations.
Develop a completed and comprehensive project plan that integrates environmental management strategies, sustainability considerations, and relevant regulatory requirements.

Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of public‑sector organisational structures, the allocation of responsibilities, and the principles underpinning contemporary employment and workforce management practices, including how these structures support effective environmental management and sustainability governance.

Demonstrate problem‑solving skills to effectively develop, deliver, manage, and monitor a specific project, incorporating environmental management principles to minimise ecological impact and enhance sustainable outcomes.

title: Environmental Sustainability in Early Childhood
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject looks at the ideas and actions that demonstrate what early childhood educational communities can do when children, teachers and parents work together to address one of the most serious issues of our time. It focuses on what early childhood education - and specifically, early childhood teacher education - can and should do to play its part in helping societies move towards sustainable living. The syllabus will examine the relationship between scientific theories of environmental management and link early childhood theory to the practices of environmental sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the value and process of being a sustainable early childhood setting.

Familiar with the various concepts, theories, priorities and practices that define sustainability, with a particular focus on contemporary debates concerning young children's relationship with their environment.
Develop a leadership culture for working towards sustainability.
Demonstrate the relationship between environmental and economic sustainability in the ECEC context.
Demonstrate practical skills in developing educational experiences that use sound scientific theories to investigate environmental issues relating to sustainable living.
Develop healthy and sustainable environments for young children and communities.
Demonstrate effective interpersonal communication skills and relationship building strategies to afford effective teams.

title: Environmental Sustainability in Early Childhood
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject looks at the ideas and actions that demonstrate what early childhood educational communities can do when children, teachers and parents work together to address one of the most serious issues of our time. It focuses on what early childhood education - and specifically, early childhood teacher education - can and should do to play its part in helping societies move towards sustainable living. The syllabus will examine the relationship between scientific theories of environmental management and link early childhood theory to the practices of environmental sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the relationship between environmental and economic sustainability in the ECEC context.

Articulate the various concepts, theories, priorities and practices that define sustainability, with a particular focus on contemporary debates concerning young children's relationship with their environment.
Demonstrate practical skills in developing educational experiences that use sound scientific theories to investigate environmental issues relating to sustainable living.
Develop leadership skills for working towards sustainability.
Articulate the value and process of being a sustainable early childhood setting.
Demonstrate effective interpersonal communication skills and relationship building strategies to afford effective teams.
Develop healthy and sustainable environments for young children and communities.

title: Envisioning the Digital Society
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn about the development of internet technologies and their impacts on the fields of communication and media. You will develop practical skills for content production while engaging in debates about the economic, political, and social implications of digital media. You will examine both current debates and historical trends to understand the emergence of the digital society.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge about the emergence and impact of digital media upon social, economic and political structures.
Produce digital content at the level of a developing professional.
Communicate your understanding of the impacts of internet technologies on media industries.
Critically examine how digital media has transformed professional practices in the fields of communication and media.

title: Equine Breeding Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject has a particular emphasis on practical horse breeding management. It will cover reproductive anatomy and endocrinology, normal and abnormal pregnancy, supervision and troubleshooting parturition, neonatal care and theoretical and practical applications of breeding mares. This subject gives students realistic scenarios and allows them to make stud management decisions based on their understanding of the subject material.
learning_outcomes: Implement appropriate management of mares to achieve maximum reproductive efficiency and perform artificial insemination using aseptic technique.
Examine the management of foals from birth to yearling age, including prevention and management of common health issues.
Examine reproductive anatomy of the mare and explain the relationship between anatomy and the endocrine system that regulates reproductive processes and associated behavioural changes.
Interpret and practically assess physiological and behavioural signs to guide foal health management.
Discuss methods used to evaluate reproductive potential and be able to compare the diagnostic tools and management of common reproductive disorders.
Explain the major events of foetal development and placentation in the horse and apply management strategies for pregnant and foaling mares.

title: Equine Disease Prevention
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject equips students with the key skills needed to optimise horse health, performance and welfare. The importance of risk factors relating to the horse, its environment, and management will be explored in relation to industry practices.
