On completing this subject, students will be able to outline how daily management challenges the horse’s natural body defences and as a result, better assess horse health and disease risk, design basic on-farm biosecurity protocols, justify choice of preventive healthcare programs and communicate this information, orally and in writing to different stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Observe and identify the influence of horse management on disease risk and justify preventative healthcare measures.
Identify and perform practical parasite control measures to customise a program managing equine internal parasites.
Recognise and explain the risk of infection and spread to equine establishments and implement practical hygiene and biosecurity measures.
Appraise and communicate information within the scientific literature and demonstrate effective collaboration with their peers.
Identify and describe risks to the horse’s natural body defence mechanisms in various horse husbandry settings.
Identify evidence-based risk factors and generate a basic causal web for common equine diseases demonstrating their multifactorial nature.

title: Equine Disease Prevention
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject equips students as potential future decision makers with the key skills needed to optimise horse health, performance and welfare. The importance of risk factors relating to the horse environment and management will be critically appraised in relation to industry practices. On completing this subject students will be able to evaluate horse health and evaluate disease risk, consider and dispel horse health myths, design basic on-farm biosecurity protocols, justify choice of preventive healthcare programs and communicate this information, orally and in writing to different audiences (lay and professional).
learning_outcomes: Justify and implement equine preventative health care.
Evaluate disease risk and develop and implement biosecurity measures for an equine property.
Critically appraise the equine scientific literature for strength of evidence and to dispel equine health myths.
Apply integrated control measures for equine internal parasites.
Identify evidence-based risk factors and generate a causal web for common equine diseases demonstrating their multifactorial nature.
prerequisites: ASC208: Equine Disease, Injury and Rehabilitation

title: Equine Breeding Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject applies information from previous reproduction subjects, with a particular emphasis on practical horse breeding management, including breeding techniques and facilities, stallion fertility and management, mare fertility and management to maximise breeding efficiency, management of the non-pregnant, pregnant, foaling and post-partum mare as well as management of the neonatal foal and developing young horse. This subject gives students realistic scenarios and allows them to make stud management decisions based on their understanding of the subject material.
learning_outcomes: explain the diagnostic tools and management of common reproductive disorders in mares and stallions;
appraise the management of foals from birth to yearling age, including prevention and management of common disorders of foals, limb deformities and general health care.

apply knowledge of equine reproductive anatomy and physiology to illustrate appropriate management of non-pregnant mares to achieve maximum reproductive efficiency, including the interpretation of ultrasound images of the mare reproductive tract;
apply knowledge of stallion behaviour and reproductive anatomy and physiology to describe and assess the management of stallions to achieve maximum reproductive efficiency;
assess and appraise the management of non-pregnant mares using appropriate information and analyse the management of pregnant and foaling mares; and
select and design breeding facilities to suit a range of different horse stud environments;

title: Equine Exercise Physiology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the physiology underlying equine athleticism building upon existing knowledge of mammalian energy production systems. Students will witness physiological changes in the horse during exercise and monitor exercise intensity to enable improvements in aerobic capacity. Students will learn how to manage performance horses within regulatory frameworks to ensure health, welfare and integrity during competition. Students will use evidence-based findings to plan training programmes and monitor equine athletic performance to uphold horse health and welfare.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply evidence-based findings to equine training protocols and explain these concepts effectively to enhance practice.
Effectively manage a competition horse before, during and after competition to ensure equine health and welfare.
Use objective monitoring to interpret changes in equine athletic capacity to determine the effectiveness of a training regimen.
Differentiate between the physical demands made on the horse in a range of equestrian sports.
Interpret the regulatory requirements of a chosen equine sport with regards to the management of the equine athlete on the national and international stage.
Observe and describe the physiological changes occurring within the horse in response to exercise.

title: Equine Disease, Injury and Rehabilitation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to develop and apply their knowledge of the anatomy and physiology of the healthy horse. Students' knowledge and competence in providing first aid and rehabilitation for sick horses will be developed. On successful completion of this subject students will be equipped with the skills to recognise common equine diseases and injuries and be able to identify and administer appropriate equine first aid and equine rehabilitation methods.
learning_outcomes: Outline the principles of evidence-based rehabilitation of horses with common injuries.
Identify available horse health professionals and review their legal limits and expertise in the context of relevant legislation.
Categorise horse disease problems by severity to assist with prioritising first aid.
Recognise typical clinical and behavioural signs of a healthy and sick horses.
Describe important equine disease states and apply this knowledge to outline the specific considerations for first aid and rehabilitation of common equid emergencies.
Explain the basic wound healing process, and outline appropriate first aid measures for a typical traumatic equine lower limb injury.

title: Equine Health and Disease
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to build on knowledge of cellular biology, basic endocrinology and anatomy and physiology developed in EQS100 Equine Life Systems. It will introduce the basics of animal health and disease with specific regard to the horse. It will cover homeostasis in the horse through adaption, endocrinology, immunology and fluid dynamics. Mechanisms of disease will be introduced as alterations of homeostasis and specific disease conditions discussed. First aid and wound management will also be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Outline and demonstrate appropriate first aid measures and practical skills for a range of conditions;
Recognise and assess severity of diseases in the horse from first principles and outline management strategies;
Outline the legal aspects of first aid management of horses under your care.
Identify and describe the disruptions to homeostasis that impact on the health of the equid;
Explain the basic wound healing process and discuss appropriate management strategies; and
Outline the processes involved in maintaining homeostasis in the horse;
prerequisites: ASC208: Equine Disease, Injury and Rehabilitation

title: Equine Industry and Welfare
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable the student to understand the extent of the growing equine industry both in Australia and globally. Throughout this subject, students will gain a working understanding of industry governance and operating processes and procedures, including workplace health and safety, legal aspects and duty of care. Common horse management and husbandry procedures will be examined and assessed in relation to globally agreed health and welfare indicators and codes of practice. During this subject, students will also be given the opportunity to examine Indigenous Australian Cultural Competence and consider how lessons learnt can be applied within the equestrian context. On successful completion of this subject, students will be able to demonstrate a full understanding of the ethical considerations associated with the management of industry resources, namely horses, humans and land.
learning_outcomes: describe and review the rationale behind common horse husbandry and management practices;
recognise and assess critical equine health and welfare indicators necessary for good horse management; and
outline legal and ethical requirements associated within the equine and allied industries;
demonstrate an understanding of the structure, scope and contribution of and influences on the horse industry by sourcing and using appropriate information resources in Australia and globally;
identify the roles that Indigenous Australian people have had interacting with horses since European settlement.
review essential human occupational health and safety practices within the equine industry;

title: Equine Life Systems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The unique evolution of the horse has enabled humans to use them for work, performance, and companionship. Equine Life Systems is designed to cover cell-based biology, microbiology, and organ-based anatomy and physiology with a focus on the unique aspects of the horse. It will cover the structure, function, and reproduction of basic and specialised cells and the embryological development from cells into a horse. This subject will cover the core anatomy and physiology of the horse, including endocrinology and how different body systems communicate. This subject is critical in developing foundation knowledge for advanced equine core subjects.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe basic mammalian cell structure and function.
Identify and describe the basic functions of equine organ systems with regard to underlying physiological processes.
Apply basic practical techniques in micro and macro anatomy and physiology.
Outline and explain how equine body systems communicate to achieve homeostasis.
Describe and relate the embryology of the horse and explain its role in healthy development and genetic diversity.
Identify and describe the basic anatomical structure of equine organ systems, using the correct anatomical terminology.

title: Equine Locomotion
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the biomechanics of equine locomotion using the latest evidence-based research and draws on students existing knowledge of equine anatomy and physiology. Throughout this subject students will develop and practice the fundamentals of gait assessment, rider analysis, saddle fit and equine podiatry. On successfully completing this subject students will possess the theoretical and practical skills that the 21st Century horse manager requires to optimise the performance of their equine athletes whilst preserving the horse's soundness and athletic longevity.
learning_outcomes: Apply biomechanical analysis to improve interactions between horse, rider and equipment.
Identify and analyse factors that impact on equine biomechanics in terms of performance and injury risk.
Deconstruct and analyse abnormal equine movement anatomically, biomechanically and physiologically.
Assess a range of human and environmental factors impacting equine locomotion using qualitative and quantitative methods as appropriate.
Assess and analyse normal equine movement anatomically, biomechanically and physiologically.
Locate, identify and evaluate the anatomical structures that support equine movement and to describe the functional linkage of anatomy to motion.

title: Equine Locomotion
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the biomechanics of equine locomotion using the latest evidence-based research and draws on students existing knowledge of equine anatomy and physiology. Throughout this subject students will develop and practice the fundamentals of gait assessment, rider analysis, saddle fit and equine podiatry. On successfully completing this subject students will possess the theoretical and practical skills that the 21st Century horse manager requires to optimise the performance of their equine athletes whilst preserving the horse's soundness and athletic longevity.
learning_outcomes: assess a range of influences on equine locomotion using qualitative and quantitative methods as appropriate
apply biomechanical analysis to improve biomechanical interactions between horse, rider and equipment.
assess and analyse normal equine movement anatomically, biomechanically and physiologically;
deconstruct and analyse abnormal equine movement anatomically, biomechanically and physiologically;
identify and analyse the anatomical, management and environmental factors that impact on equine biomechanics in terms of performance and injury risk; and

title: Equestrian Industry Governance
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Australian equestrian competitions rely heavily on volunteer labour regardless of equine discipline. The exceptions are the two racing industry codes. This brings up additional challenges not faced by paid workforce. Levels of volunteerism continue to fall in all sports, not just equestrian. In an industry that is under increasing scrutiny regarding animal use, it is imperative that organisations and participants exercise good governance. The aim of this subject is to investigate the ethical, legal, safety and risk management of staging an equestrian event in accordance with competition rules to ensure the welfare and safety of all participants including the horses. This subject will also explore First Nations peoples relationships with horse and the horse industry since the arrival of horses in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Explore worldwide cultural relationships with horses and the impact of engagement within equine related industries.
Examine legal, safety and risk management factors in the context of horse-related activities.
Interpret rules of competition in an official capacity for a relevant equine discipline.
Compare and contrast Australian equestrian industries with international equestrian industries.
Implement strategies for effective running of organisations and events based on volunteer labour.
Demonstrate the importance of appropriate insurance compliance.

title: Equine Nutrition
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the basic principles and application of feeding horses. The feeding of all horse classes will be studied in depth and include examination and evaluation of nutritional problems that may arise as a result of horse diet. From this, feeding management strategies will be developed which can be applied to a range of contexts depending on horse type and use. The role of nutritional supplements and use of commercial feedstuffs will be explored and evaluated. Least cost rations will be formulated for a range of horses. Other factors that influence equine nutrition such as toxic plants will also be covered. Solution-based problem solving will be used to enable students to experience a hands-on approach to the theory taught in this subject. On successful completion of this subject, students will be able to formulate comprehensive nutrition plans tailored to individual equids and the conditions (natural or artificial) in which they are kept.
learning_outcomes: formulate rations, at least cost, for all classes of horses according to NRC (2007) requirements;
appraise a range of feeding practices and evaluate their impact on equine health and welfare;
critique the literature and contemporary research findings into equine nutrition.
devise feeding strategies that enhance equine health and welfare;
identify plants that are toxic to horses and develop management strategies to avoid toxicity; and
evaluate the quality of feedstuffs and commercially available products;

title: Equine Nutrition
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Throughout this subject students will explore the basic principles and application of feeding horses with an emphasis on optimal health, welfare and body condition score. The feeding of all horse classes will be studied, including the identification of nutritional and/or health problems that may arise because of a horse’s diet. From this, feeding management strategies will be developed which can be applied to a range of contexts depending on horse type and use. The role of nutritional supplements and the use of commercial feedstuffs will be explored and analysed. Least cost rations will be formulated for a range of horses. The grazing management of pastures for horses will be investigated with the use of pasture growth measurements to calculate a yearly feed budget to ensure optimal management of pasture. On successful completion of this subject, students will be able to formulate rations tailored to individual equids and the conditions (natural or artificial) in which they are kept.
learning_outcomes: Compare the quality and nutritive value of feedstuffs and discuss the effects of processing of commercially available products on their nutritive value.
Discuss feeding strategies that enhance equine welfare for all classes of horse.
Utilise the National Research Council Nutrient requirements for horses (2007) to formulate least cost rations for all classes of horse.
Measure pasture growth to implement pasture-based feed budgets to make informed decisions about managing horses at pasture.
Examine a range of feeding practices and interpret their impact on equine health and welfare.

title: Equine Reproduction
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on content studied in biology and provides the opportunity to study the functional anatomy and physiology of the equine reproductive systems. Topics covered include anatomy of the mare and stallion reproductive tract, endocrine control of reproduction, seasonality, mare oestrous cycles, gametogenesis, physiology of the equine pregnancy and parturition, as well as basic genetic inheritance. On successfully completing this subject students will possess an understanding of the science behind the management decisions required when breeding horses and raising foals.
learning_outcomes: Describe the endocrine mechanisms that regulate equine reproduction and explain the physiological and behavioural changes that occur during the oestrous cycle and with changing seasons.
List and explain the major events of foetal development, placentation and parturition in the horse.
Identify and describe the reproductive anatomy of the mare and stallion and discuss its function.
Describe common genetic disorders of horses and carry out basic calculations to predict the possible outcomes for coat colour and genetic disorders for given examples.
Describe the processes of gametogenesis and fertilisation in the horse.
Explain the basic mechanisms of inheritance.

title: Essay Writing - Style and Structure
school: School
syllabus_overview: Essay Writing - Style and Structure aims to provide students with the key skills required to write essays successfully at university. The subject content covers the broad academic categories of style and structure, with a focus on complexity and formality, referencing, punctuation, grammar, as well as writing an essay introduction, body, and conclusion. There is an emphasis on practice activities and short online tests to check for understanding of the concepts presented.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective strategies for note taking.
Write a coherent body paragraph that includes a topic sentence, elaboration and evidence.
Write a variety of simple, compound and complex sentences.
Find resources or services that support further development in academic writing skills.
Identify some basic grammatical terms and understand their relevance to formal academic writing.
Demonstrate the ability to write formal and complex structures, where appropriate.
Use the conventions of academic writing to produce texts.
Plan and structure a text that presents and supports a point of view based on research.
Use punctuation to organise meaning in a text and be able to edit a text to ensure that correct punctuation is used.
Identify the features of academic writing.
Critically evaluate evidence.
Write a concluding paragraph.
Write an introduction to an academic essay.
Demonstrate the ability to integrate sources into a body paragraph.
Demonstrate an understanding of the purpose of referencing at university and be able to produce correct in-text citations and an end-of-text reference list.
prerequisites: SSS034: Essay Writing - Style and Structure

title: Equity and Trusts
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the historical development of equity and its relationship to common law, the assignment and other dispositions of property in equity, the obligation of confidence in equity with respect to information, and fiduciary duties. A substantial component of the subject is dedicated to the study of trust law. Students will consider the nature of a trust; legal requirements in establishing a trust; as well as the rights, duties and powers associated with trusts. Students will also be introduced to remedial constructive trusts.
learning_outcomes: Articulate important legal concepts in a logical and persuasive manner.
Identify and evaluate equitable doctrines and remedies and apply them to practical scenarios.
Evaluate the use of equitable doctrines and remedies in scenarios concerning Indigenous people and communities, and those disadvantaged before the law.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the legislative framework surrounding unconscionable conduct.
Critique the roles of trustee and beneficiary in respect to important case law.
Evaluate critically the role played by equity in common law jurisdictions.
Engage critically with the philosophies behind equitable relief.
Analyse critically different types of trusts, including remedial constructive trusts, and reflect upon social policies underpinning this area of the law.
Demonstrate awareness of the principles of equity and trusts and their relationship to the broader Australian legal landscape, including property law and the law of contract.
prerequisites: LAW116: Writing and Communication for Legal Professionals

title: Essay Writing 1 - Style
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Essay Writing 1 - Style aims to provide students with the key skills required to write essays successfully at university. The subject content covers the broad academic category of style with a focus on complexity and formality, referencing, punctuation and grammar. There is an emphasis on practice activities and short online tests to check for understanding of the concepts presented.This subject is the foundation subject for the writing of essays at university level. It is recommended that students progress beyond this subject to Essay Writing 2: Structure and then Essay Writing 3: Putting it into Practice. Each subject provides a building block in preparation for the writing of essays at university level.
learning_outcomes: Identify the purpose of referencing at university
Write formal and complex structures, where appropriate
Write a variety of simple, compound and complex sentences
Find resources or services that support further development in academic writing skills
Use punctuation to organize meaning in a text and be able to edit a text to ensure that correct punctuation is used
Identify some basic grammatical terms and understand their relevance to formal academic writing
Identify the features of academic writing
Use the conventions of academic writing to produce texts
Apply the principles of referencing correctly to produce correct in-text references and an end-of-text reference list

title: Essay Writing 2 - Structure
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Essay Writing 2 - Structure aims to provide students with the key skills required to write essays successfully at university. The subject content covers the broad academic category of structure, with a focus on writing an essay introduction, body, and conclusion. There is an emphasis on practice activities and short online tests to check for understanding of the concepts presented.This subject is the second in a series on the writing of essays at university level. Each subject provides a building block in preparation for the writing of essays at university level.
learning_outcomes: Identify the purpose of referencing at university
Integrate sources into a body paragraph
Write an introduction to an academic essay
Find resources or services that support further development in academic writing skills
Write a concluding paragraph
Identify the features of academic writing
Plan and structure a text that presents and supports a point of view based on research
Apply the principles of referencing correctly to produce correct in-text references and an end-of-text reference list
Write a coherent body paragraph that includes a topic sentence, elaboration and evidence
Use the conventions of academic writing to produce texts

title: Essay Writing 3 - Putting it into Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Essay Writing 3 - Putting it into Practice is an extension subject that aims to provide students with opportunities to practice the key skills required to write essays successfully at university. The subject content applies learning about essay writing to the production of an essay. Students are able to choose a topic and practice writing an essay. They are provided with the opportunity to gain feedback and learn from that feedback to develop their essay writing skills. This subject is designed as part of a sequence of subjects focused on essay writing. It is recommended that students have completed SSS077 - Essay Writing 1: Style and SSS078 - Essay Writing 2: Structure prior to enrolling in this subject. This is the third stage of the sequence, which is focused on student-directed learning and the application of skills. Students attending the weekend workshop for SSS031 - Academic Writing Skills will also find that workshop provides appropriate background for this subject.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of referencing correctly to produce correct in-text references and an end-of-text reference list
Interpret and apply feedback to the development of academic writing
Use evidence to develop and support an argument
Identify the features of academic writing
Use the conventions of academic writing to produce a complete essay
Plan and structure a text that presents and supports a point of view based on research
Find resources or services that support further development in academic writing skills

title: Essential Clinical Pharmacology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore pharmacology, which is the study of how drugs affect the body and provides insight into why drugs are used to treat certain pathological conditions. This will lead into clinical pharmacology which covers the safety and efficacy of treatment and why individuals may have different outcomes when treated with the same drug. You will investigate case studies to develop their problem solving and decision making skills with regard to medication management. Employing these process will also reveal the range of drugs and drug classes that can be used to treat a given medical condition. You will also research and educate your colleagues on the pharmacology of a newly released medication.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and collaborate effectively in a group.
Explain medication related outcomes in terms of the principles of drug receptor interactions.
Identify and justify evaluation and monitoring steps to minimise patient harm and ensure effective use of medicine.
Detect medication related issues and justify medication related decisions to ensure the quality use of medicine.
Identify adverse drug reactions and drug interactions, explain their mechanisms (if known), describe their consequences and recommend steps to manage or minimise their impact.
Interpret patient information and make recommendations to improve a patient's medication regimen.
Explain how drugs can alter the progression of a pathophysiological condition or reduce the signs and/or symptoms associated with that condition.

title: Essential Communication Skills
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Being able to communicate effectively with a range of people using a variety of modes of communication is important for success in university study and in life. This subject is designed to introduce the communication skills that are essential at a tertiary level. In this subject students will learn how to engage with study materials that are presented in a range of different formats, and will learn how to work with and communicate with staff and with peers using a range of different forms of communication. In addition, students will learn principles for developing responses and demonstrating knowledge using different modes of communication as required by assessment tasks and learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Use written communication for university purposes
Engage in verbal communication for relationship building and study purposes
Develop and use strategies for active listening
Identify the nature of communication at university level
Communicate using multimodal forms of communication
Read a range of study materials for meaning

title: Essential Nursing Care: Managing the Deteriorating Patient
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will expand on the knowledge and skills developed in Essential Nursing Care: Acute Care, with a focus on the provision of safe, evidence-based nursing care to children and adults experiencing acute serious or life-threatening illness. Using a case-based approach, students will explore the pathophysiology, recognition and collaborative management of cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological, mental health and paediatric emergencies and their associated complications. During weekly clinical simulation laboratory sessions and workplace learning, students will have the opportunity to further develop their assessment skills as they perform comprehensive assessment of the relevant body systems (for distance education students this will involve a 4 day intensive). Students will also develop clinical skills relevant to the management of the seriously ill adult or child including venepuncture, intravenous cannulation, administration of blood products and management of central venous access devices.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively with individuals, groups and members of the interdisciplinary team in the acute care environment (NMBA 1.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 7.4, 7.5, 7.6, 7.7, 9.1, 9.2, 9.3, 9.4, 10.2, 10.4).

Demonstrate a broad knowledge which links the underlying pathophysiology of serious cardiac, respiratory and neurological presentations to their clinical manifestations (NMBA 2.6, 3.1, 3.4, 4.1, 7.4).

Apply theoretical knowledge to safely perform selected procedural skills including venepuncture, intravenous cannulation, administration of blood products and management of central venous access devices, required for the care of patients experiencing serious or life-threatening illness (NMBA 1.2, 2.5, 7.1, 7.2, 7.4).
Analyse the legal and ethical considerations associated with the management of the deteriorating patient (NMBA 1.1, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 7.4, 7.5, 7.6, 9.3, 9.5).

Collect, interpret and document subjective and objective data in the seriously ill or deteriorating person (aligns with Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia National Competency Standards for the Registered Nurse: 1.1, 1.2, 2.5, 4.1, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 7.4, 8.1, 8.2).

Apply theoretical knowledge, critical thinking and the use of best evidence to contribute to the planning and implementation of appropriate nursing interventions for the person experiencing a serious or life-threatening illness (NMBA 1.2, 2.5, 2.6, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1, 6.1, 6.2, 6.4, 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, 7.7, 7.8, 8.1, 8.2, 10.3).
prerequisites: NRS223: Essential Nursing Care: Chronic and Complex Nursing

title: Essential Nursing Care: Theory to Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will allow students to consolidate and further apply the knowledge and skills they have acquired throughout their degree as they prepare to make the transition from student to graduate Registered Nurse. Using authentic scenarios, students will have the opportunity to integrate their theoretical knowledge with their critical thinking and problem solving abilities as they undertake comprehensive assessments in order to plan deliver and evaluate safe, evidence-based nursing care in a range of contexts. An elective clinical placement will allow students to refine and consolidate the application of their clinical skills while exploring an area of speciality practice that is of interest to them. The importance of time management and active participation in the multi-disciplinary team will be emphasised on this placement as students work towards managing an appropriate patient load with minimal supervision.
learning_outcomes: Apply theoretical knowledge, critical thinking and clinical decision making skills to provide safe, person-centred nursing care in a workplace learning experience (NMBA 1.2, 2.2, 2.3, 2.5, 2.6, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, 7.7, 7.8, 8.1, 8.2, 9.3, 9.4, 9.5, 10.3).
Conduct and document a comprehensive health assessment and physical assessment (NMBA 1.2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.6, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 7.4, 8.1).
Access health information and research, and critically evaluate its application to address complex problems in the clinical setting (NMBA 2.6, 4.1, 5.1, 5.3, 9.3).
Describe, implement and evaluate strategies to teach a colleague (NMBA 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, 6.4, 9.2, 9.5, 10.3).
Critically reflect on their own practice and the practice of others with the aim of improving quality of care and patient/client outcomes (NMBA 2.5, 3.5, 4.1, 4.4).
Apply theoretical knowledge to the safely administer and monitor the effects of medications, intravenous fluids and blood products (NMBA 1.2, 2.5, 7.2, 7.4, 9.3, 9.5).

Demonstrate a broad foundational knowledge of the legal, ethical and professional knowledge required for safe and accountable practice (aligns with Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia National Competency Standards for the Registered Nurse: 1.1, 1.2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.6, 9.3, 9.5).
prerequisites: NRS312: Essential Nursing Care: Managing the Deteriorating Patient

title: Essentials of Islamic Spirituality
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the importance of self-development based on the teachings of the Qur'an and hadith (prophetic narratives). It covers foundational Islamic spirituality concepts, such as ihsan (spiritual excellence), ikhlas (sincerity), istiqama (balance) and taqwa (righteousness). These concepts will be discussed alongside ibada (worship) to appreciate the relationship between all these concepts. It will also explore the spiritual meaning of the five pillars of Islam; what each practice signifies; their relationship with one another within the framework of purification of the nafs (ego); and how the five pillars assist in the practitioner's spiritual development. The importance of the sunnah (practical teachings of the Prophet Muhammad) in the everyday life of a Muslim will also be discussed, with a particular focus on their application in contemporary times.
learning_outcomes: Discuss ibadah (worship) in relation to its key components.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of spiritual concepts in various life scenarios.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including research, writing and communication skills.
Critically articulate the relationship between levels of self-development from an Islamic perspective.
Critically evaluate the significance of the five pillars in relation to Islamic spiritual development.

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Cardiology
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the theoretical knowledge and understanding of cardiac conditions applicable to paramedics in an out-of-hospital environment. The subject reviews cardiac anatomy, physiology, and pharmacology as appropriate for the level of graduate entry into paramedicine. Emphasis is placed on obtaining a high level of understanding of the pathophysiology of cardiac conditions, including managing acute coronary syndromes, dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest in the adult, paediatric and neonatal populations in the out-of-hospital setting. Evidence-based theories and practices of cardiac management strategies will be used to develop student's skills in leadership and management of cardiac patients.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate safe and competent management for adult, paediatric and neonatal advanced life support (ALS) resuscitation of non-traumatic cardiac arrest, including the NSQHS standard communicating for safety in accordance with evidence-based practice and current guidelines.
Manage cardiac care in the out-of-hospital environment based on specialised knowledge of the pathophysiology and aetiology of acute cardiovascular emergencies.
Analyse the current management guidelines of cardiovascular emergencies and develop evidence-based treatment plans relevant to paramedic practice.
Integrate autonomous judgement, accountability, and leadership in the management of out-of-hospital cardiac clinical care.

Evaluate complex data from patient and technologically derived sources (e.g. point of care) to inform decision-making about the clinical care of acute cardiovascular emergencies in the out-of-hospital environment.

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Clinical Placement
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Using the Registered Nurse Standards for Practice and nursing experience as a foundation, this subject gives students the opportunity to exhibit the Paramedic Professional Capabilities in a supervised paramedic practice environment. During their Work Integrated Learning (WIL), students will demonstrate ethical and professional practices, including effective communication and interprofessional collaboration. The focus will be on assessing and formulating treatment plans for patients, emphasising a culturally safe and collaborative approach to healthcare delivery that aligns with National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) standards and the quality use of medications. Students will also engage in reflective practice to identify professional learning and development opportunities as paramedics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate diagnostic or monitoring procedures, treatment, therapy, or other actions safely informing clinical decision making and quality use of medications.
Demonstrate ethical and professional practice, consistent with relevant legislation and regulatory requirements whilst providing dignity and care to the patient.
Demonstrate appropriate communication skills and interprofessional collaboration with emergency service personnel and other health practitioners during safe patient management.
Identify and reflect on professional learning, clinical practice, development needs and opportunities from the placement experience.
Formulate comprehensive and appropriate patient care following NSQHS standards, and demonstrating a logical and systematic approach in a culturally safe framework.
prerequisites: CLS400: Essentials of Paramedicine: Medical Emergencies
CLS405: Essentials of Paramedicine: Traumatic, environmental and toxicological emergencies

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Medical Emergencies
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on students’ previous knowledge and experience to integrate their understanding of pathophysiology with patient assessment and history findings to identify potential differential diagnoses and formulate a working diagnosis for patients with acute medical emergencies. Students will propose ethical and culturally safe, evidenced-based paramedic treatment plans that are supported by the use of clinical practice guidelines. This subject also focuses on clinical decision-making, interprofessional communication and the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) guidelines to recognise and respond to deteriorating patients, preventing and controlling infections and communicating for safety.
learning_outcomes: Apply a knowledge of pathophysiology and aetiology (characteristics and consequences) of acute medical emergencies in the out of hospital environment.
Apply ethical and culturally safe care to adult patients experiencing an acute medical emergency in the out of hospital environment.
Apply the principles of interprofessionalism in the out of hospital environment.
Analyse management guidelines of acute medical emergencies and develop evidence based treatments plans for the out of hospital environment.

Apply the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) standards, recognising and responding to acute deterioration, preventing and controlling infections, and communicating for safety standards, to safely and effectively manage patients.
Evaluate complex data from patient and technologically-derived sources (e.g. point of care) to inform decision making about clinical care in acute medical emergencies.

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Mental Health and Primary Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the theoretical knowledge and understanding of medical conditions applicable to paramedics in the out-of-hospital environment. The subject reviews a range of patient conditions that may require alternative transport decisions and non-hospital alternatives to traditional management pathways. Mental health conditions will be considered in relation to risk assessment and appropriate treatment pathways. Students also consider the contexts of health and wellbeing for First Nations peoples and examine the role of paramedics in addressing inequities and supporting improved health outcomes for First Nations people across their lifespans. Students will learn the role of paramedics in diagnosing and treating older people and those who are frail or vulnerable and be able to evaluate complex conditions to provide rationalised patient care.
learning_outcomes: Perform assessments appropriate for both mental health disorders and conditions specific to vulnerable, frail, and/or older populations encountered in paramedic practice.

Develop skills in responding to people with mental illness, including providing support and early intervention for self and other paramedics experiencing early indicators of mental distress and trauma, and promoting resilience in paramedic practice.

Apply knowledge of diverse populations, vulnerability, and mental health to demonstrate ethical practice in paramedic practice, and to plan the delivery of culturally safe healthcare to First Nations Peoples.
Apply knowledge of both mental health disorders and conditions specific to vulnerable, frail, and/or older populations encountered in paramedic practice.

Identify skills for developing effective therapeutic relationships with First Nations Peoples and for applying culturally appropriate care and communication with First Nations clients and families, and those from culturally diverse backgrounds.

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Paediatrics and Maternal Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the knowledge to manage paediatric and maternal emergencies in the out-of-hospital environment. The subject reviews anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology for normal and complex presentations as appropriate for the level of graduate entry into paramedicine. There is a focus on paramedic care that enhances and does not inhibit the physiological processes of pregnancy, labour, birth and the postnatal period. Evidence-based person-centred management strategies will develop skills in assessing and managing medical and traumatic emergencies for both paediatric and maternal populations.
learning_outcomes: Apply the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) Comprehensive Care Standard while providing ethical and culturally safe care in the out-of-hospital environment.
Apply the knowledge of pathophysiology and aetiology (characteristics and consequences) of paediatric medical and traumatic emergencies in the paramedic setting.
Analyse management guidelines of paediatric and maternal emergencies and develop evidence-based treatment plans relevant to paramedicine.
Assess and implement woman-centred maternal and newborn care during normal and complex presentations while protecting and supporting physiological birth.
Describe key anatomical and physiological differences in infants and children with the ability to demonstrate age appropriate assessment and history taking techniques.
prerequisites: PHC401: Paramedic Intensive Care for Paediatrics
PHC401: Paramedic Intensive Care for Paediatrics

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Pharmacology
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will expand upon the student's general understanding of pharmacology from their nursing education and professional experience. Students will then apply further learning and knowledge from these principles to paramedic practice. Students will be introduced to medications used to manage various clinical conditions encountered in out-of-hospital settings. Students will provide provisional diagnoses of patient conditions, make sound clinical decisions, and safely administer medications to treat these conditions. This subject will enable students to identify possible drug interactions when considering medication administration.
learning_outcomes: Identify strategies to safely and effectively administer medication to patients in out-of-hospital settings in accordance with the NSQHS Medication Safety Standards.
Explain the relevant pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the most common medications used in paramedic practice.

Identify common prescription and over-the-counter medications and describe possible interactions with medications administered by paramedics, as identified in Clinical Practice Guidelines, to inform decision-making and medication administration.
Develop medication treatment plans in accordance with Clinical Practice Guidelines for patients with a variety of medical complaints.

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Transition to Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject sets the foundation for future clinical practice by requiring students to integrate and consolidate knowledge and skills developed in preceding subjects and to demonstrate that they have autonomous clinical judgement and evidence-informed decision-making skills that apply to real-world situations. Students will practice making autonomous clinical judgements about culturally safe, appropriate patient-centred care in the treatment of First Nations peoples of Australia and patients from diverse populations. This subject focuses on ensuring students are prepared and can demonstrate the requirements to successfully transition into professional paramedic practice. Students will be required to attend a compulsory Intensive school in order to demonstrate and be assessed in applying professional clinical judgement and practical skills in relation to appropriate patient-centred care.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on and apply knowledge from previous and current professional studies to the development and improvement of paramedic practice, and analyse individual learning needs to facilitate the transition to professional practice.
Practise with accountability evidenced by the application of knowledge of legal and ethical frameworks, patient information systems, and regulatory requirements in paramedic settings.
Evaluate own preparedness for practice against the Paramedicine Board's Professional Capabilities and the Code of Conduct for registered paramedics.

Make evidence informed autonomous clinical judgements about culturally safe, appropriate patient centred care in treating patients from diverse populations including First Nations peoples of Australia and people with disabilities.

Apply skills and knowledge learnt during the course in a simulated paramedic environment, utilising a simulation ambulance and all other paramedic equipment to assess, plan and treat various patient presentations, including the maintenance of patient records.
Apply the principles of patient advocacy in out of hospital settings within the legal, ethical, and regulatory contexts of paramedicine.

title: Estate Planning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the concepts involved in estate planning that are explained in subject FIN560, placing particular attention to the application of various law, processes and principles which are involved in dealing with a client's needs for wealth preservation and transfer. Financial and estate planning operations are explained within a broader professional occupation of estates practice. The subject introduces students to the tasks associated with the identification of wealth preservation and transfer needs of clients as well as the development of estate administration plans, and prepares students for a professional career in estate planning and administration.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on the structure, regulation and participants in the private wealth management sector.
Analyse and evaluate various approaches to the estate planning process.

Use effective communication skills and estate planning principles to establish client needs and objectives and develop an estate administration plan then sets out the proposed method of administration of the client's estates that is proposed to meet the client's needs and objectives.
Conduct technical research to complete estate planning work.
Create, present, and interpret a professional-quality Statement of Advice that includes a detailed estate administration proposal.

title: Ethical Hacking
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to key concepts and practices related to ethical hacking, emphasising an ethical approach through the use of an isolated test environment. Topics covered include footprinting, reconnaissance, network scanning, enumeration, malware, sniffing, and social engineering. Students will learn how to identify vulnerabilities in systems and understand how these vulnerabilities can be exploited by an attacker. Moreover, students will acquire basic skills in hacking into systems and cracking passwords in an isolated test environment. Additionally, the subject will briefly explore hacking countermeasures to enhance students' understanding of defensive techniques.
learning_outcomes: Intercept (sniff) network traffic that is traversing a network.
Identify vulnerabilities in systems and exploit them.
Use methods to compromise a computer system’s security in an isolated test environment.
Perform reconnaissance, footprinting, network scanning, and enumeration.
Compare effective countermeasures to prevent harm being done by malicious hackers.

title: Essentials of Paramedicine: Traumatic, environmental and toxicological emergencies
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on students’ previous knowledge and experience to integrate the principles of pathophysiology with patient assessment and history findings to identify potential differential diagnoses and formulate a working diagnosis for patients with traumatic injuries or exposed to environmental or toxicological emergencies. Students propose and implement ethical and culturally safe evidenced-based treatment plans that are supported by the use of clinical practice guidelines. There is a focus on out-of-hospital concepts of interprofessional collaboration in healthcare and with allied emergency services, multi-casualty incident management, as well as the safe application of clinical skills and paramedic equipment as appropriate for the level of graduate entry into paramedicine.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate safe use of paramedic equipment in simulated (out-of-hospital) environments, and safe clinical skills performance, including application of the NSQHS standard for preventing and controlling infections.
Plan and implement ethical and culturally safe care to adult patients experiencing traumatic, environmental, or toxicological emergencies in the out-of-hospital environment.

Analyse the current management guidelines of trauma, multi-casualty traumatic, environmental and toxicological emergencies to develop evidence-based treatments plans for the out of hospital environment.
Develop and implement safe and effective treatment plans for complex patient presentations involving trauma, multi-casualty traumatic, environmental and toxicological emergencies.
Communicate and act in a professional manner with patients, bystanders, paramedics, interprofessional healthcare teams and allied emergency service personnel;.

Apply knowledge of pathophysiology and aetiology (characteristics and consequences) of trauma, multi-casualty traumatic emergencies, environmental and toxicological emergencies in the out-of-hospital environment.

title: Ethics
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to a range of theories of ethics and central moral notions, including autonomy, justice, utility and sympathy. This theory is deployed in the interpretation and analysis of professional life. Students are introduced to the notion of a moral dilemma, and, more generally, the way in which theoretical notions can inform concrete ethical decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Have an advanced theoretical understanding of the central moral notions deployed in these theories.
Have an advanced understanding of a range of ethical theories.
Deploy complex theoretical ethical notions in concrete decision making.
Have a deep understanding of the notion of a moral dilemma.
Have an advanced understanding of research principles and methods employed in ethical theorising.

title: Ethics
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to a range of theories of ethics and central moral notions, including autonomy, justice, utility and sympathy. This theory is deployed in the interpretation and analysis of professional life. Students are introduced to the notion of a moral dilemma, and, more generally, the way in which theoretical notions can inform concrete ethical decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Have an advanced theoretical understanding of the central moral notions deployed in these theories.
Have a nuanced understanding of the moral bases of the professions, and the relevance of ethical theory to professional life.
Have an advanced understanding of a range of ethical theories.
Deploy complex theoretical ethical notions in concrete decision-making.
Have a deep understanding of the notion of a moral dilemma.

title: Ethics and Current Issues in Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject gives students an in-depth understanding of the key ethical and professional responsibilities and intellectual debates central to being a psychologist today. It aims to promote critical thinking and reflexivity in both their academic and practical dimensions. The subject has two areas of focus. First it examines the ethical context of, and current issues in psychological practice by examining current laws, codes and standards pertaining to professional conduct. It also aims to develop the problem solving skills necessary for professional and responsible practice in all fields of Psychology. The second focus is on various current theoretical, methodological and applied debates within Psychology and the ethical issues raised by these debates.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate familiarity with state and national codes of ethics and ethical guidelines for psychologists.
Demonstrate understanding of current debates about theory, method, and application of psychology.
Demonstrate understanding of professional practice issues.
Demonstrate familiarity with Australian legislation and laws that relate to the practice of psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding of the process of professional regulation for psychologists.
Demonstrate how an understanding of all of the above components of the subject form part of the discipline's calling to reflective, critical and ethical practice.
Apply an ethical decision making model to ethical dilemmas.
Demonstrate comprehension of the political history and sociocultural context of psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding of the critical importance of reflexivity in psychology.

title: Ethics and Professional Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to understand and examine a wide range of ethical and professional practice issues and concepts in the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) field. Students will analyse ethical issues and concepts surrounding the ICT profession as well as the current practices involving ICT. Different types of widely used principles and the mechanisms that are used to realise these principles will be examined. Various ethical implications will also be explored, especially with respect to privacy. Aspects of Information Technology (IT) professional practices will be investigated.
learning_outcomes: Discuss various philosophical theories of ethics and how these relate to the ethical and legal issues raised by current practices involving ICT.
Discuss professionalism and critically analyse and apply various concepts of professional ethics, in the context of the ICT profession.
Critique prevalent ICT related ethical issues, such as, privacy, intellectual property, and regulating the cyberspace.
Analyse and evaluate indigenous socio-professional ethical issues and principles.
Analyse ethical challenges of emerging and converging technologies.
Apply ethical theories and concepts to analyse ICT related ethical dilemmas.
prerequisites: ITC506: Topics in Information Technology Ethics

title: Ethics and Professional Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the intersection of ethics, professional practice and financial crime within organisational settings. It examines various means by which corrupt and unethical conduct can be combated within these settings. It analyses relevant ethical theories and perspectives and uses those to analyse case studies and develop professional and ethical responses to financial crime problems.
learning_outcomes: Interpret key ethical issues arising in the corporate and public sectors.
Analyse personal and organisational responses to ethical issues.
Design and justify a sustainable integrity system to address ethical issues in corporate and public sectors.
Identify and analyse structural and cultural features conducive to money laundering, terrorism financing, financial crime, corruption and serious ethical misconduct.
Demonstrate the communication, literacy, numeracy, research and digital skills required of a competent professional financial crime control practitioner.

title: Ethics
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students are introduced to a range of ethical theories, which they will apply to important moral questions. Central theoretical questions include: ‘Must we always bring about the morally best outcome?', ‘Are we ever permitted to prioritise ourselves over others?', and ‘Does the duty to bring about the best outcome ever conflict with the moral rights of others?'. Students are given the option to choose a specialised module, where ethical theory is applied to address real-world dilemmas. Dilemmas will be chosen from a range of contexts, including: criminal justice, climate change, resource allocation, care for vulnerable individuals, and biomedical ethics.
learning_outcomes: Find solutions to moral dilemmas.
Apply theoretical ethical notions in concrete decision making.
Critically evaluate a range of ethical theories.
Employ moral reasoning skills in evaluating a relevant field of practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of the central moral notions deployed in these theories.

title: Ethics and Social Work Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject critically explores the relationship between ethical theory, ethical principles, and professional practice. The overarching theme is the service ethic in social work theory and its implications for practice. Advanced reasoning skills will be developed as an essential foundation for critical thinking and ethical practice. The value and adequacy of professional codes as guides to practice will be considered, as well as the conflict between personal and professional values and the legal and organisational context of practice. The notion of moral risk and ethical responsibility, and ethical dilemmas will be considered. The subject will conclude with a discussion of ethical decision making and some common practice issues.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the relationship between ethical theories and principles, professional codes, and professional values.
Explain and critique the organisation, legal and human rights context of social work and their implications for professional practice.
Critically discuss particular ethical issues in professional practice.
Develop reasoned solutions to ethical dilemmas encountered in professional practice, based on evaluation of the application of ethical theories, principles and professional codes.
Apply the processes of ethical reasoning and ethical judgement.
Explain, apply and analyse the ethical theories and principles that form the basis of professional social work practice.

title: Ethics for a Dangerous World
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject students consider ethical issues concerning a range of emerging catastrophic risks that threaten the future of our society. These risks include pandemic diseases, terrorism, rising inequality, climate change, weapons of mass destruction, artificial intelligence, nanotechnology, disinformation and conspiracy theorizing. Students learn to apply ethical theorizing, combined with an understanding of the philosophical difficulties raised by consideration of potential catastrophic risks, to develop practical solutions to address these potential catastrophic problems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a significant degree of understanding of philosophical theories about the management of potentially catastrophic risks.

Apply skills of analysis and understanding of both philosophical ethics and philosophical theories about the management of potentially catastrophic risks to advance the clarification and resolution of particular moral issues addressed in the syllabus.
Demonstrate a significant degree of understanding of the practice of addressing ethical problems.
Demonstrate a significant degree of understanding of philosophical techniques of analysis and argument.

title: Ethics in Sport
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: While sport can have enormous benefits to both the practitioner and the community, such as creating unity and promoting positive social values, there are also practices within sport which can be considered to be highly questionable, even unethical. This subject explores the ethical dimensions of a practitioner's role within sport, by developing the student's awareness and appreciation of such issues.This subject will develop the student's ability to critically analyse many issues, practices and relationships within the sport profession, such as performance enhancing drugs and the ethical use and misuse of technology. The aim of this subject is to promote an ethical understanding of the practices of sport and the student functioning within those roles.Through successful completion of the subject, the student will have the ability to question their own morals, integrity and suppositions as future exercise science, sports media and sports management professionals.
learning_outcomes: Question and analyse their own cultural values and assumptions in regards to issues such as gender, sexuality and equality (through ethical enquiry).
Determine the significant relationship between ethics, the individual, social practice, and lifelong learning.
Critically explore the ethical theories as they pertain to sport, exercise, competition and professional practice.
Critically reflect on the nature and significance of both modern and post-modern ethical inquiry in sport.
Critically examine the ethical implications of professional practice in the field of Exercise Science, Sports Media and Sports Management.
Interrogate contemporary sporting discourses and practices to identify the global issues in sport and the role of the media.

title: Ethics of Corporate Governance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is about the governance of corporations and ethical issues relating to the control of corporations and their behaviour. It examines the inter-section of governance techniques with regulation, corporate law and ethical theories. The subject will examine how differing theories of the corporation impact on corporate governance, and how issues such as corporate social responsibility and the impact of recent events on the governance of a corporation.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate ethical principles, values, concepts and theories and apply these within a corporate governance context.
Describe and analyse how internal systems of control are developed and enforced and their relationship to external regulatory frameworks.
Evaluate the impact of recent events on corporate governance of Australian and foreign corporations.
Synthesise the conceptual arguments surrounding the ideas of governance, regulation and the theoretical models of the corporation.
Critically discuss the principles, modes and techniques of corporate governance and evaluate how these are applied in Australian companies.

title: Ethics Research Dissertation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The student will write a dissertation at Masters level which involves determining a topic in ethics studies, identifying a methodology, and carrying out supervised research into the topic in accordance with the methodology, reaching a conclusion which is located within a body of existing literature. The methodology may be empirical, legal, historical or theoretical.
learning_outcomes: Conduct a literature survey.
Present a logically structured paper on the scale of a long research article.
Undertake ethics research.

title: Ethics Research Dissertation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The student will write a dissertation at Masters level which involves determining a topic in ethics studies, identifying a methodology, and carrying out supervised research into the topic in accordance with the methodology, reaching a conclusion which is located within a body of existing literature. The methodology may be empirical, legal, historical or theoretical.
learning_outcomes: Undertake ethics research.
Conduct a literature survey.
Present a logically structured paper on the scale of a long research article.

title: Ethics, Advocacy and Human Rights
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject will critically evaluate law, ethics and human rights and their relationship in and to case management. Particular emphasis will be given to understanding the concept of advocacy and the ways in which graduates might positively influence legal and formal processes and outcomes for vulnerable and disadvantaged people. Students will be able to apply a decision-making framework that incorporates ethics, legal considerations, human rights and risk management in the context of operational management and budgetary responsibility.
learning_outcomes: Apply a decision-making framework that incorporates ethics, legal considerations, human rights and risk management in the context of operational management and budgetary responsibility.
Examine and apply the different types of advocacy required when working with people with reduced decision-making capacity and people facing discrimination.
Identify and analyse ethical approaches relevant to case management.

Identify and analyse value conflicts and ethical dilemmas that occur in a case management and care coordination setting and apply frameworks that are informed by legal statutory and ethical principles to resolve those issues.
Understand and critique how international human rights law has shaped government policy and impacts on individuals' rights.
Identify and apply the principles, skills and strategies involved in case management advocacy.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the values, principles and standards of practice articulated in the professional codes of ethics.

title: Ethics, Governance and Developments in Accounting Thought
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students examine, through the lens of ethics and governance, the developments in accounting theory and professional standards. Through an investigation of the prior research the subject provides insight into the search for a conceptual framework, the evaluation and comparison of various accounting models and discussion of contemporary management accounting and financial reporting issues.
learning_outcomes: Critique the role of theory in the nature and development of accounting as a discipline.

Compare and contrast the diverse perspectives which can be used to explain the development of accounting and the accounting profession including the impact of social change on accounting and vice versa.
Discuss and critically reflect on the role of ethics, professionalism and corporate governance theories to support the role of accounting as a profession.
Critically research and evaluate selected contemporary financial reporting and management accounting issues.
Critically appraise the objectives of accounting and relate them to the various concepts of accounting discussed in earlier subjects including attempts to develop and apply a conceptual framework.
prerequisites: ACG513: Contemporary Cost Accounting for Management Decision-making

title: Ethics, Identity and Colonisation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This interdisciplinary subject applies a decolonising lens to understand significant social, political, and philosophical questions about the self. The subject provides students with the opportunity to examine the impact of Australia’s colonisation on their understanding of Indigenous and non-Indigenous people’s experiences of self and relationship to others. Students will analyse the role of historical and contemporary forms of identification such as race, nation, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, class, and cultures in organising people's experience of everyday life and politics. Drawing on contemporary analytic metaphysics, students consider philosophical issues concerning the very nature of the self, the persistence of the self through time, and the relationship between selfhood and moral agency.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the role of identity within political, cultural, and socio-economic contexts, both Australian and international.
Examine the impact that colonialism and neo-colonialism has in Australia on a diverse range of conceptions of the self.
Critically evaluate the role of the self in moral agency, and interpersonal and intercultural relations.
Investigate how the metaphysics of survival illuminates colonising hegemonies which secure or disrupt one's self-conception.
Critically examine the complexity of individual and collective identity politics applying an Indigenist standpoint lens.
Critically evaluate contemporary philosophical and ethical theories about the nature of the self.

title: Ethics, Sustainability and Culture
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject students explore the nature of ethics. Major ethical theories are studied and applied to a range of business issues, including corporate social responsibility, ethics in the workplace, and discrimination. The subject includes a study of organisational and diverse societal cultures, and an examination of Indigenous histories, cultures and contemporary realities of Indigenous People in Australia. Environmental sustainability is considered from ethical, business and cultural perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the responsibility that business has to conduct its operations in a manner that does not threaten environmental sustainability.
Outline ethical theories in western moral philosophy and apply them in organisational contexts.
Describe the issues and debates associated with the concept of corporate social responsibility.
Critically reflect on their role as business professionals and how their future actions as business professionals can affect society in positive and negative ways.
Apply ethical theories to assess how successive Australian governments have treated Indigenous Australians, and discuss how an understanding of ethics can assist in creating a more equitable society.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of Indigenous Australian relationships to land.
Solve real life ethical dilemmas.

Demonstrate knowledge of the historical policies and practices that resulted in the marginalisation of Indigenous Australian peoples and critically discuss the links between past and present Indigenous socio-economic disadvantage.
Describe what constitutes a just society, and outline opposing arguments about justice and economic distribution.

title: Ethics, Law and Medical Science
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to acquaint students with current ethical and legal issues in biomedical, and science research and health care practice. Using a number of ethical principles, the subject examines the role of ethics and law, paying particular attention to issues such as genetic engineering and recombinant DNA research, human and foetal experimentation and reproductive technology. The subject also considers the rights of patients in medical research and treatment and the role of the law. The subject concludes with an examination of codes of ethics and the role and functioning of Institutional Ethics Committees.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the way in which the law protects individuals who are patients or subjects of research.
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of Institutional Ethics Committees in the regulation of research.
Apply these principles to case studies arising within biomedical research and health care practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of ethical principles derived from ethical theory and relevant to biomedical research and health care practice.
prerequisites: LAW131: Legal and Ethical Issues in Health

title: European Art 1850-1920
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the study of European art, focussing on those developments which established the foundations of modern art. The subject identifies some of the major concepts, themes, movements and stylistic developments in art during the period 1850-1920. Aspects of the history of the decorative arts and design and of photography are included.
learning_outcomes: Possess skills required for and confidence in analysing works of visual art.
Demonstrate knowledge of the major developments in art, design and photography in Europe during the period studied.
Be aware of some of the wider social, literary and philosophical backgrounds to the production of art during the period studied.

title: European Customs Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces students to the relationship between the Union Customs Code (UCC) and the consequential responsibilities of the European customs services and traders in respect of goods crossing national borders. The unit examines the scope of the legislation; the procedural context; and the relevant policy and practice that results in streamlined, uniform and simplified customs procedures, legal certainty and electronic environment. There is a particular focus on customs procedures for compliant and trustworthy economic operators (AEO).
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate critically customs law issues and their implications for regulatory practice including customs procedures for compliant and trustworthy economic operators.
Analyse issues that may arise in the customs environment in the context of legal requirements.
Make high level, independent judgements concerning the administration of customs procedures in conformity with the rules of European customs law.
Apply and assess critically the principles of European customs law to situations that they may face as customs officials.
Identify the sources of customs law including the UCC and key international instruments affecting Customs operations.
