Demonstrate an ability to contribute to policy-making processes which impact on customs practice and procedure with appropriate reference to relevant UCC provisions and national application.

title: Evaluating Health Care Services
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students develop and justify an evaluation plan for a health service or an aspect of health service delivery. As part of this, Students select and explain an evaluation model and implement an evaluation project. They also explore the place and value of implementation science related to health services and reflect on their personal capacity for undertaking future enquiry within the management role. The subject concludes with the submission of an evaluation business report or a publishable article.
learning_outcomes: be able to develop and justify an evaluation plan for a health service or an aspect of service delivery;
be able to report the results of an evaluation project via a business report or journal article.
be able to discuss the place and value of implementation science; and
be able to reflect on and critique their personal capacity for undertaking future enquiry within the health management or leadership role;
be able to discuss evaluation as a function of management;
be able to compare various approaches to evaluation and performance improvement in health service organisations;

title: Evaluating Human Resources
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is focused on examining the importance of measuring the effectiveness of the human resource management (HRM) function, and individual human resource activities. It provides an introduction to specific human resource measurement techniques.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine the importance of measuring HRM initiatives to demonstrate the value of HRM activities.
Describe and evaluate the application of various evaluation techniques.
Identify and apply the main ethical considerations in relation to evaluating the HRM function and activities.
Design and propose tailored solutions to Human Capital Analytics to meet specific business needs.
Offer viable and justifiable solutions in relation to identified business problems.

title: Evaluation in Clinical Education
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject applies the principle of transformative learning to explore the role of evaluation in the planning and delivery of education in a clinical context. The sources of information that can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of clinical education will be reviewed. Students will also learn how to appraise existing assessment tools and learning resources. A variety of learning and teaching models will be evaluated. Students will critically reflect on their own individual strengths and areas for development in the delivery of clinical education, including examining the possibility of bias as an assessor, and reflecting on specific challenges to the role of the clinical educator. Finally, students will learn about the role of continuing professional development for the clinical educator and establish a professional portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise the reliability and validity of a range of contemporary clinical assessment tools.
Outline strategies to plan and document continuing professional development to maintain clinical proficiency and teaching and learning practices.
Critically appraise the currency, reliability and relevance of existing learning resources for a specific learning need.
Apply evidence-informed critical reflection models to develop own teaching and assessment practices.
Critically evaluate the impact of a clinical education initiative on the learning needs of clinicians.
Evaluate a range of clinical education models (clinical supervision, preceptorship, mentoring and clinical facilitation).
prerequisites: HLT542: Professional Practice in Clinical Education
HLT542: Professional Practice in Clinical Education

title: Doctorate Research Plan
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject provides students with training in research methods and study design. Through professional workplace exposures and discussion with the supervisory team, students identify gaps in the existing knowledge and formulate research questions and hypotheses for the clinical research project of the Doctor of Veterinary Studies and will develop a proposal and planning for the project. The students will undertake a critical analysis of (1) theoretical knowledge, existing knowledge and professional practice in the field of investigation, (2) the identified research questions and (3) available research methods and prepare a literature review. Students will provide a presentation of the research proposal and plan. Candidates obtain all the necessary approvals for the project.
learning_outcomes: Identify and communicate research questions to develop new knowledge for professional practice.
Demonstrate advanced cognitive skills and expert understanding of theoretical and current knowledge and critical reflection on that knowledge and professional practice.
Demonstrate an advanced level of knowledge at the frontier of a field of work relevant to the identified research question.
Design, critique and communicate appropriate research plans for clinical research to provide original contributions to knowledge in the context of professional practice.

title: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop a critical knowledge of English language and literacy as socio-cultural practice and investigate the everyday literacy practices of human beings, particularly young children. Students will develop an understanding of evidence-based practices across the following elements: oral language, phonemic awareness, comprehension, vocabulary, phonics and fluency. They will learn how oral language is acquired, and explore the relationships between language, literacy and literature. They will explore the features of texts (oral, written, visual and multimodal) which support literacy learning and teaching of reading for young children between 0 and 8 years of age.
learning_outcomes: Articulate knowledge about phonics and phonemic awareness and their relationship to everyday language and literacy practices of young children.
Dxplain how texts (literary, factual, multimodal and digital) support the literacy learning of young children between 0 and 8 years of age.
Discuss transitions (for example, to preschool, to school, to new social contexts) as related to language, learning and literacy practices.
Articulate knowledge of English language and literacy as socio-cultural practice.
Describe the relationship between language, literacy and literature.
Explain connections between play, language and learning.
Describe different aspects of reading and writing as these relate to language, learning and literature, and everyday literacy practices.
Discuss oral language acquisition and the everyday language and literacy practices of young children.
prerequisites: EMC203: Play and Investigation as Curriculum (Literacy)
EML110: English 1: Language as Social Practice
EML449: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice
EPT174: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice

title: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop a critical knowledge of English language and literacy as sociocultural practice and investigate the everyday literacy practices of human beings, particularly young children. Students will develop an understanding of evidence-based practices across the following elements: oral language, phonemic awareness, comprehension, vocabulary, phonics and fluency. They will learn how oral language is acquired in first and additional languages, and explore the relationships between language, literacy and literature. Students will explore the features of oral, written, visual and multimodal texts and the ways these variously support language and literacy learning and the teaching of reading and writing for young children between 0 and 8 years of age. Students will also plan appropriate and targeted professional learning goals, with an early opportunity to evaluate, reflect on and improve their personal literacy levels measured against the standards required for Australian teachers.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of English language and literacy as sociocultural practice.
Critique ways different texts (literary, factual, multimodal and digital) support the language and literacy learning of young children between 0 and 8 years of age.

Explain the complexities of different kinds of social and educational transitions (for example, to preschool, to school, to new social and cultural contexts) as related to language, learning and literacy practices.

Demonstrate a critical understanding of oral language acquisition and the everyday language and literacy practices of young children and First Nations children and those for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D).
Explain succinctly the connections between play, language and learning.
Transmit knowledge about phonics and phonemic awareness and their relationship to everyday language and literacy practices of young children.
Describe the relationship between language, literacy and literature.
Evaluate how different aspects of reading and writing relate to language, learning and literature, and everyday literacy practices.
prerequisites: EML106: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice

title: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop a critical knowledge of English language and literacy as socio-cultural practice and investigate the everyday literacy practices of human beings, particularly young children. Students will develop an understanding of evidence-based practices across the following elements: oral language, phonemic awareness, comprehension and vocabulary. They will learn how oral language is acquired, and explore the relationships between language, literacy and literature. They will explore the features of texts (oral, written, visual and multimodal) which support literacy learning and teaching of reading for young children between 0 and 8 years of age.
learning_outcomes: Explain connections between play, language and learning.
Articulate knowledge about phonemic awareness and its relationship to everyday language and literacy practices of young children.
Describe different aspects of reading and writing as these relate to language, learning and literature, and everyday literacy practices.
Describe the relationship between language, literacy and literature.
Articulate knowledge of English language and literacy as socio-cultural practice.
Discuss oral language acquisition and the everyday language and literacy practices of young children.
Explain how texts (literary, factual, multimodal and digital) support the literacy learning of young children between 0 and 8 years of age.
Discuss transitions (for example, to preschool, to school, to new social contexts) as related to language, learning and literacy practices.
prerequisites: EMC203: Play and Investigation as Curriculum (Literacy)
EML106: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice
EML110: English 1: Language as Social Practice
EML449: Everyday Language and Literacies: Learning and Practice

title: Evidence and Investigation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the process of identifying, recovering and presenting evidence obtained in the course of investigations. Using recent case studies and court decisions from a number of different jurisdictions, the subject examines in detail the ethical and legal complexities surrounding the gathering and presenting of evidence. Students are challenged to ensure that evidence is gathered in a manner which avoids common pitfalls often experienced by investigators. Emphasis is placed on the need to locate all facts in an investigation, both inculpatory and exculpatory. The subject also explores management processes that ensure an ethical investigation is carried out, and the ethical actions of those involved in all stages of the investigation.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the importance of maintaining the integrity of evidence from crime scene to court.
Apply knowledge and skills to plan, lead and conduct criminal investigations in accordance with ethical, legal, operational and organisational frameworks.
Identify and discuss legal constraints for lawful facilitation of evidence collection and use in criminal proceedings.
Critically analyse the importance of ethics in the investigation of criminal matters.
Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.

title: Evidence Based Practice in Podiatry
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides final year students with the opportunity to critically appraise and reflect on contexts and issues relevant to the contemporary practice of podiatry. Students will extend foundational knowledge of research to critically evaluate the value of podiatry practice knowledge. Critique of a range of relevant research methodologies will enable students to further develop skills in evaluating the evidence base. Students will have the opportunity to research a contemporary issue of relevance to the podiatry profession and will undertake a review of the literature. This subject will facilitate the student's communication skills through oral presentation of a literature review to a group of peers, academics and practitioners. The purpose of this subject is to facilitate skill development in the use of online databases, critical analysis of the literature and writing for research, to encourage students to consider their role as potential practitioner-researchers. This subject enables students to transition from the role of student to the role of new graduate podiatrist.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the role of research and evidence-based practice in informing practice knowledge.
Critically reflect on and self-evaluate their contribution to practice as a new graduate podiatrist.
Communicate a critical review of practice knowledge effectively to an audience of peers, academics and practitioners.
Critically analyse the use of a range of research methodologies used to explore podiatric practice.
Demonstrate the graduate entry-level podiatry professional capabilities for language, literacy and numeracy.
Critique a contemporary practice issue in podiatry from a quality improvement perspective.
prerequisites: POD415: Evidence Based Practice in Podiatry
POD415: Evidence Based Practice in Podiatry
HIP202: Evidence-Based Health Practice and Research
HIP102: Research Foundations for Health, Sports and Exercise Sciences

title: Evidence in Practice 2
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds directly from the previous Evidence in Practice Subject. Students integrate knowledge of human anatomy and physiology across the lifespan when undertaking the skills and techniques required to safely obtain, interpret and document a range of systematic assessments. Students develop medication calculation skills and apply clinical reasoning for the safe, legal and evidence-based administration of medications via oral and parenteral routes. Students will demonstrate readiness for their next professional experience placement subject through practising within the framework of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice and the Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) in the simulation learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Describe their actions, behaviours, attitudes, decisions, judgements, assumptions and scope of practice and identify areas for further development to support future professional experience placements and registered nurse practice.
Explain the principles of clinical risk and patient safety in acute care environments.
Demonstrate safe, legal and evidence-based preparation and administration of medications.
Explain the patient's condition(s) to justify the administration of medications.
Systematically collect, evaluate and compare focused subjective and objective assessment data and use clinical reasoning to determine the next appropriate steps.
Adapt communication techniques to meet the varying needs of people.

title: Evidence in Practice 3
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds directly from the previous Evidence in Practice subjects. A systems based approach is used to support students develop the psychomotor skills required to undertake person-centred, comprehensive and evidence-based assessments and interventions for people experiencing common health conditions across the lifespan. There is a specific focus on developing skills required for rural and remote practice. Students develop capacity to apply industry policies, pathways, guidelines and evidence-based resources for translation into practice. Students further develop medication calculation skills and apply clinical reasoning for the safe, legal and evidence-based administration of medications and fluids via the intravenous route. Students will demonstrate readiness for their next professional experience placement subject through practising within the framework of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice and the Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) in the simulation learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate safe, legal and evidence-based preparation and administration of intravenous medications and fluids.
Integrate clinical reasoning when undertaking interventions for people experiencing a range of conditions.
Explain the person's condition(s) to justify selected interventions including the administration of intravenous medications and fluids.
Apply a reflective framework to analyse individual practice and identify areas for further development to support future professional experience placements and practice as a registered nurse.
Integrate technology and data to improve work practices and support patient interaction with healthcare services and information.

title: Evidence in Practice 5
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds directly from the previous Evidence in Practice subjects. Students focus on coordination of care for people across the lifespan within a diverse range of acute health settings. Students are exposed to multiple responsibilities and are challenged to undertake timely, skilled and comprehensive patient assessments, critically examine patient assessment data to identify and prioritise patient needs, clinically reason to determine appropriate next steps and evaluate outcomes of interventions with consideration to clinical risk and patient safety. Students are challenged to enhance their skills for effective communication within a range of complex and time sensitive clinical situations, including during virtual assessment in rural and remote settings. Students will demonstrate readiness for their next professional experience placement subject through practising within the framework of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice and the Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) in the simulation learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on personal and professional practice to establish goals for future professional development.
Demonstrate complex psychomotor skills to deliver safe, timely and quality nursing care as part of a broader plan for care.
Critique patient assessment data to identify and prioritise patient needs and clinically reason to determine appropriate next steps within the context of clinical deterioration.
Develop comprehensive and person-centred plans for coordinating care in acute health settings.
Demonstrate effective communication and teamwork within complex and time sensitive clinical situations.

title: Evidence in Practice 6
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds directly from the previous Evidence in Practice subjects and is the final simulation based learning subject in the Bachelor of Nursing program. Students apply leadership skills and are challenged to build on their communication for effective interprofessional collaboration across a variety of health contexts and settings. Students will apply safe delegation and supervision skills when coordinating care for multiple people across the lifespan. Students will demonstrate readiness for professional practice through practising within the framework of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice and the Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) in the simulation learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate leadership when communicating with a variety of stakeholders across a range of interdisciplinary health contexts.
Plan and implement person-centred, comprehensive, evidence based and holistic assessments and interventions.
Demonstrate leadership when coordinating care across a range of interdisciplinary health contexts.
Critically reflect to demonstrate that individual practice meets the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia Registered Nurse Standards for Practice.

title: Evidence Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the practical and theoretical knowledge required for aspects of evidence and procedure within the criminal justice system in New South Wales. It explores the major evidential and procedural issues involved in underpinning the prosecution of criminal matters, including the rules governing the admissibility of evidence. The Evidence Act 1995 (NSW) and the Uniform Evidence Law form the backbone of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and discuss the interaction of evidence law and substantive criminal law.
Evaluate critically the function of judicial discretion within the context of the NSW adversarial system.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of public policy reform and developments in international law on evidentiary law within NSW.
Evaluate the historical, social, political, and ethical factors that impact upon the contemporary adversarial system.
Demonstrate critical awareness of the problems associated with the imposition of the rules of admissibility of evidence.
Analyse and synthesise relevant factual, legal and policy issues relating to evidence.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the major principles of evidence as they apply in the state of New South Wales.
Apply rules of evidence, and standards of admissibility, in order to resolve problem-based scenarios.

title: Evidence-Based Practice in Clinical Leadership
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the advanced principles and philosophy underpinning evidence-based practice (EBP) and the role EBP plays in provisioning clinical leadership. In that context, this subject develops insights and capability in the application of EBP in shaping thinking, education and action that drives leadership within the clinical domain. This subject focuses on the development of capability for identifying clinical uncertainty, acquiring relevant evidence, appraising evidence in the context of the problem, application and integration of information in decision making, and critically evaluating and reflecting on the learning. To that end, the subject includes high-level problem solving, critical thinking and appraisal, clinical judgement and decision making, reflection and reflective practice, and synthesis of new knowledge in complex environments.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and reflect on the role of EBP in improving practice and in implementing innovation in practice.

Analyse and address a clinical problem through enquiry and rigorous critical appraisal to develop and evaluate an EBP practice initiative within the context of their own practice and communicate findings to contribute to professional practice.
Apply knowledge and evidence to evaluate grounded practice.
Retrieve relevant information from reliable sources and apply advanced cognitive and research skills in analysis and synthesis of information for problem solving in complex environments.
Develop, justify and apply an appraisal framework within the context of practice.

title: Evolution of Australian Sport
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will critically examine the historical, political and social significance of elite and professional sport in Australia. Beginning with the emergence of international competition in the late nineteenth century, students will explore the evolution and development of Australian sport at national and international levels. Students will specifically examine the significance of Australia's participation in major sporting events such as the Olympic and Commonwealth Games.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the historical significance of leisure, clubs, pubs and public spaces to the evolution of sport in Australia.
Discuss the historical factors relevant to the emergence of elite and professional sports in Australia.
Articulate the role and significance of Australia's participation in major sporting events such as the Olympic and Commonwealth Games.
Explain the connection between Australian national identity and international sporting success.
Discuss the emergence and growth of Australian sport at a national and international level.

title: Evolving Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a foundational understanding of biomechanics and properties of human tissues, applied to the practice of physiotherapy. Students will build on their foundational skills in physiotherapy practice and client care in the context of functional human movement. Using an evidence-based practice framework, students will utilise their foundational knowledge of anatomy and physiology to learn about the mechanical properties of tissues, bones and ligaments how this relates to physiotherapy assessment and management. Students will learn how materials in the human body respond to the use of selected electrophysical agents used in contemporary physiotherapy practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the concepts of contemporary pain science in the application of electro-physical agents, including ice and heat.
Discuss the application of electro-physical agents, including ice and heat in contemporary physiotherapy practice.
Search, find and apply evidence to physiotherapy scenarios and create and present the information in multimodal digital formats.
Demonstrate skills in observation and digital technologies to assess, measure and analyse human movement.
Describe the properties of soft tissues and their components in relation to development, aging, injury, pathology and physiotherapy management.
Describe the properties of bone, fracture healing, joint replacements and fracture fixation and the impacts on physiotherapy management.

title: Executive Command
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The student is required to conduct research into a current problem/issue relevant to their profession. Students will report the findings of their research as portfolios. A portfolio consists of a compilation of scholarly documents written by the student which can include academic or professional journal articles and conference papers, plans, and reports and policy documents. The portfolio is submitted with an analysis/exegesis which integrates the research within the profession while demonstrating academic and professional development over the course of study. The maximum length for the analysis/exegesis that is presented to support the portfolio shall be 30,000 words.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate a range of case studies in varying styles of executive leadership.
Analyse and evaluate a range of case studies in the application of executive leadership to actual situations both internal and external to policing.
Identify and discuss their professional development needs.
Demonstrate an understanding of organisational behaviour.
Demonstrate an understanding of a range of practical approaches to executive leadership.
Demonstrate an understanding of the major theoretical approaches to executive leadership.
Demonstrate an understanding of the processes of executive leadership as gained from experienced senior mentors.
Conduct research and reflect on policing problems.
Demonstrate an understanding and analyse differences and similarities that exist in executive leadership within law enforcement and other government security and emergency roles.
Evaluate organisational issues.

title: Excise
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an in-depth study of the principles and workings of excise taxation. The course examines the significance of excise to providing governments with secure streams of revenue, as well as the growing trend to use excise taxation as a means of implementing other policy objectives.
learning_outcomes: Explain and discuss critically the rights and responsibilities of States in using excise to achieve certain policy objectives.

Conduct a comparative analysis of relevant excise compliance models including analysing and critically assessing the regulatory frameworks of different countries against best practice and established international standards.
Formulate appropriate and well-developed policy and legal advice for border managers and/or regulators on excise administration and to be able to communicate that advice to others.
Explain and discuss critically the main principles which govern excise taxation.

Locate and use key international instruments and research appropriate compliance responses to excise taxation and apply that research to practical and theoretical situations that they may face as border regulators and/or managers.

Identify and explain the practical impact of excise beyond revenue generation including analysing and critically assessing the regulatory frameworks of different countries against best practice and established international standards.

title: Executive Leadership in Law Enforcement and Security
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject analyses the principles, dimensions and qualities of contemporary executive leadership in the context of policing, law enforcement, emergency service and security organisations. There will be particular emphasis on the challenges and dynamics of strategic leadership in the public sector. It explores the dynamics of operational demands from the leadership perspective and examines the impact of political and social influences.
learning_outcomes: Apply established leadership theories to the law enforcement and security context and critically analyse the application of these with reference to your professional practice.

Plan and execute a substantial piece of scholarship which demonstrates a capacity to locate and analyse relevant theory and research in the field of leadership in law enforcement and security and apply that theory and research to professional leadership practice.

Demonstrate an ability to analyse the contextual influences on leadership in the law enforcement and security contexts and to develop a strategic leadership approach capable of being communicated to a range of professional and high level audiences.
Investigate, analyse and synthesise the broad body of knowledge of the history and context of leadership in law enforcement and security, including relevant developments overseas.

Demonstrate mastery of the key theoretical underpinnings in leadership generally, public sector leadership, and law enforcement and security leadership, and critically reflect on the impact of these on professional practice.

title: Exercise for Health and Fitness
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Health and wellness are enhanced through participation in regular physical activity and improved fitness. In this subject, students will develop their capacity to plan and deliver safe and effective exercise programs to achieve fundamental health and fitness outcomes. Students will examine concepts of health and wellness, define and distinguish between physical activity and exercise, and explore the health-related components of fitness. Communication with clients, collaborative goals, health screening and risk appraisals are key areas of study. Students will develop practical skills for various fitness modalities and exercise instruction for both individuals and groups.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a variety of physical conditioning activities with technical proficiency.
Perform pre-screening and consultations to establish client risk for exercise prescription, goals and needs.
Provide safe and effective instructions to clients when delivering individual and group exercise sessions.
Discuss the influence of physical activity, exercise, and fitness on dimensions of health, wellness, and quality of life.
Design and deliver a short-term exercise program using a variety of exercise modalities to achieve health and fitness outcomes.
Identify and explain the use of appropriate assessments and exercise intervention requirements relative to clients' needs and goals.
prerequisites: EHR221: Exercise for Health and Fitness

title: Exercise for Metabolic and Mental Health Conditions
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: The prevalence of metabolic, renal and mental health conditions in Australia has increased rapidly in recent years, with a significant impact on both the quality of life and life expectancy. In this subject students will investigate physiological mechanisms involved in the pathophysiology of metabolic, renal and mental health conditions. Students will develop their ability to apply evidence-based strategies to manage clients with a range of metabolic, renal and mental health conditions. Students will develop the knowledge and skills required to perform initial assessments, interpret assessment outcomes and apply safe and effective exercise interventions for people with metabolic, renal and mental health conditions. Students will develop the skills to deliver culturally relevant assessments and interventions for a broad range of clients. Students will develop practical skills pertinent to the assessment and management of clients with complex metabolic, renal and/or mental health presentations.
learning_outcomes: Describe the pathophysiology of metabolic, renal and mental health conditions and evaluate pertinent outcomes when assessing people living with complex needs.
Develop and apply safe and effective assessments for clients living with metabolic, renal and/or mental health conditions.

Use inclusive and culturally responsive practices to communicate professionally and interact empathetically with a diverse range of people living with metabolic, renal and/or mental health conditions.
Develop evidence-based exercise prescription, interventions, and recommendations for the management of metabolic, renal and mental health conditions.
Identify and respond appropriately to considerations and contraindications when applying exercise assessments and interventions for people living with metabolic, renal and mental health conditions.

title: Exercise for Neurological and Neuromuscular Conditions
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In Australia, more than one in three people will experience a neurological or neuromuscular condition in their lifetime which may impact significantly on both their quality of life and life expectancy. Students will develop the knowledge, skills and competencies required to work safely and effectively with clients with neurological and neuromuscular conditions. Students will develop knowledge and comprehension of the structure and function of the sensory-motor system, pathophysiology, motor dysfunction, investigation and treatment, including exercise. After completing this subject, students will be able to design, deliver, and adapt safe and effective exercise interventions to enhance health status and functional outcomes in persons with a wide range of movement disorders.
learning_outcomes: Explain the structure and function of sensory-motor systems and their contributions to movement control and functional performance.
Use knowledge of sensory-motor pathophysiology to recognise implications for health status and movement dysfunction.

Demonstrate critical thinking and reflective practice when designing, adapting, and evaluating inclusive and culturally responsive interventions to provide value-based care for a diverse range of people living with movement disorders.
Select, apply, and interpret appropriate assessments relevant to persons living with sensory-motor impairments and use data obtained to inform clinical decision making and person-centred care.
Describe the investigative techniques and holistic management strategies for a range of movement-related disorders.

title: Exercise Prescription for Cancer Management
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Cancer is the leading cause of total disease burden in Australia, with a significant impact on both the quality of life and life expectancy for many Australians. Students will develop the knowledge, skills and competencies required by graduate exercise physiologists to work safely and effectively with clients with a cancer history. Emphasis is placed on developing knowledge and comprehension of cancer pathophysiology, investigation and treatment, and evidence-based applications for exercise prescription for cancer management. After completing this subject, students will be able to conduct effective initial consultations to evaluate the exercise needs of clients with a history of cancer. Students will also be able to design and deliver safe exercise assessments and lifestyle interventions to evaluate and improve the physical fitness, health, and wellbeing across all phases of cancer treatment and management.
learning_outcomes: Use inclusive and culturally responsive practices to apply knowledge of the effects of exercise and lifestyle factors on cancer prevention and management to improve health status and quality of life when working with diverse populations.
Demonstrate the ability to design and deliver effective, person-centred exercise interventions across the cancer journey using sound clinical reasoning.
Apply behavioural strategies to demonstrate empathy and promote exercise motivation and adherence in persons experiencing psychosocial distress.
Describe the investigative techniques and treatment strategies for a broad range of cancers.
Explain the pathophysiology of cancer, risk factors, disease development, reoccurrence and survival.
Perform effective initial consultations and appropriate assessments for people living with cancer to identify needs and establish goals for exercise participation.

title: Exercise Prescription for Cardiopulmonary Conditions
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Cardiopulmonary diseases are a significant disease and cost burden to the health care system in Australia. Students will develop the knowledge, skills, and competencies to work safely and effectively with clients with cardiopulmonary conditions. Knowledge and comprehension of cardiopulmonary pathophysiology, including aetiology and risk factors, diagnostic procedures, treatments and applications will be used for exercise prescription for the management of cardiopulmonary conditions. After completing this subject, students will be able to conduct effective initial consultations, design and deliver safe and effective exercise assessments and lifestyle interventions in a culturally safe manner, evaluate physical fitness, and improve health and wellbeing of people with chronic and complex cardiopulmonary conditions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the capacity to promote inclusion and apply culturally responsive practices when working with diverse populations.
Formulate evidence-based exercise interventions and recommendations to improve health status for people living with cardiopulmonary conditions.
Formulate, critique and interpret results of person-centred assessments of cardiopulmonary function.
Describe diagnostic techniques and the effect of treatments on acute and chronic exercise responses in people living with cardiopulmonary conditions.
Explain the pathophysiology of cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions as it relates to exercise physiology.
Outline the risk factors, complications and contraindications that must be accounted for when prescribing exercise interventions to people living with cardiopulmonary conditions.

title: Exercise, Health and Disease
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the relationship between physical activity and health. Emphasis is placed on examining evidence justifying the application of exercise prescription in the primary, secondary and tertiary prevention of selected cardiovascular, metabolic, respiratory, neurological and musculoskeletal diseases. The subject will investigate a range of topics including pathophysiology, risk assessment and exercise testing and programming with a particular focus on the exercise dose response. Physical activity, health and exercise prescription issues in pregnancy and older adults are also addressed.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the contributions of health-related agencies and the impact of public policy on physical activity and sedentary behaviours at the population level.
Explain the role of sedentary behaviour and physical activity in the aetiology, prevention and management of lifestyle-related chronic diseases.
Utilise an exercise management approach in developing individualised and community-based exercise interventions for the prevention of selected lifestyle-related chronic diseases.
Relate the benefits and risks of physical activity and apply evidence-based best practice to recommend appropriate levels of physical activity for various populations and sub-groups.
Analyse and evaluate the impact of the social determinants of health in relation to population characteristics and needs, using these to inform development of appropriate interventions.
Apply evidence-based guidelines for optimising physical activity and reducing sedentary behaviour throughout the lifespan.

title: Experiencing Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject explores contemporary scientific concepts utilizing common resources that students can modify in their future careers to inspire the next generation of scientists. Students will study science as a human activity that has progressed over time to answer interesting and important questions and contribute to culture and society. The subject provides students with experiences in scientific process, develops their scientific knowledge, and expands skills in applying scientific methodology to everyday applications. Further, the subject will allow students to experience the scientific process in exciting ways to develop a relationship with the natural world.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of what constitutes scientifically valid evidence and how it is obtained.
Demonstrate the capacity to engage in scientific inquiry using the scientific method and logical reasoning.
Demonstrate a capacity to engage proactively with issues related to public perception of science and to scientific ethics.
Conduct observational scientific investigations independently.
Demonstrate the application of science content.
Identify the differences between scientific and general knowledge as well as between science and pseudo-science, and evaluate how science and societal values interact.
Identify and critique alternative conceptions associated with science, including critique of science for validity.

title: Experimental Design
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore ways of combining digital applications with a variety of creative techniques and processes. The emphasis will be on developing a thorough analysis of a design challenge and exploring form, function and approach leading to innovative and imaginative solutions. The students will document and critically examine all stages of the project from their initial concepts through to completion. Sustainability, as well as cultural and ethical issues, will be considered throughout the design process.
learning_outcomes: Research, design, develop and produce a resolved design outcome in the context of contemporary design practice.
Apply the principles involved in design for a wide variety of outcomes including a sensitivity to environmental, cultural and ethical issues.
Critically analyse and validate various experimental techniques and processes as a means to producing design solutions.
Demonstrate an understanding of a broad range of design options and associated skills and their application in design.
Critically evaluate ideas from various perspectives (designer, client and consumer) throughout the design process using prototyping, user testing, self-evaluation and critiquing.
Apply technical, creative and theoretical skills to take an idea from concept to production ready artwork.

title: Experimental Design and Analysis
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Proper experimental design is a prerequisite to the efficient and cost effective resolution of comparative quantitative research questions. This subject introduces experimental design and analysis by examples and by the study of the underlying linear model. Use of appropriate computer packages allows testing of assumptions and investigation of advanced topics. Extensions of the basic methodology are explored.
learning_outcomes: Communicate results and justify interpretations in terms of the original problem.
Perform the analysis of such experiments using appropriate statistical protocols.
Perform design and analysis tasks on recognised software platforms.
Identify situations for which a linear model is appropriate.
Design, and check the design of, basic experiments.
Critically test any assumptions underpinning the use of the linear model.

title: Experimental Design and Analysis (PG)
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Proper experimental design and sampling is a prerequisite to the efficient and cost effective resolution of comparative quantitative research questions. This subject introduces experimental design based analysis and sampling techniques through the use of examples from research and professional settings. It also extends the basic methodology with applications. Students will gain experience in using software packages, and in evaluating and presenting results in the form of a standard statistical report as used in professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Perform the analysis of such experiments using appropriate statistical protocols.
Evaluate and present results, with an integrated understanding of the underlying theory, in the form of a standard statistical report.
Critically test any assumptions underpinning the use of the linear model.
Design, and check the design of, standard experiments reflective of professional practice.
Demonstrate basic knowledge of survey methods and its application to a wide range of problems.
Perform design and analysis tasks on recognised software platforms.
Communicate results and justify interpretations in terms of the original problem with logic and precision.

title: Experimental Photography
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the practice of analogue photography and the role that it played in shaping modern photographic practices. This will be underpinned by critical analyses of historical and contemporary photographic practices and an exploration of the analogue camera. Students will experience hands-on learning that will immerse thems in analogue and experimental photographic techniques. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
learning_outcomes: Determine appropriate photographic techniques and independently operate in a range of environments.
Skilfully demonstrate the fundamentals of representation, aesthetics and meaning in photographic imagery.
Proficiently prepare photographic work for presentation in a range of analogue formats.
Critically analyse photographic works in terms of their historical and contemporary provenance.
Demonstrate a deep knowledge of the principles and workings of selected analogue photographic processes.
Employ current concepts of photographic analysis.

title: Experimental Production and Applied Theatre
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject students research, analyse, plan and produce a range of collaborative productions responding to a range of social and cultural issues. Students are exposed to a broad survey of historic and contemporary productions including screen based drama, drama in non-traditional settings, and socially engaged performance practices.
learning_outcomes: Describe a range of cultural, political, environmental or economic drivers that inform innovative production.
Critique their own work and the work of their peers.
Test and evaluate ideas from various perspectives (author and audience) through user testing, self-evaluation and critique.
Critically analyse and validate various exploratory techniques and processes as a means of producing experimental innovative productions.
Apply technical, creative and theoretical skills to take an idea from concept to production in innovative and socially engaged dramatic contexts.

title: Exploring Communication Practice
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the knowledge, skills and abilities required to understand the commonalities and differences between the specialised fields of strategic communication, news and media, and design and content creation. Students apply the communication planning cycle in a multidisciplinary context to develop their understanding of practice.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on and review their developing understanding of practice.
Apply the communication planning cycle.
Work effectively in a multidisciplinary project team.
Understand how to plan and manage the production of communication content.
Explain the practical commonalities and differences between strategic communication, news and media, and design and content creation.

title: Exploring Literature
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop professional skills in the appreciation and critical evaluation of literature through immersion in a wide variety of genres, explicit instruction in theories and frameworks, critical analysis of research and reflexive transformation of their practice. Exploration requires movement from the known to the unknown and in this sense the student will examine their existing approaches to literature and challenge these with new models, forms and modes. Students will design a web folio of literature-based learning and connections.
learning_outcomes: Understand the unique and essential role of literature in the curriculum of the twenty-first century.
Demonstrate a grounded understanding of narratology and literary theory.
Exhibit professional judgement and creativity in the selection of literary texts.

title: Extended Care Clinical Management
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the students' knowledge and experience as a paramedic as a number of clinical situations are contextualised to the extended care paramedic setting. During this subject the student will learn about analgesia and sedation, trauma, mental health, infections, wound care management, and palliative care. This subject will address these topics with a focus on primary health care patient assessment, treatment, case management and identification of transport, referral or field care options.
learning_outcomes: Be able to implement safe and appropriate patient assessment and management strategies derived from current evidence based knowledge to palliative care in the extended care paramedic setting.
Be able to apply a complex knowledge of the pharmacology of analgesia and sedation to the safe and effective provision of extended care interventions.
Be able to apply a complex and current knowledge of advanced wound care management principles as applicable to extended care paramedics.

Be able to make informed and safe clinical decisions based on a knowledge of the pathophysiological processes of trauma conditions and commonly encountered infections in the extended care paramedic setting.

Be able to implement safe and appropriate patient assessment, therapeutic intervention, and management strategies derived from current evidence based knowledge to mental health care in the extended care paramedic setting.
Be able to apply a knowledge of pharmacology to the safe and effective selection and administration of medications for commonly encountered infections in the extended care paramedic setting.

title: Exploring the Breadth of Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will facilitate an integrated approach to building clinical knowledge and skills across areas of physiotherapy. Students will build on their clinical knowledge and skills in acute care, rehabilitation and community physiotherapy. Students in this subject will extend their knowledge around the business of physiotherapy in terms of sustainable practice, scope of physiotherapy practice and other key understandings around the practice of physiotherapy.
learning_outcomes: Advocate for physiotherapy that is supported by evidence, including best available research evidence.
Apply the concepts of sustainable practice to the business of physiotherapy.

Demonstrate adaptive, respectful and responsive communication (in all forms) to reflect the purpose, context, culture, literacy, ethical, legal and/or professional requirements of the task or interaction.
Create and share information in multimodal digital formats.
Analyse situations that are outside the physiotherapy scope of expertise or competence and take appropriate action.
Locate, evaluate, use and integrate evidence-based information to inform decision making, and develop and guide their own knowledge, learning and practice.
Justify physiotherapy options to manage a client's presenting problems.
prerequisites: PHS406: Advanced Preparation for Physiotherapy Practice
PHS406: Advanced Preparation for Physiotherapy Practice

title: Extended Care Skills
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to enable students in the Extended Care Stream of the Master of Paramedicine to make a successful transition to the role of an extended care paramedic. The subject will build on students' previous paramedic qualifications and experience to focus their clinical practice on the extended care skills implemented by advanced paramedics. Students will have an opportunity to integrate theory into practice under supervision in controlled environments, including high fidelity clinical simulation.
learning_outcomes: Describe and demonstrate situational awareness, scene safety and effective communication with allied health care professionals.
Implement and justify problem solving and clinical decision making skills that allow them to identify, analyse and apply appropriate knowledge to new problems.
Demonstrate the ability to complete advanced extended care paramedic skills.
Critically evaluate and implement extended care management of trauma and medical presentations in a variety of settings.
Demonstrate clinical competence of extended care paramedic skills in a simulated environment.
Critically analyse and apply debriefing and reflection in clinical practice.

title: Extended Essay in Information Studies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject offers students the opportunity to demonstrate an advanced understanding of a topic area in Information Studies though the writing of an extended essay with a view to possible publication. Students select a topic from a wide-ranging list, and, under the supervision of a lecturer, but working independently, devise an essay title, draft an applicable, annotated bibliography, and then submit a 5,000-word composition that critically addresses the relevant theoretical and practical issues, with reference to the literature.
learning_outcomes: Critically review and synthesize the literature in this topic area.
Write a scholarly and engaging essay.
Identify and analyse the key theoretical and practical issues pertaining to this topic area.
Demonstrate in-depth knowledge of a particular topic area, and its literature, in Information Studies.

title: Extension
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on how people and communities influence change in the agricultural and equine industries, using extension as a key concept—defined as "facilitated change in an environment that has social, economic and technical complexity" (APEN, 2020). Students explore the role of social sciences in these industries, examining how social relationships, networks, and community knowledge interact with physical and biological systems. Through communication and social science theories and methods, students gain insight into the forces and processes of change, and develop practical skills to support and lead change in rural and industry contexts.
learning_outcomes: Design an effective extension plan.
Analyse and review extension practice in relation to theory.
Discuss the social dimensions of relevant rural sectors in relation to extension.
Discuss innovation and/or practice change through systems thinking.

title: External Communication Strategies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops student understanding of external communication strategies. Students examine common forms of corporate public communication including websites, social media, press releases, and media announcements with a view to developing basic skills in each of these areas and executing external communication strategies to support wider strategic objectives. This subject is designed with adaptable delivery models, which may include combinations of condensed online sessions and one-off workshops.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of an integrated public communication strategy consisting of website/s, social media and other forms of media.
Develop a strategy for public communication that supports the organisation's wider strategic objectives.

title: External Reporting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject begins with an introduction to the sources of international financial reporting regulation and an overview of the conceptual framework, both crucial to informing the global debate regarding financial reporting standard formulation and application. The remainder of the subject applies selected financial reporting standards to specific real world business issues including the raising of capital, impairment of assets and management of long-term construction contracts. Students will gain an appreciation of the dynamic and contested arena of financial reporting standard setting. This subject is the first of two with an exclusive focus on financial accounting.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the form and content of published financial reports.
Outline the nature of financial reporting regulations that exist for reporting entities and companies in general.
Explain the role of the financial reporting conceptual framework and apply its components to practical situations.

Apply generally accepted accounting principles and specific financial reporting standards relating to concepts of recognition, measurement, disclosure, revaluation and impairment of financial statement elements.
Critically analyse current issues relating to the global development and application of financial reporting standards.

title: Fairytales, Superheroes and Literary Greats
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys exciting and influential literary texts that have social, cultural, and historical resonance. Important theoretical concepts are introduced in order to elicit critical and creative responses to texts that include adopting postcolonial and feminist reading strategies and techniques.
learning_outcomes: Describe key concepts and debates in literature.
Analyse and evaluate a range of popular and literary texts.
Conduct research into the relationships between texts and historical and cultural contexts.
Demonstrate a critical approach to a range of texts and genres.

title: Facilitating Change
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Change is a dynamic and perpetual process, and this subject introduces students to a range of theoretical and practical perspectives that facilitate a critical awareness of organisational change. The relationship between the organisation and the staff affected by change is examined through contemporary change management thinking. Knowledge gained is applied to analyse organisational change issues and explore alternative courses of action.
learning_outcomes: Identify, examine and critically analyse approaches to organisational change, and assess the outcomes from a range of theoretical perspectives.
Work collaboratively as part of a team or individually propose, justify and communicate ethical recommendations that contribute to the success of a change initiative.
Identify drivers of organisational change.
Examine stakeholder responses to change.
Analyse and assess the ethical and sustainability issues surrounding organisational change.
Work collaboratively as part of a team or individually assess an organisational change management program in relation to organisation and performance goals.

title: Facilitating Positive Behaviours
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores how to give positive behavioural support to people with distressed or 'challenging’ behaviours because of intellectual disability: cognitive impairment or dementia. Students will focus on one of these two groups. The subject adopts a critical and holistic biopsychosocial approach to understanding the functions of behaviour and its relationship to communication. This includes social, environmental, psychological, economic, political and personal determinants of human behaviour, which are considered in relation to vulnerable people from these groups. The subject explores values and ethics, how to create enabling environments, how to facilitate positive communication, and how we can provide positive support to the client and family. Issues including the social impact of stigma and labelling are considered. Specific concepts of care and tools for assessing and working with behaviours of concern are critically evaluated.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the potential impacts of challenging behaviours on staff, organizations and family caregivers.
Demonstrate the skills to facilitate positive behaviours as a primary approach to practice, with behaviour management as a secondary approach.
Demonstrate an understanding of how human rights, legal perspectives and the concept of ability can be applied in practice in relation to behaviour change.

Utilise the concepts of functional analysis, functional assessment and the use of charting (ABC - Antecedent Behaviour and Consequence) as tools for predicting, understanding and analysing behaviours.
Demonstrate understanding of, and ability to utilise a range of behavioural change models.
Appropriately utilise the terminology of behaviours of concern, challenging behaviour and positive behavioural approaches.
Assess the respective roles of behavioural, social, environmental, psychological, economic, political and personal aspects, including staff interactions, as influences on behaviour.
Demonstrate an understanding of behavioural principles and of behaviour as a means of communication.
Demonstrate an understanding of the bio-psycho-social model of healthcare intervention and its application to working with people demonstrating challenging behaviours.

title: Family Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to family law in a multicultural Australia. Students explore family law issues such as marriages, de facto relationships, divorce, property settlement and children under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth). Issues of same-sex relationships and Indigenous perspectives on family law are also canvassed. In addition, underlying social issues such as child abuse and domestic violence are examined, including the recognition of children's rights. A number of these issues within the family law setting are canvassed within the context of gender and gender inequalities.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate legal mechanisms relating to the resolution of family disputes.

Demonstrate an understanding of family law within the context of gender, and the links between gender, family violence and the economic consequences of relationship breakdown, including gender inequalities associated with property settlements and financial arrangements.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the historical context of family law, including the links between sociological, historical, philosophical and political perspectives on the developments in areas of family law.
Identify restraints imposed on the powers of the family law courts by the Australian Constitution.
Reflect on Indigenous people's perspectives on family law, including addressing critical issues pertaining to Indigenous people's access to justice in the family law courts.
Articulate and apply the current law relating to parental responsibility, children, access, and custody, including making professional judgement decisions, and identifying any pre-action procedures.
Critically discuss the development and role of family law in multicultural Australia.

Articulate and critically evaluate the role of law reform in the areas of child abuse and domestic violence; domestic and international laws targeting the crime of parental child abduction; and international developments in respect to the protection of children, including demonstrating an understanding of the best interests of the child principle.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) and the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), especially in relation to irretrievable breakdown of marriage, relationship breakdown, separation, divorce, property, and financial settlement arrangements.

title: Fields of Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the social work profession and the human services sector as well as providing an overview of some fields of practice in social work. The subject content encourages students to consider critical issues relating to a range of social work practice contexts.
learning_outcomes: Understand and participate in discussions that reflect the contested nature of social services.
Demonstrate knowledge of the range of vulnerabilities and contexts of practice.
Identify and draw on relevant foundation knowledge, ethical principles and current debates to inform professional practice.
Identify and draw on relevant foundation knowledge from other disciplines that inform professional practice.
Engage in current debates surrounding professional intervention in a variety of contexts.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of practice in the social services and the historical development of social service practice and the social work profession.
Identify and discuss ethical and practice issues and dilemmas that arise in specific fields of practice.
prerequisites: SWK326: Fields of Social Work Practice

title: Final Professional Experience: Consolidating Practice in the Primary Context
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject draws on teacher education students' cumulative learning across the course and includes preparation for and completion of the final professional experience placement of up to 240 hours. During this professional experience placement students demonstrate the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST) at graduate level. Specific attention is given to the value of critical reflection and critical inquiry into their teaching practice. As a component of the subject, students complete the Graduate Teacher Performance Assessment (GTPA), an authentic task whereby students are required to plan, teach and assess a curriculum aligned sustained learning sequence. Students will integrate evidence from this sequence to complete the GTPA submission which requires evaluation of the impact of their teaching on school students' learning through the five GTPA Practices: planning, teaching, assessing, reflecting, and appraising. Students are required to pass both components of the Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education (LANTITE) before commencement of the final professional experience placement as part of the accreditation requirements of the Master of Teaching Primary. Students satisfactory completion of the final placement and the GTPA, are both requirements for graduation from an accredited teacher education program.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate achievement of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST) at graduate level during professional experience in a primary classroom and through satisfactory completion of the GTPA.
Select and apply quality and fit for purpose diagnostic, formative, summative, formal and informal assessment strategies which address principles of inclusion.
Organise classroom activities and provide clear directions.
Plan and evaluate teaching and learning sequences constructively aligned to curriculum documentation using a range of evidence and data.
Critically reflect on and appraise the impact of their teaching practice on student outcomes to modify and improve future teaching and progress student learning.
Apply current models of pedagogy and strategies appropriate to the context and stage, to cater for the diverse needs of learners.
Identify professional development needs and goals and seek advice, constructive criticism and support from colleagues.
Justify and evaluate pedagogical decisions.
prerequisites: EPT510: Professional Experience: Positive Primary Classroom Environments
EEE505: Aligning Learning, Teaching and Assessment
EMM503: Mathematics in the Primary Years
EPT521: Professional Experience: Consolidating Effective Teaching and Assessment in the Primary Years

During this professional experience placement students demonstrate the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST) at graduate level. Specific attention is given to the value of critical reflection in, on and of practice. learning_outcomes: Select and apply quality and fit for purpose diagnostic, formative, summative, formal and informal assessment strategies which address principles of inclusion.
Identify professional development needs and goals and seek advice and support from colleagues.
Organise classroom activities and provide clear directions.

Demonstrate achievement of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST) at graduate level during professional experience in a primary classroom and through satisfactory completion of the GTPA.
Reflect on and appraise the impact of their teaching practice on student outcomes to modify and improve future teaching and progress student learning.
Apply current models of pedagogy and strategies appropriate to the context and stage, to cater for the diverse needs of learners.
Plan teaching and learning sequences constructively aligned to curriculum documentation using a range of evidence and data.
Justify and evaluate pedagogical decisions.

title: Finance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to the principles of financial management from a corporate perspective. The approach is to present and examine the theories and practices of investment, financing and dividend decision-making; and to examine the application of a range of analytical techniques appropriate to contemporary financial decision making.
learning_outcomes: Employ analytical techniques, using contemporary electronic aids appropriate to financial decision making.
Analyse the impact of economic, legal and tax changes on the financial position of the firm.
Identify, analyse and solve financial problems confronting business enterprises, particularly problems relating to corporate investment, asset management and financing decisions.
Demonstrate critical evaluation and communication skills relating to the scope, methodology, role, objectives and ethics of financial management within business organisations.

title: Financial Accounting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject, which builds upon the introduction to financial accounting provided in the prerequisite subject, begins with an introduction to the regulatory environment for financial reporting and an overview of the conceptual framework for financial reporting principles and standards. The major focus is the form and content of published financial reports and the application of generally accepted accounting principles and specific financial reporting standards relating to concepts of recognition, measurement, disclosure, revaluation and impairment of financial statement elements.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and apply generally accepted accounting principles and specific financial reporting standards relating to concepts of recognition, measurement, disclosure, revaluation and impairment of key financial statement elements.
Discuss critically and comprehensively the statutory and professional requirements upon which published financial statements are based.
Explain the form and content of financial statements.
Prepare basic financial statements for reporting entities.

title: Financial Accounting 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject deals with the accounting and reporting requirements of corporations set down by legislation and the professional accounting bodies in Australia. It follows on from ACC514 Financial Accounting, concentrating on accounting for different forms of business combinations, including parent-subsidiary relationships, foreign subsidiaries, and associated companies.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess and report upon the information contained within published financial statements.
Discuss the relevant accounting standards and statutory reporting requirements for foreign currency dealings, segment reporting, and leases.
Prepare accounts for each of the above-mentioned business combinations in accordance with relevant professional and statutory reporting requirements.
Explain the relationships that exist between a parent company and its subsidiary(ies), an investor and its investee, a company and its overseas subsidiaries.

title: Financial Accounting A
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In an international context this subject deals with company formation, changes in a company's capital structure and the statutory and professional financial reporting requirements of incorporated reporting entities. An understanding of the overview of the conceptual framework and the role of accounting standards leads to the study of the definition, measurement and recognition of assets, liabilities and owner's equity items and to the disclosure of these items in financial statements.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure of accounting standards and be able to recognise structural differences.
Outline the nature of the statutory, listing and professional regulations placed on reporting entities and companies in general.
Describe the procedures and be able to perform the accounting entries required to form a company having both share and debt capital.
Explain the role of the conceptual framework for financial reporting and apply its components to practical situations.
Apply generally accepted accounting principles and relevant accounting standards relating to the concept of disclosure (eg accounting policies, materiality, after reporting date events).
Apply generally accepted accounting principles and specific accounting standards relating to concepts of recognition and measurement of financial statement elements.
Explain why some standards only deal with disclosures.
Describe how the accounting standard process developed and how it currently operates.
Describe alternative concepts of measurement in accounting.
Describe the place of national statutory, listing and professional regulations in the context of international reporting.

title: Financial Accounting and Reporting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the ability to analyse and interpret accounting information developed in ACC127 Accounting & Financial Literacy. Students will use manual and automated accounting information systems to process accounting information and prepare financial reports. All aspects of the financial statement preparation process are covered with a focus on accounting for key assets with reference to International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and their Australian equivalents (AASB).
