learning_outcomes: Prepare financial statements for reporting entities in accordance with relevant professional and statutory reporting requirements.
Describe and explain how technologies and accounting systems such as Enterprise Resources Planning and cloud based computing can support data analysis for decision making and risk mitigation.
Appreciate how new technologies may impact the future of accounting and enhance and improve efficiency in communication.
Interpret and apply generally accepted accounting principles.
Calculate, account for and report values of key assets including: receivables, inventory; and property, plant, equipment.
Record accounting transactions using manual and automated accounting information systems.

title: Financial Accounting B
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In the context of the internationalisation of accounting this subject deals with the corporate form of business organisation, the form and content of corporate financial statements, how to account for: taxation of company profits; acquisition of another entity; and expansion into an economic entity (parent-controlled entity; and investor-investee relationships). Consolidation, including the elimination of inter-entity transactions, direct outside recognition and an introduction to indirect outside equity interest are studied. Foreign currency transactions and translation of foreign currency statements are also covered in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Account for company income tax.
Discuss the accounting implicaitons for corporate entities in an international environment.
Account for and prepare the financial report disclosures required for investments in associated companies.
Demonstrate a detailed knowledge of relevant accounting standards and statutory reporting requirements in Australia.
Account for the acquisition of assets and other entities.
Recognise the form and content of Australian published corporate financial reports, viz., balance sheets, income statements, cash flow statements, interim reports and concise financial reports.
Prepare a consolidated statement of cash flows, including its accompanying notes for a parent and its controlled entities.

Prepare consolidated balance sheets and income statements for economic entities where there is 100% control; where a direct outside equity interest is involved; and, introduce the concept of indirect outside equity interest.
Recognise that corporate accounting operates in both a national and international environment.
Translate the financial statements of an overseas controlled entity which have been denominated in a foreign currency.
Account for foreign currency transactions.

title: Financial Crime
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to contemporary fraud and financial crime, exploring how these offences occur across industries and countries, and how technology and regulation have shaped their evolution. Through real-world case studies, students examine the impact of digital innovations, leadership, and organisational culture on financial wrongdoing. The subject develops skills in risk assessment, detection, and prevention, preparing students for further study or careers in investigations, compliance, or law enforcement.
learning_outcomes: Apply prevention and detection strategies to identify cause for concern in financial systems, transactions, and governance structures.
Evaluate how technological advancements, regulatory frameworks, and organisational cultures contribute to or mitigate financial crime risks.
Compare the characteristics and methods of modern financial crimes across industries and jurisdictions, and analyse and classify fraud typologies using real-world case studies.
Assess and present the societal and economic consequences of financial crime through comparative analysis of its impacts on individuals, businesses, and national economies.
Critique responses to financial crimes in contemporary case studies, proposing evidence-based improvements to existing prevention and enforcement approaches.

title: Financial Crime Control and Risk Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The subject examines organisational, contextual and cultural risk factors that give rise to fraud and financial crime opportunities. The subject evaluates commonly adopted fraud and financial crime prevention mechanisms and frameworks drawn from around the world and evaluates their effectiveness in light of an evolving crimescape. The subject explores national and international best practice guidance designed to aid organisations in reducing their exposure to financial crime abuse.
learning_outcomes: Review and apply risk management theories, models and frameworks.
Describe the functionality of financial crime prevention mechanisms and frameworks.
Evaluate and recommend fraud and financial crime prevention mechanisms and frameworks to address specific fraud and financial crime risks.
Identify and analyse organisational, contextual and cultural risk factors.

title: Financial Crime Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Students will examine financial intelligence and its role in supporting the wider financial crime control functions. Students will explore foundational knowledge and analytical methods at both strategic and operational levels to inform decision making. Students will also critique contemporary issues in financial crime intelligence and their impact on current and future operations.
learning_outcomes: Examine analytical methods available for strategic and operational analysis of financial crime activity, including the use of typologies and red flags.
Reflect on the integration of current and emerging issues in financial crime intelligence into operational practice.
Explore financial intelligence frameworks within the context of financial crime programs, and how it informs corporate, government and investigative decision-making at a practitioners level.

title: Financial Institutions Lending
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the principles and techniques of lending in financial institutions. Students will develop skills in the techniques involved in the analysis and application of financial data for lending together with approaches for effective credit risk management.
learning_outcomes: Assess current issues in lending and financial assessment techniques.
Utilise financial data in lending transactions.
Apply effective techniques for credit risk management.
Analyse and interpret financial reports.
Apply sound and practical lending techniques.

title: Financial Institutions and Markets
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the nature and operation of financial institutions and markets in Australia as well as the economics of the financial system in which they operate. A wide range of financial institutions, markets and securities are examined in detail, together with such concepts as financial intermediation, interest rate and exchange rate determination.
learning_outcomes: Explain and evaluate the role and impact of Government policy on the financial system.
Explain the causes of change in financial conditions.
Explain the nature and operation of Australia's financial institutions and markets.
Apply analytic skills to the interpretation of developments and changes in financial markets.

title: Financial Literacy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Financial Literacy is vital in all workplaces and professions. This subject addresses the basics of interpreting and using financial information in professional environments to ensure that students are well prepared for future study and employment. It focuses on practical uses of financial literacy in differing professions and workplaces.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the information conveyed in standard budgeting tools such as a cash flow statement, profit and loss statement and a balance sheet.
Understand and apply the principles of the time value of money and opportunity cost.

title: Financial Literacy for Decision Makers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop skills that enable them to analyse and interpret accounting reports and to communicate the results of this analysis to interested parties. The subject focuses on the use of accounting information and students will learn various tools and techniques to enable them to make effective business decisions.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe sources of business finance.
Use a spreadsheet to assist in the preparation of business information; and,.
Analyse and interpret a range of accounting and financial transactions and reports.
Generate and analyse a range of business results and reports.

title: Financial Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to the principles of financial management from a corporate perspective. The approach is to present and examine the theory and practice of investment and financing decision-making. The application of a range of analytical techniques appropriate to contemporary financial decision-making is used to evaluate business options.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the impact of economic, legal and tax changes on the financial position of the firm.
Identify, analyse and solve financial problems confronting business enterprises, particularly problems relating to corporate investment, asset management and financing decisions.
Demonstrate critical evaluation and communication skills relating to the scope, methodology, role, objectives and ethics of financial management within business organisations.
Employ analytical techniques, using contemporary electronic aids appropriate to financial decision making.

title: Financial Management in Health Services
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the complexities of healthcare finance, focusing on funding models, budget management, and financial decision-making. Students will critically evaluate global and emerging funding approaches, apply financial tools to operational and capital budgeting, and address contemporary challenges such as fraud and waste. Through analysis and synthesis of financial data, learners will develop strategies to support sustainable and equitable health service management. Practical case studies will enhance understanding of financial governance and accountability in healthcare settings.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse contemporary challenges in healthcare finance and propose practical solutions.
Critically evaluate current and emerging healthcare funding models considering their implications for sustainability and equity.
Evaluate financial information to support evidence-based decision making in health service management.
Analyse and respond to budgetary challenges in healthcare settings by adopting accounting principles.
Justify strategies for operational and capital budget management.

title: Financial Management of Small Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the nature and characteristics of small business, and develops the key financial skills and abilities needed for the effective financial management of small business. This subject will be of particular interest to existing or potential small business owners. A key learning outcome will be the production of a business plan.
learning_outcomes: Describe the components of basic accounting reports and use accounting reports and tools such as budgeting and cost-volume-profit analysis for decision-making.
Collate data from many sources and create information in the form of reports for a small business.
Analyse and evaluate accounting reports using financial ratios and trend data that highlight the profitability, liquidity and solvency/gearing of a small business.
Identify the sources of finance available to a small business.
List and define the key characteristics and issues involved in starting and running a small business.

title: Financial Management of Small Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject requires students to investigate and put into practice the key financial skills and abilities needed for the effective financial management of small business. Students will simulate the experience of starting up a small business, sourcing finance and advice, research, marketing and management of a product. A key learning outcome will be the production of a detailed business plan and a presentation on the concept of the business to specialist audiences. This subject will be of interest to existing or potential small business owners.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the key characteristics and issues involved in starting and running a small business.
Analyse and evaluate accounting reports using financial ratios and trend data that highlight the profitability, liquidity and solvency/gearing of a small business.
Evaluate the sources of finance available to a small business, and outline the sources of business advice and assistance.
Explain the components and application of basic accounting reports, and use accounting reports and tools such as budgeting and cost-volume-profit analysis for decision making.
Analyse and synthesise data from many sources to create various reports for a small business and specialist audiences.

title: Financial Markets and Institutions
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the nature and operation of financial institutions and markets in Australia as well as the economics of the financial system in which they operate. A wide range of financial institutions, markets and securities are examined in detail, together with such concepts as financial intermediation, interest rate and exchange rate determination.
learning_outcomes: Explain the causes of change in financial conditions.
Explain the nature and operation of Australia's financial institutions and markets.
Apply analytic skills to the interpretation of developments and changes in financial markets.
Explain and evaluate the role and impact of Government policy on the financial system.

title: Financial Markets and Instruments
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the nature and operation of financial institutions and markets in Australia as well as the economics of the financial system in which they operate. A wide range of financial institutions, markets and securities are examined in detail, together with such concepts as financial intermediation, and interest rate and exchange rate determination. The emphasis is on how markets and the instruments used in them can be employed to manage financial risks which businesses, individuals and governments face.
learning_outcomes: Investigate, explain and analyse the causes of changes in interest and exchange rates on business and financial markets.
Critically analyse and provide informed comment on recent developments in the organisation and structure of the financial system, various financial markets and the instruments of these markets.

Identify the impact of exchange rates and interest rates on financial markets, instruments and business and demonstrate how appropriate use of instruments and techniques can be used to manage and mitigate financial risks.

title: Financial Planning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the concepts involved in personal financial planning, placing particular attention to the various processes and principles which are involved. It provides an overview of the laws and regulations relating to the financial planning industry, the forms of government assistance to individuals, the choice of investments available, and the role of insurance and superannuation. The subject will introduce students to the tasks associated with the development of financial plans and develop their ability to construct financial plans through the study materials, case studies and practical workshops.
learning_outcomes: Create, present, and interpret a professional-quality Statement of Advice that includes documentation of the decision process and a detailed action plan.
Reflect critically on the structure, regulation and participants in the financial planning industry.
Evaluate sources of consumer credit and apply investment strategies for wealth accumulation.
Analyse and evaluate various approaches to the financial planning process.
Apply risk management and taxation strategies for wealth protection.
Use effective communication skills and financial planning principles to establish client goals and risk profile and develop a strategic statement that will form the basis of the financial plan.
Demonstrate an understanding of legal, social security, and retirement-related rules associated with financial planning.

title: Financial Planning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the concepts involved in personal financial planning, giving particular attention to the various processes and principles which are involved. It provides an overview of the laws and regulations relating to the financial planning industry, the forms of government assistance to individuals, the choice of investments available, and the role of insurance and superannuation. The subject will introduce students to the tasks associated with the development of financial plans and develop their ability to explain and discuss financial plans.
learning_outcomes: Apply risk management and taxation strategies for wealth protection.
Compare sources of consumer credit and apply investment strategies for wealth accumulation.
Use effective communication skills and financial planning principles to establish client goals and risk profiles, which will then form the basis of the financial plan.
Explain the structure and regulation of the financial planning industry.
Analyse various approaches to the financial planning process.
Categorise stakeholders in the financial planning industry.
Discuss legal, social security, and retirement-related rules associated with financial planning.

title: Financial Statement Analysis and Valuation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Finance professionals will, at some stage in their career, need to source, critically analyse and make decisions using externally available financial information and economic data. This may be, for example, in relation to constructing, reviewing or defending possible merger, takeover or partnership/joint venture transactions. Others may use financial statement analysis skills for recommending investment in stock/equity markets. This subject is designed to develop the student's abilities to act as an analytical user of externally-available financial and economic information. Throughout the subject reference is made to the impact of different financial reporting rules on the comparability/usefulness of published financial information. The emphasis of the subject is on applying frameworks and techniques to listed companies, to ensure that students can practically apply the knowledge gained in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse the role, uses and limitations of external financial reports.
Explain the impact of choices from among permissible accounting methods on figures reported in financial statements.
Apply analytical techniques using financial reports and other externally available information to critically evaluate company viability, performance and valuation.
Critique various valuation techniques.

title: Fiqh (Islamic Law) of the Five Pillars
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the study of Islamic law or jurisprudence (fiqh) relating to the five pillars of Islam (the declaration of faith (shahadah), the daily prescribed prayers (salat), fasting during the month of Ramadan (sawm), purifying alms (zakat), and the pilgrimage (hajj)), together with the textual evidence for the basis of the rulings. The rituals related to these practices will be studied together with the criteria and method for practice. Physical cleansing in Islam will also addressed. The Hanafi school of Islamic law will be the primary school studied, however, views and evidence from Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools of law will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Explain the cleansing process needed for different circumstances and different practices.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Cite textual evidence for ritual practices of Islam.
Describe the practice of the five pillars of Islam.
Explain the jurisprudence (fiqh) related to their practice.

title: Fire Ecology and Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Australia is the most fire-prone continent in the world, and its flora and fauna have evolved in the presence of fire over millions of years. Yet altered fire regimes imperil many species, and fire management is a critical component of conservation in Australia. This subject explores ecological aspects of fire in the Australian environment including fire as a physical disturbance (fire behaviour) and the fire regime (including timing, frequency, severity and spatial patterning). The subject explores changes in Australian fire regimes over time, from Indigenous use of fire prior to European colonisation, through to contemporary fire management (including the continuation and resumption of Indigenous fire regimes). Students will explore the ways in which plants and animals have adapted to particular fire regimes, and how changes in fire regimes affect ecosystems and the biota inhabiting them. Students will discuss current issues in fire ecology and learn how to apply ecological principles to fire management. Finally, we explore the effects of global climate change on fire regimes, and the flow on effects of changes in fire regimes on ecosystems.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of key fire concepts and fire ecology to develop appropriate fire management strategies.
Discuss Indigenous Australian fire practices and the effects of cultural fire on ecosystems.
Describe the key elements of fire behaviour and the fire triangle, including the relationship between weather and fire behaviour.
Evaluate how fire management plans and strategies are developed, and how they need to address relevant legislation, policy frameworks and practical requirements.
Define and use terminology, methods and concepts common in fire ecology, and disturbance ecology in general.
Develop sampling design and data collection to examine fire impacts on biota.
Describe anthropogenic climate change and its potential impacts on current and future fire regimes.
Discuss the characteristics used to describe fire regimes.
Discuss plant and animal responses to fire and the fire regime.

title: Fire-Setting Behaviour, Legal Issues and Investigative Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Knowledge of fire-setting behaviours is an important tool for fire investigators. This subject will examine the psychological theories and motives of fire-setting behaviour and the evidence derived from them. It will analyse the common sub-groups of fire-setters and the prevention and intervention strategies applying to each of them. Students will also gain an understanding of specific legal issues relating to incendiary fires as well as investigative practices for identifying, analysing and presenting expert evidence in relation to such fires.
learning_outcomes: Be familiar with the psychological theories of fire setting behaviour.
Relate fire-setting behaviours and motive to evidence at a fire scene.
Demonstrate a general knowledge of various prevention and intervention strategies for each fire-setting sub-group.
Recognise a range of motives for fire-setting.
Prepare for and present expert evidence in relation to incendiary fires.
prerequisites: JST416: Fire Investigation 2 (Fire Investigation Process and Law)
JST417: Fire Setting Behaviour and Legal Issues in Investigative Practice

title: First Nations and Media: Seeing Knowledge, Seeing Power
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject critically investigates non-Indigenous understandings and mediated constructions of First Nations peoples. The subject explores how we see and know ourselves and others through a variety of media including memes, gifs, video games, news, films and television shows. The historical role of media in rationalising settler colonisation and its use by First Nations peoples to challenge colonial and racial stereotyping will be outlined. The subject explores the differences between First Nations and non-Indigenous produced media and the ethical, cultural, and political implications of this.
learning_outcomes: Enact media and racial literacies with a critical understanding of standpoint in relation to First Nations' experiences of Australian media and history.
Reflexively critique racial stereotyping in representations of First Nations peoples across a variety of media.
Critically investigate the media as multi-modal racialising space for both First Nations and non-Indigenous peoples.
Research and develop a research topic on the historical and colonial contexts of First Nations and non-Indigenous produced media.

Apply theoretical approaches developed by First Nations scholars and media practitioners to analyse the construction of media identities and institutional knowledges and their impact of First Nations lives.
Rewrite and deconstruct media with an awareness of the ethical, cultural, and political implications of media representations of First Nations peoples.
prerequisites: IKC403: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australian Cultures, Histories and Contemporary Realities
IKC404: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australians and the Politics of Control

title: First Nations Australians and Psychology: An Introduction
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students to engage with all First Nations Australians by teaching them the knowledge and skills to work respectfully and effectively. The pedagogical approach, Yindyamaldhuray Yalbilinya Mawan, gives an insight into the traditional ways of learning that have been handed down through the generations by Elders. This subject will provide knowledge of First Nations Australian cultures and information which assists students to deconstruct and reconstruct Australian culture, the discipline of Psychology, the First Nations Australian backstory, and the implications of this for contemporary professional practice. Students will be guided through Yindyamaldhuray Yalbilinya Muwang to incorporate these elements into discipline-specific approaches, respectful communication, self-reflection and an understanding of generic cultural manners, which are required to work respectfully and effectively in First Nations Australian contexts.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their own culture and examine the culture of the discipline of Psychology and its historical development in Australia.
Describe pre-invasion Australian First Nations cultures and explain how cultural practices sustained psychological health and well-being over time.
Describe social justice and explain its importance when working in the field of Psychology.

Apply relevant knowledge and skills; respectful communications, self-reflection, and generic cultural manners to facilitate respectful and effective engagement with First Nations Australians when working in the field of Psychology.

Explain the impact of invasion and the political policies and practices that followed, including the impact of the Stolen Generations and other historical traumas on the psychological health and well-being of First Nations Australians.

Examine cultural bias, the way that the concept of White Privilege evolved and consider their effects on socioeconomic disadvantage and the psychological health and well-being of First Nations Australians.

title: First Nations Education: Knowing, Relating, Connecting
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to enable students to explore First Nations Australian Education and its role and place in Australian educational settings. Using Indigenist Standpoint and decolonising lenses, teacher education students will critically reflect on their cultures and values and examine media, policy, and curriculum and pedagogy practices relevant to their own educational contexts. Students will undertake research and/or experiences to learn about and apply First Nations Australian protocols for developing locally relevant First Nations content and to facilitate the participation of First Nations peoples in education. This subject develops students' knowledge, understandings and skills relating to culturally responsive and relational pedagogical approaches to addressing Focus Areas 1.4 and 2.4 of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers. Students will evaluate their role in contributing to social justice and reconciliation within Australian education contexts.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their own developing First Nations cultural responsiveness and articulate how this has influenced decisions that strengthen relational practice.
Select and evaluate knowledge from a range of sources relating to the knowledge, understandings and skills required by teachers to engage effectively with First Nations Australian peoples.
Apply principles of decolonisation and describe how this realises human rights and social justice agendas in education contexts.

Critically analyse the influence of social, cultural and institutional influences on one's own standpoint, popular discourse about First Nations Australian peoples, and the relationships between First Nations Australian and non-Indigenous Australian peoples.

Identify and apply protocols for developing culturally appropriate First Nations curriculum content relating to local First Nations Australian knowledges and knowledge sources, spirituality, beliefs and values, concepts of kinship and culturally sensitive issues.
Explain the impact of past and present Australian educational policies to articulate how these have influenced education and educational practices in relation to First Nations Australian students.
Apply culturally responsive pedagogies for all learners and explain how these are effective for First Nations learners.
prerequisites: EEB435: Indigenous Australian Studies for Teachers
EEB446: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Cultural Education Program
EED422: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development

title: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of Indigenous Australian peoples' varied and diverse realities. It will enhance understandings of the effects of historical and contemporary policy and practices on the lives of First Nations Australians. It examines a range of social, cultural, historical, and institutional factors that impact on the contemporary experiences of Indigenous Australian and non-Indigenous Australian peoples using a relational framework. It develops skills in critical thinking, reflection, and analysis for reflexive practice within diverse professions.
learning_outcomes: Investigate, compare and reflect on standpoint to explain Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples' historical positioning.

Critically reflect on the factors that have shaped historical and contemporary engagement with Indigenous communities and Indigenous peoples and critique deficit paradigms as they relate to Indigenous Australians.
Refine, review, relate and map new knowledge and understandings to demonstrate ethical professional practice, and to explore principles for respectful partnerships with Indigenous communities.
Describe, analyse and theorise individual and collective standpoint in relation to Indigenous peoples' experiences of Australian history.
Examine how racialised power and privilege influence historical and contemporary structures of Australian society and its institutions.
prerequisites: IKC101: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country

title: First Nations Foods and Diets
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to some of the traditional foods and diets of First Nations people from around the world. Using a module framework, students will review and analyse the intersection of nutrition, health and well-being within societies and explore examples of medicinal or functional foods in various contexts. Intellectual property (IP) of First Nations people is discussed with respect to biopiracy, including protection and fair and equitable sharing of IP as outlined in the Nagoya Protocol.
learning_outcomes: Explain how traditional bio-processing methods provide biodiversity conservation.
Describe traditional methods for processing indigenous foods.
Describe functional foods and their contributions to health and well-being.
Classify foods on the basis of physical form, chemical composition and nutritional functions.
Identify traditional foods and medicines from First Nations people around the world.
Compare medicinal, cultural and social non-nutritional uses of food.
Critically evaluate the role of international conventions in regulating use of traditional knowledge.
Identify traditional foods and medicines used by Australian First Nations people.
Discuss novel food products of the future.
Critically evaluate health-benefit claims of products originating from indigenous plants.
Describe functional foods of First Nations people that are now used globally.
Discuss how foods can be used as medicines and factors influencing use of food for medicinal purposes.

title: First Nations Education: Knowing, Relating, Connecting
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject is designed to enable students to explore First Nations Australian Education and its role and place in Australian educational settings. Using Indigenist Standpoint and decolonising lenses, teacher education students (TES) will critically reflect on their cultures and values and examine media, policy, and curriculum and pedagogy practices relevant to their own educational contexts. TES will undertake research and/or experiences to learn about and apply First Nations Australian protocols for developing locally relevant curriculum content and to facilitate the participation of First Nations peoples in education. This subject develops TES knowledge, understandings and skills relating to culturally responsive and relational pedagogical approaches to addressing Focus Areas 1.4 and 2.4 of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers. TES will evaluate the roles of various stakeholders in contributing to social justice and reconciliation within Australian education contexts.
learning_outcomes: Examine the impact of past and present Australian educational policies to articulate how these have influenced education and educational practices in relation to First Nations Australian students.
Apply culturally responsive pedagogies for all learners and analyse how these are effective for First Nations learners.
Apply principles of decolonisation and explain how this realises human rights and social justice agendas in education contexts.
Critically reflect on their own developing First Nations cultural responsiveness and articulate how this has influenced decisions that strengthen relational practice.

Evaluate and apply protocols for developing culturally appropriate First Nations curriculum content relating to local First Nations Australian knowledges and knowledge sources, spirituality, beliefs and values, concepts of kinship and culturally sensitive issues.

Select and evaluate knowledge from a range of sources to articulate scholarship on the knowledge, understandings and skills required by teachers to engage effectively with First Nations Australian peoples.

Critically analyse the influence of social, cultural and institutional influences on one's own Standpoint, popular discourse about First Nations Australian peoples, and the relationships between First Nations Australian and non-Indigenous Australian peoples.
prerequisites: EED422: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development
ESS440: Teaching and Learning in the Differentiated Classroom
EEB505: Indigenous Australian Studies for Teachers
EEB435: Indigenous Australian Studies for Teachers
EEB446: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Cultural Education Program

title: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of Indigenous Australian peoples' varied and diverse realities. It will enhance understandings of the effects of historical and contemporary policy and practices on the lives of First Nations Australians. It examines a range of social, cultural, historical, and institutional factors that impact on the contemporary experiences of Indigenous Australian and non-Indigenous Australian peoples using a relational framework. It develops skills in critical thinking, reflection, and analysis for reflexive practice within diverse professions.
learning_outcomes: Investigate, compare and reflect on standpoint to explain Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples' historical positioning.

Critically reflect on the factors that have shaped historical and contemporary engagement with Indigenous communities and Indigenous peoples and critique deficit paradigms as they relate to Indigenous Australians.
Critically examine how racialised power and privilege influence historical and contemporary structures of Australian society and its institutions.
Refine, review, relate and map new knowledge and understandings to demonstrate ethical professional practice, and to explore principles for respectful partnerships with Indigenous communities.
Describe, analyse and theorise individual and collective standpoint in relation to Indigenous peoples' experiences of Australian history.
prerequisites: IKC107: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country

title: First Nations Ways of Knowing, Being and Doing in Research
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students consider the colonial foundations of Western knowledge paradigms and research practices and how these impact on Australian First Nations peoples. Students will increase their understanding and awareness of Indigenous and Indigenist research methods and methodologies and critically analyse the research practices of their future discipline. Through reflexive analysis of their own standpoint, students are encouraged to question their assumptions about research and consider how to conduct respectful research in Australian contexts.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critically reflect on historical and contemporary research practices relating to Australian First Nations peoples and critically evaluate the social, historical, and political discourses that informed them.
Identify Indigenous and Indigenist research frameworks and methodologies, their cultural relevance, ethical implications and application within academic contexts.
Select and critically review scholarly literature to provide insights into relationships between First Nations considerations, the researcher and future research practice.
Recognise the importance and value of community engagement, cultural protocols, reciprocity and shared decision making in research partnerships.
prerequisites: IKC501: Indigenous Research Methods and Methodologies

title: Fish Ecology and Conservation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Fish are the most diverse group of vertebrates on earth. In this subject students will gain in-depth knowledge about the global biodiversity and conservation of fishes. Students will learn fundamental principles of fish biology, ecology and evolution and how this knowledge can be used in conservation management. Students will gain experience in field and laboratory sampling techniques for fish and the analysis of data. Students complete this subject with an in-depth understanding of fish biodiversity and the links to ecosystems, fisheries and people.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the ecological functions of major external and internal features of fish and how they vary among species and environments.
Integrate communication and critical thinking skills needed to explore, interpret and present basic fish ecology data.
Apply animal welfare principles to humanely handle and study fish.
Analyse the threats to fish biodiversity and the fundamental concepts that underpin conservation approaches.
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of fish biodiversity and how it is globally distributed.
Assess and apply a range of field and laboratory methods to safely sample fish.

title: Fish Movement and Migration
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Fish are important components of biodiversity and sources of food and income. Fish have an inherent need to migrate or move for spawning, feeding and dispersal; however, river development is known to adversely affect fish and fisheries by blocking important movement and migration pathways. There is an unprecedented global boom in irrigation and hydropower infrastructure projects and in many areas these are leading to significant fish declines. This subject draws on decades of research and development that have provided a suite of policy and engineering tools that can mitigate the impacts of river development on fish populations. Students will learn how to identify potential problems associated with river development activities and how to develop solutions. Students will learn relevant concepts and gain practical experience to recognise and tackle sustainability issues related to fish movement, biology, river hydrology and development.
learning_outcomes: Assess the potential impact of river development and identify migration barriers.
Describe the importance of different types of fish movement and migration.
Explain the need for strong policies and guidelines.
Analyse and discuss the design and operation of various types of mitigation strategies.
Articulate the importance of short term research and long term monitoring in conserving global fish stocks.

title: Flower Crop Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the sustainable production of commercial cut flower and foliage crops including examples of traditional, popular, native, and exotic crops. Utilising a rose project case study, students will develop their knowledge and understanding of the biology, principles, and practices of cut flower production in protected structures, focusing on both pre-harvest and post-harvest physiology and production techniques to maintain extended vase life. Students will apply what they are learning to the development of a flower crop project proposal.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe the range and diversity of cut flower crops.
Justify pre-harvest and post-harvest procedures for optimal production of flower crops.
Apply knowledge about the growth cycle of flower crops to describe the optimal management of the vegetative and reproductive phases of flower crops.
Discuss the principles of hydroponic and indoor systems for growing flower crops and explain how these growth systems are utilised to maximise production efficiencies.
Design and develop a flower enterprise proposal, including budgets.
Compare and contrast current and new technologies used in the production of flower crops.

title: Five Industry Certification Credits
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Administration Credit subject only

title: Fluid Mechanics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a foundational understanding and practical skills in fluid mechanics. Students will explore the principles of fluid statics and dynamics, engaging with important concepts such as pressure distribution, hydrostatic forces, and the dynamics of fluid flow.
learning_outcomes: Calculate pressure drops, flow rates, and pipe diameters for flow in pipes and channels, considering Reynolds number and flow regimes.
Understand the significance of boundary layers in fluid flow over surfaces and analyse their impact on drag and lift forces.
Analyse and apply principles of fluid statics to solve engineering problems related to pressure distribution and hydrostatic forces.
Utilise principles of fluid dynamics to analyse fluid flow in engineering contexts, including applications of Bernoulli's equation and conservation laws.

title: Food and Beverage Engineering
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the core concepts of food process engineering relevant to practitioners in the wine and other beverage industries. Students will develop knowledge and skills in mass and energy balances; fluid and solids handling; solid-liquid separations; heat transfers, including refrigeration; motors, drives, sensors and control; and hygienic design and operation of beverage and food plants.
learning_outcomes: Perform engineering calculations relevant to the design, selection and operation of food and beverage manufacturing processes.
Assign correct units to engineering quantities and convert between different systems of units.
Explain and apply the principles of hygienic design and the sanitary operation of food and beverage plants.
Describe the operating principles of motors, drives and sensors used in food processing.

Explain the principles of operation of equipment used in food and beverage processing for fluid and solids handling, solid-fluid separation, and heat transfer, and recommend appropriate equipment for a specific application.
Perform simple mass and energy balances relevant to food and beverage processing operations.
Explain the principles of automated control of food processing operations.

title: Food Environment and Culture
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will examine and analyse the social, cultural, ethical and anthropogenic climate change issues that shape agri-food systems at local and global levels. By prioritising First Nations Peoples perspectives, aspirations and rights for self-determination, students will explore the impact of settler-colonialism on First Nations Peoples of Australia and agroecosystems management, food sovereignty and caring for Country. Students will develop a range of professional communication styles and independent research skills.
learning_outcomes: Explain a number of the core concepts that define the major contemporary challenges for global agricultural production and examine the potential future implications of one of these challenges.
Use ethical models to review and analyse the complexity of ethically challenging issues in agriculture.
Communicate, in a professionally appropriate manner, about contemporary agricultural challenges by considering multiple perspectives to arrive at a justified viewpoint.
Examine how our own and others cultural values and beliefs affect professional communication and practice, and the strategies that can be employed to enhance communication across cultures.
Recognise the inter-relationship between cultural, environmental, social and economic sustainability and discuss issues that arise for global sustainability in Agricultural contexts.

Analyse the impact of settler-colonialism on First Nations Peoples of Australia, specifically in relation to agroecosystems management, food sovereignty and caring for Country, by prioritising First Nations Peoples perspectives, aspirations and rights for self-determination.
prerequisites: IKC101: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country

title: Food Processing and Preservation
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The applications of common food preservation and processing operations are examined through selected case studies. The subject focuses on the principles of the food processing technologies commonly employed and how these may be optimised to best assure the safety, nutritional and sensory quality of food products. New technologies that offer improved sensory or nutritional outcomes are also introduced.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the principles underpinning common food processing and preservation processes.

Discuss the expected effects of different food processing operations on sensory and nutritional properties of foods and how these operations may be optimised through manipulation of the processing conditions.
Evaluate the rationale for the application of specified food processing operations to selected food products.
Analyse and apply the use of new technologies for food processing.

title: Food and Nutritional Chemistry
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will investigate the structure and chemistry of major (water, proteins, carbohydrates, lipids) and minor nutrients (vitamins and other bioactive compounds) in foods and their nutritional impact. Chemistry of reactions, both beneficial and degradative, of food nutrients that impact the quality, safety, nutrition and sensory properties of foods during food processing and storage will be explored as well as the use of enzymes to modify food properties and nutritional values. Further to this, how major food components modify the structure, texture, physicochemical and flow behaviour of foods will be explored. Selected examples of chemical and instrumental methods for characterising physicochemical and other properties of foods will be undertaken. Students will gain a practical appreciation of the food components, their functions in food processing and impact on food nutritional value.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret laboratory data and relate the outcomes to food and nutritional chemistry.
Describe and use appropriate chemical and instrumental methods to determine composition of and physical characteristics of food.
Explain the nature and mode of action of thickeners, gelling agents, emulsifiers, and foaming agents for manipulating structure, texture and functions of foods.
Apply the structure and chemical properties of food components to their nutritional and health status.
Discuss how chemical reactions and enzymes bring about desirable or undesirable changes in foods.
Relate the structures and chemical properties of food components to their physicochemical and functional properties in foods.
Describe the chemical, structural and functional characteristics of water, proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and vitamins and other bioactive compounds in foods.

title: Food Product Development
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject introduces a structured approach to the design and development of new and improved food products to meet specific market and nutritional requirements. Students will integrate the stages and processes employed in the development of a new food product, from idea generation through to product launch. Issues considered include concept development, market research, product formulation and shelf life, legislation, manufacturing and quality control protocols, packaging and labeling requirements, the product launch and post-launch product management.
learning_outcomes: Clearly define and justify the rationale for development of a new or improved food product based on the integration of the consumer behaviour, market trends and nutritional requirements.
Professionally pitch a new product concept and justify the choices made.

Integrate prior knowledge and skills in food science and nutrition, food safety, formulation and processing, and quality assurance to plan the development of new or improved food product with acceptable sensory qualities and shelf life that satisfy regulatory requirements.
Discuss the factors that will influence future trends in new product development.
Critically discuss the steps and systems required to develop or improve a food product in response to an identified market need or opportunity.

title: Food Microbiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the fundamentals of microbiology, focusing on the structure, function, and classification of microorganisms, such as bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites. Students will examine their roles in food production, processing, and storage, and their impact on foodborne diseases, human health, and environmental systems.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the importance of microorganisms to human health, the environment and food systems.
Explain the principles underlying the microbiological quality and safety of foods.
Describe the microbial contamination of foods, food spoilage and food preservation and microbial borne diseases.
Apply the roles of microorganisms in food production and processing.
Demonstrate practical skills in microbial detection and handling techniques.
Describe the structure and function of microorganisms, kinetics of microbial growth and how microorganisms can be cultivated and assayed.

title: Food Safety and Quality Management
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students develop a deeper understanding of application of food quality and safety concepts in the context of food business. Students consider the principles, implementation and management of quality and safety in the food industry. They explore modern quality management principles (eg. Total Quality Management, ISO9001, etc) and how objective and subjective food quality factors are perceived by different stakeholders within the food value chain. The implementation and management of food quality will draw on frameworks and tools that support the planning and delivery of quality such as customer-centred design, process management, including continuous improvement and statistical process control. Special attention is placed on the assurance of quality and safety in food business through the implementation of Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) and Food Safety plans. Using these principles, students develop the skills to plan, monitor and sustain a quality management system in a food environment.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss cues and attributes that contribute to the perception of food quality, including safety and reliability, sensory properties, nutritional and health outcomes, provenance and authenticity, cost and convenience, and production systems.
Apply the principles of Total Quality Management to design a quality management system appropriate to a food manufacturing service or retail environment.
Analyse quality attribute data using the appropriate statistical techniques and recommend actions to assure processes remain in control and products remain within specifications.
Design and implement a Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) and food safety plan for a food business.
Integrate food manufacturing requirements and quality assessment techniques into an effective quality management system.
Apply Australian and international food legislation to design and evaluate food quality management systems.

title: Food, Nutrition and Sociology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will reflect on the complex range of factors that influence food choices, diet and lifestyle. These include personal, social, cultural, psychological, environmental, economic and political factors. Students will develop the knowledge and skills to analyse contemporary issues affecting food and eating within society and evaluate systems through a variety of lenses, with the ultimate aim of developing an ethical, culturally responsive and socially just approach to working in the food and nutrition field.
learning_outcomes: Discuss what is meant by cultural safety and social justice in relation to food and nutrition issues with particular emphasis on First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD) communities.
Describe and demonstrate the application of reflective practice in contributing to professional development and excellence in practice.
Identify evidence based literature relevant to food and nutrition issues.

Analyse the methods of food and nutritional monitoring, food systems and nutrition policy, and investigate the influence of food policy, food marketing, food technology and ecological issues on the food supply chain.
Analyse the complex range of factors that impact individual food choice throughout the life cycle.

title: Forecasting and Risk Assessment
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the identification, measurement and management of risk using multi-disciplinary techniques. The role of the decision maker and the role of decision making heuristics and bias are studied together with key qualitative and quantitative techniques used to model, measure and treat risk. The subsequent treatment of risk through risk retention, self insurance or the transfer and avoidance of risk is also examined. The subject allows students to identify these concepts from the perspective of a risk manager, e.g., establish risks in relation to individuals, property and legal liability. Whenever possible, study examples will be based on the real-world problems encountered in the work environment of students.
learning_outcomes: Assess and critically evaluate the role of the decision maker in risk and the influences of decision making heuristics, bias and risk preference in the risk management process.
Critically interpret the risk management concept and discriminate and appraise different definitions of risk and risk management.
Interpret risk through modelling techniques.
Design and implement strategies to diminish risk through the potential to self insure, or to transfer risk using different product solutions.
Determine the probability, frequency and consequences of a risk event occurring.

title: Forensic Accounting, Asset Tracing and Recovery
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to methods of forensic accounting and asset recovery as they are applied during financial investigations. Students will develop knowledge of basic accounting concepts and principles; and explore the role of business, both as victims of financial crime, as well as vehicles by which financial crimes are committed. In considering financial systems and businesses as both a victim and vehicle, students will learn what forensic accounting can offer a financial crime investigation and the circumstances under which they should be engaged. Students will also gain experience analysing financial crime case data and producing forensic financial crime reports.
learning_outcomes: Apply their knowledge of the work and scope of the forensic accountant in tracing the proceeds of financial crime, and the current model of expert witness statements, to prepare a brief of evidence for prosecution.
Apply the expert witness statement to secure the order to restrain, forfeit and / or seize assets under current relevant legislation.
Make recommendations to improve business practices to prevent financial crime.
Demonstrate their knowledge of the role of a forensic accountant in an investigation, as both an investigator and expert witness, by designing a financial crime investigation plan.

title: Forensic Investigation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will acquire an understanding of the principles of forensic investigation and the complexities involved in conducting forensic investigations in a contemporary context. Students will develop a deeper understanding of the methods for acquiring digital evidence from more contemporary, non-traditional, digital systems (such as social media sites, virtualised systems and multimedia platforms) using practical examples, case studies and activities. Students will also learn principles of investigating malware and ransomware attacks and how to resolve potential investigatory difficulties in these contexts.
learning_outcomes: Describe key terms, concepts and implementation considerations of fundamental cyber security systems, processes, and tools in a contemporary business context.
Analyse and describe vulnerabilities, threat actors and threat vectors within a contemporary context.
Analyse approaches to implementing secure networks, firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems and identity and access management systems.
Formulate approaches for incident analysis and response, risk management and disaster recovery/business continuity.
Analyse typical cyber security requirements, formulate and implement technical and procedural strategy to provide enhanced security solutions.

title: Forensic Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the interface between psychology and the justice system. It builds on areas of psychology such as social, clinical, cognitive and developmental psychology as well as incorporating material from other relevant disciplines such as criminology. The emphasis in the subject is on the critical evaluation of theory and research and the ability to apply it to issues such as the development of criminal behaviour and approaches to dealing with it.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate a range of theories relevant to forensic psychology.
Outline the scope of forensic psychology and describe the interface between psychology and the judicial system.
Use the psychological literature to develop and support arguments.
Apply theory and research critically and appropriately to issues in the justice system.
Recognise ethical issues involved in forensic psychology.
Write a policy type report.
Demonstrate a basic knowledge of some of the psychological tests used in forensic situations.

title: Foundation Mathematics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for students who enter university without a strong background in mathematics and who need to raise their knowledge and skills in mathematics to a higher standard.
learning_outcomes: Solve problems involving uncertainty using the basic principles of probability.
Make and justify informed decisions about financial situations based on appropriate models.
Construct and use diagrams to solve mathematical problems.
Describe and model patterns in mathematical terms.
Demonstrate the purposes and functions of mathematics in the community.
Successfully apply mathematical skills and processes across a wide range of topic areas.
Communicate mathematical ideas and reasoning clearly and effectively using symbols, numbers, words, diagrams and graphs.
prerequisites: MTH101: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Foundation Mathematics
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will review foundation skills in mathematics including order of operations, signed numbers, fractions, decimals and percentages, index numbers, scientific notation & significant figures, algebra, equations solving, graphs, trigonometry with right angle triangles, and problem solving strategies. The subject is particularly relevant to those students needing to update their skills and confidence before studying a mathematics or mathematics related subject.
learning_outcomes: Understand and work with algebraic expressions.
Use a calculator confidently and correctly.
Understand and work with arithmetic.
Understand concepts of functions, variables and graphs.
Apply problem solving skills to practical problems.

title: Foundation Physics 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This micro subject is one of two Physics offerings in the Studylink suite of subjects. It introduces students to measurement, vectors, force, motion and energy. Waves (Electromagnetic, Light and Sound), Electricity and Atomic and Nuclear Physics. Following completion, students may undertake Foundation Physics 2.
learning_outcomes: Explain equilibrium and momentum
Calculate the displacement, velocity and acceleration of objects using the laws of Kinematics
Describe how heat is transferred
Explain Newtons Laws of motion
Calculate potential energy, kinetic energy and elastic potential energy
Identify vector and scalar quantities, including vector addition
Describe how uncertainty arises with physical measurements
Explain the law of conservation of energy

title: Foundation Maths
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Foundation Maths is one of four modular subjects in the Access Charles Sturt Entry course. It explicitly teaches the foundational numeracies required for successful university study across a range of disciplines. Each module builds on the last to progressively support the development of numerical communication, confidence and curiosity. Students will perform numerical operations using efficient mental strategies or a calculator. They will be able to communicate solutions to simple and unfamiliar mathematical problems. They will be supported to ask good questions to clarify understanding and be able to reflect on their experience with maths to identify their own strengths as well as their opportunities for growth.
learning_outcomes: Apply maths learning strategies to solve problems independently and cooperatively by contributing to the maths learning community.
Perform numerical operations using efficient mental strategies or a calculator.
Ask good questions to clarify understanding.
Reflect on experience with maths to identify strengths and opportunities for growth.
Communicate solutions to simple and unfamiliar mathematical problems.

title: Foundational Pharmacology and Pathophysiology for Allied Health Practice
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will apply their knowledge of basic chemistry, biochemistry and human physiology to the study of pharmacology. This foundation subject provides students with an introduction to pathophysiology and fundamental concepts of pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and polypharmacy, with an emphasis on the cardiac, renal and respiratory systems. Students will analyse a range of pharmacological treatments for diabetes, to contextualise the effects of chronic disease on multiple organ systems. This subject also introduces students to the concept of pharmacological manipulation of the immune system and reviews the pharmacology of anti-inflammatory drugs.
learning_outcomes: Explain the mechanism of action and properties of pharmacological agents used for the treatment of cardiac, respiratory, renal, endocrine and inflammatory pathology.
Analyse the implications of polypharmacy, drug-drug and drug-disease interactions when taking a client history.
Apply foundational knowledge of pathology and pharmacology to explain the clinical management of chronic disease.
Appropriately apply the professional language associated with medical and pharmacological practice.

title: Foundation Physics 2
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This micro subject is one of two Physics offerings in the Studylink suite of subjects. It introduces students to Waves (Electromagnetic, Light and Sound), Electricity and Atomic and Nuclear Physics. It is advised that students first complete Foundation Physics 1.
learning_outcomes: Describe how medical imaging equipment such as Ultrasound, MRI, X-Ray, CT and PET utilise the waves and atomic physics
Explain and apply the relationship between current, resistance and voltage in electrical circuits
Explain the physics of wave motion, both Light and sound
Demonstrate understanding of magnetism and its relationship to electricity
Describe the electromagnetic spectrum
Explain the physics of atomic and nuclear physics

title: Foundations and Techniques in Biochemistry
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an outline of the structure and function of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids); the major metabolic and bioenergetic pathways within cells; and practical experience in common techniques used in biochemistry. It provides the basis for further studies in metabolism, molecular and cell biology, genetics, immunology and microbiology, physiology, plant science, biotechnology and disease processes.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure and function of the four major classes of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids) and understand the relationship between structure and function.
Describe common techniques used in the study of biochemistry.
Perform basic techniques in biochemistry such as spectrophotometric protein assays, chromatography, electrophoresis, and enzyme kinetics assays.
Describe the properties of enzymes as biological catalysts.
Describe the major metabolic pathways used to synthesise and consume ATP.
Describe the role of energy in living cells, with particular reference to the concept of free energy and the role of ATP.

title: Foundations for Information Studies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with the contextual, professional, scholarly and technological foundations of the body of knowledge underpinning the information disciplines and professions. Professional information settings including libraries, archives, records repositories and other information centres and organizations will be discussed. An introduction to information scholarship and research and current issues in library and information studies practice will follow. The subject will orient students to the MIS program and enable them to develop and refine their individual educational and professional objectives.
learning_outcomes: Identify, evaluate and communicate about developments arising from major issues, questions and trends that define the information fields.
Compare and contrast how libraries and information agencies fit into constantly evolving information technology and infrastructure contexts.
Describe and investigate information professions, information users, and the discipline and fields comprising library and information studies.
Apply IT skills to a range of contexts related to the information studies field and the roles of IT in enabling the management of information.
Identify and explain ethical, legal and policy issues relevant to the information sector.
Investigate and critically analyse libraries and information agencies in their historical, social, cultural, economic, and political contexts.
Demonstrate comprehension of the diversity of library and information scholarship, including the professional and theoretical discourse of library and information studies.

title: Foundations for Pastoral and Spiritual Care of Older People
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a theoretical basis for pastoral and spiritual care of older people within a holistic framework. It introduces students to biblical-theological, spiritual, psychosocial and ethical perspectives on ageing. Taking into account pluralist socio-cultural and religious context(s) of contemporary Australia, it pays attention to: concepts of human being and personhood; understandings of body, mind and spirit; psychosocial and spiritual development in later life, including life review, narrative and spiritual reminiscence; the gifts and challenges of later life, including the search for wisdom and meaning, self-transcendence, role changes, isolation, suffering, illness and disability; and particular ethical issues associated with ageing.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on relevant literature and their own beliefs about the gifts and challenges associated with ageing.
Demonstrate the ability to reflect critically on the ageing process from several points of view: biblical-theological, spiritual, psychosocial and ethical.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of ethical aspects of ageing in contemporary society.
Evaluate critically various models of spiritual and faith development in later life.
Outline and discuss critically processes of life review, narrative and spiritual reminiscence in relation to the search for meaning in later life.
Demonstrate an understanding of pertinent issues relating to theological anthropology, including personhood, embodiment, ageing and dying.
Articulate, both sympathetically and critically, approaches to ageing in Christian, other-faith, indigenous and humanistic traditions.
Demonstrate specialised knowledge of psychosocial and spiritual development in later life.

title: Foundations in Clinical Procedures and Veterinary Nursing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the knowledge and skills associated with veterinary clinical procedures and veterinary nursing. Students will develop knowledge and skills in veterinary imaging, laboratory procedures and the maintenance and preparation of a range of medical and diagnostic equipment and procedures. Students will also develop self-reflection and self-assessment skills to develop professional habits for lifelong learning. ASC182 is the second of four subjects which are used for the basis of the awarding of a Certificate IV in Veterinary Nursing.
learning_outcomes: Collect biological samples and perform pathology procedures, including maintaining the integrity of samples and preparing consignments for diagnostic laboratories.
Implement and complete imaging routines, including radiography, ultrasound and endoscopy, according to industry and practice policies and procedures.
Identify animal anatomy and physiological functions, and compare and describe animal classification, body systems, and external anatomical features to recognise normal health.
Provide high quality nursing care for patients treated or housed in a veterinary practice, including provision of advice to clients, monitoring of patients and providing first aid as required.
Implement medical nursing routines, including the preparation and handling of animal patients and equipment for specific routines.
prerequisites: ASC180: Animal Handling and Health Care

title: Foundations in Social Policy
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: SPE211 provides a historical perspective on political social policy debates that helps us to understand contemporary developments in which social provisions are distributed and social conduct is regulated. The first part of this subject provides an introduction to politics, government and the Australian political system. This is aimed at providing a foundation for Part 2 which focuses more specifically on the role of governments in shaping society towards the achievement of social and economic goals. In the second part of this subject we explore the controversial and contested territory of the pursuit of social well-being through government social policies. The focus will be on the role of governments in shaping society and thereby creating a social environment in which individual citizens and whole sectors of the population enjoy more, or less, social opportunities and rewards. You are encouraged to participate in the SPE211 subject online by discussing and sharing your learning about subject topics and its application to debates in the media.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the impacts social policies can have on diverse sectors of the population.
Understand the concepts of liberal and democratic as they relate to a Liberal democratic political system.
Demonstrate how Liberal Democratic Political Systems Enhance or limit the wellbeing of citizens.
Demonstrate an understanding of rights and freedoms in a Liberal Democracy.
prerequisites: SPE101: Introduction to Politics and Social Policy
SPE201: Politics and Social Policy in Australia
SPE301: Critical Issues in Social Policy

title: Foundations in Veterinary Surgical Nursing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to veterinary surgical nursing and nursing support. Students will develop knowledge and skills in the pre-, intra- and post-operative procedures involved in surgical support. Students will learn to provide support for the animal patient whilst maintaining high standards of veterinary surgical nursing. Students will engage in topics such as admission, surgical preparation, anaesthesia, patient recovery and discharge. ASC183 is the third of four subjects which are used for the basis of the awarding of a Certificate IV in Veterinary Nursing. This subject requires 15 days of work placement.
learning_outcomes: Prepare for and monitor anaesthesia and analgesics in patients (animals) for surgical procedures.
Coordinate surgery schedules and prepare the surgical environment.
Identify, clean, prepare and pack surgical instruments for sterilisation.
Provide support for the veterinary surgeon for routine and non-routine surgical procedures.
Perform dental prophylaxis and assist with simple extractions.
prerequisites: ASC182: Foundations in Clinical Procedures and Veterinary Nursing

title: Foundations of Agriculture
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
