syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the Australian agricultural landscape, emphasising the unique characteristics of agricultural industries and addressing sustainability issues to promote growth and resilience. Students will develop practical skills in information literacy, critical thinking, and academic writing while gaining an understanding of agricultural practices through theoretical knowledge and hands-on experience, enabling them to make informed decisions on agricultural production systems.
learning_outcomes: Apply effective academic skills and professional practice competencies.
Identify and appraise the Australian agricultural landscape.
Identify, analyse, and appraise sustainability issues impacting agricultural growth and resilience.
Review and evaluate literature and data to facilitate planning, problem-solving, and decision-making in agriculture.

title: Foundations of Biochemistry and Human Molecular Genetics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The study of biochemistry and genetics provides the background for understanding the underlying pathophysiology of numerous diseases. This subject provides an outline of the structure and function of the major macromolecules and how their metabolic pathways have intertwined bioenergetic pathways within cells. The broad field of genetics will also be introduced covering genetic regulation and the central dogma, which is the process of transcribing DNA into mRNA and translating mRNA into proteins. The role of genetic analysis in guiding diagnosis and treatment of diseases affected by genetic variations will also be explored.
learning_outcomes: Discuss how DNA technology can direct diagnosis and treatment of human disease into the future.
Explain how genetic variation occurs and how it contributes to human disease, using examples of inherited disorders.
Explain how cells store and provide energy for enzymatic processes using alternate metabolic pathways to synthesis ATP.
Outline the processes of DNA replication, transcription, translation, mutation, repair and heredity.
Describe DNA and chromatin structure.
Describe the structure and function of the major classes of biological macromolecules and explain how structure impacts their function.

title: Foundations of Big Data Analytics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to big data analytics as a tool for addressing and applying new analytical methods and algorithms to process large volumes of data in the context of information technology. Students will be introduced to the key practical concepts behind big data analytics. Students will also learn how to successfully extract value from massive volumes of structured and unstructured data to contribute towards informed decision making processes. Students will be provided an overview of the methods and techniques that help automate data analysis such as data mining, machine learning and artificial intelligence. Students will also be introduced to well-known software analytic tools used in this area.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the challenges associated in harvesting value from big data to empower decision making processes.
Extract value from large data sets for informed decision making by utilizing some well-known software tools.
Discuss the basic concepts behind big data analytics and recognise the various types and sources of big data.
Interpret machine learning and artificial intelligence concepts in the context of big data analytics.
Explain the major stages of big data analytics life cycle.

title: Foundations of Biology 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Foundations of Biology 1 is one of a suite of non-award short subjects offered on the Study Link platform and designed for students who may not have studied biology in the later years of secondary school. This is the first in a series of four subjects introducing students to the building blocks of biology. Students are supported to develop an understanding of biology through an introduction to the structure and function of cells. This is contextualised against a framework which establishes the role of biology in society, including discipline specific pathways. Students will also develop skills in scientific thinking and communication. This subject provides foundation knowledge for future science studies, and the first step into additional Study Link biology subjects.
learning_outcomes: Explain the basics of biology and cell structure and function
Apply skills in scientific thinking and communication in learning situations.
Identify the role of biology in society including in discipline contexts

title: Foundations of Business Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundation into the concepts and skills of business analysis. The subject covers the entire process from problem investigation through requirements and information gathering to solution engineering. It also examines stakeholder communication and buy-in principles as part of the solution process, as well as change management and implementation.
learning_outcomes: Appropriately apply the functions of business analysis tools and techniques.
Integrate solution design with typical business solution implementation processes.
Devise a stakeholder buy-in and alignment strategy, and to manage and influence the stakeholder decision process.
Design and create suitable solutions to business challenges using the typical tools of business analysis.
Compare and contrast the elements of the Business Analysis International Qualifications (BAIQ) framework.
Critically analyse the role, purpose and function of business analysis as a professional discipline.

title: Foundations of Clinical Education
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject applies the principle of transformative learning to provide an introductory exploration of education in a clinical health context. In this subject, students will explore the impacts of the clinical setting to evaluate strategies which address institutional barriers to the provision of effective healthcare education. Students will reflect on the role of the clinical educator and how this differs from other health professionals; identifying the key attributes and responsibilities that the educator requires to be effective in their profession. The principles of adult learning will be applied to real world contexts, emphasising the need for educators to adapt to diverse, individual learning needs of clinicians and students. Finally, students will learn about the clinical educator's role in the use of technology for clinical education.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the opportunities and challenges that a specific clinical environment presents as an education setting.
Discuss a range of contemporary technologies used in clinical education.
Apply the principles of adult learning to accommodate diverse learning styles, cultural backgrounds and levels of experience for adult learners.
Differentiate the responsibilities and attributes of the clinical educator from other health professionals.
Examine the role of clinical education in bringing about person-centred changes in a clinical setting.
prerequisites: HLT539: Foundations of Teaching and Learning in Clinical Education

title: Foundations of Clinical Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces foundational skills and principles for safe and effective paramedic care in paramedicine practice settings. Students will develop situational awareness, apply work health and safety (WHS) and infection control protocols, and manage scenes safely. Emphasis is placed on building rapport through active listening and empathy while performing primary and secondary surveys tailored to medical and trauma contexts. Students will also explore basic trauma care and develop essential skills for managing cardiac arrest, including clinical decision-making and collaborative handovers. Students will acquire a strong foundation for safe, professional, and person-centred paramedic practice.
learning_outcomes: Describe evidence-informed foundational trauma care.
Implement safe and effective interventions to provide basic life support.
Perform foundational medical and trauma assessments, interventions, and apply clinical handover skills.
Explain the principles of work health and safety practices, including infection control, for both self and the health consumer.
Discuss and apply effective communication strategies to foster rapport, convey empathy, and show respect.

title: Foundations of Corruption and Misconduct
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the different approaches to integrity assurance and corruption prevention in the public sector. The subject highlights the suitability of different approaches of particular challenges arising within the context of public service organisational corruption. It initially focuses upon the nature of the public service ethos, and on some of the key challenges to its operation in practice. The subject then examines the nature of corruption and misconduct and considers definitions, costs and consequences of corruption as well as examining different explanations for why corruption and misconduct occur. It looks at major forms of corruption and misconduct, and uses case studies to develop student understandings of how corruption and misconduct can occur and continue unchecked
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the foundations of the public service ethos.
Recognise institutional, political and individual factors associated with corruption and misconduct within public sector organisations.
Demonstrate familiarity with the main forms of corruption and misconduct.
Apply theoretical perspectives to the understanding of why corruption and misconduct can arise, within the context of particular case studies.
Recognise different ethical frameworks applicable to the delivery of public services.

title: Foundations of Clinical Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will be introduced to the foundations of scene control, infection control, patient assessment, history taking, basic patient management, maths and medical terminology. Students will start to formulate a field impression and implement a treatment plan for the patient with introductory medical complaints. These competencies are fundamental skills required for the progression through their paramedic career.
learning_outcomes: explain basic work health and safety practices and safely perform manual handling, defibrillation, and infection control in the non-traumatic paramedic environment; and
apply the (evidence based) principles of basic scene assessment in the non-traumatic paramedic environment;
apply (evidence based) management techniques for patients requiring basic life support and/or fracture immobilisation, in the non-traumatic paramedic environment;
accurately and safely calculate medication dosages of common medications used in paramedicine;
perform a verbal patient handover.
demonstrate (evidence based) patient assessment skills required to perform primary and secondary surveys, and patient interviews;

title: Foundations of Crime Scene Investigation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles of crime scene investigation, focusing on protocols for securing, documenting, and processing scenes to preserve evidence integrity. Using simulations and case studies, students will analyse the consequences of poor scene management and evaluate best practices for digital documentation and chain-of-custody compliance. The subject explores ethical and legal responsibilities in evidence handling and develops skills in hypothesis testing and procedural critique for technology-driven forensic environments.
learning_outcomes: Practice identifying basic patterns in simulated crime scenes, comparing simple case studies to recognise differences between authentic and staged crime scenes with the intention of developing an initial hypothesis.
Apply best-practice, systematic methods for documenting, searching and collecting various forms of evidence.
Analyse and apply crime scene management protocols, including roles, responsibilities, and contamination prevention strategies, to preserve evidence integrity.
Assess investigative methods by identifying forensic opportunities in practical scenarios to understand how mistakes influence the admissibility of evidence.
Evaluate the ethical and legal considerations in the handling of crime scenes for evidence to be admissible in court, including continuity/chain of evidence.

title: Foundations of Critical Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students' previous education and experience to advance the knowledge and skills required to provide advanced paramedic practice. Students will investigate models of clinical reasoning, critical thinking, and decision-making to apply them to current and future paramedic practice. Theories and frameworks for leading self and others will be explored alongside strategies to further develop communication skills and manage risk in critical care paramedicine. Students will also learn to integrate the knowledge of safe, ethical, patient-centred and inclusive practice including for First Nations peoples into critical care paramedicine while developing their ability to collaborate as part of an interprofessional team.
learning_outcomes: Integrate paramedic knowledge of safe, ethical, patient-centred and inclusive practice in the context of critical care paramedicine.
Apply interprofessional and collaborative practice in critical care Paramedicine.
Apply self and team leadership skills alongside communication strategies in critical care Paramedicine.
Integrate clinical reasoning, critical thinking and decision making in the context of critical care paramedicine.

title: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 1
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: In this subject, novice level aspects of pre-clinical dentistry through theory, laboratory exercises and pre-clinical simulation will be introduced. This training will commence with concepts around work, health and safety and infection control according to the latest guidelines and legal requirements. Students are also introduced to the social and biomedical impacts on health and oral health. Simple concepts in caries pathophysiology and disease risk assessment will be introduced. Instruction in basic dental laboratory skills and techniques will also be an integral part of this unit along with pre-clinical simulation training, which will introduce students to the ongoing study and manipulation of dental materials and restorative cavity preparation techniques. Early knowledge in dental radiation science and radiographic technique will be provided. This novice level training will also assess manual dexterity and spatial sense.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the dynamic and emerging scope of dental practice in Australia and the cultural and societal influences on patient care, and social justice and access to dental care.
Demonstrate skills in specified cavity preparations and their restorations and specific skills in dental laboratory including evidence of developing manual dexterity and spatial sense.
Describe dental caries and periodontal disease and their etiological and preventative factors.

Explain the fundamentals of dental ethics, Australian health care system and legislation, oral health care team, and the relationship between the dentist and society, the dentist and patients and the dentist and colleagues.
Describe radiation sciences and radiographic techniques relevant to dentistry.
Describe current work, health and safety legislation and infection control guidelines related to the practice of dentistry and apply this knowledge in the simulation clinic.

Discuss the physical, chemical and mechanical properties that are foundational to the selection and use of dental materials and equipment in the dental technology laboratory and pre-clinical simulation clinic.
Explain the application of forces, levers and other principles of physics relevant to dental practice.
Demonstrate a basic knowledge of effective communication skills, clinical records keeping, clinical history taking and clinical data collections.

title: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 2
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject will continue the development of basic dental diagnostic and clinical management skills related to both simple restorative (operative) and periodontal procedures in the clinical dental environment. Students will learn differential diagnosis of simple oral conditions, appropriate to a novice-level clinician, and the management of simple restorative and periodontal procedures in the clinical dental environment. There will be a focus upon associated dental processes, the aetiology, diagnosis, differential diagnosis and immunopathogenesis of caries and periodontal diseases are presented in lecture and discussion sessions.
learning_outcomes: Explain the basic clinical procedures involved in the examination of the dental patient, including history, exam and diagnosis.
Apply foundation knowledge of oral condition, and basic clinical procedures in a clinical environment.
Describe the aetiology, diagnosis, differential diagnosis and immunopathogenesis of periodontal disease.
Describe the aetiology and differential diagnosis of common oral conditions.
Describe the aetiology, diagnosis, differential diagnosis and immunopathogenesis of dental caries.
prerequisites: DOH254: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 2
CHM102: Chemistry for Dental and Veterinary Sciences
DOH254: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 2

title: Foundations of Digital Infrastructure
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the foundational concepts, components, and operations of contemporary digital infrastructure in modern computing environments. In this subject, students will explore how digital systems exchange and manage data, how networked technologies support secure communication and connectivity, and how cloud and artificial intelligence technologies enable contemporary digital services and computing environments. Students will develop an understanding of core concepts related to data communications, networking, cyber security, cloud computing, and emerging digital technologies through practical activities and guided exploration.
learning_outcomes: Describe the fundamental concepts of digital infrastructure, including data communications, networking, cyber security, and cloud computing.
Explain how devices, networks, and applications exchange and manage data across interconnected systems.
Describe the role of cyber security, connectivity, and emerging technologies in contemporary digital environments.
Demonstrate basic skills in network configuration, cloud environments, and digital infrastructure tools through guided exercises.
Reflect on how cloud, artificial intelligence, and emerging digital technologies influence modern computing and society.

title: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 3
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide students with the opportunity to participate in the provision of patient-centred dental clinical care. There is a strong emphasis on diagnosis and evidence-based treatment planning and the completion of simple clinical procedures, including the administration of oral local anaesthetics, non-complex periodontic and restorative procedures, the relief of pain and the provision of uncomplicated removable dental prostheses.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate foundation knowledge and apply clinical skills relevant to the diagnosis and management of a patient presenting with pain.

Demonstrate foundation knowledge and an understanding of evidence-based practice and patient-centred care in the management of patients that fall into the scope of practice for a novice student practitioner.

Demonstrate foundation knowledge and apply clinical skills relevant to the management of simple restorative, periodontic, endodontic and removable prosthodontic cases (at the level of a novice student practitioner).

Demonstrate a consistent pattern of patient assessment, diagnosis and management planning including appropriate history taking (including medical assessment), examination, diagnostic analysis and the use of diagnostic aids.
prerequisites: DOH233: Pathological Basis of Human Disease
DOH335: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 3
DOH335: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 3

title: Foundations of Fire Investigation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the concepts and principles of fire investigation which will be enlarged upon in later subjects. It will present the types of investigations to be carried out at fire scenes in order to determine the origin and cause of the fire. Emphasis is placed on fire scene preservation, examination and the early identification of fraud indicators, as well as exhibit handling. Students will be introduced to the behaviour of fire and the effects that fire has on materials and structures, in addition to workplace health and safety issues associated with working on a fire ground. The aim is to develop a world best-practice methodical scientific and professional approach to fire scene investigation.
learning_outcomes: Apply investigative techniques such as observation, collection of evidence, and document the scene by note-taking and photography, to inform the production of final reports/statements.
Apply an understanding of fire ignition, combustion principles, fire dynamics and interpretation of fire patterns to conduct an initial investigation.

Apply a foundational/introductory understanding of the different types of fire events (structural fires, motor vehicle accidents and fires, electrical fires, explosions and wildfires) and human motivation and behaviour, to inform a fire investigation.
Analyse all the evidence to determine the fire origin and develop and test an hypothesis of the cause of the fire in order to prepare a brief and give evidence in a courtroom.
Apply fundamental principles of scene and evidence preservation whilst establishing and maintaining a safe working environment.
Recognise the differences between accidental, natural, incendiary/arson and undetermined fire cause classifications, with attention to fraud indicators.

title: Foundations of Health Management and Leadership
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the Australian healthcare system and equips them with the knowledge and skills necessary for effective leadership and management in the healthcare industry. Students will delve into key concepts such as leadership theories, organisational culture, professional resilience, evidence-based decision making, and reflective practice. Through a combination of theoretical study and practical application, students are prepared to navigate the complex landscape of healthcare management while fostering personal growth and professional development. In addition, students will acquire a comprehensive toolkit to excel in the complex and dynamic field of healthcare management. By embedding management and leadership concepts and the recognition of evidence-based decision making, students complete the subject with the skills and knowledge necessary to lead effectively and drive positive change within healthcare organisations.
learning_outcomes: Analyse evidence-based decision making within the healthcare industry.
Describe organisational culture within healthcare organisations.
Apply leadership and management theory to professional practice.
Discuss the Australian and international healthcare systems and structures.
Incorporate professional resilience and reflection into practice.

title: Foundations of Inclusive Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject teacher education students will develop their understandings of inclusion and inclusive teaching practices that supports learner agency and effectively teach all students, including students with a disability, in disability affirming ways, in school and early childhood education settings. This includes understanding the intent and enactment of the relevant legislation and policies pertaining to the education of students with disabilities, contemporary thinking around inclusive education and the evidence-based foundations of inclusive teaching. Students will also develop strategies to engage and collaborate with other professionals, support services, students, parents and/or caregivers in planning for inclusion and participation in safe and positive classroom environments that maximise the potential for a wide range of learner variability. The subject includes a focus on responsive teaching, learner variability, explicit teaching, differentiation and universal design for learning, with a specific focus on supporting the literacy and numeracy needs of learners. The potential of digital technologies to be used for supporting participation and engagement is also explored.
learning_outcomes: Apply the essential characteristics of explicit teaching and other effective teaching strategies to support academic inclusion of students with disabilities with a specific focus on supporting literacy and numeracy.
Explain the research-based evidence of a tiered approach to differentiation as a reasonable adjustment, and describe its applicability.

Outline the implications for teaching and learning arising from legislative requirements and policies that support the inclusion and participation of children and young people with disabilities in educational settings.
Describe disability affirming and trauma informed approaches to behaviour support for all children including those with complex learning profiles

Describe strategies and processes for collaborating with learners, parents/caregivers and other professionals in planning for inclusion and participation of children and young people with disabilities.
Develop a lesson using the principles of universal design for learning in order to teach to a wide range of learner variability.
Describe ICT and other strategies in their planning to support inclusive learner participation and engagement.
Describe appropriate learning goals and actions to support learner variability (including disability, learning difficulties and giftedness), based on an IFSP/ILP meeting.
prerequisites: ESS306: Programming, Teaching and Learning in Inclusive Settings

title: Foundations of Intelligence Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This micro subject provides an introduction to the fundamentals of intelligence. It examines the purpose and use of intelligence in the private sector, law enforcement, national security and military contexts. The subject explains the types of intelligence such as tactical, operational, and strategic, and teaches basic analytical techniques. The subject is suitable for those new to intelligence, needing to use intelligence in the workplace, or with interest in exploring a career in the intelligence sector.
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically, evaluate and transform information to complete a range of activities.
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of intelligence and the application of intelligence in law enforcement, national security and the private sector.

title: Foundations of Learning and Teaching in Higher Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: EEL522 develops the capacity to teach effectively, introducing learning and teaching theory and practice skills relevant in higher education. Participants will enhance the student learning experience through transformative teaching approaches, practices, and innovative design that support the diversity of students represented in the Higher education sector. Subject learning activities highlight the need for deliberate and reflexive practice, informed by scholarly activity and the development of a personal professional learning planning. Assessments in this subject are authentic, and the learning and assessment process includes opportunity for constructive, and timely feedback to learners. The cohesive assessment regime sequences assessments to support learners as they progressively develop knowledge and skills.
learning_outcomes: Design and evaluate assessment tasks to demonstrate constructive alignment within the subject, as well as alignment with institutional policies and a recognition of student diversity.
Demonstrate reflective practice, professionalism, and academic integrity to make informed judgements and decisions on the student learning experience.

Plan and design quality teaching and learning experiences that are informed by a scholarly understanding of student diversity, using disciplinary, practice-based, and multi-modal pedagogies to enhance the learner experience.
Critically evaluate the social, cultural and historical dimensions of teaching in Higher Education in Australia using Indigenist Standpoint methodology.
Analyse their individual learning and development priorities and develop a professional development plan to guide their professional practice.
prerequisites: EEL416: Learning and Teaching at CSU
EEL516: Foundations of Learning and Teaching in Higher Education
EEL409: Developing as a Teacher in Higher Education

title: Foundations of Learning and Teaching in Higher Education
school: Division of Learning and Teaching
syllabus_overview: EEL516 Foundations of Learning & Teaching in Higher Education introduces participants to professional development planning and to the key issues and challenges in planning, designing and facilitating learning in higher education. The subject addresses the needs of academic probation at CSU and is based on the criteria for becoming a Higher Education Academy (HEA) Associate Fellow. Participants prepare a Professional Development Plan that helps them identify their teaching strengths and development needs and to choose a pathway through a menu of modules structured around three HEA Areas of Activity. Participants complete authentic assessments related to their teaching practice and develop a reflective narrative on their learning and achievement with respect to the subject learning outcomes. Participants are required to demonstrate completion of the Indigenous Cultural Competency Program as an essential component of this subject.
learning_outcomes: Develop an ongoing professional development plan, informed by experience and scholarship.
Demonstrate effective preparation and performance in teaching and supporting student learning that is informed by scholarship and reflective practice.
Plan and design quality teaching and learning experiences that are informed by a scholarly understanding of student learning and pedagogies.
Reflect on their learning from the Indigenous Cultural Competency Program and its influence on their teaching ideals and practices.
Evaluate and revise assessment tasks to demonstrate alignment with CSU policies and scholarly practices.
Reflect on their learning experiences and demonstrate their achievement of the subject learning outcomes.
prerequisites: EEL409: Developing as a Teacher in Higher Education
EEL416: Learning and Teaching at CSU

title: Foundations of Law and Criminology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a preliminary examination of the Australian Legal System and its institutions, with particular emphasis on social justice concepts, theories and historical analysis.
learning_outcomes: be able to describe the evolution of the Australian Criminal Justice systems and the institutions;
be able to describe the institutions of criminal justice in Australia;
to be able to describe the criminal justice laws;
be able to apply a knowledge of the processes and practices of criminal justice systems in Australia through analysis of state justice systems;
to be able to describe the basic theories of justice;
be able to demonstrate the ability to undertake research and academic writing and display professional communication and conduct with academic staff and students.
be able to evaluate the effects of cultural norms and expectations on the criminal justice systems; and

title: Foundations of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn the fundamental principles and practical skills for the physiotherapy management of musculoskeletal presentations (including sports injuries) across the lifespan. Students will learn to use a problem-solving approach in the assessment and management of specific presentations that may affect the musculoskeletal system. Learning in this subject will focus initially on the lower limb and progress to the thoraco-lumbar spine. Communication, professional and ethical behaviour, and other elements of professional practice including reflection and critical analysis will be a focus of this subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional and ethical behaviour appropriate to musculoskeletal physiotherapy practice.
Reflect on professional practice and recommend actions to improve their own skills and knowledge.
Demonstrate foundational clinical reasoning processes which explore, explain and analyse assessment findings.
Use risk stratification tools to identify patients at risk of a poor outcome and alter management plans appropriately for these patients.
Communicate effectively to involve the client and relevant others in the planning and implementation of musculoskeletal physiotherapy practice.

Plan and implement safe and effective physiotherapy management for disorders of the lower limb and lumbar spine across the lifespan, and recognise when physiotherapy management is no longer required, or referral to another practitioner is appropriate.
Locate, evaluate and use evidence-based information to inform decision making and develop and guide their own knowledge, learning and practice.

Plan and apply a range of physiotherapy assessment and evaluation techniques using tests, imaging, tools and outcome measures relevant to the lower limb and lumbar spine for people across the lifespan.
Critically analyse resources, synthesise the information and communicate effectively according to the context and audience.
prerequisites: BMS172: Functional Anatomy of the Vertebral Column, Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb

title: Foundations of Oral Surgery
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with an opportunity to develop their knowledge and skills in the management of simple dental extractions incorporating diagnosis, treatment planning, execution, and post-operative follow up. This learning will be underpinned by discussion of the surgical principles and biological processes that accompany any surgical intervention and further supported by a focus on understanding the general principles of pharmacology with relevance to dental care, pain control and administering local anaesthetics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the general principles of pharmacology and pharmacotherapeutics with relevance to dental care.
Apply knowledge and skills relevant to the provision of simple, safe and effective local anaesthesia.

Demonstrate the professional knowledge and surgical skills necessary to manage cases appropriate to their level of training and abilities, recognising the boundaries of their scope of practice as a novice practitioner.
prerequisites: DOH233: Pathological Basis of Human Disease

title: Foundations of Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the application of assessment principles to inform physiotherapy management, including the use of e-health digital technologies for rural and remote physiotherapy practice. Students will learn the principles of goal setting and client education for common health conditions. Students will develop their skills in interprofessional practice by beginning to consider other health professional roles in client care. Students will begin to learn about the role of physiotherapists across the lifespan and basic principles of human development. This subject will also enable students to further develop their understanding of the business of physiotherapy in local and global settings and sustainable practice in the context of physiotherapy.
learning_outcomes: Use clinical reasoning processes to set goals for client recovery.
Outline the role of a physiotherapist across the lifespan.
Communicate effectively in written and verbal forms with clients and colleagues, in the planning and implementation of physiotherapy management strategies.
Explain the business of physiotherapy in local and global settings and sustainable practice in the context of physiotherapy.
Use evidence-based practice and current research to guide the development of professional knowledge and clinical decision-making in physiotherapy.
Demonstrate foundational collaborative practice skills as a basis for teamwork and interprofessional practice.
Demonstrate ethical, safe and effective person-centred physiotherapy management.
Describe the roles of other health professionals in managing people with diverse clinical presentations, including individuals living in rural and remote communities.
prerequisites: PHS100: Introduction to Physiotherapy Clinical Practice

title: Foundations of Professional Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the core competencies required to practice as a professional psychologist. It focuses on the development of competence in evidence-based practice, ethical decision-making, basic interviewing and counselling skills, assessment and diagnosis of psychopathology, and in generating socio-culturally informed individualised formulations and treatment plans.
learning_outcomes: Discuss an understanding of the issues relevant to inter-professional learning and practice.
Critically analyse and synthesise a large body of literature in order to discuss the history and characteristics of the major taxonomic systems for psychopathology.
Synthesise complex information in order to develop individualized culturally informed formulations and treatment plans for disorders commonly encountered in professional practice.
Reflect on current levels of competence in order to further develop and enhance demonstration of basic counselling skills.

Analyse critically and synthesize a large body of complex information in order to support the application of ethical decision-making theories and practices to ethical dilemmas commonly encountered in professional practice.
Reflect on current levels of competence in order to develop and/or enhance diagnostic interviewing skills in the assessment of psychopathology.

title: Foundations of Psychology 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: PSY101 Foundations of Psychology 1 and PSY102 Foundations of Psychology 2, together, provide a thorough introduction to the discipline of psychology. PSY101 Foundations of Psychology 1 includes the following topic areas: i) introduction to the science of psychology, ii) research methods, iii) biological aspects of behaviour, iv) sensation and perception, v) consciousness, vi) learning, memory, vii) cognitive processes and language, and viii) intelligence. Fundamental principles, theories, methods, and research findings are studied for each topic. A key aim of the subject is to develop students' competencies in critical thinking and essay writing following the American Psychological Association (APA) conventions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate foundational knowledge in the following core areas of psychology; i) history and development of psychology, ii) research methods, iii) biological aspects of behaviour, iv) sensation and perception, v) consciousness, vi) learning, vii) memory, viii) cognitive processes and language, and ix) intelligence.
Develop and apply critical thinking skills in evaluating psychological literature and questioning claims that arise from myth, stereotype, pseudoscience or untested assumptions.
Understand and apply a range of psychological theories, concepts, principles, and research findings, with the ability to communicate this effectively to others in various formats.
Demonstrate the ability to critically reflect on and understand the ethical and practical aspects and processes of psychological research.
Demonstrate theoretical knowledge of the nature and the historical and philosophical development of psychology as a scientific discipline and as a profession.
Correctly apply the structure and formatting conventions of an academic essay following the guidelines of the American Psychological Association (APA).

title: Foundations of Psychology for Health and Human Services
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the general field of psychology, its scientific and professional development. It examines some important areas of psychology including learning, developmental psychology, social psychology, personality, health psychology and psychological disorders. The subject is specifically designed for students who contemplate careers in health and human services. Students should note that this subject does not contribute to an Australian Psychology Accreditation Council accredited major in psychology.
learning_outcomes: Apply psychological theories and concepts to relevant issues and real world situations.
Understand and recount key concepts and theories in the discipline of psychology which are relevant to health and human services.

Apply academic skills developed throughout the subject including: sourcing, reading and evaluating scientific research articles and academic literature; academic writing; referencing; and critical thinking.

title: Foundations of Psychology 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: PSY102 Foundations of Psychology 2 complements with the introduction of core areas of psychology commenced in PSY101 Foundations of Psychology 1. PSY102 Foundations of Psychology 2 includes the following topic areas: i) motivation and emotion, ii) personality, iii) human development, iv) health, stress, and coping, v) psychological disorders and treatments, vi) social psychology, vii) cross-cultural psychology, and viii) Indigenous psychology with a focus on Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Fundamental principles, theories, methods and research findings are studied. This subject also introduces students to basic statistics and research methods. A key aim of the subject is to develop students' competencies in interpreting basic statistical concepts and reporting research projects following the American Psychological Association guidelines.
learning_outcomes: Correctly apply the structure and conventions of a psychological research report following the guidelines of the American Psychological Association (APA).
Demonstrate theoretical knowledge of the nature and the historical and philosophical development of psychology as a scientific discipline and as a profession.
Develop and apply critical thinking skills in evaluating psychological literature and questioning claims that arise from myth, stereotype, pseudoscience or untested assumptions.

Demonstrate foundational knowledge in the following core areas of psychology: i) motivation and emotion, ii) personality, iii) human development, iv) health, stress, and coping, v) psychological disorders and treatments, vi) social psychology, vii) cross-cultural psychology, and viii) Indigenous psychology with a focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Understand and apply a range of psychological theories, concepts, principles, and research findings, with the ability to communicate this effectively to others in various formats.
Demonstrate an understanding of basic statistical and research methods concepts and apply these to communicate the outcomes of a psychological research study.
Demonstrate foundational knowledge and critically reflect on cross-cultural and Indigenous psychology with a focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Demonstrate an ability to critically reflect on and understand the ethical and practical aspects and processes of psychological research.

title: Foundations of Restorative Dentistry
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to develop the novice student dental practitioner’s knowledge and skills in restorative dentistry, including the development of manual dexterity skills and hand-eye coordination. The preclinical simulation component comprises intra-coronal anterior and posterior tooth cavity preparations and their restoration using contemporary direct restorative materials. Practical aspects related to the contemporary management of dental caries will also be covered. The lecture content will support the topics covered in the practical classes and introduce students to several concepts of clinical significance including caries management systems and minimum intervention dentistry. These foundation level skills and understanding will be further developed in the clinical subjects later in the program.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the clinical significance of tooth conservation and contemporary restorative dental practice, at the level of a novice student dental practitioner.
Demonstrate the ability to take accurate dental impressions and create appropriate jaw records using a simulated model.
Demonstrate appropriate preparation of cavities for direct restorations in a simulated environment, at the level of a novice student dental practitioner.

Demonstrate and explain the application of restorative materials and techniques for the placement of direct restorations in a simulated environment, at the level of a novice student dental practitioner.
prerequisites: CHM102: Chemistry for Dental and Veterinary Sciences

title: Foundations of Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students extend their knowledge of typical communication and swallowing development and the models of practice speech pathologists apply in everyday practice with different populations (e.g., Evidence Based Practice (EBP), Family Centred Practice (FCP), Person Centred Practice (PCP), and Interprofessional Collaborative Practice (IPCP). This knowledge is then applied to the context of ageing, identifying and differentiating processes of typical ageing from disease processes. Students learn about speech pathology assessment and intervention through exploration of speech pathology documents, the use of online technologies, and through practice education experiences. In addition, students develop their professional and academic communication and reasoning skills, integrating information from a range of contexts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the development of professional communication skills including conversation, interview and client data collection with children, caregivers and people with communication difficulties.
Demonstrate research skills to collect, synthesise and critique information to evaluate clinical processes and/or models of practice in the context of individual, social and cultural variation.

Describe and differentiate between speech pathology practice frameworks (e.g., Evidence Based Practice (EBP), Family Centred Practice (FCP), Person Centred Practice (PCP), Interprofessional Collaborative Practice (IPCP), etc.).
Integrate knowledge of speech pathology practice areas and key associated disorders to identify and describe typical communication and swallowing across the lifespan.
Identify and describe processes for speech pathology assessment and intervention in clinical contexts.

title: Foundations of Trauma Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students apply their knowledge of anatomy and physiology to formulate a field impression and implement a treatment plan for the trauma patient. Students will continue to develop their foundation of clinical practice in a trauma environment. The focus will include scene control, assessment of the trauma patient, introduction to managing multi-casualty incidents, extrication techniques, triage principles and treatment integration.
learning_outcomes: explain the mechanisms of injury to body systems and their affect on patients health status;
prioritise and assess patients in the trauma environment;
accurately and safely calculate medication dosages of medications used in the paramedic trauma environment only if it is specifically needed.
apply the principles of scene assessment in the paramedic trauma environment;
apply (evidence based) management techniques for patients requiring basic life support relating to shock and traumatic injury;
work within scope of practice with other members of a multidisciplinary team to respond to a simulated mass casualty incident; and
explain public health models and organisational policies and guidelines for responding to multi-casualty or major incidents;
perform appropriate patient immobilisation, packaging and extrication, adhering to safe practices of patient manual handling;

title: Four Industry Certification Credits
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Administration Credit subject only

title: Fraud and Financial Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject explores current fraud and financial crime methodologies. Drawing on contemporary case studies the subject provides necessary information upon which further study is based. It explores variations in criminal offending from a range of industries and international jurisdictions and how those methodologies have evolved over time. It also examines the role of leadership in some of the world's most significant financial crime related failures.
learning_outcomes: Classify financial crimes by common characteristics.
Evaluate and discuss current and evolving financial crime risks.
Analyse and discuss the opportunities for crime created by individual, leadership and organisational failures.
Describe the nature and scale of financial crime.

title: From Grimm to Ghibli: A Journey Through Children's Literature
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Drawing on a broad range of examples from across the globe, LIT124 serves as an introduction to the wonderful world of children’s literature and focuses on narrative in fairy tales, picture books, films, poetry, and fantasy texts. It explores the evolving concept of the child and how literature for children responds to these changes, but it also considers ideas of age-appropriateness and subversion, as well as literature for children which engages with environmental, historical, and cultural questions. Students can expect to engage with a rich range of stories from the likes of the Brothers Grimm, Walt Disney, Hayao Miyazaki, and more.
learning_outcomes: Discuss some of the significant scholarship in the field of children's literature.
Analyse texts written or produced for children from a range of positions.
Describe selected texts produced for children.
Demonstrate a critical approach to a range of children's texts.

title: Functional Anatomy and Human Performance
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide a comprehensive coverage of kinesiological principles necessary to understand individual joint structure and function and apply kinanthropometrical knowledge of the human body. Students will learn to identify the elements of the neuro-musculoskeletal system and study the role of the bony segments, joint related connective tissue structures, muscles and the external forces applied to those structures. Practical components will involve anthropometry, posture and movement analysis with application including the effects of ageing, reduced use, and injury on the neuro-musculoskeletal system and the role physical activity and exercise plays in preventing functional decline.
learning_outcomes: Perform movement analysis on basic movement patterns used for exercise.
Evaluate results from anthropometric, flexibility and posture testing and provide appropriate exercise prescription recommendations.
Understand and explain the functional linkage of anatomy to motion.
Describe the effects of ageing, reduced used, injury and deconditioning on the neuro-musculoskeletal system and discuss the role of physical activity and exercise for preventing functional decline.
Identify and explain joint structure and function of all the major joints.
Utilise measurement techniques used to collect objective data in the functional anatomy field.
Describe the impact of body proportions on body composition, function, sports performance and talent identification.
Locate and identify selected anatomical features and describe function and adaptations that can occur during exercise.

title: Functional Anatomy of the Head, Neck, Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limb
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focusses on the functional anatomy of the head, neck, pectoral girdle, and upper limb. In addition, the anatomy of the thoracic and abdominal walls are discussed in detail. Topics covered include limb motion related to joint mobility and surface anatomy, and the anatomical relationships of bones, muscles, blood vessels and nerves within each of the body regions covered. Students undertaking this subject will be assumed to have a basic understanding of anatomical terminology, the general organisation of the body as a whole, and have an introductory level knowledge of the gross anatomy of the musculoskeletal system. Students completing this subject as an online education enrolment will be required to attend an intensive school.
learning_outcomes: Describe the relationship between upper limb motion and joint mobility.
Describe the effects of posture, respiratory phase and pregnancy on relevant anatomical structures.
Identify and interpret surface features of the normal living body.
Explain the anatomical basis of relevant practical diagnostic procedures and treatments commonly performed by health professionals.
Describe the structure of the thoracic and abdominal walls.
Describe how the integumentary system, fascia, muscles and bones can protect underlying structures in the body.
Describe the relationship between surface features of the upper limb and joint motion.
Describe the anatomical relationships between bones, muscles, nerves and blood vessels of the pectoral girdle.
Describe the anatomical relationships between bones, muscles, nerves and blood vessels of the upper limb.
Describe the anatomical relationships between bones, muscles, nerves, soft tissues and blood vessels in the head and neck.
Identify and interpret key features of radiological images.
Describe the normal anatomical variation between individuals due to age, gender, and body build.

title: Fundamental Design Approaches
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject delivers theoretical knowledge of fundamental design principles through creative practice. The major emphasis of this subject is on studio practice as it relates to the diversity of the Creative Industries. It encourages an ethical, critical and reflexive approach to practice that is grounded in research and development, and embraces experimentation across a range of analogue and digital media. Students gain an understanding of design principles as they apply to spatial, temporal and emotive affect.
learning_outcomes: Undertake basic visual research, design development and iteration via a range of design processes and contexts.
Analyse and selectively engage analogue and/or digital tools as appropriate to particular design tasks.
Develop an adaptable and strategic approach to design processes as they apply to a range of contexts.
Assign interrelated aspects of visual design to a range of visual communication contexts.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the underlying factors that have shaped changing conventions and developments in design.
Apply the basic principles and theories of design via applied design processes.

title: Functional Anatomy of the Vertebral Column, Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a comprehensive overview of the functional anatomy of the vertebral column, pelvic girdle, pelvic floor, and lower limbs. Topics covered include limb motion related to joint structure and mobility, relevant aspects of surface anatomy, and the anatomical relationships between bones, muscles, blood vessels, and nerves in these body regions. Students undertaking this subject will be assumed to have a basic understanding of anatomical terminology, the general organisation of the body as a whole, and have an introductory level knowledge of the gross anatomy of the musculoskeletal system.
learning_outcomes: Describe the relationship between key surface features of the lower limb and motion and joint mobility.
Identify and interpret key features of radiological images.
Describe the anatomy of the pelvic floor and the vertebral column.
Describe how the integumentary system, fascia, muscle and bone can protect underlying structures in the body.
Describe the normal anatomical variation between individuals due to age, gender and body build.
Explain the anatomical basis of relevant practical diagnostic procedures and treatments commonly performed by health professionals.
Identify and interpret surface features of the normal living body.
Describe the anatomical relationship of bones, muscles, blood vessels, nerves of the pelvic girdle and lower limb.
Describe the effects of posture, respiratory phase and pregnancy on anatomical structure.

title: Fundamentals of Adult Neurological Physiotherapy
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will build on a student's knowledge of normal movement, biomechanics, neuroscience, exercise physiology and the principles of motor control, in order to analyse neurological pathology in the adult population. Students will extend their practical skills in neurological and musculoskelatal assessment, relevant to clients with neurological disorders. This subject will provide students with the opportunity to apply their skills in problem solving to undertake holistic assessment of, and develop management plans for, adults with movement disorders that arise from changes in the neurological and related musculoskeletal systems. Students will be expected to demonstrate ethical decision making to inform safe, effective and evidence based physiotherapy practice. Through this subject, students will have the opportunity to demonstrate skills in producing well-argued and carefully constructed accounts of complex thinking relevant to the evaluation of neurological physiotherapy scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively with and involve clients, peers and relevant others in the planning and implementation of adult neurological physiotherapy.
Plan, deliver and document safe and effective evidence-based physiotherapy interventions relevant to adult neurological physiotherapy practice.
Demonstrate skills in producing well-argued and carefully constructed accounts of complex thinking relevant to the evaluation of neurological physiotherapy scenarios.
Evaluate and use evidence-based information to inform decision making and develop and guide their own knowledge, learning and practice.
Demonstrate professional and ethical behaviour appropriate to adult neurological physiotherapy practice.
Reflect critically on their clinical reasoning and professional practice in order to propose actions for continuous improvement.
Safely and effectively apply a range of physiotherapy assessment tests, tools, and evaluation or outcome measures, relevant to adult neurological physiotherapy practice.
prerequisites: BMS271: Functional Anatomy of the Head, Neck, Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limb
BMS172: Functional Anatomy of the Vertebral Column, Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb

title: Fundamentals of Cloud Computing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the core cloud computing concepts, service models, deployment models, and foundational architectural principles. Students will explore how organisations use cloud platforms to deliver computing, storage, networking, and application services at scale. Through practical examples and guided activities, students will learn to evaluate and select appropriate cloud solutions at a conceptual level, compare cloud and on-premises approaches, and understand shared responsibility, cost considerations, and basic security principles. Emphasis is placed on conceptual understanding, decision-making, and cloud literacy, rather than technical implementation.
learning_outcomes: Describe common cloud deployment models and their use cases
Identify foundational security, privacy, and responsibility considerations in cloud environments
Communicate cloud solution concepts to anon-technical audience using appropriate professional terminology.
Explain fundamental cloud computing concepts, terminology, and service models
Analyse the benefits and limitations of cloud computing compared to traditional infrastructure

title: Fundamentals of Law Enforcement Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a sound knowledge of the fundamentals of the use of intelligence in the law enforcement field. It will equip the student with an understanding of intelligence basics, critical reasoning and analysis, ethics in intelligence in law enforcement, operational intelligence practice, along with some of the modern techniques and tools utilised in obtaining the intelligence product.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse the range of contemporary intelligence issues in relation to law enforcement and security.
Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Make independent analysis and judgments in a range of intelligence contexts and generate intelligence assessments.
Analyse and compare the roles and use of intelligence in the fields of criminal, national security, and military law environments.

title: Fundamentals of Nuclear and Radiation Physics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students explore and examine the fundamental theoretical principles of nuclear and radiation physics that support further studies in nuclear science. They will learn about the atomic and nuclear structures, and gain knowledge about charged particle and photon interactions with matter and their real-world applications.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate theoretical understandings of real-world applications.
Use units, terminology and nomenclature appropriately.
Apply fundamental physics principles within the context of national and international regulatory frameworks.
Interpret and solve nuclear science calculation-based problems.
Explain the theoretical concepts that support principles of nuclear and radiation physics.
Describe and appraise principles, procedures and instruments used in nuclear science.
prerequisites: PHY211: Fundamentals of Nuclear and Radiation Physics

title: Fundamentals of Nuclear and Radiation Physics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students explore and examine the fundamental theoretical principles of nuclear and radiation physics that support further studies in nuclear science. They will learn about the atomic and nuclear structures and gain knowledge about charged particles and photons interactions with matter and their real-word applications.
learning_outcomes: Use units, terminology and nomenclature appropriately.
Describe and differentiate principles, procedures and instruments used in nuclear science.
Interpret and solve nuclear science calculation-based problems.
Explain the theoretical concepts that support principles of nuclear and radiation physics.
Demonstrate theoretical understandings of real-world applications.

title: Fundamentals of Nuclear Science and Safety
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the fundamental concepts, innovations and safety associated with nuclear science. It will examine the principles and applications of nuclear science and safety with an emphasis on the underlying principles. The content is delivered in four modules specifically addressing the fundamental principles associated with nuclear physics, radiation physics, radiation safety and managing a radiological emergency. The subject provides the foundation understanding in nuclear science and safety as a pathway for further studies in the medical radiation or nuclear science sectors.
learning_outcomes: Describe and differentiate principles, procedures and instruments.
Demonstrate understanding of core principles through connection and exploration of real-world applications.
Explain the principles of nuclear physics, radiation physics and radiation safety.
Use units, terminology and nomenclature appropriately.
Explain the principles of radiation safety and radiation emergency management, and identify appropriate radiation emergency planning and response.
Interpret and solve core calculation-based problems.
prerequisites: PHY115: Physics for Medical Radiation Science

title: Fundamentals of Plant Protection
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Yield loss due to pests (from weed, pathogen, invertebrate and vertebrate species) is one of the largest costs to agricultural production. Pest management is also a major source of commercial revenue within the Industry. In this subject, students familiarise themselves with the types of pests affecting plant production systems in Australia and globally. Students will learn about the biology and ecology of common pests and use strategies for assessing their impact on plant production in broadacre, horticultural and irrigated contexts. Social, regulatory, integrated management approaches to their control will also be considered including the development of a basic understanding of agri-chemical groups and application techniques.
learning_outcomes: Assess pest impact on production.
Identify chemical and non-chemical approaches to the management of pests, and explain how these may be effectively integrated.
Describe the biology and ecology of key pests.
Identify key pests affecting plant production including weeds, invertebrate and disease-causing agents.

title: Fundamentals of Radiation Safety and Management
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will explore the fundamental theories of radiobiology, radiation protection, safety and management. They will examine radiation safety concepts with an emphasis on risk identification, risk planning, risk mitigation and risk response. Two modules are provided: Fundamentals of Radiation Safety, and Fundamentals of Emergency Management in the Nuclear Sector. Students will develop their foundational understandings to support further studies in the nuclear science sector.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and identify radiation exposure risk and procedures for risk reduction and mitigation.
Differentiate principles, related procedures and instruments used in radiation safety and apply understandings of foundational principles to real-world applications.
Interpret and solve calculation-based problems associated with radiation safety and exposure.
Use units, terminology and nomenclature appropriately.
Apply communication skills for risk identification and incident management planning within the context of national and international regulatory frameworks.
Explain the theoretical concepts of radiobiology, exposure protection and safety.
prerequisites: PHY212: Fundamentals of Radiation Safety and Management

title: Fundamentals of Radiation Safety and Management
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will explore the fundamental theories of radiobiology, radiation protection, safety and management. They will examine radiation safety concepts with an emphasis on risk identification, risk planning, risk mitigation and risk response. Two modules are provided: Fundamentals of Radiation Safety, and Fundamentals of Emergency Management in the Nuclear Sector. Students will develop their foundational understandings to support further studies in the nuclear science sector.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate principles, related procedures and instruments used in radiation safety and apply understandings of foundational principles to real-world applications; and.
Demonstrate communication and teamwork skills for risk identification and incident management planning.
Interpret and solve calculation-based problems associated with radiation safety and exposure.
Analyse and identify radiation exposure risk and procedures for risk reduction and mitigation.
Explain the theoretical concepts of radiobiology, exposure protection and safety and be capable of using units, terminology and nomenclature appropriately.

title: Fundamentals of Strategic Planning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to provide students with the knowledge, understanding and skills relating to strategic planning processes within organisations. The subject examines the factors which influence strategic planning processes such as decision making, management, communication, leadership and innovation. These key issues will be explored in detail to enable students to develop their own thinking and analytical skills through synthesis and critical reflection in the context of strategic planning.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and reflect on the interface between leadership and strategy.
Define and use the decision-making process in an organisational context.
Understand and apply relevant theoretical concepts of strategic planning.
Assess effective practices of innovation in an organisation, identify key issues and formulate and apply appropriate innovation strategies for enhancing the performance of an organisation.
Examine and criticise the role of communication in the strategic context.
Critically analyse current strategic planning issues in a world of constant change.

title: Fundamentals of Veterinary Biology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a brief introduction to taxonomy and phylogeny, and basic science and measurement concepts. It then introduces cell biology incorporating applied aspects of basic cell structure and function including aspects of introductory organic chemistry, biochemistry, microbiology, and cell physiology with particular emphasis on biochemical and genetic functions of cells. It provides foundations in membrane transport and cell signalling. This subject will prepare students for advanced study in physiology, pathophysiology, microbiology and histology. Previous basic knowledge of chemistry and biology is assumed.
learning_outcomes: Describe cell information storage and regulation using DNA and its control of the cell cycle, explaining how recombinant DNA technology and neoplasia change function, giving examples in animal health and production.
Use phylogenetic and taxonomic principles to explain major differences between eukaryote and prokaryote organisms including microbes, plant and animal cells.
Utilise principles of research, measurement and analysis to demonstrate an awareness of scientific method and an emerging ability to communicate research findings and conclusions appropriately.

Explain the structure and functions of cell membranes and their integral proteins and describe the role these play in cellular communication, including chemical transport and detailed explanations of development of membrane potential and the action potential.
Describe the families of biological molecules essential for life (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids) and outline the relationships of their anabolic and catabolic pathways.
Describe and apply concepts of thermodynamics, solution, diffusion, equilibrium and normality to physiological systems.
Demonstrate a basic understanding of the structure, function and pathogenicity of various classes of micro-organisms, and to culture and identify them.
Describe the basic structure of cells, including various subcellular structures in relation to their function and tissue types.

title: Fundamentals of Water Resources and Environmental Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles and practices of water resources and environmental engineering, focusing on the interaction between human activities, water resources and the environment. Topics covered include open‑channel hydraulics, engineering hydrology, flood estimation and urban drainage design. Students will develop an understanding of the scientific foundations and core principles that underpin these fields and build the capability to apply hydraulic and hydrological methods to real‑world engineering problems. Prior knowledge of fluid mechanics is extended and contextualised within water engineering applications.
learning_outcomes: Apply basic principles of hydraulics and hydrology in urban water resources and environmental projects.
Analyse hydrologic data to estimate runoff and floods for water resource applications.
Discuss environmental issues and the role of environmental engineering in civil engineering projects.
Apply the principles of hydraulics to analyse flow conditions and perform design calculations for open channels and simple hydraulic structures.

title: Funds Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the construction, management and protection of an investment fund in the contemporary financial environment. Students will apply their learning from previous finance subjects to the process of managing an international portfolio comprising both financial and real assets. Students will also examine institutional aspects of the managed fund sector in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Apply portfolio management techniques to restructure portfolios in light of new information or revised objectives.
Implement various techniques to preserve and enhance portfolio returns.
Establish portfolio objectives with respect to risk and return and construct investment portfolios that best meet these objectives.
Gain an appreciation of a range of contemporary issues in portfolio management and acquire knowledge of the institutional framework of the funds management sector.

title: Games 1 - Games Design
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the fundamental ideas behind the design of electronic and non-electronic games. It touches on formal fields like systems theory and game theory. Game design also includes basic interactive design, including interface design, information design and human computer interaction. Perhaps most important for game design is a detailed study of how games function to create experiences. This includes examining how rule design, play mechanics, game balancing, and social game interaction integrate with visual, audio, tactile and textual elements into the total game experience. More practical aspects of game design such as game design documentation and playtesting are also covered.
learning_outcomes: Integrate knowledge of the basic principles of game design to propose and design an original game.
Explain the nature, significance of play and factors involved in making a game fun.
Explain the notion of gameplay, flow and the role of narrative in games.
Apply knowledge of the basic principles of game design to analyse, discuss, and evaluate existing games.
Describe the broad history of the digital game industry and identify some of the major technological events affecting the digital game industry.
Identify and describe the fundamental characteristics, basic components and structure of games.
Articulate a game concept in a game design document and construct a playable prototype from the game design document.
Explain the notion of game balance and describe the processes and roles involve in creating a digital game.
Explain the system dynamics of a game.

title: Future Directions in Social Work
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject requires Master of Advanced Social Work Practice students to integrate and consolidate their learning (knowledge, values and skills) from across the degree, developing a deeper level of applied scholarship to revitalise and sustain professional identity and engagement, incorporating a clear vision for future professional practice for themselves and the profession.
learning_outcomes: Develop a portfolio that includes reflection on their learning in the Master of Advanced Social Work Practice, including exploration of social work values, professional skills, knowledge and contexts.
Explain developments in their professional identity as social workers and to discuss the contribution social work makes to their chosen field of practice.
