Integrate a range of complex anthropological ideas, and demonstrate ability to derive a theological position against the background of human and theoretical difference.

title: God and Humanity
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the development, critique and reformulation of theological ideas regarding humanity and humanity's relation to God and creation. Traditional themes in theological anthropology are considered, including creation, the imago dei, sin, grace, salvation and vocation. Challenges to historical formulations, including the challenge of difference, are brought into conversation with contemporary approaches such as feminist, postcolonial, ecological, queer and liberation discourses.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Assess critically recent constructive theological anthropologies and their societal and cultural relevance.
Engage critically with contemporary challenges to Christian theological anthropology, including difference.
Discuss key theological ideas regarding humanity and humanity's relation to God and creation in historical and contemporary contexts.

title: Governance and Decision Making
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will investigate the principles of good governance, the internal controls and structures that underpin good governance and discuss the benefits of governance in decision making. The benefits of governance for organisations of all types will be examined and students will be exposed to the pitfalls of poor governance frameworks and how internal controls within organisations can support decision making.
learning_outcomes: Describe and analyse how internal systems of control support an organisations governance and aid in decision making.
Analyse situations of when governance or lack thereof lead to poor decision making and undesirable outcomes.
Describe and critically discuss the principles and techniques of governance and their importance in decision making within all types of organisations.

title: Government and Police
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop an understanding of the relationship between government and policing, with particular emphasis on policing in liberal democracies. While the main focus will be on Australian police organisations and Australian governments, there will be some comparative analysis, including the relationship between policing and government in the USA and the UK.
learning_outcomes: be able to demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between liberal democratic government and policing
be able to demonstrate an understanding of the Police Commissioner's role
be able to explain modern Australian policing in its institutional context
be able to demonstrate an understanding of the sources of legitimacy of the police officer's role

title: Grammar Essentials for Writing at University
school: School
syllabus_overview: Grammar Essentials for Writing at University is an online and self-paced subject that allows student discussion and interaction to assist students towards more effective academic writing. The Subject Coordinator will be available to support and facilitate student learning in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Explain parts of speech in written sentences.
Identify structural, grammatical and punctuation errors in writing.
Find resources or services that support further development in effective academic writing.
Use grammatical structures appropriate to the writing task.
Produce a short written text that is grammatically correct.

title: Grammar Essentials 1: The Basics of Grammar
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop the knowledge and skills of students in the fundamental area of grammatical accuracy in academic writing. It is an online and self-paced subject that allows student discussion and interaction to assist students towards more effective academic writing. Topics covered include the role of grammar in communication, parts of speech, writing a grammatically correct sentence, features of an effective paragraph, punctuation, spelling rules and strategies, and where to find help.
learning_outcomes: be able to understand academic literacy;
be able to explain parts of speech in written sentences;
be able to understand the role of grammar in academic writing;
be able to identify structural, grammatical and punctuation errors in writing;
be able to produce a short written text that is grammatically correct; and
be able to identify resources or services that support further development in effective academic writing.
be able to identify and apply grammar rules;
be able to use grammatical structures appropriate to the writing task;

title: Grammar Essentials: Applying Grammar in University Study
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to further develop and extend the knowledge and skills of students in the area of grammatical accuracy in academic writing. Common grammatical errors made in undergraduate studies will be highlighted and correct forms practised in context. It is an online and self-paced subject that allows student discussion and interaction to assist students towards more effective academic writing. Topics focus on common problems encountered in academic writing at university level.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic literacy to a range of types of tasks
Identify resources or services that support development in effective and grammatically accurate academic writing
Produce a short-written text that is grammatically correct
Identify common university tasks that require correct use of grammar
Recognise the role of grammar in academic writing

title: Grape and Wine Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce students to the principles of grape and wine production, and the factors influencing viticultural and winemaking practices in Australia and around the world. Students will develop knowledge of the basic winemaking processes and the major wine types. Students will examine the biology, anatomy and life cycle of the grapevine. The use of hybrids and rootstocks in viticulture and wine production is covered particularly in relation to the development of grapevines for the future. Students will also be introduced to vineyard management practices, and basic scientific experimentation and statistics as applied to grape and wine production.
learning_outcomes: Identify phenological stages of the grapevine and describe the vegetative and reproductive structures of a grapevine.
Apply basic methodology in data processing and analysis as it relates to grape and wine production.
Explain common vineyard management practices.
Describe historical and geographical factors that affect the Australian and International Wine Industries.
Describe the essential differences and outline basic production steps of the wine making process to produce the major wine types.
Discuss hybrid grapevines, the use of rootstocks and the concept of grapevines of the future.

title: Grief, Loss and Change
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares the student for working with clients through the processes of loss, grief, and change. Issues related to changes in health status, bereavement, relationship loss, migration and cultural status are considered.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate their understanding of normal human reactions when confronted with loss and the influence of personal and social variables in shaping these.
Evaluate and critically discuss a range of conceptualisations of the experience of grief, loss and change.
Demonstrate a sound understanding of what is involved in assessing for issues of grief, loss and change in situations where these may, or may not, be relevant.
Demonstrate an appropriate level of self-awareness around how their own history of grief, loss and change may enhance or interfere with their provision of effective psychosocial support/counselling.

title: Groundwater Hydrology and Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students are introduced to a wide range of practical and theoretical concepts pertinent in the science and management of groundwater. Topics covered include: the water cycle, hydrogeology, groundwater recharge / discharge determination, groundwater conceptual modelling, an array of monitoring and sampling methods, groundwater microbiology, groundwater geophysics, groundwater pollution, and groundwater and soil remediation. Students are then introduced to a range of groundwater management approaches including resource allocation, quality protection, and sustainability. This subject has no intensive. On completion students will be able to critically apply a variety of conceptual and practical frameworks that are commonly used to underpin current approaches to addressing groundwater problems in a mining or primary production context.
learning_outcomes: Will be able to critically apply a variety of conceptual and practical frameworks that are commonly used to underpin current approaches to addressing groundwater problems in a mining or primary production context.

Have an in-depth understanding of the key concepts associated with groundwater including groundwater and its relationship to the hydrological system, the movement of water in the earth, and the properties of, and flows associated with groundwater.
Have specialised skills in the practical aspects of groundwater analysis and management.
Have an in-depth understanding of theories and tools associated with estimation of groundwater flows and volumes.

title: Growth, Motor Development and Ageing
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject focuses on the basic developmental principles, theoretical approaches and issues related to the study of human growth, motor development and ageing across the life span. The subject introduces prominent motor development theories and explores prenatal, infant, adolescent and adult growth and motor skill development. It explores how growth and maturation impact motor skill performance and exercise, and the development of fitness, strength, flexibility, ballistic, locomotor and manipulative skills. The subject introduces Newell’s Model of Interacting Constraints as the basis for understanding how structural, functional, task, sociocultural and psychosocial constraints affect physical activity, exercise and motor development.
learning_outcomes: Outline factors relevant to perceptual-motor development across the lifespan.
Understand and differentiate the concepts of somatic growth, development, maturation and motor development, including the role of puberty and the adolescent growth spurt in motor skill performance.
Describe key components of prenatal, childhood growth, early motor development, and the development of locomotor, manipulative and ballistic skills.
Describe changes in motor function across the lifespan and apply them to the critical observation of exercise interventions.
Critically reflect on the maturity bias in sport.
Understand and apply common motor development theories.
Understand the role played by weight status, fitness, physical activity and exercise, psychosocial and cultural constraints in growth and motor development across the life span.

title: Group and Peer Supervision
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles and practice of group and peer supervision which complement individual professional and pastoral supervision. Students will be helped to grow in the skills of facilitating group and peer supervision. Students will learn how group and peer supervision can optimise reflective learning processes, provide supervisors with opportunities continuing professional development in their supervision practice, and enhance the importance of collaborative peer networks for advanced professional supervisors.
learning_outcomes: Relate principles of relational and inter-personal dynamics to group and peer supervision.
Define and differentiate between individual, group and peer supervision.
Analyse current models of group and peer supervision, and relate theories of group and peer supervision to their own professional and ministry setting.
Develop a personal approach to group and peer supervision supported by current literature and research.
Demonstrate an understanding of reflective practice to group and peer supervision and its relationship to models of professional/pastoral supervision.
Evaluate their strengths and areas for growth in the provision of group and peer supervision in the light of feedback from lecturers and fellow students.

title: Guided Arabic Reading
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to explore various aspects and considerations when perusing Arabic texts. Students will explore frequently used words, phrases and expressions in the Arabic language. Different genres of texts from Arabic fiction and non-fiction will be studied, compared and contrasted to demonstrate the students' comprehension. Students will continue to advance their knowledge in vocabulary, syntax and morphology as well as continue to access non-vowelised texts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate comprehension of texts by comparing and contrasting content from the same genre.
Identify and demonstrate understanding of frequently used Arabic phrases and expressions.
Use various kinds of dictionaries to understand meanings of words in their context of use.
Demonstrate an advanced-low proficiency in analysis and composition of sentences and paragraphs.

title: Guided Research
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject is provides experience in guided research for students who intend to continue from the Bachelor of Islamic Studies to Bachelor of Islamic Studies (Honours). As a result, enrolment in this subject requires the approval of the Subject coordinator. The subject allows for the research of an approved topic in a chosen Islamic Studies sub-discipline, to be determined in consultation with the Subject coordinator. Students are expected to demonstrate the use of appropriate methodology, research, writing and communication skills through the presentation of a major essay in their topic area.
learning_outcomes: Discuss critically issues in a chosen Islamic Studies subdiscipline arising from the investigation of an approved research topic.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate consultative and communications skills in developing and exploring an appropriate research project.

title: Guided Research in Islamic Studies
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students to conduct independent guided research on an approved topic in the field of Islamic studies. Students are expected to develop an effective research design in consultation with their supervisors after critically examining all the components of a research project. This includes identifying a suitable methodology and theoretical framework. The subject improves researcher candidates’ skills with advanced critical and analytical thinking as well as academic writing skills. The scaffolded assessments lead to the completion of a thesis by instilling students with confidence to conduct major research projects and deliver them in an academic setting.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced critical thinking, analytical thinking and research writing skills.
Demonstrate independent research, organisational and written communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research paper on a topic related to Islamic studies.
Assess and use the best theoretical framework and research method for the research project.
Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and communication skills through interaction with a supervisor and multiple reviewers.
Discuss critical issues on selected topics from the Islamic studies field.
Critically analyse and demonstrate in-depth understanding of literature relevant to the research question.
prerequisites: ISL599: Guided Research in Islamic Studies

title: Guided Research
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This is a guided research subject at the Masters level. In consultation with their supervisor, students will select an appropriate topic and write a research essay of approximately 10-12,000 words discussing critically their research question. Students are expected to demonstrate competence in the use of appropriate research methodology together with advanced written and oral communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research essay. Students will be required to present their research at a 'Masters Research Seminar' prior to final submission of their paper.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and communication skills through interaction with a supervisor.
Demonstrate independent research, organisational and written communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research essay in a select theological field.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the literature relevant to their research question.
Reflect critically on the literature relevant to their research question.
Discuss, at postgraduate level, critical issues arising from study in a select theological field.

title: Guided Research in Islamic Studies
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject is an independent guided study and research on an approved topic in a chosen field of Islamic Studies. Students are expected to demonstrate competence in the use of appropriate research methodology together with advanced written and oral communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research paper on a topic agreed to in consultation with a supervisor.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the literature relevant to their research question.
Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and communication skills through interaction with a supervisor.
Demonstrate independent research, organisational and written communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research essay in a select Islamic studies field.
Discuss critical issues arising from study in a selected Islamic Studies theological field.
Reflect critically on the literature relevant to their research question.

title: Guided Research in Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: The principal purpose of this subject is to provide students intending to progress beyond the Graduate Diploma of Theology to the Master of Theology with an experience in guided research. As a result, enrolment in this subject requires the approval of the Subject Coordinator. The subject facilitates the exploration of an approved topic in a chosen theological subdiscipline, to be determined in consultation with the Subject Coordinator. Students are expected to demonstrate the use of appropriate methodology, research, writing and communication skills, normally through the preparation of a substantial essay.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced dialogical skills in developing and exploring an appropriate research project.
Demonstrate critical appraisal of literature relevant to their research topic.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of an issue in a particular theological subdiscipline arising from the investigation of an approved research topic.

title: Guided Research in Ministry
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject is the guided research subject in the Master of Ministry course. Research is undertaken on an approved topic in a chosen field of professional ministry. The student will be expected to demonstrate the use of appropriate research methodology, critical reflection, and written and oral communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research paper.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and synthesise an argument.

Demonstrate independent research, organisation, and written and oral communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research paper in the chosen field of professional ministry.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the literature relevant to their research question.
Demonstrate the practical application of their research findings to the professional practice of ministry.
Demonstrate professional academic relationship skills through interaction with their supervisor.
Reflect critically on the literature relevant to their research question.
Discuss, analyse, and reflect critically on issues arising from their study in the chosen field of professional ministry.

title: Guided Research in Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: The principal purpose of this subject is to provide students intending to progress beyond the Bachelor of Theology to the Bachelor of Theology (Honours) or Master of Theology with an experience in guided research. As a result, enrolment in this subject requires the approval of the Subject coordinator. The subject facilitates the exploration of an approved topic in a chosen theological subdiscipline, to be determined in consultation with the Subject coordinator. Students are expected to demonstrate the use of appropriate methodology, research, writing and communication skills, normally through the preparation of a substantial essay.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate sound dialogical skills in developing and exploring an appropriate research project.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss critically an issue in a particular theological subdiscipline arising from the investigation of an approved research topic.
Demonstrate critical appraisal of literature relevant to their research topic.

title: Gymnastics and Dance
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the teaching and practice of gymnastics and dance, considering these in a variety of contexts and examining the different ways in which they contribute to life long participation in physical activity. The subject focusses on developing, engaging, safe, age-appropriate gymnastics and dance experiences, drawing on a number of teaching styles and processes. Through this approach, a strong foundation of theory will support practice. Students will devise experiences that develop the ability to adapt, improvise, transfer, refine, compose, perform and appreciate movement.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and examine various theories in gymnastics and dance, reflecting on how these can strengthen and enrich their future pedagogical decisions and general practice in the gymnastics-dance domain.
Develop skills, knowledge and understanding of movement as a physical art form that can embody expression, communication and meaning.

Discuss and debate the relevance of gymnastics and dance for children and young people in contemporary Australia, by considering and reflecting on pedagogical and philosophical changes across significant historical epochs.

Analyse relevant theory, applying knowledge and understanding gained to develop, plan, deliver and manage creative, age-appropriate, inclusive and safe experiences in gymnastics and dance, with an awareness of risk assessment and safety issues in a variety of contexts.

Compose, perform and appraise movement in gymnastics and dance contexts, as well as engage with and construct compositional and aesthetic criteria which are useful to assess, appraise and appreciate gymnastics and dance skill performance or the performance of a gymnastics-dance sequence.

Explore a range of learning, teaching and assessment strategies and educational processes in gymnastics and dance contexts, transferring theory and practice from the university context to a school context.

title: Haematology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to haematology and examines the structural and functional attributes of cellular and non-cellular constituents of blood in healthy and disease states. Morphological and functional characteristics of the blood cells at different stages of production, differentiation and maturation are considered in detail. Also, the haemostatic system, which comprises primary haemostasis, secondary haemostasis and the fibrinolytic system will be covered. Furthermore, blood disorders including anaemias, leucocyte disorders (benign and malignant), and disorders of the haemostasis are discussed at clinical, pathophysiological and laboratory diagnostic levels.
learning_outcomes: List and describe the components of the haemostatic system and explain their functions.
Define and describe the disorders of the haemostatic system.
Define and describe the disorders of blood cells.
Compare and contrast the development of blood cells and describe structure and functions of the blood producing tissues/organs.
Explain principles that underpin routine haematological tests.
List, describe and explain the morphological and functional attributes of blood cells.

title: Hacking Countermeasures
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will learn how to test computing systems for vulnerabilities and secure them against hacking. Students will learn how attackers find weaknesses in a computing environment, and be asked to critically evaluate system defences intended to prevent such attacks. Students will become familiar with perimeter and endpoint defences, before learning how to scan and attack networks. Students will also become familiar with the material they need to prepare for the EC-Council Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) industry certification exam during this subject.
learning_outcomes: Prioritise and implement countermeasures to prevent attackers causing harm to information systems.
Use reconnaissance and analysis tools and techniques to understand an environment and identify threats.
Compare and effectively utilise open source threat intelligence resources when analysing possible threats.
Identify and analyse information system weaknesses, and demonstrate how these make an environment vulnerable to attack.
Analyse and compare common web application attack techniques, and justify defences that mitigate these attacks.

title: Haematology 1 (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to haematology and examines the structural and functional attributes of cellular and non-cellular constituents of blood in healthy and disease states. Morphological and functional characteristics of the blood cells at different stages of production, differentiation and maturation are considered in detail. Also, the haemostatic system, which comprises primary haemostasis, secondary haemostasis and the fibrinolytic system will be covered. Furthermore, blood disorders including anaemias, leucocyte disorders (benign and malignant), and disorders of the haemostasis are discussed at clinical, pathophysiological and laboratory diagnostic levels.
learning_outcomes: Define and describe the disorders of the haemostatic system.
Compare and contrast the development of blood cells and describe structure and functions of the blood producing tissues/organs.
Define and describe the disorders of blood cells.
List, describe and explain the morphological and functional attributes of blood cells.
List and describe the components of the haemostatic system and explain their functions.
Explain principles that underpin routine haematological tests.

title: Haematology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth study of advanced haematological concepts in areas of blood cell kinetics and regulation of cell cycle, haemopoietic malignancies, anaemias, and disorders of haemostatic systems (primary haemostasis, coagulation system and fibrinolytic system). Furthermore, quality control and quality assurance measures related to haematology are integrated into this subject.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the current impact of advances in molecular techniques relevant to haematology.
Evaluate the key issues regarding quality control and quality assurance in the haematology laboratory.
Explain the pathogenesis, clinical findings, laboratory diagnosis and treatment of anaemias.
Demonstrate high levels of academic literacy.

Analyse, interpret and apply the results of haematological tests, as well as some clinical findings, to problem-solving activities including but not limited to case studies in regard to haematological disorders.
Explain the pathogenesis, clinical features, classification, laboratory diagnosis, and principles of treatment of haemopoietic malignancies.
Explain the pathogenesis, classification, clinical features, laboratory diagnosis, and treatment of disorders of the haemostatic system.

title: Haematology 2 (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth study of advanced haematological concepts in areas of blood cell kinetics and regulation of cell cycle, haemopoietic malignancies, anaemias, and disorders of haemostatic systems (primary haemostasis, coagulation system and fibrinolytic system). Furthermore, quality control and quality assurance measures related to haematology are integrated into this subject.
learning_outcomes: Explain the pathogenesis, clinical findings, laboratory diagnosis and treatment of anaemias.
Explain the pathogenesis, classification, clinical features, laboratory diagnosis, and treatment of disorders of the haemostatic system.

Analyse, interpret and apply the results of haematological tests, as well as some clinical findings, to problem-solving activities including but not limited to case studies in regard to haematological disorders.
Evaluate the key issues regarding quality control and quality assurance in the haematology laboratory.
Explain the pathogenesis, clinical features, classification, laboratory diagnosis, and principles of treatment of haemopoietic malignancies.
Analyse the current impact of advances in molecular techniques relevant to haematology.

title: Head and Neck Anatomy
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop their understanding of the structure and function of the head and neck, as a foundation for specialist study in communication and swallowing. Students will develop knowledge of head and neck anatomy; bones, joints, muscles, vascular and neural structures in the region. Changes in structure and function across the lifespan will also be covered. This subject will assist students to identify anatomical features of the head and neck region, and empower students to apply this knowledge in order to explain (dys)function of the communication, auditory, swallowing and respiratory systems.
learning_outcomes: Identify the bones, joints and cavities of the skull and cervical spine.
Explain normal development and relevant developmental abnormalities of the head and neck across the lifespan.
Describe the neurovascular anatomy of the head and neck.
Identify the face muscles and their relation to facial expressions and movements.

Identify the musculoskeletal anatomy of the larynx, pharynx, palate, oral cavity, temporomandibular joint, ear, nasal cavity and thorax and explain relevant functions and their role in communication, auditory, swallowing and respiratory functions.
Identify the functional anatomy of the central nervous system and cranial nerves and explain their role in communication, auditory, swallowing and respiratory functions.

title: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the skills and knowledge to conduct an analysis of hazards and risk assessment for a community/enterprise. This will include developing an understanding of hazard identification, hazard characteristics and description, community/ enterprise characteristics and description, interaction consequences of hazards on the community/ enterprise, risk assessment and vulnerability.
learning_outcomes: Specify the characteristics of hazards and risks, including appropriate specific hazard and risk descriptions.
Identify, analyse, evaluate, and prioritise risk treatment options.
Describe and apply the concept of vulnerability assessment including risk prioritisation.
Determine the impact of hazards on a community/enterprise.
Identify the hazards and risks relating to a community/enterprise.
Specify the characteristics of a community/enterprise, including appropriate specific community/enterprise descriptions.

title: Head and Neck Anatomy
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide students with the opportunity of learning the functional and clinical anatomy of the head and neck and to continue to develop their basic anatomical knowledge. The subject will cover the skeletal, muscular, vascular and nervous tissue components of the head and neck with a strong emphasis on function as it relates to dentistry and a special focus on clinical anatomy relevant to minor oral surgery and the administration of local anaesthetics.
learning_outcomes: Describe the topographical and functional anatomy of the head and neck, in particular the arrangement, relations and functions of the major skeletal, ligamentous, muscular and neurovascular components of the head and neck.
Identify and describe the bones and osteological features of the skull and its articulations, the hyoid bone and the vertebral column, and identify these structures on radiographic images.

Describe the detailed structural and functional anatomy of the oral cavity and demonstrate the clinical anatomical knowledge of the region that is foundational to clinical dental practice, in particular minor oral surgery and the administration of local anaesthetics.

Describe the embryology of the head and neck, in particular the embryological development of the oral and nasal cavities, the larynx and pharynx, and relate the embryology to the functional anatomy of these regions.

title: Healing Our Spirit: Grief, Loss and Yarning
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an understanding of the historical issues that impact on contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. These issues have created significant grief, loss and trauma for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and have been identified as major contributors to emotional and physical illness within these communities. The subject will examine the stages of loss and grief and explore and discuss the healing processes and the significance of healing for communities. The subject will also introduce students to the counselling (yarning) processes and the theories and models used in an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander context. Holistic health encompasses spirituality as well as the physical, social, and emotional wellbeing of the individual and community.
learning_outcomes: differentiate between different models of counselling through expression in role plays and various mediums.
investigate the difference between an interview, counselling (yarning) process and therapy; and
define the terms associated with grief, loss and trauma through research and /or lived experiences;
examine the stages of the grieving process and its significance to healing;
critically discuss the concepts of healing and analyse the experiences of loss, grief and trauma as factors contributing to the impairment of health and wellbeing;
implement the fundamental principles of the counselling (yarning) process including confidentiality, ethics and legal issues;
describe and reflect upon the impact of trans-generational grief on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities;

title: Health and Physical Activity
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the contemporary nature and role of health and physical activity in the lives of children. Teacher education students will explore some of the factors that impact on children's health, well-being, resilience and participation in physical activity. Students will learn about, and learn to develop children's movement skills through opportunities for expressive and rhythmic movement, minor and modified games, and initiative and nature-based challenge activities. Students will investigate contemporary children's health issues such as personal safety, child protection, healthy eating, drug use, sexual and mental health.
learning_outcomes: Describe key children's health issues including healthy eating, sexual health, safety, drug education, child protection, interpersonal relationships and healthy choices.
Describe the measures needed to establish a safe, inclusive, challenging and participatory movement environment for children's physical activity.
Use the theories of children's growth and development to identify and justify a range of fundamental movement skills for children.
Explain the benefits of physical activity participation and health promotion strategies in supporting the health, resilience and wellbeing of children.
Describe a range of structured physical activities highlighting the components of fitness developed by children by participating in each of these physical activities.
Identify and describe factors that influence the health, resilience, wellbeing and physical activity status of Australian children, including groups at risk.
prerequisites: EHR334: Games, Sport and Contemporary Physical Activities 2
EHR101: Sociocultural Foundations of Human Movement

title: Health and the Human Body: Cells, Immunity and Musculoskeletal System
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory subject which will familiarise students with the foundational concepts of chemistry and biology as they relate to physiology. The subject begins by introducing physiology at a molecular level and continues through cells, tissues and some organ systems, including skeletal and integumentary systems. There is a focus on basic microbiology as it pertains to infection and control of cross infection. Students apply their knowledge of cellular communication to neurophysiology, endocrine and immune systems as a preparation for further studies in pathophysiology, as they prepare for their future careers as allied health professionals.
learning_outcomes: Explain the relevance of microbiology, immunology and control of cross infection for allied health professionals.
Apply knowledge of cellular communication to inform a foundational understanding of the neurophysiological, endocrine and immune systems.
Describe the organisation of cells into tissues.
Describe how cells function and communicate to become the fundamental building blocks of living organisms.
Describe the structure and function of skin, nervous system, muscle and bone at a foundational level.

title: Health and Wellbeing Across the Lifespan
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore biopsychosocial health and wellbeing across the lifespan. Students will examine and critique various models of health, including biomedical, social and individualised models and will gain an understanding of the impact of social determinants of health on individuals and communities. Developmental and other sources of disability will be examined and social constructions of disability and ageing will be critiqued. Human services practice in health settings applicable to different life stages will be explored and relevant approaches to health and wellbeing support examined.
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss health and wellbeing issues, including disabilities, associated with different stages of development throughout the lifespan.
Describe the bio-medical/individualised and social models of health and discuss the use and implications of these for human services practice in various health settings.
Demonstrate critical awareness of social determinants of health including the impacts and complexity of poverty, discrimination and inclusion, on health and wellbeing.
Identify and describe human service roles relevant to different health settings.
Identify, discuss and form a beginning critique of social constructions of disability and ageing.

title: Health Assessment and Intervention: Chronic and Complex Pathophysiology
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students examine the pathophysiology of Australia’s most common chronic and complex health conditions to inform evidence-based nursing care. Students examine the psycho-social factors affecting quality of life, autonomy and wellbeing for people across the lifespan living with chronic disease, their families and carers. Students evaluate health service navigation and contemporary frameworks and models for chronic care with a focus on formulating person-centred discharge plans.
learning_outcomes: Critique health system and service navigation for people with chronic and complex conditions, with an emphasis on person-centred discharge planning and the role of the registered nurse within collaborative healthcare teams.
Examine factors that affect quality of life, autonomy and wellbeing for people living with chronic and complex conditions, their families and carers.
Formulate person-centred care plans for individuals living with chronic conditions.
Evaluate contemporary frameworks and models of care for people living with chronic and complex conditions.
Analyse the pathophysiology of common chronic conditions and impact of comorbidities to inform evidence-based nursing care.
prerequisites: NUR200: Health Assessment and Intervention: Acute Pathophysiology
NRS171: Health Challenges 1: Acute Care A

title: Health Assessment and Intervention: Acute Pathophysiology
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students extend their foundational knowledge of human anatomy and physiology to explore the pathophysiology of common acute health conditions experienced across the lifespan, including the assessment and management of pain associated with these conditions. A systems-based approach supports students to be able to explain the link between assessment findings and underlying pathophysiology, and explain how selected interventions address underlying pathophysiological processes.
learning_outcomes: Analyse expected assessment findings for people across the lifespan presenting with acute physiological changes.
Analyse evidence-based approaches that underpin the care of people across the lifespan requiring acute pain management.
Explain how interventions address the underlying pathophysiology of common acute health conditions.
Explain the underlying pathophysiology of common acute health conditions.
prerequisites: NRS171: Health Challenges 1: Acute Care A
BMS175: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses 2

title: Health and Wellbeing Across the Lifespan (postgraduate)
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines the domains of social work and human services practice and the experiences of people accessing those services across the lifespan. Students will gain an understanding of the impact of social determinants of health on individuals and communities and examine and critique various models of health, including biomedical, psychological, social, cultural and individualised models. Developmental and other sources of disability will be examined and social constructions of disability and ageing will be critiqued. Social work and human services practice in health settings applicable to different life stages will be explored and relevant approaches to health and wellbeing examined.
learning_outcomes: Compare the bio-medical/individualised and social models of health, including social constructions of disability, mental health and ageing, and evaluate the use and implications of these for social work and human services practice in various health settings.
Critically evaluate social work and human services roles in diverse health settings across the lifespan".
Demonstrate critical awareness of social determinants of health including the impacts of poverty, discrimination and inequality.
Identify and analyse health and wellbeing issues associated with different stages of development throughout the lifespan for diverse groups in Australia.

title: Health Assessment and Intervention: Mental Health
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students explore assessments, expected assessment findings, interventions and evaluation methods for the care of people across the lifespan experiencing common mental health conditions. There is a focus on people living in rural, regional and remote settings. Students will integrate strategies for delivering culturally safe mental health care in Partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Students will also examine the legal and ethical aspects of mental health service delivery. This subject also supports students to develop strategies to support personal and professional resilience and maintenance of their own mental health as a registered nurse.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a range of assessments and interventions that relate to mental health for people across the lifespan.

Analyse strategies for delivering culturally safe mental health care that reflects individual, cultural and linguistic diversity and addresses potential challenges in the delivery of responsive health care practice.
Critique contemporary models of mental health care including consumer collaboration, and how their application optimises care for people experiencing mental health conditions.
Explain factors that contribute to mental health, including genetic, social, cultural, physical and environmental factors.
Explore evidence-based strategies to work in Partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health professionals, organisations and communities to respectfully explore cultural information.
prerequisites: NRS384: Health Challenges 3: Mental Health Care

title: Health Assessment for Advancing Nursing Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates students' previous experience to develop advanced knowledge and skills in health and physical assessment across the lifespan, with a focus on factors impacting health assessment in the rural and remote setting. Students will further develop skills in clinical reasoning to integrate assessment data, knowledge of relevant anatomy and physiology, and evidence-informed practice, as they work in collaboration with the interdisciplinary team to develop patient-focused solutions in a range of clinical situations. In addition to physical assessment, students will also develop their knowledge and skills in health assessment as they evaluate social and cultural considerations to determine care priorities in the context of culturally safe assessment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the impact of the rural and remote environment on the health of the consumer and care provision.
Apply relevant legal and ethical frameworks in the conduct of health and physical assessment in advanced nursing practice.
Analyse changing assessment priorities, techniques and findings for specific populations across the lifespan, including infants, children and older adults.
Apply advanced communication skills to obtain health information and effectively communicate assessment findings and/or care priorities to health consumers and members of the interprofessional team.
Evaluate social and cultural considerations to implement person-centred and culturally safe assessment.

Integrate clinical reasoning processes with knowledge of relevant anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology to interpret a range of health and physical assessment data across the lifespan and identify priorities of care.
Apply advanced health assessment and clinical examination techniques to collate information from health consumers across the lifespan.

title: Health Challenges 1: Acute Care A
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces foundational knowledge to prepare students to use creative, scientific problem-solving approaches for the nursing care of people with health challenges related to the integumentary, nervous, cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine and exocrine systems. Students will also consider the links between the pathophysiology of illness and assessment findings; and explore how nursing care sustains the patient, enhances patient outcomes, and assures patient safety.
learning_outcomes: Explain the alterations to health for body systems including integumentary, nervous cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine and exocrine systems.
Demonstrate an understanding of the application of nursing care and collaborative care to prevent and/or manage exacerbations of fluid and electrolyte health challenges.

Explain the underlying pathophysiology of abnormal assessment findings in the context of selected health challenges to the integumentary, nervous, cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine and exocrine systems.
Explain alterations to fluid and electrolytes balances during health challenges.

Demonstrate an understanding of the application of nursing care and collaborative care to prevent and/or manage exacerbations of health challenges to the integumentary, nervous, cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine and exocrine systems.
prerequisites: BMS165: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses 1

title: Health Challenges 2: Acute Care B
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide the essential knowledge for students to use creative scientific problem-solving approaches for the nursing care of people with health challenges related to infection, inflammation, the immune system, the musculoskeletal system, the gastrointestinal system, the haematological system, the renal / urinary system and the reproductive system.
learning_outcomes: Explain the alterations to health for body systems including immune, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, haematological, renal / urinary, and reproductive systems.

Explain the underlying pathophysiology of abnormal assessment findings in the context of selected health challenges to the immune, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, haematological, renal / urinary, and reproductive systems.

Demonstrate an understanding of the application of nursing care and collaborative care to prevent and /or manage exacerbations of health challenges including the processes of infection and inflammation, and wound healing.

Demonstrate an understanding of the application of nursing care and collaborative care to prevent and /or manage exacerbations of health challenges affecting the immune, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, haematological, renal / urinary, and reproductive systems.
Explain common alterations in health including the processes of infection and inflammation, and wound healing.
prerequisites: NRS171: Health Challenges 1: Acute Care A

title: Health Challenges 3: Mental Health Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the use of mindful communication and capacity for human connectedness and legal and ethical aspects of care. It will examine and explore mental health and well-being, mental disorder and mental illness, and treatment modalities in all settings where nurses practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse factors that impact on the mental health of vulnerable groups with relation to individualising nursing care.
Explain the assessment of mental health challenges, such as distress, crisis, trauma and emergency.
Analyse emerging modalities for the provision of mental health care in regional and rural settings.
Examine the legal and ethical aspects of mental health service delivery and the application of these to practice.
Discuss and evaluate contemporary theories of mental health and mental illness.
prerequisites: NRS211: Essential Nursing Care: Acute Care
NRS274: Health Challenges 2: Acute Care B

title: Health Challenges 4: Complex Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject supports students to analyse and apply creative scientific problem-solving approaches to nursing care for people with complex health challenges related to stress responses, shock, cancer, ageing, and end of life. Students examine the pathophysiology of these complex health challenges and develop appropriate nursing care to enhance patient outcomes and assure patient safety.
learning_outcomes: Plan, justify, and evaluate the nursing care required for the person who receives pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for complex health challenges.
Explain and justify collaborative care for the person experiencing complex health challenges.
Discuss and link the pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, and nursing interventions for people with complex health challenges.
Evaluate the impact of multiple comorbidities on complex health challenges.
prerequisites: NRS384: Health Challenges 3: Mental Health Care
NRS274: Health Challenges 2: Acute Care B

title: Health Challenges 5: Chronic Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject supports students to analyse and apply creative scientific problem-solving approaches to nursing care for people with chronic health conditions related to recurring and continuous health challenges. This includes examination of the pathophysiology of these chronic health challenges, recognition of clinical manifestations, and the development of appropriate nursing care to enhance patient outcomes and assure patient safety. Students are also supported to create opportunities for interprofessional contributions to the care of the person with chronic health challenges, locally, nationally and globally.
learning_outcomes: Plan, justify, and evaluate the nursing care required for the person who receives pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for chronic health challenges.
Evaluate the impact of multiple comorbidities on chronic health challenges.
Examine frameworks and models of care for the management of chronic health challenges.
Discuss and link the pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, and nursing interventions for people with chronic health challenges.
Explain and justify interprofessional care for the person experiencing chronic health challenges.
prerequisites: NRS384: Health Challenges 3: Mental Health Care
NRS274: Health Challenges 2: Acute Care B

title: Health Promotion Project Management
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will design a health promotion project in collaboration with a community based organisation, working in partnership with stakeholders to facilitate a person and community-focused approach to care. The focus of the project will be on community health, wellness, or rehabilitation and students will apply the PRECEDE/PROCEED model of health promotion to inform ethical practice in project planning, implementation and evaluation. Students will work closely with a community organisation in the design of the project with a focus on integrated healthcare and ensuring sustainable healthy communities. This subject will further develop students' skills in academic and digital literacies, and extend their knowledge of research methods, biomedical and social sciences.
learning_outcomes: be able to present the completed project proposal to the identified community and demonstrate successful collaboration with the community stakeholders
be able to complete a critical evaluation of relevant literature to inform project development
be able to apply the PRECEDE/PROCEED model to design the project on behalf of an identified community, working in partenrship with the key stakeholders to adopt a community-focused approach to care
be able to assess the health and wellbeing needs of an identified community, working in partnership with the key stakeholders
be able to justify a project that addresses a complex rehabilitation or health and wellbeing need of the identified community
be able to reflect critically on the project development process

title: Health Research Dissertation
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop their research skills through undertaking original independent research. With guidance from experienced mentors, they will evaluate existing findings and gather, analyse, and interpret new data to create new knowledge. The end product of this intensive research process will be a dissertation or a publishable journal article.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the research project verbally to professional audiences.
Conduct a research project, and prepare a manuscript for publication in a peer reviewed journal in accordance with the journal's publication guidelines or prepare a dissertation.
Undertake independent scholarship and/or research applicable to health related sciences.
Apply ethical research practices.
prerequisites: HSC505: Research and Evidence Based-Practice in Health Sciences

title: Health, Society and Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to the social determinants of health and how social inequity affects a person's chances in life. The learning for students emphasises the health of First Nations people and those living in remote and rural areas. Students will explore social factors and sociological theories that create categories within the population. Students will conduct an independent enquiry to investigate the social determinants of health in a specific town or region using advanced academic and information literacy.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced academic and information literacy to conduct an independent research project.
Analyse the social determinants of health that impact various groups of Australians including First Nations people.
Explain the social factors that create specific categories of clients in health services.
Use sociological theory to explore the health impact of social inequity.

title: Health Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: The subject investigates psychological aspects of health and health care. It examines the influence of stress and certain risk behaviours on health, and people's reactions to illness and medical treatment. The subject also discusses psychological approaches to health care. Students should note that this subject does not contribute to an APAC (Australian Psychology Accreditation Council) accredited sequence in psychology.
learning_outcomes: Outline and compare major models of health and illness.
Critically evaluate psychological factors associated with certain risk behaviours, such as substance abuse.
Evaluate psychological approaches to changing risk behaviours, and outline methods of health promotion.
Identify the influence of personality and social factors on health.
Analyse reactions to illness, disability, pain and medical treatment.
Define the concept of stress, and discuss physiological and psychological reactions to stress.
prerequisites: PSY317: Psychology of Health and Illness

title: Health, Wellbeing and Family Care in Later Life
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines the concepts of health, wellbeing and ill-health as experienced by a range of older adults. Age related physical, psychological and cognitive changes are examined and differentiated between those associated with healthy ageing and those associated with medical conditions. A range of age-associated medical conditions are examined to identify risks and preventative strategies for healthy ageing and the social, cultural and psychological implications of these are also considered. Issues around the provision of informal/family care are explored in relation to the carer, the person being cared for and social and cultural structures that support these roles.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the differences between age-related cognitive and physical changes in healthy ageing from those associated with illness.
Critically examine and apply bio-psycho-social and cultural perspectives to age related physical, psychological and cognitive changes experienced by older adults.
Apply knowledge of preventive strategies to minimise health risks to older adults.
Critically analyse the socio-cultural context and health and well-being implications of family/informal care.

title: Health, Wellbeing and Family Care in Later Life
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines the concepts of health, wellbeing and ill-health as experienced by a range of older adults. Age related physical, psychological and cognitive changes are critically analysed and differentiated between those associated with healthy ageing and those associated with medical conditions. Students will develop and apply advanced knowledge of a range of age-associated medical conditions to identify and critically evaluate risks and preventative strategies for healthy ageing, taking account of the social, cultural and psychological implications. Issues around the provision of informal/family care are critically examined in relation to the carer, the person being cared for and social and cultural structures that support these roles.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced knowledge and specialised skills to critically evaluate evidence- informed preventative strategies to minimise complex health risks to older adults within diverse care contexts.
Critically analyze and synthesise advanced research-based knowledge to distinguish age-related cognitive and physical changes in healthy ageing from those associated with illness.
Critically evaluate and integrate advanced knowledge of complex socio-cultural contexts and their health and well-being implications for family/informal care.
Critically examine and apply advanced knowledge of bio-psycho-social and cultural perspectives to age related physical, psychological and cognitive changes experienced by older adults.

title: Heat Transfer
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles and mechanisms of heat transfer in engineering systems. Emphasis is placed on understanding fundamental principles and applying them to analyse and solve engineering problems related to heat transfer phenomena.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of convective heat transfer to analyse internal and external flow situations.
Examine the principles of radiation heat transfer and its applications in engineering systems.
Compare mathematical models and computational tools to solve heat transfer problems.
Analyse one-dimensional and multi-dimensional heat conduction problems.
Compare the fundamental principles and mechanisms of heat transfer, including conduction, convection, and radiation.

title: Hebrews and the General Epistles
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the genre, literary structure, provenance and distinctive theological features of Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John and Jude, focusing especially on the exegesis and interpretation of Hebrews, James and 1 Peter. An important dimension of this subject is the study of these New Testament writings as diverse expressions of early Christianity and alternative voices to Paul and the Gospel writers.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Identify features of Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John and Jude that provide clues to their provenance.
Demonstrate critical appreciation of distinctive theological features of these New Testament texts, especially Hebrews, James and 1 Peter.
Discuss the genre and literary structure of these New Testament writings and to demonstrate familiarity with the history of interpretation of these texts.
Demonstrate a critical and informed understanding of issues relating to the interpretation of Hebrews and the General Epistles.
Demonstrate advanced competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts through critical engagement with primary biblical materials and constructive engagement with secondary literature.
Discuss major theological and ethical themes in Hebrews and the General Epistles and critically evaluate their contemporary relevance.

title: Hebrews and the General Epistles
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the genre, literary structure, provenance and distinctive theological features of Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John and Jude, focusing especially on the exegesis and interpretation of Hebrews, James and 1 Peter. An important dimension of this subject is the study of these New Testament writings as diverse expressions of early Christianity and alternative voices to Paul and the Gospel writers.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the genre and literary structure of these New Testament writings and to demonstrate familiarity with the history of interpretation of these texts.
Identify features of Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John and Jude that provide clues to their provenance.
Demonstrate a critical and informed understanding of issues relating to the interpretation of Hebrews and the General Epistles.
Demonstrate critical appreciation of distinctive theological features of these New Testament texts, especially Hebrews, James and 1 Peter.
Demonstrate advanced competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts through critical engagement with primary biblical materials and constructive engagement with secondary literature.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss major theological and ethical themes in Hebrews and the General Epistles and critically evaluate their contemporary relevance.

title: High Level Facilitation for Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the concepts of learning through facilitation. This is a practicum subject that requires students to put theory into practice during a 200 hour supervised professional placement. The subject provides students with an opportunity to apply learning and teaching theory and encourages observation, reflection and analysis of learning in various workplace and education contexts. This subject requires students to complete professional experience activities that can contribute to supervised teaching practice requirements for some workplace purposes. The practicum placement includes a minimum 50 hours of supervised teaching practice, observed and evaluated by a qualified teacher or educator; plus a minimum of 50 hours observing the teaching practice of others; plus a minimum of 100 hours of engagement in other professional activities, such as developing course and/or teaching materials, evaluating training, participating in assessment validation, mentoring students and/or peers, undertaking other professional development activities. Appropriate evidence demonstrating these requirements includes (but may not be limited to) verified journals, timesheets, minutes of meetings, course materials, reports, reviews, reference letters, etc.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and discuss strategies used to accommodate the needs of different groups of learners and teaching contexts.
Develop and present a portfolio of teaching practice with evidence.
Develop and implement innovative facilitation strategies and approaches to teaching and learning in their own professional practice.
Adapt and implement teaching methods to suit a variety of teaching and learning situations.
Analyse teaching and learning approaches in relation to the planning, implementation and evaluation of facilitation methods.
prerequisites: EPT320: High Level Facilitation for Adult and Vocational Education

title: Highly Effective Teaching: Primary Arts, Humanities and Languages
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This is a core subject to meet the requirements for a primary specialisation in Arts, Humanities and Languages. Teacher education students' understandings of best practice in primary teaching and learning will be developed through inquiry-based learning and assessment. Arts, HASS/HSIE students will conduct an inquiry into a topic in their area of focus from the Arts/HSIE curriculum. Language students will conduct an individual inquiry into a topic of language-specific curriculum and pedagogical studies. All students will expand their understanding of and skills in curriculum integration including literacy, numeracy and critical and creative thinking, and importantly, ways to promote understanding and respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories, cultures and languages in the primary context. A deeper engagement with constructivist pedagogy through inquiry-based learning will occur and students will pay particular attention to the use of ICTs to support student and teacher professional learning.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and use a range of resources, with specific attention to ICT-based materials.
Identify and critique a range of global and local topics and issues relevant to best practice primary teaching and learning in the Australian context.

Construct multiple ways to integrate the primary curriculum.

title: Highly Effective Teaching: Issues in Primary English
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will extend their English discipline and curriculum knowledge through examining issues and topics relevant to effective primary English and literacy instruction. Students will learn and apply inquiry skills to independently locate, analyse, synthesise and evaluate sources of information addressing an issue or topic. Students will develop skills as reflective practitioners through generating implications from their inquiry for their future classroom practice. They will learn to construct a high quality report encompassing current theory, research, policy and practice in English education and lead a seminar presentation to contribute to the learning of their peers in the area of primary English.
learning_outcomes: Plan and conduct seminars to promote peer learning about the ways research informs effective English and literacy instruction.
Explain the implications of contemporary issues and topics for teaching and learning English and literacy for a diversity of contexts in primary education.
Communicate the outcomes of inquiry through coherent and accessibly written, spoken and digital texts.
Implement inquiry-based skills in English and literacy classrooms through engagement in the inquiry process and reflection on it.
Critique through peer assessment, the effectiveness of presentations to communicate research on effective English and literacy instruction.
Articulate connections between issues and topics in English and literacy education and relevant theories of pedagogy, practice and processes for teaching and learning English and literacy.

Source, analyse and synthesise high quality scholarly academic literature and other key relevant materials that support multiple perspectives on issues and topics in English language and literacy education.
Identify, critique, and respond to a range of global and local issues and topics relevant to the teaching and learning of English in the Australian context for the diverse range of learners.
prerequisites: EML447: Highly Effective Teaching: Issues in Primary English
