title: Highly Effective Teaching: Primary PDHPE
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject further develops teacher education students' knowledge of and skills in teaching PDHPE by developing their skills in curriculum integration, including the embedding of Australian Curriculum general capabilities into K-6 learning programs. Students investigate the five propositions underpinning the NESA K-10 PDHPE syllabus documents, and draw on contemporary research relating to children's health, wellbeing, resilience and physical activity status, in order to inform the design of quality health and movement learning experiences. In this subject, students explore how current models of health promotion can encourage community engagement, and assist in developing K-6 learners' health and physical literacy. Quality authentic assessment theories and practices will be explored and applied to the design and grading of learners' assessment samples in both health and movement contexts. The subject will further assist students to critique the efficacy and the cultural responsiveness of educational resources, including digital technologies, designed to support the teaching and learning of health and movement concepts.
learning_outcomes: Critique and safely and ethically use digital resources to develop learners' digital literacy and support learning of health and movement concepts.
Apply NESA assessment requirements to design authentic assessment tasks and provide meaningful feedback that celebrates learner achievement, and assist K-6 learners to establish learning goals.

Effectively integrate K-10 PDHPE syllabus inclusions with other Key Learning Areas, 'learning across the curriculum' priorities and general capabilities to design stage appropriate, challenging and inclusive health and movement learning opportunities for K-6 learners.
Identify and critique contemporary evidence-based research and policy and apply their implications to teaching and learning in health and movement contexts.
Adopt a health promoting schools approach to develop learners' health and physical activity knowledge, skills and values.

Use a strengths-based approach to design and differentiate the categories of movement opportunities to challenge K-6 learners, develop their physical literacy and assist them to achieve syllabus outcomes and movement success.
prerequisites: EMR501: Highly Effective Teaching: Primary PDHPE

title: Highly Effective Teaching: Primary PDHPE
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides opportunities for students to critique scholarship and policy directions relating to Australian children's health and movement. Further, students will apply the implications of research to the design of quality, contemporary PDHPE learning experiences for children in K-6 contexts, and communicate their understandings with the profession. In this subject, students explore how current models of health promotion can assist in curriculum integration, inform broader school policy and practices and encourage community engagement aimed at promoting the adoption of healthy, safe and active lives of children, their families and communities. The subject further allows students to investigate the Health and Physical Education curriculum structures, and explore the inclusions, programming and integration possibilities. Using the Australian curriculum proposition of critical inquiry, students investigate the concept of physical literacy and propose strategies to embed the development of physical literacy in Physical Education learning experiences. Quality authentic assessment theories and practices will be critiqued and applied to the design of assessment of health and physical literacy. The subject will further assist students to select and critique the appropriateness of educational resources, including digital technologies, to support the teaching and learning of health and movement concepts, and the development of literacy, numeracy and digital literacy skills.
learning_outcomes: Explore and apply health promotion and advocacy approaches to broader school health and physical education practices.

Apply NESA assessment requirements to design authentic health and movement assessment tasks and provide meaningful feedback that celebrates learner achievement, and assist K-6 learners to establish learning goals.

Critique contemporary evidence-based research and policy relating to Australian children's health and movement and apply the implications to the design and implementation of PDHPE programs, and professional learning opportunities for future colleagues.
Critique and safely and ethically use digital resources and to develop learners' digital literacy, literacy and numeracy and support learning of health and movement concepts.
Apply Australian Health and Physical Education curriculum inclusions to the design of quality, integrated, educative teaching and learning experiences for K-6 learners.
Develop educative movement experiences that promote physical literacy in Physical Education programs.
prerequisites: EMR409: Highly Effective Teaching: Primary PDHPE

title: Highly Effective Teaching: Primary STEM
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: STEM education integrates the areas of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) in an interdisciplinary and applied approach to learning and teaching. STEM draws on knowledge and skills of the scientific and technical disciplines to pose, ponder and solve complex, real-world problems. To be successful in STEM, children need to be skilled investigators, innovative thinkers, problem solvers and communicators, as well as have confidence in their abilities in STEM, and view STEM as personally relevant and important. In this subject, students will be required to develop engaging STEM learning experiences that integrate syllabus content which is applied in project, problem or inquiry-based learning situations that are authentic and contextual. Students will also explore a strengths-based approach to differentiate their practice and strategies to integrate the general capabilities such as: critical and creative thinking, information and communication technology capability and personal and social capability into STEM learning experiences.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and present to peers emergent research and policy directions that inform effective STEM instruction.
Design STEM units of work using a framework for effective STEM education and incorporating appropriate use of ICT and digital technologies, and assessment to facilitate and evaluate learning.
Describe and promote effective strategies to foster children's STEM capabilities, including knowledge, creativity and innovation, and higher-order thinking skills, within authentic STEM contexts.
Apply a strengths-based approach to design STEM units of work that support diverse learners and inclusive student participation in STEM learning activities.
Identify cross-curricular links and describe pedagogical approaches to integrating the learning areas of Mathematics and Science and Technology, as well as the general capabilities in STEM education.

Present an argument for adopting an integrated, real world approach to STEM education and justify the strategies that could be used to foster student and educator engagement and self-efficacy in STEM.
Develop, promote and evaluate quality STEM learning experiences that use integration, inquiry and project-based learning strategies.
prerequisites: EMS407: Highly Effective Teaching: Primary STEM

syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the theory and practice of histological techniques; including surgical cutup, fixation, processing, embedding, sectioning and staining of tissues using routine and specialised techniques. Students will also develop an understanding of the normal histologic structure of cells and tissues within the human body. This subject contains a compulsory 4-day intensive school where students will learn practical skills in histological techniques.

title: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives of Sport Communication
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the historical and contemporary connections between sport and the media and serves as a foundation for further study in this field. Sport and media have a unique connection, and it is impossible to describe sport and media as discreet independent social institutions. They are, rather, overlapping and corporate organisations. This subject explores prominent sports journalists in history and their reporting style, the impact of television on sports, the media’s portrayal of historical mega-sporting events, investigative sports journalism, milestone shifts in media and the notion of sports media as the 'toy department' of news. The subject provides students with knowledge of the complex interrelationship between sport and media throughout history.
learning_outcomes: Describe the ways in which sports media has been historically inclusive or exclusionary toward journalists and athletes of diverse backgrounds and genders.
Investigate and explain the ways that recent developments in technology, such as digital cultures, are reshaping sports media.
Describe the ways in which sport influences media landscapes.

Describe the changing landscape of sports media as a professional practice.

title: Historical and Social Contexts of Early Childhood Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will survey historical, philosophical, and sociological understandings of early child education. Children, childhood, and families are examined in their different historical, cultural, and social contexts with attention to both perspectives and practice. The subject will consider, historical perspectives on children and childhood; the development of early childhood education and care in Australia; practical approaches and philosophies in early childhood; early childhood policy and provision; and ethical responsibilities in early childhood education. In today's world, teacher's work is increasingly complex. Teachers must be cognisant of the complexity of social and cultural factors that influence children and their family, and resultant social justice issues. Issues specifically related to social class, gender, and ethnicity, will also be examined. Students will be able to critically evaluate existing knowledge and scholarship, and identify theoretical perspectives and philosophy in practice, enabling reflection and reflexivity as they develop as teachers.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic writing and APA style referencing.
Articulate ideas and information clearly and appropriately for the given context, audience and ICT.
Explain how contexts, policy, and frameworks affect children and families in early childhood education.
Explain the role of ethics, reflection, and reflexive practice as students and teachers in early childhood education to address social justice issues.
Discuss ways that educational philosophies affect curriculum, pedagogy and service provision in early childhood contexts.
Describe how philosophical approaches to the care and education of children have changed over time.

Describe the historical and contemporary development of early childhood education and care in Australia.

title: Historical Sociology: Migration and Human Relocation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the various historical and contemporary forces that cause people to migrate and relocate. Topics covered include colonialism and imperialism, the mass migration of the post war years, refugee movements caused by war and civil conflict, other forms of forced displacement, including human trafficking, and those seeking political or religious asylum. As an example of historical sociology the subject is interdisciplinary in nature.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse historical source material.
Identify different causes for migration and human relocation and situate these in space and time.
Interrogate the interpretative differences in secondary sources.
Articulate the main principles of historical sociology.
Apply competent research and writing skills to a significant topic relevant to the subject matter.

title: History of Christianity in China
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject will discuss critically the contextualisation of Christianity in China. Historically and theologically acceptable definitions of contextualisation, accommodation, indigenisation and enculturation will be considered, together with key movements and figures involved in the contextualisation of Christianity in China. Christian texts, music, art and literature will be examined from differing critical perspectives and interpretations. Within the broader history of Christianity in China, this subject will emphasise three key figures from the twentieth century: the theologian T. C. Chao; the activist Christian leader Y. T. Wu; and the church leader Bishop K. H. Ting. Other important figures will be introduced by way of comparison and contrast. Each figure will be closely examined based on his own writings in dialogue with the times. The emphasis throughout this subject is on social and intellectual history, and its interpretation for today.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the relevance of the history of Christianity in China to theological understanding and contextualisation in the Church today.
Demonstrate systematic knowledge of and critical engagement with the history of Christianity in China with an emphasis on the contextualisation process and its relevance for the Church Today.

Demonstrate intellectual flexibility in the analysis and critique of Chinese Christian institutions and theological ideas, individuals and communities, in relationship to Chinese social, cultural and intellectual history.
Demonstrate creativity in the critical application of historical and theological sources for the contextualisation of Christianity in China.
Demonstrate a critical theological and historical engagement with subjects central to the study of history and Christian tradition in China and their relevance to the Church today.
prerequisites: THL346: History of Christianity in China

Demonstrate intellectual flexibility in the analysis and critique of Chinese Christian institutions and theological ideas, individuals and communities, in relationship to Chinese social, cultural and intellectual history.
Demonstrate the relevance of the history of Christianity in China to theological understanding and contextualisation in the Church today.
Demonstrate creativity in the critical application of historical and theological sources for the contextualisation of Christianity in China.
prerequisites: THL556: History of Christianity in China

title: History of Prophets: Adam to Jesus
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject looks at the history of prophets and monotheism from the perspective of the Qur'an spanning the human legacy from the first man and the first Prophet Adam (pbuh) to the last Prophet Muhammad (pbuh). The Qur'anic narratives will be given in order to see how prophets influenced the world history. Main topics that will be covered are: Qur'anic approach to prophetic stories; Adam, the first man and the first Prophet, prophets up to Noah and the flood, the Prophet Abraham and his fight against paganism, the Prophet Joseph, the Prophet Moses, prophets sent to Bani Israel after Moses and Jesus.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Articulate an understanding of how religion develops within the context prophetic history.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the prophetic history of as described in Islamic sources.
Understand critically the relevance of prophetic stories in contemporary times and people.
Analyse and discuss critically to theological matters related to each Qur'anic prophet and their history.

title: History, Social and Emotional Wellbeing
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of history, social and emotional wellbeing issues, and mental health problems in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. This theory is underpinned by an understanding and acknowledgment of the history of colonisation and the effects on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples throughout Australia. These include psychological and spiritual effects on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, the value of traditional Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander belief systems, the community, societies, healing and lore/law. This subject will explore the importance of being connected to the land and Dreaming (spirituality). Importantly this subject will investigate appropriate ways of healing within Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in a contemporary context. Holistic health encompasses spirituality as well as the physical, social, and emotional wellbeing of the individual and community.
learning_outcomes: Discuss historical and cultural backgrounds of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities.
Explain legislation, policies and practices that have impacted on the identity, culture and health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Demonstrate the social and emotional wellbeing issues which have arisen in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander society since colonisation utilising digital medium.
Define social and emotional wellbeing and holistic health and wellbeing.

Describe relationships between historical, cultural, legislative, policy and practice factors that affect the health and wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and implications for health care provision.

title: Homiletics
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles and practice of homiletics. It explores issues of biblical interpretation in the homiletic context, the theology of proclamation and the spiritual and vocational orientation of the preacher. This subject also provides students with analytical tools for evaluating homilies.
learning_outcomes: Prepare and deliver a biblically and theologically literate homily/sermon for a prescribed setting.
Identify and to articulate the main elements of the Christian homiletic/preaching tradition.
Demonstrate an advanced capacity for individual and collective critique of homilies/sermons in terms of their theological clarity, overall presentation and contextual suitability.
Identify and to analyse critically the role of the community in the homiletical interpretation of Scripture.
Demonstrate in-depth knowledge of both pastoral responsibilities and public accountabilities associated with the homiletic/preaching task in contemporary cultural and technological contexts.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.

title: Holistic Eco-Social Approaches in Mental Health
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores mental health practice in the context of the global environmental crisis, which is having disproportionate impacts on human health and wellbeing. Conventional approaches to mental health based on Euro-Western ideology are challenged, and a holistic environmental framework is presented to include social and ecological dimensions. Drawing from a range of worldviews and knowledges, the psychological and emotional responses to environmental loss and decline, as well strategies and approaches for promoting mental health in a range of contexts are examined. This subject is relevant to health and human service practitioners interested in understanding how to adapt to a changing climate and practice context.
learning_outcomes: Explain the psychological and emotional responses to environmental loss and decline.
Describe the holistic attributes of human wellbeing and mental health.
Apply holistic environmental approaches to mental health practice, including being (ontology), thinking (epistemology) and doing (methodology).
Identify a range of worldviews that influence environmental sustainability and holistic conceptualisations of mental health.

title: Honours Dissertation Proposal and Literature Review
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop a research question, design a project to respond to it, and then explain the design as part of a research proposal. Students are expected to critically analyse existing literature related to their research question to write a literature review that explains how their planned research will build on existing knowledge and its contribution to the field. Students will examine the ethical considerations of research and the requirements of a human research ethics application.
learning_outcomes: Complete a human ethics application for a research project.
Clearly communicate key ideas and concepts.
Demonstrate skills in reviewing, critiquing and synthesising research literature.
Design a small-scale project that uses appropriate ideas, methods and concepts.
Construct and build an argument for their research.
Articulate an understanding of research methods and processes in the form of a written research proposal.

title: Honours in Science Fundamentals (16)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will build foundational knowledge, skills, and confidence to pursue a research project. Through engaging in the development of their research project, students will develop their knowledge, skills, and confidence as a novice researcher. This will include knowledge and skills to develop and application and obtain the research ethics approval when appropriate. Through regular communication with their supervisor(s), students will also have opportunities to reflect on their research practices, experiences, and learning. With guidance and feedback from their supervisor(s), students will identify a clear research question and design a research study, which they will explain and defend in a written research proposal. Students will also critically review existing literature to support development of their research question, explaining (a) how their planned research will build on existing knowledge and (b) why their planned research is worth undertaking. Acceptable formats for the final submitted Honours include: a dissertation or a publishable report ready for peer review or a publishable journal article ready for journal peer review. HRS425 (24 Points), HRS426 (16 points) and HRS427 (8 points) are the same subject with different point values that reflects the subject hours allocated to that subject code: 8 points requires 140-160 hours, 16 points requires up to a maximum of 320 hours and 24 points requires up to a maximum of 480 hours. These variations occur to allow those in integrated Honours programs to include advanced discipline subjects in their honours program and reflects the intended depth of study required for the Honours project design. They also enable accommodation of a specific elective as part of the BSc(Hons) program as agreed and approved in consultation with their project supervisors, Honours Advisors and the Course Director. Course Documentation determines whether a student enrols in HRS425, HRS426 or HRS427.
learning_outcomes: With supervisor approval, identify a clear, specific research question, which can feasibly be addressed in an Honours-level research project.
With supervisor guidance, explain how their research question will be addressed, explicitly acknowledging relevant time and resource constraints and any contingency planning.
With guidance, justify their choice of sample, recruitment strategy, data collection, and/or data analysis plan, as relevant, in relation to their question and any relevant ethical considerations.
Succinctly report on their research progress in a way that shows increasing independence as a novice researcher.
With supervisor guidance, develop, submit an ethics application and obtain ethical approval (where appropriate) and begin collecting and/or analysing data to address a research question.
In regular supervision conversations, reflect on their research progress, including strengths and skills they are developing, issues they have encountered, and problem-solving they have engaged in.
Strategically acquire and critically review existing research on a given topic to support a research proposal.
Construct a convincing written argument regarding (a) how a proposed study will build on or strengthen existing research and (b) why this study should be conducted.
prerequisites: HRS425: Honours in Science Research Fundamentals  (24)

school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, Students will be guided by their supervisor(s) to develop their knowledge, skills, and confidence as a researcher, particularly in relation to data analysis and interpretation. Through regular communication with their supervisor(s), students will have opportunities to reflect on their collected data, analyses, and interpretations. Students will develop practical insights into real-world research writing and dissemination processes. Students will develop a deeper understanding of the world of professional research by working through the process of writing a dissertation, or a research report for (potential) publication, under the guidance of their research supervisor(s). Students will also present this research orally to an audience of interested end-users or stakeholders. Explain factors that can influence a researcher's choice of knowledge dissemination methods, including the selection of a suitable scholarly journal.

school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on developing students' understanding of research methods that will be integral for the completion of their dissertation. Students' methodological knowledge and skills will be developed through analysing and evaluating published research studies in their discipline. Students will consider broad approaches to research (qualitative, quantitative, and pragmatic), question-clarity, specific designs, sampling decisions/techniques, recruitment strategies, data collection and analysis methods, and conclusion validity. Overall, this subject will introduce students to concepts and skills that are important for designing and conducting methodologically sound research in their discipline area.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast research designs, sampling, data collection and data analysis methods used by researchers in their discipline area.
Identify examples of qualitative and quantitative research in their discipline area, and compare and contrast the associated strengths of each approach.
Appraise the reliability and validity of published research, considering the reported methods and results to support the formulation of a study.
Critically engage with the role of ethics in the research process.
Evaluate the appropriateness of methodological choices in relation to a study's research question/s.

Demonstrate data analysis skills relevant to their planned Honours research.
Evaluate the formulation of research questions for methodological planning.
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of qualitative, quantitative and/or mixed methods research.
Appraise the validity of conclusions in published research articles.

title: Horse Behaviour and Training
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to examine horse behaviour and training methods in detail. Students will be able to thoroughly appraise the importance of stimulus control for horse welfare and human safety and experience the use of established training strategies and theories in order to achieve a specified goal. The role of humans associated with horse management and training will also be considered, with particular reference to forms of stockmanship including the Indigenous Australian Stockmen. On successfully completing this subject students will become proficient in identifying a wide range of behavioural signs that may indicate inadequacies and/or anomalies in the horse's behavioural repertoire and be able to produce a well-reasoned plan for addressing these and consequently ensuring that the horse's welfare needs are met.
learning_outcomes: analyse causes of difficulties in training and provide behavioural strategies for their resolution;
assess the importance, and demonstrate implementation of stimulus control within equitation training;
appraise the limitations of equine learning abilities and establish underpinning training principles;
deconstruct the horse-trainer-rider relationship in order to facilitate effective horse training;
analyse and determine effectiveness of real-life training methods in a range of horse uses and equestrian disciplines;

differentiate and appraise the relationships between contributing factors such as tradition, culture and within Australia, Indigenous Australian impact with respect to horse welfare and quality of life; and
identify and employ appropriate communication modes depending on the context (of the conversation), the nature of the recipient audience and the topic under discussion.

title: Horse Behaviour and Training I
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Throughout this subject students will develop and enhance their understanding of horse evolution, domestication and behaviour, and its relationship to equine welfare and quality of life. Students will learn evidence-based training principles and how learning theory can be applied to horse-human interactions to ensure safe handling. On successful completion of this subject students will be able to demonstrate theoretical and practical knowledge of horse behaviour, welfare, and horse-human interactions and be able to apply learning theory principles to a range of situations.
learning_outcomes: Describe the implications of evolution and domestication on horse behaviour.
Identify and explain the appropriate use of learning theory in a range of training situations.
Recognise and demonstrate practical skills in safe horse handling practices to allow Workplace Health and Safety requirements to be met.
Discuss the importance of stimulus control within equine training and be able to practically demonstrate this concept throughout horse-human interactions.
Identify factors essential for a comprehensive assessment of equid welfare and quality of life.

title: Horse Behaviour and Training II
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Throughout this subject, students will build on their knowledge of horse behaviour and training covered in EQS120. This subject will further develop their understanding of the mechanisms by which horses learn with respect to their neurophysiology and cognitive capabilities and their ability to resolve problem behaviours. This will be discussed in relation to appropriate management, handling and training practices currently employed within the equine industry and contrasted against other animal industries for evaluation of industry sustainability and ethical practice. On successful completion of this subject, students will be able to demonstrate a developed understanding of learning theory and its application to horses, as well as being able to appraise common husbandry and training practices with regard to sustainable horse use, the horse-human relationship and public perception.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the causes of difficulties in training and provide strategies for their resolution consistent with learning theory principles.
Discuss the effectiveness of training methods in a range of horse uses and disciplines and practically apply evidence-based training practices.
Describe the limitations of equine learning with respect to their ethology and cognition.
Discuss the horse-human relationship and its influence on effective horse training.
Identify appropriate communication methods for use in the discussion of equine training and behaviour and be able to communicate effectively both orally and/or in writing.
prerequisites: EQS120: Horse Behaviour and Training I

title: Horse Breeding Technologies
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will cover the reproductive anatomy and physiology of the stallion and explore the theory and application of assisted equine reproductive technologies. As part of this subject, students develop practical skills in stallion semen collection, evaluation and processing, semen transport, semen freezing and thawing, and embryo vitrification. Oestrous synchronisation and advanced reproductive technologies such as embryo transfer, oocyte pickup, epididymal semen collection, Gamete Intrafallopian Transfer (GIFT), and Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI) are also studied. This subject provides students with valuable hands-on skills while broadening their knowledge of more advanced and emerging technologies in equine reproduction.
learning_outcomes: Assess the legal and practical aspects of reproductive management of horses in artificial breeding programs to maximise the pregnancy rates.
Demonstrate and explain procedures for the appropriate processing and management of transported stallion semen to maximise sperm longevity and survival.
Appraise the various methods of oestrous synchronisation and explain the process of embryo collection and transfer in the mare.
Apply knowledge of stallion behaviour, reproductive anatomy and physiology to describe and assess the management of stallions to achieve maximum reproductive efficiency.
Describe and practically demonstrate the processes of stallion semen collection, semen evaluation and the influence of semen extenders.
Differentiate and describe the various advanced reproductive technologies available for use in horses and compare and contrast their use.

title: Horse Breeding Technologies
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on previous studies of equine reproduction and explores the theory and application of assisted equine reproductive technologies. As part of this subject, students develop practical skills in stallion semen collection, evaluation and processing, semen transport, semen freezing and thawing and artificial insemination of mares. Oestrous synchronisation and advanced reproductive technologies such as embryo transfer, oocyte pickup, Gamete Intrafallopian Transfer (GIFT) and Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI) are also studied. This subject provides students with valuable hands-on skills, while broadening their knowledge of more advanced and emerging technologies in equine reproduction.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate and outline the processes of stallion semen collection, evaluation, processing, chilling, freezing, storage and thawing using scientifically developed calculations to maximise sperm longevity and survival.
describe procedures for the appropriate management and transport of frozen and chilled stallion semen;
distinguish and describe the various different methods of oestrous synchronisation in mares;
assess the legal and ethical aspects of reproductive management of horses.
differentiate and describe the various advanced reproductive technologies available for use in horses and compare and contrast their use in practice; and

outline the management of mares for an artificial insemination program to maximise the pregnancy rate (this includes performing artificial insemination of a mare in an aseptic manner), and devise management plans for given broodmare scenarios;

title: Hospital and Rural Pharmacy Practice
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses pharmacy practice within hospital and rural environments. Hospital-based pharmacy practice: the role of the clinical pharmacist in the health care team, and the approach to medication management within diverse hospital settings are examined. Quality use of medicines, patient safety and quality improvement principles will inform the study of medication utilisation within a range of clinical categories and address current medication priority areas. Rural pharmacy practice: issues affecting rural healthcare are explored to gain an understanding of the complexities and challenges of rural practice. Issues specific to rural health are examined, including mental health, zoonotic disease, and the impact of environmental factors. The health of Australian First Nations people is explored, including an epidemiological overview, consideration of health priorities, and evidence-based models of pharmaceutical care. Students studying this subject are assumed to have completed the first three years of the pharmacy program, and to be concurrently studying final year professional practice and clinical therapeutics. As part of this subject students will complete 4 weeks of placement.
learning_outcomes: Apply a patient-centred, culturally responsive approach to medication management to deliver safe, effective care.
Identify, analyse and reflect on health priorities of Australian First Nations people.
Research, critically analyse and synthesise information to deliver evidence-based care.
Analyse and assess clinical service provision to deliver continuous improvement in quality and safety.
Apply principles of quality use of medicines to medication management within the hospital setting.
Identify, analyse and reflect on health priorities of rural people.
prerequisites: HLT417: Indigenous Perspectives on Health and Wellbeing
PHM490: Hospital and Rural Pharmacy Practice
PHM490: Hospital and Rural Pharmacy Practice

title: How and Why: Consumers and their Behaviour
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: To make strategic marketing decisions, organisations need to understand the individual, social, organisational, and cultural factors that influence customer behaviour. This subject examines the buyer decision process in both consumer and business markets. The topics draw on concepts derived primarily from psychology and sociology, where decision making is considered from a number of angles including perception, learning, motivation, attitudes, culture, values, lifestyles and situational influences. These various theoretical concepts are applied and integrated with regard to market segmentation and positioning and implementation of marketing strategies.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and justify which consumer behaviour theories are needed to support marketing decisions in different contexts.
Critically analyse key consumer trends and evaluate the potential impact on marketing strategy.
Apply consumer behaviour theories and concepts to develop solutions to marketing problems in a variety of contexts.
Critically analyse different consumer behaviour for different consumer types.
Identify the fundamental processes and influences of consumer behaviour.

title: HSIE: Teaching About People, Places and the Past
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides teacher education students with the curriculum and pedagogical knowledge that will enable them to be teachers of Humanities and Social Sciences K-6. In this subject, teacher education students will specifically engage with the knowledge and understandings, skills and values of the NSW Human Society and its Environment (HSIE) learning area and examine how these are represented in mandated syllabuses. Teacher education students will develop an understanding of teaching and assessment strategies and resources (including digital resources) and design HSIE curriculum teaching and learning sequences. Students will create authentic learning experiences that are informed by understandings of inquiry-based learning, place-based pedagogies and cross-curriculum priorities.
learning_outcomes: Design meaningful learning experiences that connect the HSIE curricula with the community.
Incorporate a range of strategies and resources for teaching and assessing primary HSIE in a sequence of learning.
Describe the cross-curriculum priorities and their relationship to the HSIE learning area, and embed the priorities and capabilities in HSIE learning sequences.
Plan learning experiences that demonstrate understanding of the NSW Human Society and Its Environment (HSIE) K-6 Syllabus, Early Stage 1 - Stage 3.
Articulate a rationale for teaching HSIE in primary classrooms, which includes inquiry-based and place-based pedagogies.
Incorporate literacy, numeracy and digital literacy capabilities in HSIE learning programs.

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the opportunity to develop and apply foundational concepts of anatomy and physiology to the human body, including the endocrine, cardiovascular, immune, respiratory, urinary, digestive and reproductive systems. Students will build on their understanding of the fundamentals of cellular physiology, develop understanding of the physiological changes related to metabolism and during pregnancy, and explore concepts of heredity.
learning_outcomes: Describe the principal structural features and normal functioning of the endocrine, cardiovascular, immune, lymphatic, respiratory, urinary, digestive and reproductive systems.
Explain how the interaction of these body systems maintains homeostasis.
Apply foundational knowledge of body systems to discipline-specific contexts.
Explain the anatomical and functional relationships between nutrition, metabolism and temperature regulation in the human body.
Discuss the relationship between genes and inheritance.
prerequisites: BMS162: Health and the Human body: systemic human physiology
BMS175: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses 2

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to foundational concepts relevant to the anatomical structure and physiological function of the human body. Students will develop an understanding of anatomy and physiology from the atomic level through to the integration of various body systems. The focus will be the nervous, skeletal, muscular, and integumentary systems.
learning_outcomes: Communicate anatomical and physiological concepts using discipline specific terminology and illustrations.
Identify and describe the principal structures and features of the nervous system, its sub-divisions and neurophysiological processes associated with communication within the body.
Identify and describe structures and features of the integumentary systems and explain their function.
Describe common disease-causing microorganisms, their classification, and how infection is transmitted and may be controlled.
Describe the structure and function of biological molecules, cells, and tissues.

Identify and describe the principal structures and functions of the musculo- skeletal system, muscle contraction and movement, and explain bone development, growth and remodelling and the physiology of muscle contraction.
prerequisites: BMS161: Health and the Human Body: Cells, Immunity and Musculoskeletal System
BMS165: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses 1

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on previous learning, to develop the students' capacity to link knowledge about human anatomy and physiology to clinical reasoning and safe nursing practice. The subject completes the examination of the body by learning about the integumentary, endocrine, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, urinary (renal), and reproductive systems. Also it will consider the importance of chromosomes, genes and DNA; and the impact of sexual maturation and ageing on anatomical and physiological systems and processes.
learning_outcomes: Identify the human anatomy and describe the physiology of specific organ systems (integumentary, endocrine, musculo-skeletal, gastrointestinal, urinary/renal as well as fluids and electrolytes, in normal body function and reproductive systems).
Explain the role of genes and inheritance.
Explain the anatomy and physiology of the ageing process.
Describe the relationship of metabolism to normal body function.
prerequisites: BMS165: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses 1

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces essential concepts of chemistry and human anatomy and physiology as students begin to construct the foundational knowledge required for understanding and implementing safe nursing practice. The subject focuses on the chemistry and anatomy and physiology of the nervous, vascular, haematological, lymphatic, pulmonary, and immune systems beginning from the cellular level then progressing through tissues to body systems. This knowledge is then applied to essential concepts such as maintaining homeostasis and interruptions to homeostasis such as inflammation, infection and pain.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure and function of biological molecules, cells and tissues.
Describe common disease-causing microorganisms and their classification.
Describe the routes of transmission of microorganisms and the methods used to control spread of infection.
Identify and describe specific organs systems (nervous, cardiovascular, haematological, lymphatic, pulmonary and immune) and explain the relationship between their structure and function.
Identify principles and applications of mechanical force, heat, electricity and radiation to health care.
Define the concept of homeostasis and explain the role of homeostasis in normal body functions.
prerequisites: BMS161: Health and the Human body: cells, immunity and musculoskeletal system
BMS162: Health and the Human body: systemic human physiology

title: Human Aspects of Cybersecurity
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to human-centric cybersecurity. It presents a comprehensive overview of security principles with a focus on human-cyber vulnerabilities. Students will learn about human factors that contribute to cybersecurity risks, cyber-criminal behaviours, and social engineering through real-world case studies. The subject challenges the notion of portraying humans as the “weakest link” in the cybersecurity chain and provides transformative mindset and strategies to effectively detect and manage cybersecurity via a human-as-a-sensor approach.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically evaluate human factors and behaviours for effective cyber resilience.
Identify and utilise fundamental concepts and principles of security and social engineering in real-world cybersecurity defence scenarios.
Synthesise and interpret findings from security analytics, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.
Design human-centric protocols to safeguard people from cyber-exploitation and risks.

title: Human Biochemistry
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an outline of the structure and function of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids); and the major metabolic and bioenergetic pathways within cells. It provides the basis for further studies in metabolism, molecular and cell biology, genetics, immunology and microbiology, physiology, plant science, biotechnology and disease processes.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure and function of the four major classes of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids) and be able to discuss and explain the relationship between structure and function.
Explain and describe the role of energy in living cells, with particular reference to the concept of free energy and the role of ATP.
Describe the properties of enzymes as biological catalysts.
Describe the major metabolic pathways used to synthesise ATP.
prerequisites: CHM111: Math, statistics, physics and advanced chemistry for Medical Science
BCM210: Foundations and Techniques in Biochemistry

title: Human Biochemistry (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an outline of the structure and function of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids); the major metabolic and bioenergetic pathways within cells. It provides the basis for further studies in metabolism, molecular and cell biology, genetics, immunology and microbiology, physiology, plant science, biotechnology and disease processes.
learning_outcomes: Explain and describe the role of energy in living cells, with particular reference to the concept of free energy and the role of ATP.
Describe the major metabolic pathways used to synthesise ATP.
Describe the properties of enzymes as biological catalysts.

Describe the structure and function of the four major classes of biological macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids) and be able to discuss and explain the relationship between structure and function.
prerequisites: BCM210: Foundations and Techniques in Biochemistry

title: Human Bioscience 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject begins the study of human bioscience. Relevant chemistry, physics and microbiology are introduced before beginning the study of normal structure and function of the human body. This subject focuses on the structure and function of the integumentary, musculoskeletal, and nervous systems.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate between the three major muscle types (skeletal, smooth, cardiac).
Identify major skeletal muscles.
Describe common applications of mechanical force, heat, electricity, fluids and radiation to health care.
Demonstrate understanding of the role the integument plays in protection, sensation, fluid balance, temperature regulation, vitamin production and immunity.
Describe the structure and function of the muscular system.
Describe the function of major cellular constituents.
Describe the structure of the cell.
Differentiate between the four tissue types (epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous) on the basis of structure, function and location.
Demonstrate understanding of neurotransmission and neurointegration.
Recognise simple chemical formulae and equations.
Recognise some important classes of chemical functional groups.
Describe the structure and function of the nervous system (central, peripheral, autonomic, special senses).
Demonstrate understanding of the process of bone growth.
Demonstrate understanding of muscle contraction.
Define homeostasis.
Describe the structure and function of the integumentary system.
Describe the nature and properties of matter.
Demonstrate understanding of the basic principles of microbiology.
Describe the human body using appropriate anatomical terminology.
Describe the structure of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
Describe the structure and function of the skeletal system.
Describe processes that maintain homeostasis.
Describe the body cavities and associated membranes.
prerequisites: BMS162: Health and the Human Body: Systemic Human Physiology
BMS161: Health and the Human Body: Cells, Immunity and Musculoskeletal System

title: Human Computer Interaction
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the Human Computer Interface (HCI) discipline and the design of usable interfaces for computer applications. The subject looks at how to gather user requirements and employ the principles of design in order to successfully develop interfaces that meet those requirements. It includes the evaluation of interfaces for usability using techniques derived from the principles.
learning_outcomes: Design a set of appropriate usability tests for a given interface.
Evaluate an interface to determine its effective usability and identify enhancements for improvement.
Interpret and evaluate usability testing results to plan interface improvements.
Identify and explain the importance of the principles of design in relation to the design of an interface.
Design a user interface to meet a given set of requirements.

title: Human Development Across the Lifespan
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an understanding of mental health development (from conception through to adolescence, adulthood and old age) across the lifespan. It will examine the developmental milestones in human physical and mental development, the theories of human development, in particular attachment theory and the significance of nature versus nurture, personality theories and the differences in gender development. In addition this subject will explore cultural and social influences on developmental stages for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders and identify relevant services that may be required for these age groups.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate a range of personality theories and identify the theorists who developed these;
identify the traditional roles of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults with contemporary roles.
explain the milestones and stages in human physical and mental development across the lifespan;
discuss cultural, social and gender influences on developmental stages for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders across the lifespan; and
debate the significance of nature versus nurture for human development;
describe the mental health disorders that can occur within each age group;
discuss a range of theories and stages of human development across the lifespan based upon reading of seminal documents and images;

title: Human Exercise Physiology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the principles by which acute and chronic exercise affect human physiology, examining how the muscular, metabolic, cardiorespiratory, and hormonal systems adapt. Students investigate the immediate physiological changes during exercise, such as increased heart rate and oxygen consumption, alongside long-term adaptations like decreases in blood pressure and enhanced aerobic capacity. Environmental conditions, such as hot and cold environments, are scrutinized for their impact on performance and response patterns. This subject provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the body's dynamic physiological adjustments to physical activity. Students will also partake in practical skill development through measuring and evaluating physiological capacities.
learning_outcomes: Explain the metabolic, muscular, hormonal and cardiorespiratory responses to exercise and adaptations to training.
Describe the fundamental principles underlying prescription, implementation and monitoring of exercise programs for healthy populations and for population groups with varying needs.
Differentiate physiological capacities and training adaptations between males and females.
Demonstrate the application and proficiency of the various techniques used in exercise physiology research and physical fitness testing.
Differentiate the physiological changes and adaptations during exercise in different environmental conditions and external influences.

title: Human Genetics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the broad field of genetics. It will cover standard Mendelian genetics, our modern understanding of molecular genetics, and the central dogma (DNA is transcribed to mRNA which is translated to protein). The role of genetics in behaviour and human evolution will be briefly explored. Modern disciplines of applied molecular technology (including proteomics and genomics), the genetic basis of molecular diseases, epigenetics and the genetics of cancer will also be examined.
learning_outcomes: Describe DNA structure, chromatin structure, DNA replication, transcription, RNA processing, translation, mutation induction, DNA repair and RNA interference.
Describe Mendelian inheritance principles and predict phenotypical outcomes using Mendelian genetics and the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
Identify, describe and explain, using genetic concepts, how genetic changes can cause or contribute to human disease by comparing the normal situation with the pathophysiology of the disease.
Evaluate the ethical and professional issues arising from testing, diagnosing, prognosticating or treating of genetic disorders.
Describe and analyse the genetics, pathophysiology, genetic testing and treatment of Mendelian inherited disorders using one Mendelian disorder as an example.

Define and discuss how DNA technology influences/furthers our knowledge of genomics and epigenetics and explain how this can direct diagnostics, prognostics and treatment of human disease (with a focus on cancer) in the future.

title: Human Nature and the Good Life
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to a number of major philosophical theories about human nature and the good life. Theories studied stretch from those that originated in ancient civilisations to those articulated during the 20th century. Connections between each theory of human nature and philosophical positions in metaphysics and epistemology are explored, and the implications for the good life are then articulated through ethics and political philosophy. Philosophical theories of human nature and the good life pre-date the modern science of psychology and provide a useful perspective on the contemporary interface between philosophy and psychology. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
learning_outcomes: Identify where underlying philosophical debates concerning central issues in relation to human nature, for example, the nature vs nurture debate, connect with philosophical theories of human nature and the good life.
Explain aspects of a number of philosophical theories of human nature and the good life.
Recall, compare, and apply philosophical theories of human nature and the good life.
Critically evaluate aspects of a number of philosophical theories of human nature and the good life.

title: Human Nutrition
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines nutrients and how the body uses nutrients including ingestion, digestion, absorption, transport, metabolism, interaction, storage and excretion. This is then extended to consider the role of diet and nutrition in therapy and disease states.
learning_outcomes: Outline the principles involved in quantitative aspects of nutritional research (e.g. distinguish epidemiological studies from experimental studies).
Calculate the energy values provided by the macro-nutrients and use these in quantifying the energy requirements for healthy nutrition.
Describe the role of nutrition in various disease states.
Demonstrate the principles of dietary analysis, and recommend appropriate strategies, as required, to result in optimal nutrition.
Identify the role of pharmaceutical agents in nutritional therapy.

Distinguish those special nutritional requirements during periods of physiological stress (eg during different stages of the life cycle including pregnancy and lactation, and during periods of physical activity).
Describe the range of nutrients and recommended nutrient intakes, where these are applicable.
Outline the digestion, absorption and transport of nutrients in the human body.
Discuss the links between diet and health.
Describe the nutritional importance of water, water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamins, minerals and trace minerals.

title: Human Reproductive Biology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will study aspects of human reproductive biology. Topics will include fertility, endocrine control of reproduction, ovarian and testicular function, fertilisation, implantation, embryonic and foetal development, parturition, lactation and neonatal development.
learning_outcomes: Describe the hormonal, tissue and behavioural changes that occur across the menstrual cycle and explain how these are regulated.
Demonstrate understanding of gamete transport, and the cellular and molecular biology of sperm-egg interactions and fertilisation.
Explain the processes of spermatogenesis, oogenesis and folliculogenesis, and be able to compare and contrast these processes.
Describe the biological principles underlying contraceptive technology, and compare and contrast the various options for control of fertility.
Explain the processes involved in lactation and assess the advantages and disadvantages of breast and bottle feeding.
Explain the origin and characteristics of common congenital malformations.
Distinguish between the main stages of embryonic, foetal and neonatal development and explain the detection and causes of foetal disorders.
Explain how sexually transmitted diseases may contribute to altered neonatal or reproductive function.
Describe the anatomical and physiological changes that occur at puberty and explain the mechanisms behind these changes. Identify factors that may influence the timing of puberty.
Examine the causation of, and compare and contrast techniques used to overcome infertility.
Demonstrate an understanding of the hormonal control of reproduction in males and how this is regulated.
Explain the maternal responses to and complications of pregnancy.
Demonstrate an understanding of the processes involved in normal and difficult births, evaluate the use of medications during labour and delivery, and compare different birthing methods.
Describe the structure of the organs of the reproductive system in males and females and indicate how this relates to function.
Describe the processes of sexual differentiation and explain some of the disorders that can occur in the process.

Describe the changes that occur with menopause and andropause, indicate the mechanisms responsible for these changes, discuss how these changes may be managed and argue the risks/benefits associated with this management.

title: Human Molecular Genetics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the broad field of genetics. It will cover standard Mendelian genetics, our modern understanding of molecular genetics, and the central dogma (DNA is transcribed to mRNA which is translated to protein). Modern disciplines of applied molecular technology (including proteomics and genomics), the genetic basis of molecular diseases, epigenetics and the genetics of cancer will also be examined.
learning_outcomes: Identify, describe and explain, using genetic concepts, how genetic changes can cause or contribute to human disease by comparing the normal situation with the pathophysiology of the disease.

Define and discuss how DNA technology influences/furthers our knowledge of genomics and epigenetics and explain how this can direct diagnostics, prognostics and treatment of human disease (with a focus on cancer) in the future.
Describe DNA structure, Chromatin structure, DNA replication, transcription, RNA processing, translation, mutation induction, DNA repair and RNA interference.
Describe Mendelian inheritance principles and predict phenotypical outcomes using Mendelian genetics and the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
Describe and analyse the genetics, pathophysiology, genetic testing and treatment of Mendelian inherited disorders using one Mendelian disorder as an example.
Discuss the ethical and professional issues arising from testing, diagnosing, prognosticating or treating of genetic disorders.

title: Human Resource Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Employees' performance and commitment are recognised as critical drivers of organisational success, and the role of Human Resource Management (HRM) in aligning people management strategies with the strategic objectives of the organisation is important in today's dynamic operating environment. This subject will provide students with foundational knowledge of HRM and its theoretical base, and will cover key activities and functions of HRM. The subject will also examine the strategic role that HRM plays in helping organisations meet the competitive pressures of modern business.
learning_outcomes: be able to critically examine the role of HRM in contributing to the realisation of business goals and satisfying employee needs;
be able to critically discuss the evolution of HRM and its theoretical base;
be able to provide recommendations for enhancing HRM practices.
be able to identify the ethical implications of HRM and critically discuss how these can be managed;
be able to explain the major functions, techniques, procedures and systems in HRM;
be able to articulate how the broad HRM function is a joint effort of all managers in the organisation;
be able to identify and critically examine the challenges facing HRM; and
prerequisites: HRM200: FOUNDATIONS OF HUMAN RESOURCES (AHRI) FOUNDATIONS OF HUM RES (AHRI)

title: Human Resource Management in Information Agencies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to the theoretical and practical foundations of human resource management (HRM) which will enable them to apply HRM strategies in their workplace. Students will learn to critically examine how HRM functions, how HRM can play a role in effective change management, and in what ways human resource issues can influence HRM strategy formulation and implementation in an information agency.
learning_outcomes: Apply human resource management concepts and theories to an information agency.
Analyse and evaluate the key issue of change and its impact on developing strategic HRM approaches in an information agency.
Explain the ways in which key human resource issues, functions and approaches may be executed with a strategic orientation.
Compare similarities and differences in human resource management practices among different cultures.
prerequisites: INF514: Human Resource Management in Information Agencies

title: Human Resource Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to human resource management in organisations with a focus on developing solutions that are practical and effective in meeting business goals. Studying this subject will provide you with the skills to make a difference to the performance of organisations. In addition, you will develop skills in critical thinking, communication, research and collaboration.
learning_outcomes: Use research skills in the formulation of business-relevant HR recommendations and solutions.
Explore methods that foster teamwork and collaboration in the organisational context.
Critically evaluate and propose plausible HR recommendations to solve business problems.
Provide sustainable, theoretically-sound and well-informed inclusive HR recommendations to achieve organisational objectives.
Employ contemporary digital platforms to develop, communicate and review HR recommendations.
prerequisites: HRM571: Managing People in the Information Age

title: Human Resource Management in Information Agencies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject presents the essential elements of human resource management (HRM). It introduces students to HRM concepts, theories and functions which will enable them to apply successful HRM strategies in their workplace. Students will examine how HRM functions and how different issues such as change management inform the process of developing and implementing a strategic human resource approach in an information agency.
learning_outcomes: Apply human resource management concepts and theories to an information agency.
Analyse, synthesise, and evaluate the key issues of change and its impact on developing strategic HRM approaches in an information agency.
Evaluate the similarities and differences in human resource management practices among different cultures.
Research, formulate and implement a strategic human resource plan for an information agency.
prerequisites: INF333: Human Resource Management in Information Agencies

title: Human Resource Planning and Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Employees' performance and commitment are recognised as critical drivers of organisational success, and the role of Human Resource Management (HRM) in aligning people management strategies with the strategic objectives of the organisation is important in today's dynamic operating environment. This subject will provide students with foundational knowledge of HRM and its theoretical base, and will cover key activities and functions of HRM. The subject will also examine the strategic role that HRM plays in helping organisations meet the competitive pressures of modern business.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically examine the challenges facing HRM.
Explain the major functions, techniques, procedures and systems in HRM.
Critically examine the role of HRM in contributing to the realisation of business goals and satisfying employee needs.
Articulate how the broad HRM function is a joint effort of all managers in the organisation.
Critically discuss the evolution of HRM and its theoretical base.
Provide recommendations for enhancing HRM practices.
Identify the ethical implications of HRM and critically discuss how these can be managed.
prerequisites: HRM200: FOUNDATIONS OF HUMAN RESOURCES (AHRI) FOUNDATIONS OF HUM RES (AHRI)

title: Human Rights and Indigenous Australians
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the United Nations and domestic systems of human rights and critically examines Australia's history of upholding the rights of Indigenous Australians. It investigates the role of various UN treaties, conventions and committees, including the International Committee for the Elimination of all Forms of Racial Discrimination, and domestic bodies such as the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission and domestic legislations such as the Racial Discrimination Act and Racial Vilification laws. It also examines the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and how this applies to Indigenous peoples of Australia.
learning_outcomes: Examine the UN Declaration of the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
Relate Australia's history of human rights to Indigenous Australians.
Summarise Australia's domestic human rights systems and apply them to Indigenous Australians.
Interpret the United Nations system of Human Rights protections and Australia's obligations under this system.
Articulate and critically examine United Nations criticisms of Australia's treatment of Indigenous Australians and the major areas of concern.

title: Human Rights and Law for the Human Services
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide theoretical understanding and context for human rights practice and the law within the human services. Employing problem-based learning and a decolonising approach, this subject covers the history and theories of human rights and draws on a human rights framework and rights-based practice. It also considers the foundational laws and legal issues required by graduates working in the broad field of the human services. Incorporating the twin themes of human rights and social justice, key topics include the legal environment and professional responsibility and accountability. Particular emphasis is given to rights-based practice and the ways that graduates might employ mechanisms that positively influence legal processes and outcomes for people from marginalised and disadvantaged backgrounds.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply human rights principles to human rights practice and demonstrate a developing understanding of rights-based practice.
Recognise legal issues and problems in professional practice in the human services.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of human rights of service users, human rights theories and instrumentalities and explain their application to human services practice.

Recognise and demonstrate an understanding of mechanisms that positively influence legal processes and outcomes for vulnerable and disadvantaged people and demonstrate some understanding on how to be rights-based in practice.
Consider, critically evaluate and engage in the wider human rights, legal, ethical, social policy debates central to the human services in Australia, including reform of the law.
Demonstrate judgment as to the appropriate role of the human service worker in relation to the legal system and their client(s).
prerequisites: HCS532: Human Rights and Law for the Human Services (postgraduate)

title: Human Rights and Law for the Human Services (postgraduate)
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide theoretical understanding and context for human rights practice and the law within social work and the human services. Employing problem-based learning and a decolonising approach, this subject covers the history and theories of human rights and draws on a human rights framework and rights-based practice. It also considers the foundational laws and legal issues required by graduates working in the broad field of social work and human services. Incorporating the twin themes of human rights and social justice, key topics include the legal environment, professional responsibility and accountability. Particular emphasis is given to rights-based practice and the ways that graduates might employ mechanisms that positively influence legal processes and outcomes for people from marginalised and disadvantaged backgrounds.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise appropriate roles of social and human service workers in relation to the legal system and their client(s).
Evaluate and apply problem-solving approaches to engage in human rights issues.
Engage in and critically evaluate the wider human rights, legal, ethical, social policy debates central to social work and the human services in Australia, including reform of the law.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of human rights and its application in practice including its historical context, theories and instrumentalities.
Evaluate mechanisms that positively influence legal processes and outcomes for vulnerable and disadvantaged people and demonstrate capacity for rights-based practice.
Analyse legal issues and problems in professional practice in social work and human services.
prerequisites: HCS221: Human Rights and Law for the Human Services

title: Human Rights and Social Justice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Human rights standards are increasingly considered as a model for best practice for the criminal justice system in both developed and developing nations. The criminal justice system plays a primary role in the protection of human rights and this subject will ensure students' familiarity with human rights concepts, standards, debates, and the applicability of human rights to the criminal justice system. Students will also look at vulnerability and discrimination within a rights based framework and will examine how a rights based approach can inform ethical professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Describe the features of a human rights based model of best practice for a criminal justice system.
Explore how concepts of vulnerability and discrimination are understood through a rights based approach.
Evaluate the debates surrounding the use of human rights based model of criminal justice.
Consider how a rights based approach can inform ethical professional practice within the criminal justice system.

title: Human Services Credit Package 72
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This credit package of 72 points applies to students who have successfully completed one of the following courses with a recognised training provider: Diploma of Community Services Diploma of Community Services (Alcohol and other Drugs) Diploma of Community Services (Alcohol and other Drugs and Mental Health) Diploma of Community Services (Case Management) Diploma of Community Services (Financial Counselling) Diploma of Community Services (Mental Health) Diploma of Community Services (Family Intervention) Diploma of Community Services Work Diploma of Community Development Diploma of Counselling Diploma of Disability Diploma of Youth Work Students may be awarded credit for the above recognised Diplomas as follows: Students eligible for 72 points credit require a Diploma (refer to list above) that is accredited with the Australian Community Workers Association (please refer to their website at http://www.acwa.org.au in the Course Accreditation section) The credit package recognises prior study in areas mapped to the Bachelor of Human Services course structure and subjects. Credit will be awarded (as a total of 72 points) HCS111 Introduction to Human Services HCS221 Human Rights and Law for the Human Services SOC102 Social Inequality WEL118 Human Resources Organisations WEL218 Cross-Cultural Competencies WEL222 Case Management WEL232 Place Learning in Human Services 1 WEL231 Holistic Eco-Social Approaches in Mental Health XYZ01C (8) One Restricted Elective or Major

title: Human Services Credit Package 80
school: School

title: Human Services and Sustainable Development
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop an understanding of sustainable development and establishes human service professionals as central players in the process of developing an environmentally sustainable society. Competing interests of science, economics and environment are examined, and social and ecological justice dimensions are analysed within a holistic sustainable development framework. Holistic approaches for re-envisioning and leading the process of sustainable development as part of human services practice are considered.
learning_outcomes: Describe the meaning of sustainable development within local, national and global contexts.
Identify discourses affecting sustainable development.
Identify holistic approaches to sustainable development, including Indigenous perspectives and ecological justice dimensions.
Explain how human service professionals can actively contribute to and lead sustainable development processes as part of practice.
