title: Human Services Organisations
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for human service professionals seeking a comprehensive understanding of the structure, purpose, and internal functioning of organisations within the sector. Students will explore the key elements that shape human service organisations, examining the legislative and policy contexts that influence their operations and practices. The subject will also focus on transformative leadership and the importance of interprofessional collaboration, equipping students with the skills necessary to foster effective teamwork and innovation in service provision. Additionally, the subject will address contemporary challenges faced by human service organisations, with particular emphasis on resource mobilisation, the integration of technology, and the pursuit of sustainability. By the end of the subject, students will have developed a nuanced understanding of the evolving landscape of human service organisations with emphasis on delivering services that promote social justice and enhance the wellbeing of individuals and communities.
learning_outcomes: Examine transformative leadership and interprofessional practice in human service organisations.
Evaluate contemporary challenges in service delivery, focusing on resource mobilisation, the integration of technology and sustainability within human service organisations.
Identify and describe the structure, purpose, and internal functioning of human service organisations.
Demonstrate an understanding of the policy and legislative context shaping human service organisations and engage in informed discussion about their implications.

title: Human Services Research Methods
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will prepare students for post-graduate human services research by examining different epistemologies and methodologies and by focussing on research methods appropriate to human services situations. Topics will include needs analysis, program evaluation and action research as well as survey research design, sampling, methods of data collection, data analysis and presentation of research findings.
learning_outcomes: Be able to differentiate between epistemologies and methodologies relevant to the human services field.
Understand types of sampling, methods of data collection and data analysis techniques appropriate to human services settings.
Understand the social and political context in which research takes place.
Have developed research proposals and written up research reports.
Understand the ethical components of human services research.
Understand the place of research as a tool for social change.
Understand the place of research in human services.

title: Human Trafficking: A Global Perspective
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the theory and research surrounding a range of transnational crimes, focusing on human trafficking and the organised groups involved in these cross-border crimes. The subject will consider the criminal supply and demand factors involved and contemporary and emerging issues such as the cross-border exploitation of vulnerable women and children. Regulatory border responses will be evaluated.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically the harms associated with the transnational exploitation of vulnerable women and children.
Analyse complex issues regarding the supply and demand factors surrounding human trafficking, including the role of women.
Evaluate critically current border responses to human trafficking and other transnational organised exploitative crimes with a view to informing and influencing professional practice.
Analyse the range of transnational organised exploitative crime, and evaluate the contemporary and emerging threats in a regional and global context, and formulate plans to prevent, or reduce it.

title: Human-Centred Design for workplace creativity
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the human-centred design methodology for collaborative and creative problem solving in the workplace. Students will use human-centred design processes and practices to explore their professional interests through the creation of collaborative, innovative and strategic solutions in a range of workplace contexts.
learning_outcomes: Implement fundamental human-centred design principles.
Apply human-centred design methodologies to devise creative solutions to a problem.

title: Humanities and Social Sciences Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the broad fields of the Humanities and Social Sciences, covering a wide range of disciplines that explore human societies, cultures, histories, and behaviours. It is built on the premise that the Humanities and Social Sciences are key to an individual’s education, enhancing their (inter)cultural literacy, sense of belonging, and ability to engage as critical thinkers and informed citizens at the community, regional, and global levels. The subject examines the historical development and current theories of knowledge, skills, and research processes across a variety of academic disciplines within the Humanities and Social Sciences. It also addresses the tension between universal and local epistemologies, exploring how knowledge is constructed and understood differently depending on cultural, historical, and geographical contexts. Students will explore perspectives on time, place, and society developed from the rich knowledge traditions of Indigenous peoples, such as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, alongside those developed from European intellectual traditions, the latter of which are often tied to colonialism. As part of this exploration, students will critically examine how past and ongoing discussions surrounding the boundaries and claims of the Humanities and Social Sciences are framed within the context of the Australian and NSW curricula for HASS/HSIE, preparing them to engage with these issues in both academic and school settings.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the role of the Humanities and Social Sciences in fostering ethical, critical, and intercultural debates and actions.
Examine how the Humanities and Social Sciences contribute to the development of individual and collective identities at local, national, and global levels.
Identify and describe key disciplines within the Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS), including their historical development and links to colonial expansion.
Critically reflect on Indigenous Australian knowledge systems that shape own and others’ Ways of Knowing, Being and Doing in relation to place, time, and people.
Apply a range of concepts and methods relevant to disciplinary thinking to investigate social issues.
Recognise and reflect on contributions from Global South societies, scholars, and traditions in shaping contemporary human and social thought and understandings of the world.

title: Humanitarian Relief
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide a broad overview of what to expect when working in the humanitarian aid sector. It is designed for students of Emergency Management, and students from any other disciplines who may be considering serving in a humanitarian capacity. Topics covered include making personal preparations, how to define socially responsible engagement, an overview of the international relief system, and a background to what is a complex emergency.
learning_outcomes: Describe and evaluate the main theoretical concepts, principles, and policies of humanitarian practice.
Identify, describe, and explain the key frameworks and organisations of the humanitarian sector.
Critically analyse the legal, ethical, and cultural issues facing contemporary humanitarian emergencies.
Critically reflect and evaluate one's own self-resilience, self-preparedness, and professional practice in relation to complex humanitarian emergencies.

title: ICT Project Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is a study of a practitioner's approach to information technology project management. It provides students with an opportunity to develop the knowledge and skills needed to understand project management principles, techniques and tools. The subject integrates previous learning in ICT (information and communications technology) and prepares students to address issues and challenges in ICT project management. Students learn important factors that help with the successful implementation of ICT projects in a given focus area.
learning_outcomes: Explain and appreciate the role of ICT project management within a professional workplace, from the viewpoint of the member/leader of the project team.

Identify and reflect on the key elements of the PMBOK (Project Management Body of Knowledge) framework, including project stakeholders, communication management, the project management knowledge areas, common tools and techniques, and project success factors.
Collaborate effectively with others in a team environment and contribute productively to team outputs.
Differentiate between a range of project life cycle models, and their appropriate application.
Critically evaluate how a practising ICT project manager applies ICT project management techniques, skills, methods and software tools in the IT profession.
Apply and analyse established ICT project management principles, skills and techniques to a case study.
Demonstrate an understanding of leadership qualities required to successfully lead a project.

title: ICT Project Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the opportunity to critically evaluate the project life cycle, and to develop the knowledge and skills needed to apply established project management principles and techniques. Students will also examine the critical risk factors in managing a project, including those that relate to scope, time and cost, and communications.
learning_outcomes: Utilise appropriate communication practices within a project management team context and contribute productively to team outputs.
Research and apply established IT project management principles, skills and techniques to a case study.

Identify, critically analyse, reflect on and synthesise the key elements of the IT project management framework, including project stakeholders, communication management, the project management knowledge areas, common tools and techniques, and project success factors.
Research and critically evaluate how a practising IT project manager applies project management techniques, project management skills and methods in the IT industry.
Critically analyse the role of project management within a professional workplace, from the viewpoint of the member/leader of the project team.

title: Identity, Values and Colonisation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This interdisciplinary subject applies a decolonising lens to understand significant social, political, and philosophical questions about the self. The subject provides students with the opportunity to examine the impact of Australia’s colonisation on their understanding of Indigenous and non-Indigenous people’s experiences of self and relationship to others. Students will analyse the role of historical and contemporary forms of identification such as race, nation, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, class, and cultures in organising people's experience of everyday life and politics. Drawing on contemporary analytic metaphysics, students consider philosophical issues concerning the very nature of the self, the persistence of the self through time, and the relationship between selfhood and moral agency. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
learning_outcomes: Understand the role of the self in moral agency, and interpersonal and intercultural relations.
Demonstrate the role of identity within political, cultural, and socio-economic contexts, both Australian and international.
Describe contemporary philosophical and ethical theories about the nature of the self.
Understand the complexity of individual and collective identity politics applying an Indigenist standpoint lens.
Investigate how the metaphysics of survival illuminates colonising hegemonies which secure or disrupt one's self-conception.
Examine the impact that colonialism and neo-colonialism has in Australia on a diverse range of conceptions of the self.

title: Ihsan (Spirituality) Essentials
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the basic spiritual concepts found within Islamic spirituality, as well as the spiritual significance of the five pillars of Islam. The subject discusses the importance of self-development with a particular focus on spiritual development. Some of the key foundational concepts that will be addressed includeihsan (spiritual excellence) andikhlas (sincerity), istiqama (straightforwardness) and taqwa (righteousness). The five pillars of Islam will be covered from a spiritual, mental and social perspective; what each practice signifies and how they assist in the development of the individual and the community. The importance of the Sunnah (practical teachings of the Prophet Muhammad) in the life of a Muslim will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Explain the Islamic concept of ibadah (worship) with its sub-categories.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including research, writing and communication skills.
Understand the role of the Sunnah (practical teachings of the Prophet Muhammad) in the life of a Muslim.
Explain the spiritual significance of the five pillars of Islam.
Understand key Islamic spiritual concepts.
Describe the three levels of self-development from an Islamic perspective.

title: Illicit Network Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The twenty-first century has been characterised by networks. The physical, information, and communication networks which have shaped contemporary society have been adopted and adapted by subnational actors, including terrorists and criminals, to serve their own ends. In this subject, you will explore the illicit networks of terrorists and criminals to comprehend the scale and complexity of the modern threat. You will explore conceptual frameworks and operational terminology, models and influences, and organisational and operational principles. You will be exposed to the real world strengths and weaknesses of illicit networks, and the various tools used to counter illicit networks. Finally, you will assess the strategic logic underlying diverse contemporary counter approaches.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the strategic logic of past illicit network counteractions to provide insight and inform contemporary counter approaches.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of illicit networks, with reference to organisations, principles, and emerging networks in order to make threat assessments.
Objectively evaluate existing approaches to illicit networks to inform professional practice and empirically-driven decision-making; and,.
Select and apply appropriate research methods and tools to investigate illicit networks in diverse terrorism and security contexts.
Communicate a complex understanding of illicit networks clearly to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Image Critique and Image Interpretation
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to formally develop fundamental image critique and interpretation skills for conventional radiographic images of the chest, abdomen and musculoskeletal system using authentic clinical scenarios. The theoretical modules of this subject are designed to enable diagnostic radiography students to critically evaluate radiographic images, identify and describe normal appearance and common abnormalities, create a descriptive interpretation and correlate the findings with relevant clinical history to help make informed clinical decisions in response to patient presentation or changing condition. Students will develop critical evaluation and reflective skills relevant to the practice of diagnostic radiography. The subject is aligned to the practicum subject Radiographic Techniques 1 so that practical experiences inform the understandings developed in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical, legislative and regulatory principles to effectively communicate information related to significant, urgent and/or unexpected findings using appropriate and accurate scientific terminology (MRPBA Domains 1.7c and 2.1a).
Critically reflect on own strengths and limitations to identify learning needed to improve professional practice and plan how to address these development needs (MRPBA Domains 4.2b and 4.2d).

Critically evaluate and justify the efficacy of planar imaging correlating with the clinical history, using evidence-based practice and with consideration of client centred care (MRPBA Domains 1.3a and 1.4a).

Exercise professional judgement and apply clinical reasoning to suggest appropriate additional/follow up imaging and/or patient management to include timely action for the immediate management of clients with urgent or unexpected x-ray findings (MRPBA Domains 1.7c, 2.1h, 2.4c, 3.2c, 4.1b and 4.1c).

Critically evaluate image quality and positioning against radiographic criteria to include assessment of exposure index, field of view and anatomical rotation for planar chest, abdomen and musculoskeletal x-rays (MRPBA Domains 1.7b; 1a and 1f).

Perform accurate oral and written interpretations using a systematic approach, to accurately identify and describe normal, variant, abnormal radiographic appearances including urgent and/or unexpected findings for planar chest, abdomen and musculoskeletal x-rays correlating with the clinical history (MRPBA Domains 1.1c and 1.7c).
prerequisites: MRS342: Image Critique and Image Interpretation
MRS341: Image Interpretation and Correlative Imaging
MRS342: Image Critique and Image Interpretation

title: Image Guided Therapy
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Image guided therapy is the use of any form of medical imaging to plan, perform, and evaluate therapeutic interventions (these include surgery, radiation therapy and medical therapies). Image guided therapy techniques help to make interventions less invasive and drives precision medicine. In the context of this subject, the focus will be on the state-of-the-art imaging technologies that comprise molecular imaging: PET, SPECT, MRI, CT and Ultrasound. This subject has an advanced practice focus to build skills and capabilities beyond the established scope of practice. The subject provides a focus on recent innovation and development in image guided therapy, detailing the theory and translational application. The subject aims to provide a rich understanding of the principles and practice within a context of capability application in advanced practice.
learning_outcomes: Develop and critically appraise robust frameworks to support decision making and application of image guided therapy.
Demonstrate advanced understanding of the principles and applications of image guided therapy.
Apply the principles of image guided therapy from the context of therapeutic intervention and patient outcomes.
Demonstrate command of and critically reflect on the legal, social and ethical implications of image guided therapy within the context of advanced practice.
Demonstrate strong conceptual understanding of technologies driving image guided therapy through knowledge synthesis.

title: Imaging Pathology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students study and explore pathology as it relates to the medical radiation sciences. The subject covers the major pathologies encountered in the clinical practice of diagnostic radiography, nuclear medicine and radiation therapy. Students develop detailed insight and understanding into prototype pathologies with translational investigational, critical appraisal and deductive skills to other less commonly encountered pathologies (or those more common to a single Medical Radiation Science specialisation). Students will explore the relationships between pathologies with respect to aetiology, pathogenesis, epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis and patient management / treatment.
learning_outcomes: Explain the aetiology and pathogenesis of commonly imaged pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.1b-c).
Describe and justify the therapeutic approaches for commonly imaged pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.3a-d).

Describe the physical characteristics and imaging appearance of major common pathologies and demonstrate knowledge and insight through synthesis for a variety of medical radiation science modalities (MRPBA Domain 1.1a-c).
Analyse the various imaging modality options and their efficacy in the diagnosis of commonly imaged pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.3a-d).
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1a-c).

title: Imaging Pathology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to fundamental pathological concepts relevant to medical radiation sciences. Students will explore the relationships between pathologies in terms of aetiology, pathogenesis, epidemiology, pathophysiology, and diagnosis. Key topics include pathological terminologies, cell pathology, mechanisms of injury and repair, necrosis, apoptosis, ischaemia, infarction, micro-organisms, immunity, fluid hemodynamic disorders and oncogenesis. Students will also gain advanced insights into neoplasia and the cardiovascular system, along with clinical correlations and diagnostic imaging/therapeutic approaches to these pathologies.
learning_outcomes: Analyse various imaging modality options and their efficacy in the diagnosis of imaging pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.3a-d).

Apply critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, collaboration, individual and group problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 3.2; MRPBA Domain 4.1a-c).
Describe and justify the therapeutic approaches for imaging pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.3a-d).
Explain the aetiology and pathogenesis of commonly imaged pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.1b-c).

Describe the physical characteristics and imaging appearance of major pathologies and demonstrate an insight through synthesis for a variety of medical radiation science modalities (MRPBA Domain 1.1a-c).

title: Imaging Pathology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the foundational knowledge acquired in previous imaging pathology studies and provides an in-depth exploration of systemic pathologies relevant to medical radiation sciences. Students will gain detailed insights into the pathology of major organ systems, including the musculoskeletal, respiratory, gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, genitourinary, endocrine/exocrine, and lymphatic systems. Students will also explore diseases of the central nervous system and integrates clinical correlations and diagnostic imaging/therapeutic approaches to diseases.
learning_outcomes: Describe the physical characteristics and imaging appearance of major pathologies and demonstrate knowledge and insight through synthesis for a variety of medical radiation science modalities (MRPBA Domain 1.1a-c).
Apply critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1a-c).
Describe and justify the therapeutic approaches for imaging pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.3a-d).
Explain the aetiology and pathogenesis of commonly imaged pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.1b-c).
Analyse various imaging modality options and their efficacy in the diagnosis of imaging pathologies (MRPBA Domain 1.3a-d).

title: Imaging Theories and Techniques
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject covers imaging theories and techniques to enable students to produce a digital portfolio of photographic works in various mediums. The major topics covered are professional photographic practice, such as print and portfolio development and gallery exhibition theory and technique, including web based image galleries.
learning_outcomes: Have a strong working knowledge of the principal theories and techniques in outputting digital imagery to print and the web.
Show creative and innovative solutions to the design and production of a digital portfolio in a variety of mediums.
Demonstrate these theories and techniques with specific reference to photographic practice.
Be aware of current and evolving methods of digital photo-image presentation and dissemination of images.

title: Immunohaematology and Blood Transfusion
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the theoretical and practical aspects of blood group serology and blood banking practice, with a comprehensive laboratory component focused on different areas of immunohaematology including pre-transfusion testing, investigation of haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn (HDFN), and investigation of transfusion reactions. Distance students will complete the required practical component of the subject at a 3 day intensive school.
learning_outcomes: explain safe transfusion requirements, transfusion-transmitted diseases, transfusion reactions, autoimmune haemolytic anaemias; haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn, and foeto-maternal allo-immune thrombocytopenia;
conduct pre-transfusion testing;

demonstrate an understanding of the organisation of blood collection centres and blood banks in regard to donor selection, blood collection, and the processing, storage and preservation of blood products;
describe features of blood products including but not limited to their preparation methods, storage, quality control and indications for use;
demonstrate high levels of academic communication and team working skills.
conduct tests used for investigation of transfusion reactions and haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn; and
explain the principles used for detection and identification of blood group antigens and antibodies and apply them to problem-solving activities including but not limited to case studies;
prerequisites: BMS318: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion
BMS341: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion
BMS441: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion
BMS336: Advanced Haematology and Blood Transfusion

title: Immigration Law, Policy and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject provides an introduction to the law, policy and practices that impact on the regulatory and facilitatory border management role for people crossing national borders. Migration Law is studied from both international and domestic perspectives. The subject considers sociological, humanitarian and demographic policy impacts. Practical issues related to visas, entry permits, border operations, and compliance will also be explored
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss and formulate perspectives on the policy drivers (humanitarian, sociological, economic, demographic) affecting the border management role in respect of people crossing national borders.
Identify, develop and articulate solutions to selected people/passenger processing issues and problems in the border management context.
Critically assess and analyse the challenges faced by customs, immigration and other border agencies in the delivery of their services.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of migration law (international and domestic) on border operations.
Demonstrate an informed understanding of immigration practices at the border.

title: Immunology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the structure and function of the mammalian immune system, dynamics of the immune response in fighting infections, and immune system dysfunction. It also focuses on immunological assays and their application in the laboratory. This subject has a compulsory 4 day intensive.
learning_outcomes: Explain the mechanisms of immune responses and of anti-microbial defences of the mammalian immune system in order to discuss immunological responses in a range of situations and compare the outcome of immune responses in normal and pathological situations.
Evaluate the range of immunological techniques capable of being employed in modern biomedical science.

Explain the pathology of the immune system with particular reference to immunodeficiency diseases, hypersensitivity reactions, infectious diseases and autoimmune diseases and discuss the suitability/importance of various assays used in the diagnosis of these conditions.
Describe the structure and properties of the tissues, cells and molecules involved in immune responses and apply this knowledge to the overall function of the immune system.
Perform a range of immunological techniques and report, interpret and analyse the data generated.
Evaluate the importance of various components of the immune system and how they interact with each other during an immune response.

title: Immunology (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the structure and function of the mammalian immune system, dynamics of the immune response in fighting infections, immune system dysfunction and theory underpinning immunological assays and their application.
learning_outcomes: Explain the structure and properties of the tissues, cells and molecules involved in immune responses and apply this knowledge to the overall function of the immune system.
Evaluate the importance of various components of the immune system and how they interact with each other during an immune response.

Explain the pathology of the immune system with particular reference to immunodeficiency diseases, hypersensitivity reactions, infectious diseases and autoimmune diseases and discuss the suitability/importance of various assays used in the diagnosis of these conditions.
Evaluate the range of immunological techniques capable of being employed in modern biomedical science.

Explain the mechanisms of immune responses and of anti-microbial defences of the mammalian immune system in order to discuss immunological responses in a range of situations and evaluate the outcome of immune responses in normal and pathological situations.

title: Immunology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the structure and function of the mammalian immune system, dynamics of the immune response in fighting infections, immune system dysfunction and theory underpinning immunological assays and their application.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the importance of various components of the immune system and how they interact with each other during an immune response.
Evaluate the range of immunological techniques capable of being employed in modern biomedical science.

Explain the pathology of the immune system with particular reference to immunodeficiency diseases, hypersensitivity reactions, infectious diseases and autoimmune diseases and discuss the suitability/importance of various assays used in the diagnosis of these conditions.

Explain the mechanisms of immune responses and of anti-microbial defences of the mammalian immune system in order to discuss immunological responses in a range of situations and evaluate the outcome of immune responses in normal and pathological situations.
Explain the structure and properties of the tissues, cells and molecules involved in immune responses and apply this knowledge to the overall function of the immune system.

title: Implant-based Prosthodontics
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the foundational knowledge developed in the co-requisite qualification - the International Team for Implantology (ITI) Curriculum Foundation Level certification program. Students will develop the knowledge and skills necessary to select patients for implant therapy and complete the fabrication of implant-supported prostheses. Students will learn both digital and analogue techniques for recording the positions of implants in simulated clinical scenarios, and how to select appropriate abutments and materials for the fabrication of prostheses. Techniques for managing single missing teeth and longer edentulous spaces will be discussed. Additionally, the use of implants to stabilise and support lower complete overdentures will be demonstrated.
learning_outcomes: Design implant supported restorations.
Describe the restorative treatment process for implant supported prostheses.
Assess patients for possible implant treatment and document the planning of such treatments.
Discuss informed consent with respect to implant dentistry.
Provide supportive care for patients undergoing implant treatment.
Describe the history and application of dental implants to patient care.
Communicate effectively with a dental laboratory when prescribing an implant supported prosthesis.

title: Implementing Change
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject extends the learning covered in MGT540 Facilitating Change and introduces students to the processes of change implementation. Students will have the opportunity to engage in authentic and practical activities to develop their skills, knowledge and expertise in managing various stages of the change process. Contemporary aspects of change are considered from disruptive, rapid and volatile operating environments to nimble, agile, dynamic recovery and data driven change responses. Ethical and human centred approaches are considered alongside strategic, policy, governance and viability issues. On completion students will be able to draw upon a personal toolkit of skills and processes to facilitate effective change initiatives within organisations.
learning_outcomes: Develop a communication plan that outlines the case for change and incorporates strategies to maximise commitment and engagement.
Evaluate the case for change drawing on internal and external factors, competitive trends and organisational strategic objectives.
Reflect on the change experience to facilitate continuous learning and innovation.
Design a change plan that balances organisational imperatives with ethical and human centred considerations.
Devise a process to monitor, evaluate and, if required, make recommendations to modify the change plan.
Assess organisational readiness for change.

title: Incident Response
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will investigate the current threats to computing systems and networks along with effective countermeasures. Students will also learn the principles and stages of an appropriate security incident response. In addition, this subject will prepare students for the Global Information Assurance Certification (GIAC) and Certified Incident Handler (GCIH) industry certification exam.
learning_outcomes: Plan and manage the incident recovery process for an organisation.
Analyse security events to determine if there has been a security incident.
Explain, analyse, and justify current industry best practice in preparing for a security incident.
Explain hacking techniques and propose relevant countermeasures.
Describe how a system or network is analysed for security vulnerabilities.
Justify an appropriate response to a security attack.
Analyse an incident and reflect on the causes and future implications.

title: Inclusive Community Engagement
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Ensuring genuine inclusion of diverse and disadvantaged sections of communities in decision-making and governance continues to be a key community engagement challenge. This subject focusses on inclusive community engagement approaches that aim to meet this challenge. Moreover, inadequate progress on social and ecological imperatives and declining trust in social institutions has led to a proliferation of regulatory and legislative obligations around community engagement and to a 'participatory turn' in theory and practice. Alongside a critical overview of core perspectives in the contested field of community engagement, this subject gives particular attention to participatory approaches in the 21st century. The subject is designed with adaptable delivery models, which may include combinations of condensed online sessions and one-off workshops.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and enact community engagement practices that enable social inclusion and robust community participation.
Identify and apply community engagement approaches that foster community leadership and resilience.

title: Inclusive Education Legislation, Policy and Resourcing
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject provides a focus on the current legislative and policy basis for inclusion with emphasis on international, national and state legislation, policies and standards. In addition, the subject provides the opportunity to write a school-based policy to promote greater awareness and application of inclusive practices in schools. Students will apply the knowledge gained in their previous coursework with reference to effective inclusive practice at the school, class and child level with new knowledge of legislation, policy and resourcing to provide appropriate services to children with additional needs. The assessment items for this subject will enable students to analyse and reflect on policy for inclusion and apply their knowledge of the provision of services to students with additional needs, to policy design and development.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the social, moral, cultural, legal, educational and political influences on the development of inclusive policy and legislation.
Write an inclusive education policy that scales up what is known from best practice in inclusion.
Define the characteristics of effective policy as reflected in the development of a policy rating scale that reflects key effectiveness criteria and is subject to peer feedback.
Analyse policy and evaluate current inclusive education policy documents using the rating scale developed in the subject.
Critically analyse relevant legislation between principles, legislation, policies and practice in inclusive education.
Describe the relationship between principles, legislation, policies and practice in inclusive education.

title: Inclusive Education Practicum
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This capstone Work-Integrated Learning subject consolidates and applies advanced knowledge in inclusive education through the integration of theory, policy, and data-informed practice. Students engage in one of two pathways: Advanced Practice–Teaching: Action Research, where they design and conduct a six-step research project in an inclusive setting, or Advanced Practice–Leadership: Program Evaluation, where they design, implement, and report on a program evaluation in an educational context. Both pathways incorporate a supervised 20-day (or equivalent) placement, allowing students to demonstrate autonomy, expert judgement, and adaptability in authentic professional contexts. Through structured mentoring and reflective consultation, students further develop advanced research, analytical, and evaluative skills, preparing them to lead, innovate, and contribute to complex and diverse educational environments.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and apply either action research or evaluation frameworks in inclusive education settings, demonstrating advanced knowledge of their principles, steps, and ethical considerations.
Communicate evaluation findings through coherent, well-structured reports, including literature synthesis, methodology, results, and evidence-based discussions and conclusions.
Meet the requirements of work-integrated learning.
Plan, conduct, and refine ethical research and/or evaluation studies by creating research designs, implementation schedules, valid tools, and strategies for iterative improvement.
Design, implement, and evaluate interventions and/or programs formulating objectives, selecting evidence-based strategies, and generating valid methods for monitoring progress.

title: Independent Knowledge Integration: Theory and Professional Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject is a core subject taken in the final session of the Masters program. It is designed to capitalise on the knowledge and skills acquired by the masters coursework student. The subject provides students with an the opportunity to showcase their learning across their course, reflect on their research, knowledge, and professional practice. Students will learn creative, cognitive, and reflective techniques, hypothesis testing, utilising global literacies and communication of ideas.
learning_outcomes: Research and apply established theories to business organisations, law enforcement and/or security contexts.
Demonstrate a knowledge of recent developments in law enforcement, security and/or financial crime regulation issues in a professional context.
Interpret and transmit knowledge, skills and ideas using global literacies to specialist and non-specialist audiences to provide insight, leadership and influence stakeholders.
Demonstrate the application of knowledge and skills with creativity and initiative to new situations in either financial crime control, law enforcement or security.
Synthesize learning from across the course, through using critical reflection to contribute to professional practice.
Demonstrate technical and communication skills to design, evaluate, implement, analyse and theorise about developments that contribute to professional practice.
prerequisites: JST530: Research Methodology and Dissertation Proposal

title: Indigenous Australian Cultures and Spiritualities
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of key aspects of Indigenous Australian cultures, including the centrality of place to the spirituality and identity of Indigenous Australians. The subject enhances critical self-reflection and inquiry for extended relational positions for Indigenous and non-Indigenous theology students. The impact of colonisation and Christian missionary endeavour on the lives, cultures and spirituality of Indigenous Australians is critically assessed. The subject evaluates practices and protocols for effective engagement and partnership between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians and critically evaluates strategies for fostering conciliation and social justice.
learning_outcomes: Devise theological perspectives on conciliation and social justice in the contexts of Indigenous Australian spiritualities and cultures.
Analyse and theorise a reflexive framework to deploy theological perspectives relational to Indigenous cultures and spiritualities.
Critically assess the impact of Christianity and the church on the lives, cultures and spiritualities of Indigenous peoples.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including research, writing and communication skills.

Critically evaluate the impact of post-invasion history, including the nature and impact of various policies and practices (e.g. Stolen Generations, deaths in custody, youth suicide and stolen wages).
Construct effective strategies and protocols for faithful engagement and partnerships of integrity between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians.
prerequisites: THL225: Indigenous Australian Cultures and Spiritualities

title: Indigenous Australian Cultures and Knowledge Systems
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines concepts of culture, and the impact of diverse worldview positions on representations of Indigenous Australian peoples and cultures. The diversity of Indigenous cultures, knowledge frameworks, and contemporary cultural practice will be examined. Students will analyse the centrality of Indigenous cultures and knowledge to Australian national identity through an Indigenist lens. Through reflection on professional standpoint, students will explore principles of practice that underpin their role as agents of change.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the diversity of Indigenous knowledges and cultures and to apply understandings as agents of change in professional practice.
Examine and reflect on their knowledge and worldviews through socio-cultural and historical lenses.
Deconstruct the legacies of colonial representations of Indigenous cultures over time and examine the impact on contemporary cultural discourses and Australian national identity.
Identify the significance of Indigenous worldviews on knowledge systems, language, kinship, and connections to Country.

title: Indigenous Australian Cultures and Spiritualities
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys key aspects of Indigenous Australian cultures, including the centrality of place to the spiritualities and identities of Indigenous Australians. The subject provokes critical self-reflection and inquiry for new relational positions for Indigenous and non-Indigenous theology students. The impact of colonisation and Christian missionary endeavour on the lives, cultures and spiritualities of Indigenous Australians is critically assessed. The subject constructs practices and protocols for effective engagement and partnership between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians and strategies for fostering conciliation and social justice.
learning_outcomes: Adopt a reflexive framework to demonstrate understanding of theological perspectives relational to Indigenous cultures and spiritualities.
Demonstrate understanding of conciliation and social justice in the contexts of Indigenous Australian spiritualities and cultures.

Critically evaluate the impact of post-invasion history, including the nature and impact of various policies and practices (e.g. Stolen Generations, deaths in custody, youth suicide and stolen wages).
Demonstrate understanding of the impact of Christianity and the church on the lives, cultures and spiritualities of Indigenous peoples.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including research, writing and communication skills.
Construct appropriate practices and protocols for effective engagement and partnership between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians.
prerequisites: THP410: Indigenous Australian Cultures and Spiritualities

title: Indigenous Australian Cultures and Spiritualities
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of key aspects of Indigenous Australian cultures, including the centrality of place to the spirituality and identity of Indigenous Australians. The subject enhances critical self-reflection and inquiry for extended relational positions for Indigenous and non-Indigenous theology students. The impact of colonisation and Christian missionary endeavour on the lives, cultures and spirituality of Indigenous Australians is critically assessed. The subject evaluates practices and protocols for effective engagement and partnership between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians and critically evaluates strategies for fostering conciliation and social justice.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the impact of post-invasion history, including the nature and impact of various policies and practices (e.g. Stolen Generations, deaths in custody, youth suicide and stolen wages).
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including research, writing and communication skills.
Devise theological perspectives on conciliation and social justice in the contexts of Indigenous Australian spiritualities and cultures.
Critically assess the impact of Christianity and the church on the lives, cultures and spiritualities of Indigenous peoples.
Construct effective strategies and protocols for faithful engagement and partnerships of integrity between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians.
Analyse and theorise a reflexive framework to deploy theological perspectives relational to Indigenous cultures and spiritualities.
prerequisites: THL225: Indigenous Australian Cultures and Spiritualities

title: Indigenous Australian Health
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of the health and well-being perspectives of Indigenous Australian peoples. It will enhance understandings of the underlying historical, political, social, economic and cultural factors that contribute to Indigenous health in a contemporary context. It examines a range of social, cultural, historical, and institutional factors that impact on the contemporary health experiences of Indigenous Australian and non-Indigenous Australian peoples using a relational framework. It develops skills in critical thinking, reflection, and analysis for reflexive practice within the health professions.
learning_outcomes: Describe, analyse and theorise individual and collective standpoint in relation to Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples' historical experiences of the health professions.
Critically examine how the invention of racial science influences historical and contemporary structures of Australian society and its health institutions.
Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of Indigenous Australian perspectives on health and wellbeing through reflection on contemporary Australian health practice and service delivery.

Relate and map new knowledge and understandings to demonstrate ethical practice in the health professions, and to explore principles for respectful partnerships with Indigenous Australian communities.

Critically reflect on historical and socio-economic factors that frame Indigenous Australian peoples' health and critique deficit paradigms and their impact on health service provision to Indigenous Australians.
Investigate, compare and reflect on health practices and the social determinants of health for Indigenous Australians.

title: Indigenous Australian Histories
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: History informs who we are and how we understand our different relationships to First Nations Country. This subject enables students to critically reflect on their own positioning in relation to Australian history. Engaging with a variety of sources, students will learn how standpoint influences the recording and re-presentation of history and how to critically analyse the different experiences of a shared Australian history. Students will investigate the impact of colonisation on the lives of Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians and critique how colonial narratives influence what is collectively known and not known about Australian history. These narratives include the history of racial science and the theories of race which were and are used to justify the colonial invasion of First Nations Country. Students will understand how Indigenous resistance to colonial and government policies contributes to Australian history and will apply their learning as agents of change to professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on own positioning in relation to Australian history.
Explain how racial science and theories of race influenced the colonisation of Australia.

Analyse the impact of colonisation on the lives and experiences of Indigenous Australian peoples including how colonial narratives influence what is collectively known and not known about Australian history.
Explain how knowledge of Indigenous resistance to colonial and early government policies increases understandings of Australian history.
Recognise the impacts of the history of colonisation in Australia and apply understandings as agents of change in professional practice.

title: Indigenous Australian Practice for Human Service Workers
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Understanding processes of colonisation and decolonisation, particularly in relation to policy and practice within Human Services, are central features of this subject, and will enable students to work effectively with Indigenous Australians. This focus on Human Services practice will be guided by the worldviews and experiences of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, including their experiences of racism and discrimination in accessing services. The subject includes an overview of national Australian Indigenous issues pertinent to Human Services, and will equip students to respond effectively, using protocols of the community/ies in which they will undertake Human Services work.
learning_outcomes: Articulate, within Human Services practice, the significance of Australian Aboriginal heritage and culture in contributing to the wellbeing of Indigenous Australians.
Apply decolonising frameworks of practice, including `thinking, doing and being', from an Indigenous Australian perspective.
Demonstrate knowledge and respect for Indigenous Australian cultures while undertaking Human Services work.
Effectively apply proficiency in the use of Indigenous Australian protocols, when undertaking Human Services work with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
Demonstrate an understanding of colonisation and its impact on Indigenous Australian peoples, families and communities, when undertaking Human Services work.
Articulate Indigenous Australian worldviews for use in Human Services practice.

title: Indigenous Australian Studies for Teachers
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject has been designed to allow students to explore Indigenous Australian Education and its benefits in primary and secondary educational settings. Students will critically reflect on their cultures and values, the relationship between Australian historical, socio-cultural, and socio-political contexts, and the cultures, histories and contemporary experiences of Indigenous Australia. They will advance their understanding of the dynamics of Indigenous Australian values, worldviews and knowledges. Students will encounter a diverse range of pedagogies and strategies that respect Indigenous Australian perspectives, orient students to reflect on Indigenous Australian cultures, histories and contexts to consider culturally responsive strategies for Indigenous Australian students. They will have the opportunity to apply their pedagogical understandings to investigate and reflect on current issues affecting Indigenous Australian people and anti-racism education policies, programs and services. They will evaluate their role in contributing to student outcomes, equity and quality within the primary or secondary education contexts.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply culturally appropriate pedagogies and programming for Indigenous learners.
Recognise the similarities and/or diversities of local Indigenous knowledge and knowledge sources, spirituality, beliefs and values, concepts of kinship and culturally sensitive issues.
Describe practices which demonstrate the importance of community consultation and the participation of Indigenous people in educational environments.
Examine past and present Australian educational policy to articulate the impact of schools and schooling on Indigenous students.

Articulate scholarship on the knowledge and skills to effectively engage with Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples and reflect on what it means to be culturally competent educator/professional.
Critically analyse the influence of media and social media on Standpoint, popular discourse about Indigenous peoples, and the relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians.
Plan developmentally appropriate and effective Indigenous perspectives across other key learning areas.
Apply principles of decolonisation to social justice strategies and critically analyse contemporary policy and practice.
prerequisites: EEB435: Indigenous Australian Studies for Teachers

title: Indigenous Australian Studies for Teachers
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject has been designed to allow students to explore Indigenous Australian Education and its benefits in primary and secondary educational settings. Students will critically reflect on their cultures and values, the relationship between Australian historical, socio-cultural, and socio-political contexts, and the cultures, histories and contemporary experiences of Indigenous Australia. They will have the opportunity to apply their pedagogical understandings to investigate and reflect on current issues affecting Indigenous Australian people and anti-racism education policies, programs and services. learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the influence of media and social media on Standpoint, popular discourse about Indigenous peoples, and the relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians.
Describe the skills and knowledge to effectively engage with Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples and reflect on what it means to be a culturally competent educator/professional.
Recognise the importance of community consultation and the participation of Indigenous people in educational environments.
Examine past and present Australian educational policy to articulate the impact of schools and schooling on Indigenous students.
Apply principles of decolonisation to social justice strategies and critically analyse contemporary policy and practice.
Plan developmentally appropriate and effective Indigenous perspectives across other key learning areas.
Recognise the similarities and/or diversities of local Indigenous knowledge and knowledge sources, spirituality, beliefs and values, concepts of kinship and culturally sensitive issues.
Apply culturally appropriate pedagogy and programming for Indigenous learners.

title: Indigenous Australians and Criminal Justice
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject has been designed to enable students to closely examine the complex relationships between Indigenous Australian peoples and the Australian criminal justice system. This subject applies a sociocultural and historical framework to enable students to critically analyse the impacts of health, education and socio-economics on these complex relationships. Students will critique dominating frameworks of Western approaches to justice, rehabilitation, and recidivism to develop a foundation for practice that is community-driven and culturally responsive. Dimensions of power, class, race and culture in Australian criminal justice will be examined through neo-colonial, decolonising, and critical race theory. Students will demonstrate advanced knowledge of protocols for working with Indigenous Australian peoples in professional contexts.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the impact of historical and socio-cultural theories and practices of criminal justice in Australia and analyse and apply contemporary theoretical perspectives in Criminology.
Critically reflect on and analyse the impact of Western perspectives of criminal justice on Indigenous communities, cultures, and peoples.
Apply culturally relevant research approaches to design a criminal justice workplace project using an Indigenist framework that respects protocols for working with Indigenous Australian peoples.
Analyse and critically reflect on the relationships between Indigenous Australian peoples and the Australian criminal justice system to identify key issues and solutions.

title: Indigenous Australians and Justice: An Introduction
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with the foundational knowledge in Indigenous Australian Studies from which to build their knowledge and skills to enhance the students' ability to work effectively with Indigenous Australian peoples across the criminal justice system. The subject takes into consideration the recommendations and findings from The Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody and applies a framework to support the development of Indigenous cultural competence. Students will examine the diversity of Indigenous Australian cultures, historical contexts and contemporary social realities that affect access to justice for Indigenous peoples in Australia. Through this examination students will gain an understanding of Indigenous community protocols and develop strategies to work effectively in Indigenous contexts related to criminal justice practice.
learning_outcomes: Examine the ways in which government responses to Indigenous Australian people affect access to justice for Indigenous Australian people.

Reflect critically on social, cultural, and institutional impact on their profession, including assumptions stemming from the history of legislation and interactions with Indigenous Australian peoples and communities.
Demonstrate knowledge of Indigenous community protocols and the major issues and strategies relevant to working effectively in Indigenous contexts.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the socio-economic and political policies, practices and ideological processes of colonisation and their impact upon Indigenous Australians and their cultures.

title: Indigenous Australians and Literatures: Critical Endeavours
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to Indigenous Australian writing, performance and cinema to explore the ways Indigenous Australian peoples use creative endeavours to express Indigenous perspectives and challenge dominant culture control over Indigenous cultural expression. Critical perspectives are applied to identify underlying constraints inherent in non-Indigenous portrayals of Indigenous Australian peoples and cultures and interprets texts produced by Indigenous Australians for their political and cultural activism. Students will consider and participate in contemporary literary spaces in which Indigenous and non-Indigenous content and perspectives are negotiated.
learning_outcomes: Explore meaning in literature as mediated by the cultures and ontologies of the writer and reader.
Contextualise Indigenous Australian texts within specificities of history and culture.
Use critical perspectives to analyse representations of Indigenous Australians and cultures in literary productions.
Identify themes and textual features and conduct structural and stylistic analysis.
Create a literary text that demonstrates negotiation of Indigenous agendas in text production.

title: Indigenous Australians and the Politics of Race and Representation
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to concepts and theories of race and outlines the historical representations of group Indigeneity in Australia. It explores the social and cultural constructions of race and national identity and aligns them with concepts of representation. It critiques the impact of media representations of Indigenous Australians on contemporary perceptions of Indigeneity and examines the intersections between such perceptions and professional cultural competencies.
learning_outcomes: Examine representations of Indigeneity in the Australian context.
Identify the social and cultural constructions of race.
Explain and apply concepts and theories of race to professional practices.
Critically review the intersections between politics, the media and representations of Indigenous Australians.
Identify the cultural construction of national group identity.

title: Indigenous Australians and the Politics of Control
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject frames policy developments in Indigenous Australian affairs since 1967 from Indigenous standpoints and critically examines Indigenous Australian politics in relation to a dominant political structure. Specific policy developments and legislative determinations are critically examined from Indigenous Australian perspectives and considered in light of Indigenous Australian pursuits of rights and self-determination. Students will become familiar with policy developments since 1967, including the discourses that formed the basis of initial federal Land Rights legislation, the constraints of self-management and will critically analyse current Government initiatives including the Northern Territory Emergency Response and Closing the Gap. This subject explores the workings of policy implementation and how this impacts on the pursuit of Indigenous Australian interests. Students will be asked to examine their position in relation to Indigenous Australian politics.
learning_outcomes: Describe Indigenous political standpoints and use them to critically analyse Australian political structures and directions in Indigenous policy.
Critically reflect on distributions of power and personal positioning in Indigenous policy development and implementation.
Explain the features of distinct policy eras and key legislation and critically evaluate the discourses that informed them.
Evaluate contemporary policies and policy implementation in Indigenous affairs and the capacity of Indigenous people to pursue their political interests.

title: Indigenous Communities, Criminal Justice and Policing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The subject focuses on a number of issues impacting on contemporary relations between Indigenous Australians and the criminal justice system with a view to understanding causal factors and identifying relevant criminal justice responses. Attention will be paid to the historical relations between the police and Indigenous Australians and the role of government in structuring those relations. Specific points of focus include institutional racism, criminal justice procedures, Indigenous community relations, including self-determination and justice reinvestment initiatives.
learning_outcomes: Examine how government responses affect the policing of Indigenous people.
Evaluate current criminal justice policies which focus on Indigenous people.
Critique key contemporary debates about the experiences of Indigenous Australians and their interaction with the criminal justice system.
Discuss the impact of colonisation on contemporary police practice, criminal justice, and Indigenous Australian relations.
Reflect on one's own worldview and the worldviews of others, and apply this to professional practice.

title: Indigenous Criminology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: Indigenous Criminology will explore the historical and contemporary constructions of criminality, deviance and victimisation in the context of Indigenous peoples. It will discuss opposing criminology theoretical frameworks and evaluate the benefits in centering Indigenous peoples’ beliefs, traditions, and understandings in the traditionally Western concepts and constructs of victimisation, crime prevention, punishment, and offender rehabilitation. Exposure to Indigenous research methods, an understanding of strengths-based research, and the ability to identify Indigenous led research, will be included in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the importance of integrating Indigenous knowledge systems into contemporary criminal justice policies.
Identify and evaluate barriers and potential solutions to Indigenous peoples’ engagement with the criminal justice system.
Analyse historical and contemporary constructions of criminality, deviance and victimisation in relation to Indigenous peoples.
Evaluate competing, cross-cultural Criminological Theories.
Identify Indigenous-led research and explain its role in shaping policy and practice in the field of criminology.

title: Indigenous Education for Social Justice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will learn how to respond ethically, respectfully and effectively to contemporary issues in Indigenous education. They will encounter Indigenous peoples' life stories to further their own cultural competence and enrich curriculum content in a learning setting. They will expand their repertoires of practice by applying pedagogies derived from Indigenous sources to benefit all children and relate these to mandated curriculum and policy outcomes. Students will map issues and teaching principles relating to Indigenous education and plan a sequence of learning experiences for children that utilises Indigenous perspectives and pedagogies to achieve mandated learning outcomes. They will develop their ability to recognise and respond to the cultural values and worldview of Indigenous children, families and communities and discuss the importance of Indigenous pedagogies.
learning_outcomes: Discuss how and why Indigenous generated pedagogical approaches should be implemented to benefit all children.
Discuss the importance of Indigenous education in contemporary Australia.
Identify the connections between languages, literacies, cultural identities, education and social futures.
Create teaching plans using Indigenous perspectives and pedagogies with a capacity to make links to mandated curriculum and policy.
Describe how to seek information respectfully on Indigenous peoples' lives.
Justify transformative personal/professional development and growth towards increasing cultural competence with respect for Country and its local custodians.
Aware of the diversity of identities, experiences and education of Indigenous children, families and communities.
prerequisites: EEP304: Diversity and Difference in Early Childhood Education

title: Indigenous Education Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to appropriate curriculum and pedagogy for teaching Indigenous children and demonstrate how Indigenous teaching and learning practices can be of benefit to all education participants. Students will gain knowledge and appreciation of the importance and implications of full consultation with local Indigenous communities within these settings. It will focus on empowering students to effectively reflect on all aspects of teaching with respect to Indigenous perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the importance of community consultation and the participation of Indigenous people in educational environments.
Developed an awareness and understanding of culturally appropriate pedagogy for Indigenous children.
Formulate culturally appropriate teaching strategies for Indigenous children.
Understand and developed aspects of a culturally safe education environment.

title: Indigenous Education Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to appropriate curriculum and pedagogy for teaching Indigenous children and demonstrate how Indigenous teaching and learning practices can be of benefit to all education participants. Students will gain knowledge and appreciation of the importance and implications of full consultation with local Indigenous communities within these settings. It will focus on empowering students to effectively reflect on all aspects of teaching with respect to Indigenous perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Formulate culturally appropriate teaching strategies for Indigenous children.
Understand and demonstrate knowledge for providing a culturally safe education environment.
Develop an awareness and understanding of culturally appropriate pedagogy for Indigenous children.
Recognise the importance of community consultation and the participation of Indigenous people in educational environments.

title: Indigenous Environmental Studies
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students critically engage with the historical foundations of current practices and processes of environmental management to develop awareness of how these impact contemporary realities for Indigenous Australian peoples. By critically reflecting on their standpoint, students examine the influence these foundations have on relationships between people and Country. Students develop an understanding of intercultural awareness and cultural responsivity by examining their own values, beliefs, and current knowledges to support a critique of past and present environmental management practices. The pivotal role Country plays in the maintenance of Indigenous Australian health and wellbeing is explored. Students develop a working knowledge of Indigenous Australian environmental practices with an understanding of their own role as social actors and identify strategies for working with diverse populations into the future. This subject is taught collaboratively by the School of Indigenous Australian Studies and the School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences.
learning_outcomes: Critique non-Indigenous relationships with Country.
Apply the concepts of environmental studies appropriate to Indigenous Australian people and their communities.
Critically reflect on own knowledge, values, and experiences to identify personal learning goals relating to the development of cultural responsiveness, and strategies for achieving those goals.
Discuss the pivotal role Country plays in the maintenance of Indigenous Australian health and well-being.
Critically reflect on how knowledge of Indigenous Australian cultures, histories and contemporary contexts, facilitate or challenge current models of environmental management in Australia.
prerequisites: IKC101: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country

title: Indigenous Health Care For Nurses
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject supports students on their learning journey through the histories, cultures, and knowledges of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, through the use of Indigenous ways of knowing, being and doing. Learning is supported by an exploration of the key concept of ‘cultural safety' in health settings to develop cultural capability and competence within the students' nursing practice. Students also consider the contexts of health and wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and examine the role of nurses in supporting improved health outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, across the lifespan.
learning_outcomes: Describe the context of health and wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, including historical and current determinants of health, human rights, principles of social justice, transpersonal caring, primary health care needs utilising strength-based approaches, and policy considerations.

Apply the principles of Caring Science and appropriate clinical decision-making models, within the role of a registered nurse, as part of a culturally responsive workforce in supporting improved outcomes in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health, across the lifespan.

Explain the meaning of cultural awareness and safety, and as a registered nurse, how to adopt culturally respectful practices that support the development of your own cultural capability with respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories, cultures and knowledges.

Discuss decolonising approaches to healthcare that involve communication and collaboration, dialogue and negotiation, power sharing, acknowledgment of privilege, with a focus on Indigenous perspectives that ensure culturally safe care.
Outline Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of knowing, the importance of sovereignty and self-determination, and cultural protocols and.

title: Indigenous or Indigenist Research Proposal
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: By placing First Nations perspectives and ways of knowing at the forefront, students will evolve their understandings of decolonised research practices to articulate a feasible, socially just and respectful research project. Students will explore the application of Indigenous or Indigenist methodologies and methods to underpin innovative, disrupting, contemporary research processes. Through critical analyses of scholarly literature, students will identify knowledge gaps to formulate a clear research question(s), that leads to the design, and writing of a small-scale research proposal. This subject is designed to be responsive to the independent needs of students whether you are a postgraduate student, and/or a professional seeking to design a workplace project outside of academia.
learning_outcomes: Clearly articulate appropriate research question/s and use initiative and judgment to develop a feasible research proposal that uses an Indigenous or Indigenist framework.
Demonstrate a commitment to decolonising research methodologies and forefronting Indigenous perspectives, priorities, aspirations and values in the field of research.
Mobilise ethical considerations and issues of significance for First Nations peoples to justify a research design.
Select and critically evaluate scholarly literature related to the discipline underpinned by First Nations research considerations.
prerequisites: IKC501: Indigenous Research Methods and Methodologies

title: Indigenous Peoples: Sport, Identity and Culture
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Using the cultural competence pedagogical framework, this subject provides students with the opportunity to examine how participation in sport and physical activity impacts upon Indigenous Australian peoples. Through the use of a comparative cultural analysis of Australian, New Zealand and North American sporting case studies, students will be challenged to reflect on, question and critique their cultural assumptions and contest Indigenous sporting stereotypes. The subject's learning design further creates spaces for students to explore the place of sport and physical activity in (re)producing the cultural identity of Indigenous peoples. In this subject, students will be engaged in learning experiences that require them to propose and advocate for policy and practices that acknowledge, accommodate and celebrate Indigenous Australian cultural diversity in sport, recreation and physical activity settings.
learning_outcomes: Critically explore the major paradigms of the sport and exercise science discipline and how these paradigms influence the impact of the profession on clients from Indigenous Australian cultures.
Demonstrate awareness of and adopt sensitivity to cultural practices beyond their own belief system.
