Interrogate current sporting policy and practice to identify cultural dissonance.
Question cultural value assumptions and challenge Indigenous Australian sporting stereotypes.
Critically analyse and differentiate between the sporting cultural practices of Indigenous Australian people in selected case study applications.
Advocate for respectful partnerships between Indigenous Australian and non-Indigenous Australian people in and through sport.
Explain how participation in play, physical activity and sport impacts upon Indigenous Australian peoples.

title: Indigenous Perspectives on Health and Wellbeing
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable students to explore health and wellbeing as a holistic concept linked to community, environment and culture in order to extend their understanding of Indigenist approaches to health. Students will reflect on their standpoint and evaluate the relevance of language, policy, workplace culture and history to professional practice. This subject will provide students with the knowledge to apply a decolonising approach to the creation and delivery of health services which are responsive to the priorities of Indigenous Australian peoples and their communities. Students will reflect on their role as a health professional with respect to Indigenous health and wellbeing, and the development of authentic sustainable partnerships to deliver culturally safe healthcare. This subject will enhance students' cultural capabilities, including strategies to manage and lead workplace change to foster secure health service environments.
learning_outcomes: Examine the core principles of culturally responsive health partnerships to explore the complexity of working with diverse Australian Indigenous communities.
Apply a decolonising framework to the collection, use, and interpretation of data in professional practice.
Identify opportunities to enhance health outcomes for Indigenous Australian peoples through advocacy and change leadership in the profession.
Apply Standpoint Theory to reflexively examine the social, cultural, historical, and institutional forces that impact their practice as a health professional.

Analyse their evolving understandings of Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australian cultures, histories and contemporary contexts to challenge the taken for granted discourses that frame contemporary health service delivery.

Explain a decolonising approach to decision-making to create innovative health services for Indigenous Australian people and their communities with due consideration of all relevant legal, professional, ethical standards and Codes of Practice.
Design strategies for continued personal and professional learning to further develop cultural capabilities for health practice.
prerequisites: HLT517: Indigenous Perspectives on Health and Wellbeing
IKC101: First Nations Foundations: Knowing, Relating and Understanding Country
IKC502: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australian Cultures, Histories and Contemporary Realities
IKC403: Critical Studies: Indigenous Australian Cultures, Histories and Contemporary Realities

title: Indigenous Perspectives on Health and Wellbeing
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable students to explore health and wellbeing as a holistic concept linked to community, environment and culture in order to extend their understanding of Indigenist approaches to health. Students will reflect on their standpoint and evaluate the relevance of language, policy, workplace culture and history to professional practice. This subject will provide students with the knowledge to apply a decolonising approach to the creation and delivery of health services which are responsive to the priorities of Indigenous Australian peoples and their communities. Students will reflect on their role as a health professional with respect to Indigenous health and wellbeing, and the development of authentic sustainable partnerships to deliver culturally safe healthcare. This subject will enhance students' cultural capabilities, including strategies to manage and lead workplace change to foster secure health service environments.
learning_outcomes: Design and justify strategies for continued personal and professional learning to further develop cultural capabilities for health practice.
Apply Standpoint Theory to reflexively examine the social, cultural, historical, and institutional forces that impact their practice as a health professional.
Examine and apply the core principles of culturally responsive health partnerships to explore the complexity of working with diverse Indigenous communities.
Apply a decolonising framework to the collection, use, and interpretation of data in professional practice.

Critically analyse their evolving understandings of Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australian cultures, histories and contemporary contexts to challenge the taken for granted discourses that frame contemporary health service delivery.

Apply a decolonising approach to decision making to create innovative health services for Indigenous Australian people and their communities with due consideration of all relevant legal, professional, ethical standards and Codes of Practice.
Identify and analyse opportunities to enhance health outcomes for Indigenous Australian peoples through advocacy and change leadership in the profession.
prerequisites: HLT417: Indigenous Perspectives on Health and Wellbeing

title: Indigenous Research Methods and Methodologies
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject an Indigenist framework is applied to examine the colonial foundations of Western knowledge paradigms and research practices in relation to Indigenous Australian peoples. It will develop students' conceptual and theoretical knowledge on the value of decolonising and anti-colonial approaches to research with Indigenous peoples and / or research on issues of significance for Indigenous Australians. The subject will enable students to critically analyse their standpoint in a research context and review the critical use of Indigenous research principles and practices. The subject culminates in the formulation of a research project that responds to a research problem with relevance to students' workplace or research.
learning_outcomes: Apply culturally competent research approaches to design a workplace or research project using an Indigenist framework.
Create a conceptual framework to mitigate the impact of Western research methodologies.
Transmit knowledge to key stakeholders on the significance of positionality to knowledge reproduction through research.
Analyse, critically reflect on and synthesise the impact of researcher standpoint and Western methodologies on Indigenous communities, cultures, and peoples.

title: Indigenous Social Work Policy and Practice
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject an Indigenist and Human Rights based framework is applied to enable students to contextualise and critically examine the social, historical, cultural and institutional conditions under which social work practice for Indigenous Australians has evolved. Students will examine the discourses through which knowledge about Indigenous Australians is constructed in order to critically analyse the impact of past and current policy on their professional practice. The subject is designed for students and practitioners to apply a relational framework for deeper understandings of cultural competence in the field.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the key social and community issues facing Indigenous communities today.
Synthesise and apply skills, attributes and knowledge integral to work with Indigenous people in social work contexts.
Engage in critical reflection on the role of social workers in working with Indigenous people and communities.
Develop and implement relational cultural competency, self-reflection, reflexivity and critical analysis.

title: Industrial / Organisational Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject emphasises the application of the principles of psychology to industrial and organisational settings. Industrial/Organisational (I/O) Psychology is concerned with behaviour in work situations and the scientific study of the relationship between humans and the world of work. Topics include major fields in I/O Psychology: Personnel, Organisational Behaviour, Human Engineering, Vocational and Career Counselling, Organisation Development and Industrial Relations. Particular focus will be on intra-individual variables such as job satisfaction and work motivation; prediction and measurement systems for employee selection and performance appraisal; and special stimulus variables like training and development, environmental conditions and information processing.
learning_outcomes: Explain the key aspects of Organisational Psychology: work teams; organisational attitudes and behaviour; stress and well being at work; work motivation; and leadership.

Demonstrate an understanding of the basic aspects of Personnel Psychology: job analysis; psychological employment assessment; recruitment selection; training and development; and performance appraisal.
Describe the foundations of Human Factor Psychology: job design; union/management relations; ergonomics and work conditions.
Demonstrate a general framework of understanding the three major fields of Industrial and Organisational Psychology: Personnel, Organisational and Human Factors.

title: Industrial Relations in Context
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject locates the Australian employment relations systems within contemporary economic and political contexts and debates. Amidst the tensions and challenges of globalisation, the subject examines the perspectives of major stakeholder groups relating to the purpose, design and outcomes of the Australian employment relations systems.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise and critically evaluate academic literature, and apply scholarly methods to address real-world problems.
Critically evaluate stakeholder perspectives relating to the purpose, design, and outcomes of the Australian employment relations systems.
Reflect on the contribution of the Australian employment relations systems to business, economic and social sustainability.
Analyse contemporary issues and debates in Australian employment relations, in the context of global economic developments.

title: Industrial Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide students with an overview of, and an introduction to, the collective aspects of industrial law in Australia. The subject covers the sources of industrial law, the constitutional basis of industrial law, the contents of a federal award, the meaning of an industrial organisation and industrial action, the purpose of enterprise agreements, and wage fixation principles. Each of these core areas shall be examined, reviewed and assessed in light of the impact of legislative changes from the Workplace Relations Act 1996 (Cth), to the Work Choices legislation in 2006 and the introduction of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).
learning_outcomes: Explain how industrial organisations play a part in industry and industrial dispute, within the restraints of common law and federal legislation.
Identify and analyse the significance of the collective aspects of industrial law in Australia.
Define the concepts 'industry' and 'industrial dispute'.
Identify, discuss and analyse the various industrial instruments used in relation to Australia's National Employment Standards, and their impact on wages and conditions of employment.
Explain the constitutional basis of industrial law.

title: Industrial Relations in Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the processes, practices and procedures in Australian industrial relations. Building on the institutional and theoretical foundations of the industrial relations system, students critically examine a range of interventions used in professional practice. The learning strategy in this subject emphasises the connections between theory, research and practice, and students will have the opportunity to develop and improve their professional skills in conducting industrial relations processes that support business goals.
learning_outcomes: Employ negotiation and advocacy skills to develop grievance and resolution procedures and reflect on the importance of following due process in all areas of industrial relations.
Compare and contrast organisational approaches to enterprise negotiations and make recommendations to facilitate agreement in a timely and amicable manner.
Utilise effective communication methods to transparently convey information on IR issues and policy to relevant stakeholders.
Evaluate tribunal practices and procedures and to make recommendations regarding preparation for presentation before a tribunal.
Evaluate the role of the IR practitioner, and describe the practical elements and application of industrial relations within the context of the current Australian workplace.

Critically analyse an organisation's approach to industrial relations and make recommendations for improvement using data driven, humane and ethical decision processes that align with an organisation's competitive advantage.

title: Industrial Technology Major
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This is a credit code for Entry Level Credit into the Bachelor of Education (Secondary) Industry Entry Program.
learning_outcomes: This is a credit code for Entry Level Credit into the Bachelor of Education (Secondary) Industry Entry Program.

title: Industry Case Based Learning in Medical Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will integrate and reinforce their understandings of specialist discipline knowledge gained through earlier theoretical studies, practicals and work placements in order to develop an in-depth understanding of medical laboratory science and its role in healthcare provision. Students will engage in the interpretation of diagnosis of clinical case studies and other issues that could impact reporting in pathology including, but not limited to, pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical factors.
learning_outcomes: Work independently and collaboratively to analyse case studies related to medical laboratory science and construct a scientific report of the findings.
Propose and justify solutions to cases and problems.
Identify and critically analyse clinical cases and other related factors to clinical outcomes inclusive of pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical issues in medical laboratory science.

title: Industry Certification Credit
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Credit Code Only

title: Industry Placement
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to extend students' employability skills and their understanding of professional practice. The subject is also aimed at developing students' self reflection and self monitoring skills to help build their efficacy and confidence in the work place. As part of this subject, students will gain practical experience and apply their academic learning in a professional setting through a work placement.
learning_outcomes: Learn and assess through reflection the required practical and technical skills required of an entry level professional:.
Explore and enhance personal brand development through academic application and self-development.
Prepare an effective job application.
Define, evaluate, and reflect on employability skills to plan appropriate professional development activities.
Explore, develop and evaluate a personal career plan.
Develop practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.
prerequisites: BUS506: Contemporary Employability Skills and Reflective Practice

title: Industry Practice
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will undertake an approved internship with a business or organisation associated with the industry relevant to their course, over a period equivalent to 15 working days. Students will investigate and reflect upon the context and processes of management and/or operations (relevant to their course) in the work environment they observe and experience; analyse outcomes; and formulate solutions to issues or opportunities they identify.
learning_outcomes: Research, identify and utilise theory to better understand observations made of a workplace.
Identify issues and opportunities within a business/organisation and formulate and communicate appropriate solutions.
Analyse and contextualise aspects of workplaces they encounter including; Work, Health and Safety, workplace culture, Human Resource Management, leadership and management, and operations.

title: Industry Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable students to demonstrate their ability to apply and synthesise technical and conceptual knowledge gained throughout their course into contemporary industry practices aligned to their chosen specialised area of IT. This subject will prepare students to apply their academic learning in a professional setting by undertaking a series of practice-based learning activities and completing a work placement with an approved organisation. The subject will allow students to enhance their IT skills and enable them to apply discipline specific knowledge to practical workplace settings while also allowing them to build valuable industry contacts.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and reflect on the application of theoretical components of the course in a professional workplace setting.
Exercise judgement to recommend appropriate solutions to real world problems taking into consideration relevant social and ethical contexts.
Develop a career plan that aligns personal skills and capabilities with industry requirements and future career aspirations.
Develop professional identity and explore potential career paths.
Research the skills and capabilities required for Information Technology (IT) professionals in their designated specialist area and conduct a personal skills audit on their own capabilities.
Identify and employ the appropriate mediums for communicating effectively to professionals in an Australian workplace context.

title: Industry Research Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: Under the guidance of a supervisor/mentor, the student will be required to undertake research and prepare a dissertation/project on an approved area of customs administration and/or international trade facilitation and regulation. The subject will require completion of a dissertation/research project of approximately 5,000 words and will require demonstration of competence in research and the capacity to present a well-written piece of work in an appropriate format which analyses or critically reviews the approved topic in depth.
learning_outcomes: Formulate a written contribution to existing knowledge/practice, or an original re-examination of existing knowledge/practice, with a coherent structure that contributes to argument.

Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of their selected topic and familiarity with, and citation of, existing quality literature and the effective relationship of their paper to other scholarship in the area.
Demonstrate appropriate research techniques, showing the use of primary and secondary sources and depth and quality of research.
Demonstrate good analytical skills and the ability to present well-developed arguments relating to the question posed and supported by logical, compelling premises/evidence, evaluation and critique.
Demonstrate literary skills at a high level.

title: Infant Pedagogy for 0-2 Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject takes an ecological approach to exploring the interactions, relationships and learning between babies and significant adults, and the learning environment in the early childhood setting. The caring and educative relationships and interactions between baby, family and early childhood educators within the early childhood setting are also examined. The guided practice aspect of this subject is designed to take into account students' previous experiences.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and demonstrate the importance of quality caring relationships between the infant, family and educators in the early childhood setting.
Use observation and documentation of babies' play to inform and honour the learning trajectory based on what is significant for the baby within an ecological framework.
Extend and refine their teaching, leadership and management skills utilising knowledge gained through their university studies, and reflection on their teaching and learning.
Articulate the roles and responsibilities of early childhood teachers in relation to the care and learning of babies.
Discuss the implications and meanings of the Early Years Learning Framework, the National Quality Standards and the Code of Ethics in relation to babies, families and the educators.
Demonstrate a working understanding of professional philosophy and knowledge, infant pedagogy and interpersonal skills.
Evaluate the many environmental factors that will influence the type of infant program to be offered within the early childhood setting.
Demonstrate competence in a range of pedagogical, social and communication skills commensurate with the professional experience setting and the student's stage in the course.
Apply or implement sensory-motor play experiences for neurological growth and ongoing learning and development.

title: Information and Investigation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Students will study the theories that attempt to explain why crime happens, and how these theories inform frameworks of information gathering and investigative practice. They will plan for the application of the frameworks to both specific investigations and, more broadly, to community policing and crime prevention. Students will also evaluate and interpret data and statistics relevant to investigative practice. They will learn to identify sources of information (including the public, the witness, the suspect, the informant, the investigative interview, the policing community, the intelligence community, and the forensic community) and will learn strategies for information gathering and exchange that are effective, legal and ethical. This subject gives students a good foundational knowledge which will be applied more practically in JST313 Investigative Interviewing and JST322 Crime Reduction.
learning_outcomes: Apply your knowledge of the theories of criminal behaviour to determine an appropriate policing framework for an investigation, community policing event or crime prevention objective and justify the framework selected with academic evidence.
Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Plan an investigation by applying a framework to source relevant information legally and ethically.
Research and interpret data relevant to a specific investigation, community policing event or crime prevention objective.

title: Information Literacy
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the concept and practice of information literacy, and the issues related to it across education, workplace and everyday contexts. Students will be encouraged to consider information literacy from a number of perspectives. They will reflect on how information literacy can be applied in relation to information practice within their specific information environments.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the importance of information literacy education across all sectors.
Show that they understand and evaluate the empirical literature related to information literacy.
Identify and describe a range of information literacy approaches and perspectives.
Analyse the issues that affect the practice of information literacy in a range of settings.
Develop an information literacy plan that is relevant to a specific setting studied.
Reflect on their information literacy practice.

title: Infectious Diseases And Applied Immunology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines important human pathogens and their interactions with the immune system. The actions of antimicrobial therapies, antibiotic resistance and disorders of the immune system will be covered in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Describe the actions and properties of antimicrobial therapies and their application to the treatment of human infections.
Explain the mechanisms involved in important disorders of the immune system.
Describe the pathogenesis of infections.
Explain microbial mechanisms of resistance to antimicrobial therapies.
Explain the interactions between important human pathogens and the immune system.

title: Information Literacy
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the concept and practice of information literacy, and the issues related to it across education, workplace and everyday contexts. Students will be encouraged to consider information literacy from a number of perspectives. They will reflect on how information literacy can be applied in relation to information practice within their specific information environments.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their information literacy practice.
Develop an information literacy plan that is relevant to a specific setting studied.
Articulate the importance of information literacy education across all sectors.
Identify and describe a range of information literacy approaches and perspectives.
Analyse the issues that affect the practice of information literacy in a range of settings.
Show that they understand and can evaluate the empirical literature related to information literacy.

title: Information Security
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a broad overview of information security concepts, with an emphasis on combatting security threats to operating systems, computer programs, databases and networked systems. Students will also study cyber security professionalism and foundational security policies that stipulate requirements about integrity, confidentiality and availability. Techniques for implementing these policies are also investigated, including memory management techniques, access control mechanisms, user authentication, and networking tools.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the security mechanisms of a trusted operating system with those used in a general purpose operating system.
Analyse privacy and security issues using a professional code of conduct such as the Australian Computer Society (ACS) Code of Conduct.
Compare and contrast foundational security policies and models that deal with integrity and confidentiality.
Investigate and justify the use of the access control mechanisms and user authentication processes.
Explain the fundamental concepts of cryptographic algorithms.
Examine malicious activities that may affect the security of a computer program and justify the choice of various controls to mitigate threats.
Justify security goals and the importance of maintaining the secure computing environment against digital threats.

title: Information Sources and Services
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the nature and structure of information work across different sectors including galleries, libraries, archives, museums, government organisations and commercial enterprises. It examines the major information sources and services used and developed by information professionals to answer various information requests in different contexts. The concepts of search strategies and critical evaluation of information are introduced. The dynamics of reference interviews in the larger reference process are studied. A variety of search strategies are examined and evaluated. Technical, cultural, ethical and legal aspects of information services are discussed. Marketing and visibility of information services are studied. Students will also evaluate and reflect on various roles of information professionals in providing quality information services.
learning_outcomes: Select between various online platforms and applications to engage and communicate with users.
Evaluate the purpose and role of the reference interview in meeting users' information needs.
Market and provide access to new information sources and services for existing and potential users.
Critically evaluate a range of information resources and approaches for the purpose of meeting users' information needs.
Generate an efficient plan to deliver information services in various contexts.
Analyse the impact of emerging technologies and social media on the roles of information professionals and information services.

title: Information Sources and Services
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the nature and structure of information work across different sectors including galleries, libraries, archives, museums, government organisations and commercial enterprises. It examines the major information sources and services used and developed by information professionals to answer various information requests in different contexts. The concepts of search strategies and critical evaluation of information are introduced. The dynamics of reference interviews in the larger reference process are studied. A variety of search strategies are examined and evaluated. Technical, cultural, ethical and legal aspects of information services are discussed. Marketing and visibility of information services are studied. Students will also evaluate and reflect on various roles of information professionals in providing quality information services.
learning_outcomes: Locate and evaluate a range of information resources for the purpose of meeting users' information needs.
Explain and conduct effective information services in various contexts.
Discuss the impact of emerging technologies on the roles of information professionals and information services.
Explain the purpose and role of the reference interview in meeting users' information needs.

title: Information Systems Analysis and Design
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an opportunity to examine information systems analysis and design techniques from a business perspective. This includes knowledge and skills in feasibility analysis, requirements gathering, domain modelling, and systems development methodologies and planning. Students will also study advanced design techniques used to build an information system from a set of business requirements.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish between requirement gathering techniques and combine these appropriately to apply to a real scenario.
Describe the context of an information system.
Model and refine various aspects of information systems within a project development environment.
Compare and contrast the different methodologies of information systems analysis and design and critically evaluate their appropriateness for different and complex situations.
Assemble the components of a requirements model using the tools and techniques of object oriented or structured systems modelling.

title: Innovation and Change Management
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides you with an opportunity to explore contemporary conceptualisations of change in health services. Innovation and change is investigated as you complete case studies in relation to your current or future health service contexts and roles. The aim is to enable health leaders to judiciously facilitate change in their workplaces.
learning_outcomes: Examine the relationship between innovation and change management.
Evaluate case studies of change in reference to their current or future health service contexts and roles.
Explain how change can be facilitated by leaders in a health service.
Analyse design thinking and co-design as applied to change management.
Analyse management and staff roles in relation to the judicious facilitation of change.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the rich chemistry associated with the elements beyond carbon and organic chemistry. Students will learn through a systematic presentation of properties and reactions of representative elements with application of chemical principles and theories related to, for instance: atomic structure; bonding; acids and bases; solid structure; coordination chemistry bonding, kinetics, and structure; and trends in main group chemistry. Students will also gain practical experience in the laboratory with synthesis, reactions, and equilibria of a range of compounds.
learning_outcomes: Apply acid/base models and properties to evaluate, predict, or appraise acid/base properties of compounds.
Use simple bonding theories and their application to predict properties of compounds, and apply these theories and models to describe molecules.

Reflect on observed chemical reactions in synthesis, and apply ligand substitution reactions, mechanisms and kinetics to validate such theories; calculate equilibria associated with ligand substitution.
Apply bonding theories to explain, predict, and draw the structures of transition metal complexes.
Apply models of solid state structures to describe or predict packing in compounds.
Apply the periodic table to predict trends in the properties of elements and their compounds.
Use knowledge of main group chemistry to describe or predict reactions of elements with hydrogen, oxygen (air), nitrogen, water, the halides, and acids/bases.
Demonstrate competence and safety in the use of instrumentation relevant to inorganic chemistry, and completing and recording synthesis reactions and modelling.
Describe coordination chemical reactions and mechanisms by nomenclature, structure, and bonding.

title: Instrumental Analysis 1
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: A study of advanced instrumental methods, techniques and applications for chemical analysis, covering topics such as theory and practice of trace analytical techniques, electroanalytical techniques, absorption spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy and flame and flameless atomic absorption spectroscopy.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the requirements, procedures and difficulties involved in trace and ultra trace analysis.
Discuss the limitations and applicability of instrumental analysis to chemical problems.
Demonstrate understanding of the inorganic applications of spectroscopic techniques.
Be competent in using a range of modern analytical techniques.
Demonstrate understanding of the analytical applications of electrochemistry.
Have further developed skills in scientific reporting and communication.
Demonstrate a range of important analytical chemistry techniques having high sensitivity and selectivity.

title: Instrumental Analysis 2
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores advanced instrumental methods, techniques and applications for chemical analysis, covering topics such as the theory and practice of advanced liquid and gas chromatography, mass spectrometry, hyphenated chromatography-mass spectrometry, infrared spectroscopy, and nuclear magnetic resonance. Students will develop skills in synthesising multidimensional data from various analytical techniques to solve complex, real-world challenges as required by practicing analytical chemists. Students will also develop knowledge and skills in laboratory and chemical safety, as well as advanced operation, optimisation and troubleshooting of high-end analytical instrumentation.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise and analyse multidimensional data to solve complex chemical problems.
Work safely in a laboratory and with advanced analytical instrumentation, ensuring correct tuning, optimisation and operation required to achieve reproducible results
Apply and adapt a range of instrumental chemistry techniques having high sensitivity and selectivity to conduct chemical investigations.
Compare and contrast the applicability and limitations of analytical techniques to chemical problems.
Present and evaluate literature and experimental data required for scientific reporting and communication.
Utilise a range of modern analytical techniques, especially chromatographic techniques including those coupled to mass spectrometers, and manipulate instrumental parameters for optimised separation.
Utilise spectroscopy techniques and interpret spectral data, including infrared, mass spectrometry and nuclear magnetic resonance.

title: Insurance Foundations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject develops the knowledge and skills required to identify and meet the insurance customers' needs and to provide and maintain quality service. It includes a study of the nature of the economic and financial environment within which insurance needs are generated.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the operation of financial markets.
Implement claims handling for clients where appropriate.
Analyse client needs.
Analyse the specific requirements of general insurance.
Develop and present appropriate strategies and solutions to the client.
Provide ongoing services to clients.
Analyse financial products in relation to the markets in which they operate.
Apply the taxation issues in relation to products and market in which they operate.
Analyse the impact of the economic environment on financial services, products and the market in which they operate.
Negotiate options and strategies with the client.
Establish relationships with clients.
Analyse the advisory function as it relates to the insurance sector.

title: Insurance Law and Regulations I
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with the knowledge and skills to comply with relevant insurance legislation to carry out operational procedures in distributing and servicing insurance products.
learning_outcomes: Comply with operational aspects of laws pertaining to insurance.
Explain changes to and implications of laws.
Comply with agency / broker agreements and professional indemnity obligations.
Maintain statutory records.

title: Insurance Law and Regulations II
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to the regulatory framework for insurance and provides them with the knowledge and skills to comply with relevant insurance regulation to carry out operational procedures in distributing and servicing insurance products.
learning_outcomes: Comply with regulatory requirements, rules and circulars pertaining to insurance at an operational level.
Identify the relevant regulatory bodies and their requirements.
Comply with relevant industry code.
Explain changes to and implications of regulations and rules and circulars.

title: Integrated Chronic Health Condition Management
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject emphasises the integrated nature of physiotherapy practice in the management of chronic health conditions. Students will develop a deeper understanding of the lived experience of people with chronic health conditions, holistic perspectives of health and wellbeing, collaborative practice and culturally responsive approaches to chronic health care and other conditions. Students undertaking this subject will develop their skills further in general physiotherapy assessment and management, evidence-based practice, and demonstrated skills in clinical reasoning. Students will develop their understandings of person-centred care through development of skills in interviewing, goal setting and physiotherapy management for people with chronic conditions living in rural and remote settings.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their performance in a manner that demonstrates professional growth.
Demonstrate effective and professional communication to interact with patients/clients and other health professionals.
Recognise the complex and interrelated factors that may impact on the client, their needs and response to physiotherapy; including for clients in rural and remote settings.
Recognise situations outside their scope of practice; and describe and justify appropriate ways in which to respond to these situations.
Plan and implement person centred, ethical, evidence based, collaborative, safe and effective individual and group physiotherapy, for people with chronic health conditions.
Demonstrate and articulate sound clinical reasoning processes which analyse assessment findings in relation to physiotherapy for chronic health conditions.
prerequisites: PHS313: Foundations of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice
PHS318: Fundamentals of Adult Neurological Physiotherapy

title: Integrated Clinical Placement 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will complete a second supervised clinical placement within a pathology setting and submit a comprehensive portfolio based on their experience. This provides students with the opportunity to integrate the theoretical knowledge gained in the subjects studied and practice and consolidate their skills in a clinical environment. Students will be required to demonstrate their ability to reflect and critically evaluate their practice. Students will complete 210 placement hours as part of this subject and this completes the placement requirements for the pathology specialisation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate problem solving and decision making skills.
Describe the procedures employed to assess the accuracy, reproducibility and validity of current laboratory methods.

Reflect on their experience and maintain a portfolio identifying clinical / practical experiences and the learning that has taken place as a result of these experiences; with specific reflection of their experience on the AIMS Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists.
Integrate information from various laboratory or other workplace sites in making decisions and to recognise appropriate responses to data discrepancies.
Demonstrate an understanding of workplace health and safety and safe work practices relevant to the discipline.
Demonstrate professional behaviour.
Explain how to collect, prepare and analyse clinical data and/or specimens.
Work independently and as a team member to solve problems and interpret data in a medical science workplace setting.
Communicate effectively in both written and oral format within a multidisciplinary workplace.

title: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will complete a supervised clinical placement and submit a comprehensive portfolio based on their experience. This provides students with the opportunity to integrate the theoretical knowledge gained in the subjects studied and practice and consolidate their skills in a clinical environment. Students will be required to demonstrate their ability to reflect and critically evaluate their practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate written and oral communication skills relevant to the discipline.
Demonstrate knowledge of workplace health and safety and safe work practices relevant to the discipline.
Demonstrate problem solving and decision making skills within a laboratory.
Reflect on clinical experiences and maintain a portfolio identifying clinical/practical experiences and the learning that has taken place as a result of these experiences.
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviour.
Describe the collection, preparation and analyses of clinical specimen or clinical data.
Operate independently and as a team member.

title: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 3
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will complete a third supervised clinical placement within a pathology setting and present on their findings and proposed ideas. This provides students with the opportunity to integrate the theoretical knowledge gained in the subjects studied and practice and consolidate their skills in a clinical environment whilst being innovate with current workplace issues. Students will be required to demonstrate their ability to reflect and critically evaluate their practice. Students will need to reflect on the AIMS Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists around the work they have completed in the placement and show the units they have been able to improve in since their second placement. Students will complete 140 placement hours as part of this subject and this completes the placement requirements for the course.
learning_outcomes: Develop and design solutions for current factors affecting daily operations within a medical science laboratory setting.
Reflect on practical experiences and present tasks undertaken whilst on placement.
Demonstrate an understanding of workplace health and safety and safe work practices relevant to the discipline.
Demonstrate general problem solving and decision making skills faced in a diagnostic laboratory.
Identify areas of proficiency within the AIMS Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists.
Work independently and as a team member to solve problems.
Demonstrate professional behaviour.
Communicate effectively in both written and oral format within a multidisciplinary workplace.
prerequisites: BMS385: Work Integrated Learning in Medical Laboratory Science 2 (10)
BMS365: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 2

title: Integrated Exercise Prescription and Coaching
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject integrates exercise science sub-disciplines to support students to develop advanced skills in exercise prescription and coaching. Students will use evidence-based practices to individualise exercise prescription and coaching methods to the specific needs of clients. Students will learn how to communicate and apply interventions that improve performance and health, and encourage behaviour change. Students will further learn and understand industry needs, practicing with integrity, and within the professional scope of practice.
learning_outcomes: understand industry needs, practice integrity as an Exercise Scientist, and adhere to ESSA Code of Professional Conduct and Ethical Practice.
prescribe exercise for diverse populations, including youth, elderly, and disabled athletes;
program advanced training for the development of strength, hypertrophy, speed, power, reactive strength, and endurance;
develop periodisation plans for client needs, considering social determinants of health and specific medical conditions;
develop and implement injury prevention strategies and understand the role of exercise professionals in rehabilitation, collaborating with healthcare professions;
analyse and interpret data for exercise prescription, to evaluate training effectiveness, and monitor client progress;
apply coaching science, communication techniques, and behavioural strategies to enhance exercise delivery; and
prerequisites: EHR226: Assessment, Design and Delivery of Exercise
EHR132: Exercise for Health and Fitness

title: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will complete a second supervised clinical placement within a pathology setting and submit a comprehensive portfolio based on their experience. This provides students with the opportunity to integrate the theoretical knowledge gained in the subjects studied and allows them to practice and consolidate their skills in a clinical environment. Students will be required to demonstrate their ability to reflect and critically evaluate their practice and also reflect on the Australian Institute of Clinical and Medical Scientists (AIMS) Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate problem solving and decision making skills within the laboratory.
Explain how to collect, prepare and analyse clinical data and/or specimens.
Communicate effectively in both written and oral format within a multidisciplinary workplace.
Demonstrate knowledge and application workplace health and safety and safe work practices relevant to the discipline.
Describe the procedures employed to assess the accuracy, reproducibility and validity of current laboratory methods.

Reflect on their experience and maintain a portfolio identifying clinical / practical experiences and the learning that has taken place as a result of these experiences; with specific reflection of their experience on the AIMS Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists.
Demonstrate professional behaviour.
Work independently and as a team member to solve problems and interpret data in a medical science workplace setting.
Integrate information from various laboratory or other workplace sites in making decisions and to recognise appropriate responses to data discrepancies.
prerequisites: BMS265: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 1

title: Integrated Marketing Communications
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Planning, developing and implementing an Integrated Marketing Communication (IMC) strategy is vital for organisations. This subject will examine how the IMC process creates and enhances relationships with customers and other stakeholders by strategically controlling and influencing messages communicated to these groups. From a practical perspective, students will be exposed to a range of evolving communication tools and the issues that practitioners would consider in applying these tools in specific marketing contexts.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate marketing communications for a range of organisations and reflect on current organisational marketing by using communications tools.
Apply theoretical frameworks that integrate various elements of marketing communication to a specific organisation communications problem to develop an IMC plan.
Examine and evaluate various elements of a contemporary communication mix.
Explain and critically discuss the role of marketing communication in the overall marketing and business strategy.
Evaluate theoretical concepts underlying integrated marketing communications.

title: Integrated Marketing Communications
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject takes an integrated approach to the planning and development of promotional programs. Buyer behaviour theory which is relevant to the marketing communication process is reviewed. A comprehensive planning model is applied to decisions about the elements of the promotion mix: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and publicity.
learning_outcomes: Examine and appraise the impact of contemporary societal and market trends underlying integrated marketing communications strategies.
Evaluate the role of marketing communications in the overall marketing strategy.
Communicate clearly and effectively in oral and written work.
Identify and evaluate communication tools and make recommendations for their use in integrated marketing communication strategies.
Analyse and apply theoretical concepts underlying integrated marketing communications programs.

title: Integrated Medical Laboratory Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In addition to looking at medical laboratory sciences from a single discipline, this subject encourages integration at an advanced level, utilizing the knowledge from different disciplines into one broad discipline, with reference to selected disease(s). This is done by e.g. analysing how the different disciplines are involved in management of particular disease(s). Technology is dynamic and latest technology is constantly added into healthcare and there also are re-emerging and 'new' diseases to contend with. The assignments afford the opportunity to demonstrate knowledge and to evaluate these, in medical laboratory sciences. Professionalism, registration and certification are topics and issues that constantly change and/or are updated. This subject therefore allows the student to keep abreast and to evaluate current issues in medical laboratory medicine. After completing this subject, a student has a deeper and wider understanding of integrated medical laboratory sciences that is useful in specialist and routine medical laboratory sciences and in research. Such knowledge is important in teaching, management and research. It is assumed that a student in this subject works or has worked in medical laboratory sciences or studied medical laboratory science or equivalent. Students from other disciplines are enrolled at the discretion of the Course Director.
learning_outcomes: Analyse how the various disciplines of medical laboratory sciences are involved in diagnosis, monitoring and management/or treatment of diseases.
Discuss and evaluate the rationale of the current and future techniques in diagnosis, monitoring and management/treatment of current and emerging/re-emerging diseases.
Discuss and evaluate the anatomical, physiological, epidemiological, pharmacological and pathological factors which contribute to diseases.
Discuss, evaluate and reflect on the current and future status and role of medical laboratory sciences in health provision.

title: Integrated Vineyard Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on concepts and key aspects acquired in earlier viticulture-related subjects. Students will focus on key areas that should be considered in managing a vineyard, including vineyard establishment, training, trellising, pruning, canopy management, irrigation, fertilisation, and pest and disease management. In addition, students will explore the principles of managing cover crops and weeds, and techniques for mitigating extreme environmental conditions. Students will also investigate the key concepts related to the management of organic and biodynamic vineyards, and the incorporation of precision viticulture for mitigating vineyard variability.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the principles and vineyard management techniques as relevant to organic, biodynamic and precision viticulture.
Develop vineyard irrigation and fertilisation strategies particularly in relation to the soil properties, and site and environmental characteristics.
Interpret and apply the scientific literature related to vineyard management.
Implement management inputs in relation to cover crops, weeds, frost, heat waves, bushfires, wildlife, and the harvesting of grapes, especially with regard to factors affecting grape quality.
Evaluate sites and grapevine planting stock as appropriate for establishing a sustainable vineyard.
Compare and contrast the different types and underlying principles of trellises and training systems, pruning techniques, and practices of canopy management.
Analyse the role of vineyard management on vine health, and develop an integrated pest and disease management program in vineyards.

title: Integrated Vineyard Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on concepts and key aspects acquired in earlier viticulture-related subjects. Students will focus on key areas that should be considered in managing a vineyard, including vineyard establishment, training, trellising, pruning, canopy management, irrigation, fertilisation, and pest and disease management. In addition, students will explore the principles of managing cover crops and weeds, and techniques for mitigating extreme environmental conditions. Students will also investigate the key concepts related to the management of organic and biodynamic vineyards, and the incorporation of precision viticulture for mitigating vineyard variability.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the different types and underlying principles of trellises and training systems, pruning techniques, and practices of canopy management.
Evaluate sites and grapevine planting stock as appropriate for establishing a sustainable vineyard.
Interpret the scientific literature related to vineyard management.
Develop vineyard irrigation and fertilisation strategies particularly in relation to the soil properties, and site and environmental characteristics.
Implement management inputs in relation to cover crops, weeds, frost, heat waves, bushfires, wildlife, and the harvesting of grapes, especially with regard to factors affecting grape quality.
Discuss the principles and vineyard management techniques as relevant to organic, biodynamic and precision viticulture.
Analyse the role of vineyard management on vine health, and develop an integrated pest and disease management program in vineyards.

title: Integrating Paramedic Medical Science
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will integrate the principles of anatomy and physiology, pathophysiology, pharmacology, psychology and sociology with assessment findings and patient histories to formulate a differential diagnosis and implement a treatment plan for the patient with a presenting medical condition. This subject will investigate disease processes in all age ranges, including paediatric, adult and geriatric patients and ensure that evidence based practice is reviewed in all treatment plans and rationale. Students will learn effective communication techniques to ensure sound ethical and professional treatment plans are developed in consultation with their patients' and their families'. Students will be encouraged to critically reflect on their own practice during simulated activities and encouraged to review evidence-based practice and promote patient-centred care.
learning_outcomes: Perform accurate differential diagnosis based on evidence gained from clinical data, paramedic science, and paramedic research for patients with medical conditions.
Critically reflect on practice and identify strategies to improve clinical reasoning and patient-centred care.
Demonstrate a sound ethical and professional disposition including effective communication with patients, bystanders, the paramedic team, and other health care professionals.
Develop and implement safe and effective treatment plans for complex patients presenting with acute and non-acute medical conditions.

title: Integrating Paramedic Trauma Science
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will integrate the principles of anatomy and physiology, pathophysiology, pharmacology, psychology and sociology with assessment findings and patient histories to formulate a differential diagnosis and implement a treatment plan for the patient with trauma, environmental or a toxicological emergency. This subject will investigate disease processes in all age ranges, including paediatric, adult, and geriatric patients. Internal students will demonstrate patient assessment, paramedic skills, judgement, communication, and decision making in the high-fidelity patient simulation environment. Online students must be engaged in paramedic clinical practice and be able to apply and reflect upon their experiences assessing and treating patients in the field.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sound ethical and professional disposition including effective communications with patients, bystanders, the paramedic team, and other health care professionals.
Develop and implement safe and effective treatment plans for complex patient scenarios involving traumatic injuries, environmental conditions, and toxicological exposures.

Perform accurate differential diagnosis based on evidence gained from clinical data, paramedic science, and paramedic research for patients with traumatic injuries, environmental conditions, or toxicological emergencies.
Critically reflect on practice and identify strategies to improve clinical reasoning and patient care.
prerequisites: CLS202: Life Span Health Issues and Paramedic Care

title: Integrating Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject further develops student capabilities in physiotherapy assessment and management for individuals presenting with common orthopaedic, cardiorespiratory, and neurological conditions. Key areas of focus include pain management, goal setting, clinical reasoning, rural and remote healthcare, and professional conduct. Students will enhance their interprofessional practice by gaining a deeper understanding of their own scope of practice, learning how to appropriately refer clients to other health professionals, and reflecting on their role within a collaborative team environment. The subject also encourages students to explore their professional values, cultural awareness, and ethical responsibilities, with particular attention to how Western values in physiotherapy practice may influence the experiences of First Nations people. This subject includes a compulsory supervised experiential learning placement. The experiential learning placement will most likely consist of a work integrated learning (WIL) placement in a health setting. Alternative experiential learning activities may include simulation-based education and/or other forms of experiential learning.
learning_outcomes: Plan and perform foundational, person-centred, and evidence-based assessments and treatment interventions in orthopaedic, cardiorespiratory, and neurological physiotherapy practice, including the safe and effective use of exercise in rehabilitation.
Demonstrate professional behaviour appropriate to physiotherapy and working in interprofessional contexts, including critical appraisal and reflection.
Use clinical reasoning processes to explore and explain assessment findings and document these findings.
Apply ethical, safe and effective physiotherapy management for people from rural and remote settings using e-health technologies such as telehealth.

Demonstrate the concept of strengths-based knowledge and communication, evaluate their communication skills with a particular focus on culturally respectful, ethical and responsive communication, and develop strategies for improvement through self-reflection.
Examine the culture of physiotherapy, and analyse the impact of this service experience for First Nations peoples.
prerequisites: BMS171: Introduction to Functional Human Anatomy

title: Integration of Theory, Knowledge and Practice
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This 32 point subject, completed over one session, will allow students to engage with the integration of theory and new/acquired knowledge into professional practice. Students will develop specialised cognitive and technical skills and critical understanding of a field of learning, leading to advancement of evidence-based professional practice. Candidates will apply theory, knowledge and technical skills to demonstrate autonomy, expert judgement, adaptability, responsibility and critical reflection for the ongoing capacity for development of new knowledge in the field of investigation and/or professional practice. In this subject, students undertake training and develop of advanced cognitive and technical skills and substantial knowledge in the selected discipline of the profession, undertake systematic investigation and critical reflection and integration of the theory and knowledge, develop communication skills to explain, conceptualise and critique theoretical propositions, knowledge advancement and application and, develop research methodologies to advance knowledge in the context of professional practice.
learning_outcomes: be able to demonstrate cognitive, technical and creative skills to investigate, analyse and synthesise complex information, problems, concepts and theories.
be able to communicate the critical appraisal and integration of theory and knowledge in professional contexts;
be able to reflect critically on theory and knowledge and the integration of current and new knowledge and evaluate common practices;
be able to demonstrate cognitive and technical skills to integrate theoretical knowledge and critical reflection of theory and the application of theory; and
be able to demonstrate advanced and integrated understanding of a complex body of knowledge in the selected discipline;

title: Intelligence and Analytics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with an understanding of data, information and analytical techniques within an intelligence context. Students will develop a working knowledge of the role and use of data and information within intelligence and its interpretation through various analytic techniques. Students will be introduced to a variety of qualitative and quantitative methods for use by intelligence and security practitioners in dealing with intelligence problems. Students will apply these techniques to an intelligence product based on a real-world challenge. The subject explores current develops relating to data, analytics, artificial intelligence and big data within the field, including challenges and opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate mastery of contemporary theoretical knowledge and discourse on data, information, analytic and knowledge discovery techniques in an intelligence context.
Use a range of analytical tools in supporting tactical/operational analysis and be able to apply appropriate analytical tools to different analytical problems.
Explain key intelligence and analytical concepts and the use of data and information within an intelligence context, including legal and ethical aspects.

Collect, analyse, consolidate and synthesise operationally relevant information to provide reports (intelligence reports) that can explain a range of security threats and provide recommendations to address these.
Demonstrates the communication, literacy, numeracy, research, and digital skills required of a competent, professional intelligence analyst.

title: Intelligence Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject equips the student with a comprehensive understanding of management principles relevant to the intelligence setting. Key general management and leadership concepts (including organisational structure, staffing issues and goal setting) will be examined, and applied to the intelligence context. Students will explore current issues and challenges in the management of intelligence functions, including staff development & training and making intelligence actionable. Intelligence Management is a subject that is relevant to leaders and managers working across different intelligence contexts; including policing, national security, defence and the private sector.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically reflect on the key challenges for manager of intelligence units, how these differ from challenges faced by practitioners, and recommend solutions.
Identify and critically reflect on challenges for intelligence managers when engaging with stakeholders and external organisations and how these might be managed.
Demonstrates the communication, literacy, numeracy, research, and digital skills required of a competent, professional intelligence analyst.
Critically evaluate and reflect on the application of contemporary leadership and management theory in the intelligence context.

title: Intelligence Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This micro subject is designed for those aspiring toward intelligence leadership roles, or further formal training in the leadership of intelligence units. The subject introduces some of the contemporary issues and practices in intelligence leadership. It provides instruction on developing leadership skills. The subject uses reflective based learning techniques as the conduit to better understand effective leadership practices relevant to the intelligence field.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate reflective techniques to inform intelligence leadership practice.
Demonstrate knowledge of intelligence leadership practices and theory.
Transmit knowledge, skills and ideas to others.
prerequisites: JST493: National Security and Intelligence Issues

title: Intensive Animal Production and Welfare
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Intensive animal production and welfare is becoming increasingly important in feeding the world's population. Animal welfare is an important and emotional issue that affects Australian animal industries, as well as companion animal owners and research establishments. Humans have an ethical responsibility to provide adequate care for animals under their control, and animal production professionals have particular obligations and responsibilities in this area. Students will explore the feedlot beef, lamb, pig, poultry, and fish industries and the role of animal production professionals in serving them. Topics examined include the economic basis of the industries, factors affecting productivity and profitability, issues related to public perception, animal welfare and environment, genetics and selection, principles of housing design, and the integration of nutrition, health, and reproduction management to attain high levels of productivity. This subject will provide opportunities for students of Livestock Production and Animal Science to integrate knowledge gained previously in animal health, behaviour and welfare, economics, genetics, reproduction and ruminant nutrition. Students will experience exposure to a professional workplace setting /intensive animal production enterprise and undertake case study activities.
learning_outcomes: Discuss principles of yard and housing design in relation to animal production, welfare and environmental constraints.
Describe the characteristics of production systems which are associated with high productivity and profitability.
Discuss important aspects of managing feedlot cattle, intensively raised pigs, poultry and fish.
Discuss the issues in feedlot beef, pig, poultry and fish production which relate to animal and human health, food quality and safety, and market sustainability.
Describe common production systems for feedlot beef cattle, pigs, poultry and farmed fish.

title: Intercultural Awareness and Muslim Community in Australia
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides intercultural awareness by informing students about practical ways of connecting with the Muslim community. Muslims in Australia come from numerous countries around the world. Such a heterogeneous community includes newly arrived refugees along with the already settled third generation Muslims. The subject aims to develop an understanding of the complex Muslim community through their commonly shared Islamic culture and their Muslim identity. Focusing on everyday religio-cultural practices of Muslims, this subject provides opportunities to critically assess, address and accommodate the needs and expectations of everyday Australian Muslims as clients, customers, co-workers, co-residents and co-citizens in multicultural Australia's everyday settings.
learning_outcomes: Perform independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of substantial work.
Analyse the main practices and concepts that are addressed in the public discourse (e.g. halal, Ramadan, Eid, mosque).
Evaluate critical misconceptions, presumptions and prejudices about Muslims and Islam and their contributing factors.
Critically assess topical issues with some level of nuance to conduct casual, safe and difficult conversations with and about Muslims.
Critically discuss nuances between religion, culture and religious identity.
Critically interpret, address and accommodate the needs and expectations of Muslims during interactions in diverse settings.

title: Interfaith Dialogue
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In the context of increasing religious plurality in Australia, this subject introduces students to the principles and practice of interfaith dialogue. It examines how such dialogue may, from a Christian perspective, assist with the building of acceptance and understanding of religious traditions other than Christianity. To promote the capacity of students to engage in interfaith dialogue, the subject examines the history, beliefs, practices and thought of one or more of the following religious traditions: Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism. It also explores challenges to Christian theology and practice that emerge from interfaith dialogue.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate knowledge of the history and impact of religious diversity in Australia and its relevance for Christian belief and practice in contemporary society.
Discuss critically the relationship between Christian theology and the practice of interfaith dialogue.
Demonstrate an understanding of the history, beliefs, practices and thought of one or more of the following religious traditions: Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism.
Demonstrate critical appreciation of the principles of interfaith dialogue and practice.
Demonstrate the capacity to engage in interfaith dialogue.

title: Interfaith Dialogue
school: School of Theology

It examines how such dialogue may, from a Christian perspective, assist with the building of acceptance and understanding of religious traditions other than Christianity. It also explores challenges to Christian theology and practice that emerge from interfaith dialogue.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the relationship between Christian theology and the practice of interfaith dialogue.
Demonstrate an understanding of the history, beliefs, practices and thought of one or more of the following religious traditions: Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism.
Demonstrate critical appreciation of the principles of interfaith dialogue and practice.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate knowledge of the history and impact of religious diversity in Australia and its relevance for Christian belief and practice in contemporary society.
Demonstrate the capacity to engage in interfaith dialogue.

title: Intermediate Arabic Grammar 1
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will continue reading the 'Stories of the Prophets' textbook whereby they further build on the knowledge of vocabulary, syntax and morphology. The higher verb forms will be introduced for the first time. Students will also acquire the knowledge of how most nouns and verbs are derived by learning the systematic approach to word derivation developed by grammarians. This subject will also continue with developing the reading, writing and composition skills acquired in the previous unit.
learning_outcomes: Formally analyse sentences incorporating the new rules of syntax and morphology.
Conjugate higher verb forms in the appropriate tense, gender, number and person.
Demonstrate understanding of the system of word derivation.
Demonstrate basic to intermediate-level comprehension of non-technical prose.
