school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will continue reading the 'Stories of the Prophets' textbook whereby they further build on the knowledge of vocabulary, syntax and morphology. The higher verb forms will be introduced for the first time. Students will also acquire the knowledge of how most nouns and verbs are derived by learning the systematic approach to word derivation developed by grammarians. This subject will also continue developing the reading, writing and composition skills acquired in the previous unit.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate basic to intermediate-level comprehension of non-technical prose.
Demonstrate understanding of the system of word derivation.
Formally analyse sentences incorporating the new rules of syntax and morphology.
Conjugate higher verb forms in the appropriate tense, gender, number and person.

title: Intermediate Arabic Grammar 2
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: In this subject, the role of theism will be further expanded upon with the multiple roles that anism mansub plays such as the maf'ool mutlaq, bihi, fihi and lahu. The 'Stories of the Prophets' textbook will be analysed at a more advanced level, specifically focusing on theism mansub as well as building on new vocabulary, new syntax and complex morphology.
learning_outcomes: Formally classify verbs according to their multiple morphological characteristics.
Formally analyse sentences incorporating the new rules of syntax.
Distinguish between the different types of mansubat.
Demonstrate intermediate level proficiency in reading and composition skills.
Demonstrate intermediate level comprehension of non-technical prose.

title: Intermediate Arabic Grammar 2
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: In this subject, the role of the ism will be further expanded upon with the multiple roles that an ism mansub plays such as the maf'ool mutlaq, bihi, fihi and lahu. The 'Stories of the Prophets' textbook will be analysed at a more advanced level, specifically focusing on the ism mansub as well as building on new vocabulary, new syntax and complex morphology.
learning_outcomes: Formally analyse sentences incorporating the new rules of syntax.
Demonstrate measurable improvement in reading and composition skills.
Demonstrate intermediate level comprehension of non-technical prose.
Distinguish between the different types of mansubat.
Formally classify verbs according to the multiple morphological characteristics.

title: International Agriproduct Trade
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to international agrifood trade policy and competitiveness. It begins with an exploration of the basic theoretical framework for understanding the benefits of trade, and will explore indepth why there are barriers to trade and why international trade rules are so important. It then examines agriproduct trade policy with a particular emphasis on new trade barriers and the role of the World Trade Organisation. The subject also looks at the importance of managing commodity prices, the various factors that affect commodity prices and analyse a risk management strategy policy.
learning_outcomes: Integrate elements of competitiveness theory and transaction cost economics to improve international agriproduct trade.
Explain and critically analyse the role of the International Trade Agreements involving agriproducts and the growth of new barriers to trade.
Explain the basis of agricultural protection and its impact on agricultural trade.
Evaluate the importance of managing commodity prices, the various factors that affect commodity prices and analyse a risk management strategy policy.
Relate the theoretical basis of international trade to contemporary trade issues.

title: International Accounting Issues
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an insight into the accounting issues associated with the global business environment. It provides an overview of the importance of international accounting and management control to the multinational enterprise and an analysis of the reasons for the diversity of operations in accounting practices across the world. The topics that are covered provide both a practical and theoretical perspective and are placed within a global context.
learning_outcomes: Explain the reasons for diversity and evaluate the ways of classifying international accounting practices.
Investigate and appraise the role of management in controlling multinational businesses.
Critically discuss the importance of accounting to international businesses.
Analyse the issues involved with foreign currency transactions and translate foreign currency financial statements.
Critically evaluate the usefulness of financial reports prepared by multinational enterprises.
Critically discuss the drivers of international harmonization of accounting practice.

title: International Air and Sea Passengers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject students examine passenger operations at airports, seaports, and land border crossings. Students will gain the technical knowledge and skills to apply relevant passenger control techniques in various operational environments, identify risk factors and solve problems associated with passenger processing.
learning_outcomes: Research, identify and detail how recent technological advances can be used in the effective processing of passengers.
Critically evaluate the effectiveness of passenger processing techniques in particular operational settings.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the international standards relating to the processing of passengers and be able to evaluate the application of such standards in their own border management environment.
Demonstrate a broad knowledge of the importance of document examination, risk assessment, questioning, and the preservation of evidence in the effective examination of both passengers and baggage.
Evaluate critically the manner in which international trends may impact on passenger processing, including emerging technologies, economic imperatives and international standards and pressures.
Identify and communicate clearly the relevant issues raised by a passenger processing scenario, analyse the implications of the issues and propose appropriate actions.
Demonstrate a broad knowledge of the processes and techniques used in effective examination of both passengers and baggage.

title: International Air Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an in-depth study of the various aspects of international air law including the contemporary aviation environment, the institutional framework and the fundamental legal principles as set out in the Chicago Convention and other multilateral and bilateral instruments.
learning_outcomes: Explain and discuss critically the main legal principles which govern civil aviation in the context of the impact on international trade flows and border regulation.

Locate and use key international instruments and research appropriate compliance responses to international air law and apply that research to practical and theoretical situations that they may face as border regulators and/or managers.

Formulate appropriate and well-developed policy and legal advice for border managers and/or regulators on the application of international conventions on different aspects of aviation, space travel and transport and to be able to communicate that advice to others.

Identify and explain the practical impact on border regulation and management of international air law including analysing and critically assessing the regulatory frameworks of different countries against best practice and established international standards.

title: International and National Perspectives on Primary Health Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will expose students to international and national perspectives of primary health care and develop their practice based experience of primary health care as a way of working that is sustainable for communities and the profession. A group project will form the basis of the experiential learning in this subject and will culminate in presentation of outcomes either as a publication suitable for submission to a peer reviewed journal or a presentation to peers and/or the broader nursing community.
learning_outcomes: Apply the values and principles of social justice and equity in health care (NMBA 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 5.3,6.1, 7.7, 7.8, 9.3, 10.1, 10.3, 10.4).
Critically analyse epidemiological concepts and data that impact on the health of communities (NMBA 1.3, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5).
Collaborate with peers to create a professional education session (NMBA 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 4.1, 9.2).
Reflect on working collaboratively in a team (NMBA 4.4, 10.1, 10.2, 10.3, 10.4).
Explain the role of government and non-government sectors in health globally and nationally (NMBA 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3).
Identify and provide evidence-based strategies that enable change and sustainability for communities (NMBA 1.2, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4.3, 9.2, 9.3, 9.4, 10.1, 10.3).
Critically analyse the influences of culture on health from international and national perspectives (NMBA 1.3, 2.3, 2.6, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3).

Critically analyse the influences of social determinants of health on communities and advocate for change in a professional manner (aligns with Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia National Competency Standards for the Registered Nurse: 2.6, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3).
prerequisites: NRS378: Health Optimisation 4: Family, Community and Rural Nursing
NRS211: Essential Nursing Care: Acute Care
NRS311: Life-stage Considerations: Child, Adolescent and Family Health

title: International Banking and Finance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an understanding of investment banking. Students will gain knowledge of business fundraising options, valuations methods and corporate financing transactions and the risks, regulations and consequences of each.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively with other finance professionals.
Evaluate and communicate the fund-raising options (debt or equity) for a business including evaluating the financial risk and consequences of the options.
Apply various valuation methods to value an asset and determine which valuation method is the most advantageous for their client.
Analyse and communicate to a client on their corporate finance transactions ensuring they meet regulatory and ethical standards.

title: International Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject presents an understanding of the business practices of Australia's major trading partners, and the range of issues and problems that managers of international business operations face on a day-to-day basis. Topics include how to choose the appropriate form and location of international operations; how to deal with the economic, sociocultural and political forces that affect organisational performance; and how to manage the ethical, legal and social responsibility issues that arise in the international context. This is achieved through guided readings, completion of case studies, and critical analysis of the international business environment.
learning_outcomes: Explain key concepts in globalisation and assess the implications for Australia in general as well as Australian and international firms and their business practices.
Research and recommend appropriate strategies for the form, location and operational strategies of an international firm.
Research and evaluate the attractiveness and viability of conducting business in specific locations around the globe.
Analyse international business environments and practices, and evaluate how they are being shaped by economic, financial, socio-cultural, political and legal forces.
Investigate different socio-cultural and ethical environments in the international arena and explain the implications for conducting business.
Identify general and specific issues as well as new trends facing managers of international business operations, and design strategies to respond to these issues.

title: International Cultural and Education Program
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is provided in recognition of students' full and compliant participation in an International Short term Program. Programs will typically consist of a 3 or 4 week cultural and educational program in an international setting involving students living in another country; engaging in studies of culture, language, history, art, etc. with visits to sites of cultural and educational significance, and intercultural engagement with local peers. Programs may include some practical experience in a school setting.
learning_outcomes: Have improved social, cultural and educational knowledge and understanding of the specific context of the international experience.
Display an improved ability to think globally and consider issues from other cultural perspectives.
Better appreciate the complex and interacting factors that contribute to notions of culture and cultural relationships.
Have improved cross cultural communication skills and some facility with local language.
Appreciate the importance of multicultural diversity to professional practice in their field of study.
Value diversity of language and culture.
Demonstrate an awareness of own culture and its perspectives, and other cultures and their perspectives.

title: International Cultural and Educational Experience
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject facilitates the student's academic inquiry associated with the participation in a Short Term International Experience Program, of at least 120 hours duration, conducted in an educational setting. The subject will deliver pre-travel orientation and study activities; and post-International program personal and professional reflection. Whilst overseas, students will live and engage with the local community and be encouraged to visit sites of cultural and historical importance. Programs should include some practical experience in an educational setting relevant to the student's education sector.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the global issues associated with their educational sector, with a particular focus on the country to be visited.
Discuss the cultural issues associated with education as it relates to the country to be visited.
Reflect on their International experience in relation to the cultural and educational differences between Australia and the country visited.
Demonstrate culturally competent behaviours during an international visit.
Reflect on their participation in a Short Term International Experience Program as it relates to their development as a teacher.
Teach, deliver training, and/or provide educational assistance in an educational setting in the country of visit.
prerequisites: EEB310: International Cultural and Education Program

title: International Cultural Experience
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: Students enrolled in this subject will typically spend time in an international setting. This will involving living in another country; engaging in studies of local culture, language, history, etc. as well as studies related to their academic discipline. It may also involve visits to sites of cultural and educational significance, and intercultural engagement with local peers. The subject will provide students with an opportunity to become more culturally aware and to develop an international perspective in relation to their academic discipline. It will also provide the opportunity to discover new strengths and abilities, conquer new challenges and solve new problems thus enhancing generic skills.
learning_outcomes: Better appreciate the complex and interacting factors that contribute to notions of culture and cultural relationships.
Demonstrate improved cross-cultural communication skills.
Display improved social, cultural and educational knowledge and understanding of the specific context of the international experience.
Display an improved ability to think globally and consider issues from other cultural perspectives.
Demonstrate an awareness of their own culture and its perspectives, and other cultures and their perspectives.
Recognise the importance of global knowledge and cultural understanding in their chosen profession.

title: International Customs Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the relationship between the domestic responsibilities of customs services and the international law obligations to which they give effect. The jurisdiction of customs authorities is examined and the international organisations and conventions that impact on customs activities, in particular the impact of the conventions of the World Customs Organization, are assessed.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically assess the sources of international customs law including key international instruments affecting Customs operations.
Make advanced level, independent judgements concerning the administration of customs procedures in conformity with the rules of international law.
Apply the principles of international customs law to situations that they may face as customs officials.
Analyse critically issues that may arise in the customs environment in the context of international legal requirements.
Demonstrate an ability to contribute to policy-making processes which impact on customs practice and procedure with appropriate reference to relevant international conventions.

Formulate appropriate and well-developed approaches to policy, practice and procedure in accordance with international legal requirements and obligations and be able to communicate those approaches to others.
Identify and evaluate critically customs law issues and their implications for regulatory practice.

title: International Dimensions of Human Resource Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines the activities and policies of human resource management in the context of international business operations. In particular, it explores how human resource management is practiced in multinational organisations in the contemporary global business world. It also identifies trends and future challenges that are likely to have an impact on international human resource management.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role and context of international industrial relations.
Explain the role of International Human Resource Management (IHRM) in sustaining the growth of international business activity and globalisation.
Draw contextually appropriate conclusions as to the cultural and organisational applications of IHRM.
Evaluate sourcing, training and development, compensation and the performance management of human resources for global markets.
Determine and explore current IHRM trends and future challenges and apply them to a contemporary workplace issue.

title: International Engagement
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject offers students the opportunity to engage in a real life international project. Students will work with a business that is either operating or has the potential to operate internationally. They will complete a project on some aspect of the business's international operations. The students will further develop their problem solving skills as they undertake independent projects that link theory and practice. This will contribute to students' understanding of international operations in a given context.
learning_outcomes: Identify and construct strategies that improve an international business.
Understand and critically evaluate the operations of real life international projects of organisations using a process model that takes into account a long-term perspective.
Identify the real life challenges while managing international projects and manage them efficiently.
Explain and critically analyse different aspects of international projects in culturally diversified environments.
Review how to plan and implement outcome-oriented international projects.

title: International Exchange
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is provided in recognition of students' full and compliant participation in an International Short Term Program. Programs will comprise 120-140 hours learning in a cultural and educational program in an international setting involving students engaging in studies of culture, language, history, art, etc. with visits to sites of cultural and educational significance, and intercultural engagement with local people. These activities may take place within the context of a professional work placement. However, workplace placements, in this subject, do not contribute to professional accreditation hours.
learning_outcomes: Develop cross-cultural communication skills and some facility with local language.
Demonstrate an awareness of their own cultures and its perspectives, and other cultures and their perspectives.
Appreciate the complex and interacting factors that contribute to notions of culture and cultural relationships.
Develope social, cultural and educational knowledge and understanding of the specific context of the international experience.
Appreciate the importance of multicultural diversity to professional practice in their field of study.
Value diversity of language and culture.
Develop an improved ability to think globally and consider issues from other cultural perspectives.

learning_outcomes: Administration subject - CSU International Study Experienc

title: International Finance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject aims to develop an understanding of a representative range of issues in international finance and global financial markets. It covers topics such as spot and forward exchange rates, interest rate parity, currency hedging and exchange rate forecasting techniques. It focuses on the internationalisation of markets, global financial crisis and on international corporate governance issues.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss the key theoretical relationships and to manipulate these relationships in both diagrammatic and arithmetic terms.
Analyse the functioning limitations and new developments in international financial markets.
Evaluate international financial market incomes.
Apply relevant theories and techniques in solving quantitative problems in international finance.
Explain the basic concepts and terms in international finance.

title: International Financial Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject examines financial decision making in the international environment. Topics covered include foreign exchange, international finance markets, risk management in international finance and foreign investment analysis in international business.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate how ongoing changes in corporate debt markets and financial regulation impact on international financial markets and businesses operating internationally.
Identify the various methods firms use to raise money in international financial markets and critically appraise the differences between these methods.
Identify relevant cost and revenue data and employ relevant methodologies to evaluate foreign investment proposals.
Identify the causes and effects of changes in exchange rates on money and capital markets.
Analyse and evaluate the financial risks faced by firms engaging in international business activities and apply appropriate management techniques to hedge these risks.
Critically analyse existing theories of the relationships between spot and forward rates, relative interest rates and inflation rates in light of recent empirical research.
Analyse the linkages between domestic and international financial markets.

title: International History from 1945
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the history of international relations from 1945. It concentrates on the origins, development and resolution of the Cold War in Europe and Asia and subsequent developments in global politics. Topics include the Korean and Vietnam Wars, the Cuban missile crisis, the external relations of China, and the post-September 2001 'war on terror'. The subject also introduces the principal traditions and theories of international relations and approaches to writing international history.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of major developments in international history from 1945.
Demonstrate enhanced skills of expression.
Demonstrate the ability to assess and interpret evidence drawn from a range of sources.
Demonstrate an understanding of the main interpretations of international history from 1945.
Demonstrate an understanding of basic concepts in the theory of international relations.

title: International Law of Cross-Border Trade
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the relationship between the domestic responsibilities of customs services and the international law obligations to which they give effect. The jurisdiction of customs authorities is examined and the international organisations and conventions that impact on customs activities, in particular the impact of the conventions of the World Customs Organization, are assessed.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically assess the sources of international customs law including key international instruments affecting customs operations.
Identify and evaluate critically customs law issues and their implications for regulatory practice.

Formulate appropriate and well-developed approaches to policy, practice and procedure in accordance with international legal requirements and obligations and be able to communicate those approaches to others.
Make advanced level, independent judgements concerning the administration of customs procedures in conformity with the rules of international law.
Apply the principles of international customs law to situations that they may face as customs officials.
Analyse critically issues that may arise in the customs environment in the context of international legal requirements.
Demonstrate an ability to contribute to policy-making processes which impact on customs practice and procedure with appropriate reference to relevant international conventions.

title: International Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject explores key issues facing managers operating in today's globalised world. These issues include the need to understand the international business environment and the need to develop skills in cross-cultural communication, negotiation, conflict resolution and global teamwork. This subject further explores how managers can respond positively to the challenges of motivating and leading a multi-cultural workforce, including expatriates, impatriates and global teams. Informed strategic decision-making and the issue of ethics and corporate social responsibility in an international/global context are also examined.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the main theories, concepts and models of culture and use these theories to make recommendations regarding management of cross-cultural communication, negotiation and conflict resolution in a multi-cultural team environment.
Identify the ethical and corporate social responsibility issues managers may face when operating internationally and develop a strategic response to these issues.
Investigate cultural differences in relation to decision making, motivation and leadership and recommend management strategies for Human Resource policy and leadership of cross-cultural teams.
Evaluate the implications for managing teams and businesses in a globalised world.
Research the political, legal and economic environment of a country and analyse managerial implications for leading teams and operating a business.
Effectively communicate recommendations regarding the viability, form and function of a firm's international operations.

title: International Economics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this subject is to provide an in-depth and systematic understanding of the concepts, theories and policies relating to international trade and finance. In particular, the subject will deal with international trade theories, commercial policies, foreign exchange, issues in international resource movements, labour and environmental standards as well as international monetary systems. Assumed knowledge in this subject is equivalent to that covered in ECO110 and ECO120 or, in ECO130.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and evaluate issues in international resource movements, and labour and environmental standards.
Describe the operation of foreign exchange markets.
Describe the concepts associated with the standard trade theories and evaluate the limitations of these theories.
Demonstrate and communicate a broad knowledge of International Monetary Systems and recent events.
Investigate the effects of commercial policies and describe the impact of international trade organisations and conventions on Australia's trading position.
Critically investigate the significance of the newer complementary trade theories in explaining the current patterns in the world.

title: International Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: International economic, cultural, political and legal environments will be studied as a prelude to planning marketing strategies for international markets. The subject will examine the role of marketing research, international finance, market entry and expansion strategies and the marketing mix in international marketing.
learning_outcomes: Plan, implement and manage international marketing strategies.
Analyse elements of the international environment and their inter-relationship and demonstrate their relevance to international marketing strategies.
Apply cultural sensitivity to create marketing strategies aligned with global citizenship principles.
Identify and assess international marketing opportunities and threats.
Formulate effective strategies for international marketing, including market entry and marketing mix strategies.

title: International Placement and Study Tour
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject offers the opportunity for students to participate in an international study tour of 2 to 4 weeks duration. The study tour may include visits to businesses, governments and non-government agencies together with workshops delivered in-country. The subject provides an opportunity for students to develop their personal and problem-solving skills in a cross cultural environment. Students will be required to complete assessments linking theory to practice on some aspect of the international business environment. Study tour locations for each calendar year will be listed on the CSU Global site.
learning_outcomes: Independently and critically examine and reflect on the impact of their experience in an international context.
Analyse and evaluate different aspects of international projects in culturally diversified environments.
Make strategic recommendations that are appropriate for the relevant international context.
Synthesise and evaluate the impact of cultural, legal, economic, political and technological forces affecting business in that environment.
prerequisites: MBA550: Entry to CSU Global Post Graduate

title: International Policing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject analyses the international deployment of police in peace keeping, capacity building and other roles. It discusses the various models of intervention and the factors which influence success or otherwise. This subject draws on case studies of international policing initiatives and the growing body of knowledge in this field. The need to create ownership of security sector reform by local populations and the challenges associated with policing across cultures, languages and organisations will also be examined along with the expectations of the home force and reintegration challenges.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to analyse the contextual influences on your organisation of International Policing and to develop a strategic approach to the issue capable of being communicated to a range of professional and high level audiences.
Investigate, analyse and synthesise the broad body of knowledge of the history and context of International Policing, including relevant developments in Australia and overseas.
Demonstrate mastery of the key theoretical underpinnings in International Policing generally and critically reflect on the impact of these on current law enforcement practice.
Demonstrate an ability to conduct case based research to enable effective analysis and critical reflection.

title: International Practical Experience
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will allow students to develop as professionals and further expand on their understanding of the range of ethical and moral responsibilities underpinning their future careers in global terms. The subject incorporates a period of study abroad or an equivalent international experience. It will provide the students with the opportunity to become more culturally aware. It will provide an opportunity to discover new strengths and abilities, conquer new challenges and solve new problems, thus enhancing generic communication and problem solving skills and allowing them to develop new ideas and perspectives and a deeper understanding with repect to themselves and their chosen profession. In addition, employers are reported to view students who have studied abroad as more self-motivated, independent, willing to embrace challenges and more able to cope with diverse problems and situations. Completion of this subject may thus enhance employment opportunities upon graduation, both in Australia's increasingly ethnically diverse workplace and abroad.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the nature and characteristics of the community in which they were based.
Critically evaluate their own professional development as a result of completing an international experience.
Recognise the range of opportunities for professional learning that the international experience provided.
Demonstrate understanding of the role of international education experiences in creating goodwill for Australia around the world and increasing international awareness.
Recognise the value of global knowledge and cultural understanding and how this forms an integral part of their education.
Recognise their role as ambassadors for their course, the university and Australia.
Feel empowered to better understand themselves and others through a comparison of cultural values and ways of life.

title: International Practical Experience 2
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to apply aspects of their learning through a period of study abroad or equivalent international experience. As such it encourages students to develop as professionals and further expand on their understanding of the range of ethical and moral responsibilities underpinning their future careers in global terms. This experience will provide students with the opportunity to become more culturally aware. It will provide an opportunity to discover new strengths and abilities, conquer new challenges and solve new problems, thus enhancing generic communication and problem solving skills and allowing them to develop new ideas and perspectives and a deeper understanding with respect to themselves and their chosen profession. Employers are reported to view students who have studied abroad as more self-motivated, independent, willing to embrace challenges, and more able to cope with diverse problems and situations. Completion of this subject may thus enhance employment opportunities upon graduation, both in Australia's increasingly ethnically diverse workplace and abroad.
learning_outcomes: Recognise a range of opportunities for professional learning that international experience can provide.
Feel empowered to better understand themselves and others through a comparison of cultural values and ways of life.
Have an understanding of the nature and characteristics of the community in which they were based and how important a cross-cultural experience is to education.
Exercise appropriate initiative, judgement , and decision making in a range of contexts.
Have an understanding of how an international experience can influence a student's professional development.
Value professionalism, citizenship, and science.
Act in the role of goodwill ambassadors for Australia, for their course, and the University around the world.

title: International Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to study business, society and culture in an international setting during a study tour. The tour can include visits to businesses, government agencies, NGOs local institutions and authorities. The subject provides students with the opportunity to develop an understanding of these areas in a cross-cultural environment.
learning_outcomes: Independently undertake and examine the impact of their experience in the international context.
Compare different aspects of international projects in culturally diverse environments.
Critically evaluate the operations of real life international and local organisations.
Differentiate between the norms in business, culture and society of the host country and Australia.

title: International Public and Private Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to public international law and its significance for Australian law. Using case studies and in-depth analysis of international human rights in Australia, this subject concentrates on key themes and emerging trends in the international community. Private international law (also known as Conflict of Laws) and its distinction to public international law is compared and contrasted. Students are also introduced to the principles by which an Australian court applies the law of another country or state.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the relationship between international and domestic law to a variety of audiences.
Apply the rules of treaty interpretation and customary law practices to solve hypothetical problems within this area of law.
Demonstrate an understanding of Australia's international human rights obligations regarding Indigenous Australians.
Undertake independent legal research to communicate informed legal opinion on issues surrounding private international law, otherwise known as the law of conflict of laws.
Discuss the elements of private international law and their distinctions with public international law.

Demonstrate reflective and critical thinking skills, together with the use of professional judgement, to discuss how international law shapes Australia's domestic laws, including rights, obligations and responsibilities.

Interpret and critically analyse treaties, declarations, and related international legal instruments, and identify areas of deficiency in the context of humanitarian law and human rights protection, including the limitations of the concept of state sovereignty.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of operative framework of international law.
Analyse critically case law pertaining to disputes between states, including critically reflecting upon the potential for international law to be a socially progressive force.
Critique the role of the United Nations, and other international bodies and tribunals, including the effectiveness of the International Criminal Court.

title: International Relations
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the political study of international relations. It introduces the basic theories, concepts and ideas which shape the globalised world today. By critically examining the various ways international issues are practised, understood and debated (from security and trade, to climate change, terrorism and nuclear weapons etc.), this subject enables future professionals to make sense of the complexities of contemporary international relations questions, and Australia's place in the world.
learning_outcomes: Identify key political actors and institutions in international relations.
Demonstrate an understanding of what international relations is and how it is represented.
Communicate and debate international political issues.
Develop a critical knowledge of key issues in contemporary international relations.
Apply various approaches to the study of international relations.

title: International Social Development
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will focus on social development as a process of social change designed to promote the wellbeing of a population as a whole. It is also an approach to social welfare which offers an effective developmental response to the situation of socially and economically deprived populations. It will emphasise elements of international social work and social welfare practice useful for socio-economic development such as self-help, mutual aid, conscientization, institution building, community social capital and developing community capacity.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine case studies of social development so as to understand programs and strategies addressing the major global issues.
Apply social development concepts and principles to social welfare policy and practice in an international context.
Prepare for an international placement and/or career in international social development.
Discuss the nature and context of social development at both international and national levels.
Explain concepts of growth and change as they relate to social development.

title: International Supply Chain Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with a conceptual and practical understanding of international supply chains and their infrastructure and regulation. The subject will examine best practice approaches to the management of supply chain issues (including the 'authorized trader' programs that have been legislated for in many countries or customs unions, regulatory compliance and security).
learning_outcomes: Analyse the issues and solve complex problems addressing the regulation of the international supply chain.
Explain and critically commentate on the key concepts of international supply chain management.

Identify and assess critically the practical impact of the key principles of the World Customs Organization (WCO) SAFE Framework of Standards on international trade and to apply those principles to both theoretical and practical situations/scenarios in respect of cross border trade and management.
Apply their knowledge of best practice supply chain management approaches to particular trading environments and situations.

title: International Study Exchange- Business 40 Band 8
school: School
syllabus_overview: Administration subject - CSU International Study Experience
learning_outcomes: Administration subject - CSU International Study Experience

title: International Trade Policy and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the international trade policies and practices that have been developed as a consequence of WTO/GATT law and other international obligations and policy settings, the implications of this policy and practice in the current international trade environment, the importance of these implications and the importance of national agendas to those administrating or participating in cross border trade.
learning_outcomes: Assess and evaluate the impact of GATT/WTO law and other international trade obligations on national trade policy objectives and implementation.
Commentate critically on current policy approaches to international trade and analyse the implications of various policy approaches on the global trading environment and the border.

Formulate appropriate analytical and well-developed approaches to border policy, practice and procedure by analysing areas of international trade that could benefit from GATT/WTO law reform and to be able to explain those approaches to others.
Explain and commentate critically on the framework and key legal principles of the GATT and WTO Agreements and other relevant international treaties.
Formulate appropriate analytical and well-developed practical responses that meet international obligations while achieving national trade policy objectives and explain those approaches to others.

Solve complex problems, in both theoretical and practical situations/scenarios of cross-border trade and management, by developing policy that addresses appropriate compliance with GATT/WTO law and other international legal obligations and other emerging and topical aspects of international trade.

title: International Trade Terms and Documentation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the international sale of goods which necessarily involves the transport of goods by sea, air or land across borders. The carriage of those goods generates both risks and costs. The contractual and documentary aspects of international trade, including how such issues, risks and costs impact on customs activities in areas such as declaration processing and customs valuation will be addressed. In addition, students will learn to identify sources of information on international business transactions and to apply this information in the workplace.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the underlying legal framework that supports international trade transactions.
Evaluate the commercial and regulatory benefits of Carnets, Single Administrative Documents (SAD) and Single Goods Declarations (SGD.
Discuss the importance of particular commercial documents to effective border management.
Discuss the contractual relationships formed in international trade transactions.
Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of the key commercial documents generated in an international sales transaction.
Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge and understanding of the terminology used in international trade, with particular emphasis on international commercial terms of trade or Incoterms.

Discuss key aspects of international trade contracts, including the relevant documents and the associated commercial risks facing the various members of the international trade and transport community, and their mitigation.

title: International Trade Treaties and Conventions
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the obligations generated in an extensive range of international trade treaties and conventions which impact on how cross-border trade is managed. These international instruments will be examined from the perspective of both the control and the facilitation of traded goods. The agreements administered by the World Trade Organization (WTO), the World Customs Organization (WCO) and the United Nations (UN) agencies will be key aspects of this subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the role of customs and border agencies play in implementing national obligations.

Integrate ideas and formulate solutions to issues and problems in the border management context that arise as a consequence of international trade treaties and conventions and apply those solutions to border management practice.

Demonstrate the application of the key principles of the international trade treaties and conventions to the development of creative and effective solutions to border management issues, e.g. prohibited and restricted goods, trade facilitation and information exchange.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the key principles of the international trade treaties and conventions which impact on border management and international trade (for example the WCOs Revised Kyoto Convention; WTOs multilateral trade agreements and the UN Drug Conventions.).
Assess critically the challenges faced by customs and other border agencies in meeting international obligations while ensuring that national obligations and policies are not compromised.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the international trade treaties and conventions which have implications for border management.

Identify the relevant international trade treaty or convention applicable to a border management scenario, and clearly and coherently articulate the implications raised and propose appropriate actions.
Review and analyse critically international, regional and national developments affecting border integrity and trade.

title: Internet of Things (IoT)
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce the foundational concepts, architectures, and applications of the Internet of Things (IoT) in contemporary digital environments. In this subject, students will explore how IoT systems are structured, connected, monitored, and secured through the interaction of devices, networks, cloud platforms, and data-driven services. Students will investigate the application of IoT technologies across sectors such as healthcare, agriculture, logistics, smart cities, and industrial automation. The subject will examine communication protocols, networked device ecosystems, cloud-connected architectures, and data flow models that support IoT operations in distributed environments. Students will develop an understanding of how IoT devices communicate, exchange data, and securely integrate with cloud-based systems.
learning_outcomes: Describe how IoT devices communicate using common networking and messaging protocols
Identify foundational security risks and mitigation strategies in IoT environments
Explain the architecture and components of Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems
Analyse data flow between edge devices, networks, and cloud platforms in IoT environments
Apply conceptual IoT architectures across a range of industry sectors

title: Internet of Things
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will equip students with the necessary knowledge and skills required to evaluate, design, and implement an Internet of Things (IoT) architecture for various applications. Starting with IoT concepts including their application and relevant standards, students will learn about IoT networking protocols and simulation tools along with the programming necessary for IoT systems. This subject will also explore topics such as the software and data management requirements for an IoT ecosystem, along with the security and privacy implications of various IoT applications.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the current and emerging IoT technologies by examining their suitability for different applications.
Evaluate the role of IoT in the modern world and its impact on various industries.
Analyse the various software and data management requirements for an IoT ecosystem.
Assess and reflect on the benefits, risks, and security implications of various IoT applications.
Propose and design IoT architecture for a given case study in a simulated environment.

title: Internet Technologies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the fundamentals of internet technologies, from underlying communication technologies to network applications. In particular, the subject covers topics such as network and data communication models, and introduces emerging internet technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT). It also explores Internet protocols and introduces fundamental cyber security concepts and technologies.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply IP addresses including IPv4 and IPv6.
Analyse the TCP/IP protocol.
Present a basic knowledge of digital data.
Explain data link protocols.
Describe and evaluate emerging internet technologies such as Internet of Things (IoT).
Define and explain various internet terminologies.
Explain fundamental cyber security concepts and technologies.

title: Interpreting and Communicating Accounting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the accounting discipline in an integrated manner using accounting concepts and underlying accounting policies and principles to develop and apply critical thinking, information technology and communication skills to business decision making. The subject provides the basis for an iterative and spiral approach to accounting, exposing students to the key areas of accounting which support an organisation‘s business and enhance decision-making capacity. Students will gain a foundation understanding of accounting as an information system, professional ethics, computer applications, business communication and report writing, through the preparation and elementary analysis of financial and management accounting reports.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the historical development of accounting and explain the role of accounting in strategy including business sustainability and risk management.

Analyse the effectiveness of internal controls relating to cash receipts and cash payments, and explain how information and communication technology controls enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of an organisations systems and processes.

Apply conceptual and technical aspects of accounting to prepare relevant business financial statements for different business structures, and evaluate accounting information for decision making purposes.
Communicate clearly and concisely in a range of formal and informal situations and settings.

Explain how information and communication technology has impacted the business environment, and discuss technological advances that support data analysis, decision making, and enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of communication.

title: Interpreting Islamic Sacred Texts
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject involves the study of selected Qur'anic verses and selected Hadith (Prophetice Narratives) from their original language at postgraduate level. Students will need to examine various tafsirs (exegeses) written on the selected Qur'anic verses. While studying the varioustafsirs, students will need to examine and analyse text-critical issues, literary and historical context, literary structure, relevant critical approach(es) (e.g., form, narrative, sociological, ideological, etc.) as appropriate to the chosen verses. Similarly, selected Hadith will be analysed alongside various Hadith commentaries where students will need to examine and analyse critically the commentaries, as well as the text at hand.
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically the various commentaries written on selected Hadith.
Demonstrate independent research, writing and communication skills through preparation and presentation of substantial exegetical work.
Analyse critically the various exegeses written on selected Quranic verses.
Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and discussion skills through interaction with the subject co-ordinator.
Provide a detailed commentary at postgraduate level of selected Hadith through the application of the methodologies studied.
Provide a detailed exegesis at postgraduate level of selected Quranic verses through the application of the methodologies studied.

title: Interpreting Islamic Sacred Texts
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject involves the study of selected Qur'anic verses and hadiths (Prophetic traditions) from their original language at postgraduate level. Students will examine various tafsirs (exegesis) written on the selected Qur'anic verses. While studying the various tafsirs, students will analyse text-critical issues, literary and historical contexts, literary structure and critical approach(es) (e.g. form, narrative, sociological, ideological) as appropriate to the chosen verses. Similarly, selected hadiths will be analysed alongside various hadith commentaries, which students will examine and critically analyse.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and discussion skills through interactive methods of teaching.
Critically analyse the various exegeses written on selected Qur'anic verses.
Provide detailed exegesis at postgraduate level of selected Qur'anic verses through the application of the methodologies studied.
Provide detailed commentary at postgraduate level of selected hadiths through the application of the methodologies studied.
Critically analyse the various commentaries written on selected hadiths.
Demonstrate independent research, writing and communication skills through preparation and presentation of substantial exegetical work.

title: Interprofessional Healthcare Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In Australia, clinical and community health teams are required to work collaboratively. Shared decision-making and interprofessional collaboration are crucial for supporting client-centred care and improving health outcomes. This subject explores the Australian healthcare system including non-government organisations, healthcare teams, self-care and resilience as healthcare workers. Topics also include the principles and importance of interprofessional collaboration in healthcare and the challenges faced within disciplines to support clients as well as a focus on understanding the determinates of health and equity. Students will explore effective communication skills, digital health, scope of practice, self-care, assessment and care planning and referrals as well as legal and ethical considerations. The application of professional frameworks such as therapeutic relationships, recovery, and professional identity are also explored. The subject will use a case-based learning approach so healthcare students from multiple disciplines can apply their knowledge to real life scenarios and understand the interprofessional implications of care.
learning_outcomes: Describe the Australian health care system and the roles of healthcare teams and how interprofessional practice contributes to improved health outcomes for clients.
Identify the foundational legal and ethical considerations for interprofessional practice.
Demonstrate effective communication skills relevant to interprofessional practice.
Describe the principles of self-care and resilience as a healthcare worker.
Explain scope of practice, professional frameworks and the role of interprofessional practice in healthcare.
prerequisites: HSM202: The Dynamics of Health Care Practice

title: Intersectionality and Communication
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines how communication, both language and images, can enable diversity and inclusion. It challenges the student to consider how different forms of communication impacts on individuals, groups and communities.
learning_outcomes: Examine the impact of language, narrative and discourse on inclusive conversation and communication.
Analyse images in different media and examine assumptions about how gender, race, age, disability and other identities are represented or omitted.

title: Intersectionality and Inclusion
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines diversity and inclusion through a human rights perspective. It examines lived-experience and well-being through inclusion and social justice perspectives to challenge discrimination applied through existing structures and systems.
learning_outcomes: Extrapolate human rights (issues) when examining the impacts of structures and systems on individuals, communities and collectives.
Apply theories, knowledge and reflections to understand the multidimensional nature of intersectionality, diversity, and inclusion.
Determine relational factors between individual identities and systems/structures to overcome a universalised and colonising approach to definitions of systemic oppression.
Compare and analyse strategic approaches to inclusion and inclusivity.

title: Intersectionality - Contemporary Theory for Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject develops knowledge of intersectionality, diversity and inclusion theory and practice. It will enhance understanding of the effects of historical and contemporary policy and practices on the lives of individuals with diverse intersections. Students will consider the specific dimensions of Indigenous peoples' experiences of intersectionality through an Indigenist lens. It examines the history of intersectionality and how it relates to the various power and structure processes across the micro, meso and macro components of society. It develops skills in critical thinking, reflection, and analysis for reflexive practice within diverse professions that enable inclusion.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how theory applies across systems and processes - micro, meso and macro.
Use a decolonising framework to examine theory and practice to consider the unique impacts of the intersection of colonisation and intersectionality for Indigenous peoples.
Develop and apply critical reflection skills to investigate complex problems and solution building to real world contexts.
Reflect on their own positionality in preparation for practice.
Describe theory relating to intersectionality, inclusion and diversity.

title: Intersectionality and Social Identity
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject challenges the notion of identity and how identity is socially constructed. It considers how structures and systems impact on individuals and collective identities. This subject will also examine the varied structural impacts for Indigenous peoples that are distinct from other intersectional identities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a proactive understanding of identities of individuals within a collective.
Identify the structural impact of colonisation on Indigenous people.
Distinguish the ways structures and systems have varying impacts on individual and collective identities.
Identify structural and systemic impacts on individuals, groups and communities through an intersectional lens.

title: Intersectionality at Work
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is a capstone subject that enables students who have undertaken the Graduate Certificate in Intersectionality, Diversity and Inclusion to integrate the theory, skills and knowledge gained into a work integrated project at their place of work. Students will apply intersectional lenses and Indigenist Standpoint principles (Phillips 2011).
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge, skills and understanding to a workplace, community, or organisational setting.
Respond to authentic, contextual professional tasks using responsive communication, relational, and reflective skills to support inclusive practice.
Reflect on the impact of structural factors on equality within a reflexive framework.
Demonstrate their ability to adopt ethical, principled and culturally safe and sensitive practices and standards in a professional context.
Synthesise and apply their knowledge of problem-based learning, to the design, implementation and evaluation of a strategy or project.
Re-examine evolving professional philosophy in relation to their developing professional identity.
Gather, analyse, synthesise industry-specific information and data to inform decisions related to inclusivity, equality.
prerequisites: HCS412: Intersectionality - Contemporary Theory for Practice

title: Intervention for Language and Cognitive Impairments in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop competence in intervention for the speech pathology practice areas language and cognition. Students develop knowledge, skills and attributes relevant to negotiating and planning intervention with clients and their carers. They develop and demonstrate practical and professional skills used in the implementation and monitoring of interventions for addressing impairments of language (verbal, written, symbolic) and cognition for clients across the lifespan. Students also critique theory, empirical research and holistic frameworks to facilitate client-centred care. This subject facilitates students' critique of speech pathology intervention practices in the context of multilingual and multidialectal Australia, and enables them to identify and justify speech pathology intervention approaches for clients from diverse cultural and social backgrounds. Clinical reasoning and communication skills are developed through communicating intervention procedures and outcomes with a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences.
learning_outcomes: Negotiate, plan and justify intervention procedures and models of service delivery for management of language (verbal, written, symbolic) and cognitive impairments, based on critical reflection, analysis and synthesis of theory, concepts and holistic client data.

Use clinical reasoning and communication skills appropriate to a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences to discuss, document and report on intervention procedures, progress and professional recommendations regarding management of language (verbal, written, symbolic) and cognitive impairments.
Monitor, evaluate, and modify intervention delivery, based on analysis, synthesis and interpretation of intervention data.

Demonstrate technical skills for delivering intervention targeting language (verbal, written, symbolic) and cognitive impairments while adhering to professional ethical standards and medico-legal requirements.
Critique current speech pathology intervention practices in the multilingual and multidialectal context of Australia.
Negotiate client centred goals for language (verbal, written, symbolic) and cognitive impairments integrating relevant current evidence, client preference and context.
prerequisites: SPH529: Intervention for Language and Cognitive Impairments in Speech Pathology
SPH513: Assessment and Analysis of Language and Cognition in Speech Pathology

title: Intervention for sensory-motor impairments in speech pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will learn about research principles and practices relevant to the planning, implementation and evaluation of intervention targeting sensory-motor functions (speech, voice, fluency and swallowing). You will undertake database searches, critiquing of empirical research, data collection and analysis, synthesis and reporting of knowledge and information. You will use frameworks for goal-setting, and planning and evaluating intervention. You will apply intervention strategies with paediatric and adult clients and their families/caregivers. This subject builds on SPH512 (Assessment and analysis of sensory motor impairments in speech pathology) and will contribute to your preparation for your workplace learning subjects (SPH515/17 and SPH525/27).You will engage with a range of case studies to develop skills in identifying and writing specific, targeted and measurable goals, selecting evidence-based and holistic intervention goals/approaches and justifying goals and approaches selected for the management of sensory-motor impairments through critical reflection on the client's reported strengths, difficulties and available resources, and an understanding of the role of socio-cultural context in the experience of sensory-motor impairment.You will participate in a range of online learning experiences that offer the opportunity for you to work through topics in small groups or pairs. You will share your ideas and knowledge and learn from others in interactive activities including structured activities and independent study. You will attend a 3-day intensive on the Albury campus where you will have opportunities to deliver, monitor and modify intervention to manage sensory-motor difficulties.To demonstrate mastery of these learning outcomes and learning experiences you will write a series of intervention plans for individuals with different sensory-motor difficulties, complete a portfolio of practical activities during the intensive and write professional reports for a specified audience, summarising the intervention procedures and progress.You will use the CSU Learning Management System, Interact2, to engage in learning activities with your peers and utilise a range of online technologies and tools to inform your assessment tasks. During the intensive, you will have face-to-face lectures and practice delivering a range of speech-language pathology procedures to manage sensory-motor difficulties in children and adults, under the guidance of certified practicing speech pathologists.
learning_outcomes: Apply research principles and procedure to the management of speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing functions in individuals across the lifespan, demonstrated by writing a series of intervention plans for individuals with speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing difficulties, completing a portfolio of practical activities, interpreting sensory-motor intervention data and writing professional reports.

Apply knowledge of speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing to select and justify intervention procedures and models of service delivery, based on holistic, evidence-based, ethical and socio-cultural frameworks, demonstrated by writing a series of intervention plans for individuals with speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing difficulties, interpreting sensory-motor intervention data and writing professional reports.

Deliver intervention strategies with professionalism and care targeting speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing functions, and analyse and synthesise intervention data to monitor, evaluate, and modify intervention delivery, based on holistic, evidence-based, ethical and cultural frameworks, and using appropriate technical skills, demonstrated by completing a portfolio of practical activities, interpreting sensory-motor intervention data provided for individual cases and writing professional reports.

Report intervention procedures, progress and professional decisions regarding speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing management, based on holistic, evidence-based, ethical and cultural frameworks, using communication, technical and creative skills appropriate to a specific audience, demonstrated by writing a series of intervention plans for individuals with speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing difficulties, interpreting sensory-motor intervention data and writing professional reports.

Write and justify goals for intervention of speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing difficulties, utilising holistic, evidence-based, ethical and cultural frameworks, demonstrated by writing a series of intervention plans for individuals with speech, voice, stuttering and/or swallowing difficulties.
prerequisites: SPH512: Assessment and Analysis of Sensory-Motor Skills in Speech Pathology

title: Intervention for Sensory-Motor Impairments in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop competence in intervention for the speech pathology practice areas of hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation. For each of these practice areas, students develop knowledge, skills and attributes relevant to negotiating and planning intervention with clients. Students develop and demonstrate practical and professional skills to implement and monitor interventions. They also critique theory, empirical research and holistic frameworks to facilitate client-centred care across the lifespan. This subject facilitates students' critique of speech pathology intervention practices in the context of multilingual and multidialectal Australia, and enables them to identify and justify speech pathology intervention approaches for clients from diverse cultural and social backgrounds. Clinical reasoning and communication skills are developed through communicating assessment procedures and outcomes with a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences. This subject also facilitates critique of the role of health promotion as a form of speech pathology intervention for individuals or communities.
learning_outcomes: Use clinical reasoning, creative and communication skills appropriate to a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences to develop and justify health promotion resources.
Integrate knowledge and skills across a range of practice areas to plan, negotiate and justify intervention/s for clients with co-occurring impairments.

Plan and justify intervention procedures and models of service delivery for management of hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation, based on critical reflection, analysis and synthesis of theory, concepts and holistic client data.

Negotiate ethical and culturally responsive client-centred goals based on evidence-based practice for clients with disorders of hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation.

Monitor, evaluate, and modify intervention delivery, based on analysis, synthesis and interpretation of data relating to interventions for hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation.

Demonstrate technical skills for delivering intervention/s targeting hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation, while adhering to professional ethical standards and medico-legal requirements.

Use clinical reasoning and communication skills appropriate to a range of specialist and non-specialist audiences to document, report on and discuss intervention procedures, progress and professional recommendations regarding management of hearing, voice, fluency, speech, and swallowing and mealtime participation.
prerequisites: SPH528: Intervention for Sensory-Motor Impairments in Speech Pathology
SPH512: Assessment and Analysis of Sensory-Motor Skills in Speech Pathology

title: Introduction to Addiction Studies
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with knowledge of a broad range of theoretical frameworks relating to the construct of addiction as well as the mechanisms of action and effects of a range of drugs and other addictions. This subject also aims to provide students with a theoretical framework to critically analyse a range of conflicting perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Describe the processes of drug absorption and distribution.
Outline and critically reflect on behavioural and social models of addiction.
Critically describe and assess the influence of psychological, social, cultural and political factors on addiction.
Critically describe and apply the mechanisms of tolerance, physical dependence and withdrawal in a range of different settings.
Describe the actions of various drugs in the Central Nervous System.

title: Introduction to Ageing
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to show students that ageing is an individual experience. The subject introduces age related biological and social factors that influence the health and wellbeing of each individual older adult. The subject promotes examination of prevailing social attitudes about ageing and the impact these have on choices, opportunities and the wellbeing of older adults. Students will have the opportunity to examine elements of the Australian health and aged care system as they relate to the experience of ageing. Students are required to reflect on personal attitudes as they relate to working with people who are ageing.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the social construction of ageing and the impact that this can have on choices, opportunities and wellbeing in later life.
Apply their knowledge of the individual experience of ageing to reflect on their own attitudes to older people.
Compare individual experiences of ageing through a biopsychosocial perspective.
Apply their knowledge of the individual experience of ageing to reflect on the Australian health and aged care systems.

title: Introduction to AI for Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a strong foundation in the principles and practical applications of artificial intelligence. Throughout this subject, students will gain the ability to articulate the core concepts of AI, including its common benefits and potential drawbacks in various contexts. They will learn to assess the feasibility of integrating AI into diverse projects, understanding both technical and strategic considerations. This subject is designed for IT literate users who need to understand and deploy AI effectively in their organisation, but do not need to program and build a full AI system from first principles.
learning_outcomes: Apply and justify AI frameworks in applied business scenarios to support decision-making.
