Evaluate the fundamental concepts of AI and identify the common benefits and drawbacks of utilising AI
Critically assess and select appropriate AI approaches or models for specific business problems
Analyse business scenarios to evaluate the feasibility of AI implementation across technical and strategic factors

title: Introduction to Anatomy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide students, who are enrolling into a first year tertiary anatomy subject, with foundation anatomy material. The subject covers anatomical terminology, and provides an introduction to the structure of the human skeleton and associated muscles. Key study skills required to gain an understanding of anatomy will be a key component of this subject also.
learning_outcomes: Correctly identify the muscles of the upper limb, lower limb and to explain muscle function
Demonstrate suitable study skills required for anatomy
Correctly identify common anatomical terminology
Correctly identify bones and major landmarks of the skeleton

title: Introduction to Animal Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce students to the many professions served by animal scientists, through an exploration of the animal industries, the roles that animals serve in society, and how cultural background may influence the interactions that occur between humans and animals. Through practical sessions, students will begin to develop an appreciation of animal management and safe handling techniques. Students will also begin to develop skills in scientific communication, critical thinking and inquiry in the context of animal science.
learning_outcomes: Apply developing literacy, numeracy, digital, professional and communication skills in obtaining evidence-based information, evaluating it to solve problems, and communicating the information to potential stakeholders.
Discuss drivers underpinning animal science and how they impact on animal management and production of domestic and/or wildlife species.
Handle a range of domestic animal species in a safe and professional manner.
Discuss how cultural background, economics and environmental factors may influence interactions between humans and animals.

title: Introduction to Arabic Reading
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for students with no prior language skills in Arabic. It presents an introduction to reading Arabic and is designed to teach students how to articulate Arabic letters, words and sentences. It will also cover writing practice of Arabic vocabulary, together with basic speaking in Arabic and basic acquisition of commonly used Arabic words. This subject provides foundations for further study in Classical Arabic.
learning_outcomes: Read a basic vowelised text in Arabic with fluency.
Demonstrate a basic vocabulary of commonly used words.
Identify and proficiently pronounce the Arabic alphabet.
Communicate in simple conversation related to greetings and introductions.
Write basic Arabic words and sentences.
prerequisites: ISL160: Arabic Language I: Language Essentials And Qur'anic Script

title: Introduction to Arabic Reading
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for students with no prior language skills in Arabic. It presents an introduction to reading Arabic and is designed to teach students how to articulate Arabic letters, words and sentences. It will also cover writing practice of Arabic vocabulary, together with basic speaking in Arabic and basic acquisition of commonly used Arabic words. This subject provides foundations for further study in Classical Arabic.
learning_outcomes: Communicate in simple conversation related to greetings and introductions.
Write basic Arabic words and sentences.
Read a basic vowelised text in Arabic with fluency.
Demonstrate a basic vocabulary of commonly used words.
Identify and proficiently pronounce the Arabic alphabet.

title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The students will learn how machines can engage in learning, reasoning and planning with a special focus on Machine Learning (ML). The subject will discuss recent developments in the areas of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision (CV). The subject will also empower students with development skills in AI system design using the Python programming language. This will help students solve everyday problems using AI techniques.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and use existing models for solving natural language processing and/or computer vision problems.
Evaluate various AI search algorithms, such as uninformed, informed, heuristic, and constraint satisfaction.
Understand the basic requirements for designing neural networks and machine learning models.
Understand the fundamental theories, evolution, and applications of AI.
Apply machine learning solutions to real-world problems.

title: Introduction to Astronomy
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to astronomy and is suitable as a basis for further studies in this field, or for students majoring in other areas, or students who wish to take the subject for general interest. It gives a basic level of training in the areas of solar system astronomy, stellar astronomy, galactic and extra galactic astronomy and cosmology as well as a grounding in astronomical instrumentation and the physics associated with these areas. Students are required to attend an intensive school.
learning_outcomes: Compare, analyse and differentiate between, some of the theories formulated in astronomy and cosmology.
Describe and explain the concept of the celestial sphere and right ascension and declination.
Conduct and report on simple astronomically related practical experiments.

Describe and discuss theories of the formation and evolution of the solar system, describe and categorise the properties of its various components including the Sun, planets, moons, comets and asteroids, and explain the origin of various astronomical phenomena such as the occurrence of eclipses.
Set up a small astronomical telescope and use it to perform simple astronomical observations.

Describe and summarise (1) stellar formation, evolution and associated theories, (2) the structure, formation, evolution and various types of, galaxies, and theories associated with them, (3) the large scale structure of the universe and associated theories, (4) the fundamentals of astrobiology and the search for extraterrestrial life, (5) the fundamentals of cosmology and associated theories.
Perform simple calculations relevant to astronomy.
Recognise astronomy as a scientific endeavour and identify it as a field requiring the scientific method.
Describe and explain the physical principles behind the scientific instruments used in astronomy such as telescopes, spectroscopes and imaging devices, and the physics associated with their use.
Describe the scale and extent of the universe and categorise its various components.

title: Introduction to Australian Society and Health
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to stimulate the student's understanding of the holistic concepts, theories and models of health and wellbeing in an Australian context. Students will be supported to develop their understanding of contemporary service delivery models and deeply reflect on their role within the health sector. Integrated throughout the subject is an exploration of the socio-cultural factors that influence the engagement of people with diverse needs seeking health care. Students will start to develop fundamental skills and capabilities that underpin professional and inter-professional practice, such as; academic literacy, professional collaboration and communication.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain how the biomedical and social models of health underpin the Australian healthcare system.
Demonstrate academic literacy skills, including identification of credible sources of information and expressing ideas using clear and concise written English.
Identify and explain how health professionals, systems, and services influence access to healthcare for people with diverse needs.
Self-reflect and explore assumptions, bias and stereotypes about culture and diversity as a foundation for professional and interprofessional collaborative practice.
prerequisites: HIP100: Introduction to Health and Rehabilitation
EHR101: Sociocultural Foundations of Human Movement

title: Introduction to Biblical Languages
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to rudimentary features of Biblical Hebrew and New Testament Greek. It acquaints students with the alphabets of both Hebrew and Greek, familiarises them with basic grammatical features of both languages and facilitates the learning of elementary vocabulary. The subject orients students to the range of grammatical and lexical tools available to support the use of scholarly resources based on Biblical Hebrew and New Testament Greek. It also raises student awareness of interpretive implications arising from cultural dimensions of biblical texts preserved in ancient languages.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a working knowledge of relevant grammatical and lexical tools.
Demonstrate recognition of elementary vocabulary in Biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek.
Translate simple phrases from Biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek into English.
Recognise and reproduce the Hebrew and Greek alphabets.
Demonstrate self-guided learning.
Demonstrate awareness of interpretive implications arising from cultural dimensions of biblical texts as ancient documents.
Demonstrate an understanding of basic Biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek grammar.

title: Introduction to Biblical Languages
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to rudimentary features of Biblical Hebrew and New Testament Greek. It acquaints students with the alphabets of both Hebrew and Greek, familiarises them with basic grammatical features of both languages and facilitates the learning of elementary vocabulary. The subject orients students to the range of grammatical and lexical tools available to support the use of scholarly resources based on Biblical Hebrew and New Testament Greek. It also raises student awareness of interpretive implications arising from cultural dimensions of biblical texts preserved in ancient languages.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of basic Biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek grammar.
Recognise and reproduce the Hebrew and Greek alphabets.
Demonstrate recognition of elementary vocabulary in Biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek.
Demonstrate self-guided learning.
Demonstrate a working knowledge of relevant grammatical and lexical tools.
Translate simple phrases from Biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek into English.
Demonstrate awareness of interpretive implications arising from cultural dimensions of biblical texts as ancient documents.

title: Introduction To Bioscience
school: School
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to provide students with foundation material relevant to studies in human bioscience. The subject covers the language of biosciences, an introduction to clinically relevant mathematics, physics and chemistry, and an introduction to the human body.
learning_outcomes: Be able to correctly use common medical and anatomical terminology
Be able to explain the primary structures and function of the body systems
Be able to explain basic chemical concepts and perform mathematical calculations relevant to bioscience

title: Introduction to Case Based Study
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will use clinical cases to bridge across discipline knowledge, placing the person at the centre of health knowledge and introduce clinical reasoning. The investigation of cases will be undertaken from multiple viewpoints to facilitate students' exploration and appreciation of multidisciplinary and preventative healthcare, medical ethics and health communication with individuals and the community.
learning_outcomes: Communicate using the language and conventions of healthcare professionals and adapt communication strategies as appropriate for the message and the audience.
Reflect on their own communication strengths and weaknesses to inform self-directed learning, and personal and professional development.

Identify the factors associated with the social determinants of health and how they may impact on design of preventative health strategies or healthcare delivery with an emphasis on rural and regional care.
Discuss aspects of multidisciplinary, interdisciplinary and preventative healthcare in rural and regional contexts.
Discuss the ethical implications of diagnostic processes and diagnostic determinism.

title: Introduction to CAD and Computing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to fundamental concepts and techniques in computer-aided drawing (CAD) and office computing. Students will learn to use industry-standard software for drafting and design as well as office productivity tools for creating and managing documents. Emphasis will be placed on practical applications and hands-on exercises to develop proficiency in CAD drafting and office computing skills.
learning_outcomes: Utilise CAD software to create 2D and 3D technical drawings.
Use office computing software for word processing, spreadsheet analysis, and presentations.
Communicate technical information through technical drawings, written reports, and presentations.
Demonstrate the use of artificial intelligence in producing engineering documentation.
Explain drafting standards and conventions used to produce professional-quality drawings.

title: Introduction to Chemistry
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to cover those concepts and skills in chemistry required by a student who is enrolling into a typical first year tertiary chemistry subject. Included in the subject is a section on basic mathematics that the student may need to review in order to cope with the rest of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Calculate percentage composition of elements in compounds;
Distinguish between ionic and molecular compounds;
Define and give examples of various chemical terms;
Understand how chemical compounds are named;
Understand basic atomic structure, chemical bonding and the formation of compounds;
Write and balance chemical equations;
Identify and name simple hydrocarbons.
Determine atomic weights and molecular weights;
Express concentration of a solution in various ways;
Distinguish between physical and chemical change;
Appreciate the diversity and complexity of organic compounds; and

title: Introduction to Christian Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject offers an introductory engagement with the major doctrines of the Christian faith, including God as Trinity, the person and work of Christ, the Spirit, humanity and the church. It explores the tasks, methods and sources of Christian theology, enabling students to develop initial skills of theological reasoning together with the capacity to use theological vocabulary. Attention is given to historical and contemporary approaches to doing theology, as well as to the relation between Christian doctrine and Christian practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the tasks, methods and sources of Christian theology.
Demonstrate an ability to articulate and to evaluate connections between Christian theology and ministerial or practical contexts.
Engage critically with both historical and contemporary approaches to doing theology.
Engage critically with the major doctrines of the Christian faith.
Identify key theologians and to demonstrate a critical understanding of their place in the development of Christian theology.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.

title: Introduction to Christian Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject offers an introductory engagement with the major doctrines of the Christian faith, including God as Trinity, the person and work of Christ, the Spirit, humanity and the church. It explores the tasks, methods and sources of Christian theology, enabling students to develop initial skills of theological reasoning together with the capacity to use theological vocabulary. Attention is given to historical and contemporary approaches to doing theology, as well as to the relation between Christian doctrine and Christian practice.
learning_outcomes: Engage critically with both historical and contemporary approaches to doing theology.
Demonstrate an ability to make connections between Christian theology and ministerial or practical contexts.
Demonstrate a basic understanding of the tasks, methods and sources of Christian theology.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills.
Identify key theologians and to demonstrate an understanding of their place in the development of Christian theology.
Engage at an introductory level with the major doctrines of the Christian faith.

title: Introduction to Clinical Practice
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the fundamental knowledge and skills required for the Bachelor of Oral Health (Therapy and Hygiene). Through classroom and simulation clinic participation, students begin to develop the cognitive and fine motor application skills needed for proficient oral health care delivery. The concepts of clinical preparation and lifelong person-centred care will be examined with a focus on the fundamentals of dental caries and periodontal diseases, instrumentation, dental materials, communication, and professionalism.
learning_outcomes: Describe and compare the physical and chemical properties of restorative, preventative and impression materials, their clinical indications and contra-indications, their chairside handling and their waste management processes, discussing their applications and implementing appropriately when required.
Describe and apply basic concepts of professionalism and ethics, reflective practice, policies, sustainable practice, infection control, and workplace health and safety procedures effectively.
Identify, describe and utilise appropriate dental instruments, materials and medicaments to perform dental procedures safely and competently in the simulation clinic.
Identify carious and non-carious tooth loss, describe its aetiology and associated risk factors.

Describe and apply the principles of radiography, including the different types of intra-oral radiographs, their indications, clinical techniques, and common errors, and accurately read and interpret radiographs.
Identify and describe the tissues of the periodontium in health and in disease, the aetiology, classification and progression of periodontal disease and risk factors associated with the disease.

Describe and apply the main components of history taking and comprehensive examinations, patient prognosis, diagnosis, treatment planning and outcomes, preventative strategies and be able to summarise key elements of patient information.

title: Introduction to Contemporary Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Contemporary Paramedic Practice provides students with the foundational knowledge and skills to identify and assess minor illnesses and injuries in paramedicine practice settings. This subject introduces the core principles of paramedic practice, enabling students to begin formulating clinical diagnoses and developing basic treatment plans for primary care presentations. They will also prepare and administer medications following the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) standards and relevant regulations. It also covers transport decisions, referral pathways, and management strategies for minor conditions and injuries, empowering students to confidently balance health consumer safety with the need for an efficient and effective healthcare system.
learning_outcomes: Describe the appropriate clinical approach to assessing primary care presentations.
Apply safe preparation and administration of medications to health consumers in accordance with NSQHS standards.
Identify appropriate management strategies for common minor illnesses or injuries in the paramedic primary care setting.
Outline the key attributes of effective clinical decision-making in the management of primary care presentations, aligning with paramedic professional capabilities and the code of conduct.
Explain the management of minor illnesses and injuries in primary care presentations, emphasising interdisciplinary collaboration with other healthcare professionals to ensure person-centred care.
prerequisites: PAR100: Foundations of Clinical Paramedic Practice

title: Introduction to Criminology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce students to the history and evolution of criminology as a discipline, offering a comprehensive overview of key theoretical approaches to understanding crime. Students will learn how to apply criminological theories to real-world crime situations, examining both the causes of crime and society’s responses to it. Throughout the subject, students will develop critical thinking skills to assess the strengths and limitations of various theoretical perspectives, preparing them for deeper exploration in later stages of their criminology studies.
learning_outcomes: Explain key criminological theories that have shaped the study of crime over the past 200 years.
Communicate criminological ideas and arguments clearly and effectively, appropriate to academic and professional contexts.
Analyse criminological theories, assessing their strengths and weakness.
Identify and articulate the historical development of criminological theories, including the influence of political and social change.

title: Introduction to Data Tools and Analytics
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with the contextual, professional, scholarly and technological foundations of the body of knowledge underpinning the Data Management analytics discipline and professions. Professional settings within organisations in which existing data sets (including big data, research data, enterprise data) reside and are analysed will be discussed. Research, current issues, and examples of practical application in the field of data analytics and technologies relevant to the Information Studies field will be introduced. The subject will orient students to the current data handling and management trends and technology, and help them learn how to select and manage the right tools and analytical applications in their work settings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate how data, including enterprise, research and 'big' data are collected and managed within organisations.
Appraise the role or information technology (IT) and analytics in relation to the use and management of data.
Identify and critically assess and apply appropriate data tools and analytics.
Investigate and critically analyse the literature regarding data in different organisations, including information agencies, in their social, cultural, economic, ethical and technological contexts.

title: Introduction to Customs Valuation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the World Trade Organization (WTO) Valuation Agreement. This Agreement is in use in or will be introduced into all WTO member countries and economies for use by Customs and industry as the method of valuing goods as they cross national borders. Students will acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to determine the value of goods under their national legislation, based on this internationally recognised system. They will examine all methods of valuation under the Agreement, including the impact of related parties, together with specific issues such as discounts, royalties and conditioned sales.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and evaluate critically practical and topical Customs valuation issues.
Locate and apply sources guiding interpretation of the Agreement to solve Customs valuation problems.
Value goods and justify their valuation decisions with reference to the provisions of the Agreement and other sources guiding interpretation of the Agreement.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the valuation methodologies provided in the WTO Valuation Agreement.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the aims, objectives, structure and relevance of the WTO Valuation Agreement.

title: Introduction to Database Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to provide a solid grounding in database theory and application, and its place within the implementation of computer-based applications. There will be an emphasis on conceptual modelling to design a secure database that is implemented and queried using Structured Query Language (SQL).
learning_outcomes: Implement a database design using Structured Query Language (SQL).
Apply database theory to the design and implementation of relational databases.
Analyse and model business database requirements using Entity Relationship Diagrams (ERD).
Analyse a database design and apply normalisation theory and techniques.
Query a database using SQL.
Investigate and propose the security requirements for a database.

title: Introduction to Digital Imaging
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the creation and manipulation of photographic digital images (access to digital manipulation software is required eg: Photoshop). Students will develop an individual aesthetic through this process that is also informed by a survey of significant photographic images from the field.
learning_outcomes: Familiar with digital imaging terminology and practice.
Demonstrate competent basic principles and workings of the digital camera.
Competently acquire digital images and demonstrate an understanding of related hardware and software.
Demonstrate preliminary emergence of an individual photo-imaging aesthetic.
Use current industry standard image processing/manipulation software.

title: Introduction to Educational Research
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This introductory subject focuses on developing the skills needed to read, understand and evaluate the relevance of educational research. As such the subject focuses upon building understandings regarding the need for educational research; providing an overview of research orientations and methods for investigating educational problems; examining research designs, their relationship to the nature of findings and appropriateness for different educational investigations; reading and critiquing research reports and studies. The subject allows students to select research articles aligned with relevant professional interests so they can critique and assess the significance of these research studies and findings for their professional practice. This subject provides a foundation for studies in EER501 Qualitative Research, EER502 Quantitative Research, ERP401 Education Honours Project/Dissertation, ERP502 Master of Education Project and ERP503 Master of Education Thesis.
learning_outcomes: Understand how research studies are designed and conducted.
Have gained an overview of different methods that may be employed in researching educational problems.
Judge when each of these research methods is appropriate and how each may be applied to educational situations.
Read and understand research literature.
Understand why educational research is conducted.
Know how to critique research and research reports.

title: Introduction to Emergency Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the scope and diversity of emergency/disaster management and its various functions. The subject also focuses on the theory and concepts of emergency prevention, preparedness, response and recovery, the roles and functions of the key organisations in emergency/disaster management and the dynamics that occur in their interrelationships.
learning_outcomes: Explain the rationale for integrated emergency management and emergency legislation.
Describe and analyse the nature of an emergency and disaster, and the distinctions between each.
Explain the need for emergency/disaster management.
Explain the framework for emergency management, prevention, preparedness, response and recovery, including analysing the effects of emergencies/disasters on people and the environment.
Explain the concepts of command and control.

title: Introduction to Energy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: An introduction to the basic concepts, principles and technology of thermodynamics, energy, fluid mechanics and heat transfer.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic concepts of fluid mechanics and their application to typical fluid flow problems and buoyancy problems.
Demonstrate an understanding of the basic concepts of thermodynamics and their application to mass and energy conservation in simple systems .
Describe the principles and methods of temperature and pressure measurement.
Demonstrate an understanding of the principles, mechanisms and laws of heat transfer and employ these laws to solve simple one-dimensional heat transfer problems.
Identify the advantages and disadvantages of energy sources with respect to their technical merits and with respect to their impact on society.

title: Introduction to Equitation Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Throughout this subject students will develop and enhance their understanding of the basic mechanisms by which horses learn and can subsequently be managed, handled and trained. The multidisciplinary nature of the equitation science discipline will also be examined and students will have the opportunity to obtain and assess interactions with horses that may impact on both horse welfare and human safety. On successful completion of this subject students will recognise the need for evidence based research in order to reach conclusions about existing and future practice within the equine industry. They will be proficient and safe horse handlers.
learning_outcomes: Outline the implications of evolution and domestication on horse behaviour.
Outline and appreciate the underpinning principles and breadth of the Equitation Science discipline with particular reference to horse and human welfare.
Employ simple assessment and measurement techniques to determine and manage the effects of humans on horses during interactions.
Recognise the importance of the principles of science and develop scientific, reading, analytical and communication skills within the context of equine-based practice and evidence-based research.
Distinguish factors essential for a comprehensive and meaningful assessment of the overall welfare and quality of life of any equid.
Handle horses safely in a range of situations using simple, classical and operant conditioning methods allowing Workplace Health and Safety requirements to be met.

title: Introduction to Environmental Practice
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject encompasses foundation level professional skills and knowledge for students studying environmental science. Students are provided with a basic understanding of the fundamental theories and concepts of how life on earth is sustained. Fundamental skills and capabilities that underpin professional and inter-professional practice, such as academic literacy, reflective practice, professional reasoning, effective communication skills and evidence-based practice are also introduced. In this subject students will start to consider and plan for their future area/s of employment and explore what it means to be a professional in their chosen discipline/s. Students will consolidate their learning, and apply their knowledge and skills, through the work integrated learning opportunities with industry and academic experts.
learning_outcomes: Discuss professional and ethical issues related to the discipline.
Explain the concepts of academic integrity, ownership, intellectual property, and copyright, and apply these concepts through correct use of attribution and referencing.
Reflect on self as a learner and identify learning opportunities which facilitate the development of lifelong learning skills.
Discuss the interactions of human activities and environment.
Locate information relevant to the discipline, evaluate the sources of that information, and select high quality evidence-based information to formulate and support their academic writing.
Recognise specific career pathways and the associated skills to support professional requirements.
prerequisites: SCI100: Professionalism and Communication in Science

title: Introduction to Equitation Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Throughout this subject students will develop their understanding and appreciation of the physical impacts experienced by horses during their interactions with humans. Students will be taught the fundamental principles of experimental design and be able to develop and explore scientific questions relating to equestrian and equitation practices. On successful completion of this subject students will be able to demonstrate theoretical and practical knowledge of a range of tools and approaches enabling the objective assessment of the impacts of equestrianism and equipment on horses and riders, including behavioural observations and physical measurements.
learning_outcomes: Design, construct and demonstrate a simple piece of equipment to enhance equitation practice.
Explain how to objectively observe and record horse behaviour in a range of husbandry and equestrian contexts.
Identify and describe humans’ direct or indirect (through equipment) physical impacts on horses.
Utilise appropriate software and technology to capture, organise and assess data.
Explain the importance of sustainable and ethical equitation for the long-term future of the horse industry.
Conduct a simple scientific experimental study to investigate an aspect of equitation practice.

title: Introduction to Food and Nutrition
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject introduces core principles in food and nutritional sciences and scientific communication skills relevant to these disciplines. You will learn about academic and digital literacy skills, critical analysis of the scientific literature and the scientific methods relevant to the food and nutrition disciplines. Topics include: the major nutrients and non-nutrients in foods and their contribution to nutrition and well-being across the lifespan; principles of food safety, food preservation and the impact of processing on food nutrients through consideration of major plant and animal food products; and, the characteristics of the modern food system with an emphasis on food and nutrition security as well as the role of food and nutrition policies, standards and regulations.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the characteristics of the modern food system, including the concept of food security and the role and development of food and nutrition policies and regulations.
Describe the major nutrients and non-nutrients present in common foods.
Describe the use of the research methods, including the scientific method, to inform food and nutrition practice.
Explain the importance of food safety and describe procedures for the safe handling of food.
Describe the typical production and processing operations underpinning the provision of common food products.
Apply communications skills appropriate for food and nutrition scientists.
Outline the contribution of major and minor nutrients to human health and well-being and identify how nutrition requirements change across the life span.

title: Introduction to Geospatial Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Geospatial Science engages students with geospatial data, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and Remote Sensing, providing the foundational knowledge and skills needed to understand and develop basic applications in Geospatial Science. The subject adopts a real-life, problem-based approach to introduce and explain key geospatial concepts. Upon completion, students will be able to identify Geospatial Science applications relevant to their course and future profession, describe fundamental concepts and methods used in geospatial data acquisition, processing, and visualisation, and evaluate the use of AI tools based on their relevance and ethical implications, including data privacy and bias.
learning_outcomes: Apply geospatial data acquisition and processing methods using GIS software to solve basic, real-world geospatial problems and clearly communicate the results.
Identify opportunities to use AI tools within basic GIS workflows and discuss the relevance and ethical implications of their outputs.
Describe and explain foundational concepts related to geospatial data, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Remote Sensing.
Identify and describe geospatial data and applications of Geospatial Science relevant to professional practice.
prerequisites: SCI200: Introduction to Spatial Science and Data Visualisation

title: Introduction to Functional Human Anatomy
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to study in human functional anatomy relevant to diagnosis, intervention and rehabilitation in allied health practice. The subject introduces students to the study of anatomy and provides a broad introduction to the anatomy of the human musculoskeletal structure and body systems. This subject provides a foundation for further detailed studies of the anatomy of regions of the body. The learning experiences in this subject involve a range of learning modalities involving theoretical and practical learning.
learning_outcomes: Describe the anatomy of the respiratory system.
Describe the anatomy of the cardiovascular system.
Define fundamental anatomical terminology and the anatomical position.
Describe the anatomy of the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Briefly describe the anatomy of the digestive, urinary and reproductive systems.
Describe the anatomy of the musculoskeletal system, including the axial skeleton, appendicular skeleton, appendicular and axial muscles, and arthrology.
Describe the relationship between the structure and function of the human body.
Describe the anatomy of tissues and list their major functions.

title: Introduction to Horticulture
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with an introduction to the basic principles and practices of production and landscape horticultural science as they are applied in a variety of Australian horticulture industries. The critical importance of plants to human health and welfare and the challenge to produce plants sustainably into the future to meet these needs is the central theme underlying the subject. Students will explore key career skills and investigate careers that are possible in horticulture as well as developing their competence in key academic skills.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on self as a learner and early career professional by identifying learning opportunities which facilitate the development of professional and lifelong learning skills .
Relate the history, trends, issues, and challenges in horticultural science to the need to bring about sustainability.
Identify, describe and explain the diversity of plant species and their interactions within the environment, particularly their importance to the health and well-being of humans.
Express ideas and communicate information and present an independent exposition of knowledge in academic writing.
Explain the environmental requirements of horticulturally valuable crops grown in Australia and outline the processes involved in consistently producing successful, sustainable crops.

title: Introduction to Health, Nutrition and Exercise Behaviour
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the benefits and considerations of physical activity, exercise and nutrition for health. Students will also learn about social-psychological theories to understanding human behaviour. The subject will explore a range of complex factors that affect physical activity and food intake behaviours, including personal attitudes, historical, cultural, psycho-social, environmental influences and demonstrate an appreciation of how these factors impact on physical and mental wellbeing. Students will explore how psychological factors influence participation in exercise and physical activity settings, and the psychological outcomes of exercise participation. The subject will also provide students with foundational principles of nutrition and the physiological, psychological and social processes involved in food and eating.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and explain key psychological factors influencing exercise participation and/or eating patterns.
Describe the basic functions of macronutrients, micronutrients, and other major dietary components and their common food sources.
Evaluate and use selected theoretical and applied approaches to explain exercise and nutrition behaviours.
Analyse and explain key psychological outcomes of exercise participation and adherence.
Evaluate current evidence-based guidelines used to provide appropriate general nutritional advice.
Explain the complex interaction between individuals and their environment and how these impact health.
Explain dietary behaviours and energy availability concerns in relation to physical activity and exercise requirements.
prerequisites: EHR109: Introduction to Sport and Exercise Behaviour

title: Introduction to Human Services
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to human services in Australia, including history and contemporary issues underpinning human service practice. Contemporary human services approaches that shape knowledges for practice will be introduced (including biopsychosocial model of health and wellbeing, eco-social framework, trauma informed practice, intersectionality, ethical practice and social justice approaches). These approaches will be linked to different fields of practice in examining the impacts and complexity of issues, such as addressing poverty and promoting equality, belonging, identity, as well as ecological and human rights and overall social development.
learning_outcomes: Articulate a developing understanding of social determinants of health and wellbeing, including the impacts and complexity of poverty, power, discrimination and inclusion, on health and wellbeing.
Articulate an understanding of foundational human service knowledges and approaches for practice applicable across and within different fields of practice.

Demonstrate an understanding of the history and characteristics of professional human services in Australia, including a knowledge base, core values and ethics, together with principles and approaches for practice.
prerequisites: HCS409: Social Welfare in Human Services

title: Introduction to Imagery and Geo-spatial Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a detailed body of knowledge relating to the application of imagery and geo-spatial intelligence collection and analytical tools to a range of intelligence contexts (national security, policing and emerging practice areas). Students will apply this body of knowledge to different generic operational intelligence scenarios in order to consolidate new skills. In particular, students will complete assessment tasks using relevant imagery and geo-spatial technology analytical skills learnt in the subject. These technical skills are directly applicable to the intelligence officer's workplace.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of key technical skills related to imagery and geo-spatial intelligence.
Demonstrate an understanding of geo-spatial theoretical concepts in different intelligence contexts.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the key ethical and professional issues relevant to imagery and geo-spatial intelligence.
Review, analyse, consolidate and synthesise knowledge in imagery and geo-spatial intelligence applications to a range of intelligence settings.
Think critically about the current and emerging intelligence environments and the challenges in using imagery intelligence.

title: Introduction to Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the key concepts, theories, histories, and models of intelligence within contemporary national and international contexts, while developing foundational skills in intelligence collection and analysis to evaluate information and support basic assessments. Students learn to communicate intelligence effectively through structured reports and oral briefings, alongside critically examining the ethical, legal, and societal implications of intelligence practice in democratic settings. The subject also highlights the role of intelligence in informing operational and strategic decision-making, particularly within law enforcement contexts, ensuring students understand both the practical and professional applications of intelligence work.
learning_outcomes: Communicate intelligence findings effectively through structured oral briefings and professionally presented intelligence reports.
Identify and apply foundational intelligence collection and analytical techniques to evaluate information and support basic intelligence assessments.
Describe and explain key concepts, theories, histories, and models of intelligence within contemporary national and international contexts.
Explain how intelligence products inform operational and strategic decision-making in law enforcement contexts.
Examine ethical, legal, and critical perspectives relating to intelligence practice and reflect on the role of intelligence in democratic societies.

title: Introduction to Insurance Classes and Products
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the various types of insurances policies, policy documents, underwriting and claims handling procedures.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the various types of insurance policies.
Interpret insurance policy conditions and wording.
Analyse company underwriting guidelines and claims handling procedures.
Describe and analyse insurance documents.

title: Introduction to Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with an introductory overview to the theory and practice of intelligence. It will equip the student with a foundational understanding of and knowledge about intelligence theory, the contexts of intelligence practice, intelligence analysis and the role of intelligence. Moreover, this subject introduces the basic skills that analysts and intelligence professionals need to meet the obligations of their role.
learning_outcomes: Make high level, independent judgments in a range of intelligence contexts, including preparing intelligence briefs and evaluating case studies.
Demonstrate highly developed written communication skills in the context of intelligence briefs and other written tasks.
Demonstrate through written intelligence products, advanced cognitive skills and the ability to evaluate complex problems.

Demonstrate application of knowledge of a range of contemporary intelligence practitioner issues and problems (particularly related to the role of intelligence, technology, ethics, management, and the role of the private sector).

title: Introduction to Internet Technologies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the fundamentals of internet technologies, from underlying communication technologies to network applications. In particular, the subject covers topics such as network and data communication models, and introduces emerging internet technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT). It also explores Internet protocols and introduces fundamental cyber security concepts and technologies.
learning_outcomes: Define and explain various internet terminologies.
Describe and evaluate emerging internet technologies such as Internet of Things (IoT).
Explain data link protocols.
Analyse the TCP/IP protocol.
Explain and apply IP addresses including IPv4 and IPv6.
Explain fundamental cyber security concepts and technologies.
Present a basic knowledge of digital data.

title: Introduction to Islamic Art and Design
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the principles and regional variations of Islamic art and design from a contemporary perspective. The content is sourced from Morocco to Indonesia, from the 7th century to the present day, representing a wide range of case studies. No prior knowledge of Islam or Arabic is required. This subject, unique to CSU, is designed to engage the Australian propensity to travel and appreciate international cultural heritage. Students will be introduced to Islamic art to enable broader cultural understanding and recognition of distinctive design principles, rather than the minutiae of historic periods and distant dynasties. Both the spectacular and the vernacular will be studied to reveal principles common to art and design, which are intrinsically linked in Islamic visual culture.
learning_outcomes: Acquire the foundations for ongoing study in this rapidly expanding international field, including familiarity with the world's major Islamic Art collections, resources, and principal theorists.

Be familiar with a broad cross-section of Islamic contributions to ornament, calligraphy, architecture, textiles, ceramics, metalwork, and glass, including their regional and unifying characteristics.

title: Introduction to Islamic Psychology
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to Islamic psychology, its context, definitions, framework and perspectives. Understandings of human nature will be explored from an Islamic perspective. The importance of the integration of psychological theories and interventions in the life of a Muslim will be discussed with a focus on the need to decolonise psychology and its content. This subject also provides a brief history of Islamic psychology and its origins, looking at early classical scholars, their worldviews and their heritage. Some of the classical scholars studied include al-Kindi, al-Farabi and Ibn Rushd (Averroes); physicians studied include al-Balkhi, al-Razi and Ibn Sina (Avicenna); and theologians studied include al-Ghazzali, Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Qayyim.
learning_outcomes: Describe key Islamic psychology concepts.
Evaluate the key contributions of early Muslim scholars and modern contributions towards Islamic psychology.
Critically discuss the relationship between Islamic scriptures and psychology.
Explain the histories of secular psychology and Islamic psychology.
Formulate a working definition of Islamic psychology.
Define, compare and contrast secular perspectives of psychology with Islamic perspectives of psychology.

title: Introduction to Mathematics (1)
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explicitly teaches numeracy skills to the level required for first year university studies. Students will learn to perform calculations, with and without calculators, using Real numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages. Students will be taught how to build mental models to solve every day mathematical problems, using statistics, probability, algebra and graphs. Skills will be consolidated through engaging with a range of real-world situations from the contexts of health, science and education.
learning_outcomes: Perform arithmetic calculations with Real numbers.
Represent and perform simple calculations related to personal finance.
Use geometry, measurement, and trigonometric skills to solve two dimensional and three dimensional mathematical problems.
Model mathematical scenarios using statistics, probability, algebra, and graphs.
Apply mathematical knowledge to solve problems with a familiar context.

title: Introduction to Learning Online
school: School
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Learning Online introduces students to the CSU online learning environment. Through authentic activities within Interact2, students will develop the skills and confidence necessary to successfully begin their studies at CSU. Practical learning activities will incorporate the key elements of online learning, including navigating the Interact2 environment, watching presentations, participating in online meetings and forum discussions, searching for and evaluating information and submitting assignments. Topics also encompass the development of a personal learning plan, time management and tips for locating additional internet based study tools and student support available. It is estimated that approximately 14 hours of personal study will be required to complete the subject.
learning_outcomes: Identify and locate resources and services to address future needs for effective online learning.
Demonstrate awareness of online tools available for note taking, bookmarking and referencing.
Develop a personal learning plan and time management strategies for effective online learning.
Demonstrate approaches that ensure meaningful participation in an online learning community.
Use Interact2 for accessing study materials and maintaining effective interactions with lecturers and fellow students.
Use search tools to locate relevant information on the Internet.
Use other CSU learning tools such as EASTS, the Online Meeting Tool and CSU Replay.

title: Introduction to Microbiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject introduces the importance of micro-organisms in the environment. It provides an overview of microbiology that encompasses the effect of microbes on human health, the environment and applied aspects of microbiology, including agricultural, industrial and food/wine microbiology. The cultivation, enumeration and identification of micro-organisms and control of microbial growth are emphasised in laboratory classes. The mechanisms by which micro-organisms cause disease in humans, plants and animals and defences against these infections are introduced.
learning_outcomes: Describe the means by which microorganisms can be cultivated and assayed.
Describe the structure and function of microorganisms.

Demonstrate a good understanding of the interactions of microorganisms with human beings, with particular emphasis on the microorganisms of importance to human and animal health, the environment and the agriculture, food and beverage industries.
Demonstrate a good understanding of the processes used to study microorganisms,.
Demonstrate knowledge of the means by which the growth of microorganisms can be controlled.

title: Introduction to Midwifery Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students are introduced to the roles and scope of midwifery practice and women-centred care and will participate in simulation experience to develop key skills in preparation for their midwifery practice experiences. Students will build on their existing knowledge of human bioscience and behavioural sciences to gain an understanding of the psychological, physiological and social aspects of childbearing and early parenthood. Students will also develop the foundational knowledge and skills required to provide safe maternity care and support the woman and her significant others during her childbearing experience from the perspective of wellness through to variations of normal.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role and scope of the midwife in the provision of woman-centred midwifery care to support the woman’s right to make informed choices and promote the safety of the mother and her baby throughout the childbearing continuum.
Demonstrate foundational midwifery knowledge and skills required for safe, woman-centred assessment and care during childbearing.
Apply knowledge of the anatomical, physiological, social and emotional changes that occur during childbearing to provide woman-centred, safe and evidence-informed midwifery care.
Identify deviations from normal childbearing and processes for consultation, referral and collaboration with other health professionals.

title: Introduction to Information Security
school: School

title: Introduction to New Testament Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the various writings that comprise the New Testament. It does so with reference to their historical context and their literary and theological features. It also introduces critical methods of New Testament interpretation, including basic exegetical skills. Attention is given to long-standing interpretive issues, including the relations between the gospels, the historical value of Acts, authenticity and pseudonymity in Paul, and apocalyptic literature.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate familiarity with key historical, cultural, literary and theological issues pertaining to the study of the New Testament.
Demonstrate a working knowledge of the contents of the New Testament and of its social, cultural and historical background.
Demonstrate an understanding of interpretive issues concerning the relationship between the two Testaments in the Christian Bible.
Engage in basic exegesis of New Testament texts and to interact with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Demonstrate familiarity with significant developments in the history of New Testament studies and with critical approaches to New Testament texts.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss the use of New Testament texts in the life of the contemporary Church.
prerequisites: THL409: Introduction to New Testament Studies

title: Introduction to New Testament Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the various writings that comprise the New Testament. It does so with reference to their historical context and their literary and theological features. It also introduces critical methods of New Testament interpretation, including basic exegetical skills. Attention is given to long-standing interpretive issues, including the relations between the gospels, the historical value of Acts, authenticity and pseudonymity in Paul, and apocalyptic literature.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the contents of the New Testament and of its social, cultural and historical background.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate advanced familiarity with key historical, cultural, literary, and theological issues pertaining to the study of the New Testament.
Discuss critically the use of New Testament texts in the life of the contemporary Church.
Engage in sound exegesis of New Testament texts and to interact critically with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of interpretive issues concerning the relationship between the two Testaments in the Christian Bible.
Demonstrate advanced familiarity with significant developments in the history of New Testament studies and with critical approaches to New Testament texts.

title: Introduction to Old Testament Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject is a foundational introduction to the contents of the Old Testament (Hebrew Bible) and to basic scholarly tools and critical methods used in Old Testament studies. It surveys the formation of the Old Testament, both as a whole and as comprising collections of books, while focusing on selected texts from the Torah (Pentateuch), Prophets, Writings and Apocrypha. It pays particular attention to issues of oral and textual transmission, historical and geographical context, religion and culture, genre and canon, exegesis, interpretation and diverse theological perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Discuss in a way that shows developing critical awareness a range of texts from the Pentateuch, Prophets, Writings and Apocrypha.
Demonstrate a working knowledge of the contents of the Old Testament and of its social, cultural and historical background.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss the use of Old Testament texts in the life of the contemporary Church.
Demonstrate familiarity with key historical, cultural, literary and theological issues pertaining to the study of the Old Testament.
Demonstrate an understanding of interpretive issues concerning the relationship between the two Testaments in the Christian Bible.
Engage in basic exegesis of Old Testament texts and to interact with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
prerequisites: THL408: Introduction to Old Testament Studies

title: Introduction to Pharmacology in Mental Health
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces a broad theoretical overview of the mechanisms of drug action of commonly prescribed and used pharmacotherapies within mental health disorders. Students will learn terminology and drug nomenclature used in the primary health care context. A focus in this subject will be on commonly prescribed and used medications in mental health, which provides the framework for the development of the necessary skills and abilities required to engage within a multidisciplinary team within the health system.
learning_outcomes: apply the skills required to effectively communicate with patient/clients and with peers and other health professionals.
describe the relationship between social, emotional and physical wellbeing and the effects of specific medications used within the mental health context;
research, identify and discuss the need for various dose forms for commonly used medications in mental health; and
research, identify and discuss the mechanism of action of drugs at a fundamental level using current digital mediums;
discuss selected drug groups specific to mental health;
prerequisites: MHP109: The Body, Illness and Health

title: Introduction to Medical Emergencies
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop the students' knowledge and skills required to care for patients experiencing a medical emergency. The students will be required to integrate pathophysiogical principles and assessment findings to implement appropriate basic treatment and management plans for the medical patient. The subject will also encourage professional interaction and communication between different health care providers along with developing the students' report writing skills.
learning_outcomes: Communicate clearly with other health care providers in verbal handovers, patient care, and patient documentation.
Treat/manage patients experiencing a medical emergency using basic and intermediate interventions.
Safely and effectively handle, prepare and administer basic medications used in paramedic practice.
Recognise/diagnose and explain the medical conditions encountered in paramedic practice.
Use a range of diagnostic tests/medical equipment and technology that provides data, formulate a differential diagnosis for a patient experiencing a medical emergency.

title: Introduction to Old Testament Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject is a foundational introduction to the contents of the Old Testament (Hebrew Bible) and to basic scholarly tools and critical methods used in Old Testament studies. It surveys the formation of the Old Testament, both as a whole and as comprising collections of books, while focusing on selected texts from the Torah (Pentateuch), Prophets, Writings and Apocrypha. It pays particular attention to issues of oral and textual transmission, historical and geographical context, religion and culture, genre and canon, exegesis, interpretation and diverse theological perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Engage in sound exegesis of Old Testament texts and to interact critically with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Demonstrate advanced familiarity with key historical, cultural, literary and theological issues pertaining to the study of the Old Testament.
Discuss critically the use of Old Testament texts in the life of the contemporary Church.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the contents of the Old Testament and of its social, cultural and historical background.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of interpretive issues concerning the relationship between the two Testaments of the Christian Bible.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss critically a range of texts from the Pentateuch, Prophets, Writings and Apocrypha.
prerequisites: THL105: Introduction to Old Testament Studies

title: Introduction to Physiotherapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces professional concepts such as group work, scope of practice, evidence-based practice, basic documentation, assessment principles, and the use of e-health technologies for example, telehealth. These concepts will be explored in order to provide students with an introductory understanding of the physiotherapy profession and practice of physiotherapy in national and international contexts, and will begin to develop the clinical reasoning, literacy, numeracy and assessment skills used in physiotherapy practice. This subject will focus on introducing students to metropolitan, rural and remote contexts of physiotherapy practice including important considerations around the business, sustainability and legalities of physiotherapy practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective communication.
Demonstrate skills in collaboration as a foundation for teamwork and interprofessional practice.
Use clinical reasoning processes and evidence based practice to begin to explore and explain assessment findings at a foundation level.
Plan and perform a person-centred physiotherapy assessment for selected clinical scenarios, at a foundation level.
Reflect upon professional practice and employ feedback to take action to improve knowledge and skills in physiotherapy practice.
Discuss the use of e-health technologies in physiotherapy assessment (for example, telehealth), particularly in the context of rural and remote physiotherapy practice.
Demonstrate and apply knowledge of the values, code of conduct, ethical and legal obligations, informed consent, and professional behaviour appropriate to physiotherapy practice.
Based on evidence, define pain as a complex multidimensional experience, recognising the individual variability in pain presentations.
prerequisites: PHS100: Introduction to Physiotherapy Clinical Practice
PHS100: Introduction to Physiotherapy Clinical Practice

title: Introduction to Pharmacy
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to the pharmacy profession and the roles and responsibilities of pharmacists in the Australian health care system. The regulatory framework governing pharmacists and their practice is explored through authentic examples of pharmacy practice. Students are introduced to core pharmacy skills for supply and management of medicines and utilisation of evidence-based health information, including effective written and oral communication. This subject includes work integrated learning.
learning_outcomes: Describe requirements for prescriptions and perform basic pharmaceutical calculations.
Identify and discuss the impact of instruments which inform the regulatory framework of pharmacy practice.
Locate, evaluate and utilise evidence -based health and medicines information.
Discuss the impact of effective communication with patients, pharmacy colleagues, and other health professionals.
Discuss the roles and responsibilities of pharmacists in the Australian health care system.

title: Introduction to Philosophy and Ethics
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This introductory subject offers a taste of central areas of philosophy, including ethics, epistemology, and metaphysics. Across the course we will explore questions such as: What is knowledge, and do we have any at all? What does it mean to be a man, woman, or some other gender? Does deception undermine sexual consent? What duties do we have in relation to climate change? Is it morally permissible for students to use AI to write their essays? Is time travel possible? These questions are not just abstract puzzles—they shape how we think about ourselves, our responsibilities, and the world we inhabit.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a grasp of basic philosophical techniques of analysis and argument.
Demonstrate a basic understanding of the practice of addressing philosophical and ethical problems.

Apply their skills of analysis and argument and their understanding of theories to the clarification and resolution of the particular philosophical and ethical problems/issues addressed in the Syllabus.

title: Introduction to Podiatric Clinical Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with the opportunity to review and interpret information in a person’s health record and discuss with the person their medical and treatment history, to develop foundation knowledge and skills for endorsement for scheduled medicines. Students will develop an understanding of control of cross infection, hand hygiene and instrument sterilisation, as preparation for observing and undertaking initial assessment in both simulated and real clinical settings. This subject provides students with the knowledge to differentiate between normal and abnormal clinical presentations of a range of conditions including neurological, vascular, basic anatomical/orthopaedic, and dermatological conditions.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate normal from abnormal parameters in a range of common dermatological pathology through description of aetiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and management.
Demonstrate appropriate infection control, instrument sterilisation, and hand washing practices with due consideration of environmental sustainability issues.
Safely perform routine skin and nail care in a simulated setting with due consideration of people and equipment.

Review and interpret information in the person’s health records and discuss with the person their medical and treatment history, to contribute to an understanding of their needs and current treatment.
Perform assessments of the neurological, vascular, musculoskeletal and dermatological systems in a simulated setting.
Develop a simulated management plan for an uncomplicated podiatric presentation.
prerequisites: POD111: Introduction to Lower Limb Assessment and Treatment

title: Introduction to Podiatric Medicine
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to general health literacy and professional practice, including professional standards and legal and ethical frameworks, which inform podiatric practice. As communication is a significant aspect of healthcare practice, and forms the basis of successful history taking, students will be introduced to verbal and non-verbal communication strategies which are inclusive, and culturally and socially appropriate. Students will reflect on their values, attitudes and perceptions of others as part of the process of learning about self-awareness, cultural humility and cultural responsiveness. Students will also gain knowledge of the anatomy and physiology of common podiatric conditions and develop skills to identify, understand, and manage a range of cutaneous pathologies relevant to podiatric practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain how professional standards, legislation and ethical considerations will impact on their course of study and inform their future and continuing practice as a podiatrist.
Describe the clinical presentation, aetiology, pathophysiology, and management of a range of cutaneous conditions relevant to podiatric practice.
Communicate using the professional discourse of health and medicine, and self-reflect on appropriate communication strategies to ensure inclusion for diverse groups.
Articulate the concept of cultural humility and cultural responsiveness as a process of lifelong learning.
Describe the role and scope of the podiatrist within the healthcare team and the broader healthcare system.

title: Introduction to Police Investigations
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide those students who intend seeking a career in a police service with a fundamental understanding of the investigative processes carried out by police. The central theme throughout is the application of those ethical and legal principles which impact on investigation practice. Investigation processes are examined with reference to logic, critical thinking and scientific method. Sources of information available to police are canvassed, with the final focus being on investigation and interviewing as evidence. Specific reference will be made to the P.E.A.C.E. model of investigative interviewing. The theoretical component is applied to investigation practice.
learning_outcomes: be able to discuss and apply ethical interviewing practice during investigations;
be able to describe the role of the general duties police officer in investigation;
be able to appreciate and articulate the necessity for ethical practice in investigation;
be able to describe the importance of proper suspect identification procedures;
be able to conduct an effective investigative interview;
be able to demonstrate the application of logic, critical thinking and scientific method to investigation;
be able to critically appraise the role of investigation as one part of the profession of policing;
be able to demonstrate understanding of the legal principles which apply to the admission of confessional evidence in court.
be able to understand the importance of ethical informant management;
be able to critically evaluate victims, witnesses, informants, physical evidence and intelligence as sources of information;

title: Introduction to Policing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the role and function of the police from a social, historical and comparative perspective. Students will consider the various forms of policing practices in Australia and other nations, allowing students to develop a foundational knowledge of policing. The structures, roles and reforms of the police are considered as well as issues such as ethical practices in policing, social diversity, community relations and debates about distinct policing strategies and their social impact. Students will explore relevant policing and allied theories as well as important concepts for policing in contemporary society. The subject introduces students to key concepts, philosophies and styles of policing that underpin policing practices. In doing so, this subject compliments the learning experiences offered in other first year policing and criminal justice subjects, encouraging critical reflection on the role, function, styles and techniques of policing.
learning_outcomes: Identify and reflect on the role of police from a social, historical and comparative perspective.
Evaluate the key theories used to inform policing practice and concepts for policing in contemporary society.
Compare and contrast the range of policing roles.
Describe various forms of policing practices in Australia and overseas.
Articulate the various policing models and strategies available.
Evaluate key issues impacting policing such as ethical practice, social diversity, community relations and debates about distinct policing strategies and their social impact.

title: Introduction to Primary Health Care: Mental Health
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: There is evidence that increasing involvement and control of health policy, health initiatives and service delivery by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people themselves delivers improved health outcomes. A Primary Health Care model is the focus of this subject, which covers the promotion of health and mental health, early intervention and the prevention of illness. The subject simplifies the dynamics of care, explaining the differences for upstream, midstream and downstream models of care, downstream being primary medical care whereas primary health care is upstream. This addresses a range of health issues that have no specific medical intervention yet impact populations as well as individual health, community involvement and the use of current technology. Holistic health encompasses spirituality as well as the physical, social, and emotional wellbeing of the individual and community. Professional skills such as literacy and locating and interpreting information necessary to understand and communicate disciplinary knowledge will be introduced.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the differences between primary, secondary and tertiary levels of health care as well as the principles of primary health care and how these address individual self-care and population health.
