Recognise how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled Organisations are involved in primary health care.
Demonstrate academic writing, referencing and literacy skills, and be able to locate and interpret information necessary to understand and communicate disciplinary knowledge.
Understand the Australian health care system in relation to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health, and how Aboriginal Torres Strait Islander mental health clinicians enhance the system.
Define primary health care, the determinants of health, health promotion, prevention and early intervention.
Identify the role of international organisations in primary health care developments; and.

title: Introduction to Reflective Practice and Clinical Reasoning in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the speech pathology profession, including the scope of practice and professional and ethical frameworks that influence and shape current practice in Australia. Within this subject, students develop skills in critical reflection and apply these to exploring their previous learning, and professional and personal experiences in the context of developing theoretical and professional knowledge. Students also reflect on their pre-existing personal and professional communicative competence and critique this in relation to theoretical models of language use in everyday and professional contexts. Students develop skills in professional communication, reflection and clinical reasoning, and set and evaluate professional learning goals in relation to these professional competencies. Learning and assessment activities within this subject are designed to support the development of digital literacy as a foundation for further learning in the Master of Speech Pathology and a tool for later clinical practice.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on personal learning styles and language use in the context of learning theory and models of communication.
Engage in, contribute to, and critically reflect on group learning and feedback processes.
Use technical, creative and communication skills, including a range of academic and digital literacy skills, to communicate with non-specialist audiences.
Reflect critically on personal skills related to professional conduct, ethical standards, life-long learning, and developing professional identity.
Explain and critically reflect on how international, professional and ethical frameworks guide and shape speech pathology practice.

Identify and justify personal learning goals, and strategies for achieving those goals, based on integration of reflection on personal experiences, learning styles, language use and developing professional competency.

title: Introduction to Research
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject discusses the role and value of research in information agencies. It looks at the role of research in evidence-based professional practice, with a focus on the evaluation of research literature and interpretation of research results. This subject introduces research concepts and practices appropriate to professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply research evaluation skills appropriate in professional environments.
Have a broad understanding of the types of research relevant to, and applied in, libraries, information agencies and other professional settings.
Critically evaluate completed research.
Have a general understanding of the principles of evidence-based practice.

title: Introduction to Science 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Science 1 is one of a suite of non-award subjects offered on the Study Link platform. This is the first of two subjects designed to familiarise students with the language, concepts and opportunities common to studying in different science disciplines. Students will work through four sequential modules focused specifically on the nature of scientific thinking, the process of the scientific method, the features of science communication and the interconnectedness between different branches of science. Throughout the subject there is a focus on problem solving, applied critical thinking, using evidence, and the development and practicing of transferable skills.
learning_outcomes: Describe the processes involved in the scientific method.
Identify different purposes of science communication.
Explain why scientific thinking is based on evidence.
Identify the interconnectedness of different branches of science.

title: Introduction to Science and Biology
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: At the end of this subject, students will have a foundational understanding of biology, including the structure and function of plant and animal cells. From learning about the cell as 'building block', students will be introduced to the structure and function of human body systems. Students will be able to transfer this knowledge of systems to explain different factors which might affect the functioning of living organisms at cellular, individual, and population level. A range of scaffolded learning tasks will enable students to develop critical thinking, academic writing, and research skills to a level consistent with the expectations of first year university. Students will be explicitly taught to assess the credibility of bioscience information and why this assessment is important. A range of learning and assessment tasks support the development of foundational skills specific to effectively communicating credible scientific information to identified audiences for specific purposes.
learning_outcomes: Describe the basic structure and function of cells and systems.
Explain the factors affecting the functioning of organisms at cellular, individual and population levels.
Apply critical thinking skills to assess the credibility of bioscience information.
Communicate credible bioscience information to identified audiences for educational purposes.

title: Introduction to Substance Use: Alcohol and Other Drugs
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces and orientates the student to the Alcohol and Other Drugs (AOD) field. It will examine the historical context and current patterns of AOD use in our society. Various models of dependence including harm minimisation as the dominant philosophy in Australia will be explored. The basic pharmacology of commonly used drugs of dependence will be detailed. The subject will cover the key components of assessment and intervention for states of intoxication, overdose and withdrawal. Finally the primary purpose and evidence supporting current specific AOD treatment interventions will be outlined. Holistic health encompasses spirituality as well as the physical, social, and emotional wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander individuals and communities.
learning_outcomes: define the terms harm minimisation and abstinence;
identify between signs and symptoms of intoxication, overdose and withdrawal, including the ability to perform clinical observations; and
describe the general principles of intervention treatment models.
discuss and apply different models of dependence;
explain the key components of substance use: alcohol and other drug assessment;
demonstrate substance use: alcohol and other drug that places the client at risk of harm;

describe the trends and prevalence of substance use: alcohol and other drugs in both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and Australian society including its effects on the financial, social and environmental sustainability;

title: Introduction to Sport and Exercise Behaviour
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to a broad range of psychological theories and research related to human behaviour in sport and exercise settings. Students will explore how psychological factors influence individual involvement and performance in sport, exercise, and physical activity settings. Students will examine how participation in sport, exercise, and physical activity influences the psychological factors of the individuals involved, as well as analyse the complex interaction between individuals and their environment. This subject provides students with the ability to acquire skills and knowledge about sport and exercise psychology that can be applied as a coach, teacher, personal trainer, exercise leader, sports psychologist, sports rehabilitator, sports administrator or sports journalist.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise, evaluate and use selected theoretical and applied approaches to explain sport and exercise behaviour.
Demonstrate their competency in reading, writing, critically analysing, comprehending and discussing sport and exercise psychology literature.
Explain and critically analyse the complex interaction between individuals and the sport and exercise setting.
Analyse and explain key psychological outcomes of participation and performance in sport and exercise.
Analyse and explain key psychological factors influencing participation and performance in sport and exercise.

title: Introduction to Statistics
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will review the necessary mathematics and statistics prerequisite skills required by students about to study subjects including Business Statistics (QBM117), Scientific Statistics (STA201), Postgraduate Scientific Statistics (STA401/501), Mathematics and Statistics in Health Sciences (MTH135), Business Data Analysis (QBM120), Foundations of Psychology 2 (PSY102) and An Introduction to Research, Ethics and Reasoning (PSY115). The topics to be covered include basic numeracy, calculator skills, introductory algebra, straight line graphs, introductory probability and statistics.
learning_outcomes: Use a calculator confidently and correctly
Explain and apply methods used in descriptive statistics
Explain and apply basic concepts of probability
Explain and apply the concepts of basic algebra
Explain and apply the concepts of basic arithmetic
Plot and interpret straight line graphs

title: Introduction to Surveying
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces fundamental theories and practices in surveying. Topics include the concept of surveying, the use of surveying equipment, error analysis and post-processing the results; the geographic information system, and the modern development of surveying. Emphasis is on the practical application of surveying concepts and tools.
learning_outcomes: Use of basic surveying equipment and post-process data with error analysis.
Apply the theory and practice of basic surveying skills.
Understand the functions of the Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and recognise modern surveying tools.

title: Introduction to Tariff Classification
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject gives students a practical grounding in the Harmonized System Convention, which provides a common international method for coding, describing and classifying goods that can be used by all bodies that are involved in the movement of goods, including freight forwarders, insurance institutions, transport associations, importers and exporters.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a working knowledge of the functions of the committees that are responsible for the maintenance of the System.
Demonstrate an indepth understanding of the aims and objectives of the Harmonized System Convention.
Discuss and demonstrate their comprehension of the classification structure of the Harmonized System Convention.
Classify goods and justify their classification decisions by reference to the provisions of Interpretative Rules and the Legal Notes.
Classify parts and accessories according to the terms of the classification descriptions and by certain Legal Notes.

title: Introduction to Teacher Librarianship
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to the role of the teacher librarian and situates this role within the broader, evolving information landscape. Particular emphasis is placed on the teacher librarian as a conduit between the school and the outside world of information, the instructional role of the teacher librarian in supporting student learning outcomes, and working in collaboration with school community members to build effective school library programs and services. A range of information process and inquiry learning models are explored. Strategies for the effective integration across the curriculum of information literacy outcomes, including digital literacies, are also examined. Students are encouraged to become reflective practitioners, employing the research and professional literature and evidence-based practice to inform their vision and understanding of the teacher librarian role. This is the keystone subject of the course, and provides the foundation for the reflective practitioner experience throughout the course.
learning_outcomes: Identify recent educational developments that impact upon the role of the teacher librarian, and the importance of accountability, research, and evidence-based practice for informing school library programs and services.
Discuss key concepts in information literacy, such as effective search strategies, resource-based learning, inquiry-based learning, digital literacy, and information fluency.
Evaluate and apply a broad range of information process models.
Articulate an understanding of the changing information landscape, digital information and the impact this has on the role of the teacher librarian.
Explain the knowledge, skills and behaviours of a reflective practitioner.
Explain the roles of the teacher librarian, including that of information professional and instructional partner, engaged in collaborative practices.

title: Introduction to Teacher Librarianship
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to the role of the teacher librarian and situates this role within the broader, evolving information landscape. Particular emphasis is placed on the teacher librarian as a conduit between the school and the outside world of information, the instructional role of the teacher librarian in supporting student learning outcomes, and working in collaboration with school community members to build effective school library programs and services. A range of information process and inquiry learning models are explored. Strategies for the effective integration across the curriculum of information literacy outcomes, including digital literacies, are also examined. Students are encouraged to become reflective practitioners, employing the research and professional literature and evidence-based practice to inform their vision and understanding of the teacher librarian role. This is the keystone subject of the course, and provides the foundation for the reflective practitioner experience throughout the course.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an understanding of the changing information landscape, digital information and the impact this has on the role of the teacher librarian.
Explain the roles of the teacher librarian, including that of information professional and instructional partner, engaged in collaborative practices.
Explain the knowledge, skills and behaviours of a reflective practitioner.
Discuss key concepts in information literacy, such as effective search strategies, resource-based learning, inquiry-based learning, digital literacy, and information fluency.
Evaluate and apply a broad range of information process models.

Identify recent educational developments that impact upon the role of the teacher librarian, and the importance of accountability, research, and evidence-based practice for informing school library programs and services.

title: Introduction to the Information Professions
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to basic concepts in information studies, to the work of information professionals and the contexts of professional practice, including libraries, archives, records repositories and other information centres and organisations. Cultural, legal, technical, social, and ethical issues currently influencing the functions and operations of professional practice are explored, and information scholarship and research introduced. The subject will orient students to the BIS program and enable them to develop and refine their individual educational and professional objectives.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of some key factors related to information literacy and information seeking behaviour.
Describe how information is organised for, and retrieved by, information agency users.
Investigate and critically analyse libraries and information agencies in their historical, social, cultural, economic, and political contexts.
Demonstrate an understanding of the historical, social and legal issues emerging from the information society, and explain the implications of these for information professionals.
Understand basic IT terminology relevant to the information studies field and the role of IT in enabling the management of information.
Describe the basic concepts and core knowledge related to information studies and the information professions.
Identify the roles and functions of the various types of information agencies and the specific needs of their users.

title: Introduction to the Australian Legal System
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a foundation in the study of law. It includes a practical overview of the structure and origins of the Australian legal system and introduces the skills of legal reasoning and analysis. Students explore the concept of law, civil law and the common law. They also look at the development of judge-made and statute law (focusing on English and Australian legal history). The subject encompasses the relationship between courts and constitutional structures; the understanding and integration of principles of judicial reasoning and statutory interpretation; the place of Indigenous law in Australia; and the development and relevance of international law.
learning_outcomes: Present persuasive and informed arguments based on leading precedents.
Plan and apply effective strategies in legal research of case law and legislation based scenarios.
Identify and explain the facts pertaining to cases and ratio decided within the Australian judicial system.
Explain the adversarial system of justice including limitations such as access to justice.
Demonstrate an historical understanding of Indigenous social justice and the contemporary context of reconciliation in Australia.
Interpret statutes and common law and identify legal problems in scenarios and cases.
Demonstrate an understanding of knowledge pertaining to international law, with a focus on human rights awareness.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the sources of law in society and the process of law making including the place of customary law in Australia.

title: Introduction to the Qur'an and Islamic Worldviews
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the fundamental beliefs and practices, central themes, scriptural parables and ethical principles from the lens of the Qur'an which shape Islamic worldviews and ways of life. The subject explores the Qur'an content on the fundamental questions of life, existence, creation, afterlife, resurrection, human suffering, wellbeing and spirituality. This subject also situates the major themes of the Qur'an within a historical and theological context in relation to other major faith traditions. Students will be able to study Islam within an "non-confessional approach".
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the revelation, preservation and interpretation of the Qur'an.
Critically differentiate text from context, changing and unchanging dynamics of Islamic worldviews with Qur'anic interpretation.
Identify four essential themes of the Qur'an and how they are reflected in the Islamic worldviews.
Perform and demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of substantial work.
Analyse the context of the Qur'an and Islamic worldviews historically and theologically.
Critically evaluate the Qur'an's responses to the fundamental questions of life and existence such as creation, afterlife, resurrection, human suffering, wellbeing and spirituality.

title: Introduction to the Registered Nurse Profession
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to their identity as a Bachelor of Nursing student as they begin their transformation toward practice as a registered nurse. Students will establish a socially constructive learning environment, develop capacity for academic writing, searching journal databases and identifying and critiquing sources of evidence. Students will also explore the professional context of the registered nurse in Australia and essential concepts of person-centred care, clinical reasoning, safety and reflection as they prepare for their first professional experience placement subject.
learning_outcomes: Explain how the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) standards and codes, the International Council of Nurses (ICN) code of ethics and legislation relevant to the practice of the registered nurse underpin nursing practice.
Describe healthcare safety and quality standards and governance.
Apply beginning level academic skills, including academic writing, database searching and identifying appropriate evidence.
Describe therapeutic and person-centred communication approaches for interacting with people and families.
Explain concepts of person-centred care, clinical reasoning, critical thinking and theories that support nursing practice.
prerequisites: NUR101 : Transition from Enrolled Nurse to the Registered Nurse Profession

title: Introduction to the Web
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the major components of modern front-end Web development, including Web page content, presentation and behaviour. It provides the students with the coding skills to build structured HTML Web pages, and to control the formatting and behaviour of Web pages using CSS and JavaScript. It also underlays the context within which front-end and back-end web applications interact to build an overall Web experience.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the Document Object Model (DOM).
Design structured Web pages using headings, paragraphs, lists and tables.
Format Web page content using Cascaded Style Sheets (CSS).
Identify and explain the structure of the Web and the anatomy of Web pages.
Create simple Web pages using basic HTML text elements.
Use JavaScript to manipulate Web page content.

title: Introduction to Theatre Performance and Production
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the interdisciplinary study of theatre including the practical and theoretical aspects of staging live and mediated performance. It introduces strategies to manage performing arts practice and students develop their understanding of technical production roles and production planning. Students explore and apply a range of collaborative and organisational communication skills for theatre, performance and production.
learning_outcomes: Apply theoretical knowledge of performance and storytelling.
Demonstrate an understanding of production roles and arts project management.
Develop strategies for collaboration and problem-solving in a creative context.
Demonstrate an understanding of theatre workplace health and safety responsibilities.

title: Introduction to Transport Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principles, methods, and applications of transport engineering within civil engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including transportation planning, traffic engineering, transportation infrastructure, and sustainable transportation systems. Emphasis is placed on understanding the relationships between transportation and society, the environment, and urban development.
learning_outcomes: Perform basic road geometric design and earthwork volume calculations.
Discuss the fundamental principles and theories of transport engineering.
Apply transportation planning and management methodologies to analyse travel demand and the effectiveness of transportation alternatives.

title: Introduction to Veterinary Technology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Veterinary Technology provides an overview of the veterinary technology profession. It equips students with essential skills and foundational knowledge necessary for success in subsequent veterinary technology subjects. Students will develop their skills in academic literacy and numeracy, academic writing, library, referencing, and selecting suitable resources, together with animal behaviour, handling and welfare, and legal and ethical considerations for those working with animals. Students will develop their capacity to work professionally within a clinical setting including communication. Professional standards and reflection will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Outline fundamental concepts in animal behaviour and animal anatomy.

Demonstrate the behaviours, values and ethical standards expected of a novice professional during class activities through interactions with academic staff and peers as an individual or working in a team.
Present written work that displays appropriate information gathering from peer-reviewed and other credible sources, appropriately and correctly referenced.
Discuss the legal and ethical frameworks influencing animal use in society.
Demonstrate emerging professional communication skills in the educational setting.
Describe how animal behaviour can be measured in a range of animal species and how this information can be used to assess welfare for animals.
Use technical skills and animal behaviour theory to safely handle a range of animal species.
Apply new knowledge from the classroom to the practical classes.

title: Introduction to Underwriting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to insurance underwriting. It examines the knowledge and skills required to assess and evaluate risk against appropriate risk criteria.
learning_outcomes: Issue contracts of insurance.
Evaluate risk and underwrite business.
Discuss the principles of hazard assessment and risk transfer.

title: Introductory Chemistry 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Introductory Chemistry 1 is one of the suites of non-award micro-subjects offered on the Study link platform. This is the first of two foundation Chemistry subjects. The content introduces Chemistry to students who have not previously studied the topic and those needing to refresh their knowledge. Students are introduced to a basic model of atomic structure and apply that model to the first 20 elements to explain their properties and bonding. The naming conventions and writing of formulas for Ionic compounds are covered using a table of ions and students are also introduced to the naming of Organic compounds and the creation of polymers.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and name simple hydrocarbons and polymers.
Explain how different types of chemical bonds form.
Explain and apply the Bohr-Rutherford atomic model.
Describe how properties are related to chemical structure.

title: Introductory Chemistry 2
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Introductory Chemistry 2 is one of the suites of non-award micro-subjects offered on the Studylink platform. Students should first complete Introductory Chemistry 1. These Chemistry micro-subjects are designed for students who have not previously studied Chemistry or who need to refresh their knowledge. Students will be introduced to calculating molecular weights, the concept of the mole, and writing molecular and empirical formulas. Students will write and balance chemical equations leading to stoichiometric calculations. The nature of solutions, solubility and acids and bases will be covered in content and assessment.
learning_outcomes: Perform stoichiometric calculations.
Calculate concentrations of solutions in various situations.
Write balanced chemical equations.
Calculate pH in acids and bases.

title: Introductory Mathematics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for students with an elementary mathematics background who are planning to enrol in subjects requiring intermediate or higher numeracy skills, such as science, finance, teaching, computing and information technology. The subject reinforces calculation skills, basic algebra, working with formulae, applications of exponential and logarithmic functions, and introductory calculus.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and write about applications of mathematics in their field of study.
Plot and interpret graphs.
Calculate the sums of arithmetic and geometric series and use them in simple financial calculations.
Use exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions in applications.
Carry out calculations and use algebra accurately.
Use the basic rules of integration and calculate integrals of polynomial functions.
Use the basic rules of differentiation and calculate derivatives of elementary functions.
Use vectors in scientific applications.
prerequisites: MTH101: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications
MTH401: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Introductory Haematology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to haematology and examines the structural and functional attributes of cellular and non-cellular constituents of blood in health and disease states. Morphological and functional characteristics of the blood cells at different stages of production, differentiation and maturation are considered in detail. Also, the haemostatic system, which comprises primary haemostasis, secondary haemostasis and fibrinolytic system, is dealt with thoroughly. Furthermore, blood diseases including anaemias, leucocyte disorders (benign or malignant), and disorders of the haemostasis are discussed at clinical, pathophysiological and laboratory diagnostic levels. The subject is highly practice oriented and prepares the students to work in pathology laboratories. The subject includes a 4 day compulsory intensive school for distance students.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate and describe the development of blood cells, and comment on structure and functions of the blood- producing tissues/organs.
Classify and describe the disorders of the haemostatic system.
Name and classify the components of the haemostatic system and explain their functions.
Classify and explain the morphological and functional attributes of blood cells.
Classify and describe the disorders of blood cells.
Explain principles behind routine haematological tests.
Demonstrate high levels of academic communication and team working skills.
Demonstrate basic skills necessary to conduct routine haematological techniques.
Interpret the results of haematological tests.

title: Introductory Mathematics
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for students with an elementary mathematics background who are planning to enrol in subjects requiring intermediate or higher numeracy skills, such as science, finance, teaching, computing and information technology. The subject reinforces calculation skills, basic algebra, working with formulae, applications of exponential and logarithmic functions, and introductory calculus.
learning_outcomes: Use the basic rules of integration and calculate integrals of polynomial functions.
Use the basic rules of differentiation and calculate derivatives of elementary functions.
Use vectors in scientific applications.
Carry out calculations and use algebra accurately.
Plot and interpret graphs.
Calculate the sums of arithmetic and geometric series and use them in simple financial calculations.
Apply exponential and logarithmic laws, and examine the behaviour of population and decay.
Interpret and write about applications of mathematics in their field of study.
prerequisites: MTH401: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Introductory Physics
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide the minimum knowledge and concepts in physics required by a student who is enrolling into a typical first year tertiary physics subject. It will include modules on mechanics, heat, wave motion, light and sound, electricity and magnetism, and atomic and nuclear physics. The subject is particularly relevant to those students pursuing a range of science courses including the Medical Radiation Science undergraduate program.
learning_outcomes: Have a basic understanding of electricity and magnetism
Have a basic understanding of heat
Have a basic understanding of wave motion, light and sound
Have a basic understanding of mechanics
Have a basic understanding of atomic and nuclear physics

title: Introductory Medical Radiation Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to the diverse array of technology required for the medical radiation sciences. A basic technological introduction to x-ray production, radiation detection and radiation safety is undertaken. Students develop an understanding of the technological requirements of quality management, safety and standards. Students explore the principles of evidence-based practice, sourcing appropriate information and assessing levels of information accuracy and reliability. Students will plan and commence their professional portfolio to support their development in their chosen specialisation.
learning_outcomes: Identify and utilise effective communication skills in a variety of settings using a variety of media.
Describe and explain, at an introductory level, the principles of patient information management systems and 3D datasets for diagnostic image production.
Describe the role of the professional portfolio to support ongoing professional development (MRPBA Domain 4).
Describe commonly used qualitative and quantitative research methods for the purposes of evidence based practice (MRPBA Domain 4.1).

Demonstrate, at an introductory level, assessment and reflective skills in a range of contexts including clinical problem solving, research and empirical practice, and academic and professional discourse (MRPBA Domain 4).
Describe and explain, at an introductory level, the principles of medical radiation physics and instrumentation including X ray production and radiation detection (MRPBA Domain 1.3).
Explain and apply the principles of evidence based practice with specific reference to resolving clinical challenges (MRPBA Domain 4).
Recognise and describe radiation safety and risk management with specific reference to safe radiation practice (MRPBA Domain 5).

title: Introductory Statistics for the Social Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will review foundation skills in mathematics and statistics such as calculator skills, basic algebra, descriptive statistics, tables and graphs, sigma notation, and the normal distribution. The subject is particularly relevant to those students studying Foundations of Psychology 1 (PSY101) and Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology (PSY201).
learning_outcomes: Calculate mathematical formula correctly.
Understand and produce statistical graphs.
Use a calculator confidently and correctly.
Develop support networks.
Utilise services available at Charles Sturt University.
Use and understand the standard normal table.
Understand and apply basic methods used in descriptive statistics.

title: Introductory Structural Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces theoretical principles and fundamentals of structural engineering, focusing on linear elastic analysis of structural systems commonly encountered in civil engineering projects. Emphasis is on developing a fundamental understanding of structural behaviour and applying engineering principles to solve simple structural engineering problems.
learning_outcomes: Use manual and computer-based approach to design basic structural elements.
Apply fundamental principles of structural mechanics to analyse the behaviour of structural elements under various loading conditions.
Use linear structural analysis methods to determine internal forces, deflections, and stability of simple structural systems.

title: Investigating Criminology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to key concepts and methods in criminology. It explores the historical development of criminological knowledge, the role of criminologists, and major debates shaping current understandings of crime and justice. Students will examine how crime is defined, measured, and researched using both quantitative and qualitative data. Through case studies, current issues, and interactive learning, students will begin developing essential skills in critical thinking, argumentation, problem solving, and foundational research. This subject provides a solid base for further criminological study by equipping students with analytical tools and communication techniques essential to understanding and investigating crime in contemporary society.
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain key criminological concepts, methods, perspectives, and debates used to define and understand crime and criminal behaviour.
Identify and communicate existing criminological literature, research, and public and official perspectives on crime and the factors that shape them.
Communicate criminological ideas, findings, and arguments clearly and effectively in both academic and professional contexts.
Apply foundational research and analytical skills to investigate criminological questions using appropriate sources, methods, and ethical considerations.

title: Investigating Financial Crime - Prosecuting Financial Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the investigation of financial crimes and the significant impact that situational and historical contexts have on how modern financial investigations are conducted. Through sharing experiences, and the examination of case studies, students will explore the planning and conduct of civil and criminal investigations and the importance of communication during the active and post investigative phases, both as investigative tools and as a means of improving investigative capacity.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how historical investigations and societal context influence modern financial crime investigations.
Communicate investigative practice and experience to a range of professional audiences towards ongoing professional development.
Justify the use of alternative investigative approaches, from a range of professional settings, to conduct a financial crime investigation.
Plan a financial crime investigation that is framed using appropriate legal prescriptions and ethical best practice.

title: Investigation: Literacy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject the acquisition of oral language and the conditions supporting emergent literacy are considered within diverse social and cultural contexts. The central role of parents, carers and teachers in guiding language and emergent literacy through interactions with children is a special focus. The potential for learning and language development through dramatic play, music and movement is examined.
learning_outcomes: Understand the key role adults can play in enhancing or impeding children's language and literacy development.
Demonstrate knowledge of and ability to plan for emergent literacy in children.
Identify environments that enhance children's language and literacy development.
Understand and be able to explain teaching strategies which assist the development of children's talk, thinking and emergent literacy.
Analyse and describe children's oral language development.
Demonstrate awareness of promoting children's language and literacy through using a range of play-based learning experiences (e.g. dramatic play, music and movement).

title: Investigation: Mathematics, Science and Technology
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject presents the development of mathematical, scientific and technological concepts by young children within a socio-cultural theoretical framework informed by an inquiry stance. Science, mathematics and technology provide tools and contexts for processing concrete, perceptual and linguistically available information to form concepts and solve problems. Students will participate in a number of practical but theoretically based experiences in order to understand the kinds of social, linguistic and imaginative contexts which facilitate young children's mathematical, scientific and technological understanding.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate their skills in planning, implementing, evaluating and reflecting upon teaching and learning experiences with the potential for facilitating mathematics, science and technology understandings.
Demonstrate skills in creating learning communities in early childhood settings with the potential for facilitating mathematics, science and technology understandings.
Expanded and consolidated their own science, mathematics and technological knowledge, and the historical and cultural sources of that knowledge.
Explain and demonstrate specific communication and teaching strategies which support children's construction of mathematical, scientific and technological knowledge.
Access the human and technological resources most appropriate for exploring and examining all aspects of the subject.
Apply professional skills and knowledge in ways which will encourage children to investigate materials and ideas regardless of cultural background and other sources of diversity.
Identify and explain opportunities for spontaneous learning where mathematics, science and technology serve the purposes of investigating a phenomenon, question or problem.

Identify and explain the ways in which the integrative nature of young children's play and other informal contexts can support their construction of knowledge and acquisition and use of early mathematics, science and technology concepts.

title: Investigations Principles
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in depth exploration of the key concepts, theories and principles underpinning contemporary investigations within the public and private sectors. Students will experience the challenges that may arise in the course of investigations by engaging with real world case studies which examine the parameters of investigation strategies in the search for truth. The potential for organisational and personal prejudices and bias, ‘noble cause' corruption, and the impacts these may have on leadership, accountability, policy and decision-making are also explored. The subject also considers the efficacy of successful outcomes through the implementation of professional and ethical standards, practices and procedures employed during investigations, and the impact these may have on the evaluation and credibility of evidence.
learning_outcomes: Acknowledge and reflect on the significance that effective leadership, accumulative experience and critical thinking can have on investigations.
Critically analyse why heuristics, biases and (noble cause) corruption have the potential to manifest within contemporary investigations, and their subsequent significance.
Contribute to the progressive processes associated with investigative strategy development and implementation.
Demonstrate the communication, literacy, numeracy, research and digital skills required of a competent Investigator.
Lead and monitor ethical practice and process and reinforce the need for accountability in achieving successful investigative outcomes.

title: Investigative Interviewing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines interviewing as an investigative tool. The subject looks back at a number of miscarriages of justice which have served to shape contemporary interviewing models in use today. With a focus on memory and the factors that affect the reliability of evidence gained from vulnerable witnesses and other interviewees, the subject looks at the investigative interviewing core skills required to secure quality accounts from interviewees in an ethical and professional manner. Practically, the subject explores the 'PEACE' model framework of investigative interviewing and looks at how the 'Free Recall' and 'Conversation Management' styles of interviewing can be used in interviews with witnesses, victims and suspects. Finally, the subject looks closely at how interviews with persons of interest can be enhanced through tactical planning and the strategic use of evidence.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.

Compare and contrast the move from the traditional investigative interviewing methods to contemporary interviewing models, having regard to persons of interest and the strategic and tactical use of evidence.

Evaluate the move from traditional investigative interviewing methods to contemporary interviewing models, having regard to vulnerable interviewees, the fragility of memory and the cognitive interviewing principles.
Apply investigative interviewing theory using contemporary models and frameworks, to ethically gain accurate and reliable interview accounts from complainants, witnesses or persons of interest.

title: Investigative Practice 1A
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop investigative skills in line with the legal requirements of the NSW Police Force and the NSW criminal justice system. The subject introduces critical and logical thinking, crime scene processes, note-taking and develops statement preparation skills. The PEACE model for investigative interviewing of victims and witnesses is introduced. There is a component that examines information gathering and the submission of Police Intelligence Reports.
learning_outcomes: Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking framework in policing scenarios.
Perform basic level investigative functions applicable to the role of a General Duties Constable.
Perform basic crime scene processes and functions.
Explain the importance of information and intelligence gathering and dissemination in the policing environment.
Explain the PEACE model of investigative interviewing relating to willing/cooperative participants at an introductory level.
Explain the investigative process applicable to the NSW Police Force.

title: Investigative Practice 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop investigative skills in line with the legal requirements of the NSW Police Force and the NSW Criminal Justice System. The subject introduces critical and logical thinking, crime scene processes, note-taking and develops statement preparation skills required for the compilation of a Brief of Evidence. The PEACE model for investigative interviewing of victims, witnesses and offenders is introduced. There is a component that examines information gathering and the submission of Police Intelligence Reports.
learning_outcomes: Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking framework in policing scenarios.
Compile a basic Brief of Evidence in accordance with the standards of the NSW Police Force and the criminal justice system.
Explain the importance of information and Intelligence gathering and dissemination in the policing environment.
Explain the PEACE model of investigative interviewing at an introductory level.
Perform basic crime scene processes and functions.
Explain the investigative process applicable to the NSW Police Force.
Perform basic level investigative functions applicable to the role of a General Duties Constable.

title: Investigative Practice 1B
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop investigative skills in line with the legal requirements of the NSW Police Force and the NSW criminal justice system. The subject continues a focus on critical and logical thinking, note-taking, developing statement preparation skills and introduces the compilation of a Brief of Evidence. The PEACE model for investigative interviewing of suspects is introduced.
learning_outcomes: Compile a basic Brief of Evidence in accordance with the standards of the NSW Police Force and the NSW criminal justice system.
Explain the PEACE model of investigative interviewing relating to unwilling/uncooperative participants at an introductory level.
Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking decision-making framework in policing scenarios.
Perform basic level investigative functions applicable to the role of a General Duties Constable.
prerequisites: PPP154: Communication and Police Professional Standards, Conduct and Values 1A

title: Investigative Practice 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject revises previously learnt interview techniques and processes and examines further interviewing techniques for victims, witnesses and suspects. There is a focus on Electronically Recorded Interview of a Suspected Person (ERISP). The subject examines the additional legal and mandatory requirements of police when investigating the offences of domestic violence, traffic offences, larceny and its associated offences, i.e. break enter and commit serious indictable offence, fraud, receiving and goods in custody. The preparation of a Brief of Evidence is an essential skill for an operational general duties police officer. This subject addresses all the details that police are required to include in a Brief of Evidence.
learning_outcomes: Compile a Brief of Evidence in accordance with the standards of the NSW Police Force and the NSW criminal justice system.
Apply systematic intelligence gathering processes as the basis of intelligence led policing in scenarios.
Explain the investigative process applicable to the NSW Police Force as applied to these prevalent offences.
Undertake investigative and recording functions applicable to the role of General Duties Constable with regards to these prevalent offences.
Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking decision-making framework in policing scenarios.
Utilise the PEACE model of investigative interviewing of victims, witnesses and suspects at a basic level in practical simulations.

title: Investments
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The principal focus of this subject is on the financing and risk management aspects of corporate finance, and security and portfolio analysis. Valuation techniques introduced in Financial Management are applied to various investment situations incorporating current theories in finance.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively about security analysis and portfolio management.
Solve financial problems within the context of a dynamic market place.
Demonstrated financial research and analytical skills.
Undertake financial research.

title: Investments Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The principal focus of this subject is the financing and risk management aspects of corporate finance, and security and portfolio analysis. The subject, incorporating current theories in finance, applies basic corporate valuation techniques to various investment types.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in financial research and analytical skills.
Communicate effectively about security and portfolio analysis.
Critically discuss and evaluate features of securities and security markets.
Solve financial problems under conditions of uncertainty.

title: iOS App Development
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will design, create, and develop native apps for Apple mobile devices using both the Objective-C and Swift programing languages. You will learn how to utilize the tools and application programming interfaces (APIs) required to build applications for the iPhone and iPad platform using the iOS software development kit (SDK). You will also learn to prepare apps for submission to the App Store.
learning_outcomes: Implement delegates, callbacks, and handlers for interactive user interface elements.
Critically analyse and compare the different types of view controller and navigation techniques and when to use them.
Design, create and test multi-touch graphical user interfaces.
Communicate with external APIs and store data locally on the device.
Publish applications for both test and deployment to the Apple AppStore.
Design and develop international applications for Apple's iOS platform.
Develop flexible layouts for multiple device resolutions.

title: Islam and Policing in the Modern World
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a strong foundational knowledge and understanding of the history, culture and contemporary challenges of Islam. Students will apply their developing knowledge of Islam and Islamic culture to inform their professional practice when understanding and applying policy, regulation and enforcement strategies.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the current direction of Islam and its impact on future legislation, policies and practices.
Identify the historical and cultural aspects of Islam that may be influencing contemporary law enforcement policies and/or other relevant sectors.
Demonstrate the communication, literacy, numeracy, research and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Analyse the historical and cultural aspects of Islam to identify which factors may be impacting on the relationships between Islam, Muslim persons, and authorities in various circumstances.

title: Islam in Politics, Society and Media
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces Islam and Muslims' relationship with politics and society. As a world religion with over 1.8 billion followers, Islam plays an important role in the world as well as national and international politics. Consequently, Islam and Muslims are on the news on a daily basis. The subject critically examines the Islamic sources, historical precedence and the socio-political climate currently at force in the Muslim world. While interrogating how Islam has been politicised and how politics has been Islamicised across different parts of the world, this subject unpacks Islam and Muslim portrayal in the global media. By providing a range of case studies from different parts of the Muslim world and by analysing Muslim minorities in the West, this subject examines Muslims' view and practice and their engagement with secularism and liberal democracy.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the international political tensions in relation to global socio-political conflicts and turmoils.
Critically examine Muslims' engagement with politics and portrayal in media as minorities in multi-faith and multicultural societies.
Critically compare and contrast the trajectory of democracy and secularism in the range of case studies covered from around the Muslim world.
Develop a grounded understanding of Islam's relationship with politics, secularism and liberal democracy from a theological, theoretical, historical and contemporary perspective.
Adapt and apply analytical tools to explain the emergence of contemporary Islamic movements and Islamic parties in relation to their socio-political circumstances.
Perform independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of substantial work.

title: Islam in the Modern World
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses contemporary issues facing Islam and Muslims in the modern world, from personal to public and local to international spheres. This subject sheds light on topics such as jihad, extremism and shari'ah, as well as examining heated debates about Islam and Muslims on topics like women's rights, Islamism as a political ideology and bioethical matters. Before delving into the aforementioned topics, colloquial and terminological meanings are delineated. Then the Islamic basis for the issues is provided by addressing the Qur'an and Sunnah. Giving historical, cultural and socio-political circumstances, issues are weighed in the contemporary local and global contexts. This subject provides well-grounded perspectives about the most debated and most controversial topics on Islam and Muslims.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate cultural and socio-political impacts on interpreting Islam, Islamic law and ethics in the contemporary world.
Provide informed views about the most debated and most controversial topics on Islam and Muslims.
Participate in and conduct an academic debate on Islam in the modern world.
Understand the impact of contemporary phenomena like modernity, postmodernity, acculturation and globalisation in the Muslim world.
Examine the Islamic basis of phenomena, issues and arguments about Islam.
Produce a comprehensive view about the proposed subjects.
Develop a scholarly response to the Muslims' contemporary challenges and issues.
Analyse the influence of contemporary issues over Muslims in the personal, local and global contexts.

title: Islam in the Modern World
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses contemporary issues facing Islam and Muslims in modern life from personal to public and local to international spheres. It sheds light on controversial topics like jihad, shari’a and extremism; examines the significant debates around Islam and Muslims such as women’s rights, Islamism as a political ideology and bioethical discussions; and explores the experiences of Muslims practising Islam under current local and global circumstances. The subject approaches these topics by delineating and clarifying colloquial and terminological meanings of key concepts and provides the Islamic bases of the issues in reference to the Qur’an and Sunnah. Giving historical, cultural and socio-political contexts and perspectives, the topics are weighed in contemporary local and global scales. Overall, the subject provides nuanced understanding of Islam in the modern world, drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives and critical analysis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the impact of contemporary phenomena such as modernity, postmodernity, acculturation and globalisation for Muslims, Muslim communities and societies.
Develop a scholarly response to contemporary challenges and issues related to Islam and Muslims.
Critically evaluate cultural and socio-political impacts on interpreting Islam, Islamic law and ethics in the contemporary world.
Critically analyse the influence of contemporary issues on Muslims in personal, local and global contexts.
Demonstrate independent research and critical writing skills.
Participate in and conduct an academic debate on Islam in the modern world.

Explore Muslims’ early roots in Australia dating back to their intermarriages with Indigenous women, their contribution to building of the Australian nation and develop an insight about the shared racism experiences that are still prevalent in the contemporary Australian society.

title: Islam Through Western Eyes
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the major approaches, issues, controversies and differing perspectives in the study of Islam and Muslim society's Western thought, scholarship and public opinion. It provides insight into the various classical and modern texts that discuss Islam 'through Western eyes.' Students explore the complex historical, socio-political and ideological factors which impact the way Islam and Muslims are viewed in the West.
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically colonisation of the Muslim world and its impact on Muslim societies.
Evaluate how Islam and Muslims are perceived in the West.
Demonstrate an understanding of the medieval discourses developed about Islam and Muslim societies.
Demonstrate an understanding of orientalism and its role and development to modern times.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of the Western view of Islam, in particular the Australian context.

title: Islam in the Modern World
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses contemporary issues facing Islam and Muslims in the modern life from personal to public and local to international spheres. It sheds light on controversial topics like jihad, extremism, fundemantalism and shari'ah; examines the significant debates around Islam and Muslims such as women rights, Islamism as a political ideology and bioethical discussions; and explores Muslims' experience in living Islam under current local and global circumstances. The subject approaches these topics by delineating and clarifying colloquial and terminological meanings of key concepts and provides the Islamic bases of the issues in reference to the Quran and Sunnah. Giving historical, cultural and socio-political circumstances and perspectives of modern scholarship, issues are weighed in the contemporary local and global contexts.
learning_outcomes: Relate critically between individual issues and develop a comprehensive perspective.
Develop a scholarly response to contemporary challenges and issues around Islam and Muslims.
Critically analyse phenomena, issues and arguments about Islam and respond from an Islamic framework.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the impact of contemporary phenomena such as modernity, postmodernity, acculturation and globalisation in the Muslim world.
Participate in and conduct an academic debate on Islam in the modern world.
Evaluate critically cultural and socio-political impacts on interpreting Islam, Islamic law and ethics in the contemporary world.
Analyse critically the influence of contemporary issues over Muslims in personal, local and global contexts.
Demonstrate independent research and writing skills.

title: Islam: Morality and Etiquette in Daily Life
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the concepts ofakhlaq (morality) and adab (etiquette) as the fourth dimension of Islam. It highlights the importance of their application in demonstrating human virtue and perfection. The subject commences withakhlaq and adab in the everyday life of a Muslim, followed by immediate family, and then other common relationships such as neighbours, work colleagues and friends. One's relationship with the environment, animals and worship are also covered. An important part of this subject is to study the traditional understanding of akhlaq and adab through the lens of the the Quran, Hadith and the views of the traditional scholars. The traditional understanding of each type of interpersonal relation will then be analysed critically, considering the benefits and the challenges of their application in the contemporary context.
learning_outcomes: Articulate critically the traditional understanding of akhlaq (morality) and adab (etiquette) in various interpersonal relation settings.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the role of religion in developing personal character.
Evaluate critically the application of the traditional understanding of akhlaq (morality) and adab (etiquette) in today's world.
Understand and apply critically the Islamic disciplines of akhlaq (morality) and adab (etiquette).
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.

title: Islamic Chaplaincy
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to educate and train students to provide pastoral care in the community setting. It explores both theoretical and applied aspects of clinical pastoral education. It is located at the intersection of Islamic theology of caring, grief and loss. The subject emphasises multidimensional assessments and the different applications of spiritual, therapeutic, supportive and educational strategies for individuals.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss Islamic concepts related to suffering, sickness, loneliness, grief and loss.
Explain spiritual care in Islam and use a variety of methods and sources for spiritual care.

Critically discuss various practical perspectives of spiritual care and its place in relation to Islamic disciplines, including tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), fiqh (jurisprudence), philosophy, ethics and Islamic spirituality.
Reflect critically on the relational dynamics occurring in pastoral conversations.
Articulate and work within the boundaries of Islamic chaplaincy role.
Employ a variety of pastoral interventions including empathy.

title: Islamic Economy, Banking and Finance
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject offers a comprehensive introduction to the principles of Islamic economy, banking and finance. It focuses on the underlying principles of economic justice and analyses the distinctive features of Islamic banking and finance. Students will evaluate the various modes of personal and business finance solutions through examination of pertinent primary and secondary Islamic sources. Additionally, the subject includes a study of the global progression of Islamic finance, along with an exploration of the challenges and opportunities inherent in the implementation of Islamic banking and finance within the context of Australia.
learning_outcomes: Describe the significant phases of global Islamic banking development and identify opportunities and challenges related to Islamic banking and finance in the Australian market.
Apply critical thinking and problem-solving skills in the application of Islamic banking and finance.
Identify and explain the features of Islamic commercial contracts, and discuss the regulatory and governance framework of Islamic banking.
Critically analyse and discuss the key principles underlying Islamic economics, including principles of economic justice, and distinguish these from conventional banking and finance practices.
Describe the Islamic legal rationale and framework governing Islamic banking and financial transactions, and analyse the essential features of Islamic financial solutions.

title: Islamic Economy, Banking and Finance
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an intensive introduction to the principles of Islamic economy, banking and finance. It focuses on the underlying principles of economic justice and analyses the features of Islamic banking and finance. Several modes of personal and business finance solutions will be outlined and evaluated by considering the relevant primary and secondary Islamic sources. The subject will also cover the global development of Islamic finance, the challenges and opportunities associated with Islamic banking and finance in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Describe the significant phases of the development of Islamic banking across the globe.
Explain and analyse the essential features of Islamic banking and financial solutions.
Identify and discuss the key principles underlying Islamic economics and the principles of economic justices.
Identify and explain the features of Islamic commercial contracts.
Distinguish and critically analyse the differences between Islamic and conventional banking and finance.
Identify and describe the opportunities and challenges of Islamic banking and finance related to the Australian market.
Describe the Islamic legal rationale and framework that govern the Islamic banking and financial transactions.
Describe and discuss the Islamic banking regulatory and governance framework.
Use critical thinking and apply problem solving skills in the application of Islamic banking and finance.

title: Islamic Family Law and Society
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on applying Islamic law to the study of family law and its branches. The perspectives of Sunni legal schools are analysed when covering family law topics, such as the conditions for a valid marriage; dissolution of a marriage; parenting and children; custody and guardianship; and alimony and maintenance. These matters are discussed in conjunction with how they evolved in the contemporary world and within a Western context. Consideration is given to the views of classical and contemporary Muslim scholars regarding how legal rulings are justified and supported with the Quran, Sunnah and jurisprudential (fiqh) literature as well as the social context of their time. Challenges and solutions to contemporary applications of Islamic family law related matters are critically analysed.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast Islamic family law and Australian statutory law in related areas.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the plurality of thought, customs and application of family law within Muslim societies in the classic era and contemporary world.
Evaluate the challenges of applying the principles of Islamic family law in statutory legislation.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, and written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Critically analyse legal conditions in topics of Islamic family law.
prerequisites: ISL411: Methodology of Islamic Law (Usul al-Fiqh)

title: Islamic Family Law
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the application of Islamic law to the study of Islamic family law. The perspective of the Hanafi legal school will be considered when covering topics such as the conditions for a valid marriage, dissolution of marriage, parenting and children, custody and guardianship, and alimony and maintenance. In addition, appropriate legal rulings of other schools will also be discussed and evaluated critically. Finally, the similarities and differences between Islamic law and Australian statutory legislation relating to family law matters will be considered.
learning_outcomes: Explain and analyse critically the Islamic law on dissolution of marriage.
Understand critically the plurality of thought, custom and application of family law within Muslim societies.
Articulate critically the challenges of applying the principles of Islamic family law in statuary legislation.
Explain and analyse critically the requirements for a valid marriage contract in Islamic law.
Explain and analyse critically Islamic law on custody, guardianship alimony and maintenance.
Compare and contrast Islamic family law and Australian statutory law in related areas.
prerequisites: ISL211: Usul al-Fiqh (Methodology of Islamic Law)

title: Islamic Family Law and Society
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on studying Islamic family law and its branches. The perspectives of sunni legal schools are explored when covering family law topics, such as the conditions for a valid marriage; dissolution of a marriage; parenting and children; custody and guardianship; and alimony and maintenance. These matters are discussed in conjunction with how they evolved in the contemporary world and within a Western context. Consideration is given to the views of classical and contemporary Muslim scholars regarding how legal rulings are justified and supported with the Qur’an, sunnah and fiqh (jurisprudential) literature as well as the social context of their time. Challenges and solutions to contemporary applications of Islamic family law-related matters are also critically analysed.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate independent research, organisation, and written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Evaluate the challenges of applying the principles of Islamic family law in statutory legislation.
Compare and contrast Islamic family law and Australian statutory law in related areas.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the plurality of thought, customs and application of family law within Muslim societies in the classic era and contemporary world.
Critically analyse legal conditions in topics of Islamic family law.
prerequisites: ISL512: Methodology of Islamic Law (Usul al-Fiqh)

title: Islamic History: Caliphate Era
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the history of Muslim societies and civilisations from the time of the death of Prophet Muhammad to the end of the Caliphate era. The periods of Rightly Guided Caliphs, the Umayyad Empire, the Abbasid Empire and the Ottoman Empire will be studied, with a focus on the significant historic events which took place during the Caliphate era. The intellectual, economic, social and cultural aspects of the Islamic civilisations will be explored, particularly the contribution to science during the golden era. The decline of the Muslim world will also be critically evaluated.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically how Crusades and the Mongol invasion of the Muslim world produced a new world order.
Discuss critically the internal and external factors responsible for the decline of the Muslim world.
Analyse critically the effects of the end of the Caliphate.
Evaluate critically the Muslim contribution to science and human civilisation.
Understand critically the major events of the Rightly Guided era and the first schism.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the intellectual, cultural, social and economic scale of the Islamic civilisation.

title: Islamic History: Caliphate Era
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject critically discusses the history of Muslim societies and civilisations from the death of Prophet Muhammad to the end of the Caliphate era. The periods of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, Umayyad Empire, Abbasid Empire, Ottoman Caliphate and other major sultanates will be studied. There will be particular focus on the major historic events as well as the intellectual, economic, social and cultural aspects of the Islamic civilisations. The Muslim contribution to science and civilisation will be evaluated critically. The decline of the Muslim world will also be analysed.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the intellectual, cultural, social and economic scale of the Islamic civilisation.
Critically discuss internal and external factors responsible for the rise and decline of the Muslim world from the 15th to 19th centuries.
Critically understand the major events of the Rightly Guided era and the first schism in Islamic history.
Critically evaluate how the Crusades and the Mongol invasion of the Muslim world produced a new world order.
Critically evaluate the Muslim contribution to science and human civilisation.

title: Islamic Law and Practice in the Contemporary World
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to Islamic law and the related issues in the contemporary world. It covers the development of principles, methods, and schools of law, and discusses Islamic law in the modern period. The implementation of Islamic law in the contemporary context, reform, renewal and change in Islamic law are also addressed. The related challenges in the modern period and the debates on re-interpretation of Islamic law will be explored, together with the accommodation of Islamic law in Muslim societies, and reflections of these issues for Muslim minorities in the west.
learning_outcomes: Discuss critically the reform of Islamic law in the modern period.
Demonstrate an understanding of the development of Islamic law, its sources and classical schools.
Demonstrate an understanding of the various components of Islamic Law including family and criminal laws.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the application of Islamic law in a contemporary context.
Analyse critically the relationship between Islamic law and secular law in the Australian context.
Discuss critically the implication of the adoption of Islamic law by Muslim minorities living in the West.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of Islamic law on minorities living in the Muslim world.

title: Islamic Jurisprudence of Five Pillars
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the study of Islamic law or jurisprudence (fiqh) relating to the five pillars of Islam - the declaration of faith (shahadah), the daily prescribed prayers (salat), fasting during the month of Ramadan (sawm), purifying alms (zakat), and the pilgrimage (hajj) - together with the textual evidence for the basis of the rulings. The rituals related to these practices will be studied together with the criteria and method for practice. Physical cleansing in Islam will also addressed. The Hanafi school of Islamic law will be the primary school studied, however, views and evidence from Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools of law will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Articulate critically the jurisprudence (fiqh) related to the practice of the five pillars of Islam.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
