Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the ritual cleansing process needed for different circumstances and different practices.
Analyse critically the evidence for the practice of the five pillars of Islam.
Show an in-depth understanding of the rituals involved in individual, congregational, Friday, eid and funeral ritual prayers.

title: Islamic Studies Honours Project/Dissertation
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This is a research subject in which the student writes a dissertation on a topic approved by an appointed supervisor, showing awareness of scholarly debate and involving critical analysis of relevant materials in one specialist Islamic Studies field. The dissertation should demonstrate the student's capacity to assemble material, argue a case at an advanced level, and demonstrate critical thinking and interpretive judgement in developing new understanding in Islamic Studies. The dissertation is written over two sessions and is to be a minimum of 15,000 and a maximum of 20,000 words in length.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced critical understanding of a specialist Islamic Studies field.
Present a clear and coherent exposition of knowledge and ideas in their chosen area of research.
Demonstrate critical thinking and interpretive judgement in developing new understanding in their field of study.
Develop an appropriate bibliography.
Demonstrate advanced competence in methods of Islamic Studies research.
Plan and execute a substantial scholarly research project with clarity and independence.

title: Islamic Psychology: Human Behaviour and Experience
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the fundamental sub-disciplines and theories in psychology and critically evaluates these theories from Islamic perspectives. The sub-disciplines of contemporary psychology including health, behavioural, developmental, personality, social and cognitive psychology are analysed using the latest research and evidence. The subject also includes Islamic perspectives in relations to human nature, experiences and behaviour. Parallels between contemporary psychological perspectives and Islamic psychology are explored.
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of psychological theories and Islamic psychological principles to various situations.
Discuss the sub-disciplines of contemporary psychological theories.
Critically analyse contemporary psychological issues in comparison to Islamic psychology perspectives.
Explain contemporary psychology as a discipline.
Explain the social and cultural-religious influences in the development of psychological theories and practices.
Identify and compare individual and cultural-religious differences.
Describe the procedures of psychological scientific inquiry.

title: Islamic Studies: Methodology and Sources
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject covers those research strategies and methods of data collection most suited to the field of Islamic Studies and its sub-disciplines. It provides an overview of contexts within which enquiry is undertaken, and introduces candidates to the role and potential of research in the specific discipline of Islamic Studies in relation to contemporary issues and/or topics which intersect with social and political sciences. The subject discusses and evaluates sources which are considered essential for the various sub-disciplines of Islamic Studies. There is also focus on research traditions and paradigms relevant to the candidate's discipline, and the nature of the research process, including planning and designing a research project.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of qualitative and quantitative research methodologies and their application to the field of Islamic Studies.
Demonstrate familiarity with the role and potential of research in the field of Islamic Studies and/or its discipline areas.
Critically apply knowledge gained to define and refine their proposed area of study.
Demonstrate the research skills and expertise necessary to prepare a Bachelors Honours dissertation or Portfolio.

Demonstrate a critical understanding of the ethical issues in research and their particular relevance to Islamic Studies, including recognising the significance of consent, confidentiality and other ethical considerations in relation to research.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the professional contexts within which the enquiry is undertaken.
Demonstrate in-depth awareness of the main sources, classical and contemporary, in their chosen field of research.

title: Islamic Theology: Classical to Contemporary Thought
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses usul al-din (systematic Islamic theology) as a foundational discipline in Islamic faith and its intellectual discourse. Islamic theology is founded on the creedal principles of the Islamic faith, which establishes the conditions of belief listed as the essential articles identified by the Qur’an and Prophet Muhammad. Theological analysis of the Islamic creed includes key topics such as the existence of God; names and attributes of God; the relationship between God and humans; the scope of God's power; the efficacy of His decree; prophethood and eschatology. These key concepts of Islamic theology will be studied according to the Ash'ari, Maturidi, Mu’tazila and Jabriyya schools of thought. This subject also examines and discusses the development of Islamic theology in response to historical events until the present day. Contemporary theological issues such as existence of God, evidence for resurrection and dealing with theodicy and suffering will be critically analysed and studied in the context of the traditional and contemporary scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss the views of major theological schools such as Ashari, Maturidi, Jabriyya and Mu’tazilite.
Critically discuss eschatological concepts in Islamic theology.
Demonstrate independent research organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of substantial work.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of Islamic theological positions on theodicy, suffering and evil and evidence for life after death.
Demonstrate comprehensive understanding of the concept of God in Islamic theology.

title: Islamic Theology: Classical to Contemporary Thought
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses Islamic theology as the foundational discipline in Islamic faith and its intellectual discourse. Key theological topics such as existence of God, names and attributes of God; the relationship between God and humans; the scope of God's power; the efficacy of His decree; prophecy and eschatology will be studied according to the mainstream Ash'ari and Maturidi theological perspectives. This subject will also discuss the development of Islamic theology in response to historical events until the present day. Contemporary theological issues such as existence of God, evolution theory, proof of resurrection and dealing with theodicy and suffering will be critically analysed and studied in the context of the traditional and contemporary scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of Islamic theological positions on evolution theory, theodicy, proof of life after death.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the concept of God in Islamic theology.
Discuss critically eschatological concepts in Islamic theology.
Discuss critically the major Islamic theological schools such as Ashari, Maturidi and Mutazilite.

title: Islamic Worldview
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the fundamental beliefs, practices, spiritual concepts, values and perspectives that shape the Islamic worldview. It focuses on how the primary texts of Islam, the Qur'an and narrations (hadith) attributed to Prophet Muhammad, cover these themes together with the views of classical and modern Muslim scholars and theologians. In particular, the monotheism of Islam, six essentials of beliefs, five pillars of Islam and Islam's views on human nature, life, universe and the Islamic response to the question of suffering are discussed.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate critically the fundamental social values of Islam.
Discuss critically the fundamental beliefs, practices, spiritual concepts, values and perspectives that shape the Islamic worldview.
Demonstrate an understanding of the Islamic religious practices and key Islamic spiritual concepts.
Carry out independent research using scholarly sources in Islamic studies.
Demonstrate an understanding of the Islamic view of monotheism.
Articulate critically the purpose of the creation of the universe and humankind in accordance with the Islamic worldview.

title: Islamic Worldview and Faith Essentials
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of Islamic fundamental beliefs and worldview with particular reference to the Qur'an and the Prophetic narrations (Hadith). This subject focuses primarily on the six essential articles of the Islamic creed and offers a theological analysis that includes the views of various schools of Islamic theology. The modules in the subject will address the Islamic concept of God and understanding of human nature, the creation story according to the Qur'an, the unseen world, revelation, prophethood and the Prophet Muhammad, and other fundamental Islamic doctrines and beliefs.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Explain the six essential beliefs of Islam.
Articulate the relationship that exists between the fundamental beliefs of Islam.
Sight textual evidence (Qur'an and hadith ) for the beliefs of Islam.
Explain the Islamic worldview.

title: Islamic Worldview and Theology
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a detailed coverage of Islamic fundamental beliefs, creed, theology and worldview with particular reference to the Qur'an and hadith as primary sources. The Islamic concept of God and the understanding of human nature will be addressed, together with the creation story according to the Qur'an. The unseen world, revelation, prophethood, the Prophet Muhammad and the question of theodicy and suffering are addressed. The approach is a balance between textual basis of theology and rational argumentation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically arguments and textual evidence (Qur'an and hadith) provided for the beliefs of Islam.
Discuss critically the relationship between the fundamental beliefs of Islam.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the Islamic worldview, six essentials of belief and mainstream creedal formulations.

title: Islamic Worldview and Theology
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides detailed coverage of the creedal fundamentals of the Islamic faith and worldview with references to the Qur'an and hadith as primary sources. It explores the essential articles of the Islamic faith from a theological perspective and supported by kalam methodology. The subject includes analysis of the Islamic concept of God and understanding of human nature, together with the creation narrative of the Qur'an. Gayb (the unseen world), wahy (divine revelation), nubuwwah (prophethood), the Prophet Muhammad and qadar (divine destiny) are examined in detail. The philosophical problem of theodicy and suffering are also critically analysed in this subject. The approach is a balance between textual basis of theology and rational argumentation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the Islamic theology and worldview, the six essentials of belief and mainstream creedal formulations.
Critically discuss the relationship between the fundamental beliefs of Islam.
Develop independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Critically analyse the key concepts of Islamic theology and creed.
Critically analyse arguments and textual evidence (Qur'an, hadith and kalam arguments) provided for the creedal beliefs of Islam.

title: Issues in Ageing and Pastoral Studies: Project
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to undertake theological reflection on ageing through a 10,000 word research project related to an issue in ageing and pastoral studies in which the student advances theoretical and/or practical foundations for ageing, spirituality and pastoral care concerns. It builds on and applies the foundations and methods acquired in THL530 Social Research Methods for Pastoral Studies.
learning_outcomes: Validate awareness and sensitivity to ethical issues arising from the project in ageing and pastoral studies.
Demonstrate effective reference and critical engagement with the relevant literature.
Demonstrate a high order of skill in planning and implementing a research project.
Produce a thorough, carefully reasoned report which demonstrates an indepth understanding of a specific area of knowledge or inquiry.
Demonstrate an advanced ability to communicate and contextualise the ageing and pastoral studies project.

title: Issues in Ageing and Pastoral Studies: Project
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to undertake theological reflection on ageing through a 10,000 word research project related to an issue in ageing and pastoral studies in which the student advances theoretical and/or practical foundations for ageing, spirituality and pastoral care concerns. It builds on and applies the foundations and methods acquired in THL530 Social Research Methods for Pastoral Studies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective reference and critical engagement with the relevant literature.
Demonstrate an advanced ability to communicate and contextualise the ageing and pastoral studies project.
Demonstrate a high order of skill in planning and implementing a research project.
Validate awareness and sensitivity to ethical issues arising from the project in ageing and pastoral studies.
Produce a thorough, carefully reasoned report which demonstrates an indepth understanding of a specific area of knowledge or inquiry.

title: Issues in Bibliographic Access
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines key issues involved in contemporary library cataloguing and the application of bibliographic standards to a wide range of resources and user contexts. The standards studied, both practically and theoretically, include Resource Description and Access (RDA), MARC 21 and BIBFRAME, Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) and Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC), covering both bibliographic and authority control. Students learn how such standards can be optimally employed in particular, local environments, and to critically evaluate policy and practice with reference to theoretical models such as those originating from the Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records (FRBR) report.
learning_outcomes: Assess the appropriateness of conceptual frameworks used to support the development of bibliographic standards and practice.
Develop local cataloguing policy with reference to specific user and library contexts.
Apply key bibliographic standards with professional judgement.
Appraise the value and functions of bibliographic and authority control.
Critically discuss key issues affecting contemporary cataloguing practice.

title: Issues in Contemporary Art
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to bring the student's study of art history up to the present. Assuming that history is what is past and has been recorded, it deals with what is happening now, and may or may not become history. It examines the extent, the functions, and the sources of funding and support for contemporary art, and how these things are shaped by practitioners, critics, theorists, journals, the popular press, and the public. Current debates about what to fund and place in galleries, the awarding of prizes, the value of the past and the place of different cultures and ideologies will be looked at. Rather than seeking definitive answers, the course will identify issues and canvass various points of view.
learning_outcomes: Explain and defend their own work and position.
Demonstrate an understanding and reply to the arguments of both "Philistines" and extreme elitists.
Follow and participate in, debate about the role of the artist and art in contemporary society.

title: Issues in Breast Imaging
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to encourage a broader understanding of breast imaging issues and their implications for practice. The subject introduces principles and suggests ways to enhance and develop skills and knowledge that will assist the students' effective practice. This subject focuses on consumer centred breast care within a multidisciplinary team environment. Topics include effective communication and counselling, law and ethics, environmental health and safety, primary health care, information sharing and health promotion as relevant to breast screening and breast care and exercises aimed at preparing the student for their future roles as mentors and educators. Students will also explore topics such as evidence-based mammography practice, the sociology of mammography, cultural safety, security and humility when working with women identifying as being from a First Nations or culturally and linguistically diverse background, or with women with disability.
learning_outcomes: Apply the psychological basis of mammography care and relate to practice those aspects of care and understanding required to deal appropriately with a client who has a disability, breast disease, or the possibility of breast disease.
Critical reflection on core elements of mammography practice to reduce the discomfort of clients being x-rayed, both physically and emotionally.
Analyse, evaluate and reflect on published research and be able to relate evidence-based breast imaging research to practice.

Demonstrate the ability to make a critically informed judgment on aspects of the quality of care delivered by different professional groups working in local breast care services from the perspective of the clients requesting or requiring the care.

title: Issues in Dementia Care and Communication
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject builds advanced professional knowledge and skills in communication and supporting people with dementia in community and residential care contexts. Students will independently research different models of dementia support and critically evaluate them to determine the efficacy of the models. Using a case study, students will integrate and apply specialised skills and knowledge to identify potential triggers and drivers that may have contributed to a described incident. Students will develop a research-informed, holistic, biopsychosocial approach to applying high-level judgement and advanced skills in assessing the individual with dementia in their environment, and its impact on behaviour, in order to facilitate professional support.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and integrate advanced theoretical and empirical evidence to apply specialised skills and knowledge to diverse models of dementia support.
Apply and justify evidence-informed strategies and specialised skills, including holistic assessment skills, to support people with dementia in varied care settings.
Critically analyse and synthesise advanced, research-informed knowledge to contextualise dementia within diverse health and aged care settings.

Critically analyse and evaluate the complex contexts influencing behaviours associated with dementia, applying advanced knowledge and skills to support evidence-based interventions and the communication of complex concepts to varied audicences.

title: Issues in Dementia Care and Communication
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject builds professional knowledge of communicating and supporting people with dementia in community and residential care contexts. Students will research different models of dementia support and critique them to determine the efficacy of the models. Using a case study, students will apply these academic skills and a biopsychosocial approach to care, to identify potential triggers and drivers that may have contributed to a described incident. Students develop a holistic approach to understanding the individual with dementia and their environment and its impact on behaviour in order to facilitate positive support.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate the context of behaviours associated with dementia.
Analyse and contextualise dementia within health and aged care settings.
Demonstrate the application of a holistic approach to develop strategies to support people with dementia in community and residential care contexts.
Critique and evaluate different models of dementia support.

title: Issues in Health Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: The subject examines three major issues in health psychology: The relationship between personality and health, health promotion and the experience of chronic illness. A comparison of the mainstream and critical approaches to health psychology will be an underlying theme in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and critically evaluate major models of health behaviour that underpin contemporary health promotion.
Discuss and compare the mainstream and critical approaches to health psychology.
Critically evaluate research into the experience of chronic illness.
Define a range of personality traits which have been linked to illness and health behaviour, and critically evaluate research into this relationship.

title: Issues in Human Resource Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: A number of factors can create issues between organisations and their people, or between people within organisations. These factors can include changing generations, increasing global competition, emerging technologies and societal and regulatory changes. This subject examines individual and organisational issues, challenges and possible solutions within the practice of human resource management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate the implications of human resource issues for individuals and organisations.
Develop and rationalise contextual solutions to selected human resource issues or challenges for specific organisational environments.
Identify, define and discuss contemporary issues in the field of human resource management.

title: Issues in Professional Learning
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The on-going professional learning of educators is recognised as central to the quality of teaching in a wide range of education and training settings. This subject examines current research, policy and practice related to the professional learning of educators. Particular attention will be paid to the links between professional knowledge, learning and practice; the ways in which professional learning can be developed and sustained in specific education and training sites; the leadership of professional learning; and professional learning innovations. Students will have opportunities to relate key ideas in the subject to their professional practice across education and training settings.
learning_outcomes: Analyse developments in professional learning practices within historical and socio-political contexts related to teaching, teachers' work and professional knowledge in education and training contexts.
Examine the development and efficacy of professional learning policies and models to justify professional learning practices in education and training contexts.
Critically evaluate underlying theories, conceptual frames and structures which shape professional learning practices/policies in education and training contexts.
Reflect critically on key professional learning concepts and ideas to promote continuous improvement across chosen education and training contexts.

title: Issues of Ethics, Access and Equity in Speech Pathology Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students extend their knowledge of frameworks of practice and critically reflect on the ways in which these frameworks interact with issues of ethics, access and equity in a range of diverse contexts. Students synthesise their understanding of the frameworks for practice with knowledge of service delivery models and the geographical, institutional and sociocultural factors which can affect the accessibility of services, in order to propose potential solutions for specific client and community case studies. Students develop research skills to inform evaluation of communication accessibility in everyday environments.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on how professional and institutional practices, frameworks for practice, and geographic and sociocultural contexts facilitate or challenge the equity of access of speech pathology services, and explain how these frameworks and contexts shape professional practice.
Observe and evaluate the barriers and facilitators to communication within a local environment.
Apply research skills to investigate the roles of geographic, institutional and sociocultural contexts, theoretically and in relation to specific client or community case studies.
Use technical, creative and communication skills, including a range of academic and digital literacy skills, to communicate with specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Reflect critically on their beliefs, attitudes and values in relation to issues of access and equity in a way that demonstrates knowledge of ethical and professional frameworks.

title: Issues of Language, Literacy and Numeracy Practice in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Through this subject, students will explore current issues in teaching literacy and numeracy in the adult and vocational educational contexts. The subject will examine a number of current theory and policy positions and their impact on teaching and learning practices.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the issues associated with literacy and numeracy teaching practices within the adult and vocational education context.
Develop a theoretical framework for programming and teaching literacy and/or numeracy to diverse groups of learners.
Engage with different positions on literacy and numeracy education put forward in political and social debates around literacy education.

title: Issues, Crisis and Reputation
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Issues and crisis management are core communication disciplines. Together they provide the framework for building, maintaining and protecting organisational reputation on and offline. This subject critically explores organisational reputation with a focus on issues and crisis. It explores principles, theory and case studies of contemporary practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate specialised skills in developing communication strategies to manage issues, respond to crises as well as building, maintaining and evaluating organisational reputation.
Demonstrate cognitive skills to critically evaluate issues, crises and reputation theory and practice.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge in the fields of issues, risk, crisis and organisational reputation.

title: IT Fundamentals
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to computing hardware and software along with the application of computing systems in a business environment. The subject commences with a discussion of computing architecture and data representation. Students are then introduced to the fundamentals of computer programming and software development as well as computer networking techniques. The subject also examines higher-level concepts, including the lifecycle phases of an information system. The subject concludes with a discussion of information system frameworks and governance requirements.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the features of various software development methodologies.
Investigate and describe the essential elements of a computer and their functionalities.
Develop an elementary computer program.
Apply an understanding of data representations and calculations to practical situations.
Discuss the principle lifecycle phases of an information system, from requirements and acquisition through to operation and maintenance.
Discuss and analyse fundamental networking concepts, protocols and standards.
Compare and contrast the role of IT service management frameworks, policies and compliance issues.

title: IT Governance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject helps students prepare for industry certification in the Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology (COBIT® 5) framework, which defines a set of generic processes for the governance of enterprise IT (GEIT). All components of COBIT® 5 will be examined along with its relationship with other popular frameworks and ISO/IEC standards. Students will explore the application of GEIT practices relevant to IT practitioners to allow them to develop the skills needed to evaluate and implement IT Governance measures across a variety of organisational types.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the relevance and influence of various frameworks which align with and support the COBIT® framework.
Explain and justify how IT Governance fits within wider corporate governance guidelines, and why it is important to the organisation.
Evaluate and apply the concepts and practices of COBIT and tailor them to suit the needs of an organisation’s strategic goals.
Critically evaluate the practices of IT Governance within the context of appropriate and relevant ISO/IEC standards including ISO/IEC 33000, 31000, 20000 and 38500.
Apply various elements of IT Governance in an organisational context.
Evaluate what is required to achieve a shared understanding of how IT is governed amongst all stakeholders.

title: IT Management Issues
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will equip students with the knowledge and skills required to analyse the impact of information systems on organisational activities as well as evaluate options for the delivery and management of information capability in an organisation. Students will learn to analyse information delivery efficiency, to manage information systems, and to develop digital strategies by employing knowledge management techniques. Upon completion of this subject, students will be able to successfully manage information systems with the aim of achieving operational excellence for an organisation.
learning_outcomes: Critique the administrative and planning processes for information systems management in an organisation.
Analyse the impact of information and communication technologies on organisational activities.
Evaluate different options for delivering and managing information capability in an organisation.
Analyse the efficiency of information delivery and manage information systems.
Develop digital strategies to achieve operational excellence for information systems using knowledge management and artificial intelligence techniques.

title: IT Professional Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn to reflect upon and practise a number of key academic and workplace professional skills. These include academic writing skills that make use of appropriate referencing techniques, as well as professional workplace behaviour. The subject also introduces several classic ethics theories and provides students with the opportunity to analyse, critique and apply these theories within an Information and Communication Technology (ICT) context. Students will also study the Australian Computer Society Code of Ethics and its application to a workplace context.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively as an ICT professional to both a professional and general audience.
Analyse and evaluate ethical problems from the viewpoint of ICT professionals using the Australian Computer Society Code of Ethics.
Critically evaluate the roles and responsibilities of an ICT professional.
Apply ethical theories to a diverse range of scenarios.

title: IT Infrastructure Management PG
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will employ a research, reporting and presentation approach using the latest ICT tools to examine and critically analyse a combination of the technical and management issues in the administration of contemporary IT infrastructure. The subject will provide students with the essential knowledge of service and quality management processes and practices. Students will learn the applied knowledge of IT Service Management (ITSM) and will be introduced to the universal “Information Technology Infrastructure Library (ITIL)” framework which provides a cohesive set of best practices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate the need for IT Service Management (ITSM) and its relevance to an organisation.
Compare and contrast the best practice frameworks for ITSM.
Investigate, critically analyse and evaluate the impact of new and current ICT services to an organisation.
Describe how effective IT Infrastructure Management requires strategic planning with alignment from both the IT and business perspectives in an organisation.
Synthesise the theoretical, technical and management issues that deliver ICT services to an organisation.

title: IT Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is the final step in your major IT project within the systems analysis, network engineering and systems administration areas. Work started in ITC306 Software Development Project 2 will be completed in this subject. This subject, and its linked subject ITC306, cover the practical application of a project management methodology in the development and delivery of a major project. In this subject, students will be working in teams to produce and release their project deliverables, including appropriate manuals. They will then be expected to review the project outcomes, artefacts and collaborative work.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively in a team environment.
Implement standard testing parameters and evaluate system performance.
Apply project management tools to assist in timely completion of milestones.
Evaluate the project process, including team management, against the project proposal.
Demonstrate technical writing skills through development of appropriate technical manuals.

title: IT Project Experience
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a project development experience at an advanced level on a topic in Information Technology as selected by a student. Students will demonstrate project management skills by selecting, planning, managing and reporting on the project. The subject is suitable for a range of project types and as preparation for a course-related capstone experience.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate project management skills during all stages of the project.
Design a detailed project plan.
Effectively use professional writing skills to report on the final outcomes of the project.
Select a project topic and analyse the benefits as they relate to the workplace and/or research (as well as professional development and personal interest).
Negotiate with the supervisor (or team leader or mentor) to determine a rubric to show how the project is to be evaluated.
Reflect upon and critically evaluate all practices and learning outcomes from the project.
Apply technical and theoretical skills of the area studied to an IT Project.

title: IT Risk Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a thorough background in IT security risk management issues. Comprehensive selections of risk management techniques for IT security are covered, including quantitative and qualitative methods. Other topics include security decision-making, risk mitigation, risk transference and business continuity planning.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the various approaches for mitigating security risk, including when to use insurance to transfer IT risk.
Apply both quantitative and qualitative risk management approaches and to compare and contrast the advantages of each approach.
Justify the goals and various key terms used in risk management and assess IT risk in business terms.
Evaluate and explain the benefits of using intrusion detection systems, firewalls and vulnerability scanners to reduce risk.
Critically evaluate IT security risks in terms of vulnerabilities targeted by hackers.

title: IT Service Quality Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject covers IT service management using the interpretation and application of the ISO/IEC 20000 standard and the Information Technology Infrastructure Library (ITIL®), including how to develop the service management capability of an organisation and assess its readiness for certification within the ISO/IEC 20000 Certification Scheme. The subject will also help students prepare for a range of ITIL® industry certifications and undertake an ISO/IEC 20000 readiness gap analysis.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the function and purpose of ITIL®, ISO/IEC 20000 and DevOps in a business context.
Critically evaluate and apply the key concepts of ITSQM.
Identify and analyse business challenges to implementing ITIL®, ISO/IEC 20000, and DevOps frameworks.
Compare and contrast the role of frameworks, policies and compliance in an IT context.
Evaluate and apply the principles of continuous delivery / continuous integration within IT service management.
Design an ITSQM implementation strategy for an organisation.

title: IT Work Place Learning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the development of the student's professional identity, knowledge and work practice. Through closer integration of theoretical constructs with work environment examples they will have the opportunity to extend their critical reflective practice, and further explore their own personal development, professional skills, and work ethic.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate personal development across a range of professional practice skills.
Critically reflect on and evaluate the application of theory in a workplace setting.
Apply knowledge of contemporary thinking in employability skills, career planning and development to enhance personal skills applicable to the work environment.

title: IT Work Placement
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the development of the student's professional identity, knowledge and work practice. Through closer integration of theoretical constructs with their current or proposed work environment they will have the opportunity to extend their critical reflective practice, and further explore their own personal development, professional skills, and work ethic. As part of this subject, students will gain practical experience and apply their academic learning in a professional setting through a work placement either with a new host organisation or by undertaking a project or higher duties in their existing workplace.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on and evaluate the application of theory in a workplace setting.
Evaluate personal development across a range of professional practice skills.
Develop practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.
Apply knowledge of contemporary thinking in employability skills, career planning and development to enhance personal skills applicable to the work environment.

title: Italian Renaissance Art
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject looks at the extraordinary flowering of Italian Renaissance art which established the conventions which dominated artistic expression until the 20th century. It traces the development from the essentially symbolic art of the Middle Ages to the ideal of the accurate representation of reality, through the use of linear and aerial perspective, architectural perspective, indoor and outdoor scenes, landscape, light sources and shadowing, the use of geometric shapes to model and arrange figures, the use of colour, and religious, civic and classical iconography.
learning_outcomes: Have developed an understanding of the relative nature of artistic conventions, and understand their origins and uses.
Recognise different periods, schools and artists by the conventions, techniques and subject matter used.

title: ITI Foundation Program Credit Package
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject represents the credit provided for the completion of the ITI Foundation Program.

title: IT Work Placement PG
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable students to apply their academic learning in a professional setting by undertaking work placement with an approved organisation or by undertaking a project or higher duties in their existing workplace. The subject will also allow students to enhance their IT skills and enable them to apply discipline specific knowledge to practical workplace settings while also allowing them to build valuable industry contacts. Students will be required to undertake work placement/internship at an approved workplace to demonstrate the links between the theoretical components of their course and the practical application of skills.
learning_outcomes: Reflect and critically evaluate the application of theoretical components of the course in a workplace setting.
Apply IT discipline knowledge and problem-solving skills to real-world practical scenarios.
Demonstrate applied proficiency through professional experience gained through IT work placement.
Develop the communication skills required for a successful career in the Australian job market.

title: Jesus the Christ
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the biblical sources and major historical developments of Christian thinking concerning the claim that Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ of God. It introduces major classical, modern (twentieth-century) and contemporary developments in the theology of the person and work of Christ. Further contemporary themes are examined, including Christology and religious pluralism, liberation Christologies and contextual Christologies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of modern (twentieth-century) and contemporary developments in the theology of the person and work of Christ.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the major classical developments in the theology of the person and work of Jesus Christ.
Analyse critically key aspects of the biblical witness that Jesus of Nazareth is the promised messiah of God.
Expound and evaluate at least one major contemporary approach to Christology.

title: Jesus the Christ
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the biblical sources and major historical developments of Christian thinking concerning the claim that Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ of God. It introduces major classical, modern (twentieth-century) and contemporary developments in the theology of the person and work of Christ. Further contemporary themes are also examined, including Christology and religious pluralism, liberation Christologies and contextual Christologies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the major classical developments in the theology of the person and work of Jesus Christ.
Expound at least one major contemporary approach to Christology.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss key aspects of the biblical witness that Jesus of Nazareth is the promised messiah of God.
Demonstrate an understanding of modern (twentieth-century) and contemporary developments in the theology of the person and work of Christ.

title: Jesus the Christ
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the biblical sources and major historical developments of Christian thinking concerning the claim that Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ of God. It introduces major classical, modern (twentieth-century) and contemporary developments in the theology of the person and work of Christ. Further contemporary themes are examined, including Christology and religious pluralism, liberation Christologies and contextual Christologies.
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically key aspects of the biblical witness that Jesus of Nazareth is the promised messiah of God.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the major classical developments in the theology of the person and work of Jesus Christ.
Expound and evaluate at least one major contemporary approach to Christology.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of modern (twentieth-century) and contemporary developments in the theology of the person and work of Christ.

title: Jihadist Terrorism
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Jihadist terrorism is the most prominent subnational security threat of the twenty-first century. Jihadist terrorism catapulted to the international security agenda with Al Qaeda's attack on the World Trade Centre and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, and altered the terrorism landscape from that point. This subject will introduce the strategic and ideological foundations that motivate the Global Jihadist Movement. It will also explore the terrorist franchises throughout the Middle East, Africa, and South East Asia. This leads into a transnational threat analysis, focusing on contemporary groups such as Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, Al Shabaab, and Islamic State - all of whom have the power to inspire terrorist attacks in the West.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced knowledge of jihadist drivers, enablers, and causes when making threat assessments particular to the international terrorism environment.
Exploit a range of information and research methods to formulate theories and make assessments.
Demonstrate professional objectivity in order to inform professional practice.
Critically evaluate jihadist concepts and theories with reference to recent developments, in order to provide insight on contemporary and emerging threats.
Clearly communicate complex knowledge regarding Contemporary Terrorism in order to influence specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Journalism - Level 5
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for the Master of Communication (generic and with specialisations) Articulated Set.
learning_outcomes: N/A.

title: Journalism Perspectives 1
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject develops students' specialist knowledge, skills and abilities to research, plan and produce content for news and other media. Students develop skills in undertaking research, analysing and interpreting information, constructing a story and content for multiple online platforms. Students develop an understanding of the media landscape and how to work professionally and ethically within that landscape as a journalist.
learning_outcomes: Identify and gather information to write and produce news content.
Plan and manage the production of news content for a variety of media channels.
Work in a team to meet a deadline.
Demonstrate the fundamental skills of a news professional.

title: Judaism and Early Christianity
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the rise of Judaism following the Babylonian exile (mid-sixth century BCE) to the second century CE. It examines the influence of Hellenism, the Maccabean revolt, Judea under Herod and Rome, the two Jewish Wars, sectarian Judaism and Jewish beliefs and institutions in the first century CE. The rise of early Christianity within the context of formative Judaism and the competing responses of these two movements to the destruction of the temple in 70 CE are examined.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical and advanced understanding of issues relating to the history and development of Judaism from the mid-sixth century BCE to the second century CE.
Discuss critically Jesus and the rise of early Christianity within the context of Second Temple Judaism.
Demonstrate advanced competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts through critical engagement with primary biblical materials and constructive engagement with secondary literature.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss the historical relationship between Second Temple Judaism and early Christianity and its significance for biblical interpretation and Christian traditions.
Identify distinguishing features of major Jewish groups and institutions in the first centuries BCE and CE and critically evaluate their impact upon the Jewish war of 66-73 CE.

title: Journalism Perspectives 2
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject continues to progress students’ knowledge, skills and abilities in the field of journalism. Students undertaking this subject will work on real-world projects to further enhance their expertise and professional practice. Students will work in a team to produce and publish news content for a range of media channels and reflect upon their practice as an emerging journalist.
learning_outcomes: Work efficiently as part of a news team in researching, producing and publishing content.
Demonstrate skills, knowledge and behaviour of a professional journalist.
Plan and manage the production of complex news content to a professional standard.
Reflect on your practice as a media professional.

title: Judaism and Early Christianity
school: School of Theology

It examines the influence of Hellenism, the Maccabean revolt, Judea under Herod and Rome, the two Jewish Wars, sectarian Judaism and Jewish beliefs and institutions in the first century CE. The rise of early Christianity within the context of formative Judaism and the competing responses of these two movements to the destruction of the temple in 70 CE are examined.
learning_outcomes: Identify distinguishing features of major Jewish groups and institutions in the first centuries BCE and CE and their impact upon the Jewish war of 66-73 CE.
Discuss the historical relationship between Second Temple Judaism and early Christianity and its significance for biblical interpretation and Christian traditions.
Demonstrate a critical and informed understanding of issues relating to the history and development of Judaism from the mid-sixth century BCE to the second century CE.
Discuss Jesus and the rise of early Christianity within the context of Second Temple Judaism.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate advanced competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts through critical engagement with primary biblical materials and constructive engagement with secondary literature.

Identify distinguishing features of major Jewish groups and institutions in the first centuries BCE and CE and critically evaluate their impact upon the Jewish war of 66-73 CE.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.

title: Justice and Punishment
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is concerned with the study of philosophical theories of justice. It analyses the concept of justice and examines theories about the meaning and content of justice with respect to social and economic arrangements, civil and criminal law, trials and punishments. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the ways in which law and justice are connected.
Express an understanding of the differences between criminal and distributive justice.
Display knowledge of a range of philosophical theories of justice.
Use the discourse of justice to analyse social and economic policy.
Articulate the idea of a fair trial.
Exhibit knowledge of competing justificatory theories of punishment, including their strengths and weaknesses.
Analyse the concept of justice and related terms.

title: Jurisprudence
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a philosophical introduction to the nature of law and the legal system, including the relationship of law to justice and morality. It introduces students to significant philosophical theorists including Austin, Bentham, Dworkin, Grotius, Hart, Kant, Kelsen, Marx and Rawls. Students study legal reasoning, the relationship between morality and law, what gives rules authority, the role of the judge, and the social and economic nature of law. This subject also explores the nature of rights and their relationship to law, ethics and morality, together with the philosophical foundations guiding judicial decision-making and legal interpretivism.
learning_outcomes: be able to discuss critically the development of Marx's theories about and ideas on law by later legal theorists
be able to articulate the interrelationship of ethics, law and rights
be able to engage critically with the principles underpinning legal realism
be able to discuss and critique the conception of rights, including human, legal and moral rights
be able to demonstrate an understanding of the processes for the determination of individual rights, and the social, political and legal institutions necessary to maintain these rights
be able to demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the terminology relevant to jurisprudence
be able to demonstrate an understanding of the role of legal theory in contemporary judicial decision making
be able to identify and discuss the philosophy grounding particular laws and legal structures in contemporary Australia
be able to discuss key issues in the philosophy of law
be able to discuss the origins of legal philosophy in ancient society and its influence on the development of contemporary jurisprudence
be able to discuss critically the influence of the major forms of feminist theory on the development of contemporary jurisprudence
be able to analyse and critically assess significant writings of selected jurists or legal theorists

title: Key Concepts in Stem 2
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Key Concepts in STEM 2 is one of a suite of non-award micro-subjects offered on the Studylink platform. This subject is the second in a series of three subjects introducing students to foundational thinking in disciplines that incorporate science, technology, engineering and maths. Students are introduced to simple systems as the next step in developing the fundamentals of logic, critical thinking and problem-solving. Students will learn to apply a range of approaches to interpret, deconstruct and integrate components of simple systems leading to the development of effective problem-solving skills. Students will be aided in building transferable skills across different contexts and begin to acquire an aptitude for knowledge construction. Students are recommended to first undertake Key Concepts in STEM 1.
learning_outcomes: Deconstruct and integrate components of simple systems to explore new ideas.
Apply knowledge of simple systems to solve problems in a range of STEM contexts.
Identify simple systems in everyday and STEM contexts.

title: Key Concepts in STEM 3
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Key Concepts in STEM 3 is one of a suite of non-award micro-subjects offered on the Studylink platform. This subject is the third in a series of three subjects introducing students to the foundational thinking in disciplines that incorporate science, technology, engineering and maths. Students are recommended to first complete Key Concepts in STEM 1 and 2. This third subject progresses to complex systems as the concluding step in establishing a foundation in logic, critical thinking and problem-solving. Students will learn to apply a range of approaches and different perspectives to interpreting complex systems leading to the development of effective problem-solving skills. Students will be aided in building transferable skills across different contexts and grow their capacity for knowledge construction.
learning_outcomes: Apply understanding of complex systems to solve problems in different STEM contexts.
Investigate complex systems from different STEM perspectives.
Identify complex systems in natural phenomena.

title: Knowledge and Reality
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject engages with a number of problems that have been central to the Western philosophical tradition. These are basic problems in what is called epistemology (the theory of knowledge) and metaphysics (the study of the nature of reality). They include: How, if at all, is knowledge possible? What is the relation between the mind and the body? Do we have free will?
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of, and competence in, modern philosophical analysis and argumentation.
Explain the central philosophical issues concerning knowledge, the mind, and free will.
Critically evaluate the main philosophical theories concerning knowledge, the mind, and free will.
Demonstrate a sound understanding of the problems addressed in the subject, and of the discussions of those problems in selected historical and contemporary sources.

title: Knowledge Management in Practice
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of Knowledge Management (KM) in an organisational context, and focuses on the strategies and processes used by organisations to identify, access, manage, and share their information assets to meet their KM needs. Motivators and drivers required to align a new KM project with organisational strategies are included. It will examine how organisations can adapt KM practices, progress to share this knowledge, and mature to develop new strategic directions. The impact of organisational culture and change management philosophies on KM implementation will demonstrate how the capture and use of organisational knowledge is influenced internally by workers such as knowledge brokers, champions, and subject experts, and externally by suppliers, customers, and so on. Technologies as drivers, processes and techniques used to capture and utilise organisational knowledge are also covered.
learning_outcomes: Apply appropriate Knowledge Management practices to real world situations.
Understand and implement Knowledge Management processes encompassing the key people, departments/sections, policies and processes prevalent in an organisation.
Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamental elements of Knowledge Management in an organisational context.
Understand and evaluate the implementation and use of the technology required for an organisational Knowledge Management strategy to succeed.
Critically analyse and document an organisation's knowledge needs for an effective Knowledge Management strategy and process development.
Identify the drivers and inhibitors of effective Knowledge Management practices.
prerequisites: INF458: Knowledge Management Strategies and Processes
INF323: Knowledge Management Processes and Systems
INF523: Knowledge Management Processes and Systems

title: Laboratory Quality Assurance
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Quality of products and services is important in healthcare thus it is important to have skills to analyse, evaluate and propose improvement. This subject therefore provides a platform to discuss, analyze and evaluate drivers of quality such as quality assurance standards and accreditation. Leadership and management and technology are important in quality and safety, therefore the assignments in this subject call for analysis, evaluation and reflection on these drivers. After completing this subject, a student has a deeper and wider knowledge of management of quality that is useful e.g. in specialist and routine pathology and in research. It is assumed that a student in this subject works or has worked in medical laboratory sciences or studied medical laboratory science or equivalent and has undergraduate knowledge or equivalent of quality and statistics for quality. Students from other disciplines are enrolled at the discretion of the Director.
learning_outcomes: Discuss, evaluate and propose improvements to management and leadership styles and management of resources in regard to quality and safety of laboratory services and products.
Discuss and evaluate issues such as technology, automation, information systems and laboratory organization and how they impact on quality and safety of services and products now and in the future.
Have the skills to investigate, analyse, synthesise and offer solutions to problems, errors or issues that compromise quality.
Discuss and analyse quality assurance, quality assurance standards and accreditation in their profession and workplace.
Discuss and evaluate quality management systems and their application in general and in their profession and workplace.

title: Labour Economics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject applies economic analysis to the labour market and complements studies in human resource management and industrial relations and applies economic principles to specific labour issues such as wage and employment determination, labour productivity and labour force participation rates. Contemporary labour market issues are explored including unemployment, wages policy and the institutional framework of Australian labour markets.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and apply economic principles and theories to labour market issues.
Evaluate labour market policies and apply these to issues relating to unemployment, wages and discrimination.
Analyse conditions in the Australian labour market, including skill shortages.

title: Landscape Design
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Landscape design is a broad discipline with a long tradition of creativity involving plants and other landscape elements. This subject is designed to give students a solid grounding in the principles and practices of landscape design as a platform for innovative and sustainable practice. The historical, aesthetic, horticultural and practical elements of landscape design will be explored. This includes Australian native and exotic plant assemblages as well as hard landscape elements. Drawing principles and graphic presentation, both essential components of any design process, will be investigated.
learning_outcomes: Identify the cultural and philosophical ideologies that influence landscape design.
Apply sustainability principles to landscape materials and design elements.
Identify a selection of plants and evaluate their suitability to fulfill a range of design elements in a given site.
Explain the features of the design process and apply them to create an original landscape design.
Describe various graphic presentation principles and formats and demonstrate how they are used.
Describe the historical evolution of landscape design and discuss how history has influenced contemporary styles of landscape design.
Justify the selection of hard landscaping elements to suit a given site.

title: Landscape Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Landscape ecology is essentially the study of spatial patterns and the way that these spatial patterns influence ecosystem processes and populations. In this subject students learn about the theoretical framework under which these large scale processes and interactions can be studied. They build on existing university knowledge of ecology and conservation to understand spatial processes within ecosystems: relationships among pattern, process and scale; and the modelling of spatial and temporal dynamics in biological systems. As such, students will combine knowledge of GIS, spatial analysis, remote sensing and ecology to analyse the biophysical properties of real landscapes for biodiversity conservation and landscape management. There is no intensive associated with this subject. Students completing this subject are able to apply their knowledge and skills to address problems and make appropriate decisions about natural resource management issues at a landscape level.
learning_outcomes: Apply their knowledge and skills to address problems and make appropriate decisions about natural resource management issues at a landscape level.
Have an in-depth understanding of key concepts, principles and issues associated with landscape ecology.
Use critical thinking and sound judgement to design appropriate research projects to test specific issues relating to the application of landscape ecology to natural resource management.
Have a variety of specialised skills in the use of landscape metrics and spatial statistics to landscape processes and interpret the results.

title: Language Learning Theories and Perspectives
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the major language and language development theories informing TESOL practices, approaches, and methods. This subject considers the importance of context for language development. It also explores recent developments in language learning theory that influence TESOL practice including power relations, identity, digitisation, and globalisation.
learning_outcomes: Understand various language learning theories and perspectives, including their historical origins.
Evaluate current language learning issues, phenomena, or practices drawing upon varied language learning theories and perspectives.
Be aware of various critiques on key language learning theories and perspectives.
Describe language as a meaning making system.

title: Language, Literacy and Numeracy in Vocational Education and Training
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the roles that language, literacy and numeracy (LLN) play in education and training. Students will learn to recognise the language, literacy and numeracy demands of training and assessment, and be able to develop training and assessment to suit individual skill levels, including accessing relevant support resources.
learning_outcomes: Design competency-based training programs and resources in accordance with a relevant Training Package and Units of Competency to meet the specific language, literacy and numeracy needs of individual learners or groups of learners.
Discuss the relationship between language, literacy and numeracy skills to the social, ethnic and economic experiences of individual learners or groups of learners in Adult and Vocational education.
Analyse and discuss theories and approaches to the teaching of adult LLN (language, literacy and numeracy) to maximise student engagement and enhance student outcomes.
Analyse and describe the language, literacy and numeracy demands of the workplace.
prerequisites: EEB201: Language, Literacy and Numeracy in Vocational Education

title: Larrikin, Rebel, Dreamer: Australian Voices
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the development of Australian literature and culture through studying a wide variety of texts including novels, plays, poetry, films, and songs. From the late nineteenth century to present-day, poetic considerations of landscape to Indigenous responses to colonisation, the texts in this subject consider Australia's diverse voices and changing cultural, political and material contexts. Through the subject, students will develop an understanding of the ways that Australian literature reflects complex social problems, contributes to significant national debates and nation-building and shapes conceptual understandings of the world and Australia's place within it.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and critically analyse a variety of Australian literary and creative works using skills derived from literary studies.
Identify and describe the social, political and cultural contexts for particular Australian literary and creative works.
Apply skills in research, communication, and writing in order to examine and compare literary texts and contexts.
Demonstrate knowledge of the ways in which Australian literary and creative works engage with key questions and debates within the Australian literary field.

title: Law of Employment
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: LAW515 equips students with a fundamental knowledge of labour law. The subject examines the contract of employment and the various sources of law that interact and have an impact upon the relationship between employers and employees. The subject fosters professional practice and facilitates career advancement through problem based learning, by using contemporary case studies that accommodate the development of research, analysis and communication skills. Students will be provided with the opportunity to develop work skills while gaining knowledge of employment law, discrimination in the workplace, and labour rights law. Employment relations will also be examined through multiple lenses including globalisation, organisational change and the interpretation and operation of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).
learning_outcomes: Evaluate workplace-related scenarios/cases by identifying the relevant issue(s), stating the relevant principles of employment law, discussing how these relate to the legal issue(s), and suggesting potential remedies.
Synthesise legal issues related to workplace relations, policies, industrial relations bodies, and other aspects of Australian employment law including dispute resolution.
Apply the legislative provisions and related common law to legal issues arising in the workplace setting.
Analyse and evaluate the principles of employment law in Australia, including its history, development, and the current constitutional and theoretical frameworks within which it operates.
Research and critique the development of modern fair work, work health and safety, workers' compensation and rehabilitation schemes, anti-discrimination and other legislative requirements.

title: Law and Ethics in Health Management and Leadership
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students consider key legislation, accountabilities, responsibilities, and policy related to health management and leadership. Underpinning these areas of inquiry are foundational ethical and philosophical frameworks and health law principles which offer students mechanisms for framing and enacting legal and ethical responsibilities in multiple contexts, including organisation governance, health care delivery, and public health.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of health law to health management and leadership.
Apply ethico-legal principles to health care delivery and to public health.
Discuss Australia’s legal system and legal framework of the Australian health care system.
Analyse accountabilities and delegations related to organisational governance.
Analyse the nature and scope of health law and ethics, including the relationship between human rights, ethics and the law.

title: Law and Ethics for Health Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will explore the legal and ethical principles essential for providing safe and effective health care, including how these principles apply to First Nations peoples and the impact of introducing Western laws and ideals. Key themes including autonomy, self-determination, and professional accountability will be examined across a range of healthcare settings and professional contexts. Students will also address legal and ethical consideration related to working with specific groups, such as First Nations peoples, children, older adults, the terminally ill, and those lacking decision-making capacity as they apply relevant principles to their areas of professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast legal, ethical and cultural principles relevant to the provision of health care for diverse groups of healthcare consumers in a range of contexts.
Evaluate ethical principles, models and theories related to the provision of health care, including in the provision of health care to First Nations peoples and communities.
Justify approaches to care that consider advocacy, autonomy, legal capacity and equitable access to health care for groups of healthcare consumers, including First Nations peoples and communities.
Apply relevant legal and ethical principles when working in partnership with First Nations peoples and communities in a range of healthcare settings and contexts.
Analyse the development of and relationship between legislation, legal principles and professional accountability in the interprofessional healthcare context.

title: Law of Employment
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject is designed to allow students to learn and apply laws relating to the individual employment relationship. In addition, students will examine and apply the law pertaining to discrimination through scenario based learning and investigate the law that applies to occupational health and safety issues.
learning_outcomes: Identify instances of discrimination and breaches of workplace health and safety, and explain the law relating to them.
Analyse the law in relation to workplace scenarios.
Apply the law covered in this subject to workplace scenarios.
Effectively communicate the application of the law to workplace scenarios.
Explain the law relating to contracts of employment.

title: Law of Torts
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundational core for the study of tort law by addressing the following questions: What are torts? What is liability? How can breaches of duty of care be compensated? Students will gain an understanding of a range of tort law topics including negligence, trespass to the person, trespass to goods, trespass to land, accidental and personal injury, breach of statutory duty, and strict and vicarious liability. In addition, the remedies and defences available for tortious liability are considered in relation to both common law and statutory schemes, along with the assessment of damages.
learning_outcomes: Explain how tort law, including the relevant defences, has been developed and modified through statutory processes in Australia.
Present clear coherent arguments based on leading tort law precedents.
Review and evaluate nuisance and trespass within the framework of Australian tort law.
Explain the basis of contributory negligence and the principles of apportionment.
Explain the law pertaining to compensation schemes within the NSW legal system.
Demonstrate an understanding of the applicability of tortious principles with respect to the duty of care owed by statutory authorities to Indigenous Australians.
Plan and apply effective strategies in legal research of tort law based scenarios.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the role of tort law and the principles governing tortious remedies.
Explain the purpose of the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW) and its relationship to the common law.
Demonstrate an understanding of the elements of tortious liability, including the rules pertaining to the recovery of damages.
Apply the sources of tort law within common law and statute based scenarios.
prerequisites: LAW112: Introduction to the Australian Legal System

title: Law Policy and Procedure 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines general duties policing within NSW and the theory of policing in a liberal democratic society. It focuses on the rule of law, with particular emphasis on criminal, traffic and drug law enforcement. It also focuses on the role of police in upholding and enforcing the law in the criminal justice system and the service role of policing in situations that do not necessarily require police legal intervention. There is a study of the primary stakeholders who come into frequent contact with NSW Police, with a particular focus on vulnerable people and people with special needs.
learning_outcomes: Identify the causes of crime within society.
Identify various offences and apply appropriate legislative solutions to them.
Outline the structure of the NSW Police Force.
Explain how social inequality, based on race, gender and socio-economic status, impacts on the policing role in NSW.
Identify legally and socially vulnerable persons in society and the policing requirements and obligations regarding them.
Explain the legislative framework that underpins policing in NSW.
Explain the role of police within the NSW criminal justice system.
Apply STOPAR as a critical thinking framework in policing scenarios.
