learning_outcomes: Discuss and apply subject-specific literacy practices in their teaching areas.
Sequence teaching and learning strategies to scaffold effective literacy development using the multiliteracies pedagogical framework.
Develop and justify the design of literacy and numeracy instruction for diverse learners that addresses the foci (resources) of the Four Resources Model.
Discuss and employ a range of research-based strategies for literacy instruction and assessment.
Teach about texts and their use to inclusively support diverse learners.
Identify and discuss digital technologies that can be used for literacy development.

title: Literature Across the Curriculum
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the role of the teacher librarian and the use of literature in education, particularly in enhancing student learning outcomes, long-term reading motivation and life-long learning. The subject examines important theory and research related to literature; the diversity of literature and multi-literate environments; and the impact of social and cultural influences on literature. This knowledge will be used to inform the creation of literature and reading experiences across the curriculum to demonstrate how school library services can enhance literature practices in the school community.
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the role of multi-literacies, including visual literacy, in the context of literature in education.
Analyse theory, research and models related to literature, and interpret the implications for education.
Identify how digital environments diversify school student experiences with literature.
Extend the role of the teacher librarian in promoting literature across the curriculum.
Predict and interpret social and cultural issues as they apply to the use of literature in education.
Evaluate a wide variety of literature, and apply such knowledge to the selection, appreciation and critical evaluation of literature in education.

title: Literature Across the Curriculum
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the role of the teacher librarian and the use of literature in education, particularly in enhancing student learning outcomes, long-term reading motivation and life-long learning. The subject examines important theory and research related to literature; the diversity of literature and multi-literate environments; and the impact of social and cultural influences on literature. This knowledge will be used to inform the creation of literature and reading experiences across the curriculum to demonstrate how school library services can enhance literature practices in the school community.
learning_outcomes: Predict and interpret social and cultural issues as they apply to the use of literature in education.
Identify how digital environments diversify school student experiences with literature.
Evaluate a wide variety of literature, and apply such knowledge to the selection, appreciation and critical evaluation of literature in education.
Analyse theory, research and models related to literature, and interpret the implications for education.
Extend the role of the teacher librarian in promoting literature across the curriculum.
Appreciate the role of multi-literacies, including visual literacy, in the context of literature in education.

title: Literature and Other Resources for Children and Young Adults
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a broad overview of literature and other resources for children and young adults from a public librarian's perspective. This subject traces the development of literature and other resources paying particular attention to the technological, cultural and social influences that have shaped this development. A range of genres and formats are explored and attention given to new and emergent trends in reading and engagement with materials and formats. The role that public libraries and librarians play in these trends will be discussed. The subject also explores the role of the library in literacy development and promoting engagement with reading for pleasure and recreation.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and discuss the cultural, creative and aesthetic values of literature and other resources.
Evaluate and apply a broad range of literacies.
Apply criteria to critically evaluate and select literature and other resources for children and young adults for programs and collections.
Assess the issues and concerns associated with the access and provision of materials in multiple formats for children and young adults.
Select and use a wide variety of literature and resources, authors and creators, and genres and formats for children and young adults.
Integrate support for literacy and language development into public library programs for children and young adults.
Identify significant historical developments and the production of materials for children and young adults worldwide.
prerequisites: INF205: Literature and Other Resources for Children and Young Adults
INF442: Trends in Literature for Children and Young Adults

title: Literature and Other Resources for Children and Young Adults
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a broad overview of literature and other resources for children and young adults from an information professional's perspective. This subject traces the development of literature and other resources paying particular attention to the technological, cultural and social influences that have shaped this development. A range of genres and formats are explored and attention given to new and emergent trends in reading and engagement with materials and formats. The role that public libraries and librarians play in these trends will be discussed. The subject also explores the role of the library in literacy development and promoting engagement with reading for pleasure and recreation.
learning_outcomes: Utilise criteria to evaluate and select literature and other resources for children and young adults for programs and collections.
Discuss the role of public library programs in supporting language and literacy development for children and young adults.
Explain the cultural, creative and aesthetic values of literature and other resources.
Describe issues and concerns with the access and provision of materials in multiple formats for children and young adults.
Identify significant historical developments and the production of materials for children and young adults worldwide.
Demonstrate a broad knowledge of literature and resources, authors and creators, and genres and formats for children and young adults.
Explain a range of literacies.
prerequisites: INF512: Trends in Literature for Children and Young Adults.
INF521: Literature and Other Resources for Children and Young Adults
INF442: Trends in Literature for Children and Young Adults

title: Literature and Society
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject uses literary sources to study English social history in the period 1914-1939. War memoirs, bestsellers, detective stories, and novels of recognised literary merit are examined for social insights.
learning_outcomes: Develop critical skills in evaluating different types of historical evidence, and in using evidence in presenting logically ordered arguments.
Demonstrate and understanding of the social history of England c. 1914-1939.

title: Literature in Digital Environments
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine literature experiences and practices in digital environments and the principles of interactivity, connectivity and access that now characterise the reading experience in the digital age. Learning and information behaviours; dynamic non-linear hyperlinked environments; and forms and formats on various devices, will be examined to understand the emerging influences and changes in reading and literacy experiences. This subject will include the use of online tools and digital resources for literacy experiences, and will allow students to experiment with creativity in connected learning environments.
learning_outcomes: Explain the value of digital storytelling in context, and apply appropriate tools and strategies to learning.
Critically discuss current and emerging text and literacy experiences in digital environments for learning and teaching.
Design and create a digital artefact or publication for online and mobile learning environments.
Explain issues in managing copyright, digital rights and licensing to manage literary devices, resources and services.
Incorporate digital media texts into reading and literacy experiences in the curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners.
Explain the features of literature and literacy in a digital environment, including information and knowledge transactions.
Critically discuss current and future developments in social-networked literature, including content creation, collaboration, interfaces and experiences.

title: Life Writing
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The primary aim of this subject is to explore how life experiences are researched, interpreted and represented. Students will also review theoretical issues relating to genre in the field, read examples of various forms of life writing - for example, autobiographies, memoirs, diaries, biographies, letters - and develop their skills in life writing by focussing on a variety of approaches.
learning_outcomes: Present the results of their research on a life in written form.
Demonstrate an understanding of the challenges of interpreting material and decisions required to choose an appropriate medium to present it.
Demonstrate an understanding of the demands of researching material, perhaps in a multiplicity of locations, for life writing.
Differentiate between different forms associated with life writing, for example, autobiography, biography, memoir.
Demonstrate an understanding of the variety of theoretical issues related to life writing.

title: Literature Review in Ministry
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the theory and skills involved in developing a literature review in ministry at the doctoral level. It requires candidates to be thoroughly conversant with the literature of the subject they intend to study, and to understand the major theories, methodological assumptions, key concepts, data-collection techniques, issues, problems, areas of neglect, and newly acquired knowledge within their selected and related disciplines. The literature review provides a rationale for research and a justification of its value and significance for the professional practice of ministry.
learning_outcomes: Apply a broad range of strategies for developing a literature review.
Understand the major theoretical frameworks in the literature of their chosen field of research.
Understand the importance and the various roles of the literature review in research.
Discuss the issues and problems identified in the literature of the approved field of research in ministry.
Articulate a specific purpose and a clear set of objectives to guide the writing of their literature review.
Demonstrate an indepth understanding and familiarity with the literature in the approved field of research.
Select, evaluate and synthesise appropriate literature for their chosen topic area and develop this into a review which critically explores the issues in depth and with balance.
Understand the major processes applied in the approved field of research in ministry as demonstrated in the literature.

title: Literature Review
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the theory and skills involved in developing a literature review at the post graduate level. At its completion, students should be thoroughly conversant with the literature of their intended area of study and understand the major theories, methodological assumptions, key concepts, issues, problems, areas of neglect, and newly acquired knowledge within their selected and related areas of study. The literature review provides a rationale for research and a justification of its value and significance for professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the importance and various roles of the literature review in research.
Demonstrate advanced critical skills to investigate, analyse and synthesize complex literature, problems, concepts and theories in a professional context.

Select, evaluate and synthesise appropriate literature for their chosen topic area and develop this into a review which critically explores the issues in their chosen topic area in depth and with balance.
Demonstrate the ability to apply a broad range of strategies for developing a literature review to a specific body of knowledge or practice and evaluate critically complex ideas at an abstract level.
Articulate a specific purpose and a clear set of objectives to guide the writing of their literature review.

title: Livestock Production Systems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to the livestock industries in Australia and the main components of management in livestock production systems. Students will link biological processes to key management practices and learn how to use appropriate technologies and practices to optimise production outcomes. Students will learn about basic scientific principles which underpin livestock systems. These include an introduction to biological interactions between animals and their environment, introductory principles in livestock digestion and nutrition, livestock reproduction and livestock health. Students will also learn about the annual management of the main livestock production systems found in Australia (Beef, Sheep and Dairy), including the development of operational calendars and identifying the critical factors required in the management of livestock production systems. Concurrently, students will also be provided with an introduction to best practice management in analysing animal performance and the methodology of meeting market specifications as efficiently as possible.
learning_outcomes: Describe the biological processes underpinning livestock production management decisions.
Compute common biophysical measures of animal performance and describe the on farm factors that impact these.
Identify the key management components of a livestock production system and apply these components to different farming contexts.
Identify market requirements and describe on farm factors that influence such requirements.
Create a calendar of operations for a livestock enterprise.

title: Livestock Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to expose students to the more detailed aspects of efficient and sustainable livestock management within a commercial production environment. Concepts developed in previous livestock subjects will continue to be expanded so that students develop practical and best practice management strategies within the main areas of livestock management that will have an impact upon profitability and sustainability of an enterprise. These include reproduction management, meeting nutritional requirements and maximising feed utilisation across the farm (including managing the impact of environmental variation on decision making in livestock management), breeding systems and genetic selection, meeting market specifications and managing livestock health. There is a focus on the interactions between decisions that are made within the entire livestock production chain and the subsequent impacts on other areas of management within the farm, as well as the marketing environment.
learning_outcomes: Suggest valid management decisions and recommendations that are supported by technically credible and scientifically sound knowledge and information and/or valid analytical processes.
Communicate research, analyses and recommendations effectively, coherently and professionally to a client in a report.
Identify, measure, analyse and prioritise the opportunities to most effectively improve the profitability and/or sustainability of a livestock production system.

Develop and evaluate further production strategies to meet customer &/or consumer specifications and improve the profitability and/or sustainability of the enterprise or respond to risks to a livestock production system.
Collect and analyse relevant property information and evaluate current management strategies in a livestock enterprise in terms of industry benchmarks.

title: Loss, Grief and Palliative Care for Older People
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students to work with older people experiencing loss and grief caused by chronic or terminal illness, loss of independence and declining capacity. It addresses physical, psychosocial and spiritual aspects of care. The subject focuses on the multidisciplinary nature of care for older people, including those requiring palliative care at the end of life. Issues of communication, spiritual need, social interaction, cultural norms and quality of life are addressed to prepare students to assist older people experiencing loss and grief, as well as their families and carers in residential and community care settings.
learning_outcomes: Assess critically community resources for bereavement support and counselling, as well as to provide relevant information regarding this support to families and friends.
Demonstrate an ability to use a palliative approach to enhance the care of the dying person and their family and friends.
Evaluate critically a range of responses to loss and grief situations involving older people.
Demonstrate an ability to recognise and articulate the needs of different cultural and ethnic communities.
Identify and assess critically individual behaviours that might indicate an abnormal response to loss and grief.
Demonstrate an ability to initiate and provide bereavement support for older people in residential and community care settings.
Discuss and evaluate critically their own practice and the practice of others in working with clients going through loss and grief responses related to older adults.

Demonstrate a critical understanding of loss and grief as experienced by older persons confronting multiple changes in health, social interaction and accommodation, including normal changes associated with ageing.
Compare and contrast theories of loss and grief applied to older people.
prerequisites: WEL322: Loss, Grief and Palliative Care for Older People

title: Local Anaesthesia and Surgery
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to surgery and the clinical use of local anaesthetic agents and other relevant medicines. The ethical and medico-legal implications of surgery will underpin students' study, with a strong emphasis on client selection, surgical assessment and post-operative care. This subject will also address general surgical principles, reinforcing and expanding the students' understanding and practice of infection control and clinical protocols. Students will study local anaesthetics in detail to ensure a comprehensive knowledge of these agents, as preparation for the practice of cutaneous surgery. Successful completion of this subject enables students to safely administer local anaesthetic drugs in topical and injectable forms. Students will develop foundational knowledge for the practice of cutaneous surgery, with a specific focus on nail surgery, electro-surgery and dry needling techniques. The theory of surgery will also encompass podiatric surgery techniques for the correction of foot deformity and the use of surgery as prophylaxis e.g. in the diabetic foot.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate competence in nail surgery procedures, and knowledge of podiatric surgery techniques for the alleviation of pain.
justify and administer topical and injectable local anaesthetics for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes in podiatric practice;
explain the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of a range of amide local anaesthetic agents;
demonstrate competence in infection control, universal precautions and clinical protocols relevant to surgery; and
evaluate the potential adverse effects, indications and contraindications for the use of local anaesthetic agents;
evaluate pre-, peri- and post-operative management strategies;
analyse the medico-legal and ethical issues associated with surgery;
prerequisites: BMS263: Foundational Pharmacology and Pathophysiology for Allied Health Practice

title: LOTE Curriculum Studies 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the theories and pedagogy of languages other than English (LOTE) for years K-10. The progression from early, to middle and upper years of schooling are addressed in the K-12 context. Students will develop an understanding of the teaching strategies appropriate to the design, implementation and assessment of high quality LOTE curriculum teaching and learning programs that cater for the needs of diverse learners.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the content and context of relevant language education syllabuses and how they are contextualised in classroom practice.
Identify, analyse and assess the major theories of language learning and the implications of this on LOTE teaching.
Explain the similarities and differences between first and subsequent language development and the implications of this on LOTE teaching.
Identify and apply theories of language learning to LOTE classrooms to assist a diversity of students backgrounds and abilities.
Effectively apply a range of teaching/learning, assessment, ICT and classroom management strategies for teaching languages in K-10 through the designing of units of work and writing of lesson plans.

title: LOTE Curriculum Studies 2
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject expands upon the fundamental theories and pedagogy of teaching languages other than English (LOTE) developed in EML451, with a particular focus on teaching Stage 6 senior students. It is concerned with the development of the LOTE program to meet syllabus demands in the context of broader educational, community and social issues. It focuses on developing greater cross-cultural awareness and intercultural competence through consideration of key concepts in intercultural communication and key issues in languages pedagogy through a 'language as culture' perspective.
learning_outcomes: Explain how LOTE curriculum content is organised, specifically for Stage 6 students.
Reflect on your role as a language teacher and the value of languages in the broader school curriculum.

Plan Stage 6 language lessons that include quality teaching, learning and assessment strategies, including ICT strategies, that provide for differentiation of learning strategies for diverse learners.
Explain how contemporary language and cultural issues (or intercultural issues) are reflected in local policy contexts.

Demonstrate an understanding of an Intercultural approach to language teaching and learning that reflects the principles of multicultural Australia through developing a position statement and choice of resources.

title: Macroeconomic Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the study of macroeconomics to encompass a model of an open economy such as Australia. Emphasis is placed on the relationship between the goods and financial sectors of the Australian economy, and the impact of various internal and external shocks to the domestic economy and its financial markets.
learning_outcomes: be able to develop a macroeconomic model of an open economy such as Australia;
be able to critically analyse the relationship between different macroeconomic and financial sector activities;
be able to apply this model to an analysis of macroeconomic problems to explain the impact of macroeconomic forces on the Australian economy;
be able to critically interpret the operation of the open macroeconomy and the problems associated with achieving simultaneous external and internal balance; and
be able to analyse and evaluate the policy prescriptions to deal with these problems.

title: Macroeconomics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the study of macroeconomics to encompass a model of an open economy such as Australia. Emphasis is placed on the relationship between the goods and financial sectors of the Australian economy, and the impact of various internal and external shocks to the domestic economy and its financial markets.
learning_outcomes: Critically interpret the operation of the open macroeconomy and the problems associated with achieving simultaneous external and internal balance.
Analyse and evaluate the policy prescriptions to deal with these problems.
Critically analyse the relationship between different macroeconomic and financial sector activities.
Apply this model to an analysis of macroeconomic problems to explain the impact of macroeconomic forces on the Australian economy.
Develop a macroeconomic model of an open economy such as Australia.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Practice And Trends
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the theoretical basis of practice in the modality of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and examines advanced techniques and new applications and future directions of MRI. Emphasis will be placed upon the scanning techniques, scan sequences and protocols, coil selection, clinical indications of the scan, pathology shown and patient management. Emerging developments whether they be in clinical practice, contrast agents, equipment, or safety practice will be examined.
learning_outcomes: Review, synthesise and apply evidence-based literature in relation to current MRI practice and Medical Radiations interdisciplinary learning.
Apply and critically discuss the technical knowledge required to undertake the specialised procedures used in clinical MRI.
Investigate safety in MRI and examine its relationship to clinical practice, patient management and professional decision making.
Undertake quality audits in the practice of MRI.
Apply knowledge and skills, and critically discuss the clinical practice of MRI in the areas undertaken in this subject.
prerequisites: MRS554: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Practice And Trends
MRS554: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Practice And Trends

title: Making Change Happen
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will learn about, and operate within Wiradjuri community protocols. Students will work with a community mentor and members of the Wiradjuri community to identify, negotiate, plan and implement a project which seeks to build the capacity of the community in practical and contributory ways. This subject includes a 50 hour community placement where students will undertake activities suggested by the community and engage with the knowledge, history, language and culture of that community, and through these activities students will gain experiential insights that will allow them to contribute to the building of better lives and futures for members of that community.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on past practices that have impacted on the Wiradjuri community.
Demonstrate knowledge of, and act according to, Wiradjuri community protocols.
Identify opportunities for community service and development, and nation rebuilding and plan, negotiate and implement a program that contributes to the realization of these opportunities.
Apply the body of knowledge relating to acting according to Wiradjuri community protocols in Wiradjuri community contexts.
Critically reflect on the intergenerational consequences of colonization, dispossession and dislocation.
Think critically and analytically about the role of leadership in the Wiradjuri community.
prerequisites: EPT454: Professional Study in Wiradjuri Community Development

title: Making it New: The Power and Influence of Modernist Literature
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores major literary works that have come to shape the zeitgeist of the early twentieth century. The time-period covered — 1890-1930 — captures a dynamic moment in history where writers and artists experimented with new forms and styles of expression. During this time, the intensification of industrialisation and the rapid rise of new technologies — photography and cinematography — transformed the landscape of representation, and the power of such innovation still reverberates today. Authors covered may include Joseph Conrad, T.S. Eliot, Virginia Woolf, and James Joyce. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge of how to read literary texts that consciously break with traditional modes of representation.
Demonstrate an awareness of historical factors that have contributed to the development of literary experimentation in the era of high modernism.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the theoretical issues at stake in thematising the concept of modernism.

title: Mammography Practice
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on experiential learning within the mammography practice setting and is delivered across three sessions. The emphasis is on reflective, consumer-centred mammographic practice, with students learning through collaboration with experienced radiographers and mammographic technologists, supervised hands-on practice, and self- and professional appraisals. Mammography practice is integrated with the theoretical components of the course, allowing students to develop their clinical practice through reflection and application of theoretical knowledge. Students are expected to demonstrate safe and competent mammography practice appropriate to their stage in the course at each appraisal. A defined set of competency-based experiences must be completed prior to graduation, with achievement of these skills documented, assessed, and critically reflected upon within this subject.
learning_outcomes: Provide/deliver mammography care, support and communication to clients and the multidisciplinary team at a professional and ethical standard, guided by best-practice and evidence-based principles.
Consistently produce and evaluate mammograms of optimal diagnostic quality, applying the ALARA principle, while ensuring minimal client discomfort.

Plan, implement and evaluate the safe and ethical practice of mammography across all examinations outlined in the Australian Society of Medical Imaging and Radiation Therapy (ASMIRT) Competency-Based Mammography skills framework, applying evidence-based principles in any mammographic setting.

Demonstrate a clear understanding of their role as a primary health care provider, integrating into practice the principles of open enquiry, environmental sustainability, workplace health and safety, equity, cultural sensitivity and diversity, social justice, self-determination, and community engagement and collaboration.
Apply reflective and critical analytical skills in clinical reasoning, decision making and in working with clients and other health professionals.

title: Management Accounting A
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Examines the way in which accountants provide financial and other information for managers to use within organisations. Focuses on the design and operation of product costing systems, on the design and operation of accounting control systems, and on contemporary management interventions to achieve world-class performance. Topics include computer financial modelling, job costing, process costing, Activity Based Costing (ABC), JIT cost allocation issues, joint costing, budgeting, variance analysis, responsibility accounting, performance measurement, theory of constraints, kaizen, business process re-engineering, economic value, balanced scorecard and international dimensions of management accounting.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate technical, computational, and analytical skills associated with the design and operation of product costing and accounting control systems.
Describe issues associated with contemporary performance measurement.
Use computer spreadsheets as an aid to product costing, budgeting and performance evaluation.
Describe cultural and international dimensions of management accounting.
Communicate effectively in designing reports for management.

title: Management Accounting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the way in which accountants provide financial and other information for managers to use within organisations. It focuses on the design and operation of product costing systems, on the design and operation of accounting control systems, and on contemporary international accounting and management interventions to drive organisational value and to achieve world-class performance. Areas and issues covered include understanding various types of costs, overhead cost allocation issues and methodologies, spreadsheet modelling, job costing, process costing, Activity Based Costing (ABC), Just-in-Time (JIT) cost allocation issues, absorption, variable, joint and operation costing, various budgeting methodologies, standard costing, variance analysis, responsibility accounting, the international dimensions of management accounting and a range of quantitative and qualitative performance measurement methodologies.
learning_outcomes: Apply technical, computational, and analytical skills to the design and operation of product costing and management accounting control systems.
Exercise critical thinking and judgement in identifying and solving management accounting problems.
Understand and communicate the impact of cultural and international dimensions on management accounting practice.
Efficiently and effectively use computer spreadsheets as an aid to product costing, budgeting and performance evaluation.
Review, critically analyse and communicate knowledge of contemporary issues around qualitative and quantitative cost performance measurement.

title: Management Accounting B
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Emphasises the role of management accounting in decision making, particularly in providing information and analysis to support strategic management activity. The focus is on evaluating existing competitive strategies, developing new strategies, and monitoring and assessing progress towards chosen strategies. Seeks to assist those involved in organisational decision-making by providing models which can be used in understanding, structuring and resolving problems.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the internationalisation of management accounting, including the nature and implications of global competitiveness, management accounting in multinational organisations, and the cultural impact of management accounting.
Work both individually and in cooperative team environments for learning, and collaborate in business problemsolving and decisionmaking exercises.
Engage in product and profit planning.
Assess problem situations, the factors involved in decision making generally, and in strategic managerial decision making in particular.
Discuss the process of strategic analysis, and demonstrate skill in using relevant techniques to analyse firm and competitor strategies.
Develop computer spreadsheet models for financial planning and to aid in decision analysis.
Analyse strategic problems and recommend appropriate strategies.

title: Management Accounting for Costs and Control
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on management accounting for cost and control purposes in an organisational context. It emphasises the use of quantitative techniques and computer software including spreadsheets. The subject includes an overview of management accounting perspectives with an emphasis on systems design and provides a framework for problem solving and analysis of conventional and modern cost accounting paradigms including job and process costing, standard costing and variance analysis, relevant costs for decisions, activity-based costing, kaizen costing, just-in-time, target costing, control systems, benchmarking, performance evaluation and balanced scorecard.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and critique the historical and ethical development of management accounting.
Critique how managers make decisions.
Explain the role of management accounting in organisational contexts and the implications for management accounting of different paradigms.
Apply cognitive skills in the design and operation of costing systems.
Critically evaluate the design and operation of performance management systems.
Create and implement computerised decision models.
Apply analytical and synthetical skills in report writing, and use quantitative techniques and computer software including using the Internet as a professional source.

title: Management Accounting for Sustainable Decision Making
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines financial and other information accountants provide for managers to use within organisations to make decisions and to understand and communicate the impact of cultural and international dimensions on management accounting practice. It focuses on the design and operation of product costing systems, on the design and operation of accounting control systems, and on contemporary international accounting and management interventions to drive organisational value in order to achieve world-class performance. Areas and issues covered include: understanding various types of cost methodologies, spreadsheet modelling, budgeting methodologies, responsibility accounting, the international dimensions of management accounting and a range of quantitative and qualitative performance measurement methodologies.
learning_outcomes: Review, critically analyse and communicate knowledge of contemporary issues around qualitative and quantitative cost performance measurement.
Apply technical, computational, and analytical skills to the design and operation of sustainable product costing and management accounting control systems.
Exercise critical thinking and judgement in identifying and solving management accounting problems.
Efficiently and effectively use computer spreadsheets as an aid to product costing, budgeting and performance evaluation.
Understand and communicate the impact of cultural and international dimensions on management accounting practice.

title: Management of Information Agencies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students are introduced to the foundational knowledge and theory of management as it applies to the running of information agencies. Emphasis is on providing students with an understanding of management issues they are likely to face in the typical operations of an information agency. Theoretical concepts such as supervision and leadership and their application to practice will also be explored.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the knowledge and skills to manage or supervise library and information services staff effectively
Apply relevant theories to complex management and leadership challenges
Critically evaluate the strategies required to manage library and information services effectively within the broader organisation, in a climate of constant change
Critically analyse the management principles and their practical application in planning, organising, leading, and evaluating activities

title: Management of Brands
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Strong brands are key assets for companies. This subject will focus on the management of brands, including developing brands that resonate with consumers, building brand equity, measuring brand performance and managing brands over time. It has been designed to provide students with the capabilities to evaluate, design and make recommendations for branding programs across a diverse range of large and small organisations.
learning_outcomes: Examine and critically evaluate current branding activities in the marketplace.
Apply relevant theoretical concepts of branding to analyse specific problems and challenges in brand management.
Make recommendations for the design and implementation of brand marketing programs.
Create and effectively communicate a brand positioning strategy.
Conduct a brand audit and use the information generated for brand planning.

title: Managerial Economics for Business Strategy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject applies managerial decision making analysis on various economic models, as well as introduces the student to optimisation techniques used in a managerial decision making environment. Economic models are related to cost and production as well as to the types of profit analyses underpinning contemporary business decision-making. The subject explores the profit/loss implications of alternative business strategies under various market conditions including competitive, monopoly and oligopoly market structures. Game theory models of business strategy are explored and applied to various business contexts. Alternative business pricing practices are reviewed. Policy issues are considered in an applied context through case studies and business applications.
learning_outcomes: Analyse strategic business decision-making using a range of contemporary models.
Discuss various economic models of managerial decision making.
Apply the business strategy analysis to several case study managerial economics models.

title: Managing Agroecosystems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Agricultural systems are managed ecosystems. This core subject will enable students to develop their understanding of natural ecosystems and how that knowledge can be applied to agricultural ecosystems. This subject will explore the relationship between the environment and the ecological suitability of agricultural enterprises. A major outcome of this subject will be to impart skills in developing and applying systems models towards the understanding of management options and their implications from the perspectives of productivity, stability, social equity, economics, and natural resource management.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a conceptual understanding of the ecological principles that drive agriculture.
Discuss sustainable agricultural system in the context of global food security.
Evaluate sustainability in the broad context of disturbance and recovery.
Develop eco-friendly models to preserve agricultural resources and evaluate the efficiency of such models.
Characterise the principles to manage and conserve complexity in agro-ecosystems.
Demonstrate management skills in generating sustainable technologies in crop ecosystems.
Analyse trials in sustainable farming practices and offer critique on them.

title: Managing and Leading Change
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject presents an integrated approach to the theory, research and practice of the leadership and management of the change process. Students will develop and apply action plans that encompass diagnosis, interventions, implementation, institutionalisation (sustaining change) and learning.
learning_outcomes: Formulate strategies and action plans for managing and leading effective change including targeting the level and types of change, change institutionalisation, and learning.
Assess political, cultural, structural and leadership factors in implementing change, considering the type, depth and scale of the change program.
Evaluate and apply appropriate methods for the diagnosis of external and internal pressures for change in organisations.
Create tactics to understand and engage stakeholders and predict their behavioural and emotional reactions.
Demonstrate a perspective on the theory and practice of organisational change.

title: Managing Broking Operations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to the role of management in a broking operation, in particular to the requirements of Policy Statement 164 Licensing: organisational capacities as necessary for an Australian Financial Services Licence.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the insurance broking industry and typical broking structures.
Develop an operational business plan for a broking organisation.
Explain the key tasks involved in human resource management of a broking organisation.
Explain the organisational requirements and other obligations of an Australian Financial Services Licensee as set out in Policy Statement 164 Licensing: Organisational capacities.
Assess market needs and develop a marketing plan for a broking organisation.

title: Managing Brands and Product Innovation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Strong brands and product innovation are important ingredients for the success of organisations in a rapidly changing world. Brands deliver value to consumers primarily through innovation, be it introducing new products and services, as well as through innovation in areas such as packaging, distribution, and product delivery. This subject will focus on the mutually dependent areas of brand management and product innovation. The subject has been designed to provide students with the capabilities to understand and apply the product development process in conjunction with brand management principles for building, enhancing and leveraging brand equity of products/services marketed by organisations.
learning_outcomes: Develop and make recommendations for specific brand strategies aimed at enhancing brand equity.
Articulate and reflect on the role of innovation in organisations and the challenges organisations face managing brands and developing new products and services.
Examine and critically evaluate branding and new product development activities in the marketplace.
Apply relevant theoretical concepts of brand and new product development strategy in a range of specific marketing contexts.
Make recommendations on the design, development and implementation of activities required to take a new product from an idea or opportunity through to a successful launch.

title: Managing Business Operations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to equip students with an understanding of an organisation's processes and operations in a changing environment. It focuses on the design, production and delivery of operations in both the manufacturing and services sectors. Students will study operations concepts, strategy, tools, techniques and systems. Students will apply quantitative and qualitative techniques to optimise operational performance.
learning_outcomes: Determine and apply appropriate tools and techniques in a variety of operations situations.
Collect, analyse and interpret operational data.
Establish standards and develop controls applicable to various processes.
Formulate and evaluate alternative approaches in operations management.
Respond to changes in the business environment by deploying the appropriate operations strategy.
Analyse and critically appraise an organisation's operations.

title: Managing Business Relationships
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Managing Business Relationships provides students with an understanding of the nature, structure and distinguishing characteristics of business-to-business markets in comparison to consumer markets. This subject presents a framework for understanding business-to-business buying behaviour and for developing relational marketing strategies that create and deliver value to targeted business-to-business markets and customers.
learning_outcomes: Analyse differences between business and consumer markets.
Make recommendations to develop and improve the management of relationships within a specific organisation's network.
Investigate and evaluate the nature, structure and distinguishing characteristics of business markets.
Evaluate how companies operate within a business network by closely examining a specific organisation's network.
Develop strategies for creating, delivering, pricing and promoting business offerings.

title: Managing Business Relationships
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the art of initiating, developing, maintaining and terminating a range of relationships in professional practice contexts. This subject also explores the interpersonal skills necessary to build relationships, including the art of listening, negotiating and managing conflict as important parts of professional practice. This subject embodies the principles of practice-based learning.
learning_outcomes: Devise a plan for managing and measuring the value of relationships in contemporary practice.
Determine and assess the interpersonal skills necessary to build relationships.
Appraise the role of communication in relationships.
Critique the theoretical constructs underpinning the management of professional relationships.

title: Managing Contemporary Farm Systems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject immerses students in the practicalities of farming. Depending on whether they are studying on-campus or online, students will spend time on the Charles Sturt farm or an approved farm developing practical skills, monitoring and reporting skills, and their general understanding of farm systems and supply chains. As part of their monitoring activities, students will develop skills in numeracy, data management and descriptive statistics. Students will also spend time exploring career pathways within the Agriculture field, auditing their own skills profiles and identifying developmental opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate developing digital literacy for professional practice and research.
Demonstrate the development of literacy and numeracy skills to understand, interpret and report information.
Demonstrate the development of skills in the recognition and mitigation of risks; associated with Workplace Health and Safety in Agricultural enterprises.
Demonstrate skills in communication and strategic questioning.
Describe a range of contemporary farm systems and their value chains.
Appraise their personal and professional capabilities through individual skills gap analysis and identify/undertake opportunities for development.
Demonstrate skills in monitoring and data collection of key farm information and the use of descriptive statistics in its presentation.

title: Managing Product and Service Innovation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In an era where established business models are being constantly challenged or disrupted, organisations need a culture of innovation and continuous improvement. This subject looks at innovation in an organisational context as well as examining the challenges companies face in developing successful new products and services. The activities involved in bringing a new product or service from an initial idea or opportunity through to a successful launch are examined in detail.
learning_outcomes: Examine and critically evaluate current new product activities in the market.
Critically reflect on the role of innovation in organisations and the challenges companies face in new product development.
Synthesise innovation literature to develop a theoretical framework for use in an audit of innovation practices of a specific organisation and make recommendations for improvement.
Evaluate the new product practices of an organisation and make recommendations for improvement that demonstrate knowledge of success factors in new product development.

title: Managing for Sustainability
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Sustainability is moving from the margins to the centre of business thinking and practice. In this subject we investigate what businesses are doing to adopt a more sustainable approach and evaluate how businesses utilise sustainability as a source of competitive advantage. Looking at a number of Australian and international case studies, the subject will attempt to analyse how individual businesses are attempting to align their activities to address global sustainability challenges such as climate change, resource scarcity and ethical conduct. After an initial introduction to sustainability and sustainable development, the subject presents a number of theories, models and strategic options for sustainable business. Subsequently this concept of corporate sustainability is analysed from the perspective of a variety of stakeholders - customers, suppliers, investors, employees, the natural environment, the broader community and civil society.
learning_outcomes: Research and evaluate the social and environmental risks and opportunities which impact on a particular business, use these to build a sustainability strategy for this business, and create a plan for improvement over the next two to three years.
Evaluate how the concepts of ethical behaviour and corporate social responsibility can be integrated into a business's sustainability strategy.
Define and explain the concepts of sustainability and sustainable development.
Identify, analyse and describe how sustainability can provide a source of innovation and competitive advantage to businesses.
Identify a range of frameworks for sustainability and assess a business's sustainability performance against these various frameworks.
Describe stakeholder theory and construct stakeholder maps for particular businesses.

title: Managing Projects and Resources
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the planning, management and evaluation of projects in environmental management. Working within an environmental sector role‑play scenario, students engage with realistic planning and budgetary constraints while exploring human resource management, organisational structures, risk assessment, budgeting and the preparation of grant applications. These themes are addressed in tandem and are woven together through a narrative based around a regional natural resource management agency. On completion, students will have demonstrated their advanced theoretical and technical knowledge of how to apply project management concepts to environmental problems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate problem solving skills to effectively develop, deliver, manage, and monitor a specific project.
Critically analyse funding opportunities available to an organisation in terms of potential organisational risk and capacity.
Apply advanced knowledge and understanding of organisational structures, the overarching assignment of duties, and employment procedures in the public sector.
Effectively communicate advanced theoretical and technical knowledge of the project management lifecycle.
Produce a coherent and fully developed project plan that integrates technical, organisational, and environmental considerations.

title: Managing Quality and Innovation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Quality Management & Innovation frameworks and techniques are used in many industries to enhanced business performance. This subject aims to introduce students to the historical theories and contemporary approaches to quality management and innovation practice. The subject encourages students to critically reflect on quality management practice with a focus on customers, organisational strategy, leadership impacts and human resource management initiatives. The students critically examine several quality management theories and models including quality control systems, continuous improvement, product and process innovation, the management of knowledge for innovation, teamwork systems and organisational restructuring for innovation and quality management.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the implementation of Quality Management systems within an organisation.
Devise appropriate solutions for Quality Management implementation issues in particular organisations.
Compare and contrast theories of Quality Management and innovation and evaluate their relevance for contemporary organisations.
Analyse the importance of customer focussed innovation for improving the competitive position of an organisation.
Evaluate the role of leadership, strategy and HRM approaches in fostering organisational commitment to a culture of quality innovation and improvement.

title: Managing Talent Productively in Health Services
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students for managing people productively in high-pressure work environments. Students learn to develop and justify a workforce plan, develop recruitment and retention strategies and apply learning theory in the creation of staff education plans. The subject also explores the role of professional development, lifelong learning, reflective practice and self-directed learning for both self and others for continuous improvement. There is also a focus on interpersonal approaches to managing people including conflict resolution, mentoring, and techniques for empowering, inspiring and enabling others.
learning_outcomes: Analyse approaches to manage workplace conflict through prevention and planning.
Apply the principles of a learning theory to training and education.
Apply strategic principles for workforce sustainability that aligns with intersectionality, inclusive practices and key organisational plans.
Describe strategies to empower, inspire and enable individuals using professional reflective practice.
Plan, develop and implement professional development, lifelong learning and mentoring to ensure continuous improvement to self and others.
Evaluate techniques to manage staff performance at all levels in the health care environments.

title: Managing the Classroom Environment
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops teacher education students' knowledge and understandings of key factors in effective classroom management including quality teaching, engagement, participation, and inclusion. Students will draw on their understandings of young peoples' physical, social, emotional and intellectual development and learn about theories and models of classroom management to facilitate learning and the management of behaviour. The importance of differentiated and culturally responsive planning, and processes to deal with challenging behaviours, including bullying and cyberbullying, will be explored. Strategies for effective communication within the education setting and beyond will also be explored. Students will also analyse legislative requirements and school based student welfare/discipline policies and/or approaches which support positive classroom management and learner welfare.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse key educational theories and models of classroom management (including Authoritarian, Mixed Method, and Egalitarian approaches), and evaluate how effective teaching practices, curriculum rigour, engagement strategies, and inclusive pedagogical approaches create positive learning environments.

Describe the physical, social, emotional and intellectual development and characteristics of students from diverse backgrounds, and analyse how these developmental factors affect learning, behaviour, and classroom interactions.

Explain the professional and legal responsibilities of teachers regarding student protection, safety, and wellbeing, and demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with school teams, families, and community stakeholders to support student learning and behaviour.

Identify, select, and implement strategies to prevent, respond to, and de-escalate challenging student behaviours, including disruptive conduct, bullying, and cyberbullying across different contexts and student cohorts, while understanding whole-school behaviour support approach.

Design evidence-based plans and strategies that apply classroom management principles to create inclusive learning environments, promote positive student behaviour and relationships, and support diverse learners through differentiated instruction, collaborative learning, and effective communication practices.

title: Managing the Learning Environment
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops teacher education students' knowledge and understandings of key factors in effective classroom management including quality teaching, engagement, participation and inclusion. Students will draw on their understandings of young peoples' physical, social, emotional and intellectual development and learn about theories and models of classroom management to facilitate learning and the management of behaviour. Students will design evidence-based plans and strategies to create effective, positive and safe classroom environments. The importance of differentiated and culturally responsive planning, processes to deal with inappropriate behaviour, including bullying and cyber-bullying, and strategies for effective communication within the education setting and beyond will be explored. Students will also critically analyse legislative requirements and school based student welfare/discipline policies and/or approaches that support positive classroom management and learner welfare.
learning_outcomes: Explain and demonstrate effective communication strategies at classroom and whole-school levels to support student engagement, while discussing professional and legal responsibilities regarding student protection, safety, wellbeing and the provision of equitable learning opportunities.

Describe, justify and evaluate educational theories and models of classroom management, analysing key factors in effective practice, including quality teaching, engagement, participation and inclusion, and appraise how these are implemented through evidence-based pedagogical approaches.

Apply theories of physical, social, emotional and intellectual development to understand student characteristics and analyse how these developmental factors affect learning behaviours, engagement patterns, and classroom interactions across diverse student populations.

Design evidence-based plans that apply appropriate classroom management theories, principles and models to create positive learning environments, facilitate effective strategies for positive student behaviour and relationships, and support diverse learners through inclusive participation and engagement in classroom and wider school settings.

Justify selected strategies and practical approaches to manage challenging student behaviours, including prevention, intervention and response to disruptive behaviour, bullying and cyberbullying across different contexts and cohorts, while evaluating whole-school behaviour support approaches and their integration with classroom management practices.

title: Managing the Learning Environment
school: School of Education
