Students will draw on their understandings of young peoples' physical, social, emotional and intellectual development to apply theories and models of classroom management to facilitate learning. Students will develop and apply knowledge of proactive and reactive management of behaviour needed to create effective, positive and safe classroom environments. The importance of differentiated and culturally responsive planning, and processes to deal with challenging behaviours, including bullying and cyberbullying, will be explored. Strategies for effective communication within the education setting and beyond will also be explored. Students will also analyse legislative requirements and school based student welfare/discipline policies and/or approaches which support positive classroom management and learner welfare.
learning_outcomes: Explain the professional and legal responsibilities of teachers regarding student protection, safety and wellbeing and demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with school teams, families and communitty stakeholders to support student learning and behaviour.

Identify and analyse key educational theories and models of classroom management, (including Authoritarian, Mixed Method, and Egalitarian approaches), and evaluate how effective teaching practices, curriculum rigour, engagement strategies, and inclusive pedagogical approaches create positive learning environments. and appraise how they are applied through pedagogical practice.

Design evidence-based plans and strategies that apply classroom management principles to create inclusive learning environments, promote positive student behaviour and relationships, and support diverse learners through differentiated instruction, collaborative learning, and effective communication practices.

Describe the physical, social, emotional and intellectual development and characteristics of students from diverse backgrounds, and analyse how these developmental factors affect learning, behaviour and classroom interactions.

Identify, select and implement strategies to prevent, respond to, and de-escalate challenging student behaviours, including disruptive conduct, bullying and cyberbullying across different contexts and student cohorts, while understanding whole school behaviour support approach.

title: Managing your Global Workforce and Business
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this subject is to develop an awareness of and the skills applicable to managing people from a cross-cultural perspective. Key areas include communication, leadership and motivation, culture, negotiation, decision making, global alliances, emerging economies, applied ethics and social responsibility. The subject then examines how these factors influence managing people within a global business.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and explain how the variables of culture interact with other national and international factors to affect managerial processes and behaviour.
Analyse and explain issues relevant to corporate social responsibility, sustainability and ethics while operating in global locations.
Evaluate cross cultural management in the context of global changes.
prerequisites: HRM386: International Dimensions of Human Resource Management

title: Mantiq (Logic) and Critical Reasoning
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: The ability to reason persuasively and analyse objectively arguments posed by others are essential skills in Islamic studies and modern academia. This subject introduces students to principles of critical reasoning and how to apply those in written and spoken works. Students will develop the skills to differentiate between valid and invalid, sound and unsound arguments. They will also practice and develop skills in constructing sound logical arguments and identifying logical fallacies. It covers the place of mantiq (logic) within Islamic scholarship. Historically Muslim logicians were able to develop a distinct system of logic, uniquely suited for examining concepts, ideas, and strictures rooted in divine revelation.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and critically analyse the reasoning of others and identify logical fallacies.
Apply critical reasoning in their spoken and written work.
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of reasoning and logic (mantiq) in Islamic studies.
Demonstrate the ability to construct sound and valid logical arguments.
Demonstrate an appreciation for Muslim scholars of mantiq (logic).

title: Mandatory Technology Contexts: Computational, Design, and Systems Thinking
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject engages students in the discipline knowledge and understandings of the four technology context areas of the Stage 4 NESA (2023) Technology 7-8 course, as well as requisite skills in computational, design, and systems thinking through application in practical and theoretical contexts. This not only forms part of teacher education students' preparation to teach Technology 7-8, it also contributes to developing knowledge and skills required to teach stage 5 and 6 Design and Technology. An important aspect of this subject is students' learning through instruction and application in practical projects how to select and safely use materials, ingredients, equipment, and tools in the four technologies contexts, and how and where the three types of thinking apply and may be taught within these contexts. Knowledge and skills gained in this subject will be extended upon in subsequent design and discipline specific studies, as well as professional placements.
learning_outcomes: Competently complete projects from each of the Technology 7-8 contexts.
Assess risk, and develop and document appropriate project processes in a safe work method statement.
Explain project-based learning and its application in teaching Technology 7-8.

Develop projects that address the requirements of the Technology 7-8 syllabus for each of the technologies contexts, including the incorporation of computational, design, and systems thinking to facilitate learning of these skills.
Select and safely use materials, ingredients, equipment and tools in a range of technology contexts.

title: Manufacturing Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject serves as an introduction to the field of manufacturing engineering, providing students with foundational knowledge and understanding of various manufacturing processes, materials, technologies and quality systems.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe common manufacturing processes and quality control methods used in industry.
Demonstrate proficiency in performing calculations related to manufacturing processes.
Recognise different materials used in manufacturing and their properties.
Discuss the basic principles and concepts of manufacturing engineering.

title: Marine Claims Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with the knowledge and skills to manage and resolve claims in Marine classes of insurance.
learning_outcomes: Participate in negotiations to settle claims.
Review claims settlement policy and procedures.
Process facultative and treaty claims.
Apply legal terms and concepts to Marine claims management.
Process claims and finalise settlement.
Evaluate nonroutine claims.
Resolve claims disputes.

title: Mapping the Field of Educational Leadership
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the literature encompassing the field of educational leadership. It examines the philosophical, ethical and historical strands which underpin educational leadership as a field. It analyses key trends in the field, both globally and across a number of Anglophone nations, such as Australia, Canada, USA and the United Kingdom. In so doing, it provides a critical examination of theories of educational leadership and their purpose within education as a profession in the 21st Century.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the philosophical, historical and ethical strands which underpin contemporary educational leadership literature.
Articulate an informed critique of the theoretical stances within the field.
Articulate links between historical and contemporary concepts of leadership and their application to students' local settings and students' own professional philosophies of leadership.
Develop an understanding of the key developments in educational leadership as a field.

title: Marine Underwriting Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the knowledge and skills to assess and underwrite risk relating to marine insurance and to survey risk exposure and review and interpret portfolio performance.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the concept of carrier in marine insurance.
Negotiate premiums.
Discuss the concept of cargo in marine insurance.
Discuss the concept of marine liability.
Draft marine policy wordings and clauses.
Evaluate quotation slips.
Analyse risk related to marine insurance.
Review operational performance of portfolio.
Provide quotations.
Discuss the concept of hull in marine insurance.

title: Maritime Enforcement
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the roles and responsibilities of maritime enforcement agencies and various international conventions and agreements, including and principally the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, that impact on maritime regulation and enforcement.
learning_outcomes: Explain and discuss critically the rights and responsibilities of States in various maritime zones of jurisdiction and the relevant legal considerations when conducting enforcement in the maritime environment.

Analyse and evaluate interagency and cooperative maritime enforcement arrangements in and between selected coastal States and apply that analysis and evaluation to practical and theoretical situations that they may face as border regulators and/or managers.
Formulate appropriate and well-developed operational strategies that address maritime enforcement challenges in different maritime settings and to be able to communicate those strategies to others.

Conduct a comparative analysis of the international and domestic laws relating to maritime regulation and enforcement including analysing and critically assessing the regulatory frameworks of different countries against best practice and established international standards.

title: Maritime Regulation and Enforcement
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the range of maritime activities undertaken at the border. The key international conventions that impact on maritime operations together with legislative and procedural aspects of maritime activities are examined using a number of case studies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of the key international legal conventions when conducting enforcement in the maritime environment.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the range of maritime activities and evaluate the procedures used in different operational settings.
Research, identify and detail how the various maritime zones are enforced within their chosen coastal State.
Assess the potential risks that may arise in planning and conducting a maritime enforcement activity and demonstrate an ability to formulate practical mitigation strategies.
Formulate strategies after undertaking a basic SWOT analysis of a planned maritime enforcement activity, operation or control checkpoint.
Evaluate critically various operational approaches to maritime enforcement and identify good practice, including the use of targeting and information management.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the roles and responsibilities of the various members of a typical coordinated maritime enforcement activity.

title: Marketing - Level 5
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for the Master of Communication (generic and with specialisations) Articulated Set
learning_outcomes: N/A.

title: Market Research
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to the principles of market research and how market research may be applied to address a management problem. The aim of this subject is to develop the skills needed to conduct or apply market research within a commercial context. The subject begins with an overview of the research design process. It then addresses fundamental qualitative and quantitative research issues including data measurement, collection and analysis, and how data can be analysed to provide strategic guidance.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the advantages, limitations, and the ethical implications of commonly used research techniques and their relevance to a research problem.
Develop and evaluate research proposals and reports within the context of a research problem.
Understand and apply the concepts and methods of market research to address a research problem.
Analyse and integrate different sources and types of data to draw conclusions.
Reflect on the biases and limitations of market data given a particular research problem.
Recognise the difference between a management problem and a market research problem.

title: Marketing for Managers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Marketing is used by managers to identify and develop markets and align the organisation's resources to achieve its business goals. The key focus of marketing activity is to research and develop an understanding of the needs and wants of consumers and the evolving nature of markets in a complex, diverse and rapidly changing globalised world. This subject will introduce managers to foundational ideas and theories that explain why marketing is an essential activity in any organisation. Students will also investigate and critically discuss how marketing practice operates within a dynamic contemporary marketplace
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically evaluate how mega trends and issues related to digital transformation, society, sustainability and business ethics might affect marketing strategy and tactics.

Apply the elements of the marketing mix including brand management to a range of audiences within business to business (B2B) and/or business to consumer (B2C) markets, and make recommendations for decision makers.
Assess and explain the nature of marketing practice in organisations.
Find and evaluate relevant and important information about organisations, their industries and marketplaces from secondary sources.
Evaluate the key marketing concepts of segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP) and analyse an organisation's approach to STP.

title: Marketing Fundamentals
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Marketing is about markets and people. Students will examine different types of markets and the interactions of clients, business customers and end consumers within those markets. The purpose of this subject is to introduce students to the principles of marketing strategy by exploring how organisations adapt their marketing activities in response to needs and wants at the individual, organisational and societal level. The subject also explores the impact of societal and cultural elements on both people and marketing practice.
learning_outcomes: be able to create and communicate marketing strategy solutions and recommendations for organisation.
be able to effectively gather and utilise secondary data research; and
be able to analyse real-life situations in the corporate, and/or small medium and entrepreneurial business sector and/or not for-profit organisations using marketing frameworks and practice;
be able to develop an overview of the business planning process for different types of organisations;
be able to define and describe marketing concepts in complex and diverse markets;
be able to examine key societal and business issues related to marketing activities;

title: Marketing of Libraries and Information Agencies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a detailed introduction to the fundamentals of marketing principles and practice to facilitate adoption of successful marketing strategies in an organisational context. Marketing concepts, theories and principles are covered, along with their application to the library and information environment. The subject examines the distinct characteristics of services enabling students to identify and develop strategic marketing initiatives and plans in order to build branding and promotional strategies.
learning_outcomes: Discuss contemporary issues such as the environment, social media and other technologies and how they may affect marketing in order to formulate a service strategy.
Prepare a strategic marketing plan with appropriate and measurable goals and objectives.
Apply the marketing mix to a specific target market.
Explain the role and value of marketing in the provision of information resources and services.
prerequisites: INF420: Current Topics in Effective Library Management

title: Marketing in Action
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to develop, evaluate and apply contemporary speciality marketing topics including global marketing and value chains, business-to-business relationships, services marketing, and contemporary models of retail marketing. This subject combines the application of marketing fundamental with practical business knowledge. This subject provides an opportunity for students to better understand how marketing is evolving in the 21st Century.
learning_outcomes: Present recommendations to a range of audiences using a variety of mediums (e.g., written reports, oral presentations).
Identify and analyse current marketing principles pertaining to marketing in a global, services, retail and B2B contexts.
Critically assess market conditions in a range of market contexts and to identify the likely impact for key stakeholders.
Conduct secondary market research.
Apply current marketing practices in a range of business contexts through the design of relevant and appropriate strategies and tactics.

title: Marketing of Libraries and Information Agencies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a detailed introduction to the fundamentals of marketing principles and practice to facilitate adoption of successful marketing strategies in an organisational context. Marketing concepts, theories and principles are covered, along with their application to the library and information environment. The subject examines the distinct characteristics of services enabling students to identify and develop strategic marketing initiatives and plans in order to build branding and promotional strategies.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse contemporary issues such as the environment, social media and other technologies and how they may affect marketing in order to formulate a service strategy.
Analyse and transmit knowledge about the relationship between strategic marketing planning and organisational strategy to deliver on stated objectives.
Evaluate and apply the marketing mix to a specific target market.
Design and produce a strategic marketing plan with appropriate and measurable goals and objectives.
Explain the role and value of marketing in the provision of information and services.
prerequisites: INF310: Marketing of Libraries and Information Agencies

title: Marketing of Services
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The global significance of the services sector has forced many organisations to re-think their business model. This subject examines the nature of services marketing in detail. Building on knowledge from MKT110, this subject explores how service organisations compete. Drawing on the services literature and industry best practice, this subject critically examines the distinct characteristics of services and how these characteristics shape marketing strategies that can deliver organisational outcomes. Central constructs such as customer satisfaction, service quality, and value are considered along with the role of technology and ethics in determining appropriate marketing strategies.
learning_outcomes: Create a service strategy for the development of new services including planning for variations in pricing, demand and capacity.
Identify the distinctive characteristics of services marketing and describe the components of the expanded marketing mix.
Describe and develop an effective service recovery process.
Design guidelines for a customer service program.
Analyse the significance of satisfaction, value and service quality and explain its role in achieving organisational service goals.

title: Master Research (Agricultural and Environmental Sciences) FT
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a research subject available only to students enrolled in an appropriate Higher Degree by Research within the School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences. Students enrolled in this subject will work directly with their supervisory team to undertake an appropriate research project, culminating in completion of a thesis/dissertation to be submitted for examination.
learning_outcomes: Disseminate their research via a range of media, and be able to coherently defend their work, to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

Demonstrate cognitive, technical and creative skills to investigate, analyse and synthesise complex information, problems and concepts and theorise and apply established theories to different bodies of knowledge and practice.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of research principles and methods applicable to their field of research.
Demonstrate an advanced level body of knowledge in the relevant field and a capacity to critically reflect on that knowledge and its application/s.
Apply knowledge and skills to plan and execute a piece of research that generates a substantial contribution to the field in the form of a research thesis.
Develop a research hypothesis or question that is soundly embedded in the context of the current body of knowledge in the field.
prerequisites: AGR602: Master Research (Agriculture and Wine) FT

title: Marketing Strategy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Marketing strategy is examined from a range of theoretical perspectives. Strategic arena analysis and the value chain provide complementary frameworks for investigation of markets and strategic options. Analytical skills are developed through the application of these frameworks to an industry environment. This is a capstone marketing subject and should be attempted towards the end of a Masters degree.
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate various theoretical approaches that have contributed to competitive strategy formation.
Critique the role of business partnerships and customer relationship management in the creation of superior customer value.
Systematically identify, evaluate and control for strategy implementation.
Analyse critical capabilities, skills and knowledge necessary for effective strategy development.

school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on foundational knowledge, skills and application of communication practice. Students from the strategic communication, news and media, and design and content creation majors will contribute to a multidisciplinary project. Students will learn how to: implement appropriate strategy, research and evaluation methods in multidisciplinary contexts; reflect on their practice; and further develop their cultural competency.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and reflect on practice.
Apply relevant methodologies to inform practice.
Work collaboratively in a multidisciplinary team to produce culturally appropriate outputs.
Apply the communication planning cycle to develop a communication solution.

learning_outcomes: Design research methodology appropriate to the research question or questions.
Understand and critically analyse the scholarly literature in order to inform the development of an appropriate research question or questions, and.
Utilize library and information technology appropriately to locate scholarly literature relevant to a phenomenon or problem of interest.

title: Masters Dissertation in Ageing and Pastoral Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will implement a research proposal and write a dissertation on their completed research in ageing and pastoral studies. It is designed to enhance academic and professional development of students working in the field of ageing and pastoral studies and to equip graduates with analytic and conceptual competencies. The program allows significant flexibility to accommodate individual student preferences and/or professional requirements. Students will be encouraged to publish their research findings in appropriate journals.
learning_outcomes: Produce a thorough, carefully reasoned dissertation which demonstrates an indepth understanding of a specific area of knowledge or enquiry.
Validate awareness and sensitivity to ethical issues arising from the dissertation in ageing and pastoral studies.
Demonstrate effective reference to the literature.
Demonstrate a high order of skill in planning and implementing a research project.
Demonstrate an advanced ability to communicate and contextualise an ageing and pastoral studies project.

title: Masters Research
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject provides students with training in research methods and study design. Through professional workplace exposures and discussion with the supervisory team, students identify gaps in the existing knowledge and formulate research questions and hypotheses for the clinical research project of the Master of Veterinary Studies and will develop a proposal and planning for the project. The students will undertake a critical analysis of (1) theoretical knowledge, existing knowledge and professional practice in the field of investigation, (2) the identified research questions and (3) available research methods, and prepare a literature review. Students will provide a presentation of the research proposal and plan. Students obtain all the necessary approvals for the project.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of research principles and methods applicable to clinical research.
Demonstrate a body of knowledge and skills relevant to conducting clinical research.
Design, critique, analyse, theorise and communicate research plans for clinical research to provide original contributions to knowledge.
Demonstrate cognitive and technical skills to design, use and evaluate research and research methods.

title: Materials and Image Development
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students' perceptions and understanding of the multi-disciplined nature of current image making practice using traditional and contemporary analogue and digital processes. Drawing to Design is the core of visual thinking that any designer or artist must have to be adaptable and flexible in their individual image development approaches across a variety of contexts. Students will acquire perceptual and observational drawing and image making skills to manage and extend a diversity of inventive and expressive visual problem solving responses. This subject is intended to challenge students' approaches to drawing and image making as well as the ideas that are explored through drawing.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to analyse and develop sequential or related developmental iterations to test idea and form towards complex resolved outcomes.

Demonstrate the development of an individual image making practice closely informed by a complementary visual research processes based upon the philosophies and approaches of traditional and contemporary designers and artists in related fields of graphic design, illustration, animation, drawing, printmaking and photography amongst others.

Recognise, interpret and organise formal strategies of composition, perspective, line, tone, colour, size and shape variations to generate inventive, predetermined visual outcomes appropriate for a range of contexts.
Demonstrate the ability to interpret and critically discuss their own and others work toward more developed understanding of the breadth of practice using design language and terminology.
Evidence a capacity to appropriately apply, integrate and adapt analogue and digital media through concepts and innovative outcomes.
prerequisites: SLV215: Interpretation and Analysis of Form
TXT205: Concept and Themes: Research and Process

title: Materials and Image Research
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to consolidate students understanding, expertise and analytical abilities through a lecture program and workshop tutorials. Students are encouraged to investigate and integrate a range of techniques and processes based on extended research and concept development.
learning_outcomes: Understand the effect of different technologies upon the process and outcome.
Demonstrate the ability to interpret a brief/assignment/commission from concept drawings to finished artwork.
Developed an individual interpretation of, and critical approach to visual problems.
Developed an individual visual language of process.
Demonstrate the ability to undertake research and investigative visual research using historical and contemporary data.

title: Maternal and Paediatric Care in Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject equips students with the knowledge and skills to provide paramedic care to paediatric and maternal populations in paramedicine practice settings. Students will develop the skills to formulate evidence-based treatment plans by integrating anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, and pharmacology, aligned with graduate paramedicine standards. The subject also builds foundational competencies for safe care across childbearing and emergency scenarios. Emphasis is placed on safe, ethical, person-centred, and culturally inclusive practices, including cultural safety for First Nations peoples and diverse populations, fostering professional paramedicine attributes.
learning_outcomes: Justify woman-centred maternal and newborn care during normal and complex presentations while advocating and supporting normal physiological birth.

Integrate knowledge of key anatomical and physiological differences in paediatrics with the ability to demonstrate age-appropriate assessment and history taking to inform paramedic clinical decision-making.
Apply the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) Standards to deliver safe, respectful, and collaborative maternal and paediatric care within paramedic practice.
Evaluate ethical and inclusive practices during paediatric, maternal and neonatal paramedic care, including culturally safe care for First Nations peoples and diverse populations.
Formulate safe, evidence-based paramedic treatment plans for paediatric, maternal and neonatal emergencies.
prerequisites: PAR200: Medical Emergencies in Paramedic Practice

title: Math, statistics, physics and advanced chemistry for Medical Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is a continuation of the study of the fundamentals of chemistry. Students will learn the underlying principles behind rates of chemical change, oxidation/reduction and electrochemistry; and be introduced to organic chemistry, with some specific applications to medical science. The subject will also include some basic statistics and physics as necessary for the understanding of medical science and the techniques used in medical science laboratories.
learning_outcomes: Describe and solve basic statistical calculations including, but not limited to, mean, standard deviation, t-test, Chi square test.
Recognise and describe a selected range of standard chemical transformations between common organic functional groups.

Describe and explain basic principles in physics that relate to equipment or processes important in medical science, including, but not limited to, microscopy, spectrophotometry, fluorometry, mass spectrometry and conductivity.
Explain the catenation ability of the element carbon, the nature of covalent molecular compounds, and identify the various forms of isomerism.
Identify the various classes of organic compounds, apply nomenclature principles and explain chemical properties.
Solve and interpret rate equations from kinetic data.
Describe and apply fundamentals of kinetics.
Balance redox equations, use the Nernst Equation and calculate equilibrium constants from electrochemical data.

title: Mathematical and Scientific Learning in the Early Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn about the development of mathematical, scientific and technological understandings from birth to five years of age. The foundation concepts and processes will be explored along with how these understandings are developed through children's everyday activities, play, and investigations, across the birth to five spectrum. The subject will explore what mathematics, science, and technology look like in these different settings, and the pedagogical approaches for recognising, supporting and extending development of these concepts and processes in each of these settings. There is a specific focus in this subject on intentional teaching for enhancing children's learning of science, mathematics and technology concepts. Students will learn how to observe, record, analyse and plan for this learning in early childhood settings.
learning_outcomes: Investigate everyday technology and digital technology for children's scientific or mathematical learning.
Apply knowledge of foundational mathematics, science and technology concepts and processes developed during the early childhood years.
Identify and implement relevant curriculum (e.g., Early Years Learning Framework) and teaching strategies which support children's construction of mathematical, scientific and technological learning.
Demonstrate an ability to use children's drawings and narratives as a starting point for planning future mathematics and science learning experiences.
Collaborate and communicate professionally in the design and evaluation of resources for teaching mathematics, science and technology in the early years.

Apply theoretical knowledge and effectively use pedagogies of play, language, modelling, and questioning to facilitate opportunities for mathematical, scientific and technological learning and developing children's emerging understandings of mathematics, science, and technology.

Observe, plan, record and analyse children's engagement in relation to the children's developing understandings of mathematical, scientific and technological concepts and processes through their everyday activities, play, and investigations.
prerequisites: EMC305: Investigation: Mathematics, Science and Technology

title: Mathematical Modelling
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' practical skills by using computer software to solve mathematical applications. The two main applications considered are the numerical solutions of differential equations (ordinary and partial); and fitting data to a model using least-squares regression (linear and non-linear).
learning_outcomes: Calculate the solutions of partial differential equations using various methods.
Write computer programs to solve real-life problems.
Determine the stability of a finite difference equation.
Adapt existing code to produce numerical solutions for differential equations.
Generate suitable finite difference equations from differential equations.
Numerically calculate the solutions of ordinary differential equations using various methods.
Fit data to a model using linear and non-linear regression techniques.

title: Mathematical Modelling
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' practical skills by using computer software to solve mathematical applications. The two main applications considered are the numerical solutions of differential equations (ordinary and partial); and fitting data to a model using least-squares regression (linear and non-linear).
learning_outcomes: Numerically calculate the solutions of ordinary differential equations using various methods.
Write computer programs to solve real-life problems.
Adapt existing code to produce numerical solutions for differential equations.
Interpret mathematical models and communicate their output to non-mathematical audiences.
Fit data to a model using linear and non-linear regression techniques.
Determine the stability of a finite difference equation.
Calculate the solutions of partial differential equations using various methods.
Generate suitable finite difference equations from differential equations.

title: Mathematics and Numeracy Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the central concepts, skills, modes of enquiry, language, and content of mathematics. Teacher education students will explore mathematical concepts with a strong emphasis on numeracy as an enjoyable and relevant way of constructing mathematical meaning and ideas. Connections between mathematical concepts and areas, as well as applications to real world scenarios and problems will be explored.
learning_outcomes: Apply mathematical knowledge, skills and processes across a wide range of topic areas to solve appropriate real-world problems and scenarios.
Solve problems involving uncertainty using the basic principles of probability.
Reflect critically on mathematical skills and understanding to improve practice.
Construct and interpret diagrams, tables and graphs to solve mathematical problems and communicate results.
Make and justify informed decisions about financial situations based on appropriate models.
Communicate, interpret and analyse data in a variety of representations.
Describe and model patterns in mathematical terms.
Communicate mathematical ideas, reasoning and solutions, clearly and effectively using appropriate symbols, notation and conventions.
prerequisites: MTH101: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Mathematics and Statistics
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Mathematics and Statistics explicitly teaches the foundational numerical skills required for initial participation in university courses involving science and engineering. Students will apply mathematical knowledge in unfamiliar contexts to solve problems. They will learn how to represent graphically and perform calculations related to exponential numbers. The subject requires students to extract, interpret and comprehend a range of mathematical information in texts, tables, diagrams, and graphs, and to analyse bivariate data to make inferences and predictions. Students are presented with a range of real-world situations from the science and engineering fields to consolidate the skills learnt.
learning_outcomes: Model everyday mathematical scenarios using statistics, probability, algebra and graphs.
Analyse bivariate data to make inferences and predictions.
Apply mathematical knowledge to solve problems with an unfamiliar context.
Extract, interpret and comprehend a range of mathematical information in texts, tables, diagrams and graphs in familiar and unfamiliar contexts.
Represent graphically and perform calculations related to exponential numbers.

title: Mathematics And Statistics In Health Sciences
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to provide students with the necessary foundation in mathematics and statistics for subjects in the health sciences. The mathematical module reinforces calculation skills, basic algebra, working with formulae and applications of exponential and logarithmic functions. In the study of statistics, the emphasis is on understanding the key concepts and applying acquired skills to data interpretation by the use of a modern software package.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate if the assumptions underlying statistical techniques are valid in a given scenario.
Summarise and interpret data graphically and numerically.
Use a statistical package to analyse data appropriately, and then interpret the output.
Plot and interpret graphs of mathematical functions.
Convert a measurement from one unit to another.
Carry out calculations and use algebra correctly.
Use exponential and logarithm functions in applications.
Calculate and interpret probabilities, and use some standard probability distributions.
Calculate confidence intervals and carry out tests of hypotheses.

title: Mathematics Difficulties: Prevention and Intervention
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the prevention of mathematics difficulties in the primary school years and in designing interventions for individual children. The subject content is grounded in the scientifically based research on mathematics teaching and learning. Explicit teaching is the pedagogy for instruction used in the teaching of mathematics in this subject. There is a specific emphasis on assessment and the role of careful instructional design and delivery in the teaching of children who are at risk for mathematics difficulties. Students will apply their understanding of assessment, explicit teaching, and instructional decision making.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate their lesson using evidence-based strategies for adapting instruction.
Develop an explicit teaching strategy for teaching a mathematics skill and then deliver the lesson which will receive peer feedback.
Identify a child's relative risk for mathematics difficulties using a reliable curriculum-based measure.
Recognise, understand and describe common mathematical difficulties experienced by diverse learners.
Understand and apply the principles of Curriculum Based Measurement and Curriculum-Based Assessment of Mathematics.
Summarise student performance and place children in a mathematics scope and sequence at their instructional level.
Deliver their math lesson including all the key features of explicit teaching.

title: Mathematics for Calculus
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will review arithmetic and algebra skills that are prerequisite knowledge in the study of a calculus based mathematics subject. It is intended to provide students with the necessary skills to successfully attempt subjects such as Computer Aided Mathematics with Applications 1 (MTH101) and Introductory Mathematics (MTH105). Topics include calculator skills, fractions, signed numbers, algebra, concepts of functions and introductory calculus.
learning_outcomes: Understand and work with algebraic expressions.
Understand concepts of functions, variables and graphs.
Use a calculator confidently and correctly.
Understand and work with arithmetic.

title: Mathematics for Engineers 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the essential mathematical concepts and techniques crucial for engineering analysis and problem-solving. Emphasis is placed on covering core topics while providing practical applications relevant to engineering disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Utilise vector calculus concepts such as vectors, dot and cross products, and vector-valued functions to analyse and solve engineering problems.
Use fundamental mathematical concepts including algebra, trigonometry, calculus and differential equations, essential for engineering analysis and problem-solving.
Interpret mathematical solutions within the context of engineering problems.
Apply mathematical techniques such as differentiation, integration, and solving differential equations to analyse and solve engineering problems.

title: Mathematics for Engineers 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will deepen students' understanding of advanced mathematical concepts and techniques relevant to engineering analysis, providing them with the mathematical tools necessary to tackle complex engineering problems in their future academic and professional pursuits.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced mathematical techniques, including multivariable calculus, Fourier analysis, and numerical methods, to analyse and solve engineering problems.
Analyse and interpret engineering systems using Fourier Analysis.
Utilise linear algebra concepts such as matrices, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors to solve systems of linear equations and ordinary differential equations.

title: Mathematics for Engineers 3
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces fundamental statistical concepts and techniques essential for engineering analysis and decision-making. Emphasis is placed on understanding statistical principles, data analysis, and interpretation of results in engineering contexts.
learning_outcomes: Examine statistical methods in real-world engineering problems, communicating findings effectively.
Apply fundamental statistical concepts and methods essential for engineering analysis.
Utilise regression analysis to model relationships between variables and predict outcomes.
Apply probability theory and distributions to analyse uncertainty in engineering systems.
Develop hypothesis tests and interpret results to make informed engineering decisions.

title: Mathematics for Out of Field Teachers
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This microcredential introduces students to the discipline of mathematics, its nature, history, philosophy and place in secondary education. It examines the Years 7-12 mathematics curriculum, and in particular the development of content from the Number and Algebra strands within the mathematics K-10 syllabus. It also extends students' knowledge and practice of mathematics teaching and learning with a focus on Year 11 and Year 12 NSW Mathematics syllabuses and the Australian Curriculum. Particular attention is devoted to the application of contemporary theories of learning in mathematics, authentic pedagogies, and assessment for learning in the planning of secondary mathematics curriculum.
learning_outcomes: Apply contemporary models of pedagogy in planning of a sequence of learning activities that develop a foundational mathematical concept.
Apply the concepts, content and structure of a Stage 6 Mathematics syllabus in the development of a detailed teaching program for a sequence of lessons.

Explain the structure and content of the mathematics 7-10 Syllabus for NSW or the Australian Curriculum, including assessment and reporting requirements and apply this in the development of a sequence of learning activities.
Identify, critique, and explain the implications of a range of issues relevant to the teaching and learning of secondary mathematics in the Australian context for a diverse range of learners.

title: Mathematics for Primary Teachers
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to enable graduate entry primary teacher education students to be confident and competent teachers of primary school mathematics, pass the national Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education Students (LANTITE) and comply with the NESA course accreditation requirements. To achieve a satisfactory grade in this subject students must complete a minimum of 90 hours of approved study in mathematics across the three content areas in the NSW Mathematics K-10 syllabus: Number & Algebra, Measurement & Geometry & Statistics & Probability.
learning_outcomes: Use problem solving, mathematical reasoning, conceptual understanding and procedural fluency in relation to calculations involving number and in basic algebraic manipulations.
Identify, interpret, evaluate, communicate and represent the mathematical information embedded in a situation.
Successfully apply mathematical knowledge and problem-solving processes across a wide range of topic areas to solve appropriate real-world problems.
Communicate mathematical ideas and reasoning clearly and effectively using common mathematical symbolism, notation and conventions, and representations such as graphs and tables.

Utilise mathematical information such as graphs, statistics and data, including planning, gathering, organising, applying data to solve problems, and communicating results through the selection of appropriate representations.
Complete a range of arithmetic and mathematical operations and transformations involving various shapes and their measurement, basic geometry, systems and units of measurement.

title: Mathematics for Teachers
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to develop teacher education students' (TESs) awareness of their personal numeracy knowledge and skills and provides teacher education students access to resources they may use to improve their numeracy capabilities. The national Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education (LANTITE) is a mandatory online assessment that examines aspects of an individual's personal literacy and numeracy skills. This zero-credit point subject is to be completed as preparation for LANTITE and to comply with NESA course accreditation requirements. To achieve a satisfactory grade in this subject TESs must complete a minimum of 90 hours of approved study in mathematics with StudyLink (complimentary short courses for CSU students) across the three content areas in the NSW Mathematics K-10 syllabus: Number & Algebra, Measurement & Geometry & Statistics & Probability.
learning_outcomes: Identify, interpret, evaluate, communicate and represent the mathematical information embedded in a situation.
Use problem solving, mathematical reasoning, conceptual understanding and procedural fluency in relation to calculations involving number and in basic algebraic manipulations.

Utilise mathematical information such as graphs, statistics and data, including planning, gathering, organising, applying data to solve problems, and communicating results through the selection of appropriate representations.
Complete a range of arithmetic and mathematical operations and transformations involving various shapes and their measurement, basic geometry, systems and units of measurement.
Communicate mathematical ideas and reasoning clearly and effectively using common mathematical symbolism, notation and conventions, and representations such as graphs and tables.
Successfully apply mathematical knowledge and problem-solving processes across a wide range of topic areas to solve appropriate real-world problems.

title: Mathematics in the Primary Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates the central concepts, modes of enquiry and structure of the content of mathematics and explicitly connects these ideas to the models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing mathematics. There is also a strong emphasis on: ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the mathematics classroom; the role and value of mathematics in the broader school curriculum; and the relationship between mathematics, numeracy and literacy.
learning_outcomes: Apply strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment in a lesson sequence to meet the diverse needs of learners in the mathematics classroom.

Apply pedagogical knowledge, informed by constructivist principles, research and current evidence-based practices associated with teaching and learning mathematics in developing learning activities to support students with a range of abilities to access the Primary Mathematics curriculum and demonstrate achievement.
Authentically assess student achievement by designing meaningful, stage appropriate tasks, which provide evidence that accurately represents a student's knowledge, understanding and skills.
Analyse various models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing mathematics as they relate to teaching for diversity in the mathematics classroom.
Prepare and apply standards-referenced marking criteria and meaningfully report learner achievement to key stakeholders.
Reflect on and justify practice using educational literature and research.
Apply knowledge of current primary mathematics syllabus documents, including the General Capabilities, in developing learning activities for primary mathematics.

title: Mathematics for the Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will review foundation skills in mathematics such as calculator skills, unit conversions using the unit factor method, mathematical operations of using algebra, decimal, fractions, percentages, area, volume, trigonometry, and graphing techniques. The subject is particularly relevant to those students studying science and agriculture subjects for which some knowledge of mathematics is required.
learning_outcomes: Understand and work with arithmetic and other basic concepts of mathematics.
Use a calculator confidently and correctly.
Interpret and apply a variety of graphical techniques.
Understand and use trigonometry in a variety of applications.
Develop support networks.
Understand and work with algebraic expressions.

title: Mathematics in the Primary Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject consolidates the central concepts, modes of enquiry and structure of the content of Mathematics, and explicitly connects these ideas to the models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing Mathematics. There is also a strong emphasis on: ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the Mathematics classroom; the role and value of Mathematics in the broader school curriculum; and the relationship between Mathematics, numeracy and literacy.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of current primary Mathematics syllabus documents, including the General Capabilities, in developing learning activities for primary Mathematics.
Apply strategies for differentiating teaching, learning and assessment in a lesson sequence to meet the diverse needs of learners in the Mathematics classroom.
Prepare and apply standards-referenced marking criteria and meaningfully report learner achievement to key stakeholders.
Authentically assess student achievement by designing meaningful, stage appropriate tasks, which provide evidence that accurately represents a student's knowledge, understanding and skills.

Apply pedagogical knowledge, informed by constructivist principles, research, and current evidence-based practices associated with teaching and learning Mathematics in developing learning activities to support students with a range of abilities to access the Primary Mathematics curriculum and demonstrate achievement.
Analyse various models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing Mathematics as they relate to teaching for diversity in the Mathematics classroom.

title: Mathematics: Content and Pedagogy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the central concepts, modes of enquiry and content structure within the K-6 mathematics continuum, highlighting the role of mathematics in everyday situations, and the importance of home and community numeracy practices. Students explore the principles and practices underpinning the teaching of mathematics and develop an appreciation and deep understanding of current syllabus documents that will inform and guide their pedagogical practice. This subject also reinforces the function of 'real world' mathematics as a numerate and literate practice and the role and value of Information and Communication Technologies [ICT] as a pedagogical tool.
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of strategies to cater for and engage primary children K-6 in mathematics, including the use of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT).
Create and evaluate investigations and open problems applying the 'working mathematically' process.
Apply knowledge of current primary mathematics syllabus documents, including the general capabilities, in developing learning activities for primary mathematics.

Apply pedagogical knowledge, informed by constructivist principles, research and current evidence-based practices associated with teaching and learning mathematics in developing learning activities and lessons for primary mathematics and justify their design with respect to pedagogical models and practices of primary mathematics.
Explain and interpret the place of primary mathematics in the K-12 continuum of learning.
Explain the function of mathematics as a numerate and literate practice to meet the cognitive, social and aesthetic needs of children.

title: Mathematics: Content and Pedagogy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the central concepts, modes of enquiry and content structure within the K-6 mathematics continuum, highlighting the role of mathematics in everyday situations, and the importance of home and community numeracy practices. Students explore the principles and practices underpinning the teaching of mathematics and develop an appreciation and deep understanding of current syllabus documents that will inform and guide their pedagogical practice. This subject also reinforces the function of 'real world' mathematics as a numerate and literate practice and the role and value of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) as a pedagogical tool.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of current primary mathematics syllabus documents, including the general capabilities, in creating learning activities for primary school mathematics.

Appraise pedagogical knowledge, informed by constructivist principles, research and current evidence-based practices associated with teaching and learning mathematics in creating learning activities and lessons for primary school mathematics, and justify their design with respect to pedagogical models and practices of primary school mathematics.
Apply a range of strategies to cater for, and engage primary school children K-6 in mathematics, including the use of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT).
Analyse the function of mathematics as a numerate and literate practice to meet the cognitive, social, cultural and aesthetic needs of children.
Create and evaluate investigations and open problems applying the 'working mathematically' process.
Explain and interpret the primary school mathematics in the K-12 mathematics continuum of learning.

title: Maths Skills 1 - Introductory
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Maths Skills 1 is an introductory subject designed for students who are concerned about the mathematics component of their course. The subject assumes minimal mathematics ability and aims to build confidence in working mathematically. The subject aims to systematically build confidence in working mathematically through the development of foundational skills in the basic arithmetic operations, place value, rounding, order of operations, directed numbers, decimals, fractions, percentages, ratios and rates. It also gives an introduction to basic algebra. The subject is taught without the use of a calculator. This subject is designed as a short 14 hour course. Students complete a diagnostic test at the point of enrolment to ensure they do not already possess the skills covered in this basic level subject.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply the concepts of basic algebra
Explain and apply the concepts of basic arithmetic

title: Maths Skills 1 Introductory B
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This maths based subject teaches strategies for solving mathematical puzzles and word problems. By giving a structure for problem solving students are provided with a method for approaching unfamiliar tasks. The use of problem solving in society is examined to showcase the method.
learning_outcomes: Use strategies to clarify mathematical problems
Understand the four stages of problem solving, Understand, Plan, Solve and Check
Identify a range of strategies that are appropriate for solving a problem and choose the most efficient
Understand how problem solving is used in STEM fields

title: Maths Skills 2 - Intermediate A
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Maths Skills 2 - Intermediate is taught as 2 sequential modules A and B, each 14 hours long. Maths Skills 2 - Intermediate A is designed for students who are entering University without a strong background in mathematics or who have limited recent practice and are planning to enrol in subjects requiring basic arithmetic skills, calculator skills and basic algebra. Some secondary level mathematics is desirable but not essential. This subject builds on the skills acquired in the Maths Skills 1 - Introductory subject so can be taken by students who have completed this subject and need to extend their mathematics knowledge further. A diagnostic test can be completed prior to the commencement of this subject for applicants who have not completed Maths Skills 1 - Introductory subject and need assistance to determine which of the two courses best fits their initial needs.
learning_outcomes: Use a calculator confidently and correctly
Carry out calculations and use algebra accurately
Explain and apply the concepts of basic arithmetic

title: Maths Skills 2 - Intermediate B
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Maths Skills 2 - Intermediate is taught as two sequential modules A and B, each 14 hours long. Maths Intermediate B builds on the content covered in Maths Intermediate A to develop more advanced algebra and problem solving skills. This subject also introduces linear and non-linear functions, graphing techniques and some simple exponentials and logarithms.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply the concepts of exponentials and logarithms
Explain and apply the concepts of functions, variables and graphs
Apply problem solving skills to practical problems involving mathematics
Carry out calculations and use algebra accurately

title: Maths Skills 3 - Advanced A
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Mathematics Skills 3 - Advanced is taught as 2 sequential modules: A and B, each 14 hours long. Mathematics Skills 3 - Advanced A and B are advanced subjects that prepare students for the commencement of undergraduate study in those courses that require a strong knowledge of mathematics. It is designed for those students who studied the equivalent of Advanced Mathematics (formerly known as 2 Unit Mathematics) at HSC or Mathematical Methods at VCE within the last 10 years, and need a refresher. It covers number systems, advanced algebra, functions and graphs, trigonometry and differential and integral calculus with applications. The subjects are recommended for students planning to study courses such as Engineering and Computer Science or a course majoring in Mathematics. It is designed as 2 x 14 hour modules. Mathematics Skills 3 - Advanced A focuses on number systems, advanced algebra, trigonometry, sketch trig functions.
learning_outcomes: Plot and interpret graphs
Explain and apply the concepts of advanced algebraic expressions
Explain and apply the concepts of trigonometry in a variety of applications
Explain and apply the concepts of different number systems

title: Maths Skills 3 - Advanced B
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Maths Skills 3 - Advanced is taught as two sequential modules A and B, each 14 hours long. Maths Skills 3 - Advanced A and B are advanced subjects that prepare students for the commencement of undergraduate study in those courses that require a strong knowledge of mathematics. It is designed for those students who studied the equivalent of Advanced Mathematics (formerly known as 2 Unit Mathematics) at HSC or Mathematical Methods at VCE within the last 10 years, and need a refresher. It covers number systems, advanced algebra, functions and graphs, trigonometry and differential and integral calculus with applications. The subjects are recommended for students planning to study courses such as Engineering and Computer Science or a course majoring in Mathematics. It is designed as two x 14 hour modules. Maths Skills 3 - Advanced B focuses on simple plane geometry, differentiation, simple curve sketching, integration and solving complex word problems that involve the setting up and solving of equations.
learning_outcomes: Apply problem solving skills to practical problems involving mathematics
Use the basic rules of differentiation and calculate derivatives of elementary functions
Use the basic rules of integration and calculate integrals of simple functions
Plot and interpret graphs

title: Maths Skills 3 - Advanced C (Matrices, Networking, Logic and Differential equations)
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Maths Skills 3 - Advanced C is one of the suites of non-award micro-subjects offered on the Studylink platform and the third of three university preparation level Advanced Maths subjects. This subject reviews and revises the mathematics which students may encounter in science-based undergraduate courses. In particular, the topics provide students with deeper experience in working with the applications of calculus then progress through simple logic (applicable to computing and electronics), matrices, networking and differential equations.
learning_outcomes: Use Boolean algebra, Karnough maps and truth tables to explain mathematical logic.
Be able to apply matrices to everyday situations
Represent networks and scheduling problems using mathematical diagrams.
Use calculus to solve differential equations related to kinematics

title: Mechanical Engineering Design Challenge
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the fundamental principles and practices of machine design. Students will learn to apply mechanical engineering concepts to the design and analysis of mechanical components and systems. The subject emphasizes design methodologies, analysis techniques, and practical considerations in creating functional and reliable machines.
learning_outcomes: Produce and interpret technical documentation, including drawings, specifications, design reports.
Develop detailed designs for mechanical components and systems based on engineering principles and real-world constraints.
Perform engineering analyses to evaluate the performance, safety, and reliability of mechanical designs.
Utilise systematic design methodologies to approach complex engineering problems and create effective solutions.

title: Meat And Fibre Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn how to assess traits of meat and fibre which affect processing performance, product quality and end use, how raw products are prepared and processed and how meat and fibre products are marketed to meet consumer preferences. Students will also develop their knowledge of the biological and processing factors that affect product quality. Students will focus on the major domestic species with practicals covering beef, pork and lamb meat quality measurement and marketing, and raw wool and mohair assessment and marketing. The subject may include field trips to local processing plants and industry guests.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe suitable marketing strategies for meat and fibre products.
Explain the market requirements for different meat and fibre product categories.
Identify and discuss the factors that impact on meat and fibre product quality.
Assess and evaluate the quality of animal meat and fibre products.
Explain and evaluate the processing and storage requirements of meat and fibre products.

title: Mechanical Engineering Experimentation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces undergraduate mechanical engineering students to the principles and techniques of experimental methods. Emphasising practical applications, the course covers experimental design, data collection, and analysis specific to mechanical engineering problems. Students will gain hands-on experience in setting up experiments, analysing results, and communicating findings effectively.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate experimental results, identifying potential sources of error and uncertainty and assessing the implications for engineering practice.
Develop and implement experimental designs to investigate mechanical engineering problems and validate engineering hypotheses.
Collect, process, and analyse experimental data using mechanical engineering tools and techniques, including statistical methods and software.
Communicate experimental methods, results, and conclusions effectively.

title: Mechanics and Thermal Physics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to physics suitable both as a basis for further studies in this field and for students whose major interest is in other areas. It gives a basic level of training in the topics of classical mechanics, elasticity, fluids and thermodynamics. The approach uses calculus as required.
learning_outcomes: Solve quantitative and numerical problems using the concepts developed in the study.
Conduct experiments which demonstrate some of the concepts developed during the study.
Appreciate the factors operating at the microscopic and macroscopic levels which determine the behaviour of materials and their response to a change in temperature.
Demonstrate an understanding of the basic principles determining the behaviour of fluids.
Appreciate the elastic behaviour of materials.
Present experimental results in an acceptable manner, indicating the likely sources and magnitudes of any errors involved.
Demonstrate an understanding of the basic principles determining the behaviour of bodies which are subjected to forces and/or torques.

title: Mechanics of Materials
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a foundational understanding of the behaviour of materials under various loading conditions. This subject covers essential concepts, theories, and analytical methods necessary for analysing and designing structures.
learning_outcomes: Apply basic theories of elasticity and plasticity to analyse the behaviour of materials under axial, torsional, and bending loads.
Explain stress, strain, and their relationship in engineering materials.
Calculate stresses, strains, and deformations in structural components subjected to various loading conditions.
Solve problems involving the mechanical properties of materials, including tensile strength, yield strength, and modulus of elasticity.

title: Mechanics of Machines
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an understanding of the principles and analysis techniques for machines and mechanisms commonly used in mechanical systems. It covers topics such as kinematics, dynamics, and mechanisms, with a focus on the analysis and design of machine elements and systems.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the kinematic behaviour of machine elements and mechanisms through position, velocity, and acceleration analysis.
Evaluate the performance of machine elements such as linkages, cams, and gears, considering factors such as efficiency, reliability, and design constraints.
Apply analytical and computational methods to solve problems related to balancing, vibration, and dynamic behaviour in mechanical systems.
Design machine elements and mechanisms to meet specified requirements, integrating principles of kinematics, dynamics, and mechanical design.

title: Mechatronics and Embedded Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive overview of the integration of mechanical, electrical, and computer engineering principles in the design and development of intelligent systems. Emphasis is placed on hands-on experimentation, project-based learning, and collaborative problem-solving.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of sensors and actuators used in mechatronic systems and their interfacing techniques.
Apply fundamental concepts and principles of mechatronics and embedded systems.
Implement, and test basic mechatronic and embedded systems.
Apply microcontroller programming using appropriate programming languages.

title: Media Production for Community Engagement
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Students undertake online study followed by a practice-based workshop on how to produce basic media content, including still images, video, and audio, for the purposes of engaging with the community and promoting events and initiatives. The subject will include on-camera instruction and practice and introductions to key media production equipment and software. This subject is designed with adaptable delivery models, which may include combinations of condensed online sessions and one-off workshops.
learning_outcomes: Produce media content for the purposes of community engagement and promotion.
Develop community engagement and promotional strategies requiring media content.

title: Media Training
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' ability to utilise words, tone and body language to communicate messages powerfully using a range of media channels. Students will learn how media operates; skills to plan, prepare for and undertake simulated interview and develop the confidence to interact with media professionally. This subject will include a virtual or physical study visit.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate use of words, tone and body language appropriate for a media channel.
Confidently and effectively interact with media professionals.
Prepare for and undertake a simulated media interview.

title: Mediation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the mediation process and explores issues requiring a detailed understanding by the mediator including: the steps of mediation, different models of mediation, the role of the mediator, ethics and values in mediation, and refining mediation for professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the steps of the mediation process and the different models of mediation and recognise disputes which can be mediated.
Evaluate the knowledge, skills and attitudes needed in mediators.
Discuss the role of power/gender in mediation.
Analyse ethical issues that may arise during the mediation process, including the ethical obligations of mediators.

title: Mediation: Processes and Uses
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the mediation process and provides an opportunity for applied learning at the intensive. The subject explores issues for which a mediator needs to have a detailed understanding including: the steps of mediation, different models of mediation, the role of the mediator, ethics and values in mediation, and refining mediation for professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the knowledge, skills and attitudes needed in mediators and describe the applications of mediation in different settings.
Plan and facilitate a mediation in a professional context and discuss the role of power/gender in mediation.
Analyse ethical issues that may arise during the mediation process, including the ethical obligations of mediators.
Explain the steps of the mediation process and apply the skills of conflict resolution to the mediation process.
Reflect on different models of mediation and recognise disputes which can be mediated.

title: Medical Critical Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students’ previous education and experience to advance the knowledge and skills needed to provide critical care paramedicine for medical emergencies. Students will further develop their ability to integrate assessment and diagnostic data, knowledge of relevant anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology, and evidence-informed practice to propose critical care paramedicine treatment plans. To foster the clinical reasoning skills required in critical care paramedicine, students will integrate critical thinking and decision-making strategies and written communication skills as part of managing medical emergencies.
learning_outcomes: Interpret clinical data derived from advanced patient diagnostics, assessment and history taking to inform clinical decision-making for medical emergencies.
Integrate critical thinking and communication skills as part of critical care management of medical emergencies.
Formulate evidence-informed critical care paramedic treatment plans for medical emergencies.
Integrate advanced knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology to critical care paramedic management of medical emergencies.

title: Medical Laboratory Management
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students develop skills and understanding of management principles that drive quality of service and product in a laboratory setting. As healthcare expands and becomes more complex, the role of medical laboratories equally expands in terms of the services, products they offer and management of resources. There is a growing expectation for quality service and product from consumers such as patients, other healthcare staff and laboratories. In a global environment, healthcare attracts staff from various cultures and serves people from varied backgrounds. Further, healthcare needs to be sensitive to cultures of First Nation peoples.
