learning_outcomes: Analyse the concepts of management and leadership in the laboratory setting, including the impact of funding and the cost of diagnostics on decision making and resource allocation.
Analyse the role of professional, licensing and accreditation bodies such as NATA, NPAAC and AIMS in medical diagnostic or medical research laboratories.

Evaluate and apply principles of cultural competence and safety in relation to Australian First Nations peoples and other cultures in the medical science laboratory with respect to patients, patient samples and staff.

title: Medical Emergencies in Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop the student's knowledge and skills required to care for health consumers experiencing a medical emergency. Students will assess and manage medical presentations in paramedic practice using basic and intermediate interventions. Students will use technology and diagnostic equipment to formulate provisional and differential diagnoses by integrating pathophysiological principles with assessment outcomes. Students will learn to formulate and implement effective person-centred management plans for common medical presentations. Additionally, they will prepare and administer medications following the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) standards and relevant regulations as part of these integrated management plans.
learning_outcomes: Prepare and administer basic medications used in paramedic practice in accordance with the NSQHS standards and relevant legislation and regulatory requirements.
Formulate provisional and differential diagnoses for health consumers experiencing medical emergencies by analysing data obtained from diagnostic equipment and technology.
Assess and apply basic and intermediate interventions to treat and manage medical emergency presentations.
Identify and describe emergency medical conditions encountered in paramedic practice.
prerequisites: PAR100: Foundations of Clinical Paramedic Practice
PAR103: Introduction to Contemporary Paramedic Practice

title: Medical Microbiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject continues students' study of medical microbiology. Studies of viral, fungal and parasitic infectious diseases of major body systems are conducted with an emphasis on viral and parasitic diseases. The host-parasite relationship and antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic chemotherapy are also studied in detail as well as multisystem infections such as vector-borne, zoonoses and infections of the compromised host. Practical sessions involve tasks which emphasise development of specialised techniques and diagnosis of viral, fungal and parasitic infections.
learning_outcomes: Outline the range of antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic chemotherapeutic agents available and their mode of action.
Perform basic virological techniques and have and explain the theoretical aspects of cell culture.
Explain the importance of world-wide viral infections, vector-borne viral and parasitic infections and multi-system zoonoses.
Analyse clinical issues and implications associated with viral, fungal and parasitic infections in a compromised host.
Describe the causative organisms, pathogenesis, epidemiology and clinical signs of viral, fungal and parasitic diseases affecting major body systems.
Analyse the nature of host-parasite relationships and be competent in the handling and identification of common parasites.
Identify medically important parasites and fungi with microscopy.

title: Medical Radiation Science Residency
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject completes the detailed development of student clinical skills that underpin professional practice in both the public and private setting. The subject finalises the Honours student's practical training and requirements for professional accreditation. In this subject, students complete supervised medical radiation science practice experiences in their chosen specialisation for a total of 36 weeks (which is approximately 870 hours and 90 hours devoted to Honours research and assessment). Practicum experience provides students with the opportunity to further refine their clinical skills; demonstrate clinical reasoning and problem solving skills; begin to work independently; build on their team and communication skills; build cultural competence; demonstrate sound radiation safety practices and demonstrate high levels of professional behaviour. Students will also develop and consolidate critical evaluation and reflective practice skills. Students are required to pass each placement and related competency tasks to pass this subject.
learning_outcomes: Exemplify highly developed teamwork and communication skills in all settings.
Consistently integrate the complexities of patient presentation and other surrounding issues in their practice.
Model professionalism in all interpersonal interactions.
Work independently with minimal direction.
Identify and solve complex clinical problems, demonstrating advanced clinical reasoning skills.
Demonstrate skills to enhance the health outcomes of Indigenous Australians.
Demonstrate skills to enhance communication with Indigenous Australians.
Demonstrate leadership potential and initiative.
Demonstrate cultural competence approaches to individual and professional models of health.
Model time efficiency in their clinical practice.
Show advanced understanding of radiation safety in all situations under immediate supervision.

title: Medical Radiation Science Residency
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject completes the detailed development of student clinical skills that underpin professional practice in both the public and private setting. The subject finalises the student's practical training and requirements for professional accreditation. In this subject, students complete supervised medical radiation science practice experiences in their chosen specialisation for a total of 36 weeks (which is approximately 1300 hours). Practicum experience provides students with the opportunity to further refine their clinical skills; demonstrate clinical reasoning and problem solving skills; begin to work independently; build on their team and communication skills; build cultural competence; demonstrate sound radiation safety practices and demonstrate high levels of professional behaviour. Students will also develop and consolidate critical evaluation and reflective practice skills. Students are required to pass each placement and related competency tasks to pass this subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills to enhance communication with Indigenous Australians.
Demonstrate cultural competence approaches to individual and professional models of health.
Model professionalism in all interpersonal interactions.
Demonstrate skills to enhance the health outcomes of Indigenous Australians.
Consistently integrate the complexities of patient presentation and other surrounding issues in their practice.
Work independently with minimal direction.
Show advanced understanding of radiation safety in all situations under immediate supervision.
Exemplify highly developed teamwork and communication skills in all settings.
Identify and solve complex clinical problems, demonstrating advanced clinical reasoning skills.
Demonstrate leadership potential and initiative.

title: Medical Science Communications and Methods
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide a firm foundation for developing skills in scientific communication. Students will learn about and develop academic, information and digital literacy skills. They will also develop numeracy and basic statistical skills relevant to their discipline of study along with an introduction to the scientific method and the critical analysis of the scientific literature. Students will explore physical principles to develop an understanding of equipment use and function relevant to medical science.This subject will also raise student awareness of evidence-based, professional and ethical issues relating to health and medical sciences.
learning_outcomes: Explain evidence-based health paradigms.
Demonstrate information, digital and academic literacy and numeracy skills appropriate for undergraduate medical sciences.
Explain basic physical principles relevant to equipment and processes in medical science.
Demonstrate skills to analyse and interpret scientific papers and appropriately communicate medical science information.
Describe and apply the scientific method, including basic statistical analysis.
Explain professional and ethical issues related to medical science including medical science research.
Demonstrate capability to solve simple mathematical and chemical calculations applicable to health sciences.

title: Medical Science Special Topic
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject considers issues that may confront a graduate medical scientist. Topics covered include methods of information retrieval from published literature and report writing. A literature survey on a selected topic from medical science will be presented both as a written report, a poster and an oral seminar.
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the organisation and structure of the scientific literature.
Apply scientific conventions commonly used both in the presentation of an oral seminar, a scientific poster and in a written report.
Collect, collate and critically review information on a specific topic.
Describe in depth a specific area of medical science through the medium of the literature review.
Apply knowledge of medical science information sources to literature searching.

title: Medicine and Surgery for Dental Practice
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will cover relevant aspects of the causes, nature and management of diseases of major body systems. This will include relevant discussion of the respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, endocrine, hematological, immunological, neurological, renal, dermatological and musculoskeletal systems. This subject will also include aspects of oral medicine where the oral health and general health nexus will be addressed.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate a knowledge of general and oral health issues of Indigenous Australians.
demonstrate a knowledge of dental management of medically compromised patient; and
demonstrate a knowledge of causes, key clinical features, diagnostic markers and principles of management of oral mucosal diseases and their impact on general health;
demonstrate a knowledge of causes, key clinical features, diagnostic markers and principles of management of diseases of body systems and their impact on oral health;

title: Medicine and Therapeutics in Dental Practice
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject explores key aspects of oral medicine, focusing on the critical connection between oral health and general health. Students will examine the aetiology and management of diseases of major body systems that impact on oral health. Similarly, the diagnosis and management of oral mucosal disease and its impact on general health will be examined. Pharmacology and therapeutic implications for dental management of medically compromised patients will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Define and discuss the oral and dental risks and management strategies for medically compromised patients.
Demonstrate the clinical application of pharmacological principles and therapeutics, with relevance to optimal oral and dental health and the management of oral disease.
Compare and contrast the presentation, diagnosis and principles of systemic diseases that impact on oral health.
Apply knowledge of the presentation, diagnosis and management of oral mucosal diseases to explain their impact on general health.
prerequisites: DOH337: Foundations of Dental Clinical Practice 3
DOH412: Medicine and Surgery for Dental Practice

title: Medieval Church History
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the history of Christianity in the countries of the classical Roman Empire and their immediate neighbours in north-western and eastern Europe and the Middle East. It covers the period from the breakup of the Western empire in the fifth century to the conquest of the Eastern Empire in the fifteenth century. Themes explored include church-state relations, concepts of Christian leadership, Christian scholarship, evangelism, pastoral care, the spiritual life in community and religious orders, and the tense relations between Eastern and Western Christendom.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge of the primary source documents of this period and be able to analyse, interpret, and critically review these documents.
Research and communicate the relevance of historical documents for understanding the historical origins of contemporary churches in Australia and Asia.
Analyse and critically evaluate historiographical approaches to the Christian faith across different cultures and ecclesial communities.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills relevant to history as a discipline.
Demonstrate broad and coherent knowledge of the development of the Christian Church from 500 to 1500 CE in both Western and Eastern traditions.
Critically review and analyse the contribution of historians from a variety of denominational and historical contexts.

title: Medieval Church History
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys the history of Christianity in the countries of the classical Roman Empire and their immediate neighbours in north-western and eastern Europe and the Middle East. It covers the period from the breakup of the Western empire in the fifth century to the conquest of the Eastern Empire in the fifteenth century. Themes explored include church-state relations, concepts of Christian leadership, Christian scholarship, evangelism, pastoral care, the spiritual life in community and religious orders, and the tense relations between Eastern and Western Christendom.
learning_outcomes: Research and communicate the relevance of historical documents for understanding the historical origins of contemporary churches in Australia and Asia.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the primary source documents of this period and be able to analyse, interpret, and critically review these documents.
Critically review and analyse the contribution of historians from a variety of denominational and historical contexts.
Analyse and critically evaluate historiographical approaches to the Christian faith across different cultures and ecclesial communities.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills relevant to history as a discipline.
Demonstrate broad and coherent knowledge of the development of the Christian Church from 500 to 1500 CE in both Western and Eastern traditions.

title: Medieval Legends and Shakespearian Legacies
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Medieval Legends and Shakespearian Legacies first examines the romantic and tragic worlds of medieval literature, for such texts not only reveal truths about our past, but also inform our contemporary imagination; the global sensation of Game of Thrones is exemplary of medievalism’s continuing relevance. After its plunge into the ‘Dark Ages’ of medieval times, the subject focuses on the ‘Golden Age’ of English literature in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries with particular attention to the work of William Shakespeare and its persistent fascination and relevance for contemporary audiences. Marie de France, Sir Thomas Malory, Geoffrey Chaucer, William Shakespeare and John Webster all epitomise Western literature's rich history of storytelling. Malory’s Arthurian legends, the dazzling virtuosity of Chaucer’s poetic and Shakespeare’s epic tragedies have inspired modern-day songwriters, poets, authors, and filmmakers alike. The powerful themes of love, death, violence, and friendship are also examined through these literary greats who continue to captivate us.
learning_outcomes: Recognise earlier forms of English and read early texts with the help of glosses and notes.
Engage with the literature from medieval times to the mid-seventeenth century.
Recognise and evaluate later developments of medieval and Renaissance forms.
Recognise, describe and critically analyse the forms and features of literary texts and genres.

title: Medieval Worlds
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Medieval World looks at the history of Europe and the Mediterranean from the 8th to the 15th centuries. The subject includes studies of church and state, of heresy and dissident movements, class structures, the crusades, the black death, economic development and urbanisation, the medieval arts and literature, and representations of the medieval world in our own time. This subject offers students the opportunity to study a distant but fascinating world, which is still the foundation of much of our culture.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an appreciation of the symbols and arts of premodern European culture.
Demonstrate an awareness of the influence of the Medieval Era on the modern world.
Describe and write about events from varied perspectives.
Interpret historical documents across time.

title: Meeting the Needs of Students with Communication Difficulties
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on meeting the needs of students who experience communication difficulties in inclusive settings. This includes understanding the nature of communication difficulties, collaboration with speech and language professionals, assessment, planning and the role of technology. Frameworks of assessment and intervention practices are applied to case examples of students with communication needs.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively with associated professionals to implement communications interventions in an inclusive learning environment .

Prioritises programming for students with complex language and communication needs, designing behavioural objectives for language development, particularly in association with communicative and brain injury needs .
Critiques communicative competence and constructs effective processes within an inclusive learning environment .
Assess and report on assistive technologies including rationale and recommendations .
Evaluates and implements appropriate and effective Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) strategies for learners with complex needs, including First Nations students .

title: Mental Health Challenges for Pastoral and Spiritual Care
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject investigates challenges in providing effective pastoral and spiritual care to older persons affected by mental health problems, including dementia. It examines mental health concerns relating to ageing and explores appropriate pastoral and spiritual care strategies to promote well-being and maximise quality of life for older people. Issues associated with understanding and dealing with dementia are integral to the subject. Questions relating to faith, spirituality and meaning provoked by mental health challenges in later life are explored. Professional and ethical standards for working with older people living with mental health difficulties and appropriate referral processes are also addressed.
learning_outcomes: Discuss critically issues relating to faith, spirituality and meaning provoked by mental health challenges in later life.
Demonstrate the ability to argue on theological and psychosocial grounds for the dignity and worth of people living with dementia.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of pastoral and spiritual needs of older people living with various mental health problems, including dementia.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of appropriate referral processes in relation to various forms of mental illness.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of mental health challenges for older people and their relevance for pastoral and spiritual care.

Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of culturally relevant pastoral and spiritual care strategies, including sensitive communication skills, to promote well-being and to maximise quality of life for older people living with various mental health challenges, including dementia.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of various current conceptions of dementia and its attendant challenges.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of ethical best practice in working with people living with dementia and other mental health problems.
prerequisites: THL464: Dementia: Challenge for Pastoral Care
THL447: Pastoral Care in Mental Health and Dementia

title: Mental Health
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide a critical introduction to the field of mental health and mental disorders and the various mental health services and programs. It will examine biological, psychological and sociological frameworks relevant to mental health and mental disorders from an evidence based perspective. It will also provide an orientation to prevention, promotion, classification (diagnosis, assessment, treatment and rehabilitation) of mental disorders. Various factors that impact upon mental disorder such as socio-economic status, race, gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation and age are discussed as well as the relationship of people with mental disorders to their families, caregivers and others in supportive and regulatory roles. HCS310 introduces gender and cultural diversity including indigenous mental health in the subject via diverse case studies. Consumer and carer perspectives are also embedded into the learning within HCS310.
learning_outcomes: Identify strategies to minimise discrimination and combat stigma.
Assess the risks and strengths of individuals, families and communities for the purposes of promoting mental health, early intervention, treatment and continuing care.
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the mental disorder classification system.
Identify the effects of oppression, discrimination and stigma on individuals with mental disorders and their families.
Demonstrate a sound understanding of the biological, psychological and sociological frameworks for understanding the etiology of mental disorders.
Present work in appropriate professional and academic style and standard.
Plan and conduct culturally competent, gender specific individual, family, group and community based capacity building and preventive interventions.
Demonstrate an understanding of mental health policy and service delivery systems, legal and ethical issues.

title: Mental Health Clinical 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will undertake Work Integrated Learning (placement) which introduces the student to the mental health environment and assists the student to gain an understanding of mental health issues that may impact on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities.
learning_outcomes: identify and apply screening tools in mental health;
apply both written and verbal communication skills in their clinical workplace learning context; and
understand how a comprehensive mental health assessment is used in clinical settings and apply it to practice.

title: Mental Health Clinical 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject communication skills, the National Practice Standards for Mental Health Workforce, law, ethics and professional boundaries will be introduced. Students will learn how to conduct a comprehensive mental health assessment, a mental status examination and a risk assessment. Documentation of assessment and progress notes within a mental health setting will be included as part of the assessment process. Screening tools for mental health will be explored and the concept of clinical formulation will also be considered. In this subject students will undertake Work Integrated Learning (placement) which introduces the student to the mental health environment and assists the student to gain an understanding of mental health issues that may impact on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities.
learning_outcomes: apply both written and verbal communication skills in their clinical workplace learning context;
describe their scope of practice as a student mental health clinician as reflected in the current National Practice Standards for the Mental Health Workforce;
understand how a comprehensive mental health assessment is used in clinical settings and apply it to practice;
understand the impact of the cultural, psychological, physical, social, environmental, spiritual and political factors on people experiencing mental health issues.
describe and apply the clinical formulation framework;
identify and apply screening tools in mental health; and

title: Mental Health Clinical 2
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will undertake Work Integrated Learning (placement) to develop greater understanding of the use of assessment and screening tools and to gain understanding of the mental health issues that may impact on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities.
learning_outcomes: implement clinical formulation and care planning to the comprehensive mental health assessment; and
explain and relate the legal and ethical issues associated with clinical practice in mental health.
develop culturally safe communication skills used while conducting a comprehensive mental health assessment;

title: Mental Health Clinical 2
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject communication skills will be analysed in the context of conducting a comprehensive mental health assessment, while applying the National Practice Standards for the Mental Health Workforce, law, ethics and professional boundaries. Aspects of the mental health assessment will be applied and analysed so that skills in clinical formulation are developed. Risk assessment and the mental status examination will be analysed further so that greater proficiency with use of these tools will be gained and care planning developed. Screening tools will be analysed and compared. In this subject students will undertake Work Integrated Learning (placement) to develop greater understanding of the use of assessment and screening tools and to gain understanding of the mental health issues that may impact on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities.
learning_outcomes: describe and explain how their clinical practice relates to professional practice expected, as reflected in the current National Practice Standards for Mental Health Workforce;
describe and implement reflective practice to mental health care.
develop culturally safe communication skills used while conducting a comprehensive mental health assessment;
explain the impact of the cultural, psychological, physical, social, environmental, spiritual and political factors on people experiencing mental health issues; and
analyse risk assessment and screening tool used in clinical practice;
explain and relate the legal and ethical issues associated with clinical practice in mental health;
implement clinical formulation and care planning to the comprehensive mental health assessment;

title: Mental Health for Paramedicine
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will equip students with evidence-based knowledge and effective skills to care for persons experiencing a wide range of mental health emergencies and/or presenting with substance-induced behavioural emergencies. This will encompass all population groups, including First Nations people and diverse populations. Paramedics need to function effectively in an increasingly demanding and complex environment that impacts physical and mental well-being which places them at increased risk of mental illnesses such as Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). This subject is designed to assist students to strengthen their capacity for self-care, strengthen their emotional resilience, recognise early signs of mental distress, engage in effective therapeutic relationships and identify how to access mental health professionals and services.
learning_outcomes: Identify a range of psychological strategies to use throughout a career in paramedicine that will support emotional wellbeing and resilience and reduce vulnerability to mental health problems such as anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Identify and analyse research related to paramedicine's role in responding to people with mental illness, to developing a resilient paramedic workforce and early intervention for front-line health professionals experiencing early indicators of mental distress and trauma.

Apply and demonstrate skills in mental state examination, mental health assessment, risk assessment, structured handover, de-escalation and behavioural management of people inclusive of First Nations people and diverse populations, who are experiencing a mental health crisis and/or are drug affected.

Describe and explain key mental health disorders/illnesses, assess their prevalence in all population groups, including First Nations people and diverse populations, clinical features, associated crises or emergencies that may arise with these conditions, evidence-based pharmacological and psychological treatments and relevant mental health services.

Describe and explain the use of current mental health legislation and underpinning ethical principles that must inform clinical practice in situations where the person may be mentally, behaviourally or cognitively impaired.

Identify and demonstrate skills for effective therapeutic relationships including the identification of barriers to effective communication and, how to engage in culturally appropriate care/communication for First Nations people and their families.
prerequisites: NRS246: Emergency Care in Mental Health

title: Mental Health Clinical 3
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will build students' skills in evaluating a comprehensive mental health assessment and applying the National Practice Standards for the Mental Health Workforce. Students will refine their skills in comprehensive mental health assessment including risk, clinical formulation and care planning, to develop proficiency in assessment, case presentation and management. Inclusion of an 8-week work placement provides students with an opportunity to apply the use of assessment and screening tools in mental health practice.
learning_outcomes: apply communication skills and interviewing techniques used while conducting a comprehensive mental health assessment and providing culturally safe care for complex mental health clients;
evaluate and compare risk assessment tools used in clinical practice and implement strategies to support clients that present as high risk;
critique the legal and ethical issues associated with clinical practice;
evaluate the impact of factors on people experiencing mental illness i.e., cultural, psychological; and
describe and evaluate how clinical practice relates to professional practice, as reflected in the National Practice Standards for the Mental Health Workforce;
implement clinical formulation and care planning after completing a comprehensive mental health assessment;
critically examine reflective practice and its application to mental health care.

title: Mental Health Theory 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject equips students with foundational knowledge and practical skills for mental health practice, aligned with the National Practice Standards for the Mental Health Workforce . Students will learn about their scope of practice, mental health screening tools, understand diverse factors influencing mental health, communication and ethical practice. Students will also describe and apply clinical formulation frameworks and develop readiness for workplace learning.
learning_outcomes: Describe and apply the clinical formulation framework.
Describe their scope of practice as a student mental health clinician as reflected in the current National Practice Standards for the Mental Health Workforce.
Understand the impact of the cultural, psychological, physical, social, environmental, spiritual and political factors on people experiencing mental health issues.

title: Mental Health Theory 2
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, communication skills will be analysed in the context of conducting a comprehensive mental health assessment, while applying the National Practice Standards for the Mental Health Workforce, law, ethics and professional boundaries. Aspects of the mental health assessment will be applied and analysed so that skills in clinical formulation are developed. Risk assessment and the mental status examination will be analysed further so that greater proficiency with use of these tools will be gained and care planning developed. Screening tools will be analysed and compared.
learning_outcomes: Analyse risk assessment and screening tools used in clinical practice.
Describe and explain how their clinical practice relates to professional practice expected, as reflected in the current National Practice Standards for Mental Health Workforce.
Explain the impact of the cultural, psychological, physical, social, environmental, spiritual and political factors on people experiencing mental health issues.

title: Mental Health, Law and Ethics
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will address legal and ethical issues pertaining to the management of people who have a mental illness or a mental health disorder. Mental health professionals are accountable for their day to day work, to the consumer and to the community. There is an expectation to practice within a standard of care framework when practising as a mental health professional. Ethical issues surrounding mental health care and treatment will be examined including the principles of autonomy, coercion, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. Legal issues such as negligence, managing information and the Privacy Act, the Crimes Act, the Inebriates Act, the Guardianship Act, the Public Health Act, Occupational Health and Safety legislation, the NT National Emergency Response Act and mandatory reporting will be explored. Most importantly, reference to the Mental Health Act/s (as they pertain to each State and Territory) will be examined as to how it governs daily practise within mental health services.
learning_outcomes: Define informed consent, mandatory reporting, and freedom of information.
Distinguish between legal and professional responsibility and code of conduct, and explain the relationship between them.
Critically discuss the legal, ethical and potential cultural issues that may arise in mental health practice.
Analyse the importance of managing information and confidentiality in oral, print and digital forms.
Critically discuss and describe duty of care and standard of care alongside negligence and legal liability.
Explain the way the legal system in Australia was established, its function and its relationship with mental health workers.
Differentiate the steps in ethical decision-making.
Explain how laws, policies and guidelines influence the practice of mental health professionals and impact on clients.

title: Mentoring, Leadership and Change
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject examines theories and models of leadership learning through coaching and mentoring. It focuses on the importance of critical reflection in, on and for practice, the change process, and the imperative for educational leaders to achieve school and/or organisational improvement. The development of conceptual, theoretical and practical understandings involves an examination of the nature and practice of coaching and mentoring across various international contexts. Research relating to effectiveness (culture, conditions and context) and evaluation of practice is considered. This subject provides the opportunity for students to analyse, reflect on current research from a global perspective and then develop a coaching and mentoring plan for structured professional development in an education and/or training setting.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the conceptual underpinnings of coaching and mentoring in leadership learning as an effective professional development tool and as a strategy for implementing change and/or organisational improvement.
Analyse staff professional development and support needs, and formulate a work-based coaching and/or mentoring program based on international best practices.
Evaluate research evidence on coaching and mentoring effectiveness relating to leadership learning in education and/or training settings from around the globe.
Examine coaching and mentoring programs both locally and internationally from a comparative perspective.
Evaluate theoretical knowledge and concepts underpinning coaching and mentoring (in, on and for practice) from across international contexts.

title: Mentoring/Workplace PD Strategies for VET
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Mentoring is increasingly recognised as an important strategy in the professional development of teachers and other educational practitioners. This subject looks at the differing modes of mentoring and other workplace professional development strategies which can be fitted to purpose and the conditions and principles that enable both mentoring and being mentored to be a positive contribution to professional growth. The subject takes a practical approach to mentoring and engages students in reflecting on mentoring programs they have been part of, or have researched.
learning_outcomes: Explain different approaches to mentoring and the role of a mentor.
Develop personal strategies to effectively mentor others.
Evaluate a mentoring program.
Analyse professional development strategies and their use within the workplace.
Design and plan for the implementation of an effective mentoring program.

title: Menu Planning for the Community
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an opportunity to develop a deeper understanding of food service provision in the community and its effect on food consumption. Students will develop skills in advocating and contributing to activities to promote the provision of a safe and nutritious food supply. Students will also gain experience in developing and communicating evidence based, sustainable, culturally and socially appropriate food-based strategies to assist individuals and communities to improve their nutritional status by making healthier food choices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the nutrition quality of recipes and menus using relevant standards and databases.
Analyse the challenges and opportunities that exist in regard to the ability of individuals and communities to make optimal food choices within specific food environments.
Select appropriate foods consistent with evidence based nutrition recommendations for a range of special dietary needs and across the lifespan.
Analyse quality management through regulatory compliance with respect to nutrition and accreditation standards within specific food environments.

Apply a critical, evidence based approach to the development of culturally, politically, environmentally and socially appropriate food-based plans to improve the food choices of individuals within specific food environments.

title: Metabolic Biochemistry in Health and Disease
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students examine the biochemistry of metabolism pertinent to the study of nutrition. Students build on their knowledge of metabolic pathways developing deeper biochemical understandings of changes in response to physiological and pathophysiological states including, but not restricted to, phenylketonuria, galactosaemia, fatty acid dysfunction, metabolic and cardiovascular diseases.
learning_outcomes: Describe the underlying principles of inherited metabolic disorders, with special reference to galactosaemia, phenylketonuria and fatty acid oxidation disorders.
Integrate metabolic knowledge from earlier biochemistry subjects to describe the metabolic adaptations (and their underlying regulation) to a range of physiological states.
Describe the influence of dietary factors on the development of common diseases such as liver disease, diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease.
Discuss the role of metabolic aberrations on the pathogenesis of common human diseases.
Acquire and analyse information from relevant scientific literature and present a synthesis of findings on a given topic relevant to nutrition, metabolism and health.
Explain the influences of reactive oxygen species and antioxidants on the pathogenesis of common human diseases.
Explain how the metabolic changes in nutritional diseases such as anorexia, marasmus and kwashiorkor result in the observed clinical symptoms for these diseases.
Analyse how metabolic changes in both physiological and pathological states may affect human nutritional requirements.

title: Metadata for Resource Discovery
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the role that metadata plays in information retrieval across a range of information environments and search contexts. It focuses on the concepts and principles involved in describing information resources, and discusses how metadata element sets and value vocabularies should be designed and applied to optimise intellectual access. Students also consider issues around metadata sharing and the future of metadata creation.
learning_outcomes: Relate different users' needs with the description of information resources and the information retrieval systems that serve these needs.
Create accurate metadata for effective retrieval of information resources in online information environments.
Explain the central role of accurate description and analysis of information resources in successful information retrieval.
Analyse and discuss different issues in the application of metadata standards in different contexts.
Apply selected metadata standards and schema to the creation of metadata for a wide range of information resources.
prerequisites: INF116: Describing and Analysing Information Resources

title: Metadata for Resource Discovery
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the role that metadata plays in information retrieval across a range of information environments and search contexts. It focuses on the concepts and principles involved in describing information resources, and discusses how metadata element sets and value vocabularies should be designed, evaluated and applied to optimise intellectual access. Students also consider issues around metadata sharing, metadata quality and the future of metadata creation.
learning_outcomes: Develop metadata element sets through designing, evaluating and modifying metadata elements according to local needs.
Appraise the relationships between different users' needs, the description of information resources and the information retrieval systems that serve these needs.
Evaluate different issues in the application of metadata standards in different contexts.
Apply selected metadata standards and schema to the creation of metadata for a wide range of information resources.

Examine the central role of accurate description and analysis of information resources in successful information retrieval.

title: Metal Technology: Workshop and Design
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the opportunity to develop introductory workshop knowledge and skills and safety procedures in the use of metal as a material for the secondary school context. An emphasis on design as it relates to Industrial Technology metal projects is also an important part of the subject. Students will consider how these skills and concepts relate to technology teaching in the secondary school. They will engage in school metal workshop projects and receive advice and demonstration of teachers' practice including issues related to Work Health and Safety (WHS) in the TAS teaching environment. They will report on these aspects of teaching to develop an applied understanding of safety, pedagogy and design, to ensure a safe technology classroom environment and consider how this supports their development as effective technology teachers. They will build on these understandings through assessment items that link theory and practice in this technology area.
learning_outcomes: Develop and put into practice WHS procedures in a metal workshop.
Apply metal technology skills content to educational goals with an emphasis on a design.
Competently use hand tools and power tools in a metal based workshop.
Discuss workshop practice in relation to school workshop safety.
Discuss their development as effective and safe technology teachers.

title: Metal Technology: Workshop and Pedagogy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on skills developed in EPI203, and provides students with the opportunity to develop more advanced workshop knowledge, skills and safety procedures. These relate to more complex equipment, techniques and processes used with metal in the secondary school context, particularly those in Stage 6/Years 11-12. An emphasis on pedagogical approaches and workshop teaching strategies appropriate to Industrial Technology Metal is also an important part of the subject. Students will engage in school metal workshop projects and receive advice and demonstration of teachers' practice including issues related to Work Health and Safety (WHS) and classroom management. They will discuss and demonstrate an applied understanding of syllabus specified requisite knowledge and skills for Stage 6/Years 11-12 Industrial Technology, and how these may be taught in the classroom and/or workshop.
learning_outcomes: Competently use power tools and equipment in a metal based workshop.
Explain and demonstrate Senior Industrial Technology Metal techniques and processes.
Discuss, develop and put into practice WHS procedures in a metal workshop.
Plan teaching of metal technology knowledge and skills using a range of appropriate strategies.
Discuss teaching metal technology knowledge and skills including project management.

title: Methodology of Islamic Law (Usul al-Fiqh)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the methodology related to the principles of Islamic jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). The development of Islamic law in the early history of Islam, the emergence of ijtihad (Islamic legal interpretation) together with the revealed and non-revealed sources of law and methodology of usul al-fiqh will also be addressed. In addition, the four primary sources of law as well as other supplementary sources of law used in the practice of ijtihad (independent legal deduction) will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Show an in-depth understanding of the methodology of Islamic law.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the development of Islamic legal theory (usul al-fiqh).
Analyse critically arguments and propositions used in Islamic legal rulings (fatwa).
Understand and apply critically the general principles of Islamic jurisprudence.
Discuss critically the primary and supplementary sources of Islamic law.

title: Methodology of Islamic Law (Usul al-Fiqh)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on usul al-fiqh (the methodology and the principles of Islamic jurisprudence). The development of Islamic law in the early history of Islam, the emergence of ijtihad (Islamic legal interpretation and independent deduction) together with the revealed and non-revealed sources of law and methodology of usul al-fiqh are also analysed. In addition, the four primary sources of law as well as other supplementary sources of law used in the practice of ijtihad are discussed. Finally, aḥkām (legal rulings) and dalālah (textual implications) are also examined. These matters are discussed within the classical usul al-fiqh framework along with the contemporary scholarly views, discussions and applications in the modern context.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss the primary and supplementary sources of Islamic law.
Evaluate the methodology of Islamic law.
Critically assess the application of the general principles of Islamic jurisprudence.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, and written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Analyse arguments and propositions used in fatwa (Islamic legal rulings) and their implementation in contemporary times.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the development of usul al-fiqh (Islamic legal theory).

title: Methodology of Prophetic Traditions (Usul al-Hadith)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the place of hadith in Islamic scholarship and the methodology of evaluating critically the authenticity of hadith narrations, as well as their classification in canonical texts. Prophet Muhammad's sayings, actions and his approvals as reported by his companions have been collected separately as multi-volume hadith books. Collection of hadith books, their classification and authentication has been an integral part of Islamic scholarship. This subject will also cover the history of development of the science of hadith critique from the time of Prophet Muhammad (7th century) to the 10th century of Islamic scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the different phases in the collating of hadith literature in the first three centuries of Islam.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding and skill in the appreciation of methods for critical analysis of hadith.
Articulate critically the difference between hadith and Sunnah.
Differentiate critically the level of authenticity between hadith narrations.
Critically discuss the methods used to classify hadith.

title: Methodology of Qur'anic Exegesis (Usul al-Tafsir)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the methodology of Qur'anic exegesis. The concept of revelation, the importance of occasions of revelation for exegesis, the concept of abrogation, and a set of tools used in textual analysis will be discussed. The history of the development of Qur'anic exegetical method and its evolution over time to produce a rich literature of exegetical works will also be addressed. In addition, modern exegetical issues concerning the Qur'an will be investigated together with a critical evaluation of how the modern history of the Muslim world influenced contemporary exegetical works.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the Qur'an through a methodical approach to its interpretation.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Recognise and evaluate critically different exegetical types.
Demonstrate a familiarity with the terminology used in Qur'anic exegesis.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the history of the development of Qur'anic exegesis.
Understand and apply critically the general principles of Qur'anic exegesis.
Apply critically exegetical methods to the interpretation of the Qur'an.

title: Methodology of Prophetic Traditions (Usul al-Hadith)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the place of hadith in Islamic scholarship and the methodology of critically evaluating the authenticity of hadith narrations, as well as their classification in canonical texts. Prophet Muhammad's sayings, actions and his tacit approvals as reported by his companions have been collected separately as multi-volume hadith books. Collections of hadith books, their classification and authentication have been an integral part of Islamic scholarship. Additionally, this subject delves into the historical development of the science of hadith critique, spanning from the time of Prophet Muhammad in the 7th century to 10th century Islamic scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate in-depth understanding and proficiency in the appreciation of methods for critical analysis of hadith.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the phases involved in the compilation of hadith literature in the first three centuries of Islam.
Critically differentiate the level of authenticity between hadith narrations.
Critically explore the key methods employed to classify hadith.
Critically articulate the distinction between hadith and sunnah.

title: Methodology of Qur'anic Exegesis (Usul al-Tafsir)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on usul al-tafsir (the methodology of Qur'anic exegesis) and ‘ul ūm al-Qur’an (Qur’anic sciences). Students will critically analyse the concept of revelation, the transmission and collection of the Qur’anic text and some major fields of Qur’anic sciences such as the inimitability of the Qur’an, occasions of revelation, clear and ambiguous verses, the concept of abrogation along with tools used in textual analysis. The subject also addresses the evolution of Qur'anic exegetical methods to produce a rich literature of exegetical works. In addition, it investigates modern exegetical issues concerning the Qur'an together with a critical evaluation of how the modern history of the Muslim world has influenced contemporary exegetical works.
learning_outcomes: Employ a methodical approach to the Qur'an's interpretation and compare different exegetical methods.
Analyse the historical development of Qur'anic exegesis and critically evaluate its general principles and major fields within Qur’anic sciences.
Use independent research skills, organisational abilities, and effective written and oral communication through the presentation of a substantial work.
Distinguish terminology used in Qur'anic exegesis and critically evaluate various exegetical types.

title: Methods for Environmental Data Analysis
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Methods for Environmental Data Analysis provides a practical introduction to the quantitative methods for environmental management and research. Environmental scientists spend considerable amounts of their time designing experimental and observational studies and evaluating existing data sets to develop solutions to the many environmental and natural resource issues facing Australia and the globe. It is often the case that there will be a need to analyse data sets to make predictions or forecasts to determine how resources are best allocated for future work. Researchers and managers must, therefore, be familiar with the types of data and how they are collected, common techniques for data analysis, and exploration and identification of patterns in data. There is no intensive associated with this subject. Students completing this subject have understanding of experimental and observational study design and the ability to interpret and communicate findings from environmental research clearly and coherently within a management context.
learning_outcomes: Undertake basic biostatistical analysis.
Have the ability to generate simple models and hypothesise relevant to environmental problems and research.
Have the ability to analyse and evaluate the utility of different types of data, how it is collected and analysed in order to make sound judgements about the quality of the research.
Have a comprehensive understanding of experimental design and observational studies in a range of contexts associated with environmental science.
Have communication skills in exploring, interpreting, and presenting data graphically.
Have the ability to interpret and communicate findings from environmental research clearly and coherently within a management context.

title: Microbiology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject covers the importance of microorganisms, the effect of microbes on human health and applied aspects of microbiology. The mechanisms by which microorganisms cause disease in humans and host defences against these infections are introduced.
learning_outcomes: Describe how the growth of microorganisms can be controlled.
Describe the structure and function of microorganisms.
Explain and apply how microorganisms interact with the human host.
Explain processes used to study microorganisms.
Describe methods by which microorganisms can be cultivated and assayed.

title: Microbiology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject continues student's study of medical microbiology largely excluding medical bacteriology. Studies of viral, fungal and parasitic infectious diseases of major body systems are conducted with an emphasis on viral and parasitic diseases. The host-parasite relationship and anti-viral, anti-fungal and anti-parasitic chemotherapy are also studied in detail as well as multi-system infections such as vector-borne zoonoses and infections of the compromised host. Students also study methodology and laboratory techniques for diagnosis of viral, fungal and parasitic infections including aspects of biological safety.
learning_outcomes: Describe the causative organisms, pathogenesis, epidemiology and clinical signs of viral, fungal and parasitic diseases affecting the major body systems.
Evaluate the problems associated with the compromised host and associated viral, fungal and parasitic infections.
Define the range of antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic chemotherapeutic agents available, describe their mode of action and justify their use.
Explain the importance of world-wide viral infections, vector-borne viral and parasitic infections and multi-system zoonoses.

title: Microbiology 2 (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject continues student's study of medical microbiology largely excluding medical bacteriology. Studies of viral, fungal and parasitic infectious diseases of major body systems are conducted with an emphasis on viral and parasitic diseases. The host-parasite relationship and anti-viral, anti-fungal and anti-parasitic chemotherapy are also studied in detail as well as multi-system infections such as vector-borne zoonoses and infections of the compromised host. Students also study methodology and laboratory techniques for diagnosis of viral, fungal and parasitic infections including aspects of biological safety.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the problems associated with the compromised host and associated viral, fungal and parasitic infections.
Explain the importance of world-wide viral infections, vector-borne viral and parasitic infections and multi-system zoonoses.
Describe the causative organisms, pathogenesis, epidemiology and clinical signs of viral, fungal and parasitic diseases affecting the major body systems.
Define the range of antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic chemotherapeutic agents available, describe their mode of action and justify their use.

title: Microbiology 3
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers a range of bacterial species involved in a wide collection of infectious diseases. It covers the structure of Gram positive and Gram negative bacteria, bacterial toxins and virulence factors, specimen handling, antibacterial chemotherapy, human microbiome, organ infections, the infections of the compromised hosts, zoonosis, and diagnostic bacteriology with an emphasis on the new molecular diagnostic techniques used for identification, quantification of bacteria found in clinical patient samples and to diagnose the aetiological agents of infection in pathology laboratories.
learning_outcomes: Explain typical structure of Gram positive and Gram negative bacteria, bacterial taxonomy, toxins and virulence factors, metabolism, growth and gene transfer.
Explain the general features of the Gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and the normal human microbiome of the GIT and evaluate the characteristics features of GIT infections caused by pathogenic bacteria.
Evaluate the methods used in diagnostic bacteriology for the identification, quantification, and antibiotic susceptibility testing of bacteria found in clinical patient samples.
Justify methods, protocols and procedures used to collect, store and transport clinical specimen.
Explain natural defences of the eye and the type of eye diseases caused by bacterial infections.
Investigate the type of bacteria that can cause infections in the upper and lower respiratory tract as well as the urinary tract.
Investigate the aetiology of sexually transmitted diseases caused by bacterial infections.
Investigate the bacterial infections of immuno-compromised hosts and identify vector-borne diseases.
Explain and justify methods used in antibacterial chemotherapies and describe the mechanism of actions of antibiotics and the ways in which bacteria develop antibiotic resistance.
Explain the anatomy of the skin, the skin microbiome and the bacterial skin infections and describe the common clinical manifestations associated with these types of infections.

school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers a range of bacterial species involved in a wide collection of infectious diseases. It covers the structure of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, bacterial toxins and virulence factors, specimen handling, antibacterial chemotherapy, human microbiome, organ infections, infections of compromised hosts, zoonosis, and diagnostic bacteriology. Emphasis is placed on new molecular diagnostic techniques used for the identification and quantification of bacteria in clinical samples and for diagnosing the aetiological agents of infection in pathology laboratories.

title: Midwifery Care for First Nations Families
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will explore how power relations and colonisation have impacted First Nations Australian families' experience of childbirth, the childbearing period and midwifery practice. Students will consider community development and social determinants of health as they analyse the role of the midwife in Closing the Gap in relation to maternal and newborn health. The concepts of cultural sensitivity and safety are explored and students will be expected to critically reflect on their own culture and attitudes and consider the impact these may have as they develop their capacity to provide woman-centred care to First Nations Australian women and families.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the impact of power relations, including power over First Nations peoples on midwifery practice in Australia.
Analyse the role of midwifery in optimising outcomes for First Nations peoples in relation to maternal and newborn health from a community development and social determinants of health perspective.
Analyse the impact of place of birth, and maternity care strategies for First Nations women and families, including issues of cultural safety and sensitivity, in woman-centred maternity care.
Discuss culturally safe ways of working with, and empowering First Nations Australian women and families.

title: Ministry Level 4
school: School
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for a Ministry Level 4 16 point credit within the Master of Ministry Articulated Set of courses
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for a Ministry Level 4 16 point credit within the Master of Ministry Articulated Set of courses.

title: Midwifery Practice Experience
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will apply theory to practice and will demonstrate achievement of all the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) competencies as well as undertake the required midwifery practice experiences. Midwifery practice experiences will include continuity of care, antenatal care, labour and birth, complex care, postnatal care, and neonatal care.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on midwifery practice as defined by the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Midwifery Standards for Practice (2018).
Assess, plan, apply and evaluate safe and effective continuity of care utilising a woman-centred focus across the childbearing continuum.
Establish, maintain and conclude therapeutic relationships with woman and their significant others across the childbearing continuum.
Demonstrate effective and accurate verbal and written communication with midwives, healthcare providers, and other professionals during consultation, referral and handover.
Identify deviations from normal childbearing and consult, refer to and collaborate with other healthcare professionals.
Adhere to scope of practice, legal, professional, and ethical boundaries, as well as local policy and procedure.

title: Mission, Evangelism and Apologetics
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the study of Christian mission, evangelism and apologetics. It explores the historical, biblical and theological perspectives on these themes. Particular focus is given to the relationship between the gospel and culture, and recent discussion regarding the missional nature of the church. Attention is also given to issues relating to the practice of mission, evangelism and apologetics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Evaluate critically the changes of understanding in mission, evangelism and apologetics that have occurred throughout the history of the church.
Engage critically with recent discussions on the relationship between gospel and culture, power and gender.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the variety of definitions of mission, evangelism and apologetics, including their interrelationship.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of issues relating to the contemporary practice of mission, evangelism and apologetics: e.g. 'missional' church.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the various biblical and theological perspectives on mission, evangelism and apologetics.

school: School

learning_outcomes: This credit code is for a Ministry Level 5 16 point credit within the Master of Ministry Articulated Set of courses.
