title: Mobile Application Development
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the theoretical and technical knowledge and skills necessary to develop various applications for small and resource-constrained devices. The Android platform is the primary focus of the subject, whilst iPhone Operating System (iOS) and Windows Mobile will also be considered in the overview of platform architectures. The concepts of Graphical User Interface (GUI), local and distributed database design will be taught to produce some sample mobile applications. Successful completion of the subject will lead participants towards developing applications relating to real-life problems, games, entertainment and education.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and discuss technology trends in rapidly evolving field of handheld devices.
Develop distributed applications for mobile devices.
Write and develop programs for different mobile platforms.
Identify and analyse requirements for mobile applications development.
Classify and distinguish the basic platforms of handheld devices.

title: Modern History of Islamic Societies
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the history of Islamic societies between the 19th and 21st centuries. It addresses the major events of the period through a critical examination of the complex interplay of internal factors (religion, race and culture) and external factors (global conflicts and Western dominance). Students will consider political and social changes attributed to the demise of the Ottoman, Mughal and Safavid Empires and the emergence of national states. The effects of European colonisation on the development of the Muslim world, and the theological, political, legal, cultural, and spiritual changes occurring during the modern era of Islamic history will be considered.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and evaluate critically the various narratives that attempt to explain the development of the Islamic nation states.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the events that shaped the current state of the Islamic societies.
Identify and discuss critically religious, cultural and geo-political factors that influenced the modern history of the Muslim world.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of how the religion of Islam has been used as a tool in political struggles.
Evaluate the internal and external factors that contributed to key events in the modern era.
Analyse and discuss the rise and decline in nationalism, secularism and socialism in the Muslim world.

title: Models of Community Development
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines what community leadership and resilience mean in the context of community development theory and practice. It gives close attention to models that attend to the power inequalities shaping leadership and resilience among communities. Practices are considered that foster community leadership, resilience and power for social action and change including organising, activism, resistance, social movements and participatory democracy and economies. The theory and practice implications of challenging the power inequalities that undermine inclusive community leadership and resilience are analysed. The subject is designed with adaptable delivery models, which may include combinations of condensed online sessions and one-off workshops.
learning_outcomes: Apply theoretical concepts to community development practice.
Explain how community development theory and practice can reproduce or resist the power inequalities shaping community leadership and resilience experiences.
Identify and discern between a range of community development models relevant to community leadership and resilience.

title: Modern History of the Muslim World (WWI to Present)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the modern history of the Muslim world from the 19th to 21st centuries. It provides students with in-depth understanding of key events and developments that have shaped the Muslim world over the past centuries. The subject begins with the decline of the Ottoman, Mughal and Safavid empires and guides students through the transformative journey of the Muslim world. The subject emphasises major regions and countries, analysing significant events within the timeframe. It takes a critical approach, examining the complex interplay of internal factors, such as religion, politics, race and culture, as well as external factors like colonisation, world wars, the Cold War, collapse of the Soviet Union, Gulf wars and Arab Spring. Students are encouraged to evaluate the development of nationalism, democracy and socio-political forces that have influenced the evolution of Islamic societies in the modern era. They will also explore the responses of Muslim scholars and activists, who have initiated Islamic revivalist movements after the abolishment of the caliphate in 1924.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate comprehensive understanding of the events that shaped the current state of the Islamic societies.
Analyse and evaluate the rise and decline in nationalism, secularism and socialism in the Muslim world.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of how the religion of Islam has been used as a tool in political struggles.
Analytically discuss and evaluate the various narratives that attempt to explain the development of the Islamic nation states.
Identify and critically discuss religious, cultural and geopolitical factors and major events that influenced the modern history of the Muslim world.
Critically evaluate the internal and external factors that contributed to key events in the modern era and how these shaped history.

title: Modern Physics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Modern Physics focuses on a body of knowledge necessary to examine the fundamental physical principles of the universe. By exploring historic experiments and utilising theories developed in classical physics, students will make amendments to classical theories and derive theories that comprise modern physics. This will be achieved through a study of electromagnetism, relativity and quantum mechanics. Practical experience is developed through experimentation with quantum processes, developing skills in data analysis, and demonstration of concepts.
learning_outcomes: Conduct experiments of both classical and modern processes with developed skills in the generation and analysis of data to demonstrate and communicate concepts.
Examine theories and experimentation in both classical and modern physics.
Utilise, identify and apply theories and equations in modern physics to conceptually/analytically solve problems, obtain values/model results and communicate information to an audience.
Apply electromagnetism, relativity and quantum mechanics to analyse and evaluate results of atomic, molecular and nuclear physics.
Establish theories/derive equations within modern physics.

title: Molecular Cell Biology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the current model of eukaryotic cell at a molecular level, detailing aspects of cellular structure and function, regulation, the cell cycle and the flow of genetic information. It links aspects of biochemistry and genetics as they pertain to cell functioning and fits this knowledge into the broader context of organism structure, cancer development and embryological development.
learning_outcomes: Describe in detail the current understanding of genomic evolution and how it relates to species differentiation.
Describe the processes of cell regulation including gene regulation, cell signalling, the cell cycle and apply these to development, cell- and tissue differentiation and programmed cell death.
Describe in detail the cell structure and function, including subcellular structure, membranes, membrane proteins , active and passive transport, the cytoskeleton and cell movement.
Perform basic molecular genetic analytical procedures.
Demonstrate an understanding of the cell as a basic unit of life including the organisation of cells and their composition.

title: Molecular Cell Biology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Molecular Cell Biology 2 will expand on Molecular Cell Biology 1, detailing advanced aspects of cellular structure and function, regulation, the cell cycle and sexual reproduction. It links aspects of biochemistry and genetics as they pertain to cell functioning and fits this knowledge into the broader context of organism structure, cancer development and embryological development.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of sexual reproduction for cells and organisms.
Evaluate their role in development, cell and tissue differentiation and programmed cell death.
Describe the processes of cell regulation including cell signalling, the cell cycle and sexual reproduction.
Describe the processes involved in cellular energy production and the cellular structures responsible for these processes.
Describe in detail, cell structure and function, including subcellular structure, membranes, membrane proteins, active and passive transport, the cytoskeleton and cell movement.

title: Molecular Cell Biology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the current model of eukaryotic cells at a molecular level, detailing aspects of cellular biochemistry, the flow of genetic information, the production of proteins and their basic functions. It links aspects of introductory biochemistry and introductory genetics as they pertain to cell functioning and fits this knowledge into the broader context of cellular function.
learning_outcomes: Describe in detail the current understanding of genomic evolution and how it relates to species differentiation.
Describe the cell as a basic unit of life including identifying the internal organisation of cells and compare their chemical composition.
Identify and describe current technologies used to analyse structure and functions of genes.
Describe the flow of information in a cell from DNA to protein and compare the molecular processes involved and explain their regulation.
List, identify, define and describe important molecular processes and their components.

title: Molecular Cell Biology 2 (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Molecular Cell Biology 2 will expand on Molecular Cell Biology 1, detailing advanced aspects of cellular structure and function, regulation, the cell cycle and sexual reproduction. It links aspects of biochemistry and genetics as they pertain to cell functioning and fits this knowledge into the broader context of organism structure, cancer development and embryological development.
learning_outcomes: Describe the processes of cell regulation including cell signalling, the cell cycle and sexual reproduction.
Describe in detail, cell structure and function, including subcellular structure, membranes, membrane proteins, active and passive transport, the cytoskeleton and cell movement.
Explain the importance of sexual reproduction for cells and organisms.
Evaluate their role in development, cell and tissue differentiation and programmed cell death.
Describe the processes involved in cellular energy production and the cellular structures responsible for these processes.

title: Molecular Pathology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will draw together the knowledge gained in their study of physiology, biochemistry, human genetics and cell biology, haematology and histopathology to examine the molecular basis of disease. This subject will take a multi-disciplinary approach to the topic and focus on the application of molecular techniques to assist in the diagnosis of disease in a medical laboratory setting and how these techniques can be used to assist in the diagnosis and treatment of emerging diseases. This subject includes a practical component; distance students will complete this component at a 3 day intensive school.
learning_outcomes: explain how cytogenetics may be used in the diagnosis of disease;
describe the molecular basis of diseases relevant to medical laboratory scientists;
explain the practice of ''molecular medicine'' and the translational aspects of molecular pathology: molecular diagnostics, molecular assessment, and personalized medicine;
justify the use of a particular diagnosis technique within a pathology setting and to assess both the benefits and limitations of the teachnique; and
critically evaluate the use of molecular techniques in the diagnosis and treatment of disease.

This subject will take a multi-disciplinary approach to the topic and focus on the application of molecular techniques to assist in the diagnosis of disease in a medical laboratory setting and how these techniques can be used to assist in the diagnosis and treatment of emerging diseases.

Explain how cytogenetics may be used in the diagnosis of disease.
Justify the use of a particular diagnosis technique within a pathology setting and explain both the benefits and limitations of the technique.
Describe the molecular basis of diseases relevant to medical laboratory scientists.

title: Molecular Pathology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will take a multi-disciplinary approach to the examination of the molecular basis of disease. The subject focus is on the application of contemporary molecular techniques to assist in the diagnosis, prognostication and treatment selection for human disease. The subject also addresses the translational aspects of molecular pathology in areas such as pharmacogenomics and personalised medicine.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the theory of precision/personalised medicine and discuss the translational aspects of molecular pathology.
Justify the use of molecular diagnostic techniques and to assess both the benefits and limitations of these methods.
Describe the molecular basis of human diseases.
Critically evaluate the scientific literature and demonstrate important skills in scientific analysis and communication.

title: Money Laundering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the criminal phenomena of money laundering and how and why its form and function varies across industries, regional and international jurisdictions. The subject analyses traditional and emerging forms of money laundering and associated crimes committed via the use of digital currencies and online platforms. It examines both the risks and rewards facing money launders who seek to move funds around the world, along with how money laundering is quantified locally and globally.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the theoretical and professional perspectives on money laundering behaviour.
Describe the nature and scale of money laundering.
Analyse and discuss the affordances of technology in shaping money laundering.
Analyse and discuss the opportunities legitimate societal and global structures offer money launderers.
Evaluate and discuss current and evolving money laundering risks.

title: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Due Diligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the development of a risk-based approach to the reduction of money laundering and terrorist financing via the implementation of organisational controls. It explores internationally informed best practice and how this manifests differently across jurisdictions. The subject analyses the effectiveness of regulatory regimes that specifically address issues of money laundering and terrorist financing.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the communication, literacy, numeracy, research and digital skills required of a competent professional financial crime control practitioner.
Evaluate AML/CTF compliance risks and apply appropriate strategies to mitigate risks at the strategic and operational level.
Communicate complex risk mitigation strategies to stakeholders.
Identify and explain the weaknesses underpinning AML/CTF systems.
Compare and analyse global approaches to the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing.

title: Morals, Minds and Decision-making
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject delves into the complexities of moral and rational decision-making. We start by examining how recent advances in psychology impact moral theorizing. We will consider, for example, the effects of cognitive bias on the reliability of moral intuitions and how neuroscience, particularly brain imaging studies, informs our understanding of morality. We will then engage with a series of case studies to navigate the challenges of practical decision-making. Through these explorations, we will critically assess whether rational decision-making is psychologically feasible and neuro-scientifically realistic and whether there are inherent limits to rationality itself. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the main philosophical theories concerning the relation between reasons and values.
Demonstrate an understanding of the major philosophical approaches to practical reason and decision making.
Determine the philosophical significance of recent findings in neuroscience and psychology.

title: Motivating and Influencing People
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject we examine three factors that assist us to understand human behaviour at work. In particular, we look at the way in which individual level factors (e.g. personality and motivation), team level factors (e.g. leadership and group dynamics) and organisational differences (e.g. structure and culture) combine to explain behaviour. Behaviour at work plays a critical role in explaining organisational outcomes such as productivity and absenteeism.
learning_outcomes: Apply techniques to motivate and influence people at work.
Critically appraise the inter-relationship between individual, team and organisational systems.
Evaluate a number of theories that explain human behaviour.

title: Motivation and Engagement
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The aim of the subject is to provide an appreciation and understanding of the motivation and engagement of staff through the lens of contemporary HR practices. Students are expected to reflect on their own experience and their organisation's practices across a range of key issues. 'Policy is generally regarded as a blunt instrument, yet it is often utilized primarily to mitigate risk rather than to equitably encourage and support desired behaviours'. This subject will explore this proposition in the policing context utilising comparative analyses and case studies.
learning_outcomes: Think critically about the motivation and engagement of people in a policing context, particularly as they relate to issues such as performance, discipline and absenteeism.

Identify and examine key challenges in human resource management and think critically about solutions to these including the application of workforce planning, demographics and organisational performance.
Review, analyse, consolidate and synthesise the theoretical concepts, philosophy and underpinnings upon which key components of contemporary HR management are based.

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Credit code for Australian Defence Force students in the Bachelor of Policing and Bachelor of Policing (Investigations).

title: Multi-Agency Investigations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Many types of incidents in the public and private sector can become ‘Critical' and by distinction have different characteristics to ‘Major Incidents'. Critical incidents are high stake, ambiguous and potentially politically sensitive situations and events, which can occur beyond normal expected organisational activity and, if not managed correctly, can have serious and wide ranging ramifications. A major incident, on the other hand, may be an event requiring a multi-agency response and can often be planned beforehand. An investigation may not always be necessary following a major incident but if at any point it becomes a ‘critical' one, then an investigation will normally ensue. Using critical incidents as examples, this subject examines organisational and multi-agency responses to, and management of, the divergent categories of an investigation in to a critical incident, exploring; the phases of a critical incident, organisational preparedness, operational risk management, community impact and post incident review and learning. Decision making models will be considered in depth, and the nuances between ‘Decision Inertia' and ‘Decision Error' will be examined alongside how ‘emotional intelligence' might affect decision making and ethical standards.
learning_outcomes: Plan, lead, co-ordinate and implement effective strategies in multi-agency investigations.
Apply professional practice and judgement and contemporary operational and risk management theories in multi-agency settings.
Demonstrate the communication, literacy, numeracy, research and digital skills required of a competent Investigator.
Critically analyse diverse compliance, regulatory, and accountability issues arising in multi-agency investigation environments.
Apply the most effective option required to achieve objectives in multi-agency settings.
Apply established decision-making models in complex operational situations.

title: Multiple Understandings
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject presents a range of theoretical perspectives on children's learning and investigates the implications of these for early childhood curriculum. Students will consider how contemporary schools of thought such as social constructionism, poststructuralism, and critical and cultural-historical theories may inspire new possibilities in working with young children and their families. The aim is to render problematic what may have been taken as the 'truth' about early childhood education: how young children learn; the role of the educator in that learning; and the role of parents and the community in the early childhood curriculum.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast a range of appropriate curriculum frameworks with the multiple perspectives and approaches to early childhood curriculum identified above.
Examine competing theories of how young children learn and demonstrate an understanding of the uncertainty, ambiguity and limits to knowledge(s) used to guide early childhood practices.
Critically reflect on the implications of different theories of learning for early childhood curriculum practices.

Distinguish among multiple perspectives on and approaches to early childhood curriculum and the effects of each position on curriculum planning, including the selection of assessment strategies and approaches.
Examine and critically reflect on their own theories of teaching and learning and what informs their practice.

Articulate their own position statement(s) on how young children learn and the role of early childhood education in society and consider the implications of these on their work in developing and enacting an equitable curriculum for and with young children and their families.
Understand and critically reflect on key concepts, theoretical approaches and assumptions that inform early childhood education.
prerequisites: EEA304: Multiple Understandings: Early Childhood Teaching and Learning

title: Multiplatform Production Project
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject the student develops a proposal for a significant major work or a significant contribution to a major collaborative project in which their contribution is appropriate to their area of specialisation. In this subject the students, individually, produce and design web based media assets for the project. This may involve any combination of digital sound, music, text, and/or video, image creation and manipulation, animation, 3D modelling or other special effects, interactive techniques and/or other multimedia processes.
learning_outcomes: Produce an independent multiplatform production using industry standard practice.
Critically engage in, and respond to, the contemporary theory and practice of interactive design and multiplatform production towards informational, artistic, educational or entertainment contexts.
Develop a proposal procedure to required industry expectation.
Apply sustainability, accessibility and ethics best practice principles as they apply to the multiplatform environment.
Critically analyse and implement the range of media platform options for a variety of conceptual tasks.

title: Multivariable Calculus
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject extends the study of calculus to functions of several variables. Partial derivatives are reviewed and double and triple integrals introduced. The subject also covers vector calculus, which includes differential operators (gradient, divergence and curl) and line and surface integrals. Vector calculus culminates in higher dimensional versions of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: Green's Theorem, Stokes' Theorem and the Divergence Theorem.
learning_outcomes: Calculate divergence and curl of a vector field.
Demonstrate if a vector field is conservative and calculate line integrals.
Calculate and apply partial derivatives, directional derivatives, the gradient, tangent planes and differentials.
Calculate surface integrals.
Classify and graph conics and simple quadric surfaces.
Demonstrate the application of Green's Theorem, Stokes' Theorem and the Divergence Theorem.
Calculate double and triple integrals.
Calculate and graph level curves and surfaces.
Demonstrate the use of multivariable calculus to applied problems.
prerequisites: MTH402: Computer Aided Mathematics 2 with Applications

Calculate line integrals and recognise a conservative field.

title: Multivariate Statistical Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to multivariate statistical modelling techniques through an applied approach to data analysis. The emphasis is on demonstration of techniques and their applicability via investigations of the various methodologies. The use of real life data and software packages is also emphasised in this subject to illustrate the power and limitations of multivariate methods.
learning_outcomes: Classify given complex problems, arising from a variety of professional or research contexts, by checking assumptions to select the appropriate analysis techniques.
Apply the chosen technique to solve the complex problem.
Use statistical packages in analysis of real data arising from a variety of professional or research contexts.
Analyse multivariate data with summary estimates and correct visualisation.
Use a variety of matrix notations and perform matrix algebra used in multivariate analysis.
Report and explain the results of the analysis to a variety of audiences, including those with or without statistical backgrounds.

title: Muslims in Australia: Past and Present
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on Muslims in the Australian context. It offers a distinct overview of their past and present, while analysing the Islamic cultural-religious and civilisation manifestations with Australian history. It also explores the impact of early cross-cultural encounters, immigration and social policies on early Muslim settlements in Australia, together with the development of Islamic communities in the Australian context. It examines the influence of multiculturalism on Muslims in Australia, their integration into mainstream society, and their encounters with global issues. Finally, it discusses possible connections between historical and contemporary Muslim migration to Australia.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the socio-historical concepts of immigration, settlement, integration, and social policies in Australia, and the plurality of the interpretations of these concepts.

Discuss critically the impact of historical events in the settlement of Muslims in Australia, and be able to analyse critically cross-cultural and civilisational encounters between Muslims and non-Muslims.
Critically interpret the past and the present within the context of the actions, values, ideals, encounters and contributions of Muslims.
Discuss critically the development of Muslim communities and institutions in Australia.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of relevant literature and important Muslim socio-historical issues in the Australian context.

title: Muslims in the West: Identity and Culture
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject discusses the various perspectives that Islam and Muslim minorities encounter in Western society. It covers the historical, social, and political development and transformation of Muslims living in the West. Students will critically analyse and examine the related issues of identity, integration and social cohesion, and analyse critically the changing dynamics of the West, and how Muslims living in the West are affected by these changes. The European, North American, and Australian contexts will also be considered.
learning_outcomes: Examine critically the consequences of divisionism (e.g. Islamic radicalism and Islamophobia) in multicultural societies and discuss preventative measures to build social cohesion in Australian multicultural and multifaith communities.
Demonstrate an understanding of the contemporary dynamics of multicultural western communities where Islam and Muslims live.
Critically analyse the varying motives, struggles and challenges of both the immigrant and host societies in the development of a multicultural society which is respectful of diverse perspectives.
Analyse and assess critically the mediation efforts between Muslims and the West and their consequences for a peaceful society.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of diverse perspectives concerning the reality of Muslims in the West, and develop means and processes of living together in a truly multicultural society.

title: Narrative: Production and Performance
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The ability to tell a story across a range of media platforms is essential for students entering careers in the fields of communication, art, design, performance and media production. This subject provides an introduction to storytelling through audio, vision and live/recorded performance, with consideration of the evolution of technologies and practices.
learning_outcomes: Construct narratives using audio, video & performance production processes.
Use a range of techniques to capture, edit and publish audio and moving images.
Reflect on the evolution of technology and how narratives can be shaped by various mediums.
Critique and apply the fundamental concepts of narrative.
Produce and critique audio visual creative works.
Appropriately use the various file formats used to publish audio and moving images.

title: National Security and Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The subject equips the student with an understanding of intelligence practice in the national security context in Australia and its ‘Five Eyes' key alliance partners (United States, United Kingdom, Canada and New Zealand). It builds on key introductory principles including critical thinking and operational intelligence theory and practice delivered in earlier subjects in the Master of Intelligence Analysis. The subject is based on three broad areas, which in turn informs the learning outcomes. First, it introduces the student to advanced strategic intelligence analysis capabilities and analytical techniques in the national security context. Second, this subject encourages students to develop a sound appreciation of the national security context, including the roles of various agencies in the National (Australian Intelligence Community), and those of the Canadian, New Zealand, US and UK. Contemporary legislation and key professional debates about intelligence are explored (e.g. the politicisation of intelligence, intelligence failures and ethics). Third, this subject places intelligence in its workings in the national security context by discussing links between intelligence doctrinal issues and their application and relevance to the increasingly complex global and transnational security environment.
learning_outcomes: Think critically about the National Intelligence Community (Australian) and their own professional practice in relation to it.
Demonstrate mastery of critical thinking and alternative analytical capabilities in the context of national security and intelligence issues.
Review, analyse, consolidate and synthesise knowledge of key theoretical and practical intelligence analysis principles that guide practitioners working with national security agencies.
Demonstrate advanced analytical and research skills and be able to appropriately apply these to a range of contemporary national security intelligence practice issues.
Critically reflect on the contemporary legal and ethical issues relating to national security intelligence, and provide recommendations for policy and management action.
Review, analyse, consolidate and synthesise a range of data in a selected area of global/transnational security area.
prerequisites: JST493: National Security and Intelligence Issues

title: Natural Resource Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Maintaining natural resources including biodiversity, minerals, and water in the face of increasing pressures and threats is a major challenge for traditional owners, other stakeholders, practitioners and scientists. This subject provides an introduction of how such resources are managed. Topics include the nature of natural resources and examinations of the organisations, approaches, methods and policies related to natural resource management. Emphasis is placed on the role of Indigenous Australian communities in past and present natural resource management. On completion, students have a broad understanding of natural resource management and the ability to apply their knowledge and skills to make sound judgements about ways to manage and protect natural resources.
learning_outcomes: Identify a natural resource and define natural resources management.
Explain the importance of Indigenous Australian natural resource management.
Review and discuss the roles of natural resource policy mechanisms and tools.
Discuss a range of natural resource management issues and approaches to managing them.
Apply knowledge and skills to explain the human dimensions underpinning natural resource management.

title: Natural Resources Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the regulatory framework governing primary production in the agricultural and mining industries. Students evaluate law and policy issues such as live export, fracking, native title and collaboration between the mining industry and Indigenous Australians.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of a range of legal instruments addressing mining and agricultural activities.
Interpret and analyse legislation, codes of conduct and policy instruments in the context of mining and agricultural production.
Demonstrate a critical awareness of ethical, social and cultural issues operating within the rural practice context.
Critically analyse case law involving disputes between mining corporations and native title claimants.
Apply legal research techniques and the rules of statutory interpretation to solve hypothetical problems relating to Indigenous cultural heritage and environmental obligations.
prerequisites: LAW312: Resources Law: Contemporary Issues in Primary Production
JST123: Indigenous Australians and Justice: An Introduction

title: Navigating the curriculum landscape
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject critically examines contemporary curriculum debates. Starting with an exploration of notions of curriculum, teaching and learning from an Indigenist Standpoint (Phillips, 2019), students then interrogate sociocultural theories of curriculum, how we understand knowledge and knowing, as well as a range of Australian and international First Peoples ways of knowing, being and doing. Students will identify and analyse the tensions between official curriculum, diverse learning needs and how these are identified, responded to and documented. Included here is a focus on Indigenist ways of knowing and being. From these investigations, students will evaluate curriculum practices in their own educational contexts and propose strategies that bring to the fore local knowledges in response to State/National curriculum requirements. This subject is focused on cultivating approaches to curriculum work that responds to situated learner and learning contexts.
learning_outcomes: Compare and critique a range of curriculum and pedagogic models relevant to a particular context.
Apply an Indigenist Standpoint framework to critically reflect on your own epistemologies and ontologies of teaching and learning.
Analyse and discuss discourses shaping contemporary curriculum priorities.
Critically review and apply sociocultural theories of curriculum.
Propose locally responsive approaches to curriculum making in context.

title: Negotiating and Managing Conflict
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the main styles of negotiation used in business environments in order to manage conflict and focus on beneficial outcomes. The subject looks at these various styles, their flaws, benefits, and the most appropriate situation in which to apply each style to enhance effective negotiation. Students will also reflect on critiques of each style and will participate in role plays involving various styles.
learning_outcomes: Apply different methods of conflict resolution during negotiations.
Explain and critically evaluate the situational appropriateness, effectiveness, and usefulness of various negotiation styles.
Effectively practice various negotiation skills in specialised settings.

title: Network Design
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide students with experience in the architectures and considerations related to designing, securing, operating, and troubleshooting enterprise networks. Concepts covered in this subject enable students to develop advanced skills related to wide area network (WAN) technologies, Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), Access Control List (ACL), Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), Network Address Translation (NAT), Internet Protocol Security (IPSec), Virtual Private Network (VPN), and Quality of Service (QoS) mechanisms for secure remote access, along with software-defined networking, virtualisation and automation concepts supporting network digitisation. This subject is the last in a series of three subjects that incorporate the Cisco Networking Academy Program.
learning_outcomes: Virtualise, secure and automate wide area networks (WANs).
Explain and evaluate the nature and operations of various WAN technologies.
Utilise network management tools.
Configure and troubleshoot enterprise networks.
Identify and protect against cybersecurity threats.
Explain, analyse software-defined networking, including controller-based architectures.
Implement application programming interfaces (APIs) to enable network automation.

title: Multimedia Design and Creation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject engages students in the process of designing and creating multimedia projects. It explores the creation of multimedia content exploring creative futures and virtual environments. Students realise their imagined multimedia construction through a media design and production project that engages diverse fields.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply divergent and convergent thinking for multimedia and design towards exploring creative futures and virtual environments.
Apply knowledge and skills in multimedia design and production.
Analyse and apply research, explorations and experimentations in order to creatively problem solve.
Work independently or collaboratively within a team environment in design concept and productions.
Apply theories and practices of innovation and creativity in multimedia project design.

title: Negotiation Skills
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the main styles of negotiation used in business environments. The subject looks at these various styles, their flaws, benefits, and the most appropriate situation in which to apply each style to enhance effective negotiation. Students will also reflect on critiques of each style and will participate in role plays involving various styles. These skills will benefit many employment sets, including, but not limited to, lawyers, human resources, sales, and management.
learning_outcomes: Gather information and write reports relevant to negotiated outcomes.
Explain and critically evaluate the situational appropriateness, effectiveness, and usefulness of various negotiation styles.
Reflect critically on theory and professional practice and scholarship of negotiation.
Effectively practice various negotiation skills in specialised settings.
Apply different methods of conflict resolution during negotiations.

title: Network Security
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: As the digital threat landscape rapidly evolves, managing information technology (IT) network risk is of paramount importance to most organisations. This subject provides students with knowledge and skills in fundamental network security principles and practices. Students will be introduced to a range of key network security concepts and network security protocols, such as types of security threats, cryptography, wireless network security, cloud and Internet of Things (IoT) security. Some of the practices related to network security management will be briefly explored, focusing on network vulnerability and risk assessment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the security threats to a network.
Evaluate and propose effective countermeasures for network security.
Explain fundamental network security concepts.
Discuss basic network security management functions, such as risk assessment, monitoring and auditing.
Identify and analyse the key components of cloud computing security.

title: Network Forensics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide students with the knowledge and skills necessary to investigate security incidents and conduct forensic analysis on computer networks. Students will learn about the tools and techniques used to capture and analyse network traffic, and how to use this information to identify potential security breaches and malware infections.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse security incidents on computer networks.
Describe the basic network protocols, including TCP/IP, HTTP, DNS, and FTP.
Capture and analyse network traffic using/employing network traffic analysis tools.
Conduct forensic analysis of network traffic and respond to security breaches and malware infections.

title: Network Security and Cryptography
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: ITC593 provides the practical knowledge and skills needed to analyse and work with network security protocols and standards, along with an in-depth introduction to the field of cryptography. The subject explores how contemporary encryption algorithms, digital signatures and cryptographic hash functions are used to implement various security goals, such as authentication, confidentiality and integrity. It also includes a comprehensive coverage of emerging security trends in modern IT infrastructure.
learning_outcomes: Analyse cryptographic algorithms, both symmetrical and asymmetrical, and explain how they are used to improve network security.
Investigate and evaluate the current and emerging trends in cryptography and network security.
Identify and explain the various digital threats to IT networks and computing devices.
Compare and contrast the features of various authentication protocols.
Design security solutions using existing authentication protocols.
Effectively communicate and justify why a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is an important component in a network security architecture.
Propose mitigating techniques against cryptographic and network security threats.

title: Networking and Building Partnerships
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the art of relationship building and its use to gain competitive advantage through initiating, developing, maintaining and terminating a range of relationships in professional practice contexts. This subject is designed with adaptable delivery models, which may include combinations of condensed online sessions and one-off workshops.
learning_outcomes: Develop strategic communication to facilitate the identification, cultivation and maintenance of relationships.
Explain the importance of relationships within community resilience and leadership practice.

title: Networking Fundamentals
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to contemporary computer networking concepts and instils the skills and knowledge required to design, configure and manage a small to medium sized network. Students will gain knowledge about the layered architectural design principles along with the technical standards required for establishing connectivity through such networks. The subject will introduce students to the current and emerging concepts in IP addressing, IP routing, switching and TCP/IP security to develop the skills required to design, implement and troubleshoot computer networks
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate the architectural design principles of internetworking.
Examine IP addressing requirements using suitable addressing schemes.
Design and troubleshoot a network architecture for optimal network management and performance.
Evaluate the requirements of IP routing and select appropriate routing methods to ensure secure and efficient data transmission.
Reflect and evaluate the historical evolution and ongoing transformations of the internet.

title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students' knowledge of conditions of a neurodevelopmental origin, including learning disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autistic spectrum disorders, and the broader range of neurodevelopmental conditions which affect cognition and behaviour throughout the lifespan. Students will examine the diagnostic classification, epidemiology and aetiology of these conditions, and learn how to enhance diagnosis and practice through the conduct of accurate psychological assessments and the selection of interventions.
learning_outcomes: Identify the presenting features of the range of neurodevelopmental disorders.
Critically analyse and synthesise a large body of complex information in order to support the assessment and differential diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders.
Produce accurate, detailed and informative psychological reports.
Conduct accurate and efficient psychological assessments of children, adolescents and adults presenting with known or suspected neurodevelopmental disorders.
Identify optimal interventions for accurate and efficient psychological assessments of children, adolescents and adults presenting with known or suspected neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Neuroethics: The Ethical Implications of Science
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject delves into the complexities of moral and rational decision-making. We start by examining how recent advances in psychology impact moral theorizing. We will consider, for example, the effects of cognitive bias on the reliability of moral intuitions and how neuroscience, particularly brain imaging studies, informs our understanding of morality. We will then engage with a series of case studies to navigate the challenges of practical decision-making. Through these explorations, we will critically assess whether rational decision-making is psychologically feasible and neuro-scientifically realistic and whether there are inherent limits to rationality itself. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the main philosophical theories concerning the relation between reasons and values.
Determine the philosophical and ethical significance of recent findings in neuroscience and psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding of the major philosophical approaches to practical reason and decision making.

title: Neuropathology and Pain
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will study the aetiology, pathophysiology, clinical assessment, and management of a range of neurological conditions to understand the role of a podiatrist in managing complex neurological and pain conditions, within a multidisciplinary team. Students will extend their knowledge of pain pathophysiology with a particular focus on the use of pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions for the management of acute and chronic pain. This subject will contribute to the student's preparation for endorsement for scheduled medicine and progression towards competence in prescribing analgesic medicines.
learning_outcomes: Explain appropriate assessment techniques and management options for a range of peripheral and central nervous system pathologies.
Justify pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions for collaborative management of acute and chronic pain.
Evaluate the aetiology, pathophysiology and clinical presentation of a range of peripheral and central nervous system pathologies.
Evaluate pain as a presenting symptom and assess the impact on a person’s functional ability.
Discuss the role of a podiatrist in multidisciplinary management of pain and nervous system pathology, including referral of a person when suitable treatment options are outside scope of practice.

title: Neuroscience of Motor Behaviour
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the neuroscience of motor control and learning. Emphasis is placed on the functional neuroanatomy, organisation and integration of the neural subsystems involved in human movement. All levels of the nervous system are examined from peripheral sensory receptors and motor nerves to the highest levels of cerebral cortical function governing cognitive aspects of movement. Sensorimotor adaptations to musculoskeletal injury, exercise training, reduced use, ageing, skill learning and motor disturbances due to neurological disease will also be addressed. Laboratory work employs electrophysiological techniques and kinetics to examine sensorimotor and/or neuromotor function in a variety of situations. This subject includes a compulsory intensive if the subject is undertaken by Distance Education.
learning_outcomes: Discuss acute and/or chronic changes in sensorimotor function associated with ageing, exercise and injury.
Discuss the role of cortical and subcortical structures in motor learning and memory.
Discuss the contribution of cortical and subcortical structures in planning, organising and executing motor commands to produce smooth, coordinated, rhythmical movement.
Describe the neuroanatomy and neurophysiology of vision and balance.
Discuss key features of the underlying pathophysiology of common neurological diseases and identify implications for motor control and/or learning.
Explain the pathway of motor signal transmission from the cortex to spinal motor neurons.
Explain the pathway of sensory signal transmission from peripheral receptors to the cerebral cortex for touch and kinesthesia.
Describe the morphology and function of different nervous system cells.
Describe the neuroanatomy and neurophysiology of touch and kinesthesia.
Discuss sensorimotor integration in joint stability, postural control, locomotion and reaching/grasping.
Discuss neuroplasticity associated with motor learning, musculoskeletal injury and chronic changes in physical activity.
Describe synaptic structure and neural communication processes.

title: Neuroscience for Health Practice
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an understanding of fundamental neuroanatomy and neurophysiology. Students will develop an understanding of the sensory, motor and autonomic nervous systems, as well as the vascularisation of the central nervous system. Higher cortical function and dysfunction are also covered. Students will apply their fundamental understanding of neuroscience to investigate the major functional categories of neurological disease, examples of common neurological disorders, and the major classes of pharmaceuticals used to modulate nervous system activity.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of the peripheral and central nervous systems to interpret clinical findings.
Determine appropriate diagnostic tests to identify neurological function / dysfunction.
Describe the parts and the function of the peripheral and central nervous systems.
Explain the pharmacological basis of the treatment of neurological and psychiatric diseases in relation to neurological structure and function.

title: New Religious Movements and Alternative Spiritualities
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the beliefs and identifying characteristics of various new religious movements, 'cults', sects, and other alternative forms of spirituality. It also explores major historical, religious, social, legal and ethical issues raised by the presence of such groups within an Australian and global context. In particular, this subject examines responses to new religious movements, 'cults' and sects from the churches, civil society, the media, judiciary, government and law enforcement agencies.
learning_outcomes: Research, critically evaluate, and articulate community and individual responses to new religious movements.
Evaluate the role and rights of new religious movements within a pluralist democratic society.
Critically and accurately discuss the beliefs, character and activities of new religious movements.
Research and communicate issues surrounding the definition of the term "cult".
Demonstrate and articulate an understanding of the relevance of the mind control/brainwashing debate and its relevance for the study of new religious movements.
Critically evaluate and articulate the role of the media in the public perception and response to new religious movements.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Analyse and articulate a basic understanding of the legal issues raised by new religious movements.

title: New Testament Greek 1
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This foundational subject develops the competence needed to begin to read the New Testament in Koine (Common) Greek. It does this by introducing students to the basic grammar and vocabulary of the Greek New Testament. The subject draws attention to the significance of New Testament Greek for biblical and theological study.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of basic Greek grammar.
Demonstrate the acquisition of a significant amount of the vocabulary of the Greek New Testament.
Demonstrate self-guided learning.
Translate relatively simple passages from the Greek New Testament into English.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the importance of New Testament Greek for further biblical and theological study.

title: Non-Emergency Clinical Placement
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores at an introductory level the 'professional self' and applies the contemporary professional model of community paramedic in a health continuum. This subject will focus on competencies that examine the professional responsibilities of paramedics in multifaceted roles within Australia: therapeutic communication, empathy, attitude, confidentiality, and patient safety. Such competencies will be learned in non-emergency clinical and community focused environments. This subject requires 100 placement hours in various clinical and community venues.
learning_outcomes: be able to describe the role of community-based and non-emergency health services in a range of environments.
be able to demonstrate continual reflection on their practice.
be able to demonstrate professionalism in a supervised clinical setting and articulate their role and tasks.
be able to develop and demonstrate communication and team building skills.
be able to maintain an effective audit trail of placement through portfolio development.

title: Non-ionising Imaging Techniques
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students explore and become familiar with the imaging modalities of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasound. Fundamental principles and clinical protocols / applications of MRI and ultrasound, and a range of non-ionising imaging modalities will be introduced. Students can expect to gain a working knowledge of the principles and application of MRI and ultrasound, facilitating increased understanding of appropriate modality choices to satisfy pathophysiological indicators. Students can expect to gain a general insight into the principles and applications of other non-ionising imaging approaches. This subject is not intended to prepare students as MRI imaging technologists or as professional sonographers, however, it will prepare students for further study in these modalities.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles and application of other non-ionising imaging techniques.
Explain and evaluate professional learning and identify professional learning needs / life-long learning (MRPBA Domain 4.2).
Describe, explain, evaluate and develop MRI and ultrasound protocols in a collaborative manner (MRPBA Domain 1.9, 1.10 and 3.2).
Describe, explain and implement professional practice with specific reference to explaining the principles and clinical applications of MRI and ultrasound (MRPBA Domain 1.9 and 1.10).
Recognise, describe and apply knowledge of radiation physics and instrumentation to operate MRI and ultrasound systems safely and effectively (MRPBA Domain 1.9 and 1.10).
Understand, explain and apply principles for appropriate MRI and ultrasound parameters and protocols based on patient presentation (MRPBA Domain 1.9 and 1.10).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1).
Explain the dataset analysis and use of datasets including demonstrating management of data (MRPBA Domain 1.9, 1.10 and 1.2).

title: Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging Residency
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This capstone residency subject consolidates learning (knowledge and skills) across the entire degree into practice-based capabilities. The subject formalises the learning, development and assessment of MRPBA defined capabilities as the minimum standards for general registration with AHPRA. The residency is underpinned by professional practice in the Nuclear Medicine clinical setting (2 x 15 weeks = 1200 hours). Students further hone their clinical skills to demonstrate work ready capabilities with appropriate professional and ethical conduct to care and advocate for their patients. Students refine existing communication skills, demonstrating cultural sensitivity with both staff and patients within a range of contexts, enabling safe working environments. Students apply their decision-making skills and critical thinking in general practice of medical radiation science, practice in Nuclear Medicine specifically, and demonstrate required radiation safety and risk management capability.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and implement outcomes of patient assessment and due diligence to deliver appropriate care inclusive of appropriate management in the event of deteriorating patient condition, urgent and/or unexpected findings (MRPBA Domain 1.7).

Apply understanding of practice in Nuclear Medicine, demonstrating critical thinking and analytical skills, with specific reference to implementing preparation of radiopharmaceuticals, explaining diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceutical biodistribution, implementing routine imaging including SPECT/CT and PET/CT, implement CT imaging, implement nuclear medicine examinations and therapies (MRPBA Domain 1B).

Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with specific reference to clear, sensitive and effective, culturally appropriate communication to create culturally safe environments and collaborating with other health practitioners (MRPBA domain 3).

Identify, explain and implement professional and ethical conduct with specific reference to global citizenship, ethical, professional and legal practice, providing appropriate care, assuming accountability and responsibility, and patient advocacy (MRPBA Domain 1).
Understand, explain and apply principles of Indigenous cultural competence and safety within the context of patient care and advocacy (MRPBA Domain 1).

Describe and apply the principles of radiation safety and risk management with specific reference to safe radiation practice, protecting/enhancing patient safety, ensuring safe operation of equipment, maintaining safety of self and others and safely managing radiation and radioactivity (MRPBA Domain 5).

Implement professional practice, demonstrating critical thinking and analytical skills, with specific reference to anatomy, physiology, pathology, physics and instrumentation principles, utilising clinical information management systems, determining appropriate procedures, patient assessment and due diligence, deliver appropriate care and stabilisation/reproducibility techniques, and manage / manipulate 3D datasets (MRPBA Domain 1).
Understand the processes of peer assessment, standard setting, mentorship, and developmental support to other members of the healthcare team. (MRPBA Domain 2.5a).
Apply understanding of practice in diagnostic CT to implement diagnostic CT imaging (MRPBA Domain 1B.4).
Perform quality evaluation of image datasets, including identifying and reporting urgent or unexpected findings in an appropriate and timely manner (MRPBA Domain 1.7b and c).

Describe and apply principles of practice in nuclear medicine with specific reference to implementing preparation of radiopharmaceuticals, explaining diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceutical biodistribution, implementing routine imaging including SPECT/CT and PET/CT, implement CT imaging, implement nuclear medicine examinations and therapies (MRPBA Domain 1 and 1B.1-2 and 4).

Identify, explain and implement professional and ethical conduct with specific reference to practising in an ethical, non-discriminatory, professional and legal manner, providing appropriate care, assuming accountability and responsibility, and patient advocacy (MRPBA Domain 2).
Describe and apply principles of practice in nuclear medicine with specific reference to describing in vivo and in vitro laboratory procedures (MRPBA Domain 1B.3).
Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with specific reference to clear, sensitive and effective communication and collaborating with other health practitioners (MRPBA Domain 3).
Recognise the need for appropriate decisions about the care of patients before, during, and after the examination/treatment. (MRPBA Domain 1.7d; 2.3a).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence-based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1) be able to recognise opportunities to develop new knowledge through research and enquiry, and contribute to the enhancement of the profession (MRPBA Domain 2.5 and 4.1d).

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject supports a student to develop a deep understanding of the principles associated with the imaging technology employed in conventional nuclear medicine, including relevant physics, electronics, counting statistics, pulse-height spectrometry and image quality. Students explore the physics and instrumentation of the gamma camera, SPECT and PET, including hybrid and pre-clinical technology. Nuclear medicine computer hardware and software, associated hardware, computer operating systems and language, computer graphics, image acquisition data analysis and image reconstruction are all explored in detail.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical, analytical, and reflective skills in a range of contexts including clinical problem solving, research and empirical practice, and academic and professional discourse related to instrumentation developments and image data reconstruction (MRPBA Domain 4).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence-based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1).

Recognise opportunities to develop new knowledge through research and enquiry, and contribute to the enhancement of the profession (MRPBA Domain 2.5 and 4.1d).

Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with specific reference to clear, sensitive and effective communication and collaborating with other health practitioners with respect to these instrumentation modalities (MRPBA Domain 3).

Describe and apply the principles of radiation safety and risk management with specific reference to safe radiation practice, protecting/enhancing patient safety, ensuring safe operation of equipment and safely managing radiation and radioactivity (MRPBA Domain 5).
