title: Nuclear Safeguards Practice
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Australia's ability to fulfill its international obligations regarding safeguards and security for nuclear materials and technologies depends on having a skilled and diverse professional workforce to monitor and enforce these, and develop a strong nuclear safeguards culture. This subject, developed in partnership with the Australian Safeguards and Non-Proliferation Office (ASNO), provides an analytical, problem-based and experientially-grounded approach to building the skills for professionals working in the area of nuclear safeguards and security . The subject includes: site and lab visit(s)* to locations where nuclear materials are used, stored, monitored and disposed of; practical instruction in the tools and techniques of nuclear regulation; and approaches to future technologies and methodologies of oversight and management. *In-person or virtual
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply advanced knowledge of the Australian legal requirements for nuclear safeguards, and the management and security of nuclear materials.

Communicate at an advanced technical level, including through a written report synthesis, the safeguards challenges for regulators and inspectors of nuclear materials likely to flow from Australia's obligations and/or emerging technologies.

Identify, explain and critically evaluate how regulatory tools such as standards, physical design and security protocols combine to ensure the safeguarding of nuclear material use, storage and disposal.
Find, understand, appraise and apply regulatory, scientific and professional sources that inform nuclear inspections and compliance protocols and practice.

Understand and apply the professional and organisational dimensions and contemporary issues of nuclear inspection, including the evaluation of strengths and limitations of the full range of regulatory tools used to secure compliance from designated sites and permit holders in Australia and internationally.

title: Nuclear Safeguards Regulation: Frameworks, Institutions and Standards
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject unpacks the implications of the Australian nuclear sector for professionals responsible for the safeguarding and security of nuclear material and technologies. It provides an overview of the history of non-proliferation, international safeguards theory, the network of treaties that are the sources of legal authority for safeguards, Australia's obligations within that framework, relevant international and domestic regulatory institutions including the International Atomic Energy Agency and Australia's role in these, as well as recent debates and negotiations catalysed by the current and emerging nuclear sector in Australia. At the regulatory level, it explores the role of standards in safeguards regulation; radiation monitoring and safeguards systems; tools and techniques of inspection and verification; enforcement and compliance; export controls; and nuclear security.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding through application of the national and international legal frameworks and institutions that regulate nuclear safeguards and security, in particular the treaty framework and Australia's international and domestic legal obligations.
Understand, assess and simulate the role and regulatory techniques of nuclear safeguards oversight, including inspection and audit.
Synthesise and communicate regulatory issues arising from the implementation of nuclear safeguards in Australia to specialist and non-specialist audiences in government, industry and the public.

Explain the principles of nuclear physics relevant to regulating nuclear technology in the context of evaluating nuclear safeguards and security standards compliance, including in relation to emerging technologies.

Analyse the role of international and domestic regulators in safeguarding and securing nuclear materials and technologies in Australia from diverse disciplinary perspectives, including Australia's relationship with the International Atomic Energy Agency and how concepts such as nuclear stewardship are applied within and outside Australia.

title: Numeracy in the Early Years
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject positions the student as a reflective and active practitioner in mathematics education. It focuses on numeracy development and planning in the 0-8 age group. Students will engage in a variety of discussions and reflective practice whilst developing their own action research into effective pedagogical practice in numeracy education.
learning_outcomes: Embed technology within their pedagogical practice surrounding numeracy.
Critically analyse current practice, research and curriculum models to gain an understanding of children's needs.
Develop the skills of action research as a means of professional learning and improving classroom practice and pedagogy.
Understand implications from educational research and the consequences for their teaching and learning numeracy.
Develop a range of pedagogical approaches that utilise and build upon children's understandings of mathematics, including knowledge from home.
Integrate reflective practice and action research into their numeracy practice.
Focus on the application of knowledge to the educational workplaces and to the community settings in which they are working.
Relate theory to individual practice.
Improve their professional teaching practice.
Identify, develop and justify an appropriate range of pedagogical strategies in which to develop effective numeracy programs.
Recognise that children's prior to school numeracy experiences are a solid foundation in which to build and develop further understandings.

title: Numerical Methods for Civil Engineers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for civil engineering students to develop proficiency in solving engineering problems using numerical techniques. It covers various numerical methods commonly employed in engineering practice, including root finding, numerical integration, differential equations solving, optimisation, and finite element analysis. Students will acquire the necessary skills to model, analyse, and solve complex engineering problems using numerical approaches.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the performance of numerical algorithms, assessing factors such as accuracy, stability, and convergence, to determine their suitability for solving engineering problems.
Select computational models to simulate and analyse engineering systems, applying numerical methods to predict system behaviour and optimise design parameters.
Compare numerical solutions for ordinary and partial differential equations, utilising appropriate numerical methods and computational tools.
Critique the effectiveness of interpolation and curve fitting techniques in approximating experimental data, considering factors such as polynomial degree and data distribution.
Compare numerical methods to accurately solve engineering problems, demonstrating proficiency in root finding, numerical integration, and curve fitting techniques.

title: Numerical Methods for Electrical Engineers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for electrical engineering students to develop proficiency in solving engineering problems using numerical techniques. It covers various numerical methods commonly employed in practice, including root finding, numerical integration, differential equations solving, optimisation, and finite element analysis. Students will acquire the necessary skills to model, analyse, and solve complex engineering problems using numerical approaches.
learning_outcomes: Select computational models to simulate and analyse engineering systems, applying numerical methods to predict system behaviour and optimise design parameters.
Critique the effectiveness of interpolation and curve fitting techniques in approximating experimental data, considering factors such as polynomial degree and data distribution.
Compare numerical solutions for ordinary and partial differential equations, utilising appropriate numerical methods and computational tools.
Compare numerical methods to accurately solve electrical engineering problems, demonstrating proficiency in root finding, numerical integration, and curve fitting techniques.
Evaluate the performance of numerical algorithms, assessing factors such as accuracy, stability, and convergence, to determine their suitability for solving electrical engineering problems.

title: Numerical Methods for Mechanical Engineers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for mechanical engineering students to develop proficiency in solving engineering problems using numerical techniques. It covers various numerical methods commonly employed in engineering practice, including root finding, numerical integration, differential equations solving, optimisation, and finite element analysis. Students will acquire the necessary skills to model, analyse, and solve complex engineering problems using numerical approaches.
learning_outcomes: Compare numerical solutions for ordinary and partial differential equations, utilising appropriate numerical methods and computational tools.
Evaluate the performance of numerical algorithms, assessing factors such as accuracy, stability, and convergence, to determine their suitability for solving mechanical engineering problems.
Compare numerical methods to accurately solve mechanical engineering problems, demonstrating proficiency in root finding, numerical integration, and curve fitting techniques.
Select computational models to simulate and analyse mechanical engineering systems, applying numerical methods to predict system behaviour and optimise design parameters.
Critique the effectiveness of interpolation and curve fitting techniques in approximating experimental data, considering factors such as polynomial degree and data distribution.

title: Nursing Workplace Learning 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the concept of workplace learning and begins to prepare students for their workplace learning experiences. Students will be introduced to the use of mindful communication in the clinical context to create caring moments to support safe care for the patient, family and community. Relevant legal and ethical principles related to scope of practice and professional boundaries will also be explored.
learning_outcomes: Describe the use of mindful communication in the delivery of patient care.
Identify the core principles of Watson's Caring Science.
Explain the scope of practice of the student nurse.
Identify key student responsibilities before, during and after workplace learning.
Locate appropriate evidence for practice.

title: Nursing Workplace Learning 4
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject establishes the core concepts and principles related to maintaining a caring environment. These include research and evidence-based practice, along with the legal and caring aspects of advocacy for the person, family and community. Workplace learning experiences incorporate the centrality of research and evidence in informing practice, together with the place of expert opinion, patient/family preferences, and the ways in which the registered nurse can act as an advocate in clinical settings.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-based practice to nursing practice in accordance with organisational policies and guidelines.
Identify and apply strategies to promote advocacy for people, family and communities.
Discuss the principles that contribute to maintaining a caring environment where registered nurses work.
Appraise research for application in health contexts.
Satisfactorily complete the workplace learning assessment for this subject.

title: Nursing Workplace Learning 2
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the learning achieved in the introductory subjects and enables students to continue on their workplace learning journey. Students are supported to establish caring environments in contexts where nurses care of the person, family(ies) and/or community. Within these environments, students focus on what it means to be mindful, work to scope of practice, maintain safety and privacy, and collaborate with other professions. Students will also explore the provision of end of life care.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence in practice.
Apply concepts related to the scope of practice of a registered nurse, including inter-professional an intra-professional collaboration.
Satisfactorily complete the workplace learning assessments for this subject.
Demonstrate patient safety, quality and privacy considerations in a caring environment.
Apply legal and ethical principles to nursing practice.
Apply concepts of mindfulness with colleagues, the patient and family or significant others including self-care.

title: Nursing Workplace Learning 5
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds upon core concepts related to caring in diverse settings, considering factors such as the physical environment and sociocultural factors, as well as the person to create an overall healing environment. Students will also consider the legal and ethical implications of caring for people in diverse settings.
learning_outcomes: Satisfactorily complete the workplace learning assessments.
Discuss the application of the Caritas® Competencies in a range of settings and contexts.
Apply legal and ethical principles to nursing practice in diverse settings and contexts.
Demonstrate the application of mindful communication in collaborative practice to create and sustain healing environments.
prerequisites: NRS223: Essential Nursing Care: Chronic and Complex Nursing

title: Nutrition for Disease Prevention
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with the opportunity to further develop their understanding of public health interventions in the prevention of nutrition-related concerns common to developed countries (with particular emphasis on the Australian context). Students will critique the links between theoretical perspectives of the food and nutrition environment, behaviour change, and the development and implementation of strategies to reduce chronic disease risk. Special consideration will be given to enhancing health outcomes for rural, disadvantaged and First Nations communities.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the evidence base that underpins the development and implementation of nutrition related chronic disease prevention and health promotion strategies.

Analyse the challenges and opportunities that exist in regard to implementing nutrition related chronic disease prevention and health promotion strategies, with a particular focus on enhancing health outcomes for Australian First Nations and rural communities.
Compare and contrast the relative benefits and challenges of developing manufactured and novel foods with healthy dietary patterns to prevent disease and promote health.
Analyse the influence of the food and nutrition environment on nutrition related health outcomes and chronic disease across the lifespan.

title: Nursing Workplace Learning 6
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this capstone subject, students apply the mindful use of digital technologies to care for people, families and communities in diverse settings. The subject also supports the student to transition to the role of registered nurse, consolidating learning related to scope of practice, caring-in-practice, use of evidence, safety in practice, clinical reasoning, and mindful communication.
learning_outcomes: Integrate and synthesise the domains of scope of practice, caring-in-practice, use of evidence, safety in practice, clinical reasoning, and mindful communication to support caring.
Analyse legal and ethical considerations related to the use of digital technologies in healthcare.
Analyse the impact of increasing digitalisation in healthcare on mindful communication, and the creation and maintenance of healing environments.
Satisfactorily complete the workplace learning assessments for this subject.
prerequisites: NRS312: Essential Nursing Care: Managing the Deteriorating Patient

title: Nursing Workplace Learning 3
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the principles of transpersonal caring and support students to develop transpersonal competencies in the workplace to enable them to care for people from diverse backgrounds, cultures or experiences. Students will also explore the use of evidence to support Clinical Reasoning and Nursing Practice.
learning_outcomes: Satisfactorily complete the workplace learning assessments for this subject.
Apply legal, ethical and organisational requirements to the care of vulnerable and culturally diverse populations.
Analyse and apply evidence in practice.
Apply principles of transpersonal care to vulnerable and culturally diverse populations.
prerequisites: NRS123: Professional Nursing: Health Law for Nurses

title: Nutrition for Health
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with foundation knowledge in food, nutrition and health. The subject commences with an overview of the basic principles of nutrition and the physiological processes involved in food and eating. Students will then broaden their thinking to develop an appreciation of the importance of food and nutrition across the life cycle and become aware of the importance of evidence in informing nutrition advice to the general public. Lastly, students will start to explore the contribution of poor nutrition to ill health and the complexity of factors that influence food choices.
learning_outcomes: Describe the key food and nutrient recommendations for health at each key lifecycle stage.
Describe general processes of digestion and metabolism in healthy individuals.

Describe the complex range of determinants of food intake, including personal attitudes, historical, cultural, psycho-social, environmental, and political influences and demonstrate an appreciation of how these factors impact on physical and mental wellbeing.
Describe the broad structure of the Australian health system, including prevention programs, at the primary, secondary and tertiary levels.
Describe the role of macronutrients and key micronutrients in energy balance and health.
Describe the role of diet in the aetiology of chronic diseases and obesity and explain the metabolic and chronic health consequences of obesity.
Evaluate current evidence-based guidelines used to provide appropriate general advice on nutrition.
Evaluate the risks to physiological and psychological health of common fad or popular diets.
Describe the basic functions of macronutrients, key micronutrients, and other major dietary components and their common food sources.

title: Nutrition for Health and Performance
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: The primary focus of this subject is to provide the scientific background, knowledge and assessment skills related to meeting the nutritional needs of healthy active people. This subject will address current concepts and controversies relating to both health and sports nutrition by linking information in the fields of exercise science and nutrition. This subject will also explore the role of nutrition in optimising training responses and adaptations, sports performance, health and well-being, and disease prevention in both children and adults.
learning_outcomes: Use current guidelines to provide appropriate general advice on nutrition for athletes and healthy individuals.
Describe the relationship between nutrition and the energy demands of athletes compared to healthy individuals.
Explain the appropriate use of nutritional supplements and ergogenic aids.
Determine appropriate referral pathways for individuals who require further specialised nutrition advice.
Critique current sports nutrition literature.
Explain the importance of fluid and electrolytes and methods of hydration monitoring.
Explain common sports related nutrition concerns to lay people.
Identify individuals at nutritional risk based on basic dietary analysis.
Recognise the varied nutritional needs of individuals with known risk factors for, or presence of, varied lifestyle diseases that are pertinent to most developed countries.

title: Nutritional Pathophysiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will explore the biological responses and alterations in function associated with nutrition. Students will develop their understanding of inter-relationships between nutrition and body systems dysfunction across the lifespan as well as nutrigenomics and the gut microbiome.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the inter-relationship between nutrition and the genitourinary system including fluid balance dysfunction.
Explain the role and inter-relationships between gene function and the gut microbiome in nutrition and pathophysiology.
Analyse the inter-relationship between nutrition and disorders of the nervous system.
Discuss regulatory mechanisms and dysfunction in metabolic disorders and the gastrointestinal system.
Analyse the inter-relationship between nutrition and metabolic disorders.
Analyse the inter-relationship between nutrition and disorders of the cardiorespiratory system.
Analyse the inter-relationship between nutrition and disorders of the skeletal system.
Define and apply common pathophysiological terms.
Analyse inter-relationship between nutrition and immune dysfunction.

title: Nutritional Physiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students undertake an in depth examination of nutrients and how the body uses nutrients, including ingestion, digestion, absorption, transport, metabolism, interaction, storage and excretion. This is then extended to consider the role of diet and nutrition during various stages of the life cycle and in exercise.
learning_outcomes: Describe the basic principles of anthropometry and growth.
Apply the nutritional needs of the body as a result of sport and physical activity.
Explain the normal physiological control and non-physiological/hedonic control of appetite and food intake.
Describe and explain energetics and thermogenesis.
Explain the anatomy and physiology of digestive processes and nutrient absorption, metabolism and excretion.
Describe and explain the role of nutrition in normal body fluid and acid-base balance.
Discuss the impact of stress on physiology.
Explain the endocrine and neural control of metabolism.
Identify and describe the nutritional requirements of different stages of the life cycle (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and aging, pregnancy, lactation).

title: Object Oriented Systems Analysis and Design
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: UML (Unified Modelling Language) is used to document requirements, analysis and design activities that are part of an iterative and incremental development process. Within this subject, students will learn how to produce UML analysis and design diagrams, to analyse and verify software system requirements, and to produce and verify UML analysis and design models. Students will also learn how to evaluate and select the most appropriate design patterns for use in a software system.
learning_outcomes: Produce and verify analysis and design models for a system.
Demonstrate use of a Computer Aided Software Engineering (CASE) tool to document the models in a system.
Describe and apply an iterative incremental software development process.
Evaluate and choose appropriate software design patterns to compose the design of a software system.
Analyse and verify system requirements.
Evaluate a problem and determine the appropriate architectural style for the solution.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment: Principles and Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop and apply skills in observation, assessment, and goal-setting for occupational therapy practice. Students will develop their knowledge of assessment theory to appraise, select and conduct assessments that are suitable for life stage and context. Assessment information will be interpreted and applied to practice, including identifying potential occupational issues, collaboratively developing person-centred, occupation-focussed goals, and measuring outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Conduct, interpret and report the results of appropriate assessments used in occupational therapy practice that are responsive to life stage and context.
Develop and write clear and measurable, person-centred, occupation-focussed goals that integrate information gathered during the assessment process.
Justify appropriate information gathering, observation, assessment and outcome measurement strategies to inform occupational therapy practice.
Describe, critically appraise and select appropriate assessments used in occupational therapy practice.
prerequisites: OCC106: Communication for Occupational Therapy Practice

title: Occupational Therapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends the foundational concepts of person, environment and occupation to develop students' skills in the application of these concepts to occupational therapy practice. Students will demonstrate foundational skills in occupational therapy practice including effective communication, manual handling and the use of lower-risk assistive technology. Students will consolidate their skills in occupation-based activity analysis by observing the occupations of people experiencing occupational disruption and/or demonstrating occupational adaption and analysing their performance to identify strengths and describe potential occupational issues.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competency in manual handling, hand hygiene, and using personal protective equipment for safe occupational therapy practice.
Conduct an occupation-based activity analysis and integrate details about the person, environment and occupation to identify a person's strengths and potential occupational issues.
Clearly explain how to use lower-risk assistive technology, and demonstrate the ability to safely adjust it for a client.
Apply foundational concepts of person, environment and occupation to occupational therapy practice.
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviours for a first-year occupational therapy student including self-management and effective written and verbal communication skills.
prerequisites: OCC104: Person, Environment and Occupation Foundations

title: Occupational Therapy Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends the foundational concepts of person, environment and occupation to develop students' skills in the application of these concepts to occupational therapy practice. Students will demonstrate foundational skills in occupational therapy practice including effective communication, manual handling and the use of lower-risk assistive technology. Students will consolidate their skills in occupation-based activity analysis by observing the occupations of people experiencing occupational disruption and/or demonstrating occupational adaption and analysing their performance to identify strengths and describe potential occupational issues. Within this subject, students will complete a work integrated learning (WIL) placement. This provides the opportunity for students to demonstrate suitable professional behaviour, self-management and communication skills within a practice context.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviours for a first-year occupational therapy student including self-management and effective written and verbal communication skills for occupational therapy practice.
Clearly explain how to use lower-risk assistive technology, and demonstrate the ability to safely adjust it for a client.
Conduct an occupation-based activity analysis and integrate details about the person, environment and occupation to identify a person's strengths and potential occupational issues.
Apply foundational concepts of person, environment and occupation to occupational therapy practice.
Demonstrate competency in manual handling, hand hygiene, and using personal protective equipment for safe occupational therapy practice.
prerequisites: OCC104: Person, Environment and Occupation Foundations

title: Occupational Therapy Workplace Learning (Honours) 2
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, honours students complete their second supervised occupational therapy work-integrated learning (WIL) placement. This placement focuses on working with people who experience occupational dysfunction and/or may focus on planning or implementing an occupation-focused project. The placement provides students with the opportunity to manage their own caseload and to practice and consolidate their assessment, intervention, and evaluation skills. Students will also develop and extend their critical evaluation and reflective practice skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competency in occupational therapy practice in a professional setting.
Plan and conduct formal and informal assessments of clients.
Design and implement appropriate and well-reasoned enabling strategies and/or occupation-focused projects.
Evaluate the effectiveness of implemented strategies and projects.
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviours and engage in reflective practice.
Demonstrate appropriate verbal and written communication strategies.
Discuss the complexities of occupational therapy practice.
prerequisites: OCC300: Enabling Strategies: Working with Individuals (Consolidation)
OCC304: Enabling Strategies: Working with Communities

title: Occupational Therapy Workplace Learning 2
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students complete their second supervised occupational therapy work-integrated learning (WIL) placement. This placement focuses on working with people who experience occupational dysfunction and/or may focus on planning or implementing an occupation-focused project. The placement provides students with the opportunity to manage their own caseload and to practice and consolidate their assessment, intervention, and evaluation skills. Students will also develop and extend their critical evaluation and reflective practice skills.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the complexities of occupational therapy practice.
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviours and engage in reflective practice.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the implemented strategies and projects.
Design and implement well-reasoned enabling strategies and/or occupation-focused projects.
Demonstrate competency in occupational therapy practice in a professional setting.
Plan and conduct formal and informal assessments of clients.
Demonstrate competent verbal and written communication strategies.
prerequisites: OCC300: Enabling Strategies: Working with Individuals (Consolidation)
OCC304: Enabling Strategies: Working with Communities

school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students complete one supervised occupational therapy work-integrated learning (WIL) placement. This placement focuses on working with people who experience occupational dysfunction and/or may focus on planning or implementing an occupation-focused project. The placement provides students with the opportunity to manage their own caseload and to practice and consolidate their assessment, intervention, and evaluation skills. Students will also develop and extend their critical evaluation and reflective practice skills.

Plan and conduct formal and informal assessments of clients with supervision.
Demonstrate competency in occupational therapy practice in a professional setting.
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviours and engage in reflective practice.

prerequisites: OCC304: Enabling Strategies: Working with Communities
OCC300: Enabling Strategies: Working with Individuals (Consolidation)

school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, honours students complete one supervised occupational therapy work-integrated learning (WIL) placement. This placement focuses on working with people who experience occupational dysfunction and/or may focus on planning or implementing an occupation-focused project. The placement provides students with the opportunity to manage their own caseload and to practice and consolidate their assessment, intervention, and evaluation skills. Students will also develop and extend their critical evaluation and reflective practice skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate verbal and written communication strategies.
Design and implement appropriate and well-reasoned enabling strategies and/or occupation-focused projects.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the implemented strategies and projects.
Plan and conduct formal and informal assessments of clients relevant to the setting, with moderate to minimal supervision.
Discuss the complexities of occupational therapy practice.
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviours and engage in reflective practice.
Demonstrate competency in occupational therapy practice in a professional setting.
prerequisites: OCC300: Enabling Strategies: Working with Individuals (Consolidation)
OCC304: Enabling Strategies: Working with Communities

title: Occupational Therapy Workplace Learning 3
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends occupational therapy competencies students have developed. In this subject, students complete one supervised occupational therapy work-integrated learning (WIL) placement. Students are expected to work towards entry-level occupational therapy practice competencies and become involved in additional tasks related to their practice setting. Students will be required to be competent in their ability to practice reflectively, critically evaluate their practice, and critically reflect on their learning during the subject. Students will manage their own case load with minimal supervision, and consolidate their skills in professional reasoning, assessment, intervention, and evaluation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competency in occupational therapy practice in a professional setting.
Implement well-reasoned and appropriate enabling strategies.
Engage in reflection and identify personal goals and learning needs related to professional practice.
Demonstrate competence in behaviours essential to being a professional.
Critique the provision of occupational therapy services and suggest potential ways to develop practice.
Critique the complexities of occupational therapy practice.
Demonstrate competent verbal and written communication strategies when engaging with people, including clients and other health professionals.
Manage a case load expected of an entry-level occupational therapist as relevant to the placement setting with minimal supervision.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the enabling strategies implemented for clients.

title: Occupational Therapy Workplace Learning 3 (Honours)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences

In this subject, students complete one supervised occupational therapy work-integrated learning (WIL) placement. Critique the provision of occupational therapy services and suggest potential ways to develop practice.

title: Occupational Therapy Workplace Learning 4 (Honours)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is the final work-integrated learning (WIL) placement subject Honours students are required to complete in the occupational therapy course. This subject builds on the WIL placement subjects students have successfully completed in their third and fourth years. In OCC431, students will be expected to achieve entry-level occupational therapy practice competencies and be pro-active in implementing strategies to ensure these competencies are achieved. Students will be required to be independent in their ability to practice reflectively, critically evaluate their practice, and critically reflect on their learning during the subject. Students will demonstrate independence in their professional reasoning, and will manage a small case load independently, consolidating their assessment, intervention, and evaluation skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate excellent behaviours essential to being a professional.
Critique the provision of occupational therapy services and suggest potential ways to develop practice.
Manage a case load expected of an entry-level occupational therapist as relevant to the placement setting independently.
Demonstrate excellent verbal and written communication strategies when engaging with people, including clients and other health professionals.
Critique and articulate the complexities of occupational therapy practice.
Implement and articulate well reasoned and appropriate enabling strategies.
Evaluate and reason the effectiveness of the enabling strategies implemented for clients.
Demonstrate competency in occupational therapy practice in a professional setting.
Identify personal goals and learning needs in relation to professional practice and describe strategies to achieve these goals and needs.

title: Occupational Therapy Workplace Learning 4
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is the final work-integrated learning (WIL) placement subject students are required to complete in the occupational therapy course. This subject builds on the WIL placement subjects students have successfully completed in their third and fourth years. In OCC421, students will be expected to achieve entry-level occupational therapy practice competencies and be pro-active in implementing strategies to ensure these competencies are achieved. Students will be required to be independent in their ability to practice reflectively, critically evaluate their practice, and critically reflect on their learning during the subject. Students will demonstrate independence in their professional reasoning, and will manage a small case load independently, consolidating their assessment, intervention, and evaluation skills.
learning_outcomes: Implement and articulate well reasoned and appropriate enabling strategies.
Manage a case load expected of an entry-level occupational therapist as relevant to the placement setting independently.
Evaluate and reason the effectiveness of the enabling strategies implemented for clients.

Demonstrate competency in occupational therapy practice in a professional setting.
Identify personal goals and learning needs in relation to professional practice and describe strategies to achieve these goals and needs.
Demonstrate excellent verbal and written communication strategies when engaging with people, including clients and other health professionals.
Demonstrate excellent behaviours essential to being a professional.
Critique the provision of occupational therapy services and suggest potential ways to develop practice.

title: Officer Safety
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject delivers the foundational operational safety and tactics skills required by the operational police practitioner. It introduces students to the ethical and professional application of officer survival techniques and skills. This is achieved by requiring students to consider the theory and practice underpinning the use of these skills and to demonstrate the application of those skills and outline the justification for their use within supervised practical sessions and assessments
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the approved operational procedures and skills in a range of scenarios such as; high risk incidents, edged weapon defence, searching, handcuffing, bomb awareness, public order policing, building approach, motor vehicle stops ILVA, TECC/CRAPE and weapon retention.
Demonstrate the use of the Tactical Options Model and articulate the criteria of use for arms and appointments in decision making processes to apply such skill in reality based training scenarios.

Demonstrate the approved use and articulate the justifications for the tactical options of: baton, tactical disengagement, Conducted Electrical Weapon (CEW), communication, contain and negotiate, firearm, oleoresin capsicum defensive spray, weaponless control and officer presence and active armed offender.

title: Officer Safety: Defensive Tactics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the operational safety and tactical knowledge and skills required by the operational police practitioner. It introduces students to the ethical, legal and professional application of a range of officer survival techniques and skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the approved operational procedures and skills in a range of practical and theoretical scenarios.
Demonstrate the use of the Tactical Options Model and articulate the criteria of use for arms and appointments in decision-making processes to apply such skill in reality-based training scenarios.
Describe the criteria required for the use of a range of tactical options by operational police officers.

title: Old Testament History and Narrative
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on Old Testament narratives from Joshua to 2 Chronicles, which relate ancient Israel's story of origins from settlement in Canaan to the Babylonian exile in 587 BCE. It examines key figures and defining events, with due consideration given to extra-biblical sources and archaeological evidence. The subject investigates the functions of narrative in the writing and rewriting of Israelite history and also explores ethical issues arising from these narratives. Attention is given to the accounts of conquest and settlement, the centralisation of Israel under the monarchy, the division of the kingdom, exile to Babylon and historical interpretation in the work of the Chronicler and in later Jewish and Christian texts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate developing competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts and critical engagement with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate familiarity with aspects of the reception history of Old Testament narratives in later Jewish and Christian texts.
Discuss in a critical way issues relating to the interpretation of history and narrative in the Old Testament.
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of archaeology, historiography and textual witness in reconstructing ancient Israelite history.
Discuss major theological and ethical themes in Israel's historical and narrative literature and assess their contemporary relevance.

Identify major periods in Israel's history and their defining events, including distinctive characteristics of the Deuteronomistic account and main features of the Chronicler's interpretation of Israel's history.
prerequisites: THP403: Old Testament History and Narrative

title: Online Pedagogies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to introduce students to a range of online tools and learning theories. Students will become acquainted with online technology integration models, and engage with pedagogical approaches that assist in the purposeful and ethical integration of technologies to support teaching and learning online. These pedagogies, frameworks, and models will be utilised to design accessible online learning and teaching experiences/activities, and to evaluate their effectiveness. The context for these will be the curriculum of New South Wales, and the Australian Curriculum and Reporting Authority and their outcomes and objectives, or the equivalent for interstate and international students.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe potential ethical issues with use of specific online technologies.
Develop pedagogically sound, curricula and capability aligned, online digital artefacts.
Evaluate online pedagogies, frameworks and models.
Design accessible, curriculum aligned, and pedagogically appropriate, online teaching and learning activities.
Apply appropriate technologies and resources to online teaching and learning.

title: Old Testament History and Narrative
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on Old Testament narratives from Joshua to 2 Chronicles, which relate ancient Israel's story of origins from settlement in Canaan to the Babylonian exile in 587 BCE. It examines key figures and defining events, with due consideration given to extra-biblical sources and archaeological evidence. The subject investigates the functions of narrative in the writing and rewriting of Israelite history and also explores ethical issues arising from these narratives. Attention is given to the accounts of conquest and settlement, the centralisation of Israel under the monarchy, the division of the kingdom, exile to Babylon and historical interpretation in the work of the Chronicler and in later Jewish and Christian texts.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the impact of the fields of archaeology, historiography and other ancient textual witnesses in the ongoing work of biblical interpretation.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, and sophisticated writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an ability to discern appropriate hermeneutical and interpretive frameworks related to particular texts and synthesise biblical response(s) to issues of contemporary relevance.
Demonstrate advanced competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts and critical engagement with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Demonstrate a critical awareness of the complexity of issues related to the nexus of Old Testament narrative and history.
Critically analyse ideological perspectives underlying Israel's historical and narrative literature.
prerequisites: THL202: Old Testament History and Narrative

title: Old Testament History and Narrative
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on Old Testament narratives from Joshua to 2 Chronicles, which relate ancient Israel's story of origins from settlement in Canaan to the Babylonian exile in 587 BCE. It examines key figures and defining events, with due consideration given to extra-biblical sources and archaeological evidence. The subject investigates the functions of narrative in the writing and rewriting of Israelite history and also explores ethical issues arising from these narratives. Attention is given to the accounts of conquest and settlement, the centralisation of Israel under the monarchy, the division of the kingdom, exile to Babylon and historical interpretation in the work of the Chronicler and in later Jewish and Christian texts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical awareness of the complexity of issues related to the nexus of Old Testament narrative and history.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, and sophisticated writing and communication skills.
Critically analyse the impact of the fields of archaeology, historiography and other ancient textual witnesses in the ongoing work of biblical interpretation.
Demonstrate an ability to discern appropriate hermeneutical and interpretive frameworks related to particular texts and synthesise biblical response(s) to issues of contemporary relevance.
Demonstrate advanced competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts and critical engagement with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Critically analyse ideological perspectives underlying Israel's historical and narrative literature.
prerequisites: THL202: Old Testament History and Narrative

title: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT)
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: With the rise in social media and online communications more and more people are leaving a digital footprint of their personal details and activities. This has drastically changed the nature of open source intelligence collection and analysis. Increasingly, law enforcement and national security agencies are relying on open source intelligence, building target profiles and conducting surveillance on persons of interest and organisations. This subject aims at teaching key areas of knowledge and skills in the field of open intelligence. It teaches the role of open source intelligence in collecting and analysing information. The subject also teaches some key skills in collecting and analysing open source intelligence. An important part of this subject is the ethics involved in collecting open source material as it discusses ethical problems such as proportionality.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate applied knowledge to understanding the role and place of open source intelligence in the wider intelligence community.
Demonstrate the application of skills to collect and analyse open source intelligence.
Demonstrate applied critical and ethical thinking to issues of collection and analysis of open source data.
prerequisites: JST493: National Security and Intelligence Issues

title: Open Space Planning
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses key principles, processes and knowledge needed for open space planning and management in Australian communities.Students will learn about the contribution open and natural space makes to our communities, and the current policies and procedures that frame the delivery and management of open space.The subject introduces them to alternative approaches to open space planning and management, and to the breadth of programs that contribute to human-nature interaction. There is no intensive associated with this subject when taken by distance. On completion students have the ability to use initiative and problem solving skills to address problems and issues associated with the design and use of open space.
learning_outcomes: The ability to analyse, consolidate and synthesise knowledge and data on open space to make appropriate management decisions.
Have a variety of specialised planning skills commonly associated with open space management.
Have broad and coherent understanding of people's relationship to open space.
Have the ability to use initiative and problem solving skills to address problems and issues associated with the design and use of open space.
Have broad and coherent understanding of what is open space and how it is managed.

title: Operational Command
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The operational command of major incidents introduces a range of additional considerations for leaders; such as acute political pressures, severe time constraints and risks to life. This environment arguably requires leaders from all relevant organisations to develop decision-making skills that incorporate risk assessments on limited information and the ability to communicate and later justify their rationale. This subject will predominantly use a case study approach to illustrate the experience of senior leaders in a multi-agency environment in crises and the themes arising from research in this area in a practical way
learning_outcomes: Review, analyse, consolidate and synthesise the history and context of decision making and operational command and the impact of this on the principles underpinning current practice.
Think critically about key professional issues in multi-agency operational command and leadership, with particular reference to the ethical, political, legal and community dimensions of operations.
Identify key challenges to leadership and operational command and suggest practical solutions to the competing risks and priorities in current administrative and operational environment.

title: Operational Intelligence
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a sound knowledge in the practice of operational intelligence, including tactical intelligence. The subject will equip students with an understanding of operational intelligence principles, and mastery of the relevant industry skill sets required to work effectively as an intelligence practitioner in tactical or operational intelligence environments.
learning_outcomes: Use and apply a range of operationally relevant analytical tools, software and research methodologies to support tactical and/ or /operational intelligence activities.
Collect, analyse, consolidate and synthesise operationally relevant information and produce intelligence products.
Determine key legal and ethical issues for the provision of effective decision making support.
Describe and explain a range of trends and threats, and provide solutions and recommendations to address trends and threats.
Reflect critically on the changes to the role of intelligence in supporting operational investigative objectives (including small and large operations) in multi-disciplinary teams.
Think critically about contemporary issues in information and knowledge management as well as their impact on the operational intelligence practitioner role.

title: Operational Policing Practice 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the probationary constable performing duties while under instruction from their Field Training and Assessment Officer (FTAO). It contextualises key police practice domains of legislation, investigation, professional practice and community engagement in the field. It synthesises knowledge gained in Year 1 and extends theoretical understandings of the key police practice domains. It provides opportunities to combine theoretical knowledge with workplace practice. It utilises authentic workplace tasks to build an Operational Portfolio of competency which demonstrates the knowledge, skills and qualities required for effective operational policing practice while under instruction of their FTAO.
learning_outcomes: Identify communication strategies used in effective operational policing.
Identify how legislation applies to different operational policing situations.
Identify support services relevant to their wellbeing.
Identify community networks and external agencies relevant to their LAC.
Identify how investigative practices apply to different operational policing situations.
Complete their individual workloads as a probationary constable under supervision.
Perform operational policing duties at a professional level as identified in the NSW Police Force Operational Portfolio.
Identify demographics of their PAC (Police Area Command)/PD(Police District) and the implications for policing.

title: Operational Policing Practice 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the probationary constable performing duties in an 'assist' role. It focuses on the application of the key police practice domains of legislation, investigation, professional practice and community engagement. The focus on application requires students to engage in problem solving and decision making in the field. It provides opportunities to combine theoretical knowledge with workplace practice. It utilises authentic workplace tasks to build an Operational Portfolio of competency which demonstrate the knowledge, skills and qualities required for effective operational policing practice in an assist role.
learning_outcomes: Render assistance as a probationary constable under supervision.
Perform operational policing duties at a professional level as identified in the NSWPF Operational Portfolio.
Apply legislation to different operational policing situations.
Apply investigative practices to different operational policing situations.
Utilise communications strategies for effective operational policing.
Complete their individual workloads as a probationary constable under supervision.

title: Operational Policing Practice 3
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject draws together the key police practice domains including legislation, intelligence, investigation, response, safety, professional practice and community engagement. It extends PPP243 studies and provides opportunities to combine theoretical knowledge with workplace practice. It utilizes authentic workplace tasks to build a portfolio of competency which demonstrate the knowledge, skills and qualities required for effective operational policing practice in a lead role. This subject is the last of three to be completed in the field during Year 2 for award of the Associate Degree in Policing Practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse operational practice as a probationary constable by extending and applying an understanding of the theoretical foundations of legislation.
Extend understanding of the theoretical foundations of intelligence gathering and investigation to critically analyse operational practice as a probationary constable.

Demonstrate competent performance of operational policing duties in a lead role, including shift preparation, undertaking patrols, ensuring operational safety, responding to incidents, managing information, and completing individual workload as a probationary constable under supervision.
Demonstrate professionalism in a lead role by synthesising theoretical knowledge from online modular learning and practical skills of operational practice as a probationary constable.
Synthesise practical knowledge and skills with online modular learning to demonstrate effective community engagement as a probationary constable in a lead role.

title: Operational Safety – Firearms
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the operational safety and tactical knowledge and skills required by operational police practitioners who carry firearms in the course of their duties. It also introduces students to the ethical, legal and professional application of a range of officer survival techniques and skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the application and approved use of police issued firearms and related tactical communication.
Articulate and justify the use/discharge police firearms in accordance with the current criteria for use/discharge of police firearms for NSW police.
Demonstrate the required level of firearms proficiency and accuracy, in line with the standards set by the NSW Police Force.

title: Operations Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to equip students with an understanding of an organisation's processes and operations in a changing environment. It focuses on the design, production and delivery of operations in both the manufacturing and services sectors. Students will study operations concepts, strategy, tools, techniques and systems. Students will apply quantitative and qualitative techniques to optimise operational performance.
learning_outcomes: Respond to changes in the business environment by deploying the appropriate operations strategy.
Analyse and critically appraise an organisation's operations.
Establish standards and develop controls applicable to various processes.
Formulate and evaluate alternative approaches in operations management.
Collect, analyse and interpret operational data.
Determine and apply appropriate tools and techniques in a variety of operations situations.

title: Oral Anatomy and Histology
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be introduced to craniofacial anatomy, the human dentitions and teeth in the contexts of form and function. The detailed anatomical morphology of teeth, microscopic structure of the dental tissues, their supporting tissues, tooth calcification, emergence-eruption, dental embryology and the structure and function of the oral mucosa, the salivary glands and the temporomandibular joint are dealt with in detail.
learning_outcomes: Apply the knowledge of general and oral embryology to explain and discuss the developmental processes of calcification, emergence and eruption sequences and timings of human dentitions in the context of dental age and chronological age.
Apply the knowledge of anatomy, histology, and embryology to explain, discuss, and identify the macroscopic and microscopic features, functions and development of oral and related tissues.
Apply discipline-specific knowledge to identify, explain, and discuss the macroscopic and microscopic features and functions of the human dentitions.
Explain the principles of evidence-based practice and epidemiology.
Use discipline-specific terminology to describe and identify the macroscopic and microscopic features of the teeth, oral tissues and related structures and their functions.

title: Operations Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to equip students with a keen appreciation of operations management - the 'real work' of the enterprise or organisation. It extends into understanding how we can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of our service and manufacturing operations in the global business environment, and details the strategic elements related to the field, such as a global orientation in sourcing resources, site selection, production and delivery and accommodating customer and environmental considerations. Various topics will focus on equipping students with a range of quantitative and qualitative tools and techniques that will permit the development of models in specific situations in manufacturing or service operations before developing relevant recommendations at strategic and operational levels.
learning_outcomes: Formulate solutions to problems which can arise in the manufacturing and service sectors.
Apply techniques, tools and models in a range of operational situations.
Analyse industry situations and make recommendations to improve operations performance.
Develop operations strategy driven by business strategy considerations.
Set standards and develop controls applicable to various industries.
Critically evaluate the performance of organisation and industry operations.

title: Optimising Health: Living well with Chronic and Complex Conditions
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the opportunity for students to examine global, national and regional perspectives on achieving optimal health for those living with chronic and complex conditions (non-communicable diseases). Students will extend their knowledge and capacity to actively engage with people living with chronic and complex conditions, families, carers and communities to maximise self-management. This will include an exploration of emerging and evidence-based models supporting development of health literacy, empowerment and enablement. Students will examine systems issues impacting on advanced nursing practice including: challenges associated with condition-specific frameworks and services for people living with multiple physical and psychological conditions; enabling integrated care across services; working with First Nations peoples and other marginalised groups.
learning_outcomes: examine individual, community, social and cultural factors impacting upon optimal health outcomes for First Nations peoples and other marginalised groups in the community.

critically evaluate the delivery of services for people experiencing chronic and complex conditions (non-communicable diseases) against international, national and regional health policy, frameworks and initiatives;

critique the underpinning assumptions of contemporary models designed to support people living with chronic and complex conditions, against factors that impact on engagement and effectiveness in self-management; and
critically analyse the evidence-base for contemporary models for advanced nursing practice focused on the provision of services for people living with chronic and complex conditions;

examine the role of the advanced practice nurse in the provision of collaborative and integrated health care across all sectors of health and community service delivery, for people living with chronic and complex conditions;
prerequisites: NRS421: Chronic and Complex Nursing Practice 1
NRS422: Chronic and Complex Nursing Practice 2
NRS420: Perspectives of Managing Chronic and Complex Conditions

title: Oral Community Health 3
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject forms the capstone for the community oral health strand of the course and introduces students to research and advanced topics in community oral health. Students will investigate the ways in which evidence is generated from research and how it is used to inform current oral health practice, in doing so they will gain an understanding of different research methodologies and associated data analysis techniques particularly as they apply to public health. Students will also cover advanced concepts of public health and the role of oral health therapist within public health and their contribution to improved community health outcomes. Students will develop advanced knowledge in models of health behaviour, cultural competency and how this can be applied in clinical and community settings. This subject will also cover transition to practice and how graduates can act as advocates for individuals and communities.
learning_outcomes: Determine and apply respectful and supported practices which demonstrate cultural competency.
Develop working relationships with other professions working in health and human services where applicable and describe their contribution to the health disciplines.
Exercise critical thinking and judgement in identifying and exploring social justice, participation and empowerment issues as it relates to oral health research.
Critically evaluate policies, programs, methods and strategies used in public dental health over the last 50 years and their impact on today's oral health.
Review, critique and apply evidence based oral health research within a range of contexts.
Apply models of theory and evidence for inducing behaviour changes to benefit oral health or general health.

Apply an in-depth awareness of social and environmental issues at both the local and wider level and their impact on oral health and how dental practitioners effect change for vulnerable communities including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
Reflect on their role as agents of change within the profession and community.

title: Oral Community Health 2
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will be introduced to the determinants of oral health from a sociological perspective and learn how these impact on oral health outcomes, including cultural perspectives of health. Key concepts of health promotion relevant for oral health practitioners will be established with an emphasis on effective community engagement. Students will gain a greater understanding of the distribution and determinants of health within populations through the study of epidemiology. A foundation of the oral health therapist's role in oral health promotion and how to implement an effective oral health promotion within a clinical and regional community setting will be established. Students are provided with the opportunity to acquire a fundamental understanding of human life processes which focuses on nutrients, nutrition and the basic metabolic processes. Special emphasis is on the relationship of nutrition to quality of health, including oral health. More complex issues of nutrition will be examined as they affect vulnerable communities. Communicating with communities with high health needs will be an emphasis. Key concepts of public oral health policy will be further established with a particular focus on Indigenous oral health. Students will expand their knowledge of key concepts in models of health behaviour and learn how to apply these in a clinical and community setting, developing the skills to be effective in improving individual and community oral health outcomes.
learning_outcomes: develop reflective practice skills when applying behaviour change models, that can be utilised in a clinical setting;
apply collaborative group approaches to learning in a community setting;
describe the significance of evaluating health and how to measure health outcomes, with the ability to re-define the promotion of health; and
describe how health can be measured from a demographic, socio-economic, epidemiological and community perspective;
describe the significance of epidemiological, demographic and behavioural evidence based data collection in relation to individual and population based prevention;
assess where psychological methods of behaviour change are relevant and be able to apply suitable approach when dealing with an oral health patient;
describe key concepts of cultural perspectives on health, and how these relate to overall health outcome.
apply key concepts in Indigenous perspectives of health and demonstrated application of these in promoting oral health and improving inequalities in health outcomes;
effectively implement an oral health promotion intervention, collecting appropriate data for evaluation;
analyse and synthesize concepts of nutrition and how they relate to general and oral health;
apply models of health behaviour: protection motivation theory, the health belief model, and the theory of planned behaviour;
prerequisites: DOH222: Nutrition and Oral Health Care Delivery
PSY111: Foundations of Psychology for Health and Human Services

title: Oral Health Challenges for Priority Populations
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: The NSW Oral Health Strategic Plan 2022-2032 identifies several Priority Populations at a distinct disadvantage with respect to oral health access and/or opportunities. This subject focuses on these groups and their specific circumstances and needs. Principal among these groups are Indigenous Australians and older people, although other groups, such as people with a disability and the socially disadvantaged, will be considered. Students will study the implications for care, care facility environments, and oral health care delivery to these groups. Students will also examine the impact of ageing on oral tissues and oral diseases of significance in older people.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of the effects of ageing on oral-maxillofacial tissues.
Analyse and discuss the general and oral health issues of Indigenous Australians.
Appraise and differentiate the requirements of populations in our community that have special oral health care needs (as identified by the NSW Oral Health Strategic Plan).
Describe the broad physiologic and disease associations of ageing.

title: Oral Health Clinical Practice 2A
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the concepts and principles introduced in the first year of the course, furthering students’ knowledge of diagnosis and treatment planning. Students will continue to develop their technical oral health practitioner skills in the simulation clinic, including more complex cavity designs and procedures. Students will then be introduced to the patient clinic environment, where they will begin applying foundation knowledge of oral conditions and basic clinical procedures in a person-centred approach to clinical practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain a differential diagnosis and appropriate management strategies for a range of dental conditions, including dentinal hypersensitivity, pulpal and periapical pathosis.
Apply foundation knowledge of oral conditions and basic clinical procedures, safely, in a clinical environment.
Describe and apply management techniques for dentino-enamel defects, caries, and non-carious tooth loss.
Demonstrate and justify the appropriate use of instruments, materials and medicaments to perform dental procedures safely and competently.
Identify individual patient risk factors for oral disease and discuss the indications, contraindications, and possible outcomes of a range of different treatment options for patients of all ages.
Discuss the indications, contraindications and procedures involved for enamel microabrasion and vital bleaching.
Demonstrate a reflective approach to clinical practice as a developing dental practitioner.
prerequisites: DOH106: Psychology and Society in Oral Health

title: Oral Health Clinical Practice 2B
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject will further develop students' knowledge and understanding of evidence-based practice and person-centred care. Differential diagnosis and management skills for periodontal disease, dental trauma and temporomandibular joint disorders will be explored and students will continue to develop their technical and clinical reasoning skills, including more complex cavity designs and procedures.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and justify the appropriate use of instruments, materials and medicaments to perform advanced oral health procedures safely and competently.
Identify temporomandibular joint disorders and discuss appropriate management strategies.
Demonstrate safe clinical reasoning and reflection on oral health care across the lifespan, including the utilisation of appropriate referral pathways.
Explain a differential diagnosis and appropriate management strategies periodontal disease.
Diagnose dental trauma and discuss appropriate management strategies.
Apply foundational knowledge of evidence-based practice and patient-centred care through examination, diagnosis and treatment planning.
prerequisites: DOH209: Applied Oral Health Psychology and Research

title: Oral Health Promotion
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject will build upon knowledge of community health to develop students' skills and understanding of oral health promotion. Students will have the opportunity to learn and simultaneously apply their skills in oral health promotion planning, implementation, and evaluation. Students will be assigned a target group for whom to design an evidence-based intervention and, working in groups, will deliver and evaluate a simulated health education presentation.
learning_outcomes: Implement an oral health promotion intervention in a community setting, applying collaborative group approaches.
Design a culturally safe health promotion intervention with respect to individual, cultural and linguistic diversity.
Analyse epidemiological, demographic and behavioural evidence-based data in relation to population-based health promotion.
Collect, analyse and present appropriate evaluation data for an oral health promotion intervention.
prerequisites: DOH209: Applied Oral Health Psychology and Research

title: Oral Health Sciences 1
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory course that begins the study of Oral Biology. This subject establishes the foundational knowledge needed in oral anatomy, histology and embryologic development. Crown and root anatomy, morphology and clinical characteristics will be examined in detail. Students will identify and differentiate oral structures. The subject is focused on the healthy development of the oral cavity at this stage of study so the student acquires sound foundational knowledge needed to distinguish health from disease and provide optimal oral health care as an oral health care practitioner.
learning_outcomes: Describe the microbiology of oral biofilm, host responses and immune responses.
Explain the clinical manifestation of defects affecting dental hard tissues.
Describe the morphology of deciduous and permanent dentition and the occlusal relationships.
Describe the morpho-and histo-differentiation stages and the interactions that lead to the development of teeth and periodontium.
Describe the basic embryological processes and their macro and microscopic interactions that lead to the development of the craniofacial complex and oral region.
Describe the histology and physiology of tooth eruption and exfoliation.
Apply anatomical knowledge in describing disease processes and clinical manifestations of congenital and developmental orofacial defects and accidental and iatrogenic injuries.
Describe the macroscopic anatomy of the head and neck structures and their functions using anatomical terminology with a focus on oral and peri-oral structures.

Describe the physical and chemical properties of restorative and impression dental materials, their clinical indications and contra-indications, their chairside handling and their waste management processes.
Describe the histology of oral and peri-oral structures.

title: Oral Health Sciences 1A
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject establishes the foundational knowledge needed in oral anatomy, histology and embryologic development. Crown and root anatomy, morphology and clinical characteristics will be examined in detail. Students will identify and differentiate oral structures. Students will develop an introductory understanding of oral biofilm, host and immune responses at a microbiological level. It will introduce saliva and the oral-biofilm, stages of biofilm formation and changes in biofilm microorganisms. The function and components of fluoride in relation to optimum oral health are also explored. The subject is focused on the healthy development of the oral cavity at this stage of study, so the student acquires sound foundational knowledge needed to distinguish health from disease and provide optimal oral health care as an oral health care practitioner.
