learning_outcomes: Identify the sources, constituents, function, and types of saliva, and discuss the role of saliva in relation to oral health and the clinical steps involved in its evaluation.
Describe sources of fluoride, and discuss its mode of action and role in oral health.
Describe the microbiology of oral biofilm, host responses and immune responses.

Recognise and describe the morpho- and histo-differentiation stages and the interactions that lead to the development of teeth and periodontium, as well as be able to describe the timing, histology and physiology of tooth eruption and exfoliation in the context of dental age and chronological age.
Describe and demonstrate the morphology of deciduous and permanent dentition and the occlusal relationships.

title: Oral Health Sciences 2A
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject continues students' knowledge of oral biology. Students will learn the pharmacology of pain management by therapeutic means and demonstrate competence in the administration of local anaesthesia in a simulated dental practice setting. Students will further learn about the pathophysiology of common medical problems and learn about the common medications used in the dental practice. Students will recognise the oral health therapist’s role in providing person-centred medical and dental care for persons with medical problems and medical emergencies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate pharmacological, anatomical and practical competence in the administration of safe and effective local anaesthesia in a simulated dental practice setting.
Describe the pathophysiological determinants of systemic health, risk factors and behaviours that influence systemic health.

Describe the oral health therapist roles and the interprofessional collaborative approaches used for providing comprehensive evidence-based, person-centred medical and dental care for medically compromised and polypharmacy patients.
Identify and manage medical emergencies in a simulated dental setting.
Describe the types, dosage, indications, interactions and adverse reactions of the medications used in dental practice.
Identify and describe the effect of tobacco-use and e-cigarettes on the development and progression of oral diseases.
Describe the type, safe dosage, indications, contraindications and complications of local anaesthetics used in the dental practice.

title: Oral Health Sciences 2
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject continues students' knowledge of oral biology. This subject further develops the knowledge needed to differentiate healthy tissue from unhealthy tissue in the oral cavity. Students will learn the pharmacology of pain management by therapeutic means and treatment modalities. Knowledge of radiography and anatomical landmarks will be further developed. It will include a more in-depth exploration of oral-biofilm, stages of biofilm formation and changes in biofilm microorganisms. The specific pathogens in destructive periodontal disease and dental caries will be studied.
learning_outcomes: identify and describe the clinically important characteristics of healthy oral tissues and how they are differentiated from unhealthy tissues;
identify and describe the effect of smoking on the development of oral diseases and identify the role of oral health therapists in counselling smoking cessation.
identify the clinical and radiological manifestations of oral lesions, identifying the role of oral health therapist in the management and referral pathways;
identify and describe the normal anatomical features and variations of normal to inform clinical tasks in oral health therapy practice;
demonstrate clinical competence in the administration of local anaesthetics in a simulated dental practice environment;
describe the types, dosage, indications, interactions and complications and identify the role of the oral health therapists in relation to the medications used in the dental practice;
identify the role of oral health therapists in the management of medically compromised patients and the referral pathways;
apply anatomical knowledge in a simulated environment in regards to the oral landmarks used for the administration of local anaesthesia;
demonstrate the current theoretical knowledge in regards to the type, dosage, indications, contraindications and complications of local anesthetics used in the dental practice;
explain the role of microorganisms and diet in the development of tooth decay and periodontal disease;
identity and manage medical emergencies in the the dental practice; and
prerequisites: PSY111: Foundations of Psychology for Health and Human Services

title: Oral Health Sciences 3
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject further develops the knowledge needed in differentiated healthy tissue from unhealthy tissue in the oral cavity with a focus on oral infection related to special need patients and systemic disease. Advanced clinical pathologic correlations will be examined. Students use the body of knowledge acquired thus far and assess the appropriateness of specific health care decisions through case study discussions. All scientific knowledge gained in the course will guide the student to practice with sound evidenced-based practice standards.
learning_outcomes: Explain the appropriate management of medical emergencies in the dental practice.
Critically analyse dental literature in relation to management of oral diseases.
Describe the pathogenesis, manifestations, diagnosis and management of oral diseases.

Describe the legislation of prescribing and prescriptions, common medications used in dental practice and alcohol and drug abuse, and to identify the role of oral health therapist in these aspects and the referral pathways.
Explain the diagnosis and management of non-accidental injuries, traumatic injuries, dental anomalies and eruption/shedding disorders from the perspective of an oral health therapist.
Describe the role of oral health therapists in the diagnosis and management of cancer patients and patients receiving radiotherapy and chemotherapy and identify the referral pathways.
Describe the role of oral health therapists in the management of patients treated under general anaesthesia and conscious sedation.
Explain the implementation of appropriate preventative strategies, predict oral health outcomes and plan phased treatment for a range of soft and hard tissue diseases affecting the oral health.
Analyse the role of modifiable and no-modifiable risk factors in relation to periodontal disease stages (active and quiescence).

Define the scope of dental practice with respect to different branches of dentistry, including endodontics, prosthodontics, periodontics and oral medicine, and explain when and how to refer patients to the appropriate health professional.
List the systemic conditions that produce oral manifestations and describe the role of oral health therapist in the management of these systemic conditions and their oral manifestations.
Justify clinical decisions with respect to paediatric endodontics and prosthodontics from the perspective of an oral health therapist.
Justify, using evidence, the clinical decisions which inform responsible and professional standards of care decisions in relation to management of oral diseases.
Describe the association between systemic conditions and periodontal disease.

title: Oral Health Sciences 2B
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject continues students' knowledge of oral biology. This subject further develops the knowledge needed to differentiate healthy tissue from unhealthy tissue in the oral cavity. Students will learn the theoretical background for the pathophysiology of oral pathologies and recognise the Oral Health Therapist’s role in managing these conditions. Students will identify and describe the interprofessional collaborative approaches used for providing comprehensive evidence-based, person-centred oral health care for patients with oral pathologies.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe the signs and symptoms of oral pathologies, their diagnoses and management from an Oral Health Therapist’s perspective.
Describe and demonstrate the interprofessional collaborative approaches and the liaison and referral pathways used for providing comprehensive evidence-based, person-centred oral health care.
Identify and describe the risk factors and behaviours that influence oral health and lead to development and progression of oral pathologies.

title: Oral Microbiology
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces micro-organisms, their characteristics and how they affect humans. Cultivation, enumeration, identification and control of micro-organisms are emphasised. Mechanisms by which medically important micro-organisms cause disease are introduced. The concepts of infection, inflammation and immunology are introduced in this subject. Infection control procedures are discussed in theory and applied in laboratory classes. An understanding of normal oral flora is developed in the subject. Hypotheses of oral disease aetiology, including specific, non-specific and ecological plaque hypotheses, are critically evaluated with respect to current peer-reviewed research findings. Practical skills developed in laboratory classes are used to solve dentistry-related case-based problems in a way that encourages independent, critical and reflective thinking.
learning_outcomes: Explain, critically analyse and discuss current hypotheses of oral disease, including the specific, non-specific and ecological plaque hypotheses.
Describe the structure and function of micro-organisms.
Describe and demonstrate how micro-organisms can be identified by biochemical and molecular methods.
Apply practical skills in microscopy, enumeration, isolation and culture of micro-organisms.
Demonstrate knowledge of the means by which the growth of micro-organisms can be controlled, including managing the spread of infection in dental clinical practice.
Demonstrate a good understanding of the interactions of micro-organisms with humans with particular emphasis on the micro-organisms of importance to dental clinical practice.

title: Oral-Maxillofacial Pathology
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the aetiology, pathogenesis, histopathological, clinical and, where relevant, the radiographic features of diseases affecting the teeth, gums, oral mucosa, subjacent oral soft tissues, the jawbones and salivary glands. Emphasis in the subject is placed on the more common or important oral-maxillofacial conditions that may be encountered in general dental practice. The basic principles of clinical management, including description of diagnostic tests and their relevance, are described in relation to the more common-important diseases
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to formulate basic differential diagnoses based on patient history and clinical-radiographic-histopathological information.
Describe or discuss the clinical management of common and important oral-maxillofacial diseases and conditions.
Describe and discuss the causes, pathology and clinical features of common and important diseases of the oral-maxillofacial region.
prerequisites: DOH233: Pathological Basis of Human Disease

title: Oral Surgery
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will continue to develop competencies in a range of minor oral surgical procedures. Students will continue to master their knowledge and skills in simple exodontia. This subject will also include a study of the role and application of therapeutics in patient care. Part of the subject will include introductory concepts in surgical aspects of implant dentistry.
learning_outcomes: be able to demonstrate the ability to apply dental therapeutics competently within the clinical setting; and
be able to demonstrate understanding and clinical competence relevant to the provision of simple minor oral surgical procedures;
be able to demonstrate foundation knowledge in assessment, diagnosis, treatment planning for surgical aspects of implant dentistry.
be able to demonstrate continued development of clinical competence relevant to the management of simple dental extractions;
be able to demonstrate the knowledge and clinical application of periodontal surgical procedures in periodontal and restorative case management.;
be able to demonstrate developing knowledge and continuing development of skills relevant to the provision of simple safe local anaesthesia;
be able to demonstrate the knowledge and clinical application of endodontic periradicular microsurgery;
be able to demonstrate the clinical application of pharmacological principles with particular relevance to optimal oral and dental health.;

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to get students acquainted with the basic methods of solving ordinary differential equations. The methods considered include exact integration, Laplace transforms and power series. The following types of equations are considered in detail: separable, Bernoulli, homogeneous, first order linear and higher order linear with constant coefficients. An important role of solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in applications is illustrated by examples of electric circuits and phenomena that involve various types of growth (eg exponential, logistic).
learning_outcomes: Investigate the convergence of a solution given by a power series.
Investigate various phenomena by using relevant ODEs.

Select and apply appropriate techniques to solve these important classes of differential equations: separable, homogeneous, first order linear, higher order linear with constant coefficients and Bernoulli equations.
Apply Laplace transforms and power series to solve linear ODEs.
Interpret mathematical models and communicate their output to non-mathematical audiences.
prerequisites: MTH402: Computer Aided Mathematics 2 with Applications

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to get students acquainted with the basic methods of solving ordinary differential equations. The methods considered include exact integration, Laplace transforms and power series. The following types of equations are considered in detail: separable, Bernoulli, homogeneous, first order linear and higher order linear with constant coefficients. An important role of ordinary differential equations in applications is illustrated by examples of electric circuits and phenomena that involve various types of growth (eg exponential, logistic).
learning_outcomes: Investigate various phenomena by using relevant ODEs.

Select and apply appropriate techniques to solve these important classes of differential equations: separable, homogeneous, first order linear, higher order linear with constant coefficients, and Bernoulli equations.
Investigate the convergence of a solution given by a power series.
Use Laplace transforms and power series to solve linear ODEs.
prerequisites: MTH102: Computer Aided Mathematics 2 with Applications

title: Organic Chemistry
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will extend their knowledge of carbon chemistry and functional group reactions beyond what they encountered in first year. Greater emphasis will be given to molecular properties such as isomerism, tautomerism, bonding theory, conformations, configurations, reaction mechanisms and electronic theory, together with applications of organic products to modern society. Students will also learn skills in organic structure determination through the use of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, mass spectrometry and infra-red spectroscopy. Laboratory skills will be further developed through safe use of instrumentation and synthesis of range of organic compounds.
learning_outcomes: Predict, draw the structures of, identify and name stereoisomers and conformers, together with drawing conformational energy diagrams and assigning energy level to conformers, and vice-versa.
Apply polarity and hydrogen bonding properties of compounds to evaluate or predict their solubility and/or boiling point.
Use a repertoire of standard organic functional group transforming reactions for synthetic design and draw reaction mechanisms.
Apply important principles and theories, including, but not restricted to, electron donating and electron withdrawing effects, resonance, inductive effect, nucleophilicity, electrophilicity.
Describe the basic operating principles of infra-red, ultra-violet-visible, nuclear magnetic resonance and mass spectroscopies, and use combinations of data to predict simple organic molecules.
Evaluate or predict acid/base properties of compounds.
Operate safely in an organic chemistry laboratory involving synthetic and instrumental methods.

title: Organic and Medicinal Agents
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the application of principles and methods of chemical analysis of drugs. Major areas include, chemical analysis, diagnostic applications, receptor structure and drug binding. It covers the medicinal chemistry of a wide range of current therapeutic agents and provides the basis for an understanding of the principles and techniques for development of future drugs.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate developing abilities in the areas of measurement and recording of data relevant to the understanding of drug structure and reactivity.
Describe the mechanisms of drug action at a molecular level.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the processes involved in rational drug design.
Demonstrate understanding of the principles and applications of pharmacognosy in drug development.
Demonstrate understanding of the relationship between chemical structure and biological activity of drugs or endogenous substances.
Identify the chemical principles underlying selected diagnostic aids relevant to pharmacy.
Demonstrate understanding of the chemical-pharmacological basis for selected herbal remedies.
Demonstrate understanding of the rationale behind the chemical manipulation of drugs to devise alternative forms of drug presentation.
Describe the structure of drug receptors and the forces involved in the binding of drugs to receptors.
Demonstrate competence in the use of spectroscopic methods to analyse and determine the structure of drugs.

title: Organisational and Personal Records
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of recordkeeping and archiving across a range of organisational contexts. It considers how regulatory, policy and funding frameworks in different sectors affect recordkeeping. The contexts covered include government agencies, international organisations, companies, indigenous organisations, not for profit organisations, religious organisations, schools and museums. There is a focus on how communities, both physical and virtual, maintain their records. The subject also considers personal records, including issues involved for stakeholders when personal and family records are donated to public collections.
learning_outcomes: Apply expert knowledge of frameworks for recordkeeping for organisational records.
Analyse and critically review complex recordkeeping and archiving challenges for organisations in the public and private sectors.
Develop and apply solutions that support effective management of community records.
Identify and critically evaluate stakeholder perspectives relating to the management of private records in public collections.
Demonstrate expert knowledge of issues and challenges for personal recordkeeping.

title: Organisational and Personal Records
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of recordkeeping and archiving across a range of organisational contexts. It considers how regulatory, policy and funding frameworks in different sectors affect recordkeeping. The contexts covered include government agencies, international organisations, companies, indigenous organisations, not for profit organisations, religious organisations, schools and museums. There is a focus on how communities, both physical and virtual, maintain their records. The subject also considers personal records, including issues involved for stakeholders when personal and family records are donated to public collections.
learning_outcomes: Explain issues and challenges for personal recordkeeping.
Demonstrate specialist knowledge of frameworks for recordkeeping for organisational records.
Identify and describe stakeholder perspectives relating to the management of private records in public collections.
Analyse and evaluate recordkeeping and archiving challenges for organisations in the public and private sectors.
Apply solutions that support effective management of community records.

title: Organisational Behaviour
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Faced with complex social organisational environments, how can we explain, predict, and influence the behaviours of employees, groups/teams which are occurring within organisations? This subject addresses a range of practical organisational challenges important to organisational leaders by using the lens of an organisational behaviour and empirical, research-based approach. Drawing on management, psychological and sociological literature, the subject explores dynamic human behaviour that is influenced by individuals, groups, as well as processes, culture and structure of organisations. You will develop awareness of the diverse facets of human behaviour and gain an insight into contingency based factors that affect organisational effectiveness and the quality of work life.
learning_outcomes: Research contemporary aspects of organisational behaviour and evaluate their impact on employee-employer relationship.
Recommend strategies to effectively manage behaviour in the workplace.
Apply organisational behaviour theories in analysing workplace or case based scenarios.
Critically reflect on their own behaviour/workplace practices based on organisational behaviour concepts and theories.

title: Organisational Behaviour
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to provide students with the knowledge, understanding and skills relating to human behaviour within organisations at the individual, group and organisational levels. The subject examines the factors which influence behaviour such as leadership, teamwork, motivation, change, power and learning. Strategies which may be adopted to increase personal and organisational effectiveness will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on your own behaviour and that of others within organisations based on OB theories and concepts.
Identify and explain the contemporary Organisational Behaviour (OB) theories and concepts about behaviour of people in organisations as individuals or as members of collective groups and cultures.
Explain what motivates individuals' behaviour in organisations and create suggestions for managing their behaviour based on OB theories and concepts.
Assess the role of work teams and groups in an organisation and recommend strategies to manage performance of teams and groups.
Assess effective practices of an organisation, identify key issues and formulate and apply appropriate managerial strategies for enhancing the performance of an organisation and its people.

title: Organisational Politics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the role of politics in the management of organisations, including change management. Students will examine the nature of organisational politics, its functional use, ethical issues and political tactics. This subject takes a largely practical approach to the study of organisational politics, and students are expected to contribute to subject interactions actively, drawing on their experiences of organisational life.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical reasoning to critique the application of political strategies in organisations.
Critically analyse the application of political strategies in organisations.
Analyse and reflect on the relevance of organisational politics and its nature in contemporary organisations.
Offer a range of possible responses to organisational issues that draw on political rationales.
Formulate political strategies to respond to specific issues arising in the management of organisations.

title: Organisational Development and Workforce Capabilities
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the theoretical and practical foundations for developing adaptive workforce capabilities. A range of approaches and models for the development and management of strategic dynamic capabilities are explored. Knowledge gained is applied through analysis of current capabilities and future needs at the organisational level.
learning_outcomes: Justify and clearly communicate proposed solutions for addressing gaps in workforce capability using theoretical frameworks.
Analyse the strategic role of workforce capabilities in achieving business goals.
Critically evaluate the contribution of HRD to organisational outcomes.
Identify capability requirements (current and future) through the use of people analytics.
Develop strategies for building workforce capabilities which are ethical and sustainable.

title: Organisational Communication
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: To operate effectively, police organisations need to communicate both internally and with the community. The public 'know' about crime and the work of the police from the media, and it is essential that police at every level in the organisation learn how to work constructively and cooperatively with the media to increase public understanding. In this subject, police accountability to the community, community satisfaction with the police, and the value of strategic inter-agency relationships, alliances and partnerships are examined, as are the wider social, legal and political context. At an applied level, good internal knowledge management and communication, and best practice use of web-based information, are examined.
learning_outcomes: Communicate complex knowledge and ideas to a variety of audiences including police and other stakeholders.
Critically evaluate how communication strategies may be able to enhance transparency, organisational cohesiveness, community consultation and operational effectiveness.
Review analyse, consolidate and synthesise research relating to communication theory and critically reflect on how this can assist in the management of operational issues in a policing context.
Identify challenges to policing and how solutions to these may be facilitated by strategic use of communication strategies.

title: Organisations and Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject offers an overview of management approaches and methods, and principles of organisational behaviour. This subject will build students' appreciation that there can be a variety of understanding surrounding organisation activities and events and that there will rarely be a single 'right way' in responding to any organisational situation. It examines various key management theories and models in the areas of planning, organising, communication, teamwork, ethics, corporate social responsibility, leadership, decision making, motivation and controlling. Students will apply theoretical concepts and models to management problems and issues in the context of the global business environment.
learning_outcomes: Research and compare various sources of information about management.
Explain their personal values and experience in relation to management theory.
Apply management theory in order to analyse management dilemmas and problems, and provide recommendations for action.
Compare and contrast the work of influential management thinkers and researchers.
Express opinions on management issues with clarity, from both personal and more objective positions that are backed up with sound evidence and analysis.

title: Organisations Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Examines the modern law of commercial enterprises with a focus upon the law of corporations. Other types of business organisations, in particular partnerships, joint ventures, trusts and sole proprietorships are given coverage and compared with the corporation. Agency is examined under both the Doctrine of Ostensible Authority and the Law of Promoters. Insolvency is examined under the law pertaining to winding up.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend the law relating to the daytoday operation of a corporation both internally and externally.
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of each type of commercial enterprise.
Identify the source and content of the law in relation to each type of organisation.
Analyse the provision of the Corporations Law relating to Winding Up, Takeovers and the Securities Industry.
Resolve hypothetical problems encountered by commercial enterprises.
Identify the most appropriate form of organisation for a business undertaking.
Explain the means of bringing into being each type of organisation.

title: Organised Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject deals with: the problems of defining organised crime; with the history, both overseas and in Australia, of traditional forms of organising crime in the vice industry; corporate crime and public sector corruption; and policy implications of contemporary debates for policing and security agencies.
learning_outcomes: Research and identify the historical development of organised crime to explain current nature and extent.
Examine the impact/relationship of globalisation on organised crime and identify its impact/relationship on trafficking, gangs, narcotics and terrorism.
Analyse and report on the impact of organised crime on democracy, outlining current practices of disruption and difficulties to still be faced.

title: Ornithological Methods
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to a range of scientific methods used commonly in the field of ornithology. The subject covers both laboratory and field methods for studying the morphology, anatomy, diversity, breeding biology, survival, movement, behaviour, ecology, life history evolution and conservation of birds. Students will learn the appropriate ways of measuring these parameters and the limitations of each study technique. This subject contains a compulsory 4-day intensive, which teaches students a range of hands-on practical skills and techniques used commonly in the field of ornithology. On completion, students will have the background knowledge and technical skills necessary to commence a career as a professional ornithologist or become involved in ornithological research.
learning_outcomes: Apply professional skills in sourcing and understanding scientific information about birds.
Develop an overview on how to design and conduct a rigorous, scientific, ornithological study.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge about a range of ornithological methods that are appropriate and ethical when studying birds.
Demonstrate extensive skills in data analysis and writing a scientific ornithological manuscript.

title: Orthodontics and Paediatric Dentistry
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: This subject will focus on the integration of the specialist discipline areas of paediatric dentistry and orthodontics. Students will gain the requisite skills in diagnosis, treatment planning and case selection for general practitioner level paediatric and orthodontic care. Students will also gain an understanding of the referral pathways essential for optimal paediatric and orthodontic specialist treatment. This subject is designed to provide students with full development of skills necessary to provide more complex and comprehensive clinical care for adults, teenagers and children as they further develop their knowledge of growth and development from earlier years.
learning_outcomes: Describe and discuss the requirements for examination, diagnosis, treatment planning and dental treatment for children.
Demonstrate basic orthodontics knowledge relevant to general dental practice, with particular focus on diagnosis, case selection and referral of patients.
Compare and contrast the specific behaviour management strategies required for the provision of optimal oral health care for children.
Differentiate the requirements for dental treatment of children and adults.

title: Outdoor Recreation Credit
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This is a credit code for the Bachelor of Outdoor Education. This credit represents the completion of training.gov.au registered package SIS40313 Certificate IV in Outdoor Recreation.

title: Paediatrics and Maternal Critical Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students’ previous education and experience to advance the knowledge and skills needed to provide critical care paramedicine for paediatric and maternal emergencies. Students will further develop their ability to integrate assessment and diagnostic data, knowledge of relevant anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology, and evidence-informed practice to propose critical care paramedicine treatment plans. To foster the professional attributes required in critical care paramedicine, students will apply safe, ethical, patient-centred and inclusive practices including the application of cultural safety to First Nations Peoples during emergent maternal care.
learning_outcomes: Integrate advanced knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology to critical care paramedic management of paediatric, maternal and neonatal emergencies.
Formulate evidence-informed critical care paramedic treatment plans for paediatric, maternal and neonatal emergencies.
Interpret clinical data derived from advanced patient diagnostics, assessment and history taking to inform clinical decision making for pediatric, maternal and neonatal emergencies.
Apply safe, ethical, patient-centred and inclusive practices to critical care Paramedicine for paediatric, maternal and neonatal patients including effective cultural safety to First Nations Peoples.

title: Palliative Care in Advanced Nursing Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will examine the principles, policy and standards of palliative care and the care needs of people who have a life-limiting condition, their families and carers, across the lifespan. Evidence-informed frameworks for the provision of person-centred care, to alleviate physical and emotional pain and symptoms throughout a life-challenging illness or condition, will be analysed. Students will strengthen their knowledge of collaborative and culturally sensitive palliative care for First Nations peoples and people from other culturally diverse groups. Sensitive and complex communication strategies underpinning nursing practice will be further developed in this subject. Ethical and legal issues involving quality end-of-life care, and the societal expectations of end-of-life care, will be critically examined.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the psychosocial factors that influence the delivery of palliative care in a range of settings.
Analyse culturally respectful palliative care for First Nations peoples and people from other culturally diverse groups.
Critically reflect on communication skills that support decision making and the empowerment of individuals and their carers.
Critique models of care for the provision of palliative care to people across the lifespan.
Critically appraise the principles, policies and standards of palliative care and current ethical and legal debates, societal values and expectations of health care.
Lead and work within interdisciplinary teams to coordinate care.
prerequisites: NRS543: Clinical Management in Palliative Care Nursing
NRS534: Foundations of Palliative Care Nursing

title: Paramedic Law and Ethics
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will be provided with an introductory understanding of the legal, ethical and professional issues that they will face in their practice, and the tools, principles and frameworks they can use to help navigate them. Students will examine and apply the legal and ethical theoretical principles for safe practice as a paramedic. The subject uses a case-based framework to support students to deliberate, discuss, critique, and reflect on real-world scenarios The themes of client autonomy and self-determination, client rights and professional responsibility will be examined within the context of out-of-hospital care and include an examination of issues relating to particular groups that paramedics work with, inclusive of First Nations people, the aged, children, the terminally ill, and those who lack the capacity to make independent decisions.
learning_outcomes: Discuss concepts of bioethics related to paramedic practice.
Critically reflect on the legal and ethical frameworks, the social determinants of health for First Nations peoples, and its impact on paramedic practice.
Describe legal and ethical issues relating to particular client, religious, cultural groups inclusive of First Nations people within the health care system.
Critically discuss the legal and ethical issues pertaining to the field of out-of-hospital care.
Discuss the relationship between legal and professional responsibility.
Identify steps in ethical decision making.

title: Paramedic Professionalism and Communication
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will explores the foundations of the paramedic profession, including its historical, sociological, and systems context, as well as the evolving role of paramedics. Key elements of practice, such as person-centred care, communication, safety, wellness, and professional standards, are examined. In this subject, students will explore health equity, how to support vulnerable populations, and the health of First Nations peoples and diverse populations, emphasising paramedics' role in accessible care. Students reflect on their identity within the profession, examining decision-making processes and core values that underpin paramedicine. They are introduced to governance frameworks, including the Code of Conduct and Professional Capabilities, to understand professional expectations and community responsibilities.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast how our own cultural values and beliefs effect the role of paramedics in providing culturally safe care to First Nations peoples and diverse populations.
Explore strategies to support wellness, safety and self-care within the individual and the importance to professional identity.
Describe the context of paramedicine and roles paramedics undertake within the community in health advocacy, equity and the care of diverse and vulnerable populations.
Explain strategies to support safe and professional practice including regulation, governance and standards including codes of conduct and professional capabilities.
Collaborate and communicate with professionals to ensure integrated, person-centred, ethical care, adapting to new situations and information.

title: Paramedic Work Integrated Learning 2
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will build upon previous Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) experiences, supporting students' professional growth and understanding of paramedic practice. Students will identify learning goals aligned with their development needs and WIL opportunities. They will explore the role of paramedics in unscheduled and emergency care, analysing their position within the broader health system. Emphasis is placed on teamwork, as students collaborate with paramedics and other health professionals to deliver safe, effective, and person-centred care. Students will apply professional capabilities, values, and ethical standards drawn from the Professional Capabilities for Registered Paramedics, the Code of Conduct, and related guidelines. Through reflective practice, students will develop strategies for continuous improvement and guide their future learning.
learning_outcomes: Employ the appropriate professional capabilities and values as reflected in the Professional Capabilities for Registered Paramedics, Code of conduct and other applicable standards.
Reflect on practice to develop effective strategies to guide future learning.
Describe the role of paramedics in unscheduled and emergency care and analyse the positionality of paramedics within the health system.
Determine appropriate goals aligned with learning needs that will support student WIL experiences.
Facilitate safe and effective person-centred care through interprofessional practice.
prerequisites: CLS206: Clinical Placement and Authentic Learning 1
PAR103: Introduction to Contemporary Paramedic Practice

title: Paramedic Work Integrated Learning 1
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This introductory Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) subject begins the WIL stream, focusing on developing students' ‘professional self’ within community-based and non-emergency health services. It highlights the professional responsibilities of paramedics across diverse roles in Australia’s health continuum. Students will enhance skills in communication, collaboration, confidentiality, safety, and reflective practice within community-focused WIL environments. They will learn to maintain a placement portfolio, develop an understanding of reflective practice, and identify and mitigate safety risks in WIL and simulated settings.
learning_outcomes: Implement and maintain a basic audit trail of placement learning to demonstrate an introductory understanding of reflective practice.
Describe the role of community-based and non-emergency health services; explaining the paramedic role and contribution to the broader healthcare system.
Identify hazards and risks to the safety and well-being of self and others in WIL and simulated learning environments, and explain the mitigation processes.
Communicate and collaborate effectively with health consumers and society and other healthcare providers in non-emergency situations.
Explain how to support health consumers while applying the Paramedicine Professional Capabilities and code of conduct.

title: Paramedic Professionalism and Communication
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This introductory paramedical subject provides a landing pad for the student into the paramedic profession, and begins the learning journey of developing core skills which include communication for paramedicine. This subject will cover a wide variety of themes that include exploring the roles of paramedics and understanding the work life balance that needs to be maintained to ensure a healthy and rewarding lifelong career.
learning_outcomes: be able to recognise and summarise foundational skills in therapeutic communication, empathetic listening, negotiation, assertiveness, and collaboration.
be able to complete accurate and compliant patient care documentation.
be able to use correct and accurate medical terminology.
be able to compare strategies of Interdisciplinary communication and effective communication in teams.
be able to recall and explain the professional role of the paramedic.
be able to recall and compare patient centred and clinician directed approaches to communication.

title: Paramedic Work Integrated Learning 3
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds upon previous Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) experiences, supporting students' professional growth and understanding of paramedicine practice. In this subject students will demonstrate professional practices, including effective communication and interprofessional collaboration. Using the Professional Capabilities for Registered Paramedics (PCFRP), and previous work-integrated learning (WIL) experience as a foundation, this subject gives students the opportunity to exhibit progressive Paramedic Professional Capabilities in a supervised paramedicine practice environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ethical, professional and social judgements about their practice in alignment with the code of conduct.
Formulate treatment plans to support person-centred care and justify appropriateness based on NSQHS standards.
Evaluate professional skills and knowledge to identify areas for improvement and opportunities from the placement experience.
Communicate and collaborate with other health professionals and service personnel to provide safe person-centred management.
Reflect on personal strengths and limitations to identify learning and development required to improve and adapt professional practice.
prerequisites: PAR200: Medical Emergencies in Paramedic Practice
CLS311: Clinical Placement and Authentic Learning 2

title: Paramedic Work Integrated Learning 4
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This final Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) subject marks the culmination of the undergraduate paramedicine program, encompassing the last placement for both internal and online students. Building on knowledge and skills gained throughout the program, students will integrate and apply their learning in paramedicine environments. The subject focuses on developing professional capabilities and attitudes, and ethical values essential for practice. Students will demonstrate growth and readiness for professional practice by completing and presenting a learning portfolio, ensuring they are prepared for ongoing development in their paramedic roles.
learning_outcomes: Reflect upon professional practice and performance, and incorporate feedback, to implement strategies for continuous improvement.
Implement safe and effective treatment plans for a variety of presentations, in a supervised paramedicine environment in alignment with the NSQHS standards.
Communicate and collaborate in diverse paramedicine environments, with other health professionals, allied emergency service personnel, members of the public, health consumers and society.
Analyse and articulate clinical reasoning to support self-development and contribute to the growth and mentorship of others.
prerequisites: CLS311: Clinical Placement and Authentic Learning 2
PAR301: Complex Care in Paramedic Practice

title: Parasitology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Parasitic diseases of animals continue to be of major economic importance to the grazing livestock industries in Australia, while in developing countries they remain a significant cause of suffering and death. Students will examine common parasites, their life cycle and associated disease processes in livestock, horses, companion animals, aquatic animals and Australian native fauna. Students will also explore prevention management and control of parasitic diseases in individual animals and in herds, as well as parasitic diseases capable of being transmitted to humans.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the concept of managing herd health.
Identify and list a range of parasitic diseases and the parasites that lead to them that are of economic importance or of significance to public health.
Explain the lifecycle of common parasites.
Discuss the prevention, identification, diagnosis, treatment and control of common parasitic diseases.

title: Past Environments: Dimensions of Historical Ecology and Environmental History
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Current global and local ecological processes do not operate in a vacuum but have been shaped by changes to the environment that occurred over time. During the late Holocene and Anthropocene some of these are due to natural climatic fluctuations but most are due to environmental modification caused by human communities. There is an abundance of evidence drawn from sub-fossil deposits, Indigenous oral traditions and knowledge, archaeological sites and historic records to reconstruct past environmental conditions and events. Approaching the topic from the perspectives of historical ecology and environmental history, the subject takes the student on a trajectory from the deep past to the present examining the evidence of past environments to understand their relevance for modern ecology and to develop an understanding of the long history of humans as agents of environmental change.
learning_outcomes: Examine the sub-fossil, Indigenous oral, archaeological and historic record and describe how it forms a valuable cultural and scientific resource to understand present conditions.
Critically discuss the long history of humans as agents of environmental change.
Interpret the role of historic ecology and describe how it influences the current understanding of ecological conditions.
Compare and contrast the value and critically discuss limitations of evidence from various data sources provided by the sub-fossil, Indigenous oral, archaeological and historic record.
prerequisites: ENM123: Past Environments: An Introduction to Historic Ecology
ENM221: Conservation in a Global Context

title: Pastoral and Spiritual Care in Residential and Community Aged Care Settings
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students for pastoral and spiritual care roles in both residential and community based aged care settings, and considers the pastoral or spiritual carer's place in multidisciplinary aged care teams. Praxis issues are identified and discussed including the differing needs and priorities of residents, their families, and staff, together with ethical issues and protocols, professional standards, reflective practice and self care. In addition, building on earlier subjects in Ageing and Pastoral Studies, students will apply knowledge and skills to evaluate and design a pastoral and spiritual care program.
learning_outcomes: Discuss critically the differing needs and priorities of residents, their families, and staff in residential and community aged care 'situations'.
Demonstrate an understanding of models of care for older adults.
Apply knowledge and skills to design and evaluate pastoral and spiritual care programs (including the provision of ritual) for a variety of aged care 'situations'.
Evaluate critically different models of pastoral and spiritual care in a range of aged care settings.
Reflect critically on professional practice, ethics and self care, and the implications for their professional practice.
Evaluate the role of the pastoral or spiritual carer within a multidisciplinary team in various aged care contexts.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of residential and community care contexts.

title: Pastoral and Spiritual Care of Older People
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: Building on the theoretical content covered in THL445 Foundations for Pastoral and Spiritual Care of Older People, this subject examines practical strategies for enhancing quality of life and well-being in later life. It further develops understanding of how older people may find meaning in later life, explores the needs of older people for pastoral and spiritual care, and addresses ways of working with older people across the health-illness continuum. The subject prepares students to work sensitively, effectively and creatively with older people in a variety of settings, and it also explores multicultural and multifaith dimensions of ageing and aged care.
learning_outcomes: Assess the needs of older adults for pastoral and spiritual care.
Articulate and apply effective models of pastoral and spiritual care when working with older people.
Articulate and evaluate critically various paradigms of well-being and coping from religious and psychological perspectives.
Recognise and articulate the religious and spiritual needs of older adults and the relationship of such needs to health and well-being.
Articulate a biblical-theological and historical framework for pastoral and spiritual care, with particular reference to the care of older people.
Demonstrate knowledge of effective communication skills with older people.
Reflect critically on the pastoral and spiritual carer as practitioner in ageing and aged care.
Identify appropriate spiritual resources and to apply them creatively to engage the older person in developing life-giving strategies across the health-illness continuum.
Identify diverse cultural and faith backgrounds of older adults and creatively apply this knowledge to the context of pastoral and spiritual care.

title: Pastoral Care
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This practical subject aims to prepare students for pastoral ministry in community and church contexts. A model of pastoral care intervention will underpin skills development, alongside an understanding of human development and interpersonal process. Communication and interpersonal skills will be applied within the context of specific pastoral situations involving such factors as crisis, fear, anxiety, suffering, grief and loss.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an informed critical insight into the nature of pastoral care and its role in Christian ministry.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate understanding of practical, professional and ethical issues within pastoral work.
Demonstrate advanced communication skills of listening, attending, reflecting and use of questions, and also to utilise these in pastoral care settings.
Apply knowledge of appropriate assessment, intervention, and referral within pastoral care situations.
Demonstrate and communicate an understanding of specific pastoral situations.
Demonstrate appropriate self-awareness and a capacity for self-reflection.

title: Pastoral Counselling Dissertation
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will implement a research proposal and write a dissertation on the completed project in pastoral counselling. It is designed to enhance academic and professional development of students working in the field of pastoral counselling and equip graduates with analytic and conceptual competencies. The program allows significant flexibility to accommodate individual student preferences and/or professional requirements. Students will be encouraged to publish their research findings in appropriate journals.
learning_outcomes: Validate awareness and sensitivity to ethical issues arising from the dissertation in pastoral counselling.
Demonstrate an advanced ability to communicate and contextualise the pastoral counselling project.
Demonstrate effective reference to the literature.
Produce a thorough, carefully reasoned report which demonstrates an in-depth understanding of a specific area of knowledge or inquiry.
Demonstrate a high order of skill in planning and implementing a research project.

title: Pastoral Counselling Professional Practice
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will find an approved pastoral counselling placement and a suitably qualified external clinical supervisor, in consultation with the subject coordinator, in order to develop and refine their practical expertise in the area of pastoral counselling. The subject will involve case study presentations, a journal, analysis of progress, reflections on aspects of internship experience and a supervisor's report.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and demonstrate the professional use of an appropriate model of pastoral counselling.
Demonstrate creativity and flexibility in the application of advanced knowledge and skills to new and complex pastoral counselling situations.
Demonstrate independent thought in the presentation of pastoral counselling cases for supervision and discussion.
Demonstrate a high order of skill in analysis of their strengths and growth areas as a pastoral counsellor.
Reflect critically on their own experiences of being a pastoral counsellor.
Evaluate critically the role, purpose and process of supervision in pastoral counselling and reflect on their own process as a supervisee.
Demonstrate a high order of skills in the analysis and critical evaluation of aspects of their pastoral counselling placement experience.

title: Pastoral Counselling Skills
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject develops professional counselling skills that are relevant to pastoral counselling situations. It includes the establishment of a therapeutic pastoral counselling relationship and environment, the use of counselling microskills within pastoral counselling situations, and professional, ethical and theological issues for pastoral counsellors. Students will be encouraged to develop self-reflective practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate use of appropriate communication skills within a pastoral setting.
Articulate knowledge of professional, ethical and theological issues relevant to pastoral counselling.
Articulate their individual strengths and growth areas as a potential pastoral counsellor.
Establish a safe pastoral counselling environment and relationship.
Set realistic goals for pastoral counselling interventions.
Demonstrate the use of counselling microskills in pastoral counselling interventions.
Reflect on their pastoral counselling work with increasing self awareness.

title: Pastoral Counselling: Crisis Intervention
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject defines and examines the nature of pastoral counselling in relation to trauma and crisis intervention. A background to understanding trauma and its potential impact on individuals is given. Models of crisis intervention are examined, together with appropriate pastoral responses, skills training and professional issues.
learning_outcomes: Articulate a variety of pastoral situations involving crises.
Apply appropriate pastoral counselling responses to crisis situations.
Reflect critically on professional issues and their own processes in crisis situations.
Recognise the symptoms of a response to crisis and any resultant trauma.
Recognise and evaluate the presence of crisis situations.
Reflect theologically on spiritual aspects of crisis and trauma.
Outline and discuss critically crisis intervention models.
prerequisites: THL420: Pastoral Counselling: Theory and Professional Issues

title: Pastoral Counselling: Grief and Loss
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the skills and theory required for pastoral counsellors in the area of grief and loss. The skills learnt are applied to specific pastoral settings and this is integrated with a critical analysis of theological and theoretical knowledge in this foundational area of pastoral ministry.
learning_outcomes: Articulate a critical awareness of their own history of grief and loss.
Articulate and critique the theoretical stages and tasks of grief.
Demonstrate skills in working with people who have suffered grief and/or loss.
Discuss critically the various models of grief counselling.
Discern when referral is necessary.
Respond to grief and loss issues in specific pastoral situations.
Reflect critically on theological responses to grief, loss and suffering.
Recognise and respond to abnormal expressions of grief.
Articulate the various roles of the pastoral counsellor in different loss and grief contexts.

title: Pastoral Counselling: Mental Health and Trauma
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to working with mental health and trauma clients within pastoral settings. Building on the foundations of THL400 and THL420 it includes an understanding of theory and assessment in mental health work; theological and spiritual perspectives on mental health and trauma; and appropriate skills for counselling in these contexts. Students will develop knowledge and skills in dealing with mental health issues, trauma, stress and anger, domestic violence, addictions, appropriate ethical and self-reflective practice, and referral processes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of and response to professional and ethical issues arising in pastoral counselling settings.
Demonstrate a knowledge of community resources within their own particular geographical settings together with the ability to refer appropriately.
Demonstrate critical application of appropriate interventions for people with a variety of presentations, including mental health issues, trauma, domestic violence and addictions.
Demonstrate an ability to assess people with cognitive, emotional, behavioural and spiritual difficulties who present in pastoral settings.
Articulate knowledge of mental health issues, including depression and anxiety.
Self-reflect on their own pastoral counselling practice and skills.
Articulate assessment processes.
prerequisites: THL420: Pastoral Counselling: Theory and Professional Issues

title: Pastoral Counselling: Relationship and Family
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to relationship and family counselling within pastoral settings. It will include an understanding of self in relationship; theological and spiritual perspectives on family and relationship; theoretical models of relationship counselling; and appropriate skills for counselling in these contexts. Students will develop knowledge and skills in dealing with separation, divorce and remarriage, communication, conflict resolution, intimacy, sex and sexuality, and parenting in traditional, blended and other family structures. Students will be encouraged to reflect on their own values and background.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate ethical practice, including referral.
Articulate a theological understanding of relationship and family.
Demonstrate the advanced skills required for working with couples and families in the pastoral counselling setting.
Demonstrate the critcial application of the various theoretical approaches and models to working with relationships and families in the pastoral counselling setting.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of interpersonal relationships and family dynamics.
Reflect critically on their own values and family backgrounds.
Apply appropriate pastoral counselling responses to complex relational situations.
Demonstrate an understanding the spiritual perspectives that may emerge when working with couples and families.
prerequisites: THL420: Pastoral Counselling: Theory and Professional Issues
