title: Pastoral Counselling: Research Proposal
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop a research proposal within a particular area of pastoral counselling. Emphasis will be given to applying the rules and principles of research design within the context of pastoral counselling issues. The student will develop skills in choosing a research topic, conducting literature reviews, initiating research design, and writing a research proposal.
learning_outcomes: Generate research questions appropriate to pastoral counselling inquiry.
Demonstrate a high order of skill in research, writing and communication skills.

Demonstrate a high order of skill in selection, analysis, critical evaluation and synthesis of literature appropriate to the chosen area of study in pastoral counselling and complete a literature review.
Demonstrate application of research methodologies, methods of enquiry and data collection appropriate to the chosen area of pastoral counselling study.
Demonstrate an ability to plan and execute a research proposal.
Present for evaluation, a defensible research proposal.
Apply an indepth understanding of the ethical issues involved in the proposed research and to complete any required submissions to the appropriate ethics committee.

title: Pastoral Counselling: Theory and Professional Issues
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines different models of Christian and psychological counselling for pastoral work in the Australian context. Pastoral counselling situations and cases requiring counselling skills are examined, and gender, multi-cultural and indigenous perspectives, and spiritual practices in pastoral counselling are considered. Professional and ethical issues such as transference, countertransference, referral and supervision are examined in their relationship to pastoral ministry.
learning_outcomes: Outline and critically discuss relevant Christian counselling models.
Demonstrate an understanding of the spiritual practices relevant for pastoral counselling situations.
Outline and critically discuss relevant psychological counselling models.
Demonstrate a foundational knowledge of professional issues arising in pastoral counselling situations (incl values, boundaries, dual relationships, transference, countertransference, and referrals).
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of gender, multi-cultural and indigenous perspectives and their critical application to pastoral counselling practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of personal awareness in the personal development of the pastoral counsellor.
Demonstrate an understanding of ethical issues arising in pastoral counselling situations and their critical application to pastoral counselling professional practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of professional supervision for pastoral counsellors.
Demonstrate research, writing and communication skills.

title: Pastures and Profits in Grazing Systems
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students of veterinary science require a basic understanding of pasture agronomy, the growth of pastures, and pastures as a source of nutrition for grazing animals. The decisions around grazing management require an understanding of data analysis, economic principles and the relationship between costs, income from animal production and the optimisation of grazing systems from both a biological and an economic viewpoint. This subject introduces students to pasture management, farm economics and financial management, veterinary health economics and related statistical analysis in an integrated context, and prepares students for later studies of animal production, nutrition, plant toxicology, and the economics of health management in animal populations.
learning_outcomes: Describe and justify the use of economic tools to evaluate farming and veterinary health interventions and strategies.
Demonstrate knowledge of, and to appropriately apply basic statistical theory and methods, in the context of pasture agronomy, farm economics and animal health interventions.
Discuss the relationship between stocking rate and profit from grazing enterprises.
Review and communicate information within the scientific literature.
Describe the major pasture species and nutritive value of these pastures for grazing livestock.
Discuss key factors associated with the assessment and management of pastures in southern Australia.
Review and interpret financial statements, budgets and reports.
Demonstrate collaboration with their peers.

title: Pastoral Practice in Ageing: Politics, Policy and Principles
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth examination of the current practice of pastoral and spiritual care in ageing within a context of policy, politics, and principles of care and practice in a multifaith and multicultural society. Historical perspectives on community attitudes to older people and their care are examined. The subject also investigates and critiques political and policy initiatives in the care of ageing people, together with the way these are influenced by ecclesial philosophy and pastoral practice. The anticipation of future needs in an ageing society and their implications for pastoral and spiritual care are analysed.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an understanding of the spirituality and religious perspectives of other faiths with respect to pastoral care in ageing.
Demonstrate a sound understanding of the historical development of aged care services within secular and church communities.
Evaluate critically and creatively develop potential solutions for emerging issues in the provision of pastoral and spiritual care for the aged.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the translation of political policy into principles and practice in aged care within a particular social and cultural context.
Articulate a philosophy of mission and ministry for pastoral and spiritual care in ageing relevant to the students' cultural and denominational settings.
Demonstrate an understanding of Christian denominational philosophy for the delivery of pastoral and spiritual care and the shaping of aged care policy.
Articulate and evaluate critically the political development of policy in aged care.
Analyse anticipated future needs in an ageing society and their implications for pastoral and spiritual care.
prerequisites: THL466: Pastoral Practice in Ageing: Politics, Policy, Principles and Practice

title: Pastures and Rangelands
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject gives students the opportunity to understand the role and function of pasture and rangeland production systems relevant to agriculture and the equine industry in southern Australia. In addition, it will introduce students to key concepts in plant ecology as related to pasture systems. This subject is presented in a way that will encourage students to conduct experiments, use decision support systems, develop presentation skills and be able to relate to on-farm management issues.
learning_outcomes: Develop skills in the estimation of pasture biomass and botanical composition.
Understand the effects of stocking rate and grazing management systems on species survival and pasture/animal production.
Identify major pasture and rangeland species.
Understand the role of pastures in current farming systems in southern Australia, including horse properties from biological, economic and social perspectives.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a topical issue in pasture and/or rangeland management.
Understand basic concepts relating to the nutritive value of pastures for grazing livestock.
Explain basic concepts in plant ecology as related to pasture and rangeland management such as inter and intraspecific competition, plant populations dynamics and the role of stress and disturbance.
Monitor and evaluate pasture/livestock systems with respect to productivity, profitability and sustainability.
Develop pasture maintenance strategies with respect to soil fertility, weed management, control of pasture pests and supplementary irrigation.
For specific environments, recommend pasture species mixtures and appropriate establishment methodologies.
Describe the dominant features of rangeland resources and define critical factors in their management.
Explain the principles that underpin supplementary forage production and the response of grazing animals to supplementation with conserved fodder, forage crops and grain.
Explain critical events in the lifecycles of key annual and perennial pasture and rangeland species.
Explain the role of climatic, edaphic and management factors that influence the distribution of pasture species.

title: Pathological Basis of Oral and Systemic Disease
school: Centre of Rural Dentistry and Oral Health
syllabus_overview: Students will develop foundational understanding of the biochemical, cellular and tissue responses that can arise as a consequence of injury to cells, tissues and body organ systems. This understanding will be developed in the context of the aetiology and pathogenesis of basic pathological processes. This includes inflammation and sequelae, immunological reactivity, hypertrophy and hyperplasia, healing and neoplasia. Students will also examine phathogenesis pathogenesis and clinical, macroscopic, and microscopic features of common and important human diseases relevant to dental practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying inflammation, immune hypersensitivity, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, wound healing, and neoplasia, and relate these mechanisms to their clinical and histopathological presentation.
Use discipline-specific pathological terminology to analyse and interpret clinical, macroscopic and microscopic findings, and to construct structured comparisons between disease entities.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of host and causative variables (for example host co-morbidities, or the virulence of infective agents) that may affect the expression of disease.
Apply knowledge of the pathological basis of disease processes to compare and explain clinical, macroscopic, and microscopic features of common oral and systemic diseases.
Demonstrate an understanding of evidence-based practice through the critical appraisal of the current knowledge of disease processes.

title: Pathology Specimen Collection
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with the foundation knowledge required for pathology specimen collection. Students will learn, and apply, the principles of pathology collection techniques (including phlebotomy), workplace health and safety, medical terminology, infection control, including compliance policies and procedures. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in the key procedures associated with venous blood collection.
Demonstrate cultural competence regarding Indigenous and other cultures in patient care.
Explain the compliance policies and procedures associated with infection control and prevention.
Identify and explain clinical risks in pathology specimen collection.
Describe workplace health and safety regulations; and relevant first aid in pathology collection.
Define medical terminologies in pathology specimen collection.

title: Pathomechanics and Exercise Prescription
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Musculoskeletal conditions and injuries are highly prevalent in Australia and place a substantial burden on individuals and communities through the need for health care services, disruption to daily life, and lost productivity. Students will be supported to apply evidence-based strategies to manage clients with a range of musculoskeletal diagnoses and movement impairments. Students will apply knowledge of functional anatomy and musculoskeletal pathophysiology and develop practical skills in physical examination and clinical movement assessment. Students will also obtain and evaluate data to guide initial exercise prescriptions and evaluate client progress. Students will develop an awareness of the psychosocial issues associated with chronic musculoskeletal and movement impairments and use this knowledge to support clients and provide effective communication. After completing this subject, students will be able to conduct effective initial consultations to evaluate client needs, assess functional movement capabilities, and design and deliver safe and effective movement interventions to improve health and functional outcomes for people with musculoskeletal conditions and injuries.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of biopsychosocial care in the management of people living with musculoskeletal conditions.
Demonstrate capacity to communicate effectively with other health professionals regarding client treatment plans and health and functional outcomes.
Describe diagnostic techniques and the effects of treatments for musculoskeletal conditions and recognise implications for exercise prescription.
Describe the role of the exercise physiologist and other allied health professions in the management of musculoskeletal conditions and injuries.
Assess clients with musculoskeletal conditions and use the information obtained to guide the development of safe and effective exercise interventions.
Perform effective initial consultations to evaluate client needs, determine risk stratification, and identify exercise contraindications.

title: Pathophysiology and Pharmacology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores pathophysiological processes contributing to disease. This subject focuses on pathophysiological processes associated with musculoskeletal, cardiovascular and respiratory dysfunction. Relevant pharmacology is integrated throughout.
learning_outcomes: Describe the pathogenesis of common respiratory dysfunctions.
Demonstrate an understanding of cellular adaptation to injury.
Outline the major haematological pathologies and malignancies.
Describe the involvement of microorganisms in disease.
Describe the major types of musculoskeletal pathology including both mechanical and physiological injuries.
Describe use of pharmacological agents in the treatment and management of respiratory pathophysiological states.
Describe the characteristics of cancerous cells.
Describe the pathogenesis of major cardiovascular system dysfunction.
Describe the four pharmacokinetic processes (absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination).
Describe the aetiology and manifestations of shock.
Describe the consequences of alterations in fluids, electrolytes and acid base balance.
Identify the interaction and relative contribution genetic and environmental factors have on health breakdown.
Demonstrate understanding of the origin and main theories of pain.
Outline key pharmacodynamic principles (eg agonist and antagonists, receptor drug interactions).
Describe characteristics and origin of different types of cellular injury.
Define common pathophysiological and pharmacological terms.
Explain the pharmacological treatment of inflammation and pain.
Name and describe the actions of the major classes of antimicrobial drugs.
Outline the primary pharmacological interventions used in the treatment of cardiovascular disease.
prerequisites: BMS263: Foundational Pharmacology and Pathophysiology for Allied Health Practice

title: Pathophysiology for Laboratory Science (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Pathophysiology explores the aberrations in physiological processes contributing to disease and the changes that are associated with, or are a result of disease or injury. This subject includes foundational or general principles of pathophysiology and the specific pathophysiological states. The focus is on pathophysiological processes associated with the main body systems or processes, with an emphasis on common diseases affecting body systems. This subject explores how the various disciplines within medical sciences (pathology) do not function in isolation but interact in diagnosis, monitoring and management of disease.
learning_outcomes: Describe the characteristics and aetiology of different types of cellular injury and how these are investigated in the diagnostic laboratory.

Explain how disorders of one body system have consequences for other body systems and show justification on how diagnositc laboratory plays a role in the diagnosis of such disorders to create a holistic view of the role of the diagnostic laboratory on the treatment of the whole patient.

Evaluate the pathogenesis of common infections, dysfunctions in the nervous, endocrine, musculoskeletal, integumentary, immune, cardiovascular, respiratory, genitourinary and gastrointestinal systems.

title: Pathophysiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Pathophysiology explores the aberrations in physiological processes contributing to disease and the changes that are associated with, or are a result of disease or injury. This subject includes foundational or general principles of pathophysiology and the specific pathophysiological states. The focus is on pathophysiological processes associated with the main body systems or processes, with an emphasis on common diseases affecting body systems. This subject explores how the various disciplines within medical sciences (pathology) do not function in isolation but interact in diagnosis, monitoring and management of disease.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the pathogenesis of common infections, dysfunctions in the nervous, endocrine, musculoskeletal, integumentary, immune, cardiovascular, respiratory, genitourinary and gastrointestinal systems; and,.
Describe the characteristics and aetiology of different types of cellular injury and how these are investigated in the diagnostic laboratory.

Explain how disorders of one body system have consequences for other body systems and show justification on how diagnostic laboratory plays a role in the diagnosis of such disorders to create a holistic view of the role of the diagnostic laboratory on the treatment of the whole patient.

title: Pathophysiology and Pharmacology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject continues the study of pathophysiological processes contributing to disease. This subject focuses on pathophysiological processes associated with dysfunction of the nervous, endocrine, digestive, urinary and reproductive systems. Immune responses and wound healing are also covered in this subject. Relevant pharmacology is integrated throughout.
learning_outcomes: Apply foundational knowledge of pathophysiology and related pharmacology to explain the management of dysfunction of the nervous, endocrine, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, integument and immune systems.
Analyse the implications of polypharmacy, drug-drug and drug-disease interactions.
Demonstrate the application of the professional language associated with medical and pharmacological practice.

Explain the mechanism of action and properties of pharmacological agents used for the treatment of dysfunction of the nervous, endocrine, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, integument and immune systems.

title: Paul and His Letters
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the New Testament material traditionally associated with Paul. It investigates aspects of Pauline biography and theology through an exploration of both Acts and the epistles attributed to Paul. An important component of this subject is the exegetical and interpretive analysis of New Testament epistolary literature, focusing especially on 1 Corinthians and Romans.
learning_outcomes: Discuss in a critically informed way issues relating to the interpretation of the Pauline corpus.
Demonstrate developing competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts and critical engagement with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Discuss major theological and ethical themes in the Pauline corpus and assess their contemporary relevance.
Demonstrate knowledge of the historical, cultural, intellectual and religious contexts in which the Pauline corpus emerged.
Demonstrate an understanding of the provenance, theological outline, principal themes and main lines of argument of Paul's letters, especially 1 Corinthians and Romans.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate a developing understanding of critical scholarly methods such as rhetorical and socio-historical criticism.

title: PDHPE Curriculum and Pedagogy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject provides opportunities for teacher education students to examine and apply the NESA K-10 Personal Development, Health and Physical Education (PDHPE) syllabus and support materials, to the design of PDHPE programs and resources that support the diverse needs of primary school students, including those learners with a disability. In this subject, students will explore contemporary models of pedagogy relating to the teaching of personal development and health issues, as well as modified games, dance, gymnastics and fitness. The subject further allows students to create learning links between the PDHPE Strands, other Key Learning Areas, and the general capabilities, including literacy, numeracy and digital literacy. Students will investigate the role and educational value of PDHPE in the broader school curriculum, drawing on knowledge of critical transitions, including prior to school and Stage 3 to 4. The subject will further support students to use digital technologies to enhance learner outcomes in primary PDHPE.
learning_outcomes: Identify the literacy and numeracy demands of primary PDHPE and integrate literacy, numeracy and digital literacy capabilities in primary PDHPE.
Design resources using digital technologies to assist learners to achieve curriculum outcomes in PDHPE.
Adopt safe, ethical and informed use of digital technologies to assist learners to achieve curriculum outcomes.
Differentiate the curriculum to assist learners with diverse needs, including those with a disability, to achieve success.
Critique, select and apply a variety of pedagogical models to design stage appropriate, challenging and inclusive learning opportunities and assessment.

Explain the nature and role of personal development, health and physical education (PDHPE) as a discipline in supporting the health, resilience and wellbeing of children, including recent theory and practice in PDHPE.
Describe the place of PDHPE in the continuum of learning from K-10, with particular emphasis on the links between prior to school and ES1 and Stage 3 and 4.
Engage with the structure, content and requirements of the PDHPE syllabus and support materials to plan and teach quality PDHPE learning activities.

school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject provides opportunities for teacher education students to examine and apply the NESA K-10 Personal Development, Health and Physical Education (PDHPE) syllabus and support materials, to the design of programs and assessment tasks, that support and celebrate primary school students' achievement, including those children with a disability. In this subject, students will explore contemporary models of pedagogy relating to the teaching of personal development and health issues, as well as modified games, dance, gymnastics and fitness. Critique, select and apply a variety of pedagogical models to design stage appropriate, challenging and inclusive learning opportunities and assessment.
Adopt safe, ethical and informed use of digital technologies to assist learners to achieve curriculum outcomes.

title: Pedagogy in Diverse Classrooms
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The principle aim of this subject is to prepare teacher education students (TES) to appropriately and effectively teach First Nations Australian students, including those and others for whom English is an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D). In order to do this, the subject addresses a range of aspects of cultural diversity, multiculturalism, and their relationship to education in light of relevant state and national policies, and the premise of creating a more equitable and just society. This entails focussing on curriculum planning and pedagogical practice that considers and responds to histories, cultures, and languages, race, religion, and socioeconomic backgrounds, and differentiation of instruction to promote equity and excellence. An examination of the ways in which cultural diversity, expectations and values can be introduced and taught within the classroom environment is a specific focus. Attention is also given to the teaching of literacy and numeracy to First Nations Australian and EAL/D students.
learning_outcomes: Identify and reflect on how policies are applied to achieve inclusive education for students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds, including First Nations Australian students.

Critically reflect on their own developing cultural responsiveness and articulate how this has influenced decisions that strengthen relational practice in First nations Australian and multicultural contexts.

Justify pedagogical strategies that consider and address the strengths and educational needs of students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic background, including First Nations Australian students.

Develop, differentiate/modify, implement and evaluate curriculum programming, strategies and resources to include and respond to diverse/multicultural perspectives including for those for whom English is an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D).
Apply culturally responsive pedagogies for all learners and explain how these are effective for First Nations learners .

title: Pedagogies in Diverse Classrooms
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops teacher education students' understanding of issues that impact on students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds. Students will recognise and respond appropriately to the needs and strengths of culturally and linguistically diverse students and effectively teach students for whom English is an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D). They will acquire the knowledge and skills necessary to create inclusive classrooms that promote student participation, engagement and success in school. The subject addresses a range of aspects of cultural diversity, multiculturalism, and their relationship to schooling in light of relevant state and national policies, with the aim of creating a more equitable and just society. There is a focus on curriculum planning and pedagogical practice that considers and responds to histories, cultures, and languages, cultural diversity, religion, and socioeconomic backgrounds, and differentiation of instruction to promote equity and excellence. In this subject students will be required to think ethically, sociologically and reflectively and develop an understanding of the interconnections between theory, research, teaching and learning to consider how schooling and teaching can contribute to a more equitable society. An examination of the ways in which empathy, values and ethical and intercultural understandings can be introduced and taught within the classroom environment will also be considered in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Identify how social policy and the provision of resources can be utilised to achieve inclusive and equitable education for students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds.
Discuss ethical issues relating to education in a diverse Australian society and how they affect practices of inclusion, equity and achievement.

Justify pedagogical strategies that consider and address the strengths and educational needs of students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds including literacy and numeracy development.
Reflect on how teachers in mainstream classrooms promote inclusive student engagement and participation.

Apply an inclusive approach to curriculum, classroom teaching and assessment by developing, differentiating/modifying and evaluating programs, strategies and resources to respond to diversity/multicultural perspectives.

title: Pedagogy of Relationships
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Through this subject students will develop an understanding of the importance and complexity of relationships within the field of early childhood education and be introduced to the mediating role of relationships in learning. The subject analyses relationships between children and the environment and materials, and among people in the early learning setting using sociocultural frames. Students will explore various approaches to include child, parent and community voices for establishing respectful and reciprocal partnerships. This subject includes an embedded practical experience of sixty (60) hours in an early childhood setting that enables students to enact subject related tasks and content as a teaching professional within their workplace.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate strategies for engaging effectively in a wide range of relationships, enacting social justice.
Give visibility to children's capacity to make relations with the environment, materials and people.
Demonstrate understanding of the nature and enactment of power in relationships.
Document their own involvement within communities of learners.
Describe the enactment of democracy in early learning settings.
Utilise sociocultural theories and frames of analysis to interpret personal, interpersonal and cultural perspectives of learning contexts and relationships.
Identify and give visibility to respectful and responsive relationships with and among children, families and communities.
Describe elements that contribute to the formation and maintenance of communities of learners.

title: Pen Testing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: A penetration test, colloquially known as a pen test, is an authorised simulated cyber attack on a computer system, performed to evaluate the security of the system. During this subject, students will learn how to use penetration testing to gain an understanding of the security posture of IT environments and then highlight short- and long-term recommendations for increasing security. Students will then develop a comprehensive report detailing the findings of a penetration test and what steps the organisation needs to take to reduce their cyber security risk profile. The subject also provides hands-on activities for students to practice their penetration testing skills by engaging in a practical exercise in which they hack into a controlled lab environment.
learning_outcomes: Develop a detailed penetration testing report at a professional level suitable for a company executive audience.
Validate and exploit common vulnerabilities located in the attack surface of systems and applications.
Determine the plausibility of a particular set of attack vectors.
Advise on how organisations can meet cyber security compliance requirements.
Assess and report on the potential impact of cyber security breaches on a company.
Identify the vulnerabilities of systems and allocate priority to activities needed to improve security and securing infrastructure.

title: Performance Planning & Review - Bachelor of Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students are supported in their final year of studies as they progress towards professional engineering practice. They will evaluate their competencies gained throughout the course, identifying strengths and areas for improvement in the context of best practice in areas including leadership and engineering practice in Indigenous communities. They will reflect on their professional engineering identity developed throughout the course, their readiness for graduate employment and the process to obtain this. Students will be supported to develop plans to independently manage their goals and workload throughout the remainder of their studies. They will look towards their professional practice and their responsibilities for lifelong learning and continued professional development.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate their own performance as reflective practitioners and identify strengths and areas for improvement.
Reflect on the ethical considerations of civil engineering practice in the context of Indigenous and other cultures in Australia and internationally and critique current industry practice.
Formulate and implement individual action plans to manage workload and develop their professional identity in the areas of industry best practice.

title: People and the Environment
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Professionals increasingly are required to deal with complex and uncertain socio-ecological issues in both their planning and practice. Social science is the body of theory, understanding and experience that deals with the human (or social) dimensions of environmental issues. This subject places social science knowledge squarely in the domain of natural resource and environmental management through a number of case studies, including the importance of knowledge and understandings of the Indigenous people of Australia in contemporary environmental and resource management issues. Students completing this subject have a broad conceptual understanding of the importance of the human dimension in natural resource/environmental management.
learning_outcomes: Critically consider some applications of social research in natural resource/environmental management.
Appreciate the importance of the human dimension for natural resource/environmental management.
Demonstrate a broad understanding the nature and philosophy of the social sciences.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the different social science disciplines.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of how different groups of people, such as Indigenous Australians relate spiritually, emotionally, psychological and physically with the environment.
Make sound judgments on the use and application of some current methods of social research.
prerequisites: PKM101: People and Parks - Social Science Dimensions
PKM105: People and Places - Social Science Dimensions

title: Performance Planning & Review - Intermediate Cadet 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students engage in reflective practice as they further develop their identity as an intermediate cadet engineer. This subject enhances the professional growth of cadets during their intermediate cadetship by emphasising project management, teamwork, leadership, and reflective practice skills. Cadets actively recognise their duties and developmental opportunities during placement, demonstrating improvement from prior performance evaluations. With guidance from their workplace supervisors, students pursue achievement of their goals through evidence-based reflection, facilitating their professional advancement.
learning_outcomes: Apply and demonstrate project management approaches in the conduct and management of engineering projects.
Discuss the legal responsibilities pertinent to emerging engineering professionals.
Demonstrate achievement of individual goals through effective planning, and managment of the learning progress in both academic and professional contexts.
Showcase competency as reflective practitioners, discerning strengths and areas for improvement in their professional practice and the engineering field.
prerequisites: ENG382: Performance Planning & Review - Intermediate Cadet 1
ENG381: Performance Planning and Review - Intermediate Cadet

title: Performance Planning & Review - Intermediate Cadet 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students engage in reflective practice as they develop their identity as an intermediate cadet engineer, focussing on developing their project management, teamwork and leadership skills. They actively identify their responsibilities as intermediate cadets and opportunities suitable for their professional development during placement which clearly shows advancement over their previous performance planning and review subjects learning experiences. Their workplace supervisor and academic mentor will guide them in this process. Students set goals and goal management plans that help them realise their professional development, thus identify and progress in these goals through an evidence-based reflection process.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competence as reflective practitioners who identify strengths and areas for improvement in their own professional practice as well as the nature of the engineering profession.
Reflect on social, cultural, ethical, global, sustainable and technical aspects and responsibilities in engineering into their practice and identity as intermediate cadet engineers.
Reflect on working effectively in diverse teams and undertaking in leadership responsibilities.
Demonstrate individual goal setting, planning and progression to manage their learning and workload in both industry and university.
prerequisites: ENG381: Performance Planning and Review - Intermediate Cadet
ENG284: Performance Planning & Review - Junior Cadet 2

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering

They set workplace learning goals in consultation with their workplace supervisors. Students then use evidence-based reflection processes to determine if they are progressing on their goals, adjusting their professional practice where necessary. They also explore their developing professional identity by reflecting on teamwork in the workplace, and the social, cultural, ethical, global, sustainable and technical dimensions of engineering practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate individual goal setting, planning and progression in managing their learning workload in both industry and academic context.
Develop and explore their identity as junior cadet engineers given consideration to the social, cultural, ethical, global, sustainable and technical dimensions of engineering practice.
Reflect on the collaborative experiences of working in teams with power differentials between members.

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering

They reflectively evaluate their progress against their goals, revising and adapting their professional approach accordingly. Additionally, they delve into their professional identity by reflecting on ethical practice, and established engineering practices in the workplace.
learning_outcomes: Exhibit proficiency in achieving individual goals and effective management of learning tasks in both industrial and academic settings.
Interpret ethical codes and implement civil engineering standards within the workplace, while identifying avenues for enhancement.
Demonstrate proactive engagement by applying established work practices effectively.

Develop and explore their identity as junior cadet engineers within the context of enhancing the quality of the social, cultural, ethical, global, sustainable and technical outcomes of engineering practice.

Execute an action plan to develop their quality of practice from reflections on industry best practice and their academic and professional performance.

title: Person, Environment and Occupation Foundations
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the occupational therapy profession, focusing on the profession's core, interrelated concepts of person, environment, and occupation. Students will explore each of these concepts in detail to understand their dynamic relationship and their impact on health and wellbeing. They will develop skills in conducting an occupation-based activity analysis, and conduct 'person-environment-occupation' analyses to practically apply these concepts to themselves and others. Students will reflect on how their analysis could be extended to demonstrate their understanding of cultural, historical, and social determinants affecting the health and wellbeing of First Nations Australians. In addition, students will develop their academic literacy skills to build the conceptual and factual foundations of occupational therapy.
learning_outcomes: Effectively conduct occupation-based activity analyses.
Describe issues that may impact the development of skills that underlie occupation.
Discuss factors which may influence First Nations Australians' occupational participation and reflect on the relationship between people, their environments, and occupation.
Define the concepts of person, environment and occupation and discuss the relationship between these concepts and health and well-being.
Gather ideas and information from careful and critical reading, to build the conceptual and factual foundations of occupational therapy.

learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to critically reflect on their current practice in order to develop future career plans.
Identify the structures they will use to manage their learning and professional performance in the future.
Reflect on their experiences of teamwork situations and the challenges associated with this type of environment.
Set individual goals and produce a plan to manage the transition from university to their initial work placement.
Adapt and revise career plans to meet changing work conditions.
Reflect on their emerging professional identity and explain the principles of engineering practice.

title: Personal Lines Claims Management

Process facultative and treaty claims.
Finalise settlement.
Apply legal terms and concepts to Personal Lines claims management.
Participate in negotiations to settle personal lines claims.
Review claims settlement policy and procedures.
Evaluate nonroutine claims.

title: Person-Centred Care in Diverse Contexts
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students develop an eco-social understanding of health and examine concepts of planetary, global, public, population and local health. Students explore the importance of working in Partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people by evaluating policy initiatives relevant to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health alongside the influence of power and politics on health equity, justice and access. Digital capability is further developed through appraisal of the impact of digital health across diverse nursing practice contexts, with a focus on Australia's rural and remote areas.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the influence of power and politics on health equity, justice and access.
Examine the role of registered nurses across diverse practice contexts.
Appraise the impact of digital health on the delivery of safe, quality and person-centred care.
Examine the concepts and priorities of planetary, global, public, population and local health to inform responsive care.
Evaluate policy initiatives aimed specifically to address Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health at state and federal levels.

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with the knowledge and skills to assess and underwrite risk relating to personal lines classes and to survey risk exposure and interpret portfolio performance.
learning_outcomes: Draft the policy document.
Relate the general principles of Underwriting to Personal Lines insurance.
Provide quotation to proposer or intermediary.
Evaluate the risk exposures inherent in Personal Lines.
Review operational performance of policies and portfolios.
Evaluate the proposal and analyse and categorise the risk.
Decide proposed basis of cover.

title: Personal Portfolio 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students draw upon their experience in industry to demonstrate that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of a Charles Sturt computing graduate. During the session students will be required to attend, participate, and collate evidence for a professional online portfolio. Progress in the portfolio will show that they are exhibiting the required graduate attributes. This is the second subject which allows students to build their portfolios over two years.
learning_outcomes: Assemble a personal portfolio of professional activities undertaken.
Select from a variety of activities offered and provide evidence for their participation/completion.

title: Personal Portfolio
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students draw upon their experience in industry to demonstrate that they are progressively obtaining the skills and attributes expected of a Charles Sturt University computing graduate. During the session students will be required to attend and participate in approved events, and then collate evidence for a professional online portfolio. The participation in a yarning circle online to share experiences and respectfully gain new knowledge from others is an essential component of this subject.
learning_outcomes: Assemble a personal portfolio of professional activities undertaken.
Select from a variety of professional activities offered and provide evidence for their participation/completion.
Reflect on experiences with community-based information technology and apply Yarning circle methodologies to demonstrate new ways of engaging with knowledge.

title: Perspectives in Photography
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is concerned with aesthetic, stylistic, historical and social aspects of photography from its invention to the present. Critical approaches of nineteenth century writers are contrasted with those of twentieth century photographic theorists and historians. Particular attention is given to evaluating changing attitudes to photography (as reflected in photographic and art magazines and the popular press), and analyzing selected works by individual photographers and artists in other related visual media.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish the characteristics of photography as fine art from other forms, such as photojournalism, documentary, commercial and popular photography.
Demonstrate a broader and deeper critical understanding of photography and its place in art history.

title: Pharmaceutics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Pharmaceutics is the pharmacy discipline concerned with dose form design, development and manufacture and includes consideration of physiochemical characteristics of drugs and excipients, how drugs are delivered to the site of action, and product stability and quality. This subject addresses pharmaceutical science concepts including dissolution and diffusion, fluid mechanics and rheology, and surface properties. Physicochemical characteristics of drugs and excipients, and the effect on dose form design, manufacture and drug delivery will be examined, as will factors contributing to medicine product quality, including polymers, packaging, stability and quality control, sustainability and environmental impacts. A range of existing and emerging dose forms and routes of administration will be studied.
learning_outcomes: Describe a range of dose forms and routes of drug administration.
Apply pharmaceutical principles and knowledge to contemporary issues of dose form development and management.
Identify and discuss the physicochemical principles that underpin dose form design, formulation, manufacture, packaging and use.
Describe factors affecting stability of drug formulations, quality assurance procedures and shelf-life determination, and basic analytical principles applied to pharmaceutical analysis.
Explain how formulations and devices influence delivery of drugs to patients.
Accurately perform pharmaceutical calculations.

title: Pharmacokinetics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop an understanding of pharmacology, pharmaceutical chemistry and human physiology, and examine pharmaceutical, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic principles pertinent to drug action, to attain therapeutic objectives. Students will also learn about typical pharmacokinetics and special cases such as disease states, pregnancy, lactation, paediatrics and geriatrics, taking into account issues of patient compliance.
learning_outcomes: Explain the significance of client/patient compliance.
Use calculations to demonstrate the importance of pharmacokinetics in determining the bioavailability and disposition of drugs.
Outline a number of pharmacokinetic models, including: single compartment, multiple compartment and non-linear pharmacokinetics.
Demonstrate an understanding of the mechanisms of drug-drug/drug-food interactions.
Understand the biological and pharmaceutical factors influencing the absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination of drugs.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the differences in individuals which influence drug action (pharmacogenetics and pharmacogenomics).

title: Pharmacology and Therapeutics for Healthcare Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to foundational pharmacological principles. Students will explore pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and major drug classes, applying this knowledge within clinical settings. Emphasis is placed on pharmacotherapy for people experiencing acute, chronic, and emergency conditions, considering mechanisms of action, drug interactions, side effects, and contraindications. Students will develop skills to assess healthcare consumer needs and integrate critical thinking and clinical reasoning to make informed decisions regarding pharmacological interventions, preparing them for safe practice across diverse and contemporary healthcare environments.
learning_outcomes: Explain pharmacodynamic principles including the mechanisms of action, indication for administration, routes of administration, dosage, side effects, and contraindications of medications.
Explain pharmacokinetic principles, including how medications are absorbed, distributed, metabolised, and excreted.

Apply evidence-based pharmacological knowledge and demonstrate clinical reasoning to assess patient needs, make informed clinical decisions, safely administer and respond to adverse administration events across diverse healthcare environments.
Demonstrate safe practice by following legal, ethical, and professional standards and ensuring adherence with the NSQHS Medication Safety Standards.
prerequisites: NUR200: Health Assessment and Intervention: Acute Pathophysiology
NRS274: Health Challenges 2: Acute Care B
NRS171: Health Challenges 1: Acute Care A
NRS281: Pharmacology and Therapeutics for Nurses

title: Pharmacology for Medical Radiation Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will apply their knowledge of science and human physiology to the study of pharmacology. This subject provides students with an introduction to the fundamental concepts of pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and their application within the context of Medical Radiation Science departments. The subject introduces mechanisms of pharmaceutical action and interaction. Students will be introduced to medications used in a wide variety of clinical scenarios encountered in Medical Radiation Science departments.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with other health practitioners with respect to pharmaceutical procedures and delivery (MRPBA Domain 3 and 1).
Describe, explain and implement professional practice with specific reference to applying knowledge of for safe and effective use of medicines (MRPBA Domain 1.8a).
Apply knowledge of pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and the potential range of reactions to drugs or agents (MRPBA Domain 1.8c).
Monitor patients after medications for effects and reactions in accordance with protocols (MRPBA Domain 1.8e and 1.7d).
Demonstrate understanding of the risks, precautions and contraindications of pharmaceutical use (MRPBA Domain 1.8b).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence-based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1).
Recognise opportunities to contribute to the development of new knowledge through research and enquiry (MRPBA Domain 4.1d).
Identify relevant state and territory legislative requirements regarding pharmaceutical administration (MRPBA Domain 2.1a-h and 1.8).
Apply safely and effectively deliver medications to patients in accordance with procedures (MRPBA Domain 1.8d).

title: Pharmacology and Therapeutics for Nurses
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject enables students to develop the knowledge and skills required for the safe administration of medications, including relevant nursing and patient education considerations. Students will explore pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and pharmacogenetics, drug groups, principles of adverse drug effects, drug interactions, side effects, and the use and abuse of prescription and non-prescription drugs.
learning_outcomes: Discuss key issues associated with drug therapies for individuals, families and communities, including the management of side-effects of these therapies.
Identify different drug groups and explain the mode of action of the drug adverse effects, drug interactions, and side effects in the context of safe nursing practice and.
Discuss the concepts of drug misuse and abuse, physical and psychological dependence, withdrawal symptoms and development of tolerance, in the context of safe nursing practice.
Describe the core concepts of drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion in the context of safe nursing practice across the lifespan.

title: Pharmacology for Midwives
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will extend their existing knowledge of pharmacology, medication administration, and the associated legal and ethical considerations in the context of midwifery practice. Students will focus on the physiological changes that occur during the childbearing period that impact pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics and apply this knowledge to medication administration. In addition to prescribed and over the counter medications, students will also consider the effects of complementary and alternative medicines, and recreational and illicit drug use on the woman, fetus and neonate during pregnancy and the postpartum period.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of the principles of pharmacology associated with midwifery practice including pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of over- the-counter and prescribed medications, and recreational and illicit drugs.
Discuss the legal and ethical obligations of the midwife regarding medication management across the childbearing continuum.
Discuss the impact of social pharmacology, illicit drug use and complementary and alternative medicines for the mother, the newborn, and foetus /placental transfers across the childbearing continuum.
Analyse how medications affect physiological, biochemical and pathophysiological processes during childbearing.

title: Pharmacotherapeutics
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The focus of this subject is pharmacotherapeutics, which is the study of the therapeutic use of medicines and their effects, both beneficial and deleterious. To successfully complete this course you will need to have a firm foundational knowledge in pharmacology and pathophysiology. The topics in this subject have also been aligned with the other 4th year Pharmacy subjects so that similar topics are delivered concurrently to help facilitate the integration of your pharmacy knowledge from other subjects. The topics and tasks included in this subject have been designed so that by the time you have finished you should be able to analyse a patient's medication regimen and design a new regimen which enhances their health outcomes. Students entering this subject are assumed to have completed the first 3 years of the Bachelor of Pharmacy.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the pharmacological impacts of a patient's medication on their health or quality of life.
Develop strategies to minimise the impact of drug dependence, resistance or tolerance on patient health outcomes.
Analyse a patient's drug regimen and develop new drug regimens to improve the patient's health and quality of life.
Identify the right drug for the right patient to obtain the right response.
Identify the pharmacological impacts of medication on patient adherence.

title: Pharmacy Practice 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will commence the detailed study of issues that underpin professional pharmacy practice in both a community and hospital setting. The subject will include extemporaneous dispensing and will relate those skills to the physicochemical principles studied in pharmaceutics. The subject will also include a development of the communication, sociological and ethical issues that were introduced earlier, as well as a detailed examination of the regulatory, legislative and occupational health and safety framework within which Pharmacists must practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the impact of and apply different communication techniques used in counselling.
Differentially diagnose common self-limiting disease states and offer appropriate management.
Discuss the impact of sociological and ethical factors on health outcomes.
Accurately and safely compound extemporaneous products and document their manufacture.
Reflect on and discuss the importance of interprofessional collaboration in the pharmacy context.
Discuss the impact of regulatory and legislative frameworks on pharmacy practice.

title: Philosophy of Prophet Muhammad's Life (Sirah)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject offers a critical examination of the life of Prophet Muhammad, encompassing aspects such as pre-Islamic Arabia, his early life before prophethood, the Meccan period, his migration to Medina and the significant events that unfolded during his life in Medina. Students will meticulously study and analyse these pivotal events and milestones in his life in the context of the modern world, enabling correlations and evaluations to be made. Furthermore, this subject explores the social transformations that occurred during the lifetime of Prophet Muhammad and their significant impact on shaping human history. It delves into the dynamics at play during that era, elucidating their relevance and significance to contemporary time. In addition to examining Prophet Muhammad’s character and personality, the subject addresses contemporary criticisms and controversial topics surrounding his life.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the social transformations during his lifetime and their implication on the contemporary Muslim world.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the different roles Prophet Muhammad assumed during his life.
Critically evaluate common misconceptions about Prophet Muhammad and his life.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the main events in the life of Prophet Muhammad and the unfolding of a Muslim community.
Develop independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.

title: Physical Activity across the Lifespan
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will focus on the role of the podiatrist in maintaining a person’s physical activity, mobility and independence across the lifespan, to ensure optimal physical and mental health. Students will explore opportunities for podiatrists to collaborate as part of an interdisciplinary rehabilitation team. Students will extend their understanding of lower limb physiology and pathology in the context of daily activity, sport and exercise. Students will develop knowledge and skills in the assessment and management of diverse groups, with an emphasis on the practical application of therapeutic modalities and digital technologies for rehabilitation and activity-based interventions. This subject will contribute to the student’s preparation for endorsement for scheduled medicine and progression towards competence in prescribing injectable corticosteroid drugs.
learning_outcomes: Discuss relevant potential benefits, harms, medicine-related and person-specific factors to inform an ethical justification for the use of drugs to treat musculoskeletal pathology.

Justify pharmaceutical and non-pharmacological management options for musculoskeletal pathology affecting the foot and leg to demonstrate adequate and current knowledge of medicines prior to prescribing.
Demonstrate correct application of therapeutic modalities and provide an ethical justification for their use.
Use an evidence-based approach when recommending activity-based interventions for acute and chronic conditions as part of a holistic person-focused rehabilitation program.
Apply fundamental principles of rehabilitation and sports medicine to maintain and enhance physical activity across the lifespan.
Explain the role of a podiatrist in an interdisciplinary rehabilitation team.
prerequisites: POD316: Sports Medicine and Electrophysical Agents

title: Physics for Engineers
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an in-depth exploration of the principles of sound, waves, optics, and light, with a focus on their applications in engineering.
learning_outcomes: Analyse optical systems, including mirrors, lenses, and optical instruments, to understand image formation and aberrations.
Describe the fundamental principles of sound, waves, optics, and light, including their characteristics and properties.
Evaluate the behaviour of sound waves and light waves in different media and engineering applications.
Use mathematical representations and equations to describe and solve wave phenomena in engineering contexts.

title: Physics for Medical Radiation Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides essential physics within the context of medical radiation science. It provides the fundamental knowledge and understanding of a wide range of topics from important physical laws and concepts relevant to medical radiation science.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate comprehension of and perform calculations involving both radiation production and interaction, and the associated radiological quantities.
Recognise and describe the principles of radiation physics.
Compute and solve problems of a conceptual and quantitative nature in the above areas of medical radiation physics.
Describe and perform calculations in atomic physics, semiconductors and solid state devices.
Demonstrate an understanding of, and perform calculations in, DC electricity, magnetism and AC electricity.

title: Physiological Sciences 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundation study of the human body using an integrated systems approach. The primary focus of this subject will be on the physiological processes underlying the function of each body system. After an introduction to anatomical terminology and cell biology, the emphasis of the subject is on the physiology of the nervous, endocrine, skeletal and muscular systems.
learning_outcomes: Apply anatomical and physiological concepts to explain how they support the normal functioning of the body.
Communicate anatomical and physiological concepts using discipline specific terminology and illustrations.
Identify and explain the principal structures, features, functions, and location of the nervous, endocrine, cutaneous, skeletal, and muscular systems.
prerequisites: BMS161: Health and the Human Body: Cells, Immunity and Musculoskeletal System
BMS162: Health and the Human Body: Systemic Human Physiology

title: Physiotherapy Capstone Placement
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy Capstone Placement provides physiotherapy students with the opportunity to undertake a 25 day sustained period of physiotherapy clinical practice in a workplace setting. Students will be required to demonstrate knowledge, skills and attributes in professional physiotherapy practice; client assessment; clinical reasoning; intervention planning; implementation of physiotherapy management; and evaluate the effectiveness of management strategies and physiotherapy management to a range of clients who present with complex care needs. The placement setting undertaken in PHS424 will differ from other workplace learning subjects to ensure students cover the full range of areas required for course completion and Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) registration. Students' learning will be enabled through direct client contact under the supervision of qualified physiotherapists and other health professionals. Students will integrate knowledge from their university studies into clinical practice. Students will be assessed for their achievement of the Australian Standards for Physiotherapy using the criteria and forms developed for use in the Assessment of Physiotherapy Practice (APP). Successful engagement in this capstone clinical placement will enhance students' abilities to apply their professional skills and knowledge and attain professional practice competency expected of a new graduate, as consistent with contemporary standards of physiotherapy clinical practice.
learning_outcomes: Effectively integrate skills in assessment, clinical reasoning, planning and implementation of physiotherapy management for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.
Deliver effective physiotherapy management to a range of clients who present with complex care needs.
Articulate and demonstrate their achievement of entry-level competency relevant to the clinical setting.
Integrate and apply knowledge gained from academic subjects for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.

Demonstrate achievement of the standards required of an entry level physiotherapist as defined by the Physiotherapy Practice Thresholds in Australia and Aotearoa, New Zealand (2023) relevant to the clinical setting.

title: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 1
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 1 provides physiotherapy students with the opportunity to undertake a 25 day sustained period of physiotherapy clinical practice in a workplace setting. The purpose of this 25 day clinical placement is to enable students to develop and consolidate knowledge, skills and attributes in: professional physiotherapy practice; client assessment; clinical reasoning; intervention planning; the implementation of physiotherapy management; and evaluation of physiotherapy management strategies. The placement setting undertaken in PHS416 will differ from other workplace learning subjects to ensure students cover the full range of areas required for registration with Ahpra (Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency) and course completion. Students' learning will be enabled through direct client contact under the supervision of qualified physiotherapists and other health professionals. Students will integrate knowledge from their university studies into clinical practice. Students will be assessed for their achievement of the Australian Standards for Physiotherapy using the criteria and forms developed for use in the Assessment of Physiotherapy Practice (APP).
learning_outcomes: Integrate and apply knowledge gained from academic subjects for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.
Effectively integrate skills in assessment, clinical reasoning, planning and implementation of physiotherapy management for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.

Demonstrate achievement of the standards required of an entry level physiotherapist as defined by the Physiotherapy Practice Thresholds in Australia and Aotearoa, New Zealand (2023) relevant to the clinical setting.
Articulate and demonstrate their achievement of entry-level competency relevant to the clinical setting.
prerequisites: PHS314: Consolidation of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice
PHS350: Integrated Chronic Health Condition Management

title: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 2
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 2 provides physiotherapy students with further opportunity to undertake a 25 day sustained period of physiotherapy clinical practice in a workplace setting. The purpose of this 25 day clinical placement is to enable students to further develop and consolidate knowledge, skills and attributes in professional physiotherapy practice; client assessment; clinical reasoning; intervention planning; implementation of physiotherapy management; identify the role of other health professionals; and evaluate the effectiveness of management strategies. The placement setting undertaken in PHS417 will differ from other workplace learning subjects to ensure students cover the full range of areas required for registration with Ahpra (Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency) and course completion. Students' learning will be enabled through direct client contact under the supervision of qualified physiotherapists and other health professionals. Students will integrate knowledge from their university studies into clinical practice. Students will be assessed for their achievement of the Australian Standards for Physiotherapy using the criteria and forms developed for use in the Assessment of Physiotherapy Practice (APP).
learning_outcomes: Integrate and apply knowledge gained from academic subjects for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.

Demonstrate achievement of the standards required of an entry level physiotherapist as defined by the Physiotherapy Practice Thresholds in Australia and Aotearoa, New Zealand (2023) relevant to the clinical setting.
Effectively integrate skills in assessment, clinical reasoning, planning and implementation of physiotherapy management for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.
Articulate and demonstrate their achievement of entry-level competency relevant to the clinical setting.
prerequisites: PHS314: Consolidation of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice
PHS350: Integrated Chronic Health Condition Management

title: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 3
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 3 provides physiotherapy students with further opportunity to undertake a 25 day sustained period of physiotherapy clinical practice in a workplace setting. The purpose of this 25 day clinical placement is to enable students to further develop and consolidate knowledge, skills and attributes in professional physiotherapy practice; client assessment; clinical reasoning; intervention planning; implementation of physiotherapy management; demonstrate leadership skills; and evaluate the effectiveness of management strategies. The placement setting undertaken in PHS418 will differ from other workplace learning subjects to ensure students cover the full range of areas required for registration with Ahpra (Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency) and course completion. Students' learning will be enabled through direct client contact under the supervision of qualified physiotherapists and other health professionals. Students will integrate knowledge from their university studies into clinical practice. Students will be assessed for their achievement of the Australian Standards for Physiotherapy using the criteria and forms developed for use in the Assessment of Physiotherapy Practice (APP).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate achievement of the standards required of an entry level physiotherapist as defined by the Physiotherapy Practice Thresholds in Australia and Aotearoa, New Zealand (2023) relevant to the clinical setting.
Integrate and apply knowledge gained from academic subjects for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.
Effectively integrate skills in assessment, clinical reasoning, planning and implementation of physiotherapy management for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.
Articulate and demonstrate their achievement of entry-level competency relevant to the clinical setting.
prerequisites: PHS314: Consolidation of Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy Practice
PHS329: Supporting Participation: Physiotherapy across the Lifespan
PHS350: Integrated Chronic Health Condition Management

title: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 4
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy Competency Placement 4 provides physiotherapy students with further opportunity to undertake one (1) placement of 25 days of physiotherapy clinical practice in a workplace setting. The purpose of this 25 day clinical placement is to enable students to further develop and consolidate knowledge, skills and attributes in professional physiotherapy practice; client assessment; clinical reasoning; intervention planning; implementation of physiotherapy management; reflect on their capacity to seek, accept and respond to feedback; and evaluate the effectiveness of management strategies. The placement setting undertaken in PHS419 will differ from other workplace learning subjects to ensure students cover the full range of areas required for course completion and registration with AHPRA (Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency). Students' learning will be enabled through direct client contact under the supervision of qualified physiotherapists and other health professionals. Students will integrate knowledge from their university studies into clinical practice. Students will be assessed for their achievement of the Australian Standards for Physiotherapy using the criteria and forms developed for use in the Assessment of Physiotherapy Practice (APP).
learning_outcomes: Articulate and demonstrate their achievement of entry-level competency relevant to the clinical setting.

Demonstrate achievement of the standards required of an entry level physiotherapist as defined by the Physiotherapy Practice Thresholds in Australia and Aotearoa, New Zealand (2023) relevant to the clinical setting.
Effectively integrate skills in assessment, clinical reasoning, planning and implementation of physiotherapy management for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.
Integrate and apply knowledge gained from academic subjects for a range of clients within the specific clinical setting.
prerequisites: PHS307: Fundamentals of Physiotherapy Clinical Experience

title: Planning Environmental Education and Interpretation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: What is the best way to get your message across to your visitors? This subject examines the important role of communication planning and in particular environmental education and interpretation in environmental management and ecotourism operations. The subject looks at the theory and practice of public communication planning for government agencies and ecotourism operations. The main issues covered include identification of the audience, the use of media, the preparation of an interpretation plan, and the use of different media. The subject has no intensive. On completion, student will be apply their knowledge and initiative to plan and design interpretive and environmental education materials in a range of contexts.
learning_outcomes: Have a critical understanding the role of interpretation and environmental education in conservation and ecotourism.
Have the ability to apply their knowledge and initiative to plan and design interpretive and environmental education materials in a range of contexts.
Have an understanding the role of communication and environmental education in raising awareness, and changing attitudes and behaviour.
Have an understanding of the principles of good public environmental communication.

title: Planning for Diverse Learners
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to understand the issues that impact on children from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds and to develop a range of teaching strategies to teach these children. The way in which teaching can contribute to a more equitable and just society, is also a component of this subject. The increasing diversity in schools and early childhood services provides both opportunities and challenges. Current and future teachers need to acquire the knowledge and skills necessary to maximise the opportunities that cultural diversity offers and minimise its challenges. In this subject students will learn how to design learning experiences for diverse learners. This includes developing knowledge and skills relating to applying culturally inclusive curriculum and pedagogical approaches, differentiating teaching approaches and assessment for a range of learners, and utilising a range of existing frameworks required for their context. Students will design a differentiated unit of instruction and complete a rationale for their design. In designing the unit they will consider the learning strengths and needs of children from specific diverse groups in the community, including Indigenous Australian children, children from culturally, linguistically and socially diverse backgrounds and gifted learners.
learning_outcomes: Have an understanding of ethical issues relating to education in a diverse Australian society.
Design a sequence of lessons that demonstrates application of culturally inclusive approaches to curriculum, classroom teaching, selecting resources and assessment.
Demonstrate knowledge of culturally inclusive pedagogy and effective teaching strategies that are responsive to the strengths and needs of diverse learners.
