Demonstrate how teachers can collaborate with a range of specialist teachers, community liaison personnel and ESL and Community Language teachers to promote inclusive student engagement and participation.
Differentiate a sequence of lessons to meet the specific needs of students and articulate the value and effectiveness of the differentiation strategies utilised in the lessons.
Identify how social policy and provision are applied to achieve inclusive education for students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds.

title: Planning for Professional Placement
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the foundation for students' professional placement. This subject is designed to develop students' employability skills and their understanding of professional practice, including the job application process. Students will be required to engage with content about the information sector and reflect on professional expectations/standards and their own potential career trajectory.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on their own potential career trajectory.
Engage effectively with industry professionals.
Contextualise and discuss professional expectations/standards.
Successfully organise a professional placement.

title: Planning Health Services
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject takes a population health approach in developing needs assessments, service plans, models of care, and strategic and facility commissioning plans. In doing this, students learn strategies for engaging with priority populations, referencing First Nations approaches to health and well-being. Students will learn how to model a positive attitude towards future health care design and delivery challenges including responsive practices when working with First Nations peoples.
learning_outcomes: Develop needs assessments, service plans and models of care.
Source and analyse organisational and health data for health service improvement, and.
Discuss strategies for engaging with priority populations for future health care design and delivery.
Describe key elements of a health-related strategic plan.
Create a plan for commissioning a health facility that is health-enhancing, fit for purpose and legislatively compliant.
Critique evidence for improving First Nations health including culturally responsive practices.

title: Planning for Professional Placement
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the foundation for students' professional placement. This subject is designed to develop students' employability skills and their understanding of professional practice, including the job application process. Students will be required to engage with content about the information sector and reflect on professional expectations/standards and their own potential career trajectory.
learning_outcomes: Engage effectively with industry professionals.
Articulate professional expectations/standards.
Reflect on their own potential career trajectory.
Successfully organise a professional placement.

title: Planning Practice-Based Research Projects in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students explore clinical research as a component of professional practice. Students identify a speech pathology practice-based topic of interest, for which they search, analyse and synthesise information from a range of sources using an evidence-based practice framework. They then identify a specific gap in knowledge and develop a research question that could form the basis of a research project focusing on prevention, education and/or promotion of communication and swallowing issues, or speech pathology assessment or intervention. This process is self-directed but supported by the subject coordinator, learning materials and a collegial forum of peers. The project is continued in SPH526 (Designing, conducting and evaluating research based projects in speech pathology).
learning_outcomes: Apply cognitive, technical and creative skills to independently investigate, analyse and synthesise information, problems, concepts and theories in order to develop, communicate and justify a clinically relevant research question.
Demonstrate knowledge of research principles and methods applicable to speech pathology practice.
Reflect critically on theoretical knowledge and professional practice.

title: Plant Physiology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on concepts introduced in first year botany and plant science subjects to explore the cellular and biochemical processes that control the development, growth, and productivity of plants. Students will learn about whole-plant physiology and structure, including how plants acquire water and nutrients, and the functioning of the plant vascular system. Students will learn about the processes of photosynthesis and respiration, and gain an appreciation for the ways these processes interact to provide plants with energy. Students will learn how plant cells control development and growth, including processes of flowering and fruit development, and the metabolism and activity of plant hormones. Finally, students will learn how environmental conditions influence plant growth and productivity, and the impact of plant symbiotic relationships.
learning_outcomes: Explain how plants interact with their abiotic and biotic environments.
Describe metabolic and structural components of plant water balance, mineral nutrition, and sugar transport.
Collect, record, interpret, and communicate experimental results related to plant physiological and developmental processes.
Describe the processes of plant vegetative and reproductive development.
Apply knowledge from discrete topics to interpret and explain whole-plant physiology.
Describe the processes of photosynthesis and respiration.

title: Plant Production Systems
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, the diversity of plant production systems is explored and the basics of plant growth and development investigated. Students will identify key plant production species and develop an understanding of the key management processes associated with significant horticultural, broad-acre and irrigated plant production species. Students will also build an understanding of key concepts associated with plant growth including adaptation, yield and positive and negative inter-species interactions.
learning_outcomes: Explain how breeding objectives and techniques are used to meet geo-climatic, market, societal and management needs.

Explain key concepts associated with plant growth and development including physiological requirements for growth, adaptation, yield and positive and negative inter-species interactions and how these features differ between species.
Identify key agriculturally significant plant production species grown in Australia including those of horticulture, broad-acre and irrigated production systems.

Describe and analyse major plant-production systems (including those of horticulture, broad-acre and irrigated production systems) in terms of their temporal and geographic distribution, their production outputs and key management processes associated with establishment, in-crop management, harvest and post-harvest management.

title: Plant Taxonomy and Systematics
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the classification, naming, identification and floral biology of plants. The taxonomy and reclassification of Australia's two largest and iconic plant groups, the acacias and the eucalypts, are emphasised. Students will develop skills in preparing and curating herbarium specimens, and in identifying native and exotic species, using conventional and computer-based keys.
learning_outcomes: Use the morphological characteristics of leaf and flower structure and arrangement to identify and classify plants.
Apply the theoretical aspects of plant taxonomy to explain the principles and purposes of biological classification.
Accurately recognise and distinguish between the major families of Australian plants.
Prepare, identify, and classify herbarium specimens of native and exotic species.
Use and construct plant identification tools, such as dichotomous keys, to successfully classify plants.

title: Play and Learning
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn theories of play and their value for young children's learning. An embedded practical experience in an early childhood setting will enable students to observe, describe and reflect on the activity of children participating in play based programs, the role of the teacher in implementing and evaluating learning based on their understanding of individual children's interests and dispositions and the impact of physical spaces on play. Students will develop and implement play based learning experiences and evaluate their planned experience, suggesting ways to improve and extend the learning of children engaged with the activity.
learning_outcomes: Define the forms of play that young children engage with and explain how development and learning is supported by play.
Describe the use of space, materials and environment and discuss these aspects as elements that impact on children's learning.
Complete a series of journal entries that explore the role of the teacher in utilising play for learning in an early childhood setting.
Make detailed observations of children playing, recording the actions, interactions and responses of children and draw links between the observations and theories.
Plan activities for children in an early childhood setting, implement them and evaluate the response to the activity, and their role in supporting children's learning through the activity.
prerequisites: EMC203: Play and Investigation as Curriculum (Literacy)
EMC204: Play and Investigation as Curriculum (Science and Mathematics)

title: Podcast Fundamentals
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the fundamental steps in making a podcast including developing a concept, choosing a format, recording, editing and uploading your content.
learning_outcomes: Be able to explain the concept for a podcast to meet specific requirements
Be able to plan, record, edit and produce podcast content

title: Podiatric Biomechanics
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a detailed understanding of the biomechanical principles associated with human movement. Students will build on their knowledge of anatomy to analyse the function of the lower limb and associated structures. This subject will provide students with the opportunity to develop skills in the assessment, evaluation and management of lower limb biomechanical disorders. Students will be required to apply this knowledge in future subjects to inform the prescription of orthomechanical devices, as part of comprehensive case management.
learning_outcomes: in a simulated setting, assess a client's lower limbs and gait to determine normal and abnormal function;
apply relevant biomechanical theory to analyse pathomechanics and inform treatment options.
explain basic kinetic and kinematic biomechanical principles such as gravity, balance, equilibrium, levers, mechanical advantage and how they relate to motion;
apply the fundamental concepts and principles of biomechanics to lower limb function;
evaluate relevant assessment information to hypothesise the cause of abnormal structure and function in the lower limb; and
prerequisites: BMS172: Functional Anatomy of the Vertebral Column, Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb

title: Podiatric Clinical Practice and Diagnostics
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends the students’ understanding of podiatric clinical practice and enables consolidation of skills in communication, assessment, and management. Students will be given the opportunity to develop their professional practice through the completion of both internal and external work-integrated learning experiences. Students will be introduced to a range of rheumatological pathologies and develop skills in the ethical application of commonly used diagnostic modalities. While considering a broad range of evidence-based management options, students will consider the use of prescription and non-prescription drugs in rheumatological medicine. This will contribute to the students' preparation for endorsement for scheduled medicines and progression towards competence in prescribing non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines and gout medicines.
learning_outcomes: prescribe diagnostic investigations correctly and ethically for a range of rheumatological and non-rheumatological conditions and analyse diagnostic images and reports to inform person-focused care;
demonstrate safe and professional management practices in a clinical environment when managing cutaneous presentations.
obtain, interpret, and apply current reliable evidence and information about medicines to inform decision making for a range of rheumatological conditions;
select and perform relevant neurological, vascular, musculoskeletal and cutaneous assessments in a clinical setting to inform a clinical diagnosis;
apply knowledge of the assessment, diagnosis and prognosis of a range of rheumatological pathologies;
evaluate a person's health record, social and medical history and communicate relevant findings effectively with others;

develop a management plan for a person with an uncomplicated podiatric presentation and communicate effectively with the patient and the healthcare team, and the continuation or variation of that plan; and
prerequisites: POD204: Podiatry and Community Health Practice

title: Podiatric Paediatrics and Orthomechanics
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a detailed understanding of the human developmental process, from conception to maturity. Students will study a range of paediatric conditions that podiatrists can assess, evaluate and manage as part of a holistic client centred approach to health. Students will be provided with the opportunity to further develop communication skills and team work skills through collaborative group work. Additionally, this subject enables students to apply their knowledge of biomechanical principles associated with human movement, to a range of orthomechanical management strategies for clients of all ages.
learning_outcomes: apply knowledge of normal physical, cognitive, social and emotional development - from conception to maturity - to a range of diagnostic scenarios;
assess, diagnose and manage a range of paediatric conditions that may present in podiatric practice;
demonstrate effective communication skills for holistic client centred health management; and
identify principles of environmental sustainability in podiatry practice.
apply knowledge of the therapeutic modalities used in biomechanical case management to develop appropriate management plans for their clients;
analyse the legal and ethical considerations relevant to podiatric practice including their role as a mandatory reporter;

title: Podiatry Capstone Placement
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the podiatry capstone placement during which students are expected to demonstrate the capability for independent practice in accordance with the Ahpra Shared Code of Conduct and the Podiatry Professional Capabilities (2022). Students will work in partnership with the patient, their carers and clinical educators to demonstrate the knowledge, skills and attitudes expected for entry-level practice. Students will complete two placements: a second external placement OR an internal placement and; a final internal consolidation placement in the on-campus clinic. Clinical practice will include opportunities to implement guidelines relevant to prescribing, to inform evidence-based decisions in the context of the person's needs.
learning_outcomes: critically reflect on personal learning and the application of this learning to future professional practice.
comply with applicable professional standards, codes of conduct and guidelines relevant to prescribing medicines to inform evidence-based decisions in the context of the patient’s needs; and
analyse indications and key issues associated with the appropriate use of prescription and non-prescription medications relevant to a range of case presentations;
apply skills in clinical reasoning to justify an evidence-based approach to the assessment and management of diverse patients in need of podiatry care;
practice in a manner that aligns with legislative and regulatory requirements and ensures patient safety is protected;
communicate effectively to educate and promote intervention and prevention strategies with the patient, their carers and the broader community;

title: Podiatry and Community Health Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable students to further develop their professional practice as a podiatry practitioner, within a real clinical setting. Students will explore opportunities to reduce barriers and facilitate meaningful engagement in healthcare for diverse groups and particularly for First Nations peoples and older people. Students will explore prevailing social attitudes about ageing and the impact these have on choices, opportunities, and wellbeing for older people. The subject also introduces various aspects of age-related health, biological and social changes, and development, and allows students an opportunity to consider how to enable a person to age well. Students will investigate elements of the Australian health system and services available to older people in the community, examining opportunities for partnership and health promotion work. This subject will also build the students’ understanding of prescription medicines relevant to a person’s needs, in the context of podiatry.
learning_outcomes: identify and develop health promotion opportunities to facilitate healthy ageing for people engaging with a podiatrist.
analyse the issues facing older people in relation to health, wellbeing, choice and independence; and
effectively apply neurological, vascular, musculoskeletal and cutaneous assessments for a range of clients and accurately record findings in a clinical setting;

gather relevant information with due consideration of a person’s cultural and social history, to explain their needs in relation to treatment with prescribed medicines and non-pharmaceutical interventions;
identify potential barriers to meaningful engagement in healthcare for diverse groups and particularly for First Nations peoples and older people;
consistently review existing management plans for low risk podiatric presentations and communicate effectively with the patient and the healthcare team the continuation of that plan;
demonstrate safe and sustainable practice in a clinical environment with due consideration of people, equipment, and the environment;
prerequisites: POD203: Introduction to Podiatric Clinical Practice
POD112: Introduction to Podiatric Clinical Practice
BMS172: Functional Anatomy of the Vertebral Column, Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb

title: Podiatry Capstone Placement (Honours)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the podiatry capstone placement during which students are expected to demonstrate the capability for independent practice in accordance with the Ahpra Shared Code of Conduct and the Podiatry Professional Capabilities (2022). Students will work in partnership with the patient, their carers and clinical educators to demonstrate the knowledge, skills and attitudes expected for entry-level practice. Students will complete a final internal consolidation placement in the on-campus clinic. Clinical practice will include opportunities to implement guidelines relevant to prescribing, to inform evidence-based decisions in the context of the person's needs.
learning_outcomes: apply skills in clinical reasoning to justify an evidence-based approach to the assessment and management of diverse patients in need of podiatry care;
communicate effectively to educate and promote intervention and prevention strategies with the patient, their carers and the broader community;
comply with applicable professional standards, codes of conduct and guidelines relevant to prescribing to inform evidence-based decisions in the context of the patient’s needs; and
critically reflect on personal learning and the application of this learning to future professional practice.
analyse indications and key issues associated with the appropriate use of prescription and non-prescription medications relevant to a range of case presentations;
practice in a manner that aligns with legislative and regulatory requirements and ensures patient safety is protected;

title: Podiatry for Chronic Disease Management
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject has a focus on chronic disease relevant to podiatry practice and national health priority areas. Students will evaluate the physiological, psychological, and emotional impact of chronic disease on the person, their family and carers, and the broader community. The impact of chronic disease e.g. diabetes, on foot health, mobility, and independence is a specific focus. Consideration of the interplay of social, cultural, historical, and institutional factors will inform the students’ capability to provide culturally responsive care and enable improved health outcomes for peoples living with chronic disease. Students will consider the roles of different stakeholders and opportunities for interprofessional collaborative practice with a person, their family and carers, health professionals and organisations, to enable agency and self-determination in chronic disease management.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the impact of chronic disease on the person, family and carers, and the broader community.
Analyse the complex interrelationship between physiological, psychological, and emotional health in chronic disease.
Evaluate the impact of chronic disease e.g. diabetes, on foot health, mobility, and independence.
Analyse the principles of culturally responsive and culturally safe practice to enable optimal health and wellbeing outcomes for First Nations peoples living with chronic disease.
Propose opportunities to work in partnership with a person, their family and carers, and other agencies to enable health promotion for chronic disease management.
prerequisites: POD308: The Diabetic Foot and Chronic Wound Management

title: Policing and the Community
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Policing and the Community examines the interactions between police, the public and community. Students in this subject will examine a range of topics including history of policing, police work, discretion and accountability, occupational culture, deviance and corruption, models of policing, contemporary developments and miscarriages of justice. The subject will examine contemporary issues and perspectives on the role of police.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast a range of policing styles.
Describe the concepts of police accountability, legitimacy, and culture and connect this to the relationship between police and the community.
Describe a range of different perspectives on the role of police in the community and society.
Explain the basis of police power and how the institutional and political power of the service also shapes the role of police.
Explain the historical development and function of the police service as a criminal justice institution in Australia.
Articulate the key debates in contemporary policing.

title: Policy and Claims Handling
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the basic knowledge and skills required to analyse and settle insurance claims
learning_outcomes: Analyse insurance claims.
Compile information in relation to claims.
Be ale to participate in negotiations related to claims payments.
Resolve claims.
Settle claims.

title: Policing and the Media.
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the role of the media in modern society and the historical and contemporary relationship that exists between policing and the media. The subject covers three main topic areas. The first discusses the history, nature and importance of police-media relations. In the second topic, students conduct a review of a policing organisation's approach to the media, both at a corporate level and in a community policing or specialist area relevant to the subject participant. The third topic focuses on the development of a media strategy to support an operational plan that addresses a localised crime or strategic policing issue.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Develop an operational or corporate media strategy to address a local organisation or policing issue.
Investigate an organisation/media or police/media relationship, aspects both positive and negative and apply to the development of a media release.
Research an organisation's media policies, the role of the media department, marketing and communication branches, and the role of the levels of the hierarchy in engaging the media.
Develop and implement effective strategies and practices for engaging with the media and proactively promote police/ organisation operational and strategic goals.

title: Policy, Power and Social Action
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: How do people change society? This subject examines how people create social change within the context of contemporary governance systems. Drawing on sociological theories of social power, change and movements, it explores political and policy structures, discourses and ideologies, and the ways in which people and organisations influence them. Particular attention is paid to social movements as social mechanisms through which people continue to drive social change. Contemporary public and policy issues concerning social justice, democracy, the economy and the environment are examined to illustrate these social processes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of social movements and related theory.
Critically evaluate the strategies of social movements.
Critically analyse current issues in terms of the social forces acting to bring change and their significance to democracy.
Discuss change processes within contemporary governance contexts.
Analyse key sociological theories of power.
prerequisites: SOC218: Policy, Power and Social Action

title: Political Ideas
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students are introduced to political philosophy: the study of politics from the perspective of philosophy. Political philosophy involves ethical or "normative" analysis of political structures. Students will think about what sorts of political institutions we "ought" to have, focusing on arguments drawn from a range of influential thinkers from ancient Greece to 19th century Europe. These disparate visions of the "just society" will each be examined with reference to their contribution to the modern political world and the cultural context in which they were conceived.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply key concepts from political philosophy.
Recognise the expansion of political ideas as they have developed over the centuries.
Recognise the contested nature of political ideas that we often take for granted.
Identify underlying themes and issues that fuel contemporary political discourse.
Identify how historical, sociological and economic facts influence the development of political ideas and institutions.
Critically evaluate political philosophies with reference to specific political questions and institutions.

title: Plant Propagation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will explore the principles and practices associated with the commercial propagation of plants. Students will develop their understanding of the biology of plant propagation by examining a range of techniques such as seed and cutting propagation, budding, and grafting, separation and division as well as micro-propagation techniques such as tissue culture. The combination of theoretical knowledge, active research in areas of interest relating to plant propagation and hands-on practical experience will provide students with real-world applications in production horticulture.
learning_outcomes: Examine a variety of plant propagation techniques within a professional enterprise and benchmark that enterprise against industry best practice.
Apply sound research skills and critically evaluate contemporary literature pertaining to plant propagation.
Investigate physical dormancy breaking mechanisms in seeds and discuss how this impacts germination.
Appraise a plant propagation technique and investigate its use within the horticultural industry both globally and within an Australian context.
Describe the theoretical aspects of a variety of sexual and asexual plant propagation techniques and relate the use of those techniques to plant anatomy and physiology.

title: Political Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores theological perspectives on, and engagements with, politics and the public sphere in Australian and international contexts. Students will reflect upon and critically assess a variety of different theological approaches and modes of engagement. The subject will also include perspectives and insights from both the wider Christian tradition and more recent scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and apply knowledge and ideas from public and political theology to concrete cases.
Develop an advanced understanding of recent scholarship in public and political theology.
Offer persuasive, theologically-derived responses to some pressing contemporary political issues and debates.
Analyse and reflect critically upon central themes in the wider tradition of Christian political theology, including Christian reflection on the nature, purpose and limits of political authority.
Reflect critically on the complexities of political life in Australian political and international contexts.

title: Political Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores theological perspectives on, and engagements with, politics and the public sphere in Australian and international contexts. Students will reflect upon and critically assess a variety of different theological approaches and modes of engagement. The subject will also include perspectives and insights from both the wider Christian tradition and more recent scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Offer persuasive, theologically-derived responses to some pressing contemporary political issues and debates.
Analyse and reflect critically upon central themes in the wider tradition of Christian political theology, including Christian reflection on the nature, purpose and limits of political authority.
Reflect critically on the complexities of political life in Australian political and international contexts.
Develop an advanced understanding of recent scholarship in public and political theology.
Interpret and apply knowledge and ideas from public and political theology to concrete cases.

title: Politics and Economics in Sport
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students examine the current and historical relationship between and among sport, politics and economics. Students will develop the skills to investigate sport and social policy, the Australian sports delivery system, sport and protest, government funding of sport and the sustainability of sport as a commercial enterprise. Students will critically examine the significance of sport to Australia's national identity and develop the skills to analyse marketing strategies and management issues and the role of the media in the sports industry within Australia and globally.
learning_outcomes: Explain the Australian political system as it relates to sport policy and funding and compare the Australian model to other international models.
Identify the political and economic processes that occur in sports and sport organisations.
Evaluate the role of communities, governing bodies and government at all levels in relation to sports delivery and sustainability in Australia.
Analyse the role of the media in the globalisation and commodification of sport.
Critically examine the history and politics related to protest in sport.
Critically analyse the growth and development of commercial sports.
Deliver clear concise and unambiguous information related to the working of the sports industry in presentation and written report styles.
Articulate the relationship between sport and local, national and international economies.

title: Population Medicine
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Population Medicine will be presented in a Problem Based Learning (PBL) format over four weeks based around case studies. It will present cases related to production animals and farm livestock, particularly illustrating the management of cases with a population focus. This subject addresses in particular the use of serological and other diagnostic tests in understanding the prevalence and spread of disease and the application of principles of risk management to disease control. This subject will assist students to develop skills in researching and applying best-evidence to result in life-long learning.
learning_outcomes: Identify risk factors for the occurrence of common diseases or conditions in production animal populations.
Identify and explain the aetio-pathogenesis of common conditions in production animal populations.
Integrate and act on information regarding client expectations, financial considerations, ethics, welfare and management specific to common scenarios in production animal populations.
Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with peers and staff.
Develop and refine the differential diagnoses associated with common presenting complaints in production animal populations.

Apply and integrate literacy and numerical knowledge from the pre-clinical and para-clinical disciplines, along with best evidence, to prevent, diagnose and manage clinical and/or subclinical cases in production animal populations.
prerequisites: VSC331: Diagnosis and Critical Thinking in Veterinary Science

title: Positive Classroom Climates
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to develop students' understanding and knowledge of creating a positive learning environment. Students will be introduced to theoretical models of classroom management and their application in relation to the physical, social and emotional developmental stages of children. The importance of incorporating appropriate strategies that respond to the learning needs of children from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socio-economic backgrounds will covered. Students will learn to maintain a supportive and safe classroom environment that deals with challenging behaviours, bullying and cyberbullying and crisis and emergency response. The professional, legislative and social responsibilities of teachers is addressed in relation to school policies, staff relationships and communication with parents and the community.
learning_outcomes: Respond to the behavioural needs of children from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socio-economic backgrounds.
Discuss how quality teaching is a key factor in effective classroom management.
Apply appropriate theories and models for a supportive, inclusive and safe learning environment.
Identify issues that can affect positive learning environments, such as bullying and cyberbullying, and strategies to deal with them.
Identify the physical, social and intellectual development and characteristics of children and how these may affect their behaviour.
Discuss positive and practical approaches to manage disruptive behaviour.
Discuss professional and legislative responsibilities of teachers with regard to protecting the safety and wellbeing of children and providing equitable opportunities for learning.

title: Post Impact Disaster Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will enhance their understanding of current emergency operations management and specifically what actions could be taken during the impact and post impact phases of any emergency/disaster to enhance the management of an emergency/disaster event. This subject analyses how an actual emergency/disaster was managed and enables the identification of appropriate changes or initiatives that could be enacted to enhance the future management of a similar emergency/disaster event. The subject also analyses the specific actions that should be taken during the post impact phase of an emergency/disaster event to facilitate its effective management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate the management of an emergency event in the post impact phase.
Identify the impacts that stress and trauma have on victims, emergency workers and individuals and identify appropriate interventions.
Examine and analyse emergency management planning, response, and recovery practices.
Explain and apply the relevant legal, ethical, and governance requirements.

title: Postgraduate Psychology International Experience
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: Students enrolled in this subject will undertake a short program in an international setting. The program requires participation in psychology-focussed activities in another country, and involves engaging in studies of the culture, language and history, as well as studies related to the discipline and application of psychology. The program may include attendance at a conference in the destination country. The international experience may also include visits to sites of cultural and educational signficance, and intercultural engagment with local peers.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an enhanced appreciation of cultural factors on human behaviour.
Recognise the importance of cultural understanding to psychological practice.
Display a greater insight into their own attitudes and behaviour.
Demonstrate a greater cultural awareness and intercultural communication skills.

title: Power and Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the role of power in the practice of leadership. Students will evaluate theoretical and contemporary approaches to power and leadership. Students will research and examine various perspectives of power relations and dynamics across personal, organisational and social dimensions. The subject seeks to optimise students' communication skills to mobilise and respond to power. Students will reflect on their sources of strength and weakness, to inform a resilient response to existent power dynamics in the context of their values and ethics.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate theories of power and leadership and how they relate to the practice of leadership.
Reflect on personal and ethical values across the continuum of influence and power.
Research and examine complex dimensions and power relations and apply these to real-world situations.
Develop and apply strategies to mobilise self, individual, team, corporate, collective and social power.
Apply a range of communication practices in the context of leadership.

title: Power Electronics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a comprehensive understanding of power electronic devices, circuits, and applications. It covers fundamental principles, characteristics, and operation of power semiconductor devices, as well as the analysis, design, and implementation of basic power electronic circuits such as rectifiers, inverters, and converters. Emphasis is placed on theoretical concepts, practical applications, and the role of power electronics in various engineering fields.
learning_outcomes: Describe power semiconductor devices and their characteristics.
Analyse power electronic circuits for various applications.
Apply an understanding of basic power electronic circuits, including rectifiers and inverters.
Discuss the principles and applications of power electronics in electrical engineering.
Discuss the importance of power electronics in modern energy conversion systems and renewable energy technologies.

title: Power Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject covers a wide range of topics including power generation, transmission, distribution, and utilisation. It also includes discussions on power system components, such as generators, transformers, transmission lines, and protection systems.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the performance of power system protection schemes.
Evaluate electrical power distribution systems.
Analyse the behaviour of power systems under different operating conditions.
Compare and contrast various methods for power generation, transmission, and distribution.

title: Power and Practice in Sports Media
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject gives students an opportunity to develop and apply skills in the area of sports media. Students will analyse critiques of the industry, including the culture and common ways in which text, sound and images are used in modern sports media. The subject also requires students to produce their own examples of sports media products. Students will critique the contemporary culture of sports media in Australia and globally, consider how cultural power works in the relationship between sport and media, contemplate how notions of gender, sexuality and discrimination affect sports media, and examine new spaces in which sports media operate (particularly online spaces). This subject provides students with the opportunity to critically reflect on the landscapes of sports media and also prepares students for ethical and professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the use of text, sound and images in sports media.
Respond to and implement feedback on their own sports media product and professional practice.
Critically reflect on the economic relationship of sport and media, and how cultural power and globalisation affects such relationships.
Critically analyse the construction of narrative and 'good writing' in sports media contexts.
Plan, develop and produce clear, and concise content in professional communication works according to the rules of the relevant genre of sports media.
Critically analyse the influence that diversity, inclusion and ethics may have on the sports media environment.

title: Power, Oppression, Violence and Trauma
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to critically examine the socio-political-economic and cultural contexts for how power, oppression and exploitation operate. The subject also aims to prepare students for trauma-informed practice. Taking an intersectional approach which recognises the ongoing impacts of colonisation, the subject addresses violence and abuse across many contexts. These include family violence, intimate partner violence, child abuse and neglect, people with disabilities, elder abuse, sexual abuse, gender-based violence and abuse, cultural and race-based violence, and abuse and systems abuse. This includes implications for practice with the individuals, groups and communities that are most affected including consideration of universal risk, protective factors, and resistance and resilience across all forms of abusive behaviour.
learning_outcomes: Develop self-awareness through understanding own positionality in relation to power, oppression, exploitation and violence.
Demonstrate an understanding of theories and principles underpinning anti-oppressive practice, social justice, and human rights.
Critically examine a range of service systems and fields of practice that address issues of power, oppression, violence and exploitation.
Examine the current context of violence in Australia across a range of practice contexts.
Critically investigate historical and current socio-political-economic and cultural contexts and theories of power, oppression and exploitation and their relationship to violence.
Critically examine the Australian legislative and policy context for addressing discrimination, oppression, exploitation, violence and trauma.
Demonstrate an understanding of and critically apply principles of trauma-informed practice across micro, meso and macro levels.

title: Power, Oppression, Violence and Trauma (postgraduate)
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to critically examine the socio-political-economic and cultural contexts for how power, oppression and exploitation operate and manifest into violence. Following trauma-informed practice, the subject takes an intersectional approach and recognises the ongoing impacts of colonisation. It addresses violence and abuse across many contexts including structures and organisations. It will consider the implications for practice with individuals, groups and communities that are most affected including consideration of universal risk, protective factors, and resistance and resilience across all forms of abusive behaviour.
learning_outcomes: Develop critical self-awareness and reflexivity through understanding own positionality in relation to power, oppression, exploitation and violence.
Examine the current context of violence in Australia across a range of practice contexts.
Critically examine the Australian legislative and policy context for addressing discrimination, oppression, exploitation, violence and trauma.
Critically examine a range of service systems and professional practice capabilities that address issues of power, oppression, violence and exploitation.
Demonstrate an understanding of theories and principles underpinning anti-oppressive practice, social justice, and human rights.
Critically investigate historical and current socio-political-economic and cultural contexts and theories of power, oppression and exploitation and their relationship to violence.
Demonstrate an understanding of and critically apply principles of trauma-informed practice across micro, meso and macro levels.

title: Power, Politics and Propaganda in the Media Today
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the power of the mass media and their role and influence in Australia and the world in the era of the Digital Age. It explores the rapid technological advancements of both media and communication, which has led to the widespread availability of information. And it investigates the notion of propaganda through government and corporate power, journalists and society through mainstream and critical perspectives. Chief among these is the idea of the Fourth Estate and the Propaganda Model devised by Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky. Various topics are critically explored: ‘fake news’ and the public relations industry, the rise of the internet, social media and the data economy, free speech and censorship, media ownership concentration, foreign news coverage, elections and the battle for ‘truth'. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
learning_outcomes: Understand the tension between ‘old’ and ‘new ‘media’.
Critically evaluate the effect of changes to media policy on the Australian media and government, and accountability to the public.
Explain the power and impact of the media on Australia and the world.
Critically assess government media policies and foreign policy objectives.
Demonstrate an understanding of the differences between the fourth estate ideal and the propaganda model.

title: Practical Clinical Biochemistry
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces units, reference ranges and specimens used in clinical biochemistry. The subject also covers the patho-physiological and patho-biochemical rationale for routine clinical biochemistry tests and the interpretation of data. Biochemical techniques associated with the various routine tests covered include principles of the methods and the analytical performance. Technology, including point of care testing is important in healthcare and it is also therefore learnt. At the end of the subject, a student will have knowledge of the requirements of the various specimens and measurements and will have theoretical skills to carry out routine testing using various methods and equipment. The student will carry out test, assess performance on the analysis (quality control) and interpret clinical biochemistry data. Such knowledge is useful for example, in further studies in this discipline, routine and specialist medical laboratory sciences, forensic sciences, biotechnology, dentistry, medicine, veterinary and animal sciences, research and in industry that develops and/or supplies diagnostic technology and consumables. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Work independently and collaboratively in measurement of analyses and to write a scientific report on experimental findings and data interpretation.
Identify, describe and justify the utility of the various specimens, conditions of specimen collection and preservation as well as other requirements for analysis.

Describe, use and evaluate the various techniques (including but not limited to chemical, enzymatic, electrometric, recognition techniques and mass spectrometry) utilised in measurement of endogenous metabolites, hormones and drugs in biological fluids/tissues in various diseases.

Carry out measurements (technical skills), to evaluate methods (including but not limited to evaluating accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, linearity), to identify and analyse sources of errors, to implement quality control and quality assurance for good analytical practice.

title: Practical Haematology 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will conduct full blood count (FBC), preparation, staining and examination of blood films, as well as coagulation screening tests. Students will perform detailed morphological examinations on blood films including anaemias and leukaemias, and will be introduced to automation in the haematology laboratory in addition to basic blood banking practices. Students will be required to demonstrate their abilities in performing routine haematology tests. This practical subject will be run in a intensive format with both internal and distance cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Perform and interpret the results of haematological tests.
Explain principles that underpin routine haematological tests.
Demonstrate academic literacy skills.

title: Practical Haematology 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will develop advanced knowledge and skills in conducting laboratory tests including but not limited to the examination of blood and/or bone marrow films, and the investigations of haemoglobin abnormalities and coagulation disorders. Furthermore, quality control and quality assurance measures related to haematology are integrated into this subject. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Conduct and interpret haematological tests including but not limited to blood film examinations, investigation of abnormalities in haemoglobin synthesis, and coagulation studies.
Demonstrate high levels of academic literacy.
Demonstrate knowledge and application of key issues regarding quality control and quality assurance in the haematology laboratory.

title: Practical Histopathology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will learn practical skills in histological techniques. This subject will examine the practice of basic routine histological techniques, including surgical cut-up, fixation, processing, embedding, sectioning and staining of tissues using routine and specialised techniques. In addition, specialised histological techniques and the science behind these techniques will be covered. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of quality assurance and health and safety procedures pertinent to the histopathology laboratory.
Demonstrate an advanced level of proficiency in the preparation of routine formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections.
Demonstrate proficiency in haematoxylin and eosin staining, selected special stains and immunohistochemical methods.
Identify the causes of technical defects in histological preparations, how to solve such defects and how they could influence the diagnostic process.
Analyse sections that have undergone special stains to enable a pathological analysis of the tissues.

title: Practical Immunology and Transfusion Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will cover the practical component of two disciplines in pathology namely Immunology and Transfusion Science. This subject covers the principles of immunology and their application in the development of assays undertaken in medical science with a focus on immunological assays. Students will have a comprehensive component focused on different areas of Transfusion Science including pre- transfusion testing, investigation of haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn (HDFN), and investigation of transfusion reactions. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and perform a range of immunological techniques employed in modern biomedical science.
Perform and interpret manual and semi-automated blood transfusion testing including blood grouping, antibody screening, identification and phenotyping.
Evaluate and perform pre-transfusion testing, transfusion reaction and Haemolytic Disease of the New born investigation.
Explain how immunological principles are applied to the development of various diagnostic tests in the pathology laboratory.
Demonstrate a high level of academic literacy.
Critically analyse immunological data and apply immunological principles in evaluating assays to diagnose immune system dysfunction.

title: Practical Internetworking
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a knowledge of fundamental networking concepts and builds the capacity of students to design, evaluate and configure various network components and protocols. Students will also prepare for Cisco industry certification exams during this subject.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and implement infrastructure management technologies across diverse contexts.
Evaluate and analyse requirements, including operational characteristics and design considerations, for a contemporary hierarchical network.
Evaluate and implement infrastructure security and service technologies across diverse contexts.
Analyse and implement LAN switching, routing, and WAN technologies in small, medium, and large deployments.

title: Practical Medical Science 1
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce foundational laboratory skills necessary for a career in medical science or research. Students will draw on foundation knowledge and skills from chemistry to create links to future medical science clinical subjects and practicals. Students will learn the principles of, and use, standard and specialised laboratory equipment. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and distance cohorts attending the practical sessions. Students will also be introduced to laboratory work, health and safety.
learning_outcomes: Use general laboratory equipment for experiments relevant to medical science.
Identify laboratory equipment and glassware and demonstrate knowledge of laboratory workplace health and safety procedures.
Demonstrate general laboratory skills important in medical science and research.
Demonstrate proficiency in making dilutions and calculating the correct dilution factors of general laboratory solutions.
Interpret and calculate experimental results.
Use general laboratory equipment for chemistry experiments like volumetric analysis, chemical equilibria, acid-base equilibria and others.
prerequisites: CHM111: Math, statistics, physics and advanced chemistry for Medical Science

title: Practical Microbiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject involves performing tasks which emphasise development of specialised techniques and diagnosis of bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic infections. Practical sessions will also include case studies to simulate 'real life' medical situations, with the emphasis on laboratory diagnostic methodology in which the student microbiologist is consulted in order to diagnose the aetiological agents of infection. This practical subject will be run in a intensive format with both internal and distance cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Identify medically important bacteria, parasites and fungi with microscopy.
Perform basic virological and bacteriological techniques and explain the theoretical aspects of cell culture.
Investigate in vitro synergy between combinations of antimicrobial agents.
Investigate bacterial enteritis.
Perform and investigate bacterial gene transfer by conjugation method.
Competently perform microbiological techniques for diagnosis of organ infection.

title: Practical Molecular Methods
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce molecular techniques as used in clinical laboratories for the diagnosis and prognostication of disease. These methods are also used in molecular and research laboratories. It will draw on foundation knowledge and skills from, amongst others, second year medical science foundation subjects. The subject will cover, but not exclusively, the following topics: cytogenetic, antibody based and high throughput molecular techniques. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Calculate, analyse and justify experimental results.
Demonstrate general laboratory skills important in medical science and research.
Use general laboratory equipment and specific molecular techniques for the analysis of proteins and nucleic acids.

title: Practical Policing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: Credit package for the Associate Degree in Policing Practice

title: Practical Medical Science 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce a range of intermediate laboratory work and skills necessary for a career in medical science or research. Students will draw on foundation knowledge and skills from microbiology, anatomy and practical medical science 1 to create links to future medical science clinical subjects and practicals. This practical subject will be run in a intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the sessions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a basic competence in microscopy and foundational staining techniques.
Demonstrate general laboratory skills and experimental data analysis important in medical science and research.
Demonstrate a basic competence in aseptic technique and specimen handling in the pathology laboratory.
Demonstrate a basic competence in gross and microscopic anatomy of blood, tissues and organs.
Demonstrate a basic competence in the morphological identification of microorganisms.

title: Practical Separation Methods
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce separation techniques used in biochemical, genetic clinical and research laboratories. It will draw on foundation knowledge and skills from, amongst others, first year medical science subjects and will provide a basis for future medical science clinical subjects and practicals. This practical subject will be run in an intensive format with both internal and online cohorts attending the practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Use general laboratory equipment for isolation, separation and analysis of proteins and nucleic acids.
Demonstrate general laboratory skills important in medical science and research.
Demonstrate proficiency in making dilutions and calculate the correct dilution factors of general laboratory solutions.
Calculate, interpret and analyse experimental data.
prerequisites: BCM210: Foundations and Techniques in Biochemistry

title: Practical Skills in Nutrition Science
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to key practical skills in nutrition science that are relevant to population health and research settings. Students will develop an appreciation of their scope of practice in regard to implementing these skills in future practice. More specifically, students will explore the methodologies available for collecting and analysing dietary data; develop skills in data interpretation; and understand the principles of nutrition education and communication strategies that accommodate the needs of specific target groups.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the relevance of current dietary data collection, analysis methods and reference standards in clinical and research settings.
Analyse and interpret food and dietary data utilising current dietary analysis methods and reference standards.
Define nutritional status and nutritional risk, and identify methods used to screen for nutritional risk.
Develop evidence based and culturally safe nutrition education and communication strategies that accommodate the needs of specific target groups.

title: Practical Studies in Liturgy and Worship
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject establishes Christian liturgical practice within a range of theological and theoretical foundations. In this it enables the worship leader to explore the integration of worship with context, including pastoral practice, the imperative for justice, culture, and critical events that affect the credibility of the church. A vital part of the subject is the opportunity for an extended review of the leader's own worship style and practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical appreciation of the implications of the ritual nature of worship.
Critically evaluate the interrelationship between theology, context and liturgical practice.
Critically reflect upon the student's own practice of creating and leading worship within the current context.
Be proficient in the development and application of tools for the evaluation of ethical worship.
Integrate the celebration of liturgy with leadership in the areas of pastoral practice and social justice.

title: Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the discipline of Practical Theology in which theory and practice are considered together across a range of areas of ministry, mission, worship and pastoral care. It examines its relationship to the biblical, systematic and historical sub-disciplines in theology. Students will develop an understanding of what is distinctive about Practical Theology and the range of methodologies appropriate to it.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the distinctive nature of Practical Theology within the discipline of theology.
Demonstrate a foundational understanding of the place of practical theology in ministry and mission.
Describe the foundational praxis models and demonstrate initial skills in reflective practice.
Articulate the relationship of Practical Theology to the biblical, systematic and historical sub-disciplines of theology.

title: Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the discipline of Practical Theology in which theory and practice are considered together across a range of areas of ministry, mission, worship and pastoral care. It examines its relationship to the biblical, systematic and historical sub-disciplines in theology. Students will develop an understanding of what is distinctive about Practical Theology and the range of methodologies appropriate to it.
learning_outcomes: Articulate critically the relationship of practical theology to the biblical, systematic and historical sub-disciplines of theology.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the discipline of practical theology.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the implications of both a lay and ordained practice-based ministry and mission.
Describe and evaluate the foundational praxis models and to demonstrate initial skills in reflective practice.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Articulate and evaluate critically methods for doing practical theology.

title: Practical Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the discipline of Practical Theology in which theory and practice are considered together across a range of areas of ministry, mission, worship and pastoral care. It examines its relationship to the biblical, systematic and historical sub-disciplines in theology. Students will develop an understanding of what is distinctive about Practical Theology and the range of methodologies appropriate to it.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Articulate critically the relationship of practical theology to the biblical, systematic and historical sub-disciplines of theology.
Describe and evaluate the foundational praxis models and to demonstrate initial skills in reflective practice.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the discipline of practical theology.
Articulate and evaluate critically methods for doing practical theology.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the implications of both a lay and ordained practice-based ministry and mission.

school: School
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 1 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 1 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program.

school: School
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 2 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 2 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program.
