syllabus_overview: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 3 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 3 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program.

title: Practical Theology Level 4
school: School
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 4 (8 point) credit within the Graduate Diploma of Theology
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for Practical Theology Level 4 (8 point) credit within the Graduate Diploma of Theology.

title: Practice Improvement Project
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' capacity to lead practice improvement in their area of clinical practice with a focus on the completion of an independent, low-risk practice improvement project. With guidance from the subject coordinator or discipline-specific delegate, students will implement the practice improvement proposal they developed in an earlier subject. The stages of the project implemented during this subject will include further critical review of the literature to articulate the theoretical perspective informing the design and outcomes, along with data collection, interpretation, and analysis. Where appropriate, students will be required to apply for ethics approval to meet the National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research requirements. Students will demonstrate their ability to disseminate the findings or outcomes from the project through an oral presentation.
learning_outcomes: Translate and communicate the project process and outcomes through documentation using a relevant reporting framework.
Communicate the project findings to a relevant clinical audience through an oral presentation.
Critically analyse the ethical implications of the project.
Initiate, plan, implement and evaluate an independent project in the field of health.
Critically analyse and reflect on the findings from the project as they apply to advancing disciplinary practice.
prerequisites: NRS567: Value Based Healthcare and Critical Inquiry

title: Practice Improvement Proposal
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop students' capacity to lead practice improvement in their area of clinical practice, with a focus on conducting a literature review and developing a practice improvement proposal. Students will identify a healthcare issue that has practical applications within their specific area of practice and then develop a proposal for an independent, low-risk, practice or quality improvement project. With guidance from the subject coordinator or discipline specific delegate, students will complete a comprehensive literature review on the selected topic before using the findings to inform the development of a proposal for a practice or quality improvement project.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and translate findings from a literature review into a practice improvement proposal.
Identify a healthcare issue of concern for investigation.
Identify, collate and analyse the literature on the selected topic.
Synthesise and critically analyse the selected literature to justify the need for practice improvement.

title: Practice-Based Research Projects in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will demonstrate mastery of a body of knowledge relating to the principles of research (research design, ethics, data collection, data analysis, interpretation and dissemination of findings). Students will apply this body of knowledge to the development of a practice-based research project that focuses on prevention, education and/or promotion of communication and swallowing issues, or speech pathology assessment and intervention. This subject will enable students to build on prior learning in order to further develop their research knowledge and skills. Students will develop a research design which is ethical, rigorous and promotes benefits for practice and consumers. Students will conduct and monitor a small research project, and analyse and interpret the study findings using rigorous quantitative, qualitative and/or mixed methods. This subject also provides students with the opportunity to disseminate research findings through a conference presentation to peers.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and reflect upon the application of the research principles to a specific practice-based problem or area of need.

Independently apply cognitive, technical and creative skills to synthesise problems from practice in order to plan, implement, evaluate and disseminate an ethical and clinically relevant rigorous research project.
Critically evaluate research principles (research design, ethics, data collection, data analysis, interpretation and dissemination of findings) as they apply to speech pathology practice.
prerequisites: SPH516: Planning Practice-Based Research Projects in Speech Pathology

title: Precision Agriculture and Data Handling
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be introduced to scientific experimentation, fundamental applied statistics and the technologies crucial to the understanding and operation of modern precision agriculture methodology within a variety of agricultural contexts. General mathematic and computer skills will be developed and further expanded to allow students to collect, analyse, convert and present spatial data within an agricultural context. These skills and the application of precision agriculture are relevant to a range of common agricultural enterprises.
learning_outcomes: Select and use various forms of data acquisition within precision agriculture (remote sensing, yield monitoring).
Describe and explain how Global Navigation Satellite System technology works and its limitations within precision agriculture.
Implement appropriate use of Geographic Information System (GIS) software for agriculturally significant issues (e.g. soil, weed and/or animal management).
Use introductory statistical tools to perform calculations, statistical analysis, and present data.
Apply ethical and scientifically sound experimental methodologies.

title: Prep for Teaching Maths 1 (Number and Algebra)
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Prep for Teaching Maths 1 (Number and Algebra) is the first in a suite of three Studylink enabling subjects designed to address core Numeracy skills required by teachers to demonstrate the minimum standard as set by the Australian Government. All students enrolled in an initial teacher education course are required to sit and pass the Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education - LANTITE. This subject covers core numeracy content in the content areas of Number and Algebra, including non-calculator skills and working mathematically, which are areas examined in such a test.
learning_outcomes: Ratios and weighted percentages
Select and use appropriate problem solving strategies
Work confidently without a calculator in the content of the subject
Graph simple non-linear relationships
Determine the midpoint, gradient and length of an interval, and graph linear relationships
Solve financial problems involving earning, spending and investing money
Operate with algebraic expressions involving positive-integer and zero indices and explain the meaning of negative indices for numerical analysis

title: Prep for Teaching Maths 2 (Measurement and Geometry)
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Prep for Teaching Maths 2 (Measurement and Geometry) is the second in a suite of three Studylink enabling subjects designed to address core Numeracy skills required by teachers to demonstrate the minimum standard as set by the Australian Government. All students enrolled in an initial teacher education course are required to sit and pass the Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education (LANTITE). This subject covers core numeracy content in the content areas of Measurement and Geometry, including non-calculator skills and working mathematically, which can assist students in preparation for such a test.
learning_outcomes: Select and use appropriate problem solving strategies
Calculate the areas of composite shapes, and the surface areas of rectangular and triangular prisms
Interpret very small and very large units of measurement, uses scientific notation, and rounds to significant figures
Use maps and plans
Apply the properties of similar figures and scale drawings
Apply trigonometry, given diagrams, to solve problems involving angles of elevation and depression
Work confidently without a calculator in the content of the subject

title: Prep for Teaching Maths 3 (Statistics and Probability)
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Prep for Teaching Maths 3 (Statistics and Probability) is the third in a suite of three Studylink enabling subjects designed to address core Numeracy skills required by teachers to demonstrate the minimum standard as set by the Australian Government. All students enrolled in an initial teacher education course are required to sit and pass the Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education (LANTITE). This subject covers core numeracy content in the content areas of Statistics and Probability, including non-calculator skills and working mathematically, which are areas examined in such a test.
learning_outcomes: Work confidently without a calculator in the content of the subject
Use statistical displays to compare sets of data, and evaluate statistical claims made in media
Read boxplots to compare sets of data
Select and use appropriate problem solving strategies
Calculate relative frequencies to estimate probabilities of simple and compound events

title: Prep for Uni 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Prep for Uni is the first of two non award micro-subjects offered on the Studylink platform. The subject guides students through a series of tasks and activities designed to develop the skills, strategies and knowledge which will support successful university study. Students are introduced to university tools and systems and become familiar with the expectations of the higher education environment. On completion of this subject, students are advised to progress to Prep for Uni 2.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply the concept of time and task management in a learning environment
Choose and apply some learning and help-seeking strategies to support successful participation in university
Access and navigate relevant university systems and digital tools
Explain the purpose and expectations of university learning and teaching

title: Prep for Uni 2
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Prep for Uni is the second of two non award micro-subjects offered on the Studylink platform. The subject guides students through a series of tasks and activities designed to develop the skills, strategies and knowledge which will support successful university study. Students will develop their understanding of university tools and systems and increase their understanding of the expectations of the higher education environment including foundational principles of academic integrity. It is recommended that students first complete Prep for Uni 1 (SSS051).
learning_outcomes: Choose and use relevant university systems and digital tools to complete administrative and learning tasks.
Explain key foundational principles of academic integrity.
Develop a personal learning plan.
Describe strategies to manage learning and assessment.

title: Preparation for Information Technology Studies
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop essential skills required for study within the Bachelor of Information Technology (Faculty of Science and Agriculture). The subject develops students? skills and confidence in information searching, critical thinking, assignment writing and academic integrity within a framework of personal learning management and reflection. Student learning is extended to the social context through compulsory participation in the subject forum. The elective component aims to develop specific skills that are required for the study of Information Technology.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant critical thinking strategies
Demonstrate an understanding of academic integrity and referencing conventions
Be able to:
Define essential study skills required for tertiary study
Use an online learning environment for communication, study and research
Identify what is expected from the tertiary student
Identify and apply foundational knowledge and skills required for study within an Information Technology course.
Apply the principles of good academic writing

title: Preparing for University Study
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to transition students into undergraduate study. Students will be supported to develop the confidence, knowledge and practical skills necessary to succeed in a higher education environment, both online and face to face. The subject enables students to become independent learners through the active use of university services and systems, the acquisition of goal setting and time management strategies, and the explicit teaching of study skills. Students will become familiar with the foundational principles of academic integrity and be provided with scaffolded opportunities to understand the purpose and expectations of assessment at university.
learning_outcomes: Identify, select and use university services and systems to participate in learning.
Recognise and apply time management and goal-setting tools in the university context.
Choose and use appropriate study skills and strategies to complete specific learning and assessment tasks.
Explain and apply foundational principles of academic integrity.

title: Preparation for Studying Business
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop essential skills required for study within the Bachelor of Business (Faculty of Commerce). The subject develops students skills and confidence in information searching, critical thinking, assignment writing and academic integrity within a framework of personal learning management and reflection. Student learning is extended to the social context through compulsory participation in the subject forum. The elective component aims to develop specific skills that are required for the study of business.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant critical thinking strategies.
Identify what is expected from the tertiary student.
Define essential study skills required for tertiary study.
Identify and apply foundational knowledge and skills required for study within a business course.
Apply the principles of good academic writing.
Demonstrate an understanding of academic integrity and referencing conventions.
Use an online learning environment for communication, study and research.

title: Preservation of Audiovisual Materials
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: The subject focuses on preservation requirements for audiovisual materials, both analogue and digital. Methods for identifying different moving image and sound materials are explored, as are measures for determining deterioration characteristics, both active and passive. Storage and handling practices such as risk and vault management are also discussed. Digitisation processes for audiovisual materials are covered and an introduction to digital preservation is provided. Ethics, professional practice, handling, occupational health and safety considerations and standards are integrated into all aspects of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate awareness of principles for managing digital audiovisual objects.
Explain how and why different audiovisual objects came into being.
Explain why audiovisual objects deteriorate and be able to recognise the type and extent of deterioration.
Implement emergency preparedness and disaster management practices.
Implement appropriate preservation and storage methods including digitisation for various types of audiovisual media.
Identify and describe approaches for duplicating audio and video materials.

title: Primary English Curriculum: Reading, Process and Pedagogy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the teaching of reading by recognising the interconnectedness of listening, talking, and writing. Diagnostic, evidence-based approaches to plan the teaching of reading through knowledge, skills, strategies and assessment will be introduced.Students will develop critical knowledge and conceptual understandings of curriculum frameworks for reading instruction, and theoretical and practical knowledge will be developed thorough opportunities to integrate skills and explicit teaching strategies in the context of the primary literacy program.The subject takes a socio-cultural and multiliteracies approach which includes understanding the nature and needs of diverse learners. It places assessment, reflective evaluation and communication with parents, at the core of the learning and teaching cycle.
learning_outcomes: Have demonstrated knowledge of the nature and function of Modelled, Shared/Guided and Independent reading opportunities in a reading program.
Describe a range of means of identifying, assessing and catering for the needs of diverse learners; especially learners in 'English as a Second language' settings.
Have articulated ways of building relationships between home/community and formal educational sites.
Identify the major sociocultural and language theories which underpin curriculum approaches to literacy and learning.
Articulate their critical knowledge and conceptual understandings of current curriculum frameworks for reading instruction and the theories that inform them.
Have demonstrated that they can plan for integration of skills and explicit teaching strategies for reading and viewing in the context of a balanced literacy program.

Provide examples of planned instruction that scaffolds the use of phonemic, semiotic and syntactic cues for reading print as well as developing visual literacy, using the five semiotic systems of meaning with multimodal texts.

title: Primary English Curriculum: Text Construction, Pedagogy and Processes
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject concerns the pedagogy of text construction with a focus on teaching writing in balanced literacy programs. The design of balanced literacy programs requires the pre-service teachers' development of knowledge and conceptual understanding of past and current theories and practices informing curriculum framework and the teaching of text construction and writing. The subject provides opportunities to develop explicit teaching strategies in the context of a balanced primary school literacy program. It will also introduce a range of analytical tools brought to planning evidence-based literacy learning approaches. Throughout the subject, assessment and communication with stakeholders are situated at the core of the leaning and teaching cycle.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a personal engagement with the writing process and text construction using linguistic and visual resources.
Have identified and understood the function of text resources, including structural and grammatical features, used in the construction of meaning in texts.
Design literacy programs informed by valid and reliable evaluative and assessment processes to meet the diverse learning needs evident in Australian classrooms.
Have articulated relationships between identity and text construction practices.
Position text construction as a subject of learning and as a technology used in learning across the school curriculum and in the wider community.

Have demonstrated an engagement with a range of theoretical frameworks informing the teaching and learning of text construction practices, processes, knowledge and skills used in first and second language learning contexts.
Articulated the dynamic relationships between text construction, reading/viewing and technology.
prerequisites: EML300: Children's Literature in the Classroom

title: Primary Health Care: Community Development
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the principles and practices of community development. It focuses on how to engage and work effectively with communities to build social capital and effective community programs that will assist in improving social and emotional well-being in families and communities. The influences of globalisation, the hegemonic nature of neoliberal political ideology, and the use of online technologies on the effectiveness of community development will be considered. Students will develop their understanding and application of the important concepts of equity, access, empowerment, community self-determination and inter-agency collaboration as well as the social, economic, cultural and political determinants of health. International perspectives on community development will also be explored. Students undertaking this subject are expected to develop a proposal for a community development mental health program for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in a primary health care context.
learning_outcomes: critically examine the influences of globalisation, neoliberal political ideology and online technologies on communities and community development;
analyse how deficit focused approaches impact on communities and the outcomes of community development; and analyse the social, economic, cultural and political determinants of health;
examine the characteristics of successful community development projects including program sustainability;
explore the underlying principles of community development;
apply and implement the skills of group planning, problem solving and decision making through the development of a proposal for a community development program.

interpret how equity, access, empowerment, social justice, community self-determination and inter-agency collaboration might be achieved within a community development project; including reviewing this from a Global perspective; and

title: Principles and Practice of Radiation Therapy 3
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject completes the students' comprehensive education in Radiation Therapy in preparation for the 4th year residency. Students undertake a 6-week clinical placement. Students explore the more advanced range of treatment regimes and patient cases; including but not limited to complex modulated cases, multi-isocentric techniques, multi-lesion treatments, and will constructively reflect on clinical practice experiences, utilising research skills, and ensure an evidence-based approach to their work.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and implement outcomes of patient assessment and due diligence to deliver appropriate care inclusive of appropriate management in the event of deteriorating patient condition, urgent and/or unexpected findings (MRPBA Domain 1).
Identify and make appropriate decisions about the care of patients before, during, and after the examination/treatment. (MRPBA Domain 1.7d and 2.3a).

Implement professional practice, demonstrating critical thinking and analytical skills, with specific reference to applying anatomy, physiology and pathology, applying the principles of physics and instrumentation, utilising patient information management systems, determining appropriate procedures, and manage / manipulate 3D datasets (MRPBA Domain 1).

Demonstrate critical, analytical, and reflective skills in a range of contexts including clinical problem solving, research and empirical practice, and academic and professional discourse (MRPBA Domains 1-5).

Apply the principles of radiation safety and risk management with specific reference to safe radiation practice, protecting/enhancing patient safety, ensuring safe operation of equipment, maintain safety of self and others and safely managing radiation and radioactivity (MRPBA Domain 5).
Understand the processes of peer assessment, standard setting, mentorship, and developmental support to other members of the healthcare team. (MRPBA Domain 2.5a).
Operate equipment and apply knowledge of laboratory procedures to practice as required. (MRPBA Domain 1.3d).
Understand, explain and apply principles of Indigenous cultural competence and safety within the context of patient care and advocacy (MRPBA Domain 2 and 3).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical and reflective thinking to resolve clinical challenges and identifying professional learning needs / life-long learning (MRPBA Domain 4).

Apply understanding of practice in radiation therapy, demonstrating critical thinking and analytical skills, with specific reference to appropriate use of stabilisation devices, application of treatment simulation techniques, knowledge and application of treatment planning and dosimetry, implement CT imaging and implementation of treatment techniques according to approved plans (MRPBA Domain 1C).

Identify, explain and implement professional and ethical conduct with specific reference to global citizenship, ethical, professional and legal practices, providing appropriate care, assuming accountability and responsibility, and patient advocacy (MRPBA Domain 2).
Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with specific reference to clear, sensitive and effective communication and collaborating with other health practitioners (MRPBA Domain 3).

Synthesise and critically evaluate information to implement social, economic and environmental sustainable practices. Understand the use of CT, MRI, and PET in the localisation of a range of cancer sites, patient presentations, and related planning procedures. (MRPBA Domain 1.3c).
prerequisites: MRS349: Principles and Practice Radiation Therapy 2

title: Principles and Practice Radiation Therapy 1
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students begin their journey in the Radiation Therapy specialisation and consolidate their developing understanding in the clinical environment (2 x 4 weeks Practicum). Students will explore professionalism, ethics and law, radiation safety, patient care and communication along with a range of radiation therapy treatments and the underlying theoretical foundations for the respiratory, digestive, genitourinary and gynaecological systems as well as breast. Further to these topics, students will develop their understanding of oncological emergencies. Practical tasks undertaken in Radiation Therapy Planning Principles subject support the study undertaken by students in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Apply digital technology and digital literacy skills for professional practice and research and demonstrate digital citizenship in online learning and professional communities (MRPBA Domain 4).
Recognise opportunities to develop new knowledge through research and enquiry, and contribute to the enhancement of the profession (MRPBA Domain 2.5 and 4.1d).

Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with specific reference to clear, sensitive and effective, culturally appropriate communication to create culturally safe environments and collaborating with other health practitioners (MRPBA Domain 3).
Perform quality evaluation of image datasets, identify limitations and recognise artefacts, including identifying and reporting urgent or unexpected findings (MRPBA Domain 1.7b and c).

Describe, explain and implement professional practice with specific reference to anatomy, physiology, pathology, physics and instrumentation principles, utilising clinical information management systems, determining appropriate procedures, patient assessment and due diligence, deliver appropriate care and stabilisation/reproducibility techniques, and manage / manipulate 3D datasets (MRPBA Domain 1).
Recognise the need for appropriate decisions about the care of patients before, during, and after the examination/treatment. (MRPBA Domain 1.7d; 2.3a).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence-based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1).

Describe and apply the principles of radiation safety and risk management with specific reference to safe radiation practice, protecting/enhancing patient safety, ensuring safe operation of equipment, maintaining safety of self and others and safely managing radiation (MRPBA Domain 5).

Describe and apply understanding of practice in radiation therapy with specific reference to appropriate use of stabilisation devices, application of treatment simulation techniques, knowledge and application of treatment planning and dosimetry, CT imaging, and of treatment techniques according to approved plans (MRPBA Domain 1 and 1C).

Identify, explain and implement professional and ethical conduct with specific reference to practising in an ethical, non-discriminatory, professional and legal manner, providing appropriate care, assuming accountability and responsibility, and patient advocacy (MRPBA Domain 2).
prerequisites: MRS252: Principles and Practice of Radiation Therapy 1

title: Principles and Practice Radiation Therapy 2
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students continue to build their knowledge and skills in radiation therapy. Students explore more advanced radiation therapy techniques for the head, neck, integumentary and endocrine systems. Students undertake a clinical placement to further their experience and develop their understandings in a clinical setting and support their study towards meeting the skills and capabilities required for graduate entry professional registration. Students will continue to develop and consolidate their skills in critical evaluation and reflective practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply understanding of practice in radiation therapy, demonstrating critical thinking and analytical skills, with specific reference to appropriate use of stabilisation devices, application of treatment simulation techniques, knowledge and application of treatment planning and dosimetry, implement CT imaging and implementation of treatment techniques according to approved plans (MRPBA Domain 1C).

Explain and apply the principles of evidence based practice and professional learning with specific reference to critical and reflective thinking to resolve clinical challenges and identifying professional learning needs / life-long learning (MRPBA Domain 4).

Synthesise and critically evaluate information to implement social, economic and environmental sustainable practices. Understand the use of CT, MRI, and PET in the localisation of a range of cancer sites, patient presentations, and related planning procedures. (MRPBA Domain 1.3c).

Identify, explain and implement professional and ethical conduct with specific reference to global citizenship, ethical, professional and legal practices, providing appropriate care, assuming accountability and responsibility, and patient advocacy (MRPBA Domain 2).
Understand the processes of peer assessment, standard setting, mentorship, and developmental support to other members of the healthcare team. (MRPBA Domain 2.5a).
Operate equipment and apply knowledge of laboratory procedures to practice as required. (MRPBA Domain 1.3d).
Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills with specific reference to clear, sensitive and effective communication and collaborating with other health practitioners (MRPBA Domain 3).

Apply the principles of radiation safety and risk management with specific reference to safe radiation practice, protecting/enhancing patient safety, ensuring safe operation of equipment, maintain safety of self and others and safely managing radiation and radioactivity (MRPBA Domain 5).

Implement professional practice, demonstrating critical thinking and analytical skills, with specific reference to applying anatomy, physiology and pathology, applying the principles of physics and instrumentation, utilising patient information management systems, determining appropriate procedures, and manage / manipulate 3D datasets (MRPBA Domain 1).

Evaluate and implement outcomes of patient assessment and due diligence to deliver appropriate care inclusive of appropriate management in the event of deteriorating patient condition, urgent and/or unexpected findings (MRPBA Domain 1).
Identify and explain appropriate decisions about the care of patients before, during, and after the examination/treatment. (MRPBA Domain 1.7d and 2.3a).

Demonstrate critical, analytical, and reflective skills in a range of contexts including clinical problem solving, research and empirical practice, and academic and professional discourse (MRPBA Domains 1-5).
Understand, explain and apply principles of Indigenous cultural competence and safety within the context of patient care and advocacy (MRPBA Domain 2 and 3).
prerequisites: MRS252: Principles and Practice of Radiation Therapy 1
MRS253: Principles and Practice Radiation Therapy 1

title: Principles of Cargo Control
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Customs and Excise Studies
syllabus_overview: In this subject students examine the concepts of Customs control as it relates to the measures applied by border managers to ensure compliance with the laws and regulations for which they have administrative responsibility in respect of cargo movements across borders. Students will gain an understanding of the essential techniques and procedures which allow border managers to accurately identify areas of high risk and concentrate resources in those areas while allowing the majority of goods to pass across the border with minimal intervention
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of how improving the flow of information between a carrier and Customs will facilitate the release of cargo.
Assess key aspects of the Revised Kyoto Convention (RKC) establishing worlds best Customs practice for cargo processing.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of how consultation and co-operation with other government agencies and industry can enhance Customs ability to manage compliance.
Evaluate critically how risk indicators serve as a practical tool to select and target cargo for potential non-compliance with Customs law.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the cargo environment and the factors influencing some of the Customs procedures and processes in that environment.
Analyse the effect that particular international organisations and treaties have on customs control in respect of how cargo is treated, moved and managed.
Identify and communicate clearly the relevant issues raised by a practical cargo processing scenario, analyse the implications of the issues and propose appropriate actions.

title: Principles of Clinical and Systematic Pathology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject follows on from Principles of Pathobiology (VSC 310), with an approach to disease through a largely body systems based approach, using the related and complimentary disciplines of Anatomical and Clinical Pathology. Here pathological changes that may induce disease in each major body system are examined eg. infection, inflammation, disorders of growth, genetic disorders, diseases of immunity. For each body system material will be presented through a number of teaching modalities eg. lectures, practicals, tutorials, interactive sessions, online presentations etc., using case based material, to lead students through the investigative and diagnostic process. Students cannot progress to Phase 2, without the completion of Phase 1 subjects.
learning_outcomes: Relate morphological and functional changes in one body system to changes in another system, in well recognised disease state/s, using measurable Clinical and Anatomical Pathological variables.

Analyse both Anatomical and Clinical Pathological data to assess the presence and degree of organ/system dysfunction, with a view to specific disease diagnosis and monitoring of disease in response to therapy.

Relate these morphological changes to diminution, loss or change in function of that specific system, and then describe, hypothesise and quantitate these functional changes in terms of measurable clinical pathological variables.

Describe and summarise the advantages and limitations of Clinical and Anatomical Pathologic assessment of specific disease states, both as they relate to each other and other diagnostic aids such as physical examination or diagnostic imaging.
Use knowledge gained from this course to inform PBL subjects.
List and describe, for each major organ system, the causes of the basic pathologic changes detailed above, and how each results in alterations in morphology.

title: Principles of Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Australian ecosystems are unique in their complexity and diversity of species. Understanding the ecology of these systems is fundamental to managing and conserving these places for future generations. The subject describes the foundations for life on Earth, introducing the fundamental concepts of biology, evolution and ecology of animals and plants that make up the diversity of ecosystems on our planet. Students will have the opportunity for hands-on learning through activities such as collecting and analysing data on biodiversity, underpinned with theoretical knowledge. On completion, students will have foundational knowledge and skills to successfully continue their studies in plant, animal, terrestrial and aquatic ecology.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles and concepts underpinning population and community ecology.
Describe the scientific method and apply it to ecology.
Describe the basic ecology of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.
Explain the principles and concepts underpinning the biological function of plants and animals.
Explain natural selection and the process of evolution.

title: Principles of Irrigation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the principles of soil-water-plant-atmosphere relationships, pressurised and non-pressurised water flows, and their applications for on-farm water management. Students will apply the principles of water-plant-atmosphere relationship to determine plant water requirement and irrigation scheduling. Students will also apply principles of open channel, pipe and pump hydraulics in the design, operation and management of gravity and pressurised irrigation systems. Students will develop their knowledge of irrigation water quality and remediation techniques to apply to irrigation-induced issues in soil and water quality.
learning_outcomes: Assess irrigation water quality in terms of physical and chemical properties.
Apply basic hydraulic principles to determine pressure requirement and head loss in pipe and open channel flow systems.
Evaluate the efficiency of a surface irrigation event and distribution uniformity of drip and sprinkler irrigation systems.
Compute plant-available soil water, interpret and explain soil-water relationships.
Calculate water requirements of horticultural and broadacre crops utilising appropriate algorithms.
Design a small-scale pressurised irrigation system, choosing appropriate dripper, sprinkler, and pump products for a particular scenario.

title: Principles of Inclusive Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this subject is to develop teacher education students' understanding of inclusion and inclusive teaching practice, and the knowledge and skills to enable them to effectively differentiate their instruction in the classroom. This includes understanding the intent of the relevant legislation and evidence-based foundations of inclusive practice, and approaches and strategies that maximise the potential for students of a range of abilities to achieve success. Important to this is the adoption of non-discriminatory approaches, and the creation of classroom environments that support, value, and encourage participation (DEEWR, 2005). Teacher education students' will build their capacity to address the wide range of student abilities including giftedness and students with learning difficulties using approaches and strategies for differentiation that focus on both the needs and capabilities of the learner. They will develop strategies to engage and collaborate with other professionals, support services, students, parents and/or caregivers in planning for inclusion and participation to create safe and positive classroom cultures. A critical part of addressing the wide range of student abilities is the development and documentation of appropriate goals, outcomes, and teacher actions. The subject includes a focus on explicit teaching and other effective teaching strategies for the teaching of literacy and numeracy and learning area content to cater for the needs of a range of student abilities. The potential of how ICTs can be used to support participation and engagement is also explored.
learning_outcomes: Explain the research-based evidence of a tiered approach to differentiation as a reasonable adjustment, and evaluate its applicability.

Develop a lesson for their teaching area using the essential characteristics of explicit teaching and other effective teaching strategies to address the specific literacy and numeracy needs for a wide spectrum of learner abilities.

Explain the implications for teaching and learning arising from legislative requirements and policies that support the inclusion and participation of students with disabilities in educational settings.
Differentiate lesson outcomes and designs using three categories of differentiation (process, product and content).
Describe in detail strategies and processes for collaborating with students, parents/caregivers and other professionals in planning for inclusion and participation.

Develop and document individualised SMART learning outcomes for students with varying abilities and characteristics (learning difficulties and giftedness), and detail actions and learning conditions that identify and respond to the students' learning goals and progress based on an ILP planning meeting.
Apply ICT and other strategies in their planning to support inclusive student participation and engagement.
prerequisites: ESS440: Teaching and Learning in the Differentiated Classroom

title: Principles of Extended Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to a primary health care model of patient care by paramedics and paramedical services. The concepts of 'extended care' and 'community paramedicine' are explored. Students will examine how extended care paramedicine systems differ from traditional paramedic services. A number of programs from Australia and internationally are examined to enable students' to understand how extended care programs have developed to meet local community needs. The subject also enables student's to develop an understanding of the role of the extended care paramedic in primary health care and how this differs from traditional emergency paramedic care. Students are introduced to case management and referral options. Other topics included are; legal, professional, ethical and legislative requirements.
learning_outcomes: Be able to compare and contrast a range of modern Australian and International paramedic systems and identify the principles underpinning their development to meet local needs.
Be able to evaluate the role of the extended scope of paramedic practice in health promotion and primary health care.

Be able to critically evaluate the role and responsibilities of the extended care paramedic in primary health care and identify the relationship that exists between paramedics and allied health care providers.
Be able to provide case management and patient care priorities including non-emergency department transfer of care options.
Be able to identify and discuss the legal, professional and ethical issues pertaining to extended care paramedicine.
Be able to compare and contrast the extended care paramedic model and compare and contrast this to traditional emergency paramedics.

title: Principles of Engineering Programming
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to computer programming tailored for engineering students. Through theoretical instruction and practical exercises, students will acquire fundamental programming skills applicable to engineering problem-solving. Emphasis will be placed on algorithm development, logical thinking, and programming best practices using common engineering programming languages.
learning_outcomes: Explain fundamental programming concepts and terminology.
Apply programming techniques to analyse and manipulate engineering data.
Apply algorithms to solve engineering problems using a high-level programming language.
Discuss the role that artificial intelligence can play in modern engineering programming.

Apply ICT and other strategies in their planning to support inclusive student participation and engagement.
Differentiate lesson outcomes and designs using three categories of differentiation (process, product and content).

title: Principles of Operations Research
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundation in basic practice of operations research, that is, solving the decision-making problems that commonly confront managers by developing mathematical models of those problems. The emphasis is on understanding the methods of developing mathematical models and the use of a software package in solving the problems.
learning_outcomes: Identify applications where operations research techniques can be used in the decision-making process.
Construct mathematical models for the various management applications.
Interpret/analyse, manually or automatically, the results from the mathematical models studied and use them in making better management decisions.
Apply software in the process of decision making.
Demonstrate the use of mathematical models. statistics and algorithms to aid in decision-making.
prerequisites: MTH401: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Principles of Market Research
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to the principles of market research and how market research may be applied to address a management problem. The aim of this subject is to develop the skills needed to conduct or apply market research within a commercial context. The subject begins with an overview of the research design process. It then addresses fundamental qualitative and quantitative research issues including data measurement, collection and analysis, and how data can be analysed to provide strategic guidance.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the difference between a management problem and a market research problem.
Reflect on the biases and limitations of market data given a particular research problem.
Analyse and integrate different sources and types of data to draw conclusions.
Understand and apply the concepts and methods of market research to address a research problem.
Develop and evaluate research proposals and reports within the context of a research problem.
Critically evaluate the advantages, limitations, and the ethical implications of commonly used research techniques and their relevance to a research problem.

title: Principles of Operations Research
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundation in basic practice of operations research, that is, solving the decision making problems that commonly confront managers by developing mathematical models of those problems. The emphasis is on understanding the methods of developing mathematical models and the use of a software package in solving the problems.
learning_outcomes: Identify applications where operations research techniques can be used in the decision making process.
Apply software in the process of decision making.
Interpret/analyse, manually or automatically, the results from the mathematical models studied and use them in making better management decisions.
Construct mathematical models for the various management applications.
prerequisites: MTH101: Computer Aided Mathematics 1 with Applications

title: Principles of Pathobiology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the study of disease processes in animals. The mechanisms by which infectious and non-infectious agents cause developmental, degenerative, circulatory, inflammatory and neoplastic diseases in animals will be studied. Genetic, microbial, parasitic, immunological, metabolic, nutritional and toxic causes of disease will be considered. Students will be introduced to the host defence and immune system and will develop the descriptive skills so necessary in gross and microscopic pathology.
learning_outcomes: Observe, recognise and describe normal and abnormal gross and histological specimens from different organs and tissues.
Summarise the important mechanisms that result in neoplastic and developmental disorders.
Write, using correct scientific terminology, accurate gross and histopathological descriptions and reports.
Recognise bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and parasites, explain the importance of the host-pathogen-environment relationship in the disease process.
Use examples to outline the importance of how life cycles are relevant to the epidemiology of key classes of parasites.
Describe the key morphological features of the major classes of microbial agents and parasites.

Describe, using appropriate examples, disease processes in animals including the mechanism of entry of aetiological agents, cell injury, circulatory disturbances, inflammation, repair and regeneration and host defence mechanisms.

title: Principles of Sports Coaching and Performance
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject takes a holistic approach to learning by offering authentic and simulated opportunities to develop and connect knowledge related to exercise delivery in a range of settings, including coaching. In this subject, students will draw on a number of related exercise science areas to prepare them to apply theoretical and practical exercise science knowledge in a real-world context. This subject will allow the student to integrate learning related to exercise testing and prescription, physiology, biomechanics, skill acquisition and other key areas of exercise and sport science in a practical way. Students will be presented with scenarios which require them to provide exercise prescription in a dynamic context. This includes being prepared to adapt exercise prescription and delivery based upon client feedback, availability of resources, and social context.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional understanding of the scope of practice for the exercise scientist in the exercise and sport context in Australia including an understanding of the roles of other exercise and sports science professionals.
Select, apply and justify integrated exercise science knowledge in specific settings, including coaching.
Analyse an exercise or an exercise program and recommend appropriate changes to meet client and industry expectations.
Recommend, prescribe, evaluate and reflect on holistic exercise organisation and delivery.
Integrate knowledge of the exercise science sub-disciplines in the screening, testing, prescription and delivery of exercise.

title: Processes of Pathology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the scientific basis of human disease with a specific focus on the underlying processes that cause cell, tissue and organ dysfunction and how this impacts on comorbidities. The subject will place these changes in the context of the interrelationships between body systems and the impact of lifestyle and other external factors on disease processes. Morphological and functional changes will be related to routine pathological investigations as it applies to patient care. The application of this understanding will add to the student's knowledge base to develop diagnostic reasoning abilities.
learning_outcomes: Describe in detail the range of pathological processes and the aetiology of human diseases.
Identify the impact of co-morbidities associated with different pathological processes.
Predict the impact of pathophysiological processes at a cell, tissue or organ level to change at a multisystem level.
Identify the morphological and functional changes associated with different pathological processes.
Apply knowledge of pathological processes to interpret the findings of routine pathological investigations.

title: Product Innovation Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Innovation is critical for organisations in an era of rapid and continual change. This subject focuses on innovation in goods and services and looks and the risks and returns associated with new product development. Organisation structure and practices that foster innovation are examined alongside a detailed focus on the activities in the new product development process that contribute to success.
learning_outcomes: Examine and critically evaluate current new product activities in the market.
Articulate and reflect on the role of innovation in organisations and the challenges companies face in new product development.
Make recommendations on the design, development and improvement of activities required to take a new product from an idea or opportunity through to a successful launch.
Apply theoretical concepts of new product and new service development and critically evaluate implementation of these in a variety of contexts.

title: Production Analysis and Optimisation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The importance of yield and productivity as key contributors to the profitability and sustainability of agricultural production systems is introduced in this subject. The subject aims to provide students with tools to investigate and analyse the influences of genetic, environmental and management factors on the yield and productivity of crop and livestock systems. The subject will cover key concepts in the design and analysis of agricultural field experiments and how models can be developed to aid decision-making and optimise production systems. Students will develop skills in presenting the outputs of experimental and model-based investigations in ways that are meaningful in an agricultural context. The aims and methods of qualitative research techniques and their use in agricultural settings will also be introduced.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of how models of different forms can be developed and used to support decision-making for and optimisation of agricultural production systems.
Demonstrate an understanding of the underlying assumptions and possible faults that could contribute to poorly designed experiments.
Describe the interactions between yield, productivity and profitability, and how these inform decision-making in agriculture at farm and sector levels.
Design, analyse and interpret the results of simple and more complex experiments and present the results of statistical analyses in ways that are meaningful in an agricultural context.
Demonstrate an understanding of the roles and use of qualitative data analysis in agricultural contexts.

title: Production Animal Medicine 1
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Production Animal Medicine 1 will be presented in a Problem Based Learning (PBL) format over four weeks based around case studies. It will present cases related to farm livestock, particularly illustrating the management of medical and/or surgical cases in the individual animal. This subject addresses in particular the integration of pre- and para-clinical principles in order to diagnose and treat disease in individual animals. This subject will assist students to develop skills in researching and applying best-evidence to result in life-long learning.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with peers and staff.
Identify risk factors for the occurrence of common conditions of individual production animals.
Integrate and act on information regarding client expectations, financial considerations, ethics, welfare and management specific to common scenarios in individual production animals.

Apply and integrate literacy and numerical knowledge from the pre-clinical and para-clinical disciplines, along with best evidence, to prevent, diagnose and manage clinical and/or subclinical cases in individual production animals.
Identify and explain the aetio-pathogenesis of common conditions of individual production animals.
Develop and refine the differential diagnoses associated with common presenting complaints in individual production animals.
prerequisites: VSC331: Diagnosis and Critical Thinking in Veterinary Science

title: Production Animal Medicine 2
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Production Animal Medicine 2 will be presented in a Problem Based Learning (PBL) format over four weeks based around case packages. It will present cases related to intensively housed production animals and farm livestock, particularly illustrating the management of disease and conditions in the intensive population. This subject addresses in particular the integration of pre- and para-clinical principles in order to diagnose and treat disease in intensively produced animals. This subject will assist students to develop skills in researching and applying best-evidence to result in life-long learning.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication with peers and staff.
Identify risk factors for the occurrence of common diseases or conditions in intensive production animal populations.
Integrate and act on information regarding client expectations, financial considerations, ethics and welfare specific to common scenarios in intensive production animal populations.

Apply and integrate literacy and numerical knowledge from the pre-clinical and para-clinical disciplines, along with best evidence, to diagnose and manage clinical cases in intensive production animal populations.
Identify and explain the aetio-pathogenesis of common conditions in intensive production animal populations.
Develop and refine the differential diagnoses associated with common presenting complaints in intensive production animal populations.

title: Professional and Practice-Based Education
school: Division of Learning and Teaching
syllabus_overview: This subject offers an introduction to the theories and practice of professional and practice-based education (P&PBE). It emphasises that P & PBE is a whole of curriculum approach that can make use of a number of pedagogical approaches such as simulations, problem-based learning, as well as workplace learning (WPL). Good practices and issues associated with the Quality Agenda in relation to P&PBE will also play a prominent role in the subject. Workplace Learning as a part of professional education will be included in the subject, with sub topics such as quality, management and strategies for the incorporation of workplace learning experiences into academic curricula. This subject explicitly focuses on learning for professional and occupational practices that occurs in academic contexts. EEL504 Workplace Learning: Theory and practice has an explicit focus on learning in workplace contexts.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss the role of P & PBE in higher education.
Identify and critique options for integrating WPL into curricula.
Critique a course with which they are associated in relation to P&PBE good practices.
Discuss the implementation and management of WPL.
Demonstrate an understanding of the nature and scope of professional and practice-based education.
Articulate and critique good practices in professional and practice-based education in the context of the quality agenda.

title: Professional and Business Pharmacy Practice
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The focus of this subject is on further developing your professional practice and identity as a pharmacist. You will enhance your pharmacy and professional practice skills and knowledge while studying self-limiting disease conditions and their management, counselling and patient education. You will explore the principles of business management and marketing and apply this by developing a business plan. You will demonstrate your new skills through reflection on work integrated learning, oral presentation and case management. This subject includes work integrated learning.
learning_outcomes: Analyse their learning needs, plan and implement a strategy to address those needs and reflect on their performance in pharmacy practice.
Supply, counsel, dispense and conduct business according to ethical and legal standards in the practice of pharmacy.
Competently compound extemporaneous products and supply proprietory non-prescription products to ensure patient safety and quality use of medicines.
Competently counsel and motivate patients to change health destructive behaviours.
Evaluate pharmacy business practice and operations and design potential strategies to optimise outcomes.
prerequisites: PHM315: Professional and Business Pharmacy Practice

title: Professional Communication
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn to reflect upon and practise a number of key academic and workplace professional skills. These include academic writing skills that make use of appropriate referencing techniques, as well as professional workplace behaviour. Students will develop ethical problem solving skills in the context of Information and Communication Technology (ICT). The subject will also introduce students to strategies to overcome communication barriers along with highlighting the importance of good interpersonal communication. Students will develop skills to recognise and adjust their communication approach according to the need and situation.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the roles and responsibilities of an Information and Communication Technology (ICT) professional.
Use appropriate written and/or verbal communication mediums to convey complex knowledge and ideas to professional and general audiences.
Analyse and evaluate ethical problems from the viewpoint of ICT professionals using the Australian Computer Society Code of Ethics.
Convey written information credibly, drawing on academic conventions of citations and referencing to evidence and substantiate an argument.

title: Professional Certificate in Educational Technologies (Practical Artificial Intelligence for Teachers)
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This micro-credential equips primary and secondary teachers to integrate contemporary digital technologies, including generative artificial intelligence, into their professional practice in ways that are inclusive, accessible, and pedagogically sound. Grounded in current research and aligned with the Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools and the technological skill sets of the Australian Skills Classification, this course develops the capacity to select and apply tools that place students at the centre of learning in both online and face-to-face contexts. Students will use technology-integration and inclusive design frameworks to analyse how evidence-based approaches to digital and generative AI technologies can inform responsive and effective classroom practice. During this course, teachers will design and evaluate curriculum-aligned lessons, programs, and resources through the critical evaluation of digital and generative AI technologies with a professional critique of the ethical, legal, and social implications of these technologies in school environments. The course also requires teachers to critically appraise emerging developments in digital technologies and AI, forecasting the opportunities, risks, and broader professional implications for contemporary schooling. By completion, graduates will be able to implement, evaluate and lead technology-enhanced learning that is future-focused, evidence-driven and designed to meet the diverse needs of their learners.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and promote safe, responsible, ethical, and equitable technology use, addressing legal, social and policy considerations for students, teachers, families, and school leadership.

Design and justify curriculum-aligned lessons, programs and resources that use digital technologies and generative AI, to extend learning opportunities for all students by incorporating accessibility and inclusion approaches.
Apply contemporary digital technologies, including generative-AI tools, to facilitate inclusive and accessible student-centred learning in online and face-to-face contexts.

Analyse and evaluate pedagogical theories, research evidence and technology-integration frameworks, including Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and accessibility standards, to inform effective classroom practices using digital technologies and generative AI.
Create, and critically evaluate digital learning artefacts that demonstrate research-informed and inclusive use of technology for K-12 outcomes.
Critically evaluate and forecast emerging developments in digital technologies and AI, articulating their potential opportunities, risks and implications for schools and the teaching profession.

title: Professional Communications
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject discusses how to communicate effectively, and efficiently in professional environments. Students who undertake this subject will gain a wide range of practical communication skills supported by the latest intellectual and psychological behavioural theory. This subject explores the details of how and why humans communicate in certain ways and will equip students to communicate at all levels of professional business for effective outcomes. Students are encouraged to challenge their own communication habits and to undergo a journey of personal change through this subject.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate current human communication theory and apply this in a business context.
Compare and contrast the role and use of digital media and communications mediums for professional and business outcomes.
Facilitate business outcomes by using effective personal communication.
Identify and analyse challenges and obstacles to effective business communications.
Design, compose and deliver a professional presentation.
Analyse and apply practical communication techniques and methods.

title: Professional Development
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this capstone subject students will demonstrate achievement of Course Learning Objectives and refine their knowledge and skills in human services and existing practice as they focus on preparing for a career in the human services profession. Reflection on professional values and ethics together with the application of skills in research and collaborative practice, are key aspects of the subject. Students are required to reflect on and apply course based knowledge to the development of their own professional identity and practice, and to the human services context in a way that promotes skills for ongoing professional development post graduation. The subject is structured for students to work both independently as enquiring and reflective practitioners and to develop their ability to work collaboratively on tasks. Students will build a portfolio that demonstrates capacity to reflect and explore ethics and values in relation to a specific practice issue, using a community of practice process to share, consolidate and demonstrate collaborative professional skills and knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Engage with human services contexts in a way that is professional and fosters sustainable practice.
Develop own professional identity and explore potential career paths.
Demonstrate and apply skills in group work and collaborative practice.
Identify and critically evaluate the professional ethics and values of other professional practitioners.
Identify and critically evaluate own professional ethics and values.
Develop and present a personal portfolio that includes reflection and exploration of values, communities of practice and professional skills and knowledge in context.
Synthesise course learning outcomes and apply these to professional practice.

title: Professional Ethics and Contemporary Financial Planning
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This is a capstone professional practice subject for financial planning students. It will draw on previous study in financial planning including such areas as superannuation, estate planning, risk and insurance, investing, taxation strategies and law. With an emphasis on the practical skills of a financial planner the subject takes the student through the complete interaction between a planner and their client from initial contact, ethical behaviour, building and maintaining client relationships and financial advice in order to prepare and deliver a Statement of Advice.
learning_outcomes: Develop skills to create a mutually respectful relationship that is built on trust and understanding.
Evaluate and analyse client needs through effective communication and interpretation of clients requirements.
Identify, analyse and apply ethical standards that allow client needs to be met.
Investigate, construct, implement and evaluate a comprehensive financial plan which combine all elements and areas of client needs, to the best advantage of the client.

title: Professional Development in Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on ‘people at work' through personal reflection on diversity, inclusion and the development of cultural competency generally. Students will develop transferable skills in the context of collaboration and cultural diversity in work-related scenarios. Preparation for future careers will be emphasised, with students applying their academic learning to a range of work related scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply appropriate knowledge and transferable skills to work-related scenarios and collaborate effectively within diverse and inclusive environments;
Demonstrate understanding of ethical, sustainable and cultural perspectives and contributions to workplace and business practices
Develop, apply and reflect on personal and technical competence in work-related contexts; and

title: Professional Experience - Introduction to the Secondary Context
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides teacher education students with the opportunity to commence exploring the relationship between practical and disciplinary knowledge of teaching. They will do this in preparation for, and during a professional experience teaching placement of up to 160 hours (as required by accreditation requirements and approved by the Course Director). As they complete the preparatory phase of the subject, teacher education students will engage with issues of teaching and learning, classroom and behaviour management, planning and assessment. Workplace Health and Safety and risk management in the teaching and learning environment will also be a focus. There is an expectation that teacher education students will ensure their developing understandings of appropriate curriculum, and adolescence and social justice issues, are reflected in the teaching placements undertaken in secondary school contexts.
learning_outcomes: Plan, implement and assess student learning in a sequence of lessons that will cater for students' learning needs.
Reflect on their development as a teacher and establish learning goals for professional experience placements.
Demonstrate beginning skills essential for clear communication, managing student learning, learning environments and professional relationships.
Display a developing awareness of a range of effective teaching strategies to cater for adolescent learners.
Have achieved an overall rating of satisfactory in a professional experience placement of up to 160 hours (as required for accreditation and approved by the Course Director).
Explain and provide evidence of development towards achieving the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers.
Identify, assess and manage risk to create a safe class environment in their area of specialisation.
prerequisites: EPT123: Implementing Professional Knowledge in TAS Classrooms
EPT113: Becoming a H/PE and Outdoor Education Professional
EMT345: Curriculum Method: Design and Technology
EMT445: Curriculum Method: Design and Technology

title: Professional Experience 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Professional experience is a foundational requirement of this degree and provides teacher education students with the opportunity to develop skills studied in curriculum method and education discipline subjects. In this first placement of up to 30 days, teacher education students will explore school practices and develop their knowledge of teaching and learning to establish professional abilities in the classroom and professional connections with parents and carers and the wider school and professional community. The placement is designed so that collaboration and feedback possibilities are scheduled on a regular basis where the supervising teachers and the teacher education student discuss lesson planning, classroom management and teaching practice. Assessment of the placement is formative and discussed with teacher education students in the middle and at the end of the placement. The portfolio provides evidence of the student's commitment to and progression in developing competence in the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers.
learning_outcomes: Successfully complete a school placement (up to 30 days).
Apply the models of productive pedagogies and quality teaching.
Apply a range of strategies and effective communication skills for managing classroom environments.
Apply a range of teaching and learning strategies.
Design learning experiences.
Demonstrate their capacity to work collaboratively.
Demonstrate growth as a teaching professional in relation to the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers.
prerequisites: EMR441: Curriculum Method 1: Health and Physical Education and Outdoor Education
EMT445: Curriculum Method: Design and Technology
EMT447: Design and Digital Technologies Curriculum

title: Professional Experience 1
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable teacher education students to integrate their knowledge and skills as emerging professionals as they prepare for and complete up to 30 professional experience placement days. This experience will provide teacher education students with an opportunity to observe, discuss, undertake, and reflect on the work of secondary school teachers. In preparation for the placement, this subject will explore the professional communication skills required for fostering positive educational partnerships with young people and families within local communities. The placement is designed so that opportunities for collaboration and feedback are scheduled on a regular basis, with the supervising teacher and the teacher education student discussing lesson planning, classroom management, and teaching practice. This feedback is designed to be formative and details about progress should be discussed at the middle and end of the placement. The final placement report then forms one of the summative tasks within this subject. The development of a portfolio provides evidence of the student's commitment to, and progression in developing competence in the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers.
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of strategies and effective communication skills for managing classroom environments.
Apply a range of teaching and learning strategies.
Apply the models of productive pedagogies and quality teaching.
Demonstrate their capacity to work collaboratively.
Demonstrate growth as a teaching professional in relation to the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers.
Design learning experiences.
Successfully complete a school placement (up to 30 days).

school: School of Education

In preparation for the placement, this subject will explore the professional communication skills required for fostering positive educational partnerships with young people and families within local communities. Plan, teach, assess, reflect and evaluate student learning in a sequence of lessons that will cater for students' learning needs.
Demonstrate high quality communication skills essential for managing student learning, learning environments and professional relationships.
Establish resources in preparation for the Graduate Teacher Performance Assessment.
Successfully complete a professional experience placement up to 240 hours (as required for accreditation and approved by the Course Director).
Demonstrate progress working towards achieving the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers.
