Students then engage with qualitative and quantitative research methods focusing on data collection, data analysis, interpretation and evaluation issues. Students will prepare a research plan incorporating a critique of existing knowledge, appropriate research methodology, suitable data collection and analysis techniques and an outline of the ethical issues specific to their research. Students engage with research traditions and paradigms relevant to their discipline.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the professional cultural and social contexts within which their research enquiry is undertaken.
Identify and justify an appropriate research methodology applicable to their research.

Demonstrate a critical understanding of the ethical issues in their research, including recognising the significance of consent, confidentiality and other ethical considerations pertinent to researching professional practice.
Systematically investigate and critically evaluate a range of applied research methodologies and approaches.

Demonstrate an understanding of qualitative, quantitative and mixed research methods in relation to their research, including relevant data collection, analysis, interpretation and evaluation methods and techniques.

title: Research Methods
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce students to research strategies in the Human Services and teach them to interpret research findings as well as conduct research in their own right. The subject will examine various methods of research, both qualitative and quantitative. Within future practice, students will often need to conduct research or oversee the research of others. This subject will introduce students to this process. By the end of the subject they should be able to write a research proposal as well as be able to make sense of the findings of others.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate research reports.
Prepare a research proposal concerning social issues.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of various research methods.

title: Research Methods
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: The subject provides an overview of context within which enquiry is undertaken, and a grounding in key research traditions, paradigms and methodologies relevant to the disciplines of the arts and social sciences. Candidates select two particular methodologies and study their application in depth.
learning_outcomes: Successfully apply the methods and approaches of particular research methodologies adopted by the arts and social sciences.
Critique the application of research methodologies, assess its effectiveness in specific contexts, and identify design limitations.
Demonstrate an understanding and appreciation of key research traditions and paradigms in the arts and social sciences.

title: Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to current methodological and statistical techniques used in psychological research. A number of methodological approaches and data collection techniques are examined and evaluated. Students are also introduced to hypothesis testing, a range of common parametric and non-parametric inferential tests, and computer analysis of data.
learning_outcomes: Select appropriate methodology(ies) for answering research questions.
Describe the applications, limitations, strengths, and weaknesses of a range of research methodologies.
Use a computer package (eg., SPSS) to analyse data.
Follow the conventions of the American Psychological Association for reporting research.
Select, compute, and interpret selected parametric and non-parametric statistics appropriate to nominated research methods.
Describe the concepts, principles, and processes involved in developing high quality research.
Demonstrate an understanding of the value of quantitative research.
Describe and apply the ethical principles to be followed in carrying out research in psychology.

title: Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to current methodological and statistical techniques used in psychological research. A number of methodological approaches and data collection techniques are examined and evaluated. Students are also introduced to hypothesis testing, a range of common parametric and non-parametric inferential tests, and computer analysis of data.
learning_outcomes: Use a computer package (e.g., SPSS) to analyse data.
Describe the applications, limitations, strengths, and weaknesses of a range of research methodologies.
Describe and apply the ethical principles to be followed in carrying out research in psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding of the value of quantitative research.
Follow the conventions of the American Psychological Association for reporting research.
Select appropriate methodology(ies) for answering research questions.
Select, compute, and interpret selected parametric and non-parametric statistics appropriate to nominated research methods.
Describe the concepts, principles, and processes involved in developing high quality research.
prerequisites: PSY201: Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology

title: Research Methods in IT
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will enable students to choose and justify a research method from a broad range of quantitative and qualitative research methodologies relevant across the Information Technology (IT) discipline. Students will prepare a research plan incorporating a critique of existing knowledge, appropriate research method, suitable data collection techniques and an outline of the ethical issues impacting their research topic. Students are provided the opportunity to write a substantial proportion of their methodology/data collection chapter and publish their preliminary work by identifying a publication outlet, such as a journal or conference, and providing the publication template.
learning_outcomes: Identify and justify an appropriate research methodology for a research problem.
Design a quantitative and/or qualitative research study for the chosen research problem.
Determine and evaluate philosophical assumptions, underpinning research approaches and strategies.
Evaluate research design approaches to data collection.

title: Research Methods in Health Sciences
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the principles of research methodology as relevant to the health sciences. It examines the context of research in professional practice in the healthcare field, and will equip students with the basic research skills necessary for their continuing professional education and for pursuing research at honours level. The subject considers concepts in both qualitative and quantitative research methodology and includes basic statistical concepts and methods, and the critical appraisal of literature in science and healthcare.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills consistent with life-long learning.
Plan for and develop a research proposal.
Identify how moral, ethical, cultural, social, political and environmental issues and responsibilities impact on research.
Apply introductory descriptive and inferential statistical concepts and techniques in the analysis of data.
Accurately describe the fundamental concepts and approaches in qualitative and quantitative research methodology.
Demonstrate skills in critical thinking by accurately synthesising new research results in science/health.
Critically review and critique the literature through the use of valid resources, and thereby provide informed opinion.
Evaluate the implications of research methodologies on evidence-based practice and on their impact on clinical practice and policy.
Apply research methodology to investigate and solve research questions raised in professional practice.

title: Research Methods in Mental Health
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students undertaking this subject will develop their capacity to understand and apply research using evidence-based practice in mental health research. Student will be provided with opportunities to engage in and explore Indigenous and Westernised Methodologies that inform culturally appropriate research. Students will develop their knowledge and skills so that they become critical consumers of research, and are prepared to participate in research projects relevant to mental health.
learning_outcomes: identify formal and informal research as it relates to practices in mental health;
identify ethical and cultural considerations relevant to research activities in primary, secondary and tertiary health care contexts;
access and analyse current literature to identify evidence which informs mental health practice;
discuss how research outcomes can be translated to mental health practice for the benefit of patient/client care.
analyse and discuss a range of methodological approaches and study designs to justify their suitability for mental health research; and

title: Research Plan in IT
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will formalise the research methodology in their research plan and extend on their literature review from ITC534 in order to understand the major concepts, issues, problems, theories, and gaps within their field of research. Students will be expected to thoroughly understand the strengths and weaknesses of the methodologies by which knowledge in the field has been acquired. In addition, this subject explores the research ethical issues relevant to the student's area of research. During this subject students will develop a framework of their research based on relevant literature and appropriate methodology, and where applicable submit an ethics application.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique a range of controversial issues drawn from literature related to the area of research.
Demonstrate advanced academic writing skills.
Identify ethical issues around a research problem.
Compare and contrast research methods in IT.
Independently and systematically explore an area of research within IT and how it interrelates with other IT issues.

title: Research Practice in Healthcare
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will extend students' understanding of research in healthcare practice and assist them to reflect critically on their position in relation to research and data. Students will evaluate a range of methodological approaches to answering a research question, developing their skills in critical appraisal of disciplinary evidence, including Australian First Nations approaches to knowledge generation. This subject will provide students with the opportunity to translate research findings to their disciplinary practice context, for the purpose of supporting the delivery of safe, quality healthcare. Students will develop knowledge and skills to reflect critically on ethical issues fundamental to all research, including Australian First Nations approaches to knowledge generation, and to build an understanding of culturally relevant practices.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on ethical principles informing research practices, including Australian First Nations approaches to knowledge generation and Indigenous data sovereignty in the Australian context.
Demonstrate critical reflexivity in appraising disciplinary research to identify knowledge gaps and propose future research questions.
Compare different research approaches to investigating research questions.
Translate research to disciplinary practice to support the delivery of safe and quality healthcare.
Critically evaluate research design and methodology including Australian First Nations approaches.
Explain the value and application of research to the advancement of safe and quality healthcare practice and policy.
prerequisites: PHM508: Pharmacy Research Methods and Proposal

title: Research Project
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students implement a piece of research in an applied setting and present a formal report of their findings. Students are exposed to the phases of quantitative and qualitative research design and issues of ethical standards in research. In conjunction with an assigned supervisor, students then develop a research proposal, implement the proposed research and present a formal report of their findings. The research projects are conducted in groups, however each individual student will produce a research proposal and final report.
learning_outcomes: be able to develop a research proposal for implementation in an applied setting
be able to demonstrate their research skills by designing, carrying out and reporting a piece of empirical research.
be able to demonstrate an understanding of why research is important to practicing psychologists

title: Research Project
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the opportunity to undertake a small-scale, supervised research project in a discipline within the arts and social sciences. Each student will investigate a topic area of their choice, applying an appropriate methodology. They will complete the project by submitting a report, dissertation, or creative work with exegesis of approximately 10,000-12,000 words or equivalent that will discuss the outcomes, implications and limitations of their project.
learning_outcomes: Apply a research methodology rigorously and critically.
Present and discuss the research according to the academic standards of the applicable discipline.
Complete a small-scale research project on schedule.
Apply knowledge of ethical requirements pertaining to a research project where applicable.

title: Research Proposal
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Through critical analyses of scholarly literature, students will identify significant researchable problems related to their discipline through a literature review and formulate a clear research question(s) that leads to the design and writing of a proposal for a feasible, small-scale research project using appropriate research methodologies and methods. This subject is designed to be responsive to the independent needs of students whether you are a postgraduate student, and/or a professional seeking to design a workplace project outside of academia. In this subject, you will work with an experienced academic to design your proposal.
learning_outcomes: Select and critically evaluate scholarly literature related to the discipline.
Clearly articulate the research questions that give rise to the study and the issues that arise from its design and conduct.
Examine ethical, social and political issues in relation to the students’ chosen discipline and determine their impact on research design.
Use initiative and judgment to conceptualise and propose a justifiable, feasible small-scale research project proposal with clearly articulated objectives.
prerequisites: IKC504: Indigenous or Indigenist Research Proposal

title: Research Proposal
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop a research project including identifying a gap in current literature, writing a research proposal, ethics applications and other applications as required. A comprehensive and critical literature review in the area of study is completed to give the student a deep and wide knowledge of the research topic. Students will be equipped with knowledge of the general requirements to carry out research, which is also useful for example, in management and in teaching as well as in research supervision role for undergraduates students. This subject requires background in basic research methodologies and methods.
learning_outcomes: Identify a gap in the relevant literature and formulate a research question.
Develop a research proposal, including completion of ethical requirements and other approvals required for research.
Locate, review, critically appraise and synthesise academic literature relevant to a specific topic.

title: Research Proposal and Presentation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In both the written proposal and the seminar presentation students are expected to draw upon their previous review of the literature and methodology chapters. Students will demonstrate their thorough knowledge of the paradigms and methodologies by which knowledge in the field of their enquiry has been advanced. Within the research proposal they must address the ethical issues associated with the conduct of their research. After supervisory approval students will submit their comprehensive research proposal for Faculty peer review and defend it in an oral presentation.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically reflect on the importance to professional practice of unresolved research problems in the particular area of research.
Communicate, in a seminar situation, the potential benefit, relevance and significance of the outcomes of the research to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Justify and defend the overall research design and attenuate potential ethical issues, and demonstrate a critical understanding of the limitations of the method/s selected.
Develop and defend a research proposal with reasoned argument drawing on the relevant literature.

title: Research Proposal in Ministry
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: Issues and questions which arise from the candidate's professional practice in ministry provide the basis of the research project. From these an extended research proposal is developed by the candidate in a collaborative learning environment and is defended by presentation to the faculty of the School of Theology and professional practitioners in the candidate's proposed area of research. Candidates also complete a research proposal form and ethics approval (if required) for submission to the University.
learning_outcomes: Develop an ethics application.
Articulate the relationship between the candidate's professional work in ministry and research in ministry.
Develop a research proposal.
Profer a defence of that research proposal.

title: Research Skills
school: School
syllabus_overview: Being able to research is important for success in university study. This subject is designed to introduce the research skills that are essential for university study and that are particularly important for the completion of assessment tasks. Through study of this subject students will learn the skills of research for tertiary study and how to utilise a range of support services.
learning_outcomes: Identify the nature, importance and role of research skills in university success.
Access and interpret information represented in a variety of forms.
Use library resources to locate information and resources.
Apply skills to the evaluation of sources.
Conduct searches and source relevant information.
Document research using Charles Sturt University's accepted APA version referencing.

title: Resilience Thinking and Ecologically Sustainable Development
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The transition to more sustainable resource use requires fundamental changes in our thinking about the environment. We need to better understand that nature and humanity are dynamic and co-evolving, and that achieving sustainability and addressing global warming is not simply about decreased consumption, but rather about increasing our capacity to meet a range of challenges. Resilience thinking focuses understanding the dynamics and development of complex social-ecological systems. It focuses on the capacity of a system to absorb disturbance and reorganise while undergoing change, so as to retain essentially the same function, structure, identity and feedbacks. Communities must seriously consider ways to foster resilience in our transformation to a more sustainable society.
learning_outcomes: Develop appropriate strategies that address a range of global environmental and social problems.
Have an in-depth understanding of the nature of complex social-ecological systems.
Review, consolidate and synthesise knowledge from a number of case studies in order to critically understand the effectiveness of various strategies associated with implementing resilience thinking.
Have an in-depth understanding of key terminology, principles, concepts and theory underpinning resilience thinking and their application in resolving environmental issues.

title: Research: Data and Insights
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject explores research methods commonly used in communication industries. The subject covers fundamental principles and concepts in communication research and methods, as well as techniques and analysis used to address contemporary industry issues and problems. Students are required to plan, propose, implement and evaluate a research project.
learning_outcomes: Propose and conduct a research project and report on your findings as part of a team.
Demonstrate an understanding of important research concepts.
Identify different methodological approaches.
Apply concepts in planning and undertaking research.

title: Resourcing the Curriculum
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the critical evaluation and provision of appropriate digital and hardcopy resources to effectively resource the curriculum and support learning and teaching within the school. The role of school library collections in the information environment is particularly addressed, as are protocols and frameworks that guide selecting, curating and promoting Indigenous Australian resources that reflect decolonising practices and respect for Indigenous Australian cultures. Assessment of needs, selection, acquisition, de-selection, collection evaluation and collection policy formulation are examined in the context of the school. Issues such as budgeting, censorship, cooperative resource provision and learning management systems are explored.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of how to select, acquire and deselect collections and resources to respond to curriculum resources needs in a timely manner.
Be aware of the role of school library collections in learning and teaching.
Identify and evaluate information sources and products to determine their relevance to the information needs of the school community.
Discuss key issues such as censorship, budgeting and cooperative resource provision.

Critically evaluate and demonstrate advanced knowledge of protocols and ethical frameworks for selecting, curating, and promoting Indigenous Australian resources that reflect decolonising practices and respect Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property in school library collections.
Provide an overview of the range of information resources available and the impact of digital resources on school library collections.
Assess information needs in the context of building school library collections and services.

title: Respiratory Critical Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students’ previous education and experience to advance the knowledge and specialised skills needed to provide critical care paramedicine for airway and respiratory emergencies. Students will further develop their ability to integrate assessment and diagnostic data, knowledge of relevant anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology, and evidence-informed practice to propose critical care paramedicine treatment plans. Students will also integrate specialised paramedic knowledge, theories and frameworks to develop the professional attributes and clinical reasoning skills required to perform advanced airway management.
learning_outcomes: Integrate knowledge of specialised technical skills and apply to evidence-informed critical care paramedic practice for airway and respiratory emergencies.

Interpret clinical data derived from advanced patient diagnostics, assessment and history taking and apply to evidence-informed critical care paramedic treatment plans for airway and respiratory emergencies.
Integrate specialised paramedic knowledge, theories and frameworks for contemporary critical care Paramedicine relevant to airway management.
Apply advanced knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology to critical care paramedic management of airway and respiratory emergencies.

title: Responsible Analytics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the principles, concepts, and fundamentals of responsible data analytics. It covers a range of challenges in striking a good balance between effective and ethical/responsible use of data science, machine learning and AI – from data collection, curation, and pre-processing to analytics and decision making/support. Students will learn about the potential risks/harms associated with the data processing pipeline and/or use of data in decision support systems via real-world case studies. The subject shall explore whether and to what extent it is possible to develop responsible and ethical algorithms for data analytics in business. Furthermore, students will be introduced to modern frameworks for algorithmic governance with the lenses of socio-cultural values and human right principles.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical principles and decision-making frameworks to analyse and resolve ethical dilemmas within real-world analytics pipelines.
Analyse and apply ethical considerations in the collection, storage, analysis, and application of data in various contexts.
Critically evaluate data sources, analytics methodologies, and results to recognise biases, limitations, and potential societal impacts.
Apply an advanced knowledge of regulatory frameworks and best practices for responsible analytics, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.

title: Responsible AI
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to responsible artificial intelligence (AI) through a comprehensive overview of the ethical, social, and legal implications of developing and deploying AI technologies. The subject employs real-world case studies in the discussion of the fundamental concepts, definitions, and open debates on the adoption of emerging AI systems, the potential benefits and risks associated with AI in everyday life and business. Students will learn about algorithmic bias and fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability; and how to effectively detect and mitigate risks associated with emerging AI technologies. The subject also highlights avenues for effective and responsible adoption and use of the new AI solutions in business, government, and industry.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate responsible AI principles, policies, and frameworks for effective and ethical business decision making.
Apply fundamental concepts in responsible AI to identify and discuss ethical, social, and legal concerns associated with the implementation of emerging AI systems.
Interpret responsible AI implications/findings, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.
Design and develop protocols for detecting ethical, social, and legal implications in the adoption of AI systems within business environments.

title: Restoration Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Restoration ecology is a rapidly advancing field of ecology that underpins efforts to repair and improve degraded or modified landscapes. This subject introduces students to the key terminology, concepts, and theoretical frameworks of the discipline, with a focus on critically evaluating principles, ecological models, and approaches to restoration. Students will also consider the limitations, uncertainties, and challenges of translating theory into practice. Applications are explored across diverse contexts, including agriculture, riverine, urban, and mining. Students will be equipped to design, justify, and communicate evidence-based restoration strategies, and to apply scientific rigour, adaptive management, and critical judgement in addressing complex restoration problems.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-based approaches to assess the effectiveness of restoration practices, with awareness of professional responsibility.
Apply key concepts, principles, and theoretical frameworks underpinning restoration ecology.
Identify and explain ecological, social, and logistical challenges involved in restoring different environments.
Apply ecological knowledge to propose context-specific restoration approaches and communicate them appropriately for the intended audience.

title: Restoration Science and Practice
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Restoration ecology is a rapidly advancing field of ecology that underpins efforts to repair and improve degraded or modified landscapes. This subject introduces students to the key terminology, concepts, and theoretical frameworks of the discipline, with a focus on critically evaluating principles, ecological models, and approaches to restoration. Students will also consider the limitations, uncertainties, and challenges of translating theory into practice. Applications are explored across diverse contexts, including agriculture, riverine, urban and mining. Students will be equipped to design, justify, and communicate evidence-based restoration strategies, and to apply scientific rigour, adaptive management, and critical judgement in addressing complex restoration problems.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced and integrated concepts, principles and theoretical frameworks underpinning restoration ecology.
Critically analyse and evaluate ecological, social, and logistical challenges in restoring diverse environments.
Evaluate and adapt restoration practices using evidence-based approaches, demonstrating professional responsibility and independent judgement.
Design, justify, and communicate context-specific restoration approaches to diverse audiences drawing on current research and best practice.

title: Restricted elective
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject is an administrative placeholder used within course structures to represent the inclusion of a restricted elective (8 credit points). It is not a subject for enrolment and does not have any associated learning or assessment requirements.

title: Right Wing Extremism and Terrorism
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Right wing extremism and terrorism is increasing around the world. The attacks in Christchurch and El Paso in 2019 by right wing terrorists have reinforced the urgency of this rising threat. In this subject, you will be introduced to theories which explain right wing extremism and terrorism, and you will explore extreme right ideologies. You will then investigate right wing terrorist strategies and attacks to advance your knowledge of the terrorism nexus. Its transnational nature will be explored through the framework of online networks, and with reference to the domestic and international environments. Finally, you will focus on the right wing extremism in specific regions to consider mechanisms for countering this threat.
learning_outcomes: Clearly communicate complex issues associated with right wing extremism to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Objectively assess right wing threats to contribute to debate and inform professional practice; and,.
Critically evaluate right wing extremism and terrorism precedent to make threat assessments.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of right wing extremism and terrorism with reference to ideology, strategies and tactics, and networks to provide threat assessments.
Use a range of research approaches and evidence types to analyse existing knowledge of right wing terrorism to substantiate assessments.

title: Rights of the Child
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an understanding of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, with particular reference to its implications for early childhood education and care. The subject will critically examine children's rights to provision, protection and participation in early childhood settings, local communities and national policies. Images of children and childhood, current practices in the early childhood education field and relevant policies are explored through the lens of children's rights. The role of early childhood educators as advocates for children as independent bearers of rights is examined.
learning_outcomes: Understand the content and scope of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and implications for and of public policy related to early childhood.
Discern the interrelationship between the legal responsibilities and ethical stances of educators and recognition of children's rights.

Use the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child as a reference point for advocacy and decision making to ensure the rights of the child are acknowledged and respected in their settings and in their communities.
Critically reflect upon the content and scope of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the implications for the experiences of children in early childhood settings.
Gain a critical awareness of the various factors that contribute to the violation of children's rights, including political, cultural and economic discrimination and / or marginalisation.
Reflect upon contemporary images of children and childhood and evaluate how these support or hinder the enactment of children's rights.

title: Risk Assessment and Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject places risk management in the context of the insurance broking environment which includes not only traditional forms of insurance but also risk identification, assessment, avoidance, treatment, financing, monitoring and review.
learning_outcomes: Explain how to negotiate complex insurance program renewals with insurers.
Describe how to formulate and recommend a loss control program.
Describe how to obtain client renewal instructions.
Explain how to assess loss reports to identify and review loss trends.
Identify insurance program requirements for clients.
Outline how to monitor and review risk management processes.
Outline how to establish a loss reporting program.
Identify appropriate risk assessment and management strategies.

title: Rights of the Child
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an understanding of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, with particular reference to its implications for early childhood education and care. The subject will critically examine children's rights to provision, protection and participation in early childhood settings, local communities and national policies. Images of children and childhood, current practices in the early childhood education field and relevant policies are explored through the lens of children's rights. The role of early childhood educators as advocates for children as independent bearers of rights is examined.
learning_outcomes: Understand the content and scope of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and implications for and of public policy related to early childhood.

Use the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child as a reference point for advocacy and decision making to ensure the rights of the child are acknowledged and respected in their settings and in their communities.
Discern the interrelationship between the legal responsibilities and ethical stances of educators and recognition of children's rights.
Critically reflect upon the content and scope of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the implications for the experiences of children in early childhood settings.
Reflect upon contemporary images of children and childhood and evaluate how these support or hinder the enactment of children's rights.
Gain a critical awareness of the various factors that contribute to the violation of children's rights, including political, cultural and economic discrimination and / or marginalisation.

title: Risk Based Audit and Assurance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the practice and theory of auditing and forensic investigation adopting a risk-based approach to auditing and assurance services. The expanding role of auditing to financial and nonfinancial reporting will provide opportunity to appreciate the changing role of the auditor and societies expectation of ethics and good governance in the role of auditing. The concept of risk management is emphasised as it permeates all functions of management, audit and corporate governance.
learning_outcomes: Design an audit plan and select and apply appropriate audit procedures for a financial statement audit.
Discuss the role of the audit professional in diverse audit teams involved in assurance of sustainability and other nonfinancial reports.

Apply risk management methodologies and identify how information communication technology supports identification, reporting and management of risk, and enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of an organisation's systems and processes and analyse the adequacy of information communication technology processes and controls and identify improvements in an audit context.
Explain how technological advances that support data analysis, decision making, can enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of communication in an audit context.
Explain the importance of collaboration, cooperation, and teamwork when working towards audit goals.
Exercise critical and reflective judgement and appreciate the value of ethical practice.
Identify and critically evaluate the expanding scope of assurance services and providers in today's international business environment including non-financial reporting.

Explain and critically evaluate influences on audit and assurance services including: Australian and international professional standards, statutory and common laws, regulatory bodies, and public expectations within a global market.

title: Risk Based Auditing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject adopts a risk-based approach to auditing and assurance services, exploring the practice and theory of auditing and forensic investigation. The expanding role of auditing to financial and nonfinancial reporting provides an opportunity for students to appreciate the changing role of the auditor and societal expectation of ethics and good governance in the role of auditing. The concept of risk management is emphasised as it permeates all functions of management, audit and corporate governance.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the role of the audit professional in diverse audit teams involved in assurance of sustainability and other non-financial reports.

Explain and critically evaluate influences on audit and assurance services including: Australian and international professional standards, statutory and common laws, regulatory bodies, and public expectations within a global market.
Discuss technological advances that support data analysis, decision making, and enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of communication in an audit context.
Exercise critical and reflective judgement and appreciate the value of ethical practice.

Apply risk management methodologies and identify how information and communication technology supports identification, reporting and management of risk, enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of an organisations systems and processes, and analyse the adequacy of information and communication technology processes and controls and identify improvements in an audit context.
Identify and critically evaluate the expanding scope of assurance services and providers in today's international business environment including nonfinancial reporting.
Design an audit plan and select and apply appropriate audit procedures for a financial statement audit.

title: Risk Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject develops a framework to assess, measure and reduce risk using qualitative and quantitative approaches. The influence of the decision maker through individual bias and decision-making heuristics is also examined. The subject is closely linked with the key industry risk management standards AS/NZS 4360 and ISO31000. Through the application of real world problems, students will become familiar with the role of the risk manager. Students will also explore the use of risk management tools and how to incorporate these into their management design and strategies.
learning_outcomes: Appraise an environment and determine the probability, frequency and consequences of a risk event occurring.
Assess and evaluate the role of the decision maker in risk situations.
Define risk, differentiate between risk and uncertainty, and analyse and explain the link between risk and change.
Design, implement and evaluate a range of strategies to diminish and manage risk.
Identify, analyse and explain the influences of decision making heuristics, bias and risk preference in the risk.

title: Risk in Security Studies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Risk is a fundamental concept in security studies, influencing decision-making across intelligence, investigations, fraud prevention, terrorism studies, and emergency management. This subject explores the theoretical and practical dimensions of risk, focusing on how security professionals assess, mitigate, and manage risks in various domains. Students will critically analyse case studies, frameworks, and methodologies to develop advanced risk assessment and mitigation strategies in complex security environments.
learning_outcomes: Apply risk assessment frameworks to security-related case studies.
Develop strategic responses to mitigate future risks in fraud, investigations, intelligence, terrorism studies, and emergency management.
Communicate risk assessment findings and recommendations effectively to diverse stakeholders.
Critically evaluate risk theories and their application in security studies.
Systematically identify and analyse threats, vulnerabilities, and consequences in different security contexts.

title: Risk Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses risk management, both in the broader context and from an organisational perspective, and takes into consideration the pro-active and reactive measures which prevent or minimise risk in public and private sectors. It draws heavily upon the Australian and New Zealand Standard, AS/NZS ISO:31000:2009 Risk Management-Principles & Guidelines, and AS/NZS 4360:2004, when examining the risk management process. Students, drawing on their own experiences, examine how risk plays a crucial role in business decision making, the ways in which risk manifests itself over time and across activities, and the methods used in managing risk across organisational policies, practices, systems and processes.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the application of risk management to a practical setting.
Effectively define risk.
Identify the various risks that can threaten organisations.
Assess and analyse the nature of the risk.
Discuss and develop strategies to minimise risk.

title: Risk Management and Insurance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the concept of personal, property, liability and business risk management. It provides a framework that allows identification of risk, the probability of risk, the cost of risk; and the means of managing risk. To the extent that risk cannot be avoided or managed, self-insurance and laying off the risk to an insurance provider is examined. The key feature of this subject is the development of needs based solutions to risk management across a full range of options and the development of personalised solutions.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse the law governing insurance as it applies to financial planning clients and be able to apply it to specific situations.
Undertake secondary research and critically evaluate the conflicting positions on recent developments in insurance and risk management trends and policies.
Critically evaluate the scope and nature of different insurance products and identify appropriate contracts which cater for client identified risk.
Critically analyse the risks faced by clients and apply the risk management process to identify the exposures to risk and the options available to handle those exposures.
Prepare appropriate insurance recommendations within a Statement of Advice that will mitigate the identified risks.

title: River and Floodplain Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students gain in-depth knowledge about rivers, how they function, and the types of animals and plants that inhabit them. In doing so, it is assumed students already have some knowledge of analysing environmental data and animal identification. This subject builds on that knowledge to teach you about the diversity of freshwater habitats and the ecological models relevant to the management of freshwater ecosystems. At a intensive students will gain experience in field sampling techniques (flora and fauna), the identification of organisms, and the statistical analysis of ecological data. Students complete this subject with an in-depth understanding of the organisms and communities in aquatic environments and the effect people can have on inland aquatic ecosystems.
learning_outcomes: Have a broad understanding of the hydrological cycle and properties of water.
Have a broad and coherent understanding of the physical, chemical and ecological processes that occur in inland water bodies.

Review, consolidate, and synthesise their knowledge about river and floodplain ecology in order to critically discuss the impacts of humans and the threatening processes affecting Australian inland waters.
Have the ability use a variety of specialised techniques to sample aquatic organisms and to assess aquatic ecosystems.
Have in-depth knowledge about the ecological models used to explain river and floodplain function.
Have specialised skills identification of organisms and communities in aquatic environments.

title: Risk Management in the Emergency Management Context
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the key themes and concepts of risk management in an emergency management context. Risk management is an important consideration in any organisational management context. However the complexity of the emergency management industry sees risk management as a crucial component as it impacts on practice in a variety of ways, from pre-event emergency management planning to emergency response and the follow up emergency recovery planning and operations.
learning_outcomes: Review, analyse, consolidate and synthesise theory and best practice in emergency risk management.
Demonstrate an understanding and mastery of the skills involved in the emergency risk management process and how this is used in preparing for major emergencies and the challenges therein.
Communicate to both academic and professional audiences critical evaluations of emergency risk management practice with recommendations for policy.
Critically reflect on risk management professional practice, identify key challenges in relation to emergency risk management, and how professional practice may be enhanced to address this.

title: River and Floodplain Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students gain in-depth knowledge and integrated understanding of rivers and their floodplains, how they function, and the types of animals and plants that inhabit them. This subject builds on knowledge of animal identification and analysis of environmental data to deepen understandings about the diversity of riverine environments, the physical, chemical and biological processes that influence them and the ecological models relevant to the functioning and management of river and floodplain ecosystems. Students will gain experience in field sampling techniques (flora and fauna), the identification of organisms, and the analysis and interpretation of ecological data. Students completing this subject will develop an in-depth understanding of the organisms, communities and habitats in, and key threats to, freshwater environments, and the approaches to the conservation and management of inland aquatic ecosystems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced competency in specialised techniques for sampling and identifying aquatic organisms, and critically interpret data to inform ecological assessment and management.
Critically analyse the hydrological cycle and evaluate the ecological significance of the properties of water.
Demonstrate an integrated knowledge of the physical, chemical and biological processes that drive river and floodplain ecosystems, in Australia and globally.
Synthesise advanced knowledge of river and floodplain ecology to critically evaluate human impacts and threatening processes on Australian inland waters.
Critically evaluate and apply ecological models used to explain river and floodplain function.

title: River and Floodplain Restoration and Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the theoretical and practical frameworks that underpin the restoration and management of riverine environments following disturbance. It is assumed students undertaking this subject already have a good knowledge of river hydrology, geomorphology and ecology. The subject covers the following specialised areas of knowledge: principles of restoration ecology; decision analysis in deciding recovery goals; restoration constraints; methodologies and techniques, monitoring, and criteria for evaluating restoration outcomes. During the intensive school, students will engage with practitioners and managers and visit a range of restoration sites. Students completing this subject have the knowledge and skills needed to make sound judgments regarding the recovery goals for a river and have an ability to critically assess existing or planned restoration projects.
learning_outcomes: Make informed and independent judgements to prioritise restoration works and set realistic recovery goals.
Use specialised practical skills to develop monitoring criteria and systems for determining rate and degree of recovery.

Review and synthesise knowledge in order to make sound independent judgments for deciding recovery goals, in the light of restoration constraints and available restoration methodologies and techniques.
Apply ecological principles to guide the restoration of river and floodplain ecosystems in Australia.
Analyse the state of riverine ecosystems and the causes and processes of degradation in riparian and floodplain systems.
Critically evaluate restoration projects in relation to ecological, social, financial, and logistical constraints.

title: River Hydrology and Geomorphology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive grounding of the major concepts in river hydrology, hydraulics and geomorphology. Students will gain knowledge about flow hydrology, hydraulic behaviour, landforms and sedimentary deposits of rivers. Practical topics include the identification and description of distinctive landforms, sediments and types of flow associated with rivers, as well as methods in analysing hydrological data and report writing. The concepts and theory are woven into case studies to develop understandings of the effects of natural flood events and river regulation on the flow regime of rivers, especially those in the Murray-Darling Basin. On completion, students will possess knowledge of hydrology, hydraulics and geomorphology of rivers, some fundamental field observation and data analysis skills, and be able to critically apply this knowledge to key river management issues.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the key terminology, concepts and theory underpinning river geomorphology, river hydrology and channel hydraulics.
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the geomorphology and hydrology of a selected Australian river system and apply this knowledge to other river systems.
Critically apply their knowledge of river hydrology, hydraulics and geomorphology combined with judgement and problem solving skills to some key river management issues.
Identify and describe the distinctive landforms, sediments and types of flow associated with rivers.
Interpret and communicate the findings of a field study clearly and coherently within a river management context.
Apply their knowledge and skills in river hydrology and geomorphology to interpret hydrologic data and discuss the effects of flow on river systems.

title: River Hydrology and Geomorphology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive grounding of the major concepts in river hydrology, hydraulics and geomorphology. Students will gain knowledge about flow hydrology, hydraulic behaviour, landforms and sedimentary deposits of rivers. Practical topics include the identification and description of distinctive landforms, sediments and types of flow associated with rivers, as well as methods in analysing hydrological data and report writing. The concepts and theory are woven into case studies to develop understandings of the effects of natural flood events and river regulation on the flow regime of rivers, especially those in the Murray-Darling Basin. On completion, students will possess knowledge of hydrology, hydraulics and geomorphology of rivers, some fundamental field observation and data analysis skills, and be able to critically apply this knowledge to key river management issues.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe the distinctive landforms, sediments and types of flow associated with rivers.
Critically apply their knowledge of river hydrology, hydraulics and geomorphology combined with judgement and problem solving skills to some key river management issues.
Apply their knowledge and skills in river hydrology and geomorphology to interpret hydrologic data and discuss the effects of flow on river systems.
Interpret and communicate the findings of a field study clearly and coherently within a river management context.
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the geomorphology and hydrology of a selected Australian river system and apply this knowledge to other river systems.
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the key terminology, concepts and theory underpinning river geomorphology, river hydrology and channel hydraulics.

title: Routing and Switching
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide students with experience on switching technologies and router operations that support small-to-medium business networks as well as Wireless Local Area Networks (WLAN) and security concepts. Concepts covered in this subject enable students to develop advanced skills related to Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs), Inter-VLAN routing, Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), Etherchannel, switch security, Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), First Hop Redundancy Protocol (FHRP), WLAN and routing. This subject is the second in a series of three subjects that incorporate the Cisco Networking Academy Program.
learning_outcomes: Describe, analyse, identify and mitigate LAN security threats.
Distinguish and analyse different routing and switching protocols.
Explain the purpose, nature and operations of routing and switching techniques.
Configure and troubleshoot networks to improve efficiency and security.
Configure, verify and solve a variety of problems involving Wireless Local Area Networks.

title: Rural Communities, Global Challenges
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the sociological study of rural places, and the everyday lives of people who live and work in rural areas. Through specific emphasis on Australia, the subject examines the diverse meanings attached to 'The Rural', the influence of different ideas and policy approaches in shaping the social and economic structure of rural areas, and the challenges and prospects for rural people and places in a globalising world. The subject will be of particular relevance to students who intend to work in non-metropolitan settings.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the processes, institutions and policy approaches that shape the social organisation of rural life.
Demonstrate skills in the written presentation of an argument, including the ways in which sociologists incorporate and acknowledge the ideas of other writers.
Understand the different frameworks through which sociologists and human geographers make sense of rural places and issues.
Explain the implications of social and environmental change for rural people and places.

title: Ruminant Production and Welfare
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject is designed to develop in students an understanding of extensive ruminant production systems as well as some of the more intensive aspects of production where relevant to particular species (excluding feedlots). It focuses on aspects of herd/flock management namely production efficiency, reproduction, market/profit drivers, husbandry and animal welfare.
learning_outcomes: Describe routine animal husbandry techniques and when they are performed.
Formulate breeding programs for different ruminants.
Discuss the constraints to optimal production.
Formulate grazing strategies and rations for grazing animals.
Demonstrate how to manage herds/flocks to maximise production efficiency.
Demonstrate an understanding of the effects of animal welfare on health and production.
Utilise computer software to develop strategies for and the management of nutrition and reproduction.

title: Rural Populations and Places
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an advanced introduction to the sociological study of rural places, and the everyday lives of people who live and work in rural areas. Through specific emphasis on Australia, the subject examines the diverse meanings attached to the rural, the influence of different ideas and policy approaches in shaping the social and economic structure of rural areas, and the challenges and prospects for rural people and places in a globalising world. It engages also with contemporary debates concerning the development of sustainable and resilient rural communities, and analyses different strategies for enhancing rural 'sustainability'. The subject will be of particular relevance to students who intend to work in non-metropolitan settings.
learning_outcomes: Analyse debates concerning the sustainability of rural industries and places.
Demonstrate skills in the written presentation of an argument, including the ways in which sociologists incorporate and acknowledge the ideas of other writers.
Explain the implications of social and environmental change for rural people and places.
Understand and apply the frameworks through which sociologists and human geographers make sense of the rural.
Recognise the processes, institutions and policy approaches that shape the social organisation of rural life.

title: Sacramental Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject traces the origins of sacramental theology from its Jewish antecedents through to the New Testament texts and early church. It then considers the rise of sacramental theology proper in the patristic period. Later developments are pursued through historical and liturgical sources, from the medieval Western church and Reformation to the divergent traditions and practices in contemporary churches. The subject addresses challenges brought to sacramental theology by the ecumenical movement and by liberation, feminist and ecological theology.
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically sacramental practice and theology in light of contemporary issues, for example, reconciliation, abuse, ecology, multiculturalism.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss and critically evaluate contemporary sacramental theologies and church practices.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of key historical developments in sacramental theology.
Give an advanced critical account of the meaning and practice of Baptism, Eucharist and Reconciliation in various contemporary ecclesial traditions.
Identify and to articulate the sacramental theology expressed in liturgical texts and their enactment.

title: Sacramental Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject traces the origins of sacramental theology from its Jewish antecedents through to the New Testament texts and early church. It then considers the rise of sacramental theology proper in the patristic period. Later developments are pursued through historical and liturgical sources, from the medieval Western church and Reformation to the divergent traditions and practices in contemporary churches. The subject addresses challenges brought to sacramental theology by the ecumenical movement and by liberation, feminist and ecological theology.
learning_outcomes: Identify the sacramental theology expressed in liturgical texts and their enactment.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss and evaluate contemporary sacramental theologies and church practices.
Discuss critically sacramental practice and theology in light of contemporary issues, for example, reconciliation, abuse, ecology, multiculturalism.
Demonstrate knowledge of key historical developments in sacramental theology.
Give an account of the meaning and practice of baptism, eucharist and reconciliation in various contemporary ecclesial traditions.

title: Science and Society
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The subject examines the relationship between science and society, focusing in particular upon the impact of technological change on society. Students are to select one topic from a range of choices for an in-depth case study.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the main issues relating to the role of scientists in society.
Demonstrate the social impact of technological change.
Demonstrate present day concerns relating to the application of science and technology.
Demonstrate the 'meaning' of science in contemporary culture.

title: River and Floodplain Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject students gain broad knowledge about rivers and their floodplains, how they function, and the types of animals and plants that inhabit them. It is assumed students already have some knowledge of animal identification and analysing environmental data. This subject builds on that knowledge to teach students about the diversity of riverine environments, the physical, chemical and biological processes that influence them and the ecological models relevant to the functioning and management of river and floodplain ecosystems. At an intensive, students will gain experience in field sampling techniques (flora and fauna), the identification of organisms, and the analysis and interpretation of ecological data. Students complete this subject with a broad understanding of the organisms, communities and habitats in, and key threats to, freshwater environments, and the approaches to the conservation and management of inland aquatic ecosystems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competency in a variety of specialised practical techniques to sample and identify aquatic organisms and to use the derived data to relate these organisms to physical, chemical and biological features of freshwater ecosystems.
Analyse the physical, chemical and ecological processes that drive river and floodplain ecosystems, in Australia and globally.
Review, consolidate, and synthesise their knowledge about river and floodplain ecology to critically discuss the impacts of humans and the threatening processes affecting Australian inland waters.
Interpret and apply ecological models used to explain river and floodplain function.
Explain the hydrological cycle and discuss the ecological significance of the properties of water.

title: Science and Technology Curriculum Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject examines Years K-6 curriculum documents for science and technology and requires students to work collaboratively in designing and developing a Science & Technology program of learning for pupils in Years K-6. Contemporary theories of learning in science and technology, including constructivist and conceptual change perspectives, will be explored. Students will apply their knowledge of learning theory, lesson and unit design and assessment of, and for, learning to develop the sequence of learning activities that use pedagogies afforded by scientific and educational technologies. Students learn how to integrate scientific and technological concepts, skills in conducting scientific investigations and designing and producing solutions, literacy, numeracy, the 5Es Learning Cycle and Learning across the Curriculum Content into a Science & Technology K-6 program of learning.
learning_outcomes: Identify opportunities to embed literacy, digital literacy and numeracy in teaching/learning activities for Science and Technology K-6.
Apply models of pedagogy within a Science and Technology K-6 program, including inquiry based and project based learning.
Use a range of assessment for learning strategies in K-6 Science and Technology lessons.
Design a detailed teaching program that develops children's knowledge and understanding in Science and Technology K-6 through the skills of Working Scientifically, and Design and Production.
Develop teaching and assessment strategies that effectively support and expand opportunities for children with diverse learning needs.

Design and produce a digital resource to facilitate children's learning of Science and Technology K-6 syllabus outcomes and justify its design drawing on contemporary theories of learning in science and technology.
Interpret Science and Technology K-6 curriculum and syllabus documents for NSW or the Australian Curriculum.
prerequisites: EMS207: Science and Technology Curriculum Studies

title: Sacramental Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject traces the origins of sacramental theology from its Jewish antecedents through to the New Testament texts and early church. It then considers the rise of sacramental theology proper in the patristic period. Later developments are pursued through historical and liturgical sources, from the medieval Western church and Reformation to the divergent traditions and practices in contemporary churches. The subject addresses challenges brought to sacramental theology by the ecumenical movement and by liberation, feminist and ecological theology.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of key historical developments in sacramental theology.
Give an advanced critical account of the meaning and practice of Baptism, Eucharist and Reconciliation in various contemporary ecclesial traditions.
Analyse critically sacramental practice and theology in light of contemporary issues, for example, reconciliation, abuse, ecology, multiculturalism.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Identify and to articulate the sacramental theology expressed in liturgical texts and their enactment.
Discuss and critically evaluate contemporary sacramental theologies and church practices.

title: Science and Technology Curriculum Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject examines K-6 curriculum documents for science and technology and requires students to work collaboratively in designing and developing a science and technology program of learning for school students in Years K-6. Students will apply their knowledge of learning theory, lesson and unit design and assessment of, and for, learning, to develop a sequence of learning activities that engage K-6 students in science and technology learning and use pedagogies afforded by scientific and educational technologies. Contemporary theories of learning in science and technology, including constructivist and conceptual change perspectives, will be explored in this subject. The teaching and learning of science and technology through learner-centered approaches and curriculum integration is promoted. Students will be required to integrate scientific and technological concepts, the skills and processes of conducting scientific investigations and designing and producing solutions, literacy, numeracy, and learning across the curriculum content into their science and technology planning and teaching.
learning_outcomes: Interpret Science and Technology K-6 curriculum and syllabus documents for NSW or the Australian Curriculum.
Identify opportunities to embed literacy, digital literacy and numeracy in teaching and learning activities for Science and Technology K-6.
Use a range of assessment for learning strategies in K-6 Science and Technology lessons.
Design a detailed teaching program that develops childrens' knowledge and understanding in Science and Technology K-6 through the skills of Working Scientifically, and Design and Production.
Apply models of pedagogy within a Science and Technology K-6 program, including inquiry based and project based learning.
Design and produce a digital resource and explain how its use will facilitate children's learning of Science and Technology K-6 syllabus outcomes, content and processes.
prerequisites: EMS406: Science and Technology Curriculum Studies

title: Science and Technology Studies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Science has a distinctive way of observing and investigating to help us understand events and phenomena from the physical and natural world. Traditional, contemporary and emerging technologies can be shaped by the environment but may also shape the built environment in this rapidly developing technological world in which we live. This subject aims to extend teacher education students' understandings of science and technology through an integrated approach, by exploring how scientific discovery and invention, including the understandings and technologies of First Nations Australians, are applied and have an impact in everyday life. This includes issues related to the public perception of science and scientific ethics. Students will develop their skills in applying the processes of science, technology and design. They will question, investigate, develop ideas, seek solutions to problems and further develop their understandings of scientific and technological concepts. This subject provides opportunities for teacher education students to explore how people interact with their environment including the complex interaction of First Nations Australians with their environment.
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the relationships between science and technology and the contributions they make to daily life and towards a sustainable future.
Identify and critique alternative conceptions associated with science, including the critique of science for validity.
Explain and apply a range of key concepts and principles in science and technology.
Apply the design and production processes, including planning, producing, testing and evaluating to seek a solution to a problem.
Examine how environments and the relationship between people, especially First Nations Australians, and the environment, can impact the development of scientific and technological innovations.
Explore elements of scientific enquiry, using the scientific method and fair testing to conduct practical scientific investigations, explain observations and communicate findings.
Investigate issues related to the public perception of science and to scientific ethics.

title: Science Communication and Methodology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide a firm foundation for developing skills in scientific communication. Students will learn academic, information, and digital literacy skills as well as numeracy skills relevant to their discipline of study. The subject will also introduce students to critical analysis of the scientific literature and the scientific method. This subject will also raise awareness in students to professional and ethical issues relating to health and medical sciences.
learning_outcomes: Describe and apply the scientific method as it applies to the featured disciplines.
Express and apply communication skills appropriate for health and medical science.
Demonstrate knowledge of professional and ethical issues related to health and medical science, including research.
Critically analyse a scientific paper.
Demonstrate information, digital and academic literacy and numeracy skills appropriate for health and medical sciences.

title: Science for Out of Field Teachers
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This microcredential explores a range of pedagogical approaches to science education in Years 7-10. It examines current Science 7-10 syllabus documents and identifies the place of science in the school curriculum. It also examines Year 11 and Year 12 NSW science syllabuses and the Australian Curriculum. A major focus is on planning teaching and learning sequences for secondary science that will provide learners with opportunities to develop science understandings through the application of Working Scientifically skills and inquiry questions. Particular attention is devoted to the application of contemporary theories of learning in science, authentic pedagogies, and assessment for learning in the context of secondary science education in diverse classes.
learning_outcomes: Implement senior secondary science curriculum and syllabus documents for NSW or the Australian Curriculum into a teaching program.
Apply contemporary models of pedagogy, including inquiry based strategies, in the planning of sequences of teaching/learning activities and assessment in science.
Apply the structure and content of the Science 7-10 Syllabus for NSW or the Australian Curriculum in the development of a sequence of lessons.

Plan teaching and learning sequences for Science 7-10 and senior secondary sciences that utilise learners’ prior experience of scientific ideas and will provide learners with opportunities to develop or apply their conceptual understandings through the application of Working Scientifically skills and open, inquiry questions.

title: Science Honours Project/Dissertation
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a research subject available only to students enrolled in certain integrated Honours courses in the Faculty of Science. Students enrolled in this subject will extend their knowledge and skills in their area of specialisation. Students will work directly with their supervisor(s) to review relevant research literature, plan and conduct a research project, and prepare a comprehensive written report on their research activities and findings.
learning_outcomes: Identify a clear research question in their area of specialisation, based on a critical review of relevant literature.
Design and conduct a research project, including the selection and application of appropriate research methods.
Demonstrate an advanced level of knowledge in their area of specialisation.
Prepare a comprehensive written report on their research activities and findings.
Obtain human/animal ethics approval (if required).

title: Science Honours Research Methods
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will broaden and deepen their awareness of research methods relevant to their discipline, including methods relevant to their planned Honours research. Students' methodological knowledge and skills will be developed through analysing and evaluating published research studies in their discipline. Students will consider broad approaches to research (qualitative, quantitative, and pragmatic), question-clarity, specific designs, sampling decisions/techniques, recruitment strategies, data collection and analysis methods, and conclusion validity. Overall, this subject will introduce students to concepts and skills that are important for designing and conducting methodologically sound research in their area of interest.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the clarity of a research question in their discipline area, and explain the importance of clear question formulation for sound methodological planning.
Evaluate the appropriateness of methodological choices in relation to a study's research question.
Demonstrate basic data analysis skills relevant to their planned Honours research.
Compare and contrast research designs, sampling, recruitment (if relevant), data collection, and data analysis methods used by researchers in their discipline area.
Appraise the validity of conclusions in published research articles, considering the reported methods and results.
Identify examples of qualitative and quantitative research in their discipline area, and the associated strengths of each approach.
prerequisites: HLT505: Research Methods in Health Science A
SCI415: Social Science Research Methods for Natural Resource Management
HLT430: Research Methods in Health Sciences

title: Science in Modern Society
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
