syllabus_overview: Scientists work in a dynamic environment involving personal and institutional negotiations with social and ethical issues. In this subject, students will examine ethical theories and apply them to various aspects and case studies of science in modern society, as well as application of professional practice and recognition of Cultural and Intellectual property of Indigenous Peoples within those ethical theories. Students will also explore global issues associated with climate change through critical analysis of the global evidence and impact on world ecosystems. Students will then examine ideas of the practice of science and scientific evidence through case studies of World and Australian Indigenous cultural practices.
learning_outcomes: Locate, evaluate, and synthesise scientific information from credible sources to support evidence-based reasoning.

Analyse contemporary and historical examples of the relationship between science and society and discuss the social, cultural, environmental and economic implications and responsibilities of science to society.

Explain and apply the ethical constructs that underpin scientific codes of conduct, and use these principles to analyse the ethical dimensions of contemporary global scientific challenges, including the protection of Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) and the protocols that govern its use.
Communicate scientific ideas clearly and appropriately for diverse audiences using written, oral, and digital modes.

Analyse Indigenous Australian scientific knowledge and contributions to scientific inquiry, and compare these with other Indigenous knowledge systems and Western science to support culturally responsible scientific practice.
Compare and evaluate professional standards and codes of practice across scientific disciplines and explain how these guide professional scientific practice.

title: Scientific Data Analysis
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Data are constantly being captured, but variability makes processing these data challenging. Statistics is the science and art of making decisions in the presence of variability. This subject provides a foundation to statistics. It includes an introduction to data science, inferential statistics as well as Bayesian statistics. The subject's orientation is towards the sciences and covers both experimental and observational data including big data. The emphasis is on understanding, critically evaluating and then reflecting on a range of vital statistical concepts and applying acquired skills to data interpretation, management and modelling by using modern software package.
learning_outcomes: Calculate and interpret probabilities, use discrete and continuous random variables and sampling distributions, and assess the suitability of these distributions in probability modelling.
Model data using Bayesian analysis; examine, present and infer the output appropriately, and analyse the differences with standard statistical inference.
Synthesise the concepts of statistical inference, correlation and multiple linear regression and apply these to real world problems.
Evaluate and present results, with an integrated understanding of the underlying theory, in the form of a standard statistical report for specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Explain data science concepts, classify and synthesise datasets and identify the challenges and benefits of micro and big data.
Examine critically and reflect on whether the statistical methodology and conclusions drawn in the media, scientific papers or reports are appropriate.
Use a statistical package to: explore various types of data, summarise and analyse data appropriately, and present and interpret the output in a clear logical manner.

title: Scientific Instrumentation (Electronics)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject deals with the analysis of circuits containing both linear and non-linear elements. It covers DC and AC circuits, solid state conduction, diodes, transistors and integrated circuits, amplifiers, op-amps, oscillators and introductory digital electronics. The emphasis is on the analysis and application of circuits, rather than circuit design. This subject has a compulsory intensive.
learning_outcomes: Compute and solve problems of a conceptual and quantitative nature in the above areas of electric circuits and devices.
Conduct experiments, analyse data and write laboratory reports on electric circuits and devices.
Outline the principles and perform calculations on the operation of solid state devices including diodes, transistors and operational amplifiers.
Explain the concepts and perform calculations in circuit analysis using network theorems.
Explain the concepts and perform calculations in principles of DC and AC circuit analysis.

title: Scientific Statistics
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundation in the basic practice of statistics, ie explaining variability. The orientation is towards the sciences covering both experimental and observational data. The emphasis is on understanding statistical concepts and applying acquired skills to data interpretation by the use of modern software packages. The modern approach to the teaching of statistics is used including group work, use of local data and small projects.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and explain graphical and numerical summaries using statistical language.
Interpret computer output from analyses and reproduce such calculations manually.
Understand the importance of experimental design in terms of inference, sample size, cost and efficiency.
Use a modern calculator and a statistical software package.
Use graphical and numerical methods to describe both quantitative and qualitative data.
Explain the relationship between probability, statistics and inference.
Identify the appropriate statistical techniques and conduct statistical analysis (both by hand and with the use of a computer).
Demonstrate an understanding of the assumptions underlying statistical techniques.

title: Scientific Statistics
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Statistics is the science and art of making decisions in the presence of variability. This subject provides a foundation in the basic practice of statistics. The subject's orientation is towards the sciences and covers both experimental and observational data. The emphasis is on understanding statistical concepts and applying acquired skills to data interpretation by the use of a modern software package.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concepts of statistical inference, and apply these to confidence intervals and tests of hypotheses.
Explain standard uses of statistics in the media and in scientific papers, and determine whether the statistical methodology and conclusions drawn are appropriate.
Use a statistical package to summarise data graphically and numerically and analyse data appropriately, and interpret the output.
Evaluate if the assumptions underlying statistical techniques are valid in a given scenario.
Calculate and interpret probabilities, and use standard discrete and continuous probability distributions.
Apply basic principles of experimental design, such as determination of appropriate sample sizes, randomisation and blocking.

title: Sectional Anatomy
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students build on foundation knowledge and understanding of anatomy to explore structures and tissues in cross section. Students will consider the normal cross-sectional anatomy of the major skeletal and soft tissue structures of the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis and limbs enabling consideration of imaging pathology. The normal image appearance of the structures and their relationships, as demonstrated in multiple sectional planes on plain and contrast x-rays, CT, MRI and, where appropriate, co-registration with physiological imaging (SPECT and PET), will be considered in detail.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical appraisal and reflective skills related to clinical imaging, problem solving and decision making (MRPBA Domain 4.1a-c).
Describe and explain the principles of patient information management systems and 3D datasets for diagnostic image production (MRPBA Domain 1.2).
Describe and apply understanding of anatomy, physiology and pathology using cross sectional imaging in CT, MRI, SPECT and PET (MRPBA Domain 1.1).

title: Search Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: During this subject students will learn the latest methods, techniques and tools for improving their organisation's search marketing and brand building efforts. They will analyse how different campaigns work and create a search marketing plan that incorporates a Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) strategy and a Pay Per Clicks (PPC) campaign.
learning_outcomes: Analyse how different campaigns are working, understand conversion analysis and apply campaign attribution and tagging, and.
Implement a Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) strategy in a technically effective way and identify common issues.
Develop, evaluate, and rationalise the commercial viability of Pay Per Click (PPC) and other paid search campaigns.
Create a formal search marketing plan.
Demonstrate an understanding of content relevance and the technical aspects of on-page optimisation.

title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject students develop knowledge of the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) and the key security principles and techniques that can be used to build secure software applications. Students will also learn and apply different tools and techniques that can be used to detect and mitigate security risks during the software development process.
learning_outcomes: Apply security tools and techniques to detect and mitigate security risks during the development process.
Identify different security threats and vulnerabilities and demonstrate how they can be mitigated.
Describe the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) and its different phases.
Implement secure coding practices and principles during the software development process.

title: Seminar in Biblical and Theological Interpretation
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses, through focused seminars, in-depth research of particular persons, movements, events, eras, topics, and themes in Biblical interpretation and theology. It traces recent developments in Biblical Studies, with particular emphasis on the development of Scriptural themes and the methods of representative contemporary Biblical scholars.
learning_outcomes: Offer an informed account of the historical and theological relevance of a particular issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.
Analyse and critique the selected topic and its impact upon particular exegetical or theological problems.
Articulate critically the contemporary significance of a relevant issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.
Demonstrate independent research, writing, and communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research essay.
Evaluate critically the particular research principles and methodology appropriate for a specific issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.
Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and discussion skills through interaction with the subject coordinator and fellow students.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a current issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.

title: Sentencing Law and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Sentencing law and practice examines sentencing law and the principles that underlie sentencing legislation. Students will be introduced to the major theories and paradigms that dominate sentencing practice in the criminal justice system. Students will learn about the different types of sentences that can be passed down by the courts. Sentences such as fines, community service, court orders, treatment orders, community corrections, restorative justice, incarceration and diversion will be examined. This subject will also consider the social and political influences that shape the application of these sentences. Students will look at the impact of sentencing practices on people, including marginalised groups, indigenous people, young people and women.
learning_outcomes: Describe and evaluate the types of sentences passed by the courts of Australia.
Describe the principles and aims of sentencing in the context of Australian sentencing laws.
Evaluate the impact of sentencing on people, including vulnerable groups.
Utilise an interdisciplinary approach to evaluate sentencing law and practice.

title: Sensory Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce students to the key principles underpinning the physiology and characteristics of the senses, with a particular focus on wine sensory assessment. Through the application and development of various sensory testing skills and procedures, students will learn to describe and identify sensations produced by major wine components, main wine varieties, styles, Australian regions and common faults.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the nature and balance of the sensory characteristics in wines and relate those features to wine type, grape variety, wine style and wine processing.
Distinguish between wine faults, and explain their causes.
Explain the physiology of the perception of taste, smell, and texture, chemesthesis and its impact on sample perception characteristics.
Apply sensory principles to wine and grape juice evaluation, to identify the important sensory characteristics and their balance.
Describe sensory testing methods and interpret sensory data.

title: Seminar in Biblical and Theological Interpretation
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses, through focused seminars, in-depth research of particular persons, movements, events, eras, topics, and themes in Biblical interpretation and theology. It traces recent developments in Biblical Studies, with particular emphasis on the development of Scriptural themes and the methods of representative contemporary Biblical scholars.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate academic engagement and discussion skills through interaction with the subject coordinator and fellow students.
Evaluate critically the particular research principles and methodology appropriate for a specific issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.
Demonstrate independent research, writing, and communication skills through the preparation and presentation of a substantial research essay.
Offer an informed account of the historical and theological relevance of a particular issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.
Articulate critically the contemporary significance of a relevant issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.
Analyse and critique the selected topic and its impact upon particular exegetical or theological problems.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a current issue in Biblical interpretation or theology.

title: Server Administration
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to enable students to plan, deploy, optimise and maintain Microsoft Servers. Students will learn how to analyse network performance and create an optimisation strategy, design and apply a network security policy, analyse and configure Core Network Services, and design and implement an Active Directory solution. Students will also prepare for Microsoft industry certification exams during this subject.
learning_outcomes: Create, critically analyse and apply a network security policy.
Create a plan for server installation.
Deploy, manage, and maintain a network server.
Design and configure an Active Directory solution.
Critically analyse and configure Group Policy and core network services.
Design and configure a cloud-enabled hybrid solution.
Critically analyse network performance and create an optimisation strategy.

title: Server Administration and Maintenance
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a general introduction to managing computers called servers that provide web, file, electronic mail, and similar kinds of networked services. Computers running the Linux operating system are studied. Students learn to operate servers via the command line, write scripts to automate management tasks, analyse and improve the performance of servers, create and manage basic information services, and assess methods required to protect data and services accessed from the internet.
learning_outcomes: Manage servers from the command line.
Write scripts to automate various server management tasks.
Analyse and improve the performance of servers.
Describe the duties and responsibilities of a systems administrator.
Formulate methods for protecting data and services accessed via the internet.
Create and manage basic information services.

title: Services Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Contemporary market economies are dominated by services. This subject helps students appreciate the distinct characteristics of services and the implications these have for developing and implementing marketing strategies in a wide range of service industries. Current issues in technology and ethics are also examined in relation to service organisations.
learning_outcomes: Describe and develop an effective service recovery process.
Articulate the importance of customer retention, and develop retention strategies.
Explain the importance of asset use and yield management and develop pricing objectives and strategies.
Formulate a service product strategy and explain the important considerations in the development of new services.
Conceptualise and explain the significance of satisfaction, value and service quality in achieving competitive advantage, and devise approaches for measuring these elements.
Design an effective customer service organisation, including implementation guidelines for a customer service program.
Identify the distinctive characteristics of services marketing and explain the expanded marketing mix.
Discuss the implications of service characteristics on marketing communications, and develop appropriate marketing communications strategies.
Describe capacity management techniques and formulate demand management strategies.

title: Sexual Assault, Family Violence and Associated Trauma
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with knowledge and insight into sexual assault, family violence and the resulting associated trauma. Students will develop an understanding of the impacts experienced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples affected by sexual assault or family violence, and the associated trauma. This subject highlights the links between mental health issues related to trauma, sexual assault and family violence. Students will develop useful practical skills and knowledge to work more effectively with individuals and communities to respond effectively and to establish safety for those people affected by sexual assault, family violence and resulting trauma.
learning_outcomes: respond appropriately and effectively to issues of sexual assault, family violence and associated trauma at a beginner practitioner level.
identify issues and barriers to reporting/disclosing sexual assault and family violence for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people;
research, analyse and critically discuss the impact and prevalence of family violence, sexual assault and associated trauma for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and their communities;
discuss the principles underpinning effective partnerships with community agencies when planning initiatives to address sexual assault, family violence and associated trauma; and
critically evaluate strategies for best practice when working in the area of sexual assault, family violence and associated trauma;

title: Signals and Systems
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a solid foundation for understanding various aspects of electrical engineering, including communication systems, control systems, and signal processing. Topics covered include signal representations, linear time-invariant systems, convolution, Fourier analysis, Laplace transforms, Z-transforms, and applications of signals and systems in engineering.
learning_outcomes: Examine the applications of signals and systems in various engineering domains.
Compare tools necessary for analysing and designing linear time-invariant systems.
Use mathematical techniques to analyse continuous and discrete signals and systems.
Apply fundamental concepts of signals and systems.

title: Sirah (Life of Prophet Muhammad)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject discusses the life of Prophet Muhammad from multiple angles. There is a focus on his character, personality, and common misconceptions about his life and work. Various time periods of his life including pre-Islamic Arabia, early life before prophethood, the Meccan period and migration to Medina are covered. The social, diplomatic and military challenges he faced are studied. The family life of the Prophet, his spirituality, his reported miracles, social transformations during his lifetime, and dynamics that were to shape human history will be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the state of pre-Islamic Arabia.
Analyse social transformations during his lifetime and relate their impact on the Muslim world today.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Demonstrate an understanding of the family life and spiritual aspects of Prophet Muhammad.
Recognise and analyse common misconceptions about Prophet Muhammad.
Demonstrate an understanding of the main events in the life of Prophet Muhammad and the unfolding of a Muslim community.

title: Sexual Assault, Family Violence and Associated Trauma
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with knowledge and insight into sexual assault, family violence and the resulting associated trauma. Students will develop an understanding of the impacts experienced by at risk communities and groups affected by sexual assault or family violence, and the associated trauma. This subject highlights the links between mental health issues related to trauma, sexual assault and family violence. Students will develop useful practical skills and knowledge to work more effectively with individuals and communities to respond effectively and to establish safety for those people affected by sexual assault, family violence and resulting trauma.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate strategies for best practice when working in the area of sexual assault, family violence and associated trauma.
Discuss the principles underpinning effective partnerships with community agencies when planning initiatives to address sexual assault, family violence and associated trauma.
Respond appropriately and effectively to issues of sexual assault, family violence and associated trauma at a beginner practitioner level.
Research, analyse and critically discuss the impact and prevalence of family violence, sexual assault and associated trauma for at risk communities and groups.
Identify issues and barriers to reporting/disclosing sexual assault and family violence for at risk communities and groups.
prerequisites: MHP312: Sexual Assault, Family Violence and Associated Trauma

title: Six Industry Certification Credits
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Administration Credit subject only

title: Skill Acquisition
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject uses a behavioural approach to explore a broad range of factors and processes affecting skilled motor behaviour. Emphasis is placed on developing general principles that exercise professionals can apply to influence motor performance and skill learning. The subject delivers concepts and theories of motor behaviour; factors influencing motor control; and motor skill assessment and intervention. After completing this subject, students will be able to analyse motor skill situations to explain behaviour, task manipulation, and environmental factors to facilitate desired performance outcomes. Students will also learn strategies to facilitate motor skill learning in a variety of settings.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and discuss the common theoretical models proposed to explain motor control and the processes of motor learning.
Identify the strengths and limitations of techniques to assess processes of motor learning and motor control.
Describe the structure and function of the neuromuscular and sensory systems as they relate to the control of voluntary and involuntary movement and motor learning.

Design motor learning environments and apply evidence-based protocols to maximise each individual's specific motor learning and control outcomes, as appropriate in physical activity and exercise contexts.

Assess aspects of an individual's motor function in physical activity and exercise contexts including applying risk management and risk assessment concepts associated with the motor learning and control of exercise science.

title: Skills for LANTITE - Writing
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Skills for LANTITE - Writing is the second of two Study Link enabling subjects designed to address core literacy skills required by teachers to demonstrate the minimum standard as set by the Australian Government. All students enrolled in an initial teacher education course are required to sit and pass the Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education - LANTITE. This subject covers core literacy content in the content area of Writing, including skills to recognise and explain punctuation, grammar and language features across a range of text types, understand the structures of writing, as well as improve spelling and vocabulary.
learning_outcomes: Recognise correct punctuation, grammar and language conventions
Identify the structural features of writing.
Identify correct and incorrect examples of spelling and vocabulary.
Explain appropriate sentence structures

title: Skills for LANTITE - Reading
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Skills for LANTITE - Reading is the first of two Study Link enabling subjects designed to address core Literacy skills required by teachers to demonstrate the minimum standard as set by the Australian Government. All students enrolled in an initial teacher education course are required to sit and pass the Literacy and Numeracy Test for Initial Teacher Education - LANTITE. This subject covers core literacy content in the content areas of Reading and Comprehension, including skills to understand and respond to increasingly complex texts, which are areas examined in such a test.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of reading and comprehension to respond to questions about a variety of text types
Comprehend increasingly complex texts
Evaluate the intended purpose of texts
Reflect on the meaning of texts at literal and inferential levels
Build capacity for increased fluency in reading and responding

title: Skills of Conflict Resolution
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is about the nature and application of the skills and processes of conflict resolution. This subject analyses the considerations related to ethical use of conflict resolution skills and it examines the strategies and approaches essential in developing conflict prevention and resolution systems in an ethically responsible manner.
learning_outcomes: Describe and analyse models of dispute resolution.
Critically evaluate ethical principles, values, concepts and theories and apply these within the context of conflict resolution.
Describe and analyse the need for organisational conflict resolution systems.
Critically discuss the principles and skills of conflict resolution.

title: Social and Sustainability Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines how to change behaviour or firmly held beliefs in a manner that benefits individuals and society at large through the application of social marketing campaigns. Examples of social and sustainability marketing areas include, campaigns to prevent or reduce alcohol consumption, recycling, the climate change debate, farm management and environmental outcomes, smoking, drug abuse, domestic violence and unsafe driving. This subject examines how to design a marketing strategy that will move the target audience from ignorance or indifference to awareness, action and ultimately maintenance. The subject uses a case study approach drawing on current and historic Australian and international campaigns.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse, discuss and evaluate social marketing strategies theories.
Examine and evaluate the impact of social marketing campaigns on behaviour.
Use secondary research skills to collect, collate, monitor and use data to support social marketing strategies.
Differentiate between commercial and social marketing, and outline the scope of social and sustainability marketing, seeking out new ideas and opportunities.
Reflect on a range of contemporary social issues using multiple perspectives.
Apply marketing techniques and theories to develop creative and well-balanced solutions for business aimed at alleviating social, economic, environmental and sustainability concerns.
Critically analyse social and sustainability trends to determine the implications and make recommendations for managerial decision-making.

title: Social Context of Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the concepts of society and the individual, and their interrelationship. A sociological and historical approach is adopted that emphasises the development of the modern industrial and post-industrial state and its complex relationship with social collectives and individuals. Emphasis is placed on the role of social institutions in shaping individual and collective difference. The subject introduces students to sociological theories and relates these to the particular adult and vocational education settings in which the students are working. It also focuses on 'dimensions of disadvantage' in both theoretical and practical contexts. Social justice and equity are also explored in the current Australian context.
learning_outcomes: Understand a variety of sociological theories relevant to the practice of adult and vocational education in Australia.
Discuss the development of the modern industrial/post-industrial society and its impact on them as teachers.

Critically discuss the role of Adult and Vocational Education organisations and practitioners developing, implementing and interpreting relevant policy in the context of economic and social development and the principles of social justice and equity in education; addressing the needs of students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic background, including First Nations Australian students.
Understand the nature of individualism and difference and their construction by social institutions.
Apply sociological theory to analyse both themselves and their teaching environments.
prerequisites: EEL120: Social Context of Vocational Education and Training
EEL220: Learning Theories for Post-compulsory Education: VET
EEL404: Information Processing and Educational Practice

title: Social Determinants of Ageing and Health
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines ageing and health in the community using broad bio-psycho-social and cultural perspectives. A theoretical model of critical social gerontology is introduced and ageism in community and health systems is identified and challenged. The social determinants of health in ageing are examined along with structural and policy issues associated with the health outcomes of older adults in the community, including older Indigenous Australians. These concepts are applied in examining key topics that show how social determinants differentially shape the health and wellbeing of older adults. Key topics include: life-long learning; nutrition, exercise and active ageing; work, retirement and income; housing, transport and environmental issues and age-friendly communities. Foundational academic skills for post-graduate study are imbedded in the subject content.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of age-friendly communities processes (as outlined by World Health Organisation) and outcomes on the health and wellbeing of older adults.
Apply appropriate academic skills for postgraduate study in this field.
Analyse the role of social determinants of health in ageing, as constructed in policy and social structures, on ageing and health in the community.
Analyse ageing and health using bio-psycho-social, cultural and critical social gerontology perspectives.
Apply knowledge of social determinants of health in ageing and evaluate the differential impact of these on health outcomes of individuals, including older Indigenous Australians.

title: Social Dimensions of Disability
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to social and human services elements of the disability sector. It will enable students to examine and critique how social and organisational processes contribute to the marginalisation of people of differing abilities, thus reinforcing a focus on "disabilities". It examines the main models of disability, including human rights based frameworks, enabling students to develop a critical analysis of the models. It also fosters a conception of differing abilities beyond these established models. Policy and program development in the disability field is analysed, informed by examination of philosophical changes, legal frameworks and critical concepts. Institutional factors which mediate disability, including contemporary policy developments and debates, are examined.
learning_outcomes: Understand the Australian disability service sector: its structures and services for people with disabilities in the light of national and international disability rights and standards.
Explore and understand a range of theories and models of disability, including how they address diversity and social processes related to disability.
Explore in depth one aspect of the disability services sector, demonstrating research and digital literacy skills.
Understand the range of disability practice roles for human service workers in the disability sector.
Compare Australian laws and policies relating to disability against the context of national and international human rights frameworks.

title: Social Impact Project: Environment
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This Micro-Credential equips learners with the knowledge, skills, and practical experiences necessary to drive meaningful change in their communities. Co-delivered with industry partners; learners gain valuable skills in working collaboratively with diverse stakeholders and will learn how to develop, plan, and execute social impact projects from inception to completion focused on developing resources to support environmental sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively in project teams with multiple stakeholders on social impact projects for communities and organisations.
Critically reflect on the impact social responsibility has on professional development.

title: Social Entrepreneurship
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Social enterprises are hybrid organizations established for a social purpose, using a for-profit business model to generate the financial resources needed to support their social missions (Miles et al., 2014: 549).” Examples of social enterprises include a church bookstore where the proceeds are used to fund community engagement or Zambrero's Plate- 4-Plate meal donation program. This subject introduces social entrepreneurship and social enterprise, along with the associated tools and processes for developing, implementing and funding solutions to real community problems. It takes a very practical and applied approach, focusing in particular on how leaders can analyse and shape the community's entrepreneurial ecosystem to better support the needs of social enterprises developing solutions for community problems. This subject is designed to develop the student's capacity to develop, lead, and support social entrepreneurs and enterprises.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, generate and transmit solutions to community resilience and leadership development issues through mapping the elements and relationships of a community's entrepreneurial ecosystem using a community capital framework.
Critically analyse, evaluate and transform information about the fundamental tools of entrepreneurship.
Transmit knowledge, skills, and ideas to community stakeholders on how to leverage the community's entrepreneurial ecosystem to support those generating solutions to community problems.

title: Social Impact Project: Disability
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This Micro-Credential equips learners with the knowledge, skills, and practical experiences necessary to drive meaningful change in their communities. Co-delivered with industry partners; learners gain valuable skills in working collaboratively with diverse stakeholders, understanding of pressing social issues, and exploring their root causes, consequences, and potential solutions. Working in teams, participants will learn how to develop, plan, and execute social impact projects from inception to completion focused on supporting people with lived experience of disability.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the impact social responsibility has on professional development.
Work collaboratively in project teams with multiple stakeholders on social impact projects for communities and organisations.

title: Social Impact Project: Digital Inclusion
school: Division of Learning and Teaching
syllabus_overview: This Micro-Credential equips learners with the knowledge, skills, and practical experiences necessary to drive meaningful change in their communities. Co-delivered with industry partners; learners gain valuable skills in working collaboratively with diverse stakeholders, understanding of pressing social issues, and exploring their root causes, consequences, and potential solutions. Working in teams, participants will learn how to develop, plan, and execute social impact projects from inception to completion focused on supporting digital inclusion for education and employability.
learning_outcomes: critically reflect on the impact social responsibility has on professional development
work collaboratively in project teams with multiple stakeholders on social impact projects for communities and organisations

title: Social Impact Project: Global Internships
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This Micro-Credential equips learners with the knowledge, skills, and practical experiences necessary to drive meaningful change in their communities. Co-delivered with industry partners; learners gain valuable skills in working collaboratively with diverse stakeholders, understanding of pressing social issues, and exploring their root causes, consequences, and potential solutions. Working in teams, participants will learn how to develop, plan, and execute social impact projects from inception to completion focused on developing resources to support Fair Trade Learning relationships with developing countries.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively in project teams with multiple stakeholders on social impact projects for communities and organisations
Critically reflect on the impact social responsibility has on professional development

title: Social Impact Project: Mental Health and Wellbeing
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This Micro-Credential equips learners with the knowledge, skills, and practical experiences necessary to drive meaningful change in their communities. Co-delivered with industry partners; learners gain valuable skills in working collaboratively with diverse stakeholders, understanding of pressing social issues, and exploring their root causes, consequences, and potential solutions. Working in teams, participants will learn how to develop, plan, and execute social impact projects from inception to completion focused on developing resources to support mental health and wellbeing.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the impact social responsibility has on professional development.
Work collaboratively in project teams with multiple stakeholders on social impact projects for communities and organisations.

title: Social Impact Project: Homelessness
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This Micro-Credential equips learners with the knowledge, skills, and practical experiences necessary to drive meaningful change in their communities. Co-delivered with industry partners; learners gain valuable skills in working collaboratively with diverse stakeholders, understanding of pressing social issues, and exploring their root causes, consequences, and potential solutions. Working in teams, participants will learn how to develop, plan, and execute social impact projects from inception to completion focused on supporting people with lived experience of homelessness.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively in project teams with multiple stakeholders on social impact projects for communities and organisations.
Critically reflect on the impact social responsibility has on professional development.

title: Social Inequality
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Inequality is one of the big social and political issues of the new millennium. This subject focuses on current patterns of social inequality in contemporary society with particular reference to Australia. Topics covered include: socio-biology, the family, age, gender, race and ethnicity, regional inequalities, income and wealth distribution, social class, social mobility, unemployment and the underclass in the UK, USA, Asia and the Pacific region.
learning_outcomes: Select and use information to investigate and analyse case studies using sociological theory.
Apply social inequality theory to current social issues.
Construct a sociological argument explaining and analysing social inequalities and communicating these orally and in writing using appropriate referencing skills.
Recognise where and how social inequality occurs in Australia and globally.

title: Social Justice, Ethics and Inclusion in Classroom Practice
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject teacher education students will acquire the knowledge and skills necessary to create inclusive classrooms that promote participation, engagement and success in primary school contexts. In order to do this, the subject requires teacher education students to think critically about a range of social justice topics such as human rights, multiculturalism, equality, racism, bias, and discrimination. Students consider how policy, curriculum planning and pedagogical practice can effectively respond to a diversity of histories, languages, cultures, religions, socio-economic backgrounds and experiences of wellbeing and trauma to achieve school outcomes that reflect equity and excellence. Also, this subject introduces principles and practices that support differentiated learning as well as exploring ways in which ethical and intercultural understandings, including empathy, can be included within the classroom environment.
learning_outcomes: Identify how social policy and the provision of resources can be utilised to achieve inclusive and equitable education for students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds.
Discuss ethical issues relating to education in a diverse Australian society and how they affect practices of inclusion, equity and achievement.

Demonstrate an inclusive approach to curriculum, classroom teaching and assessment by developing, differentiating/modifying, and evaluating programs, strategies and resources to respond to diversity/multicultural perspectives.

Justify pedagogical strategies that consider and address the strengths and educational needs of children from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds including literacy and numeracy development.
Reflect on how teachers in mainstream classrooms promote inclusive student engagement and participation.

title: Social Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject examines how to change attitudes, beliefs and behaviours that benefit individuals and society at large. Examples of social marketing include campaigns to prevent or reduce alcohol consumption, smoking, drug abuse, domestic violence and unsafe driving. This subject examines how to design a marketing strategy that will move the target audience from indifference to action and ultimately maintenance. The subject uses a case study approach drawing on current and historic Australian and international campaigns. The subject also examines the importance of social marketing in the area of environmental sustainability and corporate social responsibility.
learning_outcomes: Implement successfully the use of written and oral skills to integrate key social marketing theoretical concepts and to create a coherent and theoretically rigorous argument relating to sustainability concepts.
Critically analyse, discuss, and evaluate social marketing strategies and use secondary research skills to collect, collate and integrate examples with theory.
Provide an appraisal of social responsibility and become familiar with the range of issues where social marketing has an impact.
Apply marketing techniques and theories to develop creative solutions to social problems acknowledging the implications of managerial decisions on society.
Differentiate between commercial and social marketing, and outline the scope of social marketing, seeking out new ideas and opportunities.
Evaluate the characteristics and needs of others in society and understand prospective challenges to social issues including environmental sustainability.

title: Social Media Strategy
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Social media is now predominant in the worlds of communication, marketing, and content. Professionals in these fields, and many others, are required to have strong expertise in devising social media strategies that work. This micro-subject delivers practical skills of use to those who need to develop social media strategies using up-to-date tools and techniques for all professional purposes.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of using social media for communication, marketing and content.
Develop and explain a social media strategy.
Produce a content plan targeting relevant social media platforms.

title: Social Networking for Information Professionals
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the concept, theory and practice of social networking technologies within the context of information organisations and in the work of information professionals. This subject requires students to immerse themselves within a range of social networking environments and evaluate their learning experiences throughout the session as both social networkers and information professionals.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the ability of social networking technologies to support the collaborative needs of workgroups, communities and organisations.
Use social networking technologies in professional settings.

Explain the social, cultural, educational, ethical, and technical management issues that exist in a socially networked world, and how information policy is developed and implemented to support such issues.
Explain concepts, theories and practices of participatory information services.
Critically examine the ability of the features and functions of various social networking tools to meet the information needs of users.

title: Social Networking for Information Professionals
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the concept, theory and practice of social networking technologies within the context of information organisations and in the work of information professionals. This subject requires students to immerse themselves within a range of social networking environments and evaluate their learning experiences throughout the session as both social networkers and information professionals.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the ability of the features and functions of various social networking tools to meet the information needs of users.
Critically judge the ability of the features and functions of social networking technologies and software to support the collaborative needs of workgroups, communities and organisations.
Compare and explain the concepts, theories and practices of participatory information services.

Evaluate the social, cultural, educational, ethical, and technical management issues that exist in a socially networked world, and how information policy is developed and implemented to support such issues.
Appraise and apply social networking technologies in professional settings.
prerequisites: INF206: Social Networking for Information Professionals

title: Social Platform Marketing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: During the subject students will study how to set up, optimise and evaluate social media campaigns using Facebook, Twitter, Linkedin, Google+ and YouTube. They will also learn how to create a social media marketing strategy and plan how to implement the strategy into an organisation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the value different social platforms represent for marketing and promotion.
Create a social platform strategy utilising a range of social media platforms to meet an organisation's communication goals.
Investigate and recommend social media management tools that meet an organisation's communication goals.
Report, analyse and measure the performance and impact of strategy activities.
Create an implementation plan to apply the strategy within an organisation.
Create a social platform strategy that expresses an organisation's identity, reaches the target audience and engages with that audience through social interactions.

title: Social Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: Social Psychology looks at the influences of society, groups and interpersonal relationships on the individual, and the individual's location within society. It provides the framework for analysis of the processes and forces we experience in our daily existence as individuals in society. This subject highlights the classic studies that have had a formative impact on Social Psychology and considers the growing body of work which critiques many of these classic studies. It also engages with the continuing debate within Social Psychology about how relevant social psychological theories are to an understanding of, and solution for, modern social problems and issues, including those relevant to Indigenous Australians.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in critical evaluation of previous research and theoretical positions via assessments, including a written assignment related to Australian Indigenous Issues.
Demonstrate familiarity with some of Social Psychology's fundamental issues and controversies.
Demonstrate an understanding of the wide range of research methodologies and techniques used in Social Psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding of the major theories within Social Psychology, and an awareness of their applications in everyday life.

title: Social Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Psychology
syllabus_overview: Social Psychology looks at the influences of society, groups and interpersonal relationships on the individual, and the individual's location within society. It provides the framework for analysis of the processes and forces we experience in our daily existence as individuals in society. This subject highlights the classic studies that have had a formative impact on Social Psychology and considers the growing body of work which critiques many of these classic studies. It also engages with the continuing debate within Social Psychology about how relevant social psychological theories are to an understanding of, and solution for, modern social problems and issues, including those relevant to Indigeneous Australians.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in critical evaluation of previous research and theoretical positions via assessments, including a written assignment related to Australian Indigenous Issues.
Demonstrate familiarity with some of Social Psychology's fundamental issues and controversies.
Demonstrate an understanding of the major theories within Social Psychology, and an awareness of their applications in everyday life.
Demonstrate an understanding of the wide range of research methodologies and techniques used in Social Psychology.

title: Social Research
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a structured introduction to social research including quantitative, qualitative and feminist methods. It explains what is involved in doing research, e.g. how research is designed, how information is collected by means of interviews, questionnaires, observation, experiments, or case studies, and how information is processed, analysed and interpreted. It demonstrates how computers are used in social research.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a basic knowledge of methods of social research and of their advantages and limitations.
Evaluate critically research findings and reports.
Prepare research reports.
Demonstrate skills for independently carrying out social research.

title: Social Research Methods for Pastoral Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject examines social research and data collection methods appropriate for research in the fields of pastoral counselling and ageing and pastoral studies. It provides a comprehensive understanding of the research strategies and data collection methods appropriate for pastoral studies, and addresses the principles and procedures that define and regulate research investigations. The primary focus of the subject is on the nature of the research process, and on the qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods traditions that underlie social research inquiry.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on professional and ethical issues relevant for research in the fields of pastoral counselling or ageing and pastoral studies.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods research models, and appropriate application of each methodology.
Demonstrate research, writing, and communication skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of the ethics review process relevant for research in the fields of pastoral counselling or ageing and pastoral studies.
Demonstrate the ability to discuss in a supervisory context the stages of planned research projects.
Apply appropriate research methods to a range of research questions.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the professional contexts within which pastoral studies research is undertaken.
Define social research methods within the context of pastoral counselling and ageing and pastoral studies.

title: Social Science Honours Dissertation FT
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop practical insights into real-world research writing and dissemination processes. Students will be enabled with supported autonomy to apply advanced knowledge and skills in research practices to produce a completed research dissertation. This will involve planning and executing a research project through the completion of a literature review, data collection and analysis of results culminating in the research dissertation.
learning_outcomes: Write a final dissertation that brings together all the parts of the project and can be understood by experts in the field.
Reflect on the research process and progress.
Complete and analyse a research project.
Communicate effectively in ways appropriate to the discipline, audience and purpose.
Critically review, appraise and synthesise academic literature relevant to the chosen research problem.
prerequisites: RES405: Social Science Honours Dissertation PT Part B
RES404: Social Science Honours Dissertation PT Part A

title: Social Science Honours Dissertation PT Part A
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will begin their planned Honours research activities, under the guidance of their Honours supervisor(s). Through engaging in their research project, students will develop their knowledge, skills, and confidence as a novice researcher. This may include knowledge and skills to obtain the ethics approval required to commence their data collection. Through regular communication with their supervisor(s), students will also have opportunities to reflect on their research practices, experiences, and learning.
learning_outcomes: Succinctly report on their research progress in a way that shows increasing independence as a novice researcher.
With supervisor guidance, obtain ethics approval (if necessary) and begin collecting and/or analysing data to address a research question.
Critically use theory in the development of an individual research dissertation.
In regular supervision conversations, reflect on their research progress, including strengths and skills they are developing, issues they have encountered, and problem-solving they have engaged in.
prerequisites: RES403: Social Science Honours Dissertation FT

title: Social Science Honours Dissertation PT Part B
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will complete their planned Honours research. Students will be guided by their supervisor(s) to develop their knowledge, skills, and confidence as a researcher, particularly in relation to data analysis and interpretation. Through regular communication with their supervisor(s), students will have opportunities to reflect on their collected data, analyses, and interpretations to produce a completed research dissertation.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate the rationale, method, and results of a research project via a research dissertation.
Demonstrate knowledge of research methods and sound study design, including how study design can impact on the interpretation of data.
Demonstrate knowledge and skills of data analysis and interpretation.
prerequisites: RES403: Social Science Honours Dissertation FT

title: Social Welfare in Human Services
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to the welfare sector in Australia and to concepts and issues underpinning welfare practice, past and present. It will advance students' knowledge and skills in professional human services work as well as enhance the students' capacity to critically analyse and reflect on current practice. An ecosocial framework is introduced to critique contemporary welfare state issues and provide an alternative pathway for the future of human services and society.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of, and critically assess the characteristics of professional human services, including a knowledge base, and core values and ethics.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the impacts and complexity of, and critically assess the origin of poverty and social exclusion.

Demonstrate advanced understanding of, and critically assess, welfare in Australia, including the history of human services, contemporary approaches to welfare provision and issues underpinning welfare.
Demonstrate an understanding of an ecosocial framework to human services and implications for practice.

title: Social Work and Human Rights
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide theoretical understanding and context for human rights practice within the human services. The subject covers the history and theories of human rights, human rights instrumentalities and human rights activists and movements. It outlines a social work practice framework that draws on a human rights framework, including anti-oppressive and anti-discriminatory practice. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concepts of anti-discriminatory and anti-oppressive practice.
Explain human rights instrumentalities, human rights activists.
Examine the history of human rights and explain their application in an international context.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of a range of human rights theories.
Explain and apply human rights principles to social work practice, including the global use of technology for research and the ethical sharing of information.
Discuss the implications of human rights for social work practice.

title: Social Work and Human Services Dissertation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for post-graduate students to research, in depth, a chosen topic within the social work/human services field and to demonstrate ability to select and apply appropriate research methods, analyse data and report findings in a Masters dissertation.
learning_outcomes: Undertake independent research in the fields of Social Work/Human Services practice and social policy analysis.
Demonstrate skills of writing, data analysis, policy analysis and critical thinking necessary to produce publishable research.
prerequisites: SWK500: Social Work and Human Services Dissertation

title: Social Work and Social Policy Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject requires students to analytically discuss important stages in policy making processes and the roles organisations and institutions play in them. Drawing on relevant knowledge and skills, it has a particular focus on the process of formulating policy issues, placing them on the agenda of policy makers and analysing contemporary policies. Further, it helps students to critically reflect on changes and challenges in the field of social policy.
learning_outcomes: Analytically explain changes and challenges in the field of social policy.
Critically discuss policy making processes and the roles organisations and institutions play in them.
Apply knowledge and skills to formulate issues and place them on the agenda of policy makers.
Critically discuss knowledge and skills of policy analysis and analyse policies.
prerequisites: SPE502: Social Work and Social Policy Practice

title: Social Work and Human Services Dissertation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to research a topic within the social work/human services field in depth and to demonstrate ability to research and report findings at postgraduate level.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills of writing, data analysis, policy analysis and critical thinking necessary to produce publishable research.
Undertake independent research in the fields of Social Work/Human Services practice and Social Policy Analysis.

title: Social Work and Social Policy Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to develop knowledge and skills required to identify social issues, set policy agenda and undertake policy analysis as part of social policy practice. By briefly discussing the concept of social policy, significance of social policy practice and a range of opportunities to engage in it, the subject focuses on identifying needs/issues, agenda building and advocacy in the first part. In the second part, the subject discusses policy analysis by introducing a policy analysis framework, policy evaluation and policy cases. Further, it looks at contemporary critical issues and influences on social policies.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply a policy analysis framework.
Critically apply knowledge and skills of agenda building and advocacy.
Discuss the concept and significance of social policy, important policy issues and factors that contribute to success of policies.
Critically analyse the institutions involved in policy making and the role of coordination and consultation in the policy making processes.
Identify and evaluate contemporary critical issues and influences on social policies.
prerequisites: SPE401: Social Work and Social Policy Practice

title: Social Work Credit Package
school: School
syllabus_overview: Credit package for the Bachelor of Social Work
learning_outcomes: N/A

title: Social Work Field Education 1
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This is the first of two field education subjects in the Master of Social Work (Professional Qualifying). Students have the opportunity to demonstrate professional practice skills, knowledge, values and develop their social work identity in a work setting. Students are required to demonstrate the entry level standards of professional practice to meet first placement expectations as specified by the Australian Association of Social Workers. The subject has two strands. The majority of students undertake the Placement Strand, which involves completing a placement of approximately 500 hours. Students who are assessed as eligible for recognition of prior learning based on relevant professional experience undertake the Professional Practice Assessment Strand. Placement Strand - Students undertake a structured, individualised period of experiential learning in an approved real-world work site, under the supervision of a qualified and experienced social worker. school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Students have the opportunity to develop research practice skills and to integrate theory and practice in a research setting, which may also be the place of their second practicum. Students move beyond the assessment stages of social work practice to specifically implementing a research methodology and engaging in critical analysis of the results and outcomes for the social work discipline. By the end of the subject students will have produced a 10,000 word dissertation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to undertake a piece of research and write it up in the form of a dissertation.

title: Social Work Literature Review
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject enables candidates to undertake a literature review relevant to their research project. Candidates will refine their literature-search, review and reporting skills. The subject requires candidates to be thoroughly conversant with the literature relevant to their research topic and to understand/identify the ontological, axiological, methodological and epistemological context of their topic. Skills of critical review, analysis and synthesis are developed. Candidates, in consultation with the supervisory team, are required to complete a draft literature review as preparation for their proposed research project.
learning_outcomes: Critique extant literature with reference to ontology, axiology, epistemology and methodology.
Write a draft literature review which includes an account of methodology and search strategies, and a critical exploration of the issues.
Critically reflect on the research process and progress to-date, in consultation with the supervisory team.
Demonstrate effective search strategies to systematically locate literature relevant to the research topic.
Identify gaps in the literature and articulate a rationale for the research topic.
Demonstrate high level critical analysis and synthesis of literature with reference to the research topic.
Articulate the importance and purposes of the literature review process in research.

title: Social Work Research Proposal
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject, candidates write a comprehensive research proposal to meet the requirements of the Faculty for confirmation of candidature. The candidate, in consultation with the supervisory team, is required to present their research proposal to a panel of reviewers, and to articulate the potential contribution of their research to knowledge in the field, taking into account principles of ethical research. Candidates, in consultation with the supervisory team, are required to engage constructively with reviewers' comments.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a high level of skill in writing a research proposal and to articulate the project's potential contribution to knowledge in the field, taking into account principles of ethical social research.
Meet, in consultation with the supervisory team, the Faculty's requirements for presentation of research proposal and the process for confirming candidature.
Critically reflect on the research process and progress to-date and to plan for the thesis phase of the professional doctorate.
Demonstrate, as part of the proposal, the methodological knowledge and skills to carry out the proposed research.

Demonstrate, as part of the proposal, a critical understanding of the key literature in the specified area of research and effective argument/s from that literature to justify the proposed approach to the research.
Engage constructively with recommendations for revision to the research proposal as articulated by reviewers and/or supervisors.
Present the research proposal to a panel of academics and peers.

title: Social Work Practice in Mental Health
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject critically explores social work practice in contemporary mental health contexts. Clinical knowledge and skills relevant to planning and conducting assessments and therapeutic interventions for a range of mental health conditions will be examined. Practice approaches that ensure respectful working partnerships with a diverse range of individuals and groups will also be explored.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on professional practice in contemporary mental health contexts.
Understand the mental health system and the various roles that social workers play in these environments.
Respectfully plan and conduct assessments and interventions relevant to common mental health conditions.
Work in partnership with individuals, families, carers and other organisations to promote and respond to mental health and wellbeing.

title: Social Work Theory and Practice 1 - Foundations of Practice
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject is the first of four core social work theory and practice subjects in the Master of Social Work (Professional Qualifying). The subject covers the origins and development of the profession, its ethics and core values, models of helping, foundational theory and basic communication skills of contemporary social work practice, including digital and informational literacy. Emphasis is on the early stages of intervention, especially in relation to engagement and assessment at individual, family, group and community levels. This subject also introduces a range of foundational concepts and explores how these relate to developing a distinct social work identity within the context of national and international professional bodies. Students are expected to develop a critical understanding of the effects of history, values and positionality on social work theory and to appreciate the place of research in social work practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the application of theory to practice through participation in face-to-face learning activities as per accreditation requirements.
Demonstrate and analyse core communication skills within a social work context.
Outline and critically analyse key aspects of the origins and development of social work as a profession.
Demonstrate critical thinking, research and reflective practice skills.
Independently research, critically analyse and explain foundational concepts and how these relate to social work practice and professional identity.
Discuss Indigenous social work, discourse and practice theory relevant to social work and be able to research, articulate and critically apply this knowledge.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of social work core values and ethics as defined by professional social work bodies.

It develops students' intervention skills with a focus on working with individuals and families and on use of self and professional identity in practice. The subject builds on the micro skills developed in Theory and Practice 1 and develops the concept of multidimensional assessment and intervention. The subject considers a variety of models for therapeutic intervention and their research and theoretical base and encourages students to critique a range of models for effective intervention.

syllabus_overview: This subject is the capstone theory and practice subject in the Master of Social Work (Professional Qualifying) course. It requires students to consolidate their knowledge and skills and to critically apply these in practice contexts to achieve systemic change across micro, mezzo and macro levels. Particular emphasis will be placed on social action and social movements. By the end of this subject, students will demonstrate advanced critically reflective practice and integration of theory and practice at the level of a new graduate. Students will develop and have an understanding of their professional identity as social workers. Students will apply high level skills in research that inform their practice. This subject draws together learning from across the entire course and integrates knowledge from many sources into a cohesive framework for practice, critical reflection and further research.

title: Sociocultural Foundations of Sport and Exercise
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the sociohistorical foundations of sport, exercise and physical education in Australia. Students are encouraged to begin to examine the social significance of exercise, sport and physical activity and reflect on their place in it. Students will also explore the social determinants affecting health, physical activity, exercise and sport including historical, cultural, psychosocial elements as well as their own personal attitudes. Students will also begin to explore the social intersections of exercise, health, physical activity and sport including health promotion.
learning_outcomes: Find, synthesise, summarise and reference academic research on sport from an historical perspective.
Discuss the relationship between exercise/sports and other aspects of society, such as individual and social identity and social determinants of health.
Identify and describe the role of an exercise scientist in the Australian healthcare system and broader professional networks.
Articulate the role, significance and promotion of sport, exercise and physical activity.
Examine and reflect on the sociocultural issues that affect inclusion and participation in sport and exercise.

title: Sociology Of Health And Health Care
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to sociology and how a sociological approach can be applied to provide a deeper understanding of current issues relating to health, illness and health care. Through the analysis of theory and research, students will engage with the various ways in which the social organisation of society shapes health care delivery and institutions, patterns of illness and health, and individual experiences of ill health. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in the written presentation of an argument, including the ways in which sociologists incorporate and acknowledge the ideas of other writers.
Explain the influence of social structure and human agency on the organisation of health care and health outcomes.
Apply sociological concepts and theories to contemporary health issues.
Demonstrate the significance of a sociological approach in making sense of health and medical issues.

title: Sociology of Islam
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: Sociology and anthropology are scientific disciplines that examine the role of religion in society from a secular perspective. Sociology studies how religion shapes and is influenced by society, primarily in the West, while anthropology explores the cultural and ethnographic aspects of religion in non-Western societies. Both fields focus on Islam and Muslims as a subject matter. In the meantime, Muslim scholars have attempted to develop an authentic enquiry into the role of religion in their societies. The knowledge–power relationships established by colonialism and modernity have led some Islamic scholars to reject conventional sociology and advocate for an Islamisation of social sciences. This subject critically reviews these attempts, debates and their outcomes, providing chronological and comprehensive understanding of how sociology and anthropology of Islam have developed and how Muslims are positioned within and contributed to conventional sociology and anthropology. Students learn about key sociological concepts, theories and research, and critique the strengths and limitations of the sociology and anthropology of Islam as well as Islamic sociology and anthropology. Additionally, the subject provides tools to synthesise conventional sociology and anthropology with their Islamic counterparts.
