school: School
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for Systematic Theology Level 3 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for Systematic Theology Level 3 (8 point) credit within the Bachelor of Theology program.

title: Systematic Theology Level 4
school: School
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for Systematic Theology Level 4 (8 point) credit within the Graduate Diploma of Theology
learning_outcomes: This credit code is for Systematic Theology Level 4 (8 point) credit within the Graduate Diploma of Theology.

title: Systems Analysis and Design
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with knowledge and skills in the areas of problem definition, feasibility analysis, requirements gathering, system analysis and systems design using object oriented modelling. In particular, students will gain experience in the object oriented approach to systems development including gathering and modelling requirements using object oriented tools and techniques and designing solutions to business problems.
learning_outcomes: Develop object oriented design models.
Describe the context of an information system.
Discuss and describe processes to systems analysis.
Perform feasibility analysis.
Gather system requirements.
Model systems requirements using object oriented tools and techniques.
prerequisites: ITC548: Information Systems Analysis and Design

title: Tax Law Concepts and Application
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: Students will interpret relevant tax law and apply legal resources to practical business scenarios, typical of those encountered by professional accountants, to produce client advice. The focus of this subject is on the application of taxation law in particular, the concepts of assessable income, allowable deductions, capital gains tax, tax rates and tax offsets. Special provisions of taxation eg. repairs, depreciation, and capital allowances are also examined. Fringe benefits tax and the Goods and Services Tax, including its impact on business, is also examined.
learning_outcomes: Communicate clearly and concisely in a range of formal and informal situations and settings appropriate for clients and other stakeholders.
Analyse legal rules so as to differentiate between possible outcomes to the legal issues arising from novel fact situations.
Demonstrate a capacity to engage and use legal research skills to apply the law to legal problems relating to taxation so as to reach a solution.
Explain how information and communication technology enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of reporting and communication with the Australian Taxation Office.

Identify and explain the rules of law and identify the potential tension between compliance with ethical principles, and the interrelationship between laws, regulations, and the public interest in the context of taxation law.
Explain the importance of active listening and effective interviewing techniques to engage with clients in order to elicit facts in respect to a tax problem.

title: Taxation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The fundamentals of income tax law and practice are covered. The basic ideas of assessable income including capital gains, allowable deductions and the essentials of tax accounting are examined in the context of their impact on businesses and taxpayers in general. Goods and Services Tax and Fringe Benefits Tax are also considered.
learning_outcomes: Use online resources including the Australian Taxation Office website.
Apply legislation, case law and administrative provisions as they relate to the underlying principles of Australian income tax law and practice.
Give professional advice regarding the taxation of personal services income and income from business.
Maintain relevant records necessary for the preparation of tax returns.

title: Taxation 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the students' understanding of the general principles of tax law covered in LAW505 and includes a study of the taxation of partnership income, trust income and corporate tax entities and their members. Superannuation, tax avoidance, tax planning techniques and international taxation issues are also covered.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the rules of law relating to advanced taxation law topics covered in the subject.
Demonstrate a capacity to engage in legal research.
Use legal research skills to apply the law to legal problems relating to taxation so as to reach a solution.
Analyse legal rules so as to differentiate between possible outcomes to the legal issues arising from novel fact situations.

title: Taxation Law (Issues)
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject builds upon student understanding of the general principles of tax law covered in LAW301 and entails a study of the taxation of partnership income, trust income, corporate tax entities and their members, consolidated groups, special taxpayers, incentive schemes and financial transactions. Corporate tax losses, net capital losses and bad debts, superannuation, retirement and termination payments, international aspects of income tax, barriers to tax avoidance, tax planning techniques as well as Goods and Services Tax are also covered.
learning_outcomes: Be equipped with sufficient knowledge in Australian taxation law to enable them to deal with business persons and legal advisors in an informed and reasoned manner, particularly in respect to taxation of partnership income, taxation of trust income, taxation of corporate tax entities and their members, corporate tax losses, net capital losses and bad debts, taxation of consolidated groups, special taxpayers and incentive schemes, taxation of financial transactions, superannuation, retirement and termination payments, international aspects of income tax, barriers to tax avoidance, tax planning techniques and goods and services tax.

Implement a methodology for solving legal problems based on the following steps: identifying the relevant facts, identifying the applicable law, identifying the legal issue/s involved, addressing the legal issue/s by applying the applicable law to the relevant facts in a logical, chronological, concise and complete manner and reaching a sound and reasoned conclusion.
prerequisites: LAW322: Tax Law Concepts and Application

title: Taxation 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The focus of this subject is on the on concepts of assessable income, allowable deductions, capital gains tax, tax rates and tax offsets. Special provisions of taxation viz repairs, depreciation, and capital allowances are also examined. Fringe benefits tax is explored, and the Goods and Services Tax including its impact on business is also examined.
learning_outcomes: Use legal research skills to apply the law to legal problems relating to taxation so as to reach a solution.
Demonstrate a capacity to engage in legal research.
Analyse legal rules so as to differentiate between possible outcomes to the legal issues arising from novel fact situations.
Identify and explain the rules of law relating to taxation law topics covered in the subject.

title: Taxation Law (Principles)
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore the law relating to the Australian taxation system. It will investigate the concepts of taxation law such as assessable income including capital gains, allowable deductions and tax formulas. The Goods and Services tax regime and Fringe Benefits Tax will also be examined. Students will learn both how to apply relevant tax laws and how to compute tax assessments with a focus on individual rather than corporate taxation.
learning_outcomes: Interpret legislation to compute taxable income and allowable deductions to determine taxation liabilities and evaluate appropriate offsets.
Critically evaluate the law relating to fringe benefits and calculate the relevant tax liabilities.
Describe and access the Australian regulatory taxation system and compliance regime.
Critically evaluate the law relating to capital gains taxation and trading stock and calculate the relevant tax liabilities.
Critically evaluate the law relating to the goods and services taxation regime and calculate the relevant tax liabilities.
Locate and analyse the sources of taxation law in Australia.

title: Taxation Principles and Application
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject presents students to Australian Taxation Law policies and principles in a practical business environment. Students will interpret relevant tax law and apply other legal resources to scenarios typical of those encountered by professional accountants to produce client advice. The focus of this subject is on the application of taxation law, in particular, the concepts of assessable income, allowable deductions, capital gains tax, tax rates and tax offsets. Special provisions of taxation eg. repairs, depreciation, and capital allowances are also examined. Fringe benefits tax is explored, and the Goods and Services Tax including its impact on business is also examined.
learning_outcomes: Communicate clearly and concisely in a range of formal and informal situations and settings to clients and other stakeholders.

Demonstrate Information & Research Literacy skills and explain how information and communication technology enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of reporting and communication with the Australian Taxation Office.
Demonstrate a capacity to engage and use legal research skills to apply the law to legal problems relating to taxation so as to reach a solution.
Analyse legal rules so as to differentiate between possible outcomes to the legal issues arising from novel fact situations.
Explain the importance of active listening and effective interviewing techniques to elicit facts in respect to a tax problem.

Identify and explain the rules of law relating to taxation law and identify the potential tension between compliance with ethical principles, and the interrelationship between laws, regulations, and the public interest.

title: Taxation Strategies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this subject is to provide students with the opportunity to apply knowledge of taxation laws to the financial services industry. Key concepts are reviewed briefly, but the emphasis is on application of both concepts and technical legal knowledge to issues relevant to the financial services industry. Matters arising under the income tax, goods and services tax and fringe benefits tax systems are considered. Ultimately, students should be able to identify appropriate taxation strategies that may be used in the financial services sectors.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the application of tax law to a range of stakeholders in the context of financial services.
Assess the application of Australian taxation laws on financial products.
Critically analyse the underlying concepts relevant to the treatment of financial products under the Australian income tax system.
Independently research and critically evaluate recent developments in taxation that are relevant to the financial services sector.

title: Teacher Librarian As Leader
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to theory and practice in the leadership role of a teacher librarian. Leadership theory is examined in the current global context of change and reform in school library organisation and services. Evolving views of educational leadership are examined with a particular emphasis on organisational culture, strategic and operational planning including disaster planning, managing for change, using policy and planning documents for advocacy and developing relationships within a 21st century school culture of inquiry.
learning_outcomes: Identify and develop strategies for using policy and planning documents for advocacy.
Develop a mission statement and identify objectives and outcomes for the delivery of the school's information services.
Relate issues in leadership theory and the decision-making process to the teacher librarian's role in the school.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of leadership theory and identify pathways to building capacity for the development of leadership roles in schools through the work of the teacher librarian.
Explain leadership within the context of a 21st century school culture of inquiry.
Apply the principles and methods of strategic and operational planning for change and identify the role of the teacher librarian within these processes.

title: Teaching and Assessing the Creative Arts
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop and demonstrate understanding of the processes of planning, learning and assessing in the creative arts, whilst considering the intent of both the K-6 Creative Arts syllabus and the Early Years Learning Framework (EYLF). They will explore various theoretical perspectives that inform creative arts education in the early childhood and primary contexts. This will lead to the development of appropriate learning experiences and assessment in creative arts, reflecting child centred and engaging learning environments.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate children's work samples to understand their learning.
Plan developmentally appropriate creative arts learning experiences for children.
Identify and understand appropriate assessment for the creative arts and how this supports teacher knowledge of a child's level of learning.
Understand and reflect on learning and creative theories for the development of effective creative arts learning experiences.
Plan and develop sequential learning experiences with relevant assessment in the creative arts.
prerequisites: EMA210: Teaching and Assessing the Creative Arts

title: Teaching and learning for democratic futures
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Education plays a significant role in developing critical thinking, pedagogies of care, and cultivating democratic participation in classrooms and beyond. This subject positions the teacher as a democratic professional and explores ways classrooms can become places of democratic possibility for all learners. It applies Dewey's proposition that education is the caretaker of democracy. Students will examine the purpose of education in times of conformity and compliance, populism, mis/and/disinformation, and economic and environmental precarity.
learning_outcomes: Propose a strategic plan to lead democratic curriculum and assessment change in a local educational setting.
Develop and justify a personal position regarding the purpose of education.
Critically review a range of perspectives regarding the purpose of education.
Analyse systems and structures of knowledge and power that maintain disadvantage.
Critically evaluate the democratic possibility of curriculum, policy and assessment approaches in a local education setting.

title: Teaching and Learning in Clinical Education
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject applies the principle of transformative learning to explore the practice of teaching others in a clinical setting. Students will learn about current educational theories and practices that educators use to facilitate learning with clinicians. The subject will include the development of planned learning experiences and the delivery of unplanned, opportunistic learning experiences. Students will consider the value of engaging with other educators to explore alternate viewpoints and reflect on personal teaching experiences as part of the peer learning process. Finally, students will plan, implement and evaluate an education session in the clinical environment.
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of communication skills to engage learners and create a safe and positive learning environment.
Actively participate in learning communities to explore and reflect personal teaching experiences and engage in constructive debate and inter-professional learning.
Plan and implement an authentic learning experience aligned to a specific participant learning outcome, using contemporary educational theories.
Develop specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-limited learning outcomes for clinicians.
Create a learning resource that is credible, current and relevant to the specific learning needs of a clinical setting.
Critique the role of the clinical educator in supporting the learning needs of clinicians across the span of a nursing career.
prerequisites: HLT541: Teaching and Learning in the Clinical Setting
HLT541: Teaching and Learning in the Clinical Setting

title: Teaching and Learning in the Differentiated Classroom
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject develops the knowledge and skills that enable teachers to build and differentiate quality instruction in the inclusive classroom. The subject is a cornerstone of the program as it provides students with an understanding of the scope, depth and quality of practice required to create a successful inclusive classroom/school/setting. This includes understanding the evidence-based foundations of inclusive practice and the design and delivery of approaches that maximise student achievement in inclusive classrooms. The subject focuses on explicit teaching and cooperative learning as examples of inclusive practice given the predominance of teacher led and group instruction in contemporary classroom practice. Students learn how to build and differentiate these approaches in an inclusive classroom setting. After learning how to build and differentiate instruction, students take up the question and challenge of getting to scale with inclusive practice and begin to explore the kind of effort required to make inclusive practice a sustainable part of a whole school/setting approach to learning and teaching.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate their lesson outcomes and designs using exemplars from the three categories of differentiation.
Position a lesson within a curriculum unit and justify its contribution as defined in the lesson justification assessment task.

Develop a series of five learner outcomes for any unit of study within a curriculum area (i.e. HSIE, science, etc.) or discrete skills such as those found in decoding or maths. The outcomes will include a statement of the condition under which the learning will occur; a clear description of the action required; a clear description of the outcome produced that includes criteria for successful completion or mastery.
Develop an applied understanding of the theoretical and research based underpinnings of inclusive teaching strategies and pedagogies as they relate to classroom practice.
Describe the empirical evidence base for direct instruction and cooperative learning as described in the requirement for the Theoretical Reflection Assessment Component.

Build two lessons using the evidence-based principles of inclusion (explicit teaching, cooperative learning) and incorporating learning strategies (e.g., task analysis, cognitive strategies, collaborative practice) to lesson design and in doing so situate these pedagogies within their own practice and experience.
Collaborate with peers to receive feedback and develop their lesson designs.
Evaluate the whole-of-organisation implications of evidence-based inclusive practice for a school and apply that evaluation to an educational setting.
Describe the Mulit-Tier Approach (MTA) and evaluate its applicability to the setting in which they work.
prerequisites: ESS306: Programming, Teaching and Learning in Inclusive Settings
ESS508: Inclusion and Early Intervention 0-8 Years

title: Teaching Literacy in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject covers skills and knowledge required to analyse and apply effective adult literacy teaching practices to meet the needs of learners in adult and vocational education contexts. Students will explore and critically analyse adult literacy theories and apply these theories through the development of teaching strategies relevant to their practice and their particular adult and vocational education context.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate effectiveness of teaching strategies.
Critically discuss adult learning principles to the teaching of adult literacy.
Evaluate teaching approaches that support the development of students' literacy skills and knowledge in authentic and relevant contexts.
Critically discuss the applicability of teaching approaches to specific needs, levels of literacy, learning styles, and contexts of those participating in literacy provision.
Identify learning resources (from traditional, new, and emerging technologies) that link to literacy learning outcomes and promote learner engagement with tasks and activities.
Analyse, and evaluate the conceptual frameworks and theories underpinning adult literacy teaching.
Source and evaluate materials relevant to social and cultural needs of students.
Select, develop and/or adapt effective learning resources to meet students' literacy needs.
prerequisites: EEB311: Teaching Adult Literacy in VET

title: Teaching Literacy in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject covers skills and knowledge required to analyse and apply effective adult literacy teaching practices to meet the needs of learners in adult and vocational education contexts. Students will explore adult literacy theories and apply these theories through the development of teaching strategies relevant to their practice and their particular adult and vocational education context.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the applicability of teaching approaches to specific needs, levels of literacy, learning styles, and contexts of those participating in literacy provision.
Discuss adult learning principles for the teaching of adult literacy.
Discuss teaching approaches that support the development of students' literacy skills and knowledge in authentic and relevant contexts.
Select, develop and/or adapt effective learning resources to meet students' literacy needs.
Analyse and evaluate the effectiveness of teaching strategies.
Identify learning resources (from traditional, new, and emerging technologies) that link to literacy learning outcomes and promote learner engagement with tasks and activities.
Analyse the conceptual frameworks and theories underpinning adult literacy teaching.
Source and evaluate materials relevant to social and cultural needs of students.
prerequisites: EEB311: Teaching Adult Literacy in VET

title: Teaching Numeracy in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject employs the central concepts, modes of enquiry, and structure of the content of numeracy to enable students to develop teaching and assessment strategies in Adult Education contexts; including vocational and community education. Students will investigate the numeracy demands associated with the study of Adult Education and apply numeracy concepts to their teaching in ways that are relevant, effective and meaningful for learners.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the purposes and functions of numeracy in the community with particular reference to students in the VET sector or Adult Community Education sector.
Analyse the effectiveness of teaching strategies.
Discuss the constructivist approach to numeracy teaching.
Select, develop and/or adapt effective learning resources to meet students' numeracy needs.
Develop an understanding the of numeracy discipline and use this understanding in their teaching.
Interpret and explain numeracy concepts and processes embedded within a variety of adult learning contexts.
Develop teaching and assessment strategies that address the numeracy demands of various professional or personal development fields and that acknowledge the numeracy levels of students.

title: Teaching Numeracy in Adult and Vocational Education
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject employs the central concepts, modes of enquiry, and structure of the content of numeracy to enable students to develop teaching and assessment strategies in Adult Education contexts; including vocational and community education. Students will critically analyse the numeracy demands associated with the study of Adult and Vocational Education and apply numeracy concepts to their teaching in ways that are relevant, effective and meaningful for learners.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the purposes and functions of numeracy in the community with particular reference to students in the VET or adult community education sectors.
Discuss the constructivist approach to numeracy teaching.
Develop teaching and assessment strategies that address the numeracy demands of various professional or personal development fields and that acknowledges the numeracy levels of students.
Critically analyse and evaluate effectiveness of teaching strategies.
Present a broad and critical knowledge of the numeracy discipline and use this understanding in their teaching.
Interpret and explain numeracy concepts and processes embedded within a variety of adult learning contexts.
Critically select, develop and/or adapt effective learning resources to meet students' numeracy needs.
prerequisites: EEB308: Teaching Adult Numeracy in VET

title: Teaching Reading in a Diverse World
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to give students an in-depth understanding of the practical and theoretical aspects of the reading processes relevant to a socially just, diverse and globally connected world. Students will examine theories of reading and contemporary issues in reading education. Based on their learning and experience, students identify and gather information on a reader for a case study. Using these data they choose between engaging in an action research project or writing a review of literature that will contribute to their e-Portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on their learning and their learning processes and the implications for the profession.
Explore a range of contemporary reading issues; research in-depth one issue by using either action research or developing a review of literature in the field.
Understand that these texts place different kinds of demands on the skills and strategies of the reader.
Understand and value that reading involves engaging with a wide range of texts including traditional linear text, visual text, digital text and in a multimodal world.
Broaden students understanding of the social justice implications for educators in ensuring students' diverse socio-cultural capital is viewed as a strength for enhancing literacy learning.
Develop a profile (case study) of a student's reading and make relevant recommendations for further learning.
Understand that readers actively construct meaning through dynamic transactions between the reader's prior knowledge, the information suggested by the text and the context of the reading situation.
Be further sensitised to their role not only as teachers and learners but as co-researchers with their students and as agents of change in their own educational settings.
Identify and use a range of ways of identifying, assessing and meeting the diverse literacy needs of students, especially English language learners.
Challenge students' current literacy pedagogy towards developing a more critical, contemporary approach to reading education.

title: Team Management and Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject will expose students to key questions in the area of management in law enforcement. This subject defines a team leader as a front line manager who leads or manages other practitioners, along with proactive and reactive law enforcement and security activities in a defined area of responsibility. Theoretical topics covered include management and leadership within organisational structures; team building and leading for outcomes; equal employment and occupational health responsibilities; performance management and competencies; planning; problem solving; and decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Manage minor projects in compliance with policy relating to human resources management, workplace diversity and industrial issues safety.
Initiate change as required, within their area of their influence and within the limits of service policy.
Demonstrate skills in research, analysis, evaluation, synthesis and problem solving related to team management issues.
Undertake workplace assessment in light of current police competencies.
Assess the implications of selected legislation and policy relating to human resource management, workplace health and safety in relation to team management and leadership.
Select appropriate strategies to provide effective leadership for team members.
Address and analyse team problems in light of relevant literature and research.

title: Technology and Financial Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the impact of technology on the evolution of fraud and financial crime. Drawing on current case studies it examines key fraud and financial crime threats and opportunities presented by the affordances of technology. The subject also explores the role of Financial Technology (FinTech) and big data in the prevention of fraud and financial crime.
learning_outcomes: Classify technology driven contemporary financial crimes by common characteristics.
Analyse current and evolving financial cybercrime threats.
Analyse the adaption of technologies to commit financial crime.
Evaluate the capacity of FinTech and big data to aid financial crime prevention programs.

title: Technology and Applied Studies Engineering
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on the foundation created by EPI204 which introduces students to a range of engineering principles and systems. EPI205 will extend beginning understandings about engineering and the work of engineers. Students will build on preliminary capabilities to calculate and explain force, motion, and energy. The ability to communicate about engineering projects via an engineering report and design and production folio will also be taught. Students will learn to use computer aided design (CAD) software to produce outputs from typical technologies available in schools.
learning_outcomes: Develop an engineering drawing for 3D printing output using CAD software.
Perform engineering calculations.
Document the conduct of an engineering project in a design and production folio.
Explain the purpose of and produce an engineering report.
Explain the role of engineers and the scope of their work.

title: Technology Capstone Thesis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject 'Technologist Capstone Thesis' permits the cadet technologist to demonstrate their civil engineering design skills by working in an engineering design team to solve a multidisciplinary integrated real engineering design challenge, identified in their final work placement. Cadets must apply their theoretical and technical knowledge gained elsewhere in the curriculum and the workplace learning to the design, and the outcomes should be delivered in both written (thesis) and oral (thesis defence) formats. Technologist Capstone thesis will be jointly supervised by an academic engineer from Charles Sturt Engineering and a supervisor from their work placement.
learning_outcomes: Use and manage information in a professional and ethical manner. Analyse raw information and draw appropriate conclusions in context with due consideration of the knowledge, methods, and assumptions within the engineering discipline.
Formulate an appropriate method for investigating an applied civil engineering problem and correctly and innovatively apply established engineering methods and design processes to create a solution.

Define a practical engineering problem accurately and comprehensively in a workplace context and creatively apply systematic approaches to the pro-active conduct and management of engineering projects as part of a team.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of engineering design practices, reflective applications and contextual factors impacting on multi-disciplinary engineering challenges and application of systematic engineering synthesis and design processes.

Communicate the problem definition, design processes and outcomes clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences and project a creative, entrepreneurial, and pro-active disposition.
Apply systems thinking and specialist engineering bodies of knowledge in sustainable and socially responsible engineering practice.

title: Technology Capstone Thesis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject helps cadet engineers to enhance their civil engineering design skills by working in an engineering design team to solve a multidisciplinary, integrated, complex, civil engineering design project, identified in their intermediate work placement. Cadets must apply their theoretical and technical knowledge gained elsewhere in the curriculum and the workplace learning to the design. The outcomes should be delivered in both written (thesis) and oral (thesis defence) formats. Engineering cornerstone thesis will be jointly supervised by an academic engineer from Charles Sturt Univeristy engineering and with a supervisor from their work placement, in addition to the subject coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Formulate an appropriate method for investigating an applied civil engineering problem and correctly and innovatively apply established engineering methods and design processes to create a solution.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of engineering design practices, reflective applications and contextual factors impacting on multi-disciplinary engineering challenges and application of systematic engineering synthesis and design processes.

Use and manage information in a professional and ethical manner. Analyse raw information and draw appropriate conclusions in context with due consideration of the knowledge, methods, and assumptions within the engineering discipline.

Communicate the problem definition, design processes and outcomes clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences and project a creative, entrepreneurial, and pro-active disposition.
Apply systems thinking and specialist engineering bodies of knowledge in sustainable and socially responsible engineering practice.

Define a practical engineering problem accurately and comprehensively in a workplace context and creatively apply systematic approaches to the pro-active conduct and management of engineering projects as part of a team.
prerequisites: ENG273: Civil Engineering Topic Tree - Junior Cadet Engineer

title: Technology for Adult Learning and Teaching
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the different types of flexible delivery available in the adult and vocational education sector, with a particular focus on online delivery. An emphasis is placed on the students developing the skills to use, evaluate and possibly modify flexible delivery resources to suit the needs and specific contexts of learners. Students will focus on the particular pedagogies of flexible and online learning.
learning_outcomes: Respond to the needs of different types of learners in different flexible delivery contexts.
Describe a range of educational technologies and position them within a learning theory framework.
Articulate the broad issues associated with the use of computer technologies in teaching and learning, particularly in terms of inclusivity.
Critically evaluate educational technology resources using criteria derived from a range of appropriate learning theories.
Display a critical perspective on the potential value of educational technologies.
prerequisites: EMT220: Flexible Delivery in the Vocational Education and Training Sector

title: Technology for the Connected Workplace
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Online technologies allow workforces to stay connected and engaged with their teams and customers, whether they are geographically dispersed or in the office next door. This subject introduces a suite of technologies that can be used to work effectively and securely online. The suite includes tools for online co-creation, data storage as well as two way and one way communication platforms.
learning_outcomes: Apply online technologies to a workplace context .
Reflect on and compare the merits, limits and effectiveness of various technologies.

title: Temperate Fruit and Nut Crop Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the principles of growing temperate climate plants that must flower before they produce fruits or nuts. There is a strong focus on climatic influences on flowering and fruiting and managing crop load. Utilising apples as a case study crop, students will study the biology, principles, and practices of deciduous fruit and nut crop production. Students will develop a crop production manual for a chosen fruit/nut crop and research innovative and sustainable improvements to the production cycle. Consideration of markets will also be utilised to inform the decision making needed to establish a new orchard.
learning_outcomes: Analyse market data to inform judgments about the establishment of new orchards.
Assess the maturity of a range of fruit and nut crops and develop a management program, including suitable post-harvest procedures for optimal quantity and quality of final product.

Describe the range of fruit and nut crops produced in Australia and discuss how the influences of climatic factors on vegetative growth & development, flowering, fruit set, and fruit growth and development determine optimal orchard management procedures.
Critically review current and new technologies used in the production of a horticultural crop and synthesise a plan to utilise a new proven technology into the orchard management cycle.

title: Technology Law
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to technology law, a new and challenging area of the law that involves the regulation of modern communication, identification and other forms of technology. Students explore the development of the legal system in response to new technology, as well as the threats posed by cybercrime and strategies that can be used to combat it. Issues that will be explored include: copyright and intellectual property, privacy law, technology-based identification of suspects in the criminal justice system, technology-based treatment in the healthcare sector and challenges associated with investigating and prosecuting technology based offences.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the investigative and jurisdictional issues relating to law and technology in Australia.
Articulate the development of new technology, its regulation in the legal system, and its relationship to traditional forms of law.
Evaluate the role of law reform in response to technological development in the criminal justice and healthcare sectors.
Articulate and apply the current law relating to unauthorised access and impairment of computers; online fraud; and offences against individuals, such as cyberbullying and harassment.
Evaluate the development of intellectual property and privacy laws in relation to information technology.
Critically evaluate possible future developments in technology and regulatory strategies.

title: Terrorism Awareness
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an understanding of the basic principles of terrorism as it relates to law enforcement and security, an understanding of terrorist group ideology, types of terrorism, types of terrorists, and the role of law enforcement in combating terrorism and acts of terrorism.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the communication literacies and digital skills required of a competent criminal justice practitioner.
Examine in detail various developments in the history of terrorism and their impact on modern day law enforcement.
Identify and analyse terrorist groups likely to operate within Australia, their ideology and objectives.
Identify and report potential terrorist activity, the motivation and modus operandi of terrorist groups and individuals, and the role of law enforcement in combating terrorism.

title: Terrorist Operations and Praxis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Terrorists represent a dynamic threat due to their ability to learn and innovate methods for strategic violence. These innovations are capable of fundamentally altering the atmosphere of counter terrorism in the Western world. This can be due to technical simplicity, such as September 11, 2001; technological expansion, such as Tokyo 1995; or strategic innovation, such as Munich 1972. This subject uses real world case studies of significant terrorist attacks, and explores the enduring impact they had on counter terrorism policy internationally. You will undertake a structured operations analysis of prominent attacks in order to develop theories regarding future terrorist threats.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess recent developments in terrorist operations and praxis to evaluate operational evolution.
Objectively appraise terrorist operations and praxis to inform professional practice with empirically-driven decision-making.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of terrorist operations and praxis, with regards to the impact subnational terrorist operations have had on counter terrorism approaches.
Clearly communicate complex theories regarding terrorist operations and praxis appropriately to inform specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Select and apply appropriate research methods to investigate terrorist operations and praxis, while exploiting available intelligence to substantiate assessments.

title: Terrorist Financing and Resourcing
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Terrorist financing and resourcing is an essential mechanism through which counterterrorism practitioners, policy makers, regulators and academics can assess the strength of a terrorist group and its network. In this subject, you will explore the murky underworld of terrorist finance and resourcing, and investigate the mechanisms through which terrorist networks raise, transfer, and expend their funds. You will also be introduced to concepts around privatisation, diversification, and globalisation within the ambit of transactional criminal and terrorist activity. Finally, study will assess the efficacy of historical counter terrorism approaches to understand the challenges in countering terrorist movements.
learning_outcomes: Select appropriate research methods to provide empirically-based assessments of current and emerging financing threats in various terrorism and security contexts.
Demonstrate leadership through rigorously and objectively analysing terrorist financing and resourcing, in order to inform and influence professional practice; and,.
Critically analyse terrorist financing and resourcing at the tactical, operational, and strategic levels in order to identify patterns and mechanisms.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of terrorist financing and resourcing practices with reference to subnational organisations, networks, and operations, to assess existing strategic responses.
Clearly communicate complex counter terrorism policies, practices and approaches to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Terrorist Propaganda and Communication
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: Publicity is the oxygen that sustains terrorist organisations. In a modern world with an increasingly swift news cycle, it is important to understand how terrorist organisations and individuals formulate propaganda, and exploit communication and information strategies to accrue attention to their cause, and achieve strategic effect. In this subject, you will explore terrorist communication and propaganda operations; strategies for recruitment; cyber terrorism, and its evolution; social media and terrorism, and its adaption by Islamic State. The dark web provides further opportunities for terrorists, and you will evaluate the challenges it poses for law enforcement and security professionals. Finally, you will assess the counter measures enacted by various security stakeholders and private industry.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate terrorist communication and propaganda strategies, concepts, and tools to identify patterns and make assessments.
Clearly communicate complex terrorist communication theory and practice to inform specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Objectively and professionally challenge established theories and contribute to current debate in order to inform professional practice.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of terrorist communication and propaganda strategies, including historical trends, contemporary strategies, and emerging developments in order to make assessments.
Select and apply appropriate research methods, in conjunction with open source intelligence, to develop theories regarding terrorist communication operations.

title: TESOL Professional Experience
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on understandings of the nature of effective pedagogical practices that encompass teaching, learning, and assessment in ESL/EFL classrooms. Students will undertake a 20-hour professional experience program, of which 6 hours must be in a face-to-face teaching context. During this experience they will be expected to critically integrate theory and practice in relation to ESL/EFL classroom management issues while exploring a range of second language acquisition teaching styles and methods to accommodate varying learning needs and contexts. Students are required to undertake ESL/EFL classroom observation, team teaching, and independent teaching to demonstrate their progress as an ESL/EFL teacher. Students are also required to develop their skills of professional reflective practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply the teaching-learning cycle within a TESOL context.
Engage in critically reflective collegial dialogue with TESOL professionals.
Plan effective English language learning sequences that reflect local contexts and the learners needs.
Explain and apply different methods and strategies for teaching English language in context.
Provide engaging learning experiences that appropriately address learner needs.
Apply contextualised classroom management strategies.
Collaborate with a TESOL professional to meet the above objectives.

title: TESOL Across Curriculum, Practice, and Pedagogy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the relationships between curriculum, pedagogy, and practice in TESOL. It introduces key theories and perspectives around TESOL curriculum planning and development. It also examines the pedagogical principles embedded in curriculum development. In so doing, it encourages students to apply their knowledge of curriculum and pedagogy to situated workplace practices such as English language teaching, program management, and consultation.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine the application of curricular and pedagogical knowledge in TESOL context.
Understand pedagogical principles in TESOL including their origins and development.
Understand TESOL curriculum theories and methods including their origins and development.
Understand skills, strategies, and competence related to TESOL practice.

title: Text Analytics and Conversational AI
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject presents emerging machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms that support the extraction of meaning from unstructured textual data, allowing analysts to discover latent patterns and themes. The subject investigates the feasibility and extent to which emerging text analytics techniques can be used in various real-world business contexts. The focus will be on understanding and leveraging the power of text analytics and conversational AI to enhance business decision-making and customer experience. Upon successful completion of this subject, students will be capable of applying modern natural language processing models to unearth insights from real-world business data. Further, students will learn how to assemble and evaluate various state-of-the-art techniques in text analytics tools, and interpret the analytics results to support effective and ethical business decision making.
learning_outcomes: Interpret insights from text extraction and conversational AI tools, and effectively communicate them to both expert and non-expert audiences.
Discuss and apply modern natural language processing models.
Setup advanced text extraction techniques for effective use in various business scenarios.
Identify and critically evaluate different conversational AI tools for various business use-cases.

title: Textiles and Design
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This credit code is required for cross institutional credit for subjects taught into the Bachelor of Education (Technology and Applied Studies) by Southern Cross University.
learning_outcomes: This credit code is to credit three subjects in Textiles and Design namely:
DES10642 Textiles & Society.
DES10641 Textiles & Design.
DES10643 Textiles Science & Innovation.

title: Textiles Technology Studies - 16 points
school: School of Education

title: Textiles Technology Studies - 8 points
school: School of Education

title: The Adult and Vocational Education System in Australia
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: Quality training and assessment requires practitioners to have a thorough understanding of the Australian Vocational Education system. This subject critically examines the theoretical, regulatory, and practical factors that influence training. The training system is examined in terms of the analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation cycle. The subject then presents a model of scholarship that allows a teacher-practitioner, to identify, investigate and propose opportunities for improvement in their teaching practice. This subject assumes background knowledge of content covered in the Certificate IV in Training & Assessment and experience working within the context of Australian Qualifications Framework Training Packages.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the vocational training system in the context of the training development cycle.
Critically analyse theoretical, regulatory, and practical factors that influence training within the Australian vocational education and training sector.
Design, conduct, and present the findings of a small basic research project focusing on one aspect of the training cycle that addresses an issue of importance in your area of professional practice.
prerequisites: EMV302: Adult and Vocational Education in Australia

title: The Advanced Practitioner in Medical Radiation Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the characteristics, complexities and challenges of Advanced Practice to prepare medical radiation science practitioners to meet future possibilities for Advanced Practice, whilst reflecting on the contemporary issues in health. The core function of an Advanced Practitioner is to engage in expert clinical practice to deliver innovative high quality, person-centred care. In this subject, students will develop an in depth understanding of Advanced Practice across current applications in healthcare and be able to critically evaluate and explore opportunities within their own clinical setting including viability and sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on their own professional development and/or contribution to the professional development of others to improve healthcare delivery within their own professional setting.
Analyse the complexities of health and healthcare delivery in relation to their own practice setting with consideration of evidence-based practice and relevant legal, social and ethical factors.
Critically evaluate the role and characteristics of Advanced Practice within medical radiation science informed by a synthesis of appropriate evidence-based literature.
Critically appraise the scope for Advanced Practice implementation and evaluation within the medical radiation sciences and their own practice setting.

title: The Arabic Script and its Sounds
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for students with no prior language skills in Arabic. It presents an introduction to reading the Arabic script and is designed to teach students how to articulate Arabic letters, words and sentences. It will also cover writing practice, together with basic speaking and acquisition of commonly used words. This subject provides foundations for further study in the language.
learning_outcomes: Identify and proficiently pronounce the Arabic alphabet.
Read basic vowelised Arabic script with fluency.
Communicate in simple conversation related to greetings and introductions.
Write basic Arabic words and sentences.

title: The Contemporary Designer
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines what it means to be a contemporary designer. It investigates the creative practice and innovations crafted by prominent designers in image-making, graphics, environmental and multimedia design. It explores cultural and historical influences in communicating meaning including philosophies of design and how they effect contemporary design thinking. The investigation of practice and the impact of technology, production techniques and the variations in consumer/user behaviour build a platform for students to develop a preliminary understanding of their own practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply visual critique within an established framework.
Combine image-making and type to generate contemporary design works.
Describe fundamental historical, cultural and philosophical influences on contemporary design thinking and making.
Analyse a range of design artefacts and identify principles and theories that influenced their production.
Describe and apply basic visual research methods including design development and iteration in a range of contexts.
prerequisites: GRP117: Graphic Design Theory, Context and Practice

title: The Creative Arts: The Creative Process
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will explore the creative process and engage in embodied learning focused on the creative arts: music, visual arts, drama, dance and media arts. Students will reflect on their own creative arts history and will use a theoretical framework to construct their personal creative narrative. They will further reflect on their individual processes and responses to each of the creative arts forms during their making and appreciating.
learning_outcomes: Create works of art from a range of stimuli.
Employ various creative processes that include composition, performance and appreciation of the creative art forms.
Articulate how the elements of visual arts, music, drama, dance and media arts informs the creative process in each of these creative art forms.
Apply a variety of creative process models to their own practice.

title: The Creative Professional
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject students undertake self-directed study towards the generation of an individual future work or study plan with potential to create materials and content for portfolio use. Students are required to explore and critique their current research and professional interests and consider how as emergent professionals they can maximise their individual impact in existing, emergent, future or speculative professions. This subject embraces the broad nature of each students' learning and provides a foundation for life-long learning.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on personal learning and achievements, as well as identify areas for future development.
Critically evaluate and speculate on the future of their discipline/s.
Engage in debates on a range of contemporary issues in creative industries including ethical, cultural and responsible practices.
Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of an area of research in creative industries relevant to their own professional practice.

title: The Diaconate
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: The order of deacon in the Christian Church has undergone great changes over the centuries. Students will examine contemporary developments in this order of ministry in the light of its history and the practice of the Church.
learning_outcomes: Communicate a diaconal mission, practice and spirituality in light of contemporary church order and mission.
Discuss the modern day re-emergence of the diaconate, examining its expression in various Christian traditions.
Articulate and to evaluate expressions of the diaconate in the New Testament.
Reflect theologically on diaconal ministry, in the light of tradition and practice.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Trace the subsequent development of church order and critically evaluate the place of the diaconate within it.

title: The Diaconate
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: The order of deacon in the Christian Church has undergone great changes over the centuries. Students will examine contemporary developments in this order of ministry in the light of its history and the practice of the Church.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the modern day re-emergence of the diaconate, examining its expression in various Christian traditions.
Communicate a diaconal mission, practice and spirituality in light of contemporary church order and mission.
Trace the subsequent development of church order and critically evaluate the place of the diaconate within it.
Reflect theologically on diaconal ministry, in the light of tradition and practice.
Articulate and to evaluate expressions of the diaconate in the New Testament.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.

title: The Diaconate
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: The order of deacon in the Christian church has undergone great changes over the centuries. Students will examine contemporary developments in this order of ministry in the light of its history and the practice of the church.
learning_outcomes: Communicate a diaconal mission, practice and spirituality in light of contemporary church order and mission.
Articulate expressions of the diaconate in the New Testament.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Reflect theologically on diaconal ministry, in the light of tradition and practice.
Discuss the modern-day re-emergence of the diaconate, examining its expression in various Christian traditions.
Trace the subsequent development of church order and critically evaluate the place of the diaconate within it.

title: The Disability Sector
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to social and human services elements of the disability sector. It will enable students to examine and critique how social and organisational processes contribute to the marginalisation of people of differing abilities, thus reinforcing a focus on "disabilities". It examines the main models of disability, including human rights based frameworks, enabling students to develop a critical analysis of the models. It also fosters a conception of differing abilities beyond these established models. Policy and program development in the disability field is analysed, informed by examination of philosophical changes, legal frameworks and critical concepts. Institutional factors which mediate disability, including contemporary policy developments and debates, are examined.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate Australian laws and policies relating to disability against the context of national and international human rights frameworks.
Critically compare and evaluate a range of theories and models of disability, diversity and social processes related to disability.
Evaluate disability practice in the human service sector in relation to disability policies and lived experience of disability.
Critically evaluate the Australian disability service sector: its structures and services for people with disabilities in the light of national and international disability rights and standards.

title: The Dynamic Information Environment
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to provide a specialist understanding of the provision of information resources and services within the learning and teaching context of the school. Search strategies, information sources and resource evaluation are examined in relation to print and digital environments. The teacher librarian's role in the creation, design, structure and flow of information in the school is explored, in particular the use of emerging technologies. The design of physical and virtual school library spaces and their relationship to the curriculum is also examined.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and use emerging technologies to provide innovative digital information resources.
Develop and evaluate highly effective search strategies and apply these to the learning and teaching context.
Link the provision of information resources and services for the school community to the development of information literacy outcomes across the school.
Investigate and explain how information is effectively sought and utilised.
Critically evaluate the learning and teaching context in which a range of resources and services are used in schools to support curriculum programs.

Critically evaluate and demonstrate understanding of good design principles to organise and develop physical and virtual spaces in the school library that meet 21st century teaching and learning needs.
Evaluate and integrate emerging technologies to develop curriculum resources that support the learning and teaching context.

title: The Dynamics of Health Care Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject frames the modern health services as a complex system, and builds on this by presenting the concepts of organisational culture and individual perception. This foundation is used to prepare students to communicate, influence, make decisions, participate in teams, and also to lead teams, successfully. The understandings emerging out of this work are then applied to the more complex matters that frequently impact on health services, including change, conflict and interdisciplinarity.
learning_outcomes: Explain how individual perception can both facilitate and hinder health professional practice.
Discuss the tension between protocol driven practice and a health service's inherent unpredictability.
Evaluate the benefits and challenges of teamwork in health care.
Analyse the relationship between organisational culture and performance.
Discuss how health professionals can use an understanding of organisational behaviour to communicate, influence and make decisions.
Describe the organisation of health services and their complex nature.

title: The Equine Athlete
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the physiology underlying equine athleticism building upon existing knowledge of mammalian energy production systems. During this subject students will develop an appreciation of the physiological capacity of the horse to adapt to exercise demands. Vulnerability to injury, breakdown and associated management challenges are examined. Students will undertake practical work and devise training programs that optimise both performance and welfare. On successfully completing this subject students will be proficient in designing and monitoring equine fitness and training programs.
learning_outcomes: evaluate the physical demands being made on the equine athlete during different equestrian sports;
critically appraise the physiological processes occurring within the equine athlete in response to exercise and training and design comprehensive training and management programs;
critically evaluate and apply published evidence-based findings to optimise equine training processes and relay these effectively in order to allow practitioners to improve/enhance their practice.
interpret the regulatory requirements of a chosen equine sport with regards to the management of the equine athlete on the national and international stage; and
apply current scientific monitoring protocols to evaluate equine athletic fitness and equestrian sport potential;

title: The Ethics of Capitalism
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject will consider how society ought to be arranged. It will consider which freedoms should be protected and how wealth ought to be distributed. The subject will pay particular attention to capitalist norms and will consider whether they are morally defensible. The subject will also consider how crime ought to be regulated in a just society and whether punishment can be morally justified.
learning_outcomes: Display knowledge of a range of philosophical and ethical theories of justice.
Appreciate the ways in which law and justice are connected.
Use the discourse of justice to analyse social and economic policy.
Express an understanding of the differences between criminal and distributive justice.
Analyse the concept of justice and related terms.
Articulate the idea of a fair trial.
Exhibit knowledge of competing justificatory theories of punishment, including their strengths and weaknesses.

title: The European Reformations
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject begins with an overview of fifteenth-century Western Christianity and society, emphasising the impact of scholasticism, Christian humanism and novel nationalism. It then explores: the reformations in continental Europe and reform movements within Roman Catholicism; the radical reformations, inquisitions and the plight of religious minorities; English and Scottish reformations from Henry VIII to Elizabeth I; Puritan influence; and the Stuart, Commonwealth and Restoration settlements. Consistent attention is given to the reformations' long-term legacies and the broader context of the early modern world, as well as socio-cultural issues such as gender and sexuality, death, witchcraft and moral discipline.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the diverse political, intellectual and social contexts of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century reform movements.
Assess critically historians' interpretations of reformation church history.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the successive settlements of religion in Britain.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of a range of views on controversial issues relating to theology, sacraments and church-state relations.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills relevant to history as a discipline.
Explain and to evaluate aspects of Protestant and Roman Catholic thought, life and culture before 1700 CE.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the contribution of major figures in these movements.
Demonstrate an advanced critical understanding of minority religious movements during this period.

title: The European Reformations
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject begins with an overview of fifteenth-century Western Christianity and society, emphasising the impact of scholasticism, Christian humanism and nascent nationalism. It then explores: the reformations in continental Europe and reform movements within Roman Catholicism; the radical reformations, inquisitions and the plight of religious minorities; English and Scottish reformations from Henry VIII to Elizabeth I; Puritan influence; and the Stuart, Commonwealth and Restoration settlements. Consistent attention is given throughout the subject to the broader context of early modern Europe and its interaction with the wider world, as well as socio-cultural issues such as gender and sexuality, death, witchcraft and moral discipline. Finally, attention is given to the reformations' long-term legacies to the present day.
learning_outcomes: Critically review and analyse the contribution of historians and historiographical perspectives from a variety of denominational and historical contexts.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including basic research, writing and communication skills relevant to history as a discipline.
Critically review and analyse the role of minority religious movements during this period.
