Create a professional learning resource explaining trade based money laundering typologies and indicative red flags.

title: Training, Design and Development
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The development and delivery of effective training within an organisational context is a key strategy in employee and organisational success. This subject explores the forces influencing Australian and international organisations in this regard, and their strategic responses. Needs assessment, learning theories, and the design, delivery and evaluation of training are also addressed in this practically focussed subject, as are evolving directions of training and development within Australian and global organisational contexts.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically evaluate the environmental forces influencing organisations and their strategic training responses.
Conduct a strategic needs analysis for an organisation.
Design and evaluate a training and development program for a specific organisational context.
Contextualise evolving directions of training and development within organisational contexts, including emerging best practices.
Recommend suitable learning theories that can be utilised in specific domestic and/or global organisational environments.

title: Transferable Skills Subject
school: School

title: Transforming Services and Operations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to service and operations management – the key activities which create value for the organisation. It examines these operations in the context of our contemporary digitalised, turbulent and disruptive environments. The focus of the subject will be on transforming operations through improving the efficiency and effectiveness of service and product delivery for organisations in our global, digitised business environment. Strategic elements such as a supply chain management, production and delivery innovation, seamless customer experience, global sustainability and environmental considerations and future proofing will be addressed. Various topics will equip students with a range of tools and techniques that can be applied in specific situations in both service and product operations. Recommendations at strategic and operational levels will be developed.
learning_outcomes: Work independently and/or collaboratively to recommend sustainable organisational improvements that enhance linkages between strategy, design, implementation and delivery.
Work independently and/or collaboratively to design control and risk management strategies to monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of operations.
Work independently and/or collaboratively to apply techniques, tools and models in a range of operational situations.
Work independently and/or collaboratively to evaluate digital operations methodologies to improve performance.
Critically evaluate the service or product operations of an organisation against its strategic and environmental context.

title: Transformative ecosocial change in human services
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the role of human service professionals in the context of the global environmental crisis. A model of transformative ecosocial practice is introduced, involving a distinct philosophical base of practice that emphasises holism and interdependence with the natural world. By exploring the influence of dominant discourses, including colonialism, modernism, patriarchy and neoliberalism, inherent contradictions of environmental sustainability are challenged. Students will be introduced to non-dominant discourses and knowledges for informing ecosocial practice, including Indigenous Australian, worldwide Indigenous, Global Southern, and eco-feminist perspectives. The foundations for incorporating a transformative ecosocial approach in practice will be examined including being, thinking and doing dimensions.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the influence of dominant discourses on ecosocial practice in human services, including colonialism, modernism, patriarchy, and neoliberalism.
Examine the impacts of the global environmental crisis on human and non-human wellbeing.
Apply the foundations of ecosocial practice in human services, including being, thinking, and doing dimensions.
Apply non-dominant knowledges for informing ecosocial practice in human services, including Indigenous Australian, worldwide Indigenous, Global Southern, and eco-feminist perspectives.

title: Transfusion Science
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the theoretical aspects of blood group serology and blood banking practice including pre-transfusion testing, investigation of haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn (HDFN), and investigation of transfusion reactions.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate features of blood products including but not limited to their preparation methods, storage, quality control and indications for use.
Evaluate the organisation of blood collection centres and blood banks in regard to donor selection, blood collection, and the processing, storage and preservation of blood products.

Explain and evaluate safe transfusion requirements, transfusion-transmitted diseases, transfusion reactions, autoimmune haemolytic anaemias; haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn, and foeto-maternal allo-immune thrombocytopenia.
Demonstrate high levels of academic literacy.
Explain the principles used for detection and identification of blood group antigens and antibodies and apply them to problem-solving activities including but not limited to case studies.
Explain the testing process associated with pre-transfusion; transfusion reaction; and haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn.

title: Transition from Enrolled Nurse to the Registered Nurse Profession
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are supported for their transition from enrolled nurse to the profession of the registered nurse and academic study at an Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) level 7. Students will draw on their previous study and industry experience to develop their identity as a Bachelor of Nursing student and explore the role and scope of the registered nurse in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Explain how the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) standards and codes, the International Council of Nurses (ICN) code of ethics and legislation relevant to the practice of the registered nurse underpin nursing practice.
Explain concepts of person-centred care, clinical reasoning, critical thinking and theories that support nursing practice.
Explain how scope of practice is determined for registered nurses and student registered nurses.
Describe the purpose of simulation, feedback and reflection for developing nursing practice.
Apply AQF level 7 academic skills, including academic writing, database searching and identifying appropriate evidence.
prerequisites: NUR100: Introduction to the Registered Nurse Profession

title: Transfusion Science (8)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the theoretical aspects of blood group serology and blood banking practice including pre-transfusion testing, investigation of haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn (HDFN), and investigation of transfusion reactions.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate features of blood products including but not limited to their preparation methods, storage, quality control and indications for use.
Explain the principles used for detection and identification of blood group antigens and antibodies and apply them to problem-solving activities including but not limited to case studies.

Explain and evaluate safe transfusion requirements, transfusion-transmitted diseases, transfusion reactions, autoimmune haemolytic anaemias; haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn, and foeto-maternal allo-immune thrombocytopenia.
Evaluate the organisation of blood collection centres and blood banks in regard to donor selection, blood collection, and the processing, storage and preservation of blood products.
Explain the testing process associated with pre-transfusion; transfusion reaction; and haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn.

title: Transition from TAFE/VET to University
school: School
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to provide TAFE/VET students entering the University with background and skills required for successful study. It is recognised that the transition to this new study environment requires an understanding of the key differences in systems and expectations so that students can begin their university studies with confidence. It designed for students from the Australian VET sector and is delivered via a face-to-face workshop.
learning_outcomes: Understand the differences between VET and University.
Begin to develop and apply critical thinking skills.
Navigate the CSU online learning environment.
Understand and begin to develop generic academic literacy skills.
Read, clarify and organise information in order to communicate their understanding of readings.
Understand the differences in academic expectations and cultures between VET and HE.
Find, extract, interpret and apply information to their learning from a broad range of sources and demonstrate practical skills in negotiating the online environment.

title: Transition to Allied Health Practice
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject provides students with the opportunity to extend their understanding of professional practice, in preparation for their transition to the workforce. Students will reflect on the knowledge, skills and attributes they have developed and evaluate their capabilities as an allied health practitioner, advocate, clinical educator, leader and lifelong learner. This subject will enable students to explore strategies for self-management to enable productive and sustainable professional lives. Students will critically analyse professional practice in the context of relevant legal requirements, codes of conduct and practice standards. Students will consolidate their skills in developing their understanding of effective interprofessional partnerships as a strong foundation for ethical practice, collective reasoning and person-focused practice. The evaluation of workplace cultures and the importance of respectful relationships will prepare students for graduate-entry practice in a range of healthcare contexts.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on, and critically analyse, one's own competency development as a lifelong learner.
Critically analyse professional practice in the context of relevant legal requirements, practice standards, and ethical and sustainable approaches.
Explore strategies for self-management and adaptability that contribute to resilience in practice.
Build effective interprofessional partnerships and teams to enable collective reasoning which enhances the health and wellbeing of people.
Evaluate their leadership and advocacy capabilities to identify opportunities and apply these in health care contexts.
prerequisites: OCC414: Professional and organisational contexts of practice
OCC414: Professional and organisational contexts of practice

title: Transition to Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is developed as the final subject for the undergraduate Bachelor of Clinical Practice (Paramedic) and the Bachelor of Paramedicine and the Bachelor of Paramedicine (Honours) programs for both internal and online education students. This subject sets the foundation for future clinical practice by requiring students to integrate and consolidate knowledge and skills developed in preceding subjects and to demonstrate that they have clinical judgement and decision making skills to apply this to real-world situations. This subject focuses on ensuring students are able to successfully transition to professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to work as part of a team to make clinical judgments, formulate and implement informed and reasoned treatment decisions, in complex simulated cases.
Continuously document, develop, and evaluate the quality of their professional knowledge, skills, and practice.
Explain the paramedics scope of practice, and standards of ethical and professional conduct and performance in paramedicine.
Use the principles of quality assurance/improvement to investigate a paramedic practice issue.
Use and critically evaluate rigorous clinical decision making processes to make evidence-based clinical decisions about patient care and the impact on patient outcomes.
prerequisites: CLS300: Advanced Cardiology and Paramedic Practice

title: Transition to Nursing Studies
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject has been developed to promote a positive transition to the university learning environment for students undertaking the Bachelor of Nursing. The fundamental aim of the subject is to prepare prospective nursing students for the academic requirements of the Bachelor of Nursing, and the implications and significance of beginning university studies. Further, it aims to provide a framework through which the prospective students can secure access to needed resources within their local communities before they commence the Bachelor of Nursing. The focus is on students' acquiring foundational knowledge and applied skills necessary for academic success, including time management, academic literacy and numeracy, basic computer literacy, independent learning and test-taking skills.
learning_outcomes: Know how to access resources available to support their studies.
Be cognisant of the nature of university learning.
Develop examination preparation techniques.
Plan their study time according to their own priorities and deadlines.
Demonstrate the application of basic numeracy in nursing.
Develop an understanding of their preferred learning styles.
Be familiar with the support structures that are available within the university, the workplace and the local community to support their studies.
Develop insights into their own learning needs.
Navigate the CSU online learning environment.
Identify the resources required to undertake university studies.
Be familiar with successful reading strategies.
Follow the structures and conventions of academic writing.

title: Transition to Policing Studies
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject welcomes students to the Charles Sturt University and Goulburn Police College and promotes a positive transition to these learning environments. The fundamental aim of the subject is to prepare prospective policing students for the academic requirements of the Diploma of Policing Practice as well as the implications and significance of beginning university studies. The focus is on students acquiring foundational knowledge and applied skills necessary for academic success, including time management, academic reading and writing, independent learning and test-taking skills.
learning_outcomes: Prepare for and manage their performance in a variety of examination formats.
Apply reading strategies appropriate to their aim and to that of the reading material.
Plan their study time according to their own priorities and deadlines.
Be aware of the structure and conventions of academic writing, appropriate to task and audience.
Have gained insights into the nature of university learning and their preferred learning preferences.

title: Transition to Professional Practice in Speech Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this capstone subject, students' learning focuses on preparation for transition to graduate speech pathology practice. Students engage with a range of current topics in speech pathology and critique current practice, research and service delivery in relation to these. Students integrate understanding of current practice in Australian and overseas contexts with a focus on ethical reasoning and cultural responsiveness. Students also develop skills in interprofessional and supervisory practice, as well as designing, managing, and evaluating speech pathology programs and services. Students critically reflect on their competency development across the duration of the Master of Speech Pathology, and identify and justify ongoing professional learning goals in preparation for transition to the workplace.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise and evidence own development of speech pathology knowledge, skills and attributes to demonstrate readiness to enter speech pathology practice.

Integrate understanding of recent developments in speech pathology practice and current professional issues to plan and execute contextually and culturally responsive speech pathology programs/practices.
Apply speech pathology and generic professional knowledge, skills and attributes, demonstrating autonomy, adaptability and responsibility in professional practice contexts.
Communicate complex synthesis of professional knowledge, skills and attributes to specialist and non-specialist audience.
Critically analyse and reflect on their own competency development and demonstrate autonomy and responsibility as a life-long learner.
prerequisites: SPH515: Integrating Speech Pathology Competency in the Workplace
SPH532: Clinical Reasoning for Integrated Client Care in Speech Pathology

title: Transition to Tertiary Study for Indigenous Students
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide Indigenous students with information and resources designed to help them make a successful transition to tertiary study. The focus will be on encouraging students to identify and utilise strategies that enable successful university learning. These include identifying and developing support networks to facilitate academic success as well as acquiring the academic skills needed to study successfully. Specifically this subject will help students recognise and harness their personal and cultural strengths as motivation for learning. Further it will show students how to plan for study and manage their time effectively; identify and apply their learning style; understand academic culture and language; read, take notes, and write for academic purposes; and use electronic resources for research and communication.
learning_outcomes: Take notes from a lecture or presentation.
Use notes and summaries to plan a response to an assignment task or topic.
Use information and communications technology within the CSU online learning environment to support learning.
Identify skills and strategies needed for successful transition to tertiary study.
Identify relevant support structures within the community and the university.
Apply the principles of academic integrity and use a number of referencing styles.
Summarise a written resource.
Prepare a time management plan to meet study and other commitments.
Read critically in response to an assessment task or topic.

title: Transition to Practice
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to further develop a student's competence and capability for practice as an intern pharmacist. This subject will include both professional experiences/learning and a capstone experience with options in both activities to allow students to develop their own value proposition in the pharmacy career market. Students studying this subject are assumed to have completed the first three years of the standard enrolment pattern, as this knowledge is critical for achieving professional milestones (assessments of competency) which are necessary to successfully pass this subject. Further, students will engage in both professional experiences and inter-professional activities which involve interaction with patients and health professionals. Subjects completed in the first three years, prior to completing this subject, provide students with the necessary knowledge in many areas such as pathophysiology of diseases, pharmacology, and pharmacokinetics, to ensure patient medication safety and protect the reputation of the University, the course, the profession and most importantly, the student.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to discuss with a wider audience intended patient management plans and rationale underlying those proposals.
Constructively collaborate with others and ethically manage conflict.
Communicate effectively and professionally with stakeholders and deliver considered and clear information or recommendations.
Research and review intended patient management plans for patient utility and safety.
Develop a learning plan or contract to meet identified needs and goals.
Effectively identify own learning needs and goals consistent with intended future practice.
Engage in the self directed evaluation of information and issues from various sources and articulate the outcomes.
Participate in and develop processes to provide a safe and secure environment for group work and collaborative practice.
Research, critically analyse and synthesise information appropriate for the audience.
Reflect on the role, practice and professional identity of the pharmacist to develop and maintain appropriate professional practice boundaries.

title: Transition to University Study
school: School
syllabus_overview: Transition to University Study is designed to better prepare students for successful study at university. This subject offers students an introduction into academic culture, and will allow them to become familiar with Charles Sturt University, its support systems and the expectations of tertiary study. Topics include university teaching and learning; managing self and time; reading, writing and reasoning; and preparing for and performing well in exams.
learning_outcomes: Write a short text that uses conventions of academic writing.
Plan study time according to priorities and deadlines.
Select a reading strategy appropriate to the text and the purpose of your task.
Find resources or services that support further development in transition to university study.
Demonstrate knowledge of effective exam preparation.
Explain the expectations of university learning.
Identify learning preferences and strategies for learning in relation to a range of teaching methods.

title: Transition to Uni Study
school: School
syllabus_overview: Transition to University Study is designed to prepare students for successful study at university. It is recognised that the transition to this new study environment requires an understanding of the key differences in systems and expectations so that students can begin their university studies with confidence. This subject offers students an introduction into academic culture, and develops familiarity with Charles Sturt University, its support systems and the expectations of tertiary study. It further provides an introduction to the basic skills of university engagement and success, such as reading and interpreting information, learning online, planning study time and effective exam preparation. This subject is delivered online.
learning_outcomes: be able to develop and apply generic academic literacy skills;
be able to read, clarify and organise information in order to communicate your understanding;
be able to explain the nature and expectations of university teaching and learning;
be able to develop and apply critical and reflective thinking skills; and
be able to identify university structures and support systems;
be able to find resources or services that support transition to university study;
be able to identify strategies for learning in relation to a range of teaching methods;
be able to plan study time according to priorities and deadlines;
be able to identify principles of effective assessment preparation;
be able to apply skills to navigating the CSU online learning environment.

title: Transition to the Profession
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students for their final year of study in Clinical Rotations, and provides a lead in to the workplace. As such it is an opportunity to examine the operation of veterinary practices including legislation, professional obligations, ethical dilemmas and introductory business management. Emphasis is given to the laws governing the practice of veterinary science, general workplace legislation, and the particular role of the Veterinary Practitioners Registration Board in maintaining governance of the profession. In addition the basic financial management of veterinary practice is covered, including costing of services, the need for public and professional liability insurance, and the basis of employment contracts and wage negotiation are presented. Ethical and welfare dilemmas are discussed during case based presentation. Students who will enter the Honours stream will be asked to write a literature review, and other students will be expected to submit an essay from a choice of topics. Students cannot progress to Phase 3 of this subject, without the completion of Phases 1 and 2 of the veterinary science program.
learning_outcomes: Set in place safety nets such as consent forms, client advice forms and to also be capable of achieving informed consent.
Demonstrate skills of critical analysis and personal reflection.
Identify and access the relevant veterinary legislation and apply this to practical situations as they apply to professional conduct, responsibilities and restrictions.
Demonstrate communication skills resulting in the ability to effectively interact with clients, staff and colleagues.
Demonstrate professional behaviour.
Identify opportunities for research and further education.
Demonstrate knowledge of the ethical frameworks influencing animal use in society.
Demonstrate developing knowledge of basic practice financial management.
Draft a weighted list of desired criteria to be considered in selecting a suitable employment position.
prerequisites: VSC451: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 4
VSC427: Companion Animal Medicine and Surgery 3

title: Transnational Organised Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: An increasingly globalised world order has brought with it an increasingly networked crime-terror nexus. Transnational Organised Crime (TOC) is a rising challenge for law enforcement, intelligence, and policy makers around the world due its complex socio-political dynamics and drivers. In this subject, you will explore transnational security threats to law and order, national security, and community cohesion at regional and international levels. You will be introduced to real world case studies regarding criminal networks, commodities and markets, cartels and networks, mafias and other organisations, to understand the implications of transnational organised crime. By analysing its evolution, you will be able to make threat assessments using regional and global perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Utilise appropriate research methods to investigate the networks and relationships in transnational organised crime groups.
Objectively evaluate responses to transnational organised crime to inform professional practice and ethical decision-making.
Critically analyse transnational organised crime, with reference to globalised networks, to provide operational, tactical, and strategic insight into diverse threats.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of transnational organised crime, with reference to theory and subnational organisations and networks to assess developing threats in regional and global scope.
Clearly communicate complex issues regarding transnational organised crime appropriately to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Transformational Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: It is difficult in today's cynical and complex world for leaders to gain trust from their stakeholders both internal and external. This subject takes a practical and applied look at transformative leadership. Transformative leadership takes a long-term, values and ethically based view of leadership that focuses on shared value for stakeholders and the broader society. This subject is an opportunity for students to explore how their leadership style may contribute to the development of community resilience. Students will examine leadership styles through a variety of conceptual lenses – transformational leadership, servant leadership charismatic leadership, principle-centred leadership, level 5 leadership and covenantal leadership – all of which contribute to transformative leadership. The subject is designed to assist students in evaluating and make recommendations for their own leadership style and the styles exhibited in their organisations.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect and make recommendations to enhance the use of transformative leadership in their own practice and in that of their organisation and /or community.
Critically analyse and evaluate leadership styles, including their own, in the context of community resilience and contemporary leadership thinking.

title: Trauma Critical Care
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject extends students’ previous education and experience to advance the knowledge and specialised skills they need to provide critical care paramedicine for traumatic and toxicological emergencies. Students will further develop their ability to integrate assessment and diagnostic data, knowledge of relevant anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology, and evidence-informed practice to propose critical care paramedicine treatment plans. Students will also integrate specialised paramedic knowledge, theories and frameworks to further develop the professional attributes and clinical reasoning skills required to provide effective leadership during a major trauma event.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced knowledge of anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology to critical care paramedic management of traumatic and toxicological emergencies.

Interpret clinical data derived from advanced patient diagnostics, assessment and history taking and apply to evidence-informed critical care paramedic treatment plans for traumatic and toxicological emergencies.
Integrate specialised paramedic knowledge, paramedic research, theories and frameworks for contemporary critical care paramedicine relevant to trauma.
Integrate knowledge of specialised technical skills and apply it to evidence-informed critical care paramedic practice for traumatic and toxicological emergencies.

title: Trauma in Paramedic Practice
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject expands on students' foundational knowledge by integrating anatomy, physiology, and pathophysiology with assessments and history findings. Students will identify differential diagnoses and formulate working diagnoses for presentations involving traumatic injuries, environmental exposures, and toxicological emergencies. They will develop and implement evidence-based treatment plans, guided by contemporary literature. The subject emphasises care in the paramedicine practice setting, including interprofessional collaboration with healthcare and emergency service teams, multi-casualty incident management, and the safe application of clinical skills, paramedic equipment, and technology aligned with graduate-level paramedicine practice.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on practice to identify and implement strategies to improve clinical reasoning skills and clinical care.

Synthesise knowledge of pathophysiology and aetiology of trauma, multi-casualty traumatic emergencies, environmental and toxicological emergencies to manage these presentations in the paramedicine environment.
Develop and implement safe and effective treatment plans for complex patient presentations involving trauma, multi-casualty trauma, environmental and toxicological emergencies.

Apply evidence-informed technical skills and interpret clinical data from assessments to formulate differential diagnoses and treatment plans in traumatic, environmental, and toxicological emergencies.
Employ an ethical and professional disposition when communicating within an interdisciplinary team, with health consumers and society.
prerequisites: PAR200: Medical Emergencies in Paramedic Practice

title: Treatment and Management of Alcohol and Other Substances Use
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will further develop their understanding of alcohol and other drug withdrawal for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and non-Indigenous peoples, evaluating the use of medication management and withdrawal scales in the acute withdrawal state. Students will examine the implications of long-term alcohol and other drug misuse, with a particular focus on cognitive impairment, physical health and mental health outcomes. The concept of dual diagnosis and treatment options for managing people who live with a complex combination of mental health, alcohol and other drug presentations will be explored. This subject will enable students to develop therapeutic skills will be considered in the treatment and management of clients in this complex field.
learning_outcomes: critically appraise therapeutic approaches used in the treatment and management of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and non-Indigenous peoples in the field of mental health and substance misuse.

differentiate between the application of withdrawal scales used for the management of acute withdrawal of substances, alcohol and other drugs, and medication regimes used for acute therapy and longer term management;
evaluate the implications of long-term substance, alcohol and other drug usage including cognitive impairment, physical disease and mental illness;
explain the concept of dual diagnosis and treatment options for people living with a complex combination of mental health, alcohol and other drug presentations: and
prerequisites: MHP115: Introduction to Substance Use: Alcohol and Other Drugs

title: Tropical and Subtropical Horticultural Crop Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the principles of growing horticultural crops that are adapted to both tropical and subtropical climates using citrus (Citrus species), as a case study crop to provide an overview of the biology, principles, and practices of tropical/subtropical horticultural crop production. Avocado, banana and mango, all of which have different tree architecture and climatic requirements, and, therefore, crop management practices for yield optimisation will be compared and contrasted with citrus production. Students will undertake an audit on a property of their choice, with a view to benchmark on-farm practices against best practice, then make recommendations based on both their findings and a critical review of the latest research literature.
learning_outcomes: Develop and benchmark orchard management systems for optimal crop production, with focus on sustainability.
Outline the various environmental attributes of tropical and subtropical regions with respect to climate and soil.
Accurately describe and justify the principles and production practices for a wide range of tropical and subtropical horticultural crops.

Describe supply chain of tropical and subtropical horticultural crops, including world and Australian production; peak industry bodies; industry programs; areas of priority and activity within individual industries.
Present specialist knowledge and advice orally in a formal setting.

Identify and critically evaluate contemporary and industry leading practices for tropical/sub-tropical horticultural crops from research literature and present recommendations for their implementation.
Distinguish between various tree architectural models, and critique management strategies for optimal crop production.

title: Two Industry Certification Credits
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Administration Credit subject only

title: Undergraduate International Study Experience
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject offers the opportunity for students to participate in an international study tour of 1 to 3 weeks duration. Depending on the discipline, the study tour may include visits to government and non-government agencies together with workshops delivered in-country. The subject provides an opportunity for students to develop their personal and problem-solving skills in a cross cultural environment. Students will be required to complete assessments linking theory to practice on some aspect of the relevant international environment. Study tour locations for each calendar year will be listed on the Charles Sturt University Global site
learning_outcomes: Make recommendations that are appropriate for the relevant international context.
Describe different aspects of international projects in culturally diversified environments.
Evaluate the impact of cultural, legal, economic, political and technological forces affecting crime and security in that environment.
Examine and reflect on the impact of their experience in an international context.

title: Understanding Australia: History, Politics and Society
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop students' broader understanding of contemporary Australian history and politics, including how history and politics affect the lived experiences of Indigenous Australians from British invasion to the present. From a political history disciplinary perspective, this subject will ask students to analyse and interpret the impact of social forces on Australian government processes and policies, influenced by factors that include migrants, women and international relations. Students will learn to investigate how history and politics are determined, by whom and for what reason. Students will develop skills to analyse and debate, interpret and communicate complex ideas and express these ideas to their student peers and in academic writing.
learning_outcomes: be able to articulate how Australian governments and democracy operate, including links to policy and influence, past and present; and

be able to analyse the key political and historical themes and influences in Australia in relation to the impact of past policy and practice on Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians from pre-invasion to today;
be able to apply knowledge and skills to communicate complex ideas in relation to history and politics using research, critical thinking and be able to demonstrate these in academic writing.
be able to analyse how power and privilege operates in relation to the self and to the experiences of Indigenous Australians, migrants and women;

title: Understanding and Using New Technologies
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine trends, issues and ideas that underpin learning and communication through new technologies. It is designed to facilitate the use of technology in an education-based learning/constructivist perspective rather than in a hardware/programming perspective. Throughout this subject, students will gain hands-on experience in working through the understanding of using technology appropriately in educational settings, with a special emphasis on integrating technology into the curriculum as well as other applications related to communications and creative opportunities/expression. Students will practice critical evaluation and effectiveness in changes in technology to remain current. Throughout this subject students will model an "approach" (versus avoidance) attitude towards technology, to develop a supportive role and/or instruct learners in the use of technology to enhance learning.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on different beliefs in relation to the use of technology in education and critically analyze how these may impact on educational practices.
Evaluate the appropriateness of different approaches to using technology in teaching and learning.

Demonstrate the understanding and skills related to the integration of technology into learning and teaching environments (e.g., be able to select, critique and evaluate content and appropriate technology).
Critique software for educational use as well as software for the purpose of assessment.
Demonstrate knowledge, skills and confidence in using technology in a learning environment.
Describe and comment upon current research into the use of technology in education.
Show an indepth understanding of how technology affects communication in educational environments.
Understand basic terms and concepts relating to technology in education.
Explain the impact of technology on teaching and learning.

title: Understanding Australian Political Life: Actors, Institutions and Policy
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the various political actors and their roles and functions in Australian political life within and outside of Australian political institutions, as well as the institutions themselves. By ‘actors' we mean the politicians, business groups, media companies, activists and interest groups that determine and influence the outcome of domestic policy at a state and federal level, as well as foreign policy decisions.
learning_outcomes: Identify the main political actors in the political process, and their impact on law-making, elections and society.
Critically evaluate the dynamics of decision-making in policy debates.
Contribute an informed perspective to social, economic, political, and cultural debates, including those about power, accountability and legitimacy.
Demonstrate an understanding of the role and function of the key institutions of state, and an understanding of the role and function of the private and public sectors.

title: Understanding Children from Adversity
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject develops an understanding of the emotions of children from adverse circumstances. How children feel in such circumstances is of paramount importance in child welfare interventions. Emotional development is explained with particular reference to individual variation. This subject considers both genetic and environmental variations in emotional development. It concentrates on the influence of adverse environments on the infant, child and adolescent. It examines current programs that address childhood adversity and builds student capacity in supporting their sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of the development (or lack of development) of the secondary social emotions in certain children to the part these emotions play in motivation in certain circumstances.
Analyse the influence of different contexts, particularly family and society, on the emotional development of children and adolescents.
Demonstrate an understanding of a child's feelings so that the actions taken are in accordance with a child's best interests.
Synthesise from evidence the emotional development of children and adolescents from adverse circumstances.
Analyse existing programs for children from adversity, and suggest modifications and adaptations for local use.
Recount in depth and critically consider issues in the emotional development of children and adolescents.

title: Understanding Healthy Communities
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject equips students with skills and knowledge about health promotion, community health and community development. Students will critically examine personal power, privilege and practice and the way in which those factors shape contemporary engagement with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and their communities. Students will learn about evaluating community needs and strengths; developing programs to meet identified needs and build on existing strengths; and how programs are planned, implemented and evaluated in a community focused, culturally competent and ethical way. This will be complemented by learning about funding sources, how to write a grant application and how to develop a project budget. This subject will assist students to develop strategies for working in collaboration with others, including building relationships with Indigenous Australian communities and other communities from a range of cultural and linguistic backgrounds. Leadership skills such as creating a common purpose, bringing people together, community engagement and community capacity building, will be discussed. Knowledge and skills developed in the subject will prepare students for working in community-based practice in a variety of health and community settings.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the interdisciplinary and contextual nature of primary health care, public health, health promotion and community development.
Utilise a variety of methods to assess community capacity and needs.
Describe strategies used when working in collaboration to build relationships with people and communities from a range of cultural and linguistic backgrounds.
Effect positive change in the context of health promotion and community development by demonstrating key leadership characteristics and capabilities.

Reflect critically on the values intrinsic to health promotion and community development including human rights, equity, equality, social justice, cultural responsiveness, empowerment and sustainable practice.
Apply information and data to different contexts to facilitate planning, implementation, funding and evaluation of a health promotion project.

title: Understanding Human Pathophysiology
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject enables students to build on their foundational knowledge of anatomy and physiology to develop their understanding of the principles of pathophysiology and how alterations in normal body function, or maladaptation, lead to clinical presentations as a result of dysregulation. The syllabus will focus on common cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, respiratory, endocrine, immune and nervous system presentations. Students are expected to develop their skills to support clinical reasoning and facilitate interdisciplinary understandings and communication for evidence-based practice.
learning_outcomes: Integrate symptomology and diagnostic information to understand pathophysiological processes.
Utilise correct scientific and clinical terminology relevant to dysregulation of the cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, respiratory, endocrine, immune and nervous systems.
Explain pathophysiological terminology, processes, signs and symptoms of common acute health conditions.

title: Understanding Research
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject assists students to evaluate knowledge sources and develop investigation skills related to the disciplines of human movement. The subject further provides an overview of the theory and practice of reviewing peer-reviewed literature in the broad field of human movement and further develop skills to read and critically analyse research. In addition to exploring the relationship between theory and practice, stages of the research process will be examined. Concepts to be addressed in this subject include accessing knowledge and critiquing sources of information, basic data collection and analysis techniques in quantitative and qualitative paradigms. Students will consider the ethics of conducting research in the field of sport and exercise, with a focus on working with First Nations people.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate peer reviewed information from scholarly databases.
Analyse different research paradigms.
Identify and discuss key aspects of research reports and analyse data sets using appropriate statistical methods.
Critique the validity of information available in the popular media.
Describe research methodologies appropriate to First Nations people and their communities.
Reference peer reviewed sources of information in a consistent and academically-recognised format.
Identify the need for principled and ethical research practices.
prerequisites: HIP202: Evidence-Based Health Practice and Research

title: Understanding the Social World
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject considers how the social world functions and how people live and interact within society. Sociology is investigative as well as theoretically driven. It concentrates on generating knowledge and understanding of social phenomena, trends, and issues. This exploration spans local and regional interests as well as national and global contexts. Issues explored by this subject are drawn from information provided in the Syllabus.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the development of critical thinking skills to understand society, social phenomena and sociological theory.
Analyse and evaluate social issues to understand the contemporary world.
Construct an argument to discuss and debate social issues.
Recognise and discuss basic concepts in sociology.

title: Underwriting - Commercial Lines Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the knowledge and skills to assess and underwrite risk relating to commercial lines (covering commercial motor and personal accident) and to survey risk exposure and review and interpret portfolio performance.
learning_outcomes: Provide quotation.
Relate the general principles of underwriting commercial lines.
Evaluate the risks exposure in commercial lines.
Negotiate premium rates.
Evaluate quotation slip.
Draft policy.
Analyse the risk.
Review operational performance of portfolio.

title: Understanding Writing
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to give students an in-depth understanding of practical and theoretical aspects of written language and the teaching of writing. Students will be encouraged to explore differing perspectives on writing in order to extend and enrich their current beliefs and approaches. Students will consider case-studies of writing and writers, across a range of learning and education contexts, and draw on their own experiences as writers and teachers of writing in order to examine the linguistic, sociocultural and ideological complexities of writing and learning to write.
learning_outcomes: Use frameworks and concepts central to writing and writing instruction as analytic tools.
Consider seminal case-studies and their contribution to writing instruction.
Employ writing frameworks for critiquing and enhancing pedagogical practices.
Discuss literature that has informed influential approaches to writing instruction.
Articulate their position on the nature of writing and learning to write.
Use writing as a tool for reflecting on own experiences of writing and writing education.
Demonstrate understanding of a range of theoretical perspectives on writing.

title: Underwriting - Risk Management
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the student with the knowledge and skills to assess and underwrite risk relating to Commercial Lines (Property, ISR, Contract Works) classes and to survey risk exposure and interpret portfolio performance.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the quotation slip, proposal, and analyse and categorise the risk.
Review operational performance of policies and portfolios.
Relate the general principles of Underwriting to Commercial Lines insurance for material damage, business interruption and contract works.
Determine the proposed basis of cover.
Draft the policy document.
Provide quotations.
Evaluate the risk exposures inherent in the above.

title: Uniting Church Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the history and theology of the Uniting Church in Australia within the international network of United and Uniting Churches and the broad catholic tradition of the Church. It examines the origins of this 'Australian' Church in the twentieth-century ecumenical movement, traces the history of Church Union in Australia, in particular, the creation of the Basis of Union in 1971 and the union of the three denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian and Congregationalist) to form the Uniting Church in 1977. The subject then explores the character of the Uniting Church as it has developed over the past half century.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the history, polity and liturgical traditions of the three churches that united in 1977 to form the Uniting Church;
Demonstrate a knowledge of the primary source documents of this period and be able to analyse, interpret, and critically review these documents.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Analyse and critically evaluate the history of the Uniting Church since 1977;
Research and communicate the relevance of historical documents for understanding the historical origins of contemporary churches in Australia, Asia, and the Pacific.
Articulate an historically informed appreciation and critique of the theology of the Basis of Union.

title: Uniting Church Studies
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the history and theology of the Uniting Church in Australia within the international network of United and Uniting Churches and the broad catholic tradition of the Church. It examines the origins of this 'Australian' Church in the twentieth-century ecumenical movement, traces the history of Church Union in Australia, in particular, the creation of the Basis of Union in 1971 and the union of the three denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian and Congregationalist) to form the Uniting Church in 1977. The subject then explores the character of the Uniting Church as it has developed over the past half century.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critically evaluate the history of the Uniting Church since 1977.
Demonstrate self-guided and collaborative learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate a broad and coherent knowledge of the history, polity and liturgical traditions of the three churches that united in 1977 to form the Uniting Church.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the primary source documents of this period and be able to analyse, interpret, and critically review these documents.
Articulate an historically informed appreciation and critique of the theology of the Basis of Union.
Research and communicate the relevance of historical documents for understanding the historical origins of contemporary churches in Australia, Asia, and the Pacific.

title: University Study Skills
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: University Study Skills is one of four modular subjects in the Access Charles Sturt Entry Course. It explicitly teaches the foundational literacies required for successful university study across four dimensions of listening, reading, writing and synthesising. Each module builds on the last, to progressively support the development of academic literacies. Students will be introduced to the principles of academic integrity and supported to apply them at a foundational level. Students will develop an iterative process incorporating feedback to synthesise ideas and produce text using academic conventions.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of academic integrity to identify and reference evidence.
Recognise, dissect and produce the language conventions and structural features of persuasive and analytic texts.
Use listening and reading strategies to curate information from a variety of sources.
Synthesise information through an iterative process that incorporates feedback.

title: Unspecified Minor
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for the Bachelor of Arts (with specialisations) Articulated Set

title: Unrestricted elective
school: School
syllabus_overview: This subject is an administrative placeholder used within course structures to represent the inclusion of an unrestricted elective (8 credit points). It is not a subject for enrolment and does not have any associated learning or assessment requirements.

title: Unspecified Specialisation
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This credit code is for the Bachelor of Arts (with specialisations) Articulated Set.

title: Using ICT with Children
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject considers the relationship between technology and children, and the use of technology in and beyond the early childhood and primary classrooms. Students will relate a child's socio-emotional development to new digital technologies as tools for learning and teaching. Media literacy in technology-supported classrooms will be emphasized through programming for learning and applying strategies for safely integrating new technologies using innovative practices. Students will become skilled in learning and teaching about children and digital technologies specifically in regard to relationships, ethical behaviours, health and wellbeing, citizenship, and play and pedagogy.
learning_outcomes: Understand the proactive adult supervision required for children's online activities, including the use of filters and restrictions on devices and networks.
Use digital technologies to promote safe and ethical social interactions and collaborative learning between children, peers and adults.
Plan learning opportunities about children's digital rights relating to socioeconomic, geographic, gender and culturally based contexts.
Model active decision making regarding digital technology mediated learning for use with and by children, collaboratively and independently.
Plan innovative opportunities for all children to explore and experiment with a diverse range of applications and digital technologies in a safe environment.

Plan digital technology experiences for children that promote health, wellbeing, creativity and learning, including tasks that explore, evaluate, collect, organise and display data according to appropriate syllabus document requirements.
Select and evaluate software for educational use as well as for the purpose of planning, assessing, student profiling and reporting.
prerequisites: EMT302: Understanding and Using New Technologies

title: Usul al-Din (Foundational Islamic Theology)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses Islamic theology (usul ad-din) as the foundational discipline in Islamic faith and its intellectual discourse. It covers the Islamic concept of God and related matters from the perspectives of differing theological schools fundamental to the study of Islamic theology. This subject also discusses the development of Islamic theology throughout history until the present day. Key concepts of Islamic theology such as ‘are actions part of faith', ‘essence of God', ‘the problem of free will' and ‘wisdom behind suffering on earth' are addressed in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Articulate a critical understanding of differences between the main Islamic theological schools.
Describe and analyse the main Islamic theological topics and their scope.
Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of God in Islamic theology.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of prophethood in Islamic theology.
Articulate an understanding of the concepts related to afterlife in Islamic theology.

title: Usul al-Fiqh (Methodology of Islamic Law)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject will address Islamic jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) methodology. The historic, social and religious factors in the development of Islamic legal schools will be discussed. The four primary sources of law will be studied together with the supplementary sources used in the practice of ijtihad (independent legal deduction).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the development of usul al-fiqh (Islamic legal theory).
Analyse the arguments and propositions used in legal rulings (fatwas).
Discuss critically the primary and supplementary sources of Islamic law.
Show an understanding of the methodology of Islamic law making.

title: Usul al-Hadith (Methodology of Prophetic Traditions)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to the place of Hadith in Islamic scholarship. The methods and rules related to the authentication and classification of Hadith narrations in canonical texts together with the application of this methodology are also addressed. This subject covers the history of the development of Hadith discipline from the emergence of documentation since its inception to major Hadith collections produced, together with the criteria adopted by scholars to authenticate a Hadith.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the Hadith types and their definitions.
Describe the difference between Hadith and Sunnah.
Differentiate the level of authenticity between Hadith narrations.
Critically discuss the methods used to classify Hadith.
Demonstrate an understanding of the different phases in the collating of Hadith literature in the first three centuries of Islam.

title: Usul al-Tafsir (Methodology of Qur'anic Exegesis)
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the methodology of Qur'anic exegesis. The history of the development of Qur'anic exegetical method and its evolution over time will be addressed, together with the concept of revelation. A set of tools used in textual analysis will be introduced and modern exegetical issues concerning the Qur'an will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the Qur'an through a methodical approach to its interpretation.
Demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of a substantial work.
Demonstrate a familiarity with the terminology used in Qur'anic exegesis.
Apply exegetical methods to the interpretation of the Qur'an.
Demonstrate an understanding of the history of the development of Qur'anic exegesis.
Recognise different exegetical types.
Analyse and evaluate interpretations of the Qur'an in text and other literature.
Demonstrate an understanding of the general principles of Qur'anic exegesis.

title: Value Based Healthcare and Critical Inquiry
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject enables students to develop their capacity to improve health outcomes through the exploration of evolving approaches to healthcare such as Learning Health Systems and Value Based Healthcare. Students will utilise critical inquiry strategies to identify, appraise, utilise and plan research focused on delivering effective and efficient care at the advanced practice level, better health outcomes and improved experiences of receiving care. Students will strengthen their capability to align care delivery with a person or group's experience of their health, to measure outcomes that matter to people accessing care, and develop integrated and comprehensive solutions to meet healthcare needs. Students are encouraged to focus on a healthcare need specific to their current clinical context and develop a person-centred, evidence-informed and outcome-focused innovation.
learning_outcomes: Investigate healthcare delivery through the lens of evolving frameworks such as Learning Health Systems and Value Based Healthcare.
Critically appraise research and professional literature relating to advanced nursing practice to review current practice and strengthen value-based clinical decision making.
Design a quality and/or safety improvement initiative to support culturally sensitive advanced nursing practice.
Analyse a range of strategies to access research evidence, measure outcomes and align advanced nursing practice with the needs of the person/group.
Select from a broad range of approaches to research inquiry to effectively investigate clinical and practice problems.
Identify clinical question/s using systematic methods.
prerequisites: NRS531: Critical Inquiry and Evidence Based Nursing Practice

title: Values and Conflict in Organisations
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the theories of morality and Western ethics and their application in the exercise of moral judgement within an organisational and/or business context. Typical ethical dilemmas that may be faced by employers and employees, including human resource managers, are highlighted and explored. This subject also deals with the theoretical bases, processes and organisational arrangements for dealing with conflict resolution in the workplace. Conflict resolution is the link between rationalising ethical decision making and the soundness of cooperative problem solving, expressed in conflict resolution, that is of benefit to the individual, workplace and the global community.
learning_outcomes: Apply the problem-solving model of conflict resolution (the win/win approach) to an organisational or business situation.
Identify and compare the characteristics and practices of an ethical and an unethical organisation in terms of its relations with all stakeholders.
Recommend organisational arrangements that need to be put in place when dealing with conflict resolution both in the workplace and at an industry level.
Explain the concepts and evaluate the debate relating to corporate agency and the moral responsibility of organisations.
Critically analyse the nature of morality, through applying the main Western theories of ethics and evaluate the impact of these theories on ethical dilemmas faced by managers.
Investigate the nature of conflict in organisations and analyse theoretical approaches to conflict resolution.

title: Vegetable Crop Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on vegetable crop biology and the principles and practices of successful commercial vegetable production including crop requirements, growth patterns and production techniques. It will explore the technology and science behind the pre-harvest and post-harvest management of fresh and processed vegetables. Benchmarking and the implementation of codes of practice, as well as associated marketing patterns of vegetable crops will be introduced. Students will conduct a basic experiment on a vegetable crop and report their findings.
learning_outcomes: Determine the various marketing options for vegetable crops and select appropriate options for a range of vegetable crops.
Apply knowledge and principles to plan for the harvesting, and post-harvest treatment of different vegetables.
Research and critically review appropriate literature on a topic, then design, conduct and communicate the findings of an investigative project.
Describe the range and diversity of vegetable crops and select a variety of crops appropriate for a specific situation.
Demonstrate how to interpret and manage the vegetative and reproductive phases of the vegetable growth cycle within a particular environment.
Define and evaluate alternative techniques to establish vegetable crops.
Explain the various techniques for improving vegetables through breeding.
Reflect on management practices and apply recently acquired knowledge to design improvements.

title: Vegetation Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Management of native vegetation is critical to ensuring Australian landscapes are managed in an ecologically sustainable way. In this subject, students will explore the major types of Australian plants and communities, the key determinants of plant distributions and how plant communities function. Students will learn about disturbances and threatening processes to plant communities such as fire, grazing, fragmentation, land clearing and weed invasions. Students will explore how climate change interacts with other threatening processes to impact on Australian vegetation. This knowledge will equip students to develop vegetation management plans for a range of different real-world scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Discuss effects of climate change on plant populations and communities and incorporate climate change into management strategies.
Evaluate evidence for the determinants of weed invasion and associated impacts, and develop management strategies for control.
Describe the key determinants of plant distributions and persistence, including major disturbances and human land-uses.
Describe key aspects of Australian vegetation communities and identify the dominant plant families.
Evaluate and apply adaptive management principles and legislative requirements related to native vegetation.
Discuss the effects of habitat fragmentation on plant populations and communities, and evaluate management strategies.
Discuss the effects of introduced stock grazing on vegetation communities, and apply knowledge of grazing ecology to management of plant communities.

title: Vegetation Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a comprehensive grounding in major concepts in vegetation ecology. Students will learn about: photosynthesis; plant reproduction and dispersal; interactions between plants, animals and the physical environment; plant population dynamics; plant community dynamics and; the effects of climate change on plant communities. Students will also learn practical skills in plant identification, vegetation field survey methods, report writing, and methods for analysing ecological data. Students will be introduced to theory and concepts relating to plant communities, including how they are surveyed, classified and described, and how ecosystems are affected by natural and human disturbances. On completion, students will possess knowledge of the key ecological factors which influence Australian ecosystems, and skills essential in environmental and conservation management.
learning_outcomes: Describe, explain, interpret and apply the key terminology, principles, concepts and theory underpinning vegetation ecology.
Describe and analyse the ecology of a selected Australian ecosystem, and be able to apply this knowledge to other ecosystem types.
Interpret and communicate the findings of a vegetation survey clearly and coherently within a management context.
Explain and evaluate the effects of disturbances on plant communities.
Obtain knowledge and practical experience in in the design and implementation of vegetation surveys, and apply the available tools and techniques used to identify plants in terrestrial communities.

title: Veterinary Anaesthesia and Surgery Nursing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will study veterinary anaesthesia to ensure a comprehensive knowledge as preparation for the practice of surgical nursing. Students will develop skills in pre-operative assessment, operating theatre management, intra-operative support, and anaesthetic monitoring. A 10-day work-integrated learning placement provides the opportunity for students to consolidate their learning with a specific focus on referral for complex surgical procedures.
learning_outcomes: Maintain surgical equipment using effective aseptic technique.
Provide support to the surgeon, for a range of surgical and ancillary procedures.
Monitor patient condition, vital signs and anaesthetic response and relate these to patient parameters.
Provide post-operative support to the patient and comprehensively advise the client on home management.
Admit a patient for routine surgeries, by anticipating patient needs prior to surgery and advising the client accordingly.
Prepare the theatre, surgical equipment and patient for anaesthesia and surgery.

title: Veterinary Anatomy
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Veterinary anatomy is the study of normal body organs and structures and will be delivered by lectures and practicals requiring systematic dissection of the dog as a type animal. Anatomical examination of live animals utilising handling skills are run in conjunction with dissection to give students an appreciation of the relationships of deep structures and organs to surface features. This topographical anatomy lays a foundation in normal animals for the clinical examinations and procedures carried out later in the course. Dissection of preserved and especially fresh animal tissues will begin the development of tissue handling skills required for surgery. Anatomy subjects run concurrently with Physiology Subjects and compliment each other. This is a Key subject in the Bachelor of Veterinary Biology, Bachelor of Veterinary Biology/Bachelor of Veterinary Science and Bachelor of Veterinary Biology/Bachelor of Veterinary Science (Honours) Degree
learning_outcomes: Use information presented on domestic species to understand and explain modifications to basic mammalian anatomy adopted by different animal species.
Utilise their understanding of normal structure to explain the anatomical basis for normal function of organs and systems.
Describe the basic embryological development of organs.
Describe the normal structure and disposition of the organs and structures of mammals and to be able to relate these to superficial features on the body of live animals.
Demonstrate familiarity with basic anatomy, and understand the relationship between form and function, for different body organs and systems.

title: Veterinary Clinical Skills
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject allows candidates to develop advanced clinical skills and knowledge in a selected discipline, develop cognitive and technical skills, abilities to synthesise and increase theoretical knowledge in professional practice and integration of research activity for investigation and development of new knowledge.
learning_outcomes: be able to demonstrate cognitive and technical skills to integrate theoretical knowledge in professional practice; and
be able to demonstrate advanced and integrated understanding of a complex body of knowledge in the chosen discipline;
be able to demonstrate communication skills relevant to professional practice.
be able to demonstrate cognitive skills and technical skills to demonstrate advanced understanding of theoretical knowledge and research skills relevant to the selected discipline;

title: Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care Nursing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: The subject extends the student's knowledge and skills in veterinary nursing to the field of emergency and critical care. This subject will cover the basics required for every general practice including triage, basic life support and shock assessment to the more advanced knowledge of trauma assessment, endocrine and metabolic emergencies including emergency surgery. Though focused on small animals, students will cover both equine and production animals, along with exotics and wildlife. Successful completion of this subject enables students to prepare for an emergency response, prepare emergency procedures to sustain life and perform nursing procedures to support critical animal patients.
learning_outcomes: Support the veterinarian to perform required emergency procedures.
Apply and maintain first aid to sustain animal life.
Effectively communicate with and coordinate the team in an emergency environment.
Perform day-one clinical skills required for high-end patient care and management.
Provide intensive care nursing support.
Conduct triage for the emergency and critical care of animals.
Prepare for an emergency response and implement critical care protocols.
prerequisites: ASC391: Veterinary Anaesthesia and Surgery Nursing

title: Veterinary Histology and Immunology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Veterinary Histology and Immunology aims to draw together the study of cellular and tissue structure and function of the four basic tissues of the body leading to more in depth examination of molecular cell biology. It is strongly integrated with Veterinary Anatomy and Physiology, Biochemistry and Veterinary Practice 2 and will provide an excellent grounding for the study of Disease Processes and Clinical Pathology.
learning_outcomes: Explain the key identifying features and function of blood cells.
Summarise the stages of haematopoiesis.
Distinguish the microscopic structure of the components of connective tissue, muscle, epithelium and nervous tissue.

Distinguish and describe the histological features of the tissues of the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, cardiovascular, lymphatic and haemopoietic systems, endocrine organs, integument and associated structures, urinary tract and the male as well as female reproductive tracts.
Explain the principle mechanisms of the innate and adaptive immune systems.
Recognise and identify the structure and function of typical cells at the light and electron microscopic levels.
Use a light microscope.
Outline the key cellular and non-cellular defence mechanisms of the body.
Relate the histological features of organs with their primary functions.

title: Veterinary Medical Nursing
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop the knowledge and skills to provide effective support for veterinarians and achieve best possible outcomes for patients. Students will develop the skills required to provide high quality care to hospitalised patients, including pre-operative preparation and infection control. A 10-day work-integrated learning placement provides the opportunity for students to consolidate their learning with a specific focus on a specialist practice area.
learning_outcomes: Monitor and record basic physiological parameters.
Demonstrate the ability to work individually and in a team.
Recognise and evaluate changes and trends in physiological parameters.
Assist in implementing a therapeutic management plan.
Provide tailored nursing care for a variety of conditions to companion animals and wildlife.
Recognise and appraise the impact of chronic health conditions on the wellbeing of companion animals.

title: Veterinary Masters Dissertation
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is undertaken over a minimum of one session and a maximum of two sessions and involves placement in professional practice.
