Students demonstrate the application of a body of knowledge and skills for research and scholarship in their chosen discipline/field of work. This subject involves placement in professional practice to systematically engage with research led/integrated practice and undertake and complete the clinical research project. Students develop advanced knowledge and research skills and apply these to conduct a clinical research project and produce a body of significant and original clinical research outcomes. Students will develop cognitive and technical skills to design, implement, analyse, theorise and communicate the clinical research, leading to significant original contributions to the discipline knowledge and professional practice. Students will produce a body of original research outcomes in the form of a dissertation for independent examination by external examiners.
learning_outcomes: Produce significant and original research outcomes.

Demonstrate skills to design, prepare, undertake and complete, analyse, theorise and communicate research that provides an important and original contribution to discipline knowledge and/or professional practice.

Demonstrate effective communication skills to present the results of original research outcomes for external examination against international standards and to communicate the results to peers, both internally and externally.

title: Veterinary Microbiology and Parasitology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject follows on from VSC310 Principles of Pathobiology which gave a brief introduction to the mechanisms of diseases caused by microbial and parasite pathogens. This subject further develops on the role of infectious organisms in animal health and pathogenesis of disease. Student cannot progress to Phase 2, without the completion of Phase 1.
learning_outcomes: Recognise infectious pathogenic agents (viruses, prions, bacteria, fungi, protozoan and metazoan parasites) and name the major diseases they cause.
Explain the concepts of virulence and virulence factors for a variety of pathogens.
Summarise the key steps that occur in the pathogenesis of parasitic and microbial diseases.
Distinguish sites with normal microbial flora present and normally sterile sites in the host animal.
Describe the chemical and physical methods of disinfection.
Explain the epidemiological, host environmental and management factors contributing to infectious and parasitological diseases.
Describe key culture requirements and characteristics of major bacterial and fungal pathogens of veterinary significance.
Make recommendations regarding effective preventative, treatment and control measures for infectious diseases.
Describe the concept of One Health - linking human, animal and environmental health and use examples.
Apply evidence based medicine principles to all conclusions and recommendations concerning infectious disease.
Demonstrate proficiency in obtaining a pure culture of a microorganism in the laboratory.
Perform and interpret common laboratory tests used for identification of infections and diseases.
Explain the life cycles of important parasites of animals.
Describe the Gram reaction and morphology of the major phenotypic groups of bacteria.
Identify the major groups of internal and external parasites of animals using identification keys.

title: Veterinary Pharmacology, Diagnostics and Therapeutics
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: VSC324 is an introduction to therapeutic and diagnostic modalities used in veterinary practice to diagnose and treat disease. Foundations of diagnostic imaging techniques such as radiology and ultrasonography, which are cornerstone instruments for veterinary clinical practice, will be introduced. The principles of drug treatment and therapeutic modalities such as antibiotics, anthelmintics and analgesia will be introduced. The principles of anaethesia and surgical interventions for both diagnosis and treatment will also be introduced. Students cannot progress to Phase 2, without the completion of Phase 1.
learning_outcomes: Confidently integrate knowledge of physiology and pathobiology to construct health management and treatment modalities.
Describe and perform common diagnostic procedures required to diagnose and manage disease in animals.
Discriminate and perform appropriate diagnostic imaging modalities for specific conditions.
Select appropriate sedation and anaesthetic agents for routine use in healthy animals.
Describe the principles of pharmocokinetics, bioavailability, drug metabolism and half-life.
Describe the major pharmaceutical classes and various routes of administration of drugs.
Explain the principles of therapeutic intervention, allometric scaling, determination of drug dose rates and drug interactions.
Describe the principles of radiography and radiology and other diagnostic imaging modalities.
Outline principles of analgesia, anaesthesia, fluid therapy and surgery.

title: Veterinary Physiology
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Physiology is the study of the normal function, control and integration of body systems. It is how animals live their daily lives. Its scope ranges from molecular, cellular, tissue and organ to whole body function and is the basis for recognition of abnormal function, which will be covered in subsequent pathology and clinical subjects. Foundations of veterinary physiology are explored by evaluation of homeostatic and control mechanisms. The workings of nerve and muscle cells, endocrine, digestive, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems and the ways that they interact to maintain homeostasis will be studied in domestic species. Practical exercises will utilise computer simulations and clinical techniques on human and animal subjects to illustrate and extend information presented in lectures. Veterinary physiology runs concurrently with Comparative Anatomy during first session of Second Year to provide parallel teaching of related content and to ensure that the interrelationships between form and function are apparent to students. Physiological processes in the different body systems, drawn from normal animal activities, will be presented to reinforce the content taught in previous, concurrent and successive subjects to reinforce understanding of integrated body functions.
learning_outcomes: Integrate information from concurrent subjects and apply this information to material covered in Veterinary Physiology.
Define homeostasis and identify regulatory mechanisms by which the body seeks to maintain its internal environment.
Apply basic statistical methods of hypothesis testing to analyse physiological data and present the findings in a scientific format.
Outline mechanisms for the control and integration of different body systems.
Utilise their understanding of normal function to explain the basis for abnormal function of organ systems covered.
Use information presented on domestic species to understand and explain modifications to basic mammalian physiology adopted by different animal species.
Explain the relationship between form (structure) and function of different body organs and systems.

title: Veterinary Practice 1
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Veterinary Practice 1 offers Veterinary Science students an introduction to the realities of the veterinary profession, and skills essential for the remainder of the veterinary course by providing a broad basis to the professional practice subjects. The subject has a strong emphasis on applying scientific information for writing. The subject includes the role of animals in societies including that of Indigenous Australian peoples, and companion animal behaviour, handling and welfare. Generic skills such as communication (with academic staff, peers, placement supervisors), effective use of scientific information in writing, and critical thinking and reflection are included. Practical animal handling sessions will be undertaken on site, utilising Charles Sturt University's Equine Centre and Pre-Clinical Centre. Visits to clinical practices will be in pairs or on a small group basis. Students are required to attend a debrief session after these visits, thus ensuring that areas of experiential learning are further discussed and reinforced.
learning_outcomes: Discuss fundamental concepts in animal behaviour through description and analysis of normal and abnormal behaviour in domesticated animal species.
Demonstrate developing skills in formal academic writing, such as appropriate literature research, correct referencing and a developing capability in interpreting and analysing texts.

Display an emerging awareness of the role and responsibilities of a veterinarian in societal context through understanding the history and development of the profession, and of human-animal relations including that of Indigenous Australian peoples.
Describe how animal behaviour can be measured in a range of production and companion animal species, and how this information can be used to assess welfare for animals.

Demonstrate the behaviours, values and ethical standards expected of a novice professional during class activities and workplace learning through discussion with workplace supervisors, academic staff and peers as an individual or working in a team.
Discuss the legal and ethical frameworks influencing animal use in society, for safe practices in workplaces and when working with animals.
Demonstrate an emerging understanding about personal and professional learning and development needs and sources of support.
Apply theory and knowledge from class and and technical skills to be able to safely handle several performance and companion animal species.

title: Veterinary Practice 2
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on previous learning in VSC122 (or VSC118) Veterinary Practice 1. Becoming a veterinarian involves learning scientific knowledge and practical skills but, equally importantly, also means engaging with complex real-world problems, understanding professional and animal ethics, and developing a professional identity. The subject content includes communication, animal welfare, professional ethics, institutions and legislation of the profession, veterinary business skills and self-care. Topics are presented separately, and subsequently integrated, drawing on authentic cases and scenarios. Professionalism is developed through practical classes and tutorials, in-class dialogue, and clinical workplace learning.
learning_outcomes: Take a thoughtful, active and courteous part in discussions based on classroom tasks or veterinary issues encountered in the workplace, including giving and receiving feedback.
Display novice oral and written professional communication skills appropriate to a variety of audiences.
Demonstrate continued development of understanding about personal and professional learning and development needs, and sources of support.
Draw on and extend classroom learning in topics such as anatomy and physiology, and apply knowledge in practical classes, and to cases seen in the workplace or case-based material.
Work according to evidence-based medicine principles and demonstrate application of these principles in relation to on campus classes and workplace learning activities.

Critically evaluate a variety of resources and perspectives on animal welfare, quality of life and euthanasia in the context of veterinary practice and animal production, including interpretation of relevant legislation and codes of practice.
Demonstrate developing knowledge of legal and ethical frameworks governing and influencing veterinary practice, animal welfare, and livestock industries.

Demonstrate and analyse the behaviours, values and ethical standards expected of a novice professional through class activities and workplace learning, and in discussion with workplace supervisors, academic staff and peers.

title: Veterinary Professional Practice
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides didactic material for students underpinning clinic rotations completed during the final phase of their degree. As such, it bridges other clinical rotation subjects, providing a foundation for reflection, the integration of theory and practice and the identification of generic information and skills relevant to diverse vocational settings. The seven night after-hours rotation roster provides experience in ICU patient care, after-hours and clinical observations. This subject provides students with opportunities to demonstrate knowledge across the scope of veterinary species and vocational settings encountered during Phase 3, and to display proficiency in practical skills across a broad spectrum of clinical activities.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the results of appropriate clinical examination and diagnostic methods to diagnose common disorders of animals, and identify appropriate treatment(s).
Apply existing knowledge to novel situations, contexts or problems in a logical and rational manner.
Communicate effectively with peers, both verbally and in writing.

Display proficiency in a range of clinical procedures commonly encountered in veterinary practice and relating to veterinary medicine, surgery, diagnostic imaging, clinical reasoning, pharmacology and therapeutics, anaesthesiology, reproduction, and the optimisation of herd / flock health and production.
Apply scientific method and principles of evidence based veterinary practice to the interpretation and implementation of veterinary literature and research findings.
Demonstrate assimilation of information from diverse sources and display appropriate clinical judgement and critical thinking to problems encountered in veterinary professional practice.
Utilise epidemiological principles and appropriate investigations to optimise production and/or to diagnose endemic and exotic disease incursions in animal populations.
Demonstrate knowledge of the ethical and legal obligations of the profession.

title: Veterinary Reproduction
school: Centre of Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Animal reproduction is a core veterinary discipline that embraces a broad spectrum of both basic and applied knowledge. This subject emphasises the variations, problems and challenges associated with different species and industries. Problem-based learning (PBL) is used to prepare students to identify and solve problems in an applied setting.
learning_outcomes: Utilise clinical skills to sample for, diagnose and treat reproductive problems.

Describe an assessment of reproductive function in male and females, including being able to perform breeding soundness evaluation of the male and pregnancy diagnosis in the female, including to specifically discriminate between pregnant and not pregnant cows, and age the duration of pregnancy.
Discuss the reproductive principles underlying assisted reproductive technologies such as oestrus synchronisation and artificial insemination, and describe methods of applying such technologies.
Discuss effective strategies and use evidence-based medicine (EBM) principles to diagnose and manage reproductive efficiency.
Describe the reproductive management of the domestic species covered in the subject.

Discuss the normal and abnormal (including disease) factors that influence reproductive processes such as a gametogenesis, puberty, mating, gamete transport, fertilisation, foetal development and placentation, parturition and lactation.
Describe normal and abnormal reproductive anatomy of domestic species and relate reproductive physiology and anatomical structure to function.

title: Vibration Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject delivers a thorough understanding of the theory, techniques, and practical applications of vibration analysis in mechanical systems. It covers topics such as single and multi-degree-of-freedom systems, free and forced vibrations, damping, and vibration isolation. Students will learn how to analyse and interpret vibration data, model mechanical systems, and mitigate vibration problems in engineering practice.
learning_outcomes: Model and simulate the vibration response of mechanical systems using analytical and computational methods.
Evaluate the effectiveness of vibration control strategies in reducing or mitigating undesirable vibrations in mechanical systems.
Interpret vibration data obtained from experimental measurements, including frequency response functions and modal parameters.
Analyse the vibration behaviour of mechanical systems using theoretical concepts such as natural frequencies, mode shapes, and damping ratios.

title: Vine Physiology and Performance
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on concepts of plant physiology and viticulture acquired in earlier plant biology-related subjects. The subject focuses on the implications of the environment and cultural practices on the field performance of grapevines. Students will examine the key physiological processes involved in grapevine vegetative and reproductive development. Students will also explore grapevine water usage, root functioning, carbohydrate assimilation and utilisation, source and sink organ physiology, and the acquisition and importance of key nutrients. In addition, students will focus on berry metabolism in relation to the accumulation of compounds with particular importance for wine production. Finally, students will investigate the implications of abiotic stresses and phytohormones on grapevine performance.
learning_outcomes: Relate berry metabolism and fruit composition to environmental factors and cultural inputs, and discuss the synthesis and accumulation of flavour and phenolic compounds.
Interpret the scientific literature related to grapevine physiology and performance.
Explain the process of carbohydrate production, transport and use in the sinks within the vine in relation to vine balance and the production of grapes fit for purpose.

Describe the effect of different abiotic stresses, including drought, heat, salinity and frost, as well as the impact of phytohormones, on the developmental processes of grapevines, with respect to vine longevity and productivity.
Evaluate the impacts of climate, water and nutrients on vine growth and development, in relation to vine balance and productivity including the quality and quantity of grape production.
Analyse the effects of the environment and cultural inputs on the vegetative and reproductive growth processes of grapevines, with respect to vine performance for grape and wine production.
Sample and conduct measurements on grapevines and laboratory analyses to compare grapevine physiological responses to various environmental conditions and management inputs.

title: Vine Physiology and Performance
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on concepts of plant physiology and viticulture acquired in earlier plant biology-related subjects. The subject focuses on the implications of the environment and cultural practices on the field performance of grapevines. Students will examine the key physiological processes involved in grapevine vegetative and reproductive development. Students will also explore grapevine water usage, root functioning, carbohydrate assimilation and utilisation, source and sink organ physiology, and the acquisition and importance of key nutrients. In addition, students will focus on berry metabolism in relation to the accumulation of compounds with particular importance for wine production. Finally, students will investigate the implications of abiotic stresses and phytohormones on grapevine performance.
learning_outcomes: Sample and conduct measurements on grapevines and laboratory analyses to compare grapevine physiological responses to various environmental conditions and management inputs.
Evaluate the impacts of climate, water and nutrients on vine growth and development, in relation to vine balance and productivity including the quality and quantity of grape production.
Explain the process of carbohydrate production, transport and use in the sinks within the vine in relation to vine balance and the production of grapes fit for purpose.
Interpret the scientific literature related to grapevine physiology and performance.
Relate berry metabolism and fruit composition to environmental factors and cultural inputs, and discuss the synthesis and accumulation of flavour and phenolic compounds.
Analyse the effects of the environment and cultural inputs on the vegetative and reproductive growth processes of grapevines, with respect to vine performance for grape and wine production.

Describe the effect of different abiotic stresses, including drought, heat, salinity and frost, as well as the impact of phytohormones, on the developmental processes of grapevines, with respect to vine longevity and productivity.

title: Virtualisation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The subject explores the installation, configuration, and management of VMware vSphere virtualization software. The subject will help students prepare to take the examination to become a VMware Certified Professional.
learning_outcomes: Manage higher availability and data protection using vCenter Server.
Monitor resource usage using vCenter Server.
Install and configure VMware virtualisation products such as ESXi and vCenter Server.
Understand the basics of VMware virtualisation technology.
Deploy and manage virtual machines in a VMware vSphere environment.
Manage security permissions and user access to the VMware infrastructure.

title: Virtualisation Technologies
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a detailed introduction to virtualisation and hypervisor technologies. It looks at how these technologies are used within an enterprise to achieve various business goals. It further explores the planning, implementation and management of these virtualisation technologies in the context of a virtual infrastructure.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate which virtualisation technology should be used in a given set of requirements.
Analyse the requirements for management of a virtual infrastructure.
Communicate the essentials of network and storage virtualisation.
Identify and evaluate the requirements to create a virtual infrastructure.
Communicate the importance of different virtualisation technologies for X86 and Unix based platforms.
Discuss and evaluate the requirements for effective Virtual Machine (VM) management.

title: Virtue Ethics: Purification of the Heart
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject critically evaluates the historical backdrop surrounding the development of Islamic spirituality and concept of tazkiyat al-nafs , which pertains to purification of the self. The investigation encompasses the period from Prophet Muhammad's era to the present day. Students analyse the extensive body of literature that has shaped and elucidated virtue ethics, character refinement and spirituality within the Islamic tradition, which significantly influenced the Muslim world during the classical and medieval Islamic epochs. A comprehensive assessment is made of the multitude of vices and ailments prevalent during those times, along with corresponding antidotes and virtues advocated by Islamic scholars. Moreover, spiritual ailments are carefully examined within the contemporary context, allowing students to formulate personal conclusions regarding the current role of tasawwuf (Sufism) in Islamic spirituality.
learning_outcomes: Explain the symptoms and treatments of the different ailments of the heart.
Critically discuss the origins and history of Islamic spirituality.
Evaluate the ailments of the heart in a contemporary context.
Assess the implications of the various ailments of the heart on one’s spiritual wellbeing.
Evaluate the development trends of moral philosophy and personal ethics in Islam.

title: Viticultural Science
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the management of grapevines with respect to how this influences grape and wine production. Students will examine the key scientific principles underpinning vine performance and balance, and viticultural factors that dictate grape and wine composition. Students will also develop skills in vineyard management, including vine propagation, canopy management, prediction of grape berry maturity, pest and disease identification and smart vineyard technologies.
learning_outcomes: Perform basic grapevine management techniques, and.
Describe emerging technologies that have the potential to change the way grapevines are managed in the future.
Describe grapevine growth and physiological basis of vine growth and fruit production.
Explain and interpret the interrelationships between grape yield, berry composition, viticultural conditions and wine produced.
Describe the basis of vineyard management with respect to irrigation, canopy management, nutrient availability and pest and disease management.
Explain how the composition of grape berries is influenced by abiotic and biotic factors in the vineyard environment.

title: Voice and Movement
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this subject students are introduced to the primary elements of performance and presentation practice with an emphasis on voice and movement. Through practical workshop activities, performance, production and critical reflection, students develop foundational skills and investigate the relationship between movement and voice to successful practice as a performer, creator and presenter.
learning_outcomes: Apply a knowledge of breathing, articulation, diction, projection, freedom and clarity within speech.
Identify and describe positive physical and vocal practice.
Demonstrate a capacity to integrate body, voice and text into performance.
Apply physical and vocal control, focus, dynamics and energy in presentation and performance.
prerequisites: ACT101: Introduction to Voice and Movement

title: Vulnerability and the Ethics of Intervention
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: People who work in the professions of health and human services, medicine, social work, teaching, and the public service frequently interact with vulnerable people. As a result, such workers face distinctive ethical challenges in their jobs. Doctors must decide whether to act against the wishes of patients if they judge that it is in the patients’ best interests, or whether they should always respect their patients’ preferences. Practitioners who are bound by client confidentiality must decide whether they should break confidentiality when a client reveals their intention to cause harm to a third party. Social workers must evaluate whether children are at risk of neglect, and whether and how to intervene to avert such risks. By investigating issues of this nature, this subject examines the ethical challenges that are faced by professionals whose job it is to interact with and care for the vulnerable.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate opposing viewpoints, and engage in productive debates, concerning law and policy regarding paternalistic intervention.

Analyse whether paternalistic intervention in the lives of vulnerable adults and children is ever morally permissible, and whether in terms of duty of care there is ever a professional responsibility to intervene.
Consider legal requirements that determine whether someone is capable of giving consent, and when intervention is permissible in cases where it is not possible to obtain consent.

Evaluate when an individual's right to self-determination entails that they must be left alone, and how human rights, more generally, govern the duty to intervene and the duty to respect others' autonomy.

Identify and evaluate ways of protecting the dignity of a vulnerable party in the course of paternalistic intervention, by harnessing the party's own agency as far as possible, and minimising distress.

Consider when it is necessary to respect the 'dignity of risk' of vulnerable parties (i.e. their right to take reasonable risks), while considering the impact on families and the wider community in allowing risky choices.
Develop and apply ethical approaches to professional practice, including a human rights approach.

title: Vulnerability and the Ethics of Intervention
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: Using a problem-based focus, this subject explores our ethical duties towards vulnerable adults and children, with a particular focus on the professional responsibilities of health and human services workers, and justice professionals. We will consider the ethics of intervention into the lives of vulnerable people, canvassing issues of legal capacity, autonomy, paternalism, coercion, privacy and human rights. The subject also examines associated legal duties of care, including good samaritanism.
learning_outcomes: Consider when it is necessary to respect the 'dignity of risk' of vulnerable parties (i.e. their right to take reasonable risks), while considering the impact on families and the wider community in allowing risky choices.

Evaluate when an individual's right to self-determination entails that they must be left alone, and how human rights, more generally, govern the duty to intervene and the duty to respect others' autonomy.
Critically evaluate opposing viewpoints, and engage in productive debates, concerning law and policy regarding paternalistic intervention.
Develop and apply an ethical approach to professional practice.

Analyse whether paternalistic intervention in the lives of vulnerable adults and children is ever morally permissible, and whether in terms of duty of care there is ever a professional responsibility to intervene.
Consider legal requirements that determine whether someone is capable of giving consent, and when intervention is permissible in cases where it is not possible to obtain consent.

Identify and evaluate ways of protecting the dignity of a vulnerable party in the course of paternalistic intervention, by harnessing the party's own agency as far as possible, and minimising distress.

title: Water and Wastewater Engineering
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject builds upon the knowledge acquired in earlier fluid mechanics subjects. It covers advanced topics in water and wastewater resources management and engineering, including groundwater hydrology, urban stormwater management, water quality modelling, and sustainable water infrastructure. Emphasis is placed on developing advanced skills and exploring innovative solutions to address contemporary challenges in water engineering.
learning_outcomes: Apply water quality modelling tools and techniques to assess and manage water contamination risks.
Design sustainable water infrastructure solutions to address climate change impacts and urbanization pressures.
Evaluate innovative stormwater management techniques to mitigate urban flooding and improve water quality.

title: Water Policy and Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn how to assess water quantity and quality, trends in water demand and supply, and risks to water resources in Australia due to climate change. Students will analyse water use and demand, the value of water to the environment, irrigation agriculture and urban uses, and water use efficiency and recycling. Students will learn how principles of water policy and planning are applied in the development of water policy, water reform, catchment-based decision-making, and develop sound independent judgement about the wise management of our water resources.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the water cycle, including variability due to climate change, risks to supply and interaction of surface and groundwater.

Critically review, consolidate, and synthesise knowledge underpinning the development of water policy in Australia, future challenges, and the roles and responsibilities of government, agencies, communities, and the industry.
Critically assess issues associated with urban and industrial water use and effluent management and recycling.
Critically assess issues associated with water use efficiency and management in sustainable agriculture.
Apply principles of integrated catchment management and regional decision-making in order to develop sound independent judgment regarding the wise management of waterways and resources.
Evaluate the value of water (quality and quantity) to different users, including water allocation for environmental sustainability.

title: Water Policy and Management (EM)
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is structured in three modules each of three Units. In Module 1, Units 1 to 3 provide the context and introduction to water quantity and quality including trends in water supply, climate change and risks to water resources in Australia. In Module 2, Units 4 to 6 explore water use and demand including the value of water to the environment, irrigation agriculture and urban uses, water use efficiency and recycling. In Module 3, Units 7 to 9 focus on water policy and planning including principles of water reform, current developments in water policy and catchment-based decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the principles of aquatic ecology and allocation of water for the environment.
Explain water use efficiency and management of water in sustainable agriculture (dryland and irrigation).
Demonstrate an understanding of the water cycle including climate change and variability, risks to supply, and interaction of surface and groundwater.
Describe key regional, national and international issues.
Demonstrate an understanding of urban and industrial water use; effluent management and recycling (rural and urban).
Describe approaches to integrated catchment management and regional decision-making in Australia.

Describe the principal issues underpinning the development of water policy in Australia, future challenges, and roles and responsibilities of government, agencies, communities, industry and individuals.
Demonstrate an understanding of the value of water (quality and quantity) to different users.

title: Web Programming in the Cloud
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an in-depth study of the issues surrounding the development of Web applications and programming in a public Cloud environment. It will examine the basic Cloud infrastructure foundations and development requirements for developing Web applications. Cloud native application design will be examined in detail together with the requirements for migration of monolithic applications. The role of the Cloud Edge will be considered for use with Cloud native programming and development. The subject will provide students with design and development experience in Web programming and will include practical sections where students will build applications that will attempt to solve business problems using a public Cloud.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop a Web application for either a standard Web environment or a Cloud Edge environment.
Explain the basic infrastructure and development foundations of public Cloud systems.
Critically analyse a proposed Web development proposal for design and development as a Cloud native application.
Explain the requirements for Cloud native applications and development.
Deploy and run a Web application in either a standard Web environment or a Cloud Edge environment.

title: Web Publishing for Information Agencies
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces a range of web technologies used to manage and publish information in the digital environment. It provides the knowledge and basic skills to create digital content online that will enable students to function effectively as information professionals. Students will learn the fundamental concepts of web design, publishing and its standards, such as security and accessibility, and will use simple tools and techniques to create a website in a real world context. A key aim of the subject is the creation of online content that relates to organisational goals. Students will also learn to design and create informative and engaging content to attract and hold the user's attention.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate, select and use appropriate web design elements for creating, organising, storing, sharing and working with information.
Analyse and apply good design techniques to improve readability and usability of online content.
Demonstrate an understanding of the issues and tools that affect web design and publishing in an organisational context.
Explain the application of accessibility, security and other standards in web design.

title: Welfare Practice with Children, Young People and their Carers
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' knowledge and skills for working with children, young people and their carers in adverse life circumstances. Adversity can have a deleterious impact upon wellbeing in terms of education, health, safety and justice. The subject enables students to integrate knowledge of psycho-emotional and social development of children within family and other care arrangements, with social work practice skills that enhance effective professional engagement and intervention.
learning_outcomes: Identify the practical needs of children, young people and their carers living in adverse situations, to promote resilience, or to rehabilitate developmental progression.

Articulate the likely impact of various forms of disadvantage and adversity experienced by children, young people and their carers upon children and young people's development and the reasons for this.
Demonstrate a range of effective community development interventions to promote children and young people's equity and access to services and support in the wider community.
Demonstrate a sound knowledge of children and young people's social, emotional and psychological development within cultural and other appropriate frames of reference such as family and community.

Demonstrate a range of effective techniques for talking with and influencing children, young people and their carers, in respect of addressing their needs and circumstances to promote resilience and/or rehabilitation.
prerequisites: WEL321: Welfare Practice with Children, Young People and their Carers

title: Wellbeing: Perspectives and Practices
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the concept of wellbeing for teachers, children and adolescents in educational settings. The dimensions of health will be examined, including the social, intellectual, physical, environmental, emotional and spiritual elements that influence wellbeing. Various evidence-based perspectives to promote wellbeing in school contexts and enhance student learning are investigated. Wellbeing frameworks along with school-based programs to support wellbeing and inclusion are explored. Whole school approaches to promote wellbeing strategies that support students are discussed to inform practice.
learning_outcomes: Describe the factors impacting teacher wellbeing and resilience.
Investigate evidence-based programs in promoting students’ social and emotional learning.
Describe frameworks and strategies that support the wellbeing of children and adolescents.
Describe the concept of wellbeing, including related dimensions of health and their impacts.
Describe the interplay between learning and wellbeing.

title: Wellbeing: Perspectives and Practices
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: In this subject, key theories of wellbeing and their relevance to education are explored. The relationship between wellbeing and learning, including how wellbeing influences student engagement, behaviour, and achievement, will also be investigated. System and whole-school approaches that support students’ wellbeing and safety are examined, along with related strategies. Evidence-based programs and approaches designed to promote student wellbeing are critically compared and evaluated. Pre-service students analyse the factors that influence teacher wellbeing and resilience, and design strategies that enhance their own wellbeing.
learning_outcomes: Explain how whole school structures, policies, and cultures may influence student wellbeing, proposing strategies that support students’ wellbeing and safety.
Critically compare and evaluate evidence-based programs and approaches that promote students’ wellbeing.
Investigate the relationship between wellbeing and learning, including how wellbeing influences engagement, behaviour, and achievement.
Explore theories of wellbeing and their relevance to education.
Analyse the factors influencing teacher wellbeing and resilience, designing strategies to support self.
prerequisites: EED422: Child and Adolescent Learning and Development

title: Wellness and Wellbeing in Early Childhood Settings
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the concept of wellness and wellbeing for staff and children in early childhood settings. A health model of wellness and wellbeing is used to provide a framework for exploring the social, intellectual, physical, environmental, emotional and spiritual dimensions of wellness for adults and children. Strategies to promote wellness and wellbeing for children and staff in early childhood settings are discussed.
learning_outcomes: Create a plan with useable ideas and experiences to improve wellness and wellbeing for early childhood centre staff that could be implemented in an early childhood setting.
Examine the socialisation and environmental influences on health issues and how they apply to children and staff in early childhood settings.
Discuss the role advocates in the early childhood profession have on ensuring conditions in early childhood settings that support the wellness and wellbeing of children and staff.
Explain the role and value of the various dimensions of wellness and wellbeing in relation to children and staff in the early childhood context.
prerequisites: EEB306: Wellness and Wellbeing in Early Childhood Contexts

title: What is Science?
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the basic principles and fundamental tools of science. Students will explore science as a philosophy of life and as a method for understanding the world, along with concepts of the scientific method, framing a hypothesis, designing an experiment, collecting and analysing data, and presenting results in a variety of formats and to a range of audiences. Students will learn to research the scientific literature and assess information and data quality in relation to scientific endeavours. Students will also examine pseudo-science and how science influences society (and vice-versa ), as well as standards of scientific professionalism and career development.
learning_outcomes: Use appropriate digital tools and technologies (e.g., data analysis software, simulation tools, AI‑assisted platforms) to generate, analyse, and communicate scientific information in written, oral, and graphical formats.
Analyse how scientific ideas influence social values and how social values shape the development and application of science, including their relevance to ethical and sustainable decision making.
Construct balanced arguments that integrate scientific, social, and ethical principles, using evidence from scientific literature to justify a position on contemporary scientific issues.
Apply problem‑management and opportunity‑development strategies to support ongoing personal, academic, and professional growth.
Explain how scientific knowledge is generated through evidence‑based inquiry, and distinguish between valid science, pseudo‑science, and other forms of knowledge.
Reflect on personal, academic, and professional capabilities and evaluate how these attributes influence employability, career development, and ongoing learning needs.
Locate, interpret, and evaluate scientific literature and data, and apply this information to support planning, problem solving, and evidence‑based decision making.
Analyse how experimental conditions influence measured outcomes.

title: White-Collar Psychopaths
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the challenges posed by corporate psychopaths in some of the world's greatest financial collapses. From Tiberius's financial crisis of 33 AD to the collapse of Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC white-collar psychopaths have inflicted significant social and financial harm on society through financial mismanagement and outright criminality. This subject approaches these challenges as a ‘wicked problem', acknowledging the difficulty in defining the nature of the problem itself, its innumerable causes and the absence of one correct answer. Drawing on the latest research and industry best practice, students will use problem-solving skills to navigate this socially complex area in new and innovative ways as they formulate recommendations, triggering deep reflections on both content and process.
learning_outcomes: Critique the representation of white-collar psychopaths across different mediums.
Critically reflect on and make recommendations to reduce the harms linked to elite white-collar criminals.
Identify the psychopathic characteristics commonly associated with elite white-collar criminals.

title: WIL 1: The Contemporary Bachelor of Arts
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject has two purposes: First, it provides an overview of the course that covers the overall course structure and progression planning; the role and structure of the specialisations and minors and advice on how to progress through them; and the unique Work Integrated Learning and transferrable skills components of the course. Second, it provides the platform for the first Work Integrated Learning experience of the course. This requires students to research potential industry and community sectors for the following information: workforce/industry expectations and standards; and the future outlook of the respective industry/sector. Students will be required to engage with this information and reflect on their own potential career trajectory.
learning_outcomes: Identify salient features of the course and articulate the correct way of progressing through the course.
Reflect on their own potential career trajectory.
Articulate workforce/industry expectations and standards.
Comment on the changing role of the Bachelor of Arts in the broader Australian context.
Identify examples of potential future industries/sectors of employment.

title: WIL 2: Engaging with Community and Industry
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the opportunity for students to undertake work integrated learning experiences that are meaningful to their discipline specialisation. The subject involves authentic work integrated learning in an external industry or community context. This activity may be as varied as engagement with a social media campaign or activism; self-initiated community engagement or advocacy project; volunteerism; community engaged creative work; return to country program; or formal work placement.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate real-world knowledge of a particular industry or community context via critical reflection on their work integrated learning experience.
Critically reflect on their experience of engaging with a particular industry or community context.
Comment on how their academic study relates to a particular industry or community context.
Articulate the norms and standards of a particular industry or community context.
Reflect on their own potential career trajectory.

title: WIL 3: The Think Well
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: In this final work integrated learning subject, students will work collaboratively on real-world problems that have been identified by external industry and community organisations. Students will analyse these real-world problems in an interdisciplinary context in order to offer possible solutions or different perspectives. Students will present their findings at an end-of-session symposium at which representatives from industry and community organisations will be available to offer real-time feedback.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate with their peers in a professional and productive manner.
Reflect on their own potential career trajectory.
Showcase the critical and creative thinking skills they have acquired throughout their studies.
Engage with representatives from industry and community organisations in a professional and knowledgeable way.
Demonstrate interdisciplinary, collaborative learning.

title: Wildfire Investigation
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: JST455 Wildfire Investigation provides a foundational background and encourages a deeper appreciation for the importance of capturing critical information relevant to wildfire investigation. Students will be equipped with an overview of the issues surrounding wildfire investigation, including the initial establishment of wildfire cause and origin, and scene preservation specific to wildfire. The subject will also provide an overview of wildfire arson and the need to engage with key stakeholders. The issue of forest sustainability will also be discussed in relation to the role of fire in local ecology, and the practice of regularly reducing fuel load to prevent wildfires destroying forests and related areas.
learning_outcomes: Be familiar with the processes of wildfire ignition identification.
Articulate a variety of perspectives relating issues of forest sustainability, weather patterns and the role of fire in vegetation.
Articulate the need to engage key stakeholders from relevant agencies to address deliberately lit wildfires.
Distinguish the elements of wildfire arson and recognise a deliberately lit wildfire.
Identify evidence relevant to a formal wildfire investigation.
Identify and describe the common causes of wildfire.
Explain the need to preserve a wildfire scene and the elements needed to preserve it.

title: Wildlife Management
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Effective wildlife management is crucial for the conservation of biodiversity and the sustainable use of natural resources. In this subject students focus on Australian wildlife management and learn how ecological principles underpin management strategies and actions. Key topics in wildlife management are explored including threatened species recovery and translocation methods, wildlife disaster mitigation, wildlife harvesting, wildlife parasitism and disease, and traditional and contemporary Indigenous Australian wildlife management approaches. Students completing this subject have the ability to develop and evaluate wildlife management strategies for the protection, control, sustainable use, or recovery of species and communities and can apply adaptive management principles to wildlife management problems.
learning_outcomes: Identify appropriate scientific methods to the study of wildlife management.
Identify appropriate environmental legislation and policy and their role in wildlife management.
Apply adaptive management principles to wildlife management.
Explain and summarise the key terminology, concepts and principles of wildlife management.
Review, consolidate and synthesise their knowledge to develop wildlife management strategies for the control, sustainable use and recovery of species and communities.
Discuss the main features of threatened species management, wildlife control, wildlife disease, wildlife disaster mitigation and sustainable use of wildlife.

title: Wine Chemistry
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is a study of the application of chemical principles to wine stability. Students will build on their knowledge of wine production and chemistry to develop their understanding of the underlying theory behind, and skills for, the use of wine fining agents such as bentonite, protein, PVPP, copper ion, blue-fining, and polysaccharides. Students will also learn about, and apply, other wine stabilisation procedures including cold stabilisation, ion-exchange processes, and the use of enzymes in winemaking.
learning_outcomes: Use chemical principles to interpret and assess the impact of winemaking conditions on wine stability.
Evaluate the action of enzyme treatments used in winemaking, particularly enzymes of microbial origin.
Compare and contrast the practical applications of fining agents and interpret their performance.
Evaluate how and why chemical principles influence the task of fining and stabilising wines.

title: Wildlife Ecology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: In a world of increasing human impact, an understanding of the roles wildlife species play in ecosystems is crucial for the conservation of biological diversity. In this subject, students build on their existing ecological knowledge to learn ecological principles specifically relating to wildlife. A strong emphasis is placed on the study of Australian wildlife species. Factors such as competition and predation, species distributions and wildlife population dynamics are discussed in detail. Wildlife survey techniques are learnt and implemented through a field trip. Students completing this subject have the ability to critically evaluate the effects that environmental factors have on wildlife species.
learning_outcomes: Explain and summarise the key concepts and principles of wildlife ecology.
Synthesize knowledge of the origins, evolution and patterns of diversity of Australian wildlife.
Critically evaluate the dynamics of wildlife species interactions.
Apply appropriate scientific methods to the study of wildlife ecology.
Analyse and interpret the factors influencing wildlife distribution and abundance.
Apply specialised skills in the design and implementation of wildlife surveys.
Interpret and evaluate wildlife population dynamics and modelling.

title: Wine Chemistry
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject is a study of the application of chemical principles to wine stability. Students will build on their knowledge of wine production and chemistry to develop their understanding of the underlying theory behind, and skills for, the use of wine fining agents such as bentonite, protein, PVPP, copper ion, blue-fining, and polysaccharides. Students will also learn about, and apply, other wine stabilisation procedures including cold stabilisation, ion-exchange processes, and the use of enzymes in winemaking.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the action of enzyme treatments used in winemaking, particularly enzymes of microbial origin.
Compare and contrast fining agents and interpret their performance.
Successfully use chemical principles to interpret and assess the impact of winemaking conditions on wine stability.
Evaluate how and why chemical principles influence the task of fining and stabilising wines.

title: Wine Microbiology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a specialised subject, covering the physiology and biochemistry of yeast and bacterial growth during wine fermentation and conservation. Students will gain knowledge to identify the different microorganisms involved in wine production and the impacts they have on wine quality. Students will gain the skills required to handle, culture and enumerate the microorganisms involved in the production of wine.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the impact of specific wine production techniques on the physiology and biochemistry of the alcoholic fermentation by wine yeasts.
Apply specific wine production techniques that impact microbial physiology and biochemistry that produce or retain positive wine sensory and chemical composition.
Conduct, and explain the rationale behind, procedures for the study and use of wine microorganisms in wine production.
Critically evaluate wine storage options for control of spoilage microorganisms during winemaking and wine conservation.
Critically evaluate the impact of altered wine chemical composition and storage conditions on the ecology and physiology of microorganisms.
Critically reflect and adjust grape chemical compositional measures to impact microbial growth during alcoholic and malolactic fermentation.

title: Wine Microbiology
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is a specialised subject, covering the physiology and biochemistry of yeast and bacterial growth during wine fermentation and conservation. Students will gain knowledge in identifying the different microorganisms involved in wine production and the impacts they have on wine quality. Students will also develop skills required to handle, culture and enumerate the microorganisms involved in the production of wine.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the impact of specific wine production techniques on the physiology and biochemistry of the alcoholic fermentation by wine yeasts.
Conduct, and explain the rationale behind, procedures for the study and use of wine microorganisms in wine production.
Evaluate wine storage options for control of spoilage microorganisms during winemaking and wine conservation.
Evaluate the impact of altered wine chemical composition and storage conditions on the ecology and physiology of microorganisms.
Apply specific wine production techniques that impact microbial physiology and biochemistry that produce or retain positive wine sensory and chemical composition.
Reflect and adjust grape chemical compositional measures to impact microbial growth during alcoholic and malolactic fermentation.

title: Wine Production 1
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a detailed study of the principles and techniques used in table wine production, particularly in relation to effects on wine composition and quality. Emphasis will be placed on the importance and relevance of ongoing quality control throughout the winemaking process. Students will produce a table wine, and detail and justify wine making decisions involved in its production. Students will also conduct wine sensory assessments to examine the relationship between production decisions and wine attributes.
learning_outcomes: Analyse factors affecting wine composition and quality based on chemical analysis and sensory assessment.
Describe, justify and practically apply the table wine production process.
Assess and evaluate the contributions of winemaking approaches and techniques to wine quality and sensory attributes.

title: Wine Production 2
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the grape requirements, production principles and winemaking techniques to produce sparkling wine and fortified wine, and the effect that these factors have on wine composition and quality. Students will examine table winemaking techniques beyond that of Wine Production 1, particularly processing techniques that develop and vary style.
learning_outcomes: Explain the optimum grape composition requirements for sparkling wine and fortified wine.
Detail, justify and apply the winemaking principles and processes used in sparkling and fortified wine production.
Compare and contrast the ability of various winemaking practices to influence the quality and style of wine.

title: Wine Science 1
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to wine microbiology and the main chemical concepts and analyses that underpin wine production, including interactions with. Students will analyse the key principles behind wine fermentation, composition and stability. Students will develop skills in the general chemical analysis of wine, with an emphasis on safety, fundamental operations of analytical techniques and accuracy in analysis. Students will also become proficient in calculations relevant to wine production.
learning_outcomes: Explain the chemical and microbiological principles involved with winemaking.
Describe and analyse the fundamentals of wine microbiology and winery sanitation.
Analyse winemaking problems and identify actions that will improve them.
Safely perform quality control analysis procedures, and interpret and report results.

title: Wine Science 2
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Wine Science 2 provides a study of advanced chemistry applications to wine production, focussing on flavour compounds and phenolic chemistry. Students will learn the key principles that underpin wine phenolic composition, their influence on wine colour and the modifications they undergo during wine production and ageing. Students will develop skills in the analysis of phenolic compounds and red wine colour during the practical component of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Identify types of wine phenolic compounds and evaluate their importance in terms of grape extraction during winemaking, subsequent modification through ageing and oxidation, and influences of wood treatment.
Evaluate the diversity of structures and origins of flavour compounds in wine, and relate to identification challenges.
Critically evaluate winemaking practices in terms of their effect on wine phenolic composition at a molecular level and assess their impact on wine quality.
Apply chemical principles of bonding, stability, reactivity and reaction mechanism to rationalise the behaviour of phenolic compounds.
Conduct instrumental measurements, through integration of the underlying analytical theory, to assess phenolic characteristics in red wine.

title: Wine Science 2
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Wine Science 2 provides a study of advanced chemistry applications to wine production, focussing on flavour compounds and phenolic chemistry. Students will learn the key principles that underpin wine phenolic composition, their influence on wine colour and the modifications they undergo during wine production and ageing. Students will develop skills in the analysis of phenolic compounds and red wine colour during the practical component of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the diversity of structures and origins of flavour compounds in wine, and relate to identification challenges.
Conduct instrumental measurements, through integration of the underlying analytical theory, to assess phenolic characteristics in red wine.
Critically evaluate winemaking practices in terms of their effect on wine phenolic composition at a molecular level and assess their impact on wine quality.
Apply chemical principles of bonding, stability, reactivity and reaction mechanism to rationalise the behaviour of phenolic compounds.
Apply chemical principles of bonding, stability, reactivity and reaction mechanism to rationalise the behaviour of phenolic compounds.

title: The Body, Illness and Health
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the student to a broad theoretical and practical overview of the major illnesses affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Students will learn of the vital organs and major systems in the human body. It explores the relationships between lifestyle and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health status. It also examines the role of health professionals. Further to this, it addresses the impact that colonisation has had on health and wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Holistic health encompasses spirituality as well as the physical, social, and emotional wellbeing of the individual and community.
learning_outcomes: recognise personal health data to understand the impact of optimal well being and the affect this has on sustained professional practice.
define the major illnesses and chronic diseases being experienced by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples today; and
discuss the human body, using appropriate anatomical terminology supported by digital technology;
identify the functions of some of the vital organs of the human body as they relate to chronic diseases specifically experienced by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples;
describe the relationship between social, emotional and physical wellbeing;

title: Wine Sensory Assessment
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject entails a study of wine assessment at an advanced level that assumes a significant knowledge of sensory science and some sensory descriptive skills. It considers both Australian and international wines, with major regions, varieties and styles being presented. Students will examine attributes of wine sensory quality in terms of wine type, origin, grape variety and potential market. Students will also explore the concept of quality as Australian wines are tasted, and 'Old World' wines are considered in terms of provenance and what that represents. Students will practise rating of wine from the perspective of the Australian wine show system, and their wine assessment skills tested, including scoring reliability, scoring discrimination, and comprehensive wine descriptions.
learning_outcomes: Present, orally, a sensory comparison of wines, and interpret their sensory difference in terms of the grape or wine production differences.

Competently use the Australian wine show scoring system, discuss the attributes and limitations of the wine show process, and compare the assessment process with other approaches, including European approaches, to the assessment of quality.
Identify and appraise common wine faults.
Formulate concise, relevant and meaningful sensory descriptions of wines.
Distinguish the nature and balance of the sensory characteristics in a wide range of wines and relate the features to wine type, grape variety, wine style and wine processing.
Assess wine reliably, and discriminate effectively between similar wines of differing quality or characteristics.

title: Winery Engineering
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Winery Engineering builds on earlier studies in wine production, with an expansion of core concepts of process engineering for wine production. There will be a focus on principles of process control and hygienic design and operation of food processing equipment. Students will develop knowledge and skills in: the principles of winery design, including decisions relating to equipment selection, capacity and scheduling; enhancing the sustainability of winery operations, including analysis of energy and water supply and their utilisation, and alternatives for waste disposal; and the design and evaluation of new technologies to meet economic, logistic and product quality requirements. Students will also learn about regulatory compliance issues within this framework.
learning_outcomes: Describe, evaluate and compare the use of selected procedures or technologies against economic, logistic and product quality constraints.
Describe and evaluate alternative options for disposal of liquid and solid wastes and justify the selection of methods appropriate to a given scenario.
Appraise and apply core concepts of process engineering for wine production.
Analyse grape supply logistics and wine making practices to select appropriate equipment of optimal capacity and recommend the scheduling of the equipment and winery services for a given scenario.
Describe and evaluate options for energy and water supply and their utilisation, and analyse and justify selected opportunities for enhancing the efficiency of energy use.

title: Winery Engineering
school: School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences
syllabus_overview: Winery Engineering builds on earlier studies in food and beverage engineering and wine production. Students will develop knowledge and skills in: the principles of winery design, including decisions relating to equipment selection, capacity and scheduling; enhancing the sustainability of winery operations, including analysis of energy and water supply and their utilisation, and alternatives for waste disposal; and the design and evaluation of new technologies to meet economic, logistic and product quality requirements. Students will also learn about workplace health and safety, and regulatory compliance issues within this framework.
learning_outcomes: Describe, evaluate and compare the use of selected procedures or technologies against economic, logistic and product quality constraints.
Describe and evaluate alternative options for disposal of liquid and solid wastes and justify the selection of methods appropriate to a given scenario.
Appraise significant workplace health and safety risks in winery operations and apply relevant legislation to develop safe work practices and winery design.
Analyse grape supply logistics and wine making practices to select appropriate equipment of optimal capacity and recommend the scheduling of the equipment and winery services for a given scenario.
Describe and evaluate options for energy and water supply and their utilisation, and analyse and justify selected opportunities for enhancing the efficiency of energy use.

title: Wiradjuri Culture and Heritage
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on developing student knowledge of the cultural heritage of the Wiradjuri people. Students will explore topics related to the restoration of Wiradjuri intellectual and cultural knowledge, as far as it is presently available, as part of the restoration of Wiradjuri freedom to be human, unique and different.
learning_outcomes: Think critically and generate ideas to provide solutions to problems associated with the concept of identity.
Critically examine the diversity of histories of Indigenous Nations through a variety of sources and perspectives, particularly Wiradjuri perspectives.
Analyse, consolidate and synthesise knowledge of Wiradjuri kinship and family relationships and apply this knowledge in a range of professional/ community contexts.
Demonstrate specialised knowledge of the depth of Indigenous systems of knowledge and apply this knowledge in a range of professional/community contexts.
Critically examine and reflect on the experiences and impact of State and Federal Government policies and practices on Wiradjuri people.

title: Wiradyuri Language Four
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on Wiradyuri language through story telling. Students will express their knowledge of their cultural heritage to develop and share their story in fluent Wiradyuri language. Students will develop skills in the transmission, teaching and passing on of Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community. Students will gain an in-depth knowledge of complex Wiradyuri language concepts embedded within cultural meanings. Students will build critical knowledge of language revitalisation to apply in diverse settings. Students will identify best practices to support their language acquisition. Students will demonstrate thinking Wiradyuri and conversational fluency through their own story on-country.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the benefits of using multi-media strategies to present Wiradyuri language stories.
Critically analyse techniques and strategies and demonstrate the transmission and passing on of Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community.
Effectively use oral, written and visual means to translate storytelling with Wiradyuri language.
Evaluate and provide strategies for long-term sustainability for Wiradyuri language revitalisation.
Demonstrate conversational and narrative fluency in Wiradyuri language.
Apply knowledge of Wiradyuri language to develop and create an innovative story telling approach to language reclamation.

title: Wiradjuri Language
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on developing the Wiradjuri language skills of students within the context of cultural heritage. Students will work together to increase their proficiency in Wiradjuri conversation and will work together to generate resources that can be made available for use by others teaching Wiradjuri Language. Students will also expand their working knowledge of the Wiradjuri language through an expansion of their vocabulary and a developing knowledge of Wiradjuri grammar. This subject will also provide students with the knowledge and understanding of the Wiradjuri language, including likely contrasts between pre-invasion and post-invasion, Wiradjuri language and a clear understanding of the influences and impact of invasion history on the Wiradjuri Nation, language and culture; including policies and practices that have threatened the loss of the Wiradjuri language.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of how to create Wiradjuri Language resources (with a particular focus on digital resources) for use in the wider community and in other educational contexts.
Demonstrate an understanding of the major differences in expressing concepts in Wiradjuri and English.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the likely contrasts between pre-invasion Wiradjuri language and the post-invasion impact on Wiradjuri language use.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of Wiradjuri sounds, words and sentences through conversation and apply and use this knowledge in professional/ community contexts.
Demonstrate the articulation of Wiradjuri sounds, words and sentences through conversation.

Demonstrate a clear and critical understanding of the influences and impact that history has had on the Wiradjuri Nation, language and culture, including the policies and practices that have threatened the loss of the Wiradjuri language and be able to generate ideas to provide practical solutions to the issue of Wiradjuri language recovery.

title: Wiradyuri Language One
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on developing the Wiradyuri language skills of students within the context of Wiradyuri ways of knowing, being and doing. Students will develop skills in transmission and passing on of Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community. Students will work together to increase their proficiency in Wiradyuri conversation and to generate resources to promote immersive language experiences. Students will develop their working knowledge of the Wiradyuri language through an expansion of their vocabulary and analysis of Wiradyuri grammar. This subject will also provide students with knowledge and understanding of Wiradyuri language being tightly woven within cultural heritage through immersive on-country learning experiences.
learning_outcomes: Create Wiradyuri language resources that promote immersive language learning experiences.
Evaluate skills in transmission, teaching and passing on of Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community.
Critically evaluate the use of Wiradyuri language on-country through immersive culturally-centred thinking.

Critically analyse the responsibility of learning Wiradyuri language for Wiradyuri people and for Wiradyuri Country, along with examining the importance of protocols influencing practices in the reclamation process of Wiradyuri language.
Analyse the articulation of Wiradyuri sounds, words, understanding of Wiradyuri grammar and sentences through conversation.
Sustain a basic fluent Wiradyuri conversation to demonstrate development of Wiradyuri grammar translation and communication.

title: Wiradyuri Language Three
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on developing student knowledge of Wiradyuri language and further developing complex conversations. Students will develop skills in the transmission, teaching and passing on of Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community. Students will investigate their own language acquisition and identify effective strategies to reflect on their learning. Students will further develop their Wiradyuri language fluency with more complex Wiradyuri language concepts. Students will analyse their daily language usage through speaking and writing in a variety of contexts and determine successful practices for language reclamation. Students will embed knowledge and understanding of Wiradyuri language through examining language through on-country immersive experiences.
learning_outcomes: Analyse transmission and teaching strategies to pass on Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community.
Critically examine their personal language journey through reflection and demonstrate understanding of thinking Wiradyuri.
Demonstrate fluent Wiradyuri conversations with thematic based learning experiences through on-country learning experiences.
Apply knowledge of Wiradyuri language to implement innovative immersive Wiradyuri language presentations.
Critically think and generate ideas to grow and sustain the use of Wiradyuri language in their daily lives.
Deconstruct complex Wiradyuri sentences and translate with Wiradyuri thinking.

title: Wiradyuri Language Two
school: School of Indigenous Australian Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on developing student knowledge of Wiradyuri language through strengthening culturally centred conversations. Students will develop skills in the transmission, teaching and passing on of Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community. Students will examine the depth of Wiradyuri language and connections to culture and Wiradyuri systems of knowing. Students will work together to expand their working knowledge of Wiradyuri language through questions to attain a deeper understanding of pronouns and verbs in the context of thematic-based approaches. Students will embed knowledge and understanding of Wiradyuri language by examining language through on-country immersive experiences.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, consolidate and synthesise knowledge of Wiradyuri language through on-country culturally immersive learning experiences.
