Critically examine and reflect on Wiradyuri language through culturally centred thinking, with consideration of the responsibilities to Wiradyuri people and Wiradyuri Country.
Demonstrate the articulation of Wiradyuri sounds, words, understanding of Wiradyuri grammar through conversations, with a focus on questioning techniques.
Implement innovative strategies to demonstrate a cultural practice to promote Wiradyuri language immersion
Demonstrate techniques in the transmission, teaching and passing on of Wiradyuri language for the Wiradyuri community.
Deconstruct Wiradyuri sentences and translate with Wiradyuri culturally-centred thinking processes.

title: Wireless Communications
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an in-depth knowledge of wireless communication systems. It starts with the discussion of wireless signals, their propagation mechanisms and the capacity of wireless systems for practical wireless communication scenarios. The subject then explores the working principles of wireless systems such as Wi-Fi and Wireless Local Area Networks. It further discusses emerging wireless communication systems and the challenging wireless security aspects for these systems.
learning_outcomes: Investigate theoretical and practical issues relating to wireless technology and communicate the results to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Investigate and evaluate emerging wireless networking technologies.
Investigate and evaluate various wireless networking protocols and standards.
Compare and contrast different wireless networks in terms of size, speed, limitations and applications.
Critically analyse wireless networking concepts and their applications in real life situations.
Identify the challenges and security issues posed by wireless networks.
Describe and analyse wireless signalling techniques and radio frequency communications.

title: Wireless Networks
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Computing, Mathematics and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an understanding of the fundamentals of wireless communications including communication protocols, radio frequencies, transmission methods, and different contemporary wireless networking standards. It also provides students with experience in current and emerging wireless communication technologies.
learning_outcomes: Explain the challenges and security issues posed by wireless networks.
Illustrate wireless signalling techniques and describe radio frequency communications.
Compare and contrast different wireless networks in terms of size, speed, limitations and applications.
Investigate and evaluate emerging wireless networking technologies.
Investigate and evaluate various wireless networking techniques, protocols and standards.
Describe wireless networking concepts and their application to real life situations.
Investigate theoretical and practical issues relating to wireless technology and communicate the results to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Wisdom and Worship Traditions
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores Israelite texts that reflect on living well and justly with one another (wisdom) and before God (worship) through life's varied circumstances. The interconnections between creation, human experience and language about God within Israel's varied wisdom and worship traditions are critically evaluated. Key texts examined include Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon, focusing on their respective literary features, socio-cultural contexts and diverse philosophical, religious and moral perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Interpret select texts in an informed and responsible way to demonstrate an appreciation of the rich theological and experiential perspectives within wisdom and worship traditions.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of the structure, literary forms and central themes of Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon.
Analyse critically human experience and language about God as reflected in wisdom and worship literature.
Discuss in a critical way issues relating to the interpretation of Israel's wisdom and worship literature.
Discuss major theological and ethical themes in Israel's wisdom and worship literature and assess their contemporary relevance.
Demonstrate developing competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts and critical engagement with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.

title: Wireless Networks
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: Wireless Networks is a comprehensive subject designed to provide students with a solid understanding of the principles, protocols, and technologies underlying modern wireless communication systems. This includes wireless channel characteristics, multiple access techniques, wireless network architectures, routing protocols, security mechanisms, and emerging technologies.
learning_outcomes: Identify the security vulnerabilities of wireless networks and propose appropriate security mechanisms to mitigate them.
Explain the propagation characteristics of wireless channels using basic models to predict signal behaviour in different environments.
Implement basic wireless networking protocols and standards to establish reliable and efficient wireless communication links in practical applications.
Compare the performance of multiple access techniques in wireless communication systems.
Design simple wireless network architectures to meet specific communication requirements and constraints.

title: Women in Islam and Islamic Cultures
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject will address critically the modern paradigms concerning women and gender roles within contemporary society. Developing arguments within a critical framework of an Islamic set of paradigms and values, it will take a fresh look at women in Islam by examining the status and role of women in scripture, exploring heroines in the mystic world, and discussing critically the authentic status of Muslim women in Islamic societies throughout the centuries. The subject will critically address the conditions of Muslim women in both contemporary Islamic and non-Islamic cultures and the contemporary debates concerning Muslim women. The subject will evaluate, critique and when relevant, synthesise multiple views including traditionalist/conservative, modernist/reformist and feminist approach to the woman question.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the gender factor in social and interpersonal space for men and women.
Articulate contemporary Muslim women's experience in social and religious activism.
Research interdisciplinary topics and apply critical reasoning while presenting arguments in oral and written forms.
Demonstrate the ability to assess critically women's status in Islam.
Analyse widely discussed issues of inheritance, divorce, hijab (veil) and polygamy in Islamic societies.
Understand critically non-Islamic factors contributing to women's status in Islamic cultures and societies.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the role of women in Islamic sources, art, history, jurisprudence and contemporary societies.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of contemporary Muslim women's experience in Islam.
Develop a critical approach to patriarchal as well as counter-patriarchal discourses regarding women's status in Islam.

title: Wisdom and Worship Traditions
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores Israelite texts that reflect on living well and justly with one another (wisdom) and before God (worship) through life's varied circumstances. The interconnections between creation, human experience and language about God within Israel's varied wisdom and worship traditions are critically evaluated. Key texts examined include Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon, focusing on their respective literary features, socio-cultural contexts and diverse philosophical, religious and moral perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate developing competence in the exegesis and interpretation of biblical texts and critical engagement with primary biblical sources and secondary literature.
Interpret select texts in an informed and responsible way to demonstrate an appreciation of the rich theological and experiential perspectives within wisdom and worship traditions.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including sound research, writing and communication skills.
Discuss in a critical way issues relating to the interpretation of Israel's wisdom and worship literature.
Analyse critically human experience and language about God as reflected in wisdom and worship literature.
Discuss major theological and ethical themes in Israel's wisdom and worship literature and assess their contemporary relevance.
Demonstrate an understanding of the structure, literary forms and central themes of Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon.

title: Women in Islam, Civilisations and Cultures
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses critically the modern paradigms concerning women and gender roles in primary and classical texts; through the Islamic history and civilisation; as well as in contemporary Muslim cultures and societies. Developing arguments from within a critical framework of an Islamic set of paradigms and values, it takes a fresh approach at women in Islam. It examines the status and role of women in scripture; explores significant women figures in mysticism, scholarship, social and political life. Muslim women are positioned in their historical and contemporary relaility with patriarchal, orientalist and feminist approaches highlighted. The subject covers cronologically the conditions and status of women in both contemporary Islamic and non-Islamic cultures. Classical, modern and feminist approaches, viewpoints and arguments are considered throughout the subject.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and evaluate Muslim women's role in society and religious activism.
Research interdisciplinary topics and apply critical reasoning while presenting arguments in oral and written (essay) forms.
Articulate critically the role of women in Islamic sources, art, history and contemporary societies.
Analyse critically circumstances and factors other than religion influencing women's status in Islamic cultures and societies.
Differenciate and critically assess paradigms related to women and their status in Islam and Muslim societies.
Discuss and evaluate critically controversial issues of inheritance, divorce, hijab (veil) and polygamy in Islamic societies.
Develop a critical approach to patriarchal as well as counter-patriarchal discourses regarding women's status in Islam.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of Muslim women's experience throughout the history of Islam.

title: Women, Gender and Family in Islam
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject critically addresses the modern paradigms concerning women and gender roles in contemporary society. Posing arguments from within an Islamic framework, it develops a fresh view of women, gender relationships in Islam and Muslim families. Considering the status and role of women in Islamic scripture, Prophetic tradition and Islamic law, this subject examines the women saints, scholars and rulers in the history of Muslim societies. The subject considers the modern historical backdrop (colonial and postcolonial) and socio-political conditions in the critical analysis of the current status of Muslim women and the rise of Islamic feminism in Muslim societies. Muslim women's conditions and development of their social and family status in the West is also examined with a specific focus on the Muslim women's agency, challenges and achievements in the Australian context.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate contemporary Muslim women's experience in Islam and social and religious activism.
Assess critically women's status in Islam.
Research interdisciplinary topics and apply critical reasoning while presenting arguments in oral and written (essay) forms.
Perform and demonstrate independent research, organisation, written and oral communication skills through the presentation of substantial work.
Identify non-Islamic factors contributing to women's status in Islamic cultures and societies.
Differentiate patriarchal and counter-patriarchal discourses regarding women's status and gender roles in Islam.
prerequisites: ISL355: Women in Islam and Islamic Cultures

title: Women in Islam, Civilisations and Cultures
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject explores scriptural foundations and examines the role models of Muslim women as depicted in the Qur’an as well as prominent women during the time of the Prophet. It delves into the spiritual and scholarly contributions of Muslim women throughout history. The subject also critically analyses modern paradigms and debates on women and gender roles while examining Muslim women's roles across different cultures and societies and how they are perceived by various Islamic streams and movements. It introduces multiple schools of thought, ranging from literalists and traditionalists to modernists and feminists, providing students with diverse perspectives. Ultimately, the subject develops a critical framework that engages with contemporary interpretations and paradigms in alignment with core Islamic values. By synthesising these diverse perspectives, the subject fosters an effective framework for Muslim individuals and families in the present day.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate in-depth understanding of Muslim women's experiences throughout the history of Islam.
Differentiate and critically assess paradigms related to women and their status in Islam and Muslim societies.
Critically analyse the role of women in Islamic sources, art, history and contemporary societies.
Critically analyse circumstances and factors other than religion that shape the gender roles and debates on Muslim women.
Develop a critical approach to patriarchal and hegemonic as well as counter-patriarchal and non-hegemonic discourses to achieve a synthesis on women's status in Islam.

title: Work Based Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Australian Graduate School of Policing Security
syllabus_overview: The emphasis of a work based project is to improve a current situation through effecting change to a process, policy or practice. There is a strong focus, supported by a progressive assessment structure, on a student's grasp of the applied research process. Students are therefore progressively assessed at major points throughout the project. Students are assigned an academic supervisor pertinent to their degree and are also required to work with an approved workplace mentor or advisor. Their project may be a part of a larger workplace project or a stand-alone one. The student's research may result in a comprehensive report, a journal article, training program, policy recommendation or something similar.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in-depth critical understanding of the body of knowledge, theory and practice in their area of research including any recent scientific, technical and technological advances in their chosen field.
Investigate, manage and synthesise complex information, problems and concepts.

Develop and refine the work based project for presentation in an acceptable format specific to the workplace or project area, e.g. a report, journal article, training program, policy recommendation or the like.
Communicate theoretical propositions, methods, conclusions and professional decisions to specialised and non specialist audiences specific to their workbased project.
Critically reflect on the connection between theoretical underpinnings and professional practice relating to the their workbased project.

title: Work Integrated Learning (Sports Media)
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an opportunity to consolidate their knowledge and skills in the workplace. Students will complete a 60 hour intensive placement in a sports media sub-discipline. Students will have the opportunity to immerse themselves in industry and develop a professional portfolio comprising sports media products. This will contribute to their professional development and graduate employability. This subject will provide students with the opportunity to work under the guidance of industry professionals in an authentic workplace, will extend the student's disciplinary knowledge and will facilitate the development of professional networks.
learning_outcomes: Engage actively ethically and morally with industry professionals and sporting personnel.
Evaluate the socio-politico-cultural and economic issues which effect the sports industry.
Discuss the diversity of sporting culture across a range of sports on a local, national and global scale.
Integrate discipline-specific technical capabilities, communication strategies and self-reflective practice relevant to industry placement.
Produce sports media product by critically analysing sporting cultures.
prerequisites: EHR320: Workplace Learning in Sport and Exercise

title: Work Integrated Learning 1
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject is the first of a series of three subjects which focus on employability skills, personal skills and career planning. The subject has a particular emphasis on enhancing professional knowledge of working in a business environment, expanding on employability skills and building on work-integrated learning principles.
learning_outcomes: Identify professional, career and life choices, go on to develop a strategy to achieve these, begin to apply them and appraise their efficacy.
Reflect on personal career and life choices.
Identify personal examples of key employability skills, evaluate where personal skills require development and create a plan of action to show how skills will be developed.
Discuss the relationship between learning and career and life development, and apply this personally.

title: Work Integrated Learning 3
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the development of your professional identity, knowledge and work practice. It provides you with an opportunity to build upon the skills, knowledge and personal insights gained from Work Integrated Learning 1 (BUS113) and Work Integrated Learning 2 (BUS221). Through integration of theoretical constructs with work environment examples you will have the opportunity to extend your critical reflective practice, and further explore your own personal development, professional skills, and work ethic.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on and evaluate the application of theory in a workplace setting.
Evaluate personal development across a range of professional practice skills.
Apply knowledge of contemporary thinking in employability skills, career planning and development to enhance personal skills applicable to the work environment.

title: Work Integrated Learning 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: The subject is designed to develop students' employability skills and their understanding of professional practice. It provides you with an opportunity to build upon the skills, knowledge and personal insights gained from Work Integrated Learning 1 (BUS113) The subject is also aimed at developing students' self-reflection and self-monitoring skills to help build their efficacy and confidence in the workplace.
learning_outcomes: Define, evaluate, and reflect on employability skills and graduate attributes to plan appropriate professional development activities.
Learn and assess through reflection.
Explore, develop and evaluate a personal career plan.
Prepare an effective job application.
Explore and enhance personal brand development through academic application and self-development.

title: Work Integrated Learning in Accounting
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will explore a range of employability skills which will enhance their future transition to professional life and assist in career planning. Students will undertake a structured learning experience to further develop employment skills. This will provide opportunities for students to consider the professional skills needed within a work environment and to develop the employability skills needed for future career progression.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively in the workplace.
Identify relevant work opportunities, prepare effective job applications, and set career goals.
Demonstrate an understanding of the obligations of a professional accountant.

title: Work Integrated Learning in Medical Laboratory Science 1 (10)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will complete their first of three work-integrated learning clinical placements and submit a comprehensive portfolio that integrates their practical experiences with the theoretical knowledge gained in earlier subjects. This placement provides students with the opportunity to apply, practise, and consolidate their clinical skills in a real-world setting. Students will also be required to demonstrate the ability to reflect on and evaluate their practice to support their professional growth.
learning_outcomes: Operate independently and as a team member.
Demonstrate problem solving and decision making skills within a laboratory.
Demonstrate written and oral communication skills relevant to the discipline.
Describe the collection, preparation and analyses of clinical specimen or clinical data.
Demonstrate knowledge of workplace health and safety and safe work practices relevant to the discipline.
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviour.
Reflect on clinical experiences and maintain a portfolio identifying clinical/practical experiences and the learning that has taken place as a result of these experiences.
prerequisites: BMS265: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 1

title: Work Place Learning in Human Services 1
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This is one of two work place learning (field work placement) subjects for students studying in the human services field. In this subject, students undertake an approved placement where they are able to develop and demonstrate practice skills, knowledge and ethical decision-making. Students will be required to demonstrate an ability to reflect and evaluate their practice in real-life working environments. Participation in this subject is a collaborative partnership which includes the student, CSU staff and industry partners. Students will explore their role in using an intentional approach encapsulated in the Wiradjuri phrase: 'Yindyamarra Winhanga-nha' 'the wisdom of respectfully knowing how to live well in a world worth living in'.
learning_outcomes: Integrate theory and knowledge to practice, in order to improve performance.
Articulate and implement an ethical framework for decision making.
Apply culturally sensitive practice to the placement experience especially in relation to Indigenous Australians.
Identify and utilise basic counselling skills or strategies for undertaking client or community work activity, or quality improvement in practice.
Reflect on own values and knowledge and identify strengths and areas for the next placement or for future practice.
Engage effectively in the learning experience of building professional relationships with all parties engaged within the placement.

title: Work Integrated Learning in Medical Laboratory Science 2 (10)
school: School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will complete their second of three work-integrated learning clinical placements, specifically within a pathology setting. They will submit a comprehensive portfolio that integrates their clinical experiences with the theoretical knowledge gained throughout their studies. This placement provides students with the opportunity to further apply, practise, and consolidate their skills in a professional clinical environment. Students are expected to demonstrate critical reflection on their practice and evaluate their performance consistent with the AIMS Competency-Based Standards for Medical Scientists.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively in both written and oral format within a multidisciplinary workplace.

Reflect on their experience and maintain a portfolio identifying clinical / practical experiences and the learning that has taken place as a result of these experiences; with specific reflection of their experience on the AIMS Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists.
Describe the procedures employed to assess the accuracy, reproducibility and validity of current laboratory methods.
Work independently and as a team member to solve problems and interpret data in a medical science workplace setting.
Demonstrate professional behaviour.
Integrate information from various laboratory or other workplace sites in making decisions and to recognise appropriate responses to data discrepancies.
Demonstrate problem solving and decision making skills within the laboratory.
Demonstrate knowledge and application workplace health and safety and safe work practices relevant to the discipline.
Explain how to collect, prepare and analyse clinical data and/or specimens.
prerequisites: BMS265: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 1
BMS275: Work Integrated Learning in Medical Laboratory Science 1 (10)
BMS365: Integrated Clinical Placement for Medical Laboratory Science 2

title: Work Place Learning in Human Services 2
school: School of Social Work and Arts

learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on own values and knowledge and apply strengths and areas for future development.
Critically evaluate own competence with an audit of skills knowledge and values for the purpose of being work ready.
Integrate theory and knowledge to practice, in order to improve performance.
Engage critically in building professional relationships with all parties engaged within the placement.
Utilise and evaluate basic counselling skills or strategies for undertaking client or community work activity, or quality improvement in practice.
Analyse and implement an ethical framework for decision making.
Apply culturally sensitive practice to the placement experience especially in relation to Indigenous Australians.

title: Work Placement
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the opportunity for students to apply the skills and knowledge developed throughout their degree in a relevant work placement. Students develop an understanding of how to manage themselves as an emerging practitioner and to navigate the professional relationships and issues they will encounter in the workplace.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on and evaluate work placements.
Prepare, complete and submit work placement documentation.
Integrate knowledge from study to perform effectively during a work placement.

title: Work Placement / Industry Project
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on ‘people at work' through personal reflection on diversity, inclusion and the development of cultural competence in general. Students will develop transferable skills in the context of collaboration and cultural diversity in the workplace. Preparation for work placement will be emphasised, with students applying their academic learning in a professional setting by undertaking 105 hours with either a new host organisation or by completing a project or higher duties in their existing workplace.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of ethical, sustainable and cultural perspectives and contributions to workplace and business practices.
Develop, apply and reflect on personal and technical competence through experience in a professional setting; and
Develop and apply appropriate knowledge and transferable skills to work and collaborate effectively within diverse and inclusive business environments;

The subject is also aimed at developing students' self-reflection and self-monitoring skills to help build their efficacy and confidence in the workplace. Students apply their academic learning in a professional setting by undertaking 35 hours of work placement either with a new host organisation or by undertaking a project or higher duties in their existing workplace.
learning_outcomes: Explore and enhance personal brand development through academic application and self-development.
Prepare an effective job application.
Explore, develop and evaluate a personal career plan.
Define, evaluate, and reflect on employability skills and graduate attributes.
Develop practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.

title: Work Placement 2
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on ‘people at work' through the development and application of a personal reflection on diversity, tolerance and forms of bias; Australian Indigenous Cultural Competency; and the development of cultural competence in general. The Indigenous Australian content in this subject builds on students' completion of IKC101 and considers Australian Indigenous perspectives and contributions to workplace and business practices. Students will also develop their language and communication skills, in the context of cultural diversity in the workplace. Students apply their academic learning in a professional setting by undertaking 70 hours of work placement either with a new host organisation or by undertaking a project or higher duties in their existing workplace.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on and question personal values and ethics in developing a social justice ethos, and in relation to areas such as tolerance, forms of bias, diversity and power.
Present an integrated view of the various disciplines of business: to understand how a multi-disciplinary perspective can be used to address issues relevant to Australian Indigenous communities.

Use self and professional critical reflexivity to develop discipline specific and culturally appropriate skills for working effectively with diverse cultures and Indigenous Australian colleagues, clients, businesses, persons and/or communities.
Use appropriate language and communication strategies to inform the resolution of workplace challenges related to cultures or diversity.
Demonstrate an understanding of Australian Indigenous perspectives and contributions to workplace and business practices.
Develop practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.

title: Work Placement 3
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: In this elective Workplace Learning subject, students apply their academic learning in a professional setting by undertaking 105 hours of work placement either with a new host organisation or by undertaking a project or higher duties in their existing workplace. Students will also complete the Charles Sturt STRIVE Leadership program online. Students who successfully complete this subject will receive a Certificate and acknowledgement of Charles Sturt University Leadership on Australian Higher Education Graduation Statement.
learning_outcomes: Develop practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.
Evaluate, and reflect on employability skills and graduate attributes to plan appropriate professional development activities.
Think and act inclusively with an awareness of diversity and equality.
Critically reflect on their own leadership capabilities in the workplace.
Explore, develop and evaluate a personal career plan.

title: Work-Integrated Learning in Sport and Exercise
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides work integrated learning opportunities for students to apply their knowledge and skills in an ethical, professional, and responsible manner in exercise science or sports media related industries (sub-discipline specific). The subject allows students to integrate and apply knowledge and skills gained during their degree toward authentic, real-world professional contexts. Students will undertake work integrated learning to consolidate development of competency in exercise assessment, prescription and delivery OR the dissemination of exercise and sports-related content through media platforms. The subject involves a minimum of 160 hours of professional placement that is supervised by an appropriate professional in the line with the Exercise and Sport Science Australian Practicum requirements (where appropriate). Upon completion, students will demonstrate competencies that align with current exercise and sport science related industries as well as various professional behaviours and tasks.
learning_outcomes: Identify and support client health needs through the application of appropriate exercise assessment, prescription and delivery.
Actively apply knowledge and skills in a minimum of two professional exercise science placements for a minimum of 160 hours.
Describe the broad structure of the Australian health system and distinguish the integration of diverse health professionals within multidisciplinary teams.
Practice with integrity within the Exercise and Sport Science Australia’s Scope of Practice and Code of Ethical Practice for exercise science professionals.
Utilise appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication techniques with clients, and families, carers and other health professionals.
prerequisites: EHR224: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives of Sport Communication

title: Workforce Essentials
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Policing Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject is an enabling course. It provides foundational knowledge and skills for lifelong learning, in the criminal justice practitioner context.
learning_outcomes: Understand and use appropriate technologies to apply knowledge of communication and communication processes for workplace and learning environments.
Recognise and describe personal resilience strategies in the practice of the chosen discipline.
Describe the principles of safe driving.
Recognise leadership and teamwork principles and describe their impact on community and organisations.
Identify relevant law, policy, procedure and ethical considerations in the practice of the chosen discipline.
Identify the needs of people and describe appropriate interactions and rapport building in diverse situations.
Describe actions of cultural awareness in interaction and communication with others.
Identify relevant Work Health and Safety policies, procedures and legislative requirements in the practice of the chosen discipline.

title: Working alongside children and young people in Indigenous Australian communities
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject begins by exploring the concept of Yindyamarra Winhanganha and its foundational principles as a way for engaging in respectful relationships with First Nations families and communities. It will explore a decolonising approach, considering the historical impact of colonisation, its policies and practices as it relates to child welfare and wellbeing within Indigenous Australian communities. It will also examine the lasting legacy of these policies as they relate to the wellbeing and treatment by the state of children in Indigenous Australian communities. The subject examines culturally responsive approaches to the protection of children and young people, including the right for self-determination for Indigenous communities and empowerment of those communities through their connection to Country. The terms Indigenous Australians and First Nations Australians will be used interchangeably throughout this subject.
learning_outcomes: Apply an Indigenous or Indigenist Standpoint Theory/ies to critically examine the historical positioning of Indigenous and non-Indigenous Peoples and practices including children and young people.
Devise/design and develop an individual practice model of ‘wise practice’ when working alongside Indigenous Australian People.
Analyse and theorise a field of practice or a model for practice, using the cultural principles of Yindyamarra Winhanghana approach, and other decolonising and critically reflexive frameworks.
Critically evaluate the impact of significant historical events and policies involving Indigenous Australians in relation to children and young people within the Australian context.

title: Working in Child Protection
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a frame of reference for the professional role of social workers, welfare workers and police officers engaged in the statutory protection of children and young people. Students will develop an integrated knowledge and skill base relevant to statutory child protection practice and be able to critically reflect upon the impact of the child protection work upon themselves, their professional practice with clients and the wider community.
learning_outcomes: Describe the roles and responsibilities of a range of professional workers and agencies in matters of child abuse and neglect.
Identify and apply the components of core child protection activities including.
Demonstrate their understanding of the impact of personal and community values upon child protection practice.
Articulate strategies to respond to the societal, organisational and professional constraints and conflicts that occur in work with matters of child abuse and neglect.
Demonstrate their understanding of the legal, social, scientific and moral frameworks governing child protection practice.
Formal and informal dispute resolution of legal and social problems.
Assessment of safety, risks and needs.
Case planning and management.
Demonstrate their understanding of the ethical considerations involved in professional intervention with children and young people and their families in relation to child maltreatment.

title: Working with Families and Diverse Communities
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the opportunity to analyse culture and diversity in the context of Australian health care. Students will explore the diversity of families in relation to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander culture, family roles, communities and service provision. This subject will enable students to enhance their knowledge and skills in providing culturally responsive mental health care and working effectively with clients, families and communities to promote emotional and social wellbeing. Students will develop ways to optimise available resources to benefit families and communities using primary care and general mental health care services, prevention initiatives, and interagency.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the impact of culture and diversity on the health of individuals, groups and society.

Discuss strategies for working effectively with individuals, families and communities in the management of mental health disorders and the implementation of emotional and social well-being strategies.
Evaluate evidence and apply best practice in mental health as it relates to working with families and diverse cultures.
Demonstrate academic literacy and critical reasoning through formal written communication.
Analyse the diversity of the Australian population including but not restricted to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to foster cross-cultural relationships.

title: Working with Communities to Develop Mental Health Care, Capacity and Resilience
school: School of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the opportunity for students to explore a diverse range of interventions supporting mental health, including promotion and prevention, early intervention, acute care, recovery and continuing care in the context of regional, rural and remote communities. Students will extend their knowledge and capabilities in responding to the mental health needs of individuals, communities and the wider population. Key principles of person-centred, trauma-informed and recovery-focused care will underpin the approach to practice development. Students will develop their understanding of systems issues including the application of the stepped-care model of service delivery in primary health settings; the Social and Emotional Wellbeing model of care for First Nations peoples; and factors that enable meaningful stake-holder engagement. Students will also analyse technological advances in healthcare and develop their capacity to utilise these to address the challenges arising in the delivery of effective care for people in rural and remote communities.
learning_outcomes: critically analyse two technological interventions that could be utilised in clinical practice.
apply the Social and Emotional Wellbeing model in the provision of collaborative care for First Nations people;
apply the principles of person-centred and trauma-informed care to the assessment and care planning of individuals presenting to a health service in their community;

critically evaluate the continuum of mental health promotion activities through prevention and early intervention, treatment, rehabilitation and recovery, and continuing care, relevant to their practice context;
discuss advanced nursing practice approaches to supporting individuals experiencing mild, moderate, or severe/complex mental illness in rural and remote communities;
evaluate the scope and accessibility of services to support migrant/refugee peoples in a relevant practice context; and

title: Working with people with disability
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject explores ethical and human rights foundations for working with people with different abilities, with particular emphasis on relational ethics and practices. The subject considers how to create enabling environments, how to engender positive communication, as well as ways to work collaboratively with people with different abilities and their supporters. It considers issues including the social impact of stigma and labelling. Specific concepts of care, support and tools for assessing and working with people with disability are critically evaluated.
learning_outcomes: Examine and apply ethically sound principles of care and support for working with people living with disability and their supporters.
Critically evaluate a range of bio-psycho-social models of health and disability.
Critically reflect on own values, case studies, lived experience of disability and disability service provision in relation to models of care and service provision, and current policy frameworks.
Critically evaluate the relational approach to working with people with disabilities and their supporters.
Evaluate a range of techniques including strength-based approaches in working with people with disabilities.

title: Working with Special and Cultural Collections
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces key knowledge and skills required for the management, preservation and care of special and cultural collections. It discusses and reflects on the ethics, standards, policies and practices required to care for these collections to ensure their long term sustainability. Students explore best practice in preventing and responding to environmental problems that might threaten special and cultural collections and the preservation and conservation approaches required to ensure these collections are cared for and made accessible. The institutional, historical, and community contexts of special and cultural collections are critically analysed in contemporary practice.
learning_outcomes: Historically contextualise special and cultural collections.
Analyse, evaluate and apply the main curatorial and management needs of special and cultural collections including organisation, conservation and access.
Critically apply major standards and best practice regarding security, storage, transport and handling of a range of materials.
Explain the complex impact that environmental conditions have on the longevity of material.
Communicate to a variety of audiences a professional understanding of the enduring value and importance of special and cultural collections.
Manage effective and ethical acquisition practices according to institutional and professional standards and values.

title: Workplace Assessment and Rehabilitation
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: Exercise physiologists increasingly have the opportunity to gain employment in workplace assessment and rehabilitation. Students will develop knowledge, skills and competencies required to perform roles in workplace injury prevention and management. Emphasis is placed on developing knowledge and comprehension of workers compensation systems, legislative requirements, injury statistics, occupational health and safety assessment, functional capacity evaluations, factors influencing return to work rates, and the application of exercise interventions in the management of clients with workplace injuries and diseases. After completing this subject, students will be able to perform functional task analyses for various workplace roles, assess an injured worker's functional capacity, evaluate the ability to perform normal duties or recommend appropriate modified duties. Students will also learn how to develop safe and effective work conditioning programs and graded return to work plans that promote return to pre-injury duties or appropriate alternate duties.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate capacity to perform functional task analyses of workplace roles and effectively evaluate employee requirements to successfully perform such duties.
Identify and select appropriate physical assessment measures that are applied in workplace settings.
Discuss core principles of ergonomics within the home and work, and outline the influence on workplace injury prevention and rehabilitation.

Describe worker compensation schemes, state and national legislation and frameworks, and recognise professional roles available to Exercise Physiologists in workplace injury prevention and management settings.
Demonstrate ability to perform functional capacity evaluations to assess an injured worker's capability to safely perform pre-injury duties or recommend appropriate modified duties.
Design safe and effective work conditioning programs and graded return to work plans that promote return to pre-injury duties or modified duties that meet the needs of all stakeholders.

title: Working Within The Community
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject draws together teacher education students' discipline-specific pedagogical content knowledge and skills in preparation for, and during, a 240-hour professional experience placement in a secondary school setting. In collaboration with their supervising teachers, students will plan, teach, assess and reflect on learning as appropriate to their classes and in alignment with secondary curriculum requirements. A key focus of the subject is supporting pre-service teachers as they work towards meeting the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers at the Graduate level. This progress will be shown through the goals they set and achieve during the professional placement, and through the portfolio they submit at the conclusion of placement. While on the professional experience placement, pre-service teachers will be able to observe interactions between school, home and community contexts, and recognise the pivotal role of education to the wellbeing of children, families and communities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an applied knowledge of and provide evidence of growth as a teaching professional in relation to the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers at the Graduate level.
Satisfactorily complete a professional experience placement (up to 240 hours).
Reflect on teaching practices, identify learning goals, and engage in professional dialogue with members of the profession and the wider school community for improving teaching and learning.
Explain the development and implementation of approaches to engaging and working with young people, families, and communities.
Apply a range of teaching and learning strategies.

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business

The subject has a particular emphasis on enhancing professional knowledge of working in a business environment, expanding on employability skills and building on practical experience. As part of this subject, students will gain practical experience and apply their academic learning in a professional setting through a work placement either with a new host organisation or by undertaking a project or higher duties in their existing workplace.

Identify personal examples of key employability skills, evaluate where personal skills require development and create a plan of action to show how skills will be developed.
Reflect on personal career and life choices.
Identify professional, career and life choices, go on to develop a strategy to achieve these, begin to apply them and appraise their efficacy.
Develop practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.

title: Workplace Communication
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: Professional and clear communication is vital in all workplaces. This subject addresses the basics of verbal and written communication in professional environments to ensure students are well prepared for both future study and employment. It focuses on practical aspects of communication in a modern workplace.
learning_outcomes: Write basic professional documents such as emails clearly and concisely.
Create a short presentation that demonstrates verbal communication and awareness of audiences.

faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences

syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the development of your professional identity, knowledge and work practice. It provides you with an opportunity to build upon the skills, knowledge and personal insights gained from Workplace Learning 1 (BUS110) and Workplace Learning 2 (BUS220). Through closer integration of theoretical constructs with your current or proposed work environment you will have the opportunity to extend your critical reflective practice, and further explore your own personal development, professional skills, and work ethic. As part of this subject, students will gain practical experience and apply their academic learning in a professional setting through a work placement either with a new host organisation or by undertaking a project or higher duties in their existing workplace.
learning_outcomes: Develop practical competence through personal professional experience by participating in work placement.
Critically reflect on and evaluate the application of theory in a workplace setting.
Evaluate personal development across a range of professional practice skills.
Apply knowledge of contemporary thinking in employability skills, career planning and development to enhance personal skills applicable to the work environment.

title: Workplace learning: Theory and practice
school: Division of Learning and Teaching
syllabus_overview: This subject offers an introduction to the theories and practice of workplace learning. It acknowledges the central role of workplaces in shaping student learning and professional identity. It illuminates the pivotal contribution of workplaces to nurturing students' development of professional practice capabilities. In this subject workplaces as physical and cultural learning environments, and role expectations of students as pre-accredited and often peripheral members of communities of practice are explored. This subject scrutinises the roles of students, workplace learning supervisors and university staff and privileges a model of reciprocity and collaboration in workplace learning. Workplace learning pedagogies, underpinned by situated and workplace learning theories are explored. These theories move the pedagogical focus away from acts of teaching in order to privilege student engagement with and participation in authentic workplace activities and relationships. Students will be assisted to reflect on and critique their current workplace learning practices with a view to enhancing those practices and improving student outcomes. As an example, the ways in which technology can be used to enhance workplace learning experiences are explored. This subject focuses on learning in workplace contexts and does not explicitly cover learning in academic contexts. This subject would be of interest to anyone involved in workplace learning including practitioners who supervise students in workplaces and academics who support students and supervisors before, during and after workplace learning placements.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the role of specific WPL stakeholders.
Identify and critique options for enhancing the student's own WPL practices.
Critically discuss the role of WPL in higher education.
Critique contemporary WPL practices in the context of workplace learning theory and research.
Analyse the characteristics of workplace learning.
Justify the implementation and management of WPL.
Identify and critique possibilities for integrating academic and WPL curricula.

title: Workplace Performance Planning and Review
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Charles Sturt University Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students engage in reflective management of their learning and teamwork performance. They plan their workload, set goals and then use evidence-based reflection processes to track their progress and learning. They learn essential skills for applying for engineering jobs, ethics and career planning.
learning_outcomes: Utilise the process of reflection and demonstrate the ability to reflect on current practice as student engineers.
Compare the core functions and responsibilities that underpin the role of engineers.
Analyse the collaborative experiences of working in student engineering teams.
Demonstrate individual goal setting, planning and progression to manage learning and prepare for work placement.

title: Workplace Relations in Australia
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School
syllabus_overview: The area of contemporary workplace relations in Australia is examined from an employer, employee, industry association, government and union perspective in order to better understand the key stakeholders and the critical dynamics between them. The background, history and theory of Australian workplace relations are also covered in this subject, along with international comparisons, real case studies, and the key evolutions and likely future state of play in this critical HR discipline.
learning_outcomes: Compare, contrast and critique features of Australian workplace relations practices with other international markets, and with contemporary Australian expectations and realities, including possible future directions for the field.
Identify the key historical and theoretical developments in Australian workplace relations in the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries, and contextualise how these influence the discipline today.
Define and explain employee relations, its key stakeholders, and their role and dynamics within the employment relationship and the human resource management field.
Reflect on and evaluate workplace relations best practices with real workplace contexts and plan and strategise changes and improvements.

title: World Literature
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject surveys important and influential literary works from around the globe. It explores the ways in which literary texts interact with the political and social conditions of empire and nationhood. Works from North and South America, Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Pacific are analysed including those from diasporic and first nations perspectives. Students are encouraged to examine literature's place within broader social and historical systems of representation and power.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of various literary texts in English (or English translation) from around the world.
Recognise and evaluate key debates and positions in the field of World Literary Studies.
Demonstrate skills in reading, writing, research, and communication.
Apply skills in literary analysis, critically examining the ways that literary texts from around the world engage with a range of cultural, political, geographical, and historical contexts.

title: World Religions and Christian Theology
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject advances students' understanding of Christianity within the broader religious contexts of Australian society and the contemporary world, through a study of the sacred texts, history, and contemporary outlook of the major world religions. This subject also introduces students to the different methodological approaches to religious studies and analyses how different Christian traditions have reflected theologically on religious pluralism.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a broad and coherent knowledge of the major tenets of contemporary world religions.
Research, contextualise and communicate differences between one religious system with another.
Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Make informed use of religious terminology which is fundamental to some religious traditions.
Critically review and analyse various Christian theological approaches to world religions.
Analyse and critically evaluate the methods of religious studies as a discipline.
Articulate the relevance and implications of contemporary manifestations of world religions.
Appreciate the variety of religious experience in the contemporary Australia.
prerequisites: THL487: World Religions and Christian Theology

learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.

Analyse and critically evaluate the methods of religious studies as a discipline.
prerequisites: THL329: World Religions and Christian Theology

title: World Religions in Australia
school: Centre of Islamic Studies and Civilisation
syllabus_overview: This subject will address the changes in the Australian religious landscape from the arrival of the First Fleet to the present time. It will also cover the core teachings, practices and history of Christianity, Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism, Aboriginal spiritualities and new age within the Australian context. The contribution of religion to the Australian way of life will also be critically discussed. Finally, the history of Muslims in Australia from the Afghan cameleers to larger waves of migration in the multicultural era will be covered.
learning_outcomes: Articulate critically how Australia's religious landscape changed over the last two centuries.
Demonstrate an understanding of new age spiritualities.
Demonstrate appreciation of the beliefs and practices of Christianity, Judaism, Buddhism and Hinduism.
Articulate critically the major events and milestones in Australian history and their impact on the religious landscape.
Demonstrate an appreciation of Aboriginal history and religious beliefs.
Discuss critically the migration of Muslims to Australia and development of the Australian Muslim community.
Demonstrate critical ability to deduct theological, legal and spiritual meanings from the Qur'anic verses by following exegetical methodology.

title: Wound Management and Vascular Pathology
school: School of Allied Health, Exercise and Sport Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will study the assessment, management and prevention of foot pathology related to acute and chronic health conditions. Students will extend their understanding of neurovascular assessment to identify foot and leg pathology, and determine the need for podiatric, medical and surgical management. Students will also explore the role of a podiatrist within a multidisciplinary high-risk foot team, with a particular focus on ulcer prevention, wound management, and limb preservation. This subject will contribute to the student’s preparation for endorsement for scheduled medicine and progression towards competence in prescribing antibacterials.
learning_outcomes: Identify the high-risk foot and assess complications related to acute and chronic health conditions.
Evaluate aetiology, pathophysiology, and clinical presentation to inform assessment of a range of neurovascular pathology affecting the lower limb.
Explain the role of a podiatrist within a multidisciplinary high-risk foot team, working with the person and other health professionals to optimise the safety and effectiveness of treatment.
Justify short- and long-term wound prevention and management strategies to reduce the risk of foot and leg amputation.
Explain appropriate podiatric, medical, and surgical management options for a range of neurovascular pathology affecting the lower limb.

Justify pharmaceutical and non-pharmacological management options for the management of wound infection with consideration of the implications to the wider community when prescribing antimicrobial agents.
prerequisites: POD308: The Diabetic Foot and Chronic Wound Management

title: Writing and Communication for Legal Professionals
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a foundation in legal research and professional legal communication skills in civil and criminal law in Australia. Students learn communication skills including drafting legal documentation and the art of persuasion, argumentation and negotiation. Students are also introduced to legal research skills.
learning_outcomes: Plan and apply effective strategies in legal research to locate legal precedents and use legal citation conventions in legal writing.
Demonstrate communication skills for professional practice, including advocacy skills.
Communicate effectively with clients, including Indigenous clients and clients from regional, rural, remote and culturally diverse backgrounds.
Draft legal documentation and apply the rules of grammar, syntax and punctuation in the drafting of legal documentation.
Reflect critically on the student's own professional practice, including their communication skills, listening skills and professional communication style.
Demonstrate an understanding of Aboriginal kinship structures and its impact on written and oral communication for legal professionals.

title: Writing and Producing for the Digital Age
school: School of Information and Communication Studies
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the purpose and components of writing to produce professional and academic texts. Students will develop an understanding of how to research, interpret and analyse information to inform decision making and approaches to their scholarship and professional practice. Well-developed writing and editing skills are essential for communicators working in strategic communication, news and media and design and content creation. This subject is one of four introductory subjects that build the theoretical and discipline specific skills essential for communication professionals.
learning_outcomes: Create mixed media storytelling for a range of platforms and channels.
Demonstrate the fundamental components of constructing a text.
Plan communication texts to engage, inform, and communicate to audiences with impact.
Develop and design communication for different platforms and environments.
Demonstrate an understanding of how to create communication for a variety of audiences and purposes.

title: Writing for Publication
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with writing experience focussed on new work such as poetry or short fiction. It allows students opportunities to develop their writing skills and capacities in the genre(s) of their choice. Practising writers will be involved in the classes and will be available for editorial advice.
learning_outcomes: Have acquired compositional skills and knowledge by working on a number of pieces of new writing in the genre(s) of their specialisation.
Have demonstrated their understanding of marketplace requirements for publishing new work in the area of their specialisation.
Have developed skills in editing and analysing their work.

title: Writing for Stage and Screen
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a practical introduction to the art of scriptwriting and screenwriting. It informs students about the fundamentals of writing across a number of aesthetic and technological platforms including stage, film and television. Students will participate in weekly writing workshops designed to equip them with creative and technical skills for writing professionally in theatrical and screen contexts. The weekly activities and workshops will address narrative structure, character creation and development, dialogue and storytelling. Please note this subject is only offered in years ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
learning_outcomes: Put creative and technical skills into practice by producing writing for stage, television and multimedia.
Demonstrate an understanding of the relevance of the audience or interactive users to whom the writing is directed.
Analyse and assess professional and peer productions/programs (stage, film and television).
Demonstrate an understanding of, and apply the appropriate formatting, drafting and architectural principles of writing for the stage and screen.
Recognise the industrial and technical requirements of stage, film and television writing.
Pitch professionally.

title: Written Communication
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to reading, writing, and academic inquiry at the tertiary level; and specifically prepares them for studying in the online education mode. Students will complete a number of specific tasks designed to develop their research and writing to assist them on their academic journey. Students will also be introduced to online communication practices.
learning_outcomes: Apply basic rules of grammar and punctuation.
Identify peer-reviewed literature and evaluate the academic quality of broader reference materials.
Cite references according to the required conventions or style manual.
Establish an online presence with their writing.
Integrate paraphrased and quoted sources in paragraph structure.
Plan an essay, develop a draft, evaluate and redraft, proofread and complete an essay.
Identify relevant information in written material.
Recognise the range of the language, the features and the structures of different texts.
Identify key argument strategies and logical problems in own writing.
Explain the purpose of academic scholarship and applied research, using the Boyer Model of Scholarship.
Describe the purpose of referencing sources of information.
Recognise and use plain English.

title: Young People and Crime
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: Centre for Law & Justice
syllabus_overview: Young People and Crime examines the relationship between young people and the criminal justice system. This subject considers how children and young people are understood and responded to by various criminal justice agents and institutions. Students will examine key legal, policy, and theoretical frameworks concerning juvenile justice and welfare agencies and will evaluate key juvenile interventions including alternative practices.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness of current juvenile justice practices, institutional frameworks and principal sites of intervention into the lives of young people including Indigenous young people.
Employ appropriate criminological theory to examine explanations and responses to juvenile offending.
Describe the historical foundations of contemporary systems of juvenile justice and child welfare.

Identify and evaluate alternatives to judicially processing young offenders, specifically focusing on pre-trial diversion, cautioning schemes, youth conferencing and other community based prevention and control initiatives.
Describe the contemporary statutory frameworks governing young people.

title: Young People and Health Advocacy
school: School of Education
syllabus_overview: This subject utilises a number of HPE syllabus documents to provide a context for health in relation to the target population of young people. The social determinants of rurality, socio-economic status and at risk populations will provide the focus for in depth case study analysis to provide students with the opportunity to explore and engage with health issues impacting on the target population. Students develop and apply knowledge and skills relating to issues that impact on the lives of young people including sexuality, emotional, relational and mental health. Schools and community groups will provide settings for investigation.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse a health promotion program designed to promote the health of young people.

Demonstrate knowledge of the concepts and processes involved with sexuality, mental health issues for children and adolescents, child protection and grief and loss as they relate to relevant curriculum documentation.
Develop personal advocacy strategies for supporting the health of young people.
Critique the support structures and resources available to young people, to restore, maintain or improve their health status, and that of their local community.
Analyse policies and legislation that impact on the health of young people in terms of giving responsibility, encouraging participation and valuing their contribution.
Argue the role of schools in developing health literacy in young people.
Accurately engage with relevant strands of HPE syllabuses to devise stage-appropriate quality learning experiences for school students which address sexual and mental health content.

Actively engage with the HPS framework to devise appropriate quality learning experiences for Stage 4, 5 and 6 students that are inclusive, celebrate difference and diversity, advocate for social justice, promote health and a sense of future; and have relevance and meaning beyond the classroom.

title: Youth, Culture and Mission
school: School of Theology
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the cultures in which young people are immersed and the impact these have on communication and religious self-understanding. Consideration is given to the way that Christian mission may be enacted within this context. The subject also examines ways of communicating the gospel to the post-Christian mindset by analysing popular culture.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate self-guided learning, including advanced research, writing and communication skills.
Demonstrate a broad and coherent knowledge of how immersion in a digital world influences young people.
Contextualize and communicate an appropriate missional response to a particular cultural group in Australia.
Critically review and analyse contemporary issues impacting on Australian culture with particular reference to youth.
Analyse and critically evaluate key features of popular culture.
Articulate the relevance of popular culture and communicate this in ministry settings.

title: Zadie Smith to Taylor Swift: The Art of Creative Writing
school: School of Social Work and Arts
syllabus_overview: This subject develops students' skills in creative writing across a range of forms including: fiction, poetry, songwriting, playwrighting, writing for performance and screenwriting. The subject consists of interactive lecture-seminars and workshops for the development of two creative works. Students will have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of genres and styles as they learn to develop their unique literary voice. The subject includes critical analysis of distinguished creative writers across forms to enable greater articulation of the craft of writing and offers a hands-on approach to collaborative development through feedback on other students' creative works.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and critically analyse a range of fiction and other forms of creative writing.
Demonstrate an understanding of the conceptual and architectural principles of writing.
Demonstrate editing skills in practice applied to the student's work and the work of other students.
Produce completed work.

title: Australian Business and its Role in the Global Economy
faculty: Faculty of Business, Justice and Behavioural Sciences
school: School of Business
syllabus_overview: This subject enables on-shore International students to study business, society and culture in a regional Australian setting. The subject will include a range of activities designed to foster student connection with industry such as visits to businesses, government agencies, NGOs, local institutions and authorities; or guest speakers from these sectors. The subject aims to enhance students' familiarity with the Australian workplace, and foster connections with businesses and stakeholders in preparation for work placement.
learning_outcomes: Independently examine the impact of their experience in the Australian context.
Research and critically analyse the drivers of Australian business and in particular those drivers unique to regional Australia.
Differentiate between and reflect upon the norms in business, culture and society in Australia and the students' home country.
Evaluate the Australian business context and its place in the global economy.
